        "id": "def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group",
        "kind": "definition",
        "domain": "mathematics",
        "title": "Linear and affine Lorentz maps, and the Lorentz group",
        "statement": "Let (V,eta) be a 4-dimensional Lorentz vector space (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia) with a chosen time orientation C^+ (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets), and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model). (a) A linear Lorentz map is a linear map L: V -> V such that eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V. The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted O(V,eta). (b) If (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is an ordered eta-orthonormal basis of V (lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis), eta_0 := diag(-1,1,1,1) is the matrix of eta in it, and M is the matrix of L in that basis (def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map), then L is a linear Lorentz map if and only if M^T eta_0 M = eta_0; every linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, and the condition does not depend on the eta-orthonormal basis used. (c) A linear Lorentz map L is proper if det L = +1 and orthochronous if L(C^+) = C^+; the set of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps is denoted SO^+(V,eta). O(V,eta) is called the (full) Lorentz group of (V,eta) and SO^+(V,eta) the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; that these are groups under composition is proved in lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure. (d) An affine Lorentz map is a map F: A -> A for which there exist p_0 in A and a linear Lorentz map L with F(p_0 + v) = F(p_0) + L v for all v in V; equivalently F(p) = F(p_0) + L(p - p_0) for all p in A, and L is then unique. F is called proper (resp. orthochronous) when L is. If x is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x(F(p)) = M x(p) + b for all p, where M is the matrix of L in the frame's ordered basis and b := x(F(o)) - M x(o) in R^4. (e) In this framework, unless stated otherwise, 'Lorentz transformation' means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map; improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly (the B-page counterexample names the parity and time-reversal matrices).",
        "strategy": "A definition item: it fixes the language of the page and makes no proof claim beyond what lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure establishes (the matrix criterion, invertibility and the group structure, which is listed as justified_by). The well-definedness obligations are: (i) the set O(V,eta) is defined by a property of linear maps on the fixed vector space V, so it is a set; (ii) the matrix criterion in (b) must be stated in an ordered eta-orthonormal basis, whose existence is the cited lemma, and its independence of that choice is part of the proved content; (iii) 'L(C^+) = C^+' is a condition on a map of sets, not a notation for an unproved continuity statement; (iv) the affine definition (d) must distinguish an active map F on the point set A from the coordinate expression in a chart, and must not conflate an affine map with a general chart change; the coordinate expression requires the identification of vectors with coordinate columns and the cited matrix conventions. The exposition may state that the linear part of an affine Lorentz map is recovered as L v = F(p+v) - F(p), independently of p.",

        "kind": "definition",

        "title": "The passive Lorentz boost with parameter beta",
        "statement": "Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), and let x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) be its coordinates, so that a vector is written x = x^0 e_0 + x^1 e_1 + x^2 e_2 + x^3 e_3 and the spatial part is the coordinate column x_vec = (x^1,x^2,x^3) of R^3 with its standard Euclidean structure (def-euclidean-inner-product). For beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1, where |beta| is the Euclidean norm, set gamma(beta) := (1 - |beta|^2)^(-1/2) >= 1, with equality exactly for beta=0 and strict inequality for beta!=0 (def-rational-power, lem-rational-power-laws). The passive Lorentz boost with parameter beta is the linear map B(beta): V -> V defined by its action on coordinates: for beta not equal to 0, x'^0 = gamma (x^0 - beta . x),  x' = x + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . x) beta - gamma beta x^0, and for beta = 0, B(0) := identity, where x' denotes the coordinates of B(beta) applied to the vector with coordinates x, and beta . x is the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) the matrix of B(beta) is B^0_0 = gamma, B^0_i = B^i_0 = -gamma beta_i for i = 1,2,3, and B^i_j = delta^i_j + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2) beta_i beta_j for i,j = 1,2,3 (with the last expression replaced by delta^i_j for beta = 0; the coefficient (gamma\u22121)/|beta|^2 tends to 1/2 as beta tends to0 through nonzero vectors, so the correction is (1/2) beta_i beta_j+o(|beta|^2) and the full spatial block tends to delta^i_j). In the 1+1 case beta = beta e_1 this reads x'^0 = gamma(x^0 - beta x^1), x'^1 = gamma(x^1 - beta x^0). The vector beta is called the boost parameter; it is dimensionless and mathematically independent of any unit convention.",
        "strategy": "A definition item, well-defined because the displayed formulas assign to every coordinate pair (x^0,x_vec) a pair (x'^0,x'_vec), and by thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis (applied through def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map) there is a unique linear map with that matrix, namely x |-> E o M o E^{-1}. The beta = 0 case is declared separately because the matrix expression ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2) is undefined there; the definition must not silently divide by zero, and the stated limit follows from the explicit rationalization below. This item asserts no Lorentz property: that B(beta) is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map and that B(-beta) is its inverse is the content of lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse, and the composition law is the content of lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition; the physical reading of c beta as a relative velocity is stated only on the physics items of this page, not here. For the gamma boundary, gamma is positive and gamma^2=1/(1\u2212|beta|^2)>=1, with equality exactly when |beta|=0, so gamma>=1 with precisely the asserted equality case. For beta!=0 the identity gamma^2\u22121=|beta|^2 gamma^2 yields (gamma\u22121)/|beta|^2=gamma^2/(gamma+1). Continuity of the positive power in [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] makes gamma tend to1 as beta tends to0, hence that coefficient tends to1/2. Multiplication by beta_i beta_j proves the leading correction and full spatial-block limit: |beta_i beta_j|<=|beta|^2, so [gamma^2/(gamma+1)\u22121/2]beta_i beta_j=o(|beta|^2). Thus B(beta) tends to the separately declared identity without a hidden division by zero. No physical velocity interpretation is added. Real and rational powers are identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. The Euclidean norm convention gives $|\\beta_i|^2\\le\\sum_k\\beta_k^2=|\\beta|^2$, hence $|\\beta_i|\\le|\\beta|$ and $|\\beta_i\\beta_j|\\le|\\beta|^2$. In the norm meaning of $\\beta\\to0$, $|\\beta|\\to0$. For $|\\beta|^2\\le3/4$ one has $1\\le\\gamma\\le2$, so $|\\gamma\\beta_i|\\le2|\\beta|\\to0$; also $\\gamma-1=|\\beta|^2\\gamma^2/(\\gamma+1)\\to0$.         "id": "def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame",
        "kind": "definition",
        "domain": "mathematics",
        "title": "Spatial rotations of an inertial frame",
        "statement": "Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model and let S := span(e_1,e_2,e_3) be its spatial three-space with delta the restriction of eta to S (def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame); delta is a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form, (e_1,e_2,e_3) is delta-orthonormal, and S = {w in V : eta(e_0,w) = 0}. A spatial rotation of the frame is a linear map R: V -> V such that R(e_0) = e_0, R(S) is contained in S (so that the restriction R|_S is an endomorphism of S; the determinant condition below forces R(S) = S) and delta(Rw,Rz) = delta(w,z) for all w,z in S, and whose restriction R|_S has determinant +1 computed in the ordered basis (e_1,e_2,e_3). Via the delta-orthonormal basis (e_1,e_2,e_3), these maps are exactly the linear maps whose matrix is a 3x3 matrix A with A^T A = I_3 and det A = +1; such matrices form the group SO(3), and the spatial rotations of the frame form a subgroup of the general linear group of V isomorphic to SO(3) (def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator, cor-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators-form-groups-and-have-unit-determinant-modulus). The extension by R(e_0) = e_0 of a spatial rotation is also written R.",

The definition must separate three objects: the geometric spatial three-space S of a named frame, the restriction R|_S which is the actual rotation, and the extension by the identity on the time direction. The determinant is taken with respect to the orientation of S induced by the ordered basis (e_1,e_2,e_3), which the frame definition fixes; a change of frame changes which maps are called spatial rotations.         "id": "lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure",
        "kind": "lemma",
        "domain": "mathematics",
        "title": "Lorentz maps are isomorphisms of determinant +-1 that preserve causal character and permute the cones; the Lorentz sets are groups",
        "statement": "Let L: V -> V be a linear map with eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V (def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group). Then: (i) L is a linear isomorphism of V; for every ordered eta-orthonormal basis the matrix M of L satisfies M^T eta_0 M = eta_0 with eta_0 = diag(-1,1,1,1), and conversely every invertible matrix M with M^T eta_0 M = eta_0 is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that basis. (ii) det L = +-1. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map; the sets SO(V,eta) := {L : det L = 1}, O^up(V,eta) := {L : L(C^+) = C^+} and SO^+(V,eta) = SO(V,eta) intersect O^up(V,eta) are subgroups of O(V,eta), which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group GL(V). (iii) eta(Lv,Lv) = eta(v,v) for all v in V; hence L preserves the causal character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the set of null vectors onto itself. If L is proper, then the oriented volume form is preserved: epsilon(Lv_0,...,Lv_3) = epsilon(v_0,...,v_3) for all v_0,...,v_3 in V (def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form); if det L = -1 the two sides differ by the sign -1. (iv) L(C^+) is one of the two components C^+, C^- of the timelike set, so exactly one of L(C^+) = C^+ and L(C^+) = C^- holds; L is orthochronous in the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and L(C^+) = C^+ holds if and only if L(C^+) is contained in C^+. (v) The affine Lorentz maps (def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group(d)) form a group under composition: the composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps, and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of A.",
        "strategy": "Proof plan. (i) If Lv = 0 then eta(v,w) = eta(Lv,Lw) = 0 for every w, so v = 0 by nondegeneracy of eta; hence L is injective and, V being finite-dimensional, an isomorphism. Writing vectors in an eta-orthonormal basis, the identity eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) becomes v^T M^T eta_0 M w = v^T eta_0 w for all coordinate columns v,w, which by nondegeneracy of the pairing is equivalent to M^T eta_0 M = eta_0; the converse direction defines L by v |-> E(M(E^{-1}(v))) and computes the same identity. (ii) Taking determinants in M^T eta_0 M = eta_0 and using det eta_0 = -1, det(M^T) = det M and thm-determinant-multiplicative gives (det M)^2 = 1, so det L = +-1. Closure of O(V,eta) under composition: eta(LMv,LMw) = eta(Mv,Mw) = eta(v,w). Identity and inverses: eta(L^{-1}v,L^{-1}w) = eta(LL^{-1}v,LL^{-1}w) = eta(v,w), using L(L^{-1}v) = v. The determinant conditions are preserved because det is multiplicative (thm-determinant-multiplicative, cor-determinant-of-an-inverse), and orthochrony is preserved because LM(C^+) = L(C^+) = C^+ and L^{-1}(C^+) = C^+ when L(C^+) = C^+. Being a subgroup of GL(V) uses that GL(V) is a group (cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group) and def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map. (iii) The first identity is the defining property evaluated on (v,v). Since the sign of eta(v,v) is unchanged, the causal class of every nonzero v is unchanged, and null vectors are exactly those nonzero v with eta(v,v) = 0. For the volume form: in the frame's basis write the columns v_j, so epsilon(v_0,...,v_3) = det([v_j]) by def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form; then epsilon(Lv_0,...,Lv_3) = det(M [v_j]) = det(M) det([v_j]) by multiplicativity, which equals epsilon(v_0,...,v_3) when det M = 1. (iv) L(C^+) is the continuous image of the connected set C^+ (lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components), hence connected, and it is contained in the timelike set because eta(Lv,Lv) = eta(v,v) < 0; a connected subset of the timelike set lies in one of its two components (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets, lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components). Since L is a bijection with L^{-1} also Lorentz, L maps the timelike set onto itself, so L(C^+) and L(C^-) are two nonempty components and hence are C^+ and C^- in some order; in particular L(C^+) = C^+ iff L(C^+) is contained in C^+. (v) If F(p) = F(p_0) + L(p - p_0) and G(p) = G(q_0) + M(p - q_0), then (G o F)(p) = G(F(p_0)) + ML(p - p_0) with ML Lorentz by closure; the inverse of F is p |-> p_0 + L^{-1}(p - F(p_0)), affine Lorentz with linear part L^{-1}, and the identity is affine Lorentz with L = id. There is no unproved step: every algebraic statement is a direct substitution, and the only topological input is the two-component structure of the timelike set, supplied by the cited predecessor lemma.",

    "statement": "Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I.     "id": "thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition",
    "kind": "theorem",
    "domain": "mathematics",
    "title": "Norms of four-velocity and four-acceleration, and the observer rest-space decomposition",
    "statement": "Let c > 0 and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space. (a) Norm of the four-velocity. Let x: I -> A be a C^1 future timelike worldline with four-velocity U (def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration). Then eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^2 for every s in I; equivalently the dimensionless four-velocity u = U/c satisfies eta(u,u) = -1, and U(s) is future timelike. Thus the four-velocity of a worldline lies on the future unit hyperboloid. (b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration. If x is C^2 at s, then eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0: the four-acceleration has no component along the four-velocity; if in addition A(s) is nonzero, then A(s) is spacelike. (c) Rest space and projection. Let n in V be future unit timelike, eta(n,n) = -1, and put n^perp := {v in V : eta(n,v) = 0}. Then n^perp is a 3-dimensional linear subspace of V, the restriction of eta to n^perp is positive definite, and the map h: V -> V, h(v) := v + eta(n,v) n, is linear, idempotent with h o h = h, has image n^perp and kernel span(n), satisfies h(n) = 0 and eta(n,h(v)) = 0 for all v in V, and every v in V has the unique decomposition v = -eta(n,v) n + h(v). Moreover |w| := sqrt(eta(w,w)) defines a norm on n^perp. (d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor. Let n and u be future unit timelike vectors, put gamma := -eta(n,u) and w := c h(u)/gamma. Then gamma >= 1, w lies in n^perp, u = gamma (n + w/c), |w|^2 = c^2 (1 - gamma^{-2}) < c^2, gamma = (1 - |w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}, and gamma = 1 if and only if u = n.         "statement": "Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the affine Minkowski space with tangent spaces canonically identified with V, and let Omega be a nonempty open subset of A. (a) Vector fields. (b) Covector and general tensor fields. For a smooth covector field alpha set (nabla_X alpha)(Y) := X(alpha(Y)) - alpha(nabla_X Y); for a type (r,s) tensor field T define nabla_X T by the derivation rule on the evaluation of T on smooth vector and covector fields, subtracting the covariant derivative of each vector argument and also subtracting the covariant derivative of each covector argument; Precisely, for $T:(V^*)^r\\times V^s\\to\\mathbb R$, $(\\nabla_XT)(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\alpha_r;Y_1,\\ldots,Y_s)=X[T(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\alpha_r;Y_1,\\ldots,Y_s)]-\\sum_iT(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\nabla_X\\alpha_i,\\ldots,\\alpha_r;Y_1,\\ldots,Y_s)-\\sum_jT(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\alpha_r;Y_1,\\ldots,\\nabla_XY_j,\\ldots,Y_s)$. In inertial coordinates every component of nabla_X T is X^b partial_b of that component, with no connection coefficients. (c) Properties. nabla is R-bilinear, C^infinity(Omega)-linear in X, satisfies nabla_X(fY) = X(f)Y + f nabla_X Y and the analogous Leibniz rules for tensor fields, is metric compatible (nabla eta = 0, because partial_a eta_{bc} = 0 in every inertial chart), is torsion-free (nabla_X Y - nabla_Y X = [X,Y], def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields and prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket) and has zero curvature (nabla_X nabla_Y Z - nabla_Y nabla_X Z - nabla_{[X,Y]} Z = 0), the last by equality of mixed partial derivatives of the components (thm-young-mixed-partial-theorem). (d) Fields along a curve. If gamma: I -> A is a C^1 curve and W: I -> V is a C^1 field along it (def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve), the covariant derivative of W along gamma is the ordinary V-valued derivative DW/ds := W' (def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral), because the canonical identification T_pA = V is independent of p; consequently parallel transport along any curve is the identity and a field is parallel exactly when it is constant. The derivative (d) is the one used for the acceleration of congruences, for Fermi-Walker transport and for the kinematic decomposition below; the model needs no Christoffel symbols or parallel-transport ODE in this formulation. (e) First-order C1 version. For C1 vector fields X,Y and C1 covector/tensor fields on Omega, the same directional/evaluation definitions are well-defined and have continuous coefficients: in an inertial chart $(\\nabla_XY)^a=X^b\\partial_bY^a$ and each tensor component is differentiated in the same way. C1 scalar multiplication satisfies the same first-order Leibniz rules, metric compatibility remains $\\nabla\\eta=0$, and the first-order torsion identity uses the continuous coordinate bracket $[X,Y]^a=X^b\\partial_bY^a-Y^b\\partial_bX^a$.         "statement": "Let n be an observer congruence on a nonempty open subset Omega of A (def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction), let nabla be the flat covariant derivative (def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space), and write n_b := eta_{bc} n^c for the associated covector field. (a) Rest metric and projection. Define h(v,w) := eta(v,w) + eta(n,v) eta(n,w) for vectors at the same point, so h = eta + n-flat (x) n-flat; then h(v,w) = eta(h(v),h(w)) where h(v) := v + eta(n,v) n is the orthogonal projection of thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition (c). At every point h is symmetric with radical spanned by n(p), and its restriction to n(p)^perp is positive definite. (b) Acceleration. The acceleration of the congruence is a := nabla_n n; then eta(n,a) = 0 pointwise, because 2 eta(n, nabla_n n) = n(eta(n,n)) = 0, so a(p) is spacelike or zero by the causal classification. In the model's physical interpretation the four-acceleration of the congruence observers is c^2 a and its magnitude is c^2 sqrt(eta(a,a)); the numerical units belong to the model's SI conventions and are not part of the affine geometry. (c) Kinematic decomposition. ### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is a rational, and that is not a matter of taste.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies $a^{r}$ for a nonnegative base and a **rational**
exponent only; real exponents do not exist at this point in the reading order,
and [[rem-real-exponents-deferred]] records exactly why. This is also why the
published Minkowski inequality [[thm-minkowski-finite]], which is what makes the
triangle inequality work below, is itself stated for rational $p \ge 1$. **No
statement on this page is written for $p$ ranging over a real interval.**

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

          "quote": "Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent

when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both

$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and

$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;

the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.",

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number

$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to

the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves

          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].",

          "quote": "Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.",

**(a) Chart and inertial chart.** A **chart** of the model is a diffeomorphism $u:U\to u(U)$ from a nonempty open subset $U\subseteq A$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]), written with components $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$. **(b) Tetrad at an event and tetrad field.** A **tetrad at $p\in A$** is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ future, $e_0\in C^+$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]): this is the basis of an inertial frame without an origin and without the orientation condition. The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the

**(a) Vector fields.** For smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $\Omega$ define the **covariant derivative of $Y$ in the direction $X$** at $p\in\Omega$ by

$$\bigl(\nabla_XY\bigr)(p):=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}Y\bigl(p+tX(p)\bigr),$$

the derivative of the $V$-valued composite $t\mapsto Y(p+tX(p))$, which is defined for $t$ in a neighbourhood of $0$ because $\Omega$ is open ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-derivative]]). In the inertial chart $x$ of any inertial frame one has $(\nabla_XY)^a=X^b\,\partial_bY^a$; the value does not depend on the inertial chart: for another inertial chart $x'=\Lambda x+b$ one has $\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b_{\ a}\,\partial_b$ and $Y'^a=\Lambda^a_{\ b}Y^b$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and $\Lambda$ is constant, so $(\Lambda^{-1})^a_{\ c}\,X'^b\,\partial'_bY'^c=X^b\,\partial_bY^a$. The field $\nabla_XY$ is again a smooth vector field on $\Omega$.

**(b) Covector and general tensor fields.** For a smooth covector field $\alpha$ set $(\nabla_X\alpha)(Y):=X(\alpha(Y))-\alpha(\nabla_XY)$ for every smooth vector field $Y$, and for a type $(r,s)$ tensor field $T$ define $\nabla_XT$ by the derivation rule on the evaluation of $T$: for $T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$,

$$(\nabla_XT)(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)=X\bigl[T(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)\bigr]-\sum_{i=1}^rT(\alpha_1,\dots,\nabla_X\alpha_i,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)-\sum_{j=1}^sT(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,\nabla_XY_j,\dots,Y_s),$$

where the vector and covector arguments are smooth fields on $\Omega$. In inertial coordinates every component of $\nabla_XT$ is $X^b\,\partial_b$ applied to that component, with no connection coefficients.

**(c) Properties.** The operator $\nabla$ is $\mathbb R$-bilinear, is $C^\infty(\Omega)$-linear in $X$, and satisfies the Leibniz rules $\nabla_X(fY)=X(f)Y+f\nabla_XY$ and the analogous rules for tensor fields; it is metric compatible, $\nabla\eta=0$, because $\partial_a\eta_{bc}=0$ in every inertial chart; it is torsion-free, $\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$, by the coordinate formula for the Lie bracket ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]); and it has zero curvature, $\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z=0$, by equality of mixed partial derivatives of the components ([[thm-young-mixed-partial-theorem]]).

**(d) Fields along a curve.** If $\gamma:I\to A$ is a $C^1$ curve and $W:I\to V$ is a $C^1$ field along it ([[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]]), the **covariant derivative of $W$ along $\gamma$** is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative $DW/ds:=W'$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), because the canonical identification $T_pA=V$ is independent of $p$; consequently parallel transport along any curve is the identity and a field is parallel exactly when it is constant. For $C^2$ vector fields the second derivatives needed for the zero-curvature identity of (c) exist, and that identity follows by equality of the continuous mixed second partials.           "quote": "An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple

   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector

   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.

  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when

changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is

Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both

$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on

that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose

$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.",

          "quote": "Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.",

          "quote": "Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be inertial frames whose bases are related by a boost along the common first spatial direction with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$:

$$e'_0=\gamma\Bigl(e_0+\frac{v}{c}e_1\Bigr),\qquad e'_1=\gamma\Bigl(e_1+\frac{v}{c}e_0\Bigr),\qquad e'_2=e_2,\qquad e'_3=e_3,$$

where $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, with charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]). Write the transition as

$$x'^0=\gamma\Bigl(x^0-\frac{v}{c}x^1\Bigr),\qquad x'^1=\gamma\Bigl(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0\Bigr),\qquad x'^2=x^2,\qquad x'^3=x^3.$$

Then:

**(i) Clock rate.** The straight worldline $y(\lambda):=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ (coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$, the worldline of a clock at rest in the frame $x'$) is future timelike, and the elapsed proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; equivalently $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ along $y$, where $t$ is the coordinate time of $x$.

**(ii) Length comparison.** For $L_0>0$ let $y_a,y_b$ be the two straight worldlines at rest in the frame $x'$ through the events with $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda,L_0,0,0)$. Then (a) at equal $x'$-times their $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$, while (b) at equal $x$-times their $x$-coordinate separation is $L_0/\gamma$, so the measuring frame $x$ assigns the length $L_0/\gamma$ to a rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$; (c) symmetrically, for two worldlines at rest in $x$ with $x$-separation $L_0$ the separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0/\gamma$. In each case the comparison uses events at equal time in the measuring frame; comparing equal times of the other frame is a different pair of events.

**(iii) Simultaneity.** If $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$; in particular simultaneity in the chart $x$ is not simultaneity in the chart $x'$ whenever $vL\ne0$.

          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.",

**(c) Rigid rotation, ambient nonintegrability and ring holonomy.** Fix real $\Omega$. In the inertial chart let $U_\Omega$ be the open timelike region $r^2=(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2<c^2/\Omega^2$ when $\Omega\ne0$, and the whole chart when $\Omega=0$. On this four-dimensional open set put $K=\partial_0+(\Omega/c)(-x^2\partial_1+x^1\partial_2)$, $\gamma(r)=(1-\Omega^2r^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and $n=\gamma(r)K$. $$\theta(s,s)=s^as^b\partial_an_b=\gamma^3q_1'(t)q_1''(t)/c^3,$$

## Definition

Let $V$ be a real vector space, with addition $+$, zero $0$, and additive
inverses ([[def-vector-space]]). An **affine space over $V$** is a nonempty set
$A$ together with a map

$$+\;:\;A\times V\longrightarrow A,\qquad (p,v)\longmapsto p+v,$$

such that

1. $(p+v)+w=p+(v+w)$ and $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$ and $v,w\in V$; and
2. for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$.

The map in clause 1 is the **action** of $V$ on $A$. The unique vector supplied
by clause 2 is written $q-p$ and is called the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**;
thus $q-p$ is the unique $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$. An affine space over the real
vector space $V$ is also called a **real affine space modelled on $V$**, and
then $V$ is its **space of displacements**.

The following identities are consequences of the two clauses, with the displayed
justification:

- $p+(q-p)=q$ for all $p,q\in A$: this restates the defining property of $q-p$
  in clause 2.
- $p-p=0$ for all $p\in A$: taking $q=p$ in the previous display gives
  $p+(p-p)=p=p+0$, and clause 2 applied to the pair $(p,p)$ gives
  $p-p=0$.
- $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$: this is clause 1.
- $(q-p)+(r-q)=r-p$ for all $p,q,r\in A$:
  $p+\bigl[(q-p)+(r-q)\bigr]=\bigl[p+(q-p)\bigr]+(r-q)=q+(r-q)=r=p+(r-p)$,
  so clause 2 applied to the pair $(p,r)$ identifies the two vectors.
- For each $p\in A$ the map $v\mapsto p+v$ is a bijection of $A$ with $V$: it is
  surjective by clause 2 applied to $q:=p+v$, and injective because
  $p+v=p+w$ gives $p+(v-w)=\bigl[p+v\bigr]+(-w)=p+w-w=p=p+0$, so clause 2
  applied to $(p,p)$ gives $v-w=0$, that is, $v=w$.

**Affine coordinate systems.** Suppose $V$ is $4$-dimensional and
$E:\mathbb R^4\to V$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]).
For a chosen point $o\in A$, define

$$x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),\qquad p\in A .$$

This is a bijection $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$: it is injective and surjective because
$E^{-1}$ is a bijection and $p\mapsto p-o$ is a bijection of $A$ with $V$ by the
bijection just proved, applied with that $o$. Such maps are the **affine
coordinate systems on $A$**; clause 2 is exactly what makes them well defined,
because it is clause 2 that attaches to each ordered pair $(o,p)$ a unique
displacement $p-o$.

## Definition

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

## Definition

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

## Statement

Let $\eta$ be a Lorentz form on a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$. There
is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. Such a basis
is called **$\eta$-orthonormal**; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the
count is the inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$.

[L1] Every symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space is
congruent to exactly one normal form $\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q,0_r)$ with
$p+q+r=\dim V$, and the numbers of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries
are independent of the diagonalizing basis ([[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]]).

[L2] $\eta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $V$, and in some basis in which its
matrix is diagonal there are exactly three positive diagonal entries, exactly
one negative diagonal entry, and no zero diagonal entry; this triple is the
inertia $(3,1,0)$ of $\eta$, independent of the diagonalizing basis
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [L1] the symmetric bilinear form $\eta$ on the finite-dimensional real space $V$ is congruent to exactly one normal form $\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q,0_r)$ with $p+q+r=\dim V=4$, and by [L2] its inertia is $(3,1,0)$; hence $(p,q,r)=(3,1,0)$ and there is a basis $v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3$ of $V$ with $\eta(v_i,v_j)=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,-1)_{ij}$ for all $i,j$. [L1, L2, choose]

2.1 Define the reordering $e_0:=v_3$ and $e_1:=v_0$, $e_2:=v_1$, $e_3:=v_2$. Then $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis of $V$, and evaluating the displayed matrix gives $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$, $\eta(e_1,e_1)=\eta(e_2,e_2)=\eta(e_3,e_3)=+1$ and $\eta(e_a,e_b)=0$ for $a\neq b$, that is, $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$: the required ordered basis exists. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Now let $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ be any ordered basis with $\eta(f_a,f_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$. Its matrix is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$, so in this diagonalizing basis the numbers of positive, negative and zero diagonal entries are $(3,1,0)$; by the uniqueness clause of [L1] the triple $(3,1,0)$ is intrinsic and equals the inertia of $\eta$ given in [L2]. In such a basis exactly one vector, $f_0$, is timelike, because $\eta(f_0,f_0)=-1<0$, and the remaining three are spacelike, because $\eta(f_i,f_i)=+1>0$ for $i=1,2,3$; and this count is exactly the inertia $(3,1,0)$. [step 2.1, L1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Two vectors $u,v\in V$ are
**$\eta$-orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, when $\eta(u,v)=0$. For a subset
$S\subseteq V$ the **orthogonal complement** of $S$ is

$$S^{\perp}:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,s)=0\text{ for every }s\in S\},$$

and for a vector $u$ one writes $u^{\perp}:=\{u\}^{\perp}$.

**Elementary properties.** For every subset $S\subseteq V$:

- $S^{\perp}$ is a linear subspace of $V$: if $v,w\in S^{\perp}$ and
  $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, then for every $s\in S$ bilinearity gives
  $\eta(v+\lambda w,s)=\eta(v,s)+\lambda\eta(w,s)=0$, so $v+\lambda w\in S^{\perp}$.
  In particular the zero vector lies in $S^{\perp}$ and $S^{\perp}$ is never
  empty.
- $S\subseteq (S^{\perp})^{\perp}$: if $s\in S$, then $\eta(v,s)=0$ for every
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ by the definition of $S^{\perp}$, and symmetry of $\eta$
  gives $\eta(s,v)=0$ for every $v\in S^{\perp}$, that is,
  $s\in(S^{\perp})^{\perp}$.
- $S^{\perp}=(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$: the inclusion
  $S\subseteq\operatorname{span}S$ gives
  $(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}\subseteq S^{\perp}$; conversely, if
  $v\in S^{\perp}$ and $u=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i$ is a finite linear combination
  with $s_i\in S$, then linearity in the second argument gives
  $\eta(v,u)=\sum_i\lambda_i\eta(v,s_i)=0$, so $v\in(\operatorname{span}S)^{\perp}$.

In particular, for every $u\in V$ one has $u\in u^{\perp}$ exactly when
$\eta(u,u)=0$, that is, exactly when $u$ is null or $u=0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**A nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.** Take a basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal with
diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$; such a basis exists by clause 2 of the definition
of a Lorentz form. Then $v:=e_0+e_1$ is nonzero while
$\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)+2\eta(e_0,e_1)+\eta(e_1,e_1)=-1+0+1=0$, so
$v\in v^{\perp}$ with $v\neq 0$. This is exactly what fails for a
positive-definite inner product and is why orthogonal complements in a Lorentz
vector space need not be positive definite.

## Definition

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.
