## Statement

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A Lorentz vector space $(V,\eta)$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and an
$\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$.

[L1] There is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$, and such a
basis is called $\eta$-orthonormal ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]).

[L2] For an ordered basis $v:n\to V$, every $x\in V$ has exactly one coordinate
list $\lambda$ with $x=\sum_{i<n}\lambda_iv_i$, and the coordinate list is attached
to the ordered basis ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]).

[L3] A vector $v$ is timelike when $q(v)<0$, null when $v\neq0$ and $q(v)=0$,
spacelike when $q(v)>0$, and causal when it is timelike or null, where
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$ is the associated quadratic form
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

[L4] The Euclidean inner product of $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ is
$\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$, with $\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$,
and it is symmetric, bilinear and positive definite
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[L5] The function induced by an inner product satisfies
$\lVert v\rVert\ge0$ with $\lVert v\rVert=0$ if and only if $v=0$,
$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert$, and
$\lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]).

[L6] A metric on a set $X$ is a function $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ with
$d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality
([[def-metric-space]]).

[L7] A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is convex when $(1-t)x+ty\in U$ for all
$x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]).

[L8] Every convex subset $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, is path-connected,
hence connected ([[ex-convex-subsets-of-rn-are-path-connected]], claim 1).

[L9] A subset $U$ of a metric space $(X,d)$ is open when for every $x\in U$
there is $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, and the collection of these sets is the
metric topology; a set is closed when its complement is open
([[def-metric-topology]]).

[L10] A separation of a topological space is an ordered pair of open, nonempty,
disjoint subsets with union the whole space; a space is connected when no
separation exists, and a subset is connected when it is connected in the
subspace topology ([[def-connected-space]]).

[L11] The open sets of the subspace topology on $C\subseteq X$ are exactly the
intersections $C\cap U$ with $U$ open in $X$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

[L12] The connected component $C_T(x)$ of a point $x$ in a space $T$ is the
union of all connected subsets of $T$ containing $x$, and it is the largest
connected subset of $T$ containing $x$
([[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]]).

[L13] If $X$ is path-connected then $X$ is connected, and a path-connected
subset of $X$ is a connected subset of $X$
([[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]], claim 2).

[L14] If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on the closed bounded interval and
$y$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(c)=y$ for some $c\in[a,b]$
([[thm-intermediate-value]]).

[L15] A time orientation of $(V,\eta)$ is a choice of one of the two components
of the timelike set $T$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $v=\sum_av^ae_a$ and $w=\sum_bw^be_b$, bilinearity of $\eta$ together with $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ from [L1] give $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$, hence $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, where $\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2=(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=\lVert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2^2$ by [L4]. The assignment $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ is a bijection $V\to\mathbb R^4$ by [L2]. By [L3] the timelike set is $T=\{v:\eta(v,v)<0\}=\{v:(v^0)^2>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\}=\{v:\lvert v^0\rvert>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}=T_+\cup T_-$, because $\lvert v^0\rvert>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ holds exactly when $v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ or $v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$. [L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

1.2 Define $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$. By [L5] applied to the Euclidean inner product of [L4], the Euclidean norm is nonnegative, vanishes only at $0$, is absolutely homogeneous, and satisfies the triangle inequality; with $c$ a bijection [L2] this shows that $d$ is a metric on $V$ in the sense of [L6]: $d(u,w)=0$ if and only if $c(u)=c(w)$, if and only if $u=w$; $d(u,w)=d(w,u)$ by $\lVert-x\rVert=\lVert x\rVert$; and $d(u,w)\le d(u,z)+d(z,w)$ by the triangle inequality applied to $(c(u)-c(z))+(c(z)-c(w))$. [L2, L4, L5, L6, algebra]

2.1 The coordinate image $c(T_+)=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_0>\lVert x_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2\}$ is convex in the sense of [L7]: if $x,y\in c(T_+)$ and $t\in[0,1]$, then the first coordinate of $z:=(1-t)x+ty$ is $z_0=(1-t)x_0+ty_0>(1-t)\lVert x_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2+t\lVert y_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2\ge\lVert(1-t)x_{\mathrm{vec}}+ty_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2=\lVert z_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2$, where the strict inequality uses $x_0>\lVert x_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2$, $y_0>\lVert y_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2$ and $t,1-t\ge0$ and the second inequality is the triangle inequality with homogeneity from [L5]; hence $z\in c(T_+)$. The same computation with reversed inequalities shows that $c(T_-)=\{x:x_0<-\lVert x_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2\}$ is convex. [step 1.1, L5, L7, algebra]

2.2 The coordinate vector of $e_0$ is $(1,0,0,0)$ and that of $-e_0$ is $(-1,0,0,0)$, by uniqueness of coordinates [L2]; hence $e_0\in T_+$ and $-e_0\in T_-$, so both sets are nonempty. If $v\in T_+\cap T_-$, then $v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\ge0$ and $v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\le0$ simultaneously, which is impossible; hence $T_+$ and $T_-$ are disjoint and $T=T_+\sqcup T_-$. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

2.3 Let $f(v):=v^0-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$. For all $u,w\in V$ one has $\lvert u^0-w^0\rvert\le d(u,w)$, because $(u^0-w^0)^2$ is one term of the sum $\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2^2$, and $\bigl\lvert\lvert u_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert-\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\bigr\rvert\le\lVert u_{\mathrm{vec}}-w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2\le d(u,w)$, the first inequality from $\lvert u_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\le\lVert u_{\mathrm{vec}}-w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rVert_2+\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ and its symmetric partner by [L5] and the second because the last three coordinate squares form a sub-sum; hence $\lvert f(u)-f(w)\rvert\le2d(u,w)$. If $f(v)>0$ and $d(u,v)<f(v)/2$, then $f(u)\ge f(v)-2d(u,v)>0$; therefore $T_+=\{v:f(v)>0\}$ is open in the metric topology of [L9], since the ball of radius $f(v)/2$ about each of its points lies in it, and the same argument with $g(v):=-v^0-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ shows that $T_-=\{v:g(v)>0\}$ is open. [step 1.2, L5, L9, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1 the sets $c(T_+)$ and $c(T_-)$ are convex subsets of $\mathbb R^4$, hence path-connected by [L8]. Let $p:[0,1]\to c(T_+)$ be a path in $c(T_+)$ and put $\gamma(t):=c^{-1}(p(t))$, a map into $T_+$ because $c$ is a bijection; then $d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))=\lVert p(s)-p(t)\rVert_2$ for all $s,t$, so for every $\eta>0$ the $\delta>0$ supplied by continuity of $p$ at $t$ gives $d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))<\eta$ whenever $\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$: thus $\gamma$ is a path in the metric space $(V,d)$, and $T_+$ is path-connected. The same argument gives that $T_-$ is path-connected. By [L13] the path-connected sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are connected subsets of $T$, and by step 2.2 they are nonempty with $T=T_+\sqcup T_-$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L5, L8, L13, algebra]

3.2 Suppose $C\subseteq T$ is a connected subset meeting both $T_+$ and $T_-$. The sets $C\cap T_+$ and $C\cap T_-$ are open in the subspace topology on $C$ by step 2.3 and [L11], they are nonempty because $C$ meets both, they are disjoint, and their union is $C$ because $C\subseteq T=T_+\sqcup T_-$ by step 1.1; thus $(C\cap T_+,C\cap T_-)$ is a separation of $C$ in the sense of [L10], contradicting connectedness of $C$. Hence every connected subset of $T$ is contained in $T_+$ or in $T_-$. [step 1.1, step 2.3, L10, L11, algebra]

3.3 The identity $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:f(v)\ge0\}$ holds for the closure in the metric topology of [L9]: if $f(v)<0$, then every $u$ with $d(u,v)<-f(v)/2$ has $f(u)<0$ by the Lipschitz bound of step 2.3, so a ball about $v$ misses $T_+=\{f>0\}$ and $v\notin\operatorname{cl}(T_+)$; conversely, if $f(v)\ge0$, then for every real $t>0$ the point $v+te_0$ has coordinates $(v^0+t,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ by [L2], hence $f(v+te_0)=f(v)+t>0$, so $v+te_0\in T_+$ and $d(v+te_0,v)=t\to0$. The same argument with $g(v)=-v^0-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ gives $\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:g(v)\ge0\}$; in coordinates these are the displayed sets $\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ and $\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$. [step 2.3, L2, L9, algebra]

3.4 Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to T$ be a path with $\gamma(0)\in T_+$ and $\gamma(1)\in T_-$, and put $h(t):=(\gamma(t))^0$. Using the bound $\lvert u^0-w^0\rvert\le d(u,w)$ of step 2.3, for every $\eta>0$ the $\delta>0$ supplied by continuity of $\gamma$ at $t$ gives $\lvert h(s)-h(t)\rvert\le d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))<\eta$ whenever $\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$; hence $h$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ in the sense required by [L14], with $h(0)>0$ because $\gamma(0)\in T_+$ and $h(1)<0$ because $\gamma(1)\in T_-$. By [L14] there is $t\in[0,1]$ with $h(t)=0$; but $\gamma(t)\in T$ gives $(h(t))^2=(\gamma(t)^0)^2>\lvert\gamma(t)_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\ge0$ by step 1.1, so $h(t)\neq0$, a contradiction. Hence no path in $T$ joins $T_+$ to $T_-$. [step 1.1, step 2.3, L14, algebra]

4.1 By step 3.1 the sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are connected, and by step 2.2 they are nonempty and disjoint with $T=T_+\sqcup T_-$. Let $x\in T_+$. By [L12] the component $C_T(x)$ is the largest connected subset of $T$ containing $x$; since $T_+$ is a connected subset of $T$ containing $x$, one has $T_+\subseteq C_T(x)$, while $C_T(x)$ is connected and contains $x\in T_+$, so step 3.2 gives $C_T(x)\subseteq T_+$; hence $C_T(x)=T_+$. The same argument with $x\in T_-$ gives $C_T(x)=T_-$. Therefore $T_+$ and $T_-$ are exactly the connected components of $T$, and since $T=T_+\sqcup T_-$ these are all of them. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, L12]

4.2 If $v\in\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$, then step 3.3 gives $v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ and $v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, hence $0\le2\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\le0$, so $\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert=0$ and $v^0=0$; all coordinates of $v$ vanish, and uniqueness of coordinates [L2] gives $v=0$. Conversely $0$ lies in both displayed sets of step 3.3, hence in both closures. Therefore $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}$. [step 3.3, L2, algebra]

4.3 The descriptions of step 3.3 also show that $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$ are convex cones and that the nonzero causal vectors are exactly the nonzero points of their union. For the cone property, if $v,w\in\operatorname{cl}(T_+)$ and $\lambda\ge0$, then $(v+w)^0=v^0+w^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert+\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}+w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ and $(\lambda v)^0=\lambda v^0\ge\lambda\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert=\lvert\lambda v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ by [L5], so $v+w,\lambda v\in\operatorname{cl}(T_+)$, and reversing the inequalities gives the same for $\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$. For the classification, every timelike vector lies in $T=T_+\cup T_-\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cup\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$ by step 1.1, and every null vector $v$ has $\lvert v^0\rvert=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ by step 1.1, hence lies in $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cup\operatorname{cl}(T_-)$ by step 3.3; conversely a nonzero $v$ in that union satisfies $\lvert v^0\rvert\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, hence $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2\le0$ by step 1.1, and is therefore timelike or null, that is, causal, by [L3]. [step 1.1, step 3.3, L3, L5, algebra]

5.1 Let $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis with coordinate map $c'$ and distance $d'(u,w):=\lVert c'(u)-c'(w)\rVert_2$; then $c'=Mc$ for the change-of-basis matrix $M$ between the two ordered bases, which is invertible because both are bases [L2]. For any real matrix $N$ put $K(N):=\bigl(\sum_a(\sum_b\lvert N_{ab}\rvert)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$; each component of $Nx$ satisfies $\lvert(Nx)_a\rvert\le(\max_b\lvert x_b\rvert)\sum_b\lvert N_{ab}\rvert\le\lVert x\rVert_2\sum_b\lvert N_{ab}\rvert$ by [L5], so $\lVert Nx\rVert_2\le K(N)\lVert x\rVert_2$, and applying this to $M$ and to $M^{-1}$ with $\kappa:=\max\bigl(K(M),K(M^{-1}),1\bigr)\ge1$ gives $\kappa^{-1}\lVert x\rVert_2\le\lVert Mx\rVert_2\le\kappa\lVert x\rVert_2$ for every $x$; hence $d'$ and $d$ determine the same open sets, the same closures and the same connected subsets, so the components of $T$ and the openness and closure claims of this lemma are intrinsic, independent of which $\eta$-orthonormal basis defines the coordinates. Since the argument of steps 1.1 through 4.3 used only that $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is $\eta$-orthonormal, it applies verbatim in the primed coordinates and shows that the primed coordinate sets $\{v:v'^0>\lvert v'_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ and $\{v:v'^0<-\lvert v'_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ are also exactly the two components of $T$; hence the primed pair coincides with the unordered pair $\{T_+,T_-\}$. By [L15] a time orientation is a choice of one of these two components, so the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the chosen $C^+$ and its complement $C^-$ in some order, possibly the reverse of a previously fixed naming; in particular the description is basis-independent up to that interchange. [step 3.3, step 4.2, L2, L5, L15, algebra] ∎

## Definition

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ consisting of the following four pieces of data.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

## Definition

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

## Statement

In every oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and for
every event $o\in A$ there exists an inertial frame with origin $o$; consequently
inertial charts are defined at every event. Explicitly: start from any
$\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ of $V$; if $f_0$ is not in
$C^+$ then replacing $f_0$ by $-f_0$ makes the first vector future, because the
timelike set is the disjoint union of $C^+$ and $C^-$ and
$\eta(-f_0,-f_0)=\eta(f_0,f_0)$; the resulting ordered basis has some orientation
class, and if that class is not the positive class selected by the fixed
orientation of $V$, then replacing $e_1$ by $-e_1$ (or interchanging $e_1$ and
$e_2$) produces a positively oriented ordered basis, without destroying
$\eta$-orthonormality and without changing the first, future vector.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and
an event $o\in A$.

[L1] There is an ordered basis $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ of $V$ with
$\eta(f_a,f_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]).

[L2] The timelike set $T$ is the disjoint union $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$, and a vector
is future timelike exactly when it lies in $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L3] For a finite-dimensional real vector space of dimension at least $1$ there
are exactly two orientations, described as equivalence classes of ordered bases
under the relation $\det P>0$; a basis in the chosen class is positively
oriented ([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

[L4] An inertial frame is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $o\in A$ and an
ordered basis that is $\eta$-orthonormal, future and positively oriented
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L5] If $T:V\to V$ is a linear isomorphism of an oriented real vector space with
$\dim V=n\ge1$, then $\det T>0$ means that $T$ carries every positively oriented
basis to a positively oriented basis, and $\det T<0$ means that it carries every
positively oriented basis to a negatively oriented one; the sign of $\det T$ is
exactly whether $T$ preserves or reverses the orientation
([[thm-determinant-sign-detects-orientation-change]]).

[L6] $\eta$ is a symmetric bilinear form, so
$\eta(-u,-w)=\eta(u,w)$ and $\eta(-u,w)=-\eta(u,w)$ for all $u,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

[L7] The two components $C^+$ and $C^-$ of the timelike set are convex and
satisfy $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ and $0\notin T$
([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [L1] choose an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ of $V$. [L1, choose]

2.1 By [L6], $\eta(-f_0,-f_0)=\eta(f_0,f_0)=-1<0$, so both $f_0$ and $-f_0$ lie in the timelike set $T$; by [L2] the set $T$ is the disjoint union of $C^+$ and $C^-$, so exactly one of $f_0$, $-f_0$ lies in $C^+$: if both lay in the same component, its convexity [L7] would put $0=\tfrac12f_0+\tfrac12(-f_0)$ in that component, contradicting $0\notin T$, and if one lay in each component then $-f_0$ is the required future vector. Define $g_0:=f_0$ if $f_0\in C^+$ and $g_0:=-f_0$ otherwise, and $g_i:=f_i$ for $i=1,2,3$. Then $g_0\in C^+$, and $(g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3)$ is $\eta$-orthonormal: $g_0$ contributes $\eta(g_0,g_0)=\eta(f_0,f_0)=-1$ by [L6], the remaining diagonal entries are $\eta(f_i,f_i)=1$, and each off-diagonal entry is either $\eta(f_a,f_b)=0$ or $-\eta(f_a,f_b)=0$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L6, L7, algebra]

3.1 By [L3] the basis $(g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3)$ lies in exactly one of the two orientation classes of $V$: either it is positively oriented or it is not. [step 2.1, L3]

4.1 Suppose first that $(g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3)$ is positively oriented. Then $(o;g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3)$ is $\eta$-orthonormal, its first vector is future, and its basis is positively oriented, so it is an inertial frame with origin $o$ by [L4]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L4]

4.2 Suppose instead that $(g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3)$ is not positively oriented. Put $e_0:=g_0$, $e_1:=-g_1$, $e_2:=g_2$, $e_3:=g_3$. Orthonormality is preserved exactly as in step 2.1, and $e_0=g_0\in C^+$ is still future. The change-of-basis linear map carrying $(g_0,g_1,g_2,g_3)$ to $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ has matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,1)$, of determinant $-1$; by [L5] it carries the positive class onto the negative class, and since it is a bijection of the set of ordered bases and there are exactly two classes by [L3], it carries the negative class, in which $(g_a)$ lies, onto the positive class; hence $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is positively oriented. Therefore $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an inertial frame with origin $o$ by [L4]. (Interchanging the two basis vectors $g_1,g_2$ would also reverse the orientation and preserve orthonormality and the first vector.) [step 2.1, step 3.1, L3, L5, L6, algebra]

5.1 In either case an inertial frame with origin $o$ exists. The origin is arbitrary in $A$, so taking $o$ any event gives an inertial frame at that event, and the construction uses at most the replacement of $f_0$ by $-f_0$ and one further reversal of orientation; both operations preserve $\eta$-orthonormality and the future character of the first vector. [step 4.1, step 4.2, L4] ∎

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ be one inertial chart. Give $A$ the **transported topology**
in which a set $U\subseteq A$ is open exactly when $x(U)$ is open in
$\mathbb R^4$; this is the unique topology making $x$ a homeomorphism onto
$\mathbb R^4$. Then:

1. $A$ is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological $4$-manifold.
2. The one-chart family $\{(A,x)\}$ is a smooth atlas, so $A$ is a smooth
   $4$-manifold, and $x$ is a diffeomorphism onto $\mathbb R^4$ carrying its
   standard smooth structure.
3. Every affine chart of $A$, that is, every map $y(p)=Mx(p)+b$ with $M$ an
   invertible $4\times4$ real matrix and $b\in\mathbb R^4$, and in particular
   every inertial chart, belongs to the same smooth structure, and its
   transition with $x$ is the smooth diffeomorphism $u\mapsto Mu+b$ of
   $\mathbb R^4$, with inverse $u\mapsto M^{-1}(u-b)$.
4. The transported topology and the smooth structure do not depend on the choice
   of the initial inertial chart $x$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$
and an inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$, with $A$ carrying the transported
topology.

[L1] The inertial chart is $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ for an inertial frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, it is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R^4$, and for another
inertial frame with chart $x'$ one has $x'=M^{-1}(x-x(o'))$ for the
change-of-basis matrix $M$ between the two ordered bases
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L2] A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection whose inverse is continuous; a
bijection $f$ is continuous exactly when $f^{-1}(V)$ is open for every open $V$,
and $f^{-1}$ is continuous exactly when $f(U)$ is open for every open $U$
([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

[L3] A topology is a family of open sets containing $\varnothing$ and $X$ and
closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections; the whole space is open
([[def-topological-space]]).

[L4] A topological $n$-manifold is a topological space that is Hausdorff,
second countable and locally Euclidean of dimension $n$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]).

[L5] A space is Hausdorff when distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods ([[def-hausdorff-space]]).

[L6] In a metric space distinct points $p\ne q$ satisfy
$B(p,d(p,q)/2)\cap B(q,d(p,q)/2)=\varnothing$, so every metric space is
Hausdorff ([[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]).

[L7] $\mathbb R^n$ with its product topology is the metric topology of
$d_\infty$ and is metrizable ([[lem-product-topology-on-rn]], claim 3).

[L8] For $n\ge1$ the rational open boxes form a countable basis for the product
topology on $\mathbb R^n$ ([[thm-rational-points-and-boxes-in-rn]]).

[L9] A space is second countable when its topology has an at most countable
basis, that is, an at most countable family such that every open set is a union
of members of the family ([[def-second-countable-space]]).

[L10] A chart on a topological $n$-manifold is a pair $(U,\varphi)$ with
$U$ open and $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ a homeomorphism onto an open subset of
$\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-manifold-chart-coordinate-domain-and-coordinate-functions]]).

[L11] Charts $(U,\varphi)$, $(V,\psi)$ are smoothly compatible when
$U\cap V=\varnothing$ or both transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and
$\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are smooth, a map between open subsets of Euclidean
spaces being smooth when every component is of class $C^k$ for every $k$
([[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]).

[L12] A smooth atlas on a topological manifold is a covering family of pairwise
smoothly compatible charts; a smooth structure is a maximal smooth atlas, and a
smooth manifold is a topological manifold with a smooth structure
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]).

[L13] Every smooth atlas is contained in exactly one maximal smooth atlas, its
generated structure; two atlases generate the same structure if and only if
their union is a smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).

[L14] A scalar map is of class $C^k$ when every iterated coordinate partial
derivative through order $k$ exists and is continuous
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]); the $j$-th partial
derivative is the directional derivative in the direction of the $j$-th
standard basis vector ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[L15] The function induced by an inner product satisfies
$\lVert v\rVert\ge0$, $\lVert v\rVert=0$ if and only if $v=0$,
$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert$ and
$\lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]).

[L16] An invertible linear map $T:V\to W$ has a unique inverse linear map
$T^{-1}$ and the two are mutually inverse bijections
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]).

[L17] An open subset $W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, is a smooth $n$-manifold
with the standard smooth structure generated by the one-chart atlas
$\{(W,\mathrm{id}_W)\}$ ([[prop-open-subsets-of-euclidean-space-have-the-standard-smooth-structure]]).

[L18] A diffeomorphism of smooth manifolds is a bijective smooth map whose
inverse is smooth; smoothness of a map between smooth manifolds is smoothness of
its coordinate representatives ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]).

## Proof

1.1 The chart $x$ is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R^4$ by [L1], and by the definition of the transported topology $x^{-1}(V)$ is open in $A$ for every open $V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ while $(x^{-1})^{-1}(U)=x(U)$ is open in $\mathbb R^4$ for every open $U\subseteq A$; hence $x$ and $x^{-1}$ are continuous by [L2], so $x$ is a homeomorphism [L2], and the transported topology is the unique topology for which this holds, its open sets being exactly the preimages of the open sets of $\mathbb R^4$ [L2, L3]. [L1, L2, L3]

1.2 Let $N$ be an invertible real $4\times4$ matrix and $c\in\mathbb R^4$, and put $g(u):=Nu+c$. Then $g$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse $g^{-1}(w)=N^{-1}(w-c)$ by [L16]. Each component is $g_l(u)=\sum_jN_{lj}u_j+c_l$; by the definition of the partial derivative [L14], $\partial_jg_l(a)=N_{lj}$ for every $a$, a constant function, and every iterated partial derivative of order at least $2$ is the partial derivative of a constant, hence exists and equals $0$; therefore each component is of class $C^k$ for every $k$ by [L14], so $g$ is smooth by [L11]. Moreover $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are continuous: $\lvert(Nx)_l\rvert\le(\max_j\lvert x_j\rvert)\sum_j\lvert N_{lj}\rvert\le\lVert x\rVert_2\sum_j\lvert N_{lj}\rvert$ by [L15], so $\lVert g(u)-g(v)\rVert_2=\lVert N(u-v)\rVert_2\le K_N\lVert u-v\rVert_2$ with $K_N:=\bigl(\sum_l(\sum_j\lvert N_{lj}\rvert)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$, which is the Lipschitz condition giving the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition of continuity, and the same estimate with $N^{-1}$ in place of $N$ applies to $g^{-1}$. [L11, L14, L15, L16, algebra]

2.1 $\mathbb R^4$ with its standard topology is metrizable by [L7], so distinct points of $\mathbb R^4$ have disjoint open neighbourhoods by [L6]. For $p\ne q$ in $A$ the points $x(p)\ne x(q)$ are distinct because $x$ is injective by step 1.1; choosing disjoint open sets $V\ni x(p)$ and $W\ni x(q)$ in $\mathbb R^4$, the preimages $x^{-1}(V)$ and $x^{-1}(W)$ are open in $A$ by step 1.1 and are disjoint, so $A$ is Hausdorff by [L5]. [step 1.1, L5, L6, L7]

2.2 The rational open boxes form a countable basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^4$ by [L8]. The family $\{x^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal B\}$ is countable and consists of open subsets of $A$ by step 1.1; and it is a basis for the transported topology: if $U\subseteq A$ is open, then $x(U)$ is open in $\mathbb R^4$ by step 1.1 and equals the union of the members of $\mathcal B$ contained in it, so $U$ is the union of the corresponding sets $x^{-1}(B)$, each open in $A$. Hence $A$ is second countable by [L9]. [step 1.1, L8, L9]

2.3 Let $y(p)=Mx(p)+b$ with $M$ invertible and $b\in\mathbb R^4$, and put $g(u):=Mu+b$. Then $y=g\circ x$ is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R^4$ by steps 1.1 and 1.2; it is continuous because for open $V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ the preimage $y^{-1}(V)=x^{-1}(g^{-1}(V))$ is open in $A$ by steps 1.1 and 1.2; and $y^{-1}$ is continuous because for open $U\subseteq A$ its preimage under $y^{-1}$ is $y(U)=g(x(U))$, open in $\mathbb R^4$ by steps 1.1 and 1.2. Therefore $(A,y)$ is a chart on $A$ by [L10]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L10]

2.4 Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame with chart $x'$. By the transition law of [L1], $x'=M^{-1}\bigl(x-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x+b$ with $b:=-M^{-1}x(o')$, where $M$ is the change-of-basis matrix between the two ordered bases and $M^{-1}$ is invertible because both families are ordered bases; this exhibits $x'$ as an affine chart with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ in the sense of the affine maps of step 1.2. [step 1.2, L1]

3.1 By step 2.1 the space $A$ is Hausdorff and by step 2.2 it is second countable. It is locally Euclidean of dimension $4$: for every $p\in A$ the whole space $A$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$ by [L3], and $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a homeomorphism onto the open subset $\mathbb R^4\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ by step 1.1. Hence $A$ is a topological $4$-manifold by [L4], proving claim 1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, L3, L4]

3.2 The transition map between the charts $(A,x)$ and $(A,y)$ of step 2.3 is $y\circ x^{-1}=g$, and its inverse transition is $x\circ y^{-1}=g^{-1}$; by step 1.2 both are smooth, so the two charts are smoothly compatible by [L11]. [step 1.2, step 2.3, L11]

3.3 Let $x'$ be another inertial chart, written $x'=g'\circ x$ with $g'$ an affine map of $\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part by step 2.4. For a subset $U\subseteq A$, openness in the topology transported by $x'$ means that $x'(U)=g'(x(U))$ is open in $\mathbb R^4$, which by step 1.2 (a homeomorphism maps open sets to open sets and reflects them) is equivalent to $x(U)$ being open in $\mathbb R^4$, that is, to $U$ being open in the topology transported by $x$ by step 1.1. Hence the two transported topologies coincide. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.4]

4.1 The pair $(A,x)$ is a chart by steps 1.1 and [L10]; the one-chart family $\{(A,x)\}$ covers $A$ and the pairwise smooth-compatibility condition is vacuous, so it is a smooth atlas by [L12]; the maximal smooth atlas it generates exists and is unique by [L13], and $A$ with this smooth structure is a smooth $4$-manifold by [L12]. [step 1.1, step 3.1, L10, L12, L13]

5.1 Every affine chart $y=Mx+b$ is smoothly compatible with the chart $(A,x)$ by step 3.2, and every inertial chart is an affine chart by step 2.4; hence each of these charts belongs to the smooth structure generated by the atlas $\{(A,x)\}$ of step 4.1, by the criterion of [L13] that two one-chart atlases generate the same structure exactly when their union is a smooth atlas. [step 2.4, step 3.2, step 4.1, L13]

5.2 $\mathbb R^4$ is an open subset of itself and carries the standard smooth structure generated by the one-chart atlas $\{(\mathbb R^4,\mathrm{id})\}$ by [L17]. With respect to the charts $(A,x)$ of step 4.1 and $(\mathbb R^4,\mathrm{id})$, the coordinate representative of $x$ is $\mathrm{id}\circ x\circ x^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^4}$ and the representative of $x^{-1}$ is likewise $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R^4}$; the identity of $\mathbb R^4$ has components $u_l$ whose partial derivatives are the constants $\delta_{lj}$ with all higher iterated partial derivatives $0$, so it is smooth by [L14] and [L11]. Hence $x$ is a smooth bijection with smooth inverse, that is, a diffeomorphism $A\to\mathbb R^4$ by [L18], proving claim 2. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, L11, L14, L17, L18]

6.1 The smooth structures generated by the one-chart atlases $\{(A,x)\}$ and $\{(A,x')\}$ of two inertial charts coincide: by step 2.4 and step 5.1 the chart $x'$ is smoothly compatible with $x$, so the union of the two one-chart atlases is a smooth atlas and [L13] gives equality of the generated maximal atlases; combined with step 3.3 this proves claim 3 for the transition and claim 4. [step 2.4, step 3.3, step 5.1, L13, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with
the smooth structure of [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]], and
let $p\in A$. For a smooth germ $[f]$ at $p$ define

$$\Phi_p(v)([f]):=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}f(p+tv),\qquad v\in V .$$

Then $\Phi_p:V\to T_pA$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$ onto the tangent space
$T_pA$; in particular $T_pA$ is canonically identified with $V$, independently
of any chart. If $x$ is an inertial chart and
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$, then the coordinate derivations satisfy
$\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An event $p$ of $A$, an inertial chart $x$ with frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$, and the map $\Phi_p$ of the
Statement.

[L1] The tangent space $T_pA$ is the set of derivations at $p$, i.e. of
$\mathbb R$-linear maps $v:C^\infty_p(A)\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$v([f][g])=f(p)v([g])+g(p)v([f])$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

[L2] A smooth germ at $p$ has a coordinate representative smooth near $x(p)$,
and composition with smooth maps is smooth: for a smooth curve
$c:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to A$ through $p$ and a smooth germ $[f]$, the
map $t\mapsto f(c(t))$ is smooth near $0$
([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]],
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

[L3] If a map $g$ between open subsets of Euclidean space has all partial
derivatives continuous at $a$, then $g$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and
$Dg(a)$ is the linear map with matrix the Jacobian of $g$ at $a$
([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]).

[L4] If $g$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $h$ at $g(a)$, then
$D(h\circ g)(a)=Dh(g(a))\circ Dg(a)$
([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[L5a] Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, $c$ a limit point of $A$, and $f,g$ differentiable at $c$; then $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ with $(fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c)$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], claim 3).

[L5] The coordinate derivations $\partial_0|_p,\partial_1|_p,\partial_2|_p,\partial_3|_p$
of a smooth chart form a basis of $T_pA$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]).

[L6] In an inertial chart $x$, the affine structure gives
$x(p+tv)=x(p)+tu$ with $u=E^{-1}(v)$ for every $v\in V$, and
$E:\mathbb R^4\to V$ is a linear isomorphism
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]).

## Proof

1.1 Fix $v\in V$ and a smooth germ $[f]$ at $p$. By [L6] the curve $c(t):=p+tv$ has coordinate representation $x(c(t))=x(p)+tu$ with $u=E^{-1}(v)$, a smooth curve in $\mathbb R^4$; hence $c$ is a smooth curve through $p$ in the chart $x$, and $t\mapsto f(c(t))$ is smooth near $0$ by [L2], so its derivative at $0$ exists. If $g$ agrees with $f$ near $p$, then $f\circ c$ and $g\circ c$ agree near $0$, so the derivative depends only on the germ $[f]$; hence $\Phi_p(v)([f])$ is a well-defined real number. [L2, L6]

2.1 With $u=E^{-1}(v)=(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$, set $F:=f\circ x^{-1}$, the smooth coordinate representative of $[f]$ near $x(p)$ [L2]. Then $f(c(t))=F(x(p)+tu)$ for $t$ near $0$, so by the chain rule [L4] applied to $t\mapsto x(p)+tu$ and to $F$, whose total derivative at $x(p)$ has matrix the Jacobian by [L3], $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\bigr|_0F\bigl(x(p)+tu\bigr)=D F(x(p))\cdot u=\sum_{a=0}^3u^a\partial_aF(x(p))$. [step 1.1, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

3.1 $\Phi_p$ is linear in $v$: by step 2.1 the value $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\sum_au^a\partial_aF(x(p))$ is a linear function of $u=E^{-1}(v)$, and $E^{-1}$ is linear by [L6]. [step 2.1, L6, algebra]

3.2 $\Phi_p(v)$ is a derivation at $p$: for smooth germs $[f],[g]$, the coordinate representatives satisfy $((fg)\circ x^{-1})=(f\circ x^{-1})(g\circ x^{-1})$, so the one-variable product rule [L5a] applied to the differentiable functions $t\mapsto F(y+te_a)$ and $t\mapsto G(y+te_a)$ gives the product rule for the partial derivatives: $\partial_a((fg)\circ x^{-1})(x(p))=f(p)\partial_a(g\circ x^{-1})(x(p))+g(p)\partial_a(f\circ x^{-1})(x(p))$, since $f(x^{-1}(x(p)))=f(p)$ and likewise for $g$; substituting into step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(v)([f][g])=f(p)\Phi_p(v)([g])+g(p)\Phi_p(v)([f])$, so $\Phi_p(v)\in T_pA$ by [L1]. [step 2.1, L1, L2, algebra]

3.3 $\Phi_p$ is injective: suppose $\Phi_p(v)=0$ with coordinate vector $u=E^{-1}(v)$. Applying $\Phi_p(v)$ to the germ of the coordinate function $x^a$ gives, by step 2.1, $\Phi_p(v)([x^a])=\sum_bu^b\partial_b(x^a\circ x^{-1})(x(p))=\sum_bu^b\delta^a_b=u^a$; hence $u=0$, and since $E^{-1}$ is injective by [L6], $v=0$. [step 2.1, L6, algebra]

4.1 $\Phi_p$ carries the basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ to the coordinate derivations: for $v=e_a$ one has $u=E^{-1}(e_a)=(\delta^a_b)_b$ by [L6], so step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(e_a)([f])=\partial_aF(x(p))=\partial_a|_p([f])$ for every smooth germ, that is, $\Phi_p(e_a)=\partial_a|_p$. By [L5] the derivations $\partial_a|_p$ form a basis of $T_pA$, so the linear map $\Phi_p$ carries a basis of $V$ to a basis of $T_pA$; hence $\Phi_p$ is surjective (its image contains a basis) and injective by step 3.3, so it is a linear isomorphism $V\to T_pA$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.3, L5, L6]

5.1 Finally, let $v=\sum_av^ae_a$; then $u=E^{-1}(v)=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$, so step 2.1 gives $\Phi_p(v)([f])=\sum_av^a\partial_aF(x(p))$, that is, $\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$. The construction uses only the affine structure $p+tv$ and the smooth structure of the model, both fixed independently of any choice of chart, so the isomorphism $\Phi_p$ is canonical. [step 4.1, L6, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with its inertial chart
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Every $v\in V$ has a unique
coordinate vector $(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v=\sum_av^ae_a$. For an ordered
$4$-tuple $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of vectors of $V$ let

$$[v_j^a]:=\begin{pmatrix}v_0^0&v_1^0&v_2^0&v_3^0\\ v_0^1&v_1^1&v_2^1&v_3^1\\ v_0^2&v_1^2&v_2^2&v_3^2\\ v_0^3&v_1^3&v_2^3&v_3^3\end{pmatrix}$$

be the $4\times4$ real matrix whose $j$-th column lists the coordinates of
$v_j$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and define

$$\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3):=\det\bigl([v_j^a]\bigr)$$

by the determinant of a square matrix
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]). Then $\epsilon$ is an **alternating
$4$-linear form** on $V$
([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]]): the determinant is multilinear and
alternating in the columns, so replacing one $v_j$ by $\lambda v_j+\mu w$
replaces the $j$-th column correspondingly and $\epsilon$ is linear in each
argument, and $\epsilon(v_0,\ldots,v_3)=0$ whenever two arguments coincide,
since then two columns coincide
([[thm-determinant-is-the-unique-normalized-alternating-multilinear-function]]).
The form $\epsilon$ is the **oriented volume form of the model**. Its
well-definedness as a form of the model, independent of the inertial frame used
in the display, is proved in [[lem-volume-form-is-independent-of-the-oriented-frame]].

**Components.** Write $\epsilon_{abcd}:=\epsilon(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ for the
components of $\epsilon$ in the inertial frame. Evaluating the determinant on
the coordinate matrix of $(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$, which is the permutation matrix
of the tuple, gives

$$\epsilon_{0123}=+1,\qquad \epsilon_{abcd}=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\ \text{ if }(a,b,c,d)=(\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\sigma(2),\sigma(3))\ \text{ for a permutation }\sigma,$$

and $\epsilon_{abcd}=0$ whenever two of the indices coincide; these are the
**permutation symbols** of the frame. Indeed the coordinate vector of $e_a$ is
the $a$-th standard basis vector, so the coordinate matrix of
$(e_a,e_b,e_c,e_d)$ is the permutation matrix of the tuple and its determinant
is $+1$ on the identity tuple, the sign of the permutation otherwise, and $0$
when two indices repeat.

**Raised components.** The **inverse metric** $\eta^{ab}$ is the inverse of the
matrix $\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, which
exists because $\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]); it is again
$\eta^{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)^{ab}$. The raised components of the
volume form are

$$\epsilon^{abcd}:=\eta^{aa'}\eta^{bb'}\eta^{cc'}\eta^{dd'}\epsilon_{a'b'c'd'}$$

(summation over repeated primed indices). Since the inverse metric is diagonal
with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$, only one term contributes to $\epsilon^{0123}$
and

$$\epsilon^{0123}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}\eta^{22}\eta^{33}\epsilon_{0123}=(-1)(+1)(+1)(+1)(+1)=-1 .$$

**Spatial symbol.** The **spatial permutation symbol** $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for
$i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ is defined by $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ together with alternation
in the three indices; explicitly $\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ for even permutations of
$(1,2,3)$, $\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ for odd permutations, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$
whenever two of $i,j,k$ coincide.

## Statement

The alternating $4$-linear form $\epsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]] does not depend on the inertial frame
used to define it. Explicitly, if $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and
$(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ are inertial frames with
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$ for the change-of-basis matrix $M$, then $\det M=+1$
(both ordered bases are positively oriented), and the coordinate matrices $X$,
$X'$ of any tuple $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ in the two frames satisfy $X'=M^{-1}X$,
so that $\det X'=\det(M^{-1})\det X=\det X$. Consequently
$\epsilon(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$ for every inertial frame, $\epsilon$ is the unique
alternating $4$-linear form on $V$ taking the value $1$ on every positively
oriented $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis, and in every inertial frame the
raised component $\epsilon^{0123}$ equals $-1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Inertial frames $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ of
$V$ with $e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, and the form $\epsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]].

[L1] $\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ is the determinant of the matrix whose $j$-th
column lists the coordinates of $v_j$ in an inertial frame; its components are
the permutation symbols with $\epsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\epsilon^{0123}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}\eta^{22}\eta^{33}\epsilon_{0123}=-1$, and the
inverse metric is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ in an inertial frame
([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]).

[L2] An inertial frame's ordered basis is $\eta$-orthonormal, future and
positively oriented, and its chart satisfies the transition law
$x'=M^{-1}(x-x(o'))$ for the change-of-basis matrix $M$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L3] In an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis the matrix of $\eta$ is
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]).

[L4] Two ordered bases are equivalent, and in the same positive class, when the
change-of-basis linear isomorphism $P$ has $\det P>0$; an orientation is one
equivalence class and a basis in the chosen class is positively oriented
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

[L5] An alternating $k$-linear map vanishes whenever two arguments coincide and
is linear in each argument separately
([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]]).

[L6] $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ for square matrices over a commutative ring
([[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]).

[L7] $\det(A^{-1})=(\det A)^{-1}$ for an invertible square matrix
([[cor-determinant-of-an-inverse]]).

[L8] The determinant is the unique column-multilinear, alternating, normalized
function on $n\times n$ matrices
([[thm-determinant-is-the-unique-normalized-alternating-multilinear-function]]).

## Proof

1.1 From $e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$ and the $\eta$-orthonormality of both frames [L2, L3], $\eta_{ab}=\eta(e'_a,e'_b)=\sum_{c,d}M^c_aM^d_b\eta(e_c,e_d)=(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{ab}$, that is, $M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta$ with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; taking determinants and using [L6] gives $(\det M)^2\det\eta=\det\eta$, and $\det\eta=-1$, so $(\det M)^2=1$. [L2, L3, L6, algebra]

2.1 Both ordered bases lie in the positive class selected by the fixed orientation of $V$ [L2], so the change of basis between them has determinant $>0$ by [L4]; together with $(\det M)^2=1$ from step 1.1 this gives $\det M=+1$. [step 1.1, L2, L4, algebra]

3.1 Let $X=(X^b_j)$ and $X'=(X'^b_j)$ be the coordinate matrices of a tuple $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ in the two frames. Substituting $e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$ into $v_j=\sum_aX'^a_je'_a=\sum_aX^a_je_a$ gives $X^b_j=\sum_aM^b_aX'^a_j$, that is, $X=MX'$, hence $X'=M^{-1}X$ and, by [L6] and [L7], $\det X'=\det(M^{-1})\det X=(\det M)^{-1}\det X=\det X$ because $\det M=1$ by step 2.1. [step 2.1, L6, L7, algebra]

4.1 By step 3.1 the two determinants that [L1] uses to define $\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ in the two frames agree, so $\epsilon$ does not depend on the inertial frame; in particular the coordinate matrix of the frame $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ in the frame $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is $M^{-1}$, so $\epsilon(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=\det(M^{-1})=1$ by [L7] and step 2.1. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L7, algebra]

5.1 The raised component: in an inertial frame [L3] gives $\eta^{aa}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\epsilon_{0123}=1$ by [L1] and step 4.1, so $\epsilon^{0123}=(-1)(+1)(+1)(+1)\cdot1=-1$; since $\epsilon$ is frame independent by step 4.1, this value is the same in every inertial frame. [step 4.1, L1, L3, algebra]

6.1 For uniqueness, let $\epsilon'$ be any alternating $4$-linear form on $V$ with $\epsilon'(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)=1$ for every positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Fix an inertial frame $(e_a)$ and a tuple $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ with coordinate matrix $X$. Expanding each $v_j=\sum_aX^a_je_a$ and using multilinearity and alternation [L5] together with the normalization and [L8], $\epsilon'(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)=\det(X)\epsilon'(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=\det X$, which equals $\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ by [L1]. Hence $\epsilon$ is the unique alternating $4$-linear form normalized to $1$ on every positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis, which completes the proof of all the displayed claims. [step 4.1, step 5.1, L1, L2, L5, L8, algebra] ∎

## Definition

This framework fixes the following SI coordinate and unit conventions for the
oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and its inertial
charts ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

1. **Adopted conversion constant.** The framework uses a positive real constant
   $c$, the **speed of light in vacuum**, with the SI unit metre per second,
   $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$. Its numerical value is an empirical parameter of the
   model, not a mathematical constant, and no measurement of it is made or
   quoted in this definition.
2. **Coordinates.** In every inertial chart $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ the temporal
   coordinate is $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is the reading of an ideal clock at rest in
   the frame with the SI unit second $\mathrm s$, and $x^1,x^2,x^3$ are measured
   in metres $\mathrm m$ along the frame's orthonormal spatial directions
   $e_1,e_2,e_3$. Thus all four coordinates $x^a$ carry the unit $\mathrm m$.
3. **Metric components.** With these coordinates the matrix of $\eta$ in an
   inertial chart is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with **dimensionless**
   entries, and the interval $I(p,q)=\eta(q-p,q-p)$ carries the unit
   $\mathrm m^2$.
4. **Proper time of a straight segment.** For a timelike displacement $q-p$ the
   number

   $$\tau:=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}$$

   has the unit second $\mathrm s$ and is the **proper time of the straight
   timelike segment from $p$ to $q$**. The factor $c^{-1}$ converts the length
   $\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}$ in metres into a time in seconds.
5. **Derived kinematic quantities.** For a timelike worldline parametrized by
   its proper time $\tau$, the four-velocity $U=\mathrm dx/\mathrm d\tau$ has
   unit $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, the four-acceleration $\mathrm dU/\mathrm d\tau$
   has unit $\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$, the four-momentum $mU$ of a particle of
   mass $m$ has unit $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, and the observer energy
   has unit joule. These units are recorded here as bookkeeping; the definitions
   of the quantities themselves belong to the later worldlines, mechanics and
   energy-momentum pages.
6. **Temporal-coordinate convention.** If instead a chart uses a temporal
   coordinate $t$ in seconds as the first coordinate, then the corresponding
   metric component is $g_{tt}=-c^2$ with unit
   $\mathrm m^2/\mathrm s^2$, the mixed time-space components acquire the unit
   $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, and formulas derived in one convention are not reused
   unchanged in the other.
7. **Natural units.** Natural units with $c=1$ may be used only together with an
   explicit restoration table for $c$; a value $c=1$ is then a convention of
   presentation, not a claim that the empirical constant equals the number $1$.

**Status.** These are conventions and dimensional bookkeeping for the model.
The numerical value of $c$ is empirical; SI unit status does not make any
quantity primitive in the theory, and the choice of unit system does not add
physical content to the affine Minkowski model.

## Postulate

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

Adopt the assumption that the equations of the specific mechanical and
electromagnetic models developed from this framework are covariant under the
inertial changes of description: each such model equation has the same form
when its events are relabelled by $F$ and its displacements and other tensors
are transformed by $L$.

## Status, scope and limitations

- **Adopted, not deduced.** Both clauses are adopted assumptions of the
  framework. They are not deduced from experiment in this item, and they are
  not derived from the verbal postulates of Einstein; together with the
  ideal-clock and ideal-light assumptions of the companion postulate they fix
  the framework's physical interpretation.
- **What covariance is claimed for.** Clause (ii) asserts covariance only for
  the equations of the mechanical and electromagnetic models developed in this
  framework from the present primitives. It does not select a force law, a
  matter model or an equation of motion, and it does not assert that every
  conceivable equation written in the coordinates of the model is covariant;
  a previously adopted background structure would not be excluded by a purely
  syntactic covariance test. The formulation is a constraint on the form of the
  models, not a derivation of dynamics.
- **Scope.** The scope of the assumption is flat classical spacetime with
  idealized events and inertial descriptions only: gravitational effects (no
  curvature of the affine model is introduced), globally accelerated or
  rotating frame structure, and quantum effects are outside it. The companion
  item [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] states the corresponding ideal-clock
  and ideal-light assumptions.
- **No claim about nature.** Covariance of the model equations under the maps
  above is a property of the specified model. It carries no claim that the
  physical world is exactly described by the model, and experimental agreement
  with a model prediction would be evidence about the specified model rather
  than a proof of this postulate.

## Postulate

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements, with the SI coordinate and unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]].

**(i) Ideal clocks.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let
$x:I\to A$ be a curve whose coordinate representation in an inertial chart is
of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]) with
everywhere future timelike coordinate derivative. An **ideal clock** carried
along $x$ reads, between parameters $a<b$ in $I$,

$$\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr)}\,\mathrm ds .$$

There is no additional acceleration-dependent term in the reading: the reading
depends only on the curve and the interval, not on the acceleration
(**clock hypothesis**). The integrand is a positive continuous function of $s$
on the compact interval $[a,b]$, so the integral is a well-defined Riemann
integral.

**(ii) Ideal light.** In vacuum, the **ideal light rays** are exactly the future
null straight lines

$$\{\,p+\lambda v:\lambda\in\mathbb R\,\},\qquad p\in A,\quad v\in V\ \text{future null},$$

parametrized at $p$ by $\lambda=0$. In every inertial chart $x$, such a ray has

$$x(\lambda)=x(p)+\lambda\,(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3),$$

and because $v$ is future null the components satisfy $v^0=\lvert v_{\text{vec}}\rvert>0$
by the orthonormal-coordinate description of the closed cones
([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]): hence the spatial coordinate
velocity of the ray has magnitude $\lvert v_{\text{vec}}\rvert/v^0\cdot c=c$ in
**every** inertial chart, with $x^0=ct$. The adopted conversion constant $c$ is
therefore the same in all inertial charts; its numerical value is an empirical
parameter of the model.

## Scope, status and limitations

- **Adopted, not proved.** Both clauses are adopted assumptions of the
  framework, with the physical interpretation fixed by
  [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. They are not experimentally proved here, and
  they carry no claim that real clocks or real light are exactly ideal.
- **Ideal apparatus, complete vacuum, geometric ray regime.** The light clause
  concerns ideal light in complete vacuum in the geometric (nondispersive) ray
  regime. No dispersive or refractive medium is described, and the ray model
  carries no wave-optics, coherence or intensity structure.
- **No quantum photon model.** No photon is assumed, and in particular the
  frequency of the ideal light is not identified with an energy by a factor
  $\hbar$ anywhere in this framework's primitive layer.
- **Later development.** Parametrization invariance of the clock reading, the
  proper-time function along general worldlines, four-velocity and
  four-acceleration are developed on the later worldlines-and-clocks page from
  its own items; the present item states the reading rule and the ray
  interpretation for the model and does not derive that theory here.
- **Empirical status.** Agreement of an experiment with predictions of this
  model would be evidence about the specified model and its auxiliary
  assumptions; it would not be a proof of this postulate, and a finite dataset
  cannot establish its exact validity.

## Definition

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.

## Status audit

This remark records the primitive and derived status of the notions introduced
on the spacetime-primitives page, as required before the page's derived claims.
It is bookkeeping: it asserts no physical law and no empirical claim.

**Primitive mathematical structure of the model.** The quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]: the affine space $A$ with
its action of $V$ and the displacement $q-p$, the Lorentz form $\eta$ of
signature $(-,+,+,+)$, the orientation of $V$ fixed as a positive ray of
$\Lambda^4V$, and the time-orientation component $C^+$ of the timelike set.

**Primitive physical interpretation and parameters adopted on this page.** The
physical event interpretation together with the covariance assumption
([[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]); the ideal-clock and ideal-vacuum-light
interpretation ([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]); and the conversion
constant $c$, whose numerical value is empirical and whose unit is fixed by
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. These are adopted assumptions
of the framework, not deductions.

**Derived (constructed, not adopted) on this page.** Displacements and
intervals; the causal classification of displacements; inertial frames and
their inertial charts ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); the smooth
structure of $A$ making it a smooth $4$-manifold and the canonical identification
$T_pA\cong V$; the oriented volume form and its components
([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); and the spatial Euclidean structure
and vector product of a named inertial frame
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). These are
mathematical constructions from the primitive structure, with the stated
frame-dependence where it occurs.

**Not introduced on this page and not primitive in its scope.** Proper time
along general worldlines, four-velocity and four-acceleration, momentum, energy,
charge, and any force or matter law. Later pages introduce their own adopted
premises and must repeat this status audit for them; a definition on a later
page is not made primitive by this page's conventions.

**Mathematical versus empirical status.** The mathematical statements of this
page concern only the stipulated geometry. They do not assert that the model
describes nature; the physical interpretation enters through the two adopted
postulates, whose empirical support would be evidence about the specified model
rather than a proof.

## Example

Worked computation of the transition between two inertial charts. Let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with
inertial frames $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ and
charts
$x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$, $x'(p)=E'^{-1}(p-o')$, and write
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$ with $M$ the change-of-basis matrix. Then for every
event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)+b,\qquad b:=-M^{-1}x(o'),$$

so the transition is an affine map of $\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part
$M^{-1}$.

**Restriction to the plane of $e_0,e_1$.** Fix an inertial frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $o$ the origin of $A$ used in the charts, and a real
parameter $r$, and put

$$e'_0:=\cosh r\,e_0+\sinh r\,e_1,\qquad e'_1:=\sinh r\,e_0+\cosh r\,e_1,\qquad e'_2:=e_2,\qquad e'_3:=e_3,$$

with $o':=o$. Then $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is again an inertial frame: the
matrix of the change of basis is the block matrix
$M=\operatorname{diag}\Bigl(\begin{pmatrix}\cosh r&\sinh r\\ \sinh r&\cosh r\end{pmatrix},I_2\Bigr)$
with $\det M=\cosh^2r-\sinh^2r=1$, and

$$M^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}\Bigl(\begin{pmatrix}\cosh r&-\sinh r\\ -\sinh r&\cosh r\end{pmatrix},I_2\Bigr).$$

Since $M$ has determinant $1$, the two bases are positively oriented together;
the new timelike vector satisfies
$\eta(e'_0,e'_0)=-\cosh^2r+\sinh^2r=-1<0$ with
$\cosh r>\lvert\sinh r\rvert$, so it is future timelike; hence the primed tuple
is an inertial frame. The transition values are
$x'(o)=0$ and $x'\bigl(x^{-1}(1,0,0,0)\bigr)=(\cosh r,-\sinh r,0,0)$. Inertial frames
exist at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], so the
computation applies with any chosen origin.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The inertial frames and charts of the Example, with
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, and the restricted basis with the hyperbolic parameter
$r$.

[L1] An inertial frame's ordered basis is $\eta$-orthonormal, future and
positively oriented; its chart is $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$, so $x(o)=0$; and for
another inertial frame with chart $x'$ the transition law
$x'=M^{-1}(x-x(o'))$ holds ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L2] $\cosh u=(e^u+e^{-u})/2>0$ and $\sinh u=(e^u-e^{-u})/2$
([[def-hyperbolic-functions]]), and
$\cosh^2u-\sinh^2u=1$ for every real $u$
([[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]).

[L3] In an $\eta$-orthonormal basis the matrix of $\eta$ is
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, so
$\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L4] A timelike vector $v$ with $\eta(v,v)<0$ and
$v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ is future timelike
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L5] The change-of-basis map between two ordered bases has $\det>0$ exactly
when the bases lie in the same positive class; a positive class is an
orientation and a basis in it is positively oriented
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

[L6] The change-of-basis matrix between two ordered bases is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]), and an expression
$u\mapsto M^{-1}u+b$ is an affine map of $\mathbb R^4$
([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct computation with the transition law and the hyperbolic identity.

1.1 For a general pair of inertial frames, substituting $E'(u)=E(Mu)$, equivalently $E'=E\circ M$, into $x'=E'^{-1}(p-o')$ and using $p-o'=E\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)$ gives $x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o')$, an affine map with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ by [L1] and [L6]. [L1, L6, algebra]

1.2 For the restricted basis, $\eta(e'_0,e'_0)=-\cosh^2r+\sinh^2r=-1$ and $\eta(e'_1,e'_1)=-\sinh^2r+\cosh^2r=1$ by [L3] and [L2], while $\eta(e'_0,e'_1)=-\cosh r\sinh r+\sinh r\cosh r=0$; also $\eta(e'_i,e'_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\in\{2,3\}$ and the mixed entries vanish. Hence $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is $\eta$-orthonormal by [L1]. [L1, L2, L3, algebra]

1.3 The matrix $M$ of the restricted change of basis is the displayed block matrix, and $\det M=\cosh^2r-\sinh^2r=1$ by [L2]; its inverse is the displayed block matrix, since multiplying the two blocks gives the identity using $\cosh^2r-\sinh^2r=1$. [L2, algebra]

2.1 By $\cosh^2r-\sinh^2r=1$ and $\cosh r>0$ one has $\cosh r=\sqrt{1+\sinh^2r}>\lvert\sinh r\rvert$ for every real $r$; with $\eta(e'_0,e'_0)=-1<0$ from step 1.2, the vector $e'_0$ is future timelike by [L4]. Since $\det M=1>0$ by step 1.3, the primed basis lies in the same positive class as the positively oriented original basis by [L5]; hence $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is an inertial frame by [L1]. [step 1.2, step 1.3, L1, L2, L4, L5, algebra]

3.1 With $o'=o$ and $x(o)=0$ by [L1], the transition law of step 1.1 gives $x'(o)=M^{-1}(x(o)-x(o'))=0$, and for the event $p=x^{-1}(1,0,0,0)$, whose coordinates in the first chart are $x(p)=(1,0,0,0)$, it gives $x'(p)=M^{-1}(1,0,0,0)=(\cosh r,-\sinh r,0,0)$ by the inverse computed in step 1.3. This completes the worked computation of the transition and its two displayed values. [step 1.1, step 1.3, L1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Worked classification in an inertial frame of the model. Let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$x$ be an inertial chart with frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, so that
$x(e_a)=(\delta_a^0,\delta_a^1,\delta_a^2,\delta_a^3)$ are the coordinates of
the basis vectors. Computing with the components
$\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$:

- $v=(1,1,0,0)$ has $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v^0=1=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, so
  $v$ is future null;
- $w=(2,1,0,0)$ has $\eta(w,w)=-4+1=-3<0$ and
  $w^0=2>1=\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, so $w$ is future timelike;
- $z=(1,2,0,0)$ has $\eta(z,z)=-1+4=3>0$, so $z$ is spacelike;
- $u=(-1,1,0,0)$ has $\eta(u,u)=0$ and $u^0=-1<0$, so $u$ is past null;
- $e_0=(1,0,0,0)$ is future timelike with $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$, and $-e_0$ is
  past timelike.

In particular no future causal displacement is spacelike, and the coordinate
descriptions $v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ (future causal) and
$v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$ (past causal) reproduce the sign
classification.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial chart $x$ of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and the coordinate vectors listed in the Example.

[L1] In an $\eta$-orthonormal basis $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$,
so $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$
([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], statement).

[L2] A vector is timelike when $\eta(v,v)<0$, null when $v\ne0$ and
$\eta(v,v)=0$, spacelike when $\eta(v,v)>0$
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

[L3] For a fixed time orientation, the closed cones are
$\operatorname{cl}(C^+)=\{v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$ and
$\operatorname{cl}(C^-)=\{v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}$, and a
nonzero null vector is future null exactly when it lies in
$\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and past null exactly when it lies in
$\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L4] An inertial frame's basis is $\eta$-orthonormal and its first vector is
future, and the frame's coordinates of $v$ are its coordinates in the ordered
basis ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct computation with the diagonal form.

1.1 The displacement $v=(1,1,0,0)$ satisfies $\eta(v,v)=-1+1=0$ and $v\ne0$, so $v$ is null by [L2]; since $v^0=1=\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, the vector lies in $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and is future null by [L3]. [L1, L2, L3, algebra]

1.2 The displacement $w=(2,1,0,0)$ satisfies $\eta(w,w)=-4+1=-3<0$, so $w$ is timelike by [L2]; since $w^0=2>1=\lvert w_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert$, it lies in $C^+$ and is future timelike by [L3]. [L1, L2, L3, algebra]
