## Statement

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let
$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be its spatial three-space with
Euclidean form $\delta$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]),
and let $L:V\to V$ be a proper orthochronous Lorentz map
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Write $u:=Le_0$, with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$ in the frame, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$ and $u^0>0$.
Then:

(i) $|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$ and the parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfies
$|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$;

(ii) the linear map $\widehat R:=B(\boldsymbol\beta)L$ satisfies
$\widehat Re_0=e_0$ and $\widehat R(S)=S$, and its restriction to $S$ is a
spatial rotation of the frame ([[def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame]]);
hence $\widehat R$ is the extension $\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ of the unique
spatial rotation $R:=\widehat R|_S$ and
$L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ is a product of a passive boost and a
spatial rotation;

(iii) conversely, for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and
every spatial rotation $R$ of the frame, the extension
$\widehat R=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map and
the product $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz
map;

(iv) the factorization $L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ of (ii) is unique: if
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta_1)\widehat R_1=B(-\boldsymbol\beta_2)\widehat R_2$ with
$|\boldsymbol\beta_i|<1$ and spatial rotations $\widehat R_i$, then
$\boldsymbol\beta_1=\boldsymbol\beta_2$ and $R_1=R_2$;

(v) $L$ is a passive boost, that is $L=B(\boldsymbol\beta')$ for some
$|\boldsymbol\beta'|<1$, if and only if the rotation $R$ in (ii) is the
identity, and then $\boldsymbol\beta'=-\boldsymbol\beta$ with
$\boldsymbol\beta$ the parameter of (i).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with spatial three-space $S$, a proper orthochronous Lorentz map $L$, and $u:=Le_0$ with coordinates $(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$ in the frame.

[L1] A linear Lorentz map is a linear $L$ with $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$; it is proper when $\det L=+1$ and orthochronous when $L(C^+)=C^+$; $O(V,\eta)$ and $SO^+(V,\eta)$ denote the corresponding sets ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[L2] A linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, satisfies $\det L=\pm1$, and has Lorentz inverse; it preserves $\eta(v,v)$ and the causal character of every nonzero vector; $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds exactly when $L(C^+)\subseteq C^+$; composition of linear Lorentz maps is a linear Lorentz map, and the proper orthochronous ones form a subgroup ([[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]]).

[L3] For $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is defined by its coordinate action, and in the frame's ordered basis it has the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\gamma&-\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta&I_3+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ with $\gamma=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]]).

[L4] For every $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$: $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with $B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$; $B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$; the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective; if $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with $u^0>0$ then $B(u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0)u=e_0$ ([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]]).

[L5] A spatial rotation of the frame is a linear $R:V\to V$ with $R(e_0)=e_0$, $R(S)\subseteq S$, $\delta(Rw,Rz)=\delta(w,z)$ for all $w,z\in S$, and $\det(R|_S)=+1$ ([[def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[L6] In an inertial frame, $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0\in C^+$; the chart is the affine coordinate map of the frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L7] $S=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\}$, $\delta=\eta|_{S\times S}$ is positive definite with $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and $V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$; hence for $v=v^0e_0+w$, $z=z^0e_0+y$ with $w,y\in S$ one has $\eta(v,z)=-v^0z^0+\delta(w,y)$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[L8] $(S,\delta)$ is a finite-dimensional real inner product space, and an endomorphism of it is a linear isometry exactly when it preserves $\delta$; orthogonal operators have determinant $\pm1$ ([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], [[cor-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators-form-groups-and-have-unit-determinant-modulus]]).

[L9] In every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis the timelike set is $T_+\cup T_-$ with $T_+=\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$, $T_-=\{x:x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$, and these are exactly the two components of $T$; in particular $\eta(x,x)=-(x^0)^2+|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L10] $C^+$ is one of the two components $T_+,T_-$ and $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$; a vector of $C^+$ is future timelike ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L11] For an operator on a finite-dimensional space, $\det T$ is the determinant of its matrix in any ordered basis, independently of the basis, and $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ with $\det(\operatorname{id})=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]], [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]).

[L12] For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring, $\det(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}$ where $\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)$ counts the pairs $i<j<n$ with $\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], [[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]).

[L13] $|x|$ denotes the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^3$, and the coordinates of $u_{\mathrm{vec}}$ in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ carry the standard Euclidean inner product ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $L$ is orthochronous and $e_0\in C^+$ by [L6], the image $u=Le_0$ lies in $L(C^+)=C^+$; by [L9] and [L10] the component $C^+$ is the coordinate set $\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ because it contains $e_0$ with coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$. Hence $u^0>|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge0$, so $u^0>0$ and $|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$. Moreover $\eta(u,u)=\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$ by [L2] and [L6], while $[L9]$ gives $\eta(u,u)=-(u^0)^2+|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2$, so $(u^0)^2-|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2=1$ and the parameter $\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2=1-1/(u^0)^2<1$; in particular $\boldsymbol\beta$ lies in the open unit ball of $\mathbb R^3$ and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is defined by [L3]. [L1, L2, L3, L6, L9, L10, L13, algebra]

1.2 For uniqueness, suppose $B(-\boldsymbol\beta_1)\widehat R_1=B(-\boldsymbol\beta_2)\widehat R_2$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta_i|<1$ and spatial rotations $\widehat R_i$, and apply both sides to $e_0$. Since $\widehat R_ie_0=e_0$ by [L5] and $B(-\boldsymbol\beta_i)e_0=\gamma_i(e_0+\beta_{i,1}e_1+\beta_{i,2}e_2+\beta_{i,3}e_3)$ by [L4], equality of the two images reads $\gamma_1(e_0+\boldsymbol\beta_1)=\gamma_2(e_0+\boldsymbol\beta_2)$ in coordinates, the time component giving $\gamma_1=\gamma_2>0$ and then the three spatial components giving $\beta_{1,k}=\beta_{2,k}$ for $k=1,2,3$; hence $\boldsymbol\beta_1=\boldsymbol\beta_2$. Composing the original equality on the left with the bijection $B(\boldsymbol\beta_1)=B(\boldsymbol\beta_2)$ and using $B(\boldsymbol\beta_i)B(-\boldsymbol\beta_i)=\operatorname{id}$ from [L4] gives $\widehat R_1=\widehat R_2$, and therefore $R_1=\widehat R_1|_S=\widehat R_2|_S=R_2$. [L4, L5, algebra]

2.1 Define $\widehat R:=B(\boldsymbol\beta)L$. It is a composition of linear Lorentz maps, hence a linear Lorentz map by [L2]; in particular it is invertible. By [L4] applied to the future timelike unit vector $u$ with $u^0>0$ from step 1.1, $B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$; therefore $\widehat Re_0=B(\boldsymbol\beta)Le_0=B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$. [L2, L4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $w\in S$, applying the Lorentz identity of $\widehat R$ and $\widehat Re_0=e_0$ gives $\eta(e_0,\widehat Rw)=\eta(\widehat Re_0,\widehat Rw)=\eta(e_0,w)=0$, so $\widehat Rw\in S$ by [L7] and $\widehat R(S)\subseteq S$. Conversely, let $y\in S$ and let $w:=\widehat R^{-1}y$; applying the same identity to the Lorentz map $\widehat R^{-1}$, whose value at $e_0$ is again $e_0$, gives $\eta(e_0,w)=\eta(\widehat R^{-1}e_0,\widehat R^{-1}y)=\eta(e_0,y)=0$, so $w\in S$ by [L7] and $y=\widehat Rw\in\widehat R(S)$; hence $\widehat R(S)=S$. For $w,z\in S$, $\delta(\widehat Rw,\widehat Rz)=\eta(\widehat Rw,\widehat Rz)=\eta(w,z)=\delta(w,z)$, so the restriction $\widehat R|_S$ is a $\delta$-isometry of $S$; it is an automorphism of $S$ because $\widehat R$ is an automorphism of $V$ preserving the splitting. [L2, L7, L8, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $A:=\widehat R|_S$ and let $\widehat M$ be the matrix of $\widehat R$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ and $M_A$ the matrix of $A$ in the ordered basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$. Because $\widehat Re_0=e_0$ and $\widehat R(S)=S$, the matrix $\widehat M$ is the block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&M_A\end{pmatrix}$ and, reading the Leibniz sum of [L12] over $\sigma\in S_4$, every term with $\sigma(0)\neq0$ vanishes; for $\sigma$ with $\sigma(0)=0$ the product equals $\prod_{j<3}(M_A)_{\sigma(j+1)-1,j}$, the permutation $\tau(j):=\sigma(j+1)-1$ of $\{0,1,2\}$ has the same inversion number as $\sigma$ (no inversion involves the index $0$ with $\sigma(0)=0$), and so the same sign, whence $\det\widehat M=\det M_A$. By [L11], $\det\widehat R=\det\widehat M=\det M_A=\det A=\det(\widehat R|_S)$. Now $\det\widehat R=\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)\det L=1\cdot1=1$ by [L4], [L1] and [L11]. Hence $\det(\widehat R|_S)=+1$, and by [L8] the restriction is an orthogonal operator; with step 3.1 and [L5] this shows that $\widehat R|_S$ is a spatial rotation of the frame, so $\widehat R$ is the extension $\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ of the spatial rotation $R:=\widehat R|_S$. Finally $L=B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}\widehat R=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ by [L4]. [L5, L8, L11, L12, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Conversely, let $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and let $R$ be a spatial rotation of the frame with extension $\widehat R=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$, so that $\widehat Re_0=e_0$ and $\widehat R|_S=R$. For $v=v^0e_0+w$ and $z=z^0e_0+y$ with $w,y\in S$, linearity gives $\widehat Rv=v^0e_0+Rw$ and $\widehat Rz=z^0e_0+Ry$, so by [L7] and the $\delta$-preservation of $R$ in [L5], $\eta(\widehat Rv,\widehat Rz)=-v^0z^0+\delta(Rw,Ry)=-v^0z^0+\delta(w,y)=\eta(v,z)$; hence $\widehat R$ is a linear Lorentz map. Its matrix in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is block diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(1,M_R)$ with $M_R$ the matrix of $R$ in $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and the same Leibniz argument as step 4.1 gives $\det\widehat R=\det R=1$ by [L5]; thus $\widehat R$ is proper. It is orthochronous because $\widehat Re_0=e_0\in C^+$ with $e_0$ future timelike, so $\widehat R(C^+)\cap C^+\neq\emptyset$, and by [L2] the image $\widehat R(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$; it must therefore be $C^+$. Finally $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map by [L4], and the product of two proper orthochronous Lorentz maps is proper orthochronous by [L2]. [L2, L4, L5, L7, L12, algebra]

5.2 For the characterization of boosts, suppose first that $L=B(\boldsymbol\beta')$ for some $|\boldsymbol\beta'|<1$. Then $u=Le_0=B(\boldsymbol\beta')e_0=\gamma'(e_0-\beta'_1e_1-\beta'_2e_2-\beta'_3e_3)$ by [L4], so $u^0=\gamma'$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0=-\boldsymbol\beta'$; hence $\widehat R=B(\boldsymbol\beta)L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta')B(\boldsymbol\beta')=\operatorname{id}$ by [L4], and $R=\operatorname{id}$. Conversely, if $R=\operatorname{id}$, then $\widehat R=\operatorname{id}$ and the factorization of step 4.1 gives $L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, a passive boost with parameter $-\boldsymbol\beta$. [L4, step 4.1]

6.1 Clause (i) is step 1.1; clause (ii) is steps 2.1, 3.1, 4.1; clause (iii) is step 5.1; clause (iv) is step 1.2; and clause (v) is step 5.2. This proves every clause of the statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 1.2, step 5.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with time orientation
$C^+$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] is the form;
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] fixes $C^+$), and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with spatial three-space $S$ and
Euclidean form $\delta$. Then:

(i) For every $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and for every unit spatial
vector $e\in S$ and all $\beta_1,\beta_2\in(-1,1)$ one has
$B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$;
in particular collinear boosts commute. For each fixed unit spatial axis $e$
and scalar $b\in(-1,1)$ the collinear boost $B(be)$ satisfies $b=\tanh(r)$
for a unique scalar **rapidity** $r\in\mathbb R$, and rapidities add for
boosts along that same fixed axis. This signed scalar rapidity statement does
not identify a vector $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with the scalar
$\tanh(r)$.

(ii) $SO^+(V,\eta)$ is a subgroup of $O(V,\eta)$, which is a subgroup of the
general linear group $GL(V)$; every passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
every spatial rotation of the frame, extended by fixing $e_0$, belongs to
$SO^+(V,\eta)$.

(iii) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ has a unique factorization
$L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and $\widehat R$
the extension of a spatial rotation of the frame; here
$\boldsymbol\beta=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ where $(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$ are the
coordinates of $u=Le_0$. Consequently every proper orthochronous Lorentz map
is the product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation, in that order, and
$L$ is itself a passive boost if and only if the rotation $\widehat R$ is the
identity.

(iv) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ preserves the interval $\eta(v,v)$, the causal
classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the
orientation, and the oriented volume form of the model:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,Lv_1,Lv_2,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]). An arbitrary
element $L$ of $O(V,\eta)$ satisfies $\det L=\pm1$ and either preserves or
interchanges the future and past cones; moreover $\det L=1$ alone does not
force $L(C^+)=C^+$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space $(V,\eta)$ with time orientation $C^+$, an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with spatial three-space $S$ and Euclidean form $\delta$, and the sets $O(V,\eta)$, $SO^+(V,\eta)$.

[L1] A linear Lorentz map is a linear $L$ with $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$; it is proper when $\det L=+1$ and orthochronous when $L(C^+)=C^+$; $GL(V)$ is the group of invertible linear maps ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[L2] Every linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, satisfies $\det L=\pm1$, preserves $\eta(v,v)$ and the causal character of every nonzero vector, and maps $C^+$ onto one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set; $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if and only if $L(C^+)\subseteq C^+$; $SO(V,\eta)=\{L:\det L=1\}$, $O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)=\{L:L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and $SO^+(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of $O(V,\eta)$, which is a subgroup of $GL(V)$; if $L$ is proper then $\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ and if $\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$ ([[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], [[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]).

[L3] For every $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the passive boost $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with $B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$; the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and $B(\mathbf 0)=\operatorname{id}_V$ ([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], [[def-lorentz-boost]]).

[L4] For every unit spatial vector $e$ and all $\beta_1,\beta_2\in(-1,1)$, $B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$ with $\bigl|\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}\bigr|<1$, and the two collinear boosts commute ([[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]).

[L5] The map $r\mapsto\tanh(r)$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $\mathbb R$ onto $(-1,1)$, and for every unit spatial vector $e$ and all $r,s\in\mathbb R$ one has $B(\tanh(r)e)B(\tanh(s)e)=B(\tanh(r+s)e)$ ([[lem-rapidity-parametrization-of-collinear-boosts]]).

[L6] For a proper orthochronous Lorentz map $L$ with $u:=Le_0$ and coordinates $(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, the parameter $\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, and $L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ with $\widehat R:=B(\boldsymbol\beta)L$ the extension $\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ of a spatial rotation of the frame; this factorization is unique among parameters in the open unit ball and spatial rotations; conversely every such $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ is proper orthochronous; and $L$ is a passive boost if and only if $\widehat R=\operatorname{id}_V$ ([[lem-boost-rotation-factorization]]).

[L7] A spatial rotation of the frame is the extension by $e_0\mapsto e_0$ of a linear map of $S$ preserving $\delta$ with determinant $+1$ on $S$; its extension is denoted $\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ in the frame's basis ([[def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[L8] In the frame the timelike set is $T=T_+\cup T_-$ with $T_+=\{v:v^0>|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and $T_-=\{v:v^0<-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$, and $T_+,T_-$ are exactly the two components; since $e_0\in C^+$ has coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), one has $C^+=T_+$ and $C^-=T_-$, with closed cones $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)=\{v:v^0\ge|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)=\{v:v^0\le-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L9] A nonzero vector is timelike when $\eta(v,v)<0$, null when $\eta(v,v)=0$, spacelike when $\eta(v,v)>0$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); the oriented volume form satisfies $\epsilon_{0123}=+1$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); $\det$ of a linear operator is the determinant of its matrix in any ordered basis and the Leibniz sum over a diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal entries ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]], [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Clause (i), first sentence: by [L3], $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ for every $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$. [L3]

1.2 Clause (i), second sentence: by [L4] the composition of two collinear boosts is the boost with parameter $\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}$ in the same direction, this parameter lies in $(-1,1)$, and the two factors commute; in particular the composition law is a collinear law and not an addition of parameters. [L4]

1.3 Clause (i), third and fourth sentences: fix a unit spatial axis $e$. By [L5], $r\mapsto\tanh(r)$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $\mathbb R$ onto $(-1,1)$; hence for each $b\in(-1,1)$ there is exactly one $r\in\mathbb R$ with $b=\tanh(r)$, so $B(be)=B(\tanh(r)e)$ has the unique rapidity $r$, and for $r,s\in\mathbb R$ the product $B(\tanh(r)e)B(\tanh(s)e)$ equals $B(\tanh(r+s)e)$, so rapidities add along the fixed axis. The rapidity $r$ is a scalar attached to the fixed axis $e$: the displayed equations concern the scalar parameters $\beta_i=\tanh(r_i)$ of boosts $B(\beta_ie)$, and no identification of a vector $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $\tanh(r)$ is made. [L5]

1.4 Clause (ii), subgroup part: [L2] states that $SO(V,\eta)$, $O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ and their intersection $SO^+(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of $O(V,\eta)$, and that $O(V,\eta)$ is a subgroup of $GL(V)$. [L1, L2]

1.5 Clause (ii), membership part: every passive boost lies in $SO^+(V,\eta)$ by [L3]. For a spatial rotation $R$ of the frame with extension $\widehat R=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$: by [L6] the product $B(\mathbf 0)\widehat R=\widehat R$ of the boost with parameter $\mathbf 0$ and the spatial rotation is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map; here $B(\mathbf 0)=\operatorname{id}_V$ by [L3], so $\widehat R\in SO^+(V,\eta)$. [L3, L6, L7]

1.6 Clause (iii): by [L6] every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ has the factorization $L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ with $\boldsymbol\beta=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ and $\widehat R$ the extension of a spatial rotation of the frame, and this factorization is unique; consequently $L$ is a product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation in that order, and [L6] also gives that $L$ is a passive boost if and only if $\widehat R=\operatorname{id}_V$. [L6, L7]

1.7 Clause (iv), preservation part: let $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$, so $L$ is Lorentz, proper and orthochronous. By [L2], $L$ preserves $\eta(v,v)$ and the causal character of every nonzero vector, and $L(C^+)=C^+$, so $Le_0$ is future timelike because $e_0\in C^+$ by [L8]. For the closed cones, first record the criterion: if $w$ is future timelike and $v\neq0$ has $\eta(v,v)\le0$, then $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ if and only if $\eta(v,w)<0$, and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ if and only if $\eta(v,w)>0$. Indeed [L8] gives $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)=\{v^0\ge|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)=\{v^0\le-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ in frame coordinates, with $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2$ and $w^0>|w_{\mathrm{vec}}|$; for nonzero $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ one has $v^0\ge|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge0$ and $v^0>0$, so $\eta(v,w)\le-v^0w^0+|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\,|w_{\mathrm{vec}}|\le v^0(|w_{\mathrm{vec}}|-w^0)<0$, while for nonzero $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ one has $-v^0\ge|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge0$ and $-v^0>0$, so $\eta(v,w)\ge(-v^0)w^0-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\,|w_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge(-v^0)(w^0-|w_{\mathrm{vec}}|)>0$; the nonzero causal vectors split into $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)\setminus\{0\}$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)\setminus\{0\}$ by [L8], so the signs are exhaustive. Since $L$ preserves the form, is an isomorphism and satisfies $\eta(Lv,Le_0)=\eta(v,e_0)$, applying the criterion with $w:=Le_0$ gives $L(\operatorname{cl}(C^+))\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $L(\operatorname{cl}(C^-))\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$; applying the same argument to $L^{-1}\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ (which exists by [L2]) gives the reverse inclusions, hence $L(\operatorname{cl}(C^+))=\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $L(\operatorname{cl}(C^-))=\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$. By [L2] again, properness gives $\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all $v_0,\dots,v_3$, which is the preservation of the oriented volume form and of the orientation. [L2, L8, L9, algebra]

1.8 Clause (iv), last sentence: for any $L\in O(V,\eta)$, [L2] gives $\det L=\pm1$ and $L(C^+)\in\{C^+,C^-\}$, so $L$ either preserves or interchanges the future and past cones. For the failure of the converse, let $\Lambda:=-\operatorname{id}_V$, with matrix $M=-\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,1)$ in the frame; its entries satisfy $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$, because the temporal diagonal entry is $(-1)(-1)(-1)=-1$, each spatial diagonal entry is $(-1)(+1)(-1)=+1$, and all off-diagonal entries vanish, so $\Lambda$ is a Lorentz map by [L1]; moreover $\det\Lambda=(-1)^4=1$, because the Leibniz sum over the diagonal matrix $M$ is the product of its diagonal entries by [L9], so $\Lambda$ is proper. On coordinates, $\Lambda$ sends a vector with coordinates $(v^0,v_{\mathrm{vec}})$ to $(-v^0,-v_{\mathrm{vec}})$, and $v^0>|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ holds exactly when $-v^0<-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|$; hence $\Lambda(T_+)=T_-$ and $\Lambda(T_-)=T_+$ with the notation of [L8], so $\Lambda$ interchanges the two components of the timelike set and $\Lambda(C^+)=C^-\neq C^+$: $\Lambda$ is a proper but non-orthochronous Lorentz map, and $\det L=1$ alone does not force $L(C^+)=C^+$. [L1, L2, L8, L9]

2.1 Clause (i) is steps 1.1-1.3; clause (ii) is steps 1.4-1.5; clause (iii) is step 1.6; clause (iv) is steps 1.7-1.8. Every clause is either a direct restatement of the cited supplier with its hypotheses (frame fixed, $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, $L$ proper orthochronous) or the displayed finite computation of step 1.8. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5, step 1.6, step 1.7, step 1.8] ∎

## Statement

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered $\eta$-orthonormal basis with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a linear map $K:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) with matrix $M$ in this basis, the following are
equivalent:

(a) $\eta(Kv,w)+\eta(v,Kw)=0$ for all $v,w\in V$;
(b) $M^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M=0$;
(c) writing $M$ in the block form
$M=\begin{pmatrix}0&u^{T}\\ u&\Omega\end{pmatrix}$ with
$u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\Omega$ a $3\times3$ real matrix, one has
$\Omega^{T}=-\Omega$.

The set
$\mathfrak g:=\{K:\eta(Kv,w)+\eta(v,Kw)=0\text{ for all }v,w\}$ is a
$6$-dimensional linear subspace of the space of linear maps $V\to V$. Define
the generators $M_{ab}$ for $0\le a<b\le3$ by
$(M_{ab})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{b\nu}
-\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{a\nu}$. Then the six maps $M_{ab}$ form a basis of
$\mathfrak g$ and satisfy
$[M_{ab},M_{cd}]=\eta_{bc}M_{ad}-\eta_{ac}M_{bd}-\eta_{bd}M_{ac}
+\eta_{ad}M_{bc}$ for all $0\le a,b,c,d\le3$, where
$[K_1,K_2]:=K_1K_2-K_2K_1$ is the commutator. If $s\mapsto L(s)$ is a
$\mathcal C^1$ curve in $O(V,\eta)$ with $L(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$, then its
derivative $K:=L'(0)$ belongs to $\mathfrak g$, and
$L(s)=\operatorname{id}_V+sK+o(s)$ as $s\to0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space $(V,\eta)$, an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_a)$ with $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, a
linear map $K:V\to V$ with matrix $M$, and the components of the matrix product
and transpose conventions below.

[L1] $\eta$ is a symmetric bilinear form
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]); in the basis $(e_a)$ one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b)=\eta_{ab}$ with $\eta_0$ diagonal, so for coordinate columns
$v,w$ of vectors of $V$ one has $\eta(v,w)=v^{T}\eta_0w$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]).

[L2] $(KM)$ has matrix product convention $(AB)_{ik}=\sum_ja_{ij}b_{jk}$ and
the identity matrix has entry $1$ on the diagonal and $0$ elsewhere
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]); $(A^{T})_{ij}=A_{ji}$
([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]).

[L3] The space $L(V,V)$ of linear maps $V\to V$ is a real vector space, and
the map sending a linear map to its matrix in a fixed ordered basis is a linear
isomorphism onto $M_4(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]],
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]).

[L4] $L:V\to V$ is a linear Lorentz map when
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$, and $O(V,\eta)$ denotes the set of such
maps ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[L5] For a curve $s\mapsto L(s)$ in the finite-dimensional space $L(V,V)$,
the derivative $L'(0)$ is the linear map with
$L(s)=L(0)+sL'(0)+o(s)$ as $s\to0$, and $s\mapsto L(s)v$ is differentiable
with derivative $L'(0)v$; sums and products of differentiable scalar functions
obey the algebra of derivatives ([[def-derivative]],
[[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $v,w\in V$ have coordinate columns $v,w$. By [L1] and [L2], $\eta(Kv,w)=v^{T}M^{T}\eta_0w$ and $\eta(v,Kw)=v^{T}\eta_0Mw$, so $\eta(Kv,w)+\eta(v,Kw)=v^{T}(M^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M)w$. If (a) holds this bilinear form vanishes for all $v,w$, and testing $v,w$ among the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb R^4$ forces every entry of $M^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M$ to vanish, which is (b); conversely (b) gives (a) for all $v,w$ by the same identity. Hence (a) and (b) are equivalent. [L1, L2, algebra]

1.2 Write $M$ in the block form $M=\begin{pmatrix}k&u^{T}\\ w&\Omega\end{pmatrix}$ with $k\in\mathbb R$, $u,w\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$, and recall $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,I_3)$. Then $M^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}k&w^{T}\\ u&\Omega^{T}\end{pmatrix}$, so $M^{T}\eta_0=\begin{pmatrix}-k&w^{T}\\ -u&\Omega^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ and $\eta_0M=\begin{pmatrix}-k&-u^{T}\\ w&\Omega\end{pmatrix}$; the sum $M^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M=\begin{pmatrix}-2k&w^{T}-u^{T}\\ w-u&\Omega^{T}+\Omega\end{pmatrix}$ vanishes exactly when $k=0$, $w=u$ and $\Omega^{T}=-\Omega$. Hence (b) and (c) are equivalent. [L2, algebra]

1.3 With the convention of [L2], $(M_{ab}M_{cd})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\sum_{\lambda}(\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{b\lambda}-\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{a\lambda})(\delta^{\lambda}_{c}\eta_{d\nu}-\delta^{\lambda}_{d}\eta_{c\nu})=\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{bc}\eta_{d\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{bd}\eta_{c\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{ac}\eta_{d\nu}+\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{ad}\eta_{c\nu}$, because $\sum_{\lambda}\eta_{b\lambda}\delta^{\lambda}_{c}=\eta_{bc}$ and $\sum_{\lambda}\eta_{b\lambda}\delta^{\lambda}_{d}=\eta_{bd}$. Interchanging the pairs $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ and subtracting, the eight resulting terms regroup as $(\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{d\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_{d}\eta_{a\nu})\eta_{bc}-(\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{c\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_{c}\eta_{a\nu})\eta_{bd}-(\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{d\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_{d}\eta_{b\nu})\eta_{ac}+(\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{c\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_{c}\eta_{b\nu})\eta_{ad}$, which is exactly $\eta_{bc}M_{ad}-\eta_{bd}M_{ac}-\eta_{ac}M_{bd}+\eta_{ad}M_{bc}$; the computation is entrywise and therefore valid for all index values, including repeated indices and the diagonal generators $M_{aa}=0$. [L2, algebra]

1.4 Let $s\mapsto L(s)$ be a $\mathcal C^1$ curve in $O(V,\eta)$ with $L(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$, and fix $v,w\in V$. The function $s\mapsto\eta(L(s)v,L(s)w)$ is constant equal to $\eta(v,w)$ because each $L(s)$ satisfies the defining identity of [L4], and $s\mapsto L(s)v$, $s\mapsto L(s)w$ are differentiable with derivatives $L'(0)v$, $L'(0)w$ by [L5]. Differentiating the constant function at $s=0$ with the product rule for the bilinear form $\eta$ gives $0=\eta(L'(0)v,w)+\eta(v,L'(0)w)$, so $K:=L'(0)$ satisfies condition (a) and lies in $\mathfrak g$; and $L(s)=L(0)+sK+o(s)=\operatorname{id}_V+sK+o(s)$ is the definition of the derivative in the finite-dimensional space $L(V,V)$ recalled in [L5]. [L4, L5, algebra]

2.1 By (c), the maps in $\mathfrak g$ are precisely those whose matrices have the form $\begin{pmatrix}0&u^{T}\\ u&\Omega\end{pmatrix}$ with $u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\Omega$ skew-symmetric; this set is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so $\mathfrak g$ is a linear subspace of $L(V,V)$ by [L3]. A skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrix is determined by its three entries above the diagonal and conversely every such triple occurs, so the skew-symmetric matrices form a $3$-dimensional subspace; adding the three free coordinates of $u$ gives $\dim\mathfrak g=3+3=6$. [step 1.2, L3, algebra]

3.1 For $0\le a<b\le3$ define $M_{ab}$ by $(M_{ab})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{b\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{a\nu}$. Reading off the matrix entries: $M_{0i}$ has $(M_{0i})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_0\delta_{i\nu}+\delta^{\mu}_i\delta_{0\nu}$, the block form with $u=e_i$ and $\Omega=0$, while for $1\le i<j\le3$ the matrix $M_{ij}$ has entries $(M_{ij})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_i\delta_{j\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_j\delta_{i\nu}$, the block form with $u=0$ and $\Omega=e_ie_j^{T}-e_je_i^{T}$ (the $i$-th row of $\eta$ restricted to spatial indices being $e_i^{T}$). Hence each $M_{ab}$ belongs to $\mathfrak g$ by (c), and the correspondence $M_{ab}\leftrightarrow(u,\Omega)$ maps the three $M_{0i}$ onto the three coordinate directions of $u$ and the three $M_{ij}$ onto the three standard skew matrices $e_ie_j^{T}-e_je_i^{T}$, which are independent; therefore the six $M_{ab}$ are linearly independent and, since $\dim\mathfrak g=6$ by step 2.1, they form a basis of $\mathfrak g$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, L3, algebra]

4.1 Steps 1.1 and 1.2 establish the equivalence of (a), (b), (c); steps 2.1 and 3.1 establish that $\mathfrak g$ is a $6$-dimensional linear subspace with basis $M_{ab}$; step 1.3 establishes the commutator identity; and step 1.4 establishes the derivative statement. This proves every clause of the statement. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

## Statement

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), fix an inertial frame
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with coordinates $x^a$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and give $V$ the Euclidean norm
$\lVert v\rVert:=\lVert x(v)\rVert_2$ of the frame coordinates. Let
$\mathfrak g$ be the six-dimensional space of $\eta$-antisymmetric
endomorphisms of [[lem-lorentz-lie-algebra-structure]]. Then:

(i) For every $K\in\mathfrak g$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$ the series
$\exp(sK):=\sum_{n\ge0}(sK)^n/n!$ converges absolutely in the operator norm on
the space of linear maps $V\to V$; the map $s\mapsto\exp(sK)$ is of class
$\mathcal C^\infty$ with $\frac{d}{ds}\exp(sK)=K\exp(sK)=\exp(sK)K$,
$\exp(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$, and
$\exp((s+t)K)=\exp(sK)\exp(tK)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$.

(ii) For every $K\in\mathfrak g$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\exp(sK)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map; equivalently
$s\mapsto\exp(sK)$ is a $\mathcal C^\infty$ curve in $SO^+(V,\eta)$ with
$\exp(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$. In particular every $K\in\mathfrak g$ arises as
the derivative at $0$ of a curve of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps. No
claim is made that every element of $SO^+(V,\eta)$ is the exponential of an
element of $\mathfrak g$.

(iii) Let $e\in S$ be a unit spatial vector of the frame, $\delta(e,e)=1$, and
write $e=\sum_{i=1}^3\hat e_ie_i$; set
$N_e:=-\sum_{i=1}^3\hat e_iM_{0i}\in\mathfrak g$. Then $N_e$ vanishes on the
$\eta$-orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{span}(e_0,e)$ and acts on that
plane by the matrix
$\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}$; and
$\exp(rN_e)=B(\tanh(r)e)$ for every $r\in\mathbb R$. In particular every
passive boost is the exponential of a generator in $\mathfrak g$, and
$\exp(rN_e)\exp(sN_e)=\exp((r+s)N_e)$ for all $r,s\in\mathbb R$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space $(V,\eta)$ with time orientation $C^+$, an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with the Euclidean coordinate norm $\lVert v\rVert=\lVert x(v)\rVert_2$, the space $\mathfrak g$ of $\eta$-antisymmetric endomorphisms, and a unit spatial vector $e\in S$.

[L1] $(V,\eta)$ is a Lorentz vector space: $\eta$ is symmetric bilinear with both radicals $\{0\}$ and inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). A linear map $K:V\to V$ lies in $\mathfrak g$ exactly when $\eta(Kv,w)+\eta(v,Kw)=0$ for all $v,w$, equivalently its matrix $M$ in an ordered $\eta$-orthonormal basis satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M=0$ with $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; $\mathfrak g$ is a $6$-dimensional linear subspace of the space of linear maps $V\to V$, the six maps $M_{ab}$ defined by $(M_{ab})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_a\eta_{b\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_b\eta_{a\nu}$ form a basis of $\mathfrak g$, and if $s\mapsto L(s)$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ curve in $O(V,\eta)$ with $L(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$ then $L'(0)\in\mathfrak g$ ([[lem-lorentz-lie-algebra-structure]]).

[L2] $T:=\{v:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ is the timelike set and $C^+$ is one of its two components; in every $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis the components are $T_+=\{v:v^0>|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and $T_-=\{v:v^0<-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$, these sets are open in the metric topology of the coordinate distance $d(u,w)=\lVert x(u)-x(w)\rVert_2$, and $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(C^-)=\{0\}$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L3] A linear Lorentz map is a linear $L$ with $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$; it is proper when $\det L=+1$ and orthochronous when $L(C^+)=C^+$; every linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, satisfies $\det L=\pm1$, and has $L(C^+)$ equal to one of the two components $C^+,C^-$; composition and inversion of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps are proper orthochronous ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]], [[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]]).

[L4] $V$ is a finite-dimensional real normed space, hence a Banach space; the space $\mathcal L(V,V)$ of linear maps $V\to V$ is a real vector space, and every such linear map is a bounded linear operator with the operator norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], [[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]).

[L5] For every bounded operator $A$ on a Banach space the series $E(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}t^nA^n/n!$ converges absolutely in operator norm and uniformly on compact $t$-intervals, $E(t)$ is bounded with $\lVert E(t)\rVert\le e^{|t|\,\lVert A\rVert}$, $E(0)=I$, $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$, $t\mapsto E(t)$ is $\mathcal C^\infty$ with $E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A$, and the difference quotients converge to $A$ ([[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]], applied on the Banach space $V$ of [L4]).

[L6] The operator norm is the least bound: $\lVert T\rVert=\inf\{C\ge0:\lVert Tx\rVert\le C\lVert x\rVert$ for all $x\}$, so $\lVert Tx\rVert\le\lVert T\rVert\,\lVert x\rVert$ for every bounded $T$ and every $x$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

[L7] In the frame the basis is $\eta$-orthonormal with $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, $e_0\in C^+$ with coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$, and the chart is $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); the matrix of a composition of linear maps is the product of their matrices and $\det(M_1M_2)=\det(M_1)\det(M_2)$ ([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]).

[L8] The spatial three-space $S=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w:\eta(e_0,w)=0\}$ carries the positive definite form $\delta=\eta|_{S\times S}$ with $\delta(w,z)=\sum_{i=1}^3w^iz^i$ in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and $V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[L9] For a real function on an order-convex interval: sums, products and scalar multiples of differentiable functions are differentiable with the usual derivative formulas, and a function continuous on the interval whose derivative vanishes at every interior point is constant ([[def-derivative]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]).

[L10] For every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is a natural $n\ge1$ with $1/n<\varepsilon$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

[L11] For a unit spatial vector $e$ and $r\in\mathbb R$ the passive boost $B(\tanh(r)e)$ acts on the ordered pair of directions $(e_0,e)$ by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cosh r&-\sinh r\\ -\sinh r&\cosh r\end{pmatrix}$ and as the identity on $\{y\in S:\delta(e,y)=0\}$; here $\sinh(r)=(e^r-e^{-r})/2$, $\cosh(r)=(e^r+e^{-r})/2$, $\tanh(r)=\sinh(r)/\cosh(r)$, and $r\mapsto\tanh(r)$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $\mathbb R$ onto $(-1,1)$ ([[lem-rapidity-parametrization-of-collinear-boosts]], [[def-lorentz-boost]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $K\in\mathfrak g$ and $s\in\mathbb R$. By [L4], $V$ is a Banach space for the frame-coordinate norm and every linear map $V\to V$, in particular $K$, is a bounded operator; hence $\mathcal B(V)=\mathcal L(V,V)$ and [L5] applies with $A=K$: the series $E(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}t^nK^n/n!$ converges absolutely in operator norm and uniformly on compact intervals, $E(t)$ satisfies $\lVert E(t)\rVert\le e^{|t|\,\lVert K\rVert}$, $E(0)=I$, $E(t+u)=E(t)E(u)$, $t\mapsto E(t)$ is $\mathcal C^\infty$ with $E'(t)=KE(t)=E(t)K$, and the difference quotients at $0$ converge to $K$. Writing $E(s)=\exp(sK)$ for $t=s$ this is exactly clause (i), including $K=\exp'(0)$. [L4, L5, given]

1.2 Let $e=\sum_{i=1}^3\hat e_ie_i\in S$ with $\delta(e,e)=1$. Since each $M_{0i}$ lies in the linear subspace $\mathfrak g$ by [L1], $N_e=-\sum_{i=1}^3\hat e_iM_{0i}$ lies in $\mathfrak g$. From $(M_{0i})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_0\eta_{i\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_i\eta_{0\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_0\delta_{i\nu}+\delta^{\mu}_i\delta_{0\nu}$ (using $\eta_{i\nu}=\delta_{i\nu}$ for spatial indices and $\eta_{0\nu}=-\delta_{0\nu}$) one reads $M_{0i}e_0=e_i$ and $M_{0i}e_j=\delta_{ij}e_0$ for $j=1,2,3$, since the components vanish unless $\mu\in\{0,i\}$ and $\nu\in\{0,j\}$. Hence $N_ee_0=-\sum_i\hat e_ie_i=-e$ and $N_ee_j=-\sum_i\hat e_i\delta_{ij}e_0=-\hat e_je_0$, so $N_ee=-\sum_j\hat e_j^2e_0=-e_0$ because $\delta(e,e)=\sum_j\hat e_j^2=1$. Every $v\in V$ decomposes as $v=v^0e_0+se+y$ with $v^0,s\in\mathbb R$ and $y\in S$, $\delta(e,y)=0$: indeed [L8] gives $v=v^0e_0+w$ with $w\in S$, and $w=\delta(e,w)e+y$ with $y:=w-\delta(e,w)e$ satisfies $\delta(e,y)=\delta(e,w)-\delta(e,w)\delta(e,e)=0$. For such $v$, linearity gives $N_ev=v^0(-e)+s(-e_0)+0=-v^0e-se_0$ and $N_e^2v=N_e(-v^0e-se_0)=v^0e_0+se$; in particular $N_ey=0$ and $N_e^2=P$, where $P$ is the projection onto $\operatorname{span}(e_0,e)$ along $\{y\in S:\delta(e,y)=0\}$. This last set is the $\eta$-orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{span}(e_0,e)$, because $\eta(v,v')=0$ for all $v'\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,e)$ holds exactly for $v\in e_0^{\perp}=S$ with $\delta(e,v)=0$; and in the ordered basis $(e_0,e)$ the map $N_e$ has the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}$. [L1, L7, L8, algebra]

2.1 Let $M(t)$ be the matrix of $\exp(tK)$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $M_K$ the matrix of $K$, so that $M_K^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M_K=0$ by [L1]. By step 1.1, $M$ is $\mathcal C^\infty$ with $M'(t)=M_KM(t)$ (the matrix of $KE(t)$ is the product of the matrices) by [L7]. Define $F(t):=M(t)^{T}\eta_0M(t)$; its entries are finite sums of products of $\mathcal C^\infty$ functions, so $F$ is differentiable and the product rule of [L9] gives $F'(t)=M'(t)^{T}\eta_0M(t)+M(t)^{T}\eta_0M'(t)=M(t)^{T}M_K^{T}\eta_0M(t)+M(t)^{T}\eta_0M_KM(t)=M(t)^{T}(M_K^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M_K)M(t)=0$. Since $F(0)=I^{T}\eta_0I=\eta_0$ and each entry has vanishing derivative on $\mathbb R$, [L9] makes each entry constant, so $F(t)=\eta_0$ for all $t$ and all $s$. Thus for all $u,v\in V$ with coordinate columns $x,y$ one has $\eta(\exp(sK)u,\exp(sK)v)=x^{T}M(s)^{T}\eta_0M(s)y=x^{T}\eta_0y=\eta(u,v)$, so $\exp(sK)$ is a linear Lorentz map. [L1, L5, L7, L9, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Since $N_e^2=P$ with $P^2=P$ by step 1.2, the powers of $N_e$ are $N_e^{2m}=P$ for $m\ge1$, $N_e^{2m+1}=N_e$ for $m\ge0$. The exponential series of the bounded operator $rN_e$ converges absolutely in operator norm by [L5]; splitting its partial sums into even and odd parts, each part is a convergent series of scalars times $P$ respectively $N_e$, and $\exp(rN_e)=I+\bigl(\sum_{m\ge1}r^{2m}/(2m)!\bigr)P+\bigl(\sum_{m\ge0}r^{2m+1}/(2m+1)!\bigr)N_e=I+(\cosh(r)-1)P+\sinh(r)N_e$ with the hyperbolic functions of [L11]. [L5, L11, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1, $\exp(sK)$ is a Lorentz map, so [L3] gives $\det\exp(sK)=\pm1$, the determinant being that of $M(s)$ by [L7]. Applying the group law of step 1.1 at $t=u=s/2$ gives $\exp(sK)=\exp((s/2)K)^2$, so by [L7] $M(s)=M(s/2)M(s/2)$ and $\det M(s)=\det(M(s/2))^2=(\pm1)^2=1$, using [L3] once more for $\det M(s/2)=\pm1$. Hence $\exp(sK)$ is proper. [L3, L7, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 By [L2] and [L7], $C^+$ is open in the coordinate-norm topology and $e_0\in C^+$ with coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$ and $\lVert e_0\rVert=1$; choose $\rho>0$ with $\{v:\lVert v-e_0\rVert<\rho\}\subseteq C^+$. By step 1.1 the map $t\mapsto\exp(tK)$ is continuous at $0$ with $\exp(0)=I$, so there is $\delta>0$ with $\lVert\exp(tK)-I\rVert<\rho/2$ whenever $|t|<\delta$. For such $t$, [L6] gives $\lVert\exp(tK)e_0-e_0\rVert=\lVert(\exp(tK)-I)e_0\rVert\le\lVert\exp(tK)-I\rVert\lVert e_0\rVert<\rho/2<\rho$, so $\exp(tK)e_0\in C^+$. By step 2.1 the map $\exp(tK)$ is a Lorentz map, so by [L3] its image of $C^+$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$; since it contains $\exp(tK)e_0\in C^+$, it equals $C^+$. Hence $\exp(tK)$ is orthochronous for every $|t|<\delta$. [L2, L3, L6, L7, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 Evaluate the formula of step 2.2 on the spanning set of step 1.2: using $N_ee_0=-e$, $N_ee=-e_0$, $N_ey=0$ and $Py=0$ for $\delta(e,y)=0$, one gets $\exp(rN_e)e_0=e_0+(\cosh r-1)e_0-\sinh r\,e=\cosh r\,e_0-\sinh r\,e$, $\exp(rN_e)e=\cosh r\,e-\sinh r\,e_0$, and $\exp(rN_e)y=y$. By [L11], $B(\tanh(r)e)$ acts on $(e_0,e)$ by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cosh r&-\sinh r\\ -\sinh r&\cosh r\end{pmatrix}$ and fixes every $y\in S$ with $\delta(e,y)=0$; both maps are linear and agree on the spanning set $\{e_0,e\}\cup\{y\in S:\delta(e,y)=0\}$ of $V$, so they are equal: $\exp(rN_e)=B(\tanh(r)e)$. [L11, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Let $s\in\mathbb R$. For $s=0$ the map $\exp(0)=I$ is orthochronous. Let $s\neq0$ and choose $n\ge1$ with $1/n<\delta/|s|$ by [L10], so $t:=s/n$ satisfies $|t|<\delta$ and $\exp(tK)$ is orthochronous by step 3.2. If $s>0$ then $s=nt$, and the group law of step 1.1 gives $\exp(sK)=\exp(tK)^n$, a finite product of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps, hence proper orthochronous by [L3]. If $s<0$ then $-s>0$, so $\exp(-sK)$ is proper orthochronous by the previous sentence; the group law at $t=s$, $u=-s$ gives $\exp(sK)=\exp(-sK)^{-1}$, and the inverse of a proper orthochronous Lorentz map is proper orthochronous by [L3]. Hence $\exp(sK)$ is orthochronous for every $s\in\mathbb R$. [L3, L10, step 1.1, step 3.2, algebra]

4.2 Let $\beta\in(-1,1)$ and let $e$ be a unit spatial vector. By [L11] there is a unique $r\in\mathbb R$ with $\beta=\tanh(r)$; step 3.3 then gives $B(\beta e)=B(\tanh(r)e)=\exp(rN_e)$, and for $\beta=0$ one has $B(0)=\operatorname{id}_V=\exp(0)$ by the definition of the boost. Writing $\boldsymbol\beta=|\boldsymbol\beta|u$ with a unit spatial vector $u$ when $\boldsymbol\beta\neq0$, this exhibits every passive boost as the exponential of a generator in $\mathfrak g$. Finally, [L5] applied to the single operator $N_e$ and the group law of step 1.1 give $\exp(rN_e)\exp(sN_e)=\exp((r+s)N_e)$ for all $r,s\in\mathbb R$. [L5, L11, step 1.1, step 3.3, algebra]

5.1 Clause (i) is step 1.1, together with the derivative statement $K=\exp'(0)$ noted there. Clause (ii) is steps 2.1, 3.1, 3.2 and 4.1: step 2.1 makes $\exp(sK)$ a Lorentz map, step 3.1 makes it proper, steps 3.2 and 4.1 make it orthochronous; combined with the $\mathcal C^\infty$ property of step 1.1 this is the curve statement in $SO^+(V,\eta)$, and every $K\in\mathfrak g$ arises as $\exp'(0)$ by step 1.1. Clause (iii) is steps 1.2, 2.2, 3.3 and 4.2. Nothing proved here asserts the converse direction (that every element of $SO^+(V,\eta)$ is an exponential of an element of $\mathfrak g$), which is exactly the disclaimer in the statement. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space with its inertial smooth
structure ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), and let
$F:A\to A$ be a map whose coordinate expression in some (equivalently, every)
inertial chart is of class $C^2$ and which satisfies

$$\eta(dF_pv,dF_pw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }p\in A\text{ and all }v,w\in V,$$

where $dF_p:T_pA\to T_{F(p)}A$ is the total derivative and the tangent spaces
are identified with $V$ by the canonical isomorphism of
[[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]. Then $F$ is an affine
Lorentz map: there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with
$F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Conversely every affine Lorentz map is
a $C^\infty$ map of $A$ satisfying the same preservation identity.
Consequently the $C^2$ isometries of the affine Minkowski model are exactly its
affine Lorentz maps, and these form a group under composition.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$, a map $F:A\to A$ that is $C^2$ in inertial charts and satisfies $\eta(dF_pv,dF_pw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $p,v,w$ under the canonical tangent identification, and an inertial chart $x$ with frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and coordinate isomorphism $E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$.

[L1] A linear map $L:V\to V$ with $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$ is a linear Lorentz map; an affine Lorentz map is a map $F:A\to A$ with $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for a linear Lorentz map $L$, and its linear part $L$ is unique ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[L2] Affine Lorentz maps are bijections and form a group under composition ([[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]]).

[L3] The model is the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with events and displacements $q-p\in V$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

[L4] For the inertial chart $x$, $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$; $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, so $\eta(Ea,Eb)=\eta_0(a,b)$ with $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; the chart is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L5] The inertial charts form a smooth atlas; the transitions between inertial charts are affine, hence smooth ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]).

[L6] The tangent space at every event is canonically identified with $V$; for an inertial chart the identification is $\Phi_p(v)=\sum_av^a\partial_a|_p$ for $v=\sum_av^ae_a$, and under this identification the total derivative of a chart-represented map is the coordinate total derivative conjugated by $E$ ([[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]).

[L7] A map between open subsets of Euclidean space is $C^k$ when all iterated partial derivatives of order at most $k$ exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[L8] $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$ with total derivative $Df(a)$ when $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

[L9] The $j$-th partial derivative of $f$ at $a$ is $\partial_jf(a)=D_{e_j}f(a)$, the directional derivative along $e_j$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[L10] If $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ then $D_vf(a)=Df(a)v$ for every $v$, in particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$, and the matrix of $Df(a)$ in the standard bases is the Jacobian matrix $(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i,j}$ ([[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[L11] If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_jf=\partial_j\partial_if$ for all coordinate indices ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

[L12] $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$ whenever the two total derivatives exist ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[L13] Sums, scalar multiples and differences of totally differentiable maps are totally differentiable with the expected total derivatives ([[thm-algebra-of-total-derivatives]]).

[L14] If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is convex and open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at every point with $Df(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then $f$ is constant on $U$ ([[cor-zero-total-derivative-on-a-convex-open-set-is-constant]]).

[L15] A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is convex when $(1-t)x+ty\in U$ for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$; $\mathbb R^m$ is convex and open ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]).

[L16] $\eta$ is a symmetric bilinear form whose radicals are $\{0\}$, so $\eta(u,z)=0$ for all $z\in V$ implies $u=0$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]); in coordinates $\eta_0(a,b)=-a^0b^0+a^1b^1+a^2b^2+a^3b^3$ by [L4].

[L17] A linear map $T:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$ with $\ker T=\{0\}$ satisfies $\dim(\operatorname{im}T)=\dim\mathbb R^4$ by rank-nullity ([[thm-rank-nullity]]), so its image is all of $\mathbb R^4$ ([[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Put $\Phi:=x\circ F\circ x^{-1}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$, the coordinate expression of $F$ in the chart $x$. By hypothesis and [L5], $\Phi$ is $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^4$; by the chain rule [L12] and the tangent identification [L6], at $u=x(p)$ the total derivative of $\Phi$ is the conjugate $D\Phi_u=E^{-1}\circ dF_p\circ E$ of the total derivative of $F$. Hence for all $u\in\mathbb R^4$ and all $a,b\in\mathbb R^4$, using $\eta(Ec,Ed)=\eta_0(c,d)$ from [L4] and the preservation identity of the Given, $\eta_0(D\Phi_ua,D\Phi_ub)=\eta(dF_p(Ea),dF_p(Eb))=\eta(Ea,Eb)=\eta_0(a,b)$. In particular, if $D\Phi_ua=0$ for some $a$, then $\eta_0(a,b)=\eta_0(D\Phi_ua,D\Phi_ub)=0$ for every $b$; testing $b=e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ gives $a^0=0$ and $a^1=a^2=a^3=0$, so $a=0$ by [L16], and $D\Phi_u$ has trivial kernel; by [L17] it is invertible, so the vectors $D\Phi_ue_0,\dots,D\Phi_ue_3$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^4$. [L4, L5, L6, L12, L16, L17, algebra]

1.2 Conversely, let $G$ be an affine Lorentz map with linear part $\widetilde L$ and $G(p)=G(p_0)+\widetilde L(p-p_0)$. Its coordinate expression in $x$ is $\Phi_G(u)=x(G(x^{-1}(u)))=x(G(p_0))+\widetilde L_x(u-x(p_0))$ with $\widetilde L_x:=E^{-1}\circ\widetilde L\circ E$ a linear map of $\mathbb R^4$, hence a polynomial map of degree at most one and consequently $C^\infty$; its total derivative at every point is the constant $\widetilde L_x$, and for $a,b\in\mathbb R^4$ the Lorentz property of $\widetilde L$ together with [L4] gives $\eta_0(\widetilde L_xa,\widetilde L_xb)=\eta(\widetilde L(Ea),\widetilde L(Eb))=\eta(Ea,Eb)=\eta_0(a,b)$, which under the identification [L6] is exactly the preservation identity $\eta(dG_pv,dG_pw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $p,v,w$. [L4, L6, L7, L8, L12, algebra]

2.1 For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ define the vector-valued map $A_j:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$ by $A_j(u):=\partial_j\Phi(u)=D\Phi_ue_j$, the equality being [L10]; each $A_j$ is $C^1$ because $\Phi$ is $C^2$. For $i,j,k$ define the real-valued function $C_{ijk}(u):=\eta_0(\partial_iA_j(u),A_k(u))=\eta_0(\partial_i\partial_j\Phi(u),\partial_k\Phi(u))$. The identity of step 1.1, $\eta_0(A_j(u),A_k(u))=\eta_{jk}$ with the constant $\eta_{jk}:=\eta_0(e_j,e_k)$, says that $u\mapsto\eta_0(A_j(u),A_k(u))$ is constant; differentiating it with the product rule for the bilinear form $\eta_0$ (which in coordinates is the displayed polynomial of [L16]) gives $C_{ijk}(u)+C_{ikj}(u)=0$ for all $u$. Clairaut's theorem [L11] applied to the components of the $C^2$ map $\Phi$ gives $\partial_i\partial_j\Phi=\partial_j\partial_i\Phi$ pointwise, hence $C_{ijk}=\eta_0(\partial_j\partial_i\Phi,\partial_k\Phi)=C_{jik}$. [L8, L9, L10, L11, L16, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 We show $C_{ijk}=0$ for all $i,j,k$. If $i,j,k$ are pairwise distinct, the two relations of step 2.1 give $C_{ijk}=C_{jik}=-C_{jki}=-C_{kji}=C_{kij}=C_{ikj}=-C_{ijk}$, where each equality is an instance of $C_{abc}=C_{bac}$ (first two indices) or $C_{abc}=-C_{acb}$ (last two indices); hence $2C_{ijk}=0$ and $C_{ijk}=0$ in $\mathbb R$. If exactly two of $i,j,k$ coincide, consider the three possible coincidences: $C_{iik}=-C_{iki}$ and $C_{iki}=C_{kii}$ and $C_{kii}=-C_{kii}$, so $C_{kii}=0$, then $C_{iki}=0$, then $C_{iik}=0$; the remaining coincidences are the same three after renaming. If $i=j=k$, then $C_{iii}=-C_{iii}$ by the last-two relation, so $C_{iii}=0$. Thus $C_{ijk}=0$ for every triple. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Fix $i,j$ and $u$, and put $w:=\partial_iA_j(u)\in\mathbb R^4$. By step 3.1, $\eta_0(w,A_k(u))=C_{ijk}(u)=0$ for $k=0,1,2,3$; since $(A_0(u),\dots,A_3(u))$ is a basis of $\mathbb R^4$ by step 1.1, expanding an arbitrary $z\in\mathbb R^4$ in that basis and using bilinearity of $\eta_0$ gives $\eta_0(w,z)=0$ for every $z$, whence $w=0$ by [L16]. Therefore $\partial_iA_j(u)=0$ for all $i,j,u$; equivalently the total derivative $DA_j(u)$, whose matrix is the Jacobian $(\partial_i(A_j)_m(u))$ by [L10], is the zero linear map for every $u$. [L10, L16, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By step 4.1 and [L14], applied on the convex open set $\mathbb R^4$ of [L15], each map $A_j:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$ is constant on $\mathbb R^4$: there are vectors $L_j\in\mathbb R^4$ with $A_j(u)=L_j$ for all $u$ and all $j$. [L14, L15, step 4.1]

6.1 Let $L:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$ be the linear map defined by $Le_j:=L_j$ for $j=0,1,2,3$ ([[def-linear-map]]); it is well defined because $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ is a basis of $\mathbb R^4$. By step 5.1 and step 2.1, $D\Phi_ue_j=A_j(u)=L_j=Le_j$ for all $u$ and all $j$, so the two linear maps $D\Phi_u$ and $L$ agree on a basis and $D\Phi_u=L$ for every $u$. Define $\Psi(u):=\Phi(u)-Lu$; by [L13] $\Psi$ is totally differentiable at every point, and since the linear map $L$ is totally differentiable with $DL(u)=L$ (substituting $L(u+h)-L(u)-Lh=0$ into [L8] verifies the defining limit), [L13] gives $D\Psi(u)=D\Phi_u-L=L-L=0$ for every $u$. Applying [L14] on the convex open set $\mathbb R^4$ again gives a vector $b\in\mathbb R^4$ with $\Psi(u)=b$ for all $u$; hence $\Phi(u)=Lu+b$ for all $u\in\mathbb R^4$. [L8, L13, L14, L15, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Evaluating the preservation identity of step 1.1 at $u=0$ and using $D\Phi_0=L$ from step 6.1 gives $\eta_0(La,Lb)=\eta_0(a,b)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R^4$. Define the linear map $\widetilde L:V\to V$ by $\widetilde L:=E\circ L\circ E^{-1}$; for $v=Ea$, $w=Eb$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R^4$, [L4] gives $\eta(\widetilde Lv,\widetilde Lw)=\eta(E(La),E(Lb))=\eta_0(La,Lb)=\eta_0(a,b)=\eta(v,w)$, so $\widetilde L$ is a linear Lorentz map by [L1]. Moreover, for every event $p$ with $u:=x(p)$, step 6.1 and the chart identity $x^{-1}(u)=o+E(u)$ of [L4] give $F(p)=x^{-1}(\Phi(u))=x^{-1}(Lu+b)=o+E(Lu+b)=o+Eb+E(Lu)=F(o)+\widetilde L(E(u))=F(o)+\widetilde L(x(p))$, and since $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ this reads $F(p)=F(o)+\widetilde L(p-o)$ for every $p\in A$: $F$ is an affine Lorentz map with linear part $\widetilde L$ and $p_0:=o$. [L1, L4, step 1.1, step 6.1, algebra, L3]

8.1 Step 1.1 sets up the coordinate expression and proves $D\Phi_u$ injective; steps 3.1 through 7.1 construct the constant linear part $\widetilde L$ and prove that it is a linear Lorentz map; step 1.2 is the converse. Hence the $C^2$ isometries of the model are exactly its affine Lorentz maps, and these form a group under composition by [L2] (with every affine Lorentz map being a bijection). [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 1.2, L3, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be two inertial frames with
charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Let $M$ be the
change-of-basis matrix defined by $e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$. Then:

(i) $M$ is the matrix, in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, of a linear
Lorentz map $L:V\to V$, that is $L(e_a)=e'_a$ for all $a$; $M$ is proper and
orthochronous: $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$, $\det M=+1$, and $M$ maps the future cone
onto the future cone. The same holds for $M^{-1}$, the matrix of $L^{-1}$.

(ii) The chart transition
$x'\circ x^{-1}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^4$ is the affine map
$u\mapsto M^{-1}(u-x(o'))$, whose linear part $M^{-1}$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz matrix; consequently it preserves the quadratic form
$q(u):=\eta_0(u,u)=-(u^0)^2+|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2$ of coordinate differences,
and it maps future causal coordinate vectors to future causal coordinate
vectors.

(iii) Conversely, for every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map
$L:V\to V$ and every point $c\in A$, the tuple
$(c;Le_0,Le_1,Le_2,Le_3)$ is an inertial frame, and for its chart $x_L$ one has
$x_L(p)=L^{-1}(x(p)-x(c))$ for all $p\in A$. Hence the transitions from the
chart $x$ are exactly the affine maps $u\mapsto L^{-1}(u-x(c))$ with $L$
ranging over the proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps and $c$ over $A$,
and the linear parts of transitions are exactly the proper orthochronous
Lorentz matrices and their inverses.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two inertial frames $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$, $(o';e'_0,\dots,e'_3)$ with
charts $x$, $x'$, and the change-of-basis matrix $M$ with
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$.

[L1] A linear Lorentz map is a linear $L$ with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$, its matrix $M$ in an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$, and $L$ is proper
when $\det L=1$ and orthochronous when $L(C^+)=C^+$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[L2] A Lorentz map is invertible, $\det L=\pm1$, $L(C^+)$ is one of the two
components $C^+,C^-$, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ if and only if
$L(C^+)\subseteq C^+$; the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map
([[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]]).

[L3] An inertial frame has an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis
($\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$), its first vector lies in
$C^+$, and its ordered basis is positively oriented; the chart is
$x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ with $E(u)=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L4] Positively oriented ordered bases are those in the fixed orientation
class of the model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]): two ordered
bases $\mathcal B,\mathcal B'$ are in the same class exactly when the
change-of-basis map $P$ with $P(b_j)=b'_j$ satisfies $\det P>0$, and the
relation is an equivalence relation.

[L5] The change-of-basis matrix satisfies $P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}
=[\operatorname{id}_V]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$, whose $j$-th column is
$[b_j]_{\mathcal C}$ ([[def-change-of-basis-matrix]]).

[L6] The determinant of an operator is the determinant of its matrix in any
ordered basis, independently of the basis
([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]).

[L7] $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ and the timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L8] In an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis, $T_+=\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$
and $T_-=\{x:x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ are the two components of $T$, with
closures $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{x:x^0\ge|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and
$\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{x:x^0\le-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$
([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L9] $|u\cdot z|\le|u|\,|z|$ for all $u,z\in\mathbb R^3$
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[L10] For two inertial frames with charts $x,x'$ one has $E'=E\circ M$ and
$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)$ for all $p\in A$, the change-of-basis
matrix $M$ being the one with $e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Define $L:V\to V$ by $L(u^0e_0+\dots+u^3e_3):=u^0e'_0+\dots+u^3e'_3$; by [L3] the coordinate maps $E,E'$ are linear isomorphisms, so $L=E'\circ E^{-1}$ is linear with $L(e_a)=e'_a$, it is unique with this property, and $M$ is its matrix in the ordered basis $(e_a)$ by [L5]. Since both bases are $\eta$-orthonormal by [L3], $\eta(Le_a,Le_b)=\eta(e'_a,e'_b)=\eta(e_a,e_b)$ for all $a,b$; expanding two general vectors in the basis and using bilinearity of $\eta$ gives $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$, so $L$ is a linear Lorentz map; in particular $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ by [L1], and $Le_0=e'_0\in C^+$ by [L3]. [L1, L3, L5, algebra]

1.2 By the transition law [L10], $x'(p)=M^{-1}(x(p)-x(o'))=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o')$ for all $p\in A$; under the identification of events with their $x$-coordinates this is the affine map $u\mapsto M^{-1}(u-x(o'))$ of $\mathbb R^4$, with linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part $-M^{-1}x(o')$. [L10, L5, algebra]

1.3 Let $L$ be a proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map and $c\in A$. The images $Le_0,\dots,Le_3$ form an ordered basis, and $\eta(Le_a,Le_b)=\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, so it is $\eta$-orthonormal; $Le_0\in C^+$ because $e_0\in C^+$ by [L3] and $L$ is orthochronous; and it is positively oriented, because the change-of-basis map from $(e_a)$ to $(Le_a)$ is $L$ itself with $\det L=+1>0$, so both ordered bases lie in one class by [L4]. Hence $(c;Le_0,Le_1,Le_2,Le_3)$ is an inertial frame. Its coordinate isomorphism $E_L(u):=\sum_au^aLe_a$ satisfies $E_L(u)=L\bigl(\sum_au^ae_a\bigr)=L(E(u))$ by linearity, so its chart is $x_L(p)=E_L^{-1}(p-c)=E^{-1}(L^{-1}(p-c))=L^{-1}(x(p)-x(c))$ for all $p\in A$. [L1, L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 By step 1.1 the matrix $M$ is the matrix of the linear Lorentz map $L$, so $\det L=\det M$ by [L6]; by [L2], $\det L=\pm1$. Both $(e_a)$ and $(e'_a)$ are positively oriented by [L3], hence lie in the same orientation class of [L4], so the change-of-basis map $P$ with $P(e_a)=e'_a$ satisfies $\det P>0$; by the uniqueness in step 1.1, $P=L$, so $\det M=\det L>0$ and therefore $\det M=+1$. [step 1.1, L2, L3, L4, L6, algebra]

2.2 By step 1.1, $Le_0=e'_0\in C^+$ lies in $L(C^+)$, so $L(C^+)\cap C^+\neq\emptyset$; by [L2] the set $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$, hence it cannot be $C^-$ and $L(C^+)=C^+$. [step 1.1, L2, L7, algebra]

3.1 By [L2] the inverse $L^{-1}$ is a linear Lorentz map, and its matrix in the ordered basis $(e_a)$ is $M^{-1}$ by [L5]; moreover $\det L^{-1}=(\det L)^{-1}=1$ by step 2.1 and the multiplicativity of the determinant, and $L^{-1}(C^+)=C^+$ because $L(C^+)=C^+$ from step 2.2 and $L$ is a bijection. Hence $M^{-1}$ is the matrix of the proper orthochronous Lorentz map $L^{-1}$, and $M^{-1}$ maps the future cone onto the future cone. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L1, L2, L5, algebra]

4.1 Let $A:=M^{-1}$ and $u$ be a future causal coordinate vector, that is $q(u)\le0$ and $u^0\ge0$, which by [L8] and [L7] is exactly the condition that $E(u)$ lies in the closed future cone $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$. Put $w:=Au$. First, $q(w)=\eta_0(Au,Au)=\eta_0(u,u)=q(u)\le0$, because $A$ is the matrix of the Lorentz map $L^{-1}$ by step 3.1 and $E(M^{-1}u)=L^{-1}(E(u))$ by step 1.1's construction $L\circ E=E\circ M$. Second, put $z:=A^{-1}e_0$, the coordinate column of $Le_0=e'_0$ in the basis $(e_a)$, a future timelike vector by step 2.2, so that $z^0>|z_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge0$ by [L8]. Since $A^{T}\eta_0A=\eta_0$ implies $\eta_0(Au,v)=\eta_0(u,A^{-1}v)$ for all coordinate columns $u,v$, we get $w^0=-\eta_0(Au,e_0)=-\eta_0(u,z)=u^0z^0-u_{\mathrm{vec}}\cdot z_{\mathrm{vec}}\ge u^0z^0-|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|\,|z_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge u^0\bigl(z^0-|z_{\mathrm{vec}}|\bigr)\ge0$, where the middle step is [L9] and the last uses $u^0\ge|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|$. Hence $q(w)\le0$ and $w^0\ge0$, so $w$ is a future causal coordinate vector: the transition maps future causal to future causal coordinate vectors, and by step 3.1 its linear part $A$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, L7, L8, L9, algebra]

5.1 Clause (i) is step 1.1 with the properness of step 2.1, the orthochrony of step 2.2 and the statements about $M^{-1}$ in step 3.1. Clause (ii) is the transition formula of step 1.2 together with the preservation of $q$ and of the future causal set in step 4.1. Clause (iii) is step 1.3, and conversely every transition arises there: given the two frames, step 1.1 produces the proper orthochronous Lorentz map $L$ with $Le_a=e'_a$, and step 1.2 writes the transition as $u\mapsto M^{-1}(u-x(o'))=L^{-1}(u-x(c))$ with $c:=o'$, so the transitions from $x$ are exactly the maps listed, and their linear parts are exactly the proper orthochronous Lorentz matrices and their inverses because step 3.1 computes the linear part of the reverse transition as $M$ for the same pair. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Adopt the postulates of the spacetime-primitives page: the oriented
time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ as the spacetime of the
framework with the equations of the specified model covariant under proper
orthochronous affine Lorentz maps, which are the inertial changes of
description ([[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]), and the ideal clock and ideal
light assumptions, including that ideal vacuum light rays are the future null
straight lines and that inertial charts use $x^0=ct$
([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]],
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]). Let $x$ and $x'$ be the
charts of any two inertial frames of the model. Then:

(i) the transition $x'\circ x^{-1}$ is an affine map $u\mapsto\Lambda u+b$
whose linear part $\Lambda$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix; in
particular for all events $p,q$ with coordinate differences
$\Delta=x(q)-x(p)$ and $\Delta'=x'(q)-x'(p)$ one has $\Delta'=\Lambda\Delta$
and $\eta_0(\Delta',\Delta')=\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$, where
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: the interval computed from the
coordinates of two events does not depend on the inertial chart used;

(ii) the causal classification of the displacement $q-p$ (timelike, null or
spacelike) and, for causal displacements, the relation "$q$ is in the future
of $p$" versus "$q$ is in the past of $p$" are independent of the inertial
chart used to compute them; likewise the sign of the interval
$I(p,q)=\eta(q-p,q-p)$ is chart-independent;

(iii) the class of future null straight lines is preserved by every inertial
transition: if a curve is a future null straight line in one inertial chart,
then its coordinate image in every other inertial chart is again a future null
straight line, and its coordinate speed computed as
$|\Delta x|/\Delta t$ equals $c$ in every inertial chart, consistently with
the light clause of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]];

(iv) the orientation and the oriented volume form of the model are invariant
under every inertial transition, and the composition of two inertial
transitions is again an inertial transition; for two transitions whose
relative parameters are $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ in a common spatial direction
the composed parameter is
$(\beta_1+\beta_2)/(1+\beta_1\beta_2)$.

**Scope and qualification.** This is a conditional statement about the adopted
model with ideal clocks, ideal light rays, flat classical spacetime and no
gravitational or quantum effects. It is not an empirical claim about nature,
it does not derive the postulates from experiment or from verbal symmetry
principles, and it inherits the idealizations of its premises; no measurement,
calibration or statistical inference is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The adopted model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with postulates [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] and [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], two inertial frames with charts $x,x'$ of the model, and the events and displacements of the Statement.

[L1] Two inertial charts satisfy $x'(p)=M^{-1}(x(p)-x(o'))$, an affine map with linear part $M^{-1}$, where $M$ is the matrix of the proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map $L$ with $Le_a=e'_a$; $M^{-1}$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix and the transition maps future causal coordinate vectors to future causal coordinate vectors; conversely every proper orthochronous linear Lorentz map and event give an inertial chart with that transition ([[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]).

[L2] For a linear Lorentz map $L$: it preserves $\eta(v,v)$ and the causal character of every nonzero vector and maps the null vectors onto themselves; $L(C^+)$ is one of the components $C^+,C^-$; a proper Lorentz map preserves the oriented volume form, $\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$; the inverse and compositions of Lorentz maps are Lorentz maps; and for the map $-\operatorname{id}$ one has $(-\operatorname{id})(C^+)=C^-$, because $-\operatorname{id}$ is a Lorentz map whose image of $C^+$ is a component different from $C^+$ (no vector of $C^+$ equals its own negative, as $0\notin C^+$) ([[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]]).

[L3] Collinear boosts compose by $B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$ and commute ([[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]).

[L4] The interval of events $p,q$ is $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)$, and events are timelike, null or spacelike when the displacement is; the model makes no physical claim until the postulates are adopted ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

[L5] An inertial chart is $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ for an $\eta$-orthonormal, future, positively oriented basis; in particular coordinate differences transform affinely, and $x^0=ct$ in the SI convention ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]).

[L6] A displacement is timelike, null or spacelike according to whether $\eta(v,v)<0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ with $v\neq0$, or $\eta(v,v)>0$; a causal vector is future or past causal according to its membership in the closed cones $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ or $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L7] The oriented volume form is $\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)=\det([v_j^a])$, the determinant of the coordinate matrix in an inertial frame ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]).

[L8] Adopted: the affine Minkowski model is the spacetime of the framework, and the inertial changes of description are the affine maps whose linear parts are proper orthochronous Lorentz maps; the model equations of the framework are covariant under them ([[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]).

[L9] Adopted: ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines $\{p+\lambda v:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$ with $v$ future null, and in every inertial chart their spatial coordinate velocity has magnitude $c$ with $x^0=ct$ ([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], the transition is $x'(p)=M^{-1}(x(p)-x(o'))$, the affine map $u\mapsto M^{-1}u-M^{-1}x(o')$ with linear part $\Lambda:=M^{-1}$, the matrix of the linear Lorentz map $L^{-1}$, which is proper orthochronous by [L1] and [L2]. For events $p,q$ the affine formula gives $\Delta'=x'(q)-x'(p)=M^{-1}(x(q)-x(p))=\Lambda\Delta$. Since the matrix $\Lambda$ of the Lorentz map $L^{-1}$ satisfies $\eta_0(\Lambda a,\Lambda b)=\eta_0(a,b)$ for all coordinate columns $a,b$ (the matrix form of the defining Lorentz property), $\eta_0(\Delta',\Delta')=\eta_0(\Lambda\Delta,\Lambda\Delta)=\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$, which is exactly $I(p,q)$ by [L4] and [L5]. Hence the interval computed from coordinates does not depend on the inertial chart, proving (i). [L1, L2, L4, L5, algebra]

1.2 For (iv), the volume form is preserved because its argument transforms by the proper linear Lorentz map with matrix $\Lambda$: writing $v_j=E a_j$ with coordinate columns $a_j$, the definition [L7] and the volume-form clause of [L2] give $\epsilon(\Lambda a_0,\dots,\Lambda a_3)=\det([(\Lambda a_j)^a])=\det(\Lambda[a_j^a])=\det(\Lambda)\det([a_j^a])=\epsilon(a_0,\dots,a_3)$, since $\det\Lambda=+1$; the same computation shows that the orientation (the sign of the transition determinant) is preserved. The composition of two inertial transitions is again an inertial transition: if $x,x',x''$ are inertial charts, both $x''\circ x'^{-1}$ and $x'\circ x^{-1}$ are bijections, so their composite is $x''\circ x^{-1}$, the transition from $x$ to $x''$, which by [L1] is affine with proper orthochronous linear part. Finally, if the two transitions have linear parts $B(\beta_1e)$ and $B(\beta_2e)$ with parameters in a common spatial direction $e$, then the composite has linear part $B(\beta_1e)B(\beta_2e)=B\bigl(\frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2}e\bigr)$ by [L3], and the reverse order gives the same result because collinear boosts commute. This proves (iv). [L1, L2, L3, L7, algebra]

2.1 The classification of $\Delta$ is read from the sign of $\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$: it is timelike when this number is negative, null when it is zero and $\Delta\neq0$, spacelike when it is positive, by [L6] and the coordinate expression $\eta(v,w)=v^{T}\eta_0w$ in an inertial frame; the zero displacement $\Delta=0$ is none of the three and remains $0$ under every linear transition, so the classification statement is trivially chart-independent in that case. By step 1.1 the number $\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$ is unchanged under the transition, so the classification, and with it the sign of the interval, is chart-independent. For the future/past distinction, the displacement $q-p$ corresponds to the coordinate column $\Delta$, which is future causal exactly when the vector $E\Delta$ lies in $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$; applying the linear map with matrix $\Lambda$ to a future causal coordinate vector gives a future causal coordinate vector by [L1], and applying the same statement to the inverse transition (whose linear part is $\Lambda^{-1}$) gives the converse, so future-relatedness is chart-independent. For the past case, $x\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ holds exactly when $-x\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$, because $(-\operatorname{id})(C^+)=C^-$ by [L2] and $-\operatorname{id}$ is a bijective linear map, so it maps closures onto closures and carries the identity on the closed cones over to the closed cones; since $\Lambda(-\Delta)=-\Lambda\Delta$, the argument of the previous sentence applied to $-\Delta$ shows that past-relatedness is chart-independent as well. This proves (ii). [L1, L2, L4, L5, L6, algebra]

3.1 Let $\gamma(\lambda)=p+\lambda v$ be an ideal vacuum light ray with $v$ future null, so that in the chart $x$ its coordinate image is $x(p)+\lambda v_x$ with $v_x$ the coordinate column of $v$, a straight line of future null coordinate direction by [L9] and step 2.1. Under the transition the image is $x'(p)+\lambda\Lambda v_x$ by step 1.1: again a straight line, with direction $w:=\Lambda v_x$. The vector with coordinates $w$ is the image under the Lorentz map $L^{-1}$ of the future null vector $v$, hence is future null by [L2]; therefore the coordinate image is again a future null straight line, and applying the same argument to the inverse transition shows that the class of such lines is preserved in both directions. The coordinate speed statement is then the content of the light clause [L9] applied in the chart $x'$: for the future null direction $w$ one has $w^0=|w_{\mathrm{vec}}|>0$, so $|\Delta x|/\Delta t=c$ in every inertial chart. This proves (iii). [L2, L9, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Clauses (i)-(iv) are steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 1.2. Every step is a conditional deduction from the adopted postulates [L8], [L9] and the mathematical suppliers; no step asserts an empirical measurement, and the idealizations listed in the Statement's qualification are carried by [L9]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, L8, L9] ∎
