## Statement

Let $x : [a,b] \to A$, $a < b$, be a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve in the sense of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], with a finite partition
$a = s_0 < \cdots < s_m = b$, $C^{1}$ on each open piece and finite one-sided
difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of each piece. Assume its tangents
are nonzero future causal at every open-piece point and at each one-sided
endpoint.

In any inertial chart ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) write
$y = (y^{0},z)$, $z \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$, for the coordinate path. On a piece
$(\alpha,\beta)$, choose $r \in (\alpha,\beta)$; for a function $g$ continuous
there, write

$$\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} g \;:=\; \lim_{u \downarrow \alpha} \int_u^{r} g \;+\; \lim_{v \uparrow \beta} \int_r^{v} g$$

when both limits are finite. Then:

**(a)** $y$ is continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$, $y^{0'} \ge |z'| \ge 0$ on
$(\alpha,\beta)$, and $y^{0'} > 0$ there.

**(b)** Every coordinate derivative is absolutely improperly Riemann integrable
(its absolute value has finite improper integral), and its signed improper
integral equals the corresponding endpoint increment. The continuous functions
$|z'|$ and $f = \sqrt{(y^{0'})^{2} - |z'|^{2}} = \sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$ have
finite nonnegative improper integrals, with
$\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} f \le \int_{(\alpha,\beta)} y^{0'} = y^{0}(\beta) - y^{0}(\alpha)$.

**(c)** The improper values are independent of $r$, additive under subdivision,
and the finite piece sums are independent of the admissible partition.

**(d)** $D = x(b)-x(a)$ is nonzero future causal: $D^{0} > 0$ and
$|D_{\mathrm{spatial}}| \le D^{0}$ in every inertial chart. If some interior or
one-sided endpoint tangent is future timelike, then $D$ is future timelike.
Coordinate time is strictly increasing on every nondegenerate subinterval. The
integrals need not be ordinary closed-piece Riemann integrals. No
derivative-limit hypothesis, Lebesgue-integration premise, clock identification,
or choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a < b$; a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve $x : [a,b] \to A$ with partition $a = s_0 < \cdots < s_m = b$, $C^{1}$ on each open piece, finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece, and nonzero future causal tangents at every open-piece point and at each one-sided endpoint; an inertial frame with chart $x_A$ and coordinate path $y = (y^{0},z)$; a piece $(\alpha,\beta)$ of the partition and a point $r \in (\alpha,\beta)$.

[L1] Weak piecewise regularity and corner continuity ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): $x$ is $C^{1}$ on each open piece, so $y$ is $C^{1}$ there and each coordinate $y^{j}$ is differentiable with $y^{j'}$ the corresponding coordinate derivative; the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at the piece endpoints exist, and their finiteness implies continuity of $x$, hence of $y$, at every corner and at $a$ and $b$; derivatives of a function differentiable on an interval are continuous there when the function is $C^{1}$ ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).

[L2] Metric in an inertial chart ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): in the chart of an inertial frame the matrix of $\eta$ in the basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the spatial form $\delta$ is the restriction of $\eta$ to $\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with norm $|z| = \sqrt{\delta(z,z)}$, and for a tangent vector $v = x'(u)$ with coordinates $y'(u) = (y^{0'}(u),z'(u))$, $-\eta(v,v) = (y^{0'}(u))^{2} - |z'(u)|^{2}$; $\eta$ is bilinear ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

[L3] The future cone in orthonormal coordinates ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]): with the first basis vector future, the future timelike set is $T_+ = \{v : v^{0} > |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|\}$, its closure is $\operatorname{cl}(T_+) = \{v : v^{0} \ge |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|\}$, and $T_+$ is open in $V$; a nonzero future causal vector $v$ satisfies $v^{0} \ge |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|$ and $v^{0} > 0$; a future timelike vector has $v^{0} > |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|$.

[L4] Truncated fundamental theorem of calculus ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]): if $\alpha < u < v < \beta$ then on $[u,v]$ each coordinate function $y^{j}$ is differentiable with continuous derivative $y^{j'}$, so $y^{j'}$ is Riemann integrable on $[u,v]$ and $\int_u^v y^{j'} = y^{j}(v) - y^{j}(u)$.

[L5] Order, additivity and linearity of the Riemann integral ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]], [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]): if $a \le c \le d$ and the functions are integrable with $g_1 \le g_2$ pointwise then $\int_c^d g_1 \le \int_c^d g_2$, and if $g \ge 0$ then $\int_c^d g \ge 0$; $\int_c^e g = \int_c^d g + \int_d^e g$ for $c \le d \le e$; and the integral is linear in the integrand.

[L6] Completeness and least upper bounds ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]): every nonempty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound, and if $S = \sup A$ then no $S - \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon > 0$ is an upper bound of $A$.

[L7] Norm inequality for vector-valued integrals and the triangle inequality ([[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]], [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]], [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]): for $c \le d$ and integrable vector-valued $f$, $\bigl\|\int_c^d f\bigr\|_2 \le \int_c^d \|f\|_2$; and $|u+w| \le |u| + |w|$ for the Euclidean norm on the spatial space, finite sums included.

[L8] Square root and continuity facts ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-rational-power-monotone]], [[thm-nth-roots-exist]], [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]): $t \mapsto t^{1/2}$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ and $a^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of $a$; if $0 < s \le t$ then $s^{1/2} \le t^{1/2}$ and $0^{1/2} = 0$; products and finite sums of continuous real functions are continuous, and the components of a continuous $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map are continuous.

[L9] The future cone is closed under sums of its elements: if $v$ is future timelike and $w$ is future causal then $v + w$ is future timelike, and a sum of two future causal vectors is future causal. This is the coordinate computation $(v+w)^{0} = v^{0}+w^{0} > |v_{\mathrm{sp}}| + |w_{\mathrm{sp}}| \ge |v_{\mathrm{sp}}+w_{\mathrm{sp}}|$, respectively the same with nonstrict inequalities, using [L3] and [L7].

[L10] Strict positivity of integrals of positive continuous functions ([[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]], [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]]): if $g$ is continuous and nonnegative on a nondegenerate compact interval $[p,q]$ and $g(u_0) > 0$ for some $u_0 \in [p,q]$, then $\int_p^q g > 0$, because $\int_p^q g = 0$ would force $g \equiv 0$ on $[p,q]$; in particular a continuous function that is strictly positive at every point of $[p,q]$ has strictly positive integral there. Moreover for a real constant $\mu$ one has $\int_p^q \mu = \mu\,(q-p)$, so $\int_p^q \mu > 0$ whenever $\mu > 0$ and $p < q$.

## Proof

1.1 The coordinate path $y$ is continuous at the corners and the endpoints of the piece by [L1] and $C^{1}$ on $(\alpha,\beta)$, so $y$ is continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$; on $(\alpha,\beta)$ each coordinate derivative $y^{j'}$ is continuous by [L1], and by the chart form [L2] one has $-\eta(x'(u),x'(u)) = (y^{0'}(u))^{2} - |z'(u)|^{2}$ for every $u \in (\alpha,\beta)$. [given, L1, L2]

2.1 At every $u \in (\alpha,\beta)$ the tangent $x'(u)$ is nonzero future causal, so by [L3] $y^{0'}(u) \ge |z'(u)| \ge 0$ and $y^{0'}(u) > 0$: the spatial inequality uses the coordinate description of the future cone, and strict positivity uses that $x'(u) \ne 0$ rules out the case $y'(u) = 0$. [step 1.1, L3]

2.2 For $\alpha < u < v < \beta$ and each $j \in \{0,1,2,3\}$ the truncated fundamental theorem gives $\int_u^v y^{j'} = y^{j}(v) - y^{j}(u)$ by [L4]. [step 1.1, L4]

3.1 Letting $u \downarrow \alpha$ in the case $j = 0$ of step 2.2, continuity of $y^{0}$ at $\alpha$ gives $\lim_{u \downarrow \alpha} \int_u^r y^{0'} = y^{0}(r) - y^{0}(\alpha)$, a finite real number; it is nonnegative because $y^{0'}(\cdot) \ge 0$ on $(u,r)$ and [L5] applies to the truncations, $y^{0}(r) - y^{0}(\alpha) \ge 0$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L1, L5]

3.2 Likewise $\lim_{v \uparrow \beta} \int_r^v y^{0'} = y^{0}(\beta) - y^{0}(r)$, finite and nonnegative. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L1, L5]

3.3 The functions $|z'|$ and $f = \sqrt{(y^{0'})^{2}-|z'|^{2}}$ are continuous on $(\alpha,\beta)$ and satisfy $0 \le |z'| \le y^{0'}$ and $0 \le f \le y^{0'}$ there: $|z'|^{2}$ is a finite sum of squares of the continuous functions $z'^{i}$, hence continuous by [L8]; writing $t := |z'|^{2}$, the composite $t^{1/2}$ is continuous where $t > 0$ by [L8], and at a point where $t(u_0) = 0$ the estimate $0 \le |z'(u)| = (|z'(u)|^{2})^{1/2} \le (\sup_{|u-u_0| < \delta}|z'|^{2})^{1/2} < \varepsilon$ for small $\delta$, using monotonicity of the square root and continuity of $|z'|^{2}$ at $u_0$, gives continuity there; the same argument applies to $f$, whose inner function $(y^{0'})^{2}-|z'|^{2}$ is continuous and nonnegative by step 2.1; and the domination $f \le y^{0'}$, $|z'| \le y^{0'}$ follows from $0 \le (y^{0'})^{2} - |z'|^{2} \le (y^{0'})^{2}$, $y^{0'} \ge 0$ and monotonicity of the square root, together with $(y^{0'})^{2}$'s unique nonnegative square root $y^{0'}$ from [L8]. [step 2.1, L3, L8]

3.4 For each $j$, step 2.2 gives $\int_u^r y^{j'} = y^{j}(r)-y^{j}(u)$ and $\int_r^v y^{j'} = y^{j}(v)-y^{j}(r)$; letting $u \downarrow \alpha$ and $v \uparrow \beta$, continuity of $y^{j}$ at $\alpha$ and $\beta$ gives the finite limits $y^{j}(r)-y^{j}(\alpha)$ and $y^{j}(\beta)-y^{j}(r)$, whose sum is $y^{j}(\beta)-y^{j}(\alpha)$: the signed improper integral of each coordinate derivative equals the corresponding endpoint increment. [step 2.2, L1]

4.1 Let $g$ be continuous on $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $0 \le g \le y^{0'}$ pointwise, and put $A(u) := \int_u^r g$ for $u \in (\alpha,r]$. For $\alpha < u_1 < u_2 \le r$, additivity and nonnegativity of the integral [L5] give $A(u_1) = A(u_2) + \int_{u_1}^{u_2} g \ge A(u_2)$, so $A$ is nondecreasing as $u$ decreases; and $A(u) \le \int_u^r y^{0'} = y^{0}(r)-y^{0}(u) \le y^{0}(r)-y^{0}(\alpha)$ by [L5] and step 3.1. The set $\{A(u) : \alpha < u \le r\}$ is nonempty and bounded above, so by [L6] it has a supremum $S$; for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the number $S-\varepsilon$ is not an upper bound, so there is $u_*$ with $A(u_*) > S-\varepsilon$, and every $\alpha < u < u_*$ then satisfies $S-\varepsilon < A(u) \le S$. Hence $\lim_{u \downarrow \alpha} A(u) = S$ exists and is finite. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L5, L6]

4.2 Symmetrically, $B(v) := \int_r^v g$ is nondecreasing in $v$ with $B(v) \le y^{0}(\beta)-y^{0}(r)$ by [L5] and step 3.2, so by [L6] $\lim_{v \uparrow \beta} B(v)$ exists and is finite. [step 2.1, step 3.2, L5, L6]

4.3 Applying steps 3.1 and 3.2 to $g := |z'|$ and $g := f$, and using step 3.1 and [L5] for the bound on $y^{0'}$, gives finite improper integrals with $\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} f \le \int_{(\alpha,\beta)} y^{0'} = y^{0}(\beta)-y^{0}(\alpha)$. [step 3.1, step 3.3, L5]

5.1 For each $j$ the absolute value $|y^{j'}|$ is continuous on $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $0 \le |y^{j'}| \le y^{0'}$ by step 2.1, so steps 3.1, 3.2 and 3.4 give $\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} |y^{j'}| \le y^{0}(\beta)-y^{0}(\alpha) < \infty$: every coordinate derivative is absolutely improperly Riemann integrable. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 4.3]

5.2 The improper value is independent of $r$: for $\alpha < r_1 < r_2 < \beta$ and any admissible $g$, the two-sided limit $\lim_{u \downarrow \alpha, v \uparrow \beta} \int_u^v g$ exists and equals $\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} g$ computed with $r = r_1$, because $\int_u^v g = \int_u^{r_1} g + \int_{r_1}^v g$ by [L5] and the two one-sided limits add; the same identity with $r_2$ exhibits the same two-sided limit as the value computed with $r = r_2$, so the two values agree. [step 4.1, step 4.2, L5]

6.1 Additivity under subdivision: for $\alpha < \gamma < \beta$ and admissible $g$, splitting $\int_u^v g = \int_u^{\gamma} g + \int_{\gamma}^v g$ and passing to the one-sided limits gives $\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} g = \int_{(\alpha,\gamma)} g + \int_{(\gamma,\beta)} g$. [step 5.2, L5]

6.2 For a piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ write $\Delta_i := y(s_i)-y(s_{i-1})$ and $\Delta_{i,\mathrm{sp}} := z(s_i)-z(s_{i-1})$. By steps 4.1 and 4.2, $\Delta_i^{0} = \int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} y^{0'} > 0$: the improper value dominates the ordinary integral of the continuous function $y^{0'}$ over any nondegenerate compact interior subinterval, and that ordinary integral is strictly positive by [L10] because $y^{0'} > 0$ at every point of the subinterval by step 2.1; and $\bigl|\Delta_{i,\mathrm{sp}}\bigr| = \bigl\|\int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} z'\bigr\|_2 \le \int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} |z'| \le \int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} y^{0'} = \Delta_i^{0}$, the first inequality by [L7] applied to the truncations and passed to the limit, the second by step 2.1 and [L5]. [step 2.1, step 4.3, step 3.4, step 5.1, L5, L7, L10]

7.1 Independence of the admissible partition: let two finite partitions of $[a,b]$ be admissible and let their union be the common refinement, whose points split each piece of either partition into finitely many subintervals; by step 6.1 the total sum over each piece equals the sum of the values over its subintervals, and inductively the total over the refined partition equals the total over each original partition, so the two finite sums agree. [step 6.1]

7.2 Summing over the finitely many pieces gives $D^{0} = \sum_i \Delta_i^{0} > 0$ and, by the triangle inequality of [L7] for the finite sum $\sum_i \Delta_{i,\mathrm{sp}}$ and by step 6.2, $|D_{\mathrm{spatial}}| \le \sum_i |\Delta_{i,\mathrm{sp}}| \le \sum_i \Delta_i^{0} = D^{0}$; hence $D$ is nonzero future causal by [L3]. [step 6.2, L3, L7]

7.3 Coordinate time is strictly increasing on every nondegenerate subinterval: for $s < t$ in $[a,b]$, the increment $y^{0}(t)-y^{0}(s)$ decomposes as a sum of increments over the pieces that meet $[s,t]$, each nonnegative by step 6.2 and at least one strictly positive because $(s,t)$ is nonempty and open and meets some piece in a nondegenerate interval, over which $y^{0'}$ is continuous and positive and hence has strictly positive integral by [L10]. [step 6.2, L5, L10]

8.1 If an interior point $c \in (\alpha,\beta)$ has $x'(c)$ future timelike, then $y^{0'}(c)-|z'(c)| > 0$ by [L3]; the function $y^{0'}-|z'|$ is continuous on $(\alpha,\beta)$ by steps 1.1 and 3.3, so there are $\delta > 0$ and $\mu > 0$ with $y^{0'}-|z'| \ge \mu$ on $[c-\delta,c+\delta] \subset (\alpha,\beta)$. Then $D^{0}-|D_{\mathrm{spatial}}| \ge \sum_i \bigl(\Delta_i^{0}-\bigl|\Delta_{i,\mathrm{sp}}\bigr|\bigr) \ge \int_{(\alpha,\beta)}(y^{0'}-|z'|) \ge \int_{c-\delta}^{c+\delta} \mu = \mu\cdot 2\delta > 0$ by steps 3.4, 6.1, 6.2, [L5] and the constant-integral value of [L10], so $D$ is future timelike by [L3]. [step 4.3, step 6.2, step 7.2, L3, L5, L10]

8.2 If a one-sided endpoint tangent is future timelike, say the right quotient of the piece at $s^{*} \in \{a\} \cup \{s_1,\dots,s_{m-1}\}$ is the future timelike vector $v = y'(s^{*}+)$, then for small $h > 0$ the quotient $\bigl(y(s^{*}+h)-y(s^{*})\bigr)/h$ is eventually future timelike, since it tends to $v$ and the future timelike set is open by [L3]; so $y(s^{*}+h)-y(s^{*}) = h\,q_h$ is future timelike. Split $D = \bigl[y(s^{*})-y(a)\bigr] + \bigl[y(s^{*}+h)-y(s^{*})\bigr] + \bigl[y(b)-y(s^{*}+h)\bigr]$: the first bracket is absent when $s^{*} = a$ and is otherwise future causal by steps 6.1 and 6.2 applied to the restriction to $[a,s^{*}]$, the middle bracket is future timelike, and the last bracket is future causal by steps 6.1 and 6.2 applied to the restriction to $[s^{*}+h,b]$; applying [L9] to the timelike middle bracket and the future causal last bracket, and then once more when the future causal first bracket is present, makes $D$ future timelike, and the cases of a left one-sided endpoint tangent are symmetric. [step 6.2, step 7.2, L3, L9]

9.1 The argument uses only finite-dimensional coordinate computations, truncated Riemann integrals and one-sided limits: no derivative-limit hypothesis on the open pieces, no Lebesgue integration, no clock identification and no choice principle are used. [step 8.1, step 8.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **The improper integrals need not be closed-piece Riemann integrals.** The derivative is not assumed to extend continuously to the corners, and no bound on $|x'|$ near a corner is assumed; the only estimate used is the coordinate domination $0 \le |z'| \le y^{0'}$, which turns the (possibly unbounded) spatial derivatives into functions dominated by the milder quantity $y^{0'}$, itself controlled by the endpoint increment through the truncated fundamental theorem.

- **Where the causal hypothesis is spent.** The sign of $\eta$ alone never enters the integrability conclusions: $\int y^{0'}$ is a finite increment because $y^{0'}$ is a derivative, and domination by $y^{0'}$ needs only $|z'| \le y^{0'}$, which is the future causal inequality. The strict positivity $y^{0'} > 0$ uses in addition that the tangent is nonzero; the strict timelikeness conclusions of clause (d) are the only place where a future timelike (not merely causal) tangent is used.

- **The statement is chart-relative for the improper integrals and chart-independent for the displacement.** The improper integrals are formed in a fixed inertial chart; the conclusions $D \in C^{+} \setminus \{0\}$, strict coordinate-time monotonicity and the timelikeness criterion are statements about the intrinsic displacement $D$ and the intrinsic tangents, since the coordinate criterion of [L3] describes the same cone in every inertial chart.

## Definition

Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.

## Remarks

- **Well-definedness.** (i) $g_x$ is the composition of the continuous
$V$-valued derivative $x'$, the quadratic form $v \mapsto -\eta(v,v)$ of
[[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] and the continuous square root; the coordinate
computation displayed above evaluates the quadratic form in an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis and needs no basis-free topology on $V$. (ii) The
integrand is defined on all of $I$ because strict positivity of $g_x$ is the
future timelike hypothesis, so no branch of the square root and no punctured
domain is needed. (iii) Existence of the integral on every compact subinterval
is [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], and the oriented convention of
[[def-oriented-integral]] makes $\tau(s_0) = 0$ and reverses the sign when the
endpoints are exchanged, so $\tau$ is a genuine function on $I$ for every choice
of base point. (iv) The base point enters only additively: for
$s_1, s_2, s \in I$ the additivity identity of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] gives
$c^{-1}\int_{s_1}^{s} = c^{-1}\int_{s_1}^{s_2} + c^{-1}\int_{s_2}^{s}$, so
changing $s_0$ adds the constant $c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s_1}$ to the whole function.
(v) The straight-segment value follows by evaluating a constant integrand:
$x' = q-p$ is future timelike, $\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}$ is its positive length,
and the integral of a constant over $[a,b]$ is the value times $b-a$.
- **What is deliberately not asserted.** The definition does not assert that
$\tau$ is differentiable or invertible (that is
[[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]) and does not assert that a physical
clock reads $\tau$ (that identification is the adopted assumption
that ideal clocks indicate proper time, an assumption of the framework, not a
mathematical consequence). No choice principle is used: the construction
selects no object from any family and all integrals are one-dimensional.

## Definition

Let $c > 0$ be the conversion constant of [[def-sr-proper-time]] and let
$x : [a,b] \to A$, $a < b$, be a piecewise $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline in
the weak sense of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]: $x$ is $C^{1}$
on each open piece of a finite partition $a = s_0 < \cdots < s_m = b$, its
interior tangents and finite one-sided difference-quotient endpoint tangents are
future timelike, and continuous extension of the derivative is not assumed.

**(i) The piecewise density.** On each open piece let

$$g_i(t) = \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(t),x'(t)\bigr)} > 0 .$$

By clause (b) of [[lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability]] the function
$g_i$ is continuous on $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and its two-ended improper Riemann
integral

$$\int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} g_i \;:=\; \lim_{u \downarrow s_{i-1}} \int_u^{r} g_i \;+\; \lim_{v \uparrow s_i} \int_r^{v} g_i$$

(for any $r \in (s_{i-1},s_i)$) is finite and nonnegative; it is positive
because $g_i$ is positive and continuous on a nondegenerate compact interior
subinterval, the improper value dominates the ordinary integral over such a
subinterval ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]), and that ordinary integral
is strictly positive: a continuous nonnegative function on a nondegenerate
compact interval whose integral vanishes is identically zero there
([[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]), whereas $g_i$ is
strictly positive at every point of the piece.

**(ii) Total proper time.** Define

$$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) \;:=\; c^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} g_i .$$

The finite sum is independent of the admissible partition, by subdivision
additivity and a common refinement (clause (c) of
[[lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability]]), and it is independent of the
inertial chart: for every truncation $s_{i-1} < u < r < v < s_i$ the ordinary
integral $\int_u^v g_i$ is intrinsic by [[def-sr-proper-time]] (applied to the
$C^{1}$ restriction), and the improper value is the limit of these intrinsic
truncation values, which is intrinsic.

**(iii) Based proper-time function.** For a distinguished $s_0 \in [a,b]$ set
$\tau_x(s) := \Delta\tau_{[s_0,s]}(x)$ for $s \ge s_0$ and
$\tau_x(s) := -\Delta\tau_{[s,s_0]}(x)$ for $s < s_0$, with
$\tau_x(s_0) = 0$, using restrictions and oriented limits
([[def-oriented-integral]], [[def-interval]]). It is strictly increasing, and
changing the distinguished base point changes it by an additive constant.

**(iv) Corner hypothesis (H).** Hypothesis (H) is the special case in which
each open-piece derivative has finite limits at both ends of its piece and hence
extends continuously to the closed piece. Under (H) the limiting values equal
the finite one-sided quotient derivatives of the curve, each $g_i$ extends
continuously and positively to the closed piece, its improper integral equals
its ordinary Riemann integral there
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]]), and the same
finite-sum formula applies. In particular, if $x$ is globally $C^{1}$ on
$[a,b]$ (the one-piece case of (H)), then
$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) = \tau(b) - \tau(a)$ of [[def-sr-proper-time]].

**(v) Straight pieces.** If on the piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the tangent is a
constant future timelike vector $d_i$, the contribution of that piece is
$c^{-1}(s_i - s_{i-1})\sqrt{-\eta(d_i,d_i)}$; a piecewise straight future
timelike worldline therefore has total proper time equal to the finite sum of
its straight-segment proper times. In every case $\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) > 0$.

**(vi) Additivity over concatenation.** For $a < d < b$, the restrictions of a
weak piecewise worldline $x$ to $[a,d]$ and $[d,b]$ satisfy
$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) = \Delta\tau_{[a,d]}(x) + \Delta\tau_{[d,b]}(x)$: insert
$d$ into the partition and use (ii).

The definition supplies metric time only; identification with an ideal clock
reading is a separate physical assumption. No global $C^{1}$ inverse, tangent at
a kink, or four-acceleration at a kink is asserted.

## Remarks

- **Well-definedness is the integrability lemma.** The finiteness of each
  improper integral, the independence of $r$, the additivity under subdivision
  and the independence of the admissible partition are clauses (b) and (c) of
  [[lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability]], not new hypotheses; the
  definition only packages the sums and the based function. Because the
  integrals are one-dimensional Riemann integrals of coordinate functions and
  no object is selected from a family, no choice principle is used.

- **Why the chart does not enter.** The two-ended improper integrals are formed
  in a fixed inertial chart, but each truncation integral is the intrinsic
  proper-time difference of a $C^{1}$ restriction, and the improper value is the
  limit of the truncation values along a monotone family; the limit of intrinsic
  numbers is intrinsic. So $\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x)$ is a function of the
  parametrized worldline alone.

- **Under (H) nothing improper remains.** If the derivative extends
  continuously to the closed piece with endpoint value $w$, then for
  $u < v$ in the piece the truncated fundamental theorem gives
  $x(v)-x(u) = \int_u^v x'$ (coordinatewise, and the value in $V$ is recovered),
  so the quotient $\bigl(x(s_{i-1}+h)-x(s_{i-1})\bigr)/h$ is the average
  $\frac{1}{h}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_{i-1}+h} x'$ of the continuous extension over a
  shrinking interval and tends to $w$; the extended endpoint value is therefore
  the one-sided quotient tangent of the curve, and similarly at the right end
  ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]). The improper
  integral over the closed piece is then an ordinary Riemann integral by its
  definition as the common limit of the two truncations.

- **Scope.** The construction covers future timelike piecewise $C^{1}$ curves;
  tangent vectors at kinks and four-accelerations at kinks are not defined here,
  and the statement asserts no clock reading, no maximality property of straight
  worldlines and no empirical content. The factor $c^{-1}$ appears once, in
  (ii); sums of the functions of this definition must not receive a further
  factor.

## Statement

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : [a,b] \to A$ be a weak piecewise $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline: $C^{1}$ on the open pieces of a finite partition
$a = s_0 < \cdots < s_m = b$, with finite future timelike one-sided
difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]). Let
$\varphi : [u,v] \to [a,b]$ be an increasing continuous surjection, $C^{1}$ on
the open pieces of a finite partition, with $\varphi' > 0$ at every interior
smooth point and finite positive one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at
both endpoints of each piece.

Then $\varphi$ is strictly increasing with continuous inverse, $y = x \circ
\varphi$ is a weak piecewise $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline, and

$$\Delta\tau_{[u,v]}(y) = \Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x)$$

in the notation of [[def-sr-piecewise-proper-time]]. The same equality holds
for every pair of corresponding restricted parameter intervals; based
proper-time functions differ only by their base-point constant. The relevant
partition of $[u,v]$ is the common refinement of $\varphi$'s partition and the
inverse images of $x$'s partition points.

This statement gives worldline and clock consequences only for positive
derivatives, including all one-sided endpoint derivatives; a zero-tangent
composition is not asserted to be a worldline.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $c > 0$; a weak piecewise $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline $x : [a,b] \to A$ with partition $a = s_0 < \cdots < s_m = b$; and an increasing continuous surjection $\varphi : [u,v] \to [a,b]$, $C^{1}$ on the open pieces of a finite partition with $\varphi' > 0$ at interior smooth points and finite positive one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at the piece endpoints.

[L1] Weak piecewise worldlines ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): $x$ is $C^{1}$ on each open piece with future timelike tangent, its one-sided difference-quotient tangents at the piece endpoints are finite and future timelike, and its finiteness gives continuity at corners; a curve with these properties is a weak piecewise $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline.

[L2] Mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]): a real function continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$ and differentiable on $(\alpha,\beta)$ satisfies $g(\beta)-g(\alpha) = g'(c)(\beta-\alpha)$ for some $c \in (\alpha,\beta)$.

[L3] Continuous inverse ([[thm-continuous-inverse]], [[def-interval]]): a continuous injective real function on an order-convex set is strictly monotone, and its inverse is strictly monotone in the same sense and continuous; a strictly increasing surjection $[u,v] \to [a,b]$ has $\varphi(u) = a$, $\varphi(v) = b$, and each point of $[a,b]$ has exactly one preimage.

[L4] Chain rule and derivatives ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]): componentwise in an inertial chart, if $s \mapsto y^{j}(s)$ is differentiable at $\sigma$ and $\varphi$ is differentiable at $w$ with $\varphi(w) = \sigma$, then $y^{j} \circ \varphi$ is differentiable at $w$ with derivative $y^{j'}(\sigma)\varphi'(w)$, with one-sided readings at endpoint points; products of these derivatives obey the algebra of derivatives, and differentiability implies continuity ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).

[L5] The future cone ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]): in a future $\eta$-orthonormal basis the future timelike set is $\{v : v^{0} > |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|\}$, and it is closed under multiplication by positive scalars.

[L6] Substitution ([[thm-substitution]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]): if $\varphi$ is differentiable on a compact interval with $\varphi'$ integrable there and $g$ is continuous on an order-convex set containing the image of that interval, then $\int_{\varphi(r)}^{\varphi(s)} g = \int_r^s (g \circ \varphi)\,\varphi'$; a continuous function on a compact interval is integrable there.

[L7] Continuity facts ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]], [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]): components of continuous vector-valued maps are continuous; composites, products, sums and scalar multiples of continuous real functions are continuous.

[L8] Bilinearity of $\eta$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): $\eta(\lambda v, \lambda w) = \lambda^{2}\eta(v,w)$.

[L9] Weak-piecewise integrability and total proper time ([[lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability]], [[def-sr-piecewise-proper-time]]): for a weak piecewise future causal curve the two-ended improper integrals over the pieces are finite and nonnegative, are independent of the cut point, are additive under subdivision and independent of the admissible partition; and $\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) = c^{-1}\sum_i \int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)}\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On each open piece of its partition, $\varphi$ is $C^{1}$ with $\varphi' > 0$; the mean value theorem [L2] applied on each closed piece gives $\varphi(\beta)-\varphi(\alpha) = \varphi'(c)(\beta-\alpha) > 0$ for its endpoints $\alpha < \beta$, so $\varphi$ is strictly increasing on every piece and, concatenating the finitely many pieces, strictly increasing on $[u,v]$; hence $\varphi$ is injective with $\varphi(u) = a$, $\varphi(v) = b$, and its inverse is continuous by [L3]. [given, L2, L3]

2.1 Let $\rho_0 < \cdots < \rho_N$ be the increasing enumeration of the partition points of $\varphi$ together with the preimages $\varphi^{-1}(s_1),\dots,\varphi^{-1}(s_{m-1})$, which exist uniquely by [L3]; this is a finite partition of $[u,v]$ (the common refinement). [step 1.1, L3]

3.1 On each open subinterval $(\rho_{k-1},\rho_k)$ the map $\varphi$ is $C^{1}$ and $x$ is $C^{1}$ on the open piece of $x$ containing $\varphi\bigl((\rho_{k-1},\rho_k)\bigr)$, so $y = x \circ \varphi$ is $C^{1}$ there with $y' = \varphi'\,(x' \circ \varphi)$ in coordinates, by the chain rule [L4]; hence every open-piece tangent of $y$ is a positive multiple of a future timelike vector and is future timelike by [L5]. [step 2.1, L5, L4]

4.1 At each endpoint $\rho_k$, the one-sided difference quotients of $y$ exist: writing $k_h := \varphi(\rho_k + h)-\varphi(\rho_k)$ for small $h$ on one side, $\bigl(y(\rho_k+h)-y(\rho_k)\bigr)/h = \bigl[\bigl(x(\varphi(\rho_k)+k_h)-x(\varphi(\rho_k))\bigr)/k_h\bigr]\cdot(k_h/h)$, where $k_h \to 0$ on the correct side, the first factor tends to the finite one-sided quotient tangent of $x$ at $\varphi(\rho_k)$ (or to the tangent $x'$ when $\varphi(\rho_k)$ is interior to an $x$-piece), and the second tends to the finite positive one-sided quotient derivative of $\varphi$ at $\rho_k$; the product is finite and, being a positive multiple of a future timelike vector, future timelike by [L5]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L5]

4.2 Let $\rho_{k-1} < r < s < \rho_k$. Then $\varphi$ is $C^{1}$ on $[r,s]$ with $\varphi'$ continuous, hence integrable; the function $f := \sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$ is continuous on the order-convex open piece of $x$ containing $\varphi([r,s])$ by [L7] (it is the composition of the continuous tangent component functions with the square root); substitution [L6] gives $\int_r^s \varphi'(w)\,f(\varphi(w))\,dw = \int_{\varphi(r)}^{\varphi(s)} f$. [step 3.1, L6, L7]

5.1 By bilinearity [L8], $-\eta(y'(w),y'(w)) = \varphi'(w)^{2}\bigl(-\eta(x'(\varphi(w)),x'(\varphi(w)))\bigr)$, so $\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')} = \varphi'(w)\,f(\varphi(w))$ on the open subinterval because $\varphi' > 0$; hence the left side of step 4.2 is the truncation integral of $y$'s length density over $[r,s]$. [step 3.1, step 4.2, L8]

6.1 Both $x$ and $y$ are weak piecewise future timelike curves (the first by hypothesis, the second by steps 3.1 and 4.1), so the improper integrals of $f$ over the pieces of $x$ and of $\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')}$ over the pieces of $y$ exist and are finite by [L9]. Letting $r \downarrow \rho_{k-1}$ and $s \uparrow \rho_k$ in step 4.2, the left side tends to $\int_{(\rho_{k-1},\rho_k)}\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')}$ by definition of the improper integral, and the right side tends to the integral of $f$ over the interval $\bigl(\varphi(\rho_{k-1}),\varphi(\rho_k)\bigr)$ contained in a single open piece of $x$, by continuity and strict monotonicity of $\varphi$; the limits are equal. [step 4.2, step 5.1, step 1.1, L9]

7.1 Summing step 6.1 over the refined pieces and using the additivity of the improper integrals [L9], the intervals $\bigl(\varphi(\rho_{k-1}),\varphi(\rho_k)\bigr)$ partition the pieces of $x$ up to finitely many cutting points, so $\Delta\tau_{[u,v]}(y) = c^{-1}\sum_k\int_{(\rho_{k-1},\rho_k)}\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')} = c^{-1}\sum_i\int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} f = \Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x)$. [step 6.1, L9]

8.1 The same argument applied to the restrictions of $x$ and $\varphi$ to corresponding restricted parameter intervals gives $\Delta\tau$ over every pair of corresponding restricted intervals; consequently the based functions $\tau_y$ and $\tau_x \circ \varphi$ differ by the base-point constant. [step 7.1]

9.1 The hypotheses used are $\varphi' > 0$ at every interior smooth point and finite positive one-sided endpoint quotients; at a point where $\varphi' = 0$ the composed tangent is zero and the composition is not a worldline, so no total proper time is asserted for it, and no inverse of $\varphi$ is used in the integral identity of step 7.1; no object is selected from a family, so no choice principle is used. [step 7.1, step 8.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Why the refined partition is needed.** The preimages of the corners of $x$ must be corners of $y$; refining by them makes $x$ smooth on the image of each open refined piece, so the truncation substitution of step 4.2 applies on compact subintervals, and only then are the improper limits taken. No derivative-limit hypothesis at the corners is used, and $\varphi'$ need not be bounded near a corner.

- **Positive derivative throughout.** The conclusion $\Delta\tau_{[u,v]}(y) = \Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x)$ is a statement about worldlines; the companion global-$C^{1}$ identity of [[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]] separately allows vanishing derivatives in the broad curve-integral identity without asserting a worldline there.

## Statement

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function
$\tau(s) = c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(u),x'(u))}\,du$ for a base point
$s_0 \in I$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]]). Then:

**(i)** $\tau$ is differentiable at every $s \in I$, with one-sided derivatives
at the endpoints of $I$, and

$$\tau'(s) = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr)} > 0$$

for every $s \in I$; since $\tau'$ is this composition of continuous maps,
$\tau$ is $C^{1}$ on $I$.

**(ii)** $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$, hence injective, and its image
$J := \tau[I]$ is an order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ with at least two
elements, so $\tau : I \to J$ is a bijection.

**(iii)** The inverse $\rho : J \to I$ of $\tau$ is continuous and strictly
increasing, and it is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of $J$ with

$$\rho'\bigl(\tau(s)\bigr) = \frac{1}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} > 0 ;$$

hence $\rho$ is $C^{1}$ on $J$.

**(iv)** The reparametrized curve $y := x \circ \rho : J \to A$ is a $C^{1}$
future timelike worldline whose tangent at the proper-time parameter $\tau(s)$ is

$$(x \circ \rho)'\bigl(\tau(s)\bigr) = \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

in particular $y$ is parametrized by its own proper time up to the additive
constant of the base point.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $c > 0$; an order-convex $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ with at least two elements; a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline $x : I \to A$; a base point $s_0 \in I$ and the proper-time function $\tau$ of [[def-sr-proper-time]]; and the integrand $h(u) := c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(u),x'(u))}$, so that $\tau(s) = \int_{s_0}^s h$ with the oriented integral.

[L1] Proper time ([[def-sr-proper-time]]): $g_x(u) = -\eta(x'(u),x'(u))$ is continuous and strictly positive on $I$, the function $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous there, and $\tau(s) = c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{g_x}$ with the oriented integral; changing the base point changes $\tau$ by an additive constant.

[L2] Intervals ([[def-interval]]): order-convex sets with at least two elements are nondegenerate, and every point of such a set is a limit point of it.

[L3] First fundamental theorem ([[thm-ftc-first-part]], [[def-derivative]]): if $f$ is continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$ and $F(t) = \int_\alpha^t f$ is its integral function, then $F$ is differentiable at every point of $[\alpha,\beta]$ with $F' = f$, the reading at the endpoints being one-sided.

[L4] Continuity facts ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]): $h$ is continuous on $I$ as a composition of the continuous maps $x'$, the quadratic form $-\eta(\cdot,\cdot)$ and the square root; sums, products and scalar multiples of continuous real functions are continuous; and a continuous real function that never vanishes has a continuous reciprocal.

[L5] The future cone ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]): a vector $v$ is timelike exactly when $\eta(v,v) < 0$; fixing a future $\eta$-orthonormal basis, the future timelike set is $C^{+} = \{v : v^{0} > |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|\}$, which is closed under multiplication by positive scalars; a tangent vector $x'(s)$ is future timelike exactly when $x$ is future timelike at $s$.

[L6] Oriented additivity ([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]): for integrable $f$ and $u,v,w$ in an interval, $\int_u^v f + \int_v^w f = \int_u^w f$, and $\int_u^u f = 0$.

[L7] Monotonicity of the integral ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]): pointwise $\le$ passes to the integral, and a nonnegative integrand has nonnegative integral.

[L8] Vanishing lemma ([[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]): a continuous nonnegative function on $[a,b]$ with zero integral vanishes identically.

[L9] Continuous image ([[cor-continuous-image-of-an-interval-is-an-interval]], claim 1): the image of an order-convex set under a continuous real function is order-convex.

[L10] Continuous inverse ([[thm-continuous-inverse]]): a continuous injective real function on an order-convex set is strictly monotone, its image is order-convex, it is a bijection onto its image, and the inverse is strictly monotone in the same sense and continuous.

[L11] Derivative of the inverse ([[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]], clause 1): if $f$ is continuous and injective on the order-convex $I$, $g$ is its inverse, $c \in I$ and $f$ is differentiable at $c$ with $f'(c) \ne 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$ with $g'(f(c)) = 1/f'(c)$.

[L12] Componentwise calculus and chain rule ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]): an $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map is differentiable (respectively $C^{1}$) exactly when all its components are, with componentwise derivatives, and a component of a continuous vector-valued map is continuous; the one-variable chain rule applies to real functions.

[L13] Algebra of derivatives ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]): differences of differentiable functions are differentiable with the difference of derivatives, and differentiability implies continuity.

[L14] Zero derivative on an interval ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]): a real function continuous on an order-convex set and differentiable with vanishing derivative at every interior point is constant there.

[L15] Bilinearity of $\eta$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): $\eta(\lambda v, \lambda w) = \lambda^{2}\eta(v,w)$ for real $\lambda$; and the inertial frame isomorphism $E$ is linear ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The integrand $h$ of [L1] is continuous on $I$; for each $s \in I$ choose reals $\alpha < \beta$ with $[\alpha,\beta] \subseteq I$, $s \in [\alpha,\beta]$ and $s_0 \in [\alpha,\beta]$, where $s$ is an endpoint of $[\alpha,\beta]$ only when it is an endpoint of $I$; then for $t \in [\alpha,\beta]$ oriented additivity [L6] gives $\tau(t) = c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{t}\sqrt{g_x} = c^{-1}\bigl(F(t) - F(s_0)\bigr)$ with $F(t) := \int_\alpha^t \sqrt{g_x}$. [given, L1, L2, L6]

2.1 By the first fundamental theorem [L3], $F$ is differentiable on $[\alpha,\beta]$ with $F' = \sqrt{g_x}$ (one-sided at the endpoints), so $\tau$ is differentiable at $s$ with $\tau'(s) = c^{-1}\sqrt{g_x(s)} = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$; since $s \in I$ was arbitrary this holds at every point of $I$ with the one-sided reading at endpoints of $I$, and $\tau'$ is continuous on $I$ by [L4]. [step 1.1, L3, L4]

3.1 For every $s \in I$ the tangent $x'(s)$ is future timelike, so $\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) < 0$ by [L5] and $\tau'(s) = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))} > 0$. [step 2.1, L5]

4.1 For $a < b$ in $I$, oriented additivity [L6] gives $\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{g_x} = \int_a^b \tau'$ (using step 2.1 for the integrand); this is $\ge 0$ by monotonicity [L7]. If it were $0$, the continuous nonnegative function $\tau'$ would vanish identically on $[a,b]$ by [L8], contradicting its strict positivity on $[a,b]$ from step 3.1; hence $\tau(b) > \tau(a)$, so $\tau$ is strictly increasing and injective. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L7, L8]

5.1 The image $J = \tau[I]$ is order-convex by [L9] applied to the continuous $\tau$, and it has at least two elements because $I$ is nondegenerate and $\tau$ is injective by step 4.1; hence $\tau : I \to J$ is a bijection. [step 4.1, L2, L9]

6.1 The inverse $\rho : J \to I$ is strictly increasing and continuous on $J$ by the continuous-inverse theorem [L10], applied to the continuous injective $\tau$ on the order-convex set $I$. [step 5.1, L10]

7.1 For $b = \tau(s) \in J$ one has $\tau'(s) > 0$ by step 3.1, so clause 1 of the inverse-derivative theorem [L11] gives that $\rho$ is differentiable at $b$ with $\rho'(b) = 1/\tau'(s) = c/\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))} > 0$. [step 3.1, step 6.1, L11]

8.1 The function $\rho'$ equals $1/(\tau' \circ \rho)$ on $J$: for $b \in J$, $\rho'(b) = 1/\tau'(\rho(b))$ by step 7.1. The composite $\tau' \circ \rho$ is continuous on $J$ (composition of the continuous maps $\rho$ and $\tau'$ of steps 6.1 and 2.1) and strictly positive there, so its reciprocal is continuous by the quotient clause of the algebra of continuous functions; hence $\rho$ is continuously differentiable ($C^{1}$) on $J$. [step 2.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, L4]

9.1 Fix an inertial frame with chart $x_A$ and coordinate path $y = x_A \circ x$, and write $E$ for the linear frame isomorphism. For each $j$ the composite $y^{j} \circ \rho$ is differentiable on $J$ with derivative $(y^{j'} \circ \rho)\,\rho'$ by the chain rule [L12] (with the one-sided reading at endpoints), and this derivative is continuous as a product of the continuous functions $y^{j'} \circ \rho$ and $\rho'$ of steps 6.1 and 8.1; by the componentwise characterisation [L12], $y \circ \rho$ is therefore $C^{1}$ with $(y \circ \rho)' = (y' \circ \rho)\,\rho'$. [step 2.1, step 6.1, step 8.1, L12]

10.1 Since $x \circ \rho = E \circ (y \circ \rho)$ and $E$ is linear, step 9.1 and [L15] give $(x \circ \rho)' = \rho' \cdot (x' \circ \rho)$; at $b = \tau(s)$ this reads $(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = \rho'(\tau(s))\,x'(s) = x'(s)/\tau'(s) = c\,x'(s)/\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$ by step 7.1. [step 7.1, step 9.1, L15]

11.1 At each $b = \tau(s) \in J$, bilinearity [L15] and step 3.1 give $\eta\bigl((x \circ \rho)'(b),(x \circ \rho)'(b)\bigr) = \rho'(b)^{2}\,\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) < 0$, so the tangent is timelike; and it is the positive multiple $\rho'(b) \cdot x'(s)$ of the future timelike vector $x'(s)$, with $\rho'(b) > 0$, so by the coordinate description of the future cone [L5] it is future timelike. Hence $y = x \circ \rho$ is a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline. [step 8.1, step 10.1, L5, L15]

12.1 Let $\tau_y$ be the proper-time function of $y$ with base point $\tau(s_0)$ (defined by [L1] since $J$ is order-convex and $y$ is a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline by step 11.1). Applying step 2.1 to $y$ gives $\tau_y'(b) = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(y'(b),y'(b))}$ for $b \in J$, and by steps 7.1, 10.1 and [L15] this equals $c^{-1}\rho'(b)\sqrt{-\eta(x'(\rho(b)),x'(\rho(b)))} = \rho'(b)\,\tau'(\rho(b)) = 1$. Hence the function $\sigma(b) := \tau_y(b) - b$ is continuous on $J$ and differentiable at every interior point with $\sigma' = 0$ by the algebra of derivatives [L13], so $\sigma$ is constant by [L14]; therefore $\tau_y(b) - \tau_y(b_0) = b - b_0$ for all $b, b_0 \in J$: the reparametrized worldline is parametrized by its own proper time up to the additive constant $\tau(s_0)$. [step 7.1, step 10.1, step 11.1, L13, L14, L15]

13.1 Every step uses one-dimensional or finite-dimensional calculus and fixed objects of the given worldline: the only "selections" are of the compact interval $[\alpha,\beta]$ around each point, made explicitly from the data, and no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 12.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **The proper-time function is the inverse of nothing yet.** Clause (i) proves that $\tau$ is differentiable with positive derivative; strict monotonicity, the inverse and its differentiability are consequences obtained in clauses (ii)-(iii), and the inverse is what makes the proper-time parametrization of clause (iv) available.

- **One-sided readings at the ends.** For a worldline on a half-open or unbounded $I$ the derivatives in clauses (i) and (iii) are one-sided limits at the points of $I$ that are endpoints of $I$; the inverse is formed on the order-convex image $J$, so the same convention applies there. No differentiability is asserted at points of $\overline{I}$ outside $I$.

- **The base point only shifts.** Changing $s_0$ adds a constant to $\tau$ (by [L1]) and hence shifts $J$ and $\rho$ by that constant, while all derivatives $\tau'$, $\rho'$ and the tangent formula of clause (iv) are unchanged.

- **Relation to the four-velocity.** The tangent formula of clause (iv),
  $(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = x'(s)/\tau'(s)$, is the object later named the
  four-velocity in [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; this lemma
  does not use that definition and asserts nothing about it.

## Statement

Let $c > 0$, let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), let $a < b$ with
$[a,b] \subseteq I$, and let $c_0 < d_0$. Let
$\varphi : [c_0,d_0] \to [a,b]$ be a strictly increasing $C^{1}$ surjection,
with one-sided endpoint derivatives as in
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]].

Then $\varphi(c_0) = a$, $\varphi(d_0) = b$ and $\varphi' \ge 0$. Put
$y = x \circ \varphi$ and $f(s) = \sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$. The $C^{1}$ curve
$y$ has tangent

$$y'(u) = \varphi'(u)\,x'\bigl(\varphi(u)\bigr),$$

which is future timelike exactly where $\varphi'(u) > 0$ and is the zero vector
where $\varphi'(u) = 0$. Its nonnegative length integrand

$$\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(y'(u),y'(u)\bigr)} = \varphi'(u)\,f\bigl(\varphi(u)\bigr)$$

is defined even when $y$ is not a worldline, and the broad substitution identity

$$\int_{c_0}^{d_0}\sqrt{-\eta\bigl(y'(u),y'(u)\bigr)}\;du \;=\; \int_a^b f(s)\;ds \;=\; c\bigl(\tau_x(b)-\tau_x(a)\bigr)$$

holds. If $\varphi'(u) > 0$ at every point, including the one-sided endpoint
derivatives, then $y$ is a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline, its proper-time
function $\tau_y$ of [[def-sr-proper-time]] is defined, and
$\tau_y(d_0)-\tau_y(c_0) = \tau_x(b)-\tau_x(a)$; more generally
$\tau_y(u)-\tau_y(v) = \tau_x(\varphi(u))-\tau_x(\varphi(v))$ for all
$v,u \in [c_0,d_0]$, so $\tau_y$ and $\tau_x \circ \varphi$ differ by a
base-point constant. No $\tau_y$ is asserted for a zero-tangent curve outside
that definition.

For a strictly decreasing $C^{1}$ surjection $\varphi$ onto $[a,b]$ one has
$\varphi(c_0) = b$, $\varphi(d_0) = a$ and $\varphi' \le 0$; the tangent of $y$
is past timelike where $\varphi' < 0$ and zero where $\varphi' = 0$, so $y$ is
not a future timelike worldline, while the nonnegative length integral still
equals $\int_a^b f$: oriented substitution gives
$\int_{c_0}^{d_0}\varphi' f(\varphi) = \int_b^a f$, and
$|\varphi'| = -\varphi'$ reverses that sign.

These are mathematical curve-integral identities; physical clock reading is a
separate premise. No inverse of $\varphi$ and no nonvanishing derivative are
needed for the broad integral identities.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $c > 0$; a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline $x : I \to A$; reals $a < b$ with $[a,b] \subseteq I$; reals $c_0 < d_0$; a strictly increasing (respectively strictly decreasing) $C^{1}$ surjection $\varphi : [c_0,d_0] \to [a,b]$ with one-sided endpoint derivatives; the composite $y = x \circ \varphi$; and $f(s) = \sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$.

[L1] Curves and reparametrizations ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], [[def-interval]]): a strictly increasing surjection $[c_0,d_0] \to [a,b]$ maps endpoints to endpoints, so $\varphi(c_0) = a$ and $\varphi(d_0) = b$ (respectively $\varphi(c_0) = b$, $\varphi(d_0) = a$ in the decreasing case); a $C^1$ increasing function has $\varphi' \ge 0$, a $C^1$ decreasing one has $\varphi' \le 0$; and the tangent of a curve is the limit of difference quotients over the relevant side.

[L2] Chart calculus ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]): in an inertial chart with coordinate path $y_{A} = x_A \circ x$ the frame isomorphism $E$ is linear, an $A$-valued curve is differentiable exactly when each coordinate component is, with componentwise derivatives, and its tangent is $E$ applied to the coordinate derivative; a map is $C^{1}$ exactly when all components are $C^{1}$.

[L3] Chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule]]): for real functions, $(g \circ \varphi)'(u) = g'(\varphi(u))\,\varphi'(u)$ whenever $g$ is differentiable at $\varphi(u)$ and $\varphi$ at $u$, with the one-sided reading at endpoints.

[L4] Bilinearity ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): $\eta(\lambda v,\lambda v) = \lambda^{2}\eta(v,v)$ for real $\lambda$.

[L5] Substitution ([[thm-substitution]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-sr-proper-time]]): if $\varphi : [c_0,d_0] \to [a,b]$ is differentiable with $\varphi'$ integrable and $g$ is continuous on an order-convex set containing $\varphi[\,[c_0,d_0]\,]$, then $\int_{\varphi(c_0)}^{\varphi(d_0)} g = \int_{c_0}^{d_0} (g \circ \varphi)\,\varphi'$; the derivative of a $C^{1}$ function on a compact interval is continuous and hence integrable; and $f$ is continuous on $I$ with $\tau_x$ as in [[def-sr-proper-time]].

[L6] Proper time ([[def-sr-proper-time]]): for $u < v$ in a worldline's domain, $\tau(v) - \tau(u) = c^{-1}\int_u^v \sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$ through the oriented integral; $\tau_y$ is defined only when $y$ is a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline.

[L7] The future and past cones ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]): in a future $\eta$-orthonormal basis the future timelike set is $C^{+} = \{v : v^{0} > |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|\}$ and the past timelike set is $C^{-} = \{v : v^{0} < -|v_{\mathrm{sp}}|\}$; both are closed under multiplication by positive, respectively negative, scalars: $\lambda v \in C^{+}$ for $\lambda > 0$ and $v \in C^{+}$, and $\lambda v \in C^{-}$ for $\lambda < 0$ and $v \in C^{+}$.

[L8] Continuity of composites ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]], [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]): components of continuous vector-valued maps are continuous, composites of continuous real functions are continuous, and products and sums of continuous real functions are continuous.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 A strictly increasing surjection carries the least point to the least point and the greatest to the greatest point of the target interval, so $\varphi(c_0) = a$, $\varphi(d_0) = b$ and (in the decreasing case) $\varphi(c_0) = b$, $\varphi(d_0) = a$; the derivative of a $C^{1}$ monotone function has the sign of the monotonicity, $\varphi' \ge 0$ or $\varphi' \le 0$, with the one-sided reading at the endpoints. [given, L1]

2.1 In an inertial chart, the coordinate path of $y$ is $y_A \circ \varphi$; each component $(y_A)^{j} \circ \varphi$ is differentiable with derivative $((y_A)^{j'} \circ \varphi)\,\varphi'$ by the chain rule [L3], and the derivatives are continuous by [L8] because $(y_A)^{j'}$ and $\varphi$ are continuous; hence $y$ is $C^{1}$ with $y'(u) = \varphi'(u)x'(\varphi(u))$ by the componentwise characterisation and linearity of $E$ [L2]. [step 1.1, L2, L3, L8]

3.1 Bilinearity [L4] gives $-\eta(y'(u),y'(u)) = \varphi'(u)^{2}\,\bigl(-\eta(x'(\varphi(u)),x'(\varphi(u)))\bigr) = \varphi'(u)^{2} f(\varphi(u))^{2}$, so the nonnegative length integrand is $\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')} = |\varphi'(u)| f(\varphi(u))$, which equals $\varphi'(u) f(\varphi(u))$ in the increasing case and $-\varphi'(u) f(\varphi(u))$ in the decreasing case. [step 2.1, L4]

3.2 At every $u$, $x'(\varphi(u))$ is future timelike because $\varphi(u) \in [a,b] \subseteq I$; by the cone description [L7], $y'(u) = \varphi'(u)x'(\varphi(u))$ is future timelike where $\varphi'(u) > 0$, is the zero vector where $\varphi'(u) = 0$, and is past timelike where $\varphi'(u) < 0$. [step 2.1, L7]

4.1 Since $\varphi'$ is continuous on $[c_0,d_0]$, hence integrable, and $f$ is continuous on the order-convex $I$ containing $\varphi[\,[c_0,d_0]\,]$, substitution [L5] applied to the increasing case gives $\int_{c_0}^{d_0}\varphi' f(\varphi) = \int_{\varphi(c_0)}^{\varphi(d_0)} f = \int_a^b f = c(\tau_x(b)-\tau_x(a))$ by [L6]; combined with step 3.1 this proves the broad identity. [step 1.1, step 3.1, L5, L6]

4.2 Where $\varphi' = 0$ the tangent $y'$ is zero, so $y$ is not a worldline of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] and no proper-time function is defined for it by [L6]; the length integrand of step 3.1 remains defined, which is exactly the content of the broad identity. [step 3.1, step 3.2, L6]

4.3 In the strictly decreasing case, step 3.2 makes every tangent of $y$ past timelike or zero, so $y$ is not a future timelike worldline; and substitution [L5] with oriented endpoints gives $\int_{c_0}^{d_0}\varphi' f(\varphi) = \int_{\varphi(c_0)}^{\varphi(d_0)} f = \int_b^a f = -\int_a^b f$, which combined with $\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')} = -\varphi' f(\varphi)$ from step 3.1 yields $\int_{c_0}^{d_0}\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')} = \int_a^b f = c(\tau_x(b)-\tau_x(a))$. [step 3.1, step 3.2, L5, L6]

5.1 If $\varphi' > 0$ at every point including the one-sided endpoint derivatives, then by step 3.2 every tangent of $y$ is future timelike, so $y$ is a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline and $\tau_y$ is defined; its endpoint increment is $\tau_y(d_0)-\tau_y(c_0) = c^{-1}\int_{c_0}^{d_0}\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')} = \tau_x(b)-\tau_x(a)$ by step 4.1. [step 4.1, step 3.2, L6]

6.1 For $v < u$ in $[c_0,d_0]$, substitution [L5] on $[v,u]$ gives $\tau_y(u)-\tau_y(v) = c^{-1}\int_{\varphi(v)}^{\varphi(u)} f = \tau_x(\varphi(u))-\tau_x(\varphi(v))$ by [L6], so the based functions $\tau_y$ and $\tau_x \circ \varphi$ differ by the base-point constant. [step 4.1, step 5.1, L5, L6]

7.1 No step forms an inverse of $\varphi$, divides by $\varphi'$, or assumes a derivative-limit hypothesis at the endpoints; and no object is selected from a family, so no choice principle is used. [step 4.1, step 4.3] ∎

## Remarks

- **The broad identity is the substitution theorem, not a proper-time theorem.** The left-hand integrand is the nonnegative square root $|\varphi'|\,f \circ \varphi$, which exists for every $C^{1}$ $\varphi$; only when $\varphi'$ is everywhere positive is this integrand the length integrand of an actual worldline $y$, and only then is $\tau_y$ defined. The zero-tangent case is deliberately separated from the worldline case.

- **Everything is a one-dimensional substitution.** The curve enters only through the continuity of $f$ and the chain rule for its coordinate components; no derivative-limit hypothesis, no improper integral and no choice principle is used.

## Definition

Let $c > 0$ and let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline with
proper-time function $\tau$ and inverse $\rho$ of
[[def-sr-proper-time]] and [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]].

**(a) Four-velocity.** The **four-velocity** of $x$ is the map $U : I \to V$
defined by

$$U(s) := \frac{x'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,x'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $U(s)$ is the tangent at parameter value $s$ of the proper-time
parametrized worldline $x \circ \rho$, read at the proper-time parameter
$\tau(s)$: by clause (iv) of [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]],
$(x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s)) = x'(s)/\tau'(s) = U(s)$. The map $U$ is continuous,
$U(s)$ is future timelike for every $s \in I$, and $U$ does not depend on the
base point chosen for $\tau$ (changing the base point adds a constant to
$\tau$).

**(b) Four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$, that is, $x'$ is differentiable
with continuous derivative ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), the
**four-acceleration** of $x$ is the map $A : I \to V$ defined by

$$A(s) := \frac{U'(s)}{\tau'(s)} = \frac{c\,U'(s)}{\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}} ;$$

equivalently, $A(s)$ is the derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter
of the four-velocity along the worldline: by the chain rule,
$A(s) = (U \circ \rho)'(\tau(s))$. The map $A$ is continuous.

**(c) Observer.** The **dimensionless four-velocity** of $x$ is $u := U/c$. A
**point observer** of the model at an event is a future unit timelike vector
$n \in V$, $\eta(n,n) = -1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); the four-velocity of the
observer's own worldline, the straight future timelike line through the event
with tangent $cn$, is $cn$ at each of its events.

**(d) Names and scope.** The names four-velocity and four-acceleration are the
model's names for $U$ and $A$; the physical interpretation, including the units
in which $U$ and $A$ are measured, is supplied with the coordinate conventions
of the framework and is not part of the affine geometry. The definition makes no
claim that $U$ has norm $-c^{2}$ or that $A$ is orthogonal to $U$; those are
proved in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

## Remarks

- **Well-definedness.** (i) The division by $\tau'(s)$ is legitimate because
  $\tau'(s) > 0$ for every $s$ by clause (i) of
  [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]. (ii) The identification
  $U(s) = (x \circ \rho)'(\tau(s))$ is clause (iv) of that lemma. (iii)
  Continuity of $U$: in an inertial chart the coordinate components of $U$ are
  $U^{j} = y^{j'}/\tau'$, quotients of the continuous functions $y^{j'}$ (the
  components of the continuous coordinate derivative) and the continuous
  positive $\tau'$, hence continuous
  ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
  [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]); by the componentwise
  characterisation of continuity for $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued maps and the
  identification of $U$ with $E(U_{\mathrm{coord}})$ this gives continuity of
  the $V$-valued map $U$. (iv) $U(s)$ is future timelike because it is the
  positive multiple $\tau'(s)^{-1}x'(s)$ of the future timelike vector $x'(s)$:
  in a future $\eta$-orthonormal basis the future timelike set is
  $\{v : v^{0} > |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|\}$, stable under multiplication by positive
  scalars ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]],
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). (v) $A$ is defined only when
  $x$ is $C^{2}$, in which case $U$ is $C^{1}$: its chart components
  $y^{j'}/\tau'$ are quotients of $C^{1}$ functions with nonvanishing
  denominator ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]), so $U'$ exists, is continuous
  ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
  [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]), and $A = U'/\tau'$ is continuous
  as another quotient. (vi) The observer clause is consistent with (a): the
  straight line with tangent $cn$ has tangent of squared $\eta$-length
  $\eta(cn,cn) = -c^{2}$, so its proper-time derivative is
  $c^{-1}\sqrt{c^{2}} = 1$ and its four-velocity is $cn$.
- **What is deliberately not asserted here.** Neither the norm of $U$ nor the
  orthogonality of $A$ with $U$ is asserted above, so the definition cannot be
  used as if those identities were definitional; they are theorems of
  [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. No choice principle is
  used: all objects are defined by explicit formulas from the given worldline.
