## Statement

Let $c > 0$ and let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Norm of the four-velocity.** Let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future
timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then
$\eta(U(s),U(s)) = -c^{2}$ for every $s \in I$; equivalently the dimensionless
four-velocity $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -1$, and $U(s)$ is future
timelike. Thus the four-velocity of a worldline lies on the future unit
hyperboloid.

**(b) Orthogonality of the four-acceleration.** If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then
$\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$: the four-acceleration has no component along the
four-velocity; if in addition $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s)$ is spacelike.

**(c) Rest space and projection.** Let $n \in V$ be future unit timelike,
$\eta(n,n) = -1$, and put $n^{\perp} := \{\,v \in V : \eta(n,v) = 0\,\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then $n^{\perp}$ is a
3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$
is positive definite, and the map $h : V \to V$, $h(v) := v + \eta(n,v)\,n$, is
linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

**(d) Relative velocity and Lorentz factor.** Let $n$ and $u$ be future unit
timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,
$\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$.
The vector $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative
to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

**(e) Coordinate form.** Let $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$ be an inertial frame and let
$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and, when $y$ is $C^{2}$, coordinate acceleration
$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the
four-acceleration is $A = \gamma_w\,\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\gamma_w(c,w)\bigr)$, so
that

$$A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{w \cdot a}{c}, \qquad A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}\,a + \gamma_w^{4}\,\frac{(w \cdot a)\,w}{c^{2}} ;$$

consequently
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2} + \gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$,
with $\eta(A,A) = 0$ if and only if $a = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$. For the
observer $n = e_0$ of the chart, clauses (c) and (d) specialize to
$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = w$.

**(f) Scope.** The statement is a theorem about the affine Minkowski model with
a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no
physical four-velocity. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $c > 0$ and an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$; a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline $x$ with four-velocity $U$ and (when $C^{2}$) four-acceleration $A$; a future unit timelike vector $n$; and, in clause (e), an inertial frame with coordinate path $t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$.

[L1] Four-velocity and four-acceleration ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]): $U = x'/\tau'$ and, when $x$ is $C^{2}$, $A = U'/\tau'$; the dimensionless four-velocity is $u = U/c$.

[L2] Proper time ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]): $\tau'(s) = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))} > 0$ everywhere, and $x'$ is future timelike.

[L3] Bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): $\eta$ is a symmetric bilinear form; $\eta(\lambda v, \lambda w) = \lambda^{2}\eta(v,w)$.

[L4] The future cone in orthonormal coordinates ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]): in a future $\eta$-orthonormal basis, $v$ is future timelike exactly when $v^{0} > |v_{\mathrm{sp}}|$, timelike exactly when $\eta(v,v) < 0$, spacelike exactly when $\eta(v,v) > 0$, and the future timelike set is closed under multiplication by positive scalars.

[L5] Orthogonal complements ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]): $S^{\perp} = \{v : \eta(v,s) = 0 \ \forall s \in S\}$ is a linear subspace, and $u \in u^{\perp}$ exactly when $\eta(u,u) = 0$.

[L6] Orthonormal bases ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]): there is an ordered $\eta$-orthonormal basis with $\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$; one basis vector is timelike and the other three spacelike.

[L7] Chart structure ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]): in an inertial chart $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; the restriction $\delta$ of $\eta$ to $S = \operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the Euclidean form with norm $|\cdot|$ and inner product written $w \cdot z := \delta(w,z)$; $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is a $\delta$-orthonormal basis.

[L8] Linearity ([[def-linear-map]]): a map $h$ is linear when $h(\lambda v + \mu w) = \lambda h(v) + \mu h(w)$.

[L9] Cauchy-Schwarz ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]): for the positive definite form $\delta$, $|\delta(u,v)| \le |u|\,|v|$, with equality exactly when $u,v$ are linearly dependent.

[L10] Calculus ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[def-rational-power]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-derivative]]): products and compositions of differentiable real functions obey the product and chain rules; $t \mapsto t^{\alpha}$ is differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ with derivative $\alpha t^{\alpha-1}$; and vector-valued derivatives are read componentwise.

[L11] Ordered-field arithmetic ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]): squares are nonnegative, a sum of nonnegative terms is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when all terms vanish, and positive quantities have positive inverses; order is total and transitive.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1] and [L2], $U = x'/\tau'$ with $\tau' = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')} > 0$; hence $\eta(U,U) = \eta(x',x')/(\tau')^{2} = \eta(x',x')\,c^{2}/(-\eta(x',x')) = -c^{2}$ by bilinearity [L3], and $u = U/c$ satisfies $\eta(u,u) = -c^{2}/c^{2} = -1$; $U$ is a positive multiple of the future timelike $x'$, hence future timelike by [L4]. [given, L1, L2, L3, L4]

1.2 Fix an $\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0$ timelike, write $n = n^{0}e_0 + n_{\mathrm{s}}$ and $v = v^{0}e_0 + v_{\mathrm{s}}$ with $n_{\mathrm{s}},v_{\mathrm{s}} \in S$, and use $\eta(n,n) = -(n^{0})^{2}+|n_{\mathrm{s}}|^{2} = -1$ and $\eta(n,v) = -n^{0}v^{0} + n_{\mathrm{s}}\cdot v_{\mathrm{s}}$ from [L6], [L7], [L3]. [given, L3, L6, L7]

1.3 In the chart of clause (e) the coordinate path is $t \mapsto (ct, r(t))$, so its coordinate derivative is $(c,w(t))$ with $w = r'$ by [L10], and $- \eta(x',x') = c^{2}-|w(t)|^{2}$ by [L7]; since $x'$ is future timelike, [L4] gives $c > |w(t)|$ and $\tau' = c^{-1}\sqrt{c^{2}-|w|^{2}} = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{1/2} = 1/\gamma_w$; hence $U = x'/\tau' = \gamma_w(c,w)$. [given, L1, L2, L4, L7, L10]

2.1 For $n$ future unit timelike, [L4] gives $n^{0} > |n_{\mathrm{s}}| \ge 0$, and from $\eta(n,n) = -1$ we get $(n^{0})^{2} = 1+|n_{\mathrm{s}}|^{2} > 0$, so $n^{0} > 0$ and division by $n^{0}$ is legitimate. [step 1.2, L4]

2.2 If $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then $U$ is differentiable at $s$ by [L1] and [L2] (a quotient of differentiable maps with positive denominator), and differentiating the constant $\eta(U,U) = -c^{2}$ of step 1.1 in an orthonormal basis gives $0 = \frac{d}{ds}\eta(U,U) = 2\eta(U,U')$ by the product rule [L10] and symmetry of $\eta$; since $A = U'/\tau'$ with $\tau' > 0$, this gives $\eta(U,A) = 0$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, L10]

2.3 For future unit timelike $n$ and $u$, [L4] gives $n^{0} > |n_{\mathrm{s}}|$ and $u^{0} > |u_{\mathrm{s}}|$ in a future orthonormal basis of [L6]; hence $\eta(n,u) = -n^{0}u^{0}+n_{\mathrm{s}}\cdot u_{\mathrm{s}} \le -n^{0}u^{0}+|n_{\mathrm{s}}|\,|u_{\mathrm{s}}| < 0$ by Cauchy-Schwarz [L9] (the last inequality because $n^{0}u^{0} > |n_{\mathrm{s}}|u^{0} \ge |n_{\mathrm{s}}||u_{\mathrm{s}}|$ with at least one strict inequality), so $\gamma := -\eta(n,u) > 0$. [step 1.2, L4, L9]

2.4 If $y$ is $C^{2}$, then $w$ is differentiable with derivative $a$, $|w|^{2} = w \cdot w$ has derivative $2\,w \cdot a$ by the product rule, and the chain rule with the power $t^{-1/2}$ [L10] gives $\frac{d}{dt}\gamma_w = \gamma_w^{3}\,(w \cdot a)/c^{2}$; collecting terms in $A = \gamma_w\frac{d}{dt}(\gamma_w(c,w))$ gives $A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}(w \cdot a)/c$ and $A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}a + \gamma_w^{4}(w \cdot a)w/c^{2}$. [step 1.3, L10]

3.1 For $v \in n^{\perp}$, $\eta(n,v) = 0$ gives $v^{0} = (n_{\mathrm{s}} \cdot v_{\mathrm{s}})/n^{0}$, hence $\eta(v,v) = -(v^{0})^{2}+|v_{\mathrm{s}}|^{2} = |v_{\mathrm{s}}|^{2} - (n_{\mathrm{s}}\cdot v_{\mathrm{s}})^{2}/(n^{0})^{2} \ge |v_{\mathrm{s}}|^{2}\bigl(1 - |n_{\mathrm{s}}|^{2}/(n^{0})^{2}\bigr) = |v_{\mathrm{s}}|^{2}/(n^{0})^{2} \ge 0$ by Cauchy-Schwarz [L9] and the identity $(n^{0})^{2} = 1+|n_{\mathrm{s}}|^{2}$; if $\eta(v,v) = 0$ then $|v_{\mathrm{s}}| = 0$ and $v^{0} = 0$, so $v = 0$: the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite. [step 1.2, step 2.1, L9]

3.2 Expanding $\eta(A,A) = -(A^{0})^{2}+|A_{\mathrm{vec}}|^{2}$ in the chart using step 2.4 and the identity $\gamma_w^{2}(1-|w|^{2}/c^{2}) = 1$ yields $\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2}+\gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2} \ge 0$ by [L11], with equality if and only if $a = 0$ (the first term vanishes only for $a = 0$ because $\gamma_w > 0$); and $\eta(U,A) = 0$ holds by step 2.2. [step 2.2, step 1.3, step 2.4, L11]

4.1 The map $\varphi : S \to n^{\perp}$, $\varphi(v_{\mathrm{s}}) := v^{0}e_0 + v_{\mathrm{s}}$ with $v^{0} := (n_{\mathrm{s}}\cdot v_{\mathrm{s}})/n^{0}$, is linear and bijective: linearity is clear from bilinearity of the inner product, injectivity from $v_{\mathrm{s}} = 0 \Rightarrow v^{0} = 0$, and surjectivity from step 3.1's computation of the first coordinate; hence $n^{\perp}$ is 3-dimensional. [step 1.2, step 3.1, L3, L8]

4.2 The map $h(v) = v + \eta(n,v)n$ is linear by bilinearity [L3] and [L8]; $\eta(n,h(v)) = \eta(n,v)+\eta(n,v)\eta(n,n) = 0$ and $h(n) = n+\eta(n,n)n = 0$; $h(h(v)) = h(v)+\eta(n,h(v))n = h(v)$; so $h$ is idempotent with image contained in $n^{\perp}$ and kernel containing $\operatorname{span}(n)$, and $v = -\eta(n,v)n + h(v)$ is a decomposition into $\operatorname{span}(n)$ and $n^{\perp}$, unique because those subspaces meet only in $0$ (a multiple $\lambda n$ with $\eta(n,\lambda n) = \lambda\eta(n,n) = -\lambda = 0$ vanishes); hence the image of $h$ is exactly $n^{\perp}$ and the kernel exactly $\operatorname{span}(n)$. [step 1.2, step 3.1, L3, L5, L8]

4.3 The restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$ is a positive definite symmetric bilinear form by steps 3.1 and 4.2, so $|w| = \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ has the norm properties on $n^{\perp}$ (positive definiteness, homogeneity and the triangle inequality, the last by Cauchy-Schwarz [L9]). [step 3.1, L9]

4.4 If moreover $A(s) \ne 0$, then $A(s) \in n^{\perp}$ for $n := U(s)/c$, a future unit timelike vector by step 1.1; the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite by step 3.1, so $\eta(A,A) > 0$ and $A(s)$ is spacelike by [L4]. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, L4]

5.1 With $h$ of step 4.2, the decomposition $u = -\eta(n,u)n + h(u) = \gamma n + h(u)$ and bilinearity give $\eta(u,u) = \gamma^{2}\eta(n,n)+\eta(h(u),h(u)) = -\gamma^{2}+|h(u)|^{2} = -1$; since $|h(u)|^{2} \ge 0$ by positive definiteness on $n^{\perp}$ (step 4.3), $\gamma \ge 1$, and with $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$ we get $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(\gamma^{2}-1)/\gamma^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$; also $u = \gamma n + h(u) = \gamma(n + w/c)$ and $(1-|w|^{2}/c^{2}) = \gamma^{-2}$, so $\gamma = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$ by [L11]. [step 4.2, step 4.3, step 2.3, L3, L11]

6.1 Since $\gamma > 0$ and $u = \gamma n + h(u)$, one has $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $h(u) = 0$ if and only if $u = n$: if $u = n$ then $\eta(n,u) = \eta(n,n) = -1$ so $\gamma = 1$, and conversely $\gamma = 1$ forces $|h(u)|^{2} = \gamma^{2}-1 = 0$, hence $h(u) = 0$ by positive definiteness and $u = n$. [step 2.3, step 5.1]

6.2 For the observer $n = e_0 = (1,0,0,0)$ of the chart, $h(u) = u + \eta(e_0,u)e_0 = u - u^{0}e_0 = (0, u_{\mathrm{s}})$ where $u_{\mathrm{s}} = w/c\,\gamma_w$ by step 1.3, and $\gamma = -\eta(e_0,u) = u^{0} = \gamma_w$; hence $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = c\,h(u)/\gamma = (0,w)$, the coordinate velocity, so clauses (c) and (d) specialize to $\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = w$. [step 5.1, step 1.3]

7.1 All arguments are finite-dimensional linear algebra and one-variable calculus in the given data; nothing is selected from a family and no choice principle is used. [step 6.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **The hard part is clause (c).** Positive definiteness of the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$ is where the signature hypothesis is spent; it is what makes $|h(u)|^{2} = \gamma^{2}-1$ a nonnegative quantity and hence $\gamma \ge 1$ and $|w| < c$ in clause (d), and it is also what makes a nonzero four-acceleration spacelike in clause (b).

- **The four-acceleration is not defined at kinks.** Clause (b) assumes $x$ is $C^{2}$ at the point in question; no tangent or acceleration is asserted at a corner of a piecewise worldline, consistently with [[def-sr-piecewise-proper-time]].

## Postulate

Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework, extending the ideal-clock
reading rule of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] to the general worldline
calculus of this page:

**(i) Free trajectories.** A massive test particle that is subject to no
interaction (a **free particle**) has as its worldline a straight future
timelike line of the affine model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]): there are
an event $p \in A$ and a future timelike vector $v \in V$ with
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)v$ for all $s$ ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).
Interactions, forces and collisions are not part of this assumption: a particle
that is not free may have any future timelike worldline admitted by its own
dynamical model, and no force law is adopted here. The kinematical consequences
of this shape for the four-velocity are derived, not assumed, in
[[pthm-sr-four-velocity-norm-and-orthogonality]].

**(ii) Clock hypothesis.** An ideal clock carried along a future timelike
worldline of the model, including an accelerated one and a piecewise $C^{1}$ one
with finitely many kinks, reads between any two parameter values the proper-time
difference of [[def-sr-proper-time]] for $C^{1}$ histories and of
[[def-sr-piecewise-proper-time]] for weak piecewise $C^{1}$ histories, with no
additional term depending on acceleration, jerk or any higher derivative. A
kink is an idealization of a finite short acceleration phase whose contribution
is included through the integral on the smooth pieces, and the reading does not
depend on an increasing regular change of parameter admitted by the curve
definition — its derivatives on smooth pieces and all finite one-sided endpoint
derivatives are positive, as in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]] and
[[lem-sr-piecewise-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]. Zero-tangent
compositions are not worldlines of this model.

**(iii) Scope and qualification.** The assumptions concern ideal point
particles, ideal clocks and flat classical spacetime. They are adopted, not
proved; they are not consequences of the affine geometry, and no experiment is
claimed here to establish them. They inherit the idealizations of
[[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]: real clocks have finite resolution,
calibration and apparatus limitations, and real particles are not exactly free.
The coordinate and unit conventions are those of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], and inertial charts are those
of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]].

## Scope and source notes

The free-trajectory clause is deliberately silent about interactions and force
laws, so it cannot be used to infer conservation laws, mass-shell relations or
collision kinematics, which require the separate momentum postulate of the
later energy-momentum page. The clock hypothesis is the assertion that ideal
clocks have no acceleration-dependent term, so it must not be presented as
following from the geometry, and its empirical content is not established here.
The weak piecewise mathematical referent is supplied by
[[def-sr-piecewise-proper-time]] and
[[lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability]], and regular increasing
weak-piecewise parameter independence by
[[lem-sr-piecewise-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]; the $C^{1}$
case uses [[def-sr-proper-time]] and
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]. This assumption repairs
the formulation of the already adopted clock assumption; it does not derive
clock behavior or extend its empirical scope.

The published sources describe the free-particle worldline and the
proper-time reading of ideal clocks in the same idealizations (Carroll,
Chapter 1 and Chapter 3; Reall, Sections 2.2-2.3; Crowell, Sections 3.5-3.7,
with the signature and unit conversions recorded in the reference list). The
adoption is stated conditionally: it is an assumption of this framework, and
the source references document where the same idealization appears in the

## Statement

Adopt the postulates of the model: [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] and
[[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] of the spacetime-primitives page, together
with [[post-sr-free-trajectories-and-clock-hypothesis]] of this page, and let
$c$ and the SI coordinates be those of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $x : I \to A$ be the
history of an ideal clock of the model, a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
($C^{2}$ where acceleration is used), with proper time $\tau$, four-velocity
$U = dx/d\tau$ and, when $x$ is $C^{2}$, four-acceleration $A = dU/d\tau$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]). Then:

**(i)** the reading of the ideal clock between parameter values $s_1 < s_2$
equals $\tau(s_2)-\tau(s_1)$;

**(ii)** $\eta(U,U) = -c^{2}$ everywhere, so $U$ is a future unit timelike
vector with the unit of a velocity;

**(iii)** if $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then $\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$ and $A(s)$ is
zero or spacelike, with the unit of acceleration;

**(iv)** if the clock is free (subject to no interaction), then its
four-velocity is constant along the worldline and $A = 0$ identically;

**(v)** for an ideal observer at the same event, described by a future unit
timelike vector $n = U_{o}/c$ with $\eta(n,n) = -1$, the clock's speed relative
to the observer is $|w| = c\sqrt{1-\gamma^{-2}}$ with
$\gamma = -\eta(n,U/c) \ge 1$, so it is strictly less than $c$, and
$\gamma = 1$ exactly when the clock's four-velocity equals the observer's.

**Scope and qualification.** This is a conditional statement about the adopted
model; it asserts no measurement outcome, contains no statistical inference, and
inherits the idealizations of the postulates (ideal point particles, ideal
clocks, flat spacetime, no gravitational or quantum effects).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The adopted postulates [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]], [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and [[post-sr-free-trajectories-and-clock-hypothesis]]; the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]; and a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline $x : I \to A$ that is the history of an ideal clock, $C^{2}$ where acceleration is used.

[A1] Free trajectories: a massive test particle subject to no interaction has as its worldline a straight future timelike line $x(s) = p+(s-s_0)v$ with $v$ future timelike; interactions and force laws are not part of the assumption ([[post-sr-free-trajectories-and-clock-hypothesis]], clause (i)).

[A2] Clock hypothesis: an ideal clock carried along a future timelike worldline reads, between parameter values, the proper-time difference of [[def-sr-proper-time]] ([[post-sr-free-trajectories-and-clock-hypothesis]], clause (ii); [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], clause (i)).

[A3] The model's postulates hold: the affine Minkowski space is the spacetime, and the model equations are covariant under inertial changes of description ([[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]); ideal clocks and ideal light are as stated in [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]].

[L1] Units ([[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]): the four-velocity $U = dx/d\tau$ has unit m/s and the four-acceleration m/s$^{2}$; the interval carries m$^{2}$.

[L2] Four-velocity and four-acceleration ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]): $U = x'/\tau'$ and $A = U'/\tau'$; the four-velocity of the observer's own straight worldline with future unit timelike $n$ is $cn$.

[L3] Mathematical content ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]): $\eta(U,U) = -c^{2}$; $\eta(U,A) = 0$ and $A$ zero or spacelike when $x$ is $C^{2}$; for future unit timelike $n$ and $u = U/c$, with $\gamma = -\eta(n,u)$, $\gamma \ge 1$, $|w| = c\sqrt{1-\gamma^{-2}} < c$ for $w = c\,h(u)/\gamma$, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$; $w$ is the velocity of a worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative to $n$.

[L4] Proper-time definition ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): $\tau' = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$, and for the straight worldline $x(s) = p+(s-s_0)v$ the difference quotients are identically $v$, so $x' = v$ and $\tau' = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$ is constant.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Clause (i): by the clock hypothesis [A2] the reading of the ideal clock between $s_1$ and $s_2$ is the proper-time difference $\tau(s_2)-\tau(s_1)$ of [L2]'s and [L4]'s definitions for a $C^{1}$ future timelike history; this is an adopted identification of clock readings with the mathematical proper time, not a geometric consequence. [given, A2, L4]

1.2 Clause (ii): $\eta(U,U) = -c^{2}$ is clause (a) of the mathematical decomposition theorem [L3], and the unit of $U$ is m/s by [L1]; $U$ is future timelike by that theorem, so it is a future unit timelike vector in the model's sense. [given, L1, L3]

1.3 Clause (iii): if $x$ is $C^{2}$ at $s$, then $\eta(U(s),A(s)) = 0$ and $A(s)$ is zero or spacelike, both by clause (b) of [L3]; the unit of $A$ is m/s$^{2}$ by [L1]. [given, L1, L3]

1.4 Clause (iv): if the clock is free, by [A1] there are $p \in A$ and a future timelike $v \in V$ with $x(s) = p+(s-s_0)v$; by [L4] $x' = v$ and $\tau' = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$ is a positive constant, so $U = x'/\tau' = v/\tau'$ is constant, $U' = 0$, and $A = U'/\tau' = 0$ identically. [given, A1, L2, L4]

1.5 Clause (v): let $n := U_{o}/c$ be the observer's future unit timelike vector, so that the observer's four-velocity is $cn$ by [L2]; the dimensionless four-velocity of the clock is $u = U/c$, and clause (d) of [L3] gives $\gamma = -\eta(n,u) \ge 1$, speed $|w| = c\sqrt{1-\gamma^{-2}} < c$ relative to the observer, and $\gamma = 1$ if and only if $u = n$; multiplying by $c$ this last equivalence reads $U = U_{o}$, the clock's four-velocity equal to the observer's. [given, L2, L3]

2.1 The interpretation of $w$ as the clock's speed relative to the observer uses the adopted idealization of observers as future unit timelike vectors and the identification in clause (d) of [L3]; the covariance postulate [A3] licenses treating observers described in different inertial charts as the same model objects, but no statement about actual apparatus or measured speeds is made. [step 1.5, A3, L3]

3.1 The conclusion is conditional on [A1]-[A3]: each clause is either the adopted clock/free-trajectory assumption or a clause of the mathematical theorem [L3], and no empirical premise, statistical inference or measurement claim is used; the idealizations (point particles, ideal clocks, flat classical spacetime) are inherited by every clause. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5, A1, A2, A3] ∎

## Remarks

- **What is assumed and what is derived.** Clauses (i) and (iv) rest on the adopted free-trajectory and clock assumptions; clauses (ii), (iii) and (v) are the mathematical content of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] read through the model's interpretation. The theorem asserts what follows from the adopted model, not that ideal clocks or free particles exist as described in nature.

- **The speed bound is relative to an ideal observer.** The bound $|w| < c$ is a statement about the model's ideal observers $n$; it is not a measurement result, and no statement is made about the accuracy of real clocks or the outcome of any experiment.

\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ consider the worldline
$x(t) = (ct, a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of a clock at rest at the spatial position

$x'(t) = (c,0,0,0)$, so $-\eta(x',x') = c^{2}$ and the proper-time function is
$\tau(t)-\tau(t_0) = t-t_0$; the four-velocity is $U = x'/\tau' = (c,0,0,0)$,
with $\eta(U,U) = -c^{2}$, and the four-acceleration vanishes, $A = 0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial chart with $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, a spatial position $(a_1,a_2,a_3) \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$, and the worldline $x(t) = (ct,a_1,a_2,a_3)$.

proper-time function of $x$ is $\tau(s) = (4/c)(s-s_0)$ for the chosen base

[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]. The broad length-integral
identity nevertheless holds: $\int_{-1}^{1} 12u^{2}\,du = 8 =
\int_{-1}^{1} 4\,ds$. No proper-time function of $y$ is invoked outside its
defining worldline domain.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial chart with $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; the displacement $d = (5,3,0,0)$; the straight worldline $x(s) = s\,d$ on $[1,8]$ and on $[-1,1]$; the map $\varphi(u) = u^{3}$ on $[1,2]$ and on $[-1,1]$; and $c > 0$.

[L1] Inertial charts ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]): in an inertial chart the matrix of $\eta$ is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, so $\eta(v,v) = -(v^{0})^{2}+(v^{1})^{2}+(v^{2})^{2}+(v^{3})^{2}$ for $v = (v^{0},v^{1},v^{2},v^{3})$.

[L2] Curves ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): the curve $x(s) = s\,d$ has difference quotients $d$ identically, hence tangent $x'(s) = d$; it is a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline exactly when $d$ is future timelike; a curve with a zero tangent at some point is not a worldline, the zero vector having no causal character ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

[L3] Proper time ([[def-sr-proper-time]]): $\tau(s)-\tau(s_0) = c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(u),x'(u))}\,du$ for a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline; a constant integrand $A$ gives the increment $c^{-1}A(s-s_0)$.

[L4] Reparametrization ([[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]): for a strictly increasing $C^{1}$ surjection with positive derivative, the reparametrized curve is a worldline with the same elapsed proper time; the broad length-integral identity holds even where the derivative vanishes.

[L5] Bilinearity ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): $\eta(\lambda v,\lambda w) = \lambda^{2}\eta(v,w)$.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], $\eta(d,d) = -25+9 = -16$, so $d$ is timelike by [L2]'s classification and $-\eta(d,d) = 16$ with $\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)} = 4$. [given, L1, L2]

1.2 The map $\varphi(u) = u^{3}$ is strictly increasing on $[1,2]$ with derivative $3u^{2} \ge 3 > 0$ there, and it maps $[1,2]$ onto $[1,8]$; the difference quotients of $y(u) = u^{3}d$ are $\bigl((u+h)^{3}-u^{3}\bigr)/h \cdot d = (3u^{2}+3uh+h^{2})\,d$, which tend to $3u^{2}d$, so $y'(u) = 3u^{2}d$. [given, L2]

2.1 On $[1,8]$ the difference quotients of $x$ are identically $d$, so $x'(s) = d$ and $x$ is a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline by [L2]; by [L3] its elapsed proper time over $[1,8]$ is $c^{-1}\int_1^8 4\,ds = 28/c$. [step 1.1, L2, L3]

2.2 On $[-1,1]\setminus\{0\}$ the difference quotients of $y(u) = u^{3}d$ are again $(3u^{2}+3uh+h^{2})d$, with limit $3u^{2}d$, and at $u = 0$ the quotient is $h^{2}d \to 0$; hence $y'(0) = 0$ and $y$ is not a worldline, since a worldline tangent must be future timelike and the zero vector has no causal character. [step 1.2, L2]

3.1 By bilinearity [L5], $\eta(y'(u),y'(u)) = (3u^{2})^{2}\eta(d,d)$, so $\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')} = 3u^{2}\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)} = 12u^{2}$ by step 1.1; hence the elapsed proper time of $y$ over $[1,2]$ is $c^{-1}\int_1^2 12u^{2}\,du = (4/c)(2^{3}-1^{3}) = 28/c$, which agrees with step 2.1 as [L4] requires. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, L4, L5]

3.2 With base point $s_0 \in [1,8]$ the proper-time function of $x$ is $\tau(s) = c^{-1}\cdot 4\cdot(s-s_0) = (4/c)(s-s_0)$ for $s \in [1,8]$, a strictly increasing affine function with $\tau(s_0) = 0$; solving $\tau = (4/c)(s-s_0)$ for $s$ gives its inverse $\rho(\tau) = s_0 + c\,\tau/4$ on the image interval. [step 2.1, L3]

4.1 The broad length-integral identity still holds on $[-1,1]$: $\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')} = 3u^{2}\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)} = 12u^{2}$ for $u \ne 0$ and both sides vanish at $u = 0$, so $\int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')}\,du = \int_{-1}^{1} 12u^{2}\,du = 4 - (-4) = 8$, while $\int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)}\,ds = 4\cdot 2 = 8$; equality holds without any worldline structure for $y$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, L4] ∎

## Remarks

- **Two independent computations of the same number.** The integrals $c^{-1}\int_1^8 4\,ds$ and $c^{-1}\int_1^2 12u^{2}\,du$ are computed separately, and their agreement is the concrete instance of [[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]; the cubic's derivative, rather than an inverse function, produces the second computation.

- **The boundary case is deliberate.** On $[-1,1]$ the derivative $3u^{2}$ vanishes at $u = 0$, so the reparametrized curve has a zero tangent there and is not a worldline; the broad integral identity survives, and no proper-time function of $y$ is claimed.

## Example

Worked computation. In an inertial chart with $\eta_0 =
\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ let $R > 0$ and let $\omega$ be real with
$R|\omega| < c$, and consider the worldline
$x(t) = \bigl(ct, R\cos(\omega t), R\sin(\omega t), 0\bigr)$, parametrized by
coordinate time: uniform circular motion in the first two spatial coordinates.
Then $w(t) = \bigl(-R\omega\sin(\omega t), R\omega\cos(\omega t), 0\bigr)$ has
$|w| = R|\omega|$, so $-\eta(x',x') = c^{2}-R^{2}\omega^{2}$ and the
proper-time factor is
$\tau' = c^{-1}\sqrt{c^{2}-R^{2}\omega^{2}} = 1/\gamma$ with
$\gamma := (1-R^{2}\omega^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$; the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma\,(c,w)$. Since $|w|$ is constant, $\gamma$ is constant; the
coordinate acceleration is
$a(t) = \bigl(-R\omega^{2}\cos(\omega t), -R\omega^{2}\sin(\omega t), 0\bigr)$,
with $|a| = R\omega^{2}$ and $w \cdot a = 0$. By clause (e) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] the four-acceleration is
$A = (0,\gamma^{2}a)$, so $A^{0} = 0$, $\eta(U,A) = 0$ and
$\eta(A,A) = \gamma^{4}R^{2}\omega^{4} \ge 0$. Its magnitude is
$\gamma^{2}R\omega^{2}$; for $R > 0$ it is spacelike exactly when
$\omega \ne 0$, while $\omega = 0$ is the static limit with $\gamma = 1$,
$U = (c,0,0,0)$ and $A = 0$. Numerical specialization: if $R\omega = 3c/5$,
then $\gamma = 5/4$ and the magnitude of the four-acceleration is
$\gamma^{2}R\omega^{2} = (25/16)R\omega^{2} = (15c\omega)/16$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial chart with $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, reals $R > 0$ and $\omega$ with $R|\omega| < c$, and the worldline $x(t) = (ct,R\cos(\omega t),R\sin(\omega t),0)$.

[L1] Chart and spatial structure ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]): in the chart $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the spatial part carries the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|$ and inner product $w \cdot z$.

[L2] Curves ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]): $x$ is $C^{1}$ with tangent $x' = (c,w)$ and is a future timelike worldline exactly when $\eta(x',x') < 0$ with $x'$ future.

[L3] Proper time and four-velocity ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]): $\tau' = c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$, $U = x'/\tau'$, and $A = U'/\tau'$ when $x$ is $C^{2}$.

[L4] Coordinate form of the decomposition ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], clause (e)): for a $C^{2}$ future timelike worldline with coordinates $t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, $w = r'$, $a = w'$, one has $|w| < c$, $U = \gamma_w(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w = (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, $A^{0} = \gamma_w^{4}(w \cdot a)/c$, $A_{\mathrm{vec}} = \gamma_w^{2}a+\gamma_w^{4}(w \cdot a)w/c^{2}$, and $\eta(A,A) = \gamma_w^{4}|a|^{2}+\gamma_w^{6}(w \cdot a)^{2}/c^{2}$, vanishing exactly when $a = 0$.

[L5] Bilinearity and the diagonal form ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): $\eta$ is bilinear, so $\eta(U,U)$ is computed from the chart matrix in [L1].

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The difference quotients of the first coordinate give $c$; those of the spatial coordinates give $w(t) = (-R\omega\sin(\omega t),R\omega\cos(\omega t),0)$, so $x'(t) = (c,w(t))$; then $|w(t)| = R|\omega|$ and, by [L1], $\eta(x',x') = -c^{2}+R^{2}\omega^{2} = -(c^{2}-R^{2}\omega^{2}) < 0$ by the hypothesis $R|\omega| < c$, with $x'$ future; hence $x$ is a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline by [L2]. [given, L1, L2]

2.1 By [L3], $\tau' = c^{-1}\sqrt{c^{2}-R^{2}\omega^{2}} = (1-R^{2}\omega^{2}/c^{2})^{1/2} = 1/\gamma$ with $\gamma := (1-R^{2}\omega^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and $U = x'/\tau' = \gamma(c,w)$. [step 1.1, L3]

2.2 The spatial path is $r(t) = (R\cos(\omega t),R\sin(\omega t),0)$, with $r' = w$ and $r'' = a(t) = (-R\omega^{2}\cos(\omega t),-R\omega^{2}\sin(\omega t),0)$; hence $|a| = R\omega^{2}$ and $w \cdot a = R^{2}\omega^{3}(\sin\cdot\cos - \cos\cdot\sin) = 0$. [step 1.1]

3.1 Since $|w| = R|\omega|$ is constant, $\gamma$ is constant and $A = \gamma_w\frac{d}{dt}(\gamma_w(c,w))$ with $\gamma_w = \gamma$; clause (e) of [L4] with $w \cdot a = 0$ gives $A = (0,\gamma^{2}a)$, so $A^{0} = 0$, and $\eta(U,A) = 0$; also $|a| = R\omega^{2}$ gives $\eta(A,A) = \gamma^{4}|a|^{2} = \gamma^{4}R^{2}\omega^{4} \ge 0$, with equality if and only if $a = 0$, i.e. if and only if $\omega = 0$ (since $R > 0$); the magnitude of the four-acceleration is then $\gamma^{2}R\omega^{2}$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L4, L5]

4.1 At $\omega = 0$ the worldline is $x(t) = (ct,R,0,0)$, the static limit: $w = 0$, $\gamma = 1$, $U = (c,0,0,0)$ and $A = 0$, so the clock is at rest in the chart and its acceleration vanishes; for $\omega \ne 0$ the four-acceleration is spacelike with $\eta(A,A) = \gamma^{4}R^{2}\omega^{4} > 0$. [step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Numerical specialization: if $R\omega = 3c/5$, then $\gamma = (1-9/25)^{-1/2} = 5/4$ and the magnitude of the four-acceleration is $\gamma^{2}R\omega^{2} = (25/16)R\omega^{2} = (25/16)(3c/5)\omega = (15c\omega)/16$, with the dimensions of acceleration because $c\omega$ has units m/s$^{2}$ when $\omega$ is an angular rate. [step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **The zero-frequency case is retained deliberately.** At $\omega = 0$ the clock is static and its four-acceleration vanishes; the acceleration square $\eta(A,A) = \gamma^{4}R^{2}\omega^{4}$ is nonnegative always and positive exactly for nonzero $\omega$ when $R > 0$.

- **Centripetal acceleration is orthogonal to the velocity.** The identity $w \cdot a = 0$ is what forces $A^{0} = 0$ and keeps the four-acceleration purely spatial; it reflects the constant speed of the motion and is not an additional dynamical assumption.

## Example

Worked computation. In an inertial chart with $\eta_0 =
\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ let the observer be $n = e_0 = (1,0,0,0)$ and
let $u = (5/4,3/4,0,0)$, a future unit timelike vector:
$\eta(u,u) = -25/16+9/16 = -1$. Then $\gamma = -\eta(n,u) = 5/4 \ge 1$,
$h(u) = u+\eta(n,u)n = u-(5/4)(1,0,0,0) = (0,3/4,0,0)$ lies in
$n^{\perp} = \operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and the relative velocity is
$w = c\,h(u)/\gamma = (0,3c/5,0,0)$. One checks
$u = \gamma(n+w/c) = (5/4)(1,3/5,0,0)$ and
$|w|^{2} = 9c^{2}/25 = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) = c^{2}(1-16/25)$. Also
$h(h(u)) = h(u)$ and $\eta(n,h(u)) = 0$. This four-velocity is the one of the
clock with coordinate velocity $(3c/5,0,0)$ in
[[ex-sr-proper-time-of-a-straight-worldline]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial chart with $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the observer $n = e_0 = (1,0,0,0)$ and the vector $u = (5/4,3/4,0,0)$.

[L1] Decomposition ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]): for future unit timelike $n,u$ the projection is $h(v) = v+\eta(n,v)n$ with image $n^{\perp}$ and $h \circ h = h$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$; $\gamma = -\eta(n,u) \ge 1$, $w = c\,h(u)/\gamma \in n^{\perp}$, $u = \gamma(n+w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$, and $\gamma = 1 \iff u = n$.

[L2] Chart ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]): the chart's observer is $e_0$, and $n^{\perp} = \operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the Euclidean spatial space of the frame with $|w| = \sqrt{\delta(w,w)}$.

[L3] Bilinearity ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): in the chart, $\eta(v,z) = -v^{0}z^{0}+v^{1}z^{1}+v^{2}z^{2}+v^{3}z^{3}$.

[L4] Observer clause ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]): the four-velocity of the observer's own worldline with future unit timelike $n$ is $cn$.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L3], $\eta(u,u) = -25/16+9/16 = -1$ and $\eta(n,n) = -1$, so both $n$ and $u$ are unit timelike; both are future because their first coordinates are positive and $u^{0} = 5/4 > |u_{\mathrm{sp}}| = 3/4$, $n^{0} = 1 > 0$; hence [L1] applies. [given, L1, L3]

2.1 Direct computation in the chart: $\gamma = -\eta(n,u) = 5/4$, and $h(u) = u+\eta(n,u)n = u-(5/4)(1,0,0,0) = (0,3/4,0,0)$. [step 1.1, L1, L3]

3.1 The vector $h(u) = (0,3/4,0,0)$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3) = n^{\perp}$ by [L2], and $\eta(n,h(u)) = -1\cdot 0+0 = 0$ by [L3]; idempotence $h(h(u)) = h(u)$ holds because $h(u) \in n^{\perp}$ is fixed by $h$ by [L1]. [step 2.1, L1, L2, L3]

4.1 The relative velocity is $w = c\,h(u)/\gamma = (0,3c/5,0,0)$ with $|w|^{2} = 9c^{2}/25$ by [L2]; the split identity gives $u = \gamma(n+w/c) = (5/4)(1,3/5,0,0) = (5/4,3/4,0,0)$ and the Lorentz-factor identity $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) = c^{2}(1-16/25) = 9c^{2}/25$, both by [L1]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L2]

5.1 By [L4] the observer's four-velocity is $c\,n = (c,0,0,0)$; since $\gamma = 5/4 \ne 1$, the criterion of [L1] gives $u \ne n$, so the clock's four-velocity $cu$ differs from the observer's and the split is nondegenerate. [step 4.1, L1, L4] ∎

## Remarks

- **The split is algebraic, not dynamic.** The computation uses only the projection $h$, the inner product and the definitions of $\gamma$ and $w$; no differentiation, no dynamics and no physical measurement is involved.

- **Companion clock.** The dimensionless four-velocity $u = (5/4,3/4,0,0)$ is
  the one of the straight clock with coordinate velocity $(3c/5,0,0)$ worked out
  in [[ex-sr-proper-time-of-a-straight-worldline]]; the split above re-derives
  that clock's relative velocity without using its worldline.

## Statement refuted

**False claim:** every regular $C^{1}$ curve of the model admits a proper-time
parametrization, with strictly increasing proper-time function and normalized
timelike four-velocity.

The claim is refuted by a straight future null line. It is a regular future
curve whose tangent is null at every point, so the proper-time integrand
vanishes identically, the proper-time function is constant and cannot
parametrize anything, and no unit timelike tangent can be attached to the
curve. The existence of this curve is exactly why
[[def-sr-proper-time]] carries the future timelike hypothesis and why null
rays need their own parametrization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A future null vector $k$ and the straight curve $x(s) := p + s\,k$ in the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model.

[L1] Causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]): $v$ is null when $v \ne 0$ and $\eta(v,v) = 0$, timelike when $\eta(v,v) < 0$, and the zero vector has no causal character.

[L2] Time orientation ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]): $v$ is future null when it is nonzero null and lies in the closure of the future timelike component.

[L3] Inertial charts ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]): in an inertial chart the matrix of $\eta$ is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, so for $v = (v^{0},v^{1},v^{2},v^{3})$ one has $\eta(v,v) = -(v^{0})^{2} + (v^{1})^{2} + (v^{2})^{2} + (v^{3})^{2}$.

[L4] Curves and worldlines ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): a curve $x(s) = p + s k$ with constant tangent $k$ is $C^{1}$ with $x'(s) = k$; it is a future null curve when $k$ is future null, and a future timelike worldline only when $k$ is future timelike.

[L5] Proper time ([[def-sr-proper-time]]): the proper-time integrand is $\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$ and the construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines.

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 In an inertial chart with $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ let $k := (1,1,0,0)$: then $\eta(k,k) = -1 + 1 = 0$ and $k \ne 0$, so $k$ is null by [L1], and its first coordinate is positive, so $k$ lies in the closure of the future timelike component and is future null by [L2]. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 The curve $x(s) := p + s k$ has difference quotients $\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h = k$ for every $h \ne 0$, so $x'(s) = k$ for every $s$ and $x$ is a regular $C^{1}$ future null curve by [L4]. [step 1.1, L4]

3.1 The proper-time integrand of [L5] is $\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))} = \sqrt{-\eta(k,k)} = 0$ identically; hence every proper-time integral over this curve is constant, the function $s \mapsto \tau(s)$ has zero derivative everywhere and is not strictly increasing, and there is no reparametrization by it. [step 2.1, L5]

4.1 No normalized four-velocity can be attached to the curve either: every tangent vector is the null vector $k$, while a four-velocity $U$ with $\eta(U,U) = -c^{2} < 0$ would be timelike, and a vector cannot be both null and timelike by [L1]. The curve does describe a light ray — in the chart its coordinate path is $(s,s,0,0)$, so with $t := s/c$ the spatial coordinate advances by $c\,t$ and the coordinate speed is $c$ — but it has no massive proper-time parametrization. [step 2.1, L1, L3] ∎

## Remarks

- **The failure is not a technicality of one formula.** The proper-time integrand is the length integrand of the metric along the curve, and along a null direction that length is zero; no rescaling of the parameter changes this, and no unit timelike tangent exists at any point of the curve.

## Statement refuted

**False claim:** the formula
$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1}\int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}\,ds$ assigns an
elapsed clock time to every regular $C^{1}$ curve of the model.

The claim is refuted by a straight spacelike line: its tangent is spacelike at
every point, so $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real
number. A spacelike interval is not elapsed clock time; the geometric spacing
along the curve is its spacelike length, a different quantity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A spacelike vector $d$ and the straight curve $x(s) := p + s\,d$ in the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model.

[L1] Causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]): $v$ is spacelike when $\eta(v,v) > 0$ and timelike when $\eta(v,v) < 0$.

[L2] Inertial charts ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]): in an inertial chart the matrix of $\eta$ is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, so for $v = (v^{0},v^{1},v^{2},v^{3})$ one has $\eta(v,v) = -(v^{0})^{2} + (v^{1})^{2} + (v^{2})^{2} + (v^{3})^{2}$.

[L3] Curves ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): the curve $x(s) = p + s d$ has constant tangent $x'(s) = d$ and is a future timelike worldline only when $d$ is future timelike.

[L4] Proper time ([[def-sr-proper-time]]): the proper-time integrand is $\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$ and the construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines; for a spacelike tangent the quantity $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative.

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 In an inertial chart with $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ let $d := (1,2,0,0)$: then $\eta(d,d) = -1 + 4 = 3 > 0$, so $d$ is spacelike by [L1]. [L1, L2]

2.1 The curve $x(s) := p + s d$ has constant tangent $x'(s) = d$ by [L3], so $-\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) = -3 < 0$ at every point; the integrand $\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$ of [L4] is the square root of a negative real number and is not defined. The proper-time construction therefore produces no real value on this curve. [step 1.1, L3, L4]

3.1 The geometric spacing along the curve is governed by the spacelike length per unit parameter, $\sqrt{\eta(d,d)} = \sqrt{3}$, not by a clock reading: this curve is not a timelike worldline, has no causal-character tangent that is timelike, and the failure is exactly the hypothesis of the timelike restriction in [L4]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L4] ∎

## Remarks

- **Spacelike length and proper time are different constructions.** The number $\sqrt{\eta(d,d)}$ measures a spatial separation in the model; $c$ times it is not an elapsed time along the curve, and no clock is associated with a spacelike displacement by this framework.

## Statement refuted

**False claim:** if a $C^{1}$ curve parametrizes a straight timelike line, then
it is a future timelike worldline of the model and the proper-time construction
gives the clock reading of its history.

The claim is refuted by orienting the parametrization backwards: the same
geometric line with the opposite parametrization has past timelike tangents, is
not a worldline of the model, and yet the proper-time integrand takes exactly
the same values as for the future-directed parametrization. This is why the
parametrization, and not merely the image of the curve, is part of the
definition of a worldline.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A future timelike displacement $d$ and the two parametrizations $s \mapsto p + s d$ and $s \mapsto p - s d$ of the same straight timelike line.

[L1] Causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]): $v$ is timelike when $\eta(v,v) < 0$; the sign of $\eta$ does not distinguish future from past.

[L2] Time orientation ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]): the timelike set is the disjoint union of the future component $C^{+}$ and the past component $C^{-}$, and a timelike vector is future or past but not both; $-v \in C^{-}$ whenever $v \in C^{+}$.

[L3] Worldlines ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): a future timelike worldline is a $C^{1}$ curve whose tangent at every parameter value is future timelike; the parametrization is part of the curve.

[L4] Proper time ([[def-sr-proper-time]]): the proper-time integrand is $\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$, which depends on the tangent through the quadratic form $\eta$ only.

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 In an inertial chart with $\eta_0 = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ let $d := (5,3,0,0)$: then $-\eta(d,d) = -(-25+9) = 16 > 0$, so $d$ is timelike, and choosing $d$ in the future component $C^{+}$ makes it a future timelike displacement; then $-d$ belongs to $C^{-}$ by [L2]. [L1, L2]

2.1 The curve $x(s) := p - s d$ on $[0,1]$ has difference quotients identically $-d$, so $x'(s) = -d$ is past timelike for every $s$; by [L3] the curve is not a future timelike worldline of the model, while the curve $s \mapsto p + s d$ has the same image and is the worldline. [step 1.1, L3]

3.1 The proper-time integrand of both curves agrees pointwise: $\sqrt{-\eta(-d,-d)} = \sqrt{-\eta(d,d)} = 4$ by bilinearity of $\eta$, so the proper-time integral alone does not distinguish the future-directed from the past-directed parametrization: by [L4] the proper-time construction is attached to the parametrized history, together with its future timelike hypothesis, and not to the bare image of the curve. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L4] ∎

## Remarks

- **Orientation is data, not geometry of the image.** The same set of events carries two opposite worldline parametrizations with identical proper-time densities; only the future-directed one is a worldline of the model, and the past-directed one is its orientation reversal.

## Definition

Work in the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) with its inertial atlas ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]) and the canonical identification of tangent spaces with $V$ ([[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]). The objects defined below are, in general, different objects, and the distinctions between them are part of the definition.

**(a) Chart and inertial chart.** A **chart** of the model is a diffeomorphism $u:U\to u(U)$ from a nonempty open subset $U\subseteq A$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]], [[def-smooth-manifold]]), written with components $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$. An **inertial chart** is the global chart $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ of an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). A general chart need not be inertial: if $x$ is an inertial chart and $N:x(U)\to\mathbb R^4$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image which is not the restriction of an affine map, then $u:=N\circ x$ is a chart that is not inertial, because if $u$ were the inertial chart of a frame then $x\circ u^{-1}=N^{-1}$ would be affine by [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]] and hence $N=(N^{-1})^{-1}$ would be affine as the inverse of an affine bijection, a contradiction; the map $N(y)=(y^0,y^1+(y^0)^2,y^2,y^3)$ on $\mathbb R^4$ is an explicit example.

**(b) Tetrad at an event and tetrad field.** A **tetrad at $p\in A$** is an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $e_0$ future, $e_0\in C^+$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]): this is the basis of an inertial frame without an origin and without the orientation condition. A **tetrad field** on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ is a tuple $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ of smooth vector fields on $\Omega$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], type $(1,0)$) whose values at every $p\in\Omega$ form a tetrad at $p$. A tetrad field is **observer-adapted** to a prescribed future timelike worldline or congruence when $E_0=U/c$ for the corresponding future timelike unit vector field $U$ with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**(c) Observer congruence.** An **observer congruence** on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ is a smooth vector field $n:\Omega\to V$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$ and $n(p)\in C^+$ for every $p\in\Omega$. Its **observers** are its maximal integral curves ([[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]], [[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]]). Each observer is a future timelike worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): its tangent at a parameter value $s$ is $n(x(s))$, which is future timelike, and it is regular because $\eta(n,n)=-1$ makes $n$ nowhere zero. **Completeness** of the integral curves, a global product structure of $\Omega$, and global synchronization are not asserted by this definition.

**(d) Adapted chart.** For a congruence $n$ on $\Omega$, an **$n$-adapted chart** is a chart $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U\to\mathbb R^4$ with $U$ a nonempty open subset of $\Omega$ whose spatial coordinates $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant along every integral curve of $n$ contained in $U$. No global adapted chart is asserted, and $u^0$ is not required to be affine.

**(e) Distinctions.** A chart need not be inertial, as in (a); a chart need not be $n$-adapted for any congruence. A tetrad field is not in general the coordinate frame of a chart: if $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ is the coordinate frame of a chart $(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$, that is, $E_a=\partial/\partial v^a$, then $[E_a,E_b]=0$ for all $a,b$ ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]), so a tetrad field whose members do not commute pairwise is not the coordinate frame of a chart; no converse is claimed here. A congruence need not be the flow of a coordinate, and its pointwise rest spaces need not assemble into hypersurfaces; that integrability question is decided later on this page. In an inertial chart the coordinate frame is simultaneously the basis of an inertial frame, a constant tetrad field and the congruence of stationary observers, but the four notions are distinct in general.

## Remarks

- **Non-inertial charts exist, and the example is checked.** The map $N(y)=(y^0,y^1+(y^0)^2,y^2,y^3)$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^4$ with the smooth two-sided inverse $z\mapsto(z^0,z^1-(z^0)^2,z^2,z^3)$. It is not the restriction of an affine map: $N(0)=0$ and $N(2e_0)=(2,4,0,0)\ne2N(e_0)=(2,2,0,0)$ for $e_0=(1,0,0,0)$, so $N$ is not linear, and with $N(0)=0$ it is therefore not affine. If $N\circ x$ were an inertial chart, the transition $x\circ(N\circ x)^{-1}=N^{-1}$ between inertial charts would be affine by [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]; the inverse of an affine bijection $z\mapsto Az+b$ of $\mathbb R^4$ is again affine, $w\mapsto A^{-1}w-A^{-1}b$ ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]), so $N$ would be affine, a contradiction. Hence $N\circ x$ is a chart that is not inertial, and being $C^\infty$ it belongs to the model's smooth structure.

- **Tetrads exist at every event, and tetrad fields are smooth by components.** [[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]] supplies an $\eta$-orthonormal basis $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ of $V$; since $\eta(f_0,f_0)=-1<0$ the vector $f_0$ is timelike, so exactly one of $f_0$ and $-f_0$ lies in $C^+$ because the timelike set is the disjoint union of the two future and past cones ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]), and negating it preserves $\eta$-orthonormality; no orientation condition is imposed on a tetrad, so this already produces a tetrad at any prescribed event. The formulation with the additional positive-orientation condition, and with an arbitrary origin, is the inertial-frame existence statement of [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]]. A tetrad field is componentwise smooth in an inertial chart by the definition of $C^k$ tensor fields on the affine model ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], [[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]).

- **Congruences have well-defined observers.** A smooth unit field $n$ on $\Omega$ is a smooth map $\Omega\to V$ with values in the future timelike cone, and [[thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point]] supplies through every point a unique maximal integral curve of $n$ ([[def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field]]); along such a curve the identity $\eta(n,n)=-1$ gives $\eta(x',x')=-1$ at every parameter value, so each observer is a future timelike worldline with future unit tangent, in particular regular ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]). Nothing about completeness of the maximal domains is asserted.

- **The commutation condition is only necessary.** If $(E_0,\ldots,E_3)$ is the coordinate frame of a chart $(v^0,\ldots,v^3)$, then $[E_a,E_b]=0$ by the coordinate formula for the Lie bracket; a tetrad field with $[E_a,E_b]\ne0$ for some $a,b$ therefore cannot be a coordinate frame. The converse (a commuting tetrad field is locally a coordinate frame) is a Frobenius-type statement and is not asserted by this definition.

## Definition

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space with tangent spaces canonically identified with $V$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]), and let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open subset. All tensor fields below are $C^k$ fields in the sense of [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], with $k=\infty$ unless a clause says otherwise.

**(a) Vector fields.** For smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $\Omega$ define the **covariant derivative of $Y$ in the direction $X$** at $p\in\Omega$ by

$$\bigl(\nabla_XY\bigr)(p):=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}Y\bigl(p+tX(p)\bigr),$$

the derivative of the $V$-valued composite $t\mapsto Y(p+tX(p))$, which is defined for $t$ in a neighbourhood of $0$ because $\Omega$ is open ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-derivative]]). In the inertial chart $x$ of any inertial frame one has $(\nabla_XY)^a=X^b\,\partial_bY^a$; the value does not depend on the inertial chart: for another inertial chart $x'=\Lambda x+b$ one has $\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b_{\ a}\,\partial_b$ and $Y'^a=\Lambda^a_{\ b}Y^b$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and $\Lambda$ is constant, so $(\Lambda^{-1})^a_{\ c}\,X'^b\,\partial'_bY'^c=X^b\,\partial_bY^a$. The field $\nabla_XY$ is again a smooth vector field on $\Omega$.

**(b) Covector and general tensor fields.** For a smooth covector field $\alpha$ set $(\nabla_X\alpha)(Y):=X(\alpha(Y))-\alpha(\nabla_XY)$ for every smooth vector field $Y$, and for a type $(r,s)$ tensor field $T$ define $\nabla_XT$ by the derivation rule on the evaluation of $T$: for $T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$,

$$(\nabla_XT)(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)=X\bigl[T(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)\bigr]-\sum_{i=1}^rT(\alpha_1,\dots,\nabla_X\alpha_i,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)-\sum_{j=1}^sT(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,\nabla_XY_j,\dots,Y_s),$$

where the vector and covector arguments are smooth fields on $\Omega$. In inertial coordinates every component of $\nabla_XT$ is $X^b\,\partial_b$ applied to that component, with no connection coefficients.

**(c) Properties.** The operator $\nabla$ is $\mathbb R$-bilinear, is $C^\infty(\Omega)$-linear in $X$, and satisfies the Leibniz rules $\nabla_X(fY)=X(f)Y+f\nabla_XY$ and the analogous rules for tensor fields; it is metric compatible, $\nabla\eta=0$, because $\partial_a\eta_{bc}=0$ in every inertial chart; it is torsion-free, $\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$, by the coordinate formula for the Lie bracket ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]); and it has zero curvature, $\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z=0$, by equality of mixed partial derivatives of the components ([[thm-young-mixed-partial-theorem]]).

**(d) Fields along a curve.** If $\gamma:I\to A$ is a $C^1$ curve and $W:I\to V$ is a $C^1$ field along it ([[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]]), the **covariant derivative of $W$ along $\gamma$** is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative $DW/ds:=W'$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), because the canonical identification $T_pA=V$ is independent of $p$; consequently parallel transport along any curve is the identity and a field is parallel exactly when it is constant. This derivative is the one used for the acceleration of congruences, for Fermi–Walker transport and for the kinematic decomposition below; the model needs no Christoffel symbols and no parallel-transport ODE in this formulation.

**(e) First-order $C^1$ version.** For $C^1$ vector fields $X,Y$ and $C^1$ covector or tensor fields on $\Omega$ the same directional and evaluation definitions are well-defined and have continuous coefficients: in an inertial chart $(\nabla_XY)^a=X^b\partial_bY^a$, and each tensor component is differentiated in the same way. The component recovery and the subtraction of all argument derivatives remain valid; $C^1$ scalar multiplication satisfies the same first-order Leibniz rules; metric compatibility remains $\nabla\eta=0$; and the first-order torsion identity uses the continuous coordinate bracket $[X,Y]^a=X^b\partial_bY^a-Y^b\partial_bX^a$. No $C^1$ closure of this bracket and no second covariant derivative of arbitrary $C^1$ data are asserted. For $C^2$ vector fields the second derivatives needed for the zero-curvature identity of (c) exist, and that identity follows by equality of the continuous mixed second partials. All smooth-field properties above and the $C^1$ along-curve derivative in (d) are retained.

## Remarks

- **Well-definedness of (a).** The composite $t\mapsto Y(p+tX(p))$ is the composition of the smooth curve $t\mapsto p+tX(p)$ (which stays in $\Omega$ for small $|t|$ because $\Omega$ is open and $X(p)\in V$ is a fixed vector) with the smooth map $Y:\Omega\to V$; its derivative at $0$ exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space $V$ by [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and the coordinate expression $(\nabla_XY)^a=X^b\partial_bY^a$ is the chain rule of [[thm-chain-rule]]. Chart independence uses the transformation laws of [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] together with the constancy of the linear part $\Lambda$ of an inertial transition ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]): the second derivatives of the transition vanish, so no inhomogeneous term appears. Smoothness of $\nabla_XY$ follows because $X^b\partial_bY^a$ is a smooth function of $x(p)$ in an inertial chart, and $C^k$ tensor fields are exactly those with $C^k$ inertial components ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]).

- **Well-definedness of (b).** In an inertial chart use the constant coordinate frame and its constant dual frame; their covariant derivatives vanish, so evaluating the derivation rule on those constant bases leaves only $X$ acting on each component of $T$. For variable arguments $\alpha_1,\dots,Y_s$ the ordinary product rule expressed by [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] produces exactly the subtracted terms displayed in (b), and all their derivatives cancel; this proves the stated coordinate formula and shows that the evaluation rule is well-defined, once the covector case $(\nabla_X\alpha)(Y)=X(\alpha(Y))-\alpha(\nabla_XY)$ is fixed by the requirement that $\nabla_X$ commute with the pairing. No connection coefficients appear because $\eta$ is constant and the inertial transition matrices are constant.

- **Well-definedness of (c).** Torsion-freeness is the coordinate identity $X^b\partial_bY^a-Y^b\partial_bX^a=[X,Y]^a$ ([[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]); metric compatibility is the constancy of the component matrix $\eta_{ab}$ of the metric in inertial charts; and the curvature identity follows from the equality of mixed second partial derivatives ([[thm-young-mixed-partial-theorem]]) after expanding the two iterated derivatives of the components. The Leibniz and linearity properties are immediate from the definitions.

- **Well-definedness of (d) and (e).** In (d) the canonical isomorphism $T_pA\to V$ is independent of $p$ ([[lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v]]), so a field along a curve is simply a $V$-valued map and its covariant derivative is its ordinary derivative; parallel transport is the identity because the equation $W'=0$ has exactly the constant solutions on an interval. In (e) a $C^1$ field $Y$ has a continuous differential, and the derivative of $t\mapsto Y(p+tX(p))$ at $0$ is $dY_p[X(p)]$, which is a continuous function of $p$ when $Y$ and $X$ are $C^1$; only first derivatives occur in the Leibniz, metric-compatibility and torsion assertions, and the second covariant derivatives in the curvature identity require the stated $C^2$ hypotheses. No choice principle is used anywhere; all objects are finite-dimensional or explicitly parametrized.

## Definition

Let $n$ be an observer congruence on a nonempty open subset $\Omega\subseteq A$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\nabla$ be the flat covariant derivative of the affine model ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]), and write $n_b:=\eta_{bc}n^c$ for the associated covector field ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]).

**(a) Rest metric and projection.** Define $h(v,w):=\eta(v,w)+\eta(n,v)\eta(n,w)$ for vectors at the same point, so that $h=\eta+n^\flat\otimes n^\flat$ in components. Then $h(v,w)=\eta(h(v),h(w))$ for the orthogonal projection $h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c). At every point $h$ is symmetric with radical spanned by $n(p)$, and its restriction to $n(p)^\perp$ is positive definite ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Acceleration.** The **acceleration** of the congruence is $a:=\nabla_nn$. Then $\eta(n,a)=0$ pointwise, because $2\eta(n,\nabla_nn)=n\bigl(\eta(n,n)\bigr)=0$; consequently $a(p)$ is spacelike or zero by the causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). In the model's physical interpretation the four-acceleration of the congruence observers is $c^2a$ and its magnitude is $c^2\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}$; the numerical units belong to the model's SI conventions and are not part of the affine geometry ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

**(c) Kinematic decomposition.** Set $\theta_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}$ and $\omega_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}$, where $\nabla_{(c}n_{d)}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d+\nabla_dn_c)$ and $\nabla_{[c}n_{d]}=\tfrac12(\nabla_cn_d-\nabla_dn_c)$. Then

$$\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab},$$

with $\theta$ symmetric, $\omega$ antisymmetric, both horizontal ($\theta_{ab}n^b=\omega_{ab}n^b=n^a\theta_{ab}=n^a\omega_{ab}=0$), and this decomposition is unique with these properties. The tensor $\theta$ is the **expansion (and shear) tensor**, $\theta:=h^{ab}\theta_{ab}$ is the **expansion scalar**, its trace-free part is the **shear**, and $\omega$ is the **vorticity 2-tensor**.

**(d) Born rigidity.** The congruence is **Born rigid** (it describes a rigid motion) when $\mathcal L_nh=0$. Since $(\mathcal L_nh)_{ab}=2\theta_{ab}$, Born rigidity is equivalent to $\theta=0$, equivalently to the projected symmetrized derivative of $n^\flat$ vanishing.

**(e) Scope.** These are kinematic definitions for a prescribed smooth field $n$ on the affine model; no dynamical equation, matter model, global synchronization or completeness is assumed, and $a$, $\theta$, $\omega$ and $h$ are local objects on $\Omega$.

## Remarks

- **Clause (a) is an expansion identity.** Using $\eta(n,n)=-1$ and bilinearity, $\eta(h(v),h(w))=\eta(v,w)+2\eta(n,v)\eta(n,w)+\eta(n,v)\eta(n,w)\eta(n,n)=\eta(v,w)+\eta(n,v)\eta(n,w)=h(v,w)$; the radical and positive-definiteness statements are clause (c) of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] together with [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]].

- **Clause (b) computes the acceleration as a derivative along $n$.** With metric compatibility of $\nabla$ ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] clause (c)) one has $n\bigl(\eta(n,n)\bigr)=\nabla_n\bigl(\eta(n,n)\bigr)=2\eta(n,\nabla_nn)$, and $\eta(n,n)=-1$ has zero derivative; hence $\eta(n,a)=0$, so $a$ is spacelike wherever it is nonzero. The identification of the observers' four-acceleration with $c^2a$ is the chain rule: parametrize an observer by the congruence parameter $s$, so that its tangent is $x'(s)=n(x(s))$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]] clause (c)); its four-velocity is $U=x'/\tau'=cn$ because $\eta(x',x')=-1$ forces $\tau'=1/c$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), and differentiating the components of $U$ along the curve in an inertial chart gives $U'(s)=c\,\partial_bn^a(x(s))x'^b(s)=c\,(\nabla_nn)^a(x(s))$, so the four-acceleration $A=U'/\tau'=c^2a$ ([[thm-chain-rule]]).

- **Clause (c) is a pointwise algebra identity.** Projecting $\nabla_an_b$: since $h_a{}^c\nabla_cn_d=\nabla_an_d+n_a\nabla_nn_d=\nabla_an_d+n_aa_d$ (because $h_a{}^c=\delta_a^c+n_a n^c$) and $n^d\nabla_an_d=\tfrac12\nabla_a(\eta(n,n))=0$, one gets $h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_cn_d=\nabla_an_b+n_aa_b$ from the identity $\eta(n,a)=0$; hence $\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab}$. Uniqueness holds because contracting with $n^a$ recovers $a_b$, after which $\nabla_an_b+n_aa_b$ is a fixed tensor whose symmetric and antisymmetric parts determine $\theta$ and $\omega$. Horizontality follows from $h_b{}^dn^b=0$, and symmetry and antisymmetry of $\theta$ and $\omega$ are part of their definitions. All indices are raised and lowered with $\eta$ and the computations are finite-dimensional pointwise algebra.

- **Clause (d) is the standard rigidity identity.** For the torsion-free metric-compatible $\nabla$ one has $(\mathcal L_n\eta)_{ab}=\nabla_an_b+\nabla_bn_a$ and $(\mathcal L_nn^\flat)_b=n^a\nabla_an_b+n_a\nabla_bn^a=a_b$, since $n_a\nabla_bn^a=\tfrac12\nabla_b(\eta(n,n))=0$. Hence $(\mathcal L_nh)_{ab}=(\mathcal L_n\eta)_{ab}+a_an_b+n_aa_b=(\nabla_an_b+\nabla_bn_a)+a_an_b+n_aa_b$, and substituting the decomposition of (c) cancels the four acceleration terms and leaves $2\theta_{ab}$; therefore $\mathcal L_nh=0$ if and only if $\theta=0$. This is the equation recorded as Definition 7/(123) of the cited Giulini section, in the $(-+++)$ convention of this library.

- **No global or dynamical assertion.** The definitions are local on $\Omega$; in particular the rest spaces $n(p)^\perp$ are not asserted to assemble into hypersurfaces, and the Frobenius integrability condition for that assembly is a separate statement on this page.

## Definition

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $n\in V$ be future unit timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

**(a) Rest space.** The **rest space** of $n$ is the hyperplane $n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(n,v)=0\}$; by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c) it is a three-dimensional linear subspace on which $\eta$ restricts to a positive-definite symmetric form, and the orthogonal projection onto it is $h(v)=v+\eta(n,v)n$ ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

**(b) Simultaneity slice.** For $p\in A$ the **simultaneity slice of $p$ relative to $n$** is the affine hyperplane $H(p,n):=p+n^\perp=\{q\in A:\eta(n,q-p)=0\}$; it contains $p$ and is three-dimensional, not a single point.

**(c) Simultaneity relation.** Define $q\sim_nq'$ if and only if $\eta(n,q'-q)=0$, that is, if and only if $q'-q\in n^\perp$. Then $\sim_n$ is an equivalence relation on $A$ whose equivalence classes are exactly the slices $H(p,n)$; reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are consequences of $n^\perp$ being a linear subspace and are not physical assumptions.

**(d) Rest distance.** For $p,q$ with $q\in H(p,n)$ define $d_n(p,q):=\sqrt{\eta(q-p,q-p)}$. This is a real number $\ge0$, symmetric in $p,q$, vanishes exactly when $p=q$, and satisfies the triangle inequality on each slice, because the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^\perp$ is a positive-definite inner product.

**(e) Dependence on $n$ and scope.** The relation $\sim_n$ and the slices $H(p,n)$ depend on the chosen future unit timelike vector $n$: an event $q$ with $\eta(n,q-p)=0$ generally has $\eta(n',q-p)\ne0$ for another future unit $n'$ (an explicit witness is given on this page). Simultaneity here is defined relative to a prescribed observer vector and is not an absolute relation. For a congruence $n(\cdot)$ one may form the pointwise slices $H\bigl(p,n(p)\bigr)$; whether these assemble into hypersurfaces is a separate integrability question settled later on this page, and no global foliation is asserted.

## Remarks

- **Well-definedness.** $n^\perp$ is three-dimensional because $\eta$ is nondegenerate and $n\ne0$ ([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]); positive definiteness of the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^\perp$, together with $h(n)=0$, $h\circ h=h$ and $\operatorname{im}h=n^\perp$, is clause (c) of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. Consequently each slice $H(p,n)$ is the translate $p+n^\perp$, an affine hyperplane of dimension three, and $\eta(n,q-p)=0$ is equivalent to $q-p\in n^\perp$, so the equivalence classes of $\sim_n$ are exactly the slices: this uses linearity of $\eta$ in each variable and linearity of $n^\perp$ as a subspace, nothing else.

- **The rest distance is an inner-product norm.** On the slice through $p$ the map $(q,q')\mapsto\eta(q-p,q'-p)$ is the positive-definite symmetric form obtained by restricting $\eta$ to $n^\perp$, transported to the affine hyperplane by subtracting $p$; the axioms of a positive-definite inner product therefore give nonnegativity, symmetry, the vanishing condition $d_n(p,q)=0\Leftrightarrow p=q$ and the triangle inequality. No choice principle is used: all objects are finite-dimensional or explicitly parametrized.

- **Dependence on the observer vector is not a defect.** Two distinct future unit timelike vectors $n\ne n'$ have distinct rest spaces $n^\perp\ne n'^\perp$ in general, and the relation $\sim_n$ is the relation of lying in a common slice of the foliation of $A$ by hyperplanes orthogonal to the fixed vector $n$. For a congruence the vector varies from point to point, and the resulting pointwise slices need not fit together; this is the integrability question decided by the Frobenius statement later on this page, and no global simultaneity is asserted by this definition.

## Definition

Adopt the ideal-clock and ideal-light assumptions of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $x:I\to A$ be a future timelike worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function $\tau$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]]), and let $s_-<s_+$ be parameter values in $I$. Suppose an event $q$ and the events $e_-:=x(s_-)$, $e_+:=x(s_+)$ satisfy: $q-e_-$ is future null and $e_+-q$ is future null ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Under the adopted ideal-light assumption an ideal ray is emitted at $e_-$, reaches $q$, and an ideal ray emitted at $q$ reaches $e_+$; the event $q$ is idealized as an instantaneous reflection that changes nothing else. The **radar protocol** of the observer assigns to $q$

(i) the **radar time** $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q):=\tfrac12\bigl(\tau(s_-)+\tau(s_+)\bigr)$, the ideal clock's reading midway between emission and reception, and

(ii) the **radar distance** $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q):=\tfrac{c}{2}\bigl(\tau(s_+)-\tau(s_-)\bigr)$, half the round-trip light time multiplied by $c$.

Two events measured by the same observer are **radar-simultaneous** when their radar times agree. The assignment does not change under increasing reparametrizations of the observer's worldline, because the proper-time function does not ([[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]).

**Conventions and scope.** (a) The protocol is a definition of an operational assignment conditional on the existence of the emission, reflection and reception events, and it assumes an available ideal reflector and ideal apparatus. (b) The split of the round trip into a "time" and a "distance" uses the symmetric convention in which half of the round-trip time is assigned to the outgoing and half to the returning segment; the protocol determines the round-trip quantity $\tau(s_+)-\tau(s_-)$ operationally, while the derived one-way assignment is a convention and does not measure a one-way light speed independently of a synchronization convention. (c) Nothing is claimed about accelerated observers, dispersive or absorbing media, finite-resolution apparatus, global single-valuedness or detector models, and no measurement outcome, statistical inference or empirical comparison is asserted.

## Remarks

- **Well-definedness.** The data $\tau(s_-)$ and $\tau(s_+)$ are real numbers determined by the worldline and the two parameters ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), so $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)$ are well defined; the existence hypotheses on $q$ are exactly the condition that $q$ is connected to the observer's history by a future null outgoing segment from $e_-$ and a future null returning segment to $e_+$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Since $\tau$ is invariant under increasing reparametrizations of the worldline ([[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]]), so are the radar time and radar distance.

- **The two null segments are the operational content of the adopted assumption.** The existence of ideal rays along the null displacements $q-e_-$ and $e_+-q$ is supplied by the ideal-light clause of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], which identifies ideal light rays in vacuum with future null straight lines; the protocol therefore describes an assignment conditional on that idealization and does not describe a physical mirror, a finite apparatus, or a medium.

- **The half-split is a convention, not a derived fact.** The protocol measures the round-trip time $\tau(s_+)-\tau(s_-)$ operationally; writing half of it as a one-way time and $c/2$ times it as a distance is the symmetric convention adopted here. For inertial observers this convention is shown to agree with the simultaneity slices of the observer in [[pthm-sr-radar-synchronization-of-inertial-observers]], while the failure of a globally consistent assignment of this kind for rotating observers is exhibited by the explicit example on this page. Neither statement is part of the definition.
