Reall, Mathematical Tripos Part III General Relativity (Cambridge, October 12, 2022 revision): Sections 2.2-2.3 pp. 27-30 (Minkowski metric, causal classification, timelike proper time, observer measurements in an inertial chart, radar coordinates); Internet Archive copy of the original https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/hsr1000/part3_gr_lectures.pdf"
      url: "https://web.archive.org/web/20230323191108id_/https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/hsr1000/part3_gr_lectures.pdf"
---

## Statement

Let $n$ be a future unit timelike vector, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), let $o$ be an event, and let $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$ be real numbers; put $e_-:=o+\lambda_-n$ and $e_+:=o+\lambda_+n$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). For an event $q$ the following are equivalent:

(i) $q-e_-$ is future null and $e_+-q$ is future null;

(ii) there is $u\in n^\perp$ with $|u|:=\sqrt{\eta(u,u)}=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$ such that $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$.

In that case $q-e_-=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n+u$ and $e_+-q=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n-u$, the affine midpoint $m:=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n=\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}$ satisfies $\eta(n,q-m)=0$ (so $q$ lies in the slice $H(m,n)$) and $|q-m|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$ ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]). In particular for fixed $e_-,e_+$ all admissible reflection events $q$ have the same midpoint $m$ and the same rest distance $(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$, and differ only in the direction $u$ of $n^\perp$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A future unit timelike vector $n$, events $o,e_-=o+\lambda_-n,e_+=o+\lambda_+n$ with $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$, an event $q$, and the two statements (i) and (ii) of the Statement ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[F1] Every $v\in V$ has the unique decomposition $v=-\eta(n,v)n+h(v)$ with $h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n\in n^\perp$, where $n^\perp=\{w:\eta(n,w)=0\}$ is a three-dimensional linear subspace on which $\eta$ restricts to a positive-definite form; $|w|=\sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ is a norm on $n^\perp$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c), [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

[F2] A nonzero null vector $v$ with $\eta(n,v)<0$ is future null: for the future unit timelike $n$ the future cone is the component of the causal set containing $n$, and the sign of $\eta(n,\cdot)$ distinguishes the two closed null cones ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

[F3] $\eta$ is bilinear and symmetric, and $\eta(n,n)=-1$; in the decomposition of [F1], $\eta\bigl(-\eta(n,v)n+h(v),-\eta(n,v)n+h(v)\bigr)=-\eta(n,v)^2+\eta(h(v),h(v))$ because $h(v)\in n^\perp$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

[F4] For a slice $H(m,n)=\{q:\eta(n,q-m)=0\}$ the rest distance is $d_n(m,q)=\sqrt{\eta(q-m,q-m)}$, and $q-m\in n^\perp$ makes $\eta(q-m,q-m)\ge0$ ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Set $d:=q-e_-$ and $r:=e_+-q$, so that $d+r=e_+-e_-=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)n$. By [F1] write $d=-\eta(n,d)n+h(d)$ with $h(d)\in n^\perp$; by [F2] and [F3] a nonzero vector $v$ is future null exactly when $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $\eta(n,v)<0$, and for such a $v$ the decomposition satisfies $\eta(n,v)^2=|h(v)|^2$ by [F3] applied to $\eta(v,v)=0$. Also $r=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)n-d=\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_-+\eta(n,d)\bigr)n-h(d)$ by [F1], because $-d=\eta(n,d)n-h(d)$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 (ii) implies (i): assume $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ with $u\in n^\perp$ and $|u|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2=:\rho$. Then $q-e_-=\rho n+u$ by the affine action, and by [F3] $\eta(q-e_-,q-e_-)=-\rho^2+|u|^2=0$ while $\eta(n,q-e_-)=-\rho<0$, so $q-e_-$ is future null by [F2]; likewise $e_+-q=\rho n-u$ satisfies $\eta(e_+-q,e_+-q)=-\rho^2+|u|^2=0$ and $\eta(n,e_+-q)=-\rho<0$, so $e_+-q$ is future null. [F2, F3]

2.1 (i) implies (ii): assume $d$ and $r$ are future null. By step 1.1 applied to $d$ one has $\eta(n,d)<0$; put $\mu:=-\eta(n,d)>0$, so $d=\mu n+h(d)$ and $|h(d)|^2=\eta(n,d)^2=\mu^2$, hence $|h(d)|=\mu$ by [F1]. Applying step 1.1 to $r$, whose expression is $\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)n-h(d)$: its future nullness gives $\eta(n,r)=\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu$ (up to the factor $-1$ from $\eta(n,n)$), namely $\eta(n,r)=-\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)<0$, and $\eta(r,r)=-\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)^2+|h(d)|^2=0$ by [F3]. Hence $\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)^2=\mu^2$, and since $\eta(n,r)=-\bigl(\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu\bigr)<0$ we have $\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu>0$, so the positive root applies: $\lambda_+-\lambda_--\mu=\mu$, that is $\mu=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$. Therefore $q=e_-+d=o+(\lambda_-+\mu)n+h(d)=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ with $u:=h(d)\in n^\perp$, $|u|=\mu=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$; this is (ii). [F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Midpoint and distance: assume (i), hence (ii) with $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ as produced in step 2.1. Put $m:=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n$; since $e_\pm=o+\lambda_\pm n$, the displacement identity $m-e_-=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n=e_+-m$ shows that $m$ is the affine midpoint $\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}$. Then $q-m=u\in n^\perp$, so $\eta(n,q-m)=0$, that is $q\in H(m,n)$; and $d_n(m,q)=\sqrt{\eta(u,u)}=|u|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$ by [F4] and step 2.1. [F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Conclusion: step 2.1 proves (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) and step 1.2 proves (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i), so the two conditions are equivalent; step 3.1 shows that whenever they hold the reflection event satisfies $q-e_-=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n+u$ and $e_+-q=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}n-u$ with the same horizontal vector $u$, lies in the slice $H(m,n)$ of the fixed midpoint $m=\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}$, and has the fixed rest distance $(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$. Since the data $e_-$, $e_+$ determine $m$ and the norm $\rho=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$, two admissible reflection events differ only by the choice of $u\in n^\perp$ with $|u|=\rho$; such $u$ exist because $n^\perp$ is three-dimensional and $\rho>0$. This is the full assertion. [step 2.1, step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **The two null conditions encode emission and reception.** The displacement $q-e_-$ is the vector from the emission event to the reflection event and $e_+-q$ that from the reflection event to the reception event; both are future null exactly when ideal rays emitted at $e_-$ and at $q$ reach $q$ and $e_+$ respectively, in the sense of the ideal-light assumption. The lemma is purely geometric and makes no claim about an apparatus.

- **The midpoint and the rest distance are exhausted.** The admissible set is $\{m+u:u\in n^\perp,\ |u|=\rho\}$, a two-sphere of radius $\rho$ in the three-dimensional rest space $n^\perp$ of the observer direction $n$; it contains $\rho e/|e|$ for any nonzero $e\in n^\perp$, so it is nonempty. No global synchronization or congruence statement is made here.

## Statement

Adopt [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] (ideal clocks read proper time; ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines) and the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with chart $x$, put $n:=e_0$ (future unit, $\eta(n,n)=-1$) and let $W:=x^{-1}(\{(\lambda,0,0,0):\lambda\in\mathbb R\})$ be the coordinate axis, a straight future timelike worldline whose proper time between the events with coordinates $(\lambda_-,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda_+,0,0,0)$ is $(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/c$ up to an additive constant ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Let $q$ be an event whose spatial coordinates $r:=\bigl(x^1(q),x^2(q),x^3(q)\bigr)$ are nonzero, and put $\lambda_\pm:=x^0(q)\pm|r|$ with $|r|$ the Euclidean norm of [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]. Then:

(i) the events $e_-:=x^{-1}(\lambda_-,0,0,0)$ and $e_+:=x^{-1}(\lambda_+,0,0,0)$ lie on $W$, and $q-e_-$, $e_+-q$ are future null; hence the radar protocol of [[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]] applies with emission $e_-$, reflection $q$ and reception $e_+$;

(ii) the radar assignments are $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=x^0(q)/c$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=|r|$ up to the additive constant of the observer's proper time: the radar time is the chart time of $q$ and the radar distance is the chart's rest-frame distance;

(iii) consequently, on the region of events with nonzero spatial part, radar simultaneity of this observer coincides with chart simultaneity (equal radar times are equal $x^0$), and the radar distance equals the rest distance in the simultaneity slice $H(m,n)$ of the midpoint event $m:=x^{-1}\bigl(x^0(q),0,0,0\bigr)$ ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]);

(iv) scope and qualification: this is a conditional statement of the adopted ideal model, showing that the operational round-trip protocol reproduces the inertial chart's time and rest distance, so the operational content of inertial simultaneity is this two-way radar convention; it asserts no one-way light-speed measurement without a synchronization convention, no empirical calibration, no result for accelerated, rotating or dispersive situations, and no deviation from the model. The idealizations of the postulates are carried into the conclusion.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The adopted ideal-clock and ideal-light postulates and SI conventions ([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]), an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with chart $x$, $n=e_0$, the axis $W$, an event $q$ with $\lambda_\pm:=x^0(q)\pm|r|$ and $|r|>0$, and the events $e_\pm:=x^{-1}(\lambda_\pm,0,0,0)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

[F1] Ideal light in vacuum: the ideal light rays are exactly the future null straight lines $\{p+\mu v:\mu\in\mathbb R\}$ with $v$ future null; ideal clocks read the proper time $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}\,ds$ ([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], [[def-sr-proper-time]]).

[F2] The radar protocol assigns $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac12(\tau(s_-)+\tau(s_+))$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac{c}{2}(\tau(s_+)-\tau(s_-))$ to an event $q$ reached by a future null segment from $e_-=x(s_-)$ and connected to $e_+=x(s_+)$ by a future null segment ([[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]]).

[F3] Radar midpoint lemma: for a future unit $n$, events $e_\pm=o+\lambda_\pm n$ with $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$ and an event $q$, the conditions $q-e_-$, $e_+-q$ future null hold if and only if $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ with $u\in n^\perp$, $|u|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$; in that case the midpoint is $m=\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}$ and $d_n(m,q)=|u|$ in the slice $H(m,n)$ ([[lem-sr-radar-midpoint-for-inertial-observer]], [[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]).

[F4] In the chart of an inertial frame, $x^0=ct$, the metric is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, and the spatial part of a displacement is measured by the Euclidean norm of [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]; the axis $W$ is the straight worldline $\lambda\mapsto o+\lambda e_0$, whose tangent $e_0$ is future unit ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 With $o:=x^{-1}(0,0,0,0)$ the axis is $W=\{o+\lambda e_0:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$ and $e_\pm=x^{-1}(\lambda_\pm,0,0,0)=o+\lambda_\pm e_0$; the tangent of $W$ is the constant vector $e_0=n$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$, so $W$ is a straight future timelike worldline and its proper-time function satisfies $\tau'(\lambda)=c^{-1}\sqrt{1}=1/c$, hence $\tau(\lambda)=\lambda/c+const$ by [F1] and [F4]. [F1, F4]

2.1 The hypotheses of the radar midpoint lemma [F3] are satisfied with $\lambda_\pm=x^0(q)\pm|r|$: since $|r|=0$ is excluded, $\lambda_-<\lambda_+$; the event $q$ has displacement $q-o=x^0(q)n+r_1e_1+r_2e_2+r_3e_3$ by [F4], so $q=o+\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2}n+u$ with $u:=r_1e_1+r_2e_2+r_3e_3\in n^\perp$ and $|u|=|r|=(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)/2$, because $e_1,e_2,e_3$ span $n^\perp$ and the norm of $u$ is the Euclidean norm of the spatial part by [F4]. By [F3] the displacements $q-e_-$ and $e_+-q$ are future null; hence the radar protocol applies with emission $e_-$, reflection $q$ and reception $e_+$ by [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 The radar assignments of clause (ii): by [F2] and step 2.1, $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac12\bigl(\tau(\lambda_-)+\tau(\lambda_+)\bigr)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac{c}{2}\bigl(\tau(\lambda_+)-\tau(\lambda_-)\bigr)$, and substituting the proper-time function of step 1.1 gives $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac{\lambda_-+\lambda_+}{2c}+const=\tfrac{x^0(q)}{c}+const$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)=\tfrac{c}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{c}=\tfrac{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}{2}=|r|$, where the additive constant is the same for all events measured by this observer. Hence the radar time is the chart time and the radar distance is the chart's rest-frame distance, up to the fixed additive constant of the following. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Clause (iii): by [F3] and step 2.1 the midpoint of the round trip is $m=\tfrac{e_-+e_+}{2}=x^{-1}\bigl(x^0(q),0,0,0\bigr)$, the displacement $q-m=u$ lies in $n^\perp$, and the rest distance in the slice $H(m,n)$ is $d_n(m,q)=|u|=|r|$, which equals $\rho_{\mathrm{rad}}(q)$ by step 3.1; and since $\tau_{\mathrm{rad}}$ differs from $x^0/c$ by a constant depending only on the observer, two events measured by this observer have equal radar times if and only if they have equal chart time $x^0$, so radar simultaneity coincides with chart simultaneity on the stated region. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Conclusion and scope: steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove (i) — the events $e_\pm$ lie on the observer's worldline and the two displacements are future null, so the operational protocol applies; steps 3.1 and 4.1 prove (ii) and (iii); clause (iv) is the honest qualification of the result: the deduction is conditional on the adopted ideal-clock and ideal-light postulates and the SI conventions, it identifies the operational content of inertial simultaneity as the two-way radar convention, and it asserts no one-way light-speed measurement without a synchronization convention, no empirical calibration and no result for accelerated, rotating or dispersive situations. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Conditional status.** The theorem is a conditional deduction inside the ideal model: the hypotheses are the adopted postulates, not experimental facts, and the conclusion is a statement about the model's own operational assignment. No measurement, calibration or statistical comparison is asserted, and the idealizations (exact proper-time readings, exact future null straight rays, instantaneous reflection) are part of the scope carried into every consumer.

- **What the symmetric split achieves.** The radar time $\tfrac12(\lambda_-+\lambda_+)/c$ is the half-sum of the emission and reception chart times, and the radar distance is half the round-trip light time times $c$; the theorem shows that these two-way quantities reproduce the chart's time coordinate and Euclidean rest distance. The one-way split into an outgoing and a returning light time is the symmetric convention fixed in [[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]] and is not measured independently.

## Statement

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be inertial frames whose bases are related by a boost along the common first spatial direction with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$:

$$e'_0=\gamma\Bigl(e_0+\frac{v}{c}e_1\Bigr),\qquad e'_1=\gamma\Bigl(e_1+\frac{v}{c}e_0\Bigr),\qquad e'_2=e_2,\qquad e'_3=e_3,$$

where $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, with charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]). Write the transition as

$$x'^0=\gamma\Bigl(x^0-\frac{v}{c}x^1\Bigr),\qquad x'^1=\gamma\Bigl(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0\Bigr),\qquad x'^2=x^2,\qquad x'^3=x^3.$$

Then:

**(i) Clock rate.** The straight worldline $y(\lambda):=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ (coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$, the worldline of a clock at rest in the frame $x'$) is future timelike, and the elapsed proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; equivalently $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ along $y$, where $t$ is the coordinate time of $x$.

**(ii) Length comparison.** For $L_0>0$ let $y_a,y_b$ be the two straight worldlines at rest in the frame $x'$ through the events with $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda,L_0,0,0)$. Then (a) at equal $x'$-times their $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$, while (b) at equal $x$-times their $x$-coordinate separation is $L_0/\gamma$, so the measuring frame $x$ assigns the length $L_0/\gamma$ to a rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$; (c) symmetrically, for two worldlines at rest in $x$ with $x$-separation $L_0$ the separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0/\gamma$. In each case the comparison uses events at equal time in the measuring frame; comparing equal times of the other frame is a different pair of events.

**(iii) Simultaneity.** If $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$; in particular simultaneity in the chart $x$ is not simultaneity in the chart $x'$ whenever $vL\ne0$.

**(iv) Velocity transformation.** Let $y:J\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline which in the chart $x$ is $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ with coordinate velocity $w(t):=r'(t)\in\mathbb R^3$, $|w(t)|<c$, and $\gamma_w:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. Then the coordinate velocity $w'$ of $y$ in the chart $x'$ is given by $w'_1=(w_1-v)/(1-vw_1/c^2)$ and $w'_\perp=w_\perp/\bigl(\gamma(1-vw_1/c^2)\bigr)$, the denominators being positive; moreover $|w'|<c$, and $|w'|=c$ exactly when $|w|=c$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two inertial frames of the affine Minkowski model with bases related by the boost above with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$, $c>0$, $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and their charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); the transition formulas displayed in the Statement ([[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]).

[F1] In the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the passive boost with parameter $\beta$ acts on coordinates by $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$, $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$, $x'^2=x^2$, $x'^3=x^3$; it is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse the boost with parameter $-\beta$, and $\gamma\ge1$ with equality exactly for $\beta=0$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[F2] A vector $u=u^0e_0+u^1e_1+u^2e_2+u^3e_3$ has $\eta(u,u)=-(u^0)^2+(u^1)^2+(u^2)^2+(u^3)^2$, and since the frame's first vector $e_0$ is future the component criterion holds: $u$ is future timelike if and only if $u^0>\sqrt{(u^1)^2+(u^2)^2+(u^3)^2}$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[F3] For $w=w^1e_1+w^2e_2+w^3e_3$, $|w|:=\sqrt{(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2}$ is the Euclidean norm of the spatial part of $w$ in the frame ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[F4] If $y$ is a $C^1$ future timelike worldline with proper-time function $\tau$, then for parameter values $a<b$ one has $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')}\,ds$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

[F5] If $y$ is $C^1$ with inertial coordinates $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ and $|r'(t)|<c$, then $r$ is $C^1$, $|r'(t)|<c$ pointwise, and $\gamma_w=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ is well defined and positive ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], [[def-derivative]]).

[F6] Chain rule and algebra of derivatives: the composite of $C^1$ maps is $C^1$ with the usual derivative, and finite sums, products and quotients with nonvanishing denominators of $C^1$ functions are $C^1$ ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[def-derivative]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Set $\beta:=v/c$, so $|\beta|<1$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}>0$, and record the transition in both directions: $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$, $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$, $x'^2=x^2$, $x'^3=x^3$ by [F1] with parameter $\beta$, and conversely $x^0=\gamma(x'^0+\beta x'^1)$, $x^1=\gamma(x'^1+\beta x'^0)$, $x^2=x'^2$, $x^3=x'^3$, because the boost with parameter $-\beta$ is the inverse of the boost with parameter $\beta$ by [F1]. A curve given in $x$-coordinates by $\lambda\mapsto(u^0(\lambda),u^1(\lambda),u^2(\lambda),u^3(\lambda))$ has tangent vector $E(u'(\lambda))$ at each $\lambda$ in the sense of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], and by [F2] a vector with components $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$ is future timelike exactly when $u^0>|(u^1,u^2,u^3)|_2$, where the spatial norm is that of [F3]. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Clock rate (i): the curve $y(\lambda)=x^{-1}(\lambda,\beta\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3)$ is $C^1$ with coordinate derivative $(1,\beta,0,0)$, so its tangent at every $\lambda$ is $e_0+\beta e_1$, whose components $(1,\beta,0,0)$ satisfy $1>|\beta|$; by step 1.1 the tangent is future timelike at every parameter value, so $y$ is a future timelike worldline. Its integrand is constant, $-\eta(y',y')=1-\beta^2=1/\gamma^2$, so $\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')}=1/\gamma$ and [F4] gives $\tau(\lambda_1)-\tau(\lambda_0)=c^{-1}\int_{\lambda_0}^{\lambda_1}(1/\gamma)\,d\lambda=(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$. Along $y$ the coordinate time of $x$ is $t=x^0/c=\lambda/c$, so $d\tau/dt=c\,d\tau/d\lambda=c/(c\gamma)=1/\gamma$, and the coordinate velocity of $y$ is $dr/dt=(dx^1/dt,dx^2/dt,dx^3/dt)=(v,0,0)$ because $dx^1/d\lambda=\beta$ and $\lambda=ct$. [F1, F4, step 1.1]

2.2 Length comparison (ii): a worldline at rest in $x'$ through $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,s,0,0)$ is $y_s(\lambda)=(x')^{-1}(\lambda,s,0,0)$; in $x$-coordinates it is, by the inverse transition of step 1.1, $\lambda\mapsto\bigl(\gamma(\lambda+\beta s),\gamma(s+\beta\lambda),0,0\bigr)$, because $x^0=\gamma(x'^0+\beta x'^1)$ and $x^1=\gamma(x'^1+\beta x'^0)$. For the two worldlines $y_a=y_0$ and $y_b=y_{L_0}$: (a) at the same $x'$-time $\lambda$ their $x'^1$-coordinates are $0$ and $L_0$, so the $x'$-separation is $L_0$. (b) At equal $x$-time $x^0=\tau$: for $y_a$ one has $\gamma(\lambda_a+0)=\tau$, hence $\lambda_a=\tau/\gamma$ and $x^1_a=\gamma(0+\beta\lambda_a)=\beta\tau$; for $y_b$ one has $\gamma(\lambda_b+\beta L_0)=\tau$, hence $\lambda_b=\tau/\gamma-\beta L_0$ and $x^1_b=\gamma\bigl(L_0+\beta(\tau/\gamma-\beta L_0)\bigr)=\gamma L_0(1-\beta^2)+\beta\tau=L_0/\gamma+\beta\tau$, using $\gamma(1-\beta^2)=1/\gamma$; therefore $x^1_b-x^1_a=L_0/\gamma$ for every $\tau$, which is the stated length assigned by the frame $x$ to the rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$. (c) Exchanging the roles of the two frames replaces $\beta$ by $-\beta$ in the same computation (the inverse transition of step 1.1 has parameter $-\beta$), so two worldlines at rest in $x$ with $x$-separation $L_0$ have $x'$-separation $L_0/\gamma$ at equal $x'$-times; also (a) and (b) refer to different pairs of events unless $\beta L_0=0$, as demanded by the statement. [F3, step 1.1]

2.3 Simultaneity (iii): if $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then applying the transition of step 1.1 componentwise gives $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=\gamma\bigl(0-\beta L\bigr)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$, since $x'$ is affine in $x$ with the displayed linear part; this is nonzero exactly when $vL\ne0$ because $\gamma>0$. [step 1.1]

2.4 Velocity transformation (iv): let $y:J\to A$ have $x$-coordinates $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ with $w=r'$ and $|w(t)|<c$ by [F5]. Composing with the transition map of step 1.1, which is linear and $C^\infty$, gives the $x'$-coordinates $x'^0(t)=\gamma\bigl(ct-\beta r_1(t)\bigr)$, $x'^1(t)=\gamma\bigl(r_1(t)-\beta ct\bigr)$, $x'^2(t)=r_2(t)$, $x'^3(t)=r_3(t)$; all four are $C^1$ in $t$ by [F6], and the $x'$-coordinate time is $t'=x'^0/c$. Its derivative is $dt'/dt=\gamma\bigl(c-\beta w_1\bigr)=\gamma c\bigl(1-\frac{vw_1}{c^2}\bigr)>0$, because $|w_1|\le|w|<c$ and $|v|<c$ give $|vw_1|/c^2<1$; hence $t\mapsto t'$ is strictly increasing with positive derivative, and the coordinate velocity $w'=d(x'_1,x'_2,x'_3)/dt'$ is well defined. The derivatives of the spatial coordinates are $dx'^1/dt=\gamma(w_1-\beta c)=\gamma(w_1-v)$, $dx'^2/dt=w_2$, $dx'^3/dt=w_3$, so dividing by $dt'/dt$ gives $w'_1=(w_1-v)/(1-vw_1/c^2)$ and $w'_2=w_2/\bigl(\gamma(1-vw_1/c^2)\bigr)$, $w'_3=w_3/\bigl(\gamma(1-vw_1/c^2)\bigr)$, which is the displayed formula for $w'_\perp$, the denominator being positive by the same bound. [F5, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 Subluminality of the transformed velocity: squaring the formulas of step 2.4 and multiplying by the positive factor $\bigl(1-\frac{vw_1}{c^2}\bigr)^2$ gives $\bigl(1-\frac{vw_1}{c^2}\bigr)^2\bigl(c^2-|w'|^2\bigr)=c^2\bigl(1-\frac{vw_1}{c^2}\bigr)^2-(w_1-v)^2-|w_\perp|^2\bigl(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\bigr)$, where $|w_\perp|^2=w_2^2+w_3^2$ and $1/\gamma^2=1-v^2/c^2$; expanding and using $|w|^2=w_1^2+|w_\perp|^2$ this equals $\bigl(c^2-|w|^2\bigr)\bigl(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\bigr)$. Hence $c^2-|w'|^2=\bigl(c^2-|w|^2\bigr)\bigl(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\bigr)\big/\bigl(1-\frac{vw_1}{c^2}\bigr)^2$, so with $|w|<c$ and $|v|<c$ both numerator factors are positive, $|w'|^2<c^2$ and therefore $|w'|<c$; conversely if $|w|=c$ the right-hand side vanishes and then $|w'|=c$, which is the asserted equality case. [step 2.4]

4.1 Conclusion: step 2.1 establishes (i) together with the equivalent rate $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$; step 2.2 establishes (ii)(a), (ii)(b) and (ii)(c) with the indicated pairs of events; step 2.3 establishes (iii); steps 2.4 and 3.1 establish (iv), including the positivity of the denominators, $|w'|<c$ and the equality case $|w'|=c\Leftrightarrow|w|=c$. This proves all four clauses of the Statement. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **The two computations use different hypotheses.** Clause (i) is the proper-time computation along a straight worldline with coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$; clause (iv) is the chain-rule computation along an arbitrary $C^1$ worldline with subluminal coordinate velocity. Clause (iv) does not assume that $y$ is straight, and clause (ii) makes no assertion about $y$.

- **The subluminality identity.** The identity proved in step 3.1, $c^2-|w'|^2=(c^2-|w|^2)(1-v^2/c^2)/(1-vw_1/c^2)^2$, is the coordinate form of the Lorentz invariance of the causal classification: the one-parameter factor in the numerator is linear in $(1-v^2/c^2)$, not quadratic, as one checks at $w=0$, where $|w'|=|v|$ and both sides must equal $c^2-v^2$.

## Statement

Adopt the ideal-clock and ideal-light assumptions of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and the inertial-covariance assumption of [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]], and the SI coordinate conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let the inertial frames and charts $x$, $x'$ related by a boost of parameter $v$ along the common first spatial direction be as in [[lem-sr-boost-time-length-and-velocity-formulas]], with $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$. Then, as statements about the ideal model and not about any actual apparatus:

**(i) Moving clocks run slow.** An ideal clock carried along the worldline $y(\lambda)=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ of clause (i) of the lemma reads between parameter values $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ the time $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$, and since the coordinate time of $x$ along $y$ is $t=\lambda/c$, this is $(t_1-t_0)/\gamma$; equivalently, between two events of the clock's history the coordinate time elapsed in $x$ is $\Delta t=\gamma\,\Delta\tau$, where $\Delta\tau$ is the clock's reading ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]). Symmetrically, with $x$ and $x'$ interchanged, a clock at rest in $x$ runs slow by the same factor in the frame $x'$.

**(ii) Length contraction.** For a rod at rest in the frame $x'$ of rest length $L_0>0$, with endpoints carried along the worldlines $y_a$, $y_b$ of clause (ii) of the lemma, the length assigned to it by the frame $x$ on a simultaneity slice of $x$ in the sense of [[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]] is $L_0/\gamma$; symmetrically, a rod at rest in $x$ has length $L_0/\gamma$ as measured by $x'$. Measured length here is defined by the stated protocol — the rest distance between the two endpoint events at equal time in the measuring frame — and it is not the optical appearance of a moving rod; no claim is made about a rod whose state of motion changes.

**(iii) Relativity of simultaneity.** If two events $p,q$ satisfy $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, with vanishing transverse coordinate difference, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\tfrac{v}{c}L$, which is nonzero whenever $vL\ne0$; hence simultaneity in $x$ is not simultaneity in $x'$ and is not an observer-independent relation. Each inertial frame's simultaneity is exactly the simultaneity relation of its time axis in the sense of [[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]], operationally reproduced by its radar protocol as established in [[pthm-sr-radar-synchronization-of-inertial-observers]].

**(iv) Velocity transformation.** For a $C^1$ future timelike worldline with coordinate velocity $w$ in the frame $x$, $|w|<c$, the coordinate velocity $w'$ in the frame $x'$ is

$$w'_1=\frac{w_1-v}{1-vw_1/c^2},\qquad w'_\perp=\frac{w_\perp}{\gamma\bigl(1-vw_1/c^2\bigr)},$$

so relative velocities are not simply added; moreover $|w'|<c$ whenever $|w|<c$. Equivalently, $w'$ is the velocity of the worldline relative to the observer with four-velocity direction $e'_0$ in the sense of clause (d) of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

**(v) Scope and qualification.** All clauses are conditional on the adopted ideal postulates (ideal clocks, ideal light, inertial covariance, flat spacetime) and on the stated measurement protocols. They carry no statistical or empirical claim; they say nothing about real clock errors, real rods, optical appearance, accelerating or deformable bodies, gravity or quantum effects; and they do not establish the exclusive truth of the model. The time, length and simultaneity assignments are protocol-relative: they involve the measuring frame and its simultaneity slice, which the radar theorem identifies operationally.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The adopted ideal-clock/ideal-light and inertial-covariance postulates and the SI conventions ([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]], [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]), two inertial frames with charts $x$, $x'$ related by the boost of parameter $v$, $|v|<c$, with $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and the data of clauses (i)-(iv) of the Statement ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[F1] Boost formulas ([[lem-sr-boost-time-length-and-velocity-formulas]]): (i) the worldline $y(\lambda)=x^{-1}(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3)$ is future timelike and its proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; (ii) for the worldlines $y_a,y_b$ at rest in $x'$ with $x'$-separation $L_0$, the $x'$-separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0$ while the $x$-separation at equal $x$-times is $L_0/\gamma$, and symmetrically with the frames interchanged; (iii) $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$, $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$ imply $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\tfrac{v}{c}L$; (iv) for a $C^1$ future timelike worldline with subluminal coordinate velocity $w$ in $x$, the coordinate velocity in $x'$ is $w'_1=(w_1-v)/(1-vw_1/c^2)$, $w'_\perp=w_\perp/\bigl(\gamma(1-vw_1/c^2)\bigr)$, and $|w'|<c$ when $|w|<c$.

[F2] Ideal clocks read proper time: an ideal clock carried along a $C^1$ future timelike curve reads between parameters $a<b$ the value $\sigma(b)-\sigma(a)=c^{-1}\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}\,ds$, with no acceleration-dependent term ([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] clause (i), [[def-sr-proper-time]]).

[F3] Radar theorem: for an inertial observer with chart $x$ and an event $q$ with nonzero spatial coordinates, the radar time is $x^0(q)/c$ and the radar distance is the chart's rest-frame distance $|r|$, up to the fixed additive constant of the observer's proper-time origin ([[pthm-sr-radar-synchronization-of-inertial-observers]], [[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]).

[F4] Simultaneity slices and rest distance: for a future unit $n$ and event $m$, $H(m,n)=\{z:\eta(n,z-m)=0\}$, and for $z\in H(m,n)$ the rest distance is $d_n(m,z)=\sqrt{\eta(z-m,z-m)}$ ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]). For the time axis $n=e_0$ of an inertial frame with chart $x$, $\eta(e_0,z-m)=-(x^0(z)-x^0(m))$, so $H(m,e_0)=\{z:x^0(z)=x^0(m)\}$ is the chart's simultaneity slice through $m$; and for two events at equal $x^0$ with spatial coordinate difference $\Delta r\in\mathbb R^3$, the rest distance is the Euclidean norm $|\Delta r|$ of [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]).

[F5] Observer-relative velocity: if $n$ is future unit timelike and $u$ is the unit four-velocity direction of a worldline, the relative velocity is $w=c\,h(u)/(-\eta(n,u))$ with $h(v)=v+\eta(n,v)n$, and in the chart of an inertial frame with time axis $n=e_0$ it coincides with the worldline's coordinate velocity in that chart ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clauses (c),(d),(e), [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

[F6] Inertial covariance: the framework's model equations have the same form under the inertial changes of description of [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]; in particular the boost relation between $x$ and $x'$ is such an inertial change of description, and the roles of the two frames in (i) and (ii) may be exchanged ([[lem-sr-boost-time-length-and-velocity-formulas]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Setup: the boost transition is $x'^0=\gamma\bigl(x^0-\tfrac{v}{c}x^1\bigr)$, $x'^1=\gamma\bigl(x^1-\tfrac{v}{c}x^0\bigr)$, $x'^2=x^2$, $x'^3=x^3$, and the inverse relation is the boost of parameter $-v$; the worldline $y$ of [F1](i) is a future timelike worldline carrying an ideal clock, and its coordinate time in $x$ is $t=\lambda/c$ by the SI convention $x^0=ct$ ([[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], [F1], [F2], [F6]). [F1, F2, F6]

1.2 Clause (i): by [F1](i) the proper time of $y$ between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$, and by [F2] the ideal clock carried along $y$ reads exactly this proper time; since $t$ runs from $\lambda_0/c$ to $\lambda_1/c$, the reading is $(t_1-t_0)/\gamma$. Writing $\Delta\tau:=(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$ for the clock's reading and $\Delta t:=t_1-t_0=\gamma\Delta\tau$, we obtain $\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau$. A clock at rest in $x$ is at rest in the primed frame at velocity $-v$, and the same computation applied to the inverse boost of parameter $-v$ gives the symmetric statement, so the factor is the same in both directions. [F1, F2, F6]

1.3 Clause (ii): let the rod at rest in $x'$ have endpoints on the worldlines $y_a,y_b$ of [F1](ii), whose $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$. At a fixed $x$-time the endpoints are two events with equal $x^0$ and $x$-separation $L_0/\gamma$ by [F1](ii); they lie in the simultaneity slice of $x$ through their midpoint in the sense of [F4], and their rest distance in that slice is the Euclidean norm of their spatial coordinate difference, namely $L_0/\gamma$. Since the measurement protocol of clause (ii) assigns to the rod exactly the rest distance between the endpoint events at equal measuring-frame time, the length assigned by $x$ is $L_0/\gamma$. Exchanging the roles of $x$ and $x'$ in [F1](ii) and repeating the argument gives the symmetric statement; the rod is modelled by two straight worldlines at rest in the measuring frame's complement, so the computation applies only to a rod in uniform motion and never to a rod whose state of motion changes. [F1, F4, F6]

1.4 Clause (iii): by [F1](iii), events with equal $x^0$ and first-coordinate separation $L$ have $x'^0$-difference $-\gamma\tfrac{v}{c}L$, which is nonzero exactly when $vL\ne0$, so the two events are not simultaneous in $x'$; this exhibits the observer dependence of simultaneity. Chart simultaneity is equality of $x^0$, which by [F4] is exactly the slice relation $H(m,e_0)$ of the frame's time axis; and by [F3] the radar protocol of the inertial observer reproduces $x^0/c$ and the chart distance on events with nonzero spatial coordinates, so these simultaneity slices have the stated operational content. [F1, F3, F4]

1.5 Clause (iv): apply [F1](iv) to the worldline of the clause, which is $C^1$ future timelike with subluminal coordinate velocity $w$ in $x$; this gives the displayed transformation and $|w'|<c$ whenever $|w|<c$. For the identification of $w'$ as a relative velocity, [F5] with $n=e'_0$ and $u=U/c$ gives $w_{\mathrm{rel}}=c\,h'(U/c)/(-\eta(e'_0,U/c))$, and clause (e) of [F5] states that for the chart of the frame this coincides with the coordinate velocity in that chart, namely $w'$. Finally, the deviation from the Galilean sum is exact: $w'_1-(w_1-v)=\frac{(vw_1/c^2)(w_1-v)}{1-vw_1/c^2}$ by a single algebraic simplification of the displayed formula, so the transformation coincides with the difference $w_1-v$ exactly when $v=0$ or $w_1=0$ or $w_1=v$, and not in general. [F1, F5]

2.1 Conclusion and scope: steps 1.2, 1.3, 1.4 and 1.5 establish clauses (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) as statements about the ideal model, each derived from the mathematical content of [F1] together with the adopted ideal-clock reading [F2], the radar identification [F3] and the observer-relative velocity identification [F5]; the symmetric halves of (i) and (ii) use the inverse boost as in [F6]. Clause (v) records the honest qualification: the deduction is conditional on the adopted postulates and stated protocols, it produces no measurement outcome, no statistical inference and no empirical comparison, it says nothing about real clocks, rods, optical appearance, accelerating or deformable bodies, gravity or quantum effects, and it does not establish the exclusive truth of the model; the assignments are intrinsic to the measuring frame and its simultaneity slice. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5] ∎

## Remarks

- **Conditional reading, not empirical claim.** The theorem converts mathematical coordinate statements of [[lem-sr-boost-time-length-and-velocity-formulas]] into the operational language of ideal clocks, rods and radar signals exactly under the adopted postulates of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. It is a conditional deduction about the model; agreement of any apparatus with it would be evidence about the model, not a proof of the postulates.

- **Length is slice-dependent; appearance is not claimed.** The contracted length $L_0/\gamma$ refers to the endpoint events at equal time in the measuring frame, so it is the rest distance in that frame's simultaneity slice by [[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]. No light-travel-time or photographic statement is made, and the two frames assign their different lengths to different pairs of events on the same two worldlines.

- **The velocity transformation is not a sum.** The exact identity $w'_1-(w_1-v)=\frac{(vw_1/c^2)(w_1-v)}{1-vw_1/c^2}$ shows precisely when the Galilean difference is recovered, namely when $v=0$, $w_1=0$ or $w_1=v$, and exhibits the correction factor $1-vw_1/c^2$ otherwise; the transverse component is additionally scaled by $1/\gamma$.

## Definition

Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline with four-velocity $U=dx/d\tau$ and four-acceleration $A=dU/d\tau$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), so that $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]), and let $X:I\to V$ be a $C^1$ field along $x$ ([[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]]).

**(a) Fermi–Walker derivative.** The **Fermi–Walker derivative of $X$** is

$$\frac{D_{\mathrm{FW}}X}{d\tau}:=X'-\frac{1}{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr),$$

where $X'$ is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative of $X$, which is the covariant derivative of $X$ along $x$ in the flat model ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]], clause (d)). The field $X$ is **Fermi–Walker transported along $x$** when $D_{\mathrm{FW}}X/d\tau=0$, that is, when

$$X'=\frac{1}{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr).$$

**(b) The four-velocity is Fermi–Walker transported.** Substituting $X=U$ and using $\eta(A,U)=0$ and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ gives $D_{\mathrm{FW}}U/d\tau=U'-c^{-2}\bigl(\eta(A,U)U-\eta(U,U)A\bigr)=A-A=0$.

**(c) Comparison with parallel transport.** If $A=0$ on an interval $J\subseteq I$, then on $J$ the Fermi–Walker equation reduces to $X'=0$ and coincides with ordinary parallel transport; if $A$ is not zero, the definition includes exactly the correction that also transports the time leg $U/c$ along the worldline.

**(d) Fermi–Walker transported tetrad.** A **Fermi–Walker transported tetrad along $x$** is a tuple $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ of $C^1$ fields along $x$ with $E_0=U/c$ and with every $E_a$ Fermi–Walker transported along $x$. Existence from a prescribed initial tetrad and preservation of the tetrad conditions under this transport are proved in the following lemma. The physical interpretation as a nonrotating spatial frame carried by an accelerated observer is not asserted here; only the transport rule is defined.

## Remarks

- **Well-definedness.** For a $C^2$ worldline the fields $U$ and $A$ are continuous and $U$ is nowhere zero, so the coefficients $\eta(A,\cdot)/c^2$ and $\eta(U,\cdot)/c^2$ of the transport equation are continuous functions along $x$; the equation $X'=c^{-2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr)$ is therefore a first-order linear differential equation for the $V$-valued field $X$ ([[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]], [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]], clause (d)). This definition fixes the rule and does not assert that solutions exist; existence, uniqueness and the preservation of the tetrad conditions are the content of the following lemma.

- **Clause (b) is a computation, not a definition.** The two identities used, $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$, are clauses (a) and (b) of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]; the cancellation displayed in (b) is then immediate from the bilinearity of $\eta$. The definition deliberately introduces no norm or orthogonality claim of its own.

- **Fermi–Walker transport of tensors along a worldline.** The same rule may be applied to any $C^1$ tensor field along $x$ by subtracting the covariant derivatives of all tensor arguments ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]); in this framework only the vector case with the fields $E_a$ and the four-velocity is used, and no additional structure (connection coefficients, Christoffel symbols, curvature) is needed because the model's covariant derivative along a curve is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative.

## Statement

Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$ and four-acceleration $A$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), let $\tau_0\in I$ and $X_0\in V$. Then there is exactly one $C^1$ field $X:I\to V$ along $x$ with $D_{\mathrm{FW}}X/d\tau=0$ and $X(\tau_0)=X_0$ ([[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]]); if $x$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$ then $X$ is $C^{k-1}$. The map $X_0\mapsto X$, from $V$ to the $C^1$ fields along $x$ satisfying the transport equation, is linear. Consequently, for every tetrad $(E_0(\tau_0),\dots,E_3(\tau_0))$ at $x(\tau_0)$ with $E_0(\tau_0)=U(\tau_0)/c$ there is a unique tuple of Fermi–Walker transported fields with those initial values; whether that tuple remains a tetrad at every time is proved in the following item.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $C^2$ future timelike worldline $x:I\to A$ with four-velocity $U$ and four-acceleration $A$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), a parameter $\tau_0\in I$, an initial vector $X_0\in V$, and the Fermi–Walker transport equation of [[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]].

[F1] The Fermi–Walker derivative is $D_{\mathrm{FW}}X/d\tau=X'-c^{-2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr)$, where $X'$ is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative of the field $X$ along $x$, equal to the covariant derivative along $x$ in the flat model ([[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]], [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] clause (d), [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]).

[F2] In the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ of an inertial frame, write $X=X^ae_a$, $U=U^ae_a$, $A=A^ae_a$ and $A_b=\eta_{bc}A^c$, $U_b=\eta_{bc}U^c$. Then $\eta(A,X)=A_bX^b$ and $\eta(U,X)=U_bX^b$, and the transport equation $D_{\mathrm{FW}}X/d\tau=0$ is equivalent to the linear system $X'^a=M^a{}_bX^b$ with $M^a{}_b=c^{-2}\bigl(U^aA_b-A^aU_b\bigr)$ ([[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]], [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[F3] If $x$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$, then $U$ is $C^{k-1}$ and $A$ is $C^{k-2}$: $U=c\,x'/\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$ and $\tau'=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$ are quotients of $C^{k-1}$ functions with nonvanishing denominator, and $A=U'/\tau'$ is a quotient of $C^{k-2}$ functions ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). Consequently, if $x$ is $C^2$ then $M$ is continuous, and if $x$ is $C^k$ then $M$ is $C^{k-2}$.

[F4] Linear matrix ODEs on a compact interval: for $I_0=[a,b]$ compact, $C:I_0\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ continuous, $t_0\in I_0$ and $Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$, the problem $Y'=C(t)Y$, $Y(t_0)=Y_0$ has a unique solution on all of $I_0$ ([[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]).

[F5] Maximal solutions: a first-order initial value problem with continuous, locally state-Lipschitz right-hand side has a unique maximal solution, whose domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]], [[def-maximal-ode-solution]]).

[F6] Calculus closure: sums, products, quotients with nonvanishing denominators and compositions of $C^j$ maps are $C^j$, with the usual derivative formulas ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[def-derivative]]).

[F7] An order-convex subset $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with at least two elements is an interval: for $s,t\in I$ the whole segment between them lies in $I$, so for any $\tau\in I$ the compact interval with endpoints $\tau_0$ and $\tau$ is contained in $I$ ([[def-interval]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Work in the inertial chart of one inertial frame and identify $V$ with $\mathbb R^4$ by its ordered basis, so that fields along $x$ are $\mathbb R^4$-valued functions; by [F1] and [F2] the transport equation is the linear system $X'=M(\tau)X$ with coefficient matrix $M^a{}_b(\tau)=c^{-2}(U^a(\tau)A_b(\tau)-A^a(\tau)U_b(\tau))$. By [F3] the entries of $M$ are continuous when $x$ is $C^2$, so $M:I\to M_4(\mathbb R)$ is a continuous matrix-valued function on the interval $I$; and if $x$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$ then $U$ is $C^{k-1}$ and $A$ is $C^{k-2}$, so $M$ is $C^{k-2}$. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Fundamental solution on $I$: let $\tau\in I$ and let $I_{\tau}$ be the compact interval with endpoints $\tau_0$ and $\tau$, which is contained in $I$ by [F7] and contains $\tau_0$; by [F4] applied with $n=4$, the matrix problem $\Phi'=M\Phi$, $\Phi(\tau_0)=I_4$ has a unique solution $\Phi_{I_\tau}$ on $I_\tau$. If $I_{\tau'}$ is another such compact interval, the two solutions agree on $I_\tau\cap I_{\tau'}$ (both restrict to solutions of the same matrix problem on that compact interval, which is an interval containing $\tau_0$ and $\tau$ as above, and [F4] gives uniqueness there), so the assignment $\Phi(\tau):=\Phi_{I_\tau}(\tau)$ is well defined; it does not depend on the chosen interval, and different intervals overlap in a neighbourhood of every common point. The resulting map $\Phi:I\to M_4(\mathbb R)$ satisfies $\Phi(\tau_0)=I_4$ and, on every compact subinterval of $I$ containing $\tau_0$ and hence at every point of $I$ in the domain-relative sense, $\Phi'(\tau)=M(\tau)\Phi(\tau)$. No choice principle is used: $\Phi$ is defined by the common value of solutions, which is unique. [F4, F7, step 1.1]

3.1 Uniqueness of the vector initial value problem: let $\tilde X:I\to V$ be a $C^1$ solution of $X'=MX$ on $I$ with $\tilde X(\tau_0)=X_0$. Let $\delta$ be the $4\times4$ matrix with $\delta^1{}_1=1$ and all other entries $0$, and let $\Psi(\tau)$ be the matrix with entries $\Psi^a{}_b(\tau)=\tilde X^a(\tau)\delta^1{}_b$, i.e. the matrix whose first column is $\tilde X(\tau)$ and whose remaining columns vanish. Then $\Psi$ is $C^1$ and $\Psi'^a{}_b=\tilde X'^a\delta^1{}_b=(M\tilde X)^a\delta^1{}_b=M^a{}_c\tilde X^c\delta^1{}_b=(M\Psi)^a{}_b$, so $\Psi'=M\Psi$, and $\Psi(\tau_0)$ is the matrix $X_0\delta$ with first column $X_0$. On the other hand $\Phi(X_0\delta)$ also solves the matrix problem $Y'=MY$, $Y(\tau_0)=X_0\delta$, because $(\Phi X_0\delta)'=\Phi'(X_0\delta)=M\Phi X_0\delta$ by step 2.1 and the derivative of a constant matrix factor; by the uniqueness in [F4] on every compact subinterval of $I$ containing $\tau_0$ (to which both sides restrict as solutions), $\Psi=\Phi(X_0\delta)$ on $I$. Comparing first columns gives $\tilde X=\Phi X_0$. In particular any two solutions of the vector problem with the same initial value agree on $I$, since each equals $\Phi X_0$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Existence and linearity: with $\Phi$ as in step 2.1 and $X:=\Phi X_0$, the field $X$ is $C^1$, satisfies $X'=\Phi'X_0=M\Phi X_0=MX$ and $X(\tau_0)=\Phi(\tau_0)X_0=X_0$; hence $X$ is a $C^1$ solution on $I$ of the transport equation with initial value $X_0$, and step 3.1 shows that it is the only one; by [F5] the maximal solution of the system is defined on an open interval containing the initial time and every other solution through the same data is its restriction, so the solution $X$ on $I$ is the maximal one and uniqueness holds on $I$. Since matrix multiplication is linear in its second factor, the map $X_0\mapsto X=\Phi X_0$ is linear from $V$ to the space of $C^1$ fields along $x$ satisfying the transport equation. [F5, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Regularity: assume $x$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$, so that $M$ is $C^{k-2}$ by step 1.1, and let $X$ be the solution of step 4.1, which satisfies $X'=MX$. One proves by induction on $j=1,\dots,k-2$ that $X$ is $C^j$: for $j=1$ this is step 4.1; if $X$ is $C^j$ with $j\le k-2$, then the product $MX$ is $C^j$ by [F6], because $M$ is $C^{k-2}$ and $j\le k-2$; hence $X'=MX$ is $C^j$, so $X$ is $C^{j+1}$. The induction ends at $j=k-2$, giving that $X$ is $C^{k-1}$. [F6, step 1.1, step 4.1]

5.2 The initial-tetrad clause: let $E_0(\tau_0),\dots,E_3(\tau_0)$ be a tetrad at $x(\tau_0)$ with $E_0(\tau_0)=U(\tau_0)/c$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]). By steps 4.1 and 3.1, for each $a$ there is exactly one $C^1$ Fermi–Walker transported field $E_a:I\to V$ along $x$ with $E_a(\tau_0)$ equal to the prescribed value. For $a=0$ the field $U/c$ is $C^1$, satisfies $D_{\mathrm{FW}}(U/c)/d\tau=0$ by clause (b) of [[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]], and has the same initial value $U(\tau_0)/c$; by the uniqueness of step 3.1, $E_0=U/c$. Hence there is a unique tuple of Fermi–Walker transported fields with the prescribed initial values, and its time component is the four-velocity up to the factor $1/c$. [step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Conclusion: step 4.1 and step 3.1 establish existence, uniqueness and linearity in the initial value for the $C^1$ solution of the Fermi–Walker transport equation on $I$; step 5.1 establishes the $C^{k-1}$ regularity when the worldline is $C^k$ with $k\ge2$ (in particular $C^1$ when $k=2$); and step 5.2 establishes the uniquely determined tuple with prescribed tetrad initial values and identifies its time component as $U/c$. Whether such a tuple remains a tetrad at every time is not claimed here and is proved in the following item. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **Where the linear ODE supplier is used.** The only analytic input is the global existence and uniqueness theorem for linear matrix systems on compact intervals, [[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]; the passage from compact subintervals to the whole parameter interval $I$ is made by patching, and uniqueness is obtained by encoding the vector equation as a matrix equation with a rank-one initial matrix. The maximal-solution formulation of the same argument is available through [[def-maximal-ode-solution]] and [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]: the right-hand side $F(\tau,X)=M(\tau)X$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in $X$ on the open domain containing $\{(\tau,X):\tau\in I\}$, and the maximal solution there coincides with the field constructed above on $I$.

## Statement

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of $A$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(i) Flow box.** If $X$ is a smooth vector field on $\Omega$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]) and $X(p)\ne0$ at a point $p\in\Omega$, then there is an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ in $\Omega$ and a chart $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3):U\to\mathbb R^4$ in which $X=\partial/\partial u^0$; the integral curves of $X$ in $U$ are therefore the $u^0$-coordinate lines up to reparametrization. In particular every observer congruence $n$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]) admits a local $n$-adapted chart, and in such a chart $n=\partial/\partial u^0$.

**(ii) Frobenius criterion.** For a smooth nowhere-zero one-form $\alpha$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]) let $D:=\ker\alpha$ be the hyperplane distribution $D_p=\{v\in V:\alpha_p(v)=0\}$. Then $D$ is integrable on $\Omega$ (through every point there passes a local hypersurface whose tangent space at each of its points is the corresponding $D_p$) if and only if $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $\Omega$ ([[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]]).

**(iii) Rest distributions of observer congruences.** Let $n$ be an observer congruence on $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]), let $\alpha:=n^\flat$, and let $\theta,\omega$ be its expansion and vorticity ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]). Then:

(a) $d\alpha=2\nabla_{[a}n_{b]}$, that is, $d\alpha(X,Y)=(\nabla_Xn^\flat)(Y)-(\nabla_Yn^\flat)(X)$ for smooth vector fields $X,Y$;

(b) for every $p$ and all $X,Y$ with $\alpha(X)=\alpha(Y)=0$ one has $d\alpha(X,Y)=2\omega(X,Y)$; consequently $(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)(p)=0$ if and only if $\omega(p)=0$, and on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega$ the following are equivalent: $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $U$, $\omega=0$ on $U$, and the rest distribution $\ker\alpha$ is integrable on $U$;

(c) when the rest distribution is integrable on $U$, its integral hypersurfaces are orthogonal to $n$ at every point and the restriction of $\eta$ to each of them is positive definite, so they are rest slices of the congruence.

**(iv) Scope.** All statements are local on $\Omega$; no global foliation, global synchronization, completeness or product structure is asserted, and no claim is made about variable-rank or non-smooth distributions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty open subset $\Omega$ of the affine Minkowski space $A$, the smooth structure of the inertial atlas, a smooth vector field $X$ on $\Omega$, a smooth nowhere-zero one-form $\alpha$ on $\Omega$, an observer congruence $n$ on $\Omega$ with $\alpha=n^\flat$, $n_b=\eta_{bc}n^c$, and its kinematic fields $\theta,\omega$ ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]], [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], [[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]).

[F1] Flow box: if $X$ is a smooth vector field on a smooth manifold $M$ and $X_p\ne0$, then there are local coordinates $(u^1,\dots,u^n)$ near $p$ in which $X=\partial/\partial u^1$ ([[thm-flow-box-theorem]]).

[F2] Codimension-one Frobenius: for a nowhere-zero one-form $\alpha$ on a smooth manifold, the hyperplane distribution $\ker\alpha$ is integrable if and only if $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ ([[cor-codimension-one-frobenius-criterion]], [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]]).

[F3] The flat covariant derivative is torsion-free, $\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$, is metric compatible, acts on functions as the directional derivative and satisfies the product rule; in inertial components $\nabla_a=\partial_a$ on components and $[X,Y]^a=X^b\partial_bY^a-Y^b\partial_bX^a$ ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]], [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]).

[F4] For a smooth one-form $\alpha$ and smooth vector fields $X,Y$, $d\alpha(X,Y)=X(\alpha(Y))-Y(\alpha(X))-\alpha([X,Y])$, and $d\alpha$ is a smooth two-form with components $d\alpha_{ab}=\partial_a\alpha_b-\partial_b\alpha_a$ in any inertial chart ([[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]).

[F5] Kinematics of the congruence: $\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab}$ with $\theta$ symmetric, $\omega$ antisymmetric, both horizontal, and $a_b=\nabla_nn_b$ ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]).

[F6] $n(p)^\perp=\{v:\eta(n(p),v)=0\}$ is three-dimensional, the restriction of $\eta$ to it is positive definite, the projection is $h(v)=v+\eta(n,v)n$, and $\alpha(v)=\eta(n,v)$ vanishes exactly on $n(p)^\perp$; $n$ is nowhere zero because $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Flow box and adapted charts: the flat model with its inertial atlas is a smooth 4-manifold ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth vector field on the open set $\Omega$, so [F1] applied on this manifold gives coordinates $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$ on an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ with $X=\partial/\partial u^0$. In such a chart the coordinate representation of a curve $\gamma$ in $U$ satisfies $\gamma'=X\circ\gamma$ if and only if $(u^a\circ\gamma)'=\delta^a_0$ for every $a$, i.e. if and only if $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant and $u^0\circ\gamma$ is affine; hence the integral curves of $X$ in $U$ are exactly the $u^0$-coordinate lines, up to reparametrization. If $n$ is an observer congruence, then $n$ is nowhere zero by [F6], so applying the flow box to $X=n$ produces a chart with $n=\partial/\partial u^0$ in which $u^1,u^2,u^3$ are constant along every integral curve of $n$ contained in $U$; this is precisely an $n$-adapted chart in the sense of [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]] clause (d). [F1, F6]

1.2 Frobenius criterion: the one-form $\alpha$ is smooth by hypothesis and nowhere zero, and $\ker\alpha$ is a hyperplane distribution by definition; [F2] gives immediately that $\ker\alpha$ is integrable on $\Omega$ if and only if $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $\Omega$. [F2]

1.3 The exterior derivative of the metric dual (iii)(a): let $X,Y$ be smooth vector fields on $\Omega$. By [F4], $d\alpha(X,Y)=X(\alpha(Y))-Y(\alpha(X))-\alpha([X,Y])$; here $\alpha(Y)=n_bY^b$ and $\alpha(X)=n_bX^b$, and with [F3] the product rule gives $X(n_bY^b)=(\nabla_Xn_b)Y^b+n_b\nabla_XY^b$ and $Y(n_bX^b)=(\nabla_Yn_b)X^b+n_b\nabla_YX^b$, while torsion-freeness gives $\alpha([X,Y])=n_b(\nabla_XY^b-\nabla_YX^b)$. Substituting, the terms $n_b\nabla_XY^b$ and $n_b\nabla_YX^b$ cancel and $d\alpha(X,Y)=(\nabla_Xn_b)Y^b-(\nabla_Yn_b)X^b=(\nabla_an_b-\nabla_bn_a)X^aY^b$; since $\nabla n$ is a tensor, this is the component identity $d\alpha_{ab}=\nabla_an_b-\nabla_bn_a=2\nabla_{[a}n_{b]}$. [F3, F4]

2.1 The horizontal form of $d\alpha$ (iii)(b), first part: let $X,Y$ satisfy $\alpha(X)=\alpha(Y)=0$ at every point, so that $X,Y$ take values in the pointwise rest spaces by [F6]. By step 1.3, $d\alpha(X,Y)=2\nabla_{[a}n_{b]}X^aY^b$, and by [F5] $\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab}$; substituting the decomposition, the $n\otimes a$ terms contribute $(n_aa_b-n_ba_a)X^aY^b$, which vanishes because $a_bY^b=\eta(a,Y)=0$ (the acceleration is horizontal and $Y$ is horizontal) and $a_aX^a=\eta(a,X)=0$; the $\theta$ contribution is $(\theta_{ab}-\theta_{ba})X^aY^b=0$ because $\theta$ is symmetric; and the $\omega$ contribution is $(\omega_{ab}-\omega_{ba})X^aY^b=2\omega_{ab}X^aY^b$ because $\omega$ is antisymmetric. Hence $d\alpha(X,Y)=2\omega(X,Y)$ for horizontal $X,Y$. [F5, F6, step 1.3]

3.1 The wedge condition (iii)(b), equivalence: let $p\in\Omega$ and let $(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ be a basis of $V$ with $v_0:=n(p)$ and $v_1,v_2,v_3\in n(p)^\perp$. At $p$ one has $\alpha(v_0)=\eta(n,n)=-1$ and $\alpha(v_i)=0$ for $i\ge1$ by [F6]; every $u\in V$ decomposes as $u=-\alpha(u)n(p)+h(u)$ with $h(u)\in n(p)^\perp$ by [F6]. Since $\alpha\wedge d\alpha$ is a three-form, it is determined by its values on basis triples: $(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)(v_0,v_i,v_j)=-d\alpha(v_i,v_j)=-2\omega(v_i,v_j)$ by alternation and step 2.1, $(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)(v_i,v_j,v_k)=0$ because all three arguments are horizontal and $\alpha$ vanishes on them, and every triple with a repeated argument vanishes by alternation. Hence $\alpha\wedge d\alpha$ vanishes at $p$ if and only if $\omega(v_i,v_j)=0$ for all $i,j\ge1$, which by horizontality of $\omega$ is equivalent to $\omega(p)=0$. Passing to the open set $U\subseteq\Omega$: $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ on $U$ if and only if $\omega=0$ on $U$ by the pointwise statement, and $\omega=0$ on $U$ if and only if $\ker\alpha$ is integrable on $U$ by steps 2.1 and 1.2, since $\ker\alpha$ is integrable exactly when $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$ there. [F2, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 Integral hypersurfaces are rest slices (iii)(c): suppose $\ker\alpha$ is integrable on $U$ and let $S\subseteq U$ be an integral hypersurface, so that $T_qS=\ker\alpha_q=\{v:\alpha_q(v)=0\}$ for every $q\in S$. Since $\alpha_q(v)=\eta(n(q),v)$, we have $T_qS=n(q)^\perp$ by [F6]; hence $n(q)$ is $\eta$-orthogonal to $T_qS$, and the restriction of $\eta$ to $T_qS=n(q)^\perp$ is positive definite by [F6]. Thus each integral hypersurface is a rest slice of the congruence in the sense of the pointwise orthogonal hyperplanes, with no global foliation asserted. [F6, step 3.1]

5.1 Conclusion: step 1.1 proves (i), including the existence of local adapted charts for an observer congruence with $n=\partial/\partial u^0$; step 1.2 proves (ii) as a direct application of the codimension-one Frobenius criterion; step 1.3 proves (iii)(a); steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the horizontal identity $d\alpha(X,Y)=2\omega(X,Y)$ and the equivalence of $\alpha\wedge d\alpha=0$, $\omega=0$ and integrability of the rest distribution on an open set; step 4.1 proves (iii)(c); and the scope clause (iv) is respected throughout, since every statement is local on $\Omega$ and none of the arguments uses a global foliation, completeness, or a variable-rank or non-smooth distribution. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎
