## Example

In the inertial chart $(x^0,x,y,z)$ with metric $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ consider $\Phi(\theta,\rho,y,z):=(\rho\sinh\theta,\rho\cosh\theta,y,z)$ on $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$, with $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\rho>0$. Then:

(a) the identities $x^2-(x^0)^2=\rho^2$ and $x=\rho\cosh\theta>0$ show that the image of $\Phi$ is the right wedge $W=\{x>|x^0|\}$, and the inverse $\rho=\sqrt{x^2-(x^0)^2}$, $\theta=\tfrac12\log\bigl((x+x^0)/(x-x^0)\bigr)$ is smooth on $W$; both maps are smooth, so $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism onto $W$;

(b) differentiating gives $dx^0=\sinh\theta\,d\rho+\rho\cosh\theta\,d\theta$ and $dx=\cosh\theta\,d\rho+\rho\sinh\theta\,d\theta$, so the pullback metric is $-\rho^2d\theta^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$;

(c) the field $n:=\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta$ satisfies $\eta(n,n)=-1$ and is future; computing with the pullback metric, the nonzero connection coefficients are $\Gamma^\rho_{\theta\theta}=\rho$ and $\Gamma^\theta_{\theta\rho}=\Gamma^\theta_{\rho\theta}=1/\rho$, so $\nabla_{\partial_\theta}\partial_\theta=\rho\,\partial_\rho$ and the congruence acceleration is $a=\nabla_nn=\rho^{-1}\partial_\rho$ with $\eta(a,a)=1/\rho^2$; for example at $\rho=2$ one has $|a|=1/2$ in reciprocal-length units;

(d) the slices $\theta=const$ are hyperplanes through the origin with induced metric $d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$, independent of $\theta$; hence the congruence is Born rigid, and it is irrotational because its rest distribution is the tangent distribution of these slices;

(e) the tetrad field $(n,\partial_\rho,\partial_y,\partial_z)$ is not a coordinate frame, since $[n,\partial_\rho]=[\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta,\partial_\rho]=+\rho^{-2}\partial_\theta=+(1/\rho)n$ is nonzero, whereas the members of a coordinate frame commute.

This realizes the Rindler congruence of [[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (b) with exact formulas.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The inertial chart of the affine Minkowski model with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), the map $\Phi(\theta,\rho,y,z)=(\rho\sinh\theta,\rho\cosh\theta,y,z)$ defined on $\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$, and the field $n=\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta$.

[L1] Hyperbolic functions: $\cosh^2s-\sinh^2s=1$, $\cosh s>|\sinh s|$ for all real $s$, $\sinh'=\cosh$, $\cosh'=\sinh$, and $\tanh=\sinh/\cosh$ ([[def-hyperbolic-functions]], [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]).

[L2] Future timelike criterion and units: in the inertial chart a vector with components $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$ is future timelike exactly when $-(u^0)^2+(u^1)^2+(u^2)^2+(u^3)^2<0$ and $u^0>0$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L3] Kinematics and Frobenius: the acceleration $a$ of a congruence, its expansion $\theta$ and vorticity $\omega$ satisfy $\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab}$ with $\theta,\omega$ horizontal; Born rigidity is $\theta=0$; and the rest distribution is integrable on an open set if and only if $\omega=0$ there ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]], [[thm-sr-local-congruence-adapted-charts-and-frobenius]] clauses (ii),(iii)).

[L4] Lie bracket: $[fX,Y]=f[X,Y]-Y(f)X$ and coordinate frame members commute, $[\partial_a,\partial_b]=0$ ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]).

[L5] Diffeomorphisms: a smooth bijection with smooth inverse between open subsets is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Bijection and inverse: $\Phi$ is smooth because its components are sums of smooth functions of $(\theta,\rho,y,z)$ by [L1]. For $(\theta,\rho,y,z)$ in the domain one has $x^2-(x^0)^2=\rho^2(\cosh^2\theta-\sinh^2\theta)=\rho^2$ and $x=\rho\cosh\theta>0$, so $\Phi$ maps into $W$. Conversely, given $(x^0,x,y,z)$ with $x>|x^0|$, put $\rho:=\sqrt{x^2-(x^0)^2}>0$ and $\theta:=\frac12\log\bigl((x+x^0)/(x-x^0)\bigr)\in\mathbb R$ (the argument of the logarithm being positive because $x\pm x^0>0$); then $e^{\theta}=\sqrt{(x+x^0)/(x-x^0)}$ and $e^{-\theta}=\sqrt{(x-x^0)/(x+x^0)}$, so $\rho\sinh\theta=\rho(e^\theta-e^{-\theta})/2=\frac{(x+x^0)-(x-x^0)}{2}=x^0$ and $\rho\cosh\theta=\rho(e^\theta+e^{-\theta})/2=\frac{(x+x^0)+(x-x^0)}{2}=x$ by [L1], which also shows the inverse is smooth. Hence $\Phi$ is a smooth bijection onto $W$ with smooth inverse, that is, a diffeomorphism by [L5]. [L1, L5]

2.1 Pullback metric: differentiating the four components of $\Phi$ and using [L1] gives $dx^0=\sinh\theta\,d\rho+\rho\cosh\theta\,d\theta$, $dx=\cosh\theta\,d\rho+\rho\sinh\theta\,d\theta$, $dy=dy$, $dz=dz$. Substituting into $-(dx^0)^2+(dx)^2+dy^2+dz^2$: the cross terms are $-2\rho\sinh\theta\cosh\theta+2\rho\cosh\theta\sinh\theta=0$, the $d\theta^2$ coefficient is $-\rho^2\cosh^2\theta+\rho^2\sinh^2\theta=-\rho^2$ and the $d\rho^2$ coefficient is $-\sinh^2\theta+\cosh^2\theta=1$; hence the pullback metric is $-\rho^2d\theta^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$. [L1, step 1.1]

3.1 Unit future field: in these coordinates $g(\partial_\theta,\partial_\theta)=-\rho^2$, $g(\partial_\rho,\partial_\rho)=g(\partial_y,\partial_y)=g(\partial_z,\partial_z)=1$ and all mixed components vanish, so $n=\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta$ satisfies $g(n,n)=-\rho^2\cdot\rho^{-2}=-1$. In the inertial chart, $\partial_\theta=\rho(\cosh\theta\,\partial_0+\sinh\theta\,\partial_1)$ by step 2.1, hence $n=\cosh\theta\,\partial_0+\sinh\theta\,\partial_1$, whose time component is $\cosh\theta>0$ and whose $\eta$-square is $-\cosh^2\theta+\sinh^2\theta=-1$; by [L2] $n$ is future timelike, so $n$ is a congruence on $W$. [L1, L2, step 2.1]

4.1 Acceleration: the inverse metric has components $g^{\theta\theta}=-\rho^{-2}$, $g^{\rho\rho}=1$, $g^{yy}=g^{zz}=1$; the Christoffel formula gives $\Gamma^\rho_{\theta\theta}=\tfrac12g^{\rho\rho}\bigl(2\partial_\theta g_{\rho\theta}-\partial_\rho g_{\theta\theta}\bigr)=\tfrac12\cdot1\cdot\bigl(0-(-2\rho)\bigr)=\rho$, $\Gamma^\theta_{\theta\rho}=\Gamma^\theta_{\rho\theta}=\tfrac12g^{\theta\theta}\bigl(\partial_\rho g_{\theta\theta}\bigr)=\tfrac12(-\rho^{-2})(-2\rho)=\rho^{-1}$, and all other components vanish; in particular $\Gamma^\theta_{\theta\theta}=0$ and $\nabla_{\partial_\theta}\partial_\theta=\rho\,\partial_\rho$. Therefore $a=\nabla_nn=\nabla_{\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta}\bigl(\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta\bigr)=\rho^{-1}\bigl(\partial_\theta(\rho^{-1})\partial_\theta+\rho^{-1}\nabla_{\partial_\theta}\partial_\theta\bigr)=\rho^{-1}\bigl(0+\rho^{-1}\rho\,\partial_\rho\bigr)=\rho^{-1}\partial_\rho$, since $\rho$ does not depend on $\theta$; and $\eta(a,a)=\rho^{-2}\eta(\partial_\rho,\partial_\rho)=\rho^{-2}$. At $\rho=2$ this is $\eta(a,a)=1/4$, that is, $|a|=1/2$. [step 2.1, step 3.1]

4.2 Rigidity, irrotationality and the coframe: the $\theta=const$ slices are hyperplanes through the origin (their inertial-coordinate images are $\{x=\coth\theta\cdot x^0$ with $x>|x^0|\}$, or $\{x^0=\tanh\theta\,x\}$), and their tangent space is spanned by $\partial_\rho,\partial_y,\partial_z$, which are orthogonal to $n$ by the metric of step 2.1; their induced metric is $d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$, independent of $\theta$. The rest distribution is therefore integrable, being the tangent distribution of the foliation by these slices; by [L3] its vorticity vanishes and the congruence is irrotational. Moreover the flow of $n$ is $\theta$-translation in these coordinates (up to the positive factor $\rho^{-1}$), which maps the slices to slices and leaves their induced metric unchanged, so the expansion vanishes and the congruence is Born rigid; equivalently, the metric components on the rest slices are constant along $\partial_\theta$, which is the content of the supplier's rigidity computation ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (b)). [L1, L3, step 2.1, step 3.1]

4.3 Non-coordinate frame: by [L4], $[n,\partial_\rho]=[\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta,\partial_\rho]=\rho^{-1}[\partial_\theta,\partial_\rho]-\partial_\rho(\rho^{-1})\partial_\theta=0+\rho^{-2}\partial_\theta=\rho^{-1}n$, which is nonzero since $n\ne0$; here $[\partial_\theta,\partial_\rho]=0$ because $\theta,\rho$ are coordinates. Hence the members of the tetrad field $(n,\partial_\rho,\partial_y,\partial_z)$ do not commute pairwise, while the members of any coordinate frame do; so this tetrad field is not the coordinate frame of any chart. [L4, step 3.1]

5.1 Conclusion: steps 1.1-2.1 verify the diffeomorphism and the exact pullback metric; step 3.1 checks that $n$ is a future unit field; step 4.1 computes the acceleration $a=\rho^{-1}\partial_\rho$ with $\eta(a,a)=\rho^{-2}$; step 4.2 verifies Born rigidity and vanishing vorticity with the explicit rest slices; and step 4.3 exhibits the nonzero commutator showing that the frame is not a coordinate frame. All identities are exact symbolic computations in the hyperbolic functions. [step 4.1, step 4.2, step 4.3] ∎

## Remarks

- **The acceleration is not constant over the congruence.** Each observer at fixed $\rho$ has constant proper acceleration $1/\rho$ in reciprocal-length units, but the family is not rigid in the sense of a single acceleration value: the acceleration grows as $\rho$ decreases, and no global statement about a rigid body extending to $\rho=0$ is made.

- **The metric is not curved.** The pullback metric is the flat metric rewritten in curvilinear coordinates, which is why $\nabla_{\partial_\theta}\partial_\theta=\rho\partial_\rho$ has the form of a connection coefficient; the model's curvature is zero, and the example uses only the flat connection of the inertial chart.

## Example

Fix $R>0$ and let $\Omega$ satisfy $\Omega R=3c/5$, so that $\gamma=(1-9/25)^{-1/2}=5/4$ and $c^2-\Omega^2R^2=(16/25)c^2$. In the inertial chart the ring observer at angular position $\phi=\phi_0+\Omega t$ (chart time $t$) has unit tangent

$$n=\gamma\bigl(1,-\tfrac35\sin\phi,\tfrac35\cos\phi,0\bigr)=\tfrac54\bigl(1,-\tfrac35\sin\phi,\tfrac35\cos\phi,0\bigr),$$

which is future unit because $\gamma^2(-1+\tfrac{9}{25})=-\tfrac{25}{16}\cdot\tfrac{16}{25}=-1$. Writing the cylinder $r=R$ in the rotating angular coordinate $\varphi:=\phi-\Omega t$, so that the point has inertial coordinates $\bigl(ct,R\cos(\varphi+\Omega t),R\sin(\varphi+\Omega t)\bigr)$, the induced metric is

$$g=-\bigl(c^2-\Omega^2R^2\bigr)dt^2+2\Omega R^2\,dt\,d\varphi+R^2\,d\varphi^2=-\tfrac{16}{25}c^2dt^2+\tfrac65cR\,dt\,d\varphi+R^2d\varphi^2 .$$

The rest-space covector of $n$ restricted to the cylinder is proportional to $-\bigl(c^2-\Omega^2R^2\bigr)dt+\Omega R^2d\varphi=-\tfrac{16}{25}c^2dt+\tfrac35cR\,d\varphi$, so a curve tangent to the rest spaces satisfies $dt/d\varphi=\Omega R^2/(c^2-\Omega^2R^2)=15R/(16c)$; integrating over one turn $\varphi\in[0,2\pi]$ gives the nonzero chart-time offset

$$\Delta t=\frac{2\pi\Omega R^2}{c^2-\Omega^2R^2}=\frac{15\pi R}{8c}\ne0 .$$

Hence the curve tangent to the rest spaces starting at the observer returns to the same rotating label at a strictly later chart time: the rest simultaneity of the rotating congruence does not close up around the ring, and no globally single-valued real rest-synchronization time with time-oriented nonzero differential exists on the whole cylinder. The ambient congruence extends to the smooth future unit rotating field $n=\gamma(r)\bigl[\partial_0+(\Omega/c)(-x^2\partial_1+x^1\partial_2)\bigr]$ on $r<c/|\Omega|$, which is Born rigid, and the three-dimensional ambient rest distribution is nowhere integrable because its Frobenius form is nonzero; the one-dimensional rest distribution on the cylinder is locally integrable, so its nonzero global holonomy checked above is a different obstruction. This preserves the distinction between ambient local nonintegrability and global ring synchronization failure.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial chart $(x^0=x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of the affine Minkowski model with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), real $\Omega$ and $R>0$ with $\Omega R=3c/5$, the ambient rotating field $n$ and the ring of the Example ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (c)).

[step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Why the numbers are exact.** The choice $\Omega R=3c/5$ makes $\gamma=5/4$ and $c^2-\Omega^2R^2=(16/25)c^2$, so the slope, the one-turn offset and the Frobenius form are all rational multiples of $R/c$; no approximation enters.

## Example

In an inertial chart let $q(t)=\bigl(\tfrac12\alpha t^2,0,0\bigr)$ with $\alpha>0$, and consider the congruence of translated worldlines $x_\xi(t)=\bigl(ct,q(t)+\xi\bigr)$ for $\xi$ in an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, defined while $|q_1'(t)|=\alpha|t|<c$ ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (d), [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Then $n=\gamma\bigl(1,\alpha t/c,0,0\bigr)$ with $\gamma=(1-\alpha^2t^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ is a smooth future unit timelike field, and $s=\gamma\bigl(\alpha t/c,1,0,0\bigr)$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $n$. Direct computation of the expansion on $s$ gives

$$\theta(s,s)=s^as^b\partial_an_b=\gamma^3\,\frac{\alpha^2t}{c^3},$$

which is nonzero for every $t\ne0$ on the subluminal domain; hence the congruence is not Born rigid on any neighbourhood of a time $t\ne0$, and the failure is already present at $t=0$ on the two sides, where $\theta(s,s)$ changes sign. Nevertheless, for every fixed chart time $t$ the separation between the member labelled $\xi_1$ and the member labelled $\xi_2$ is $|\xi_1-\xi_2|$, constant in $t$: the congruence has constant launch-frame separation while failing Born rigidity. This is the Bell-type translated congruence of the cited theorem; a physical conclusion about a breaking thread or rod would additionally require an elasticity model and a failure criterion and is not drawn here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial chart of the affine Minkowski model with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), the number $\alpha>0$, the worldline $t\mapsto(ct,\tfrac12\alpha t^2,0,0)$ and its translates $x_\xi(t)=(ct,q(t)+\xi)$ for $\xi$ in an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, and the field of the Example ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (d)).

[L1] Supplier clause (d): for a $C^2$ function $q$ with $|q_1'|<c$ the translated congruence has $n=\gamma(1,q_1'/c,0,0)$, $\gamma=(1-q_1'^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, unit longitudinal rest vector $s=\gamma(q_1'/c,1,0,0)$, and first-order projected deformation $\theta(s,s)=s^as^b\partial_an_b=\gamma^3q_1'(t)q_1''(t)/c^3$, nonzero exactly when $q_1'q_1''\ne0$; when $q$ is smooth these formulas agree with the smooth congruence definitions of [[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]. For every fixed chart time the members labelled $\xi_1,\xi_2$ have separation $|\xi_1-\xi_2|$ ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (d)).

[L2] Born rigidity of a congruence means the vanishing of the expansion, $\theta=0$ ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]).

[L3] The four-velocity of a future timelike worldline $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ with $|r'|<c$ is $U=\gamma_w(c,r')$ with $\gamma_w=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and $n=U/c$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (d)).

[L4] Chain rule and one-variable algebra: with $\beta:=\alpha t/c$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ one has $\dfrac{d\gamma}{dt}=\gamma^3\beta\beta'=\gamma^3\alpha^2t/c^2$ and $\dfrac{d(\gamma\beta)}{dt}=\gamma^3\beta'=\gamma^3\alpha/c$, and $1-\beta^2=\gamma^{-2}$ ([[thm-chain-rule]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 With $q_1(t)=\tfrac12\alpha t^2$ one has $q_1'(t)=\alpha t$ and $q_1''(t)=\alpha$, so the field of the Example is $n=\gamma(1,\alpha t/c,0,0)$ and $s=\gamma(\alpha t/c,1,0,0)$, where $\gamma=(1-\alpha^2t^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ is defined and positive on the subluminal domain $|t|<c/\alpha$. Evaluating the diagonal form gives $\eta(n,n)=\gamma^2(-1+\alpha^2t^2/c^2)=-1$, $\eta(s,s)=\gamma^2(-\alpha^2t^2/c^2+1)=1$ and $\eta(n,s)=\gamma^2(-\alpha t/c+\alpha t/c)=0$; hence $n$ is a future unit timelike field and $s$ a unit rest vector. [L1, L3, algebra]

2.1 Direct computation of the contraction: with $n_b=\eta_{bc}n^c=(-\gamma,\gamma\beta,0,0)$ and $s=\gamma(\beta,1,0,0)$, and with $n$ depending only on $t=x^0/c$, one has $\partial_1n_b=\partial_2n_b=\partial_3n_b=0$ and $\partial_0= \frac1c\frac{d}{dt}$; by [L4], $\partial_0n_0=-\gamma^3\beta\beta'/c=-\gamma^3\alpha^2t/c^3$ and $\partial_0n_1=\frac1c\frac{d}{dt}(\gamma\beta)=\gamma^3\beta'/c=\gamma^3\alpha/c^2$. Hence $s^as^b\partial_an_b=(\gamma\beta)^2\partial_0n_0+(\gamma\beta)(\gamma)\partial_0n_1=\gamma^5\beta^2\bigl(-\beta\beta'\bigr)/c+\gamma^5\beta\beta'/c=\gamma^5\beta\beta'(1-\beta^2)/c=\gamma^3\beta\beta'/c=\gamma^3\alpha^2t/c^3$, where $1-\beta^2=\gamma^{-2}$ and only the cross term $(a,b)=(0,1)$ occurs because $\partial_1n_0=0$; this reproduces the supplier formula of [L1]. Since $\alpha>0$ and $\gamma\ge1$ on the domain, $\theta(s,s)=0$ exactly at $t=0$ and is nonzero for every $t\ne0$, with opposite signs on the two sides of $0$. By [L2] the congruence is therefore not Born rigid on any neighbourhood of any $t\ne0$, and at $t=0$ the rigidity condition fails immediately on both sides. [L1, L2, L4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The translated members at a fixed chart time $t$ have positions $q(t)+\xi_1$ and $q(t)+\xi_2$ in the spatial coordinates, so their Euclidean separation is $|\xi_1-\xi_2|$, independent of $t$; equivalently, in the three-dimensional spatial coordinates the congruence is a translation family at each instant even though $\theta\ne0$ off $t=0$. Thus constant instantaneous separation of the labels and Born rigidity are different requirements, which is the content of [L1]. [L1, step 1.1]

3.1 Conclusion and scope: the computation exhibits the exact expansion $\gamma^3\alpha^2t/c^3$, nonzero for $t\ne0$ and zero at $t=0$, so the translated congruence is not Born rigid while its labels keep constant separation $|\xi_1-\xi_2|$. No statement is made about a material rod, a thread or a fracture: a breaking or stretching conclusion would require an elasticity model, a constitutive law and a failure criterion, none of which is part of the kinematic model, and no such conclusion is drawn. [step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Remarks

- **The failure is first order in the transverse label.** The expansion is linear in $t$ near $t=0$ and vanishes exactly there, so the congruence is momentarily rigid at the launch time but not rigid on any time neighbourhood; this is the kinematic counterpart of the Bell-type setup, and the constant separation of the labels is a statement about the labelling, not about the metric distances in the rest spaces.

- **Exact data.** Only the rational functions of $t$ and $\alpha$ arise; at $c=1$, $\beta=\alpha t$, $\beta'=\alpha$ the formula reads $\theta(s,s)=\gamma^3\beta\beta'$, an exact algebraic expression with no approximation.

## Statement refuted

**False claim:** every smooth Born-rigid future unit timelike field $n$ ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]], [[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]) is locally a positive multiple of a Killing field: there is a positive smooth function $f$ on a neighbourhood of every point with $\mathcal L_{fn}\eta=0$ ([[thm-sr-smooth-local-herglotz-noether]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski space with an inertial chart $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ in which $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the flat covariant derivative differentiates components ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]), the kinematics of a congruence with acceleration $a$, expansion $\theta$ and vorticity $\omega$ ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]]), a length scale $L_0>0$, and the functions and curves of the Construction below.

[L1] Killing equation ([[thm-sr-smooth-local-herglotz-noether]], [F10] and steps 9.1, 10.1 there): for a smooth future unit timelike field $n$ with expansion $\theta$, acceleration one-form $a^\flat$ and the Lie derivative of the metric, $\mathcal L_n\eta=2\theta-\bigl(n^\flat\otimes a^\flat+a^\flat\otimes n^\flat\bigr)$; and for a positive smooth $f$, $\mathcal L_{fn}\eta=f\mathcal L_n\eta+df\otimes n^\flat+n^\flat\otimes df$, so $\mathcal L_{fn}\eta=0$ if and only if $\nabla_a(fn)_b+\nabla_b(fn)_a=0$.

[L2] Hyperbolic functions: $\cosh^2s-\sinh^2s=1$, $\cosh s>0$, $\cosh'\!=\sinh$, $\sinh'\!=\cosh$, $\sinh 0=0$, $\cosh 0=1$ ([[def-hyperbolic-functions]], [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]).

[L3] Fundamental theorem of calculus: if $F(\lambda)=\int_0^\lambda g(s)\,ds$ for a continuous $g$, then $F$ is differentiable with $F'=g$ ([[thm-ftc-first-part]]).

[L4] Choice-free inverse function theorem: a smooth map on an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ whose derivative at a point is invertible restricts to a diffeomorphism between open neighbourhoods ([[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]]).

[L5] Exterior derivative: $d^2=0$ on smooth differential forms ([[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]]).

[L6] Future timelike coordinate criterion: in an inertial chart a vector with components $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$ is future timelike exactly when $-u^0{}^2+u^1{}^2+u^2{}^2+u^3{}^2<0$ and $u^0>0$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Construction of the data: fix $L_0>0$ and put $\psi(\lambda):=\lambda^2/(2L_0^2)$, $k(\lambda):=\psi'(\lambda)=\lambda/L_0^2$, $e_0(\lambda):=(\cosh\psi(\lambda),\sinh\psi(\lambda),0,0)$ and $e_1(\lambda):=(\sinh\psi(\lambda),\cosh\psi(\lambda),0,0)$ in the inertial coordinates, and let $z(\lambda):=\bigl(\int_0^\lambda\cosh\psi(s)\,ds,\int_0^\lambda\sinh\psi(s)\,ds,0,0\bigr)$; these are smooth in $\lambda$, $z(0)=0$, and $z'=e_0$ by [L3]. By [L2], $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-\cosh^2\psi+\sinh^2\psi=-1$, $\eta(e_1,e_1)=-\sinh^2\psi+\cosh^2\psi=1$ and $\eta(e_0,e_1)=-\cosh\psi\sinh\psi+\sinh\psi\cosh\psi=0$, so $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an orthonormal frame at every $\lambda$; moreover $e_0$ is future by [L6] because its time component $\cosh\psi>0$ and $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$. At $(\lambda,\xi,y,\zeta)=0$ these four vectors are $e_0(0)=(1,0,0,0)$, $e_1(0)=(0,1,0,0)$, $e_2=(0,0,1,0)$, $e_3=(0,0,0,1)$, so the derivative matrix is the identity and is invertible; by [L4] $\Phi$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from an open neighbourhood of $0$ onto an open neighbourhood $W$ of $\Phi(0)=0$. Therefore $da^\flat=d(k/N)\wedge d\xi$ with $\partial_\lambda(k/N)=\bigl(k'N-k\,\partial_\lambda N\bigr)/N^2=\bigl(k'N-k^2\xi\bigr)/N^2=k'/\ N^2$, where $k'=1/L_0^2$ and $N-k\xi=1$; since $d\xi\wedge d\xi=0$, $da^\flat=\bigl(1/(L_0^2N^2)\bigr)\,d\lambda\wedge d\xi$, which is nowhere zero on $W$ because $N>0$. 6.1 Conclusion and clarifications: steps 1.1-5.1 construct a smooth future unit timelike field $n$ on the open set $W$ that is Born rigid ($\theta=0$) and irrotational ($\omega=0$), and step 5.1 shows that for every positive smooth $f$ the field $fn$ fails the Killing equation on every nonempty open subset; hence the claim of the Statement refuted section is false. The Rindler congruence is not a counterexample of this kind: its metric $-\rho^2d\theta^2+d\rho^2+dy^2+dz^2$ is independent of $\theta$, so $\partial_\theta$ is a Killing field and the unit field $\rho^{-1}\partial_\theta$ is a positive multiple of it ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (b)). The rotational classification of [[thm-sr-smooth-local-herglotz-noether]] is untouched, because the present congruence is irrotational: the counterexample concerns the irrotational branch of Born-rigid motions. [step 5.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **What fails and what survives.** The false claim would make every Born-rigid motion Killing up to a positive rescaling on a neighbourhood. Here the obstruction is exact: the acceleration one-form is closed precisely for Killing rescalings (by [L1] the Killing condition forces $d\log f=a^\flat$), and $a^\flat$ is not closed on any nonempty open subset of $W$ because $da^\flat=(1/L_0^2N^2)d\lambda\wedge d\xi$ is nowhere zero. ## Statement refuted

**False claim:** the simultaneity relation $\eta(n,q-p)=0$ between events of the affine model is independent of the future unit timelike vector $n$ ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]).

**Counterexample.** In an inertial chart let $p:=x^{-1}(0,0,0,0)$ and $q:=x^{-1}(0,1,0,0)$, so that $d:=q-p$ is spacelike with $\eta(d,d)=1$, and let $n:=e_0=(1,0,0,0)$ and $n':=\gamma\bigl(e_0+\tfrac35e_1\bigr)=\tfrac54(1,\tfrac35,0,0)$, a boost of speed $3c/5$ along the first axis. Then $\eta(n',n')=\tfrac{25}{16}\bigl(-1+\tfrac{9}{25}\bigr)=-1$, so $n'$ is also a future unit timelike vector; $\eta(n,d)=0$, so $p$ and $q$ are simultaneous relative to $n$ and lie in the slice $H(p,n)$; and $\eta(n',d)=\tfrac54\cdot\tfrac35=\tfrac34\ne0$, so $p$ and $q$ are not simultaneous relative to $n'$ and lie in different slices for $n'$. The two slices $H(p,n)$ and $H(p,n')$ are distinct three-dimensional affine hyperplanes through $p$. Hence simultaneity in the sense of [[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]] depends on the observer vector and is not an observer-independent relation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski model with an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its chart $x$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]), the events $p=x^{-1}(0,0,0,0)=o$ and $q=x^{-1}(0,1,0,0)=o+e_1$, the displacement $d=q-p=e_1$, the future unit vectors $n=e_0$ and $n'=\gamma(e_0+\tfrac35e_1)$ with $\gamma=(1-\tfrac{9}{25})^{-1/2}=\tfrac54$, and the slices $H(p,n)=p+n^\perp$, $H(p,n')=p+n'^\perp$ ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]]).

[L1] $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for the inertial frame's basis, so $\eta$ is evaluated on coordinate vectors by $\eta(u,v)=-u^0v^0+u^1v^1+u^2v^2+u^3v^3$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

[L2] The future unit timelike vectors are the vectors $n$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$ and $n\in C^+$; the first basis vector $e_0$ of an inertial frame is future unit, and proper orthochronous Lorentz maps preserve the causal classification and the time orientation ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[L3] The passive boost with parameter $\beta$, $|\beta|<1$, is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse the boost with parameter $-\beta$, and its matrix in the inertial basis has entries $B^0{}_0=B^1{}_1=\gamma$ and $B^0{}_1=B^1{}_0=-\gamma\beta$ on the first two coordinate directions, so $B(-\beta)e_0=\gamma(e_0+\beta e_1)$ for the first basis vector, with $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]]).

[L4] For a future unit $n$, $n^\perp=\{v:\eta(n,v)=0\}$ and $H(p,n)=p+n^\perp=\{z:\eta(n,z-p)=0\}$; the slice contains $p$ and is a three-dimensional affine hyperplane ([[def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance]], [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c), [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The displacement is $d=q-p=e_1$ by [L1], and $\eta(d,d)=\eta(e_1,e_1)=1$, so $d$ is spacelike; the vector $n=e_0$ is future unit by [L2]; the vector $n'=\tfrac54(e_0+\tfrac35e_1)$ is the image $B(-3/5)e_0$ of $e_0$ under the boost with parameter $\beta=3/5$ by [L3], hence $n'$ is future timelike by [L2], and its norm is $\eta(n',n')=\tfrac{25}{16}\bigl(\eta(e_0,e_0)+\tfrac65\eta(e_0,e_1)+\tfrac{9}{25}\eta(e_1,e_1)\bigr)=\tfrac{25}{16}(-1+\tfrac{9}{25})=-1$ by [L1], so $n'$ is future unit; in components $n'=\tfrac54 e_0+\tfrac34 e_1$. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 Simultaneity relative to $n$: $\eta(n,d)=\eta(e_0,e_1)=0$ by [L1], so $q-p\in n^\perp$ and $q\in H(p,n)$ by [L4]; the events $p,q$ are simultaneous relative to $n$. [L1, L4, step 1.1]

2.2 Non-simultaneity relative to $n'$: $\eta(n',d)=\tfrac54\eta(e_0,e_1)+\tfrac34\eta(e_1,e_1)=0+\tfrac34=\tfrac34\ne0$ by [L1] and step 1.1, so $q-p\notin n'^\perp$ and $q\notin H(p,n')$ by [L4]; the events $p,q$ are not simultaneous relative to $n'$. [L1, L4, step 1.1]

2.3 The two slices are distinct: the vector $e_1$ satisfies $\eta(n,e_1)=0$, so $e_1\in n^\perp$, while $\eta(n',e_1)=\tfrac34\ne0$, so $e_1\notin n'^\perp$; hence $n^\perp\ne n'^\perp$ as subspaces of $V$. Both $H(p,n)=p+n^\perp$ and $H(p,n')=p+n'^\perp$ are three-dimensional affine hyperplanes through $p$ by [L4], and since their direction subspaces differ they are distinct sets. [L1, L4, step 1.1]

3.1 Conclusion: the single pair of events $p=x^{-1}(0,0,0,0)$, $q=x^{-1}(0,1,0,0)$ is simultaneous relative to the future unit vector $n=e_0$ by step 2.1 and not simultaneous relative to the future unit vector $n'=\tfrac54(e_0+\tfrac35e_1)$ by step 2.2, and the corresponding slices through $p$ are distinct by step 2.3. Therefore the simultaneity relation defined by $\eta(n,q-p)=0$ is not independent of the observer vector $n$, and the claim of the Statement refuted section is false. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3] ∎

## Remarks

- **Exact rational data.** The boost speed $3c/5$ was chosen so that $\gamma=5/4$ and the two pairings $\eta(n,d)=0$, $\eta(n',d)=3/4$ are exact rational numbers; no numerical approximation is involved.

- **The witness for distinctness of the direction subspaces is $e_1$.** The vector $e_1$ lies in $n^\perp$ and not in $n'^\perp$; the two rest spaces of distinct future unit vectors are in fact always distinct, since $n\in n'^\perp$ would give $\eta(n',n)=0$ while a pair of future timelike vectors has $\eta(n',n)<0$.

## Example

In an inertial chart with metric $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ let $\alpha>0$ and consider the worldline $x(\tau)=\frac{c^2}{\alpha}\bigl(\sinh(\alpha\tau/c),\cosh(\alpha\tau/c),0,0\bigr)$, parametrized by $\tau$; write $\theta:=\alpha\tau/c$. Its derivatives are $U:=x'=c(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0)$ and $A:=U'=\alpha(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)$, and one computes $\eta(U,U)=c^2(-\cosh^2\theta+\sinh^2\theta)=-c^2$, $\eta(A,A)=\alpha^2(-\sinh^2\theta+\cosh^2\theta)=\alpha^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=c\alpha(-\cosh\theta\sinh\theta+\sinh\theta\cosh\theta)=0$; thus $\tau$ is a proper-time parameter (up to an additive constant) and $U$ is the four-velocity of a uniformly accelerated worldline. Put $X_0:=U/c=(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0)$ and $X_1:=(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)$; then $\eta(X_0,X_0)=-1$, $\eta(X_0,X_1)=0$ and $\eta(X_1,X_1)=1$, so $(X_0,X_1)$ is an orthonormal pair. A direct substitution into the Fermi-Walker rule shows that both are Fermi-Walker transported: $X_0'=A/c$ equals $\frac1{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X_0)U-\eta(U,X_0)A\bigr)=\frac1{c^2}\bigl(0+cA\bigr)=A/c$, and $X_1'=\frac{\alpha}{c}X_0$ equals $\frac1{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X_1)U-\eta(U,X_1)A\bigr)=\frac1{c^2}\bigl(\alpha U-0\bigr)=\frac{\alpha}{c}X_0$. Moreover $X_1$ is not parallel transported, since $X_1'=\frac{\alpha}{c}X_0\ne0$ for $\alpha>0$; Fermi-Walker transport therefore differs from parallel transport for accelerated motion. The norm $\eta(X_1,X_1)=1$ is constant along the worldline, an instance of the preservation clause of [[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]], and adjoining the constant fields $\partial_y,\partial_z$ gives a Fermi-Walker transported orthonormal tetrad $\bigl(U/c,X_1,\partial_y,\partial_z\bigr)$ along the hyperbolic worldline.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial chart of the affine Minkowski model with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), the number $\alpha>0$, the curve $x(\tau)=\frac{c^2}{\alpha}(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)$ with $\theta=\alpha\tau/c$, and the fields $U=x'$, $A=U'$, $X_0=U/c$, $X_1=(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)$ of the Example ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

[L1] Fermi-Walker transport ([[def-sr-fermi-walker-transport]] clauses (a),(b),(c)): a $C^1$ field $X$ along a $C^2$ future timelike worldline is Fermi-Walker transported exactly when $X'=\frac1{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A\bigr)$; the four-velocity $U$ is always Fermi-Walker transported; and on an interval where $A=0$ the rule coincides with parallel transport, which in the flat model means $X'=0$.

[L2] Preservation and tetrads ([[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] clause (a), [[lem-sr-fermi-walker-transport-existence-and-uniqueness]]): Fermi-Walker transport preserves $\eta(X,Y)$ for transported pairs; and the unique transported family with initial values a tetrad whose first vector is $U/c$ is an orthonormal observer-adapted tetrad at every parameter.

[L3] Four-velocity and proper time ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[def-sr-proper-time]], [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clauses (a),(b)): for a $C^1$ future timelike worldline parametrized by proper time, $U=x'$ satisfies $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and, when $x$ is $C^2$, $\eta(U,A)=0$; conversely a parameter is a proper-time parameter exactly when $\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}=c$ along the curve.

[L4] Hyperbolic functions and the chain rule: $\cosh^2s-\sinh^2s=1$, $\cosh s>0$, $\sinh'=\cosh$, $\cosh'=\sinh$ ([[def-hyperbolic-functions]], [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]), and differentiation of the composite $\tau\mapsto(\sinh\theta(\tau),\cosh\theta(\tau))$ with $\theta=\alpha\tau/c$ uses the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Derivatives and causal character: by [L4], $x'(\tau)=\frac{c^2}{\alpha}\cdot\frac{\alpha}{c}\bigl(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0\bigr)=c\bigl(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0\bigr)=U$, so $U$ is $C^1$ and $x$ is $C^2$; further $U'=c\cdot\frac{\alpha}{c}(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)=\alpha(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)=A$. Evaluating the diagonal form, $\eta(U,U)=c^2(-\cosh^2\theta+\sinh^2\theta)=-c^2$, so $x$ is future timelike with $U$ future (time component $c\cosh\theta>0$) and $\tau$ is a proper-time parameter by [L3]; $\eta(A,A)=\alpha^2(\cosh^2\theta-\sinh^2\theta)=\alpha^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=c\alpha(-\cosh\theta\sinh\theta+\sinh\theta\cosh\theta)=0$; in particular $A\ne0$ because $\alpha>0$. [L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 Orthonormal pair: $X_0=U/c=(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0)$ and $X_1=(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)$ satisfy $\eta(X_0,X_0)=-\cosh^2\theta+\sinh^2\theta=-1$, $\eta(X_0,X_1)=-\cosh\theta\sinh\theta+\sinh\theta\cosh\theta=0$ and $\eta(X_1,X_1)=-\sinh^2\theta+\cosh^2\theta=1$ by [L4]; and $X_0' = U'/c=A/c$. [step 1.1, L4]

2.2 $X_1$ is Fermi-Walker transported: $X_1'=\frac{\alpha}{c}(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0)=\frac{\alpha}{c}X_0$, and $\frac1{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X_1)U-\eta(U,X_1)A\bigr)=\frac1{c^2}\bigl(\alpha U-0\bigr)=\frac{\alpha}{c}X_0$, because $\eta(A,X_1)=\alpha(-\sinh^2\theta+\cosh^2\theta)=\alpha$ and $\eta(U,X_1)=c(-\cosh\theta\sinh\theta+\sinh\theta\cosh\theta)=0$ by [L4]; the right-hand side equals $X_1'$, so $X_1$ is transported. [L1, step 1.1, L4]

3.1 $X_0$ is Fermi-Walker transported: by [L1] and steps 1.1-2.1, $\frac1{c^2}\bigl(\eta(A,X_0)U-\eta(U,X_0)A\bigr)=\frac1{c^2}\bigl(0-(-c)A\bigr)=A/c=X_0'$, because $\eta(A,X_0)=\eta(A,U)/c=0$ and $\eta(U,X_0)=\eta(U,U)/c=-c$. [L1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Difference from parallel transport and norm preservation: $X_1'=\frac{\alpha}{c}X_0\ne0$ since $\alpha>0$ and $X_0\ne0$, so $X_1$ is not parallel transported by [L1]; Fermi-Walker transport therefore differs from parallel transport along this accelerated worldline. The norm is preserved: $\eta(X_1,X_1)=1$ is constant, in agreement with the preservation clause [L2]. [L1, L2, step 2.2]

4.1 Tetrad: the constant fields $\partial_y=(0,0,1,0)$ and $\partial_z=(0,0,0,1)$ have $\partial_y'=\partial_z'=0$ and $\eta(A,\partial_y)=\eta(U,\partial_y)=0$, likewise for $\partial_z$, so the right-hand side of the Fermi-Walker rule vanishes and both are transported by [L1]. Hence $\bigl(U/c,X_1,\partial_y,\partial_z\bigr)=\bigl(X_0,X_1,\partial_y,\partial_z\bigr)$ is an orthonormal tetrad every member of which is Fermi-Walker transported, as asserted in the Example; this also realizes the observer-adapted tetrad of [L2]. [L1, L2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2]

5.1 Conclusion: steps 1.1-2.1 verify the kinematic data, steps 3.1 and 2.2 verify that both legs $X_0=U/c$ and $X_1$ satisfy the Fermi-Walker rule, step 3.2 exhibits the nonzero derivative $X_1'=\frac{\alpha}{c}X_0$ showing that Fermi-Walker transport is not parallel transport for $\alpha>0$, and step 4.1 completes the transported orthonormal tetrad. All identities are exact evaluations in the hyperbolic functions and the diagonal form. [step 3.1, step 2.2, step 3.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **Why the correction term matters.** The Fermi-Walker rule subtracts exactly the acceleration-dependent term $c^{-2}(\eta(A,X)U-\eta(U,X)A)$; along this worldline the term rotates $X_1$ at the rate $\alpha/c$ while keeping $X_0$ transported, which is what makes the pair $(X_0,X_1)$ a nonrotating orthonormal frame in the Fermi-Walker sense.

- **Uniform acceleration.** The worldline has constant acceleration magnitude $\sqrt{\eta(A,A)}=\alpha$ and lies in the region $x^0{}^2<x^1{}^2$; the example uses only the local differential identities and no horizon or coordinate-singularity statement, which belongs to the accelerated-observers page.

first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.

same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$

**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.

the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of

restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.

          "quote": "Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]): $A$ is a nonempty affine space over
the $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ with displacement vectors $q-p$ and
translations $v \mapsto p+v$ ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]), and $C^+$
is one of the two connected components of the timelike set
$T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, chosen as the time orientation, with
$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ the other component
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Write
$\overline{C^+}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and
$\overline{C^-}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ for the future and past closed cones.
A vector $v\in V$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal according to the sign
of $\eta(v,v)$ as in [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; in
particular the zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike and hence is
not causal, and the causal vectors are exactly the nonzero elements of
$\overline{C^+}\cup\overline{C^-}$.

**The closed cones and their boundaries.** By
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] the sets
$\overline{C^+}$ and $\overline{C^-}$ are convex cones with
$\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$. By
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], applied in an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis whose first vector lies in $C^+$, the closure of the
component $\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ of the timelike set is
$\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ with boundary points exactly $0$ and the nonzero null
vectors of $\overline{C^+}$. Writing $N^+$ and $N^-$ for the sets of nonzero
future and past null vectors ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]),
this gives

$$\overline{C^+}=C^+\cup N^+\cup\{0\},\qquad \overline{C^-}=C^-\cup N^-\cup\{0\}.$$

**The objects fixed by this definition.**

**(a) Causal and chronological reachability.** For events $p,q\in A$ set
$p\le q$ if and only if $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$, and $p<q$ if and only if
$q-p\in C^+$. The first relation is read "$q$ is causally reachable from $p$"
and the second "$q$ is strictly (chronologically) reachable from $p$"; both are
relations on the set of events, and neither is asserted here to have any
property beyond being a relation.

**(b) Futures and pasts.** For an event $p\in A$ set

$$J^+(p):=\{q\in A:p\le q\}=p+\overline{C^+},\qquad I^+(p):=\{q\in A:p<q\}=p+C^+,$$

$$J^-(p):=\{q\in A:q\le p\}=p+\overline{C^-},\qquad I^-(p):=\{q\in A:q<p\}=p+C^-.$$

The displayed equalities hold because $q\in J^+(p)$ says exactly that the
displacement $q-p$ lies in $\overline{C^+}$, that is $q=p+v$ for some
$v\in\overline{C^+}$; here $p+v$ is the affine translation of
[[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]. Since $0\in\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}$
one has $p\in J^+(p)\cap J^-(p)$, and since $0$ is not timelike one has
$p\notin I^+(p)$ and $p\notin I^-(p)$. The sets
$J^\pm(p)$ and $I^\pm(p)$ are called the causal and chronological future and
past of $p$.

**(c) Causal diamonds.** For events $p,q\in A$ with $p\le q$, the causal diamond
of the ordered pair $(p,q)$ is the set

$$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)=\{r\in A:p\le r\le q\}.$$

The diamond is defined only under the hypothesis $p\le q$; some of its
properties are computed in the examples page of this pair.

path is a piecewise $C^1$ curve $x:[a,b]\to A$ on a compact interval with

whose tangents are future causal: at every interior point of every open smooth
piece the tangent $x'(s)$ exists and is future causal, and at every partition
point of $[a,b]$ and at the endpoints $a$ and $b$ both one-sided
difference-quotient tangents that exist there exist and are future causal
vectors in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. For events $p,q\in A$, say

$p\ne q$ and there are real numbers $a<b$ and a piecewise $C^1$ future causal

events reachable from $p$ in this sense; thus $p\in R^+(p)$ by the first clause.

structure of $A$, the form $\eta$ and the time orientation alone: no chart, no
choice of origin, no spatial orientation of $V$ and no unit convention enters

beyond their being well-defined sets and relations: the reflexivity of $\le$ is

monotonicity of inertial coordinate time along future causal paths and the
invariance of these objects under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps are
proved later on this page and are not used here. No choice principle is used:
all objects are subsets or finite data built from a finite-dimensional real
vector space.",

$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted

$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in

$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ the other component

$\overline{C^+}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and
$\overline{C^-}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ for the future and past closed cones.

of $\eta(v,v)$ as in [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; in
particular the zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike and hence is
not causal, and the causal vectors are exactly the nonzero elements of
$\overline{C^+}\cup\overline{C^-}$.

[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] the sets
$\overline{C^+}$ and $\overline{C^-}$ are convex cones with
$\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$. By

$\eta$-orthonormal basis whose first vector lies in $C^+$, the closure of the
component $\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ of the timelike set is

future and past null vectors ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]),
this gives

$$\overline{C^+}=C^+\cup N^+\cup\{0\},\qquad \overline{C^-}=C^-\cup N^-\cup\{0\}.$$

past of $p$.

$$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)=\{r\in A:p\le r\le q\}.$$

properties are computed in the examples page of this pair.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.",

          "quote": "Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space

space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.

the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of

$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on

continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$

curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.",

          "quote": "Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$

3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws

5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of

   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.",

A vector $v\in V$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal according to the sign
of $\eta(v,v)$ as in [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; in
particular the zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike and hence is

[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] the sets
$\overline{C^+}$ and $\overline{C^-}$ are convex cones with
$\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$. By

vectors of $\overline{C^+}$. Writing $N^+$ and $N^-$ for the sets of nonzero
future and past null vectors ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]),
this gives

$$\overline{C^+}=C^+\cup N^+\cup\{0\},\qquad \overline{C^-}=C^-\cup N^-\cup\{0\}.$$

**The objects fixed by this definition.**

**(a) Causal and chronological reachability.** For events $p,q\in A$ set
$p\le q$ if and only if $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$, and $p<q$ if and only if
$q-p\in C^+$. The first relation is read "$q$ is causally reachable from $p$"

relations on the set of events, and neither is asserted here to have any

**(b) Futures and pasts.** For an event $p\in A$ set

$$J^+(p):=\{q\in A:p\le q\}=p+\overline{C^+},\qquad I^+(p):=\{q\in A:p<q\}=p+C^+,$$

past of $p$.

difference-quotient tangents that exist there exist and are future causal
vectors in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and

events reachable from $p$ in this sense; thus $p\in R^+(p)$ by the first clause.

choice of origin, no spatial orientation of $V$ and no unit convention enters

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

$\overline{C^+}=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $C^-=\{v:-v^0>|v_s|\}$ and

($k\ge 1$), then $v_1+\cdots+v_k\in\overline{C^+}$; if in addition at least one
$v_i$ lies in $C^+$, then the sum lies in $C^+$; and if $v+w=0$ with
$v,w\in\overline{C^+}$, then $v=w=0$.

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$

the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.

give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain

sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Convergence in $V$ is understood through
an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

If $x_A : A \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is the global chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is

[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by

In each momentary inertial rest frame of the traveler the stay-at-home clock runs slow by the factor 1/gamma, and the traveler may legitimately apply the time-dilation relation between events that are simultaneous in that momentary frame (lem-sr-boost-time-length-and-velocity-formulas (i), def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance). An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);

3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),

**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

          "quote": "Let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space

$\mathbb{R}$ with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]); a **curve** of the
model is a map $x : I \to A$.

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Convergence in $V$ is understood through
an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

If $x_A : A \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is the global chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

### Causal character

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike
worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s \mapsto x(-s)$, which
is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by
an explicit formula.",

          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain

symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads

$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.",

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);

3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

          "quote": "Let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space

$\mathbb{R}$ with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]); a **curve** of the
