### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Convergence in $V$ is understood through
an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

If $x_A : A \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is the global chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

### Causal character

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike
worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s \mapsto x(-s)$, which
is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by
an explicit formula.",

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with

3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because

chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the

first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$

an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of

that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

### Causal character

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike
worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s \mapsto x(-s)$, which
is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by
an explicit formula.",

          "quote": "Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.",

          "quote": "Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be inertial frames whose bases are related by a boost along the common first spatial direction with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$:

$$e'_0=\gamma\Bigl(e_0+\frac{v}{c}e_1\Bigr),\qquad e'_1=\gamma\Bigl(e_1+\frac{v}{c}e_0\Bigr),\qquad e'_2=e_2,\qquad e'_3=e_3,$$

$$x'^0=\gamma\Bigl(x^0-\frac{v}{c}x^1\Bigr),\qquad x'^1=\gamma\Bigl(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0\Bigr),\qquad x'^2=x^2,\qquad x'^3=x^3.$$

Then:

**(i) Clock rate.** The straight worldline $y(\lambda):=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ (coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$, the worldline of a clock at rest in the frame $x'$) is future timelike, and the elapsed proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; equivalently $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ along $y$, where $t$ is the coordinate time of $x$.

**(ii) Length comparison.** For $L_0>0$ let $y_a,y_b$ be the two straight worldlines at rest in the frame $x'$ through the events with $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda,L_0,0,0)$. Then (a) at equal $x'$-times their $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$, while (b) at equal $x$-times their $x$-coordinate separation is $L_0/\gamma$, so the measuring frame $x$ assigns the length $L_0/\gamma$ to a rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$; (c) symmetrically, for two worldlines at rest in $x$ with $x$-separation $L_0$ the separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0/\gamma$. In each case the comparison uses events at equal time in the measuring frame; comparing equal times of the other frame is a different pair of events.

**(iii) Simultaneity.** If $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$; in particular simultaneity in the chart $x$ is not simultaneity in the chart $x'$ whenever $vL\ne0$.

          "quote": "Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $n\in V$ be future unit timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

**(b) Simultaneity slice.** For $p\in A$ the **simultaneity slice of $p$ relative to $n$** is the affine hyperplane $H(p,n):=p+n^\perp=\{q\in A:\eta(n,q-p)=0\}$; it contains $p$ and is three-dimensional, not a single point.

**(c) Simultaneity relation.** Define $q\sim_nq'$ if and only if $\eta(n,q'-q)=0$, that is, if and only if $q'-q\in n^\perp$. Then $\sim_n$ is an equivalence relation on $A$ whose equivalence classes are exactly the slices $H(p,n)$; reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity are consequences of $n^\perp$ being a linear subspace and are not physical assumptions.

**(d) Rest distance.** For $p,q$ with $q\in H(p,n)$ define $d_n(p,q):=\sqrt{\eta(q-p,q-p)}$. This is a real number $\ge0$, symmetric in $p,q$, vanishes exactly when $p=q$, and satisfies the triangle inequality on each slice, because the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^\perp$ is a positive-definite inner product.

**(e) Dependence on $n$ and scope.** The relation $\sim_n$ and the slices $H(p,n)$ depend on the chosen future unit timelike vector $n$: an event $q$ with $\eta(n,q-p)=0$ generally has $\eta(n',q-p)\ne0$ for another future unit $n'$ (an explicit witness is given on this page).           "quote": "Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.",

          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of

          "quote": "Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.",

$x : [a,b] \to A$, $a < b$, be a piecewise $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline in

interior tangents and finite one-sided difference-quotient endpoint tangents are
future timelike, and continuous extension of the derivative is not assumed.

**(i) The piecewise density.** On each open piece let

$$g_i(t) = \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(t),x'(t)\bigr)} > 0 .$$

By clause (b) of [[lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability]] the function

$$\int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} g_i \;:=\; \lim_{u \downarrow s_{i-1}} \int_u^{r} g_i \;+\; \lim_{v \uparrow s_i} \int_r^{v} g_i$$

compact interval whose integral vanishes is identically zero there

strictly positive at every point of the piece.

**(ii) Total proper time.** Define

$$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) \;:=\; c^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} g_i .$$

The finite sum is independent of the admissible partition, by subdivision

inertial chart: for every truncation $s_{i-1} < u < r < v < s_i$ the ordinary

each open-piece derivative has finite limits at both ends of its piece and hence
extends continuously to the closed piece. Under (H) the limiting values equal
the finite one-sided quotient derivatives of the curve, each $g_i$ extends
continuously and positively to the closed piece, its improper integral equals
its ordinary Riemann integral there
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]]), and the same
finite-sum formula applies. In particular, if $x$ is globally $C^{1}$ on
$[a,b]$ (the one-piece case of (H)), then
$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) = \tau(b) - \tau(a)$ of [[def-sr-proper-time]].

**(v) Straight pieces.** If on the piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the tangent is a
constant future timelike vector $d_i$, the contribution of that piece is
$c^{-1}(s_i - s_{i-1})\sqrt{-\eta(d_i,d_i)}$; a piecewise straight future
timelike worldline therefore has total proper time equal to the finite sum of
its straight-segment proper times. In every case $\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) > 0$.

**(vi) Additivity over concatenation.** For $a < d < b$, the restrictions of a
weak piecewise worldline $x$ to $[a,d]$ and $[d,b]$ satisfy
$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) = \Delta\tau_{[a,d]}(x) + \Delta\tau_{[d,b]}(x)$: insert
$d$ into the partition and use (ii).

reading is a separate physical assumption. No global $C^{1}$ inverse, tangent at

        "title": "Affine phase functions and wave covectors on affine Minkowski space",
        "statement": "Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model), with displacements q - p in V (def-affine-space-and-displacement). (a) A map theta: A -> R is an affine phase function if there are q in A and a covector k in V* (def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional) with theta(p) - theta(q) = k(p - q) for all p in A; the covector k is then unique (the differential d theta of theta), and for each fixed q the map theta |-> (k, theta(q)) is a bijection onto V* x R, with theta(p) = k(p - q) + theta(q). In the inertial chart x of a frame (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) one has theta(p) = k_a x^a(p) + theta(o) with k_a := k(e_a) the components of k in the frame (thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis), and theta(o') = theta(o) + k(o' - o) for two origins. (b) Constant-phase directions: for v in V one has k(v) = 0 if and only if theta is constant on the line p + R v for every p in A, since theta(p + s v) = theta(p) + s k(v); if k is nonzero, the direction subspace ker k := {v in V : k(v) = 0} is a 3-dimensional linear subspace and every nonempty level set Sigma_t := {p in A : theta(p) = t} is the affine hyperplane p_0 + ker k through any of its points p_0; if k = 0 then theta is constant and Sigma_t is empty or all of A. For every C^1 curve gamma: I -> A one has (theta o gamma)'(s) = k(gamma'(s)) (thm-chain-rule, def-derivative). (c) A wave covector on (A,V,eta) is a nonzero element k of V*, and with k^sharp the raised vector of lem-sr-metric-duality-on-lorentz-vector-space k is called null, timelike or spacelike when eta(k^sharp,k^sharp) is zero, negative or positive, and future, past, future null, past null or causal when k^sharp is respectively future causal, past causal, future null, past null or causal in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets; a future null wave covector is one that is both future and null. These definitions are well posed because the causal classification of a nonzero vector is by the sign of eta and by membership in the closed cones, and k^sharp = 0 exactly when k = 0 (duality lemma). (d) This item introduces mathematical objects and terminology only: it excludes the zero covector from 'wave covector', it fixes no units and no physical interpretation, and no claim that light or any physical wave is described by such a phase is made here; that identification is adopted in post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model.         "statement": "Adopt post-sr-inertial-covariance, post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light and post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model, and the conventions of def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions. Let x and x' be inertial charts whose transition is x' = B(beta) x + b with beta in R^3, |beta| < 1, b in R^4 and B(beta) the passive boost of def-lorentz-boost; write gamma := (1 - |beta|^2)^(-1/2) and beta_hat := beta/|beta| for beta nonzero, so that the frame x' moves with velocity v = c beta relative to the frame x in the direction beta_hat. Then, conditionally on the adopted model: (i) Frame data in x'. The data of the same covector k in x' is (omega',s') with omega' = gamma(1 - beta . s) omega > 0 and s' = [s + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . s) beta - gamma beta]/[gamma(1 - beta . s)] for beta nonzero (and omega' = omega, s' = s for beta = 0), so |s'| = 1 and k'_a = (-omega'/c, (omega'/c)s'_1, (omega'/c)s'_2, (omega'/c)s'_3) in x'. In the axis case beta = b e_1 with b in (-1,1): s'_1 = (s_1 - b)/(1 - b s_1) and (s'_2,s'_3) = (s_2,s_3)/(gamma(1 - b s_1)). (ii) Reading and frequency ratios. The rest observers of x and x' (four-velocities c e_0 and c e'_0) read angular frequencies omega = -c k(e_0) and omega' = -c k(e'_0); the linear frequencies and wavelengths of the two descriptions satisfy nu' = gamma(1 - beta . s) nu and lambda' = lambda/[gamma(1 - beta . s)]. More generally, an ideal observer whose coordinate velocity in x is w (a vector of the frame's spatial three-space with |w| < c) reads omega_o = gamma_w(1 - (w . s)/c) omega, where gamma_w := (1 - |w|^2/c^2)^(-1/2); equivalently omega_o = gamma_w(1 - beta_w . s) omega with beta_w := w/c. (iii) Longitudinal cases. If s = beta_hat then omega' = omega sqrt((1 - |beta|)/(1 + |beta|)) < omega, nu' = nu sqrt((1 - |beta|)/(1 + |beta|)) and lambda' = lambda sqrt((1 + |beta|)/(1 - |beta|)): the observer moving in the direction of propagation (away from a source at rest in x and located behind it) reads a red-shifted frequency and lengthened wavelength. If s = -beta_hat then omega' = omega sqrt((1 + |beta|)/(1 - |beta|)) > omega and lambda' = lambda sqrt((1 - |beta|)/(1 + |beta|)): blue shift for an observer moving opposite to the propagation direction (toward such a source). (iv) Transverse protocols. If beta . s = 0 (propagation direction perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame x) then omega' = gamma omega; this is greater than omega when beta!=0 and equals omega when beta=0. If beta . s = |beta|^2, for beta!=0 equivalently s' . beta_hat = 0 (propagation direction perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame x'), then omega' = omega/gamma; this is less than omega when beta!=0 and equals omega when beta=0.         "statement": "Let $(A,V,\\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski model, $c>0$, and let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with stationary observer $n:=e_0$; let $E_n,q_n$ be as in [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]].\n(a) For every $P\\in\\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ the coordinate components of $P$ in the frame are $(P^0,P^1,P^2,P^3)=(E_n(P)/c,\\,q^1,q^2,q^3)$, where $q_n(P)=\\sum_{i=1}^3q^ie_i$; if $P$ is future timelike then $E^2=m(P)^2c^4+c^2\\sum_{i=1}^3(q^i)^2$ with $E=E_n(P)$.\n(b) Let $x:I\\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline whose chart coordinate path is $t\\mapsto(ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w:=r'$ and $\\gamma_w:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$; then $|w|<c$, the four-velocity is $U=\\gamma_w(c,w)$ by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\\,(e), and for $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant the components are $P=m\\gamma_w(c,w)$, that is $E_n(P)=m\\gamma_wc^2$ and $q_n(P)=\\sum_{i=1}^3m\\gamma_ww^ie_i$.\n(c) Let $B(\\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] with parameter $\\beta=v/c$, $|v|<c$, along a spatial direction $s$, and let $P'$ denote the components of the same vector $P$ after the coordinate change $x'=B(\\beta)x$; write $\\mathbf p=(P^1,P^2,P^3)$ and split it into its components $\\mathbf p_\\parallel$, $\\mathbf p_\\perp$ with respect to $s$. Then\n$$P'^0=\\gamma_v\\bigl(P^0-\\beta\\,s\\cdot\\mathbf p\\bigr),\\qquad \\mathbf p'_\\parallel=\\gamma_v\\bigl(\\mathbf p_\\parallel-\\beta P^0\\bigr),\\qquad \\mathbf p'_\\perp=\\mathbf p_\\perp,$$\nequivalently $E'=\\gamma_v(E-v\\,p_\\parallel)$, $p'_\\parallel=\\gamma_v(p_\\parallel-vE/c^2)$, $p'_\\perp=p_\\perp$.         "statement": "Let $(A,V,\\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski model, $c>0$, and let $x:I\\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline with proper-time function $\\tau:I\\to J$ and inverse $\\rho:J\\to I$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]).\n(a) For a $C^1$ map $P:I\\to V$ define its proper-time derivative $\\dot P:I\\to V$ by\n$$\\dot P(s):=\\frac{P'(s)}{\\tau'(s)},$$\nwhere $P'$ is the derivative of $P$ with respect to the worldline parameter, taken componentwise in any affine basis of $V$; the result does not depend on the basis because two affine bases differ by a constant invertible linear map. Equivalently $\\dot P(s)=(P\\circ\\rho)'(\\tau(s))$, so $\\dot P$ is the derivative of the proper-time parametrised field $P\\circ\\rho$. Since $\\tau'(s)>0$ by [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]], $\\dot P$ is well defined and continuous whenever $P$ is $C^1$.\n(b) If $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant and $U$ the four-velocity of $x$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), then $F:=\\dot P$ is called the four-force on the particle; in an inertial frame $F$ has the components of the derivative of the four-momentum with respect to proper time.\n(c) This item introduces a derivative and a name only. A datum is on-shell if every leg is massive with a recorded mass or null; a mass-specified datum records the mass $m>0$ of each massive leg or the value $0$ for each null leg. The mass sum of a side is the sum of the recorded positive masses of its massive legs; a side is massive-only if all its legs are massive.\n(c) A datum is causal if every leg lies in $\\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$; two-leg if both sides have two legs; equal-mass if in addition both sides are two-leg and the recorded masses agree pair by pair.\n(d) The definition is purely mathematical: it neither asserts that any datum describes a physical process, nor that a conserving datum exists for a prescribed list of legs, nor any law of nature. (b) Fix the positive numerical constant $c$ and, in each inertial chart, define the component families $\\varepsilon_x:=T^{00}$, $\\pi_x^i:=T^{0i}/c=T^{i0}/c$ and $S_x^{ij}:=T^{ij}$. These are numerical component and scaling conventions; their transformation is inherited from $T$. No physical units or measurement interpretation form part of this mathematical definition. (c) When $k\\ge1$, the \\emph{four-force density} of $T$ is the $C^{k-1}$ field with inertial components $f^b:=\\partial_aT^{ab}$, where $\\partial_a$ are the coordinate partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. By [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\\,(iv) the components $\\partial_aT^{ab}$ transform as a vector, so $f$ is a well-defined vector field on $\\Omega$, independent of the inertial chart. For $k\\ge1$, one says that $T$ is \\emph{locally conserved}, or \\emph{balanced}, on $\\Omega$ when $f=0$ on $\\Omega$, and that $T$ is balanced against the four-force density $f$ when $\\partial_aT^{ab}=f^b$. (d) The definition asserts no conservation of any prescribed symmetric field $T$: whether a given $T$ is conserved, whether it arises from an action or a matter model, and whether any of its integrals over a slice converges are separate hypotheses stated elsewhere.     "title": "Proper acceleration of a massive worldline and its agreement with the acceleration of an observer congruence",
    "statement": "Let c > 0 and let x: I -> A be a C^2 future timelike worldline with four-velocity U = dx/dtau and four-acceleration A = dU/dtau (def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration), so that eta(U,U) = -c^2 and eta(U,A) = 0 pointwise, and A(tau) is spacelike whenever it is nonzero (thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition (a),(b)). (a) Definition. The proper acceleration of x at the parameter value tau is the real number a(tau) := sqrt(eta(A(tau),A(tau))), the nonnegative square root of def-rational-power. This is well defined for every tau in I: if A(tau) = 0 then eta(A,A) = 0, and if A(tau) is nonzero then it is spacelike and eta(A,A) > 0 (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors); in both cases the argument of the square root is nonnegative, so a(tau) is a nonnegative real number. With the SI coordinate and unit conventions of def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions, in which x^0 = c t with t in seconds and the spatial coordinates are in metres while eta has the dimensionless matrix diag(-1,1,1,1) in an inertial chart, the components of A carry the unit metre per second squared and eta(A,A) carries the unit (metre per second squared)^2, so a carries the unit metre per second squared. The worldline is uniformly accelerated when a is constant on I. (b) Agreement with the acceleration of a congruence. Let Omega be a nonempty open subset of A and let n: Omega -> V be an observer congruence with acceleration field a_cg := nabla_n n, where nabla is the flat covariant derivative of def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space (def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics (b)). If x is a flow line of n and U = c n along x, then A = c^2 a_cg along x, and consequently a = c^2 sqrt(eta(a_cg,a_cg)) along x: the proper acceleration is c^2 times the magnitude of the congruence acceleration. In particular the proper acceleration of a congruence worldline is determined by the congruence field alone, and such a worldline is uniformly accelerated exactly when eta(a_cg,a_cg) is constant along it. (c) Reading and scope. This item defines a quantity of the model and fixes its name, its unit and its physical reading. The model reads a(tau) as the magnitude that an ideal accelerometer carried along the worldline would register at tau; this ideal-instrument identification is adopted with the model in the same sense as the framework's ideal-clock reading of proper time and is not derived here. No accelerometer response law, calibration, frequency dependence, force law or interaction is specified or asserted; the definition asserts nothing about which bodies follow which worldlines; no measurement outcome and no statistical, uncertainty or empirical claim is made.     "domain": "mathematics",
    "title": "The uniformly accelerated worldline: hyperbolic motion, constant four-acceleration magnitude, and identification as a Rindler flow line",
    "statement": "Let c > 0 and alpha > 0, set R := c^2/alpha, and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the affine Minkowski space with an inertial chart x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3), x^0 = c t (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model, def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart). Let x: R -> A be the curve x(tau) := x^{-1}(R sinh theta, R cosh theta, 0, 0), where theta := alpha tau/c. (a) Regularity, causal character and parametrization. x is C^infinity, and x'(tau) = c(cosh theta, sinh theta, 0, 0) is future timelike for every tau (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets), so x is a future timelike worldline (def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline). Since eta(x',x') = -c^2 is constant, the parameter tau is a proper-time parameter of the curve: the proper-time function tau of def-sr-proper-time satisfies tau(b) - tau(a) = b - a for all a < b in R (def-sr-proper-time, lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization), and the four-velocity is U := dx/dtau = c(cosh theta, sinh theta, 0, 0) with eta(U,U) = -c^2 (def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration, thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition (a)). (b) Constant four-acceleration magnitude. The four-acceleration A := dU/dtau = alpha(sinh theta, cosh theta, 0, 0) satisfies eta(A,A) = alpha^2 and eta(U,A) = 0. The chart coordinate velocity is dx^1/dt = c tanh theta, so |dx^1/dt| < c for every tau, and x^1 = R cosh theta > R|sinh theta| = |x^0| for every tau: the worldline lies in the right wedge W := {x^1 > |x^0|} and its speed in the chart tends to c only as tau -> +-infinity. (c) Rindler flow line. Let Phi(theta,rho,y,z) := (rho sinh theta, rho cosh theta, y, z) on R x (0,inf) x R^2 and let n := rho^{-1} partial_theta be the Rindler congruence of thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples (b), whose pullback metric is -rho^2 dtheta^2 + drho^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 and whose congruence acceleration a_cg := nabla_n n is rho^{-1} partial_rho, with eta(a_cg,a_cg) = rho^{-2} (def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space, def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics). Then x is exactly the flow line Phi(., R, 0, 0) reparametrized by theta = alpha tau/c, and along x one has A = c^2 a_cg: the four-acceleration of the worldline is c^2 times the congruence acceleration, and eta(a_cg,a_cg) = 1/R^2 = alpha^2/c^4 on the flow line rho = R. In the special initially resting case $q\\prime(0)=0$, the initial length is $L$ and every state with $q\\prime(t)\\ne0$ has stretch factor $\\gamma(t)>1$.     "statement": "Statement refuted: 'In the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with the inertial chart x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3), the null plane H := {x^1 = x^0}, is a boundary of the model in the following three senses: (i) no future causal curve crosses from {x^1 > x^0} to {x^1 < x^0}; (ii) H separates all causal relations, so no event of {x^1 > x^0} is causally related to any event of {x^1 < x^0}; and (iii) the metric degenerates on H, so that H is a singular boundary of the spacetime on which the model fails.' Here H is the full causal-past boundary of the accelerated congruence; only its half-plane {x^1 = x^0 >= 0} belongs to the boundary of the right wedge W={x^1>|x^0|}. Counterexample: (a) A future timelike crossing refutes the causal separation claims. Let p := x^{-1}(-1,0,0,0) and q := x^{-1}(3,1,0,0), and let y: [0,1] -> A be the affine segment y(s) := p + s(q-p). The displacement q - p has chart components (4,1,0,0), so eta(q-p,q-p) = -16 + 1 = -15 < 0 and the time component is 4 > 0: the segment is a future timelike curve (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets). Its coordinate function x^0 - x^1 takes the values -1 at s = 0 and +2 at s = 1, hence vanishes at s = 1/3, at x^{-1}(1/3,1/3,0,0): a future timelike curve crosses H, refuting (i). ## Definition

Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]): $A$ is a nonempty affine space over
the $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ with displacement vectors $q-p$ and
translations $v \mapsto p+v$ ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]), and $C^+$
is one of the two connected components of the timelike set
$T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, chosen as the time orientation, with
$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ the other component
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Write
$\overline{C^+}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and
$\overline{C^-}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ for the future and past closed cones.
A vector $v\in V$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal according to the sign
of $\eta(v,v)$ as in [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; in
particular the zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike and hence is
not causal, and the causal vectors are exactly the nonzero elements of
$\overline{C^+}\cup\overline{C^-}$.

**The closed cones and their boundaries.** By
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] the sets
$\overline{C^+}$ and $\overline{C^-}$ are convex cones with
$\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$. By
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], applied in an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis whose first vector lies in $C^+$, the closure of the
component $\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ of the timelike set is
$\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ with boundary points exactly $0$ and the nonzero null
vectors of $\overline{C^+}$. Writing $N^+$ and $N^-$ for the sets of nonzero
future and past null vectors ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]),
this gives

$$\overline{C^+}=C^+\cup N^+\cup\{0\},\qquad \overline{C^-}=C^-\cup N^-\cup\{0\}.$$

**The objects fixed by this definition.**

**(a) Causal and chronological reachability.** For events $p,q\in A$ set
$p\le q$ if and only if $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$, and $p<q$ if and only if
$q-p\in C^+$. The first relation is read "$q$ is causally reachable from $p$"
and the second "$q$ is strictly (chronologically) reachable from $p$"; both are
relations on the set of events, and neither is asserted here to have any
property beyond being a relation.

**(b) Futures and pasts.** For an event $p\in A$ set

$$J^+(p):=\{q\in A:p\le q\}=p+\overline{C^+},\qquad I^+(p):=\{q\in A:p<q\}=p+C^+,$$

$$J^-(p):=\{q\in A:q\le p\}=p+\overline{C^-},\qquad I^-(p):=\{q\in A:q<p\}=p+C^-.$$

The displayed equalities hold because $q\in J^+(p)$ says exactly that the
displacement $q-p$ lies in $\overline{C^+}$, that is $q=p+v$ for some
$v\in\overline{C^+}$; here $p+v$ is the affine translation of
[[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]. Since $0\in\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}$
one has $p\in J^+(p)\cap J^-(p)$, and since $0$ is not timelike one has
$p\notin I^+(p)$ and $p\notin I^-(p)$. The sets
$J^\pm(p)$ and $I^\pm(p)$ are called the causal and chronological future and
past of $p$.

**(c) Causal diamonds.** For events $p,q\in A$ with $p\le q$, the causal diamond
of the ordered pair $(p,q)$ is the set

$$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)=\{r\in A:p\le r\le q\}.$$

The diamond is defined only under the hypothesis $p\le q$; some of its
properties are computed in the examples page of this pair.

**(d) Reachability by future causal paths.** A piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path is a piecewise $C^1$ curve $x:[a,b]\to A$ on a compact interval with
$a<b$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) all of
whose tangents are future causal: at every interior point of every open smooth
piece the tangent $x'(s)$ exists and is future causal, and at every partition
point of $[a,b]$ and at the endpoints $a$ and $b$ both one-sided
difference-quotient tangents that exist there exist and are future causal
vectors in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. For events $p,q\in A$, say
that $q$ is reachable from $p$ by a future causal path when $p=q$, or when
$p\ne q$ and there are real numbers $a<b$ and a piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path $x:[a,b]\to A$ with $x(a)=p$ and $x(b)=q$. Write $R^+(p)$ for the set of
events reachable from $p$ in this sense; thus $p\in R^+(p)$ by the first clause.

**(e) Conventions and scope.** All objects above are defined from the affine
structure of $A$, the form $\eta$ and the time orientation alone: no chart, no
choice of origin, no spatial orientation of $V$ and no unit convention enters
their definition. This item asserts no property of these objects
beyond their being well-defined sets and relations: the reflexivity of $\le$ is
part of (b), while the transitivity of $\le$, the identification
$R^+(p)=J^+(p)$, the antisymmetry "$p\le q$ and $q\le p$ imply $p=q$", the
monotonicity of inertial coordinate time along future causal paths and the
invariance of these objects under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps are
proved later on this page and are not used here. No choice principle is used:
all objects are subsets or finite data built from a finite-dimensional real
vector space.

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) and use
the reachability objects $J^+$, $I^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]. Let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with chart $x$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$$
be the Euclidean norm of the spatial part $v_s:=v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ of a
vector $v=v^0e_0+v_s$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Then:

**(a) Cone description.** $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$,
$\overline{C^+}=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $C^-=\{v:-v^0>|v_s|\}$ and
$\overline{C^-}=\{v:-v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; moreover every $v\in\overline{C^+}$ with
$v\ne 0$ satisfies $-\eta(v,e_0)=v^0>0$ and $|v_s|\le v^0$, and $v$ is future
null exactly when $|v_s|=v^0>0$.

**(b) Finite sums.** If $v_1,\dots,v_k$ lie in $\overline{C^+}$
($k\ge 1$), then $v_1+\cdots+v_k\in\overline{C^+}$; if in addition at least one
$v_i$ lies in $C^+$, then the sum lies in $C^+$; and if $v+w=0$ with
$v,w\in\overline{C^+}$, then $v=w=0$.

**(c) Coordinate criterion.** For events $p,q\in A$ put
$D^a:=x^a(q)-x^a(p)$ and $D_s:=(D^1,D^2,D^3)$. Then: $q\in J^+(p)$ if and only
if $D^0\ge|D_s|$; $q\in I^+(p)$ if and only if $D^0>|D_s|$; $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ if and only if $D^0\ge|D_s|$ and $D^0>0$; and for $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ one has $0<D^0$ and $|D_s|\le D^0$. The criteria are stated for the
chart of any inertial frame, because every inertial basis is
$\eta$-orthonormal with future first vector.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma is a statement about the affine model and the fixed
time orientation; it attaches no physical meaning to $\le$, $J^+$ or $I^+$ and
uses no choice principle.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$, an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with chart $x$, and for a vector $v=\sum_a v^ae_a$ the spatial part $v_s=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with norm $|v_s|=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$.

[L1] In an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ one has $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+|v_s|^2$, and the timelike set $T=\{v:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ is the disjoint union $T=T_+\cup T_-$ with $T_+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ and $T_-=\{v:v^0<-|v_s|\}$, these being exactly the two connected components of $T$; moreover $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-|v_s|\}$ and $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L2] $C^+$ is one component of $T$, $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ is the other; a vector is future timelike, future null, future causal exactly by membership in $C^+$, or nonzero null in $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$, or the union of the two; past notions are the same with $C^-$; $\overline{C^+}$ and $\overline{C^-}$ are convex cones with $\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$, and a causal vector is future or past but not both ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L3] An inertial frame is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $o\in A$ and $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ an $\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ with $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, whose first vector $e_0$ lies in $C^+$ and which is positively oriented; its chart is $x(r)=E^{-1}(r-o)$ with $E(u)=\sum_a u^ae_a$, and in particular $x(r)-x(s)=E^{-1}(r-s)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L4] For a fixed inertial frame the spatial part $S=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ carries the positive-definite form $\delta=\eta|_S$, $|w|:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}$ is a norm on $S$, and for $w=w^1e_1+w^2e_2+w^3e_3$ one has $|w|=\sqrt{(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2}$ and $\eta(w,e_0)=0$; the Euclidean scalar product on the coordinate space is the positive-definite inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[L5] For the norm of [L4] the triangle inequality $|w+z|\le|w|+|z|$ holds for all $w,z\in S$ ([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]).

[L6] A vector $v$ is timelike when $\eta(v,v)<0$, null when $v\ne 0$ and $\eta(v,v)=0$, and spacelike when $\eta(v,v)>0$; every nonzero vector has exactly one causal character ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

[L7] For events $p,q\in A$: $q\in J^+(p)$ iff $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$; $q\in I^+(p)$ iff $q-p\in C^+$; $J^+(p)=p+\overline{C^+}$ ([[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The component $C^+$ is one of $T_+$, $T_-$ by [L2], and the coordinates of $e_0$ in the basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ are $(1,0,0,0)$, so $e_0\in T_+$; since $e_0\in C^+$ by [L3], it follows that $C^+=T_+$ and $C^-=T_-$, that is $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ and $C^-=\{v:-v^0>|v_s|\}=\{v:v^0<-|v_s|\}$. Taking closures with [L1] gives $\overline{C^+}=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $\overline{C^-}=\{v:-v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ and $\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$; also $C^-=-C^+$, because $-(T_+)=T_-$, whence $\overline{C^-}=-\overline{C^+}$ and the description $-v^0\ge|v_s|$ agrees with $-v\in\overline{C^+}$. [given, L1, L2, L3]

2.1 Let $v=v^0e_0+v_s\in\overline{C^+}$. Then $v^0\ge|v_s|\ge 0$, and $-\eta(v,e_0)=v^0$ because $\eta(v,e_0)=v^0\eta(e_0,e_0)+\eta(v_s,e_0)=-v^0+0$ by the orthonormality and spatial orthogonality of [L3] and [L4]. If $v\ne 0$ then $v^0>0$: if $v^0=0$ then $|v_s|\le 0$, so $v_s=0$ and $v=0$, a contradiction. Finally $v$ is future null exactly when $|v_s|=v^0>0$: by [L6] nullity of $v$ is the conjunction $v\ne 0$ and $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+|v_s|^2=0$, which by [L1] means $|v_s|=v^0$, and by the preceding sentence this forces $v^0>0$. [step 1.1, L1, L3, L4, L6, algebra]

2.2 Let $v,w\in\overline{C^+}$. Then $(v+w)^0=v^0+w^0\ge|v_s|+|w_s|\ge|v_s+w_s|$ by [L5] applied to the spatial parts, so $v+w\in\overline{C^+}$ by the description of step 1.1; if in addition $v\in C^+$, that is $v^0>|v_s|$, the first inequality is strict and $(v+w)^0>|v_s+w_s|$, so $v+w\in C^+$; the same holds if $w\in C^+$. [step 1.1, L5, algebra]

2.3 Let $v,w\in\overline{C^+}$ with $v+w=0$. Then $w=-v$ and $v\in\overline{C^+}$, so $w\in-\overline{C^+}=\overline{C^-}$ by step 1.1; hence $w\in\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$ by step 1.1, that is $w=0$ and $v=-w=0$. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 Let $k\ge 1$ and $v_1,\dots,v_k\in\overline{C^+}$. For $k=1$ the membership claim is the hypothesis and the strict claim is the hypothesis $v_1\in C^+$; for the passage from $k-1$ to $k$ put $s':=v_1+\cdots+v_{k-1}$ and $s:=s'+v_k$, where $s'\in\overline{C^+}$ by the induction hypothesis, so $s\in\overline{C^+}$ by step 2.2 applied to $s'$ and $v_k$. If some $v_i$ with $i<k$ lies in $C^+$, the induction hypothesis gives $s'\in C^+$ and the strict case of step 2.2 gives $s\in C^+$; if none of $v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}$ is in $C^+$ but $v_k$ is, the strict case of step 2.2 applies directly to $s'$ and $v_k$. Induction on $k$ therefore proves both claims; finite sums are defined by recursion on $k$, so no choice is used. [step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 Let $p,q\in A$ and $D:=x(q)-x(p)$, so that $D$ is the coordinate column of $q-p$ by the linearity clause of [L3]. By [L7] and step 1.1, $q\in J^+(p)$ iff $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ iff $D^0\ge|D_s|$, and $q\in I^+(p)$ iff $q-p\in C^+$ iff $D^0>|D_s|$. Moreover $D=0$ iff $q-p=0$ iff $q=p$, because $E^{-1}$ is injective; hence $q\in J^+(p)$ with $q\ne p$ iff $D^0\ge|D_s|$ and $D\ne 0$. For $D\in\overline{C^+}$ this is equivalent to $D^0\ge|D_s|$ and $D^0>0$ by step 2.1, which is the third criterion; the fourth is the same statement as read off from step 2.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L3, L7, algebra]

4.1 Clause (a) is steps 1.1 and 2.1, clause (b) is steps 2.2, 2.3 and 3.1, and clause (c) is step 3.2. Every inertial chart has the same description because each inertial basis is $\eta$-orthonormal with first vector $e_0\in C^+$ ([L3]), so the criteria hold in the chart of any inertial frame. The objects $\le$, $J^+$ and $I^+$ are those of the affine model and no physical meaning, synchronization procedure or empirical claim is attached to them here; no choice principle is used, the only analytic input being the triangle inequality [L5] and the finite-dimensional algebra of the coordinates. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, step 3.2, given] ∎
