## Statement refuted

The following universal claim is false. Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented
time-oriented affine Minkowski space.

**(U1)** The reversed Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
$-\eta(v,w)\ge\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}$ holds for every pair of
vectors $v,w\in V$ that are individually timelike, regardless of their time
orientations.

**(U2)** The analogous reversed form
$|\eta(v,w)|\ge\sqrt{\eta(v,v)}\,\sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ holds for every pair of
spacelike vectors $v,w\in V$.

First witness, refuting (U1): in the inertial chart with diagonal metric
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ take $v:=(5,3,0,0)$, which is future timelike,
and $w:=(-5,3,0,0)$, which is past timelike. Then $\eta(v,w)=34>0$, so
$-\eta(v,w)=-34$, while
$\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}=4\cdot4=16$, and the asserted inequality
$-34\ge16$ is false; the sum $v+w=(0,6,0,0)$ is spacelike. Second witness,
refuting (U2): $v:=(0,1,0,0)$ and $w:=(0,1,1,0)$ are spacelike with
$\eta(v,v)=1$, $\eta(w,w)=2$, $\eta(v,w)=1$, so
$|\eta(v,w)|=1<1\cdot\sqrt2=\sqrt{\eta(v,v)}\,\sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$. Hence the
same-orientation hypothesis of
[[lem-sr-reverse-cauchy-schwarz-for-future-timelike-vectors]] cannot be dropped,
and the spacelike reversed inequality is not universal.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with chart $x$ and coordinates $(u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3)$ of a vector $u=u^0e_0+u^1e_1+u^2e_2+u^3e_3$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L1] Coordinates and pairing: in the frame's ordered basis $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, and by bilinearity $\eta(u,u')=-u^0u'^0+u^1u'^1+u^2u'^2+u^3u'^3$ for all $u,u'\in V$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

[L2] Cone coordinates: $T_+=\{u:u^0>|u_s|\}$ and $T_-=\{u:u^0<-|u_s|\}$ are exactly the two components of the timelike set, and in a frame with $e_0\in C^+$ one has $C^+=T_+$, $C^-=T_-$; hence $u$ is future timelike exactly when $u^0>|u_s|$ and past timelike exactly when $u^0<-|u_s|$, where $|u_s|=\sqrt{(u^1)^2+(u^2)^2+(u^3)^2}$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L3] Causal classification: $u$ is timelike when $\eta(u,u)<0$, spacelike when $\eta(u,u)>0$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

[L4] The reversed Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and its equality case: for future timelike $v,w$ with $a:=\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$, $b:=\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}$ one has $-\eta(v,w)\ge ab$, with equality exactly for positive proportional pairs; the same inequality holds for past timelike pairs ([[lem-sr-reverse-cauchy-schwarz-for-future-timelike-vectors]]).

[L5] Square roots and monotonicity of squaring: every real $c\ge0$ has a unique $\sqrt c\ge0$ with $(\sqrt c)^2=c$, in particular $\sqrt1=1$; for $x,y\ge0$ one has $x<y\iff x^2<y^2$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[L6] Order of $\mathbb{R}$: the order is transitive, so $x<y<z$ implies $x<z$ ([[def-ordered-field]]).

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 In the given inertial frame evaluate the four vectors of the two witnesses: $\eta(v,v)=-25+9=-16<0$ and $\eta(w,w)=-25+9=-16<0$ for $v=(5,3,0,0)$ and $w=(-5,3,0,0)$; and $\eta(v,w)=25+9=34$ for this pair; for the second pair $v'=(0,1,0,0)$, $w'=(0,1,1,0)$ one has $\eta(v',v')=1>0$, $\eta(w',w')=1+1=2>0$ and $\eta(v',w')=1$. [given, L1, algebra]

2.1 Both $v$ and $w$ are timelike by [L3]; since $v^0=5>3=|v_s|$ and $w^0=-5<-3=-|w_s|$, [L2] identifies $v$ as future timelike and $w$ as past timelike, so the pair $(v,w)$ is individually timelike with opposite time orientations. [step 1.1, L2, L3]

2.2 The sum $v+w=(0,6,0,0)$ has $\eta(v+w,v+w)=36>0$, so it is spacelike by [L3]; the failure of (U1) for this pair is therefore exactly the failure of the future timelike set to contain the sum of two oppositely oriented timelike vectors. [step 1.1, L1, L3, algebra]

2.3 For the second pair, [L3] makes $v'$ and $w'$ spacelike, and $\sqrt{\eta(v',v')}\,\sqrt{\eta(w',w')}=\sqrt1\cdot\sqrt2=1\cdot\sqrt2=\sqrt2$ by [L5]; since $1<2$ and $1,\sqrt2\ge0$, strict monotonicity of squaring gives $\sqrt2>1$; hence $|\eta(v',w')|=1<\sqrt2=\sqrt{\eta(v',v')}\,\sqrt{\eta(w',w')}$, so (U2) is refuted. [step 1.1, L3, L5, algebra]

2.4 The span of the second pair is $\{(0,s,t,0):s,t\in\mathbb{R}\}$, on which $\eta((0,s,t,0),(0,s,t,0))=s^2+t^2$ vanishes only for $s=t=0$: the subspace spanned by the two spacelike witnesses contains no null direction, so the failure of (U2) is not an artifact of a null direction in the span. [step 1.1, L1, algebra]

3.1 For this pair $\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}=\sqrt{16}=4=\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}$, so the right-hand side of (U1) is $16$, while the left-hand side is $-\eta(v,w)=-34<0$; since $0<16$, transitivity gives $-34<16$, so $-34\ge16$ is false and (U1) is refuted. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L5, L6, algebra]

4.1 The two witnesses therefore refute the claimed universality: the reversed Cauchy-Schwarz inequality requires the same (future) time orientation of the pair, and the spacelike reversed form fails even on a spacelike plane with no null direction; neither witness contradicts the positive results [L4], which are stated for same-orientation timelike pairs. [step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, step 3.1, L4] ∎

## Statement refuted

The following claim is false: if a piecewise $C^1$ curve
$x:[\alpha,\beta]\to A$ with nonzero timelike tangents runs from an event $p$ to
an event $q$ and attains the endpoint bound
$\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}$ in the length-integral sense, that is
$\int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}\,\mathrm ds=\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}$, then
its tangents must be future timelike, so that $x$ is a worldline of the model.

Counterexample: in the inertial chart with diagonal metric
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ let $d:=(5,3,0,0)$, a future timelike
displacement with $\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)}=4$, and put
$p:=x^{-1}(0,0,0,0)$, $q:=x^{-1}(-5,-3,0,0)=p-d$ and $x(s):=p-s\,d$ for
$s\in[0,1]$. Then $x(0)=p$, $x(1)=p-d=q$, and $x'(s)=-d$ is past timelike for
every $s$, so $x$ is not a future timelike worldline; but its length integrand
is $\sqrt{-\eta(-d,-d)}=\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)}=4$ and its length integral over
$[0,1]$ equals $4$, while $\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}=\sqrt{-\eta(-d,-d)}=4$: the
bound is attained with equality by a past-directed parametrization. Attainment
of the length bound therefore does not force the future time orientation; that
orientation enters only through the model's clock interpretation, which attaches
readings to future timelike worldlines ([[def-sr-proper-time]],
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]). Within the future timelike
worldline class the equality case is characterized by
[[thm-sr-endpoint-proper-time-bound-and-flat-maximum]] (ii).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial frame with chart $x$ and $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; the coordinate vector $d=(5,3,0,0)$; the events $p=x^{-1}(0,0,0,0)$, $q=x^{-1}(-5,-3,0,0)$; and the curve $x(s)=p-s\,d$ on $[0,1]$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L1] Pairing in the frame: $\eta(r,r')=-r^0r'^0+r^1r'^1+r^2r'^2+r^3r'^3$ for coordinate vectors, by the diagonal form and bilinearity ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

[L2] Causal classification and cone coordinates: $r$ is timelike when $\eta(r,r)<0$, spacelike when $\eta(r,r)>0$; in a frame with future first vector, $r$ is future timelike exactly when $r^0>|r_s|$ and past timelike exactly when $r^0<-|r_s|$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L3] Worldlines ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]): a future timelike worldline is a $C^1$ curve all of whose tangents are future timelike; the parametrization is part of the curve, and the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s\mapsto x(-s)$, which is not a worldline of the model.

[L4] Straight-segment length ([[def-sr-proper-time]]): for a curve with constant tangent $w$ on an interval of length $b-a$, the length integral is $(b-a)\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}$ whenever $w$ is timelike.

[L5] Square roots ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[def-ordered-field]]): $\sqrt{16}=4$, and $4>0$.

[L6] The endpoint bound and its equality case ([[thm-sr-endpoint-proper-time-bound-and-flat-maximum]]): for a weak piecewise $C^1$ future timelike worldline from $p$ to $q$, $c\Delta\tau\le\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}$ with equality exactly for the strictly increasing reparametrizations of the straight segment; the theorem is stated for future timelike worldlines and attaches no reading to past-directed curves.

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], $\eta(d,d)=-25+9=-16<0$ and $\eta(-d,-d)=-16<0$, while $d^0=5>3=|d_s|$ and $(-d)^0=-5<-3=-|(-d)_s|$; by [L2] $d$ is future timelike and $-d$ is past timelike, so $\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)}=\sqrt{16}=4$ by [L5] and $q-p=-d$. [given, L1, L2, L5, algebra]

2.1 The curve $x(s)=p-s\,d$ is $C^1$ (indeed affine) on $[0,1]$ with $x(0)=p$ and $x(1)=p-d=q$; its constant tangent is $x'(s)=-d$, which is nonzero and timelike but past-directed at every $s$, so by [L3] $x$ is not a future timelike worldline of the model, although it satisfies the 'piecewise $C^1$ with nonzero timelike tangents from $p$ to $q$' hypothesis of the refuted claim. [step 1.1, L3]

3.1 Its length integral is $\int_0^1\sqrt{-\eta(-d,-d)}\,\mathrm ds=\sqrt{-\eta(-d,-d)}=4$ by [L4] and step 1.1, and the endpoint bound is $\sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}=\sqrt{-\eta(-d,-d)}=4$; hence the length integral equals the endpoint bound, with equality. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L4, algebra]

4.1 The witness therefore refutes the claim: the length bound can be attained with equality by a past-directed parametrization with no future timelike tangent, so attainment of the bound does not force the future time orientation. This does not contradict [L6], which is stated for future timelike worldlines and whose equality case characterizes the strictly increasing reparametrizations within that class; it records precisely why the future-orientation hypothesis belongs to the clock reading rather than to the length inequality. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L3, L6] ∎

## Example

$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $d:=(5,3,0,0)$, a future timelike
coordinate vector with $-\eta(d,d)=25-9=16$, so
$T:=\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)}=4$ and $n:=d/T=(5/4,3/4,0,0)$.

**(a)** $n$ is future unit timelike: $\eta(n,n)=-25/16+9/16=-1$ and
$n^0=5/4>3/4=|n_s|$.

**(b)** The boost parameter $\beta:=n_s/n^0=(3/5,0,0)$ has
$|\beta|=3/5<1$ and $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}=5/4$, and the passive boost
$B(\beta)$ of [[def-lorentz-boost]] sends $n$ to $e_0$, as clause (iv) of
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]] requires, since
$\gamma(1,3/5,0,0)=(5/4,3/4,0,0)=n$.

**(c)** The basis
$(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3):=\bigl(n,\ B(-\beta)e_1,\ B(-\beta)e_2,\ B(-\beta)e_3\bigr)$
has coordinate columns
$e'_0=(5/4,3/4,0,0)$, $e'_1=(3/4,5/4,0,0)$, $e'_2=(0,0,1,0)$,
$e'_3=(0,0,0,1)$; the checks
$\eta(e'_0,e'_0)=-1$, $\eta(e'_1,e'_1)=-9/16+25/16=1$,
$\eta(e'_0,e'_1)=-(5/4)(3/4)+(3/4)(5/4)=0$,
$\eta(e'_2,e'_2)=\eta(e'_3,e'_3)=1$ and $\eta(e'_i,e'_j)=0$ for the remaining
pairs show that $(o;e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is an inertial frame with first
vector $n$.

**(d)** Its chart $x'$ assigns to $d$ the coordinates $(4,0,0,0)$: indeed
$d=4n=4e'_0$, so $E'^{-1}(d)=4E'^{-1}(e'_0)=(4,0,0,0)$; in particular the two
endpoints of any displacement $4n$ have equal spatial coordinates in $x'$ and
time coordinates differing by $4$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with chart $x$, $\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the coordinate vector $d=(5,3,0,0)$, $T=\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)}$, $n=d/T$, and the boost parameter $\beta=n_s/n^0$ of [[def-lorentz-boost]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L1] Pairing in the frame: $\eta(r,r')=-r^0r'^0+r^1r'^1+r^2r'^2+r^3r'^3$ for coordinate vectors $r,r'$, and $\eta$ is symmetric and bilinear ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

[L2] Causal classification and cone: $r$ is timelike when $\eta(r,r)<0$ and future timelike exactly when $r^0>|r_s|$ in a frame with future first vector ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L3] Rest-frame lemma: for a future timelike displacement $d$ with $T=\sqrt{-\eta(d,d)}$ and $n=d/T$, the vector $n$ is future unit timelike, and for every event $o$ there is an inertial frame with first vector $n$; in any such frame the chart assigns to $d$ the coordinates $(T,0,0,0)$ ([[lem-sr-rest-frame-of-a-future-timelike-displacement]]).

[L4] Boosts: for $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^3$ with $|\beta|<1$ the passive boost $B(\beta)$ acts on coordinates by $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta\cdot x)$, $x'=x+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot x)\beta-\gamma\beta x^0$, with $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$; $B(\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\beta)$, and if $u$ is future unit timelike with coordinates $(u^0,u_s)$ then $B(u_s/u^0)u=e_0$; for $\beta\cdot x=0$ and $x^0=0$ the formula returns $x$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[L5] Square roots and monotonicity: every real $c\ge0$ has a unique $\sqrt c\ge0$ with $(\sqrt c)^2=c$, so $\sqrt{16}=4$ and $\sqrt{9}=3$; for $x,y\ge0$, $x<y\iff x^2<y^2$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[L6] Order arithmetic: the order is trichotomous and transitive, and multiplication by a positive real preserves inequalities ([[def-ordered-field]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], $\eta(d,d)=-25+9=-16$, so $-\eta(d,d)=16>0$ and $T=\sqrt{16}=4$ by [L5]; hence $n=d/T=(5/4,3/4,0,0)$ and $n_s=(3/4,0,0)$. [given, L1, L5, algebra]

2.1 For (a): $\eta(n,n)=-(5/4)^2+(3/4)^2=-25/16+9/16=-1$ by [L1], so $n$ is timelike, and $n^0=5/4>3/4=|n_s|$, so $n$ is future unit timelike by [L2] and [L3]. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, algebra]

3.1 For (b): $\beta=n_s/n^0=(3/5,0,0)$ with $|\beta|=3/5$ and $|\beta|^2=9/25<1$, so $B(\beta)$ is defined; $\gamma=(1-9/25)^{-1/2}=(16/25)^{-1/2}=5/4$, because $(5/4)^2=25/16$ and $5/4>0$ by [L5]; and $\gamma(1,3/5,0,0)=(5/4)(1,3/5,0,0)=(5/4,3/4,0,0)=n$, which is the displayed application of clause (iv) of [L4] to the future unit timelike vector $n$. [step 2.1, L4, L5, L6, algebra]

4.1 For (c): the coordinate action of [L4] with parameter $-\beta$ gives $B(-\beta)e_1$ the column $(3/4,5/4,0,0)$: from $-\beta=(-3/5,0,0)$ and $x=e_1$, with spatial part $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(1,0,0)$, one gets $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-(-\beta)\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})=\gamma(0+\frac35)=\frac54\cdot\frac35=\frac34$ and $x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}((-\beta)\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})(-\beta)-\gamma(-\beta)x^0=(1,0,0)+\frac{1/4}{9/25}\cdot\bigl(-\frac35\bigr)\cdot\bigl(-\frac35,0,0\bigr)=(1,0,0)+(\frac14,0,0)=(\frac54,0,0)$, that is $B(-\beta)e_1=(3/4,5/4,0,0)$; for $x=e_2$ and $x=e_3$ one has $\beta\cdot x=0$ and $x^0=0$, so the formula returns $x$, giving $B(-\beta)e_2=e_2$ and $B(-\beta)e_3=e_3$; and for $x=e_0=(1,0,0,0)$ it gives $x'^0=\gamma=5/4$ and $x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=-\gamma(-\beta)x^0=\gamma\beta=(3/4,0,0)$, so $B(-\beta)e_0=(5/4,3/4,0,0)=n=e'_0$; these are the coordinate columns of the basis of the example, and $e'_a=B(-\beta)e_a$ for every $a=0,1,2,3$. [step 3.1, L4, L6, algebra]

5.1 For the orthonormality checks of (c): $\eta(e'_0,e'_0)=-25/16+9/16=-1$, $\eta(e'_1,e'_1)=-9/16+25/16=1$, $\eta(e'_0,e'_1)=-(5/4)(3/4)+(3/4)(5/4)=0$, $\eta(e'_2,e'_2)=1$, $\eta(e'_3,e'_3)=1$, and the remaining cross pairings vanish by the diagonal form [L1]; since by step 4.1 the basis $(e'_0,\dots,e'_3)$ is the image of the inertial basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ under the proper orthochronous Lorentz map $B(-\beta)$ of [L4], orthonormality also follows from metric preservation, the first vector $e'_0=n$ is future timelike by step 2.1, and the basis is positively oriented because $B(-\beta)$ is proper and preserves the oriented volume form and the orientation class; therefore $(o;e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is an inertial frame with first vector $n$, as [L3] predicts. [step 4.1, L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

6.1 For (d): $d=Tn=4e'_0$ by step 1.1 and step 4.1, so for the chart $x'=E'^{-1}(\cdot-o)$ of the frame of step 5.1 linearity gives $x'(o+\lambda d)=E'^{-1}(\lambda d)=\lambda\,E'^{-1}(d)=\lambda(4,0,0,0)$ because $E'^{-1}(e'_0)=(1,0,0,0)$; in particular $x'$ assigns to $d$ the coordinates $(4,0,0,0)$, and the two endpoints of any displacement $4n$ have equal spatial coordinates and time coordinates differing by $4$. [step 5.1, L3, algebra]

## Statement

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]): $\eta$ is symmetric and bilinear, nondegenerate in the sense that both radicals are $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and of inertia $(3,1,0)$. Let $V^*$ be the algebraic dual ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]). Then:

**(a)** The map $\Phi:V\to V^*$, $\Phi(v)(w):=\eta(v,w)$, is linear, and it is injective: $\Phi(v)=0$ means $\eta(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in V$, that is $v\in\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{0\}$.

**(b)** $\dim V^*=\dim V=4$ ([[thm-dual-family-is-a-basis-in-finite-dimension]]), so $\Phi$ is a linear bijection; equivalently $\operatorname{nullity}\Phi=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}\Phi=4$ ([[thm-rank-nullity]], [[def-rank-and-nullity]]).

**(c)** Consequently for every covector $k\in V^*$ there is a unique vector $k^\sharp\in V$ with $\eta(k^\sharp,w)=k(w)$ for all $w\in V$; the assignment $\sharp:V^*\to V$, $k\mapsto k^\sharp$, is linear and is the inverse of $\Phi$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]), so $(v^\flat)^\sharp=v$ for $v^\flat:=\Phi(v)$ and $(k^\sharp)^\flat=k$ for every $k\in V^*$; in particular $k^\sharp=0$ if and only if $k=0$.

**(d)** If $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]) and $k_a:=k(e_a)$ are the values of $k$ on that basis, then

$$k^\sharp=-k_0e_0+k_1e_1+k_2e_2+k_3e_3,$$

that is $(k^\sharp)^0=-k_0$ and $(k^\sharp)^i=k_i$ for $i=1,2,3$ in this basis, and

$$\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=-(k_0)^2+(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2.$$

Hence, for $k\neq 0$ the vector $k^\sharp$ is nonzero and, in the sense of ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]), it is null exactly when $(k_0)^2=(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2$, timelike exactly when $(k_0)^2>(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2$ (equivalently $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)<0$), and spacelike exactly when $(k_0)^2<(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2$ (equivalently $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)>0$); for $k=0$ one has $k^\sharp=0$, which has no causal character.

No orientation, time orientation or affine structure is used, and no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$, a Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, and the map $\Phi(v):=\eta(v,\cdot)$.

[L1] $V$ is $4$-dimensional, and $\eta$ is symmetric and bilinear with $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{0\}$ and inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], [[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]).

[L2] $V^*=\mathcal L(V,\mathbb R)$ is the algebraic dual of $V$, and the assignment $B\mapsto B^\flat$ with $B^\flat(v)(w)=B(v,w)$ is a linear bijection from the bilinear forms on $V$ onto $\mathcal L(V,V^*)$; in particular $B^\flat$ is a linear map for every bilinear form $B$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]], [[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]], [[def-linear-map]]).

[L3] If $B=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ is a basis of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space, then its dual family is a basis of the dual space; consequently $\dim V^*=\dim V$ ([[thm-dual-family-is-a-basis-in-finite-dimension]]).

[L4] There is an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$, that is, $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]).

[L5] For a linear map $T$ with finite-dimensional domain, $\dim V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T$, where $\operatorname{nullity}T=\dim(\ker T)$ and $\operatorname{rank}T=\dim(\operatorname{im}T)$ ([[thm-rank-nullity]], [[def-rank-and-nullity]]).

[L6] A linear map $T$ is invertible, equivalently a linear isomorphism, when there is a linear map $S$ with $S\circ T=\operatorname{id}$ and $T\circ S=\operatorname{id}$; such an $S$ is unique and written $T^{-1}$, and $T$ is bijective ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]).

[L7] A vector $v\in V$ is timelike, null or spacelike according as $\eta(v,v)<0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ with $v\neq 0$, or $\eta(v,v)>0$; the zero vector has none of these characters, and every nonzero vector has exactly one ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The map $\Phi$ is linear, and $\ker\Phi=\{0\}$. Since $\eta$ is a bilinear form on $V$, its associated map $\eta^\flat$ lies in $\mathcal L(V,V^*)$ and $\eta^\flat(v)(w)=\eta(v,w)=\Phi(v)(w)$ for all $v,w$, so $\Phi=\eta^\flat$ is linear by [L2]. If $\Phi(v)=0$, then $\eta(v,w)=0$ for every $w\in V$, so $v$ lies in the left radical of $\eta$, which is $\{0\}$ by [L1]; conversely $\Phi(0)=0$ by linearity (equivalently $\eta(0,\cdot)=0$), so $\ker\Phi=\{0\}$. [L1, L2, given]

1.2 The map $\Phi$ is surjective. Fix an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ [L4], with dual family $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$, a basis of $V^*$ by [L3]. For all $a,b$ one has $\Phi(e_a)(e_b)=\eta(e_a,e_b)=\eta_{aa}\delta_{ab}$ with $\eta_{aa}\in\{-1,1\}$, by [L4], and the functional $\eta_{aa}e^a$ takes the same values on the basis $(e_b)$; two linear functionals that agree on a basis agree on every vector, so $\Phi(e_a)=\eta_{aa}e^a$, which exhibits $e^a=\eta_{aa}\Phi(e_a)$ as a scalar multiple of $\Phi(e_a)$ (here $\eta_{aa}^{-1}=\eta_{aa}$). Hence every element of the basis $(e^a)$ of $V^*$ lies in the linear span of $\Phi(e_0),\dots,\Phi(e_3)$, so that span is all of $V^*$; therefore $\Phi$ is surjective. [L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 The map $\Phi$ is a linear bijection, $\dim V^*=\dim V=4$, and the inverse assignment $\sharp$ exists with the stated properties. By step 1.1 $\Phi$ is injective and by step 1.2 it is surjective, hence bijective; by [L3] and [L1], $\dim V^*=\dim V=4$; and [L5] applied to the linear map $\Phi$ gives the same picture independently, $\operatorname{nullity}\Phi=\dim\ker\Phi=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}\Phi=4=\dim V^*$, with $\operatorname{rank}\Phi=\dim\operatorname{im}\Phi$ and $\operatorname{im}\Phi=V^*$ by step 1.2. By [L6] the inverse $\Phi^{-1}:V^*\to V$ is a well-defined linear map, unique, and satisfies $\Phi^{-1}\circ\Phi=\operatorname{id}_V$ and $\Phi\circ\Phi^{-1}=\operatorname{id}_{V^*}$. Writing $k^\sharp:=\Phi^{-1}(k)$ for $k\in V^*$, we get $\eta(k^\sharp,w)=\Phi(k^\sharp)(w)=k(w)$ for every $w\in V$; any $c$ with $\eta(c,w)=k(w)$ for all $w$ satisfies $\Phi(c)=k$, hence $c=k^\sharp$ by injectivity of $\Phi$, which is the asserted uniqueness. The two inverse equations are exactly $(v^\flat)^\sharp=v$ for $v^\flat=\Phi(v)$ and $(k^\sharp)^\flat=k$, and $k^\sharp=0$ holds if and only if $k=\Phi(k^\sharp)=\Phi(0)=0$. This proves (a), (b) and (c). [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L3, L5, L6]

3.1 Component formula. Let $k\in V^*$ and keep the orthonormal basis $(e_a)$ of step 1.2; put $c^0:=-k_0$ and $c^i:=k_i$ for $i=1,2,3$, where $k_a=k(e_a)$, and set $c:=c^0e_0+c^1e_1+c^2e_2+c^3e_3$. For every basis vector $e_b$, bilinearity and orthonormality [L1, L4] give $\eta(c,e_b)=\sum_a c^a\eta(e_a,e_b)=c^b\eta_{bb}$; hence $\eta(c,e_0)=-c^0=k_0=k(e_0)$ and $\eta(c,e_i)=c^i=k_i=k(e_i)$ for $i=1,2,3$. The functionals $w\mapsto\eta(c,w)$ (linear in its second argument by [L1]) and $k$ agree on the basis $(e_b)$, hence on all of $V$; therefore $\Phi(c)=k$, and uniqueness in step 2.1 yields $c=k^\sharp=-k_0e_0+k_1e_1+k_2e_2+k_3e_3$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, L1, L4, algebra]

4.1 Quadratic form and causal trichotomy. With $k^\sharp=\sum_a c^ae_a$ from step 3.1, bilinearity and orthonormality give $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=\sum_{a,b}c^ac^b\eta(e_a,e_b)=\sum_a(c^a)^2\eta_{aa}=-(c^0)^2+(c^1)^2+(c^2)^2+(c^3)^2=-(k_0)^2+(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2$, because $(c^0)^2=(k_0)^2$ and $c^i=k_i$. If $k\neq 0$ then $k^\sharp\neq 0$ by step 2.1, so [L7] applies: $k^\sharp$ is null exactly when this value is $0$, that is when $(k_0)^2=(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2$; timelike exactly when it is negative, that is when $(k_0)^2>(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2$; and spacelike exactly when it is positive, that is when $(k_0)^2<(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2$. If $k=0$ then $k^\sharp=0$ by step 2.1 and the zero vector has no causal character by [L7]. No orientation, time orientation or affine structure was used, and no choice principle was used. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L4, L7] ∎

## Definition

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with displacements $q-p\in V$ ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]).

**(a) Affine phase functions.** A map $\theta:A\to\mathbb R$ is an **affine phase function** when there are $q\in A$ and a covector $k\in V^*$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]) with

$$\theta(p)-\theta(q)=k(p-q)\qquad\text{for all }p\in A .$$

The covector $k$ is then unique: if $k'$ also satisfies the identity, then $(k-k')(p-q)=0$ for all $p\in A$, and as $p$ runs over $A$ the displacements $p-q$ run over all of $V$, so $k-k'=0$ as a functional. This unique covector is called the **wave covector** of $\theta$, also written $\mathrm d\theta$. Conversely, for every $q\in A$, every $k\in V^*$ and every $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$, the formula

$$\theta(p):=k(p-q)+\theta_0$$

defines an affine phase function with $\mathrm d\theta=k$ and $\theta(q)=\theta_0$; hence for each fixed $q$ the map $\theta\mapsto(\mathrm d\theta,\theta(q))$ is a bijection from the set of affine phase functions onto $V^*\times\mathbb R$. In the inertial chart $x$ of an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), writing $k_a:=k(e_a)$, one has

$$\theta(p)=k_ax^a(p)+\theta(o)$$

because $p-o=\sum_ax^a(p)e_a$ with unique coordinates $x^a(p)$ ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and $k$ is linear; for a second origin $o'$ one has $\theta(o')=\theta(o)+k(o'-o)$.

**(b) Constant-phase directions and level sets.** For $v\in V$, $p\in A$ and $s\in\mathbb R$ one has $\theta(p+sv)=\theta(p)+sk(v)$ by the defining identity, so $k(v)=0$ if and only if $\theta$ is constant on the line $p+\mathbb Rv$ for every $p\in A$. If $k\neq 0$, the **direction subspace**

$$\ker k:=\{v\in V:k(v)=0\}$$

is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace of $V$: it is the kernel of the nonzero linear functional $k$, and choosing $v_0$ with $k(v_0)\neq 0$ gives every $v\in V$ the unique decomposition $v=\bigl(k(v)/k(v_0)\bigr)v_0+w$ with $w\in\ker k$, so $V=\ker k\oplus\mathbb Rv_0$ and $\dim\ker k=4-1=3$; every nonempty level set

$$\Sigma_t:=\{p\in A:\theta(p)=t\}$$

is then the affine hyperplane $p_0+\ker k$ through any of its points $p_0$, and the level set is empty when $t$ is not a value of $\theta$. If $k=0$ then $\theta$ is constant and $\Sigma_t$ is either empty or all of $A$. Finally, for every $C^1$ curve $\gamma:I\to A$ one has $(\theta\circ\gamma)'(s)=k\bigl(\gamma'(s)\bigr)$ for all $s\in I$: in the coordinates of any inertial chart this is the identity $\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm ds}\bigl(k_ax^a(\gamma(s))+\theta(o)\bigr)=\sum_ak_a\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm ds}x^a(\gamma(s))$ for a finite real linear combination of differentiable real functions, the one-variable case covered by the chain rule and the derivative of a constant ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[def-derivative]]), while the right-hand side is the same linear combination read in the coordinates of $\gamma'(s)$.

**(c) Wave covectors.** A **wave covector** on $(A,V,\eta)$ is a nonzero element $k\in V^*$. With $k^\sharp$ the raised vector of [[lem-sr-metric-duality-on-lorentz-vector-space]] (so that $\eta(k^\sharp,w)=k(w)$ for all $w\in V$, and $k^\sharp=0$ exactly when $k=0$), the covector $k$ is called **null**, **timelike** or **spacelike** when $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)$ is zero, negative or positive, and **future**, **past**, **future null**, **past null** or **causal** when $k^\sharp$ is respectively future causal, past causal, future null, past null or causal in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]; a **future null wave covector** is one that is both future and null. These terms are well posed: a wave covector has $k\neq0$, hence $k^\sharp\neq0$, and a nonzero vector has exactly one causal character and is future or past exactly when it is causal.

**(d) Mathematical scope.** This item introduces mathematical objects and terminology only. It excludes the zero covector from the term wave covector, it fixes no units and no physical interpretation, and it does not claim that light or any physical wave is described by such a phase; that identification is adopted in post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model. No choice principle is used.

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space, let $n,v\in V$, and recall that a nonzero $v$ with $\eta(v,v)\le 0$ is causal ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Then:

**(a)** if $n$ is future timelike and $v$ is nonzero future causal, then $\eta(n,v)<0$;

**(b)** if $n$ is future timelike and $v$ is nonzero past causal, then $\eta(n,v)>0$;

**(c)** consequently, for a nonzero null vector $v$ and any future timelike $n$, $v$ is future null if and only if $\eta(n,v)<0$, and $v$ is past null if and only if $\eta(n,v)>0$; the sign of $\eta(n,v)$ does not depend on the choice of the future timelike $n$;

**(d)** if $n_{\mathrm{hat}}:=n/\sqrt{-\eta(n,n)}$ is the normalization of a future timelike $n$, then $n_{\mathrm{hat}}$ is future unit timelike, $\eta(n_{\mathrm{hat}},n_{\mathrm{hat}})=-1$, and $\eta(n,v)=\sqrt{-\eta(n,n)}\,\eta(n_{\mathrm{hat}},v)$ for every $v$, so the sign statements hold for $n_{\mathrm{hat}}$ as well.

The statement is pure affine Minkowski geometry, and no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and vectors $n,v\in V$.

[L1] A vector is timelike when $\eta(v,v)<0$, null when $v\ne 0$ and $\eta(v,v)=0$, spacelike when $\eta(v,v)>0$, and causal when it is timelike or null; the zero vector has no causal character and every nonzero vector has exactly one character ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

[L2] $C^+$ is one of the two connected components of the timelike set, and future timelike means membership in $C^+$, future null means nonzero null membership in $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$, and future causal means future timelike or future null; the closed cones $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are convex cones meeting only at $0$, and every causal vector is future or past but not both ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L3] In an $\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0$ timelike, writing $x=x^0e_0+x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ and $|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|:=\sqrt{(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2+(x^3)^2}$ and $\eta_{00}:=\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$, the timelike set splits into $T_+=\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and $T_-=\{x:x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$, these are exactly its two connected components, $\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{x:x^0\ge|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and $\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{x:x^0\le-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L4] For every event $o\in A$ there is an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, so its ordered basis is $\eta$-orthonormal with $e_0\in C^+$ ([[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L5] For an inertial frame, with $S=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $\delta:=\eta|_S$ the positive-definite spatial form, the coordinate triple $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ satisfies $\delta(x_{\mathrm{vec}},y_{\mathrm{vec}})=\sum_ix^iy^i$ and $|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|=\sqrt{\delta(x_{\mathrm{vec}},x_{\mathrm{vec}})}$; bilinearity and $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ give $\eta(x,y)=-x^0y^0+\delta(x_{\mathrm{vec}},y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[L6] For real lists, $|\sum_{k<n}a_kb_k|\le\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}a_k^2}\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}b_k^2}$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]), which in the coordinates of [L5] reads $|\delta(x_{\mathrm{vec}},y_{\mathrm{vec}})|\le|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\,|y_{\mathrm{vec}}|$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Frame and coordinates. Fix an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ [L4] and write every $x\in V$ as $x=x^0e_0+x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ in its basis; then $\eta(x,y)=-x^0y^0+\delta(x_{\mathrm{vec}},y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ with $|\delta(x_{\mathrm{vec}},y_{\mathrm{vec}})|\le|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\,|y_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ by [L5, L6]. Because $e_0\in C^+$ and $e_0\in T_+$, the component $T_+$ of [L3] is $C^+$, so $C^+=\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)=\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{x:x^0\ge|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ [L2, L3]. [L2, L3, L4, L5, L6]

2.1 Clause (a). Let $n$ be future timelike and $v\ne 0$ future causal. By [L2] and step 1.1 the future causal vectors are $C^+\cup(\operatorname{cl}(C^+)\setminus\{0\})$, so in the frame of step 1.1, $n^0>|n_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ and $v^0\ge|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge0$; $v\ne0$ rules out $v^0=0$, so $v^0>0$. Then $\eta(n,v)=-n^0v^0+\delta(n_{\mathrm{vec}},v_{\mathrm{vec}})\le-n^0v^0+|n_{\mathrm{vec}}|\,|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\le-n^0v^0+|n_{\mathrm{vec}}|\,v^0=-(n^0-|n_{\mathrm{vec}}|)v^0<0$, because $|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\le v^0$, $|n_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge0$, $n^0-|n_{\mathrm{vec}}|>0$ and $v^0>0$. [step 1.1]

3.1 Clause (b). If $n$ is future timelike and $v$ is nonzero past causal, then $-v$ is nonzero future causal: $v\in C^-$ or $v$ is past null, and negating does not change $\eta(v,v)$, while $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)=-\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $T_-=-T_+$ show $-v$ lies in $C^+$ (timelike case) or is nonzero null in $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ (null case) [L2, L3]. By step 2.1, $\eta(n,-v)<0$, and bilinearity gives $\eta(n,-v)=-\eta(n,v)$, so $\eta(n,v)>0$. [step 2.1, L2, L3]

4.1 Clause (c). Let $v$ be nonzero null and $n$ future timelike. If $v$ is future null then $v$ is nonzero future causal and step 2.1 gives $\eta(n,v)<0$; if $v$ is past null then step 3.1 gives $\eta(n,v)>0$. Since a causal vector is future or past but not both [L2] and a nonzero null vector is causal, exactly one of these two cases occurs, so conversely $\eta(n,v)<0$ forces $v$ future null and $\eta(n,v)>0$ forces $v$ past null; the sign is therefore determined by $v$ alone and is independent of the future timelike $n$ used. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L2]

5.1 Clause (d). For future timelike $n$, $-\eta(n,n)>0$ by [L1], so $\lambda:=\sqrt{-\eta(n,n)}$ is a positive real number and $n_{\mathrm{hat}}:=n/\lambda$ is defined. By step 1.1, $n^0>|n_{\mathrm{vec}}|\ge0$; multiplying by $\lambda^{-1}>0$ gives $n_{\mathrm{hat}}^0>|n_{\mathrm{hat,vec}}|$, so $n_{\mathrm{hat}}\in T_+=C^+$ is future timelike; bilinearity gives $\eta(n_{\mathrm{hat}},n_{\mathrm{hat}})=\lambda^{-2}\eta(n,n)=-1$ and $\eta(n,v)=\eta(\lambda n_{\mathrm{hat}},v)=\lambda\,\eta(n_{\mathrm{hat}},v)$ for every $v$. Hence $\eta(n_{\mathrm{hat}},v)$ has the same sign as $\eta(n,v)$ for every $v$, and the sign statements of steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 hold with $n$ replaced by $n_{\mathrm{hat}}$; this proves (a)-(d). The argument used only the affine Minkowski geometry of the cited items, and no choice principle was used. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, L1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space, let $k$ be a future null wave covector ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]) and let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Define

$$\varpi:=-k(e_0),\qquad s_i:=\frac{k(e_i)}{\varpi}\quad (i=1,2,3),$$

and write $s:=(s_1,s_2,s_3)\in\mathbb R^3$ with Euclidean norm $|s|$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

**(a)** $\varpi>0$;

**(b)** $|s|=1$;

**(c)** for every $v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ in $V$ one has $k(v)=\varpi(-v^0+s_1v^1+s_2v^2+s_3v^3)$; equivalently the components of $k$ in the frame are $(k_0,k_1,k_2,k_3)=(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$;

**(d)** the raised vector is $k^\sharp=\varpi(e_0+s_1e_1+s_2e_2+s_3e_3)$, with frame coordinates $\varpi(1,s_1,s_2,s_3)$; it is nonzero and future null, and $k(k^\sharp)=\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=0$;

**(e)** conversely, if a covector $k\in V^*$ has frame components $(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$ with $\varpi>0$ and $|s|=1$ in some inertial frame, then $k$ is a future null wave covector, and the construction of (a)-(b) applied to $k$ in that frame returns the same $\varpi$ and $s$;

**(f)** the pair $(\varpi,s)$ is uniquely determined by $k$ and the frame, and two future null wave covectors with the same pair agree; it is thus the complete frame description of a future null wave covector.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$, a future null wave covector $k$, and an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

[L1] A wave covector is a nonzero covector, and $k$ is future null, so its raised vector satisfies $k^\sharp\neq0$, $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=0$, $k^\sharp$ is future null, and $k(w)=\eta(k^\sharp,w)$ for every $w\in V$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]], [[lem-sr-metric-duality-on-lorentz-vector-space]]).

[L2] An inertial frame has $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$, with $e_0$ future ($e_0\in C^+$), and its vectors are linearly independent with every vector having unique coordinates in the basis ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]).

[L3] If $n$ is future timelike and $v$ is nonzero future causal, then $\eta(n,v)<0$ ([[lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative]], clause (a)).

[L4] A nonzero vector has exactly one causal character, and it is causal exactly when it is timelike or null; a causal vector is future or past but not both; future causal means future timelike or future null, and future null means nonzero null in $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

[L5] In the frame, writing $v=v^0e_0+v_{\mathrm{vec}}$ with $v_{\mathrm{vec}}=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and $\delta$ for the positive-definite spatial form, $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+\delta(v_{\mathrm{vec}},w_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and $\delta(v_{\mathrm{vec}},w_{\mathrm{vec}})=\sum_iv^iw^i$, so $|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2=\sum_i(v^i)^2$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[L6] For the components $k_a:=k(e_a)$ of a covector, the raised vector is $k^\sharp=-k_0e_0+k_1e_1+k_2e_2+k_3e_3$, and in the frame $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=-(k_0)^2+(k_1)^2+(k_2)^2+(k_3)^2$ ([[lem-sr-metric-duality-on-lorentz-vector-space]], clause (d)).

[L7] The frame's first vector is future, so $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)=\{v:v^0\ge|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

[L8] $|s|^2=\sum_i s_i^2$ for the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Clause (a). Since $e_0$ is future and $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$, it is future timelike, and $k^\sharp$ is nonzero future causal by [L1]; [L3] gives $\eta(e_0,k^\sharp)<0$. By [L1] and symmetry of $\eta$, $k(e_0)=\eta(k^\sharp,e_0)=\eta(e_0,k^\sharp)<0$, so $\varpi=-k(e_0)>0$. [L1, L2, L3]

1.2 Clause (c). For $v=\sum_av^ae_a$ with unique coordinates and $k$ linear [L2], $k(v)=\sum_av^ak(e_a)=v^0k(e_0)+\sum_iv^ik(e_i)=-\varpi v^0+\sum_i\varpi s_iv^i=\varpi(-v^0+s_1v^1+s_2v^2+s_3v^3)$, using the definitions of $\varpi$ and $s_i$; the component statement is the same identity read on the basis. [L2]

1.3 Clause (e). Let $k$ have components $(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$ with $\varpi>0$ and $|s|=1$ in the given inertial frame. Then $k(e_0)=-\varpi\neq0$, so $k\neq0$; by [L6], $k^\sharp=-k_0e_0+\sum_ik_ie_i=\varpi(e_0+s_1e_1+s_2e_2+s_3e_3)$. Its frame coordinates are $\varpi(1,s)$, so $v:=k^\sharp$ satisfies $v^0=\varpi=\varpi|s|\ge0$ and $|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|=\varpi|s|=\varpi=v^0$ by [L5, L8]; hence $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)\setminus\{0\}$ by [L7], and $\eta(v,v)=-\varpi^2+\varpi^2|s|^2=0$ by [L5, L6, L8], so $v$ is null; by [L4] $v$ is future null, and again by [L4] the covector $k$ is a future null wave covector. The construction of (a)-(b) returns $-k(e_0)=\varpi$ and $k(e_i)/\varpi=\varpi s_i/\varpi=s_i$. [L5, L6, L7, L8, L4]

2.1 Clause (b). By [L6], $k^\sharp=-k_0e_0+k_1e_1+k_2e_2+k_3e_3$ with $k_0=k(e_0)=-\varpi$ and $k_i=k(e_i)=\varpi s_i$, so $k^\sharp=\varpi e_0+\sum_i\varpi s_ie_i$. Orthonormality of the frame [L2] and bilinearity give $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=-\varpi^2+\sum_i(\varpi s_i)^2=\varpi^2\bigl(|s|^2-1\bigr)$ by [L8]; by [L1] this value is $0$, and $\varpi>0$ by step 1.1, so $|s|^2=1$ and $|s|=1$. [step 1.1, L2, L6, L8]

2.2 Clause (d). Step 1.2 and $k_i=\varpi s_i$, $k_0=-\varpi$ give $k^\sharp=-k_0e_0+k_1e_1+k_2e_2+k_3e_3=\varpi(e_0+s_1e_1+s_2e_2+s_3e_3)$ by [L6]; the coefficient of $e_0$ is $\varpi>0$ and the coordinates are $\varpi(1,s_1,s_2,s_3)$, so $k^\sharp\neq0$; [L1] gives that $k^\sharp$ is future null and $k(k^\sharp)=\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=0$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L6]

3.1 Clause (f). By definition $\varpi=-k(e_0)$ and $s_i=k(e_i)/\varpi$ are determined by $k$ and the frame (with $\varpi>0$ by step 1.1), so the pair is unique for $k$; conversely, if two covectors have the same frame data, they take the same values on each $e_a$, hence agree on all of $V$ by linearity and [L2]. Clause (c) exhibits the data of every future null wave covector, clause (e) shows every admissible pair arises from one, and steps 2.1 and 2.2 record $|s|=1$ and the raised vector; this proves (a)-(f). No choice principle was used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space, let $x$ and $x'$ be inertial charts whose transition is $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ for some $\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\beta|<1$ and some $b\in\mathbb R^4$, where $B(\beta)$ is the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] and $\gamma:=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$, and let $k$ be a future null wave covector with frame-$x$ data $(\varpi,s)$ as in [[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], so that $k$ has components $(k_0,k_1,k_2,k_3)=(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$ in $x$. Then:

**(i)** the components of the same covector $k$ in $x'$ are $k'_a=\bigl(B(-\beta)\bigr)^b{}_ak_b$, that is

$$k'_0=\gamma\bigl(k_0+\beta\cdot k_{\mathrm{vec}}\bigr),\qquad k'_{\mathrm{vec}}=k_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot k_{\mathrm{vec}})\beta+\gamma\beta k_0$$

for $\beta\ne0$ (and $k'=k$ for $\beta=0$), where $k_{\mathrm{vec}}:=(k_1,k_2,k_3)$;

**(ii)** with $\varpi':=-k'_0$ and $s'_i:=k'_i/\varpi'$ the frame-$x'$ data of $k$ is

$$\varpi'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi>0,\qquad s'=\frac{s+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)\beta-\gamma\beta}{\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)}$$

for $\beta\ne0$ (and $\varpi'=\varpi$, $s'=s$ for $\beta=0$); moreover $|s'|=1$, so $k'_a=(-\varpi',\varpi's'_1,\varpi's'_2,\varpi's'_3)$ in $x'$;

**(iii)** in the axis case $\beta=be_1$ with $b\in(-1,1)$: $s'_1=(s_1-b)/(1-bs_1)$, and $s'_2=s_2/\bigl(\gamma(1-bs_1)\bigr)$, $s'_3=s_3/\bigl(\gamma(1-bs_1)\bigr)$;

**(iv)** $\beta\cdot s'=(\beta\cdot s-|\beta|^2)/(1-\beta\cdot s)$; in particular $\beta\cdot s'=0$ if and only if $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$, and $\beta\cdot s'=-|\beta|^2$ if and only if $\beta\cdot s=0$;

**(v)** applying the transformation with $\beta$ replaced by $-\beta$ returns the original data $(\varpi,s)$, since $B(-\beta)$ is the inverse of $B(\beta)$.

The statement is pure algebra of $\eta$ and the boost; no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Inertial charts $x,x'$ with $x'=B(\beta)x+b$, $\beta\in\mathbb R^3$, $|\beta|<1$, $b\in\mathbb R^4$, $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$, and a future null wave covector $k$ with frame-$x$ data $(\varpi,s)$.

[L1] $B(\beta)$ has matrix entries in the frame basis $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$, $B^i{}_j=\delta^i_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$ for $i,j=1,2,3$ and $\beta\ne0$, while $B(0)=\operatorname{id}$; $\gamma\ge1$ with equality exactly when $\beta=0$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]]).

[L2] $B(\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with $B(-\beta)=B(\beta)^{-1}$, and the transition $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ of inertial charts has proper orthochronous linear part ([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]], [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

[L3] For a constant covector field $k$ on $A$ (of class $C^\infty$, in particular $C^1$) the components in the two charts satisfy $k'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ak_b$, where $\Lambda$ is the linear part of the transition; here $\Lambda=B(\beta)$ and $\Lambda^{-1}=B(-\beta)$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]], clause (ii), [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[L4] Frame data of a future null wave covector in any inertial frame: for the frame of $x'$, the numbers $\varpi':=-k(e'_0)$ and $s'_i:=k(e'_i)/\varpi'$ satisfy $\varpi'>0$, $|s'|=1$ and $k'_a=(-\varpi',\varpi's'_1,\varpi's'_2,\varpi's'_3)$ ([[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], clauses (a)-(d)).

[L5] In the frame of $x$, $k_a=(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$, $\varpi>0$ and $|s|=1$, with coordinates taken in the frame's orthonormal basis and the Euclidean scalar product $\beta\cdot k_{\mathrm{vec}}=\sum_i\beta_ik_i$ ([[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[L6] $|\beta\cdot s|\le|\beta|\,|s|=|\beta|<1$, so $1-\beta\cdot s>0$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Clause (i). Regard $k$ as the constant covector field on $A$; by [L3] its primed components are $k'_a=(B(-\beta))^b{}_ak_b$. For $\beta\ne0$ the matrix of $B(-\beta)$ has entries $(B(-\beta))^0{}_0=\gamma$, $(B(-\beta))^0{}_i=\gamma\beta_i$, $(B(-\beta))^i{}_0=\gamma\beta_i$ and $(B(-\beta))^i{}_j=\delta^i_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$ by [L1]; therefore $k'_0=\gamma k_0+\gamma\sum_i\beta_ik_i=\gamma(k_0+\beta\cdot k_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and $k'_i=\gamma\beta_ik_0+k_i+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}\beta_i(\beta\cdot k_{\mathrm{vec}})$, which is the displayed vector identity. For $\beta=0$ one has $B(0)=\operatorname{id}$ by [L1], so $k'=k$. [L1, L2, L3, L5]

2.1 Clause (ii). By step 1.1 and [L5], $k'_0=\gamma(k_0+\beta\cdot k_{\mathrm{vec}})=\gamma(-\varpi+\beta\cdot\varpi s)=-\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi$, hence $\varpi'=-k'_0=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi$, and this is positive because $\gamma\ge1$, $\varpi>0$ and $1-\beta\cdot s>0$ by [L6]; this also agrees with $\varpi'>0$ asserted by [L4]. Dividing the vector component of step 1.1 by $\varpi'$ gives $s'_i=k'_i/\varpi'=\bigl[s_i+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)\beta_i-\gamma\beta_i\bigr]/\bigl[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\bigr]$ for $\beta\ne0$, which is the displayed $s'$. For $\beta=0$, $k'=k$ gives $\varpi'=\varpi$ and $s'=s$. The normalization $|s'|=1$ and the component form $k'_a=(-\varpi',\varpi's')$ are clauses (a)-(d) of [L4] applied in the frame of $x'$. [step 1.1, L4, L5, L6]

3.1 Clause (iii). Let $\beta=be_1$ with $b\in(-1,1)$ and $\gamma=(1-b^2)^{-1/2}$. If $b\ne0$, substituting $\beta_1=b$, $\beta_2=\beta_3=0$ and $\beta\cdot s=bs_1$ into step 2.1 gives $s'_1=\bigl[s_1+\frac{\gamma-1}{b^2}(bs_1)b-\gamma b\bigr]/\bigl[\gamma(1-bs_1)\bigr]=(s_1-b)/(1-bs_1)$, because $s_1+(\gamma-1)s_1-\gamma b=\gamma(s_1-b)$, and $s'_2=s_2/\bigl[\gamma(1-bs_1)\bigr]$, $s'_3=s_3/\bigl[\gamma(1-bs_1)\bigr]$. If $b=0$ then $\gamma=1$ and $s'=s$ by step 2.1, which is the same as the displayed formulas at $b=0$. [step 2.1]

3.2 Clause (iv). For $\beta\ne0$, step 2.1 gives $\beta\cdot s'=\bigl[\beta\cdot s+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)(\beta\cdot\beta)-\gamma|\beta|^2\bigr]/\bigl[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\bigr]=\bigl[\beta\cdot s+(\gamma-1)(\beta\cdot s)-\gamma|\beta|^2\bigr]/\bigl[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\bigr]=\bigl[\gamma(\beta\cdot s)-\gamma|\beta|^2\bigr]/\bigl[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\bigr]=(\beta\cdot s-|\beta|^2)/(1-\beta\cdot s)$; for $\beta=0$ both sides are $0$, so the identity holds always. Since $1-\beta\cdot s>0$ by [L6], $\beta\cdot s'=0$ holds exactly when $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$, and $\beta\cdot s'=-|\beta|^2$ holds exactly when $\beta\cdot s-|\beta|^2=-|\beta|^2(1-\beta\cdot s)$, that is $\beta\cdot s(1-|\beta|^2)=0$, which by $|\beta|<1$ is exactly $\beta\cdot s=0$. [step 2.1, L1, L6]

4.1 Clause (v). The transition $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ inverts to $x=B(-\beta)x'+b'$ with $b':=-B(-\beta)b$, whose linear part $B(-\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with $|-\beta|=|\beta|<1$ by [L2]; applying step 2.1 to the chart pair $(x',x)$ with parameter $-\beta$ computes the frame-$x$ data of $k$ from its frame-$x'$ data, and that frame-$x$ data is $(\varpi,s)$ by hypothesis. Directly, $\varpi''=\gamma\bigl(1-(-\beta)\cdot s'\bigr)\varpi'=\gamma(1+\beta\cdot s')\varpi'$ and step 3.2 gives $1+\beta\cdot s'=\bigl(1-\beta\cdot s+\beta\cdot s-|\beta|^2\bigr)/(1-\beta\cdot s)=(1-|\beta|^2)/(1-\beta\cdot s)$, so $\varpi''=\gamma\cdot\frac{1-|\beta|^2}{1-\beta\cdot s}\cdot\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi=\gamma^2(1-|\beta|^2)\varpi=\varpi$; the vector part of the same instance returns a unit vector $s''$ with $k$'s frame-$x$ data equal to $(\varpi'',s'')$, and by the uniqueness of frame data in [L4] applied to the frame of $x$, $(\varpi'',s'')=(\varpi,s)$, so $s''=s$. This proves (i)-(v); the argument is pure algebra of $\eta$ and the boost, and no choice principle was used. [step 2.1, step 3.2, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $\theta$ be an affine phase function with wave covector $k$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]). Then:

**(a)** for every $C^1$ curve $\gamma:I\to A$ one has $(\theta\circ\gamma)'(s)=k\bigl(\gamma'(s)\bigr)$ for all $s\in I$;

**(b)** if $x:I\to A$ is a future timelike worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function $\tau$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]]) and four-velocity $U=\mathrm dx/\mathrm d\tau$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), then $\mathrm d(\theta\circ x)/\mathrm d\tau=k(U)$ along the worldline, the derivative being taken in the proper-time parametrization, whose inverse exists by [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]];

**(c)** if $k$ is moreover a future null wave covector, then $k(U)<0$ at every point, so $\theta$ is strictly decreasing in proper time along every future timelike worldline; the positive number $-k(U)$ is the quantity given physical meaning in def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency;

**(d)** if $k$ is a future null wave covector and $x$ is the straight worldline of an inertial observer, so that $U=cn$ for a future unit timelike vector $n$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$, then $k(U)=ck(n)$ and $-k(U)=-ck(n)>0$; conversely every future timelike worldline has $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]).

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An affine phase function $\theta$ with wave covector $k$ on the affine Minkowski space, and a $C^1$ curve $\gamma:I\to A$.

[L1] $\theta(p)-\theta(q)=k(p-q)$ for all $p,q\in A$, and for every $C^1$ curve $\gamma:I\to A$ one has $(\theta\circ\gamma)'(s)=k(\gamma'(s))$ for all $s\in I$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]], clauses (a) and (b)).

[L2] A future timelike worldline $x:I\to A$ is a $C^1$ curve whose tangent $x'(s)$ is future timelike for every $s$, and the parametrization is part of the curve ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

[L3] The proper-time function $\tau$ of a future timelike worldline is $C^1$ and strictly increasing with $\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0$; its inverse $\rho:J\to I$ is $C^1$ with $\rho'(\tau(s))=1/\tau'(s)$, and $y:=x\circ\rho$ is a $C^1$ future timelike worldline with $y'(\tau(s))=x'(s)/\tau'(s)$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]).

[L4] The four-velocity is $U(s)=x'(s)/\tau'(s)=cx'(s)/\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}$, it is future timelike, and $\eta(U(s),U(s))=-c^2$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], clause (a)).

[L5] A future null wave covector has $k^\sharp$ nonzero future causal, and for a future timelike vector $n$ and a nonzero future causal vector $v$ one has $\eta(n,v)<0$; moreover $k(w)=\eta(k^\sharp,w)$ for every $w$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]], [[lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative]], clause (a)).

[L6] The one-variable chain rule and the definition of the derivative ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[def-derivative]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Clause (a). This is exactly the chain-rule identity recorded in [L1] for $C^1$ curves: $(\theta\circ\gamma)'(s)=k(\gamma'(s))$. [L1]

1.2 Clause (c). Let $k$ be a future null wave covector and let $x$ be a future timelike worldline, a $C^1$ curve with future timelike tangent by [L2], with four-velocity $U$ as in [L4]. By [L4], $U(s)$ is future timelike, hence nonzero; by [L5], $k^\sharp$ is nonzero future causal and $k(U(s))=\eta(k^\sharp,U(s))=\eta(U(s),k^\sharp)<0$. It follows that $\theta$ is strictly decreasing in proper time along the worldline by clause (b), and the positive number $-k(U(s))$ is the quantity referred to in the statement. [L2, L4, L5]

2.1 Clause (b). By [L3] the inverse $\rho:J\to I$ of $\tau$ exists and is $C^1$, and the proper-time parametrized worldline $y:=x\circ\rho$ satisfies $y(\tau(s))=x(s)$ and $y'(\tau(s))=x'(s)/\tau'(s)=U(s)$ for every $s\in I$, the last equality by [L4]. The real function $\theta\circ x$ on $I$ equals $(\theta\circ y)\circ\tau$; differentiating at $s$ with the chain rule [L6] gives $(\theta\circ x)'(s)=(\theta\circ y)'(\tau(s))\,\tau'(s)$, and clause (a), applied to the $C^1$ curve $y$ [L1, L3], gives $(\theta\circ y)'(\tau(s))=k\bigl(y'(\tau(s))\bigr)=k(U(s))$. Hence $\mathrm d(\theta\circ x)/\mathrm d\tau:=\frac{(\theta\circ x)'(s)}{\tau'(s)}=(\theta\circ y)'(\tau(s))=k(U(s))$, since $\tau'(s)\neq0$ [L3]. [step 1.1, L1, L3, L4, L6]

3.1 Clause (d). If $U=cn$ with $n$ future unit timelike, then $k(U)=ck(n)$ by linearity of $k$, and $k(n)=\eta(k^\sharp,n)=\eta(n,k^\sharp)<0$ by [L5] applied to the future timelike vector $n$ and the nonzero future causal vector $k^\sharp$; hence $-k(U)=-ck(n)>0$. The converse claim is clause (a) of [L4], valid for every future timelike worldline. Together with steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1 this proves (a)-(d); no choice principle was used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, L4, L5] ∎

## Definition

Adopt the SI coordinate and unit conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]: in every inertial chart $x^0=ct$ with $c>0$ in metres per second and spatial coordinates in metres, so $c$ is the model's conversion constant. Let $k$ be a future null wave covector and $\theta$ its affine phase ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]).

**(a) Frame data as wave data.** In the inertial chart of a frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) let $(\varpi,s)$ be the frame data of $k$ given by [[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], so $\varpi=-k(e_0)>0$ and $|s|=1$. Define the **angular frequency** $\omega:=c\varpi$ (unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$), the **linear frequency** $\nu:=\omega/(2\pi)$ (unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$, hertz), the **wave vector** $\kappa:=(\omega/c)s$ (unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, with $|\kappa|=\omega/c$), the **wavelength** $\lambda:=2\pi/|\kappa|=2\pi c/\omega=c/\nu$ (unit $\mathrm m$), and the **propagation direction** $s$ (dimensionless). In these conventions the phase is $\theta(p)=-\omega t+\kappa\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}(p)+\mathrm{const}$ with $t:=x^0(p)/c$ the coordinate time in seconds, so the components of $k$ in the chart are

$$k_a=\bigl(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3\bigr).$$

**(b) Observer frequency.** For an ideal observer whose four-velocity is $U_o=cn$ with $n\in V$ future unit timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]), define the **observer angular frequency** of the wave as

$$\omega_n:=-ck(n)=-k(U_o)\qquad(\text{unit }\mathrm s^{-1}),$$

and the **observer linear frequency** as $\omega_n/(2\pi)$. By [[lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline]] this is minus the rate of change of the phase with respect to the observer's own proper time, and the sign convention makes it positive.

**(c) Well-definedness.** $\varpi=-k(e_0)>0$ and $|s|=1$ in every inertial frame, hence $\omega>0$ and $\lambda>0$ are well defined and independent of the choices made in their computation (frame-data lemma); $\omega_n>0$ for every future unit timelike $n$ and every future null wave covector $k$ ([[lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative]], [[lem-sr-metric-duality-on-lorentz-vector-space]]), so every ideal observer reads a positive angular frequency, and $\omega_n$ depends only on $k$ and the observer vector $n$. The classification of $k$ as future null is the one of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(d) Scope.** This item fixes definitions, units and sign conventions only. It does not assert that any physical light is described by such a phase; that identification is adopted in post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model. It contains no quantum identification of energy with $\hbar\omega$, no amplitude or intensity content, no medium or dispersion model, no source or detector model, and no measurement or empirical claim. No choice principle is used.

## Postulate

Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework, extending [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] (ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines, with coordinate speed $c$ in every inertial chart) and [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] (the affine Minkowski model, with the model's equations covariant under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps):

**(i) Ideal plane wave.** An ideal monochromatic light wave in vacuum is modeled, in any inertial chart, by a dimensionless affine phase $\theta$ with future null wave covector $k$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]], [[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]]): the level sets of $\theta$ are the wave fronts, every line $p+\mathbb Rk^\sharp$ has constant phase, and the rays of this ideal wave are the future null straight lines $p+\mathbb R_{\ge0}k^\sharp$, consistently with the general ideal-light clause that the ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines. The model is one ideal plane wave: constant wave covector, no medium, no dispersion, no absorption, no modulation or envelope, no boundary or source model, no intensity or polarization model.

**(ii) Frequency reading.** An ideal observer of the model with four-velocity $U_o=cn$ ($n$ future unit timelike) that receives this wave reads the angular frequency $\omega_n:=-ck(n)=-k(U_o)$ and the linear frequency $\omega_n/(2\pi)$ of [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]], that is, minus the rate of change of the phase with respect to the observer's own proper time with the sign convention that this number is positive ([[lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline]], [[lem-sr-future-causal-pairing-negative]]). The reading is attached to the observer's worldline at the event of reception.

**(iii) Frequency comparisons.** Comparing the frequency of one wave between two ideal observers or between two inertial descriptions means comparing $\omega_n$ at specified reception events, or the frame data $(\omega,s)$ of the same phase function in specified inertial charts; this postulate asserts no Doppler or aberration formula, and comparing events requires propagating the phase along the specified observer worldlines.

**(iv) Scope and exclusions.** These are adopted idealizations, not deductions from experiment and not claims about nature. No quantum photon model and no identification of energy with $\hbar\omega$ is made (excluded by the conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]); no claim is made that real light, real clocks, real receivers or real sources are exactly described; dispersive, absorbing, nonlinear or modulated media, finite line width, intensity, polarization, source and detector physics, gravitation, quantum effects and accelerated-observer reception are outside the model. Empirical tests of the model belong to the framework's experimental work and are not asserted here.

No choice principle is used in this formulation; the postulate is an adopted assumption of the model, not a proved assertion.

## Statement

Adopt [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]], [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and [[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]], and the conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $x$ and $x'$ be inertial charts whose transition is $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ with $\beta\in\mathbb R^3$, $|\beta|<1$, $b\in\mathbb R^4$ and $B(\beta)$ the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]]; write $\gamma:=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}:=\beta/|\beta|$ for $\beta\ne0$, so that the frame $x'$ moves with velocity $v=c\beta$ relative to the frame $x$ in the direction $\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ (step 1.1 records this). Let the ideal wave of the model have phase $\theta$ with future null wave covector $k$ and frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$ in the sense of [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]: $\omega>0$, $s\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|s|=1$ and $k_a=(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3)$ in $x$. Then, conditionally on the adopted model:

**(i) Frame data in $x'$.** The data of the same covector $k$ in $x'$ is $(\omega',s')$ with

$$\omega'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\,\omega>0,\qquad s'=\frac{s+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)\beta-\gamma\beta}{\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)}$$

for $\beta\ne0$ (and $\omega'=\omega$, $s'=s$ for $\beta=0$), so $|s'|=1$ and $k'_a=(-\omega'/c,(\omega'/c)s'_1,(\omega'/c)s'_2,(\omega'/c)s'_3)$ in $x'$. In the axis case $\beta=be_1$ with $b\in(-1,1)$: $s'_1=(s_1-b)/(1-bs_1)$ and $(s'_2,s'_3)=(s_2,s_3)/[\gamma(1-bs_1)]$.

**(ii) Reading and frequency ratios.** The rest observers of $x$ and $x'$ (four-velocities $ce_0$ and $ce'_0$) read angular frequencies $\omega=-ck(e_0)$ and $\omega'=-ck(e'_0)$; the linear frequencies and wavelengths of the two descriptions satisfy $\nu'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\nu$ and $\lambda'=\lambda/[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)]$. More generally, an ideal observer whose coordinate velocity in $x$ is $w$ (a vector of the frame's spatial three-space with $|w|<c$) reads

$$\omega_o=\gamma_w\Bigl(1-\frac{w\cdot s}{c}\Bigr)\omega,\qquad \gamma_w:=\Bigl(1-\frac{|w|^2}{c^2}\Bigr)^{-1/2};$$

equivalently $\omega_o=\gamma_w(1-\beta_w\cdot s)\omega$ with $\beta_w:=w/c$.

**(iii) Longitudinal cases.** If $s=\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ then $\omega'=\omega\sqrt{(1-|\beta|)/(1+|\beta|)}<\omega$, $\nu'=\nu\sqrt{(1-|\beta|)/(1+|\beta|)}$ and $\lambda'=\lambda\sqrt{(1+|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|)}$: the observer moving in the direction of propagation (in the interpretation of a source at rest in $x$ located behind the observer) reads a red-shifted frequency and lengthened wavelength. If $s=-\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ then $\omega'=\omega\sqrt{(1+|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|)}>\omega$ and $\lambda'=\lambda\sqrt{(1-|\beta|)/(1+|\beta|)}$: blue shift for an observer moving opposite to the propagation direction (toward such a source). Both statements are trivial at $\beta=0$.

**(iv) Transverse protocols.** If $\beta\cdot s=0$ (propagation direction perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame $x$) then $\omega'=\gamma\omega$; this is greater than $\omega$ when $\beta\ne0$ and equals $\omega$ when $\beta=0$. If $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$, equivalently $s'\cdot\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}=0$ for $\beta\ne0$ (propagation direction perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame $x'$), then $\omega'=\omega/\gamma$; this is less than $\omega$ when $\beta\ne0$ and equals $\omega$ when $\beta=0$. Both configurations are called transverse Doppler configurations in the literature, and the two factors differ for $\beta\ne0$: the direction and size of the shift are not determined by the word "transverse" without specifying the frame in which transversality holds.

**(v) Aberration.** For $\beta\ne0$, if $\theta_x,\theta_{x'}\in[0,\pi]$ are the angles between the propagation directions $s,s'$ and the boost axis $\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$, then

$$\cos\theta_{x'}=\frac{\cos\theta_x-|\beta|}{1-|\beta|\cos\theta_x};$$

the map $u\mapsto(u-|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|u)$ is a strictly increasing bijection of $[-1,1]$ onto itself, and in particular $\cos\theta_x=0$ gives $\cos\theta_{x'}=-|\beta|$.

**(vi) Scope and protocol.** All clauses concern one ideal plane wave and ideal observers, and frequencies are compared through the phase model at specified reception events; the results are conditional on the adopted postulates (ideal plane wave, ideal clocks, inertial covariance, flat classical spacetime) and are not empirical claims about nature, sources or apparatus. They exclude media and dispersion, modulation and signal speeds, intensity and polarization, real line widths, accelerating observers, gravitation and quantum effects; no statistical or measurement statement is made. If $\beta=0$ the transition is the pure translation $x'=x+b$: the inertial axes and wave-covector frame data agree, with $\omega'=\omega$ and $s'=s$, while the affine phase constant is transformed as in the covector and phase law.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Inertial charts $x,x'$ with $x'=B(\beta)x+b$, $\beta\in\mathbb R^3$, $|\beta|<1$, $b\in\mathbb R^4$; $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$; and an ideal plane wave with phase $\theta$, future null wave covector $k$ and frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$.

[A1] Adopted ideal plane-wave model: the level sets of $\theta$ are the wave fronts, the lines $p+\mathbb Rk^\sharp$ have constant phase, the rays are the future null straight lines $p+\mathbb R_{\ge0}k^\sharp$, and an ideal observer with four-velocity $U_o=cn$ reads the angular frequency $-ck(n)=-k(U_o)$ at the reception event ([[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]]).

[A2] Adopted ideal light: ideal vacuum light rays are exactly the future null straight lines, with coordinate speed $c$ in every inertial chart, and real clocks and light are not claimed to be exactly ideal ([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]).

[A3] Adopted inertial covariance: the inertial changes of description of the model are the affine maps with proper orthochronous Lorentz linear part, and covariance is asserted only for the specified model equations ([[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]).

[L1] With the SI conventions $x^0=ct$, the frame data $(\varpi,s)$ of $k$ in a frame and the wave data are related by $\varpi=\omega/c$, $|s|=1$, $\omega>0$, $k_a=(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3)$, $\nu=\omega/(2\pi)$, $\lambda=c/\nu$; and an ideal observer with four-velocity $U_o=cn$ ($n$ future unit timelike) reads $\omega_n=-ck(n)=-k(U_o)>0$, which is minus the phase rate along the observer's worldline ([[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]], [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], [[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], [[lem-sr-phase-rate-along-worldline]], [[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]).

[L2] Boost transformation of the frame data: for the chart pair of the Given, with $\varpi=\omega/c$ and $\beta\ne0$, the frame-$x'$ data $(\varpi',s')$ satisfies $\varpi'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi$, $s'=\bigl[s+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)\beta-\gamma\beta\bigr]/\bigl[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\bigr]$, $|s'|=1$ and $k'_a=(-\varpi',\varpi's')$; for $\beta=0$, $\varpi'=\varpi$, $s'=s$; in the axis case $\beta=be_1$, $s'_1=(s_1-b)/(1-bs_1)$, $s'_2=s_2/[\gamma(1-bs_1)]$, $s'_3=s_3/[\gamma(1-bs_1)]$; and $\beta\cdot s'=(\beta\cdot s-|\beta|^2)/(1-\beta\cdot s)$, with $\beta\cdot s'=0$ if and only if $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$ ([[lem-sr-null-covector-boost-transformation]]).

[L3] $\gamma\ge1$ with equality exactly when $\beta=0$, $B(0)=\operatorname{id}$, and the matrix entries of $B(\beta)$ and $B(-\beta)$ are as displayed in [[def-lorentz-boost]]; the transition $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ of inertial charts has proper orthochronous linear part ([[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]), and $B(-\beta)=B(\beta)^{-1}$ ([[lem-sr-null-covector-boost-transformation]], clause (v)).

[L4] In an inertial frame the basis vectors satisfy $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with $e_0$ future, so $e_0$ and $e'_0$ are future unit timelike; the four-velocity of an observer at rest in a frame is $c$ times its first basis vector, and a point observer is a future unit timelike vector $n$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

[L5] Frame and component relations between the charts: the transition $x'=\Lambda x+b$ has linear part $\Lambda=B(\beta)$, the new frame's basis vectors satisfy $e'_a=\sum_b(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ae_b$, and the components of a covector satisfy $k'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ak_b$ with $\Lambda^{-1}=B(-\beta)$; in the chart of any inertial frame an affine phase with wave covector $k$ has the form $\theta(p)=k_ax^a(p)+\theta(o)$ ([[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]], [[lem-sr-null-covector-boost-transformation]], [[def-lorentz-boost]], [[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]).

[L6] Relative velocity and coordinate form: for future unit timelike $n,u$, with $\gamma_{rel}:=-\eta(n,u)$ and $h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$, the vector $w:=ch(u)/\gamma_{rel}$ lies in $n^\perp$ and is the velocity of the worldline with four-velocity $cu$ relative to the observer $n$; a worldline with coordinate velocity $w$ in an inertial chart, $|w|<c$, has four-velocity $U=\gamma_w(c,w_{\mathrm{vec}})$ with $\gamma_w=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, so $n=U/c=\gamma_w(1,w/c)$ is future unit timelike ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], clauses (a), (c), (d), (e)).

[L7] The spatial three-space of an inertial frame carries the positive-definite form $\delta$, and the vectors $\beta,s,w$ of the statement are vectors of that space with Euclidean norms and scalar products; in particular $s'\cdot\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}=(\beta\cdot s')/|\beta|$ for $\beta\ne0$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). The factor $1-\beta\cdot s$ is positive because [L2] exhibits $\varpi'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi$ with $\varpi,\varpi',\gamma>0$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Setup, and the relative velocity of the frames. By [L1] the frame-$x$ data of $k$ is $(\varpi,s)$ with $\varpi=\omega/c>0$. By the frame relation of [L5], $e'_0=\sum_b(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_0e_b$ is the first column of $B(-\beta)$, namely $(\gamma,\gamma\beta_1,\gamma\beta_2,\gamma\beta_3)$ by [L3], so $e'_0=\gamma(e_0+\sum_i\beta_ie_i)$. Then $\eta(e_0,e'_0)=\gamma\eta(e_0,e_0)=-\gamma$ and $h(e'_0)=e'_0+\eta(e_0,e'_0)e_0=\gamma e_0+\gamma\sum_i\beta_ie_i-\gamma e_0=\gamma\sum_i\beta_ie_i$; by [L6] with $n=e_0$ and $u=e'_0$, the velocity of the $x'$-rest observer relative to the $x$-rest observer is $ch(e'_0)/(-\eta(e_0,e'_0))=c\gamma\sum_i\beta_ie_i/\gamma=c\beta$, of magnitude $c|\beta|$ in the direction $\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ when $\beta\ne0$. [L3, L4, L5, L6]

2.1 Clause (i). By the covector component law [L5] and [L3], $k'_a=(B(-\beta))^b{}_ak_b$; with $k_0=-\omega/c$ and $k_i=(\omega/c)s_i$ from [L1] and the matrix entries of $B(-\beta)$, this gives $k'_0=\gamma(k_0+\beta\cdot k_{\mathrm{vec}})=-\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\omega/c$, with $1-\beta\cdot s>0$ by the positivity clause of [L2], and $k'_i=k_i+\gamma\beta_ik_0+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}\beta_i(\beta\cdot k_{\mathrm{vec}})=\frac{\omega}{c}\bigl[s_i-\gamma\beta_i+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)\beta_i\bigr]$ for $\beta\ne0$ (and $k'=k$ for $\beta=0$). By the frame-data lemma [L2] the frame-$x'$ data is $(\varpi',s')$ with $\varpi'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\omega/c$, $s'=\bigl[s+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)\beta-\gamma\beta\bigr]/\bigl[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\bigr]$, $|s'|=1$ and $k'_a=(-\varpi',\varpi's')$; in wave data this is $\omega'=c\varpi'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\omega>0$ and the displayed $s'$, and the axis case is the axis clause of [L2]. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L3, L5, L7]

3.1 Clause (ii). By [L1] the rest observer of $x$ has four-velocity $ce_0$ and reads $\omega_{e_0}=-ck(e_0)=c\varpi=\omega$, and the rest observer of $x'$ has four-velocity $ce'_0$ by [L4] and reads $\omega_{e'_0}=-ck(e'_0)=c\varpi'=\omega'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\omega$ by step 2.1, so $\nu'=\omega'/(2\pi)=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\nu$ and $\lambda'=c/\nu'=\lambda/[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)]$ by the relations $\nu=\omega/(2\pi)$, $\lambda=c/\nu$ of [L1]. For the general observer, [L6] gives $U_o=\gamma_w(c,w_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so $n=U_o/c=\gamma_w(1,w/c)$ is future unit timelike and, using linearity of $k$ and $k(e_0)=-\omega/c$, $k(e_i)=(\omega/c)s_i$ [L1], $\omega_o=-ck(n)=-c\gamma_w\bigl[k(e_0)+\sum_i(w_i/c)k(e_i)\bigr]=\gamma_w\omega\bigl(1-(w\cdot s)/c\bigr)$; with $\beta_w=w/c$ this is $\gamma_w(1-\beta_w\cdot s)\omega$. [step 2.1, L1, L4, L6]

3.2 Clause (iii). If $s=\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ then $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|$ by [L7], so step 2.1 together with $\omega=c\varpi$ and [L2] gives $\omega'=\gamma(1-|\beta|)\omega$, and since $0\le|\beta|<1$, $\gamma(1-|\beta|)=(1-|\beta|)/\sqrt{1-|\beta|^2}=\sqrt{(1-|\beta|)/(1+|\beta|)}$, which is $<1$ for $|\beta|>0$ and $=1$ for $\beta=0$; substituting $s=\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ in the formula of [L2] gives $s'=\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$, so the propagation direction relative to the boost axis is unchanged. The wavelength and frequency ratios are $\nu'=\omega'/(2\pi)=\gamma(1-|\beta|)\nu$ and $\lambda'=c/\nu'=\lambda/[\gamma(1-|\beta|)]=\lambda\sqrt{(1+|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|)}$ by $\nu=\omega/(2\pi)$, $\lambda=c/\nu$ [L1] and $\omega'=\gamma(1-|\beta|)\omega$. If $s=-\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ the same computation with $-\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ gives $\omega'=\gamma(1+|\beta|)\omega=\omega\sqrt{(1+|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|)}>\omega$ for $|\beta|>0$, $s'=-\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}$ and $\lambda'=\lambda\sqrt{(1-|\beta|)/(1+|\beta|)}$; the source language in the statement is an interpretation of these factors, the model carrying no source. [step 2.1, L1, L2, L7]

3.3 Clause (iv). If $\beta\cdot s=0$, step 2.1 gives $\omega'=\gamma\omega$, which is greater than $\omega$ exactly when $\gamma>1$, that is exactly when $\beta\ne0$, and equals $\omega$ when $\beta=0$, by [L3]. If $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$, then by [L2] $\beta\cdot s'=0$, and for $\beta\ne0$ this is equivalent to $s'\cdot\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}=(\beta\cdot s')/|\beta|=0$; conversely $s'\cdot\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}=0$ with $\beta\ne0$ gives $\beta\cdot s'=0$ and hence $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$ by [L2]. With $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$ step 2.1 gives $\omega'=\gamma(1-|\beta|^2)\omega=\omega/\gamma$, which is less than $\omega$ when $\beta\ne0$ and equals $\omega$ when $\beta=0$. [step 2.1, L2, L3, L7]

3.4 Clause (v). For $\beta\ne0$ put $u:=\cos\theta_x=\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}\cdot s=(\beta\cdot s)/|\beta|$ and $u':=\cos\theta_{x'}=\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}\cdot s'=(\beta\cdot s')/|\beta|$ by [L7]; by the formula for $s'$ of step 2.1, equivalently by [L2], $u'=\bigl(\beta\cdot s-|\beta|^2\bigr)/\bigl[|\beta|(1-\beta\cdot s)\bigr]=(u-|\beta|)/(1-|\beta|u)$. Write $b:=|\beta|$ and $f(u):=(u-b)/(1-bu)$; since $0\le b<1$ one has $1-bu\ge1-b>0$ for every $u\in[-1,1]$, so $f$ is defined on $[-1,1]$. The map $g(y):=(y+b)/(1+by)$ is likewise defined on $[-1,1]$, and the comparisons $1+by-(y+b)=(1-b)(1-y)\ge0$ and $1+by+(y+b)=(1+b)(1+y)\ge0$ show $-1\le g(y)\le1$, so $g$ maps $[-1,1]$ into itself; direct expansion of the rational expressions gives $f(g(y))=\bigl[(y+b)-b(1+by)\bigr]/\bigl[(1+by)-b(y+b)\bigr]=\bigl[y(1-b^2)\bigr]/(1-b^2)=y$ and symmetrically $g(f(u))=u$ for all $u,y\in[-1,1]$, so $f$ is a bijection of $[-1,1]$ onto itself with inverse $g$. For $v>u$ in $[-1,1]$ one has $f(v)-f(u)=\bigl[(v-b)(1-bu)-(u-b)(1-bv)\bigr]/\bigl[(1-bv)(1-bu)\bigr]=(v-u)(1-b^2)/\bigl[(1-bv)(1-bu)\bigr]>0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing; in particular $f$ is the stated strictly increasing bijection of $[-1,1]$ onto itself, with $f(-1)=-1$ and $f(1)=1$, and $u=0$ gives $u'=f(0)=-b=-|\beta|$. [step 2.1, L2, L7, algebra]

4.1 Clause (vi), $\beta=0$, and scope. If $\beta=0$ then $B(0)=\operatorname{id}$ by [L3], so $x'=x+b$ is a pure translation; by [L2] the frame data agree, $\varpi'=\varpi$ and $s'=s$, whence $\omega'=\omega$ and the x- and x'-inertial axes carry the same wave data, while the affine phase constant changes as follows: since $\beta=0$ gives $x'^a=x^a+b^a$ and [L5] gives $k'=k$, comparing the two chart forms $\theta(p)=k_ax^a(p)+\theta(o)$ and $\theta(p)=k'_ax'^a(p)+\theta(o')$ of the affine phase yields $\theta(o')=\theta(o)-k'_ab^a$.
