## Remark

Remark on the conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] and [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]], for use with [[pthm-sr-null-wave-doppler-and-aberration]]. The frame data and wave data of a future null wave covector are related as in [[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], and the symbols below have the meanings fixed there and in [[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]].

**(a) Units in the adopted coordinates $x^0=ct$.** The phase $\theta$ is dimensionless; the coordinates $x^a$, the wavelength $\lambda$ and all distances are in metres; the components $k_a$ of a wave covector, the wave vector $\kappa$ and $\varpi=-k(e_0)$ are in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the angular frequencies $\omega$ and $\omega_n$ and the linear frequencies $\nu$ are in $\mathrm s^{-1}$ ($\nu$ also in hertz); $c$ is in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$; and $s$, $\beta$, $\beta_w$ and $\gamma$ are dimensionless. These assignments are consistent with the identities $\omega=c\varpi$, $\kappa=(\omega/c)s$, $\lambda=2\pi c/\omega=c/\nu$ and phase $=\theta$ dimensionless.

**(b) Two coordinate forms.** In the adopted coordinates $\theta=-\omega t+\kappa\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\mathrm{const}$ and $k_a=(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3)$; in a chart whose time coordinate is $t$ in seconds directly, so that the metric component $g_{tt}=-c^2$ carries $\mathrm m^2\mathrm s^{-2}$ and the time-space components carry $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$, the same phase is $\theta=-\omega t+\kappa\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\mathrm{const}$ with the same $\omega$ and $\kappa$, and the component tuple $(-\omega,(\omega/c)s)$ carries mixed units $(\mathrm s^{-1},\mathrm m^{-1})$ because it is read in the coordinate basis $(\partial_t,\partial_{x^i})$ rather than in the dimensionless frame basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Formulas derived in one convention are not reused unchanged in the other; this is the general warning of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] specialized to the wave covector.

**(c) Natural units and restoration.** In natural units $c=1$ with $x^0=t$ one has $k_a=(-\omega,\omega s)$, $\lambda=2\pi/\omega$, and the Doppler and aberration factors $\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)$ and $\sqrt{(1\mp|\beta|)/(1\pm|\beta|)}$ are unchanged; restoring dimensions means replacing $k_0$ by $-\omega/c$, $k_i$ by $(\omega/c)s_i$, writing every velocity as $v=c\beta$ with the dimensionless $\beta$, and replacing $\lambda$ by $2\pi c/\omega=c/\nu$. The dimensionless factors $\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)$ and the longitudinal square roots need no $c$ restoration because they contain only $\beta$, $s$ and $\gamma$; the $c$ restoration affects the map between $\omega$, $\nu$, $\lambda$ and the components of $k$, not the shift factors themselves.

**(d) Scope.** This remark introduces no quantum identification of energy with $\hbar\omega$, no amplitude or intensity content and no measurement claim; it is a units and convention statement carrying the scope of the items it cites. No choice principle is used.

Let $x$ and $x'$ be inertial charts with $x'=B(\beta)x+b$, $\beta=(3/5)e_1$ and $\gamma=5/4$, and let an ideal plane wave have frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$ with $\omega>0$.

**(a)** If $s=e_2$, so $\beta\cdot s=0$ and the propagation direction is perpendicular to the relative velocity in $x$, then [[pthm-sr-null-wave-doppler-and-aberration]] gives $\omega'=\gamma\omega=(5/4)\omega>\omega$ and $s'=(-3/5,4/5,0)$, which has $|s'|=1$; the frequency read by the $x'$-rest observer is blue-shifted by the factor $5/4$.

**(b)** If $s=(3/5,4/5,0)$, so $\beta\cdot s=9/25=|\beta|^2$ and equivalently $s'\cdot e_1=0$, the propagation direction is perpendicular to the relative velocity in $x'$, and the theorem gives $\omega'=\gamma(1-9/25)\omega=(5/4)(16/25)\omega=(4/5)\omega=\omega/\gamma<\omega$ and $s'=e_2$; the frequency read by the $x'$-rest observer is red-shifted by the factor $4/5$.

In neither case is $\omega'=\omega$ for the nonzero $\beta$, and the two exact factors differ; a statement of a transverse Doppler shift is therefore incomplete until the frame in which the direction is transverse is specified. ## Example

This worked example computes the geometry of the phase level sets of a future null wave covector. Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space, let $k$ be a future null wave covector with frame data $(\varpi,s)$ in an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]]), so that $\varpi>0$, $|s|=1$ and $k$ has components $k_a=(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$ in this frame, and let $\theta$ be an affine phase function with wave covector $k$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]). Then:

**(a)** $k(k^\sharp)=\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=0$, since the raised vector is $k^\sharp=\varpi(e_0+s_1e_1+s_2e_2+s_3e_3)$; hence $\theta$ is constant on every line $p+\mathbb Rk^\sharp$.

**(b)** The direction subspace $\ker k=\{v:k(v)=0\}=\{v:v^0=s\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}}\}$ is $3$-dimensional; for $v\in\ker k$ one has $\eta(v,v)=|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2-(s\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}})^2\ge0$ by the finite Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, with equality exactly when $v_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is a real multiple of $s$, that is exactly when $v$ lies in the line $\operatorname{span}(k^\sharp)$; hence the restriction of $\eta$ to $\ker k$ is positive semidefinite with radical the line $\operatorname{span}(k^\sharp)$, and the only null direction contained in $\ker k$ is the line through $k^\sharp$, with future ray $k^\sharp$ and past ray $-k^\sharp$.

**(c)** Every nonempty level set $\Sigma=\{p:\theta(p)=\theta(p_0)\}$ is the affine hyperplane $p_0+\ker k$ through $p_0$, whose normal covector is the null covector $k$; it contains the two null rays $p_0+\mathbb R_{\ge0}k^\sharp$ and $p_0+\mathbb R_{\le0}k^\sharp$, and all its other direction vectors are spacelike.

The verification is exact algebra; no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$, a future null wave covector $k$ with frame data $(\varpi,s)$ in an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, and an affine phase function $\theta$ with $\mathrm d\theta=k$.

[L1] $\varpi>0$, $|s|=1$, $k_a=(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$, $k^\sharp=\varpi(e_0+s_1e_1+s_2e_2+s_3e_3)$, and $k^\sharp$ is nonzero future null with $k(k^\sharp)=\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=0$ ([[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], clauses (a)-(d)).

[L2] $k(v)=\varpi(-v^0+s_1v^1+s_2v^2+s_3v^3)$ for every $v=v^0e_0+v_{\mathrm{vec}}$, and $k(v)=0$ if and only if $\theta$ is constant on every line $p+\mathbb Rv$ ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]], clauses (b)-(c)); $\ker k$ is a $3$-dimensional linear subspace when $k\neq0$.

[L3] For the frame, $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+\delta(v_{\mathrm{vec}},w_{\mathrm{vec}})$ with $\delta(v_{\mathrm{vec}},w_{\mathrm{vec}})=\sum_iv^iw^i$ and $|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2=\delta(v_{\mathrm{vec}},v_{\mathrm{vec}})$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]).

[L4] Cauchy-Schwarz in root form: $|\sum_{k<n}a_kb_k|\le\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}a_k^2}\sqrt{\sum_{k<n}b_k^2}$, with equality in the squared form exactly when the two lists are proportional in the sense that some $(\lambda,\mu)\ne(0,0)$ has $\lambda a_k=\mu b_k$ for all $k$; in the frame this gives $|s\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}}|\le|s|\,|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ with equality exactly when $s$ and $v_{\mathrm{vec}}$ are proportional ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[L5] A vector is spacelike when $\eta(v,v)>0$, null when nonzero with $\eta(v,v)=0$, and the zero vector has no causal character ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

[L6] $k^\sharp$ is future null and $-k^\sharp$ is past null, and every nonzero vector in $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ is future causal ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Clause (a). By [L1], $k^\sharp=\varpi(e_0+\sum_is_ie_i)$ with $\varpi>0$ and $|s|=1$, so $\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=\varpi^2\bigl(-1+\sum_is_i^2\bigr)=\varpi^2(|s|^2-1)=0$ by [L1, L3], and $k(k^\sharp)=\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)$ by [L1]. For every $p\in A$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ the defining identity of the phase gives $\theta(p+\lambda k^\sharp)=\theta(p)+\lambda k(k^\sharp)=\theta(p)$, so $\theta$ is constant on the lines $p+\mathbb Rk^\sharp$. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 Clause (b), kernel and sign. By [L2] and $\varpi>0$, $v\in\ker k$ is equivalent to $v^0=s\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}}$, and $\ker k$ is a $3$-dimensional subspace [L2]. For $v\in\ker k$, substituting $v^0=s\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}}$ into [L3] gives $\eta(v,v)=-(s\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}})^2+|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2$; by [L4] with $|s|=1$ this is $\ge0$, and it is $0$ exactly when $|s\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}}|=|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, which by the equality clause of [L4] holds exactly when $v_{\mathrm{vec}}=\lambda s$ for some real $\lambda$. For such a $v$, $v^0=s\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}}=\lambda$, so $v=\lambda(e_0+\sum_is_ie_i)=\lambda\varpi^{-1}k^\sharp$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(k^\sharp)$; conversely every multiple of $k^\sharp$ lies in $\ker k$ because $k(k^\sharp)=0$ by step 1.1. Hence $\eta|_{\ker k}$ is positive semidefinite, its radical is $\operatorname{span}(k^\sharp)$, and its only null elements are the nonzero multiples of $k^\sharp$. [step 1.1, L2, L3, L4]

3.1 Clause (b), null directions. By [L1] and [L6] the vector $k^\sharp$ is future null and $-k^\sharp$ is past null, so the nonzero multiples of $k^\sharp$ are exactly the two rays $\mathbb R_{>0}k^\sharp$ (future null) and $\mathbb R_{>0}(-k^\sharp)$ (past null) of the line $\operatorname{span}(k^\sharp)$; combined with step 2.1 and [L5], the line through $k^\sharp$ is the only null direction contained in $\ker k$. [step 2.1, L1, L5, L6]

4.1 Clause (c). By [L2] and step 2.1 the kernel of the nonzero functional $k$ is the $3$-dimensional subspace $\ker k$, and the level set $\Sigma=\{p:\theta(p)=\theta(p_0)\}$ is the affine hyperplane $p_0+\ker k$ through $p_0$; its direction subspace is $\ker k$, whose normal covector is $k$ (the linear functional defining the direction subspace), and $k$ is null by hypothesis. Since $k^\sharp\in\ker k$ by step 1.1, both rays $p_0+\mathbb R_{\ge0}k^\sharp$ and $p_0+\mathbb R_{\le0}k^\sharp$ lie in $\Sigma$; every other direction vector of $\Sigma$ lies in $\ker k$ outside $\operatorname{span}(k^\sharp)$ and is spacelike by steps 2.1 and 3.1 and [L5]. This proves (a), (b) and (c). The computation is exact algebra and no choice principle was used. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, L2, L5] ∎

## Statement refuted

The following universal claim is refuted: "if the propagation direction of an ideal plane wave is perpendicular to the relative velocity of two inertial frames, then the frequency read by the observer at rest in one frame equals the frequency read by the observer at rest in the other, $\omega'=\omega$."

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Inertial charts $x$ and $x'$ with $x'=B(\beta)x+b$, $\beta=(3/5)e_1$, and an ideal plane wave with frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$, $\omega>0$, $|s|=1$, in the ideal plane-wave model.

[A1] Adopted ideal plane-wave model: the wave is a dimensionless affine phase with future null wave covector, and the rest observers of $x$ and $x'$ read $\omega$ and $\omega'$ as defined in the model ([[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]], [[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]).

[L1] For the chart pair of the Given, the theorem gives $\omega'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\omega>0$ with $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$, and in the axis case $\beta=be_1$: $s'_1=(s_1-b)/(1-bs_1)$, $s'_2=s_2/[\gamma(1-bs_1)]$, $s'_3=s_3/[\gamma(1-bs_1)]$ ([[pthm-sr-null-wave-doppler-and-aberration]], clause (i)).

[L2] Transverse protocols of the theorem: if $\beta\cdot s=0$ then $\omega'=\gamma\omega$; if $\beta\cdot s=|\beta|^2$, equivalently $s'\cdot\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}=0$ for $\beta\ne0$, then $\omega'=\omega/\gamma$; in both cases $s$, $s'$ are unit and the shift is not one when $\beta\ne0$ ([[pthm-sr-null-wave-doppler-and-aberration]], clause (iv)).

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First witness. With $\beta=(3/5)e_1$ one has $|\beta|^2=9/25$ and $\gamma=(1-9/25)^{-1/2}=(16/25)^{-1/2}=5/4$. Take $s=e_2$; then $\beta\cdot s=(3/5)(0)=0$, so the propagation direction is perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame $x$, and [L2] gives $\omega'=\gamma\omega=(5/4)\omega\neq\omega$ because $\omega>0$. Thus the antecedent of the refuted universal claim holds in $x$ while its conclusion fails. [A1, L2, algebra]

1.2 Second witness. Take $s=(3/5,4/5,0)$; then $|s|^2=9/25+16/25=1$ and $\beta\cdot s=(3/5)(3/5)=9/25=|\beta|^2$, so by [L2] $s'\cdot\beta_{\mathrm{hat}}=0$, the propagation direction is perpendicular to the relative velocity in the frame $x'$, and [L2] gives $\omega'=\gamma(1-9/25)\omega=(5/4)(16/25)\omega=(4/5)\omega\neq\omega$. Explicitly, the axis formulas of [L1] give $s'_1=(3/5-3/5)/(1-9/25)=0$, $s'_2=(4/5)/[(5/4)(16/25)]=(4/5)/(4/5)=1$ and $s'_3=0$, so $s'=e_2$. [A1, L1, L2, algebra]

2.1 Conclusion. Each witness satisfies the antecedent of the refuted claim — transversality in $x$ in step 1.1 and transversality in $x'$ in step 1.2 — and yields $\omega'\neq\omega$; the two factors $(5/4)$ and $(4/5)$ differ and neither equals $1$ for the stated nonzero $\beta$, so the universal claim is false in the ideal model, and the direction and size of the shift depend on the protocol (the frame in which transversality is required). The counterexample is conditional on the adopted idealizations, performs no measurement and claims no empirical falsification; no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, A1] ∎

## Example

This worked example computes the frame data of a future null wave covector and its passive boost. In an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ let $\varpi>0$ and $s=(0,3/5,4/5)$, and let $k$ be the covector with frame components $(k_0,k_1,k_2,k_3)=(-\varpi,0,3\varpi/5,4\varpi/5)$. Then:

**(a)** $|s|=1$ and $k$ is a future null wave covector; its raised vector is $k^\sharp=\varpi\bigl(e_0+(3/5)e_2+(4/5)e_3\bigr)$ and $k(k^\sharp)=0$.

**(b)** Let $x'$ be the inertial chart with $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ and $\beta=(3/5)e_1$. The frame-$x'$ data of the same covector is $(\varpi',s')$ with $\varpi'/\varpi=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)=(5/4)(1-0)=5/4$ and $s'=(-3/5,12/25,16/25)$.

**(c)** Applying the transformation with $\beta$ replaced by $-\beta$ to $(\varpi',s')$ returns $(\varpi,s)$: $\varpi''/\varpi'=(5/4)(16/25)=4/5$, so $\varpi''=\varpi$, and $s''=(0,3/5,4/5)$.

The verification is exact rational algebra; no physical interpretation of the data is used, and no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, a real $\varpi>0$, $s=(0,3/5,4/5)$, and the covector $k$ with components $(k_0,k_1,k_2,k_3)=(-\varpi,0,3\varpi/5,4\varpi/5)$.

[L1] If a covector has frame components $(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$ with $\varpi>0$ and $|s|=1$, then it is a future null wave covector; its raised vector is $k^\sharp=\varpi(e_0+s_1e_1+s_2e_2+s_3e_3)$ with $k(k^\sharp)=\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=0$ ([[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]], clauses (d) and (e), [[lem-sr-metric-duality-on-lorentz-vector-space]]).

[L2] For inertial charts with $x'=B(\beta)x+b$, $|\beta|<1$, and a future null wave covector with frame-$x$ data $(\varpi,s)$, the frame-$x'$ data satisfies $\varpi'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi$, $s'_i=\bigl[s_i+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\beta|^2}(\beta\cdot s)\beta_i-\gamma\beta_i\bigr]/\bigl[\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\bigr]$ for $\beta\ne0$, and in the axis case $\beta=be_1$: $s'_1=(s_1-b)/(1-bs_1)$, $s'_2=s_2/[\gamma(1-bs_1)]$, $s'_3=s_3/[\gamma(1-bs_1)]$; applying the transformation with $-\beta$ returns the original data ([[lem-sr-null-covector-boost-transformation]], clauses (ii), (iii), (v)).

[L3] $B(\beta)$ is the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] with $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$, and $B(\beta)$ is proper orthochronous with $B(-\beta)=B(\beta)^{-1}$ ([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]]); the frame is an inertial frame with an inertial chart ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Clause (a). Here $\varpi s=(0,3\varpi/5,4\varpi/5)=(k_1,k_2,k_3)$ and $k_0=-\varpi$, so the components of $k$ are exactly $(-\varpi,\varpi s)$ with $\varpi>0$; and $|s|^2=0+(3/5)^2+(4/5)^2=9/25+16/25=1$. By [L1] the covector $k$ is a future null wave covector with $k^\sharp=\varpi\bigl(e_0+(3/5)e_2+(4/5)e_3\bigr)$, and $k(k^\sharp)=\eta(k^\sharp,k^\sharp)=-\varpi^2+\varpi^2(0+9/25+16/25)=0$. [L1, given, algebra]

2.1 Clause (b). With $\beta=(3/5)e_1$ one has $|\beta|=3/5$ and $\gamma=(1-9/25)^{-1/2}=(16/25)^{-1/2}=5/4$ [L3, algebra], while $\beta\cdot s=(3/5)\cdot 0+0\cdot 3/5+0\cdot 4/5=0$. By [L2] the frame-$x'$ data is $\varpi'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\varpi=(5/4)(1-0)\varpi=5\varpi/4$, and the axis formulas with $b=3/5$, $s_1=0$, $\gamma=5/4$ give $s'_1=(0-3/5)/(1-0)=-3/5$, $s'_2=(3/5)/((5/4)(1-0))=(3/5)\cdot(4/5)=12/25$ and $s'_3=(4/5)\cdot(4/5)=16/25$. As a check, $|s'|^2=9/25+144/625+256/625=9/25+16/25=1$, in agreement with $|s'|=1$ in [L2]. [step 1.1, L2, L3, algebra]

3.1 Clause (c). Apply [L2] to the chart pair $(x',x)$, whose transition has parameter $-\beta=-(3/5)e_1$, and to the data $(\varpi',s')$ of step 2.1. Since $\beta\cdot s'=(3/5)(-3/5)=-9/25$, the factor is $\gamma\bigl(1-(-\beta)\cdot s'\bigr)=(5/4)(1+\beta\cdot s')=(5/4)(1-9/25)=(5/4)(16/25)=4/5$, so $\varpi''=(4/5)\varpi'=(4/5)(5/4)\varpi=\varpi$. Hence the round trip returns $\varpi''=\varpi$ and $s''=(0,3/5,4/5)$, in agreement with clause (v) of [L2]. This proves (a), (b) and (c); all steps are exact rational arithmetic, no physical interpretation of the data was used, and no choice principle was used. [step 2.1, L2, L3, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $c>0$, and $n\in V$ is future unit
timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Write
$n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(n,v)=0\}$ for the rest space of $n$,
$h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ for the rest
projection and $|w|:=\sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ for the norm on $n^\perp$
([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c)); recall from that
clause that $h$ is linear with image $n^\perp$ and kernel $\mathrm{span}(n)$,
that $V=\mathrm{span}(n)\oplus n^\perp$, and that the restriction of $\eta$ to
$n^\perp$ is positive definite.

**(a) Observer energy, spatial momentum and invariant mass.** For every $P$ in
the future closed cone $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ define

$$E_n(P):=-c\,\eta(P,n), \qquad q_n(P):=h(P),$$

and, when $P$ is nonzero future causal, define the **invariant mass** of $P$ by

$$m(P):=\frac{\sqrt{-\eta(P,P)}}{c} .$$

Then $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$, $\eta(n,P)=-E_n(P)/c$, and

$$P=\frac{E_n(P)}{c}\,n+q_n(P)$$

is the unique decomposition of $P$ as a real multiple of $n$ plus a vector of
$n^\perp$: a vector $P$ has $P=\lambda n+w$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and
$w\in n^\perp$ if and only if $\lambda=E_n(P)/c$ and $w=q_n(P)$. Equivalently,
$E_n(P)$ and $q_n(P)$ are the unique pair consisting of a real number and a
vector of $n^\perp$ with that property. The pair $(E_n,q_n)$ is the
restriction to $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ of the pair of linear maps
$P\mapsto -c\,\eta(P,n)$ and $P\mapsto h(P)$ on $V$. For future null $P$ the
formula for $m(P)$ gives $m(P)=0$, because $\eta(P,P)=0$.

**(b) Rest-mass parameter, rest energy and kinetic energy.** Let $m>0$ and let
$P=mU$ with $U$ future timelike and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, the four-velocity
normalisation of [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]. Then call $m$
the **rest-mass parameter** of $P$ as written, $mc^2$ its **rest energy**, and

$$T_n(P):=E_n(P)-mc^2$$

its **kinetic energy** relative to the observer $n$ and the parameter $m$. The
kinetic energy is defined only after $m$ has been fixed: it is a function of
the triple $(P,n,m)$ and not a function of $P$ and $n$ alone.

**(c) No positivity, inequality or measurement claim.** This definition claims
no positivity of $E_n$, no inequality or vanishing property of $T_n$, and no
physical measurement. The names observer energy, spatial momentum, invariant
mass, rest energy and kinetic energy, and the units joule, kilogram metre per
second and kilogram, belong to the unit conventions of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] and to the physical postulates
of this framework; the mathematical content asserted here is only the explicit
dependence of the five quantities on $P$, $n$ and $m$.

**(d) What the objects depend on.** $E_n$ and $q_n$ are functions of the pair
$(P,n)$: $q_n(P)$ is an element of the vector space $V$, not a coordinate
triple, and no basis of $V$ enters its definition, while
$E_n(P)=-c\,\eta(P,n)$ uses the Lorentz form alone. $m(P)$ depends on the
scalar $\eta(P,P)$ alone and hence on no observer and no basis; $T_n(P)$
depends additionally on the chosen real number $m$. No choice principle is
used.

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), $c>0$, let $n\in V$ be future unit
timelike, $\eta(n,n)=-1$, and let $E_n,q_n,m,T_n$ be the quantities of
[[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]].

**(a)** If $P$ is nonzero future causal, then $E_n(P)>0$, $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$
and

$$\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))=\frac{E_n(P)^2}{c^2}+\eta(P,P)\ \ge\ 0 .$$

Consequently: (i) if $P$ is future null, then $\eta(P,P)=0$ and
$E_n(P)=c\,|q_n(P)|>0$; (ii) if $P$ is future timelike with invariant mass
$m(P)$, then $\eta(P,P)=-m(P)^2c^2$ and the mass-shell identity

$$E_n(P)^2=m(P)^2c^4+c^2\,|q_n(P)|^2$$

holds. The invariant mass $m(P)$ depends only on the scalar $\eta(P,P)$ and
therefore on no observer $n$ and no basis, while $E_n$ and $q_n$ do depend on
$n$.

**(b)** Let $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant, let $U$ be future timelike with
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ (the four-velocity normalisation of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), and put
$\gamma:=-\eta(U/c,n)\ge1$ and $w:=c\,h(U/c)/\gamma\in n^\perp$, the
relative velocity of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(d)
applied to the future unit vector $u=U/c$; equivalently $w=h(U)/\gamma$. Then

$$E_n(P)=mc^2\gamma,\qquad T_n(P)=mc^2(\gamma-1)\ \ge\ 0,\qquad q_n(P)=m\gamma w,$$

and $m(P)=m$. Moreover $T_n(P)=0$ if and only if $\gamma=1$, that is $U=cn$,
equivalently $P=mcn$ (the particle is at rest relative to $n$). Finally
$|q_n(P)|=m\gamma|w|=mc\sqrt{\gamma^2-1}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; a real number $c>0$; a
future unit timelike $n\in V$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$; clause (a): a nonzero
$P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$; clause (b): a real $m>0$ and a future timelike
$U\in V$ with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, with $P=mU$.

[F1] The definition of the observer quantities
([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]], Definition): for
$P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ one has $E_n(P)=-c\,\eta(P,n)$ and
$q_n(P)=h(P)=P+\eta(P,n)n\in n^\perp$, and $\eta(n,P)=-E_n(P)/c$; for nonzero
future causal $P$ the invariant mass is
$m(P)=\sqrt{-\eta(P,P)}/c$; for $P=mU$ with $m>0$ and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ the
kinetic energy is $T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$; and $|w|=\sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ on
$n^\perp$.

[F2] [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], clauses (c) and (d):
$h$ is linear with image $n^\perp$ and kernel $\mathrm{span}(n)$, the
restriction of $\eta$ to $n^\perp$ is positive definite, and
$V=\mathrm{span}(n)\oplus n^\perp$; and for future unit timelike $n,u$ one has,
with $\gamma:=-\eta(n,u)$ and $w:=c\,h(u)/\gamma$, the relations
$\gamma\ge1$, $w\in n^\perp$, $u=\gamma(n+w/c)$,
$|w|^2=c^2(1-\gamma^{-2})$, and $\gamma=1$ if and only if $u=n$.

[F3] [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: $\eta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on
$V$, so $\eta(v,w)$ is additive and homogeneous in each argument and
$\eta(v,w)=\eta(w,v)$; in particular polarisation gives
$\eta(v+w,v+w)=\eta(v,v)+2\eta(v,w)+\eta(w,w)$ and
$\eta(\lambda v,\mu w)=\lambda\mu\,\eta(v,w)$ for real $\lambda,\mu$.

[F4] [[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]: there is an ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$.

[F5] [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]] with
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]: in the oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski space there exists, for every event $o$, an inertial frame with
origin $o$, and an inertial frame's basis is an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered
basis whose first vector lies in $C^+$; in particular such a basis of $V$
exists.

[F6] [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]: in every
$\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis whose first vector is timelike, writing
$v=v^0e_0+v_s$ with $v_s\in S:=\mathrm{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and
$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$, one has
$\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+|v_s|^2$, $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ (for the appropriate
naming of the two components) and
$\mathrm{cl}(C^+)=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$.

[F7] [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]: for an inertial
frame, $S=\mathrm{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ equals $e_0^\perp$, the restriction
$\delta$ of $\eta$ to $S$ is positive definite, and
$|w|=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}$ is a norm on $S$; in coordinates
$\delta(v_s,w_s)=v_s\cdot w_s=\sum_{i=1}^3v^iw^i$.

[F8] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]]: for real numbers $a_i,b_i$,
$|\sum_{i=1}^3a_ib_i|\le\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^3a_i^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^3b_i^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.

[F9] [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]: a vector $v$ is causal exactly
when $\eta(v,v)\le0$ (it is timelike when $\eta(v,v)<0$ and null when
$v\ne0$ and $\eta(v,v)=0$), and $C^+$ is a component of the timelike set with
closed cone $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$.

[F10] [[def-rational-power]] and [[lem-rational-power-laws]]: for $a,b>0$ and
rationals $r,s$ the power $a^r$ is the positive real number defined there, with
$(ab)^r=a^rb^r$, $(a^r)^s=a^{rs}$ and $a^{1/2}$ the unique nonnegative square
root of $a$; in particular $\sqrt{\lambda^2}=\lambda$ for $\lambda>0$ and
$\gamma\sqrt{1-\gamma^{-2}}=\sqrt{\gamma^2-1}$ for $\gamma\ge1$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** fix orthonormal coordinates, prove the algebraic identity
and positivity there, then specialise to $P=mU$ using the relative-velocity
decomposition.

1.1 By [F1], $q_n(P)=P+\eta(P,n)n\in n^\perp$, $\eta(P,n)=-E_n(P)/c$, $m(P)^2=-\eta(P,P)/c^2$ for nonzero future causal $P$, and $T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ in the setting of (b). Expanding with [F3] and $\eta(n,n)=-1$ gives $\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))=\eta(P,P)+2\eta(P,n)^2+\eta(P,n)^2\eta(n,n)=\eta(P,P)+\eta(P,n)^2=\eta(P,P)+E_n(P)^2/c^2$. The formula $m(P)^2=-\eta(P,P)/c^2$ involves only the scalar $\eta(P,P)$, so $m(P)$ depends on no observer and no basis, whereas $E_n$ and $q_n$ are built from $\eta(P,n)$ and $h$ and depend on $n$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Choose by [F4] and [F5] an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0\in C^+$; write $v=v^0e_0+v_s$ with $v_s\in S=\mathrm{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $|v_s|$ as in [F6]. Bilinearity [F3] extends the quadratic form of [F6] to $\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+\delta(v_s,w_s)$ with $\delta(v_s,w_s)=v_s\cdot w_s$ the Euclidean inner product of [F7]. By [F6], $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ and $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; hence $n^0>|n_s|\ge0$ and $P^0\ge|P_s|\ge0$, while $\eta(n,n)=-1$ gives $(n^0)^2=1+|n_s|^2$. By [F8], $|P_s\cdot n_s|\le|P_s|\,|n_s|$. [F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8]

1.3 In the setting of (b), put $u:=U/c$. Since $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$, bilinearity [F3] gives $\eta(u,u)=c^{-2}\eta(U,U)=-1$, so $u$ is future unit timelike, and [F2] clause (d) applies: with $\gamma:=-\eta(n,u)\ge1$ and $w:=c\,h(u)/\gamma$ one has $w\in n^\perp$, $u=\gamma(n+w/c)$, $|w|^2=c^2(1-\gamma^{-2})$, and $\gamma=1$ if and only if $u=n$; equivalently $U=cn$, and $P=mU=mc\,n$ when $\gamma=1$. [F2, F3, F7]

2.1 Positivity of $E_n$: using [step 1.2], $c^{-1}E_n(P)=-\eta(P,n)=P^0n^0-P_s\cdot n_s$, so $c^{-1}E_n(P)\ge P^0n^0-|P_s||n_s|\ge|P_s|n^0-|P_s||n_s|=|P_s|(n^0-|n_s|)\ge0$, where the first inequality uses [F8], the second uses $P^0\ge|P_s|$ and $n^0>0$, and the last uses $n^0>|n_s|$ of [step 1.2]; if $|P_s|>0$ the last term is strictly positive, while if $|P_s|=0$ then $P\ne0$ forces $P^0>0$ and $c^{-1}E_n(P)=P^0n^0>0$, so $E_n(P)>0$ in both cases. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F8]

2.2 Nonnegativity of the spatial-momentum norm: by [F9], $P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ gives $\eta(P,P)\le0$, so substituting into [step 1.1] yields $\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))=\eta(P,P)+E_n(P)^2/c^2\ge0$; since $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$ by [step 1.1] and $|q_n(P)|^2=\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))$ for $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$ by [F1] and [F2], this is exactly the displayed inequality of (a). [step 1.1, F1, F2, F9]

2.3 The energy and momentum of $P=mU$: by [step 1.1] and [step 1.3], $E_n(P)=-c\,\eta(mU,n)=-mc^2\eta(U/c,n)=mc^2\gamma$ and $q_n(P)=h(mU)=m\,h(U)=mc\,h(u)=m\gamma w$, the last equality because $h(u)=h(\gamma(n+w/c))=\gamma\,h(w/c)=\gamma\,w/c$ by linearity of $h$ and $h(n)=0$ in [F2]. [step 1.1, step 1.3, F2, F3]

3.1 The null case: if $P$ is future null then $\eta(P,P)=0$ by [F9], so [step 2.2] gives $\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))=E_n(P)^2/c^2>0$ by [step 2.1], and since $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$ the norm of [F1] gives $|q_n(P)|=\sqrt{\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))}=E_n(P)/c$, that is $E_n(P)=c\,|q_n(P)|>0$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F1, F9]

3.2 The timelike case and the mass shell: if $P$ is future timelike, then $\eta(P,P)=-m(P)^2c^2$ by the definition of $m(P)$ in [F1]; substituting this into [step 2.2] and multiplying by $c^2$ gives $E_n(P)^2=c^2\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))+m(P)^2c^4=c^2|q_n(P)|^2+m(P)^2c^4$, using $|q_n(P)|^2=\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))$ for $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$. [step 1.1, step 2.2, F1]

3.3 The kinetic energy: by [step 2.3] and $T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ of [F1], $T_n(P)=mc^2\gamma-mc^2=mc^2(\gamma-1)\ge0$ because $\gamma\ge1$ in [step 1.3]; moreover $T_n(P)=0$ if and only if $\gamma=1$, which by [step 1.3] is equivalent to $u=n$, that is to $U=cn$, that is to $P=mU=mcn$, and conversely $P=mcn$ gives $\gamma=1$ and $T_n(P)=0$. [step 1.3, step 2.3, F1]

3.4 The momentum magnitude: by [step 2.3] and [step 1.3], $|q_n(P)|=m\gamma|w|=m\gamma\,c\sqrt{1-\gamma^{-2}}$, and since $\gamma\ge1$, [F10] gives $\gamma\sqrt{1-\gamma^{-2}}=\sqrt{\gamma^2(1-\gamma^{-2})}=\sqrt{\gamma^2-1}$, so $|q_n(P)|=mc\sqrt{\gamma^2-1}$. [step 1.3, step 2.3, F10]

4.1 Collect the conclusions and evaluate the invariant mass of $P=mU$: by [step 1.1], $m(P)^2=-\eta(P,P)/c^2$, and for $P=mU$ with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ bilinearity [F3] gives $\eta(P,P)=m^2\eta(U,U)=-m^2c^2$, so $m(P)^2=m^2$ and, since both $m(P)$ and $m$ are nonnegative and $c>0$, $m(P)=m$; together with [step 2.1] and [step 3.1] this proves clause (a) including (i), with [step 3.2] proving clause (a)(ii), and with [step 2.3], [step 3.3] and [step 3.4] it proves clause (b), the vanishing statement of (b) included by [step 3.3]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.3, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 3.4, F3] ∎

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), $c>0$, and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with stationary observer $n:=e_0$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); let $E_n,q_n$ be the observer
quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]].

**(a)** For every $P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ the coordinate components of $P$ in
the frame are $(P^0,P^1,P^2,P^3)=(E_n(P)/c,\,q^1,q^2,q^3)$, where
$q_n(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3q^ie_i$; if $P$ is future timelike then
$E^2=m(P)^2c^4+c^2\sum_{i=1}^3(q^i)^2$ with $E=E_n(P)$.

**(b)** Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) whose chart coordinate path is
$t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w:=r'$ and
$\gamma_w:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]],
[[def-rational-power]]); then $|w|<c$, the four-velocity is
$U=\gamma_w(c,w)$ by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(e),
and for $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant the components are $P=m\gamma_w(c,w)$, that
is $E_n(P)=m\gamma_wc^2$ and $q_n(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3m\gamma_ww^ie_i$.

**(c)** Let $B(\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] with
parameter $\beta=v/c$, $|v|<c$, along a spatial direction $s$, and let $P'$
denote the components of the same vector $P$ after the coordinate change
$x'=B(\beta)x$; write $\mathbf p=(P^1,P^2,P^3)$ and split it into its
components $\mathbf p_\parallel$, $\mathbf p_\perp$ with respect to $s$. Then

$$P'^0=\gamma_v\bigl(P^0-\beta\,s\cdot\mathbf p\bigr),\qquad \mathbf p'_\parallel=\gamma_v\bigl(\mathbf p_\parallel-\beta P^0\bigr),\qquad \mathbf p'_\perp=\mathbf p_\perp,$$

equivalently $E'=\gamma_v(E-v\,p_\parallel)$,
$p'_\parallel=\gamma_v(p_\parallel-vE/c^2)$, $p'_\perp=p_\perp$. The quadratic
combination is invariant,
$E'^2-c^2|\mathbf p'|^2=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p|^2=m(P)^2c^4$ for future timelike
$P$, while for future null $P$ one has $E=c|\mathbf p|$ and
$E'=c|\mathbf p'|$ in both coordinate systems; in particular the invariant
mass is frame-independent.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; $c>0$; an inertial
frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $n=e_0$; $P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ for (a); a
$C^1$ future timelike worldline $x$ with chart path $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ for
(b); a passive boost $B(\beta)$ with $\beta=v/c$, $|v|<c$, direction $s$,
for (c).

[F1] ([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]], Definition): for
$P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$, $P=(E_n(P)/c)n+q_n(P)$ is the unique decomposition
with $q_n(P)\in n^\perp$; for nonzero future causal $P$,
$m(P)=\sqrt{-\eta(P,P)}/c$; and $q_n(P)$ is an element of $V$, not a
coordinate triple.

[F2] ([[lem-sr-energy-momentum-observer-identities]], Statement): if $P$ is
nonzero future causal, then $E_n(P)>0$ and
$\eta(q_n(P),q_n(P))=E_n(P)^2/c^2+\eta(P,P)$; if $P$ is future null, then
$E_n(P)=c\,|q_n(P)|$; if $P$ is future timelike with invariant mass $m(P)$,
then $E_n(P)^2=m(P)^2c^4+c^2|q_n(P)|^2$; and $m(P)$ depends only on the
scalar $\eta(P,P)$.

[F3] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], Definition): the inertial
chart $x$ sends $p$ to the coordinates relative to $(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$, so a
vector of $V$ has components $P^a$ with $P=\sum_{a=0}^3P^ae_a$.

[F4] ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], clause (e)): for a
$C^1$ future timelike worldline with chart path $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$,
coordinate velocity $w=r'$ and
$\gamma_w=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, one has $|w(t)|<c$ and
$U=\gamma_w(c,w)$.

[F5] ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]], Definition):
$S=\mathrm{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=e_0^\perp$, the restriction $\delta$ of $\eta$ to
$S$ is positive definite, $|w|=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}$ is a norm, and with
$w=\sum w^ie_i$ one has $\delta(w,z)=w\cdot z=\sum_iw^iz^i$ and
$|w|^2=\sum_i(w^i)^2$; the cross product is not used here.

[F6] ([[def-rational-power]] and [[lem-rational-power-laws]]): for $0\le q<c^2$
the expression $(1-q/c^2)^{-1/2}$ is a positive real number whose square is
$(1-q/c^2)^{-1}$; with $q=|w|^2$ this gives
$\gamma_w^2(1-|w|^2/c^2)=1$ and $\gamma_w>0$ for $|w|<c$.

[F7] ([[def-lorentz-boost]], Definition): $B(\beta)$ is the linear map with
matrix $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i_j+((\gamma-1)/|\beta|^2)\beta_i\beta_j$ in the basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, where $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$.

[F8] ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]], clauses (i) and (vi)):
under the coordinate change $x'=\Lambda x+b$ the components of a vector
transform as $P'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bP^b$; for $\Lambda=B(\beta)$ this gives
$P'^0=\gamma(P^0-\beta\cdot\mathbf p)$ and the displayed spatial formula.

[F9] ([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], clauses (i) and
(iii)): $B(\beta)$ preserves $\eta$, is invertible, and maps $C^+$ onto
$C^+$.

[F10] ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], Definition): $\eta$ is bilinear, so
for a vector $P=\sum_aP^ae_a$ in an $\eta$-orthonormal basis,
$\eta(P,P)=-(P^0)^2+|\mathbf p|^2$ where $|\mathbf p|^2=\sum_i(P^i)^2$ by
[F5].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** read the decomposition of the observer definition in the
frame basis, then transform components with the boost matrix and cancel the
quadratic combination algebraically.

1.1 Since $n=e_0$, the decomposition of [F1] reads $P=(E_n(P)/c)e_0+q_n(P)$; as $q_n(P)\in n^\perp=S=\mathrm{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ by [F5], write $q_n(P)=\sum_iq^ie_i$, so the coordinate components of $P$ in the basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ are $(P^0,P^1,P^2,P^3)=(E_n(P)/c,q^1,q^2,q^3)$ by [F3]. [F1, F3, F5]

1.2 Under the hypotheses of (b), [F4] gives $|w|<c$ and $U=\gamma_w(c,w)$, so the chart components of $U$ are $U^0=\gamma_wc$ and $U^i=\gamma_w w^i$; since $w^i$ are the components of $w\in S$, the norm identity $|w|^2=\sum_i(w^i)^2$ of [F5] holds and $\gamma_w>0$ with $\gamma_w^2(1-|w|^2/c^2)=1$ by [F6]. [F4, F5, F6]

1.3 Under the hypotheses of (c), write $p_\parallel:=s\cdot\mathbf p$ and $\mathbf p_\perp:=\mathbf p-p_\parallel s$, so that $\mathbf p=p_\parallel s+\mathbf p_\perp$ with $s\cdot\mathbf p_\perp=0$; the boost $B(\beta)$ with $\beta=(v/c)s$ has the matrix of [F7] with $|\beta|=|v|/c$, $\beta\cdot\mathbf p=(v/c)p_\parallel$ and $((\gamma_v-1)/|\beta|^2)(\beta\cdot\mathbf p)\beta=(\gamma_v-1)p_\parallel s$, and [F8] gives $P'^a=B(\beta)^a{}_bP^b$; hence for every $v$ with $|v|<c$, $\mathbf p'=\mathbf p+(\gamma_v-1)p_\parallel s-\gamma_v(v/c)sP^0=\mathbf p_\perp+\gamma_v\bigl(p_\parallel-(v/c)P^0\bigr)s$ and $P'^0=\gamma_v\bigl(P^0-(v/c)p_\parallel\bigr)$. [F7, F8]

2.1 From [step 1.1], $|q_n(P)|^2=\sum_i(q^i)^2$ by [F5] and $E_n(P)=cP^0$, so for future timelike $P$ the mass-shell identity of [F2] becomes $E^2=m(P)^2c^4+c^2\sum_i(q^i)^2$; this is the second claim of (a). [F2, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 For $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant, the components of $P$ are $m$ times those of $U$, so by [step 1.2] $P^0=m\gamma_wc$ and $P^i=m\gamma_ww^i$; [step 1.1] identifies $E_n(P)=cP^0=m\gamma_wc^2$ and $q_n(P)=\sum_im\gamma_ww^ie_i$, which is (b). [step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.3 Specialise [step 1.3] and use $E=cP^0$, $E'=cP'^0$ of [step 1.1]: reading the components, $E'=\gamma_v(E-v\,p_\parallel)$ and $s\cdot\mathbf p'=\gamma_v(p_\parallel-vE/c^2)$ because $(v/c)P^0=vE/c^2$, while $\mathbf p'_\perp=\mathbf p_\perp$ because $s\cdot\mathbf p_\perp=0$; this is the component law of (c). [F5, step 1.1, step 1.3]

3.1 Invariance of the quadratic combination: with the formulas of [step 2.3], $\gamma_v^2\bigl[(E-vp_\parallel)^2-c^2(p_\parallel-vE/c^2)^2\bigr]=\gamma_v^2(1-v^2/c^2)\bigl[E^2-c^2p_\parallel^2\bigr]=E^2-c^2p_\parallel^2$ by $\gamma_v^2(1-v^2/c^2)=1$ from [F6], so $E'^2-c^2|\mathbf p'|^2=E^2-c^2p_\parallel^2-c^2|\mathbf p_\perp|^2=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p|^2$; by [F10] and [F2] this equals $-c^2\eta(P,P)=m(P)^2c^4$ for future timelike $P$ (and $0$ for future null $P$, since $\eta(P,P)=0$). [F2, F6, F10, step 2.3]

4.1 The null case and the coordinate statements: if $P$ is future null, then $E=c|\mathbf p|$ by [F2] applied in the unprimed frame, and $P'=B(\beta)P\ne0$ is future null by [F9] with $E'=c|\mathbf p'|$ by [F2] applied in the primed frame, which is again an inertial frame; both identities hold because $\eta(P',P')=0$ and $c|\mathbf p'|=|E'|$ with $E'>0$ from [F2]'s positivity and nonvanishing of $P'$. Since $m(P)$ is a function of the scalar $\eta(P,P)$ alone by [F2], and both frames compute the same invariant combination by [step 3.1], the invariant mass is frame-independent. This completes (c). [F2, F9, step 3.1]

5.1 Clause (a) is [step 1.1] with [step 2.1], clause (b) is [step 2.2], and clause (c) is [step 2.3] with [step 3.1] and [step 4.1]; hence all assertions of the lemma hold. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Definition

Throughout, $c>0$ and $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is the oriented time-oriented affine
Minkowski model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], with displacement space
$V$; $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and $x:I\to A$ is a $C^1$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) with proper-time function
$\tau:I\to J$ and inverse $\rho:J\to I$
([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]]). By that
lemma $\tau$ is $C^1$ with

$$\tau'(s)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0 \qquad (s\in I),$$

$\tau$ is strictly increasing, $J=\tau[I]$ is an interval with at least two
elements, and $\rho:J\to I$ is $C^1$ with $\rho'(\tau(s))=1/\tau'(s)>0$ for
every $s\in I$.

**(a) The proper-time derivative.** Let $P:I\to V$ be a $C^1$ map, its
derivative $P'$ being the derivative of a $V$-valued function of one real
variable, read componentwise in any ordered basis of $V$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The **proper-time
derivative of $P$** is the map $\dot P:I\to V$ defined by

$$\dot P(s):=\frac{P'(s)}{\tau'(s)} .$$

This is well defined because $\tau'(s)>0$ for every $s\in I$, so the scalar
division by $\tau'(s)$ is a legitimate vector-space operation on $V$. The
definition does not depend on the basis of $V$ in which $P'$ is read: a change
of basis acts on the coordinates of $P'(s)$, and hence on those of
$\dot P(s)$, by the same constant invertible linear map, which commutes with
multiplication by the scalar $1/\tau'(s)$. Since $P'$ and $1/\tau'$ are
continuous, $\dot P$ is continuous; equivalently, the proper-time derivative of
a $C^1$ field is a continuous field.

**The proper-time reading.** Since $\tau$ is a strictly increasing bijection
$I\to J$ with inverse $\rho$, one has $\rho(\tau(s))=s$ and therefore
$(P\circ\rho)\circ\tau=P$ on $I$. Fix $s\in I$; the components of $P$ in a
basis of $V$ are differentiable at $s$ and $\rho$ is differentiable at
$\tau(s)$, so the scalar chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule]]) applied to each
component of $P\circ\rho$ gives

$$P'(s)=(P\circ\rho)'(\tau(s))\,\tau'(s), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \dot P(s)=(P\circ\rho)'(\tau(s)) .$$

At an endpoint of $I$ this is the one-sided reading of the derivative, as in
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. Thus $\dot P$ is exactly the
derivative with respect to the proper-time parameter of the field $P$ read
along the parametrisation $s\mapsto\tau(s)$; for every $u\in J$ the chain rule
on $J$ gives $(P\circ\rho)'(u)=P'(\rho(u))\rho'(u)=\dot P(\rho(u))$.

**(b) The four-force notation.** Let $m>0$ be constant and suppose the
four-velocity $U:I\to V$ of $x$ is $C^1$
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]); by that definition $U$ is
always continuous, and $U$ is $C^1$ whenever the worldline $x$ is $C^2$. Then
$P:=mU$ is a $C^1$ map $I\to V$ and $F:=\dot P$ is called the **four-force**
on the particle. In an inertial frame the components of $F$ are the
derivatives of the components of the four-momentum with respect to the
proper-time parameter: writing $P^a(u)$ for the components of $P$ as a
function of the proper-time parameter $u=\tau(s)$, one has
$F^a(s)=\frac{d}{du}P^a(u)\big|_{u=\tau(s)}$.

**(c) Scope.** This item introduces a derivative and a name only. It asserts no
force law, no field equation, no equation of motion and no existence or
uniqueness of solutions of any equation of motion; in particular the
hypothesis that $U$ be $C^1$ is a regularity hypothesis on the given
worldline, not a dynamical statement. The identities satisfied by $F$ for a
stipulated four-momentum field are proved in
[[lem-sr-four-force-and-work-energy-identities]], and a physical force law
requires the separate model premise [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]].
The names four-momentum and four-force, and the units in which the components
of $P$ and $F$ are measured, belong to the framework's coordinate and unit
conventions ([[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]); the
mathematical content asserted here is the derivative construction (a) and the
notation (b) alone. No choice principle is used.

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), $c>0$, and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with $n:=e_0$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Let $x$ be a $C^2$ future
timelike worldline whose chart coordinate path is $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$, with
coordinate velocity $w:=r'$, coordinate acceleration $a:=w'$ and
$\gamma:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]); let $m>0$ be
constant, $P:=mU$ with $U=\gamma(c,w)$ the four-velocity
([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(e)), $E:=E_n(P)$,
$\mathbf p:=q_n(P)$ with coordinates $m\gamma w$, $F:=\dot P$ the four-force
of [[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]] and
$\mathbf f:=\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf p$ the coordinate three-force.

**(a)** $F=mA$, where $A$ is the four-acceleration, and $\eta(P,F)=0$;
equivalently $\eta(U,F)=0$ and the mass shell $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$ has
vanishing proper-time derivative.

**(b)** $\frac{dE}{dt}=\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w$, the Euclidean inner product
of the coordinate vectors.

**(c)** $F=\gamma\,(\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w/c,\ \mathbf f)$, that is
$F^0=\gamma\,\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w/c$ and $F^i=\gamma\mathbf f^i$ for
$i=1,2,3$.

**(d)** If instead $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ is $C^1$ and $P=mU$ with this variable
parameter, then $\eta(P,F)=-mc^2\,\frac{dm}{d\tau}$, the derivative being taken
with respect to the proper-time parameter.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; $c>0$; an inertial
frame with $n=e_0$; a $C^2$ future timelike worldline $x$ with chart path
$t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$; a constant $m>0$ with $P=mU$; for (d) a $C^1$ function
$m:I\to(0,\infty)$ with $P=mU$.

[F1] ([[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]], Definition): for a
$C^1$ field $P:I\to V$ along $x$ the proper-time derivative is
$\dot P(s)=P'(s)/\tau'(s)$; when $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant and $U$ of class
$C^1$, $F:=\dot P$ is the four-force.

[F2] ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], Definition):
$U=x'/\tau'$ and, for $C^2$ worldlines, $A=U'/\tau'$; $U$ and $A$ are
continuous and $U$ is future timelike.

[F3] ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], clauses (a), (b) and
(e)): $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$; if $x$ is $C^2$ then $\eta(U,A)=0$; and in the chart,
$|w|<c$, $U=\gamma_w(c,w)$ and
$\tau'=c^{-1}\sqrt{c^2-|w|^2}=1/\gamma_w$, so $dt/d\tau=\gamma_w$.

[F4] ([[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]], Statement): $\tau'>0$, $\tau$ is
$C^1$ and strictly increasing, and the proper-time parametrisation is
related to the chart parametrisation by the chain rule; for a $C^1$ field $Q$
along $x$, $\dot Q=\gamma_w\,dQ/dt$ in the chart parametrisation of [F3].

[F5] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] and
[[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]): in the frame the
components of a vector are read in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, the spatial part lies
in $S=e_0^\perp$ with positive definite restriction, and $s\cdot t$ is the
Euclidean inner product there, with $|w|^2=w\cdot w$.

[F6] ([[lem-sr-four-momentum-in-inertial-frame]], clause (b)):
$E_n(P)=m\gamma_wc^2$ and $q_n(P)=\sum_im\gamma_ww^ie_i$.

[F7] ([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]], Definition):
$E_n(Q)=-c\,\eta(Q,n)$ and $q_n(Q)=h(Q)$ for $Q\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$.

[F8] ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]],
[[thm-chain-rule]] and [[def-rational-power]]): sums, scalar multiples and
products of real differentiable functions and the positive power
$t\mapsto(1-t/c^2)^{-1/2}$ are differentiable with the usual rules; with
$t=|w|^2$ and $w$ of class $C^1$ this gives
$\gamma_w'=\gamma_w^3(w\cdot a)/c^2$ and
$\gamma_w^2(1-|w|^2/c^2)=1$.

[F9] ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], Definition): a
$V$-valued or $\mathbb R^3$-valued function of one real variable is
differentiable exactly when all its components are, and then the derivative is
componentwise; the coordinate vector $\mathbf p$ of [F6] is differentiable
when $w$ and $\gamma_w$ are.

[F10] ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], Definition): $\eta$ is symmetric and
bilinear, so for differentiable $P$ the product rule gives
$\frac{d}{d\tau}\eta(P,P)=2\eta(P,\dot P)$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** differentiate the explicit frame components
$E=m\gamma_wc^2$, $\mathbf p=m\gamma_w\mathbf w$ in chart time, then translate
to proper time with $dt/d\tau=\gamma_w$.

1.1 By [F3] and [F4], in this chart parametrisation $\tau'=1/\gamma_w$, hence $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma_w$ and $dt/d\tau=\gamma_w$; therefore for every $C^1$ field $Q$ along $x$, $\dot Q=\gamma_w\,dQ/dt$, and in particular $A=U'/\tau'=\gamma_w\,dU/dt$ and $F=\dot P=\gamma_w\,dP/dt$ by [F1] and [F2]. Since $x$ is $C^2$, $w$ is $C^1$ and $\gamma_w$ is $C^1$ by [F8], so $U=\gamma_w(c,w)$ is $C^1$ and $F$ exists as a continuous field. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F8]

1.2 By [F3], $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$; since $P=mU$ with $m$ constant, [F10] gives $\eta(P,P)=m^2\eta(U,U)=-m^2c^2$, so the mass shell of the statement holds. [F3, F10]

1.3 By [F3], $|w|<c$ and $\gamma_w^2(1-|w|^2/c^2)=1$ by [F8], while [F6] and [F7] give $E=m\gamma_wc^2$ and the coordinate vector $\mathbf p=m\gamma_w\mathbf w$; differentiating in $t$ by [F9] and [F8], $\frac{dE}{dt}=mc^2\gamma_w'=m\gamma_w^3(w\cdot a)$ and $\mathbf f=\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}=m\gamma_w'\mathbf w+m\gamma_w\mathbf a$, with $\mathbf a$ the coordinate vector of $a$. [F3, F6, F7, F8, F9]

2.1 Clause (a): since $m$ is constant, $F=\gamma_w\,\frac{dP}{dt}=\gamma_w\,m\frac{dU}{dt}=mA$ by [step 1.1] and [F9]; hence $\eta(P,F)=m^2\eta(U,A)=0$ by [step 1.2], equivalently $\eta(U,F)=0$ after dividing by $m>0$; and [F10] with $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$ of [step 1.2] gives $\frac{d}{d\tau}\eta(P,P)=2\eta(P,\dot P)=2\eta(P,F)=0$, so the mass shell has vanishing proper-time derivative. [F9, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 Clause (b): from [step 1.3], $\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w=m\gamma_w^3(w\cdot a)\frac{|w|^2}{c^2}+m\gamma_w(a\cdot w)=m\gamma_w(w\cdot a)\bigl(\gamma_w^2\frac{|w|^2}{c^2}+1\bigr)$; since $\gamma_w^2(1-|w|^2/c^2)=1$ gives $\gamma_w^2|w|^2/c^2=\gamma_w^2-1$ by [F8], this is $m\gamma_w(w\cdot a)\gamma_w^2=m\gamma_w^3(w\cdot a)=\frac{dE}{dt}$, which is (b). [F5, F8, step 1.3]

2.3 Clause (d): let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ be $C^1$ and $P=mU$, so that $P$ is $C^1$ and $F=\dot P$ exists by [F1]; along the worldline $\eta(P,P)=m^2\eta(U,U)=-m(t)^2c^2$ by [step 1.2], and differentiating with respect to proper time using [F10] and the product and chain rules [F8] gives $2\eta(P,F)=\frac{d}{d\tau}\eta(P,P)=-2mc^2\,\frac{dm}{d\tau}$, hence $\eta(P,F)=-mc^2\,\frac{dm}{d\tau}$. [F1, F8, F10, step 1.2]

3.1 Clause (c): by [step 1.1], $F=\gamma_w\frac{dP}{dt}$ with $P=m\gamma_w(c,\mathbf w)$, so $\frac{dP}{dt}=(mc\gamma_w',\,m\gamma_w'\mathbf w+m\gamma_w\mathbf a)$; substituting $\gamma_w'=\gamma_w^3(w\cdot a)/c^2$ from [F8] gives $F^0=\gamma_wmc\gamma_w'=\gamma_w\,\frac{m\gamma_w^3(w\cdot a)}{c}=\gamma_w\frac{\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf w}{c}$ and $F^i=\gamma_w(m\gamma_w'w^i+m\gamma_wa^i)=\gamma_wf^i$, where the first equality uses [step 2.2]; this is (c). [F8, F9, step 1.1, step 2.2]

4.1 Collecting: clause (a) is [step 2.1], clause (b) is [step 2.2], clause (c) is [step 3.1], clause (d) is [step 2.3]; no force law, no equation of motion and no measurement is used, the identities being conditional on the stated four-momentum field. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and $c>0$.

**(a) Total four-momentum.** For a finite list $(P_1,\dots,P_N)$, $N\ge0$, of
vectors of $V$, define the **total four-momentum**
$P_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i$ as the finite sum of
[[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive group $(V,+)$ of
the vector space $V$; the empty sum is $0$. The sum uses the vectors $P_i$
alone: no event, no position and no simultaneity datum enters it, and the
order of the list does not affect $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ because addition in $V$
is commutative.

**(b) Invariant mass of the total.** If $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is future timelike
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), define the **invariant
mass** of the system and its **rest energy** by

$$M:=M(P_{\mathrm{tot}}):=\frac{\sqrt{-\eta(P_{\mathrm{tot}},P_{\mathrm{tot}})}}{c}>0$$

and its rest energy is $Mc^2$.

The square root is a real number because
$\eta(P_{\mathrm{tot}},P_{\mathrm{tot}})<0$ for a timelike vector, and it is
strictly positive, so $M>0$ ([[def-rational-power]]). If
$P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is future null, set $M:=0$ and say that the system has no
rest frame. For $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ equal to zero, spacelike or past causal,
this convention defines no invariant mass.

**(c) Center-of-momentum frame.** A **center-of-momentum frame** of a nonzero
$P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) whose first vector satisfies

$$q_{e_0}(P_{\mathrm{tot}})=0,$$

that is, the total spatial momentum vanishes for the observer stationary in
that frame ([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]). Since
$q_{e_0}(P)=h(P)=P+\eta(P,e_0)e_0$, the condition is equivalent to
$P_{\mathrm{tot}}=-\eta(P_{\mathrm{tot}},e_0)e_0$, i.e. to
$P_{\mathrm{tot}}\in\mathrm{span}(e_0)$; if $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is future
timelike this holds exactly when $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\lambda e_0$ with
$\lambda>0$, and then $E_{e_0}(P_{\mathrm{tot}})=Mc^2$ for $M$ as in (b).

**(d) Comparison with the single-vector convention.** For a single future
timelike vector $P$, the invariant mass $M$ of (b) coincides with $m(P)$ of
[[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; in particular if
$P=mU$ with $m>0$ and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ (the four-velocity normalisation of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), then $M=m$. Both quantities
are functions of the scalar $\eta(P,P)$ alone.

**(e) Scope.** This definition asserts no existence of a center-of-momentum
frame (that is [[lem-sr-center-of-momentum-frame]]), no physical conservation
law and no dynamics; only the total vector carries the invariant mass, and the
individual summands need not be causal for the sum to be defined. No choice
principle is used.

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and $c>0$.

**(a)** If $v,w\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$, then $v+w\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$; if in
addition $v\in C^+$ or $w\in C^+$, then $v+w\in C^+$. Moreover
$-\eta(v,w)\ge0$ for $v,w\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$, with equality if and only if
$v=0$, or $w=0$, or both $v$ and $w$ are nonzero future null and
$w=\lambda v$ for some $\lambda>0$.

**(b)** If $P_1,\dots,P_N$ with $N\ge1$ are nonzero future causal vectors,
then $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i$
([[def-sr-total-four-momentum-and-invariant-mass]]\,(a)) is a nonzero future
causal vector; if at least one $P_i$ is future timelike, then
$P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is future timelike. The converse implication does not
hold: two future null vectors that are not parallel have a future timelike
sum.

**(c)** For every future unit $n$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) and all
$P_1,\dots,P_N\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$,

$$E_n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}E_n(P_i),\qquad q_n\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_n(P_i),$$

where $E_n,q_n$ are the observer quantities of
[[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; if the $P_i$ are
nonzero future causal, then $E_n(P_{\mathrm{tot}})>0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; $c>0$; vectors
$v,w\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ for (a); nonzero future causal
$P_1,\dots,P_N\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$, $N\ge1$, for (b) and (c); a future unit
$n$ for (c).

[F1] ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], Statement): in an
$\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis whose first vector is timelike, writing
$v=v^0e_0+v_s$ with $v_s\in S=\mathrm{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and
$|v_s|=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$, one has
$\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+|v_s|^2$, and the timelike set is the disjoint union of
the convex cones $T_+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ and $T_-=\{v:v^0<-|v_s|\}$; the time
orientation names $C^+$ as one of $T_\pm$, so
$\mathrm{cl}(C^+)=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ for the appropriate naming, and the two
closed cones meet only at $0$.

[F2] ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], Statement): the closed
cones $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ and $\mathrm{cl}(C^-)$ are convex cones meeting only
at $0$, a causal vector is future or past but not both, and a nonzero vector
has exactly one causal character.

[F3] ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], Definition): $v$ is
timelike when $\eta(v,v)<0$, null when $v\ne0$ and $\eta(v,v)=0$, spacelike
when $\eta(v,v)>0$, and causal when it is timelike or null.

[F4] ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], Definition): $\eta$ is symmetric and
bilinear, so $\eta(v+w,v+w)=\eta(v,v)+2\eta(v,w)+\eta(w,w)$ and
$\eta(\lambda v,w)=\lambda\eta(v,w)$ for real $\lambda$.

[F5] ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], Statement): for real $a_i,b_i$,
$|\sum_{i=1}^3a_ib_i|\le(\sum_{i=1}^3a_i^2)^{1/2}(\sum_{i=1}^3b_i^2)^{1/2}$,
with $(\sum_{i=1}^3a_ib_i)^2=(\sum_{i=1}^3a_i^2)(\sum_{i=1}^3b_i^2)$ if and
only if the two lists are proportional, that is there is a pair
$(\lambda,\mu)\ne(0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_i=\mu b_i$ for every $i$;
consequently $|v_s+w_s|\le|v_s|+|w_s|$ for the Euclidean norm on $S$.

[F6] ([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]], Definition):
$E_n(P)=-c\,\eta(P,n)$ and $q_n(P)=h(P)$, the restrictions to
$\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ of a linear map and of $h$, for $P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$.

[F7] ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], clause (c)): $h$ is
linear with image $n^\perp$ and kernel $\mathrm{span}(n)$.

[F8] ([[lem-sr-energy-momentum-observer-identities]], Statement (a)): if $P$
is nonzero future causal and $n$ is future unit, then $E_n(P)>0$.

[F9] ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]) and
([[thm-induction-principle]]): the finite sum
$\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i$ of the abelian group $(V,+)$ is defined by recursion, so
$\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}P_i+P_N$, and a statement about all
$N\ge1$ follows from the base case $N=1$ and the induction step.

[F10] ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]] and
[[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]]): there is an $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ with $e_0\in C^+$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** fix an orthonormal basis with future first vector, prove
the two pointwise inequalities by Cauchy-Schwarz, then close (b) by induction
and (c) by linearity.

1.1 Choose by [F10] an $\eta$-orthonormal basis with $e_0\in C^+$, so that $C^+$ is the set $T_+$ of [F1] and $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$. For $v,w\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ one has $v^0\ge|v_s|\ge0$ and $w^0\ge|w_s|\ge0$, hence $v^0w^0\ge|v_s||w_s|$ and, by [F5], $v_s\cdot w_s\le|v_s||w_s|$; therefore $-\eta(v,w)=v^0w^0-v_s\cdot w_s\ge|v_s||w_s|-v_s\cdot w_s\ge0$ by [F4]. If $v=0$ or $w=0$ equality is clear. Conversely, suppose $v,w\ne0$ and $-\eta(v,w)=0$; then both inequalities above are equalities, so $v^0w^0=|v_s||w_s|$ and $v_s\cdot w_s=|v_s||w_s|$. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz [F5] makes $v_s,w_s$ collinear with a nonnegative factor, and since $v^0w^0=|v_s||w_s|$ with $v^0\ge|v_s|$, $w^0\ge|w_s|$ and $v^0,w^0>0$, one gets $v^0=|v_s|$ and $w^0=|w_s|$; hence $v$ and $w$ are future null, $w_s=\mu v_s$ with $\mu=|w_s|/|v_s|>0$, and $w=\mu v$. Thus equality holds exactly in the three cases listed in (a). [F1, F4, F5, F10]

1.2 Under the same choice of basis, for $v,w\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ the first coordinate of $v+w$ satisfies $(v+w)^0=v^0+w^0\ge|v_s|+|w_s|\ge|(v+w)_s|$ by [F5], so $v+w\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$; if $v\in C^+$ then $v^0>|v_s|$ and the first inequality is strict, giving $(v+w)^0>|(v+w)_s|$, that is $v+w\in C^+$, and symmetrically for $w\in C^+$. [F1, F5, F10]

1.3 By [F9] the finite sums of (b) and (c) are defined recursively with $\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}P_i+P_N$ for $N\ge2$, so a claim for all $N\ge1$ may be proved by induction on $N$ with base case $N=1$ and the recursive step. [F9]

1.4 Base case of the induction for (b): for $N=1$ one has $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=P_1\ne0$ by hypothesis, $P_1$ is future causal, and $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is future timelike if $P_1$ is; the assertion of (b) therefore holds for $N=1$. [F2, F3, base]

2.1 Inductive step for (b): assume as induction hypothesis that for every list of $N-1\ge1$ nonzero future causal vectors the sum is nonzero future causal, and future timelike if at least one entry is; given nonzero future causal $P_1,\dots,P_N$, put $S:=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}P_i$ with $N\ge2$, so $S\ne0$ is future causal and future timelike if some $P_i$, $i<N$, is timelike. By [step 1.2] applied to $S$ and $P_N$, $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=S+P_N\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$, and $P_{\mathrm{tot}}\in C^+$ if $S\in C^+$ or $P_N\in C^+$. If $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ were $0$, then $S=-P_N\in-\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ while $S\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$, so [F2] gives $S=0$, contradicting $S\ne0$; hence $P_{\mathrm{tot}}\ne0$. This proves the assertion for lists of length $N$, and [F9]'s induction principle closes the proof of (b) except its final sentence. [F2, F9, step 1.2, ih]

2.2 The final sentence of (b): in the basis of [step 1.1], set $P_1=e_0+e_1$ and $P_2=e_0+e_2$. Both satisfy $v^0=1=|v_s|$, so by [F1] and [F3] they are future null and not parallel, since $P_1\ne\lambda P_2$ for every $\lambda$ (their second and third coordinates differ). By [F4], $\eta(P_1+P_2,P_1+P_2)=\eta(P_1,P_1)+2\eta(P_1,P_2)+\eta(P_2,P_2)=0+2(-1)+0=-2<0$, and $(P_1+P_2)^0=2>|(P_1+P_2)_s|=\sqrt2$, so $P_1+P_2$ is future timelike; this witnesses the failure of the converse. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Prove (c): by [F6] and [F7], $E_n$ and $q_n$ agree on $\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ with linear maps into $\mathbb R$ and $n^\perp$, so additivity over the recursive sums [step 1.3] gives $E_n(\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}E_n(P_i)$ and $q_n(\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_n(P_i)$ for all $P_i\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$, again by induction on $N$; if the $P_i$ are nonzero future causal, then [step 2.1] makes $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ nonzero future causal and [F8] gives $E_n(P_{\mathrm{tot}})>0$. [F6, F7, F8, step 1.3, step 2.1]

4.1 Clause (a) is [step 1.1] together with [step 1.2], clause (b) is the induction of [step 1.4] and [step 2.1] together with the counterexample of [step 2.2], and clause (c) is [step 3.1]; hence all the assertions of the lemma hold, the induction hypothesis of [step 2.1] having been discharged by its proof of the successor case. ## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), $c>0$, and let $Q\in V$ be future
timelike with invariant mass $M:=\sqrt{-\eta(Q,Q)}/c$
([[def-sr-total-four-momentum-and-invariant-mass]]\,(b)); put
$n_Q:=Q/(Mc)$, so that $\eta(n_Q,n_Q)=-1$, $n_Q\in C^+$ and $Q=Mc\,n_Q$.

**(a)** There exists an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0=n_Q$;
in every such frame $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$, $E_{e_0}(Q)=Mc^2$ and the components of
$Q$ are $(Mc,0,0,0)$. Such a frame is a center-of-momentum frame of $Q$ in the
sense of [[def-sr-total-four-momentum-and-invariant-mass]]\,(c).

**(b)** Conversely, if an inertial frame satisfies $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$, then
$e_0=n_Q$. Hence the time vector of a center-of-momentum frame of $Q$ is
unique, and two center-of-momentum frames of $Q$ differ only by the choice of
origin and by a positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal change of the spatial
basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $n_Q^\perp$; in particular the center-of-momentum
frame is unique up to spatial rotations.

**(c)** If $Q$ is a nonzero future null vector, then no inertial frame
satisfies $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$: a nonzero future null vector has no
center-of-momentum frame.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; $c>0$; a future
timelike $Q\in V$ with invariant mass $M=\sqrt{-\eta(Q,Q)}/c$ and
$n_Q:=Q/(Mc)$; for (c) a nonzero future null $Q$.

[F1] ([[def-sr-total-four-momentum-and-invariant-mass]], Definition): for
future timelike $P$ the invariant mass is
$M(P)=\sqrt{-\eta(P,P)}/c>0$; a center-of-momentum frame of a nonzero $P$ is
an inertial frame with $q_{e_0}(P)=0$, equivalently
$P\in\mathrm{span}(e_0)$, and the condition is equivalent to
$P=-\eta(P,e_0)e_0$.

[F2] ([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]], Definition):
$E_n(P)=-c\,\eta(P,n)$ and $q_n(P)=h(P)=P+\eta(P,n)n\in n^\perp$ for
$P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ and future unit $n$.

[F3] ([[lem-sr-energy-momentum-observer-identities]], Statement (a)): if $P$
is nonzero future causal and $n$ future unit, then $E_n(P)>0$; if $P$ is
future timelike with invariant mass $m(P)$, then
$m(P)^2=-\eta(P,P)/c^2$.

[F4] ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]], clause (c)): for
future unit $n$, the map $h$ is linear with image $n^\perp$ and kernel
$\mathrm{span}(n)$, $V=\mathrm{span}(n)\oplus n^\perp$, and the restriction of
$\eta$ to $n^\perp$ is positive definite; hence $\eta$ restricted to
$n^\perp$ is an inner product.

[F5] ([[cor-finite-dimensional-inner-product-spaces-have-orthonormal-bases]],
Statement): every finite-dimensional real inner product space has an
orthonormal basis.

[F6] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], Definition): an inertial
frame is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $o\in A$ and $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$
an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis of $V$ that is future and positively
oriented; its inertial chart sends $p$ to the coordinates relative to
$(o;e_0,\dots,e_3)$.

[F7] ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], Definition): the oriented volume
form $\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ is the determinant of the coordinate matrix in
an inertial frame, an alternating $4$-linear form; replacing one basis vector
by its negative changes the determinant's sign.

[F8] ([[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], Statement): in every
oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and for every event $o$ there
exists an inertial frame with origin $o$; explicitly, from an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis an orientation may be corrected by negating one
spatial vector without destroying $\eta$-orthonormality or the future first
vector.

[F9] ([[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], Statement): in an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis whose first vector is timelike, the timelike set is
the disjoint union of $T_+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ and $T_-=\{v:v^0<-|v_s|\}$, which
are its two connected components, are convex and are closed under
multiplication by positive reals; $\mathrm{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$,
$\mathrm{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-|v_s|\}$, and the two closed cones meet only at
$0$; the time orientation names $C^+$ as one of $T_\pm$.

[F10] ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], Definition): $\eta$ is a symmetric
bilinear form: $\eta(\lambda v,\mu w)=\lambda\mu\,\eta(v,w)$ for real
$\lambda,\mu$.

[F11] ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], Definition): a vector
$v$ is timelike when $\eta(v,v)<0$, null when $v\ne0$ and $\eta(v,v)=0$, and
causal when it is timelike or null.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** build the frame along $n_Q$ by an explicit orthonormal
basis of $n_Q^\perp$ and an orientation correction, then compare any
center-of-momentum time vector with $n_Q$ algebraically.

1.1 Since $Q$ is future timelike, $-\eta(Q,Q)>0$ and hence $M>0$ and $n_Q=Q/(Mc)$ is defined; by [F10] and $\eta(Q,Q)=-M^2c^2$, $\eta(n_Q,n_Q)=(M^2c^2)^{-1}\eta(Q,Q)=-1$ and $Q=Mc\,n_Q$ with $Mc>0$, so $Q$ is a positive multiple of the unit vector $n_Q$. Moreover $\eta(Q,n_Q)=Mc\,\eta(n_Q,n_Q)=-Mc$, whence $h(Q)=Q+\eta(Q,n_Q)n_Q=Mc\,n_Q-Mc\,n_Q=0$ and $E_{n_Q}(Q)=-c\,\eta(Q,n_Q)=Mc^2$ by [F2]. [F2, F10]

1.2 By [F9] the future component $C^+$ of the timelike set is one of the two convex cones $T_\pm$, each closed under multiplication by positive reals; since $Q\in C^+$ and $n_Q=(Mc)^{-1}Q$ with $(Mc)^{-1}>0$, [F10] gives $n_Q\in C^+$. [F9, F10]

1.3 By [F4] the restriction $\delta$ of $\eta$ to $n_Q^\perp$ is positive definite, so by [F5] there is a $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $n_Q^\perp$; setting $e_0:=n_Q$, the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is $\eta$-orthonormal, because $\eta(e_0,e_0)=\eta(n_Q,n_Q)=-1$, $\eta(e_0,e_i)=0$ by $e_i\in n_Q^\perp$, and $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$. [F4, F5, F10]

1.4 For the converse, let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$. By [F1] and [F2], $Q=-\eta(Q,e_0)e_0$ and $\eta(Q,e_0)=-E_{e_0}(Q)/c$, and [F3] gives $E_{e_0}(Q)>0$ because $Q$ is nonzero future causal, so $\lambda:=-\eta(Q,e_0)>0$ and $Q=\lambda e_0$. Then $\eta(Q,Q)=\lambda^2\eta(e_0,e_0)=-\lambda^2$ by [F10] and $\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1$, while $\eta(Q,Q)=-M^2c^2$ by definition of $M$, so $\lambda^2=M^2c^2$ and $\lambda=Mc$ because $\lambda>0$ and $Mc>0$. Substituting $Q=\lambda e_0=Mc\,e_0$ into $Q=Mc\,n_Q$ and dividing by $Mc\ne0$ gives $e_0=n_Q$. [F1, F2, F3, F10]

1.5 If $Q$ is a nonzero future null vector and an inertial frame satisfied $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$, then [F1] gives $Q=-\eta(Q,e_0)e_0=\lambda e_0$ with $\lambda\ne0$ because $Q\ne0$; then $\eta(Q,Q)=\lambda^2\eta(e_0,e_0)=-\lambda^2<0$ by [F10], contradicting $\eta(Q,Q)=0$ for a null vector in [F11]. Hence no inertial frame satisfies $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$, which is (c). [F10, F11, F1]

2.1 The ordered basis of [step 1.3] has some orientation class; if that class is negative, replace $e_1$ by $-e_1$, which leaves $\eta$-orthonormality and the first vector unchanged and reverses the sign of the determinant of the coordinate matrix, hence changes the orientation class, by [F7] and [F8]. The resulting $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is $\eta$-orthonormal, future (its first vector is $e_0=n_Q\in C^+$ by [step 1.2]) and positively oriented, so it is the basis of an inertial frame by [F6]. [F6, F7, F8, step 1.2, step 1.3]

2.2 Two inertial frames whose first vectors both equal $n_Q$ differ by their choice of origin $o$, which is arbitrary, and by their spatial triples $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(f_1,f_2,f_3)$; both triples are $\delta$-orthonormal and positively oriented bases of the same oriented Euclidean space $n_Q^\perp$, so the change-of-basis map between them preserves $\delta$ and the induced orientation, that is it is a spatial rotation. Together with [step 1.4] this gives the uniqueness statement of (b): the time vector is forced to be $n_Q$. [step 1.3, step 1.4]

3.1 In the frame of [step 2.1] the first vector is $e_0=n_Q$, so $q_{e_0}(Q)=q_{n_Q}(Q)=0$ and $E_{e_0}(Q)=Mc^2$ by [step 1.1]; by [F1] this frame is a center-of-momentum frame of $Q$, and the components of $Q=Mc\,n_Q=Mc\,e_0$ are $(Mc,0,0,0)$. This proves (a). [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Applying the spatial-rotation freedom of [step 2.2] to the frames produced by [step 2.1], two center-of-momentum frames of $Q$ differ only by origin choice and a spatial rotation, and by [step 1.4] no other time vector is possible; this completes (b). [step 1.4, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 By [step 3.1] clause (a) holds, by [step 3.2] clause (b) holds, and by [step 1.5] clause (c) holds; hence an inertial frame with $e_0=n_Q$ exists, its time vector is unique up to the stated rotations, and a nonzero future null vector has no center-of-momentum frame. [step 1.5, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Definition

Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and $c>0$.

**(a) Collision datum and conservation.** A **collision datum** is a triple
$(p;(P_1,\dots,P_N);(P'_1,\dots,P'_K))$ consisting of an event $p\in A$, a
finite nonempty list $(P_1,\dots,P_N)$, $N\ge1$, of vectors of $V$, called the
incoming legs, and a finite nonempty list $(P'_1,\dots,P'_K)$, $K\ge1$, of
vectors of $V$, called the outgoing legs. Its **side totals** are the finite
sums of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive group
$(V,+)$, formed as in [[def-sr-total-four-momentum-and-invariant-mass]]:

$$Q_{\mathrm{in}}:=\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_i,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{out}}:=\sum_{j=1}^{K}P'_j .$$

The datum **conserves** when $Q_{\mathrm{in}}=Q_{\mathrm{out}}$. The two sides
are compared only through these totals: if two data have the same incoming
legs and the same outgoing legs, their conservation behaviour is the same, and
for a datum with a single leg on each side conservation is exactly
$P_1=P'_1$.

**(b) Legs, mass data and mass sums.** A leg $P$ is **massive with mass**
$m>0$ if there is a future timelike $U\in V$ with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ (the
four-velocity normalisation of [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]])
and $P=mU$; a leg is **null** if it is a nonzero future null vector
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). For a massive leg both $U$
and $m$ are determined by $P$: $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$ forces
$m=\sqrt{-\eta(P,P)}/c$, the invariant mass $m(P)$ of
[[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]], and then $U=P/m$; so
the recorded mass of a massive leg is necessarily its invariant mass. A datum
is **on-shell** if every leg is massive or null; a **mass-specified** datum is
an on-shell datum together with the recorded mass $m>0$ of each massive leg
and the recorded value $0$ for each null leg. The **mass sum** of a side of a
mass-specified datum is the sum of the recorded positive masses of its
massive legs, and the side is **massive-only** if all its legs are massive.

**(c) Special classes of data.** A datum is **causal** if every leg lies in
$\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$; **two-leg** if $N=K=2$; and **equal-mass** if, in addition
to being two-leg, the recorded masses agree pair by pair, that is the
incoming masses $(m_1,m_2)$ equal the outgoing masses $(m'_1,m'_2)$ under the
identification of the pairing.

**(d) Scope.** The definition is purely mathematical: it neither asserts that
any datum describes a physical process, nor that a conserving datum exists for
a prescribed list of legs, nor any law of nature. Position, simultaneity,
mechanism and interaction strength are not part of a datum; only the event,
the two finite lists and their recorded masses are. In particular
conservation here is an equation between two vectors of $V$ and is not the
adopted conservation law of a physical model, which is a separate postulate;
the existence question for prescribed masses is answered only in special
cases by [[lem-sr-collision-necessary-conditions]]. No choice principle is
used.
