## Statement

Work in an inertial chart $x$ of the affine Minkowski model, identifying a nonempty open $\Omega\subseteq A$ with its image in $\mathbb R^4$; all integrals are Riemann (Darboux) integrals. (a) If $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and $\int_\Omega g\,\psi\,d^4x=0$ for every smooth compactly supported $\psi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, then $g=0$ on $\Omega$. (b) If $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is $C^1$ and compactly supported and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is $C^1$, then for each $a$, $\int_\Omega(\partial_af)g\,d^4x=-\int_\Omega f(\partial_ag)\,d^4x$, provided $g$ is $C^1$ on $\Omega$ and the products are extended by zero outside $\operatorname{supp}f$. (c) If $F:(-s_0,s_0)\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is continuous with continuous $\partial_sF$ and there is a compact $K\Subset\Omega$ with $F(s,z)=0$ for $z\notin K$ and all $s$, then $s\mapsto\int_\Omega F(s,z)\,d^4z$ is $C^1$ on $(-s_0,s_0)$ with derivative $\int_\Omega\partial_sF(s,z)\,d^4z$. The lemma is choice-free and is stated for the exact Riemann integration theory on bounded rectangles; no distribution theory, no $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ hypothesis and no choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with an inertial chart $x$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), a nonempty open $\Omega\subseteq A$ identified with its image $x(\Omega)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, and coordinates $x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3$ whose partial derivatives $\partial_a$ are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For a continuous $h:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ vanishing outside a compact subset of $\Omega$, the symbol $\int_\Omega h\,d^4x$ denotes the compactly supported Riemann integral over $\mathbb R^4$ of the zero extension $\widetilde h$ ([[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]); a closed nondegenerate rectangle is called a box.

[F1] Compactness of the support and a bounding box: a compact set $K\subseteq\Omega$ is contained in the interior of some box, and every box in $\mathbb R^4$ with pairwise distinct side endpoints has positive volume. A finite union of boxes is compact and bounded. ([[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]], [[lem-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-is-well-defined]])

[F2] If $\widetilde h$ is Riemann integrable on one box whose interior contains $\operatorname{supp}\widetilde h$, it is integrable on every such box and all the integrals agree. ([[lem-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-is-well-defined]])

[F3] The multidimensional integral is linear, monotone and satisfies $|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$; cutting a box along a coordinate hyperplane that meets its interior splits the integral additively. ([[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]])

[F4] Every continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann integrable. ([[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]])

[F5] For a constant $c$ on a nondegenerate box $Q$, every lower and upper Darboux sum equals $c\operatorname{vol}(Q)$, so $\int_Qc=c\operatorname{vol}(Q)$; for a nondegenerate closed box $Q_1\subseteq Q$, the zero-extended indicator of $Q_1$ is integrable on $Q$ with integral equal to the content of $Q_1$, which is its volume. ([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]], [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]])

[F6] If $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ are nondegenerate closed rectangles and $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable, then the iterated integral in an order in which every section is integrable equals $\int_{A\times B}f$. ([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]])

[F7] If $G:[u,v]\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at every point of $[u,v]$ as a function on that interval, then $\int_u^vG'=G(v)-G(u)$ whenever $G'$ is integrable on $[u,v]$. ([[thm-ftc-second-part]])

[F8] The one-variable sum, scalar multiple and product rules hold for coordinate derivatives: $\partial_a(fg)=(\partial_af)g+f(\partial_ag)$ for $C^1$ functions on $\Omega$. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]])

[F9] For every compact $K$ inside an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ there is a smooth $\rho:\mathbb R^4\to[0,1]$ with $\rho=1$ on $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq U$. ([[lem-euclidean-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]])

[F10] If $g,h:[u,v]\times[w_1,w_2]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(u,v)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$ for every $t$, then $G(x)=\int_{w_1}^{w_2}g(x,t)\,dt$ has $G'(x)=\int_{w_1}^{w_2}h(x,t)\,dt$. ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]])

[F11] A continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous. ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]])

[F12] Sums, scalar multiples and products of continuous real-valued maps on a topological space are continuous where defined; in particular the product $g\psi$ of a continuous $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and a smooth real-valued $\psi$ on $\Omega$ is continuous, and the nonnegativity of a product of a nonnegative and a nonnegative function is pointwise. ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Preliminary zero-extension claim. Let $h:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and vanish outside a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. Then its zero extension $\widetilde h$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^4$: off $K$ it vanishes on the open set $\Omega\setminus K$ and is zero outside $\Omega$, while at any $x\in\partial K$ one has $h(x)=0$, because $h(x)\ne0$ would put a whole neighbourhood of $x$ inside $\{h\ne0\}\subseteq K$ and make $x$ interior to $K$. Hence $h=0$ on $\partial K$, and $\widetilde h$ is continuous and compactly supported with support contained in $K\subseteq\Omega$; by [F4] it is Riemann integrable on every box containing its support, so $\int_\Omega h\,d^4x$ is well defined and, by [F2], independent of the bounding box. [given, F2, F4]

1.2 For (a), suppose $g(p)\ne0$ for some $p\in\Omega$. [given, choose]

1.3 For (b), let $K:=\operatorname{supp}f$, a compact subset of $\Omega$. By [F1] there is a box $Q$ with $K\subseteq\operatorname{int}Q$; write the chart coordinates as $(x^a,y)$ and $Q=[u_a,v_a]\times Q'$. For fixed $y\in Q'$ the function $t\mapsto f(t,y)g(t,y)$ is $C^1$ on $[u_a,v_a]$ as a function on that interval, with derivative $\partial_af(t,y)g(t,y)+f(t,y)\partial_ag(t,y)$ by [F8]; this derivative is continuous, hence integrable on $[u_a,v_a]$ by [F4]. Since $K\subseteq\operatorname{int}Q$, the points $(u_a,y)$ and $(v_a,y)$ lie outside $K$, so $f$ and hence $fg$ vanish at both endpoints. [given, F1, F4, F8]

1.4 For (c), fix $S>0$ with $[-S,S]\subseteq(-s_0,s_0)$ and a box $Q$ with $K\subseteq\operatorname{int}Q$, $K$ as in the hypothesis; write $Q=[u_a,v_a]\times Q'$ and define $H(s,y):=\int_{u_a}^{v_a}F(s;t,y)\,dt$ for $(s,y)\in[-S,S]\times Q'$. For each $s$ the function $z\mapsto F(s,z)$ is continuous on the box $Q$, hence integrable by [F4], and all its sections along the $a$-th coordinate are continuous, hence integrable; so [F6] gives $\int_QF(s,z)\,d^4z=\int_{Q'}H(s,y)\,dy$. Moreover $H$ is continuous on $[-S,S]\times Q'$, since $|H(s,y)-H(s_0,y_0)|\le(v_a-u_a)\sup_{t}|F(s;t,y)-F(s_0;t,y_0)|$ and $F$ is uniformly continuous on the compact box $[-S,S]\times Q$ by [F11]. [given, F4, F6, F11]

1.5 For fixed $y\in Q'$, [F10] applied to $(s,t)\mapsto F(s;t,y)$ on $[-S,S]\times[u_a,v_a]$ shows that $s\mapsto H(s,y)$ is differentiable with $\partial_sH(s,y)=\int_{u_a}^{v_a}\partial_sF(s;t,y)\,dt$; then [F7] applied to $\tau\mapsto H(\tau,y)$ gives, for $s\ne s_0$, $$\frac{H(s,y)-H(s_0,y)}{s-s_0}=\frac1{s-s_0}\int_{s_0}^s\partial_sH(\tau,y)\,d\tau,\qquad \Big|\frac{H(s,y)-H(s_0,y)}{s-s_0}-\partial_sH(s_0,y)\Big|\le\sup_{\tau\in[s_0,s]}|\partial_sH(\tau,y)-\partial_sH(s_0,y)|.$$ [F7, F10, given]

2.1 Preliminary positivity claim. Let $h:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and nonnegative, vanish outside a compact subset of $\Omega$, and satisfy $h\ge a>0$ on a nondegenerate closed box $Q_1\subseteq\Omega$. Choose a box $Q$ whose interior contains $\operatorname{supp}\widetilde h\cup Q_1$, and cut $Q$ successively along the coordinate hyperplanes carrying the faces of $Q_1$, so that $Q_1$ becomes one cell of a grid partition of $Q$. By step 1.1 and the additive splitting of [F3], together with monotonicity on the $Q_1$-cell and [F5], $$\int_\Omega h\,d^4x=\int_Q\widetilde h\ge\int_{Q_1}h\ge a\operatorname{vol}(Q_1)>0,$$ because $\widetilde h\ge0$ on $Q$. [given, F1, F3, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 In the situation of step 1.2, replacing $(g,\psi)$ by $(-g,-\psi)$ preserves the hypothesis and the conclusion, so assume $g(p)>0$. Continuity gives $\delta>0$ with $g>g(p)/2$ on the closed ball $\bar B_\delta(p)\subseteq\Omega$; choosing a nondegenerate closed box $Q_1$ with centre $p$ and all vertices in that ball gives $g\ge a:=g(p)/2>0$ on $Q_1$. Apply [F9] to the compact set $Q_1$ inside the open set $B_\delta(p)$ to obtain a smooth $\rho:\mathbb R^4\to[0,1]$ with $\rho=1$ on $Q_1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq B_\delta(p)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $\psi:=\rho|_\Omega$. Then $\psi$ is smooth and compactly supported in $\Omega$, and by [F12] the product $g\psi$ is continuous, nonnegative on $\Omega$, supported in the compact set $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq\Omega$, and equal to $g\ge a$ on $Q_1$. [F9, F12, step 1.2, choose]

2.3 For (b), both products $(\partial_af)g$ and $f(\partial_ag)$ are continuous on $\Omega$ and vanish outside $K=\operatorname{supp}f$; by step 1.1 their zero extensions are continuous and compactly supported, and by [F2] $$\int_\Omega(\partial_af)g\,d^4x=\int_Q(\partial_af)g\,d^4x,\qquad \int_\Omega f(\partial_ag)\,d^4x=\int_Qf(\partial_ag)\,d^4x.$$ [given, F2, step 1.1, step 1.3]

2.4 For (c), the functions $z\mapsto F(s,z)$ and $z\mapsto\partial_sF(s,z)$ are, for each fixed $s\in[-S,S]$, continuous on $\Omega$ and vanish outside the compact $K$; by step 1.1 their zero extensions are continuous and compactly supported, and by [F2] $$\int_\Omega F(s,z)\,d^4z=\int_QF(s,z)\,d^4z,\qquad \int_\Omega\partial_sF(s,z)\,d^4z=\int_Q\partial_sF(s,z)\,d^4z.$$ [given, F2, step 1.1, step 1.4]

2.5 For every $y\in Q'$, [F7] applied to the function $t\mapsto f(t,y)g(t,y)$ of step 1.3 gives $$\int_{u_a}^{v_a}\big(\partial_af\,g+f\,\partial_ag\big)\,dt=(fg)(v_a,y)-(fg)(u_a,y)=0.$$ [F7, step 1.3]

2.6 Let $\varepsilon>0$. The continuous $\partial_sF$ is uniformly continuous on the compact box $[-S,S]\times[u_a,v_a]\times Q'$ by [F11]; choose $\delta>0$ so that $|s-s_0|<\delta$ implies $|\partial_sF(\tau;t,y)-\partial_sF(s_0;t,y)|<\varepsilon$ for every $\tau$ between $s_0$ and $s$, every $t\in[u_a,v_a]$ and every $y\in Q'$. Then $|\partial_sH(\tau,y)-\partial_sH(s_0,y)|\le(v_a-u_a)\varepsilon$ for all such $\tau,y$, and step 1.5 gives $$\Big|\frac{H(s,y)-H(s_0,y)}{s-s_0}-\partial_sH(s_0,y)\Big|\le(v_a-u_a)\varepsilon\qquad(y\in Q').$$ [F11, step 1.5, choose]

3.1 By step 2.1 applied to the nonnegative continuous $h=g\psi$ of step 2.2, $\int_\Omega g\psi\,d^4x\ge a\operatorname{vol}(Q_1)>0$, contradicting the hypothesis $\int_\Omega g\psi\,d^4x=0$. Hence $g(p)=0$ for every $p\in\Omega$, proving (a). [step 2.1, step 2.2]

3.2 For (c), continuity of the derivative function: by [F4] the function $z\mapsto\partial_sF(s,z)$ is integrable on $Q$ for every $s$, and [F3] and [F5] give, for $s,s_0\in[-S,S]$, $$\Big|\int_Q\partial_sF(s,z)\,d^4z-\int_Q\partial_sF(s_0,z)\,d^4z\Big|\le\operatorname{vol}(Q)\sup_{z\in Q}|\partial_sF(s,z)-\partial_sF(s_0,z)|,$$ which tends to $0$ as $s\to s_0$ by the uniform continuity [F11] of $\partial_sF$ on the compact box $[-S,S]\times Q$. Hence $s\mapsto\int_\Omega\partial_sF(s,z)\,d^4z$ is continuous on $[-S,S]$ by step 2.4. [F3, F4, F5, F11, step 2.4]

3.3 For (b), the integrands $(\partial_af)g$ and $f(\partial_ag)$ are continuous on the box $Q=[u_a,v_a]\times Q'$, hence integrable by [F4], and their sections along the $a$-th coordinate are continuous, hence integrable; by [F6] the box integrals equal the iterated integrals. Integrating the identity of step 2.5 over $Q'$ and using [F3] linearity gives $0=\int_Q(\partial_af)g\,d^4x+\int_Qf(\partial_ag)\,d^4x$, that is $\int_\Omega(\partial_af)g\,d^4x=-\int_\Omega f(\partial_ag)\,d^4x$ by step 2.3. This proves (b). [F3, F4, F6, step 2.3, step 2.5]

4.1 For (c), let $G(s):=\int_\Omega F(s,z)\,d^4z$. By steps 2.4 and 1.4, $G(s)=\int_{Q'}H(s,y)\,dy$ for $s\in[-S,S]$. For $s\ne s_0$, linearity [F3] gives $\frac{G(s)-G(s_0)}{s-s_0}=\int_{Q'}\frac{H(s,y)-H(s_0,y)}{s-s_0}\,dy$; by step 2.6 the integrands converge to $\partial_sH(s_0,\cdot)$ uniformly on $Q'$ as $s\to s_0$, so [F3] (absolute-value estimate) and [F4] yield $\lim_{s\to s_0}\frac{G(s)-G(s_0)}{s-s_0}=\int_{Q'}\partial_sH(s_0,y)\,dy$. By step 1.5 and [F6] applied to the continuous $\partial_sF(s_0,\cdot)$ this equals $\int_Q\partial_sF(s_0,z)\,d^4z=\int_\Omega\partial_sF(s_0,z)\,d^4z$, the last equality by step 2.4. Thus $G$ is differentiable on $[-S,S]$ with derivative $s\mapsto\int_\Omega\partial_sF(s,z)\,d^4z$, which is continuous by step 3.2; hence $G$ is $C^1$ on $[-S,S]$. Since every $s\in(-s_0,s_0)$ lies in some such $[-S,S]$, the map $s\mapsto\int_\Omega F(s,z)\,d^4z$ is $C^1$ on $(-s_0,s_0)$ with the stated derivative, proving (c). [F3, F4, F6, step 1.4, step 1.5, step 2.4, step 2.6, step 3.2]

5.1 Clauses (a), (b) and (c) are proved in steps 3.1, 3.3 and 4.1. Every choice made is finite (finitely many boxes, a bump from [F9], a finite grid cut); neither the Axiom of Choice nor countable choice is used, and no distribution theory or local-integrability hypothesis enters. [step 3.1, step 3.3, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open set with an inertial chart $x$, let $K>0$, let $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and let $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth real scalar field ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]). For every smooth compactly supported $h:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ define the first variation $$\delta S(\varphi)[h]:=-\frac{K}{c}\int_\Omega\Big(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\varphi\,\partial_bh+V'(\varphi)h\Big)\,d^4x,$$ a finite Riemann integral by compact support of $h$ ([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]\,(c)). Then (a) $\delta S(\varphi)[h]=\dfrac{K}{c}\int_\Omega\big(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi)\big)h\,d^4x$, where $\Box\varphi:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\varphi$; (b) $\delta S(\varphi)[h]=0$ for every such $h$ if and only if $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ on $\Omega$. The equation in (b) is called the scalar-field equation of this model. The statement is the first variation of the action on compactly supported variations; it asserts nothing about convergence of $S$ on unbounded domains, no boundary term, no dynamics beyond the equivalence in (b) and no empirical fact. No choice principle is used. Precisely, with $L(\phi):=\tfrac12\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\partial_b\phi+V(\phi)$, define the relative action $S_h(s):=-(K/c)\int_\Omega[L(\varphi+sh)-L(\varphi)]\,d^4x$. Its integrand has support in $\operatorname{supp}h$, so it is defined for every real $s$ even when either background action diverges; $S_h\prime(0)=\delta S(\varphi)[h]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with a fixed inertial chart $x$ and its coordinate partial derivatives $\partial_a$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), a nonempty open $\Omega\subseteq A$, a numerical constant $K>0$, a smooth $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, a smooth real scalar field $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]), and smooth compactly supported real $h:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. In the inertial chart the metric components are the constant matrices $\eta_{ab}=\eta^{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, with $\eta^{ab}=\eta^{ba}$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). We write $\Box\varphi:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\varphi$ and $L(\phi):=\tfrac12\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\partial_b\phi+V(\phi)$ for a smooth scalar function $\phi$.

[F1] Compactly supported differentiation under the integral sign: if $F:(-s_0,s_0)\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is continuous with continuous $\partial_sF$ and there is a compact $K\Subset\Omega$ with $F(s,z)=0$ for $z\notin K$ and all $s$, then $s\mapsto\int_\Omega F(s,z)\,d^4z$ is $C^1$ on $(-s_0,s_0)$ with derivative $\int_\Omega\partial_sF(s,z)\,d^4z$. ([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]\,(c))

[F2] Compact-support integration by parts: if $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is $C^1$ and compactly supported and $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is $C^1$, then for each $a$, $\int_\Omega(\partial_af)g\,d^4x=-\int_\Omega f(\partial_ag)\,d^4x$. ([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]\,(b))

[F3] Fundamental lemma: if $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and $\int_\Omega g\psi\,d^4x=0$ for every smooth compactly supported $\psi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, then $g=0$ on $\Omega$. ([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]\,(a))

[F4] Chain rule for total derivatives: if $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$, then $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

[F5] Real one-variable sum, scalar multiple and product rules for derivatives. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]])

[F6] If a map is totally differentiable at a point, then all its directional derivatives exist there and equal the total derivative evaluated on the direction; in particular coordinate partial derivatives are the entries of the Jacobian. ([[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]])

[F7] Sums, scalar multiples and products of continuous real-valued maps on a topological space are continuous where defined, so every finite polynomial expression in continuous real-valued maps is continuous; a composite of continuous maps is continuous, and pulling a continuous real-valued function back along the coordinate projection $(s,z)\mapsto z$ preserves continuity, both immediately from the definition of continuity through preimages of open sets and from the descriptions of the product and subspace topologies. Consequently the maps $(s,z)\mapsto\partial_a\varphi(z)$, $(s,z)\mapsto\partial_ah(z)$, $(s,z)\mapsto h(z)$, $(s,z)\mapsto s$, $(s,z)\mapsto\varphi(z)+s\,h(z)$ and the composites $V(\varphi(z)+sh(z))$ and $V'(\varphi(z)+sh(z))$ are continuous on $\mathbb R\times\Omega$. ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]], [[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix a smooth compactly supported $h$. For every real $s$ and every $z\in\Omega$ set $\Phi_s(z):=L(\varphi+sh)(z)-L(\varphi)(z)$ and $F(s,z):=-(K/c)\Phi_s(z)$. Differentiating the real function $s\mapsto L(\varphi+sh)(z)$ with the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules [F5], the chain rule [F4] and the Jacobian identification [F6] gives $$\partial_s\Phi_s(z)=\eta^{ab}\partial_a(\varphi+sh)(z)\,\partial_bh(z)+V'(\varphi(z)+sh(z))\,h(z),$$ and the right-hand side equals $\eta^{ab}\partial_a\varphi(z)\partial_bh(z)+V'(\varphi(z))h(z)$ at $s=0$. Both $\Phi_s$ and $\partial_s\Phi_s$ are continuous on $\mathbb R\times\Omega$: each is a finite sum of products of the continuous maps $(s,z)\mapsto\partial_a\varphi(z)$, $(s,z)\mapsto\partial_ah(z)$, $(s,z)\mapsto h(z)$, $(s,z)\mapsto s$, $(s,z)\mapsto\varphi(z)+sh(z)$ and of the composites of the last of these with the continuous one-variable functions $V$ and $V'$, and [F7] gives continuity of all these sums, products and composites; both functions also vanish at every $z\notin\operatorname{supp}h$, because $\varphi+sh=\varphi$ there. [given, F4, F5, F6, F7]

2.1 Apply [F1] to $F$ on $(-1,1)\times\Omega$: the relative action $S_h(s)=-(K/c)\int_\Omega\Phi_s\,d^4x$ is $C^1$ on $(-1,1)$ with $S_h'(0)=-(K/c)\int_\Omega\partial_s\Phi_0\,d^4x=\delta S(\varphi)[h]$, using the value of $\partial_s\Phi_s$ at $s=0$ from step 1.1; the integrand of $S_h(s)$ is supported in $\operatorname{supp}h$ for every $s$, so $S_h(s)$ is a finite Riemann integral for every real $s$ and $S_h'(0)=\delta S(\varphi)[h]$. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 Claim (a): [F2] with $f=h$ and $g=\eta^{ab}\partial_b\varphi$ (here $\eta^{ab}$ is constant in the inertial chart) gives $\int_\Omega\eta^{ab}\partial_a\varphi\,\partial_bh\,d^4x=-\int_\Omega h\,\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\varphi\,d^4x=-\int_\Omega(\Box\varphi)h\,d^4x$. Substituting into the definition of $\delta S(\varphi)[h]$ from step 2.1 yields $\delta S(\varphi)[h]=\frac Kc\int_\Omega(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))h\,d^4x$. [F2, step 2.1, given]

4.1 Claim (b), forward direction: assume $\delta S(\varphi)[h]=0$ for every smooth compactly supported $h$. By step 3.1 the continuous function $g:=\frac Kc(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))$ satisfies $\int_\Omega g\psi\,d^4x=0$ for every smooth compactly supported $\psi$; [F3] gives $g=0$, i.e. $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ on $\Omega$. [F3, step 3.1]

4.2 Claim (b), reverse direction: if $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ on $\Omega$, then for every smooth compactly supported $h$ step 3.1 gives $\delta S(\varphi)[h]=\frac Kc\int_\Omega(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))h\,d^4x=0$, because the integrand is the zero function. [step 3.1]

5.1 Step 3.1 proves (a), steps 4.1 and 4.2 prove the two directions of (b), and step 2.1 identifies the first variation as the derivative of the relative action at $0$. No background action on $\Omega$ need converge, no boundary term and no choice principle is used; the displayed equation is an equivalence on $\Omega$ and asserts no dynamics. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be any nonempty open set with inertial chart $x$, let $c,K>0$ be numerical constants, and let $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. For each smooth symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor $h$ with compact support, set $g_{ab}(s)=\eta_{ab}+s h_{ab}$. Choose $s_0>0$ so that these matrices are nondegenerate with negative determinant for $|s|<s_0$; outside $\operatorname{supp}h$ they equal $\eta$. Put $D_h(s,x):=[\tfrac12 g^{ab}(s,x)\partial_a\varphi(x)\partial_b\varphi(x)+V(\varphi(x))]\sqrt{-\det g(s,x)}$ and define the relative action $$\mathcal A_h(s):=-\frac Kc\int_\Omega[D_h(s,x)-D_h(0,x)]\,d^4x.$$ This is the integral of a compactly supported density difference, without assuming either background density has a finite integral. (a) $\mathcal A_h$ is differentiable at $0$ and $$\mathcal A_h\prime(0)=\frac1{2c}\int_\Omega T^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x,\qquad T^{ab}:=K[\partial^a\varphi\partial^b\varphi-\eta^{ab}(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi))],$$ with indices raised by $\eta$. (b) $T$ is smooth and symmetric, and is the unique continuous symmetric $(2,0)$ field for which $\int_\Omega T^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x=2c\mathcal A_h\prime(0)$ for every such $h$. It is called the Hilbert stress-energy tensor of this scalar-field density. (c) The result holds on unrestricted open $\Omega$, uses only compactly supported metric variations, and imposes no convergence or boundary condition at infinity. If the full background action happens to exist, the relative action is its variation difference and gives the same derivative. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with a fixed inertial chart $x$ and coordinate partial derivatives $\partial_a$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), a nonempty open $\Omega\subseteq A$, constants $c,K>0$, smooth $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and smooth $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]). In the chart the metric is the constant matrix $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with inverse $\eta^{ab}=\eta^{ba}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\det\eta=-1$; for a smooth symmetric $(0,2)$ field $h$ with compact support we write $h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$ and raise index pairs of $\partial_a\varphi$ by $\eta$, so $\partial^a\varphi=\eta^{ab}\partial_b\varphi$ and $\partial^a\varphi\partial^b\varphi\,h_{ab}=h^{ab}\partial_a\varphi\partial_b\varphi$.

[F1] Compactly supported differentiation under the integral sign: if $F:(-s_0,s_0)\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is continuous with continuous $\partial_sF$ and there is a compact $K\Subset\Omega$ with $F(s,z)=0$ for $z\notin K$ and all $s$, then $s\mapsto\int_\Omega F(s,z)\,d^4z$ is $C^1$ on $(-s_0,s_0)$ with derivative $\int_\Omega\partial_sF(s,z)\,d^4z$. ([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]\,(c))

[F2] Fundamental lemma: if $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and $\int_\Omega g\psi\,d^4x=0$ for every smooth compactly supported $\psi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, then $g=0$ on $\Omega$. ([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]\,(a))

[F3] The Leibniz determinant is column-multilinear, alternating and normalized; in particular $\det(\eta)=-1$ and, with $A$ invertible, $\det(A^{-1})=\det(A)^{-1}$. ([[thm-leibniz-determinant-is-alternating-multilinear-and-normalized]], [[cor-determinant-of-an-inverse]])

[F4] Adjugate identity and Cramer's rule: $A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\operatorname{adj}(A)A=\det(A)I_n$, and if $\det(A)$ is a unit then $A^{-1}=\det(A)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(A)$; the adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix and its entries are the cofactors of $A$. ([[thm-adjugate-identity-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[cor-inverse-matrix-by-adjugate]], [[def-matrix-minors-cofactors-and-adjugate]])

[F5] Real one-variable derivative rules: sum, scalar multiple and product rules; and for $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ with derivative $\alpha x^{\alpha-1}$. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-rational-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]])

[F6] Chain rule for total derivatives. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

[F7] Sums, scalar multiples, products and, where the denominator is nowhere zero, quotients of continuous real-valued maps on a topological space are continuous; hence every finite polynomial expression in continuous real-valued maps is continuous. A composite of continuous maps is continuous, and pulling a continuous real-valued function back along the coordinate projection $(s,x)\mapsto x$ preserves continuity; both assertions follow immediately from the definition of continuity through preimages of open sets and from the descriptions of the product and subspace topologies. Consequently the maps $(s,x)\mapsto\det g(s,x)$, $(s,x)\mapsto\operatorname{adj}(g(s,x))^{ab}$ and $(s,x)\mapsto g^{ab}(s,x)$, being finite polynomial expressions in the continuous entries $g_{ab}(s,x)=\eta_{ab}+s\,h_{ab}(x)$ with the nowhere-zero denominator $\det g$, are continuous on $(-s_0,s_0)\times\Omega$, and with the continuous $\sqrt{\cdot}: (0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ the function $D_h$ of step 1.1 is continuous there. ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]], [[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]])

[F8] Matrix addition, scalar multiplication, products and transposes obey the usual associative, distributive and identity laws. ([[thm-ring-matrix-arithmetic-laws]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix a smooth symmetric compactly supported $(0,2)$ field $h$ and set $g_{ab}(s,x):=\eta_{ab}+s\,h_{ab}(x)$ for $s\in\mathbb R$, $x\in\Omega$. Since $h_{ab}=0$ off $\operatorname{supp}h$, one has $g(s,x)=\eta$ off $\operatorname{supp}h$. The function $(s,x)\mapsto\det g(s,x)$ is, by [F3], a polynomial in $s$ with coefficients continuous in $x$ and equals $-1$ at $s=0$; for each $x$ continuity in $(s,x')$ at $(0,x)$ yields $\varepsilon(x)>0$ and a neighbourhood $U(x)$ of $x$ with $\det g(s,x')<0$ for $|s|<\varepsilon(x)$, $x'\in U(x)$, and compactness of $\operatorname{supp}h$ gives finitely many such sets and a common $s_0>0$ with $\det g(s,x)<0$ for all $|s|<s_0$, $x\in\Omega$. Hence for $|s|<s_0$ the matrix $g(s,x)$ is invertible, its inverse entries are $g^{ab}(s,x)=\det(g(s,x))^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(g(s,x))^{ab}$ by [F4], and $D_h(s,x):=[\tfrac12g^{ab}(s,x)\partial_a\varphi\partial_b\varphi+V(\varphi)]\sqrt{-\det g(s,x)}$ is defined; the maps $(s,x)\mapsto g^{ab}(s,x)$ and $(s,x)\mapsto\det g(s,x)$, being polynomials in the continuous entries and quotients with nowhere-vanishing denominator $\det g$, are continuous on $(-s_0,s_0)\times\Omega$ by [F7], and so are $\sqrt{-\det g(s,x)}$ by [F5] and $D_h(s,x)$ by [F7], and $D_h(s,x)=D_h(0,x)$ whenever $h_{ab}(x)=0$, in particular off $\operatorname{supp}h$. [given, F3, F4, F7]

1.2 Derivative identities at $s=0$. (i) Differentiating the components of the identity $g(s,x)g(s,x)^{-1}=I$ with respect to $s$ at $s=0$ by [F5] and [F8], and using $g_{ab}(0)=\eta_{ab}$, $g^{ab}(0)=\eta^{ab}$ and $\eta_{ac}\eta^{cb}=\delta_a^b$, gives $\partial_sg^{ab}(0,x)=-h^{ab}(x)$, where $h^{ab}:=\eta^{ac}\eta^{bd}h_{cd}$. (ii) Column multilinearity [F3] expands $\det(\eta+sh)=\det\eta+s\,\Sigma+s^2(\cdots)$ with $\Sigma:=\sum_j\det(\eta\text{ with its }j\text{-th column replaced by the }j\text{-th column of }h)$; expanding each such determinant along the replaced column shows $\Sigma=\sum_{i,j}h_{ij}C_{ij}(\eta)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(\eta)h)$, and by [F4] $\operatorname{adj}(\eta)=\det(\eta)\eta^{-1}=-\eta^{-1}$, so $\Sigma=-\operatorname{tr}(\eta^{-1}h)=-\eta^{ab}h_{ab}$, because $\operatorname{tr}(\eta^{-1}h)=\eta^{ac}h_{ca}=\eta^{ab}h_{ab}$ by symmetry. (iii) Hence $\frac{d}{ds}\det g(0,x)=-\eta^{ab}h_{ab}(x)$, and since $-\det g(0,x)=1$ the chain rule [F6] with the power rule [F5] gives $\frac{d}{ds}\sqrt{-\det g(s,x)}\big|_{s=0}=\frac{1}{2}\eta^{ab}h_{ab}(x)$. [given, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8]

1.3 The field $T^{ab}:=K[\partial^a\varphi\partial^b\varphi-\eta^{ab}(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi))]$ is smooth on $\Omega$, because $\varphi$ and $V$ are smooth, $V(\varphi)$ is a smooth composition, and $\eta^{ab}$ is constant; it is symmetric, because $\eta^{ab}=\eta^{ba}$ and $\partial^a\varphi\partial^b\varphi=\partial^b\varphi\partial^a\varphi$. [given]

2.1 Apply [F1] to $F(s,x):=-\tfrac Kc[D_h(s,x)-D_h(0,x)]$ on $(-s_0,s_0)\times\Omega$: step 1.1 shows that $F$ is continuous with the stated compact support in $x$ for every $s$, and $\partial_sF$ is continuous by the same arguments applied to the derivative of $D_h$; hence $\mathcal A_h$ is $C^1$ and $\mathcal A_h'(0)=-\tfrac Kc\int_\Omega\partial_sD_h(0,x)\,d^4x$. By the product and chain rules [F5], [F6] and step 1.2, $$\partial_sD_h(0,x)=-\tfrac12h^{ab}\partial_a\varphi\partial_b\varphi+\tfrac12\eta^{ab}h_{ab}\big(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi)\big).$$ Therefore $\mathcal A_h'(0)=\frac K{2c}\int_\Omega\big[h^{ab}\partial_a\varphi\partial_b\varphi-\eta^{ab}h_{ab}(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi))\big]d^4x=\frac1{2c}\int_\Omega T^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x$, since $h^{ab}\partial_a\varphi\partial_b\varphi=\partial^a\varphi\partial^b\varphi\,h_{ab}$. [F1, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3]

3.1 Uniqueness in (b). Let $Q$ be a continuous symmetric $(2,0)$ field with $\int_\Omega Q^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x=0$ for every smooth symmetric compactly supported $h$. Fix index pairs and a smooth compactly supported $\psi$: for $a=b$ take $h_{aa}:=\psi$; for $a\ne b$ take $h_{ab}:=h_{ba}:=\psi$ and all other components zero. In the first case $\int_\Omega Q^{aa}\psi\,d^4x=0$, in the second $\int_\Omega 2Q^{ab}\psi\,d^4x=0$ by symmetry of $Q$; in both cases the continuous function $Q^{ab}$ pairs to zero against every smooth compactly supported $\psi$, so $Q^{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$ by [F2]. All sixteen components vanish, hence $Q=0$. Applying this to the difference of two continuous symmetric fields with the same pairing against every $h$ shows that the field $T$ of steps 1.3 and 2.1 is the unique such field satisfying $\int_\Omega T^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x=2c\,\mathcal A_h'(0)$. [F2, step 1.3, step 2.1]

4.1 Claim (a) is step 2.1, claim (b) is steps 1.3, 2.1 and 3.1, and claim (c) is a statement about the hypotheses used: the argument allows any nonempty open $\Omega$, integrates only the compactly supported density difference $D_h(s,\cdot)-D_h(0,\cdot)$ (identically zero off $\operatorname{supp}h$), requires no convergence of $D_h(0,\cdot)$ on $\Omega$ and invokes no boundary condition; if the background action $\int_\Omega D_h(0,x)\,d^4x$ converges, $\mathcal A_h$ is the difference of the two actions and yields the same derivative. Every choice made is finite; no choice principle is used. [step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

In the setting of [[lem-sr-scalar-field-hilbert-stress-energy]], with $\varphi$ smooth and $T$ the Hilbert stress-energy tensor of the scalar-field action, $$\partial_aT^{ab}=K\big(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi)\big)\partial^b\varphi\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$ where $\partial^b=\eta^{bc}\partial_c$ and $\Box\varphi=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\varphi$. In particular every solution of the scalar-field equation $\Box\varphi=V\prime(\varphi)$ has conserved tensor, $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$. Conversely conservation implies the scalar-field equation at every point where $d\varphi\ne0$, and hence throughout an open set on which $d\varphi$ is nowhere zero. In full generality conservation is equivalent to the pointwise product condition $(\Box\varphi-V\prime(\varphi))d\varphi=0$; it need not imply the scalar equation where $d\varphi=0$. Off shell the balance holds with the four-force density $f^b=K(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))\partial^b\varphi$. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The setting of [[lem-sr-scalar-field-hilbert-stress-energy]]: the affine Minkowski model with inertial chart $x$, constant metric components $\eta_{ab}=\eta^{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, smooth $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and smooth $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ on an open $\Omega$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]), and the field $$T^{ab}=K\big[\partial^a\varphi\partial^b\varphi-\eta^{ab}\big(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi)\big)\big]$$ with $\partial^a\varphi=\eta^{ab}\partial_b\varphi$ and $\Box\varphi=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\varphi$. The force density of a $C^1$ symmetric field is $f^b=\partial_aT^{ab}$ ([[def-sr-stress-energy-tensor-and-force-density]]), and only the coordinate partial derivatives $\partial_a$ of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] are used.

[F1] The Hilbert tensor of the scalar-field density is the field displayed in the Given, and it is smooth and symmetric. ([[lem-sr-scalar-field-hilbert-stress-energy]])

[F2] Product, sum and constant-multiple rules for coordinate partial derivatives: $\partial_a(fg)=(\partial_af)g+f(\partial_ag)$, and $\partial_a(\eta^{ab}\Phi)=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\Phi$ for constant $\eta^{ab}$. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]])

[F3] Young's theorem: if the first partials of a function defined on a disk about a point exist there and are totally differentiable at the point, then the two mixed second partials at the point agree. In particular, for a smooth function all mixed second partials commute at every point. ([[thm-young-mixed-partial-theorem]])

[F4] The scalar-field equation of this model is $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ on $\Omega$. ([[lem-sr-scalar-field-euler-lagrange]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Differentiating the Hilbert tensor. By [F1] and [F2], using that the components $\eta^{ab}$ are constant, $$\partial_aT^{ab}=K\big[\partial_a\big(\partial^a\varphi\,\partial^b\varphi\big)-\partial^b\big(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi)\big)\big]=K\big[(\Box\varphi)\partial^b\varphi+\partial^a\varphi\,\partial_a\partial^b\varphi-\partial^b\big(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi)\big)\big].$$ [F1, F2]

2.1 Cancellation of the second-order terms. For a smooth $\varphi$ the two second-order terms of step 1.1 coincide: the first is $X^b:=\partial^a\varphi\,\partial_a\partial^b\varphi=\eta^{ad}\eta^{bc}\partial_d\varphi\,\partial_a\partial_c\varphi$, while expanding the derivative of the kinetic term by [F2] gives $\partial^b\big(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi\big)=\eta^{de}\partial_d\varphi\,\partial^b\partial_e\varphi=:Y^b$ and adding $V'(\varphi)\partial^b\varphi$ for the potential term; after substituting $\partial^b\partial_e\varphi=\eta^{bc}\partial_c\partial_e\varphi$ and relabelling the dummy indices, both $X^b$ and $Y^b$ equal the same contraction $\eta^{ad}\eta^{bc}\partial_a\varphi\,\partial_c\partial_d\varphi$, the identification of the mixed second partials $\partial_a\partial_c\varphi=\partial_c\partial_a\varphi$ being [F3]. Hence the second-order terms cancel and $\partial_aT^{ab}=K(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))\partial^b\varphi$ on $\Omega$. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Consequences. If $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ then the right-hand side vanishes, so $T$ is conserved; conversely if $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ for all $b$ then $(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))\partial^b\varphi=0$ for all $b$, and since $\partial^b\varphi=\eta^{bc}\partial_c\varphi$ with $\eta^{bc}$ invertible this is equivalent to $(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))\partial_c\varphi=0$ for every $c$, i.e. to the vanishing of the pointwise product of the scalar $\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi)$ with the covector $d\varphi$; at a point where some $\partial_c\varphi\ne0$ this forces $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ there, hence on any open set on which $d\varphi$ is nowhere zero. Off shell the identity is a balance with the four-force density $f^b=K(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))\partial^b\varphi$. [F4, step 2.1]

4.1 The divergence identity and all its consequences are proved in steps 2.1 and 3.1; the identity holds for every smooth $\varphi$, the on-shell statement is the specialization of [F4], the converse is stated with its exact $d\varphi=0$ caveat, and no choice principle is used. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be open, let $\rho:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ with $\rho>0$, let $n:\Omega\to V$ be a $C^1$ field which is future timelike and satisfies $\eta(n,n)=-1$ everywhere (a future unit timelike field, [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c)), and set $T^{ab}:=\rho\,n^an^b$ (a $C^1$ symmetric $(2,0)$ field). Then, on $\Omega$, (a) $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ if and only if both $\partial_a(\rho n^a)=0$ (continuity) and $n^a\partial_an^b=0$ (inertial flow); (b) if $\rho\ge0$ is allowed to vanish, the implication $\partial_aT^{ab}=0\Rightarrow n^a\partial_an^b=0$ is asserted only on the open set $\{\rho>0\}$, and no assertion is made where $\rho=0$; (c) Under the conservation hypothesis $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ in (a), if $J$ is an interval and $x:J\to\Omega$ is a $C^2$ curve with $x'(s)=n(x(s))$ for all $s$ (an integral curve of $n$), then $x''(s)=0$: the flow lines of an inertial unit field are affine straight lines in the affine structure of $A$. For the nonnegative-density branch in (b), the same conclusion holds for an integral curve whose image lies in $\{\rho>0\}$, under conservation there. The lemma is the exact mathematical content of the dust equations; it asserts no matter model, no interaction and no empirical fact. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski model $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with fixed inertial chart $x$ and coordinate partial derivatives $\partial_a$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), an open $\Omega\subseteq A$, $C^1$ fields $\rho:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $n:\Omega\to V$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$; $n_a:=\eta_{ab}n^b$ and indices are raised and lowered with the constant $\eta$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c)). For a $C^1$ field $n$ the expression $n^a\partial_an^b$ is the coordinate form of the flat covariant derivative $\nabla_nn$ ([[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]). For a $C^1$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ field $T$ one writes $f^b=\partial_aT^{ab}$ and calls $T$ conserved when $f=0$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]).

[F1] Product rule for coordinate partial derivatives of products of $C^1$ functions: $\partial_a(\rho n^an^b)=(\partial_a\rho)n^an^b+\rho(\partial_an^a)n^b+\rho n^a\partial_an^b$. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]])

[F2] If $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval and $g:I\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $I$ and differentiable at every interior point with $g'=0$ there, then $g$ is constant on $I$. ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]])

[F3] Chain rule: a $C^1$ curve composed with a $C^1$ field is $C^1$ and its derivative is obtained by composing the derivative of the field with the curve derivative; concretely $\frac{d}{ds}n^b(x(s))=\partial_an^b(x(s))\,x'^a(s)$. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Algebraic identity. Since $\rho$ and $n$ are $C^1$, [F1] gives $\partial_aT^{ab}=\partial_a(\rho n^an^b)=C\,n^b+\rho\,n^a\partial_an^b$ with $C:=\partial_a(\rho n^a)$, the continuity expression. [F1, given]

1.2 Contraction identity. Because $n_bn^b=\eta(n,n)=-1$ is constant, its derivative vanishes: $0=\partial_a(n_bn^b)=2n_b\partial_an^b$, hence multiplying by $n^a$ and summing, $n^an_b\partial_an^b=0$; likewise $n_bC\,n^b=-C$ and $n_b\,n^a\partial_an^b=0$. [given]

2.1 Forward direction of (a) and clause (b). Assume $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$. Contracting the identity of step 1.1 with $n_b$ and using step 1.2 gives $0=C\,n_bn^b+\rho\,n_bn^a\partial_an^b=-C$, hence $C=0$. Substituting back gives $\rho\,n^a\partial_an^b=0$ for every $b$. If $\rho>0$ everywhere, division by $\rho$ gives $n^a\partial_an^b=0$ on $\Omega$; if only $\rho\ge0$ is assumed, the same conclusion holds on the open set $\{\rho>0\}$ and no claim is made where $\rho=0$. [step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 Reverse direction of (a). Conversely, if $C=\partial_a(\rho n^a)=0$ and $n^a\partial_an^b=0$ on $\Omega$, then step 1.1 gives $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$. [step 1.1]

3.1 Clause (c). Let $x:J\to\Omega$ be a $C^2$ curve with $x'(s)=n(x(s))$. By [F3], $x''^b(s)=\partial_an^b(x(s))\,x'^a(s)=n^a\partial_an^b(x(s))$, which vanishes under the conservation hypothesis by step 2.1 (or, in the nonnegative-density branch, at every $s$ with $x(s)\in\{\rho>0\}$ by step 2.1 applied there). Hence every component $(x^b)'$ has zero derivative at every interior point of $J$, and [F2] gives that $(x^b)'$ is constant; applying [F2] to the function $s\mapsto x^b(s)-x^b(s_0)-(x^b)'(s_0)(s-s_0)$, whose derivative vanishes, gives $x^b(s)=x^b(s_0)+(x^b)'(s_0)(s-s_0)$ for all $s\in J$ and every $b$. Thus $x$ is an affine straight line and $x''=0$ on $J$. [F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Steps 2.1 and 2.2 prove (a), step 2.1 proves the restricted implication (b), and step 3.1 proves (c) and its branch on $\{\rho>0\}$. The argument is a pointwise component computation with the product rule and the constancy of $\eta(n,n)$; it asserts no matter model, no interaction, no dynamics of $\rho$ beyond the displayed equations and no empirical fact, and it uses no choice principle. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be open, let $\varepsilon,P:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, let $n:\Omega\to V$ be a $C^1$ future unit timelike field ($\eta(n,n)=-1$) and set $T^{ab}:=(\varepsilon+P)n^an^b+P\eta^{ab}$. Write $D\varepsilon:=n^a\partial_a\varepsilon$, $\vartheta:=\partial_an^a$, $a^b:=n^a\partial_an^b$ and $h^{bc}:=\eta^{bc}+n^bn^c$ (these formulas define the first-order expansion scalar, acceleration and raised rest projection for the stipulated $C^1$ field; they agree with [[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]] and [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] when the field is smooth). Then the identity $$\partial_aT^{ab}=n^b\big(D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta\big)+\big((\varepsilon+P)a^b+h^{bc}\partial_cP\big)$$ holds on $\Omega$, and consequently $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$ if and only if $D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta=0$ and $(\varepsilon+P)a^b+h^{bc}\partial_cP=0$ on $\Omega$. The two equations are the energy-balance and Euler equations of the model; the lemma asserts no equation of state, no thermodynamic relation and no causality condition. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski model with inertial chart $x$, constant $\eta_{ab}=\eta^{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and coordinate partials $\partial_a$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); open $\Omega$, $C^1$ functions $\varepsilon,P$, a $C^1$ future unit timelike field $n$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c), [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]); $T^{ab}=(\varepsilon+P)n^an^b+P\eta^{ab}$ is a $C^1$ symmetric field with force density $f^b=\partial_aT^{ab}$ and conservation means $f=0$ ([[def-sr-stress-energy-tensor-and-force-density]]). The scalar $\vartheta=\partial_an^a$ and vector $a^b=n^a\partial_an^b$ are the coordinate forms of the expansion and acceleration of the field ([[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]], [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]]).

[F1] Product rule and constancy: $\partial_a(\Phi n^a)=(\partial_a\Phi)n^a+\Phi\,\partial_an^a$ for $C^1$ functions and fields, and $\partial_a\eta^{bc}=0$. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]])

[F2] Since $n_bn^b=\eta(n,n)=-1$ is constant, $n_bn^a\partial_an^b=\tfrac12n^a\partial_a(n_bn^b)=0$; hence $a^b=n^a\partial_an^b$ lies in $n^\perp$, as does $h^{bc}\partial_cP$ because $n_bh^{bc}=\eta^{bc}n_b+n^bn^cn_b=0$. ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 First expansion. By [F1], using that $\eta^{ab}$ is constant, $$\partial_aT^{ab}=\partial_a\big[(\varepsilon+P)n^an^b\big]+\eta^{ab}\partial_aP=n^b\,\partial_a\big[(\varepsilon+P)n^a\big]+(\varepsilon+P)\,n^a\partial_an^b+\partial^bP,$$ where $\partial_a[(\varepsilon+P)n^a]=(\partial_a\varepsilon+\partial_aP)n^a=D\varepsilon+DP$ with $DP:=n^a\partial_aP$, while $n^a\partial_an^b=a^b$ and $\partial_an^a=\vartheta$. [F1, given]

2.1 Reconstruction of the stated identity. Because $h^{bc}=\eta^{bc}+n^bn^c$, one has $h^{bc}\partial_cP=\partial^bP+n^b\,DP$; substituting into step 1.1 shows that the terms $DP\,n^b$ and $n^b\,DP$ from $\partial_a[(\varepsilon+P)n^a]$ and $\partial^bP$ combine as $$(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta\,n^b+(\varepsilon+P)a^b$$ together with $D\varepsilon\,n^b$, so $\partial_aT^{ab}=n^b(D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta)+(\varepsilon+P)a^b+h^{bc}\partial_cP$. By [F2] the vector $Y^b:=(\varepsilon+P)a^b+h^{bc}\partial_cP$ lies in $n^\perp$, so $n_bY^b=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Equivalence with the two equations. Contracting the identity of step 2.1 with $n_b$ gives $n_b\partial_aT^{ab}=n_bn^b(D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta)+n_bY^b=-(D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta)$ because $n_bn^b=-1$ and $Y\in n^\perp$. Hence conservation $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ implies $D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta=0$, and substituting this back into the identity of step 2.1 gives $Y^b=0$; conversely, if both $D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta=0$ and $Y=0$ hold, then the identity of step 2.1 gives $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$. The two equations displayed are exactly the energy-balance equation and the Euler equation. [step 2.1]

4.1 The divergence identity and the equivalence with the two conservation equations are proved in steps 2.1 and 3.1. The argument holds for any $C^1$ data with $\eta(n,n)=-1$ and asserts no equation of state, no thermodynamic relation, no positivity of $\varepsilon$ or $P$, no energy condition and no causality condition; all operations are finite component computations and no choice principle is used. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $x$ be an inertial chart of the affine Minkowski model with coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, let $B:=\prod_{a=0}^{3}[c_a,d_a]$ with $c_a<d_a$ be a closed axis-parallel box, and let $T$ be a $C^1$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ tensor field on an open neighbourhood of $B$; put $f^b:=\partial_aT^{ab}$ (continuous on $B$) as in [[def-sr-stress-energy-tensor-and-force-density]]. (a) (Box identity.) For each $b$, with $F_a^+:=\{x\in B:x^a=d_a\}$, $F_a^-:=\{x\in B:x^a=c_a\}$ and each face integral the Riemann integral over the remaining three coordinates, $$\int_B f^b\,d^4x=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\Big(\int_{F_a^+}T^{ab}\,d^3x-\int_{F_a^-}T^{ab}\,d^3x\Big).$$ (b) (Slice balance.) Write $K:=\prod_{i=1}^{3}[c_i,d_i]$ and, for $s\in[c_0,d_0]$, $Q^b(s):=\int_K T^{0b}(s,x)\,d^3x$; this is finite and continuous in $s$. For $c_0\le s_1<s_2\le d_0$, $$Q^b(s_2)-Q^b(s_1)=\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K} f^b\,d^4x-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\Big(\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^+}T^{ib}\,d^3x-\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^-}T^{ib}\,d^3x\Big),$$ where $K_i^\pm$ are the two faces $x^i=d_i$, $x^i=c_i$ of $K$. (c) (Finite-flux conservation.) If $f=0$ on $[s_1,s_2]\times K$ and $T^{ib}=0$ on the side faces $[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^\pm$ for $i=1,2,3$, then $Q^b(s_1)=Q^b(s_2)$ for every $b$. The theorem concerns finite axis-parallel boxes in one inertial chart and is proved by the fundamental theorem of calculus. It does not assert a flux identity for arbitrary regions or hypersurfaces, does not assert that $Q^b$ transforms as a four-vector under a change of inertial chart, and asserts no conservation without the stated side-flux hypothesis; no noncompact or limiting statement is made. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The affine Minkowski model with an inertial chart $x$ ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), a closed nondegenerate axis-parallel box $B=\prod_{a=0}^3[c_a,d_a]$, and a $C^1$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ field $T$ on an open neighbourhood $U\supseteq B$ ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]); the components $T^{ab}$ are $C^1$ functions on $U$ and $f^b=\partial_aT^{ab}$ with $\partial_a$ the coordinate partial derivatives. For a face $F_a^\pm$ of a box, its face integral is the Riemann integral of the restricted continuous function over the product of the remaining three coordinate intervals.

[F1] Fundamental theorem of calculus, second part: if $G:[u,v]\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at every point of $[u,v]$ as a function on that interval and $G'$ is integrable on $[u,v]$, then $\int_u^vG'=G(v)-G(u)$. ([[thm-ftc-second-part]])

[F2] Fubini on product rectangles: if $A$, $B$ are nondegenerate closed rectangles and $f$ is Riemann integrable on $A\times B$, then the iterated integral in an order in which every section is integrable equals the multiple integral. ([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]])

[F3] Linearity, monotonicity, the absolute-value estimate $|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$ and additivity under coordinate-slice cuts of the multidimensional Riemann integral. ([[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]])

[F4] Every continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann integrable. ([[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]], [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]])

[F5] If $n\ge1$ and $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on a nondegenerate box $Q=\prod_{j<n}[a_j,b_j]$, then for every permutation of the coordinates the corresponding repeated Riemann integral exists and equals $\int_Qf$. ([[cor-repeated-riemann-integrals-on-rectangles]])

[F6] A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded above and below and attains a maximum and a minimum. ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Claim (a). Fix $b$ and $a$. For each fixed tuple $y$ of the remaining three coordinates, the function $t\mapsto T^{ab}(t,y)$ is $C^1$ on $[c_a,d_a]$ as a function on that interval, with derivative $\partial_aT^{ab}(t,y)$, which is continuous and hence integrable by [F4]; [F1] gives $\int_{c_a}^{d_a}\partial_aT^{ab}(t,y)\,dt=T^{ab}(d_a,y)-T^{ab}(c_a,y)$. The function $(t,y)\mapsto\partial_aT^{ab}(t,y)$ is continuous on the box $B$, so its repeated integral in this order exists and equals $\int_B\partial_aT^{ab}\,d^4x$ by [F5] and [F2]; substituting the pointwise identity above gives $\int_B\partial_aT^{ab}\,d^4x=\int_{F_a^+}T^{ab}\,d^3x-\int_{F_a^-}T^{ab}\,d^3x$. The integrands are continuous on the box $B$, hence integrable by [F4]; summing the identities over $a=0,1,2,3$ with the linearity part of [F3] yields the box identity (a). [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5]

1.2 Claim (b), finiteness and continuity of $Q^b$. For each $s\in[c_0,d_0]$ the function $x\mapsto T^{0b}(s,x)$ is continuous on the compact box $K$, hence bounded and integrable by [F4] and [F6], so $Q^b(s)$ is a finite real number. For $s,r\in[c_0,d_0]$ and each $x\in K$, [F1] applied to $t\mapsto T^{0b}(t,x)$ gives $T^{0b}(s,x)-T^{0b}(r,x)=\int_r^s\partial_0T^{0b}(t,x)\,dt$; integrating over $K$ with [F2] and [F5] gives $Q^b(s)-Q^b(r)=\int_K\int_r^s\partial_0T^{0b}(t,x)\,dt\,dx$. By [F6] the continuous $|\partial_0T^{0b}|$ is bounded on the compact box $B$ by some $M_1<\infty$, so the absolute-value estimate [F3] and the constant integral give $|Q^b(s)-Q^b(r)|\le M_1\operatorname{vol}(K)|s-r|$, and $Q^b$ is (Lipschitz) continuous on $[c_0,d_0]$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6]

2.1 Claim (b), slice-balance identity. The sub-box $[s_1,s_2]\times K$ is a closed nondegenerate axis-parallel box contained in $B$, and $T$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $B$, hence on a neighbourhood of the sub-box. Applying the box identity of step 1.1 to this sub-box, the two faces with $a=0$ give $\int_K T^{0b}(s_2,x)\,d^3x-\int_K T^{0b}(s_1,x)\,d^3x=Q^b(s_2)-Q^b(s_1)$, and for $i=1,2,3$ the faces $F_i^\pm$ are the side faces $[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^\pm$ with the displayed signs; with the sub-box's interior equal to $(s_1,s_2)\times\operatorname{int}K$, this is exactly the stated identity. [step 1.1, given]

3.1 Claim (c). If $f=0$ on $[s_1,s_2]\times K$ then its integral there vanishes, and if $T^{ib}=0$ on the side faces $[s_1,s_2]\times K_i^\pm$ then the three side-flux differences vanish; step 2.1 then gives $Q^b(s_2)-Q^b(s_1)=0$, so $Q^b(s_1)=Q^b(s_2)$, for every $b$. [step 2.1]

4.1 Claims (a), (b) and (c) are proved in steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1, and 3.1. The argument uses only the fundamental theorem of calculus, Fubini's theorem for continuous functions on boxes and the elementary integral estimates; it concerns one inertial chart and finite axis-parallel boxes, asserts nothing for arbitrary regions, hypersurfaces or noncompact slices, and asserts no conservation without the stated side-flux hypothesis. All choices are finite; no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $(V,\eta)$ be the oriented Lorentz vector space of the affine Minkowski model with orientation and volume form $\varepsilon$ of [[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], and let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be an alternating bilinear form ([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]], [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Define the Hodge dual by $(*F)_{ab}:=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ and set $(\alpha\wedge\beta)_{ab}:=\alpha_a\beta_b-\alpha_b\beta_a$. Use the standard form normalization $F=\tfrac12\sum_{a,b}F_{ab}\theta^a\wedge\theta^b$ in the dual coframe $\theta^a(e_b)=\delta^a_b$ of an oriented orthonormal frame, and define $(F\wedge F)(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3):=2[F(v_0,v_1)F(v_2,v_3)-F(v_0,v_2)F(v_1,v_3)+F(v_0,v_3)F(v_1,v_2)]$, the alternating four-form exterior square. Let $n\in V$ be future unit, $\eta(n,n)=-1$, and put $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$. (a) $e(n)=b(n)=0$, and $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$ with $n^\flat:=\eta(n,\cdot)$; also $*(*F)=-F$, so the Hodge dual squares to $-1$ on two-forms. (b) In an oriented orthonormal frame with $n=e_0$: $e_i=F_{i0}$, $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$, $F_{0i}=-e_i$ and $F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$; hence the six components of $F$ are exactly the six components of the pair $(e,b)$ and the reconstruction in (a) is equivalent to these component formulae. (c) The quadratic invariants are $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|b|^2-|e|^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=-4\,(e\cdot b)$, where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are those of the spatial structure of the frame ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]); also $F\wedge F=2(e\cdot b)\varepsilon$. The two scalar expressions $I_1:=\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}$ and $I_2:=F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}$ form a basis of the homogeneous quadratic polynomials in the six components of $F$ invariant under the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; the square-wedge expression is dependent, $F\wedge F=-\tfrac12 I_2\varepsilon$. $I_2$ is an oriented pseudoscalar and changes sign if the chosen orientation is reversed with the metric and $F$ held fixed. (d) (Optional SI identification.) Let $c>0$. If in an inertial frame one identifies $F^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ for spatial vector fields $E,B$, then $e_i=-E_i/c$ and $b_i=B_i$, the invariants of (c) read $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$ and $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=4\,(E\cdot B)/c$, and $F\wedge F=-2(E\cdot B)\varepsilon/c$. If $\kappa:=(F\wedge F)(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=(F\wedge F)_{0123}$, then $E\cdot B=-c\kappa/2$. Under the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] along $e_1$ with parameter $\beta\in(-1,1)$ one has $E'_1=E_1$, $B'_1=B_1$, $E'_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$ and $B'_\perp=\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$ where the cross product is the right-handed product ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), with $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ and $v=\beta c$ along $e_1$. (e) The theorem is algebra on the oriented Lorentz vector space with the stated index and duality conventions; clause (d) is an explicitly optional identification of the components of $F$ with fields the electromagnetic framework names $E,B$, and the theorem asserts no field equation, no dynamics, no measurement and no transformation beyond the stated component law. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The oriented Lorentz vector space $(V,\eta)$ of the affine Minkowski model with its fixed orientation and oriented volume form $\varepsilon$, normalized by $\varepsilon(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=+1$ in every positively oriented orthonormal frame ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]], [[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]); the raised volume form is $\varepsilon^{abcd}=\eta^{aa'}\eta^{bb'}\eta^{cc'}\eta^{dd'}\varepsilon_{a'b'c'd'}$, so $\varepsilon^{0123}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}\eta^{22}\eta^{33}\varepsilon_{0123}=-1$. An alternating bilinear form $F$ with components $F_{ab}=-F_{ba}$ ([[def-alternating-k-linear-map]], [[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]); a future unit $n\in V$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); and the conventions $(*F)_{ab}:=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$, $(\alpha\wedge\beta)_{ab}:=\alpha_a\beta_b-\alpha_b\beta_a$, the dual coframe $\theta^a(e_b)=\delta^a_b$ ([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]), and $(F\wedge F)(v_0,\dots,v_3):=2[F(v_0,v_1)F(v_2,v_3)-F(v_0,v_2)F(v_1,v_3)+F(v_0,v_3)F(v_1,v_2)]$. The spatial inner product of the frame is the restriction of $-\eta$ to $n^\perp$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$.

[F1] Observer rest space: for future unit $n$ the subspace $n^\perp=\{v:\eta(n,v)=0\}$ is three-dimensional and $\eta$ restricts to a positive definite form on it; the map $h(v)=v+\eta(n,v)n$ has image $n^\perp$ and satisfies $h^a{}_bn^b=0=n_ah^a{}_b$. ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c))

[F2] Gram–Schmidt: every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis. ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]])

[F3] Tensor transformation and invariance of the volume form: for a proper orthochronous Lorentz map $L$ the components of a $(0,2)$ form satisfy $F'_{ab}=L_a{}^cL_b{}^dF_{cd}$, the alternating covariant laws hold on each slot, and $\varepsilon'_{abcd}=\varepsilon_{abcd}$ (the oriented volume form is invariant); the boosts $B(\beta)$ are proper orthochronous with $B(\beta)^{-1}=B(-\beta)$ and every spatial rotation extension $\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map. ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iii),(v), [[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], [[lem-boost-rotation-factorization]]\,(iii))

[F4] Passive boost: for $\beta\in(-1,1)$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ the boost along the spatial axis $e_1$ has the matrix $\Lambda^0{}_0=\Lambda^1{}_1=\gamma$, $\Lambda^0{}_1=\Lambda^1{}_0=-\gamma\beta$, and identity on the other two spatial directions; it is proper orthochronous with $B(\beta)^{-1}=B(-\beta)$. ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]])

[F5] The right-handed cross product of $\mathbb R^3$: $(u\times v)_i=\epsilon_{ijk}u_jv_k$ with $\epsilon_{123}=+1$. ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Adapted oriented frame. By [F1] the rest space $n^\perp$ is a three-dimensional inner product space; [F2] gives an orthonormal basis $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $n^\perp$. The ordered frame $(n,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ is orthonormal; if its orientation class is negative, replace $u_3$ by $-u_3$, which keeps orthonormality and makes the frame positively oriented. Writing $e_0:=n$, $e_1,e_2,e_3$ for this frame, the components satisfy $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$. Only finitely many choices are made. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 Hodge dual on the six basis forms. Let $\theta^a$ be the dual coframe and set $a_i:=\theta^0\wedge\theta^i$ and $s_1:=\theta^2\wedge\theta^3$, $s_2:=\theta^3\wedge\theta^1$, $s_3:=\theta^1\wedge\theta^2$. Evaluating the definition $(*F)_{ab}=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ on the basis forms, using $\varepsilon^{0123}=-1$ and the antisymmetry of $\varepsilon$, gives $$(*a_i)=-s_i,\qquad (*s_i)=a_i\qquad(i=1,2,3).$$ Indeed the only nonzero contributions come from the complementary index pair, and $\varepsilon_{0i}{}^{jk}=+\epsilon_{ijk}$ and $\varepsilon_{ij}{}^{0k}=-\epsilon_{ijk}$ for spatial indices. Consequently $*(*F)=-F$ on every two-form, since $*^2=-1$ on each of the six basis forms. For $F=\tfrac12F_{ab}\theta^a\wedge\theta^b$ the dual is $(*F)=e_i s_i-b_i a_i$ whenever the components $e_i=F_{i0}$ and $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$ are used, by direct substitution into the definition. [given]

2.1 Components of $e$ and $b$ and reconstruction (a),(b). With $n=e_0$ one has $n^a=\delta^a_0$, $n_a=-\delta_a^0$, so $e_0=F_{00}=0$, $e_i=F_{i0}$ and $b_0=(*F)_{00}=0$, $b_i=(*F)_{i0}=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$ by step 1.2. Hence $e(n)=e_0=0$ and $b(n)=b_0=0$. Antisymmetry gives $F_{0i}=-F_{i0}=-e_i$, and inverting the relation $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$ with the identity $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{ijl}=2\delta_{kl}$ gives $F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$. Comparing components with $n^\flat\wedge e$ (whose only nonzero components are $(n^\flat\wedge e)_{0i}=-e_i$) and with $*(n^\flat\wedge b)$ (whose only nonzero components are $*(n^\flat\wedge b)_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$, computed as in step 1.2) gives $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$, and $*(*F)=-F$ by step 1.2. The map $F\mapsto(e,b)$ is thus a linear isomorphism from the six-dimensional space of alternating bilinear forms onto $n^\perp\oplus n^\perp$, with inverse given by these component formulae. [step 1.2, given]

3.1 Invariants (c). Raising indices with the diagonal metric, $F^{0i}=e_i$, $F^{i0}=-e_i$ and $F^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$, while $(*F)^{0i}=b_i$, $(*F)^{i0}=-b_i$ and $(*F)^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}e_k$; counting both orders in each antisymmetric pair, $$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=\tfrac12\big(-2|e|^2+2|b|^2\big)=|b|^2-|e|^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=-2(e\cdot b)-2(b\cdot e)=-4\,(e\cdot b).$$ Evaluating the normalized alternating four-form on $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, only the three terms $2[F_{01}F_{23}-F_{02}F_{13}+F_{03}F_{12}]=2[e_1b_1+e_2b_2+e_3b_3]$ survive, so $F\wedge F=2(e\cdot b)\varepsilon$. [step 2.1, given]

4.1 Invariance and the boost action on $(e,b)$. Let $L$ be a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with matrix $\Lambda$, and let $F'$ have components $F'_{ab}=\Lambda_a{}^c\Lambda_b{}^dF_{cd}$; then $e'_a,b'_a$ computed from $F'$ and $n'=\Lambda n$ satisfy the same component formulae. For a spatial rotation of the frame, $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ with $R\in SO(3)$ proper, direct substitution into step 2.1 gives $(e',b')=(Re,Rb)$. For the passive boost along $e_1$ with parameter $\beta$, by [F4], [F3] and step 2.1 direct substitution gives $e'_1=e_1$, $b'_1=b_1$ and $$e'_2=\gamma(e_2+\beta b_3),\quad e'_3=\gamma(e_3-\beta b_2),\quad b'_2=\gamma(b_2-\beta e_3),\quad b'_3=\gamma(b_3+\beta e_2).$$ Because [F3] gives $\varepsilon'=\varepsilon$ and the component law on each slot, the three expressions of step 3.1 — $I_1$, $I_2$ and the coefficient of $F\wedge F$ — are invariant under every proper orthochronous change of oriented orthonormal frame. [F3, F4, step 2.1]

4.2 Optional identification (d). Let $c>0$ and suppose that in the frame one has $F^{i0}=E_i/c$, $F^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ for spatial data $E,B$. Then $F_{i0}=\eta_{ii}\eta_{00}F^{i0}=-E_i/c$, so $e_i=-E_i/c$; and $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}(-\epsilon_{jkl}B_l)=B_i$ by step 2.1. Substituting into step 3.1 gives $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$, $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=4(E\cdot B)/c$ and $F\wedge F=-2(E\cdot B)\varepsilon/c$, so $\kappa=(F\wedge F)_{0123}=-2E\cdot B/c$ and $E\cdot B=-c\kappa/2$. Under the passive boost along $e_1$ the component law $F'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$ of [F3] and [F4], evaluated directly on the six components of $F$, gives $F'^{10}=E_1/c$, $F'^{20}=\gamma(E_2/c-\beta B_3)$, $F'^{30}=\gamma(E_3/c+\beta B_2)$, $F'^{23}=-B_1$, $F'^{13}=\gamma(B_2+\beta E_3/c)$ and $F'^{12}=\gamma(-B_3+\beta E_2/c)$; translating back by the identification and writing $v=\beta c$ this is exactly $E'_1=E_1$, $B'_1=B_1$, $E'_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$, $B'_\perp=\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$, which are the stated vector formulae under the right-handed cross product [F5]. At $\beta=0$, $\gamma=1$ and the identities are immediate. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 The invariant quadratic polynomials. Let $P$ be a homogeneous quadratic polynomial in the six components of $F$ that is invariant under all proper orthochronous maps; by the isomorphism of step 2.1, $P$ is a quadratic form in $(e,b)$, say $P=e^{\mathsf T}Ae+b^{\mathsf T}Bb+e^{\mathsf T}Cb$ with $A,B$ symmetric. Invariance under the rotations $R\oplus R$ of step 4.1 means $R^{\mathsf T}AR=A$, $R^{\mathsf T}BR=B$ and $R^{\mathsf T}CR=C$ for every $R\in SO(3)$. The half-turns $R=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)$ and $R=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ are proper rotations, and since $R$ is diagonal the conditions read $R_{ii}M_{ij}R_{jj}=M_{ij}$ entrywise; together they force every off-diagonal entry of $A$ and of $B$ to vanish, while the cyclic permutation matrix (a proper rotation) forces the surviving diagonal entries to be equal, so $A=aI_3$ and $B=bI_3$. The same two half-turns force every off-diagonal entry of $C$ to vanish, and the cyclic permutation forces its diagonal entries to agree, so $C=cI_3$. Hence $P=a|e|^2+b|b|^2+c\,(e\cdot b)$ for real $a,b,c$. Invariance under the boost of step 4.1 applied to $e=(0,1,0)$, $b=0$, which is sent to $e'=(0,\gamma,0)$, $b'=(0,0,\gamma\beta)$, gives $a=a\gamma^2+b\gamma^2\beta^2$, i.e. $(a+b)\gamma^2\beta^2=0$, hence $a+b=0$ for $\beta\ne0$ (and by continuity of the polynomial identity in $\beta$ also for $\beta=0$). Thus $P=a(|b|^2-|e|^2)+c\,(e\cdot b)=-a\,I_1-\tfrac c4\,I_2$, so $I_1$ and $I_2$ span the invariant quadratic polynomials. They are linearly independent: at $b=0$, $e\ne0$ one has $I_1=-|e|^2\ne0$, $I_2=0$, and at $e=b\ne0$ one has $I_1=0$, $I_2=-4|e|^2\ne0$. Finally $F\wedge F=2(e\cdot b)\varepsilon=-\tfrac12I_2\varepsilon$, and $I_2=F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}$ changes sign if the orientation is reversed with $\eta$ and $F$ held fixed, because then $\varepsilon$ is replaced by $-\varepsilon$ and hence $*F$ by $-*F$. 6.1 Clauses (a) and (b) are steps 1.2 and 2.1, clause (c) is steps 3.1 and 5.1, and clause (d) is step 4.2. ## Postulate

Adopt, on top of the flat spacetime postulates [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] and [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]], the SI conventions [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] and the particle premises [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]], the following classical continuum matter models on an open set $\Omega\subseteq A$ of the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(i) Scalar field.** A real smooth dimensionless field $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, a smooth potential $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with values in inverse square metres ($\mathrm m^{-2}$) and a constant $K>0$ in joule per metre ($\mathrm J/\mathrm m$) have the field equation $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ — the Euler–Lagrange equation of the adopted local action density, with stationarity defined by the finite relative action for compactly supported field variations ([[lem-sr-scalar-field-euler-lagrange]]); the model's stress-energy tensor is the Hilbert tensor of [[lem-sr-scalar-field-hilbert-stress-energy]].

**(ii) Dust.** A $C^1$ rest energy density $\rho>0$ (joule per cubic metre) and a $C^1$ future unit timelike field $n$ ($\eta(n,n)=-1$) satisfy $\partial_a(\rho n^a)=0$ and $n^a\partial_an^b=0$; the stress-energy tensor is $T=\rho\,n\otimes n$.

**(iii) Perfect fluid.** $C^1$ fields $\varepsilon$ (energy density) and $P$ (pressure), both in joule per cubic metre, and a $C^1$ future unit timelike field $n$ satisfy the energy-balance and Euler equations of [[lem-sr-perfect-fluid-conservation-equations]]; an equation of state or evolution equation determining $P$ is part of the model and is not supplied by this postulate; the stress-energy tensor is $T=(\varepsilon+P)n\otimes n+P\eta$.

**(iv) Additivity.** The total stress-energy tensor of a composite system is the sum of the stress-energy tensors of its constituents (tensor-field addition on $\Omega$).

**(v) Adopted observer readings and units.** For a tensor physically assigned to matter in this model, all inertial components $T^{ab}$ have units joule per cubic metre. In length coordinates $x^0=ct$, an ideal observer with future unit direction $n$ and four-velocity $U=cn$ reads the numerical contractions of [[lem-sr-observer-stress-energy-decomposition]] as energy density $\varepsilon_n=T^{ab}n_an_b$, momentum density $\pi_n^a=-c^{-1}h^a{}_bT^{bc}n_c$ and rest stress $S_n^{ab}=h^a{}_ch^b{}_dT^{cd}$, where $h(v)=v+\eta(n,v)n$. In an adapted inertial frame these are $T^{00}$, $T^{0i}/c$ and $T^{ij}$ respectively, and the energy-flux components are $cT^{i0}=c^2\pi_n^i$. Momentum density has units kilogram per square metre per second, energy flux has units watt per square metre, and rest stress has units joule per cubic metre. These identifications are adopted model readings, not mathematical facts about an arbitrary symmetric tensor and not reported measurements. If $f^b=\partial_aT^{ab}$ is assigned to external exchange, the spatial components $f^i$ are force per volume and $cf^0$ is power per volume; the corresponding numerical balances are $\partial_t(T^{00})+\partial_i(cT^{i0})=cf^0$ and $\partial_t(T^{0j}/c)+\partial_iT^{ij}=f^j$. Neither assignment selects a force law or asserts conservation.

## Scope and status

This postulate adopts model equations and tensor identifications only. It does not assert conservation of the tensors — that is derived from these equations in [[pthm-sr-local-stress-energy-conservation]] — does not select any force law, interaction, equation of state, thermodynamic or dissipative behaviour, does not claim that these models exhaust physical matter, and contains no empirical premise, measurement or uncertainty statement. The dimensionless scalar field, the potential with its stated units and the constant $K$ are adopted primitive data of the scalar model; the SI conventions and the identification of the coordinate $x^0$ with $ct$ are those of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], and the observer congruence vocabulary agrees with [[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]] for smooth fields ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]).

## Postulate

Adopt as the boundary and isolation premise of the continuum framework the following.

**(i) Total tensor.** In every conservation or integration statement of this framework the tensor used is the total stress-energy tensor of the system considered, including every constituent that carries energy-momentum — matter, fields and supporting structures present in the region — assembled by the additivity clause of [[post-sr-matter-models-and-evolution]].

**(ii) Localisation.** Whenever conservation of a slice four-momentum over a coordinate-time interval $[s_1,s_2]$ is asserted in an inertial chart, the model assumes that during that interval the total tensor is $C^1$ and symmetric on a neighbourhood of a closed box $[s_1,s_2]\times\bar K$ ([[def-sr-stress-energy-tensor-and-force-density]], [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), that its components satisfy the zero side-flux condition $T^{ib}=0$ on the spatial faces of the box for $i=1,2,3$, and that the slice integrals converge; equivalently, the system is isolated inside the chosen region for the chosen interval.

**(iii) Failure of isolation.** If the side flux does not vanish, only the exact finite-flux balance of [[thm-sr-stress-balance-and-finite-flux]] is asserted; no conservation of a slice integral is inferred and no limiting procedure at spatial infinity is adopted.

**(iv) Unmodelled matter.** For a matter system not governed by one of the models of [[post-sr-matter-models-and-evolution]], conservation of its stress-energy tensor is not inferred; if used it must be adopted or derived separately.

**(v) Exclusion caution.** Removing a constituent — a support, a field or a container — from the total tensor can make the side-flux condition fail; the premise concerns the total tensor of the system, not an arbitrary partial tensor.

## Scope and status

This premise is an idealisation of an isolated bounded system in flat spacetime; it is not a measurement and makes no apparatus, statistical or empirical claim. The localisation clause is a boundary hypothesis on a finite box in a single inertial chart; it neither supplies an equation of motion for the total tensor nor implies the vanishing of the force density $f^b=\partial_aT^{ab}$, which is a separate hypothesis of the integration statements that use this postulate.
