## Example

Adopt the SI conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], the vocabulary of [[def-sr-experiment-interface-vocabulary]] and the ideal plane-wave model of [[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]]. Consider the longitudinal configuration of [[pthm-sr-null-wave-doppler-and-aberration]]: inertial charts $x$ and $x'$ whose transition is $x'=B(\beta e_1)\,x$ for a real $\beta\in(-1,1)$, where $B(\cdot)$ is the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]], so that the frame $x'$ moves with velocity $c\beta e_1$ relative to $x$; an ideal emitter at rest in $x$, represented by the straight rest curve through the common origin with tangent $e_0$; an ideal plane wave whose frame-$x$ data are $(\omega,s)$ with angular frequency $\omega>0$ and $s=e_1$; and the rest observer of $x'$, whose four-velocity is $c f_0$ for the future unit timelike vector $f_0$ constructed below. By clauses (i) and (ii) of that theorem this observer reads $\omega_o(\beta)=\gamma_\beta(1-\beta)\omega$ with $\gamma_\beta=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$, so the *Doppler ratio* is

$$F(\beta):=\frac{\omega_o(\beta)}{\omega}=\sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}},\qquad \beta\in(-1,1),$$

the rational power being that of [[def-rational-power]].

(a) Let $S:=\Theta:=(-1,1)$, $\theta:=\mathrm{id}$, let $D(\beta)$ be the run description comprising the inertial charts $x$ and $x'$, the emitter's straight rest curve, the future null wave covector with frame-$x$ data $(\omega,e_1)$ and its affine phase, and the observer's rest vector $f_0$, and let $F$ be as displayed. Then $M:=(S,\Theta,\theta,D,F)$ is an operational model for the dimensionless ratio $\omega_o/\omega$ in the sense of clause (b) of [[def-sr-experiment-interface-vocabulary]]: condition $(*)$ holds with the prediction supplied by the cited Doppler theorem, and $d=1$. The map $F$ is strictly decreasing on $(-1,1)$, and for every real $r>0$ there is exactly one $\beta\in(-1,1)$ with $F(\beta)=r$, namely

$$\beta(r)=\frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2};$$

consequently $F$ is a strictly decreasing bijection of $(-1,1)$ onto $(0,\infty)$.

(b) Let $z\in(0,1]$ and $\varepsilon\in[0,z)$ be real, so that $0<z-\varepsilon\le z+\varepsilon$, and let $R$ be the declared one-point record with $N=1$, $z_1=z$, $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon$ and condition annotation "longitudinal Doppler ratio of the moving observer in the propagation direction" in the sense of clause (c) of the vocabulary. Then the set of parameters consistent with $R$ and $M$,

$$C(R,M):=\{\beta\in(-1,1):F(\beta)\in[z-\varepsilon,z+\varepsilon]\},$$

equals the closed interval $[\beta(z+\varepsilon),\beta(z-\varepsilon)]$; it is nonempty, and every element of it satisfies the declared bound of $R$. If $\varepsilon=0$, it is the singleton $\{\beta(z)\}$. If $\varepsilon>0$, its endpoints are strictly ordered and its exact positive length is

$$\beta(z-\varepsilon)-\beta(z+\varepsilon)=\frac{8z\varepsilon}{[1+(z-\varepsilon)^2][1+(z+\varepsilon)^2]}>0.$$

Thus the strict inequality between the record endpoints and the positive-length conclusion apply exactly when the declared uncertainty is positive.

(c) Illustrative instance (declared illustrative values, not a measurement report): $z=9/10$ and $\varepsilon=1/100$. Then $\beta(91/100)=1719/18281\approx0.094032$ and $\beta(89/100)=2079/17921\approx0.116009$, and $C(R,M)=[1719/18281,\ 2079/17921]$, an interval of exact length $7200000/327613801$ in $\beta$, whose endpoints satisfy $F(1719/18281)=91/100$ and $F(2079/17921)=89/100$.

(d) Scope. Every number in (c) is a declared illustrative value supplied to instantiate the vocabulary's clauses and their arithmetic; the example asserts no apparatus, no calibration correctness, no measurement, no sampling model, no statistical inference and no empirical support or refutation of the Doppler theorem or of any postulate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with its inertial chart $x$, a real number $\omega>0$, real numbers $z\in(0,1]$ and $\varepsilon\in[0,z)$, and the illustrative one-point record $R$ with $N=1$, $z_1=z$, $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon$ and annotation "longitudinal Doppler ratio of the moving observer in the propagation direction".

[F1] The experimental-interface vocabulary: an operational model is a tuple $M=(S,\Theta,\theta,D,F)$ with $S$ nonempty, $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ nonempty, $\theta:S\to\Theta$ surjective, $D$ assigning run descriptions and $F:\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ a prediction map whose components are required, by the declared interpretation $(*)$, to be numbers the framework assigns to $D(s)$ with every intermediate quantity, frame, event, sign and unit declared; a data record $R=(N,z,\varepsilon,a)$ declares that each value lies in the closed box $\prod_j[z_{k,j}-\varepsilon_{k,j},z_{k,j}+\varepsilon_{k,j}]$ in the declared units ([[def-sr-experiment-interface-vocabulary]]).

[F2] Doppler theorem clauses (i) and (ii): for inertial charts whose transition is $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ with $\beta\in\mathbb R^3$, $|\beta|<1$, the same future null wave covector $k$ with frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$ has frame-$x'$ data $(\omega',s')$ with $\omega'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\omega$, where $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$; and the rest observers of $x$ and $x'$, of four-velocities $c e_0$ and $c e'_0$, read the angular frequencies $\omega=-c k(e_0)$ and $\omega'=-c k(e'_0)$ ([[pthm-sr-null-wave-doppler-and-aberration]]).

[F3] Observer angular frequency and wave data: the observer of four-velocity $U_o=c n$, with $\eta(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ future, reads $\omega_n:=-c k(n)=-k(U_o)$ in the SI convention $x^0=ct$; a future null wave covector has frame components $k_a=(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3)$ with $\omega>0$ and $|s|=1$ ([[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]).

[F4] Frame-data lemma clauses (a),(b),(e): for a future null wave covector in a frame, $\varpi:=-k(e_0)>0$ and $|s|=1$; conversely, a covector whose frame components are $(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$ with $\varpi>0$ and $|s|=1$ is a future null wave covector ([[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]]).

[F5] Passive boost: for $\beta$ with $|\beta|<1$ the map $B(\beta)$ is defined in an inertial frame's coordinates by $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta\cdot x)$ and $x'=x+((\gamma-1)/|\beta|^2)(\beta\cdot x)\beta-\gamma\beta x^0$ for $\beta\neq0$, with $B(0)$ the identity, so that in the axis case $\beta=\beta e_1$ one has $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$, $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]]); it is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, $B(\beta)^{-1}=B(-\beta)$, and $B(\beta)e_0=\gamma(e_0-\beta_1 e_1-\beta_2 e_2-\beta_3 e_3)$ ([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]]).

[F6] Inertial frame and chart: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consists of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis of $V$ that is $\eta$-orthonormal, future and positively oriented; its chart is $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ with $E(u)=\sum_a u^a e_a$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[A1] Adopted ideal plane-wave model: an ideal monochromatic light wave in vacuum is modeled in any inertial chart by a dimensionless affine phase with future null wave covector, and an ideal observer of four-velocity $U_o=c n$ receiving this wave reads the frequency $\omega_n=-c k(n)$ ([[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]]).

[F7] SI conventions: in every inertial chart $x^0=ct$ with $c>0$ in metres per second, spatial coordinates in metres, and the matrix of $\eta$ equal to $\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ ([[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]).

[F8] Rational powers and their laws: $a^r:=(a^{1/n})^m$ for $a>0$ and $r=m/n$, and $(a^r)^s=a^{rs}$, $(ab)^r=a^r b^r$, $a^{r+s}=a^r a^s$, $a^r>0$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]).

[F9] Strict monotonicity in the base: for rational $r>0$ the map $a\mapsto a^r$ is strictly increasing on the positive reals ([[lem-rational-power-monotone]] claim 2); and in an ordered field, if $c>0$ then $a<b$ if and only if $ac<bc$ ([[lem-of-sign-rules]] claim 4).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $\omega>0$ and let $k$ be the covector whose frame-$x$ components are $(-\omega/c,\omega/c,0,0)$, so $\varpi=\omega/c>0$ and $s=e_1$ with $|s|=1$; by [F4] the covector $k$ is a future null wave covector with frame-$x$ data $(\omega,e_1)$; equip it with the affine phase $\theta(p):=k(p-o)$, whose differential is $k$. For each real $\beta\in(-1,1)$ put $x':=B(\beta e_1)\circ x$ and $f_a:=B(\beta e_1)^{-1}e_a$; by [F5] the map $B(\beta e_1)$ is proper orthochronous with inverse $B(-\beta e_1)$, and [F5] applied to $-\beta e_1$ gives that $B(-\beta e_1)$ also preserves $\eta$, the future cone and the orientation, so $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)=(B(-\beta e_1)e_0,\dots,B(-\beta e_1)e_3)$ is again $\eta$-orthonormal, future and positively oriented and $(o;f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ is an inertial frame by [F6], with chart $x'$ because $E_f=E\circ B(\beta e_1)^{-1}$ gives $E_f^{-1}(p-o)=x'(p)$. The transition is $x'=B(\beta e_1)x$ with parameter $\beta e_1$ of modulus $|\beta|<1$, so [F2] clause (i) with $s=e_1$ gives the frame-$x'$ data $(\omega',s')$ of the same covector $k$ with $\omega'=\gamma_\beta(1-\beta)\omega$ and $\gamma_\beta=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$, this being the reading of the rest observer of $x'$ by clause (ii); and $\gamma_\beta(1-\beta)=(1-\beta)^{1/2}(1+\beta)^{-1/2}=((1-\beta)/(1+\beta))^{1/2}$ by [F8], the positive square root. Hence the dimensionless ratio $F(\beta):=\omega'/\omega$ equals $((1-\beta)/(1+\beta))^{1/2}$ for every $\beta\in(-1,1)$. [construct, A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8]

1.2 The map $F$ is strictly decreasing on $(-1,1)$: for $-1<\beta_a<\beta_b<1$ the difference of the two radicands is $\frac{1-\beta_a}{1+\beta_a}-\frac{1-\beta_b}{1+\beta_b}=\frac{2(\beta_b-\beta_a)}{(1+\beta_a)(1+\beta_b)}>0$, since the numerator and both denominator factors are positive by [F9], and applying the strictly increasing map $u\mapsto u^{1/2}$ of [F9] to that positive difference gives $F(\beta_a)>F(\beta_b)$. [F8, F9, algebra]

1.3 For every real $r>0$ the equation $F(\beta)=r$ is equivalent to $\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}=r^2$, because $u\mapsto u^{1/2}$ is injective on positives and $(u^{1/2})^2=u$ by [F8]; solving, $\beta=\frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2}=:\beta(r)$, which lies in $(-1,1)$ because $1+\beta(r)=\frac{2}{1+r^2}>0$ and $1-\beta(r)=\frac{2r^2}{1+r^2}>0$; and $F(\beta(r))=r$ again by [F8]. Thus $F$ is a strictly decreasing bijection of $(-1,1)$ onto $(0,\infty)$ with inverse $\beta(\cdot)$, and $\beta(\cdot)$ is itself strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$. [F8, F9, algebra]

2.1 Let $S:=\Theta:=(-1,1)$, $\theta:=\mathrm{id}$, and let $D(\beta)$ comprise the frames $x$ and $x'$ with their charts, the real boost parameter $\beta$, the wave covector $k$ with its affine phase, the emitter's straight rest curve $\rho\mapsto o+\rho e_0$ and the observer vector $f_0$; then $M=(S,\Theta,\theta,D,F)$ with the map $F$ of step 1.1 is an operational model in the sense of [F1] with $d=1$, because each component of $F(\beta)$ is assigned to $D(\beta)$ by [F2] clause (i) under the adopted idealization [A1], with the frame, sign and unit conventions declared, so condition $(*)$ holds. This is the model claimed in part (a) of the Example. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

2.2 Since $F$ is strictly decreasing with inverse $\beta(\cdot)$ by steps 1.2 and 1.3, $F(\beta)\in[z-\varepsilon,z+\varepsilon]$ holds if and only if $\beta\in[\beta(z+\varepsilon),\beta(z-\varepsilon)]$; the set is nonempty because $z-\varepsilon>0$ puts $z\pm\varepsilon$ in the range $(0,\infty)$ of $F$, and every element of it satisfies the declared bound of the record $R$ because its prediction lies in the declared closed interval, so $C(R,M)=[\beta(z+\varepsilon),\beta(z-\varepsilon)]$ as claimed in part (b). For $\varepsilon=0$ the two endpoints run together and $C(R,M)=\{\beta(z)\}$ by step 1.3, the singleton claimed; for $\varepsilon>0$ we have $0<z-\varepsilon<z+\varepsilon$ and strict decrease of $\beta(\cdot)$ in step 1.3 gives the strict endpoint order $\beta(z-\varepsilon)>\beta(z+\varepsilon)$, with length $\beta(z-\varepsilon)-\beta(z+\varepsilon)=\frac{1-(z-\varepsilon)^2}{1+(z-\varepsilon)^2}-\frac{1-(z+\varepsilon)^2}{1+(z+\varepsilon)^2}=\frac{2(z+\varepsilon)^2-2(z-\varepsilon)^2}{[1+(z-\varepsilon)^2][1+(z+\varepsilon)^2]}=\frac{8z\varepsilon}{[1+(z-\varepsilon)^2][1+(z+\varepsilon)^2]}>0$, where the numerator identity is algebra and the final sign uses $z>0$, $\varepsilon>0$ and the positivity of the two denominator factors by [F9]. [F1, F8, F9, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 For the illustrative values $z=9/10$ and $\varepsilon=1/100$ we have $z+\varepsilon=91/100$ and $z-\varepsilon=89/100$, so by step 1.3 $\beta(91/100)=\frac{1-8281/10000}{1+8281/10000}=\frac{1719}{18281}$ and $\beta(89/100)=\frac{1-7921/10000}{1+7921/10000}=\frac{2079}{17921}$, both in $(-1,1)$, and $F(\beta(91/100))=91/100$, $F(\beta(89/100))=89/100$; the consistency set is $[1719/18281,2079/17921]$ by step 2.2, and its length is $\frac{8\cdot(9/10)\cdot(1/100)}{[1+7921/10000][1+8281/10000]}=\frac{7200000}{327613801}$ by step 2.2, using $17921\cdot18281=327613801$. ## Statement refuted

A declared one-point data record of the vocabulary with positive declared uncertainty determines the parameter of an operational model uniquely: if a record $R$ of clause (c) of [[def-sr-experiment-interface-vocabulary]] is consistent with two parameters $\beta_1,\beta_2$ of one operational model $M$, then $\beta_1=\beta_2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ with its inertial chart $x$, a real number $\omega>0$, and the illustrative record $R$ with $N=1$, $z_1=9/10$, $\varepsilon_1=1/100$ and annotation "longitudinal Doppler ratio of the moving observer in the propagation direction". These are declared illustrative values, not measurements.

[F1] The experimental-interface vocabulary: an operational model is a tuple $M=(S,\Theta,\theta,D,F)$ with $S$ nonempty, $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ nonempty, $\theta:S\to\Theta$ surjective, $D$ assigning run descriptions and $F:\Theta\to\mathbb R^d$ a prediction map whose components are required, by the declared interpretation $(*)$, to be numbers the framework assigns to $D(s)$ with every intermediate quantity, frame, event, sign and unit declared; a data record $R=(N,z,\varepsilon,a)$ declares that each value lies in the closed box $\prod_j[z_{k,j}-\varepsilon_{k,j},z_{k,j}+\varepsilon_{k,j}]$ in the declared units; and clause (f) makes a consistency or comparison claim between a record and a model a separate claim requiring an explicitly declared comparison rule ([[def-sr-experiment-interface-vocabulary]]).

[F2] Doppler theorem clauses (i) and (ii): for inertial charts whose transition is $x'=B(\beta)x+b$ with $\beta\in\mathbb R^3$, $|\beta|<1$, the same future null wave covector $k$ with frame-$x$ data $(\omega,s)$ has frame-$x'$ data $(\omega',s')$ with $\omega'=\gamma(1-\beta\cdot s)\omega$, where $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}$; and the rest observers of $x$ and $x'$, of four-velocities $c e_0$ and $c e'_0$, read the angular frequencies $\omega=-c k(e_0)$ and $\omega'=-c k(e'_0)$ ([[pthm-sr-null-wave-doppler-and-aberration]]).

[F3] Observer angular frequency and wave data: the observer of four-velocity $U_o=c n$, with $\eta(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ future, reads $\omega_n:=-c k(n)=-k(U_o)$ in the SI convention $x^0=ct$; a future null wave covector has frame components $k_a=(-\omega/c,(\omega/c)s_1,(\omega/c)s_2,(\omega/c)s_3)$ with $\omega>0$ and $|s|=1$ ([[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]).

[F4] Frame-data lemma clauses (a),(b),(e): for a future null wave covector in a frame, $\varpi:=-k(e_0)>0$ and $|s|=1$; conversely, a covector whose frame components are $(-\varpi,\varpi s_1,\varpi s_2,\varpi s_3)$ with $\varpi>0$ and $|s|=1$ is a future null wave covector ([[lem-sr-null-covector-frame-data]]).

[F5] Passive boost: for $\beta$ with $|\beta|<1$ the map $B(\beta)$ is defined in an inertial frame's coordinates by $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta\cdot x)$ and $x'=x+((\gamma-1)/|\beta|^2)(\beta\cdot x)\beta-\gamma\beta x^0$ for $\beta\neq0$, with $B(0)$ the identity, so that in the axis case $\beta=\beta e_1$ one has $x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$, $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]]); it is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, $B(\beta)^{-1}=B(-\beta)$, and $B(\beta)e_0=\gamma(e_0-\beta_1 e_1-\beta_2 e_2-\beta_3 e_3)$ ([[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]]).

[F6] Inertial frame and chart: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consists of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis of $V$ that is $\eta$-orthonormal, future and positively oriented; its chart is $x(p)=E^{-1}(p-o)$ with $E(u)=\sum_a u^a e_a$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]).

[A1] Adopted ideal plane-wave model: an ideal monochromatic light wave in vacuum is modeled in any inertial chart by a dimensionless affine phase with future null wave covector, and an ideal observer of four-velocity $U_o=c n$ receiving this wave reads the frequency $\omega_n=-c k(n)$ ([[post-sr-ideal-plane-wave-model]]).

[F7] SI conventions: in every inertial chart $x^0=ct$ with $c>0$ in metres per second, spatial coordinates in metres, and the matrix of $\eta$ equal to $\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ ([[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]).

[F8] Rational powers and their laws: $a^r:=(a^{1/n})^m$ for $a>0$ and $r=m/n$, and $(a^r)^s=a^{rs}$, $(ab)^r=a^r b^r$, $a^{r+s}=a^r a^s$, $a^r>0$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]).

[F9] Strict monotonicity in the base: for rational $r>0$ the map $a\mapsto a^r$ is strictly increasing on the positive reals ([[lem-rational-power-monotone]] claim 2); and in an ordered field, if $c>0$ then $a<b$ if and only if $ac<bc$ ([[lem-of-sign-rules]] claim 4).

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $\omega>0$ and let $k$ be the covector whose frame-$x$ components are $(-\omega/c,\omega/c,0,0)$, so $\varpi=\omega/c>0$ and $s=e_1$ with $|s|=1$; by [F4] the covector $k$ is a future null wave covector with frame-$x$ data $(\omega,e_1)$; equip it with the affine phase $\theta(p):=k(p-o)$, whose differential is $k$. For each real $\beta\in(-1,1)$ put $x':=B(\beta e_1)\circ x$ and $f_a:=B(\beta e_1)^{-1}e_a$; by [F5] the map $B(\beta e_1)$ is proper orthochronous with inverse $B(-\beta e_1)$, and [F5] applied to $-\beta e_1$ gives that $B(-\beta e_1)$ also preserves $\eta$, the future cone and the orientation, so the ordered basis $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)=(B(-\beta e_1)e_0,\dots,B(-\beta e_1)e_3)$ is again $\eta$-orthonormal, future and positively oriented and $(o;f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ is an inertial frame by [F6]; its chart is $x'$, because the frame isomorphism $E_f=E\circ B(\beta e_1)^{-1}$ gives $E_f^{-1}(p-o)=B(\beta e_1)(E^{-1}(p-o))=x'(p)$, and $f_0$ is future unit timelike. [construct, F4, F5, F6, F7]

1.2 The transition between the inertial charts $x$ and $x'$ is $x'=B(\beta e_1)x$ with parameter $\beta e_1$ of modulus $|\beta|<1$; [F2] clause (i) with $s=e_1$ therefore gives the frame-$x'$ data $(\omega',s')$ of the same covector $k$ with $\omega'=\gamma_\beta(1-\beta)\omega$, where $\gamma_\beta=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$; and $\gamma_\beta(1-\beta)=(1-\beta)^{1/2}(1+\beta)^{-1/2}=((1-\beta)/(1+\beta))^{1/2}$ by [F8], so the dimensionless ratio $F(\beta):=\omega'/\omega$ is the positive real number displayed. [F2, F8, algebra]

1.3 The map $F$ is strictly decreasing on $(-1,1)$: for $-1<\beta_a<\beta_b<1$ the difference of the two radicands is $\frac{1-\beta_a}{1+\beta_a}-\frac{1-\beta_b}{1+\beta_b}=\frac{2(\beta_b-\beta_a)}{(1+\beta_a)(1+\beta_b)}>0$, since the numerator and both denominator factors are positive by [F9], and applying the strictly increasing map $u\mapsto u^{1/2}$ of [F9] to that positive difference gives $F(\beta_a)>F(\beta_b)$. [F8, F9, algebra]

1.4 For every real $r>0$ the equation $F(\beta)=r$ is equivalent to $\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}=r^2$, because $u\mapsto u^{1/2}$ is injective on positives and $(u^{1/2})^2=u$ by [F8]; solving, $\beta=\frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2}=:\beta(r)$, which lies in $(-1,1)$ because $1+\beta(r)=\frac{2}{1+r^2}>0$ and $1-\beta(r)=\frac{2r^2}{1+r^2}>0$; and $F(\beta(r))=r$ again by [F8]. Thus $F$ is a strictly decreasing bijection of $(-1,1)$ onto $(0,\infty)$ with inverse $\beta(\cdot)$. [F8, F9, algebra]

2.1 Let $S:=\Theta:=(-1,1)$, $\theta:=\mathrm{id}$, and let $D(\beta)$ be the finite run description comprising the frames $x$ and $x'$ with their charts, the real boost parameter $\beta$, the wave covector $k$ with its affine phase, and the observer vector $f_0$; let $F$ be the map of step 1.2. Then $M=(S,\Theta,\theta,D,F)$ is an operational model in the sense of [F1] with $d=1$: each component of $F(\beta)$ is the rest-observer frequency ratio $F(\beta)=-c\,k(f_0)/\omega$ in the sense of [F3], assigned to $D(\beta)$ by clause (i) of [F2] under the adopted idealization [A1], with the frame, sign and unit conventions declared, so condition $(*)$ holds. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.2]

2.2 Declare the comparison rule that a parameter $\beta$ is consistent with the one-point record $R$ exactly when its prediction $F(\beta)$ lies in the record's declared closed interval $[z_1-\varepsilon_1,z_1+\varepsilon_1]$; by [F1] clause (f) such a rule must be declared separately, and this is the declared rule of the present algebraic reading. By strict decrease and the inverse of steps 1.3 and 1.4, the consistency set is $C(R,M)=\{\beta\in(-1,1):F(\beta)\in[z_1-\varepsilon_1,z_1+\varepsilon_1]\}=[\beta(z_1+\varepsilon_1),\beta(z_1-\varepsilon_1)]$, a nonempty closed interval. [F1, step 1.3, step 1.4]

3.1 With $z_1=9/10$ and $\varepsilon_1=1/100$ the declared interval is $[89/100,91/100]$, and the two distinct parameters $\beta_1:=\beta(91/100)=1719/18281$ and $\beta_2:=\beta(89/100)=2079/17921$ satisfy $F(\beta_1)=91/100$ and $F(\beta_2)=89/100$ by step 1.4, hence both lie in $C(R,M)$; they are distinct because $\beta_2-\beta_1=\frac{2079\cdot18281-1719\cdot17921}{17921\cdot18281}=\frac{7200000}{327613801}>0$, the denominator being positive and the numerator a positive integer difference. Since $R$ is a one-point data record of [F1] clause (c) with positive declared uncertainty, the uniqueness assertion of the Statement refuted is false: a declared bounded one-point record need not determine the parameter of an operational model. This is an algebraic consistency computation on declared illustrative values; it asserts no measurement, calibration, probability model, statistical inference or empirical conclusion about any model or postulate. [F1, F8, F9, step 1.4, algebra] ∎

          "quote": "Let $4:=\{0,1,2,3\}$ and let $V:=\mathbb R^4$ be the set of all functions
$4\to\mathbb R$, with the pointwise vector-space structure of
[[def-function-space]]; so $V$ is the function space $F^X$ of
[[def-function-space]] at $F=\mathbb R$ and $X=4$, and its elements are written
$v=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v^a:=v(a)$ for $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, the components
being indexed from $0$ and written with an upper index; the index conventions
used throughout this item are fixed below. Let $A$ be the same set
$\mathbb R^4$, whose elements are
now called **points**, together with the map

$$V\times A\to A,\qquad (v,p)\mapsto v+p,$$

given by pointwise addition of functions. Then the following three conditions
hold.

1. $(v+v')+p=v+(v'+p)$ for all $v,v'\in V$ and all $p\in A$.
2. $0+p=p$ for every $p\in A$.
3. For all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $v+p=q$, namely
$v=q-p$.

Conditions 1 and 2 are read at each of the four coordinates from the field
axioms of $\mathbb R$, and condition 3 holds because $q-p$ satisfies
$(q-p)+p=q$ coordinatewise while any $v$ with $v+p=q$ agrees with $q-p$ at every
coordinate ([[def-vector-space]]). A triple consisting of a set $A$, a vector
space $V$ and a map $V\times A\to A$ satisfying 1–3 is called an **affine
space** with **translation space** $V$; the three conditions are its definition,
so by 1–3 the set $A$ above is an affine space with translation space $V$.

For $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ let $e_a\in V$ be given by $e_a(b):=1$ for $b=a$ and
$e_a(b):=0$ for $b\ne a$. Then $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis of $V$
([[def-linear-basis]]): every $v\in V$ equals $v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$, because
the two sides have the same value at each $b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$; and if
$c^0e_0+\dots+c^3e_3=0_V$ then evaluating at $b$ gives $c^b=0$, so the list is
linearly independent. We write $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ and use the coordinate
columns of [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]] with respect to
this ordered basis.

**The Minkowski form.** Define

$$\eta(v,w):=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3,\qquad v,w\in V .$$

This is the standard bilinear form $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i<n}x_iy_i$ of
[[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]] with the sign of the first
coordinate reversed, together with the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the last three coordinates; directly from the
formula, for fixed $w$ the assignment $v\mapsto\eta(v,w)$ is a linear combination
of the component functions $v\mapsto v^a$, hence linear, and similarly in $w$,
so $\eta$ is a bilinear form, and $\eta(v,w)=\eta(w,v)$ for all $v,w$, so it is
symmetric ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Its matrix in
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is

$$(\eta(e_a,e_b))_{a,b}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1),$$

and this matrix is its own inverse, the product of
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with itself being the identity matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]); in particular it is invertible, so
$\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]).

**Index conventions.** The components $v^a$ of a vector are the numbers in its
expansion $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, and
for a linear map $T:V\to V$ one writes $(Tv)^a$ for the components of $Tv$ and
$T^a{}_b$ for the matrix entries, so that $(Tv)^a=\sum_bT^a{}_bv^b$. Write
$\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)$, so that
$(\eta_{ab})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let $(\eta^{ab})$ denote the
inverse matrix of $(\eta_{ab})$, that is, $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=1$ when
$a=c$ and $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=0$ when $a\ne c$. The **lowered** components
of $v$ are $v_a:=\sum_b\eta_{ab}v^b$, and the operation is inverted by
$v^a=\sum_b\eta^{ab}v_b$, because $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is its own
inverse; explicitly $v_0=-v^0$ and $v_i=v^i$ for $i=1,2,3$. In these
conventions $\eta(v,w)=\sum_{a,b}\eta_{ab}v^aw^b=\sum_av_aw^a$ for all
$v,w\in V$.

**Causal classification.** Let $v\in V$ with $v\ne0$. Then $v$ is
**timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$, and
**spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$. If the
nonzero $v$ is causal, then $v^0\ne0$: the inequality
$-(v^0)^2+(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2\le0$ gives
$(v^0)^2\ge(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2$, and $v^0=0$ would force
$(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=0$, hence $v^1=v^2=v^3=0$ and $v=0$, contrary to the
hypothesis. A nonzero causal $v$ is therefore **future-directed** when $v^0>0$
and **past-directed** when $v^0<0$, and exactly one of these two alternatives
holds for a nonzero real $v^0$ ([[def-real-order]]). The **future causal cone**
is

$$C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\},$$

whose elements are exactly the future-directed causal vectors; the zero vector
is not in $C^+$, because it fails $v^0>0$.

**Orientation.** The **standard orientation** of $V$ is the orientation class of
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

**Lorentz maps.** A **Lorentz map** is a linear map $L:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) that is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) and satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V .$$

Writing $M:=[L]_{(e_0,\dots,e_3)}\in M_4(\mathbb R)$ for the matrix of $L$ in the
ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), $M^{\mathsf T}$ for its
transpose ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]), and $\eta$ also for the matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the condition is the matrix identity

$$M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta .$$

Expanding $Lv$ and $Lw$ in the basis gives
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\sum_{c,d}(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}v^cw^d$, whereas
$\eta(v,w)=\sum_{c,d}\eta_{cd}v^cw^d$, and the two sides agree for all $v,w$
exactly when $(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}=\eta_{cd}$ for every $c,d$, since
inserting the basis vectors $v=e_c$, $w=e_d$ gives the converse
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Equivalently, the matrix of $\eta$
in the basis $(Le_0,\dots,Le_3)$ is again
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; this is the change-of-basis congruence of
[[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] for the basis change
from $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ to its image under the invertible map $L$. The
invertibility requirement in the definition of a Lorentz map is in fact
automatic: if $L$ satisfies the displayed identity and $Lv=0$, then
$\eta(v,w)=\eta(Lv,Lw)=0$ for every $w$, so $v$ lies in the left radical of

the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is

$$(\eta(e_a,e_b))_{a,b}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1),$$

and this matrix is its own inverse, the product of
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with itself being the identity matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]); in particular it is invertible, so
$\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]).

**Index conventions.** The components $v^a$ of a vector are the numbers in its
expansion $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, and
for a linear map $T:V\to V$ one writes $(Tv)^a$ for the components of $Tv$ and
$T^a{}_b$ for the matrix entries, so that $(Tv)^a=\sum_bT^a{}_bv^b$. Write
$\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)$, so that
$(\eta_{ab})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let $(\eta^{ab})$ denote the
inverse matrix of $(\eta_{ab})$, that is, $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=1$ when
$a=c$ and $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=0$ when $a\ne c$. The **lowered** components
of $v$ are $v_a:=\sum_b\eta_{ab}v^b$, and the operation is inverted by
$v^a=\sum_b\eta^{ab}v_b$, because $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is its own
inverse; explicitly $v_0=-v^0$ and $v_i=v^i$ for $i=1,2,3$. In these
conventions $\eta(v,w)=\sum_{a,b}\eta_{ab}v^aw^b=\sum_av_aw^a$ for all

**timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$, and
**spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$. If the
nonzero $v$ is causal, then $v^0\ne0$: the inequality
$-(v^0)^2+(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2\le0$ gives
$(v^0)^2\ge(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2$, and $v^0=0$ would force
$(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=0$, hence $v^1=v^2=v^3=0$ and $v=0$, contrary to the
hypothesis. A nonzero causal $v$ is therefore **future-directed** when $v^0>0$
and **past-directed** when $v^0<0$, and exactly one of these two alternatives
holds for a nonzero real $v^0$ ([[def-real-order]]). The **future causal cone**
is

$$C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\},$$

whose elements are exactly the future-directed causal vectors; the zero vector
is not in $C^+$, because it fails $v^0>0$.

the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

**Lorentz maps.** A **Lorentz map** is a linear map $L:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) that is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) and satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V .$$

Writing $M:=[L]_{(e_0,\dots,e_3)}\in M_4(\mathbb R)$ for the matrix of $L$ in the
ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), $M^{\mathsf T}$ for its
transpose ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]), and $\eta$ also for the matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the condition is the matrix identity

$$M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta .$$

Expanding $Lv$ and $Lw$ in the basis gives
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\sum_{c,d}(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}v^cw^d$, whereas
$\eta(v,w)=\sum_{c,d}\eta_{cd}v^cw^d$, and the two sides agree for all $v,w$
exactly when $(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}=\eta_{cd}$ for every $c,d$, since
inserting the basis vectors $v=e_c$, $w=e_d$ gives the converse
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Equivalently, the matrix of $\eta$
in the basis $(Le_0,\dots,Le_3)$ is again
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; this is the change-of-basis congruence of
[[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] for the basis change
from $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ to its image under the invertible map $L$. The
invertibility requirement in the definition of a Lorentz map is in fact
automatic: if $L$ satisfies the displayed identity and $Lv=0$, then
$\eta(v,w)=\eta(Lv,Lw)=0$ for every $w$, so $v$ lies in the left radical of
$\eta$, which is $\{0\}$ because $\eta$ is nondegenerate; thus $L$ is injective,
and an injective linear endomorphism of the four-dimensional space $V$ is
surjective by [[thm-rank-nullity]] together with
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], so $L$ is a bijection, and its inverse

$S(ax+by)=aS(x)+bS(y)$; thus $L$ is invertible

**proper** when $\det L=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** when $L(C^+)=C^+$.

**Frames.** A **frame** of $A$ is a point $o\in A$ together with an ordered
basis $(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ such that
$\eta(u_a,u_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ and
$u_0\in C^+$. The **coordinates** of $p\in A$ in that frame are the unique
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^4$ with
$p=o+x^0u_0+x^1u_1+x^2u_2+x^3u_3$; uniqueness holds because
$(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ is an ordered basis, and $p-o$ is the unique element of $V$
carrying $o$ to $p$.

**Tensors and components.** A **tensor of type $(p,q)$** on $V$ is a multilinear
map $(V^*)^p\times V^q\to\mathbb R$
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]), not an array: covectors are the
$(0,1)$ case, a vector $v$ is regarded as the $(1,0)$ tensor
$\theta\mapsto\theta(v)$ through the canonical evaluation of $V$ in its double
dual, and two-forms are the skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ case. Under the coordinate
change $x'=Lx$ of the frame by a Lorentz map
$L$ — that is, when the coordinates of the same point in a new frame are
$x'=Lx$ with the origin unchanged, so that the new basis vectors are
$L^{-1}u_a$ — the components of a vector $v$, a covector $\theta$ and a two-form
$F$ satisfy

$$v'=Lv,\qquad \theta'=(L^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\theta,\qquad F'(v,w)=F(L^{-1}v,L^{-1}w),$$

where $(L^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$ is the transpose map of
[[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]] applied to $\theta$; these are the component
readings of the displacement law $v'=Lv$, of $\theta'=\theta\circ L^{-1}$ for a
covector, and of $F'=F\circ(L^{-1}\times L^{-1})$ for a two-form. The basis
$(L^{-1}u_0,\dots,L^{-1}u_3)$ is again a frame whenever $L$ is orthochronous.

Finally, a fixed positive real $c$ is separate extra structure: the coordinate
$x^0$ has the dimension of length, and the time coordinate is $t:=x^0/c$. No
physical claim is made here; in particular the identification of $A$ with
physical spacetime, of $C^+$ with the future light cone, and of $c$ with the
speed of light in vacuum are later physical premises.

$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

          "quote": "Let $4:=\{0,1,2,3\}$ and let $V:=\mathbb R^4$ be the set of all functions
$4\to\mathbb R$, with the pointwise vector-space structure of
[[def-function-space]]; so $V$ is the function space $F^X$ of
[[def-function-space]] at $F=\mathbb R$ and $X=4$, and its elements are written
$v=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v^a:=v(a)$ for $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, the components
being indexed from $0$ and written with an upper index; the index conventions
used throughout this item are fixed below. Let $A$ be the same set
$\mathbb R^4$, whose elements are
now called **points**, together with the map

$$V\times A\to A,\qquad (v,p)\mapsto v+p,$$

given by pointwise addition of functions. Then the following three conditions
hold.

1. $(v+v')+p=v+(v'+p)$ for all $v,v'\in V$ and all $p\in A$.
2. $0+p=p$ for every $p\in A$.
3. For all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $v+p=q$, namely
$v=q-p$.

Conditions 1 and 2 are read at each of the four coordinates from the field
axioms of $\mathbb R$, and condition 3 holds because $q-p$ satisfies
$(q-p)+p=q$ coordinatewise while any $v$ with $v+p=q$ agrees with $q-p$ at every
coordinate ([[def-vector-space]]). A triple consisting of a set $A$, a vector
space $V$ and a map $V\times A\to A$ satisfying 1–3 is called an **affine
space** with **translation space** $V$; the three conditions are its definition,
so by 1–3 the set $A$ above is an affine space with translation space $V$.

For $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ let $e_a\in V$ be given by $e_a(b):=1$ for $b=a$ and
$e_a(b):=0$ for $b\ne a$. Then $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis of $V$
([[def-linear-basis]]): every $v\in V$ equals $v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$, because
the two sides have the same value at each $b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$; and if
$c^0e_0+\dots+c^3e_3=0_V$ then evaluating at $b$ gives $c^b=0$, so the list is
linearly independent. We write $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ and use the coordinate
columns of [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]] with respect to
this ordered basis.

**The Minkowski form.** Define

$$\eta(v,w):=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3,\qquad v,w\in V .$$

This is the standard bilinear form $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i<n}x_iy_i$ of
[[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]] with the sign of the first
coordinate reversed, together with the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the last three coordinates; directly from the
formula, for fixed $w$ the assignment $v\mapsto\eta(v,w)$ is a linear combination
of the component functions $v\mapsto v^a$, hence linear, and similarly in $w$,
so $\eta$ is a bilinear form, and $\eta(v,w)=\eta(w,v)$ for all $v,w$, so it is
symmetric ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Its matrix in
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is

$$(\eta(e_a,e_b))_{a,b}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1),$$

and this matrix is its own inverse, the product of
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with itself being the identity matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]); in particular it is invertible, so
$\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]).

**Index conventions.** The components $v^a$ of a vector are the numbers in its
expansion $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, and
for a linear map $T:V\to V$ one writes $(Tv)^a$ for the components of $Tv$ and
$T^a{}_b$ for the matrix entries, so that $(Tv)^a=\sum_bT^a{}_bv^b$. Write
$\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)$, so that
$(\eta_{ab})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let $(\eta^{ab})$ denote the
inverse matrix of $(\eta_{ab})$, that is, $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=1$ when
$a=c$ and $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=0$ when $a\ne c$. The **lowered** components
of $v$ are $v_a:=\sum_b\eta_{ab}v^b$, and the operation is inverted by
$v^a=\sum_b\eta^{ab}v_b$, because $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is its own
inverse; explicitly $v_0=-v^0$ and $v_i=v^i$ for $i=1,2,3$. In these
conventions $\eta(v,w)=\sum_{a,b}\eta_{ab}v^aw^b=\sum_av_aw^a$ for all
$v,w\in V$.

**Causal classification.** Let $v\in V$ with $v\ne0$. Then $v$ is
**timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$, and
**spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$. If the
nonzero $v$ is causal, then $v^0\ne0$: the inequality
$-(v^0)^2+(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2\le0$ gives
$(v^0)^2\ge(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2$, and $v^0=0$ would force
$(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=0$, hence $v^1=v^2=v^3=0$ and $v=0$, contrary to the
hypothesis. A nonzero causal $v$ is therefore **future-directed** when $v^0>0$
and **past-directed** when $v^0<0$, and exactly one of these two alternatives
holds for a nonzero real $v^0$ ([[def-real-order]]). The **future causal cone**
is

$$C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\},$$

whose elements are exactly the future-directed causal vectors; the zero vector
is not in $C^+$, because it fails $v^0>0$.

**Orientation.** The **standard orientation** of $V$ is the orientation class of
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

**Lorentz maps.** A **Lorentz map** is a linear map $L:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) that is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) and satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V .$$

Writing $M:=[L]_{(e_0,\dots,e_3)}\in M_4(\mathbb R)$ for the matrix of $L$ in the
ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), $M^{\mathsf T}$ for its
transpose ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]), and $\eta$ also for the matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the condition is the matrix identity

$$M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta .$$

Expanding $Lv$ and $Lw$ in the basis gives
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\sum_{c,d}(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}v^cw^d$, whereas
$\eta(v,w)=\sum_{c,d}\eta_{cd}v^cw^d$, and the two sides agree for all $v,w$
exactly when $(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}=\eta_{cd}$ for every $c,d$, since
inserting the basis vectors $v=e_c$, $w=e_d$ gives the converse
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Equivalently, the matrix of $\eta$
in the basis $(Le_0,\dots,Le_3)$ is again
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; this is the change-of-basis congruence of
[[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] for the basis change
from $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ to its image under the invertible map $L$. The
invertibility requirement in the definition of a Lorentz map is in fact
automatic: if $L$ satisfies the displayed identity and $Lv=0$, then
$\eta(v,w)=\eta(Lv,Lw)=0$ for every $w$, so $v$ lies in the left radical of
$\eta$, which is $\{0\}$ because $\eta$ is nondegenerate; thus $L$ is injective,
and an injective linear endomorphism of the four-dimensional space $V$ is
surjective by [[thm-rank-nullity]] together with
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], so $L$ is a bijection, and its inverse
$S:=L^{-1}$ is linear: for all $x,y\in V$ and all reals $a,b$, linearity of $L$
gives $L(aS(x)+bS(y))=ax+by$, and applying $S$ gives
$S(ax+by)=aS(x)+bS(y)$; thus $L$ is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]). The map $L$ is
**proper** when $\det L=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** when $L(C^+)=C^+$.

**Frames.** A **frame** of $A$ is a point $o\in A$ together with an ordered
basis $(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ such that
$\eta(u_a,u_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ and
$u_0\in C^+$. The **coordinates** of $p\in A$ in that frame are the unique
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^4$ with
$p=o+x^0u_0+x^1u_1+x^2u_2+x^3u_3$; uniqueness holds because
$(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ is an ordered basis, and $p-o$ is the unique element of $V$
carrying $o$ to $p$.

**Tensors and components.** A **tensor of type $(p,q)$** on $V$ is a multilinear
map $(V^*)^p\times V^q\to\mathbb R$
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]), not an array: covectors are the
$(0,1)$ case, a vector $v$ is regarded as the $(1,0)$ tensor
$\theta\mapsto\theta(v)$ through the canonical evaluation of $V$ in its double
dual, and two-forms are the skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ case. Under the coordinate
change $x'=Lx$ of the frame by a Lorentz map
$L$ — that is, when the coordinates of the same point in a new frame are
$x'=Lx$ with the origin unchanged, so that the new basis vectors are
$L^{-1}u_a$ — the components of a vector $v$, a covector $\theta$ and a two-form
$F$ satisfy

$$v'=Lv,\qquad \theta'=(L^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\theta,\qquad F'(v,w)=F(L^{-1}v,L^{-1}w),$$

where $(L^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$ is the transpose map of
[[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]] applied to $\theta$; these are the component
readings of the displacement law $v'=Lv$, of $\theta'=\theta\circ L^{-1}$ for a
covector, and of $F'=F\circ(L^{-1}\times L^{-1})$ for a two-form. The basis
$(L^{-1}u_0,\dots,L^{-1}u_3)$ is again a frame whenever $L$ is orthochronous.

Finally, a fixed positive real $c$ is separate extra structure: the coordinate
$x^0$ has the dimension of length, and the time coordinate is $t:=x^0/c$. No
physical claim is made here; in particular the identification of $A$ with
physical spacetime, of $C^+$ with the future light cone, and of $c$ with the
speed of light in vacuum are later physical premises.

          "quote": "Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable

at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read

published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

          "quote": "Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,

          "source": "def-compact-space",
          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is a family
  $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ of open sets with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$,
  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$
  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], and no item of this library may use
the ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading makes
compactness a property of the topological space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ alone.
Hence it is preserved when $A$ is embedded homeomorphically as a subspace, or
when another ambient space induces the same topology on $A$; it need not be
preserved if the induced topology changes. This is exactly the convention already fixed for
metric spaces by [[def-metric-compactness]], and the agreement of that
definition with this one is [[thm-compactness-agrees-with-metric-compactness]].

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. Every
space listed as $\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ is compact too: given a cover, each $x_i$
lies in some member, and finitely many members named in this way already cover.
So every finite space is compact, whatever its topology, and in particular the
discrete topology on a finite set is compact while the discrete topology on an
infinite set is not ([[def-standard-topologies]]).

**The finiteness convention.** "Finite" above is the listing form. It agrees with
the definition of finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number
([[def-countable]]), in both directions, and the agreement is the one already
discharged in [[def-metric-compactness]]: a nonempty set equinumerous with
$m \ge 1$ is listable, and a set listed as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$ injects into
$\sigma(n)$ by sending $x$ to the least $i \le n$ with $a_i = x$. Neither
direction uses a choice principle; the second selects nothing, taking a least
index instead.

**Quasicompact is not used here.** Some authors, following Bourbaki, reserve
*compact* for a space that is both compact in the above sense and Hausdorff, and
call the open-cover condition alone *quasicompact*. This library follows the more
widely adopted convention: **compact** means the open-cover condition and nothing
more, and a Hausdorff hypothesis is always written out. The fork is recorded in
[[rem-compactness-conventions-and-choice-ledger]].",

          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

- A **separation** of $X$ is an ordered pair $(U, V)$ of **open**, **nonempty**,
  **disjoint** subsets of $X$ with $U \cup V = X$.
- $X$ is **disconnected** when a separation of $X$ exists, and **connected** when
  none does.
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **connected subset** of $X$ when the space
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is connected, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the subspace topology
  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). "Disconnected subset" is read the same way.

Since $U$ and $V$ are complementary in $X$, each of them is closed as well as
open; so a separation is the same thing as a partition of $X$ into two nonempty
clopen pieces ([[def-topological-space]]). The **clopen** subsets of $X$ are
those that are both open and closed, and $\varnothing$ and $X$ are always among
them.

Neither admits a separation: a separation requires two nonempty disjoint sets
whose union is the whole space, and neither $\varnothing$ nor a singleton can be
written as such a union. So both are connected under the definition above,
without any special clause. **This is a live convention fork** and the competing
choice is recorded in [[rem-connectedness-conventions]]; nothing on this page
depends on which is taken except the reading of the word "connected" applied to

above mentions only $(X,\mathcal{T})$. When it is applied to $A \subseteq X$ it
is applied to the space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$, so it does not change if $A$ is
regarded as a subspace of some other space inducing the same topology on $A$; in
particular a subset of $A$ is connected as a subset of $A$ exactly when it is
connected as a subset of $X$, by transitivity of the subspace topology

**Spelled out for a subset.** $A \subseteq X$ is disconnected exactly when there

**Separated sets.** Two subsets $A_1, A_2 \subseteq X$ are **separated in $X$**
when

$$\overline{A_1} \cap A_2 = \varnothing \qquad \text{and} \qquad A_1 \cap \overline{A_2} = \varnothing,$$

Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.",

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. This is the same convention [[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]]
records for metrics.

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.",

$\Omega$ with the preimage of $\Omega$ under the homeomorphism
$x\mapsto x+he_i$. The **$i$-th difference quotient of $u$ of size $h$** is
$$\delta_h^iu(x):=\frac{u(x+he_i)-u(x)}{h},\qquad x\in\Omega_{i,h},$$
read on the almost-everywhere classes
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]); the
**difference-quotient vector** is
$$\delta_hu:=(\delta_h^1u,\dots,\delta_h^nu),$$
defined on the open intersection $\Omega_h:=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\Omega_{i,h}$,
while each component is defined on its own shrunken set $\Omega_{i,h}$.

Throughout this page the translation notation is the published one of
[[def-translation-of-a-function-on-rn]], namely
$\tau_hu(x)=u(x-h)$; consequently the forward shift that occurs in the
product rule is the translate by $-he_i$:
$$u(x+he_i)=(\tau_{-he_i}u)(x),\qquad \delta_h^iu=\frac{\tau_{-he_i}u-u}{h}\quad\text{on }\Omega_{i,h}.$$

For the open upper half-space
$H=\{x_n>0\}$ and a **tangential**
index $j<n$, the translation $x\mapsto x+he_j$ maps $H$ onto $H$; hence
$\delta_h^ju$ is defined on all of $H$. For the **normal** index $n$ and
$h>0$ one has $H_{n,h}=H$ (since $x_n>0$ implies $x_n+h>0$), while for
$h<0$ one has $H_{n,h}=\{x\in H:x_n>|h|\}$, a proper subset of $H$.

**Well-definedness.** Both values $u(x)$ and $u(x+he_i)$ in the numerator are
defined for every $x\in\Omega_{i,h}$, and
$$|\delta_h^iu(x)|\le\frac{|u(x+he_i)|+|u(x)|}{|h|},$$
so $\delta_h^iu\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega_{i,h};\mathbb K)$: on a compact
$K\Subset\Omega_{i,h}$ the first term is controlled by
$\int_K|u(x+he_i)|\,dx=\int_{K+he_i}|u(y)|\,dy<\infty$, because
$K+he_i$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$, and the second term is controlled
on $K\Subset\Omega$. Further, the definition depends only on the class of
$u$: if $u=\widetilde u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $E\subseteq\Omega$
is a null set with $u=\widetilde u$ on $\Omega\setminus E$, then
$\delta_h^iu\ne\delta_h^i\widetilde u$ only at points of
$(\Omega_{i,h}\cap E)\cup(\Omega_{i,h}\cap(E-he_i))$, a null set because
$E$ is null and $E-he_i$ is null by the choice-free translation invariance of
Lebesgue measure
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Two warnings, part of the definition.** First, a difference quotient is
defined on the shrunken set $\Omega_{i,h}$ inside $\Omega$, which may equal
$\Omega$ when the shift preserves it; in particular it may be undefined on a strip of width $|h|$
along the boundary, so no estimate below differentiates a Sobolev class
across the boundary. Second, extending a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ by zero
does not enlarge the domain of its difference quotient: the quotient of the
extension agrees with $\delta_h^iu$ on $\Omega_{i,h}$, while values outside
$\Omega_{i,h}$ use points not both in $\Omega$ and are not values of the
original quotient. In the upper half-space, $\Omega_{n,h}=H$ for $h>0$,
whereas $\Omega_{n,h}=\{x\in H:x_n>|h|\}$ for $h<0$. This is why every
boundary argument on this page uses only
tangential quotients of compactly supported localisations, for which the
shrunken domain is the whole half-space and no extension across
$\partial\Omega$ is invoked.",

          "source_section": "Statement",
          "quote": "Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$,

$\Omega_{i,-h}=\{x\in\Omega:x-he_i\in\Omega\}$
([[def-first-difference-quotient]]), so that
$\Omega_{i,-h}=\Omega_{i,h}+he_i$. Then:

(i) **Integration by parts, two-domain form.** Whenever the displayed
integrals converge absolutely,
$$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx+\frac1h\Big(\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}uv\,dx-\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}uv\,dx\Big).$$
Consequently, if
$$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}uv\,dx=\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}uv\,dx,$$
in particular if $uv$ vanishes almost everywhere outside

$\Omega$ and $|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}(uv),\partial\Omega)$
— or if $\Omega_{i,h}=\Omega_{i,-h}$, then
$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx.$$

$$\delta_h^i(uv)=\big(\tau_{-he_i}u\big)\,\delta_h^iv+\big(\delta_h^iu\big)\,v=u\,\delta_h^iv+\big(\delta_h^iu\big)\big(\tau_{-he_i}v\big),$$

          "quote": "Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.

> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],

a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is

[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed

          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.",

          "quote": "An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ consisting of the following four pieces of data.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by

[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.",
