          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $I$ be an order-convex subset of
$\mathbb{R}$ with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]); a **curve** of the
model is a map $x : I \to A$.

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Convergence in $V$ is understood through
an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

If $x_A : A \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is the global chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

### Causal character

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike
worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s \mapsto x(-s)$, which
is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by
an explicit formula.",

          "quote": "Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]).

  where $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.

  that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \varnothing$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,\mathcal{T})$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite
  subcover: for every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \varnothing$ and the
  empty subfamily covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the subspace
  $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact topological space, $\mathcal{T}_A$ being the
  subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ and its own open
sets, not about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do
agree, but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is

2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical natural $\iota(n) \in \mathbb{R}$ ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$

          "quote": "Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$,

$\Omega_{i,-h}=\{x\in\Omega:x-he_i\in\Omega\}$
([[def-first-difference-quotient]]), so that
$\Omega_{i,-h}=\Omega_{i,h}+he_i$. Then:

(i) **Integration by parts, two-domain form.** Whenever the displayed
integrals converge absolutely,
$$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx+\frac1h\Big(\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}uv\,dx-\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}uv\,dx\Big).$$
Consequently, if
$$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}uv\,dx=\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}uv\,dx,$$
in particular if $uv$ vanishes almost everywhere outside
$\Omega_{i,h}\cap\Omega_{i,-h}$ — for instance when $uv$ has compact support in
$\Omega$ and $|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}(uv),\partial\Omega)$
— or if $\Omega_{i,h}=\Omega_{i,-h}$, then
$\int_{\Omega_{i,h}}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\Omega_{i,-h}}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx$,
with the integrals taken over their respective shrunken sets. For $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$
and $u\in L^p(\Omega)$, $v\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ with $1\le p\le\infty$ and
$p'$ the Hölder conjugate exponent of [[def-conjugate-exponents]]
($1/p+1/p'=1$), both sides are absolutely convergent and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\delta_h^iu\,v\,dx=-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\delta_{-h}^iv\,dx.$$

(ii) **Product rule.** If $uv\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, then a.e. on
$\Omega_{i,h}$,
$$\delta_h^i(uv)=\big(\tau_{-he_i}u\big)\,\delta_h^iv+\big(\delta_h^iu\big)\,v=u\,\delta_h^iv+\big(\delta_h^iu\big)\big(\tau_{-he_i}v\big),$$

          "quote": "Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this

$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$

the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided

$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$

$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the

$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,

$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives

have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary

        "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$), inherited from the surface-integral conventions used by [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]].\n\n(i) (Causality without passivity.)         "statement": "Let $c>0$ and let $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3\\times\\mathbb R$ be open. For such a pair with $k\\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are $$E(\\varphi,A):=-\\nabla\\varphi-\\partial_tA,\\qquad B(\\varphi,A):=\\operatorname{curl}A,$$ where $\\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and $\\operatorname{curl}$ and $\\operatorname{div}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]; both $E(\\varphi,A)$ and $B(\\varphi,A)$ are maps $\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$. For $k\\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function $$G(\\varphi,A):=\\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\\partial_t\\varphi,$$ also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\\Omega$ when $G(\\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\\Omega$. For $k\\ge2$ and a $C^k$ function $\\chi:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$ (a **gauge function**) the **gauge transform** of the pair is $$T_{\\chi}(\\varphi,A):=(\\varphi-\\partial_t\\chi,\\ A+\\nabla\\chi),$$ again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$. ## Definition

Fix a vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, a parameter $\omega>0$ and amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Here $\mathbb C^3$ is the set of functions $\{0,1,2\}\to\mathbb C$ under componentwise operations, the complex analogue of the convention for $\mathbb R^n$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; we write the coordinates of $\mathbf e$ as $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and those of $\mathbf b$ as $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. For $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], the real number $\sum_{j<3}k_jx_j$; for $t\in\mathbb R$ put

$$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. The exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), which is what makes the encoded expressions differentiable in the plane-wave form; derivations that differentiate them use [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and the chain rule for holomorphic maps where they are applied.

Complex notation here is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. No electromagnetic interpretation, equation of motion or physical identification is part of this definition.

## Definition

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty finite elementary Green region in the sense of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], written as $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N$ with its supplied decomposition into elementary Green regions of pairwise disjoint interiors and with the shared-arc structure of that definition, and let $\partial D$ be its positive boundary chain ([[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]]). We require in addition that $D$ be Jordan measurable; this is explained below and holds for every finite elementary Green region. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let

$$r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$$

be a map that extends to a $C^2$ map ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on an open neighbourhood of $D\times I\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Write $p=(u,v)$ for the parameter point, write $r_u(p,t),r_v(p,t),r_t(p,t)\in\mathbb R^3$ for the partial derivatives of that $C^2$ extension at $(p,t)$, and require

$$r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\ne0\qquad\text{for every }(p,t)\in D^\circ\times I^\circ,$$

the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. For every $t\in I^\circ$ the slice $r(\cdot,\cdot,t)$ is therefore a regular parametrized patch over $D$ in the sense of [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]; at an endpoint of a nondegenerate interval $I$, and when $I$ is a singleton, the condition is vacuous and no regularity of that slice is asserted.

The **swept set** of the family is

$$S:=\bigcup_{t\in I}r(D\times\{t\})\subseteq\mathbb R^3 .$$

A **velocity field for $r$** is a pair $(W,v)$ consisting of an open set $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $S\subseteq W$ and a map $v:W\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$ such that

$$v\bigl(r(p,t),t\bigr)=r_t(p,t)\qquad\text{for every }(p,t)\in D\times I .$$

Such a pair is required to exist: the standing hypothesis of this definition is that a velocity field for $r$ is given, and $v$ denotes it. The equality above is what single-valuedness means here: whenever two parameter points map to the same spatial point, the corresponding time derivatives agree, so that $v$ is a well-defined function on the swept set.

Finally let $B:V\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ field on an open set $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ containing $S$. The **flux of $B$ through the patch at time $t\in I$** is

$$\Phi(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B\bigl(r(p,t),t\bigr),\,r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dv,$$

the integral being the Riemann integral over the compact Jordan measurable set $D$ of the displayed continuous integrand, and the pairing being the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For fixed $t$, $\Phi(t)$ is the flux of $B(\cdot,t)$ through the regular patch $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t))$ in the orientation induced by the parametrization ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]), with $r_u\times r_v$ the oriented area vector in place of the unit normal.

If the family is intended to describe an actual material sheet, one requires in addition that $r(\cdot,\cdot,t):D\to\mathbb R^3$ be injective for every $t\in I$, so that each spatial slice is an embedded sheet; this condition is not part of the standing hypotheses and is not used by the flux formula above.

### Well-definedness and conventions

*Jordan measurability of $D$.* Each piece $D_i$ is compact and Jordan measurable ([[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]]), so its boundary has content zero ([[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]); the boundary $\partial D$ is contained in the finite union of the $\partial D_i$ together with the shared arcs and endpoints, a null set ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]); being a compact null set, this union has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $\partial D$ has content zero and the bounded set $D$ is Jordan measurable ([[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]). Finite additivity of Jordan content over the pieces is the statement of [[cor-jordan-content-finite-additivity]].

*Extension independence of the spatial partials, and of $r_t$ for nondegenerate $I$.* If $r$ has two $C^2$ extensions $\tilde r_1,\tilde r_2$ to open neighbourhoods of $D\times I$, then they agree on $D\times I$. For the spatial partials, fix $(p,t)\in D\times I$: if $p\in D^\circ$ then for small $h$ the points $(p+h e_u,t)$ and $(p+h e_v,t)$ lie in $D\times I$, so the difference quotients agree and $\partial_u\tilde r_1(p,t)=\partial_u\tilde r_2(p,t)$, likewise for $\partial_v$; if $p\in\partial D$, choose $p_n\in D^\circ$ with $p_n\to p$, observe $\partial_u\tilde r_1(p_n,t)=\partial_u\tilde r_2(p_n,t)$ for every $n$, and pass to the limit using continuity of both first partials on a common neighbourhood. Hence $r_u$ and $r_v$ on $D\times I$ are determined by $r$ alone in every case. For $r_t$, the same limit argument with points $(p_n,t_n)$, $p_n\in D^\circ$, $t_n\in I^\circ$, $t_n\to t$, determines $r_t$ by $r$ alone whenever $t$ is a limit of interior points of $I$, that is, whenever $I$ is nondegenerate. If $I=\{t_0\}$ is a singleton, then $I^\circ=\varnothing$ and $r_t$ may genuinely depend on the extension: the zero map on $D\times\{t_0\}$ has the two $C^2$ extensions $0$ and $(t-t_0)\chi(p)$ with $\chi$ any smooth function, whose time derivatives at $t_0$ differ. The integrand below involves only $r_u\times r_v$, so it is unambiguous in every case.

*Integrability.* For fixed $t\in I$, the map $p\mapsto B(r(p,t),t)$ is continuous on $D$ as a composition of continuous maps, the maps $p\mapsto r_u(p,t)$ and $p\mapsto r_v(p,t)$ are continuous on $D$, and the cross product and inner product are continuous bilinear operations; hence the integrand is continuous on the compact set $D$. A continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set is Riemann integrable over it ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]), so $\Phi(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$.

*Degenerate time domains.* If $I$ is empty then $D\times I$ is empty, the family is vacuous and no flux value is asserted. If $I=\{t_0\}$ is a singleton, the compatibility condition still reads $v(r(p,t_0),t_0)=r_t(p,t_0)$, but it can always be met: choosing the extension $\tilde r(p,t):=r(p,t_0)$, which is constant in the time variable, gives $r_t\equiv0$ and admits the compatible $C^1$ velocity field $v\equiv0$. With a different extension the compatible velocity field is correspondingly different; as explained above, $r_t(p,t_0)$ is not determined by $r$ alone in this case. The flux $\Phi(t_0)$ involves only $r_u\times r_v$, so it is the flux of the fixed patch $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t_0))$ and does not depend on that choice. The condition $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ is imposed only on $D^\circ\times I^\circ$, so rank failures on the boundary of the parameter region (seams) are permitted exactly as in [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], and at an endpoint time of a nondegenerate $I$ the definition asserts no regularity of the slice.

*No physical assertion.* This is a definition of a mathematical object: a regular time-dependent parametrized patch, a velocity field compatible with it, and the flux integral. It asserts nothing about electromagnetic fields, about which vector fields occur in nature, or about the derivative of $\Phi$; the transport identity for $\Phi'$ is proved separately.

## Definition

Throughout, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and the domains of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] are developed under that convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Now $F$ is continuous on the open set $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$; for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ the set $K\setminus S$ is compact, so $|F|$ is bounded on $K\setminus S$ and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le\sup_{K\setminus S}\lVert F\rVert_2\cdot\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. The definition is stated under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ because the surface measure it invokes is; the positivity of the surface measure of nonempty open pieces of $S$, and the finite-order estimates above, are its only uses here.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]).

**Integral form.** Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous. For a measurable $V\subseteq U$ write, componentwise,

$$\int_V g\,d\lambda_n:=\Bigl(\int g_1\chi_V\,d\lambda_n,\ \dots,\ \int g_m\chi_V\,d\lambda_n\Bigr),$$

each component being the Lebesgue integral of the measurable function $g_i\chi_V$ ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). A ball $V\subseteq U$ is **compactly contained** in $U$ when its closure is a compact subset of $U$; for a Euclidean ball this means $\overline V\subseteq U$. If $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$, then $g=0$ on $U$.

**Disc form.** Let $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:W\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. For $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, $q\in W$ and $r>0$ put $e_{i+1}:=e_{(i\bmod 3)+1}$ cyclically, i.e. $e_{i+1}\times e_{i+2}=e_i$ in the cyclic order, and

$$\varphi_{i,q}(s,t):=q+s\,e_{i+1}+t\,e_{i+2},\qquad D_r:=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:s^2+t^2<r^2\},$$

with $\overline{D_r}$ the closed disc. If for every $i$, every $q\in W$ and every $r>0$ with $\varphi_{i,q}(\overline{D_r})\subseteq W$ one has

$$\int_{\overline{D_r}}(F_i\circ\varphi_{i,q})\,d\lambda_2=0,$$

then $F=0$ on $W$.

**Conventions.** The displayed disc condition is the vanishing of the flux of $F$ through the flat disc $\varphi_{i,q}(\overline{D_r})$ in the orientation with unit normal $e_i$: the affine parametrization is a regular patch whose tangent vectors $e_{i+1},e_{i+2}$ have cross product $e_i$ of norm one ([[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), so the flux of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]] is the Riemann integral $\int_{\overline{D_r}}(F_i\circ\varphi_{i,q})\,d(s,t)$; that integral equals the displayed Lebesgue integral because the integrand is continuous on the compact Jordan region $\overline{D_r}$ ([[cor-disc-jordan-content-is-pi-r-squared]], [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[lem-bounded-borel-riemann-integrands-on-boxes-have-equal-lebesgue-integrals]]). Both clauses are pointwise conclusions on their open domains. The first clause is the converse from universal integral relations to a pointwise equation; a single vanishing integral over one ball or one disc supplies no conclusion, and the hypothesis ranges over the full family described.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice; integers $n,m\ge1$; an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a continuous $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ with $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$; an open $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a continuous $F:W\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the disc condition of the Statement; and, inside the contradiction argument below, either a point $p\in U$ with $g(p)\ne0$ or a point $x\in W$ with $F(x)\ne0$.

[F1] Metric balls and continuity at a point: $B_X(a,\rho)=\{y\in X:d_X(y,a)<\rho\}$, and $f$ is continuous at $a$ when for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $f[B_X(a,\delta)]\subseteq B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F2] Open subsets of a metric space: $U$ is open exactly when every $x\in U$ has $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-topology]]).

[F3] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty$ ([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]).

[F4] Integral of signed and nonnegative functions: for measurable real $u$ with at most one of $\int u^+$, $\int u^-$ equal to $+\infty$ one sets $\int u\,d\lambda:=\int u^+d\lambda-\int u^-d\lambda$, and $u$ is integrable when both are finite, equivalently $\int|u|\,d\lambda<\infty$; then $\int(-u)\,d\lambda=-\int u\,d\lambda$; and for nonnegative measurable $f$ the integral over $E$ is $\int_Ef\,d\lambda=\int f\chi_E\,d\lambda$ ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

[F5] Monotonicity and nonnegative homogeneity for the nonnegative integral: if $0\le f\le h$ are measurable then $\int f\,d\lambda\le\int h\,d\lambda$, and if $c>0$ then $\int cf\,d\lambda=c\int f\,d\lambda$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F6] Simple integral: for a nonnegative simple measurable function $s=\sum_{j\le N}c_j\chi_{E_j}$ one has $\int s\,d\lambda=\sum_{j\le N}c_j\lambda(E_j)$ with $0\cdot\infty=0$, and the nonnegative integral of a nonnegative simple measurable function equals its simple integral; hence $\int c\chi_E\,d\lambda=c\lambda(E)$ for $c\ge0$ and measurable $E$ ([[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F7] Measurability: every continuous map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is Borel measurable under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the Borel $\sigma$-algebra is generated by the open sets, so indicators of open sets are Borel ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

[F8] Extreme values: a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded above and below and attains a maximum and a minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction; assume the Statement fails, and contradict in turn a nonzero value of $g$ (cases (A)) and, under the disc hypothesis, a nonzero value of $F$ (case (B)).

1.1 Suppose the Statement fails. Then either (A) $g(p)\ne0$ for some $p\in U$, or (B) the disc condition holds and $F(x)\ne0$ for some $x\in W$; if neither holds then $g=0$ on $U$ and, whenever the disc condition holds, $F=0$ on $W$, which is exactly the Statement. We contradict (A) and (B) in turn. [given, assume-contra]

2.1 In case (A): choose a component index $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ with $g_i(p)\ne0$ and put $u:=g_i$. Replacing the $i$-th component of $g$ by its negative preserves the hypothesis, since $\int_V(-g_i)\,d\lambda=-\int_Vg_i\,d\lambda$ by [F4], and does not change whether $g$ vanishes; hence we may suppose $u(p)=2c$ with $c:=u(p)/2>0$. By [F1] applied to the continuous $u$ at $p$ with $\varepsilon=c$ there is $\delta_0>0$ with $|u(y)-u(p)|<c$ for all $y\in B(p,\delta_0)$; by [F2] and $p\in U$ there is $\delta_2>0$ with $B(p,\delta_2)\subseteq U$; put $\delta:=\min\{\delta_0,\delta_2\}>0$. Then the ball $V:=B(p,\delta/2)$ satisfies $\overline V\subseteq B(p,\delta)\subseteq U$, so $V$ is compactly contained in $U$, and $u(y)>u(p)-c=c$ for every $y\in V$. The hypothesis gives $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$, whose $i$-th component is $\int u\chi_V\,d\lambda=0$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.2 In case (B): choose $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ with $F_i(x)\ne0$ and put $\varphi:=\varphi_{i,x}$, $W':=\varphi^{-1}[W]=\{(s,t):\varphi(s,t)\in W\}$ and $h:=F_i\circ\varphi:W'\to\mathbb R$, so that $h(0,0)=F_i(x)\ne0$. Then $W'$ is open in $\mathbb R^2$, $h$ is continuous, and for every $r>0$ with $\overline B((0,0),r)\subseteq W'$ the disc hypothesis with centre $x$ gives $\int_{\overline B((0,0),r)}h\,d\lambda_2=0$. Indeed, the standard unit vectors are orthonormal ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), so $\lVert\varphi(s,t)-\varphi(s',t')\rVert_2=\lVert(s,t)-(s',t')\rVert_2$ for all $(s,t),(s',t')$; hence $\varphi$ is continuous and $W'$ is open by [F2], while for $(s_0,t_0)\in W'$ and $\varepsilon>0$, continuity of $F_i$ at $\varphi(s_0,t_0)\in W$ gives $\rho>0$ with $|F_i(y)-F_i(\varphi(s_0,t_0))|<\varepsilon$ whenever $d(y,\varphi(s_0,t_0))<\rho$, and then $d((s,t),(s_0,t_0))<\rho$ gives $|h(s,t)-h(s_0,t_0)|<\varepsilon$ by the isometry identity; finally, when $\overline B((0,0),r)\subseteq W'$ the disc $\varphi(\overline B((0,0),r))$ lies in $W$, so the Statement's condition applies with centre $x$ and radius $r$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

3.1 In case (A): the function $u\chi_V$ is Borel and nonnegative, and $0\le c\chi_V\le u\chi_V$ pointwise, because $u>c>0$ on $V$ by step 2.1 while $u\chi_V=0$ off $V$, and $u$ is continuous while $V$ is open [F7]. Moreover $\overline V$ is a nonempty compact metric space, so $M:=\max_{\overline V}|u|$ is finite by [F8], and $|u\chi_V|\le M\chi_{B(p,\delta)}$ with $\int M\chi_{B(p,\delta)}\,d\lambda=M\lambda(B(p,\delta))<\infty$ by [F5], [F6] and [F3]; hence $u\chi_V$ is integrable and $\int u\chi_V\,d\lambda$ is a finite real number by [F4]. Monotonicity [F5] and the simple-integral rule [F6] give $\int u\chi_V\,d\lambda\ge\int c\chi_V\,d\lambda=c\,\lambda(V)>0$ by [F3], contradicting $\int u\chi_V\,d\lambda=0$ from step 2.1. Therefore case (A) is impossible: the integral hypothesis forces $g=0$ on $U$. [step 2.1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

4.1 In case (B): apply the arguments of steps 2.1 and 3.1 with $(U,u,p)$ replaced by $(W',h,(0,0))$, whose hypotheses hold by step 2.2 — $W'$ is open, $h$ is continuous and $h(0,0)=2c'$ with $c':=h(0,0)/2>0$, and the required vanishing ball integral is supplied by the disc hypothesis at centre $x$ — and with the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_2$ in place of $\lambda_n$. They produce a ball $V$ compactly contained in $W'$ with $\int_Vh\,d\lambda_2\ge c'\lambda(V)>0$ while the same hypotheses give $\int_Vh\,d\lambda_2=0$, a contradiction. Therefore case (B) is impossible: whenever the disc condition holds, $F=0$ on $W$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 Cases (A) and (B) both end in contradiction, so no failure of the Statement occurs: the integral hypothesis forces $g=0$ on $U$, and the disc hypothesis forces $F=0$ on $W$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Remarks

- The proof uses, for each clause, the hypothesis only on balls centred at the point where the function is assumed nonzero and with radius half of a continuity threshold; the full family in the Statement is what makes the lemma a localization statement, but no choice from the family is made, and the argument is choice-free apart from the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ used by the surface and measurability suppliers.
- The disc clause is not a statement about a single loop or box: one special disc carries no information, and the components must be tested in all three coordinate directions at all admissible centres and radii.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\lambda_3)$ be a real or complex valued Lebesgue integrable function on $\mathbb R^3$ that vanishes $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside the closed ball $B_a:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2\le a\}$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-metric-ball]]). Put

$$Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3,\qquad p:=\int y\,\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3\in\mathbb C^3,\qquad \lVert\rho\rVert_1:=\int\lvert\rho\rvert\,d\lambda_3,$$

the vector $p$ being defined componentwise; if $\rho$ is real-valued then $Q$ is real and $p\in\mathbb R^3$, while $R(x)$ below is real in that case and complex in general. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ with $r:=\lVert x\rVert_2\ge2a>0$,

$$\int\frac{\rho(y)}{\lVert x-y\rVert_2}\,d\lambda_3(y)=\frac Qr+\frac{\langle p,x\rangle}{r^3}+R(x),\qquad R(x):=\int_{B_a}\rho(y)\Bigl(\frac1{\lVert x-y\rVert_2}-\frac1r-\frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{r^3}\Bigr)d\lambda_3(y),$$

and the remainder satisfies the explicit bound

$$\lvert R(x)\rvert\le\frac{16\,a^2\,\lVert\rho\rVert_1}{r^3}.$$

All integrals are Lebesgue integrals; the closed ball $B_a$ is Borel and $\chi_{B_a}\rho$ is integrable. The constant $16$ is permissible but not sharp, and $Q$, $p$ and $\lVert\rho\rVert_1$ are finite. No derivative of the remainder in $x$ is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice; a real $a>0$; a real or complex $\rho\in L^1(\lambda_3)$ vanishing $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside $B_a=\{y:\lVert y\rVert_2\le a\}$; and a fixed $x\in\mathbb R^3$ with $r=\lVert x\rVert_2\ge2a$.

[F1] Euclidean inner product and norm: $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<3}x_ky_k$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$; Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert\le\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F2] Chain rule and algebra of derivatives for Euclidean maps, with the $C^k$ convention for vector and scalar fields ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F3] Fundamental theorem with interior derivative: if $G:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,1)$ and $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$ with $f=G'$ on $(0,1)$, then $\int_0^1f=G(1)-G(0)$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

[F4] Monotonicity and two-sided bounds for the Riemann integral: if $f\le g$ on $[0,1]$ then $\int_0^1f\le\int_0^1g$, and $m\le f\le M$ gives $m\le\int_0^1f\le M$ ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]).

[F5] $L^1(\lambda_3)$ is a complex vector space and the Lebesgue integral is complex-linear on it: $\int(\alpha f+\beta g)=\alpha\int f+\beta\int g$; integrable functions are measurable ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]).

[F6] Triangle inequality for the Lebesgue integral: $\lvert\int f\,d\lambda\rvert\le\int\lvert f\rvert\,d\lambda$ for $f\in L^1(\lambda_3)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

[F7] Monotonicity and nonnegative homogeneity of the nonnegative integral, and the integral over a measurable set: for measurable $0\le f\le h$ one has $\int f\le\int h$, for $c>0$ one has $\int cf=c\int f$, and $\int_Ef\,d\lambda=\int f\chi_E\,d\lambda$ for nonnegative measurable $f$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

[F8] Almost everywhere equality: the definition of a property holding $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere, and the equivalence, for $f,g\in L^1(\lambda_3)$, of $f=g$ a.e. with $\int_Af=\int_Ag$ for every measurable $A$ ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

[F9] Measurability: continuous maps $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ are Borel measurable under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and the Borel $\sigma$-algebra contains the open sets and hence the closed sets ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; reduce the kernel to a one-variable function on the parameter segment, apply the fundamental theorem twice to obtain a Taylor identity with explicit second-derivative bound, then integrate against the density.

1.1 Fix $y\in B_a$ and define $w(s):=x-sy$ and $h(s):=\lVert w(s)\rVert_2^{-1}$ for real $s$. For $0\le s\le1$ one has $\lVert w(s)\rVert_2\ge r-s\lVert y\rVert_2\ge r-a\ge r/2>0$ by [F1], so $h$ is of class $C^2$ on an open neighbourhood of $[0,1]$ and, by [F2], $h'(s)=\langle w(s),y\rangle\lVert w(s)\rVert_2^{-3}$ and $h''(s)=-\lVert y\rVert_2^2\lVert w(s)\rVert_2^{-3}+3\langle w(s),y\rangle^2\lVert w(s)\rVert_2^{-5}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By Cauchy-Schwarz [F1], $\lvert\langle w(s),y\rangle\rvert\le\lVert w(s)\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$, so the terms of step 1.1 give $\lvert h''(s)\rvert\le\lVert y\rVert_2^2\lVert w(s)\rVert_2^{-3}+3\lVert y\rVert_2^4\lVert w(s)\rVert_2^{-5}=4\lVert y\rVert_2^2\lVert w(s)\rVert_2^{-3}$. Since $\lVert w(s)\rVert_2\ge r-a$ and $r-a\ge r/2$ for $r\ge2a$, this is at most $4\lVert y\rVert_2^2(r-a)^{-3}\le32\lVert y\rVert_2^2r^{-3}$ for every $s\in[0,1]$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 Put $G(s):=(1-s)h'(s)+h(s)$ on $[0,1]$. $G$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1)$ with $G'(s)=(1-s)h''(s)$, a continuous hence Riemann integrable function on $[0,1]$; the fundamental theorem [F3] applied to $G$ and $f:=(1-s)h''(s)$ therefore gives $R_y(x):=\int_0^1(1-s)h''(s)\,ds=G(1)-G(0)=h(1)-h(0)-h'(0)$. Consequently $\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{-1}=h(1)=\lVert x\rVert_2^{-1}+\langle x,y\rangle r^{-3}+R_y(x)$, with $h(0)=r^{-1}$ and $h'(0)=\langle x,y\rangle r^{-3}$ by step 1.1; and monotonicity [F4] applied to $-|h''|\le(1-s)h''\le|h''|$ together with step 2.1 gives $\lvert R_y(x)\rvert\le\int_0^1(1-s)\lvert h''(s)\rvert\,ds\le32\lVert y\rVert_2^2r^{-3}\int_0^1(1-s)\,ds=16\lVert y\rVert_2^2r^{-3}\le16a^2r^{-3}$. [step 2.1, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 The numbers $Q$, $p$, $\lVert\rho\rVert_1$ and the remainder are finite and well defined. Indeed $\lvert\rho y_i\rvert\le a\lvert\rho\rvert$ for every $y\in B_a$, so $y\rho\in L^1(\lambda_3)$ and $p$ is finite by [F5] and [F7]; for the remainder, the function $y\mapsto\chi_{B_a}(y)\bigl(\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{-1}-r^{-1}-\langle x,y\rangle r^{-3}\bigr)$ is Borel on $\mathbb R^3$, because the bracket is continuous on the open set $\{\lVert y\rVert_2<r\}\supseteq B_a$ by [F9] (the denominator $\lVert x-y\rVert_2\ge r-a>0$ is bounded away from zero there) and $\chi_{B_a}$ is the indicator of a closed hence Borel set, and it is bounded on $\mathbb R^3$ by $\lvert\rho\rvert$ times the finite constant $C:=a^{-1}+r^{-1}+ar^{-2}$, since $\lVert x-y\rVert_2\ge r-a\ge a$ and $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert r^{-3}\le ar^{-2}$ on $B_a$; hence the product with $\rho$ lies in $L^1(\lambda_3)$ by [F5] and [F7]. [given, step 3.1, F1, F5, F7, F9, algebra]

5.1 The stated expansion holds. Replacing $\rho$ by its representative $\chi_{B_a}\rho$ changes $Q$, $p$, $\lVert\rho\rVert_1$ and the left-hand integral by nothing, by [F8], so it suffices to prove the identity for $\chi_{B_a}\rho$, for which the pointwise identity of step 3.1 holds at every $y\in B_a$. For that representative, writing the left-hand integrand as $\rho(y)\chi_{B_a}(y)\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{-1}$ and using $\chi_{B_a}=\chi_{B_a}^2$, linearity [F5] of the Lebesgue integral on the space of integrable functions gives $\int\rho(y)\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{-1}d\lambda_3(y)=r^{-1}\int\rho\,d\lambda_3+r^{-3}\sum_{i<3}x_i\int y_i\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3+R(x)=Q/r+\langle p,x\rangle r^{-3}+R(x)$, with $R(x)$ as displayed in the Statement; the three summands are integrable by step 4.1 and the linear combination is legitimate. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

6.1 The bound holds: by the triangle inequality [F6] and monotonicity [F7], $\lvert R(x)\rvert\le\int_{B_a}\lvert\rho(y)\rvert\bigl\lvert\lVert x-y\rVert_2^{-1}-r^{-1}-\langle x,y\rangle r^{-3}\bigr\rvert d\lambda_3(y)\le16a^2r^{-3}\int\lvert\rho\rvert\,d\lambda_3=16a^2\lVert\rho\rVert_1r^{-3}$, the middle inequality being the pointwise bound $16a^2r^{-3}$ for the bracket on $B_a$ from step 3.1 and the final equality the definition of $\lVert\rho\rVert_1$. Hence the expansion and the explicit remainder bound hold for every $r\ge2a$. [step 3.1, step 5.1, F6, F7, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The hypothesis is almost-everywhere support in the closed ball, not continuity of $\rho$ and not compact support in the topological sense; the moments and the integral are unchanged by modification on null sets, and the remainder bound is valid for every admissible representative.
- Only the explicit kernel and a one-variable second-order Taylor identity are used; no decay theorem for Newtonian potentials and no derivative estimate of the remainder in $x$ is invoked, and none is proved here.

## Statement

**Set form.** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $n\ge1$; a compact measurable $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$; reals $a<b$; an open $N\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with $K\times[a,b]\subseteq N$ and a real-valued $f\in C^1(N)$ whose partial derivative in $t$ is $\partial_tf$; and, for the surface form, a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface $S$ in $\mathbb R^m$ with a corresponding $f$ on a neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$.

[F1] Mean value theorem: for $a<c<d<b$-type real intervals, a function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable in its interior attains its average rate of change at an interior point; in particular, for fixed $x$ and $s,u\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne u$ there is $\tau$ strictly between $s$ and $u$ with $f(x,u)-f(x,s)=\partial_tf(x,\tau)(u-s)$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F2] Integrability of bounded measurable functions on finite-measure sets, and the triangle inequality for the integral: a bounded measurable real function $g$ on measurable $K$ with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$ is integrable, and $\lvert\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n\rvert\le\int_K\lvert g\rvert\,d\lambda_n$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

[F3] Linearity, monotonicity and nonnegative homogeneity of the Lebesgue integral: $\int_K(\alpha g+\beta h)\,d\lambda_n=\alpha\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n+\beta\int_Kh\,d\lambda_n$ for integrable $g,h$ and real $\alpha,\beta$, and for measurable $0\le g\le h$ one has $\int g\,d\lambda\le\int h\,d\lambda$, with $\int c\,g\,d\lambda=c\int g\,d\lambda$ for $c>0$; moreover $\int_Ec\,d\lambda_n=c\,\lambda_n(E)$ for $c\ge0$ and measurable $E$, in particular $\int_K\eta\,d\lambda_n=\eta\,\lambda_n(K)$ ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F4] Compactness and uniform continuity: $K\times[a,b]$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-compactness]]), and every continuous map on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], [[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

[F5] Surface measure: the surface integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure, independent of the finite charts and partitions used, continuous and monotone on nonnegative functions, and linear on signed functions integrable against it ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; represent the difference quotient by the mean value theorem as an average of $\partial_tf$ and estimate it by uniform continuity on the compact product.

1.1 The function $F(t):=\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is defined and finite for every $t\in[a,b]$: for fixed $t$ the map $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is continuous on $K$, hence bounded and Borel measurable, and $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, so it is integrable by [F2]. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne t$ and put $g(x):=\frac{f(x,s)-f(x,t)}{s-t}$ for $x\in K$; then $g$ is continuous on $K$, hence bounded, Borel measurable and integrable by [F2]. For every $x\in K$ the mean value theorem [F1] applied to the one-variable function $u\mapsto f(x,u)$ on the closed interval with endpoints $t$ and $s$ supplies a point $\tau$ strictly between $t$ and $s$ with $f(x,s)-f(x,t)=\partial_tf(x,\tau)(s-t)$, that is, $g(x)=\partial_tf(x,\tau)$; no point $\tau$ is selected as a function of $x$ anywhere below, only the pointwise inequality $|g(x)-\partial_tf(x,t)|<\eta$ that such an existential $\tau$ yields, together with the separately defined continuous function $g$. By linearity of the integral [F3] applied to the integrable functions $f(\cdot,s)$ and $f(\cdot,t)$ of step 1.1, $F(s)-F(t)=\int_K\bigl(f(x,s)-f(x,t)\bigr)d\lambda_n(x)=(s-t)\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n(x)$, so the difference quotient is $\int_Kg\,d\lambda_n$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 Given $\varepsilon>0$, put $\eta:=\varepsilon/(1+\lambda_n(K))>0$; the function $\partial_tf$ is uniformly continuous on the compact set $K\times[a,b]$ by [F4], so there is $\delta>0$ such that $\lvert\partial_tf(x,u)-\partial_tf(x,v)\rvert<\eta$ whenever $(x,u),(x,v)\in K\times[a,b]$ with $\lvert u-v\rvert<\delta$. Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $0<\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$ and let $g$ be the continuous function of step 2.1. For every $x\in K$ the mean value point $\tau$ supplied by [F1] lies strictly between $t$ and $s$, so $\lvert\tau-t\rvert<\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$ and therefore $\lvert g(x)-\partial_tf(x,t)\rvert=\lvert\partial_tf(x,\tau)-\partial_tf(x,t)\rvert<\eta$; the function $h:=g-\partial_tf(\cdot,t)$ is continuous on $K$, hence bounded and Borel measurable, so by [F2] and [F3] $\bigl\lvert\frac{F(s)-F(t)}{s-t}-\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\bigr\rvert=\bigl\lvert\int_Kh\,d\lambda_n\bigr\rvert\le\int_K\lvert h\rvert\,d\lambda_n\le\int_K\eta\,d\lambda_n=\eta\,\lambda_n(K)=\frac{\varepsilon\lambda_n(K)}{1+\lambda_n(K)}<\varepsilon$; the case $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is covered by the same chain, both sides vanishing. No choice is made anywhere in this estimate. [step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 Step 3.1 shows that for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$ the difference quotients converge to $\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$: for interior $t$ this is differentiability with the stated derivative, and at $t=a$ (respectively $t=b$), where only $h_k>0$ (respectively $h_k<0$) is admissible, it is the relative derivative there; because $N$ is open, $\partial_tf(x,t)$ is the genuine two-sided partial derivative, so the relative endpoint derivative exists and equals the displayed integral. This proves the set form. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Surface form: let $G(t):=\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$, a finite real number for each $t$ by [F5]. Fix $s,t\in[a,b]$ with $s\ne t$ and put $g(\sigma):=\frac{f(\sigma,s)-f(\sigma,t)}{s-t}$; $g$ is continuous on the compact $S$, hence $\sigma\mapsto g(\sigma)-\partial_tf(\sigma,t)$ is continuous, bounded and integrable against $dS$, and by linearity of the surface integral [F5] on the integrable functions $G(s)-G(t)=\int_S\bigl(f(\sigma,s)-f(\sigma,t)\bigr)dS(\sigma)=(s-t)\int_Sg\,dS(\sigma)$. For every $\sigma\in S$ the mean value theorem [F1] supplies $\tau$ strictly between $t$ and $s$ with $g(\sigma)=\partial_tf(\sigma,\tau)$, and again no $\tau$ is selected as a function; uniform continuity of $\partial_tf$ on the compact set $S\times[a,b]$ by [F4], the finiteness of the surface measure $S(S)$ and the monotonicity and triangle inequality for the surface integral [F5] then give, for $0<\lvert s-t\rvert<\delta$ with the $\delta$ of step 3.1 applied to $\eta:=\varepsilon/(1+S(S))$, the pointwise bound $\lvert g(\sigma)-\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\rvert<\eta$ and hence $\bigl\lvert[G(s)-G(t)]/(s-t)-\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)\bigr\rvert=\bigl\lvert\int_S\bigl(g-\partial_tf(\cdot,t)\bigr)dS\bigr\rvert\le\eta\,S(S)<\varepsilon$, exactly as in steps 2.1 and 3.1 with $S$ in place of $K$ and $dS$ in place of $d\lambda_n$. Passing to the limit as in step 4.1 gives the surface form, including the relative endpoint derivatives. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The proof is the difference-quotient argument of the published rectangle theorem in the more general setting of a compact measurable parameter set and of a fixed compact $C^1$ surface; the finite measure (or finite surface measure) of the parameter set is what makes the uniform error bound convert into an integral error bound.
- No moving set is treated. For a moving surface the parametrization itself depends on $t$ and additional terms appear; that transport identity is proved separately using the moving-patch definition on this page.

## Statement

**Proper-graph branch.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory, put $\gamma(t):=(z(t),t)$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open with $\gamma[I]\subseteq\Omega$. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$ is **proper**: $\gamma^{-1}[K]$ is a compact subset of $I$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,$$

the second integral being vector-valued with components $\langle J_i,\psi\rangle=q\int_Iz_i'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. Then $\rho$ and $J$ are distributions on $\Omega$ ([[def-distribution]]) and, with the distributional derivative of [[def-distributional-derivative]],

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega).$$

Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, and also if $I=\mathbb R$.

**Endpoint branch.** Suppose instead that $I=(a,b)$ is bounded with finite endpoints, that $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, that the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b\lVert z'(t)\rVert_2\,dt$ is finite, and that both endpoint events $(z(a),a)$ and $(z(b),b)$ belong to $\Omega$. Then the same formulas, with the integrals understood as improper integrals over $(a,b)$, define distributions $\rho$ and $J$ on $\Omega$, and

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\,\delta_{(z(b),b)},$$

the Dirac distributions being those of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]].

Mere graph containment $\gamma[I]\subseteq\Omega$ does not make the pulled-back tests compactly supported, and it does not by itself give the source-free identity: in the endpoint branch the endpoint terms are present exactly as displayed, and they vanish on a test only when that test vanishes at the corresponding endpoint event. No Maxwell equation, no point self-force and no physical interpretation of $\rho$ or $J$ is asserted; only the distributional identities for the prescribed support are proved.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$; a $C^1$ trajectory $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$; the graph map $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ mapping $I$ into an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, proper in the first branch; a real $q$; and, in the endpoint branch, $I=(a,b)$ with continuous extension of $z$ to $[a,b]$, finite $\int_a^b\lVert z'\rVert_2$, and $(z(a),a),(z(b),b)\in\Omega$.

[F1] Test functions and distributions: $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ consists of smooth functions with support compact in $\Omega$; a distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional on it; a complex-linear functional is a distribution if and only if on each $\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ it obeys a finite-order estimate $\lvert u(\psi)\rvert\le Cp_m(\psi)$, in particular a bound by $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K\lvert\psi\rvert$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distribution]], [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], [[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]).

[F2] Distributional derivative and Dirac distributions: $\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$; $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ and its derivatives are distributions ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

[F3] Compactness: closed subsets of compact metric spaces are compact, continuous images of compact sets are compact, and compact subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ are closed and bounded; in $\mathbb R$ closed and bounded is compact ([[lem-closed-subset-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]], [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]], [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F4] $C^1$ calculus: the chain rule $D(\psi\circ\gamma)(t)=D\psi(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)$ and the algebra of derivatives for sums and products; with the Euclidean coordinates of $\mathbb R^4$ written $(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$ and the Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F5] Fundamental theorem and integral algebra: if $G$ is continuous on $[u,v]$ and differentiable on $(u,v)$ with Riemann integrable derivative, then $\int_u^vG'=G(v)-G(u)$; the integral is additive over subintervals and linear on integrable functions ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]).

[F6] Improper integrals at finite endpoints: one-ended improper integrals as limits of proper truncations, with a mixed interval split finitely and each singular-end piece required to converge separately; the comparison test: if $\lvert f\rvert\le g$ eventually and $\int g$ converges, then $\int f$ converges absolutely, and absolute convergence implies convergence with $\lvert\int f\rvert\le\int\lvert f\rvert$ on a one-ended interval ([[def-improper-integral-at-a-finite-endpoint]], [[def-mixed-improper-integral]], [[thm-comparison-test-for-improper-integrals]], [[thm-absolute-improper-convergence-implies-convergence]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; write the pairing of the divergence as minus the integral of the derivative of the pulled-back test along the trajectory, and evaluate that integral by the fundamental theorem, first with compact support and then with the truncated improper integral in the endpoint branch.

1.1 The graph map $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is $C^1$ on $I$ and injective, with values in $\Omega$; for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ the pullback $\varphi:=\psi\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb C$ is $C^1$, and $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq\gamma^{-1}[\operatorname{supp}\psi]$: if $\varphi(t)\ne0$ then $\gamma(t)\in\operatorname{supp}\psi$. In the proper branch $\gamma^{-1}[\operatorname{supp}\psi]$ is compact, so $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ is a closed subset of a compact set, hence compact in $I$; thus $\varphi\in C_c^1(I)$ and $\varphi'$ is continuous. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 In the proper branch, $\rho$ is a distribution. Let $K\subseteq\Omega$ be compact and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K$, so that $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq C_K:=\gamma^{-1}[K]$, a compact subset of $I$; if $C_K=\varnothing$ then $\varphi=0$. Otherwise $u:=\min C_K$ and $v:=\max C_K$ lie in $I$ with $C_K\subseteq[u,v]\subseteq I$, and $\lvert\varphi\rvert\le p_0(\psi)$ on $[u,v]$ because $\psi$ vanishes off $K$ and $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K\lvert\psi\rvert$; hence $\lvert\langle\rho,\psi\rangle\rvert\le\lvert q\rvert\int_u^v\lvert\varphi\rvert\,dt\le\lvert q\rvert(v-u)p_0(\psi)$ by [F5], a finite-order estimate of order zero, so $\rho$ is a distribution by [F1]. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

2.2 The automatic properness claims hold. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$ and $K\subseteq\Omega$ is compact, then the time projection $\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$ is a compact subset of $I$ by [F3] and $\gamma^{-1}[K]$ is closed in $I$ (preimage of the closed set $K$ under the continuous map $\gamma$) with $\gamma^{-1}[K]\subseteq\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$; being closed in $I$ and contained in $\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$, it is closed in the subspace $\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$, hence compact as a closed subset of a compact metric space by [F3]. If $I=\mathbb R$, then $\gamma^{-1}[K]$ is closed and contained in the bounded set $\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$, hence compact in $\mathbb R$ by [F3]. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

3.1 In the proper branch, $J$ is a distribution: with the notation of step 2.1, $\lvert z'\rvert$ is continuous on $[u,v]$, hence bounded there by $M_K<\infty$, and $\lvert\langle J,\psi\rangle\rvert\le\lvert q\rvert\int_u^v\lVert z'(t)\rVert_2\lvert\varphi(t)\rvert\,dt\le\lvert q\rvert M_K(v-u)p_0(\psi)$, again a finite-order estimate of order zero. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

3.2 Endpoint branch, well-definedness: let $I=(a,b)$, with $z$ extending continuously to $[a,b]$, $\int_a^b\lVert z'\rVert_2<\infty$ and both endpoint events in $\Omega$. Then $\varphi=\psi\circ\gamma$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$ with $\lvert\varphi\rvert\le p_0(\psi)$ and $\lVert z'\varphi\rVert_2\le p_0(\psi)\lVert z'\rVert_2$ on $(a,b)$; by the comparison test [F6] the improper integrals $\int_a^b\varphi$ and $\int_a^b z'\varphi$ converge absolutely (the first against the constant $p_0(\psi)$, the second against $p_0(\psi)\lVert z'\rVert_2$), so $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_a^b\varphi$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_a^bz'\varphi$ are well-defined finite values; they are linear in $\psi$ by linearity of the truncated integrals and passage to the limit [F5, F6], and for $\psi\in\mathcal D_K$ they obey $\lvert\langle\rho,\psi\rangle\rvert\le\lvert q\rvert p_0(\psi)(b-a)$ and $\lvert\langle J,\psi\rangle\rvert\le\lvert q\rvert p_0(\psi)\int_a^b\lVert z'\rVert_2$, so they are distributions by [F1]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F5, F6, algebra]

4.1 For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ in the proper branch, the pairing of the divergence is $\langle\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle=-\langle\rho,\partial_t\psi\rangle-\langle J,\nabla\psi\rangle=-q\int_I\bigl(\partial_t\psi(\gamma(t))+\langle z'(t),\nabla\psi(\gamma(t))\rangle\bigr)dt$, the components of $\nabla\psi$ being the spatial partial derivatives and $\operatorname{div}J$ the sum of the coordinate distributional derivatives of the components of $J$ by [F2]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, F4, algebra]

5.1 By the chain rule [F4], $\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(t)=D\psi(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)=\partial_t\psi(\gamma(t))+\langle\nabla\psi(\gamma(t)),z'(t)\rangle$, since $\gamma'=(z',1)$; hence the integrand of step 4.1 is exactly $\varphi'$. [step 4.1, F4, algebra]

6.1 Since $\varphi\in C_c^1(I)$ by step 1.1, there are $u<v$ in $I$ with $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq[u,v]$ and $\varphi(u)=\varphi(v)=0$; by [F5] applied to the subinterval and by additivity of the integral over subintervals, $\int_I\varphi'=\int_u^v\varphi'=\varphi(v)-\varphi(u)=0$. Therefore $\langle\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle=0$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, which is the identity $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ of distributions. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F5, algebra]

7.1 Endpoint branch, identity: applying [F2] and the chain rule as in steps 4.1 and 5.1 gives $\langle\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle=-q\int_a^b\varphi'(t)\,dt$, where $\varphi'$ is continuous on $(a,b)$ and $\lvert\varphi'\rvert\le C(1+\lVert z'\rVert_2)$ for a constant $C$ depending on the fixed test, so the improper integral converges absolutely by the comparison test [F6]; for $0<\varepsilon<(b-a)/2$ the proper fundamental theorem [F5] gives $\int_{a+\varepsilon}^{b-\varepsilon}\varphi'=\varphi(b-\varepsilon)-\varphi(a+\varepsilon)$, and the mixed improper integral is the limit of these truncations as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ [F6]; continuity of $\varphi$ at the endpoints gives $\varphi(b-\varepsilon)-\varphi(a+\varepsilon)\to\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)=\psi(z(b),b)-\psi(z(a),a)$. Hence $\langle\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle=q\psi(z(a),a)-q\psi(z(b),b)=\langle q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)},\psi\rangle$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ by [F2], which is the endpoint identity. [step 5.1, step 6.1, step 3.2, F2, F5, F6, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **The endpoint terms are real.** For $I=(0,1)$, $z\equiv0$ and $\Omega=\mathbb R^4$ the trajectory is constant, $\int_0^1\lVert z'\rVert_2=0$ and the identity reads $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(0,0)}-q\delta_{(0,1)}$: the static point charge on a finite time window is not source-free as a spacetime distribution, and the two endpoint contributions have opposite signs. The claimed free identity for this configuration would be false.
- **Where properness is used.** In the proper branch properness makes every pulled-back test compactly supported, which is what allows the fundamental theorem without endpoint terms and gives the order-zero estimates. Neither graph containment alone nor compactness of the ambient test alone replaces this hypothesis, and no physical existence of the sources is asserted.

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with coordinates $x_1,x_2,x_3$, partial derivatives $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x_j$, Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and norm $\lvert\cdot\rvert_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), divergence and curl as in [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and cross product as in [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Put

$$Q_{ij}:=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert_2^2,\qquad \delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad (\operatorname{div}Q)_i:=\sum_{j<3}\partial_jQ_{ij}.$$

Then $Q$ is a $C^1$ tensor field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}Q=F\,\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F .$$

Moreover, writing $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for the Levi-Civita symbol ($\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $0$ if two indices coincide), every symmetric tensor $Q$ (that is, $Q_{kj}=Q_{jk}$ for all $j,k$) satisfies

$$\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0\qquad(i\in\{1,2,3\}),$$

the sum over $j,k$ being the nine-term sum with each pair counted separately. Finally, if $\Pi$ is a $C^1$ symmetric tensor field on $U$, if $g:U\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuous, and if $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ holds at every point of $U$ for a continuous $f:U\to\mathbb R^3$, where $(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i=\sum_{\ell<3}\partial_\ell\Pi_{i\ell}$ and $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}:=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$ with the sum over $j,k$, then the vector field $x\times g$ and the tensor field $x\times\Pi$ satisfy

$$\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f .$$

No symmetry of $Q$ beyond the displayed form is assumed, and no boundary integral is asserted: these are pointwise identities on $U$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$; the $C^1$ field $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ with $Q_{ij}=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert_2^2$; a symmetric tensor $Q$ in the second claim and a $C^1$ symmetric tensor field $\Pi$ with continuous $g,f$ satisfying $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ in the third claim.

[F1] Cross product: for $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\,u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[F2] Divergence and curl: $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_{i<3}\partial_iF_i$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=(\partial_2F_3-\partial_3F_2,\ \partial_3F_1-\partial_1F_3,\ \partial_1F_2-\partial_2F_1)$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]).

[F3] Inner product and norm: $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{i<3}u_iv_i$ and $\lvert F\rvert_2^2=\langle F,F\rangle$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F4] Product rule and differentiability of products of $C^1$ functions, with the partial-derivative convention for maps on open Euclidean sets ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; expand the divergence of the quadratic tensor in coordinates, match the resulting expression with $-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$, cancel symmetric terms in the Levi-Civita contraction, and differentiate the cross-product products in the angular-balance identity.

1.1 The entries $Q_{ij}=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\langle F,F\rangle$ are sums of products of $C^1$ functions, hence $C^1$ on $U$ by [F3] and [F4], so both sides of the first identity are defined; moreover $\partial_j\langle F,F\rangle=\partial_j\sum_{l<3}F_lF_l=2\sum_{l<3}F_l\,\partial_jF_l$ by the product rule [F4]. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 For fixed $i$, $\sum_{j<3}\partial_jQ_{ij}=\sum_{j<3}\partial_j(F_iF_j)-\tfrac12\sum_{j<3}\delta_{ij}\partial_j\langle F,F\rangle=\sum_{j<3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i+F_i\partial_jF_j\bigr)-\sum_{l<3}F_l\partial_iF_l=F_i\operatorname{div}F+\sum_{j<3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i-F_j\partial_iF_j\bigr)$ by step 1.1, the product rule [F4] and the divergence formula [F2]. [step 1.1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.2 For a symmetric tensor and fixed $i$, the nine-term sum $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}$ vanishes: terms with $j=k$ have $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$, and for $j\ne k$ the pair $(j,k)$ and the pair $(k,j)$ contribute $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}+\epsilon_{ikj}Q_{jk}=\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}-\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0$, because $\epsilon$ changes sign under exchange of its last two indices and $Q$ is symmetric. This is the second claim. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The first coordinate of $F\times\operatorname{curl}F$ is, by [F1] and [F2], $F_2(\partial_1F_2-\partial_2F_1)-F_3(\partial_3F_1-\partial_1F_3)=F_2\partial_1F_2+F_3\partial_1F_3-F_2\partial_2F_1-F_3\partial_3F_1$; adding and subtracting $F_1\partial_1F_1$ shows that $-\bigl(F\times\operatorname{curl}F\bigr)_1=\sum_{j<3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_1-F_j\partial_1F_j\bigr)$, and the same expansion in the second and third coordinates gives $-\bigl(F\times\operatorname{curl}F\bigr)_i=\sum_{j<3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i-F_j\partial_iF_j\bigr)$ for every $i$. Substituting this into step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{div}Q=F\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$, which is the first identity. [step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]

3.2 The field $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$ is $C^1$, and differentiating the product in $x_\ell$ and summing over $\ell$ gives $(\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi))_i=\sum_{\ell<3}\partial_\ell(\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell})=\epsilon_{ijk}\sum_{\ell<3}\bigl(\delta_{j\ell}\Pi_{k\ell}+x_j\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}\bigr)=\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}+\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\sum_{\ell<3}\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_k$, where the term $\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}$ vanishes by step 2.2 applied to the symmetric field $\Pi$; here $\delta_{j\ell}$ is the Kronecker symbol and the product rule [F4] was used in each summand. [step 2.2, F4, algebra]

4.1 Substituting $\partial_tg_k=-f_k-(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_k$ and differentiating the product with the time-independent factor $x_j$ gives $\partial_t(x\times g)_i=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\partial_tg_k=-\epsilon_{ijk}x_jf_k-\epsilon_{ijk}x_j(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_k=-(x\times f)_i-(\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi))_i$ by step 3.2; hence $\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f$, which is the third claim. [step 3.2, F4, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The identity $\operatorname{div}Q=F\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$ requires only first derivatives and no interchange of mixed partials, so the $C^1$ hypothesis is the natural one; the symmetry claim for $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}$ is a purely algebraic statement about symmetric tensors.
- The angular-balance identity is local; passing to an integral balance over a region requires a divergence theorem and boundary terms, which are not asserted here. The case $\Pi=Q$ and $g=F$ with $\partial_tF=F\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$ is the intended application, but that evolution equation is not assumed.
