## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $(S,\Omega_-,\Omega_+,n)$ be a two-sided presentation of a compact embedded $C^2$ interface in $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-em-surface-distribution]]: $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ are the two open sides and $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ is the continuous unit normal pointing from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$. Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately, with one-sided $C^1$ traces on $S$: $F$ and each first partial derivative $\partial_iF$ extend continuously from each side to $S$, and the traces $F_+,F_-\in C^0(S;\mathbb R^3)$ give the jump $[F]=F_+-F_-$.

Let $\{\partial_iF_j\}$, $\{\operatorname{div}F\}$ and $\{\operatorname{curl}F\}$ denote the locally integrable fields equal on $\Omega_\pm$ to the corresponding classical derivative of $F$; these are regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). Then, away from the edge $\partial S$ of the interface and in the distributional sense,

$$\partial_iF_j=\{\partial_iF_j\}+n_i\,[F_j]\,\delta_S\qquad(i,j\in\{1,2,3\}),$$

and consequently

$$\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S,\qquad \operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[F]\,\delta_S,$$

as distributions on the open set $\Omega\setminus\partial S$: for every test function $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap\partial S=\varnothing$ the pairings of both sides agree. Here $\delta_S$ is the surface distribution of [[def-em-surface-distribution]], $n\cdot[F]=\sum_i n_i[F_i]$, and $n\times[F]$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. A moving interface with $\partial_tS\ne0$ requires additional terms and is not covered; the stationary jump formulas may not be reused for a moving interface. Nothing is asserted at the edge $\partial S$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$; a two-sided compact embedded $C^2$ interface $S$ with sides $\Omega_\pm$ and unit normal $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$; a field $F$ of class $C^1$ on each side with one-sided $C^1$ traces; and a test function $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap\partial S=\varnothing$.

[F1] Surface distributions and jumps: $\delta_S(\varphi)=\int_S\varphi\,dS$, the density functional and the jump $[F]=F_+-F_-$ are those of [[def-em-surface-distribution]]; a field $C^1$ on each side with one-sided continuous traces has locally integrable components, and the traces extend continuously to $S$.

[F2] Distributional derivative and regular distributions: $\langle\partial_i u,\varphi\rangle=-\langle u,\partial_i\varphi\rangle$ for $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]]), and a locally integrable function defines a distribution by integration ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-distribution]]).

[F3] Divergence theorem and domains: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a bounded open set with a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation admits the divergence theorem $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}G=\sum_j\int_{S_j}G\cdot\nu_j\,dS$ for $G\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]], [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[F4] Localization: compactly supported smooth cutoffs and smooth partitions of unity subordinate to a given open cover of an open set exist ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F5] Derivative conventions: divergence and curl are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]; the cross product satisfies $(u\times v)_k=\epsilon_{kij}u_iv_j$ in the right-handed convention of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], and the Euclidean inner product is that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; products and one-sided derivatives follow the usual product and chain rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; reduce to a local single-patch computation by a partition of unity, integrate by parts on each side with the divergence theorem, and read off the jump terms.

1.1 By [F1] the components of $F$ and of its one-sided first derivatives are locally integrable on $\Omega$, the piecewise fields $\{\partial_iF_j\}$ are locally integrable, and $[F_j]$ is continuous on $S$; hence all the distributions displayed in the Statement are defined, and $n_i[F_j]\delta_S$ is the surface distribution of the continuous density $n_i[F_j]$ of [F1]. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Reduction to a single patch: let $\mathcal B$ be the family of open balls $B$ with $\overline B\subseteq\Omega$, $\overline B\cap\partial S=\varnothing$, and with $S\cap\overline B$ contained in one regular $C^1$ parameter patch on which one side is the subgraph; near such $B$ the intersections $\Omega_\pm\cap B$ are bounded open sets with the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation whose interface face is $S\cap\overline B$ and whose remaining faces lie in $\partial B$. The hypothesis on $\psi$ and [F4] give finitely many $B_1,\dots,B_N$ covering $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap S$ and a smooth partition of unity $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_N$ with $\operatorname{supp}\chi_k\subseteq B_k$ and $\sum_k\chi_k=1$ on a neighbourhood of $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap S$; writing $\psi=\sum_k\chi_k\psi+(1-\sum_k\chi_k)\psi$, the last summand vanishes on a neighbourhood of $S$, where the pairing identity reduces to the classical equality of $\partial_iF_j$ with the piecewise derivative. It therefore suffices to prove, for each $k$ and each test supported in $B_k$, the pairing identity $\langle\partial_iF_j,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega\{\partial_iF_j\}\varphi+\langle n_i[F_j]\delta_S,\varphi\rangle$. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Local computation: let $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ have support in a ball $B=B_k$ as in step 1.2. By [F2], $\langle\partial_iF_j,\varphi\rangle=-\int_{\Omega}F_j\partial_i\varphi=-\int_{\Omega_+}F_j\partial_i\varphi-\int_{\Omega_-}F_j\partial_i\varphi$. On each side apply the divergence theorem [F3] to the field $G^\pm:=F_j\varphi\,e_i$, which is $C^1$ on the closure of $\Omega_\pm\cap B$ with one-sided traces on the interface face and which vanishes identically near the faces lying in $\partial B$ because $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq B$; the outward normal of $\Omega_+$ on the interface face is $-n$ and that of $\Omega_-$ is $+n$, so $\int_{\Omega_+}\partial_i(F_j\varphi)=-\int_{S\cap B}(F_j)_+\varphi\,n_i\,dS$ and $\int_{\Omega_-}\partial_i(F_j\varphi)=\int_{S\cap B}(F_j)_-\varphi\,n_i\,dS$. Substituting $\int_{\Omega_\pm}F_j\partial_i\varphi=\int_{\Omega_\pm}\partial_i(F_j\varphi)-\int_{\Omega_\pm}(\partial_iF_j)\varphi$ gives $\langle\partial_iF_j,\varphi\rangle=\int_{\Omega}\{\partial_iF_j\}\varphi+\int_{S}((F_j)_+-(F_j)_-)\varphi\,n_i\,dS=\int_{\Omega}\{\partial_iF_j\}\varphi+\langle n_i[F_j]\delta_S,\varphi\rangle$, which is the componentwise identity. [step 1.2, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 Summing step 2.1 over $i$ (and using the definitions of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and of the piecewise fields) gives $\langle\operatorname{div}F,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega\{\operatorname{div}F\}\varphi+\langle n\cdot[F]\delta_S,\varphi\rangle$ for every test supported in some $B_k$, hence, by the finite partition of step 1.2, for every test with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap\partial S=\varnothing$; this is the divergence identity on $\Omega\setminus\partial S$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F5, algebra]

4.1 Antisymmetrizing step 2.1 gives the curl identity: by [F5], $(\operatorname{curl}F)_k=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iF_j=\epsilon_{kij}\{\partial_iF_j\}+\epsilon_{kij}n_i[F_j]\delta_S=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_k+(n\times[F])_k\delta_S$ for each $k$, since $\epsilon_{kij}\{\partial_iF_j\}$ is the classical $k$-th component of the piecewise curl and $\epsilon_{kij}n_i[F_j]=(n\times[F])_k$ in the stated convention; hence, for every test with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap\partial S=\varnothing$, $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[F]\delta_S$. [step 3.1, F1, F5, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The sign convention is the one fixed by the normal: because $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, the outward normal of $\Omega_+$ on the interface is $-n$ and that of $\Omega_-$ is $+n$, which produces the difference $F_+-F_-$. Reversing $n$ reverses both $n$ and $[F]$, leaving $n\cdot[F]$ and $n\times[F]$ unchanged, as it must.
- The computation is local on $\Omega\setminus\partial S$; at the edge the interface need not be a regular patch and no formula is asserted. A moving interface contributes an additional term proportional to the normal velocity, not covered here.

## Statement

**Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $k\in\mathbb N$. A map on $U\times I$ is **jointly $C^k$** when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; it is **jointly $C^\infty$** when it is the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open $I$ these are exactly the usual open-domain classes; at included endpoints of a nondegenerate interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton $I$ the convention still asserts extension existence and the spatial identities below, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. The convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded $I$.

**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the fields $B(\cdot,t)$ and $C(\cdot,t)$ need not be continuous in $t$ at endpoints beyond the stated one-sided convention.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open star-shaped $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with centre $a$; an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$; an integer $k\ge1$; a jointly $C^k$ field $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$; and, for the scalar witness, a jointly $C^k$ field $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$.

[F1] Star-shapedness: $a+s(x-a)\in U$ for every $x\in U$ and $0\le s\le1$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]).

[F2] Radial vector potential: if $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ is open and star-shaped with centre $a$ and $B:U\to\mathbb R^3$ is $C^1$ divergence-free, then $A(x)=\int_0^1t\,B(a+t(x-a))\times(x-a)\,dt$ is a vector potential for $B$ in the sense of [[def-vector-potential-of-a-c1-vector-field]]: it is $C^1$ and $\operatorname{curl}A=B$ ([[thm-a-divergence-free-c1-field-on-a-star-shaped-open-set-has-a-vector-potential]]).

[F3] Poincaré lemma and closedness: on a star-shaped open set every closed $C^1$ field $F$ (that is, $\partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j$) is exact, with $C^2$ potential $\phi(x)=\int_0^1\langle F(a+t(x-a)),x-a\rangle\,dt$; exactness means $F=\nabla\phi$ ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]], [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]]).

[F4] $C^k$ calculus: the $C^k$ class on open Euclidean sets is closed under sums, products and composition, with the chain and product rules for total derivatives ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F5] Differentiation under the integral over a compact parameter interval: if $g,h:[c,d]\times[\alpha,\beta]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and $g(\cdot,s)$ is differentiable with derivative $h(\cdot,s)$ for each $s$, then $x\mapsto\int_\alpha^\beta g(x,s)\,ds$ is differentiable with derivative $\int_\alpha^\beta h(x,s)\,ds$, relative and one-sided at the endpoints ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]]); the proof method is that of [[lem-em-parameter-integrals]].

[F6] Uniform bounds: continuous real functions on compact metric spaces are uniformly continuous ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]), closed bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and $\lvert\int_u^vf-\int_u^vg\rvert\le\eta\lvert v-u\rvert$ when $\lvert f-g\rvert\le\eta$ on the interval ([[lem-uniform-integral-error-bound]]).

[F7] Fundamental theorem: if $G$ is continuous on $[u,v]$ and differentiable on $(u,v)$ with Riemann integrable derivative, then $\int_u^vG'=G(v)-G(u)$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; extend the data to a neighbourhood of $U\times I$, prove joint regularity of the radial integrals on an open radial-admissibility set by induction on the derivative order using differentiation under the integral sign, and verify the spatial field identities slice by slice.

1.1 Extension and radial-admissibility. By the joint $C^k$ convention there are an open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$ and a $C^k$ map $\widetilde B:N\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\widetilde B|_{U\times I}=B$; for the scalar witness take $N$ to be the intersection of the two neighbourhoods and let $\widetilde C$ be the corresponding $C^k$ extension, which exists on that intersection. Put $P:=\{(x,t)\in N:\ (a+s(x-a),t)\in N\text{ for every }s\in[0,1]\}$; then $U\times I\subseteq P$ by [F1], and $P$ is open: if $(x,t)\in P$, the radial image $R:=\{(a+s(x-a),t):0\le s\le1\}$ is compact and contained in the open set $N$, so the distance from $R$ to the closed complement $\mathbb R^4\setminus N$ is positive — indeed finitely many balls centred at points of $R$ and contained in $N$ cover $R$, and if points $y_n\notin N$ approached $R$ then a compactness argument would place a cluster point in both $R$ and the closed set $\mathbb R^4\setminus N$ — and we put $\rho:=\tfrac12\operatorname{dist}(R,\mathbb R^4\setminus N)>0$. The map $\Phi(x',t',s)=(a+s(x'-a),t')$ satisfies $\lVert\Phi(x',t',s)-\Phi(x,t,s)\rVert_2\le\lVert x'-x\rVert_2+\lvert t'-t\rvert$ uniformly in $s$, so for $\lVert x'-x\rVert_2+\lvert t'-t\rvert<\rho$ every point of the radial image of $(x',t')$ lies within distance $\rho$ of $R$, hence in $N$, and $(x',t')\in P$. [given, F1, F4, F6, algebra]

2.1 Joint regularity of the radial integrals on $P$: for every compact box $Q\times J\subseteq P$ and every multi-index $\alpha$ in the variables $(x,t)$ with $\lvert\alpha\rvert\le k$, the partial derivative $\partial^\alpha$ of the integral $\widetilde A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,\widetilde B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\,ds$ exists on $Q\times J$ and equals $\int_0^1\partial^\alpha\bigl[s\,\widetilde B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\bigr]ds$, and this is jointly continuous on $Q\times J$; the same holds for $\widetilde\Psi(x,t):=\int_0^1\langle\widetilde C(a+s(x-a),t),x-a\rangle\,ds$. Indeed, on the compact set $(Q\times J)\times[0,1]$ every radial argument $(a+s(x-a),t)$ lies in a compact subset of $N$, and each integrand is a sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $\widetilde B$, $\widetilde C$ composed with the smooth map $(x,t,s)\mapsto(a+s(x-a),t)$, the polynomial factor $s$ and the polynomial vector $x-a$, hence is $C^k$ jointly in $(x,t,s)$ by [F4]. Induction on $\lvert\alpha\rvert$: for $\lvert\alpha\rvert=0$ joint continuity of the $s$-integral follows from uniform continuity of the integrand on the compact product and [F6]; if the claim holds for $\alpha$, then differentiating the integral in one further spatial or time variable under the integral sign is legitimate by [F5] applied with parameter $s\in[0,1]$ and the other variables frozen at values in $Q\times J$, and the resulting integral is again jointly continuous by the same uniform-continuity argument; at an included endpoint of a nondegenerate $J$ this gives the relative derivative, as stated there. [step 1.1, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

3.1 Restriction to $U\times I$: since $U\times I\subseteq P$ and the extensions agree with $B$ and $C$ there, the maps $A=\widetilde A|_{U\times I}$ and $-\widetilde\Psi|_{U\times I}$ are the restrictions of the $C^k$ maps $\widetilde A$ and $-\widetilde\Psi$ on the open set $P$, hence are jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$; the restricted integrals are exactly the formulas displayed in the Statement because $\widetilde B|_{U\times I}=B$ and $\widetilde C|_{U\times I}=C$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Field identities at each fixed time. Fix $t\in I$. The slice $B(\cdot,t)$ is $C^1$ on $U$ (as $k\ge1$) and divergence-free, and $A(\cdot,t)$ coincides with the radial witness of [F2] for that slice; hence $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ by [F2]. For the scalar witness put $\Psi_C(x,t):=\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-a\rangle\,ds$, so that $\phi=-\Psi_C$; the slice $C(\cdot,t)$ is $C^1$ and closed on $U$. Differentiating $\Psi_C$ in $x_j$ under the integral sign, legitimate by step 2.1 with $\lvert\alpha\rvert=1$, gives $\partial_j\Psi_C(x,t)=\int_0^1\bigl[C_j(a+s(x-a),t)+s\sum_i(x-a)_i\,\partial_jC_i(a+s(x-a),t)\bigr]ds$; closedness of the slice replaces $\partial_jC_i$ by $\partial_iC_j$, so the integrand is $\frac{d}{ds}\bigl[s\,C_j(a+s(x-a),t)\bigr]$ by the chain and product rules [F4], and the fundamental theorem [F7] gives $\partial_j\Psi_C(x,t)=C_j(x,t)-0\cdot C_j(a,t)=C_j(x,t)$; hence $\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$. [step 3.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, algebra]

5.1 Jointly $C^\infty$ data: if $B$ and $C$ are jointly $C^\infty$, choose one smooth extension of each on a common neighbourhood, repeat steps 1.1 through 4.1 for every $k$, and conclude that the same radial integrals are jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ for every $k$, hence jointly $C^\infty$, with the same field identities at every $t$. [step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Degenerate and unbounded time domains: for $I=\varnothing$ the statements over $U\times I$ are vacuous; for $I=\{t_0\}$ any $C^k$ extension of the restricted data to $U\times(t_0-\varepsilon,t_0+\varepsilon)$ exists and the construction of steps 1.1 through 4.1 produces the two potentials with the stated spatial identities at $t_0$, while the values of the extension away from $t_0$ are not determined by the original data, so no unique time jets are asserted; for unbounded $I$ the set $P$ is constructed from the given neighbourhood $N$ of $U\times I$ without any fixed uniform enlargement, and the argument applies verbatim. Hence both witnesses are jointly $C^k$ with the stated identities, which is the Statement. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The corrected sign convention is the one proved here: the positive radial integral $\int_0^1\langle C,x-a\rangle\,ds$ has gradient $+C$, so the scalar witness is its negative; the vector identity $\operatorname{curl}A=B$ keeps the positive sign because the cross product and curl conventions are the ones of the cited definitions. For $C=e_1$ the formula gives $\phi=-(x_1-a_1)$ and $\nabla\phi=-e_1$, as required.
- The construction is local on a star-shaped $U$ even when the surrounding open set has holes: on a ball the radial segment stays inside the ball. No global potential on an arbitrary open set and no uniqueness of the potentials are asserted.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). In the setting of [[def-em-moving-patch]]: $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a finite elementary Green region with positive boundary chain $\partial D$, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, $r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ extends to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I^\circ$, $(W,v)$ is a $C^1$ velocity field with $v(r(p,t),t)=r_t(p,t)$, and $B$ is a $C^1$ field on an open set containing the swept set $S=\bigcup_{t\in I}r(D\times\{t\})$, with flux

$$\Phi(t)=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(p,t),t),\,r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\bigr\rangle\,dp .$$

If $\operatorname{div}B=0$ on its domain, then $\Phi$ is differentiable on $I$, with relative one-sided derivatives at included endpoints, and for every $t\in I$ whose slice is regular, that is $r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\ne0$ for all $p\in D^\circ$,

$$\Phi'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r .$$

By the standing hypothesis on $D^\circ\times I^\circ$ the slice is regular at every interior time $t\in I^\circ$, so for open $I$ the identity holds at every $t\in I$; at an included endpoint of a nondegenerate interval it is asserted exactly when the endpoint slice is regular as well, and no assertion is made when it is not. Here $S(t)=r(D\times\{t\})$ carries the orientation induced by the parametrization, $n$ is the induced unit normal ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]), and the boundary integral is taken around the induced boundary chain $\varphi(\partial D)$ of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]] with the positive orientation of [[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]] and the line integrals of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. Without the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}B=0$ the additional term

$$\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot n)\,\operatorname{div}B\,dS$$

appears on the right-hand side. The identity is local in $t$ and is a statement about the parametrized mathematical object; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data $(D,I,r,v,B,\Phi)$ of the Statement, times $t\in I$ that are interior or whose slice is regular (the two cases needed below), and the notation $w:=r_u\times r_v$, $N:=w/\lVert w\rVert_2$ on $D^\circ$ at a regular slice, and $\tilde v(p,t):=r_t(p,t)=v(r(p,t),t)$.

[F1] Moving patch: the flux is the integral displayed in the Statement over the compact Jordan measurable region $D$; the velocity field is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set and satisfies $v(r(p,t),t)=r_t(p,t)$; $r$ extends $C^2$ to a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ ([[def-em-moving-patch]]).

[F2] Differentiation under the integral sign over the compact measurable set $D$: if a real-valued function and its partial $t$-derivative are continuous on a neighbourhood of $D\times[a,b]$, then $t\mapsto\int_Df(p,t)\,dp$ is differentiable with the stated relative endpoint derivatives and derivative $\int_D\partial_tf(p,t)\,dp$ ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]).

[F3] Calculus rules: chain rule for total derivatives, the product rule, equality of mixed partials for $C^2$ maps, and the $C^k$ conventions ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F4] Cross product and mixed product: $u\times v$ is bilinear and alternating and $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, so the scalar triple product is multilinear and alternating in its three arguments ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]); the Euclidean inner product is that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

[F5] Rigidity of alternating column-multilinear matrix functions: if $F:M_3(\mathbb R)\to\mathbb R$ is column-multilinear in the sense of [[def-multilinear-alternating-normalized-and-antisymmetric-matrix-functions]] and alternating (it vanishes whenever two columns are equal), then $F(M)=F(I_3)\det(M)$ for every $M$; in particular a column-multilinear alternating $F$ with $F(I_3)=0$ vanishes identically ([[lem-rigidity-of-alternating-multilinear-matrix-functions]]).

[F6] Cross-product differential identity: for $C^1$ fields $F,G$, $\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F$ with divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] ([[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]]).

[F7] Stokes for patches: for a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region and a $C^1$ field $G$ on a neighbourhood of its image, $\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}G\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_D\langle(\operatorname{curl}G)\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\rangle$ with the induced boundary chain and orientation ([[thm-the-classical-stokes-theorem-for-a-c2-surface-patch]], [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]], [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]).

[F8] Surface integrals: for a regular patch, $\int_Sq\,dS=\int_D(q\circ\varphi)J_\varphi$ with area density $J_\varphi=\lVert\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\rVert_2$, and the flux in the induced orientation is $\int_D\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\rangle$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; differentiate the parametrized flux under the integral sign, express the derivative of the area vector by the determinant identity, convert the resulting curl term into a boundary circulation by Stokes, and identify each term with the corresponding surface integral.

1.1 Preliminaries. The integrand $W(p,t):=\langle B(r(p,t),t),w(p,t)\rangle$ is defined for $(p,t)$ in a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ and is continuous there together with $\partial_tW$: $r$ and its first derivatives are continuous, $B$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, and sums, products and compositions of continuous maps are continuous. Moreover $\tilde v(p,t)=r_t(p,t)=v(r(p,t),t)$ is $C^1$ in $(p,t)$, so $D_xv$ denotes the spatial Jacobian of the velocity field, evaluated at $r(p,t)$, and $\operatorname{div}v$ its spatial divergence; on $D^\circ\times I$ the vector $w=r_u\times r_v$ does not vanish, so the unit normal $N=w/\lVert w\rVert_2$ is defined there. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Algebraic identity for the area vector. For every $3\times3$ real matrix $A$ and all $B_0,u_1,u_2\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle B_0,(Au_1)\times u_2\rangle+\langle B_0,u_1\times(Au_2)\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A)\langle B_0,u_1\times u_2\rangle-\langle AB_0,u_1\times u_2\rangle$. To prove it, let $M=[m_1\ m_2\ m_3]$ range over $3\times3$ matrices and put $E(M):=\langle m_1,(Am_2)\times m_3\rangle+\langle m_1,m_2\times(Am_3)\rangle-\operatorname{tr}(A)\langle m_1,m_2\times m_3\rangle+\langle Am_1,m_2\times m_3\rangle$. Each of the four terms is linear in each column separately: the triple product is trilinear by [F4] and multiplication by the fixed matrix $A$ is linear, so $E$ is column-multilinear. Writing the four terms as the determinants $T_1=\det[m_1,Am_2,m_3]$, $T_2=\det[m_1,m_2,Am_3]$, $T_3=-\operatorname{tr}(A)\det[m_1,m_2,m_3]$ and $T_4=\det[Am_1,m_2,m_3]$ by [F4], each interchange of two of the columns $m_1,m_2,m_3$ carries every $T_i$ to $\pm$ one of the four terms in such a way that the total reverses sign: for example exchanging the first two columns sends $T_1$ to $-T_4$, $T_4$ to $-T_1$, and $T_2,T_3$ to their own negatives, so $E\mapsto-E$; the other two interchanges are verified by the same determinant expansion. Hence $E$ is alternating as well. Therefore [F5] gives $E(M)=E(I_3)\det(M)$ for every $M$, and $E(I_3)=A_{22}+A_{33}-\operatorname{tr}(A)+A_{11}=0$, because $\langle e_1,Ae_2\times e_3\rangle=A_{22}$, $\langle e_1,e_2\times Ae_3\rangle=A_{33}$ and $\langle Ae_1,e_2\times e_3\rangle=A_{11}$ computed from the coordinate formula of [F4]. Hence $E\equiv0$, which is the displayed identity at $(B_0,u_1,u_2)=(m_1,m_2,m_3)$. [given, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Differentiation of the flux. Since $W$ and $\partial_tW$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ and $D$ is compact with finite measure, [F2] applies with $K:=D$ and gives that $\Phi$ is differentiable on $I$, with relative one-sided derivatives at included endpoints, and $\Phi'(t)=\int_D\partial_tW(p,t)\,dp$. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

2.2 The derivative of the integrand. Since $r_t=\tilde v$ and $\tilde v(p,t)=v(r(p,t),t)$, the chain rule [F3] gives $\partial_tr_u=\partial_u r_t=(D_xv)r_u$ and $\partial_tr_v=(D_xv)r_v$, so, using equality of mixed partials for the $C^2$ map $r$, $\partial_tw=((D_xv)r_u)\times r_v+r_u\times((D_xv)r_v)$; and $\partial_t\bigl[B(r(p,t),t)\bigr]=\partial_tB(r(p,t),t)+(D_xB)r_t$ by the chain rule. Hence, multiplying out and evaluating the spatial derivatives at $r(p,t)$, $\partial_tW=\langle\partial_tB+(D_xB)\tilde v,w\rangle+\langle B,\partial_tw\rangle=\langle\partial_tB+(D_xB)v+(\operatorname{div}v)B-(D_xv)B,\ w\rangle$, the last equality by step 1.2 with $A:=D_xv$, $B_0:=B$, $(u_1,u_2):=(r_u,r_v)$. [step 1.2, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 Conversion by the cross-product identity. By [F6] with $F:=v$ and $G:=B$, $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=(\operatorname{div}B)v-(\operatorname{div}v)B+(Dv)B-(DB)v$, where $(Dv)B=(D_xv)B$ and $(DB)v=(D_xB)v$; substituting into step 2.2 gives $\partial_tW=\langle\partial_tB+v\,\operatorname{div}B-\operatorname{curl}(v\times B),\ w\rangle$. [step 2.2, F6, algebra]

4.1 Identification of the terms. Fix $t\in I$ with a regular slice, so that $w=r_u\times r_v$ is nonvanishing on $D^\circ$ and $N=w/\lVert w\rVert_2$ is defined there. Writing $w=N\lVert w\rVert_2$ on $D^\circ$, the first term of the integral is $\int_D\langle\partial_tB(r,t),w\rangle\,dp=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot N\,dS$ by the surface integral formula [F8], since $w$ may degenerate only on the boundary of the Jordan region, which has content zero and does not affect the integral; the middle term gives $\int_D\langle v,w\rangle\operatorname{div}B\,dp=\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot N)\operatorname{div}B\,dS$ by the same formula; and the last term gives $\int_D\langle\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)\circ r,\ r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dp=\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ by Stokes [F7], applicable because $v\times B$ is $C^1$ on the neighbourhood $W\cap V$ of the swept set and $r(\cdot,\cdot,t)$ is a $C^2$ patch over the finite elementary Green region $D$ with $w\ne0$ on $D^\circ$. Substituting into $\Phi'(t)=\int_D\partial_tW\,dp$ from step 2.1 and step 3.1 yields $\Phi'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot N\,dS+\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot N)\operatorname{div}B\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ for every such $t$; when $\operatorname{div}B=0$ the middle term vanishes, which is the Statement. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, F7, F8, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- **Sign bookkeeping.** The boundary term appears with a minus sign because Stokes converts the flux of the curl into the circulation in the induced orientation; the additional term $(v\cdot n)\operatorname{div}B$ is absent exactly when the field is divergence-free. The example on the companion page checks both signs by direct computation.
- **Hypotheses used.** The $C^2$ regularity of $r$ is used for the equality of mixed partials, the single-valued $C^1$ velocity makes $\tilde v$ well defined, and the nonvanishing of $r_u\times r_v$ on the interior identifies the orientation; nothing is asserted for a moving interface with corners or for a velocity field that is only locally defined in space.

## Statement

Let $\omega>0$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega>0$.

**Scalar form.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr).$$

**Vector forms.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, write the same symbols for the componentwise complex-bilinear extensions of the Euclidean inner product and of the cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] to $\mathbb C^3$, and let $\operatorname{Re}$ act componentwise. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl\langle\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\langle a,\overline d\rangle\bigr),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\times\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\times\overline d\bigr),$$

the integrals of the real vector-valued integrands being componentwise. The real-valued functions $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$ are the time-dependent factors of the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] at a fixed position, with the phase absorbed into $a$ and $d$; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation: the left-hand side of the scalar identity is not $\frac12\operatorname{Re}(ad\,e^{-2i\omega t})$ in general, and the two expressions differ already at $t=0$ for $a=d=1+i$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $\omega>0$, $T=2\pi/\omega$; complex numbers $a,d\in\mathbb C$ and, in the vector forms, $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$ with the componentwise conventions of the Statement.

[F1] Complex exponential and its calculus: $\exp z=\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$ has $\exp 0=1$, is entire with $\exp'=\exp$, and satisfies the addition law $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$; for real $x,y$ one has $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$, so $|e^{i\theta}|=1$ for real $\theta$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[F2] Coordinates, conjugation and modulus: $z=a+bi$ has $\operatorname{Re}z=a$, $\operatorname{Im}z=b$, $\overline z=a-bi$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]); conjugation is a real-field automorphism with $\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w$, $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$, $\overline{\overline z}=z$, and $z\overline z=|z|^2$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]); in particular $\overline i=-i$, $\overline r=r$ for real $r$, and the field axioms of [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]] hold. Consequently, for real $\theta$, $e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta}=e^0=1$ by [F1] and $|e^{i\theta}|=1$ by [F1], so $\overline{e^{i\theta}}=\overline{e^{i\theta}}\cdot e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta}=|e^{i\theta}|^2e^{-i\theta}=e^{-i\theta}$; replacing $\theta$ by $-\theta$ gives $\overline{e^{-i\theta}}=e^{i\theta}$.

[F3] Kernel of the exponential: $\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z$, so $e^{2\pi in}=1$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$; in particular $e^{-4\pi i}=1$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]).

[F4] Real and imaginary parts of differentiable paths: identifying $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$, the maps $\operatorname{Re},\operatorname{Im}:\mathbb C\to\mathbb R$ are real-linear, so for a differentiable path $z:J\to\mathbb C$ on an interval $J$ the functions $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}z(t)$ and $t\mapsto\operatorname{Im}z(t)$ are differentiable with derivatives $\operatorname{Re}z'(t)$ and $\operatorname{Im}z'(t)$ by the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); in particular $\frac{d}{dt}e^{-2i\omega t}=-2i\omega\,e^{-2i\omega t}$, since $t\mapsto-2i\omega t$ is real-linear with derivative $-2i\omega$ and $\exp'=\exp$ by [F1].

[F5] Fundamental theorem of calculus: if $G:[\alpha,\beta]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$ and differentiable on $(\alpha,\beta)$, and $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[\alpha,\beta]$ with $f=G'$ on $(\alpha,\beta)$, then $\int_\alpha^\beta f=G(\beta)-G(\alpha)$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

[F6] Additivity of the real part: $\operatorname{Re}(u+v)=\operatorname{Re}u+\operatorname{Re}v$ for $u,v\in\mathbb C$, hence the same for every finite sum, and $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda u)=\lambda\operatorname{Re}u$ for real $\lambda$; these are the coordinate rules of the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ of [F2].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; expand each real part with $\operatorname{Re}z=(z+\overline z)/2$, exhibit an explicit antiderivative whose real part has the integrand as derivative, and evaluate it by the fundamental theorem using the period $2\pi i$ of the exponential.

1.1 Scalar algebraic identity. Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$ and $t\in\mathbb R$. By [F2], $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})=\frac12(ae^{-i\omega t}+\overline a\,\overline{e^{-i\omega t}})=\frac12(ae^{-i\omega t}+\overline a\,e^{i\omega t})$, and likewise $\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})=\frac12(de^{-i\omega t}+\overline d\,e^{i\omega t})$. Multiplying the two real expressions and using the conjugation rules of [F2] throughout gives $4\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})=ad\,e^{-2i\omega t}+a\overline d+\overline a\,d+\overline a\overline d\,e^{2i\omega t}$. Since $\overline{ad\,e^{-2i\omega t}}=\overline a\overline d\,e^{2i\omega t}$ and $\overline{a\overline d}=\overline a\,d$ by [F2], the first and fourth terms are conjugate, as are the second and third, so the last display equals $2\operatorname{Re}(ad\,e^{-2i\omega t})+2\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d)=2\operatorname{Re}(ad\,e^{-2i\omega t}+a\overline d)$ by [F6]; hence $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(ad\,e^{-2i\omega t}+a\overline d)$. [given, F2, F6, algebra]

2.1 Antiderivative. Define $\Phi(t):=\dfrac{ad\,e^{-2i\omega t}}{-2i\omega}+a\overline d\,t$ for $t\in\mathbb R$; the division is by the nonzero complex number $-2i\omega$, and $\Phi$ is differentiable with $\Phi'(t)=ad\,e^{-2i\omega t}+a\overline d$ by [F1], [F4] and the algebra of derivatives: the derivative of $e^{-2i\omega t}$ is $-2i\omega\,e^{-2i\omega t}$ because $\exp'=\exp$ ([F1]) and the parameter map is real-linear. Hence the real function $G:=\operatorname{Re}\Phi$ is continuous on $[0,T]$ and differentiable on $(0,T)$ with derivative $G'(t)=\operatorname{Re}\Phi'(t)=\operatorname{Re}(ad\,e^{-2i\omega t}+a\overline d)=2\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})$ by [F4] and step 1.1; in particular $G'$ is continuous, hence Riemann integrable on $[0,T]$. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra]

3.1 Scalar identity. Since $2\omega T=4\pi$, the kernel computation of [F3] gives $e^{-2i\omega T}=e^{-4\pi i}=1$; therefore $\Phi(T)=\dfrac{ad}{-2i\omega}+a\overline d\,T$ and $\Phi(0)=\dfrac{ad}{-2i\omega}$, so $\Phi(T)-\Phi(0)=a\overline d\,T$. The fundamental theorem [F5] applied to $G$ and $G'$ gives $\int_0^TG'=G(T)-G(0)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\Phi(T)-\Phi(0)\bigr)=T\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d)$ by [F6]. Since $G'=2\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})$ by step 2.1, dividing the identity $\int_0^TG'=T\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d)$ by $2T>0$ gives the scalar form of the Statement. [step 2.1, F3, F5, F6, algebra]

4.1 Vector forms. Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$ and $F(t):=\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$, $G(t):=\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})$, both in $\mathbb R^3$. Fix $t\in\mathbb R$. Step 1.1 applied to the complex pairs $(a_j,d_k)$ gives $F_jG_k=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a_j\overline{d_k}e^{-2i\omega t}+a_j\overline{d_k})$ for all $j,k$, so by finite additivity and real homogeneity of $\operatorname{Re}$ [F6] and the component formulas of the complex-bilinear inner product and cross product, $\langle F,G\rangle=\sum_{j<3}F_jG_j=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\langle a,\overline d\rangle e^{-2i\omega t}+\langle a,\overline d\rangle)$, and $(F\times G)_i=\sum_{j,k<3}\epsilon_{ijk}F_jG_k=\frac12\operatorname{Re}((a\times\overline d)_i\,e^{-2i\omega t}+(a\times\overline d)_i)$ for $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, where $(a\times\overline d)_i=\sum_{j,k<3}\epsilon_{ijk}a_j\overline{d_k}$ and the real factors $\epsilon_{ijk}\in\{-1,0,1\}$ pass through $\operatorname{Re}$ by [F6]. Each of these two real functions of $t$ is of the form $\operatorname{Re}(ce^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\omega t})$ with the complex number $c:=\langle a,\overline d\rangle$ respectively $c:=(a\times\overline d)_i$, as step 1.1 applied to the pair $(c,1)$ shows; applying the one-variable argument of steps 2.1 and 3.1 with that pair gives $\frac1T\int_0^T\langle F,G\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\langle a,\overline d\rangle$ and $\frac1T\int_0^T(F\times G)_i\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}((a\times\overline d)_i)$ for every $i$, which is the componentwise statement of the vector forms. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F6, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The conjugation in $\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d)$ is essential and cannot be absorbed into the amplitudes: at $t=0$ with $a=d=1+i$ one has $\operatorname{Re}(a)\operatorname{Re}(d)=1$ while $\frac12\operatorname{Re}(ad)=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(2i)=0$, so the real quadratic form and the complex square differ even pointwise.
- The proof uses no choice principle: only the power-series exponential, its kernel, the fundamental theorem and real-linear algebra of $\operatorname{Re}$ enter, and the integrand is a continuous real function on a compact interval.

## Statement

Let $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$ be real for $j=1,2$, put $Z_j:=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}$ for the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]], and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfy the two linear equations

$$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad \frac{E_i-E_r}{Z_1}=\frac{E_t}{Z_2}.$$

Then

$$\frac{E_r}{E_i}=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1},\qquad \frac{E_t}{E_i}=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2},$$

and the real numbers $R:=\bigl\lvert E_r/E_i\bigr\rvert^2$ and $T:=\bigl(Z_1/Z_2\bigr)\bigl\lvert E_t/E_i\bigr\rvert^2$ satisfy

$$R+T=1 .$$

The two displayed equations are assumptions, not derived from any wave or field model; the ratio definitions of $R$ and $T$ are algebraic, and no electromagnetic validity is asserted. Oblique incidence, complex impedance and anisotropic media require further systems and branch conventions and are outside this statement.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Real numbers $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$ for $j=1,2$, the square roots $Z_j=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}$, and complex numbers $E_i,E_r,E_t$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfying $E_i+E_r=E_t$ and $(E_i-E_r)/Z_1=E_t/Z_2$.

[L1] Square roots and positivity: for real $x\ge0$ there is a unique $s\ge0$ with $s^2=x$, written $\sqrt x$, and $x>0$ implies $\sqrt x>0$; also $\sqrt{x^2}=x$ for $x\ge0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]). Order and field arithmetic in $\mathbb R$ are those of [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: sums and products of positive reals are positive, a positive real is nonzero, and $\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb C$ under the embedding of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], on which the field operations of $\mathbb C$ restrict to those of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

[L2] Modulus and conjugation: for $z\in\mathbb C$, $|z|^2=z\overline z$, and if $z$ is real then $\overline z=z$, so $|z|^2=z^2$ for real $z$; also $|zw|=|z||w|$ and $|z|\ge0$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; solve the two linear equations by substitution, then substitute the resulting ratios into the algebraic expressions defining $R$ and $T$.

1.1 Positivity and invertibility. Since $\mu_j>0$ and $\varepsilon_j>0$, the quotients $\mu_j/\varepsilon_j$ are positive by [L1], so $Z_j=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}>0$ for $j=1,2$; in particular $Z_1,Z_2\ne0$ and $Z_1+Z_2>0$, so $Z_1+Z_2$, $Z_1Z_2$ and $E_i$ are invertible complex numbers. [given, L1, algebra]

2.1 Solving the system. Substituting the first equation $E_t=E_i+E_r$ into the second gives $\dfrac{E_i-E_r}{Z_1}=\dfrac{E_i+E_r}{Z_2}$; multiplying by the nonzero number $Z_1Z_2$ and collecting terms yields $Z_2E_i-Z_2E_r=Z_1E_i+Z_1E_r$, that is, $E_r(Z_1+Z_2)=E_i(Z_2-Z_1)$. Dividing by the nonzero numbers $E_i$ and $Z_1+Z_2$ gives $\dfrac{E_r}{E_i}=\dfrac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_1+Z_2}$, and then $\dfrac{E_t}{E_i}=1+\dfrac{E_r}{E_i}=\dfrac{Z_1+Z_2+Z_2-Z_1}{Z_1+Z_2}=\dfrac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}$ by the field arithmetic of [L1]. Both ratios are real numbers, since all $Z_j$ are real. [step 1.1, L1, algebra]

3.1 The balance $R+T=1$. Because the ratios of step 2.1 are real, [L2] gives $\bigl\lvert E_r/E_i\bigr\rvert^2=\bigl(\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_1+Z_2}\bigr)^2$ and $\bigl\lvert E_t/E_i\bigr\rvert^2=\bigl(\frac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}\bigr)^2$, so $R=\frac{(Z_2-Z_1)^2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}$ and $T=\frac{Z_1}{Z_2}\cdot\frac{4Z_2^2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}=\frac{4Z_1Z_2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}$, and therefore $R+T=\frac{(Z_2-Z_1)^2+4Z_1Z_2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}=\frac{Z_2^2-2Z_1Z_2+Z_1^2+4Z_1Z_2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}=\frac{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}=1$ by the expansion $(Z_1+Z_2)^2=Z_1^2+2Z_1Z_2+Z_2^2$ and the invertibility of $Z_1+Z_2$ from step 1.1. [step 2.1, L1, L2, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- In the period-averaged reading of the amplitudes as time-harmonic complex phasors, [[lem-em-period-average]] with $a=d=A$ gives $\frac1{T_0}\int_0^{T_0}\operatorname{Re}(Ae^{-i\omega t})^2\,dt=\frac12|A|^2$ for $\omega>0$ and $T_0=2\pi/\omega$, so $\bigl\lvert E_r/E_i\bigr\rvert^2$ is the ratio of the mean squares of the real reflected and incident fields and $T$ differs from the corresponding transmitted mean-square ratio by the real factor $Z_1/Z_2$; the identity $R+T=1$ itself is the algebraic consequence proved above and does not rest on any field model.
- Neither the system nor the conclusion involves $\mathrm{AC}$ or any choice principle; it is finite algebra in $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$. The equations are satisfied by $E_t=E_i$, $E_r=0$ exactly when $Z_1=Z_2$, in which case $R=0$, $T=1$.

## Example

Take the unit square $D=[0,1]^2$ as parameter region, an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, a function $a\in C^2(I)$ with $a>0$ everywhere, and

$$r(u,v,t):=\bigl(a(t)u,\ a(t)v,\ 0\bigr),\qquad B:=e_3,\qquad v(x,t):=\frac{a'(t)}{a(t)}\,(x_1,x_2,0).$$

Then $r$ is of class $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2\times I$, the tangent vectors are $r_u=(a,0,0)$ and $r_v=(0,a,0)$ with $r_u\times r_v=(0,0,a^2)\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I^\circ=D^\circ\times I$, the field $B$ is constant with $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and $v$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3\times I$ with $v(r(u,v,t),t)=(a'(t)u,a'(t)v,0)=r_t(u,v,t)$; so the data satisfy the standing hypotheses of [[def-em-moving-patch]]. For every $t\in I$ the parametrized flux is $\Phi(t)=a(t)^2$, hence $\Phi'(t)=2a(t)a'(t)$; the fixed-time surface integral of $\partial_tB$ is $0$; and $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=-2(a'(t)/a(t))\,e_3$, so patch Stokes gives $\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r=-2a(t)a'(t)$, exactly the sign in the formula of [[lem-em-moving-flux]]. Dropping the term $-\oint(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ — that is, treating the moving patch as fixed — would leave $\Phi'=0$, which the direct derivative contradicts whenever $a'(t)\ne0$. All maps are of the stated regularity and no singular support is involved; the example verifies the sign convention and the necessity of the motion term, and asserts no physical law.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The unit square $D=[0,1]^2$; an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$; a function $a\in C^2(I)$ with $a>0$; the maps $r$, $B$, $v$ displayed in the Example; and a fixed time $t\in I$.

[L1] Moving patch and transport identity: in the setting of [[def-em-moving-patch]] with $\operatorname{div}B=0$ on its domain, the flux $\Phi(\tau)=\int_D\langle B(r(p,\tau),\tau),r_u(p,\tau)\times r_v(p,\tau)\rangle\,dp$ is differentiable on $I$ and, at every $\tau\in I$ at which $r_u\times r_v$ is nonvanishing on $D^\circ$, satisfies $\Phi'(\tau)=\int_{S(\tau)}\partial_\tau B\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(\tau)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$, with the induced orientation and boundary chain ([[lem-em-moving-flux]]).

[L2] The unit square is an elementary Green region: with $a_0=0$, $b_0=1$, $\alpha\equiv0$, $\beta\equiv1$ on $[0,1]$, the set $D$ has both the Type I description $\{(x,y):0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le1\}$ and the analogous Type II description, so it is a compact elementary Green region, hence a finite elementary Green region, and it is compact and Jordan measurable; its volume is $\operatorname{vol}(D)=(1-0)(1-0)=1$ ([[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], [[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]).

[L3] Integrals of constants over $D$: for every constant $c$, the Riemann integral over the Jordan set $D$ is $\int_Dc\,du\,dv=c$. Indeed $D$ is its own nondegenerate bounding rectangle, so by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]] $\int_Dc$ is the Darboux integral of $c$ over $D$; on every cell of every grid partition both the infimum and the supremum of $c$ equal $c$, so every lower and upper Darboux sum equals $c\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=c\operatorname{vol}(D)=c$ by [[def-multidimensional-darboux-sums]], [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]] and [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]], whence the common value is $c$ ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]).

[L4] Calculus and vector analysis rules: $a>0$ makes $a'/a$ of class $C^1$ on $I$ and $v$ of class $C^1$ jointly in $(x,t)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); the product rule gives $(a^2)'=2aa'$, and the time derivative of the constant field $B$ satisfies $\partial_tB\equiv0$; the partial derivatives, divergence, curl, cross product and Euclidean inner product are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[L5] Patch Stokes: for a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region and a $C^1$ field $G$ on a neighbourhood of its image, $\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}G\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_D\langle(\operatorname{curl}G)\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\rangle$, with the induced boundary chain, the positive boundary orientation and the line integrals as cited ([[thm-the-classical-stokes-theorem-for-a-c2-surface-patch]], [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]], [[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]], [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]], [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct; evaluate the parametrized flux and its derivative, evaluate the two terms of the transport identity by explicit vector calculus and Stokes, and compare.

1.1 Setting and regularity. The map $r(u,v,t)=(a(t)u,a(t)v,0)$ is of class $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2\times I$, since it is polynomial in $(u,v)$ with $C^2$ coefficients, with $r_u=(a,0,0)$, $r_v=(0,a,0)$ and $r_u\times r_v=(0,0,a^2)\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I$ because $a>0$; further $v(x,t)=\frac{a'(t)}{a(t)}(x_1,x_2,0)$ is $C^1$ jointly, and $v(r(u,v,t),t)=\frac{a'}{a}(au,av,0)=(a'u,a'v,0)=r_t(u,v,t)$, while $\operatorname{div}B=0$ for the constant field $B=e_3$. So all hypotheses of [L1] hold, and $D$ is the elementary Green region of [L2]. [given, L1, L2, L4, algebra]

2.1 The flux and its derivative. At each $\tau$, $\langle B(r),\ r_u\times r_v\rangle=\langle e_3,(0,0,a(\tau)^2)\rangle=a(\tau)^2$, a constant in $(u,v)$; hence by [L3] $\Phi(\tau)=\int_Da(\tau)^2\,du\,dv=a(\tau)^2$. Therefore $\Phi'(t)=2a(t)a'(t)$ for every $t\in I$ by the product rule of [L4]. [step 1.1, L3, L4, algebra]

2.2 The two terms on the right-hand side. Since $B$ is constant, $\partial_tB\equiv0$ and the surface integral $\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS$ vanishes. For the boundary term, [L4] gives $v\times B=\frac{a'}{a}(x_1,x_2,0)\times(0,0,1)=\frac{a'}{a}(x_2,-x_1,0)$ and then $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=\bigl(0,0,\partial_1(-\tfrac{a'}{a}x_1)-\partial_2(\tfrac{a'}{a}x_2)\bigr)=(0,0,-2\tfrac{a'}{a})=-2\tfrac{a'}{a}e_3$ at time $t$; consequently $(\operatorname{curl}(v\times B))\circ r=-2\tfrac{a'}{a}e_3$ is constant on $D$, and patch Stokes [L5] together with the constant-integral fact [L3] gives $\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_D\langle-2\tfrac{a'}{a}e_3,(0,0,a^2)\rangle\,du\,dv=-2\tfrac{a'}{a}a^2\int_Ddu\,dv=-2a(t)a'(t)$. [step 1.1, L3, L4, L5, algebra]

3.1 Comparison. Substituting steps 2.1 and 2.2 into the identity of [L1] gives $2a(t)a'(t)=0-(-2a(t)a'(t))$, so the transport identity of [[lem-em-moving-flux]] holds exactly, with the boundary term contributing $+2a(t)a'(t)$ to $\Phi'$; if that boundary term is dropped, the identity would read $\Phi'(t)=0$, contradicting step 2.1 whenever $a'(t)\ne0$. The example therefore checks the sign convention and the necessity of the motion term at a fully smooth, singular-free configuration, and it asserts no physical law. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- When $a$ is constant, $\Phi(t)=a^2$ is constant, both terms of the identity vanish, and the contrast with the fixed-patch reading disappears; the example's discriminating case is therefore any $t$ with $a'(t)\ne0$.
- The computation uses no choice principle; it is finite algebra and one application of the published Stokes theorem for a patch over the unit square.

## Definition

Let $4:=\{0,1,2,3\}$ and let $V:=\mathbb R^4$ be the set of all functions
$4\to\mathbb R$, with the pointwise vector-space structure of
[[def-function-space]]; so $V$ is the function space $F^X$ of
[[def-function-space]] at $F=\mathbb R$ and $X=4$, and its elements are written
$v=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v^a:=v(a)$ for $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, the components
being indexed from $0$ and written with an upper index; the index conventions
used throughout this item are fixed below. Let $A$ be the same set
$\mathbb R^4$, whose elements are
now called **points**, together with the map

$$V\times A\to A,\qquad (v,p)\mapsto v+p,$$

given by pointwise addition of functions. Then the following three conditions
hold.

1. $(v+v')+p=v+(v'+p)$ for all $v,v'\in V$ and all $p\in A$.
2. $0+p=p$ for every $p\in A$.
3. For all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $v+p=q$, namely
$v=q-p$.

Conditions 1 and 2 are read at each of the four coordinates from the field
axioms of $\mathbb R$, and condition 3 holds because $q-p$ satisfies
$(q-p)+p=q$ coordinatewise while any $v$ with $v+p=q$ agrees with $q-p$ at every
coordinate ([[def-vector-space]]). A triple consisting of a set $A$, a vector
space $V$ and a map $V\times A\to A$ satisfying 1–3 is called an **affine
space** with **translation space** $V$; the three conditions are its definition,
so by 1–3 the set $A$ above is an affine space with translation space $V$.

For $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ let $e_a\in V$ be given by $e_a(b):=1$ for $b=a$ and
$e_a(b):=0$ for $b\ne a$. Then $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis of $V$
([[def-linear-basis]]): every $v\in V$ equals $v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$, because
the two sides have the same value at each $b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$; and if
$c^0e_0+\dots+c^3e_3=0_V$ then evaluating at $b$ gives $c^b=0$, so the list is
linearly independent. We write $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ and use the coordinate
columns of [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]] with respect to
this ordered basis.

**The Minkowski form.** Define

$$\eta(v,w):=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3,\qquad v,w\in V .$$

This is the standard bilinear form $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i<n}x_iy_i$ of
[[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]] with the sign of the first
coordinate reversed, together with the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the last three coordinates; directly from the
formula, for fixed $w$ the assignment $v\mapsto\eta(v,w)$ is a linear combination
of the component functions $v\mapsto v^a$, hence linear, and similarly in $w$,
so $\eta$ is a bilinear form, and $\eta(v,w)=\eta(w,v)$ for all $v,w$, so it is
symmetric ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Its matrix in
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is

$$(\eta(e_a,e_b))_{a,b}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1),$$

and this matrix is its own inverse, the product of
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with itself being the identity matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]); in particular it is invertible, so
$\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]).

**Index conventions.** The components $v^a$ of a vector are the numbers in its
expansion $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, and
for a linear map $T:V\to V$ one writes $(Tv)^a$ for the components of $Tv$ and
$T^a{}_b$ for the matrix entries, so that $(Tv)^a=\sum_bT^a{}_bv^b$. Write
$\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)$, so that
$(\eta_{ab})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let $(\eta^{ab})$ denote the
inverse matrix of $(\eta_{ab})$, that is, $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=1$ when
$a=c$ and $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=0$ when $a\ne c$. The **lowered** components
of $v$ are $v_a:=\sum_b\eta_{ab}v^b$, and the operation is inverted by
$v^a=\sum_b\eta^{ab}v_b$, because $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is its own
inverse; explicitly $v_0=-v^0$ and $v_i=v^i$ for $i=1,2,3$. In these
conventions $\eta(v,w)=\sum_{a,b}\eta_{ab}v^aw^b=\sum_av_aw^a$ for all
$v,w\in V$.

**Causal classification.** Let $v\in V$ with $v\ne0$. Then $v$ is
**timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$, and
**spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$. If the
nonzero $v$ is causal, then $v^0\ne0$: the inequality
$-(v^0)^2+(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2\le0$ gives
$(v^0)^2\ge(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2$, and $v^0=0$ would force
$(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=0$, hence $v^1=v^2=v^3=0$ and $v=0$, contrary to the
hypothesis. A nonzero causal $v$ is therefore **future-directed** when $v^0>0$
and **past-directed** when $v^0<0$, and exactly one of these two alternatives
holds for a nonzero real $v^0$ ([[def-real-order]]). The **future causal cone**
is

$$C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\},$$

whose elements are exactly the future-directed causal vectors; the zero vector
is not in $C^+$, because it fails $v^0>0$.

**Orientation.** The **standard orientation** of $V$ is the orientation class of
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

**Lorentz maps.** A **Lorentz map** is a linear map $L:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) that is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) and satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V .$$

Writing $M:=[L]_{(e_0,\dots,e_3)}\in M_4(\mathbb R)$ for the matrix of $L$ in the
ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), $M^{\mathsf T}$ for its
transpose ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]), and $\eta$ also for the matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the condition is the matrix identity

$$M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta .$$

Expanding $Lv$ and $Lw$ in the basis gives
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\sum_{c,d}(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}v^cw^d$, whereas
$\eta(v,w)=\sum_{c,d}\eta_{cd}v^cw^d$, and the two sides agree for all $v,w$
exactly when $(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}=\eta_{cd}$ for every $c,d$, since
inserting the basis vectors $v=e_c$, $w=e_d$ gives the converse
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Equivalently, the matrix of $\eta$
in the basis $(Le_0,\dots,Le_3)$ is again
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; this is the change-of-basis congruence of
[[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] for the basis change
from $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ to its image under the invertible map $L$. The
invertibility requirement in the definition of a Lorentz map is in fact
automatic: if $L$ satisfies the displayed identity and $Lv=0$, then
$\eta(v,w)=\eta(Lv,Lw)=0$ for every $w$, so $v$ lies in the left radical of
$\eta$, which is $\{0\}$ because $\eta$ is nondegenerate; thus $L$ is injective,
and an injective linear endomorphism of the four-dimensional space $V$ is
surjective by [[thm-rank-nullity]] together with
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], so $L$ is a bijection, and its inverse
$S:=L^{-1}$ is linear: for all $x,y\in V$ and all reals $a,b$, linearity of $L$
gives $L(aS(x)+bS(y))=ax+by$, and applying $S$ gives
$S(ax+by)=aS(x)+bS(y)$; thus $L$ is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]). The map $L$ is
**proper** when $\det L=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** when $L(C^+)=C^+$.

**Frames.** A **frame** of $A$ is a point $o\in A$ together with an ordered
basis $(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ such that
$\eta(u_a,u_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ and
$u_0\in C^+$. The **coordinates** of $p\in A$ in that frame are the unique
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^4$ with
$p=o+x^0u_0+x^1u_1+x^2u_2+x^3u_3$; uniqueness holds because
$(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ is an ordered basis, and $p-o$ is the unique element of $V$
carrying $o$ to $p$.

**Tensors and components.** A **tensor of type $(p,q)$** on $V$ is a multilinear
map $(V^*)^p\times V^q\to\mathbb R$
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]), not an array: covectors are the
$(0,1)$ case, a vector $v$ is regarded as the $(1,0)$ tensor
$\theta\mapsto\theta(v)$ through the canonical evaluation of $V$ in its double
dual, and two-forms are the skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ case. Under the coordinate
change $x'=Lx$ of the frame by a Lorentz map
$L$ — that is, when the coordinates of the same point in a new frame are
$x'=Lx$ with the origin unchanged, so that the new basis vectors are
$L^{-1}u_a$ — the components of a vector $v$, a covector $\theta$ and a two-form
$F$ satisfy

$$v'=Lv,\qquad \theta'=(L^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\theta,\qquad F'(v,w)=F(L^{-1}v,L^{-1}w),$$

where $(L^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$ is the transpose map of
[[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]] applied to $\theta$; these are the component
readings of the displacement law $v'=Lv$, of $\theta'=\theta\circ L^{-1}$ for a
covector, and of $F'=F\circ(L^{-1}\times L^{-1})$ for a two-form. The basis
$(L^{-1}u_0,\dots,L^{-1}u_3)$ is again a frame whenever $L$ is orthochronous.

Finally, a fixed positive real $c$ is separate extra structure: the coordinate
$x^0$ has the dimension of length, and the time coordinate is $t:=x^0/c$. No
physical claim is made here; in particular the identification of $A$ with
physical spacetime, of $C^+$ with the future light cone, and of $c$ with the
speed of light in vacuum are later physical premises.

## Remarks

- **Sign convention.** The form has signature $(-1,1,1,1)$: with the index
conventions of the Definition, $v^0$ is the time component and $v^1,v^2,v^3$
are the spatial components of $v$; the lowered time component $v_0=-v^0$
carries the opposite sign, while $v_i=v^i$ for $i=1,2,3$.
- **What is not asserted.** The affine space, the form, the cone and the
transformation laws are mathematical data and conventions; the physical readings
of these objects, and any statement that some physical trajectory or force
equation has this form, are separate premises that this item does not supply.

## Statement

Let $0\le\beta<1$ and put $\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}>0$
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). Define
$\Lambda_\beta:V\to V$ by $(\Lambda_\beta v)^0=\gamma(v^0-\beta v^1)$,
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^1=\gamma(v^1-\beta v^0)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)^2=v^2$,
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^3=v^3$. Then $\Lambda_\beta$ is linear
([[def-linear-map]]), $\Lambda_\beta$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map,
and more precisely: (a) $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$ for
all $v,w\in V$; (b) $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; (c) $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$;
(d) $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$. In particular a future causal vector
has future causal image and $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=\eta(v,v)$
for every $v$ ([[def-real-order]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]]). The hypothesis
$0\le\beta<1$ is not removable: at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $\beta$ with $0\le\beta<1$, the number
$\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$, the map $\Lambda_\beta:V\to V$ defined in the
statement, and the Minkowski space $(V,\eta)$ of
[[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]].

[L1] On $V=\mathbb R^4$ the form
$\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$ is bilinear and symmetric with matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; the future causal cone is
$C^+=\{v:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\}$; a Lorentz map is an invertible linear
$L:V\to V$ with $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$; the map $L$ is proper
when $\det L=1$ and orthochronous when $L(C^+)=C^+$
([[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]).

[L2] For $a>0$ and rationals $r,s$ the powers of [[def-rational-power]]
satisfy $a^r>0$, $a^{r+s}=a^ra^s$ and $a^{-r}=(a^r)^{-1}$
([[lem-rational-power-laws]]). With $a:=1-\beta^2$, which is positive by the
hypothesis, this gives $\gamma=a^{-1/2}>0$ and
$\gamma^2a=a^{-1/2}a^{-1/2}=a^{-1}=1/a$, so $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$.

[L3] For $a,b\ge0$ one has $a\le b$ exactly when $a^2\le b^2$
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]), and the order of $\mathbb R$ is total, with
$|x|=x$ for $x\ge0$ ([[def-real-order]]); in particular $0\le\beta<1$ gives
$\beta^2<1$ and $1-\beta>0$.

[L4] In an ordered basis the $j$-th column of the matrix of a linear map $T$ is
the coordinate column of $T(b_j)$, and the coordinate column of $v$ records the
coefficients in $v=\sum_jx_jb_j$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]).

[L5] The determinant of an operator on a finite-dimensional space is the
determinant of its coordinate matrix in any ordered basis
([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]).

[L6] If $A=[T]_{\mathcal B}$ is row-reduced to an upper triangular matrix $U$
using only row additions, then the determinant is unchanged by each addition and
$\det(U)$ is the product of the diagonal entries of $U$
([[cor-operator-determinant-by-row-reduction]]).

[L7] An invertible linear map has a unique inverse linear map $T^{-1}$ with
$T^{-1}\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V$ and
$T\circ T^{-1}=\operatorname{id}_V$
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]).

[L8] A map $T:V\to V$ is linear when $T(av+bw)=aT(v)+bT(w)$ for all
$a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $v,w\in V$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $\Lambda_\beta$ is linear: in components $(\Lambda_\beta u)^0=\gamma u^0-\gamma\beta u^1$, $(\Lambda_\beta u)^1=-\gamma\beta u^0+\gamma u^1$, $(\Lambda_\beta u)^2=u^2$, $(\Lambda_\beta u)^3=u^3$, so each component of $\Lambda_\beta u$ is a real linear combination of the components of $u$, and since addition and scalar multiplication in $V$ are pointwise, $\Lambda_\beta(au+a'u')=a\Lambda_\beta u+a'\Lambda_\beta u'$ for all reals $a,a'$; this is linearity in the sense of [L8]. [given, L8, algebra]

1.2 (a) For all $v,w\in V$ one has $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$, and the same computation holds with $-\beta$ in place of $\beta$: substituting the displayed components into the form of [L1] gives $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\gamma^2[-(v^0-\beta v^1)(w^0-\beta w^1)+(v^1-\beta v^0)(w^1-\beta w^0)]+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$, the bracket expands to $-(1-\beta^2)v^0w^0+(1-\beta^2)v^1w^1$, and $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ by [L2], so the whole expression equals $-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3=\eta(v,w)$; only $\beta^2$ occurs, so the computation with $-\beta$ is identical. [given, L1, L2, algebra]

1.3 (d) $\Lambda_{-\beta}\circ\Lambda_\beta=\operatorname{id}_V=\Lambda_\beta\circ\Lambda_{-\beta}$: the map $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ is given by the same formulas with $-\beta$ and is linear by the same component computation as the one displayed for $\Lambda_\beta$, and using $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ one computes $(\Lambda_{-\beta}(\Lambda_\beta v))^0=\gamma((\Lambda_\beta v)^0+\beta(\Lambda_\beta v)^1)=\gamma(\gamma(v^0-\beta v^1)+\beta\gamma(v^1-\beta v^0))=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)v^0=v^0$ and likewise $(\Lambda_{-\beta}(\Lambda_\beta v))^1=\gamma((\Lambda_\beta v)^1+\beta(\Lambda_\beta v)^0)=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)v^1=v^1$, while both maps fix the last two components; the composite $\Lambda_\beta\circ\Lambda_{-\beta}$ is the same computation with $\beta$ and $-\beta$ interchanged. Hence $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ is a two-sided inverse of $\Lambda_\beta$, and by the uniqueness of the inverse in [L7], $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$. [given, L2, L7, algebra]

1.4 At $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ is undefined: there $1-\beta^2=0$, while $a^{-1/2}$ is defined for $a>0$ and $0^r$ only for rational $r>0$ [L2], so the hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ cannot be dropped. [given, L2]

1.5 (b, matrix) The matrix $M$ of $\Lambda_\beta$ in the basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ has first column the coordinate column $(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)$, second column $(-\gamma\beta,\gamma,0,0)$ and last two columns those of the identity matrix (the matrix is symmetric, so these are also its first two rows): by [L4] its columns are the coordinate columns of the images of the basis vectors, and the displayed component formulas give $\Lambda_\beta e_0=\gamma e_0-\gamma\beta e_1$, $\Lambda_\beta e_1=-\gamma\beta e_0+\gamma e_1$, $\Lambda_\beta e_2=e_2$, $\Lambda_\beta e_3=e_3$. [given, L4, algebra]

2.1 (b) $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$: replacing the second row of the matrix of step 1.5 by (second row) $+\beta$(first row) changes only its first entry, $-\gamma\beta+\beta\gamma=0$, and leaves an upper triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are $\gamma$, $\gamma-\beta^2\gamma=\gamma(1-\beta^2)$, $1$, $1$; row additions leave the determinant unchanged and the determinant of an upper triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries [L6], so $\det\Lambda_\beta=\gamma\cdot\gamma(1-\beta^2)\cdot1\cdot1=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$, the last step using that the determinant of the operator is the determinant of its coordinate matrix [L5] and that $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ [L2]. [step 1.5, L2, L5, L6, algebra]

2.2 (c, inclusion) Both $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)\subseteq C^+$ and $\Lambda_{-\beta}(C^+)\subseteq C^+$: if $v\in C^+$ then $v^0>0$ and $(v^1)^2\le(v^0)^2$, so $|v^1|\le v^0$ by [L3], and since $0\le\beta<1$ one has $(\Lambda_\beta v)^0=\gamma(v^0-\beta v^1)\ge\gamma(v^0-\beta|v^1|)\ge\gamma(1-\beta)v^0>0$ and $(\Lambda_{-\beta}v)^0=\gamma(v^0+\beta v^1)\ge\gamma(1-\beta)v^0>0$, while $\eta(\Lambda_{\pm\beta}v,\Lambda_{\pm\beta}v)=\eta(v,v)\le0$ by step 1.2; these are exactly the two defining conditions of $C^+$. [step 1.2, L2, L3, algebra]

3.1 (c) $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$: step 2.2 gives the inclusion $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)\subseteq C^+$ and also $\Lambda_{-\beta}(C^+)\subseteq C^+$, which by $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$ from step 1.3 says $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}(C^+)\subseteq C^+$; for $u\in C^+$ the vector $v:=\Lambda_\beta^{-1}u$ then lies in $C^+$ and satisfies $u=\Lambda_\beta v$, so $C^+\subseteq\Lambda_\beta(C^+)$, and with the inclusion the two sets are equal. [step 1.3, step 2.2]

3.2 In particular every future causal vector has future causal image, namely the inclusion from step 2.2, and $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=\eta(v,v)$ for every $v$ is step 1.2 with $w=v$. [step 1.2, step 2.2]

4.1 $\Lambda_\beta$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map: it is linear by step 1.1, it satisfies $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$ by step 1.2, and it has the two-sided inverse $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ by step 1.3, so it is a Lorentz map in the sense of [L1]; $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$ by step 2.1 makes it proper and $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$ by step 3.1 makes it orthochronous. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L7]

5.1 All claims of the statement are established — linearity in step 1.1, (a) in step 1.2, (d) in step 1.3, the excluded endpoint in step 1.4, (b) in steps 1.5 and 2.1, (c) in steps 2.2 and 3.1, the proper orthochronous Lorentz property in step 4.1 and the consequence for future causal vectors in step 3.2 — so the hypothesis is exactly as stated. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1] ∎
