## Statement

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]) and let
$z:J\to\mathbb R^4$ be of class $C^1$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))<0$ and
$z^0{}'(s)>0$ for every $s\in J$; $z'$ is the derivative of the vector-valued
curve ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) and such a $z$ is called a
$C^1$ future timelike curve. Put $g(s):=-\eta(z'(s),z'(s))>0$, fix $s_0\in J$,
and define $\tau(s):=c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{g(u)}\,du$ for $s\in J$. Then:
(1) $g$ is continuous on $J$ and so is $s\mapsto\sqrt{g(s)}$, where
$\sqrt{\cdot}$ is the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]],
[[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); (2) $\tau$ is differentiable on
$J$ with $\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}>0$, hence $\tau$ is strictly increasing on
$J$, injective, and continuous
([[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]],
[[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]); (3) the inverse
$\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to J$ is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of the
interval $\tau[J]$, with $(\tau^{-1})'(\tau(s))=c/\sqrt{g(s)}$
([[thm-continuous-inverse]], [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]]); (4) the
reparametrized curve $z\circ\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to\mathbb R^4$ is differentiable
at every $\tau(s)$, with tangent $U(\tau(s)):=c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$ satisfying
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[thm-chain-rule]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]); (5) if instead
$\eta(z'(s),z'(s))=0$ for all $s\in J$, then $g=0$, $\tau\equiv0$ on $J$ and
$\tau$ is not injective, so a null curve carries no proper-time parametrization
([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]); (6) if $z(s)=p+sv$ with
$\eta(v,v)<0$ and $v^0>0$, then
$\tau(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,(s-s_0)$ and
$U=c\,v/\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$ is constant
([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[def-derivative]]). The
identification of such straight lines with inertial motion is a physical premise
and is not asserted here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a $C^1$ future
timelike curve $z:J\to\mathbb R^4$ with $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))<0$ and
$z^0{}'(s)>0$ for all $s\in J$, the function $g(s):=-\eta(z'(s),z'(s))>0$, a
point $s_0\in J$, and the function $\tau(s):=c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{g(u)}\,du$
of the statement.

[L1] On $V=\mathbb R^4$ the form $\eta$ is symmetric and bilinear with matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $c$ is a fixed positive real
([[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]).

[L2] A nonempty open interval is order-convex, its defining inequalities are
strict, so each of its points has a neighbourhood contained in it and it has at
least two elements ([[def-interval]]).

[L3] A map into $\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when all its components are of
class $C^k$; for $k=1$ this means that every component has a continuous first
derivative ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[L4] For a curve $f$ into $\mathbb R^m$ and a limit point $c$ of its domain, $f$
is differentiable at $c$ exactly when every component is, and then
$f'(c)_i=f_i'(c)$; sums and scalar multiples of differentiable curves are
differentiable with the expected derivatives
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]).

[L5] Every real $a\ge0$ has a unique $\sqrt{a}\ge0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2=a$
([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[L6] For $a,b\ge0$ one has $a\le b$ exactly when $a^2\le b^2$
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[L7] Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values and quotients (where
defined) of functions continuous at a point are continuous there, and constant
functions and $x\mapsto x^n$ are continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]).

[L8] If $I$ is order-convex and $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and injective,
then $f$ is strictly monotone, $f[I]$ is order-convex, $f:I\to f[I]$ is a
bijection, and the inverse is continuous ([[thm-continuous-inverse]]).

[L9] Composites of continuous functions are continuous
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]).

[L10] On an order-convex set $I$ with at least two elements, a continuous
$f:I\to\mathbb R$ has, for every base point $c_0\in I$, the primitive
$F(x)=\int_{c_0}^x f$; any two primitives differ by a constant; and for $a<b$ in
$I$ one has $\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a)$ for every primitive $G$ of $f$
([[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]]).

[L11] If $f$ is continuous on an order-convex $I$ and $f'>0$ at every interior
point of $I$, then $f$ is strictly increasing on $I$
([[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]).

[L12] Differentiability at a limit point of the domain implies continuity there
([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).

[L13] For $c$ a limit point of the domain, $f'(c)$ is the limit of
$(f(x)-f(c))/(x-c)$ as $x\to c$ ([[def-derivative]]).

[L14] If $I$ is order-convex with at least two elements, $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is
continuous and injective with inverse $g:f[I]\to I$, $c\in I$ and $b:=f(c)$, then
$c$ and $b$ are limit points, and if $f$ is differentiable at $c$ with
$f'(c)\ne0$ then $g$ is differentiable at $b$ with $g'(b)=1/f'(c)$
([[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]]).

[L15] If $g$ is differentiable at $c$, $b:=g(c)$ is a limit point of the domain
of $f$, and $f$ is differentiable at $b$, then $f\circ g$ is differentiable at
$c$ with $(f\circ g)'(c)=f'(b)g'(c)$ ([[thm-chain-rule]]).

[L16] If $f$ is continuous on an order-convex $I$ and differentiable with
$f'=0$ at every interior point of $I$, then $f$ is constant on $I$
([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]).

[L17] For the oriented integral, $\int_u^u f=0$ and
$\int_u^v f=-\int_v^u f$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $J$ is order-convex with at least two elements, and every point of $J$ is a limit point of $J$ and lies in its interior: $J$ is a nonempty open interval and so has one of the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$, $\mathbb R$ with strict defining inequalities, so a sufficiently small neighbourhood of any $s\in J$ is contained in $J$, whence a punctured neighbourhood of $s$ meets $J$ again, and $J$ contains two distinct points. [given, L2, algebra]

2.1 $g$ is continuous on $J$: by [L3] each component $z^a$ of the $C^1$ curve is $C^1$, so $z^a$ and its derivative $z^a{}'$ are continuous on $J$; by [L7] each $(z^a{}')^2$ is continuous, and by [L1] one has $g(s)=-\eta(z'(s),z'(s))=(z^0{}'(s))^2-\sum_{i=1}^{3}(z^i{}'(s))^2=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\epsilon_a(z^a{}'(s))^2$ with $\epsilon=(-1,1,1,1)$, a finite sum of continuous functions, hence continuous by [L7]. [step 1.1, L1, L3, L7, algebra]

3.1 $s\mapsto\sqrt{g(s)}$ is continuous on $J$: on $[0,\infty)$ the map $x\mapsto x^2$ is continuous by [L7], strictly increasing by [L6], and its image is $[0,\infty)$ by [L5]; hence its inverse, which is $\sqrt{\cdot}$ by the uniqueness in [L5], is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ by [L8], and composing with the continuous $g$ gives a continuous function by [L9]. [step 2.1, L5, L6, L7, L8, L9]

4.1 $h(s):=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}$ is continuous on $J$: it is the scalar multiple of the continuous function $\sqrt{g}$ by the constant $c^{-1}$, which exists because $c>0$, and scalar multiples of continuous functions are continuous by [L7]. [step 3.1, L1, L7]

5.1 $\tau$ is a primitive of $h$ on $J$, so $\tau$ is differentiable on $J$ with $\tau'(s)=h(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}$ for every $s\in J$, and $\tau$ is continuous on $J$: $J$ is order-convex with at least two elements by step 1.1 and $h$ is continuous by step 4.1, so the primitive assertion of [L10] applies to $h$ on $J$ with base point $s_0$, giving the derivative everywhere on $J$, and differentiability at the limit point $s$ of $J$ gives continuity at $s$ by [L12]. [step 1.1, step 4.1, L10, L12]

6.1 $\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}>0$ for every $s\in J$: by step 5.1, $\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}$; here $g(s)>0$ by hypothesis, so $\sqrt{g(s)}>0$ because $\sqrt{g(s)}$ is the nonnegative square root of $g(s)$ [L5], and $c^{-1}>0$ because $c>0$ [L1]; the product of two positive reals is positive. [step 5.1, L1, L5, algebra]

6.2 Null case: if $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))=0$ for all $s\in J$, then $g=0$ by its definition and $h=0$; by step 5.1, $\tau$ is a primitive of the zero function on $J$, so $\tau'=0$ at every point of $J$ and $\tau$ is constant on $J$ by [L16]; moreover $\tau(s_0)=\int_{s_0}^{s_0}\sqrt{g(u)}\,du=0$ by [L17], so the constant is $0$ and $\tau\equiv0$ on $J$; a constant function on $J$ is not injective because $J$ has at least two elements, so a null curve carries no proper-time parametrization. [step 1.1, step 5.1, L16, L17, algebra]

7.1 $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $J$, hence injective: $\tau$ is continuous on $J$ by step 5.1, $J$ is order-convex and every point of $J$ is interior to $J$ by step 1.1, and $\tau'(s)>0$ at every $s\in J$ by step 6.1, so [L11] applies; a strictly increasing function is injective. [step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, L11]

8.1 $\tau[J]$ is an interval (order-convex), the map $\tau:J\to\tau[J]$ is a bijection with inverse $\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to J$, and $\tau^{-1}$ is continuous on $\tau[J]$: this is [L8] applied to the continuous injective map $\tau$ on the order-convex set $J$, whose image is $\tau[J]$ by definition; the order-convexity of $J$ and continuity of $\tau$ are steps 1.1 and 5.1, and injectivity is step 7.1. [step 1.1, step 5.1, step 7.1, L8]

9.1 $\tau^{-1}$ is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of $\tau[J]$, with $(\tau^{-1})'(\tau(s))=1/\tau'(s)=c/\sqrt{g(s)}$: the inverse $\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to J$ is the one supplied by step 8.1 from [L8], and [L14] applies to $\tau$ with $c$ there equal to $s$ and $b=\tau(s)$; its hypotheses are the order-convexity of $J$ with at least two elements (step 1.1), continuity (step 5.1) and injectivity (step 7.1), and $\tau'(s)\ne0$ by step 6.1, so the derivative is $1/\tau'(s)=c/\sqrt{g(s)}$ by step 5.1. [step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, L14, algebra]

10.1 For each $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the composite $z^a\circ\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at $\tau(s)$ with derivative $z^a{}'(s)\cdot c/\sqrt{g(s)}$: $z^a$ is differentiable at the limit point $s$ of $J$ by [L3] and step 1.1, $\tau^{-1}$ is differentiable at $\tau(s)$ by step 9.1, and $\tau(s)$ is a limit point of $\tau[J]$ by [L14] as used in step 9.1, so the chain rule [L15] applies and gives the displayed derivative by [L4]. [step 1.1, step 9.1, L3, L4, L15, algebra]

11.1 The reparametrized curve $z\circ\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to\mathbb R^4$ is differentiable at every $\tau(s)$, with tangent $U(\tau(s))=c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$: by [L4] applied to the components of step 10.1, the curve is differentiable exactly when its components are and its derivative has those components, so $U(\tau(s))$ is the vector with components $z^a{}'(s)c/\sqrt{g(s)}$, which is $c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$. [step 10.1, L4, algebra]

12.1 $\eta(U(\tau(s)),U(\tau(s)))=-c^2$: by step 11.1, $U(\tau(s))=c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$, and bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$ [L1] give $\eta(U,U)=(c^2/g(s))\,\eta(z'(s),z'(s))=-(c^2/g(s))\,g(s)=-c^2$, since $g(s)=-\eta(z'(s),z'(s))>0$. [step 11.1, L1, algebra]

12.2 Straight-line case: assume $z(s)=p+sv$ with $\eta(v,v)<0$ and $v^0>0$, so $z'$ is the constant $v$ and $g$ is the constant $k:=-\eta(v,v)>0$, and $h$ is the constant $c^{-1}\sqrt{k}$ by step 5.1; the function $G(s):=c^{-1}\sqrt{k}(s-s_0)$ is a primitive of $h$ on $J$, its difference quotient at any $c\in J$ being the constant $c^{-1}\sqrt{k}$ by [L13], so for $s>s_0$ the evaluation formula of [L10] gives $\tau(s)=G(s)-G(s_0)=G(s)$, for $s=s_0$ one has $\tau(s_0)=\int_{s_0}^{s_0}h=0=G(s_0)$ by [L17], and for $s<s_0$ antisymmetry [L17] gives $\tau(s)=-\int_s^{s_0}h=-(G(s_0)-G(s))=G(s)$; hence $\tau(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}(s-s_0)$, and the tangent of step 11.1 is the constant $U(\tau(s))=c\,v/\sqrt{k}=c\,v/\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$. [step 5.1, step 11.1, L1, L10, L13, L17, algebra]

13.1 All six claims are established: claim (1) by steps 2.1 and 3.1; claim (2) by steps 5.1 (differentiability and derivative), 6.1 (strict positivity), 7.1 (strict increase and injectivity) and 5.1 (continuity); claim (3) by steps 8.1 and 9.1; claim (4) by steps 10.1, 11.1 and 12.1; claim (5) by step 6.2; and claim (6) by step 12.2; the identification of straight lines with inertial motion is not asserted. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 6.2, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, step 11.1, step 12.1, step 12.2] ∎

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/gr-qc/9712019"

## Statement

Let $(V,\eta)$ be the four-dimensional real Minkowski vector space of
[[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], with the fixed form of signature
$(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form,
$F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$
([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is
nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$
([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]],
[[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and
$\Phi:V\to V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); with
$F_{\alpha\beta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_\beta)$ in the fixed ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]] and $(\eta^{\mu\alpha})$
the inverse matrix of $(\eta_{\alpha\beta})$, one has
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, the
index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in
components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu=0$, where
$u_\mu:=\sum_\alpha\eta_{\mu\alpha}u^\alpha$ and
$F^\mu{}_\nu:=\sum_\alpha\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\nu}$. Consequently, if
$J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a
nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J\to V$ is differentiable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on
$J$ for some real $m\ne0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on
$J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). The same norm-conservation conclusion
holds for a family of skew forms $F_s$ and their pointwise operators $\Phi_s$
defined by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, when $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$: no
derivative of $F_s$ is required. In particular one may evaluate a varying field
$F_x$ along a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$. This is a conditional statement
about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any
particle.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The four-dimensional Minkowski vector space $(V,\eta)$ of
[[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]] with fixed ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, a skew-symmetric bilinear form $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$, a
nonempty open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a differentiable curve
$U:J\to V$, and real numbers $m\ne0$ and $q$.

[L1] $\eta$ is symmetric and bilinear with matrix
$\eta_{\alpha\beta}=\eta(e_\alpha,e_\beta)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ in the
basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, that matrix is its own inverse, and $\eta$ is
nondegenerate ([[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]).

[L2] A bilinear form $F$ is skew-symmetric when $F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v$,
and then $F(u,u)=0$ for every $u$
([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]], [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]).

[L3] A bilinear form $B$ on a finite-dimensional space is nondegenerate exactly
when its flat map $B^\flat:V\to V^*$, $B^\flat(u)(v)=B(u,v)$, is an isomorphism
([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]).

[L4] The assignment $B\mapsto B^\flat$ is a linear bijection from bilinear forms
on $V$ to linear maps $V\to V^*$
([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]]).

[L5] A map $T:V\to V$ is linear when $T(av+bw)=aT(v)+bT(w)$
([[def-linear-map]]).

[L6] A curve $U$ into $\mathbb R^4$ is differentiable exactly when all its
components are, and then $U'_a=(U^a)'$
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]).

[L7] Sums, scalar multiples and products of differentiable real functions are
differentiable, with $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[L8] Differentiability at a limit point of the domain implies continuity there
([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).

[L9] If $f$ is continuous on an order-convex set $I$ and $f'=0$ at every interior
point, then $f$ is constant on $I$
([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]).

[L10] A nonempty open interval is order-convex, and every point of it is
interior to it and is a limit point of it ([[def-interval]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For each $u\in V$ the map $w\mapsto F(w,u)$ is linear: by bilinearity of $F$ [L2] one has $F(aw+a'w',u)=aF(w,u)+a'F(w',u)$ for all reals $a,a'$ and all $w,w'\in V$, so $F(\cdot,u)\in V^*$. [given, L2, algebra]

1.2 The flat map $\eta^\flat:V\to V^*$, $\eta^\flat(x)(w):=\eta(x,w)$, is a bijection: $\eta$ is nondegenerate on the four-dimensional space $V$, so by [L3] its flat map is an isomorphism; equivalently, no nonzero $x$ satisfies $\eta(x,w)=0$ for all $w$. [given, L1, L3, L4]

2.1 For each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$, namely $\Phi(u):=(\eta^\flat)^{-1}\bigl(F(\cdot,u)\bigr)$: the functional $F(\cdot,u)$ lies in $V^*$ by step 1.1 and $\eta^\flat$ is a bijection by step 1.2, so exactly one $x\in V$ satisfies $\eta^\flat(x)=F(\cdot,u)$, that is $\eta(x,w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L3, L4]

3.1 $\Phi:V\to V$ is linear: for all $u,u'\in V$, all reals $a,a'$ and every $w\in V$, bilinearity of $F$ and $\eta$ [L1, L2] gives $\eta(\Phi(au+a'u'),w)=F(w,au+a'u')=aF(w,u)+a'F(w,u')=a\eta(\Phi(u),w)+a'\eta(\Phi(u'),w)=\eta(a\Phi(u)+a'\Phi(u'),w)$; since $w$ is arbitrary, the uniqueness in step 2.1 gives $\Phi(au+a'u')=a\Phi(u)+a'\Phi(u')$, which is linearity in the sense of [L5]. [step 2.1, L1, L2, L5]

3.2 Coordinate formula: writing $F_{\alpha\beta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_\beta)$ and letting $\eta^{\nu\alpha}$ denote the entry of the inverse of the matrix $(\eta_{\alpha\beta})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, one has $\Phi(u)^\nu=\eta^{\nu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, the sum running over $\alpha,\beta\in\{0,1,2,3\}$: substituting this candidate into the defining pairing gives $\eta_{\mu\nu}\eta^{\nu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta=\delta_\mu^\alpha F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta=F_{\mu\beta}u^\beta=F(e_\mu,u)$, because $\eta_{\mu\nu}\eta^{\nu\alpha}=\delta_\mu^\alpha$ is the inverse-matrix identity and the matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is its own inverse [L1]; the candidate therefore satisfies the defining property in step 2.1, and uniqueness gives the formula, that is $\Phi(u)^0=-F_{0\beta}u^\beta$ and $\Phi(u)^i=F_{i\beta}u^\beta$ for $i=1,2,3$. [step 2.1, L1, algebra]

3.3 $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$: symmetry of $\eta$ [L1] and the defining equation of step 2.1 give $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=\eta(\Phi(u),u)=F(u,u)$, which is $0$ by the skew-symmetry of $F$ [L2]. [step 2.1, L1, L2, algebra]

4.1 Component form: $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu=0$, where $u_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\alpha}u^\alpha$ and $F^\mu{}_\nu:=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\nu}$; indeed $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu=u^\alpha\eta_{\alpha\mu}\eta^{\mu\beta}F_{\beta\nu}u^\nu=u^\beta F_{\beta\nu}u^\nu=F(u,u)=0$ by [L2], the middle equality using the inverse-matrix identity of step 3.2 and the last equally following from step 3.3 with the coordinate formula, since $u^\beta F_{\beta\nu}u^\nu=\eta(u,\Phi(u))$. [step 3.2, step 3.3, L1, L2, algebra]

4.2 Norm conservation for a constant form: assume $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on $J$ with $m\ne0$; then $f(s):=\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$. Indeed, by [L1] and [L6], $f(s)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\epsilon_a(U^a(s))^2$ with $\epsilon=(-1,1,1,1)$ is differentiable on $J$ with $f'(s)=\sum_a2\epsilon_aU^a(s)(U^a)'(s)=2\eta(U(s),U'(s))$, using the product rule and sum rule [L7]; the equation gives $\eta(U(s),U'(s))=(q/m)\eta(U(s),\Phi(U(s)))=0$ by step 3.3, so $f'=0$ everywhere on $J$; $f$ is continuous on $J$ by [L8] and the interval $J$ is order-convex with every point interior [L10], so [L9] gives that $f$ is constant on $J$. [step 3.3, L1, L6, L7, L8, L9, L10, algebra]

5.1 Varying-form clause: let $F_s$, $s\in J$, be skew-symmetric bilinear forms and let $\Phi_s$ be defined pointwise by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, with $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$ on $J$; then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is again constant on $J$. Indeed the computation of step 4.2 applies verbatim — it differentiates only $U$, never $\Phi_s$ or $F_s$ — giving $f'(s)=2\eta(U(s),U'(s))$, while at each fixed $s$ one has $\eta(U(s),\Phi_s(U(s)))=F_s(U(s),U(s))=0$ by the skew-symmetry of $F_s$ [L2]; hence $\eta(U,U')=(q/m)\eta(U,\Phi_s(U))=0$ and $f'=0$ on $J$, so [L9] gives that $f$ is constant as in step 4.2. In particular, for a varying field $F_x$ and a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$ one may take $F_s:=F_{x(s)}$ and the corresponding pointwise operator $\Phi_s$. [step 4.2, L2, L6, L7, L9, algebra]

6.1 Conclusion: for every $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)$ with $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w$ (step 2.1); $\Phi$ is linear (step 3.1) and has the index-raised coordinate formula $\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$ (step 3.2); $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ (step 3.3), in components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu=0$ (step 4.1); and both $mU'=q\Phi(U)$ and its varying-form version $mU'=q\Phi_s(U)$ make $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ constant on the nonempty open interval $J$ (steps 4.2 and 5.1). The statement is conditional on the displayed equation and asserts nothing about particles. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1] ∎

## Example

With $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: (i) the vector $v$ with components
$(1,0,0,0)$ is future timelike and unit, $\eta(v,v)=-1$. (ii) For $0<\beta<1$
the boost $\Lambda_\beta$ of
[[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]] sends $v$ to the vector with components
$(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)$,
whose $\eta$-norm is $-\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=-1$ and whose time component
$\gamma$ is positive; at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined, so the
hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ cannot be dropped. (iii) The null line
$z(s)=(s,s,0,0)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, has $\eta(z',z')=0$, so the proper-time
construction of [[lem-em-proper-time-reparametrization]] gives $\tau\equiv0$,
which is not an invertible parameter: the timelike hypothesis cannot be weakened
to causal. (iv) For the symmetric nonzero form $F:=\eta$ one has
$\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ and $\eta(v,\Phi(v))=\eta(v,v)=-1\ne0$, so the antisymmetry
hypothesis of [[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]] is genuine. (v) For
the skew form with $F_{01}=1$, $F_{10}=-1$ and other coefficients zero, the
operator of [[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]] sends $e_0$ to $-e_1$:
$\eta(-e_1,w)=-w^1=F(w,e_0)$. Thus its invariant pairing and standard
raised-index formula have the same sign, and $\eta(e_0,\Phi(e_0))=0$. No
physical clock premise or experimental claim is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Minkowski vector space $(V,\eta)$ of
[[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]] with its basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, the vector
$v=e_0$, whose components are $(1,0,0,0)$, a real $\beta$ with $0<\beta<1$, the
boost $\Lambda_\beta$
and the number $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ of
[[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]], the null line $z(s)=(s,s,0,0)$ on
$J:=\mathbb R$, and the forms $F:=\eta$ and the skew form with
$F_{01}=1$, $F_{10}=-1$ and other coefficients zero.

[F1] On $V=\mathbb R^4$ the form
$\eta(v,w)=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$ is symmetric and bilinear with matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, it is nondegenerate, the vectors
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are the standard ordered basis, and $C^+$ consists of the
nonzero causal vectors with positive time coordinate
([[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]).

[L1] For $0\le\beta<1$ the map $\Lambda_\beta$ with
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^0=\gamma(v^0-\beta v^1)$,
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^1=\gamma(v^1-\beta v^0)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)^2=v^2$,
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^3=v^3$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, its inverse is
$\Lambda_{-\beta}$, and at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined
([[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]]).

[L2] For a nonempty open interval $J$ and a $C^1$ curve $z$ with
$\eta(z',z')<0$ and $z^0{}'>0$ the function
$\tau(s)=c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^s\sqrt{g}$ with $g=-\eta(z',z')$ has
$\tau'>0$ and gives the tangent $U(\tau(s))=c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$ with
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$; and if $\eta(z',z')=0$ on $J$, then $g=0$, $\tau\equiv0$ and
$\tau$ is not injective
([[lem-em-proper-time-reparametrization]]).

[L3] For a skew-symmetric bilinear form $F$ and each $u$ there is exactly one
$\Phi(u)$ with $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w$, the map $\Phi$ is linear,
$\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$, and in a frame
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$ with
$F_{\alpha\beta}=F(e_\alpha,e_\beta)$ and $(\eta^{\mu\alpha})$ the inverse of
$(\eta_{\alpha\beta})$ ([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]).

[L4] $\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval, and a nonempty open interval is
order-convex ([[def-interval]]).

[L5] For $a>0$ and rationals $r,s$ one has $a^r>0$, $a^{-r}=(a^r)^{-1}$ and
$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 (i) η(v,v)=η(e_0,e_0)=−1<0 and v^0=1>0, so v is a future timelike vector with η(v,v)=−1, that is, a unit future timelike vector. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 (ii, coordinates) For 0<β<1 the boost of [L1] sends v=e_0 to (γ(1−β·0),γ(0−β·1),0,0)=(γ,−γβ,0,0). [given, L1, algebra]

1.3 (iii, null tangent) The line z(s)=(s,s,0,0) has z'=(1,1,0,0) identically, so η(z',z')=−1+1=0; this is the null alternative of [L2]. [given, F1, L2, algebra]

1.4 (iv, symmetric form) For F:=η one has η(w,u)=η(u,w) for all w by symmetry [F1], so Φ(u):=u satisfies η(Φ(u),w)=η(u,w)=F(w,u) for every w; uniqueness of the solution of this equation (nondegeneracy of η [F1], as used in [L3]) gives Φ=id, and then η(v,Φ(v))=η(v,v)=−1≠0. [given, F1, L3, algebra]

1.5 (v, skew sign witness) For the skew form with F_{01}=1, F_{10}=−1 and other coefficients zero one has F(w,e_0)=w^1F(e_1,e_0)=−w^1 and η(−e_1,w)=−η(e_1,w)=−w^1 for every w, so Φ(e_0)=−e_1 by the uniqueness in [L3]; the raised-index formula of [L3] gives Φ(e_0)^μ=η^{μα}F_{αβ}(e_0)^β=η^{μ1}F_{10}=−η^{μ1}, which is −1 for μ=1 and 0 for μ≠1, again −e_1; both computations therefore have the same sign, and η(e_0,Φ(e_0))=η(e_0,−e_1)=0. [given, F1, L3, algebra]

1.6 (ii, excluded endpoint) At β=1 one has 1−β²=0, so γ=(1−β²)^{−1/2} is undefined, as the statement of [L1] records; hence the hypothesis 0≤β<1 cannot be dropped. [given, L1]

2.1 (ii, norm) With the image (γ,−γβ,0,0) of step 1.2, η(Λ_β v,Λ_β v)=−γ·γ+γβ·γβ=−γ²(1−β²)=−1, the last equality because γ²(1−β²)=(1−β²)^{−1/2}(1−β²)^{−1/2}(1−β²)=(1−β²)^{−1}(1−β²)=1 by [L5] with a:=1−β²>0; the time component γ is positive by [L1] and [L5]. [step 1.2, L1, L5, algebra]

2.2 (iii, conclusion) J:=R is a nonempty open interval by [L4], and the curve z(s)=(s,s,0,0) is C¹ with η(z',z')=0 identically by step 1.3, so the null clause of [L2] applies: g=0, τ≡0 on J and τ is not injective; thus the timelike hypothesis cannot be weakened to causal. [step 1.3, L2, L4]

3.1 All five checks are established — (i) in step 1.1, (ii) in steps 1.2, 2.1 and 1.6, (iii) in steps 1.3 and 2.2, (iv) in step 1.4, and (v) in step 1.5 — with no physical clock premise and no experimental claim. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5, step 1.6, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous. If $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^m)$, then $g=0$ on $U$. Here $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product and $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda$ is the finite sum $\sum_{i<m}\int_U g_ih_i\,d\lambda$ of integrals of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). The scalar case is $m=1$: a continuous $g$ with $\int_Ugh\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ vanishes on $U$. The vector case is deduced from the scalar case componentwise, each component tested separately. The conclusion is pointwise on $U$, and the hypothesis is the full family of compactly supported smooth test functions. The Axiom of Countable Choice is declared because the localization lemma [[lem-em-continuous-localization]] and the measurability fact [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]] used in the recorded proof assume it; no other choice principle enters.

**Conventions.** $C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^m)$ is the space of smooth $\mathbb R^m$-valued functions with compact support in $U$, defined componentwise in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] and [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Each product $g_ih_i$ is continuous on $U$ and vanishes outside a compact subset of $U$, and $\int_U g_ih_i\,d\lambda$ denotes the Lebesgue integral of its zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$, where $\lambda=\lambda_n$ is $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]); [F5] and [F6] below record that this is a finite real number and that for a nonnegative integrand it agrees with the nonnegative integral over the measurable set $U$ of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; naturals $n,m\ge1$; an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$; a continuous $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ with $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^m)$; and, inside the contradiction argument below, a point $p\in U$ with $g(p)\ne0$.

[F1] Cutoff lemma, in ZF: for a compact set $K\subseteq\Omega$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$ ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F2] Localization, under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: if $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ is continuous on an open set $U$ and $\int_VG\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$, then $G=0$ on $U$ ([[lem-em-continuous-localization]], where $\int_VG$ is the componentwise integral over the measurable set $V$). Below we use only its contrapositive form: if $G(q)\ne0$ for some $q\in U$, then some ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$ has $\int_VG\,d\lambda_n\ne0$.

[F3] Order and scalar rules for the nonnegative integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]): for nonnegative measurable $f\le h$ one has $\int f\,d\lambda\le\int h\,d\lambda$, and for $c>0$ one has $\int cf\,d\lambda=c\int f\,d\lambda$, while the zero function has integral $0$; the nonnegative integral over a measurable set of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] is an instance of this integral.

[F4] Continuity of pairings: if $f,w:U\to\mathbb R^m$ are continuous then $x\mapsto\langle f(x),w(x)\rangle$ is continuous ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]], clause 3); for $m=1$ this is the ordinary product of two continuous real functions under [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. In particular the components $g_i$ of $g$ are continuous, and for $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ the function $\psi e_i$ lies in $C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^m)$ and has $\langle g,\psi e_i\rangle=g_i\psi$.

[F5] Signed integral ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]): for measurable real $F$ with at most one of $\int F^+\,d\lambda$, $\int F^-\,d\lambda$ equal to $+\infty$, one sets $\int F\,d\lambda:=\int F^+\,d\lambda-\int F^-\,d\lambda$; $F$ is integrable when both parts are finite. If $F\ge0$ then $F^-=0$ and the signed integral of $F$ equals its nonnegative integral, which over a measurable set $E$ is the integral of $F\chi_E$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]); and $\int(-F)\,d\lambda=-\int F\,d\lambda$ is definitional from $(-F)^+=F^-$ and $(-F)^-=F^+$.

[F6] Compactly supported continuous functions have finite integrals: let $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with compact support $K$. If $K=\varnothing$ then $F=0$ and $\int F\,d\lambda=0$; otherwise $K$ is a nonempty compact metric space, so $M:=\max_K|F|$ is finite ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]), $K$ is bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) hence contained in a closed box $Q$ with $\lambda(Q)<+\infty$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]), $F$ is Borel measurable ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), and $|F|\le M\chi_Q$, so $\int|F|\,d\lambda\le\int M\chi_Q\,d\lambda=M\lambda(Q)<+\infty$ by [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]] and [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]]; thus $F$ is integrable by [F5]. In particular each integrand $g_ih_i$ of the hypothesis has a continuous compactly supported zero extension by [F4], and each pairing in the hypothesis is a finite real number.

[F7] Continuity in balls ([[def-metric-continuity]], [[def-metric-ball]]): $u$ is continuous at $p$ when for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $u[B(p,\delta)]\subseteq B(u(p),\varepsilon)$; and $B(p,\delta)=\{x:d(p,x)<\delta\}$ for $\delta>0$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction; assume a point where $g\ne0$, reduce to a scalar continuous function with a vanishing test pairing, and construct a nonnegative compactly supported test function whose integral is both $0$ and positive.

1.1 Suppose the conclusion fails: $g(p)\ne0$ for some $p\in U$. If $m=1$, put $u:=g$; then $u$ is continuous and the hypothesis reads $\int_Uu\psi\,d\lambda=0$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$. If $m\ge2$, choose $i<m$ with $g_i(p)\ne0$ and put $u:=g_i$; for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ the function $\psi e_i$ lies in $C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^m)$ with $\langle g,\psi e_i\rangle=g_i\psi$ by [F4], so the hypothesis gives $\int_Uu\psi\,d\lambda=0$. In both cases $u:U\to\mathbb R$ is continuous with $u(p)\ne0$, and replacing $u$ by $-u$ preserves the vanishing pairing because $\int_U(-u)\psi\,d\lambda=-\int_Uu\psi\,d\lambda$ by [F5]; hence we may assume $u(p)>0$. [given, F4, F5, assume-contra]

2.1 Continuity of $u$ at $p$ with $u(p)>0$ yields $\delta>0$ with $B(p,\delta)\subseteq U$ and $u(x)\ge u(p)/2$ for every $x\in B(p,\delta)$: taking $\varepsilon:=u(p)/2>0$ in [F7] gives $\delta_0>0$ with $|u(x)-u(p)|<u(p)/2$ for $d(p,x)<\delta_0$, and since $U$ is open one may shrink $\delta_0$ to a $\delta>0$ with $B(p,\delta)\subseteq U$, the bound remaining valid on the smaller ball. [step 1.1, F7, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F1] with $\Omega:=B(p,\delta)$ and $K:=\{p\}$: there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B(p,\delta))$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $p$. Extended by zero, $\chi$ lies in $C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subseteq B(p,\delta)$. [step 2.1, F1]

4.1 Put $\varphi:=u\chi$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^n$. Then $\varphi$ is continuous and compactly supported in $U$ by [F4] and [F1], satisfies $\varphi\ge0$ on $U$ because $\varphi=0$ where $\chi=0$ and $\varphi(x)=u(x)\chi(x)\ge(u(p)/2)\chi(x)\ge0$ for $x\in B(p,\delta)$ by step 2.1, and has $\varphi(p)=u(p)>0$; hence $\varphi$ is not the zero function. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F4, algebra]

5.1 The hypothesis at the admissible test function $\chi$ gives $\int_Uu\chi\,d\lambda=0$, that is $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=0$: since $\varphi\ge0$, the signed integral equals the nonnegative integral of $\varphi$ over the measurable set $U$ by [F5], and that integral is a finite real number by [F6]. [step 3.1, step 4.1, given, F5, F6]

5.2 By the contrapositive localization [F2] applied to the continuous function $\varphi$ with $\varphi(p)\ne0$, there is a ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$ with $\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda\ne0$; as $\varphi\ge0$, monotonicity in [F3] applied to the zero function below $\varphi\chi_V$ gives $\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda\ge0$, so this integral is strictly positive. [step 4.1, F2, F3]

6.1 Since $V\subseteq U$, the nonnegative measurable functions $\varphi\chi_V$ and $\varphi\chi_U$ satisfy $\varphi\chi_V\le\varphi\chi_U$ pointwise, so monotonicity in [F3] gives $\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda\le\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=0$, contradicting step 5.2; therefore no point $p\in U$ with $g(p)\ne0$ exists and $g=0$ on $U$. [step 5.1, step 5.2, F3, discharge-contradiction] ∎

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; a bounded open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$; an open $N\supseteq\overline U$; a real $\kappa>0$; smooth maps $A,J:N	o V=\mathbb R^4$; the Minkowski form $\eta$ and conventions of [F1]; $F_{\mu

## Example

Two exact boundary checks. (i) Stationarity is first order. On $\mathbb R^2$ the polynomial $S(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ has differential $0$ at $(0,0)$, while $S(\varepsilon,0)=\varepsilon^2>0$ and $S(0,\varepsilon)=-\varepsilon^2<0$ for every $\varepsilon\ne0$; a point where the first variation vanishes need not be a minimum. Consequently the equivalence of [[lem-em-compact-field-variation]] between stationarity and the coefficient equation, and the conversion by [[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]] of a vanishing first variation into pointwise equations, are first-order conditions: they carry no minimality and no existence content, and the example involves no adopted physical action. (ii) Compact support of the variation is essential. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for this Lebesgue-functional branch, exactly as in the compact-field supplier; the polynomial branch (i) remains choice-free. Take $U=(-1,1)^4$, $\kappa=1$, $J=0$ and the smooth field $A$ with $A_0(x)=(x^1)^2$ and $A_1=A_2=A_3=0$, in the conventions of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]. Then $F_{01}=-2x^1$ and $F^{01}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}F_{01}=2x^1$, all other components vanishing, so $\partial_\mu F^{\mu0}=\partial_1F^{10}=-2\ne0$ and the coefficient equation $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=-\kappa J^\nu$ fails at $\nu=0$. Nevertheless the variation $h$ with $h_0\equiv1$ and $h_1=h_2=h_3=0$ is smooth but not compactly supported in $U$; along it $A_0+sh_0=(x^1)^2+s$, so $F_{01}$ and the integrand $L=2(x^1)^2$ are independent of $s$ and $S[A+sh]=\int_U2(x^1)^2\,d\lambda$ is constant in $s$, with first variation $0$ although the field equation fails. For the complementary stationarity-boundary check take instead $A_0=x^1$, the other covariant components zero, $J=0$, and $h_0=x^1$, $h_i=0$ (so $A^0=-x^1$, $h^0=-x^1$). Here $F_{01}=-1$ is constant, so the coefficient equations all hold, but this smooth noncompact direction gives $S[A+sh]=8(1+s)^2$ and derivative $16\ne0$ at zero. Thus extending the compact stationarity condition to all smooth noncompact directions would invalidate the converse. These two witnesses show that the stated compact-support hypothesis cannot simply be removed: its coefficient conversion has no boundary term precisely in its declared compact class. Other variation classes require their own boundary hypotheses.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the two computational branches of the Example: part (i) with $S(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$; part (ii) with $U=(-1,1)^4$, $\kappa=1$, $J=0$, and the two fields $A$ and variations $h$ displayed there, in the covariant-component conventions of [L1]. The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is assumed in part (ii), exactly as in [[lem-em-compact-field-variation]]; part (i) of the Example uses no choice principle.

[L1] Minkowski conventions: $\eta_{\mu\nu}=\eta^{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{\mu\nu}$ in the standard basis, so raising a covariant component reverses the sign of the zeroth coordinate: $m^0=-m_0$ and $m^i=m_i$ for $i=1,2,3$ ([[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]).

[L2] Functional and derivative conventions: for smooth $A$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline U$, $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, $F^{\mu\nu}=\eta^{\mu\alpha}\eta^{\nu\beta}F_{\alpha\beta}$, $L=-\frac{1}{4\kappa}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}+J^\nu A_\nu$ and $S[A]=\int_U L\,d\lambda$; the partial derivative $\partial_\mu$ is the directional derivative in the standard direction and agrees with the ordinary derivative of the corresponding coordinate line ([[lem-em-compact-field-variation]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[L3] Derivatives of constants and powers: a constant function has derivative $0$ at every point, $x\mapsto x^2$ has derivative $2x$, and $x\mapsto x$ has derivative $1$; hence $\partial_1(x^1)^2=2x^1$, $\partial_1x^1=1$ and $\partial_0x^1=\partial_0(x^1)^2=0$, so the differential of $(x,y)\mapsto x^2-y^2$ at $(0,0)$ vanishes because $\partial_1S(x,y)=2x$ and $\partial_2S(x,y)=-2y$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], clauses 1 and 2).

[L4] The open box $U=(-1,1)^4$ has $\lambda(U)=16$, the constant $c\ge0$ on $U$ has $\int_Uc\,d\lambda=c\lambda(U)$, and $\int_U2(x^1)^2\,d\lambda\le\int_U2\,d\lambda=32$; these integrals of the continuous integrands over the bounded open $U$ are finite real numbers, the integrands being continuous hence Borel measurable and every Borel set being Lebesgue measurable under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct; exact finite computations in the conventions of [L1] and [L2].

1.1 Part (i): by [L3] the partial derivatives $\partial_1S(x,y)=2x$ and $\partial_2S(x,y)=-2y$ both vanish at $(0,0)$, so the differential of $S$ at the origin is $0$, while $S(\varepsilon,0)-S(0,0)=\varepsilon^2>0$ and $S(0,\varepsilon)=-\varepsilon^2<0$ for every $\varepsilon\ne0$; a point of vanishing first variation is therefore neither a minimum nor a maximum, the stationarity equivalence in (c) of [[lem-em-compact-field-variation]] and the coefficient extraction through [[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]] are first-order conditions carrying no minimality and no existence content, and this branch is choice-free. [given, L3, algebra]

1.2 Part (ii), first witness: for $A_0=(x^1)^2$ and $A_1=A_2=A_3=0$, so that $A^0=-(x^1)^2$ by [L1], [L2] and [L3] give $F_{01}=\partial_0A_1-\partial_1A_0=-2x^1$ and $F_{10}=2x^1$ with all remaining $F_{\mu\nu}$ zero; raising both indices by the constant matrix $\eta^{\mu\nu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}$ of [L1] gives $F^{01}=2x^1$, $F^{10}=-2x^1$ and all remaining $F^{\mu\nu}$ zero, hence $\partial_\mu F^{\mu0}=\partial_1F^{10}=-2$, which differs from $-\kappa J^0=0$, so the coefficient equation fails at $\nu=0$. The variation with $h_0\equiv1$ and $h_1=h_2=h_3=0$ has $h^0\equiv-1$ and is smooth but not compactly supported in $U$. Along it $(A+sh)_0=(x^1)^2+s$ and $(A+sh)_i=0$, so $F_{01}(s)=-2x^1$ and $F(s)_{\mu\nu}F(s)^{\mu\nu}=-8(x^1)^2$ are independent of $s$, whence $L(s)=2(x^1)^2$ for every $s$ by [L2] with $\kappa=1$ and $J=0$; the integral $S[A+sh]=\int_U2(x^1)^2\,d\lambda$ is therefore independent of $s$ by [L4], so this smooth noncompact direction has first variation $0$ although the field equation fails. [given, L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra]

2.1 Part (ii), second witness: for $A_0=x^1$, $A_1=A_2=A_3=0$ and $J=0$, one has $F_{01}=\partial_0A_1-\partial_1A_0=-1$ constant, so every $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=0$ and the coefficient equations $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=-\kappa J^\nu$ all hold; the variation with $h_0=x^1$ and $h_1=h_2=h_3=0$ has $h^0=-x^1$ by [L1]. Along it $(A+sh)_0=(1+s)x^1$, so $F_{01}(s)=-(1+s)$ and $F(s)_{\mu\nu}F(s)^{\mu\nu}=-2(1+s)^2$, whence $L(s)=\frac12(1+s)^2$ by [L2]; since $\lambda(U)=16$ by [L4], $S[A+sh]=8(1+s)^2$, whose derivative at $s=0$ is $16\ne0$. Thus the converse direction in (c) of [[lem-em-compact-field-variation]] would fail if the compactly supported variation class were extended to all smooth directions, so the compact-support hypothesis is essential exactly for the boundary-free coefficient conversion, and part (ii) is the branch that carries $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [given, L1, L2, L3, L4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $\theta_0\in I$, and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on $I$ in the sense that $f$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ and $f'$ is continuous on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]). Assume $f(\theta_0)=0$ and that $f'(\theta)\ge m>0$ for every $\theta\in I$. Let a recorded scalar $\hat y\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\hat y|\le s$ with $s\ge0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), and let a separately specified calibration-error model bound be $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$ with $\delta\ge0$ for a value $y$ assigned to the same quantity. If a model requires $y=f(\theta)$ for some $\theta\in I$, then every $\theta\in I$ compatible with those two simultaneous bounds satisfies

$$|\theta-\theta_0|\le\frac{s+\delta}{m};$$

equivalently, if a proposed $\theta$ violates this bound, then the specified model-plus-error-bound pair is incompatible with the premises. The conclusion is a deterministic conditional statement about the stated bounds; it is not a sampling law, a statistical inference, or a claim about the historical reports of the causal-response page.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with at least two elements, a point $\theta_0\in I$, a function $f:I\to\mathbb R$ differentiable at every point of $I$ with $f'$ continuous on $I$, the normalisation $f(\theta_0)=0$, the lower bound $f'\ge m>0$ on $I$, a recorded scalar $\hat y\in\mathbb R$ with $|\hat y|\le s$, $s\ge0$, a calibration bound $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$, $\delta\ge0$, and the model requirement $y=f(\theta)$ for a point $\theta\in I$.

[L1] Every interval is order-convex: if $x,y\in I$ and $x\le z\le y$ then $z\in I$ ([[def-interval]]). Hence for any two points $a<b$ of $I$ the whole closed interval $[a,b]$ is contained in $I$.

[L2] For an ordered field $F$ and $x,y\in F$ one has $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$ ([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]]), with the absolute value of [[def-abs-value]]: $|u|=u$ for $u\ge0$, $|u|=-u$ for $u<0$, so $|u|\ge0$ with equality only for $u=0$.

[L3] A function differentiable at a limit point $c$ of its domain is continuous at $c$, and consequently a function differentiable at every point of a set is continuous at every point of that set ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]). Since $I$ has at least two elements, every point of $I$ is a limit point of $I$ ([[def-interval]]): given distinct $x,y\in I$, an arbitrary small one-sided step from $x$ towards $y$ stays in $I$.

[L4] Differentiation is a local operation and continuity is preserved by restriction ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]): for $a<b$ in $I$, a punctured neighbourhood of an interior point $c\in(a,b)$ lies in $[a,b]$, so the difference quotient of the restriction $f|_{[a,b]}$ at $c$ agrees with that of $f$ and the restriction is differentiable at $c$ with the same derivative $f'(c)$; and by [L3] the restriction is continuous at every point of $[a,b]$.

[L5] Mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]): if $a<b$ and $g:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$, then there is $\xi\in(a,b)$ with $g(b)-g(a)=g'(\xi)(b-a)$.

## Proof

1.1 Write $y=\hat y+(y-\hat y)$ and apply the triangle inequality of [L2] together with the two assumed bounds: $|y|\le|\hat y|+|y-\hat y|\le s+\delta$. [L2, algebra]

1.2 If $\theta=\theta_0$ then $|\theta-\theta_0|=0\le (s+\delta)/m$, because $s\ge0$, $\delta\ge0$ give $s+\delta\ge0$ and $m>0$ makes $(s+\delta)/m\ge0$. [L2, algebra]

1.3 Suppose $\theta\ne\theta_0$ and put $a=\min(\theta,\theta_0)$, $b=\max(\theta,\theta_0)$, so $a<b$ and $\{a,b\}=\{\theta,\theta_0\}$. By [L1] the closed interval $[a,b]$ is contained in $I$; by [L3] the function $f$ is continuous on $I$, and by the restriction clause of [L4] the restriction $g=f|_{[a,b]}$ is continuous on $[a,b]$; by the locality clause of [L4] $g$ is differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ with $g'=f'$ there. The mean value theorem [L5] therefore yields $\xi\in(a,b)$ with $g(b)-g(a)=g'(\xi)(b-a)$. Since $g(b)-g(a)$ equals $f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)$ up to the sign that reverses $b-a$ as well, and $g'(\xi)=f'(\xi)$, this is exactly $f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)=f'(\xi)(\theta-\theta_0)$. [L1, L3, L4, L5]

2.1 At the intermediate point of step 1.3 one has $f'(\xi)\ge m>0$, so $f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)$ has the sign of $\theta-\theta_0$, and therefore $|f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)|=f'(\xi)\,|\theta-\theta_0|\ge m\,|\theta-\theta_0|$. [step 1.3, L2, algebra]

3.1 Since $y=f(\theta)$ and $f(\theta_0)=0$, step 2.1 gives $m|\theta-\theta_0|\le|y|$, and step 1.1 gives $|y|\le s+\delta$. Hence $m|\theta-\theta_0|\le s+\delta$, and dividing by $m>0$ yields $|\theta-\theta_0|\le(s+\delta)/m$. [step 2.1, step 1.1, algebra]

4.1 Every $\theta\in I$ compatible with the model requirement and the two bounds falls under one of the two cases: $\theta=\theta_0$ satisfies the bound by step 1.2, and $\theta\ne\theta_0$ satisfies it by step 3.1. Equivalently, if a proposed $\theta$ has $|\theta-\theta_0|>(s+\delta)/m$, then no assignment satisfying both stated bounds can also satisfy $y=f(\theta)$, so the specified model-plus-error-bound pair is incompatible with the premises; no probability, sampling, or statistical inference has been used. [step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

For $z\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi\bigl[z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\,\cos\theta\bigr]^l\,d\theta$, $l\in\mathbb N_0$. Then $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $|P_l(z)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_l(1)=1$, and for $|q|<1$ the series $\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ with

$$(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}q^lP_l(z),$$

where the branch is the analytic square root equal to $1$ at $q=0$ ([[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]]). Consequently, for $r>|y|$ with $n=x/|x|$ and $N\in\mathbb N_0$,

$$\bigl|\,|x-y|^{-1}-\sum_{l=0}^{N}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\bigr|\le|y|^{N+1}|x|^{-N-2}(1-|y|/|x|)^{-1},$$

uniformly on $|y|\le a<r$ (with $y=0$ interpreted by the zero higher terms), and after integrating against an $L^1$ source the corresponding multipole expansion converges with that error times its $L^1$ norm. For the integrated $L^1$-source and every-spatial-derivative assertions, assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) through the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate interfaces. On an observation compact set disjoint from $\overline{B_a(0)}$ every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly, uniformly also over $|y|\le a$, by harmonicity of the coefficient terms and [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]. The initial finite-Riemann polynomial/generating assertions are choice-free. This lemma supplies the convergent zonal kernel; it does not by itself prove a spherical $L^2$ basis or boundary convergence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $z\in[-1,1]$, an integer $l\in\mathbb N_0$, a complex $q$ with $|q|<1$, the function $w(\theta)=z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta$ on $[0,\pi]$, a compact observation set $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, a radius $a\ge0$ with $\inf_K|x|>a$, a real $L^1$ density $\rho$ vanishing outside the closed ball of radius $a$, and Countable Choice for the integrated-source and derivative assertions.

[L1] **Interval integrals of $\mathbb C$-valued functions.** Under the identification $\Phi:\mathbb C\to\mathbb R^2$, $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$, of [[thm-complex-numbers-are-the-real-coordinate-plane]], with $|z|=\lVert\Phi(z)\rVert_2$ by [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], the integral of a $\mathbb C$-valued function on $[a,b]$ is the componentwise one of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]; it is linear in the integrand ([[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]] applied componentwise), it is additive over adjacent intervals ([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] claim 3), and by [[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]] $\bigl|\int_a^b f\bigr|\le\int_a^b|f|$ for $a\le b$. For real-valued integrands, [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] gives nonnegativity, monotonicity, and the two-sided bound $m(b-a)\le\int_a^b f\le M(b-a)$ when $m\le f\le M$.

[L2] **Uniform convergence and termwise integration.** With the conventions of [[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]] states: if $|f_k|\le M_k$ and $\sum M_k<\infty$, then $\sum f_k$ converges absolutely and uniformly. By [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]] a series of $\mathbb C$-valued functions converges uniformly exactly when its real and imaginary parts do; and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-riemann-integration]] gives $\int_a^b f_k\to\int_a^b f$ for a uniformly convergent sequence of integrable functions on $[a,b]$, applied to those two real components.

[L3] **Holomorphy, power series and the identity theorem.** [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]: a function is holomorphic on an open set when it is complex differentiable at every point; a complex domain is nonempty, connected and open ([[def-complex-domain]]). [[thm-termwise-differentiation-of-complex-power-series]]: a power series is holomorphic on its disc of convergence with termwise derivative. Sums, products, scalar multiples and, where the denominator is nonzero, quotients of functions complex differentiable at a point are complex differentiable there, with the usual rules ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]). [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]]: two holomorphic functions on a complex domain that agree on a set with an accumulation point **in that domain** agree everywhere.

[L4] **Substitution, additivity and inverse tangent.** [[thm-substitution]]: for $c<d$, $\varphi$ differentiable on $[c,d]$ with integrable derivative and $f$ continuous on an order-convex interval containing $\varphi([c,d])$, $\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)}f=\int_c^d(f\circ\varphi)\varphi'$, the left side being oriented. [[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]]: $\arctan' x=(1+x^2)^{-1}$ and $\arctan x=\int_0^x(1+t^2)^{-1}dt$. [[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]: $\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\to\mathbb R$ is a strictly increasing bijection with inverse $\arctan$. [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]]: cotangent is the quotient $\cot x=\cos x/\sin x$ where defined, and $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$.

[L5] **Trigonometric values used.** [[lem-wallis-integrals-recurrence-and-squeeze]]: $I_m:=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^mt\,dt$ satisfies $I_0=\pi/2$, $I_1=1$, $I_m=\frac{m-1}{m}I_{m-2}$ for $m\ge2$, and $I_{2j}=\frac{\pi}{2}\prod_{k=1}^{j}\frac{2k-1}{2k}$. [[thm-cofunction-supplementary-and-reflection-identities]]: $\cos(\pi/2-x)=\sin x$, $\cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x$, $\tan(\pi/2-x)=\cot x$. [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]: $\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y$. [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]: $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$ where defined. The same cofunction identities give $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^mt\,dt=I_m$ by the cofunction substitution.

[L6] **Binomial expansion.** [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]]: for $u,v\in\mathbb C$ and $l\in\mathbb N_0$, $(u+v)^l=\sum_{k=0}^l\binom lk u^kv^{l-k}$.

[L7] **Harmonic functions and their estimates.** Assume Countable Choice where these suppliers declare it. [[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]]: for the Laplace fundamental solution $\Phi$ in dimension $3$, $x\mapsto\Phi(x-y)$ is smooth and harmonic on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{y\}$ (so $x\mapsto|x-y|^{-1}$ is smooth and harmonic off $y$). [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]: partial derivatives commute for $C^2$ functions. [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]: for harmonic $u$ with $B_r(x)\Subset\Omega$, $|D^\alpha u(x)|\le C_{3,\alpha}r^{-3-|\alpha|}\int_{B_r(x)}|u|$. [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: a continuous function with integrable interior derivative is recovered from its derivative by the integral.

[L8] **Parameter integrals, power-series coefficients and Choice.** [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] with its displayed hypotheses: an integrand differentiable in the parameter with an integrable majorant for the partial derivative has differentiable parameter integral with the expected derivative. [[cor-power-series-sums-are-smooth-with-coefficient-formula]]: a real power series with positive radius is smooth inside its disc and $a_m=f^{(m)}(c)/m!$. [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: $L^1$ is a complex vector space and its integral is complex-linear; [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: monotonicity and the scalar rule for nonnegative integrals. [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through these Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate interfaces.

## Proof

1.1 For $z\in[-1,1]$ put $w(\theta)=z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta$. Then $|w(\theta)|^2=z^2+(1-z^2)\cos^2\theta\le z^2+1-z^2=1$, so $|w(\theta)|\le1$, and the complex binomial theorem [L6] gives $w(\theta)^l=\sum_{k=0}^{l}\binom lk z^{l-k}\bigl(i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta\bigr)^k$ for every $l\in\mathbb N_0$ and $\theta\in[0,\pi]$. [L6, algebra]

1.2 The cosine integrals are $\int_0^\pi\cos^k\theta\,d\theta=0$ for odd $k$ and $\int_0^\pi\cos^{2j}\theta\,d\theta=2I_{2j}=\pi\prod_{i=1}^{j}\frac{2i-1}{2i}$ for $k=2j$. Indeed, [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]] splits $\int_0^\pi=\int_0^{\pi/2}+\int_{\pi/2}^\pi$; the substitution $\theta=\pi-t$ of [L4] on $[\pi/2,\pi]$, with $\cos(\pi-t)=-\cos t$ from [L5], turns the second integral into $(-1)^k\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^kt\,dt$; the cofunction identity $\cos t=\sin(\pi/2-t)$ and the same substitution identify $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^kt\,dt$ with $I_k$; and the values of $I_k$ are those of [L5]. [L4, L5, algebra]

1.3 For real $a>|b|\ge0$ put $I(a,b)=\int_0^\pi(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta$. Then $(a^2-b^2)I(a,b)^2=\pi^2$. Indeed, on $[0,\pi/2]$ substitute $\theta=2\arctan t$, $t\in[0,1]$, which is legitimate by [L4] because $t\mapsto2\arctan t$ has continuous derivative $2(1+t^2)^{-1}$ and $(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}$ is continuous on $[0,\pi]$; by [L5] and [L4], $\cos(2\arctan t)=\cos^2(\arctan t)-\sin^2(\arctan t)=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$, because $\cos^2 x=(1+\tan^2x)^{-1}$ at $\tan(\arctan t)=t$; hence $\int_0^{\pi/2}(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\int_0^1\frac{2\,dt}{(a+b)+(a-b)t^2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}\arctan c$ with $c=\sqrt{(a-b)/(a+b)}>0$. On $[\pi/2,\pi]$ the reflection $\theta=\pi-t$ ([L5]) turns the integrand into $(a-b\cos t)^{-1}$ and the same substitution gives $\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\int_0^1\frac{2\,dt}{(a-b)+(a+b)t^2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}\arctan\frac1c$. Since $\tan(\pi/2-x)=\cot x$ ([L5]) and $\cot(\arctan c)=1/\tan(\arctan c)=1/c$ ([L4]), with both angles in $(0,\pi/2)$ where $\tan$ is injective ([L4]), $\arctan c+\arctan(1/c)=\pi/2$; adding the two halves by [L1] gives $I(a,b)=\pi/\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$, hence $(a^2-b^2)I(a,b)^2=\pi^2$. [L1, L4, L5, algebra]

1.4 Fix $\rho\in(0,1/4)$, real $b$ with $|b|<\rho$, and complex $a$ with $|a-1|<\rho$; then $\operatorname{Re}a>3/4>|b|$, so $a+b\cos\theta\ne0$ on $[0,\pi]$, and $I(a,b)=\int_0^\pi(a+b\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta$ is well defined as a $\mathbb C$-valued integral [L1]. The map $a\mapsto I(a,b)$ is holomorphic on $|a-1|<\rho$: for $h\ne0$ small, the difference quotient equals $-\int_0^\pi\bigl((a+b\cos\theta)(a+h+b\cos\theta)\bigr)^{-1}d\theta$ by the elementary identity $\frac{1}{A+h}-\frac1A=-h\,\frac{1}{A(A+h)}$, and the integrands converge uniformly on $[0,\pi]$ to $-(a+b\cos\theta)^{-2}$ because $|a+b\cos\theta|\ge\operatorname{Re}a-|b|>1/2$ and, for $|h|\le\rho$, $|a+h+b\cos\theta|>1/4$; [L2] applied to real and imaginary parts therefore gives complex differentiability at every such $a$, hence holomorphy [L3]. The same computation in the second variable shows that for each fixed $a$ with $|a-1|<\rho$ the map $b\mapsto I(a,b)$ is holomorphic on $|b|<\rho$. [L1, L2, L3]

2.1 Inserting step 1.1 into the defining integral and using step 1.2 with the linearity of [L1], only the terms with even $k=2j$ survive, and $i^{2j}=(-1)^j$ gives $P_l(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor}(-1)^j\binom{l}{2j}W_j\,(1-z^2)^jz^{l-2j}$ with $W_j=\prod_{i=1}^{j}\frac{2i-1}{2i}$ and $W_0=1$. Each summand is a real polynomial of degree $l$, so $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$; at $z=1$ every term with $j\ge1$ carries the factor $(1-z^2)^j=0$, so $P_l(1)=W_0=1$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, algebra]

2.2 Taking moduli in the defining integral, $|P_l(z)|=\pi^{-1}\bigl|\int_0^\pi w(\theta)^l\,d\theta\bigr|\le\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi|w(\theta)|^l\,d\theta\le1$ by the norm inequality of [L1] and $|w|\le1$ from step 1.1. [step 1.1, L1]

2.3 For each real $b$ with $|b|<\rho$ the function $F_b(a)=(a^2-b^2)I(a,b)^2-\pi^2$ is holomorphic on the disc $|a-1|<\rho$ (products and differences of holomorphic functions, [L3]); by step 1.3 it vanishes for every real $a\in(1-\rho,1+\rho)$, since there $a>1-\rho>|b|$; that interval has accumulation points in the disc, so [[thm-identity-theorem-holomorphic-functions]] gives $F_b\equiv0$ on the disc. For each fixed $a$ with $|a-1|<\rho$, the function $b\mapsto(a^2-b^2)I(a,b)^2-\pi^2$ is holomorphic on $|b|<\rho$ by step 1.4, and it vanishes for every real $b$ with $|b|<\rho$ by the first part; the identity theorem applied on the disc $|b|<\rho$ therefore gives $(a^2-b^2)I(a,b)^2=\pi^2$ for all such $a$ and all complex $b$ with $|b|<\rho$. [step 1.3, step 1.4, L3]

3.1 For $|q|<1$ the series $\sum_lq^lw(\theta)^l$ has the majorant $\sum_l|q|^l<\infty$ and converges uniformly on $[0,\pi]$ to $(1-qw(\theta))^{-1}$; by [L2] it may be integrated term by term, so $G_z(q):=\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ satisfies $G_z(q)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi(1-qw(\theta))^{-1}d\theta$, and the majorant $|q|^l$ also gives absolute convergence and uniform convergence on $[-1,1]$ of $\sum_lq^lP_l(z)$ because $|P_l|\le1$ by step 2.2. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L1, L2]

4.1 $G_z(q)=\sum_lq^lP_l(z)$ is a complex power series whose coefficients are bounded (step 2.2), so its radius of convergence is at least $1$; by [L3] it is holomorphic on $|q|<1$, and $G_z(0)=P_0(z)=1$ because $P_0(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi1\,d\theta=1$. The constructions of steps 1.1-4.1 use no Choice. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L3]

4.2 Fix real $q$ with $|q|<\rho$ and set $a=1-qz$, $b=-iq\sqrt{1-z^2}$; then $|a-1|=|qz|\le|q|<\rho$ and $|b|\le|q|<\rho$, and $a^2-b^2=(1-qz)^2+q^2(1-z^2)=1-2qz+q^2$. Since $a+b\cos\theta=1-q\bigl(z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta\bigr)=1-qw(\theta)$, step 3.1 gives $\pi G_z(q)=\int_0^\pi(1-qw(\theta))^{-1}d\theta=I(a,b)$; hence step 2.3 yields $(1-2qz+q^2)G_z(q)^2=1$ for every real $q$ with $|q|<\rho$. [step 2.3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Define $\Psi(q)=(1-2qz+q^2)G_z(q)^2-1$ on $|q|<1$; by step 4.1 and [L3] the function $\Psi$ is holomorphic there, and by step 4.2 it vanishes on the interval $(-\rho,\rho)$, which has accumulation points in the disc. The identity theorem [L3] gives $\Psi\equiv0$, that is $(1-2qz+q^2)G_z(q)^2=1$ for every $|q|<1$. The polynomial $1-2qz+q^2$ has the two roots $q=z\pm i\sqrt{1-z^2}$ of modulus $\sqrt{z^2+(1-z^2)}=1$, and equals $1$ at $q=0$, so it is nonzero and holomorphic on the connected disc $|q|<1$, and $G_z$ satisfies $G_z(0)=1$ and $G_z^2=(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1}$ there; if $S$ is any holomorphic function on the disc with $S(0)=1$ and $S^2=(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1}$, then $(G_z-S)(G_z+S)\equiv0$ while $G_z+S$ is continuous with value $2$ at $0$, hence nonzero near $0$, so $G_z=S$ near $0$ and then on the whole connected disc by the identity theorem. Thus $G_z$ is exactly the analytic square root of $(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1}$ equal to $1$ at $q=0$. [step 4.1, step 4.2, L3]

6.1 For $x\ne0$, $y\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|x|>|y|$, write $r=|x|$, $n=x/|x|$, $q=|y|/r<1$; if $y\ne0$ and $\hat y=y/|y|$, then $|x-y|^{-1}=r^{-1}\bigl(1-2q(n\cdot\hat y)+q^2\bigr)^{-1/2}=r^{-1}\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(n\cdot\hat y)=\sum_{l\ge0}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)$ by the generating identity of step 5.1, since $n\cdot\hat y\in[-1,1]$. The remainder satisfies $\bigl|\sum_{l>N}q^lP_l(n\cdot\hat y)\bigr|\le\sum_{l>N}q^l=\frac{q^{N+1}}{1-q}$ by step 2.2, which after multiplication by $r^{-1}$ gives the stated bound, uniformly on $|y|\le a$ whenever $|x|\ge r>a$; for $y=0$ the formula reduces to $|x|^{-1}$ with all higher terms zero, consistently with $c_l=|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(\,\cdot\,)$ vanishing for $l\ge1$ at $y=0$. [step 5.1, step 2.2, algebra]

7.1 Fix $x$ with $|x|>|y|$. Applying step 6.1 with the variable $t$ in place of $y$ (i.e. $x-ty$, $|t||y|<|x|$) gives the real power series $|x-ty|^{-1}=\sum_{l\ge0}t^l\,c_l(x,y)$ with $c_l(x,y)=|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(x\cdot y/(|x||y|))$ and radius at least $|x|/|y|>1$; by [L8] its coefficients are the derivatives at $t=0$, $c_l(x,y)=\frac{1}{l!}\,\partial_t^l\bigl|_{t=0}|x-ty|^{-1}$, and each $c_l(\,\cdot\,,y)$ is the degree-$l$ homogeneous polynomial in $y$ obtained by expanding $|y|^lP_l(x\cdot y/(|x||y|))$, the solid harmonic coefficient. [step 6.1, L8]

8.1 For fixed $x\ne0$ and small real $t$ the function $(x,t)\mapsto|x-ty|^{-1}$ is smooth and harmonic in $x$ off $x=ty$ by [L7]; since mixed partials commute ([L7]) the operator $\Delta_x$ commutes with $\partial_t^l$, so $\partial_t^l|x-ty|^{-1}$ is harmonic in $x$ on the open set where $x\ne ty$; restricting to $t=0$ and using step 7.1, every $c_l(\,\cdot\,,y)$ is smooth and harmonic on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$. Replacing $x$ by $y$ in the same computation, $\Delta_y|x-ty|^{-1}=t^2\Delta_x|x-ty|^{-1}=0$, shows that the degree-$l$ solid polynomial $y\mapsto c_l(x,y)$ is harmonic in $y$ for each fixed $x\ne0$. [step 7.1, L7]

9.1 Fix a nonempty compact $K$ with $\inf_K|x|>a$; choose $\delta>0$ and an open bounded neighbourhood $K_+$ of $K$ with $\inf_{K_+}|x|>a$ and every closed $\delta$-ball centred at a point of $K$ contained in $K_+$. For $|y|\le a$ and $x\in K_+$ the tail $v_N(x,y)=\sum_{l>N}c_l(x,y)$ is harmonic in $x$ by step 8.1 and satisfies $|v_N(x,y)|\le a^{N+1}\bigl(\inf_{K_+}|x|\bigr)^{-N-2}\bigl(1-a/\inf_{K_+}|x|\bigr)^{-1}\to0$ uniformly on $K_+\times\overline{B_a(0)}$ by step 6.1. Hence for every multi-index $\alpha$ the interior derivative estimates of [L7] give $|D^\alpha v_N(x,y)|\le C_{3,\alpha}\delta^{-3-|\alpha|}|B_\delta|\sup_{K_+}|v_N(\,\cdot\,,y)|\to0$ uniformly on $K$, uniformly for $|y|\le a$. Each sequence $N\mapsto D^\alpha S_N$ of derivatives of the partial sums is therefore uniformly Cauchy, and its uniform limit is identified with $D^\alpha$ of the kernel along short coordinate segments by [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]; thus every fixed spatial derivative series of the kernel converges uniformly on $K$, uniformly for $|y|\le a$. Countable Choice is used only through the harmonic-estimate interface [L7]; the empty $K$ case is vacuous. [step 6.1, step 8.1, L7]

10.1 For a density $\rho$ vanishing outside $\overline{B_a(0)}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $\bigl||x-y|^{-1}-\sum_{l\le N}c_l(x,y)\bigr|\le\varepsilon$ for all $x\in K$ and $|y|\le a$ by step 9.1, so $\bigl|\int\rho(y)\bigl[|x-y|^{-1}-\sum_{l\le N}c_l(x,y)\bigr]dy\bigr|\le\varepsilon\|\rho\|_1$; the partial-sum integrals equal $\sum_{l\le N}\int\rho(y)c_l(x,y)dy$ by the complex linearity of the Lebesgue integral [L8], and hence $\int\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}dy=\sum_{l\ge0}\int\rho(y)c_l(x,y)dy$ with the remainder bounded by $\|\rho\|_1\sup_{|y|\le a}\bigl||x-y|^{-1}-\sum_{l\le N}c_l(x,y)\bigr|$ and, on $|x|\ge r>a$, by $\|\rho\|_1|a|^{N+1}r^{-N-2}(1-r^{-1}a)^{-1}$ (step 6.1, with [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] for the $L^1$ factor). Moreover, on a small open coordinate interval $J$ with $\overline J\subset K_+$ every derivative $D^\alpha_x|x-y|^{-1}$ is bounded on $J\times\overline{B_a(0)}$ by a constant $C_\alpha$, since $|x-y|\ge\inf_{K_+}|x|-a>0$ there; the majorant $C_\alpha|\rho(y)|$ is integrable, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applies (with empty exceptional set) and identifies every spatial derivative of $x\mapsto\int\rho(y)|x-y|^{-1}dy$ on $J$ with $\int\rho(y)D^\alpha_x|x-y|^{-1}dy$, i.e. with the corresponding termwise-differentiated multipole series. [step 6.1, step 9.1, L8]

11.1 Collecting the results: $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $P_l(1)=1$ and $|P_l|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$ (steps 2.1, 2.2); for $|q|<1$ the series $\sum_lq^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ and equals the analytic inverse square root of $1-2qz+q^2$ by steps 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1; the exterior expansion and its geometric remainder hold uniformly on $|y|\le a<r\le|x|$ by step 6.1, with $y=0$ handled by the zero higher terms; the integrated $L^1$-source expansion converges with error at most $\|\rho\|_1$ times the geometric tail, and every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly on observation compacta, uniformly over $|y|\le a$, with derivatives of the integral identified directly by differentiation under the integral sign (steps 9.1, 10.1); the coefficient terms are smooth and harmonic in $x$ away from the origin and are solid harmonics in $y$ (step 8.1). The finite-Riemann polynomial and generating assertions use no Choice (step 4.1); Countable Choice enters only through the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate interfaces [L7, L8]. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, step 10.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$, and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$, its derivatives are $\partial_t s=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $c>0$ and $0\le v_*<c$, a $C^1$ map $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$, and a point $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. The Euclidean norm $|\cdot|$ is that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]].

[L1] [[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]: if $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^m$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ and $\|f'\|\le M$ there, then $\|f(u)-f(v)\|\le M|u-v|$ for all $u,v\in[a,b]$; and if $f'$ is integrable then $\int_a^bf'=f(b)-f(a)$.

[L2] [[lem-reverse-triangle-inequality-in-a-normed-space]]: $\bigl|\|u\|-\|v\|\bigr|\le\|u-v\|$; [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] makes $|\cdot|$ a norm on $\mathbb R^3$, so this reverse triangle inequality and the ordinary triangle inequality hold for $|\cdot|$.

[L3] Continuity of the data and of $g$: [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] and [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] make $C^k$ maps and their derivatives componentwise, and [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] with [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]] make a differentiable $\mathbb R^3$-valued map continuous. [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] and [[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]] give continuity of sums, scalar multiples and composites. In particular $z$ is continuous, $s\mapsto x-z(s)$ is continuous, the norm is $1$-Lipschitz and continuous, and $g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$.

[L4] [[thm-intermediate-value]]: a continuous real function on a closed bounded interval takes every value between its endpoint values.

[L5] [[thm-parametrized-implicit-function-theorem-with-higher-regularity]]: for $k,m,n\ge1$, $p\in\mathbb N$, open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n+p}$ and $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ of class $C^k$, if $F(a,b,\lambda_0)=0$ and $D_yF(a,b,\lambda_0)$ is invertible, then near $(a,\lambda_0)$ the equation $F(x,y,\lambda)=0$ is equivalent to $y=\varphi(x,\lambda)$ for a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi$, and $D\varphi=-D_yF^{-1}D_{(x,\lambda)}F$. [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]: finite sums, products and composites of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$.

[L6] [[thm-higher-regularity-of-local-inverses]]: a $C^k$ map with invertible derivative at a point has $C^k$ local inverses there. [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]: $(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}$ on $(0,\infty)$, in particular $(d/dh)h^{3/2}=(3/2)h^{1/2}$ for $h>0$; [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums, scalar multiples, products and quotients of differentiable functions are differentiable with the usual rules.

## Proof

1.1 For all $s_1,s_2\in\mathbb R$ the restriction of $z$ to the interval with endpoints $s_1,s_2$ is continuous with derivative bounded by $v_*$ at interior points, so [L1] gives $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\le v_*|s_2-s_1|$; consequently $z$, and by [L3] each map $s\mapsto g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$, is continuous. [L1, L3]

2.1 For $s_2>s_1$ the reverse triangle inequality [L2] gives $|x-z(s_2)|\ge|x-z(s_1)|-|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|$, so by step 1.1 $g_x(s_2)-g_x(s_1)\ge(s_2-s_1)-\frac{v_*}{c}(s_2-s_1)=(s_2-s_1)\bigl(1-\frac{v_*}{c}\bigr)>0$: the map $g_x$ is strictly increasing and $g_x(s)\ge s$ for every $s$. Moreover $|x-z(s)|\le|x-z(0)|+|z(s)-z(0)|\le|x-z(0)|+v_*|s|$, so for $s<0$ one has $g_x(s)\le s+\frac{|x-z(0)|-v_*s}{c}=s\bigl(1-\frac{v_*}{c}\bigr)+\frac{|x-z(0)|}{c}$. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 Given $t$, put $C=|x-z(0)|/c$ and choose $s_+=\max(t,0)+1$ and $s_-=\min\bigl(t,\frac{t-C}{1-v_*/c}\bigr)-1$, so that $s_-<t<s_+$; step 2.1 gives $g_x(s_+)\ge s_+>t$ and $g_x(s_-)<t$. Since $g_x$ is continuous by step 1.1, [[thm-intermediate-value]] on the nondegenerate interval $[s_-,s_+]$ supplies a root $s$ of $g_x(s)=t$, i.e. of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. If $s_1<s_2$ were two roots then $g_x(s_1)=g_x(s_2)$ would contradict the strict increase of step 2.1, so this root is unique; it satisfies $s\le t$ because $g_x(s)\ge s$, with $s=t$ if and only if $|x-z(t)|=0$, that is if and only if $x=z(t)$. Hence off the instantaneous trajectory, where $x\ne z(t)$, one has $s<t$ and $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the set $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ is open because $z$ is continuous. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L3, L4, algebra]

4.1 Fix $(x_0,t_0)\in D$, let $s_0=s(x_0,t_0)$, $r_0=|x_0-z(s_0)|=c(t_0-s_0)>0$, $n_0=(x_0-z(s_0))/r_0$, $\beta_0=z'(s_0)/c$ and $\kappa_0=1-n_0\cdot\beta_0$. Since $|n_0|=1$ and $|\beta_0|\le v_*/c<1$, one has $1-v_*/c\le\kappa_0\le1+v_*/c$ and $\kappa_0>0$. [step 3.1, L1, algebra]

5.1 Define $F(x,\tau,y)=c^2(\tau-y)^2-|x-z(y)|^2$ on $\mathbb R^5$. Each component of $z$ is $C^k$ and the expression is a finite sum of products of $C^k$ functions composed with $z$, so $F$ is $C^k$ by [L5]. At the base point of step 4.1, $F(x_0,t_0,s_0)=c^2(t_0-s_0)^2-r_0^2=0$, and computing the partial $y$-derivative along the differentiable curve $y\mapsto z(y)$ gives $\partial_yF(x_0,t_0,s_0)=-2c^2(t_0-s_0)+2(x_0-z(s_0))\cdot z'(s_0)=-2cr_0+2r_0\,c\,\beta_0\cdot n_0=-2cr_0\kappa_0\ne0$. The parametrized implicit function theorem [L5] (with $y=s$, parameters $(x,\tau)$) therefore gives open neighbourhoods $P\ni(x_0,t_0)$, $Q\ni s_0$ and a unique $C^k$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ with $F(x,\tau,\varphi(x,\tau))=0$ on $P$ and $D\varphi=-D_yF^{-1}D_{(x,\tau)}F$. [step 4.1, L5, algebra]

6.1 By [L3] the map $(x,\tau)\mapsto\varphi(x,\tau)-\tau$ is continuous and negative at $(x_0,t_0)$ because $\varphi$ is continuous with $\varphi(x_0,t_0)=s_0<t_0$; shrinking $P$ if necessary, $\varphi(x,\tau)<\tau$ there. On that neighbourhood $F=0$ reads $c^2(\tau-\varphi)^2=|x-z(\varphi)|^2$ with $\tau-\varphi>0$, hence $\tau-\varphi=|x-z(\varphi)|/c$, that is $g_x(\varphi)=\tau$; by uniqueness of the root (step 3.1) $\varphi=s$. Thus $s$ is $C^k$ on a neighbourhood of $(x_0,t_0)$; since $(x_0,t_0)\in D$ and $k\ge1$ were arbitrary (and a smooth $z$ is $C^k$ for every $k$), $s$ is $C^k$ on $D$, and smooth when $z$ is smooth. [step 5.1, step 3.1, L3, L5]

6.2 Reading off the displayed derivative formula at the base point of step 5.1, $\partial_\tau F(x_0,t_0,s_0)=2c^2(t_0-s_0)=2cr_0$ and $\partial_{x_i}F(x_0,t_0,s_0)=-2(x_0-z(s_0))_i=-2r_0n_{0,i}$, so $\partial_ts=\partial_\tau\varphi=-\partial_\tau F/\partial_yF=1/\kappa_0$ and $\partial_{x_i}s=-\partial_{x_i}F/\partial_yF=-n_{0,i}/(c\kappa_0)$; since the point was arbitrary in $D$, the same formulas hold on all of $D$, with $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$ by step 4.1. [step 4.1, step 5.1, L1, algebra]

7.1 For the sharpness clause choose $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $(-1,1)$ and $\chi=0$ outside $(-2,2)$, and put $f(s)=\chi(s)|s|^{3/2}$. Then $f$ is $C^1$: on $(0,\infty)$ it equals $s^{3/2}$ with derivative $(3/2)s^{1/2}$, on $(-\infty,0)$ it equals $(-s)^{3/2}$ with derivative $-\frac32(-s)^{1/2}$ by [L6], and at $0$ the difference quotient is $|h|^{3/2}/h=\operatorname{sgn}(h)|h|^{1/2}\to0$, so $f'(0)=0$; $f'$ is bounded by some $C_f<\infty$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ with $\varepsilon C_f<c/2$ and set $z(s)=(\varepsilon f(s),0,0)$, a $C^1$ trajectory with $|z'|\le v_*:=\varepsilon C_f<c$; fix $L>2\varepsilon\sup_s f(s)$ and $x=(L,0,0)$, so $|x-z(s)|=L-\varepsilon f(s)$ and the equation $g_x(s)=t$ reads $s+\bigl(L-\varepsilon f(s)\bigr)/c=:g(s)=t$. One has $g'(s)=1-\varepsilon f'(s)/c\ge1-\varepsilon C_f/c>1/2>0$, so $g$ is strictly increasing, and the root map $s$ is the inverse of $g$. At $0$ one has $g(0)=L/c=:t_0$ and $g'(0)=1-\varepsilon f'(0)/c=1$, hence $s'(t_0)=1/g'(0)=1\ne0$; if $s$ were $C^2$ near $t_0$, then by [L6] (applied to the $C^2$ map $s$ with invertible derivative $1$ at $t_0$) its local inverse, namely $g$, would be $C^2$ near $0$. But $f'(h)=(3/2)h^{1/2}$ for small $h>0$, so $\bigl(g'(h)-g'(0)\bigr)/h=-\frac{\varepsilon}{c}\cdot\frac{(3/2)h^{1/2}}{h}=-\frac{3\varepsilon}{2c}h^{-1/2}\to-\infty$ as $h\downarrow0$: $g$ is not twice differentiable at $0$, a contradiction. Hence a merely $C^1$ trajectory need not give a $C^2$ root. [step 6.2, L6, algebra]

8.1 Collecting: existence, uniqueness, $s\le t$ with equality exactly on $x=z(t)$, and the open domain $D$ with $s<t$, $r>0$ are step 3.1; $C^k$ (hence $C^1$, and smooth for smooth $z$) regularity on $D$ is step 6.1; the derivative formulas and the bound $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$ are steps 4.1 and 6.2; the non-improvement witness for a merely $C^1$ trajectory is step 7.1. No Choice principle is used anywhere. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 6.2, step 7.1] ∎
