## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$ and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (entrywise integrability), and let

$$\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds\qquad(\operatorname{Im}z>0)$$

be the matrix response function. Here locally absolutely continuous means that each real entry restricted to every compact interval $[a,b]\subseteq[0,\infty)$ satisfies the finite disjoint-interval condition of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]: for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\sum_\ell(v_\ell-u_\ell)<\delta$ implies $\sum_\ell|K_{jk}(v_\ell)-K_{jk}(u_\ell)|<\epsilon$ for every finite family with disjoint interiors. $K\prime$ denotes the almost-everywhere derivative, with any measurable zero extension on its null exceptional set. Then the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic functions on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-domain]]), continuous and $C^1$ on its real boundary, bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K'_{jk}\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and the entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas hold: for real $\omega$,

$$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi .$$

The sharper bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le(|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K\prime_{jk}\|_1)/|z|$ holds for every nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. Here $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$ means $\lim_{R\to\infty}\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}(\int_{\omega-R}^{\omega-\eta}+\int_{\omega+\eta}^{\omega+R})F(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$; the tails converge absolutely, so the choice of centering at infinity does not change the limit. For an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define the total transfer function $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$; the formulas then apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Causality alone supplies neither growth assumptions beyond those stated nor the passivity quadratic-form condition, which is a separate model assertion.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $d\ge1$, a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ entrywise, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, and the response $\chi$ as in the statement. Write $k=K_{jk}$ for a fixed real entry.

[L1] **Absolute continuity, its calculus and integrability.** [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]] defines absolute continuity on a compact interval by the finite disjoint-interval condition; [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]] gives that a $C^1$ function on $[a,b]$ in the endpoint-extension sense is Lipschitz, hence absolutely continuous. Under Countable and Dependent Choice, [[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] gives, for $k$ absolutely continuous on $[0,N]$, the a.e. derivative $k'\in L^1[0,N]$ and the identity $k(s)=k(0)+\int_0^sk'(u)\,du$; [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] gives $\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a)$ for absolutely continuous $F,G$.

[L2] **Convergence and parameter integrals.** [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: if $f_n\to f$ a.e. and $|f_n|\le g$ a.e. with $\int g<\infty$, then $\int|f_n-f|\to0$ and $\int f_n\to\int f$. [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: monotonicity and the scalar rule for nonnegative integrals; in particular a nonnegative function bounded below by a positive constant on sets of unbounded measure has infinite integral. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]: with an integrable majorant for the parameter derivative, the parameter integral is differentiable with the expected derivative.

[L3] **Complex analysis tools.** [[def-complex-domain]]: the upper half-plane $H=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ and its translates are nonempty connected open sets. [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]]: a function with continuous first partials satisfying $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ at every point is holomorphic. [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]] and [[cor-ml-estimate-for-complex-line-integrals]]: line integrals of continuous integrands over rectifiable contours exist and satisfy $|\int_\gamma f|\le ML(\gamma)$ when $|f|\le M$ on the trace. [[cor-cauchy-theorem-star-shaped-domain]]: a holomorphic function on an open star-shaped set has zero integral over every closed rectifiable contour in it; [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] records the same conclusion for null-homotopic loops in general open sets. [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]]: on a fixed rectifiable contour, uniform convergence of continuous integrands passes to the integral. [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]: a continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous, so continuity on the closed upper half-plane gives uniform convergence on compact pieces under vertical shifts. [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]] are the declared choice assumptions of [L1].

## Proof

1.1 Fix an entry $k=K_{jk}$. On each $[0,N]$ the FTC representation of [L1] gives $k(s)=k(0)+\int_0^sk'(u)\,du$ for every $s\in[0,N]$. Since $k'\in L^1(0,\infty)$, the limit $\ell:=k(0)+\int_0^\infty k'(u)\,du$ exists and $k(s)\to\ell$ as $s\to\infty$, because $|k'(u)|\mathbf 1_{[0,s]}(u)\le|k'(u)|$ and dominated convergence [L2] applies. If $\ell\ne0$ there is $s_0$ with $|k(s)|\ge|\ell|/2$ for all $s\ge s_0$, so monotonicity of the nonnegative integral [L2] gives $\int_0^N|k|\ge(|\ell|/2)(N-s_0)\to\infty$, contradicting $k\in L^1$; hence $\ell=0$ and $k(s)\to0$. [L1, L2]

1.2 For $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ the integral defining the entry $\chi_{jk}(z)=\int_0^\infty k(s)e^{izs}ds$ converges absolutely with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\int_0^\infty|k(s)|e^{-\operatorname{Im}z\cdot s}ds\le\|k\|_1$, and it is continuous on the closed upper half-plane: if $z_n\to z$ in $\{\operatorname{Im}\ge0\}$, then $k(s)e^{iz_ns}\to k(s)e^{izs}$ pointwise with majorant $|k(s)|$, so [L2] gives $\chi_{jk}(z_n)\to\chi_{jk}(z)$. [L2]

1.3 Write $z=x+iy$ on $H$. The parameter derivatives of the integrand $k(s)e^{izs}$ in $x$ and $y$ are $isk(s)e^{izs}$ and $-sk(s)e^{izs}$, whose absolute values are bounded by the measurable function $s|k(s)|$, integrable by hypothesis; [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied on a bounded rectangle around any point of $H$ therefore gives $\partial_x\chi_{jk}(z)=\int_0^\infty isk(s)e^{izs}ds$ and $\partial_y\chi_{jk}(z)=-\int_0^\infty sk(s)e^{izs}ds$, and both partials are continuous on $H$ by [L2]. Since $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=i\int_0^\infty sk(s)e^{izs}ds=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}$, the Cauchy-Riemann equations hold with continuous partials, and [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]] makes $\chi_{jk}$ holomorphic on the upper half-plane. [L2, L3]

2.1 Along the real boundary, fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$: for $t$ in a bounded interval around $\omega$ the integrand $k(s)e^{its}$ has $t$-derivative $isk(s)e^{its}$, bounded by the integrable $s|k(s)|$, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] gives $\chi_{jk}'(t)=\int_0^\infty isk(s)e^{its}ds$ for every such $t$, and this derivative is continuous in $t$ by dominated convergence [L2]. Thus $\chi_{jk}$ is continuous on the closed upper half-plane (step 1.2) and $C^1$ on its real boundary. [step 1.2, L2]

2.2 For $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ and $N>0$, apply [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] on $[0,N]$ to the absolutely continuous pair $(k,\operatorname{Re}e^{izs})$ and to $(k,\operatorname{Im}e^{izs})$; the function $s\mapsto e^{izs}$ is $C^1$ hence absolutely continuous by [L1], and combining the two real identities gives $\int_0^Nk(s)e^{izs}ds=\frac{k(N)e^{izN}-k(0)}{iz}-\frac{1}{iz}\int_0^Nk'(s)e^{izs}ds$. Since $|e^{izN}|\le1$ for $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ and $k(N)\to0$ by step 1.1, dominated convergence [L2] with majorant $|k'|$ gives, in the limit $N\to\infty$, $\chi_{jk}(z)=-\frac{k(0)}{iz}-\frac{1}{iz}\int_0^\infty k'(s)e^{izs}ds$; hence $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\frac{|k(0)|+\|k'\|_1}{|z|}$ for every nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, in particular $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|k(0)|+\|k'\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$, and $\chi_{jk}(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on the closed upper half-plane. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 Let $F=\chi_{jk}$, which is holomorphic on $H$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane and $O(1/|z|)$ there by steps 1.3, 1.2 and 2.2. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, choose $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$, and let $\gamma$ be the closed contour consisting of the real segments $[\omega-R,\omega-\eta]$ and $[\omega+\eta,\omega+R]$ traversed from left to right, the clockwise small upper semicircle $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle $z=\omega+Re^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ increasing from $0$ to $\pi$; every piece is rectifiable and the contour is closed. For $\delta>0$ put $f_\delta(z)=F(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on the open set $D_\delta=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$: this set is star-shaped about $\omega+iA$ for $A>1$, because the removed ray lies in $\{\operatorname{Im}\le0\}$ while every point of $\gamma$ has $\operatorname{Im}\ge0$ and different from $\omega$, so the segment from $\omega+iA$ to it stays in $D_\delta$. On $D_\delta$ the function $F(\cdot+i\delta)$ is holomorphic (translate of a holomorphic function) and $1/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic off $\omega$, and $\gamma$ lies in $D_\delta$; [[cor-cauchy-theorem-star-shaped-domain]] therefore gives $\int_\gamma f_\delta=0$. As $\delta\downarrow0$ the integrands $f_\delta$ converge uniformly on the trace of $\gamma$ to $F(z)/(z-\omega)$: the trace is compact, all shifted points lie in a compact subset of the closed upper half-plane, and $F$ is uniformly continuous there by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]; so [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] gives $\int_\gamma F(z)/(z-\omega)dz=0$. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.2, L1, L3]

4.1 Estimate the pieces of the identity of step 3.1, using $|F(z)|\le C/|z|$ from step 2.2. On the large arc $|z-\omega|=R$ and $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$, so the integrand is at most $C/(R(R-|\omega|))$ and [[cor-ml-estimate-for-complex-line-integrals]] bounds the contribution by $\pi RC/(R(R-|\omega|))\to0$ as $R\to\infty$. On the small arc, parametrizing $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $\int=-i\int_0^\pi F(\omega+\eta e^{i\theta})\,d\theta\to-i\pi F(\omega)$ as $\eta\downarrow0$ by continuity of $F$. The two real segments contribute $\int_{\eta<|t|<R}F(\omega+t)/t\,dt$ with $t$ real; writing $F(\omega+t)=F(\omega)+[F(\omega+t)-F(\omega)]$, the constant term integrates to $0$ on the symmetric punctured interval and the remainder is bounded on $|t|\le1$ because $F$ is $C^1$ on the real boundary (step 2.1) with the difference quotient tending to $F'(\omega)$, while for $|t|\ge1$ it is dominated by $O(1/|t|^2)$ using $|F|\le C/|t+\omega|$; hence its $\eta\downarrow0$ limit is the absolutely convergent principal value. Passing to the limit first in $\eta$ and then in $R$ in the identity $\int_\gamma F/(z-\omega)=0$ therefore yields $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{F(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi=i\pi F(\omega)$, and the tails converge absolutely, so the centering at infinity does not affect the limit. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, L3]

5.1 Write $F=u+iv$ with $u=\operatorname{Re}F$, $v=\operatorname{Im}F$. Splitting the identity of step 4.1 into real and imaginary parts gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{u(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi+i\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{v(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi=i\pi(u(\omega)+iv(\omega))=-\pi v(\omega)+i\pi u(\omega)$; comparing parts, $u(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{v(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi$ and $v(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{u(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi$. [step 4.1]

6.1 Each entry $k=K_{jk}$ is locally absolutely continuous with $k,k'\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $sk(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ by the hypotheses on $K$, so steps 1.3, 2.1, 2.2 and 5.1 apply to it: the entries of $\chi$ are holomorphic on the upper half-plane, continuous on the closed upper half-plane and $C^1$ on the real boundary, obey $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le(|k(0)|+\|k'\|_1)/|z|$ for nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ (hence $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|k(0)|+\|k'\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$), and satisfy the two displayed principal-value dispersion formulas. For an instantaneous real matrix $\chi_\infty$ the identities applied to $\chi=\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty$ give the stated form of the total transfer function; the scalar case is $d=1$. Nothing in the argument uses or produces a passivity quadratic-form condition, and no growth assumption beyond the stated integrability of $K,K',sK$ is made. [step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 5.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice (used through the smooth-up-to-the-boundary density theorem below) and the Axiom of Countable Choice (declared by the flattening and Sobolev suppliers). The axiom interfaces are [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain in the graph sense ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[def-connected-space]]); its closure is compact, so the boundary has a finite cover by boundary charts ([[def-compact-space]]). There is a constant $C_\Omega$, depending only on $\Omega$, with

$$\|v-v_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1(\Omega),\qquad v_\Omega:=\frac1{|\Omega|}\int_\Omega v\,dx .$$

Here $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the weak coordinate derivatives, and $\nabla v$ denotes the weak gradient. The estimate is the mean-zero (Poincare) inequality needed for weak Neumann solvability, where the mean-zero subspace carries the gradient norm.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A bounded connected $C^1$ domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ in the graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, and a function $v\in H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. For a measurable $A\subseteq\Omega$ with $|A|>0$ write $v_A=|A|^{-1}\int_Av$.

[L1] **Sobolev conventions.** [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] (Countable Choice): $W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is the set of $L^2$ classes whose weak coordinate derivatives $D^\alpha v$, $|\alpha|\le1$, exist as $L^2$ classes; for the multi-index $e_i$, $D^{e_i}v$ is the weak gradient component $\partial_iv$, and $\|\nabla v\|_2=(\sum_i\|\partial_iv\|_2^2)^{1/2}$. [[lem-bounded-restriction-and-cutoff-localisation-in-sobolev-spaces]] (Axiom of Choice): restriction to an open $U\subseteq\Omega$ maps $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$ contractively into $W^{1,2}(U)$.

[L2] **One-dimensional absolute continuity and product integration.** [[thm-acl-characterisation-of-w-one-p]]: a $W^{1,2}$ function on a box is, after modification on a null set, absolutely continuous on almost every line parallel to each coordinate axis, with the one-variable fundamental theorem and the $L^2$ derivative along that line. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: iterated integrals of nonnegative and $L^1$ functions over product domains agree. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]: $\int|fg|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$; in particular $\bigl|\frac1{|A|}\int_A h\bigr|^2\le\frac1{|A|}\int_A|h|^2$ for $h\in L^2(A)$.

[L3] **Charts, flattening, density and change of variables.** [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]: about each boundary point there is a $C^1$ flattening chart $\Phi$ of the local graph, with $C^1$ inverse, mapping the local piece of $\Omega$ exactly onto the half-box $\{t<0\}$; on compact patches the chart and its inverse have bounded first derivatives. [[lem-c-k-boundary-flattening-preserves-wkp-locally]] (Countable Choice, $k=1$, $p=2$): composition with such a chart is a bounded operation on $W^{1,2}$ between the compact patches, in both directions when the patches correspond. [[thm-smooth-up-to-the-boundary-density-on-smooth-domains]] (Axiom of Choice, $k=1$, $p=2$): the restrictions to $\Omega$ of compactly supported smooth functions are dense in $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]] (Countable Choice): a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T$ gives $\int f\,d\lambda=\int(f\circ T)|\det DT|\,d\lambda$ for nonnegative measurable $f$.

[L4] **Topology.** [[def-compact-space]] and [[def-connected-space]]: the closure of a bounded graph domain is compact, continuous images of compact sets are compact, and a topological space is connected when it has no partition into two nonempty relatively open sets.

[L5] **Choice.** [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is used exactly once, to invoke the density theorem of [L3]; [[def-countable-choice]] is declared by the Sobolev, flattening and change-of-variables interfaces of [L1] and [L3].

## Proof

1.1 Let $R=\prod_{i=1}^3I_i$ be a closed box of positive side lengths (an axis-parallel product of bounded intervals) and let $u\in W^{1,2}(R^\circ)$. Then $\int_R\int_R|u(x)-u(y)|^2dx\,dy\le C_R|R|\int_R|\nabla u|^2dx$ with a constant $C_R$ depending only on the side lengths. Indeed, $|u(x)-u(y)|^2\le3\sum_{i=1}^3|u(x)-u(x^{(i)})|^2$ where $x^{(i)}$ is $x$ with its $i$-th coordinate replaced by $y_i$ (the telescoping identity with three intermediate points); along almost every line parallel to the $i$-th axis the one-variable fundamental theorem of [L2] gives $|u(x)-u(x^{(i)})|^2\le|I_i|\int_{I_i}|\partial_iu|^2$, and integrating this over the remaining coordinates (Tonelli [L2]) yields $\int_R\int_R|u(x)-u(x^{(i)})|^2dx\,dy\le|R|\,|I_i|^2\int_R|\partial_iu|^2dx$; summing the three terms gives the claim with $C_R=3\max_i|I_i|^2$. [L1, L2]

2.1 For a box $R$ and $u\in W^{1,2}(R^\circ)$ one has $\int_R|u-u_R|^2\le C_R'\int_R|\nabla u|^2$ with $C_R'$ depending only on the side lengths: for almost every fixed $x\in R$ the mean-value identity $u(x)-u_R=|R|^{-1}\int_R(u(x)-u(y))dy$ holds, and the averaged Cauchy-Schwarz inequality of [L2] gives $|u(x)-u_R|^2\le|R|^{-1}\int_R|u(x)-u(y)|^2dy$; integrating in $x$ and inserting step 1.1 gives $\int_R|u-u_R|^2\le C_R'|R|^{-1}\cdot|R|\int_R|\nabla u|^2$ with $C_R'=C_R$. The identical argument applies to a half-box $H=\{x\in R:x_3<0\}$: the segment joining two points of the convex half-box stays in the half-box, and the one-dimensional statements hold for almost every such segment. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 The same estimate transfers to each patch of $\Omega$. For a boundary chart patch $U=\Omega\cap W$ with flattening chart $\Phi$ and half-box $H=\Phi(U)$: if $v$ is smooth on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, then $w=v\circ\Phi^{-1}\in C^\infty(\overline H)$ satisfies by step 2.1 and the chain rule $\int_U|v-v_U|^2\le C_U\int_H|\nabla w|^2\le C_U\int_U|\nabla v|^2$ with $C_U$ depending only on the patch and the chart bounds; here the change of variables of [L3] transports the integrals and the bounded Jacobians of $\Phi,\Phi^{-1}$ on the compact patch compare $\nabla w$ with $\nabla v$. For an interior patch $U$ chosen as a box with $\overline U\subset\Omega$, step 2.1 gives the same inequality directly. The constants are uniform over the finitely many patches. [step 2.1, L3]

4.1 Choose a finite cover $\Omega=\bigcup_{j=1}^N U_j$ by the chart and interior patches of step 3.1, all open with $|U_j|>0$, whose intersection graph (vertices $j$, an edge when $|U_j\cap U_k|>0$) is connected. Compactness gives a finite cover: $\overline\Omega$ is compact ([L4]) and is covered by the chart neighbourhoods and the interior boxes; discard redundancies and shrink patches so that every overlap retained has positive measure, and refine the graph by adding intermediate small boxes between components if necessary. If the resulting graph had at least two components, the unions of the patches in different components would be disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets of $\Omega$ whose union is $\Omega$, contradicting the connectedness of $\Omega$ ([L4]); hence the graph is connected. Then every $v\in H^1(\Omega)$ satisfies, on each patch, the estimate of step 3.1 applied to the local restriction and to smooth approximations: by the density theorem of [L3] there are smooth $v_m\to v$ in $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$, and the estimates $\int_{U_j}|v_m-(v_m)_{U_j}|^2\le C_j\int_{U_j}|\nabla v_m|^2$ pass to the limit because restriction, the mean, and both sides are continuous in $W^{1,2}$ norm [L1]; this yields $\int_{U_j}|v-(v)_{U_j}|^2\le C_j\int_{U_j}|\nabla v|^2$ for every $v\in H^1(\Omega)$. [step 3.1, L1, L3, L4]

5.1 The patch means of such a $v$ differ controllably across overlapping patches: if $|U_j\cap U_k|>0$ then, pointwise on the overlap, $|(v)_{U_j}-(v)_{U_k}|^2\le2|(v)_{U_j}-v(x)|^2+2|v(x)-(v)_{U_k}|^2$, and integrating over $U_j\cap U_k$ and dividing by its measure gives $|(v)_{U_j}-(v)_{U_k}|^2\le\frac{2}{|U_j\cap U_k|}\bigl(\int_{U_j}|v-(v)_{U_j}|^2+\int_{U_k}|v-(v)_{U_k}|^2\bigr)$ (using [L2] for the averaged terms). Along a finite spanning tree of the connected intersection graph of step 4.1, the triangle inequality iterated over the tree path bounds $|(v)_{U_j}-(v)_{U_1}|^2$ by a finite constant depending only on the cover times the sum of the squared edge differences, hence by $C''\sum_k\int_{U_k}|\nabla v|^2\le C''\int_\Omega|\nabla v|^2$ using step 4.1. [step 4.1, L2]

6.1 Finally $v_\Omega$ minimises the constant term: $\int_\Omega|v-v_\Omega|^2=\min_{a\in\mathbb R}\int_\Omega|v-a|^2\le\int_\Omega|v-(v)_{U_1}|^2=\sum_j\int_{U_j}|v-(v)_{U_1}|^2\le2\sum_j\int_{U_j}|v-(v)_{U_j}|^2+2\sum_j|U_j|\,|(v)_{U_j}-(v)_{U_1}|^2\le C_\Omega^2\int_\Omega|\nabla v|^2$, with $C_\Omega$ built from the finitely many patch constants, the cover geometry and the measure of $\Omega$ only. Taking square roots gives $\|v-v_\Omega\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ for every $v\in H^1(\Omega)$. The Axiom of Choice is used only through the density theorem of step 4.1 and the localization of [L1]; Countable Choice is used through the Sobolev, flattening and change-of-variables interfaces; no other choice principle is invoked. [step 4.1, step 5.1, L1, L5] ∎

## Statement

For $l\in\mathbb N_0$ and $z>0$ set

$$h_l(z)=(-i)^{l+1}\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\sum_{j=0}^{l}\frac{i^j\,(l+j)!}{j!\,(l-j)!\,(2z)^j}.$$

Then $h_l$ is a complex-valued $C^2$ function of $z>0$ solving

$$h_l''(z)+\frac2z h_l'(z)+\Bigl[1-\frac{l(l+1)}{z^2}\Bigr]h_l(z)=0,$$

it never vanishes on $(0,\infty)$, and its Wronskian-type identity $\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_l(z)}\,h_l'(z)\bigr)=z^{-2}$ holds. For $k>0$ and $R>0$ the spherical Dirichlet-to-Neumann coefficient

$$t_l=\frac{k\,h_l'(kR)}{h_l(kR)}$$

satisfies the exact bounds

$$\operatorname{Re}t_l\le-\frac1R,\qquad |\operatorname{Re}t_l|\le\frac{l+1}{R},\qquad 0<\operatorname{Im}t_l\le k .$$

These are exact identities and inequalities for the displayed explicit functions, not asymptotic formulas; the argument uses only elementary differentiation and a constant Wronskian, so no large-$l$ asymptotic input is required.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $l\in\mathbb N_0$, the explicit function $h_l$ of the statement on $(0,\infty)$, and reals $k>0$, $R>0$. Complex-valued functions of the real variable $z$ are handled componentwise under the identification $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$ of [[rem-complex-plane-euclidean-dictionary]], with derivative and integral as in [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

[L1] **Differentiation.** [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]: the complex exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$. [[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]: sums, scalar multiples, products and (where the denominator is nonzero) quotients of complex differentiable functions are complex differentiable with the usual rules; in particular $z\mapsto e^{iz}P(z)$ and $z\mapsto e^{iz}P(z)/z$ are holomorphic on their domains for polynomial $P$, hence $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ along the real axis. [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: the same rules hold for real-valued functions, and (componentwise) for the real and imaginary parts of a complex-valued differentiable function: if $y=u+iv$ with $u,v$ real differentiable on an interval, then $y'=u'+iv'$, $\operatorname{Re}y'=(\operatorname{Re}y)'$, $\operatorname{Im}y'=(\operatorname{Im}y)'$.

[L2] **Constants from a vanishing derivative.** [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]: a real-valued function continuous on an order-convex set, with derivative zero at every interior point, is constant; and two such functions with equal derivatives differ by a constant.

## Proof

1.1 Write $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{l}c_jz^{-j}$ with $c_j=\frac{i^j(l+j)!}{j!\,(l-j)!\,2^j}$, so that $h_l=(-i)^{l+1}e^{iz}P(z)/z$, and put $y=zh_l=(-i)^{l+1}e^{iz}P(z)$. Substituting $y=e^{iz}P$ into the equation $y''+(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})y=0$, which is equivalent to the stated radial equation because $h=y/z$ gives $h''+\frac2zh'+(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})h=\frac{1}{z}\bigl(y''+(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})y\bigr)$, produces by the product rule [L1] the equation $P''+2iP'-l(l+1)z^{-2}P=0$ for $P$. Inserting the finite expansion $P=\sum_jc_jz^{-j}$ and matching the coefficient of $z^{-m-2}$ gives $\bigl[m(m+1)-l(l+1)\bigr]c_m-2i(m+1)c_{m+1}=0$, that is $c_{m+1}=\frac{i(l-m)(l+m+1)}{2(m+1)}c_m$, and the displayed factorials satisfy this recursion because $\frac{c_{m+1}}{c_m}=\frac{i(l-m)(l+m+1)}{2(m+1)}$; the recursion terminates with $c_{l+1}=0$, so $P$ is exactly this polynomial and $y$, hence $h_l$, satisfies the stated equation and is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$. The leading term is $(-i)^{l+1}e^{iz}/z$ with remainder $O(z^{-2})$. [L1, algebra]

2.1 With $y=u+iv$, $u=\operatorname{Re}y$, $v=\operatorname{Im}y$, put $W=uv'-vu'=\operatorname{Im}(\overline y\,y')$. The componentwise real and imaginary parts of the equation of step 1.1 give $u''+(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})u=0$ and $v''+(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})v=0$; the product rule [L1] gives $W'=uv''-vu''=u\bigl[-(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})v\bigr]-v\bigl[-(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})u\bigr]=0$ on $(0,\infty)$, so $W$ is constant by [L2]. Since $P(z)\to c_0=1$ and $P'(z)\to0$ as $z\to\infty$, $y=e^{iz}(1+o(1))$ and $y'=ie^{iz}(1+o(1))$, so $\overline y\,y'=|y|^2(i+o(1))$ and $W\to\operatorname{Im}i=1$; hence $W\equiv1$. Consequently $\operatorname{Im}(\overline{h_l}\,h_l')=\operatorname{Im}\bigl((\overline y/z)(y'/z-y/z^2)\bigr)=W/z^2-|y|^2\operatorname{Im}(1/z^3)=z^{-2}$, which is nonzero for every $z>0$; therefore $h_l(z)\ne0$ on $(0,\infty)$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, algebra]

3.1 Put $F=|y|^2$ and $c(z)=1-l(l+1)z^{-2}$. By step 2.1 the complex quantity $A=\overline y\,y'$ has $\operatorname{Im}A=1$, so $A'=\operatorname{Re}(A)'=\frac12F''$ is real (componentwise product rule [L1]); on the other hand $A'=|\overline{y'}|^2+\overline y\,y''=|y'|^2-cF$. Differentiating $\frac12F''=|y'|^2-cF$ gives $\frac12F'''=2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{y'}y'')-c'F-cF'$; since $y''=-cy$, $\operatorname{Re}(\overline{y'}y'')=-c\operatorname{Re}(\overline{y'}y)=-c\frac{F'}{2}$, and with $c'=2l(l+1)z^{-3}$ this yields the linear third-order equation $F'''+4(1-l(l+1)z^{-2})F'+4l(l+1)z^{-3}F=0$. Since $P=\sum_jc_jz^{-j}$ with $c_j=i^j(\text{real})$, all cross terms of $|P|^2=\sum_{j,k}c_j\overline{c_k}z^{-j-k}$ with $j-k$ odd cancel in the sum over $(j,k)$ and $(k,j)$, so $F=|P|^2$ is a finite even polynomial in $z^{-1}$, $F=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jz^{-2j}$ with real $a_j$ and $a_0=1$; matching the coefficient of $z^{-2m-3}$ in the third-order equation gives $-4m(m+1)(2m+1)a_m+8ml(l+1)a_m+4l(l+1)a_m-8(m+1)a_{m+1}=0$, i.e. $a_{m+1}=\frac{(2m+1)[l(l+1)-m(m+1)]}{2(m+1)}a_m$, whose positive solution is $a_j=\frac{(2j)!\,(l+j)!}{2^{2j}(j!)^2(l-j)!}$ for $0\le j\le l$ and $a_j=0$ for $j>l$, because the factor $[l(l+1)-j(j+1)]$ vanishes at $j=l$. In particular $a_j>0$ for $j\le l$, $a_0=1$, and $|h_l(z)|^2=F(z)/z^2=\sum_{j=0}^l a_jz^{-2j-2}\ge z^{-2}$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L1]

4.1 On $(0,\infty)$ one has $\frac{h_l'}{h_l}=\frac{\overline{h_l}\,h_l'}{|h_l|^2}$ and, from step 3.1 and $\overline y\,y'=\frac{F'}{2}+i$ (step 2.1), $\operatorname{Re}(\overline{h_l}\,h_l')=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\frac{\overline y\,y'}{z^2}-\frac{|y|^2}{z^3}\bigr)=\frac{F'}{2z^2}-\frac{F}{z^3}=-\frac1{z^3}\sum_{j=0}^l(1+j)a_jz^{-2j}$ and $\operatorname{Im}(\overline{h_l}\,h_l')=z^{-2}$; dividing by $|h_l|^2=F(z)/z^2$ gives $\operatorname{Re}\frac{h_l'(z)}{h_l(z)}=-\frac1z\,\frac{\sum_{j=0}^l(1+j)a_jz^{-2j}}{\sum_{j=0}^l a_jz^{-2j}}$ and $\operatorname{Im}\frac{h_l'(z)}{h_l(z)}=\frac1{F(z)}$. With $z=kR$ and weights $a_j(kR)^{-2j}\ge0$, the real part of $t_l=k\,h_l'(kR)/h_l(kR)$ is $-\frac1R$ times a weighted average of the numbers $1+j$, $j=0,\dots,l$, so $-(l+1)/R\le\operatorname{Re}t_l\le-1/R$; the imaginary part is $k/F(kR)$, and since $F(kR)=\sum_{j\ge0}a_j(kR)^{-2j}\ge a_0=1$ and $F<\infty$, one has $0<\operatorname{Im}t_l\le k$. This proves all the stated bounds, and the bounds are exact identities for the displayed $h_l$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Collecting: step 1.1 gives the $C^2$ solution property and the explicit leading term; step 2.1 gives the constant Wronskian $\operatorname{Im}(\overline{h_l}h_l')=z^{-2}$ and nonvanishing; steps 3.1 and 4.1 give the positive coefficient representation $|h_l|^2=z^{-2}\sum_ja_jz^{-2j}\ge z^{-2}$ and the exact bounds $\operatorname{Re}t_l\le-1/R$, $|\operatorname{Re}t_l|\le(l+1)/R$, $0<\operatorname{Im}t_l\le k$ for the Dirichlet-to-Neumann coefficient. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. Define the reflection boundary class by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2,x_3$-walls, and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$; extend $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$, cyclically for $B_2,B_3$. Work on the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ in the real $L^2$ fields with these parities and distributional $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$. For smooth fields the parity class gives $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Then: (i) the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in this class, and the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]); (ii) for every initial datum in the class there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class ([[def-distributional-derivative]]); (iii) the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant along the solution. This is an explicit weak PEC model; it supplies neither trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields nor completeness in lossy, open or non-rectangular guides.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Positive constants $L_1,L_2,L_3,\varepsilon,\mu$; the box $Q=(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)\times(0,L_3)$; the torus $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/(2L_1\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb R/(2L_2\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb R/(2L_3\mathbb Z)$ with its normalized product measure $\nu$ and the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; and the parity conventions of the statement.

[L1] **Torus characters and Fourier expansion.** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Under the scaling identification of $\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ with the unit-period torus, the characters $x_j\mapsto e^{i\pi n_jx_j/L_j}$, $n_j\in\mathbb Z$, form an orthonormal basis of the one-dimensional complex $L^2$ space ([[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and the Fourier partial sums converge in mean square ([[thm-l-two-fourier-series-converges-in-mean-square]]). Hence the product characters $\Phi_n(x):=\prod_{j=1}^3e^{i\pi n_jx_j/L_j}$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and Parseval's identity holds for every $f$ in that space.

[L2] **Product integration.** Fubini and Tonelli for $\sigma$-finite product spaces ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) permit iterated integration and interchange of the order of integration for nonnegative and integrable functions, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality of [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] bounds $L^2$ pairings by the product of the norms.

[L3] **Ordinary differential equations.** Every initial-value problem $z'=F(t,z)$ with continuous globally state-Lipschitz $F$ has a unique global solution ([[cor-globally-lipschitz-odes-have-global-solutions]]); the maximal-solution theorem ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]) is the local existence and uniqueness input.

[L4] **Distributional derivatives.** The distributional derivative is defined by $\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]]), and distributional differentiation commutes; a $C^k$ function is a regular distribution whose distributional derivatives are its classical ones ([[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]). A distribution on the connected open set $\mathbb R$ with all first derivatives zero is a constant ([[thm-a-distribution-with-zero-derivatives-on-a-connected-open-set-is-constant]]). Moreover continuous functions on compact intervals are Riemann integrable ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]), their oriented integral functions are $C^1$ with the integrand as derivative ([[thm-ftc-first-part]]), and a differentiable function with integrable derivative is recovered from its derivative ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

## Proof

Throughout, "the class" means the closed subspace $\mathcal C\subseteq L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R^3)\times L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R^3)$ of pairs $(E,B)$ that are real vector fields with the parity patterns of the statement and satisfy $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ in the distributional sense. The fixed factor $8L_1L_2L_3$ relating the torus measure $\nu$ to Lebesgue measure on $Q$ is positive and constant, so preservation of $\varepsilon\|E\|^2+\|B\|^2/\mu$ is equivalent to (iii).

1.1 A smooth field on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the parity pattern of the statement restricts to $Q$ as a tangential-electric and normal-magnetic perfect-conductor field: at the wall $x_1=0$ (and $x_1=L_1$), $E_1$ is even in $x_1$ while $E_2,E_3$ are odd, so $E_2=E_3=0$ there, which is $n\times E=0$; $B_1$ is odd and $B_2,B_3$ even, so $B_1=0$ there, which is $n\cdot B=0$; the cyclic coordinates are identical. The parity conditions are closed linear conditions in $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R^3)$ because a sign change of a torus coordinate preserves $L^2$ convergence and distributional derivatives, and $\operatorname{div}=0$ is the closed condition that the distribution annihilates all divergence-free tests, so $\mathcal C$ is a closed real subspace of the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R^3)^2$. The weak formulation used below is: $(E,B)\in C(\mathbb R;\mathcal C)$ is a weak solution when for every pair of smooth periodic vector fields $\Psi,\Theta$ compactly supported in $t$, $\iint E\cdot\partial_t\Psi\,d\nu\,dt+(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\iint B\cdot\operatorname{curl}\Psi\,d\nu\,dt=0$ and $\iint B\cdot\partial_t\Theta\,d\nu\,dt-\iint E\cdot\operatorname{curl}\Theta\,d\nu\,dt=0$, which is exactly the statement that the two equations hold for $\partial_t$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]] (the spatial sign convention in $\operatorname{curl}$ is the distributional one, and for smooth periodic fields the pairing identities of the definition reduce to the displayed ones). [L1, L4]

2.1 The characters $\Phi_n$ of [L1] are orthonormal in $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$: orthogonality factors as a product of one-dimensional character pairings, and each factor equals one by the one-dimensional completeness theorem of [L1]. They are complete: if $f\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ is orthogonal to every $\Phi_n$, fix $n_2,n_3\in\mathbb Z$ and set $g(x_1):=\int f(x_1,x_2,x_3)e^{-i\pi(n_2x_2/L_2+n_3x_3/L_3)}\,d\nu_2d\nu_3$, an $L^2$ function of $x_1$ by Cauchy-Schwarz; its one-dimensional character coefficients all vanish, since they are the $\Phi_n$ pairings of $f$ with $n_1$ varying, so $g=0$ a.e. by the one-dimensional completeness of [L1]; applying this for all $n_2,n_3$ and iterating in the other two coordinates, with a countable union of exceptional null sets, gives $f=0$ a.e., so the closed span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$. Parseval and mean-square convergence of finite partial sums follow from [L1] applied componentwise to the six real components of a pair of fields. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 Passing to the complexified expansion $f=\sum_n\widehat f(n)\Phi_n$ componentwise, the parity conditions of the statement select the symmetric combinations of the $\pm n$ coefficients that produce the real separated modes: for $E_1$ the products $\cos(\pi n_1x_1/L_1)\sin(\pi n_2x_2/L_2)\sin(\pi n_3x_3/L_3)$ with $n_1\ge0$, $n_2,n_3\ge1$, and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$; for $B_1$ the products $\sin(\pi n_1x_1/L_1)\cos(\pi n_2x_2/L_2)\cos(\pi n_3x_3/L_3)$ with $n_1\ge1$, $n_2,n_3\ge0$, and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$. These finite products are smooth, lie in $\mathcal C$ when their vector amplitude satisfies $k_n\cdot\widehat E_n=k_n\cdot\widehat B_n=0$ with $k_n=(\pi n_1/L_1,\pi n_2/L_2,\pi n_3/L_3)$, and are dense in $\mathcal C$: an element of $\mathcal C$ is fixed by the parity symmetrizations, and expanding it in the complete character system of step 2.1 exhibits it as an $L^2$ limit of finite sums of exactly these symmetrized products; the divergence constraints pass to the distributional limit. Grouping the symmerized products by the unordered pair $\{n,-n\}$ gives, for each wavevector $k=k_n$, a finite-dimensional real modal space $P_k$ of amplitude pairs $(v,w)$ with $k\cdot v=k\cdot w=0$ and the reality/parity conditions, and Parseval says that for $(E,B)\in\mathcal C$ the quantities $\varepsilon\|E\|^2+\|B\|^2/\mu=\sum_{k}\bigl(\varepsilon|v_k|^2+|w_k|^2/\mu\bigr)$ agree, the sum over one representative of each pair $\{k,-k\}$ being absolutely convergent. The modal operator $\Lambda_k(v,w)=\bigl(i(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}k\times w,-ik\times v\bigr)$ maps $P_k$ into itself because $k\cdot(k\times z)=0$ for every $z$; and it preserves the modal quadratic form $Q_k(v,w)=\varepsilon|v|^2+|w|^2/\mu$: indeed $\frac{d}{dt}Q_k$ along the flow equals $\frac{2}{\mu}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(i[\overline{k\times w}\cdot v-\overline{k\times v}\cdot w]\bigr)=0$, since the scalar triple product $k\cdot(z\times z')$ is alternating in its last two arguments, and complex conjugation of the second argument reverses the sign, so the two bracket terms are complex conjugates and their difference is purely imaginary. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2, algebra]

4.1 Enumerate the unordered wavevector pairs occurring in the modal decomposition of $\mathcal C$ as $k^{(1)},k^{(2)},\dots$, so that every mode belongs to exactly one $P_{k^{(m)}}$, and let $A_m$ denote the real matrix of $\Lambda_{k^{(m)}}$ in a fixed real basis of $P_{k^{(m)}}$. Each $A_m$ is bounded, so the finite-dimensional linear system $z_m'=A_mz_m$ has a unique global solution through every real initial vector $z_m(0)$, by the global Lipschitz corollary of [L3]; no choice is needed for one system. For $M\ge1$ let $(E_M,B_M)$ be the sum of the first $M$ modal solutions with the initial amplitudes inherited from the given initial datum $(E_0,B_0)\in\mathcal C$. Each $(E_M,B_M)$ is a finite sum of smooth modes, hence smooth and in $\mathcal C$, solves the two equations pointwise, and satisfies $\varepsilon\|E_M(t)\|^2+\|B_M(t)\|^2/\mu=\sum_{m\le M}Q_{k^{(m)}}(0)$ for all $t$ by the modal invariance of step 3.1. The omitted modes carry the nonnegative initial partial energies $R_M:=\sum_{m>M}Q_{k^{(m)}}(0)$, which decrease to $0$ because the total initial energy $\sum_mQ_{k^{(m)}}(0)=\varepsilon\|E_0\|^2+\|B_0\|^2/\mu$ is finite. For $M<M'$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon\|(E_{M'}-E_M)(t)\|^2+\|(B_{M'}-B_M)(t)\|^2/\mu=\sum_{M<m\le M'}Q_{k^{(m)}}(t)\le R_M$, because each omitted modal energy is constant; hence $(E_M,B_M)$ is Cauchy uniformly in $t$ in $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R^3)^2$, and its uniform limit $(E,B)\in C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ exists and takes values in the closed subspace $\mathcal C$ of step 1.1, with $\varepsilon\|E(t)\|^2+\|B(t)\|^2/\mu=\lim_M\bigl(\varepsilon\|E_M(t)\|^2+\|B_M(t)\|^2/\mu\bigr)=\sum_mQ_{k^{(m)}}(0)$ for every $t$. [step 3.1, step 1.1, L3, algebra]

4.2 Let $(E,B)\in C(\mathbb R;\mathcal C)$ be any weak solution in the sense of step 1.1, and fix a mode index $m$ together with a real mode function $\varphi$ in the finite-dimensional space of modes belonging to the pair $k^{(m)}$ (a smooth periodic vector field). Testing the two weak equations with $\psi(t)\varphi(x)$, where $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ is arbitrary, gives, in the sense of distributions on $\mathbb R$, the scalar equations $c_\varphi'=(\text{the corresponding finite linear combination of the other modal coefficients})$, where $c_\varphi(t)=\langle\varphi,(E,B)(t)\rangle$ is the coefficient pairing; these are continuous functions of $t$ because $(E,B)$ is continuous into $L^2$ and the pairing is continuous. Assembling the finitely many coefficients belonging to $k^{(m)}$ into a real vector $Z_m(t)$ gives a finite linear system $\partial_tZ_m=A_mZ_m+G_m$ with continuous right-hand side; applying the primitive construction componentwise on a compact interval $[a,b]$, every component of $A_mZ_m+G_m$ is continuous, hence Riemann integrable [L4], its oriented primitive $G$ is $C^1$ with $G'=g$ [L4], and the regular-distribution compatibility clause of [L4] (whose use here is covered by the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) transfers this to distributional derivatives; subtracting the primitive from $Z_m$ shows that the difference has zero distributional derivative, hence is constant on the connected set $\mathbb R$ [L4]; continuity makes the equality pointwise. Therefore every modal coefficient is a classical $C^1$ solution of its finite linear system. Since $Z_m$ solves a linear constant-coefficient ODE, its value at every time is determined by $Z_m(0)$ by the global uniqueness part of [L3]; hence the weak solution $(E,B)$ is uniquely determined by its initial datum $(E(0),B(0))$, because the modal coefficients determine the fields by the completeness in step 3.1. [step 3.1, step 1.1, L4, L3]

5.1 The energy of the constructed solution is constant. By step 4.1, for every $t$ one has $\varepsilon\|E(t)\|^2+\|B(t)\|^2/\mu=\sum_mQ_{k^{(m)}}(0)$, the same value at every $t$; and $\sum_mQ_{k^{(m)}}(0)=\varepsilon\|E_0\|^2+\|B_0\|^2/\mu$ by the Parseval identity of step 3.1, while the normalized torus measure and Lebesgue measure on $Q$ differ by the fixed factor $8L_1L_2L_3$. Hence the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ of the constructed solution equals its initial value at every time. By the uniqueness of step 4.2, every $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution in the class with the same initial datum is this solution, so energy conservation holds for every weak solution. [step 4.1, step 4.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.2 The limit $(E,B)$ of step 4.1 is a weak solution in the sense of step 1.1. Indeed, each truncation $(E_M,B_M)$ solves the equations pointwise, hence also in the pairing formulation, because for smooth periodic fields the distributional pairings coincide with the integral pairings and the cur sign convention is the same. For a smooth periodic test pair $(\Psi,\Theta)$ compactly supported in $t$, the differences satisfy $|\iint(E_M-E)\cdot\partial_t\Psi\,d\nu\,dt|\le\sup_{t}\|(E_M-E)(t)\|_{L^2}\cdot\int\|\partial_t\Psi(t)\|_{L^2}\,dt$, and $\int\|\partial_t\Psi(t)\|\,dt<\infty$ because $\Psi$ is compactly supported in time and continuous, so the bound tends to $0$ by the uniform convergence of step 4.1; the pairings with $\operatorname{curl}\Psi$ and $\operatorname{curl}\Theta$, and the corresponding pairings of $B_M$, are handled identically. Passing to the limit in the two displayed identities therefore shows that $(E,B)$ is a weak solution. The divergence constraints hold in the limit because the class $\mathcal C$ is closed, as recorded in step 1.1. [step 4.1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

6.1 Collecting the results: step 3.1 proves claim (i), namely that the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the class and that the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing; steps 4.1 and 5.2 construct, for every initial datum in the class, a $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution in the class, and step 4.2 proves that it is the only one, which is claim (ii); step 5.1 proves the energy constancy of claim (iii) for every weak solution. Countable Choice is used exactly through the torus-character, Fourier-convergence, Hilbert-space and regular-distribution suppliers of [L1] and [L4]; the finite-dimensional modal systems and the energy identity use no further choice. This proves every assertion of the statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, step 5.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ and let

$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,dy .$$

Then $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ the spatial derivative satisfies $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$. In particular, for smooth compactly supported $\rho$ the field $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth. The statement is about the explicit integral transform of compactly supported smooth data and does not assume smoothness of the kernel at the pole; the distributional identity $-\Delta Nf=f$ is the one supplied by the Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]), upgraded here from a distributional to a pointwise identity for smooth data.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A constant $\varepsilon_0>0$ and a function $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$; the function $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$, whose point value at $0$ is arbitrary and whose class is the Newtonian kernel of [[def-newtonian-potential]] and [[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]].

[L1] **Newtonian potential.** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). For compactly supported $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$, the potential $Nf$ of [[def-newtonian-potential]] depends only on the $L^1$ class, is finite a.e. and locally integrable, and its regular distribution satisfies $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]).

[L2] **Differentiation under the integral sign.** Let $X$ be a measure space, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an open interval, and $h:X\times I\to\mathbb C$ such that for each $t$ the section $x\mapsto h(x,t)$ is integrable, for almost every $x$ the map $t\mapsto h(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$, the extended derivative is measurable in $x$, and $|\partial_th(x,t)|\le g(x)$ a.e. with $g$ integrable. Then $H(t)=\int h(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$ is differentiable with $H'(t)=\int\partial_th(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$ ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]).

[L3] **Distributional versus classical derivatives.** If $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, then the distributional derivative of the regular distribution $T_u$ is the regular distribution of the classical derivative ([[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]).

[L4] **Bumps and positive measure.** For $0<r<R$ there is $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $0\le\rho\le1$, $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq B_R(0)$ ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]). Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, Lebesgue measure is the positive-density measure of density $1$, so every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ has positive measure ([[cor-positive-density-measures-assign-positive-volume-to-nonempty-open-sets-and-metric-balls]]).

[L5] **Fundamental lemma.** If $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ satisfies $\int g\varphi=0$ for every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then $g=0$ almost everywhere ([[lem-fundamental-lemma-of-the-calculus-of-variations]]).

## Proof

1.1 Substituting $z=x-y$ gives $Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi(z)f(x-z)\,dz$, an absolutely convergent integral for every $x$: $f$ is bounded with support in some closed ball $\overline B_R(0)$, so the integrand is supported in $x-\overline B_R(0)$ and bounded there by $\|f\|_\infty|\Phi(z)|$ with $\Phi\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$. The same substitution exhibits $Nf$ as the Newtonian potential of [L1], so the distributional identity $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ of [L1] holds. [L1, algebra]

2.1 Fix a multi-index $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$ and a point $x$, and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a compact set containing $x$ in its interior. For $z$ in the fixed compact set $K-\operatorname{supp}f$ and $x'\in K$, the function $z\mapsto\Phi(z)D^\alpha f(x'-z)$ is bounded by $\|D^\alpha f\|_\infty|\Phi(z)|$, integrable on that compact set, and $z\mapsto\Phi(z)D^{\alpha+e_j}f(x'-z)$ likewise; moreover $D^\alpha f$ is uniformly continuous on the compact set $K-\operatorname{supp}f$ shifted appropriately. Applying the differentiation-under-the-integral-sign theorem [L2] successively in the three coordinates (the parameter being one coordinate of $x$ and the measure space $\mathbb R^3$ with the dominated bounds above) gives $D^\alpha Nf(x)=\int\Phi(z)D^\alpha f(x-z)\,dz=N(D^\alpha f)(x)$ at every $x$, and the resulting function is continuous in $x$ because the bound $\|D^\alpha f(x-z)-D^\alpha f(x'-z)\|_\infty|\Phi(z)|$ on the compact $z$-set is uniform in $x,x'$ near $x$ and tends to $0$. Hence $Nf$ has continuous derivatives of every order, so $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, and the identity $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$ holds for every multi-index $\alpha$; in particular the classical Laplacian $\Delta Nf=\sum_{j=1}^3N(\partial_j^2f)$ is a continuous function, and it is the classical Laplacian of the smooth function $Nf$. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 By [L3] the distributional Laplacian of the smooth function $Nf$ is the regular distribution of the classical Laplacian, so the identity $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ of step 1.1 says that $\int_{\mathbb R^3}(f(y)+\Delta Nf(y))\varphi(y)\,dy=0$ for every test function $\varphi$. The function $g:=f+\Delta Nf$ is continuous by step 2.1, so it is locally integrable and the fundamental lemma [L5] gives $g=0$ almost everywhere. A continuous function vanishing almost everywhere vanishes everywhere: if $g(x_0)\ne0$, continuity gives $r>0$ with $|g|>|g(x_0)|/2>0$ on the nonempty open ball $B_r(x_0)$, which has positive Lebesgue measure by [L4], contradicting $g=0$ a.e.; hence $g(x_0)=0$ for every $x_0$. Therefore $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L3, L4, L5]

4.1 For smooth compactly supported $\rho$, the derivative identity of step 2.1 with $\alpha=e_j$ shows that $\nabla N\rho$ is a smooth field, and $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth because $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ is a constant. Countable Choice is inherited from the exact statement of the Newtonian-potential theorem [L1] and from the positive-density-measure corollary [L4]; the differentiation and upgrade arguments use no further choice. This proves the smoothness of $Nf$, the pointwise Poisson identity and the derivative identity $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$, and hence the smoothness of $E$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L1, L4] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); in particular the hypothesis is met under the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-complete-metric-space]]), let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb R$ be a symmetric bounded bilinear form ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]]) with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for every $v\in H$ and some $\alpha>0$, and let $\ell:H\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded linear functional with operator norm $\|\ell\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). Then there is exactly one $u\in H$ with

$$a(u,v)=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$

and it satisfies $\|u\|\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$. The argument minimises the explicit functional $J(v)=\tfrac12a(v,v)-\ell(v)$; no Lax-Milgram theorem, Zorn-type argument or unproved minimiser existence is invoked, and the only choice use is the selection of one point from each of the countably many nonempty sublevel sets $\{v\in H:J(v)<m+1/(n+1)\}$.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A real Hilbert space $H$ with norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$, a symmetric bounded bilinear form $a:H\times H\to\mathbb R$, a constant $\alpha>0$ with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for every $v\in H$, a bounded linear functional $\ell:H\to\mathbb R$, and the functional $J(v)=\tfrac12a(v,v)-\ell(v)$.

[F1] **Hilbert norm and completeness.** $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and the induced metric $(v,w)\mapsto\|v-w\|$ is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ converges in norm to a point of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-complete-metric-space]]).

[F2] **Parallelogram law.** $\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2$ for all $x,y\in H$ ([[thm-parallelogram-law]]).

[F3] **Bounded symmetric bilinear form.** $a$ is linear in each argument, $a(v,w)=a(w,v)$, and there is a real $C\ge0$ with $|a(v,w)|\le C\|v\|\,\|w\|$ for all $v,w\in H$ ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]]).

[F4] **Operator norm.** $\|\ell\|=\sup\{|\ell(v)|:\|v\|\le1\}$ is finite and $|\ell(v)|\le\|\ell\|\,\|v\|$ for every $v\in H$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

[F5] **Infima.** Every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ bounded below has an infimum, and $m=\inf S$ is characterised by: $m\le s$ for all $s\in S$, and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $s\in S$ with $s<m+\varepsilon$ ([[def-infimum]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[lem-inf-epsilon]]).

[F6] **Countable choice.** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ provides, for every family $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets, a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb N$ and $f(n)\in X_n$ for all $n$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For every $v\in H$ one has $\tfrac12a(v,v)\ge\tfrac\alpha2\|v\|^2$ by the coercivity hypothesis and $\ell(v)\ge-|\ell(v)|\ge-\|\ell\|\,\|v\|$ by [F4], hence $J(v)\ge\tfrac\alpha2\|v\|^2-\|\ell\|\,\|v\|$. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 Expanding with bilinearity and symmetry of $a$ (the same expansion as the parallelogram identity [F2], applied to the quadratic form $v\mapsto a(v,v)$) gives $a\bigl(\tfrac{v+w}2,\tfrac{v+w}2\bigr)=\tfrac12a(v,v)+\tfrac12a(w,w)-\tfrac14a(v-w,v-w)$, hence $J\bigl(\tfrac{v+w}2\bigr)=\tfrac{J(v)+J(w)}2-\tfrac18a(v-w,v-w)$ for all $v,w\in H$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Completing the square gives $\tfrac\alpha2\|v\|^2-\|\ell\|\,\|v\|=\tfrac\alpha2\bigl(\|v\|-\tfrac{\|\ell\|}\alpha\bigr)^2-\tfrac{\|\ell\|^2}{2\alpha}\ge-\tfrac{\|\ell\|^2}{2\alpha}$, so the image $S=\{J(v):v\in H\}$ is nonempty and bounded below in $\mathbb R$, and its infimum $m=\inf S\in\mathbb R$ exists by [F5]. [step 1.1, F5, algebra]

3.1 For each $n\in\mathbb N$ the set $X_n:=\{v\in H:J(v)<m+\tfrac1{n+1}\}$ is nonempty: otherwise $m+\tfrac1{n+1}$ would be a lower bound of $S$ larger than $m$, contradicting [F5] (equivalently, [F5] with $\varepsilon=\tfrac1{n+1}$ produces $v$ with $J(v)<m+\tfrac1{n+1}$). Applying $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [F6] to the family $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ gives a sequence $(v_n)$ in $H$ with $J(v_n)<m+\tfrac1{n+1}$ for all $n$; since $m$ is a lower bound of $S$, also $J(v_n)\ge m$, so $J(v_n)\to m$. [step 2.1, F5, F6, choose]

4.1 Since $m$ is a lower bound of $S$ one has $J\bigl(\tfrac{v_n+v_k}2\bigr)\ge m$, so step 1.2 and the coercivity bound $a(v_n-v_k,v_n-v_k)\ge\alpha\|v_n-v_k\|^2$ give $\tfrac\alpha8\|v_n-v_k\|^2\le\tfrac{J(v_n)+J(v_k)}2-m\le\tfrac12\bigl(\tfrac1{n+1}+\tfrac1{k+1}\bigr)$; the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $n,k\to\infty$, so $(v_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $H$. [step 3.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

5.1 By completeness [F1] there is $u\in H$ with $\|v_n-u\|\to0$. [step 4.1, F1]

6.1 The functional $J$ is continuous in the norm: for $v,w\in H$ one has $|J(v)-J(w)|\le\tfrac12|a(v,v)-a(w,w)|+|\ell(v-w)|=\tfrac12|a(v+w,v-w)|+|\ell(v-w)|\le\bigl(\tfrac C2\|v+w\|+\|\ell\|\bigr)\|v-w\|$ by [F3] and [F4], which tends to $0$ as $v\to w$; hence $J(u)=\lim_nJ(v_n)=m$. [step 5.1, step 3.1, F3, F4, algebra]

7.1 Fix $v\in H$ and consider $g(s)=J(u+sv)$; expanding with bilinearity and symmetry gives $g(s)=J(u)+s\bigl(a(u,v)-\ell(v)\bigr)+\tfrac{s^2}2a(v,v)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$. Since $J(u)=m$ is the minimum of $J$, $g(s)\ge g(0)$ for all $s$: for $s>0$ division by $s$ gives $a(u,v)-\ell(v)+\tfrac s2a(v,v)\ge0$, and letting $s\to0^+$ gives $a(u,v)-\ell(v)\ge0$, while for $s<0$ the same division gives $a(u,v)-\ell(v)+\tfrac s2a(v,v)\le0$, and letting $s\to0^-$ gives $a(u,v)-\ell(v)\le0$. Therefore $a(u,v)=\ell(v)$, and since $v\in H$ was arbitrary, $u$ solves the variational equation. [step 6.1, given, algebra]

8.1 Uniqueness: if $u_1,u_2\in H$ both satisfy the equation, then testing the difference at $v=u_1-u_2$ gives $a(u_1-u_2,u_1-u_2)=0$, and coercivity gives $\alpha\|u_1-u_2\|^2\le a(u_1-u_2,u_1-u_2)=0$, so $\|u_1-u_2\|=0$ and $u_1=u_2$ by [F1]. [step 7.1, given, F1, algebra]

9.1 Estimate: testing the equation at $v=u$ gives $a(u,u)=\ell(u)$, and coercivity together with [F4] gives $\alpha\|u\|^2\le a(u,u)=\ell(u)\le\|\ell\|\,\|u\|$; if $\|u\|=0$ then $0\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$ holds, and otherwise division by $\alpha\|u\|>0$ gives $\|u\|\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$. This proves existence, uniqueness and the estimate, and identifies the sole use of $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as the selection in step 3.1. [step 7.1, step 8.1, given, F1, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be a closed embedded $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length with period $L>0$: $\gamma(s+L)=\gamma(s)$ and $|\gamma'(s)|=1$ for every $s$, and the induced map $\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ is injective. Let $I\in\mathbb R$ and $\mu_0>0$, and for $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)=:\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$j(\psi)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,$$

with the complex-bilinear Euclidean pairing (no conjugation) of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; restricted to real-valued $\psi$ this is the stated real functional. Then $\operatorname{div}j=0$ in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]]). For any family $(\eta_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of nonnegative smooth radial kernels with $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\eta_\varepsilon=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_\varepsilon\subseteq\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$ — including the rescalings $\eta_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\eta(x/\varepsilon)$ of a chosen nonnegative unit-mass radial kernel supported in $\overline B_1(0)$ — the mollified fields $j_\varepsilon$ defined by the distribution pairing $j_\varepsilon(x):=j(\eta_\varepsilon(x-\cdot))=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))\,ds$ are smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, and their Biot-Savart fields converge, with every derivative uniformly on every nonempty compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ disjoint from $\gamma$, to

$$B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds$$

([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). In addition, assigning arbitrary finite values on the curve gives a representative $B\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, smooth off $\gamma$, with $\operatorname{div}T_B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}T_B=\mu_0j$ globally; the first identity is tested on scalar $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and the second on vector $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. If $\gamma([0,L])\subseteq B_a(0)$ for some $a>0$, then $|B(x)|\le\mu_0|I|L/\bigl(4\pi(|x|-a)^2\bigr)$ for $|x|>a$, so $B$ decays at infinity. For the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ and a point $z e_3$ on its axis the value is $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/\bigl(2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}\bigr)$. Nothing is asserted about the divergent line self-energy or about fields on the curve itself.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; a closed embedded $C^2$ arc-length curve $\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\gamma(s+L)=\gamma(s)$, $|\gamma'(s)|=1$; constants $I\in\mathbb R$, $\mu_0>0$; the sign-normalized Newtonian kernel $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ with an arbitrary finite assigned value at $0$; nonnegative smooth radial kernels $\eta_\varepsilon$ with $\int\eta_\varepsilon=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_\varepsilon\subseteq\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$; and the distribution $j$ of the Statement.

[F1] **Chain rule.** If $g$ is differentiable at $\gamma(s)$ and $\gamma$ is differentiable at $s$, then $s\mapsto g(\gamma(s))$ is differentiable at $s$ with derivative $\nabla g(\gamma(s))\cdot\gamma'(s)$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the same holds componentwise for vector-valued $g$.

[F2] **FTC and Lipschitz bounds.** If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^m$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ with $f'$ integrable, then $\int_a^bf'=f(b)-f(a)$; if moreover $\|f'\|\le M$ on $(a,b)$, then $\|f(t)-f(s)\|\le M|t-s|$ for all $s,t\in[a,b]$ ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]). A continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]), so the derivatives of the $C^1$ composites below are integrable.

[F3] **Differentiation under the integral sign.** For an open interval $I$, a measure space $X$ and $h:X\times I\to\mathbb C$ with integrable sections, a.e.-differentiable parameter dependence and an integrable dominating function for $\partial_th$, the function $t\mapsto\int h(x,t)d\mu(x)$ is differentiable with the expected derivative ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]). It is applied below with the measure space $X=[0,L]$ carrying Lebesgue measure and the parameter running in an open interval, coordinatewise in the parameter; the bounded derivatives of the smooth kernels on compact sets supply the dominating functions.

[F4] **Distributions.** $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) and the distributional derivative is $\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]]). A complex-linear functional $u$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is a distribution exactly when for every compact $K$ there are $m_K\ge0$, $C_K\ge0$ with $|u(\varphi)|\le C_Kp_{m_K}(\varphi)$ on $\mathcal D_K$ ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]). The regular-functional map embeds $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo a.e. equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). Constant-coefficient distributional derivatives commute ([[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]).

[F5] **Tonelli and Fubini.** Nonnegative measurable integrands may be integrated in either order, and absolutely integrable integrands satisfy the Fubini identity ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); translation is measure preserving, so $\int g(x-c)dx=\int g$ ([[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]).

[F6] **Polar integration and the kernel integrals.** For nonnegative Borel $q$, $\int_{\mathbb R^3}q=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^2}q(r\omega)r^2d\sigma(\omega)dr$ with the chart surface measure equal to the polar measure and $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]). Consequently $\int_{B_R}|\Phi|=R^2/2$, $\int_{B_R}|\nabla\Phi|=R$ and $\int_{B_R}|z|^{-2}dz=4\pi R$ for every $R>0$, where $\Phi$ is the kernel above and $\nabla\Phi(z)=-z/(4\pi|z|^3)$ for $z\ne0$.

[F7] **Fundamental solution.** The kernel $\Phi$ is locally integrable and $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$, and for every $y$ the translated kernel satisfies $-\Delta_xT_{\Phi(\cdot-y)}=\delta_y$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], [[lem-laplace-fundamental-kernel-is-locally-integrable]], [[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]]).

[F8] **Divergence theorem and surface integrals.** On a bounded piecewise $C^1$ domain with a finite face presentation and outward normals, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$ for $C^1$ fields on $\overline\Omega$, with the surface integrals of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and finite face areas ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]]); the sphere $S_r$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface whose outward normal at $z$ is $z/r$ and whose area is $4\pi r^2$.

[F9] **Integral bounds.** $|\int g\,d\mu|\le\int|g|\,d\mu$ for integrable $g$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]), and monotonicity and scalar rules hold for the nonnegative integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F10] **Nullity tools.** Finite subadditivity of measures ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]), the volume $|B_r|=\tfrac43\pi r^3$ of Euclidean balls ([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]), and completeness of Lebesgue measure, so that arbitrary changes on a null set preserve measurability ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

[F11] **Compactness and distance.** $[0,L]$ is compact ([[thm-heine-borel-r]]), continuous images of compact sets are compact ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]), compact subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ are closed and bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), closed bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and disjoint nonempty compact and closed sets in a normed space have a positive distance gap ([[lem-relative-compact-closed-sets-have-a-positive-distance-gap]]).

[F12] **Cross product.** $u\times v$ is the complex-bilinear alternating product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], and $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2\le\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2$ ([[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]]); the pointwise divergence and curl are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]].

[F13] **Sine and cosine.** $(\sin)'=\cos$ and $(\cos)'=-\sin$, $\sin0=0$, and $\sin$ and $\cos$ have fundamental period $2\pi$ ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ the bound $|j(\psi)|\le|I|\int_0^L|\psi(\gamma(s))|ds\le|I|L\,p_0(\psi)$ holds, with $p_0$ the supremum seminorm over any compact set containing the bounded set $\gamma([0,L])$; the constant does not depend on the compact set $K$ supporting $\psi$, so [F4] makes $j$ a vector distribution of order $\le0$, supported in $\gamma([0,L])$. [given, F4, F11, algebra]

1.2 Put $A_k(x)=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\Phi(x-\gamma(s))ds$ for $x\notin\gamma$ and $A_k=0$ on $\gamma$. For a compact $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ choose $R$ with $Q-\gamma([0,L])\subseteq B_R(0)$; Tonelli [F5] and [F6] give $\int_Q|A_k|\le\mu_0|I|\int_0^L\int_{B_R}|\Phi|=(\mu_0|I|L R^2)/2$ and $\int_Q|\partial_jA_k|\le\mu_0|I|\int_0^L\int_{B_R}|\nabla\Phi|=\mu_0|I|LR$, so $A_k$ and each first partial derivative $\partial_jA_k$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and define regular distributions by [F4]. [given, F4, F5, F6, F9, algebra]

1.3 For scalar $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$ with support in $B_R(0)$ and $0<\delta<R$, the divergence theorem [F8] on the annulus $\{\delta<|z|<R\}$, presented by the six signed-maximal-coordinate regular graph faces of each boundary sphere whose seam arcs have zero surface measure, applied to the $C^1$ field $\Phi\varphi\,e_j$ gives $\int_{\delta<|z|<R}\partial_j(\Phi\varphi)=\int_{S_R}\Phi\varphi\frac{z_j}{R}dS-\int_{S_\delta}\Phi\varphi\frac{z_j}{\delta}dS$, where the outer term vanishes and the inner term is bounded by $\|\varphi\|_\infty\frac{4\pi\delta^2}{4\pi\delta}=\|\varphi\|_\infty\delta\to0$; expanding $\partial_j(\Phi\varphi)=\partial_j\Phi\,\varphi+\Phi\,\partial_j\varphi$ and letting $\delta\to0$ with the absolutely integrable limits of [F6] yields $\langle\partial_jT_\Phi,\varphi\rangle=-\int\Phi\partial_j\varphi=\int(\partial_j\Phi)\varphi$, that is $\partial_jT_\Phi=T_{\partial_j\Phi}$ with $\partial_j\Phi(z)=-z_j/(4\pi|z|^3)$. [given, F4, F6, F8, F9, algebra]

2.1 For scalar $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$ one has $\langle\operatorname{div}j,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_kj_k(\partial_k\varphi)=-I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla\varphi(\gamma(s))ds$ by [F4]; the chain rule [F1] gives $\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla\varphi(\gamma(s))=(d/ds)(\varphi\circ\gamma)(s)$, and $s\mapsto(\varphi\circ\gamma)(s)$ is $C^1$ with continuous derivative on $[0,L]$, hence integrable, so the second FTC [F2] and the periodicity $\varphi(\gamma(L))=\varphi(\gamma(0))$ give $\int_0^L(d/ds)(\varphi\circ\gamma)ds=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{div}j=0$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.2 The pairing $j_\varepsilon(x)=j(\eta_\varepsilon(x-\cdot))$ uses the test function $y\mapsto\eta_\varepsilon(x-y)\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$, and expanding the definition of $j$ gives $j_\varepsilon(x)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))ds$ for every $x$; this is the mollified field of the Statement. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.3 The translated identity $\partial_jT_{\Phi(\cdot-y)}=T_{\partial_j\Phi(\cdot-y)}$ follows from step 1.3 because the pairing is translation invariant [F5]; applying it under the absolutely integrable $s$-integral of step 1.2 gives $\partial_jT_{A_k}=T_{\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\partial_j\Phi(x-\gamma(s))ds}$, and with the componentwise distributional curl $\operatorname{curl}_ku=\sum_{i,j}\varepsilon_{kij}\partial_iu_j$ of [F12] one obtains $\operatorname{curl}T_A=T_B$ for the stated $B$, since $\varepsilon_{kij}\gamma_j'(s)\partial_i\Phi(x-\gamma(s))=\varepsilon_{kij}\gamma_j'(s)\frac{-(x-\gamma(s))_i}{4\pi|x-\gamma(s)|^3}=\frac{(\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s)))_k}{4\pi|x-\gamma(s)|^3}$ by [F12]. [step 1.2, step 1.3, F4, F5, F12, algebra]

2.4 For scalar $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$ set $H(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi(z)\varphi(z+y)dz$, which is smooth near the compact curve $\gamma([0,L])$ by differentiation under the integral sign [F3] against the locally integrable $\Phi$; then $\langle\operatorname{div}T_A,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T_A,\nabla\varphi\rangle=-\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\Bigl(\int\Phi(z)\nabla\varphi(z+\gamma(s))dz\Bigr)ds=-\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla H(\gamma(s))ds$, the interchange being justified by the Tonelli bound of step 1.2, and the chain rule together with the FTC and periodicity of $s\mapsto H(\gamma(s))$ gives $\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla H(\gamma(s))ds=0$; hence $\operatorname{div}T_A=0$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

2.5 Componentwise, [F7] gives $-\Delta T_{A_k}=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\delta_{\gamma(s)}ds$: for a scalar test $\varphi$, Fubini [F5] and the translated fundamental-solution identity of [F7] yield $\langle-\Delta T_{A_k},\varphi\rangle=-\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\int\Phi(x-\gamma(s))\Delta\varphi(x)dx\,ds=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\varphi(\gamma(s))ds$; applying this to the components of a vector test $\psi$ gives $\langle-\Delta T_A,\psi\rangle=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))ds=\mu_0j(\psi)$, that is $-\Delta T_A=\mu_0j$. [step 1.2, F5, F7, algebra]

3.1 For every multi-index $\alpha$ the integrand $\gamma'(s)D^\alpha\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))$ is smooth in $x$ with $s$-independent bound $\sup|D^\alpha\eta_\varepsilon|$ over the compact parameter interval $[0,L]$, so differentiation under the integral sign [F3] coordinatewise gives $D^\alpha j_\varepsilon(x)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)D^\alpha\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))ds$ and $j_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$; the integrand vanishes unless $x\in\gamma([0,L])+\operatorname{supp}\eta_\varepsilon\subseteq\gamma([0,L])+\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$, a closed bounded and hence compact set by [F11], so $\operatorname{supp}j_\varepsilon$ is compact. [step 2.2, F3, F11, algebra]

3.2 Since $T_B=\operatorname{curl}T_A$ by step 2.3 and constant-coefficient distributional derivatives commute [F4], the alternating-symbol cancellations give $\operatorname{div}T_B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}T_A=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}T_B=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}T_A=\nabla\operatorname{div}T_A-\Delta T_A=0+\mu_0j=\mu_0j$; this proves the global distributional identities for $T_B$ without any limit through the singular support. [step 2.3, step 2.4, step 2.5, F4, algebra]

3.3 On $\mathbb R^3\setminus\gamma$ the field $B$ is given by the absolutely convergent integral of the Statement, with $|B(x)|\le\frac{\mu_0|I|}{4\pi}\int_0^L|x-\gamma(s)|^{-2}ds$ because $|\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))|\le|x-\gamma(s)|$ by [F12]; the same Tonelli computation as step 1.2 gives $\int_Q|B|\le\mu_0|I|LR$ on every compact $Q$, so $B\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $T_B$ is its regular distribution by [F4]; the curve is Lebesgue-null because for every $h>0$ the Lipschitz bound [F2] with $|\gamma'|=1$ covers $\gamma([0,L])$ by the $\lceil L/h\rceil$ balls of radius $h$ about the equally spaced points $jL/\lceil L/h\rceil$, whose total volume $\lceil L/h\rceil\frac43\pi h^3$ tends to $0$ as $h\to0$ by [F10], and arbitrary finite values assigned on that null set therefore give the same locally integrable class and a measurable representative; on a compact subset of the complement the distance gap of [F11] bounds the kernel and all its $x$-derivatives uniformly, so differentiation under the integral sign [F3] makes $B$ smooth off $\gamma$. [step 2.3, step 1.2, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F9, F10, F11, F12, algebra]

4.1 For every fixed $x$ one has $\operatorname{div}j_\varepsilon(x)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))ds=-I\int_0^L(d/ds)\bigl[\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))\bigr]ds=0$: the chain rule [F1] identifies the integrand with the negative $s$-derivative, the composite is $C^1$ on $[0,L]$ with integrable derivative [F2], and periodicity gives equal endpoint values. [step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra]

4.2 If $\gamma([0,L])\subseteq B_a(0)$ and $|x|>a$, then $|x-\gamma(s)|\ge|x|-a$ for every $s$, so step 3.3 gives $|B(x)|\le\frac{\mu_0|I|}{4\pi}\frac{L}{(|x|-a)^2}$, the stated decay at infinity. [step 3.3, F12, algebra]

4.3 Let $K$ be nonempty compact with $d=\operatorname{dist}(K,\gamma([0,L]))>0$ by [F11], let $0<\varepsilon<d/2$, and let $A_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{j_\varepsilon(y)}{|x-y|}dy$ be the Newtonian potential of the smooth compactly supported $j_\varepsilon$; differentiating under the integral sign [F3] on $K$, where $|x-y|\ge d/2$ for $y\in\operatorname{supp}j_\varepsilon$ by step 3.1, gives the Biot-Savart field $B_\varepsilon(x)=\operatorname{curl}A_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{j_\varepsilon(y)\times(x-y)}{|x-y|^3}dy$; substituting the formula of step 2.2 for $j_\varepsilon$, applying Fubini [F5] and translating $y=\gamma(s)+u$ with the measure-preserving change of variables [F5] yields $B_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\int_{\overline B_\varepsilon(0)}\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s)-u)}{|x-\gamma(s)-u|^3}\eta_\varepsilon(u)\,du\,ds$, all integrals absolutely convergent because $|x-\gamma(s)-u|\ge d-\varepsilon>0$. [step 2.2, step 3.1, F3, F5, F11, algebra]

5.1 For every multi-index $\alpha$ and $x\in K$, differentiate the absolutely convergent formulas of steps 3.3 and 4.3 under the integral signs [F3] and write $F_s(w)=\gamma'(s)\times w/|w|^3$: $D^\alpha B_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\int D^\alpha F_s(x-\gamma(s)-u)\eta_\varepsilon(u)duds$ and $D^\alpha B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^LD^\alpha F_s(x-\gamma(s))ds$; on the annulus $|w|\ge d/2$ one has $|D_wD^\alpha F_s(w)|\le C_\alpha|w|^{-3-|\alpha|}$ uniformly in $s$ because $|\gamma'(s)|=1$ and the derivatives of $w/|w|^3$ are homogeneous of the corresponding degrees, so the Lipschitz bound [F2] applied along the segment from $x-\gamma(s)$ to $x-\gamma(s)-u$ gives $|D^\alpha F_s(x-\gamma(s)-u)-D^\alpha F_s(x-\gamma(s))|\le C_\alpha(d/2)^{-3-|\alpha|}|u|$; integrating against the unit-mass kernel supported in $\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$ gives $|D^\alpha B_\varepsilon(x)-D^\alpha B(x)|\le\frac{\mu_0|I|L}{4\pi}C_\alpha(d/2)^{-3-|\alpha|}\varepsilon$, which tends to $0$ uniformly over $x\in K$ as $\varepsilon\to0$: the Biot-Savart fields converge with every derivative uniformly on $K$. [step 3.3, step 4.3, F2, F3, F5, F9, algebra]

6.1 For $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ and $x=z e_3$, step 3.3's formula has numerator $\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))=(z\cos(s/a),z\sin(s/a),a)$ and denominator $(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}$, so $B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\int_0^{2\pi a}(z\cos(s/a),z\sin(s/a),a)\,ds$; with $ds=a\,d\theta$, the transverse entries integrate to $0$ and the third entry integrates to $2\pi a^2$, because $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos=\int_0^{2\pi}\sin=0$ by the FTC and the fundamental period of [F13]; hence $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/\bigl(2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}\bigr)$, while no value of the singular line integral on the curve and no self-energy is asserted. [step 3.3, F2, F13, algebra] ∎
