## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), used to invoke the published Sobolev completeness theorem through its Countable-Choice interface ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open for some $L>0$, and write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H_0^1(\Omega):=W_0^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ in that norm ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then $H^1(\Omega)$ is complete, $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace and is complete, the $W^{1,2}$ quadratic norm is a Hilbert norm (its coordinate $L^2$ pairings satisfy the parallelogram law), and

$$\|v\|_{L^2}^2\le(2L)^2\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2}^2\le(2L)^2\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2\qquad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega).$$

In particular $\|v\|_{L^2}\le2L\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ and the gradient norm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm on $H_0^1(\Omega)$. The argument needs neither a smooth domain nor a general boundary-trace theorem, and no choice beyond the completeness interface is used.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice $\mathrm{AC}$ (so Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ holds), a number $L>0$, and a bounded open $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$. Write $H^1=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $H_0^1=W_0^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, with $\|u\|_{W}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2+\sum_{j=1}^3\|\partial_ju\|_2^2$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] **Sobolev spaces and norm.** For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $L^p$ classes whose weak derivatives up to order $k$ are $L^p$ classes, the $D^\alpha u$ are well-defined classes and $\|u\|_{W^{k,p}}=(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p}^p)^{1/p}$ for $p<\infty$; at $k=1$, $p=2$ this is $\|u\|_W^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2$, and the norm axioms hold by the norm theorem cited there ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[F2] **Zero-boundary space as a closure.** $W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the metric closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ in $W^{k,p}$, so $u\in W_0^{k,p}$ exactly when for every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}}<\delta$; no boundary trace is asserted ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

[F3] **Completeness.** Under the Axiom of Choice, $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with the displayed norm is a complete normed space; at $k=1$, $p=2$, $H^1$ is complete ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]]).

[F4] **Hilbert structure of real $L^2$.** Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, real $L^2(\Omega)$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int fg$ is a real Hilbert space and $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$ ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]); in every real inner-product space the parallelogram law $\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2$ holds ([[thm-parallelogram-law]]).

[F5] **Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$.** $\int|fg|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ for $f,g\in\mathcal L^2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]); applied to $g=\mathbf 1_{(-L,L)}$ this gives $(\int_{-L}^L|f|)^2\le2L\int_{-L}^L|f|^2$.

[F6] **Newton-Leibniz with interior derivative.** If $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f$ is Riemann integrable with $f=G'$ on $(a,b)$, then $\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a)$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

[F7] **Tonelli.** A nonnegative measurable function on a $\sigma$-finite product may be integrated in either order ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F8] **Norm axioms.** A norm satisfies $\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|$ and $\|x\|=0\Rightarrow x=0$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), so a limit of a sequence in a subspace that exists in an ambient complete space and is approached by elements of the subspace lies in its closure whenever the closure is closed for the norm topology.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F3] the space $H^1$ is complete for $\|u\|_W^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2$; the Axiom of Choice assumed here is used only to supply Countable Choice for that theorem by [A1]. [given, A1, F1, F3]

1.2 Let $v\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^3$; fix $(x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb R^2$ and let $G(s)=v(s,x_2,x_3)$. Since $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ and $v$ vanishes outside $\Omega$, $G$ is continuous on $[-L,L]$, differentiable on $(-L,L)$ with $G'=\partial_1v(\cdot,x_2,x_3)$ Riemann integrable, and $G(-L)=0$; hence [F6] gives $v(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\int_{-L}^{x_1}\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)\,ds$ for every $x_1\in(-L,L)$. [given, F6]

2.1 $H_0^1$ is a closed subspace of $H^1$ and is complete: if $(u_m)\subseteq H_0^1$ is $\|\cdot\|_W$-Cauchy, [F3] gives $u\in H^1$ with $\|u_m-u\|_W\to0$; given $\delta>0$ choose $m$ with $\|u_m-u\|_W<\delta$ and then, because $u_m\in H_0^1$, a test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $\|u_m-\varphi\|_W<\delta$ by [F2]; the triangle inequality [F8] gives $\|u-\varphi\|_W<2\delta$, so $u\in H_0^1$ by the characterization [F2], and $\|u_m-u\|_W\to0$ in the subspace norm; the identical argument with $H_0^1$ in place of the arbitrary subspace shows closedness of $H_0^1$ in $H^1$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F8, algebra]

2.2 The $W^{1,2}$ norm is a Hilbert norm: writing $\|u\|_W^2=\sum_{|\alpha|\le1}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2$ by [F1], each summand $\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2$ is the squared norm of the real Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega)$ by [F4], so the parallelogram law [F4] holds for each summand and, summed over the finite index set $\{|\alpha|\le1\}$, for $\|\cdot\|_W^2$ itself; combining this with the completeness of step 1.1 exhibits $H^1$ and its closed subspace $H_0^1$ as real Hilbert spaces for the coordinate $L^2$ pairings. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra]

2.3 For such $v$ and every $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, step 1.2 and the Cauchy-Schwarz bound [F5] give $|v(x)|^2\le\bigl(\int_{-L}^L|\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)|ds\bigr)^2\le2L\int_{-L}^L|\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)|^2ds$. [step 1.2, F5, algebra]

3.1 Integrating the inequality of step 2.3 over $(-L,L)^3$ and applying Tonelli [F7] to the nonnegative integrand gives $\|v\|_{L^2}^2\le2L\int_{(-L,L)^3}\int_{-L}^L|\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)|^2ds\,dx=(2L)^2\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2}^2$, because the $x_1$-integration contributes the length $2L$ and $v$ vanishes outside the box. [step 2.3, F7, algebra]

4.1 Pass the bound to $v\in H_0^1$: choose $\varphi_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $\|\varphi_n-v\|_W\to0$ by [F2]; then [F1] gives $\|\varphi_n\|_2\to\|v\|_2$, $\|\partial_1\varphi_n\|_2\to\|\partial_1v\|_2$ and $\|\nabla\varphi_n\|_2\to\|\nabla v\|_2$, and passing to the limit in step 3.1's inequality $\|\varphi_n\|_2\le2L\|\partial_1\varphi_n\|_2$ yields $\|v\|_{L^2}\le2L\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2}$; squaring and using $\|\partial_1v\|_2\le\|\nabla v\|_2$ gives the displayed chain $\|v\|_2^2\le(2L)^2\|\partial_1v\|_2^2\le(2L)^2\|\nabla v\|_2^2$. [step 2.2, step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra]

5.1 Equivalence of norms on $H_0^1$: $\|\nabla v\|_2\le\|v\|_W$ is immediate from $\|v\|_W^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|\nabla v\|_2^2$ by [F1], while step 4.1 gives $\|v\|_W^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|\nabla v\|_2^2\le\bigl(1+(2L)^2\bigr)\|\nabla v\|_2^2$; the gradient norm is therefore equivalent to the full $W^{1,2}$ norm on $H_0^1$, both operators being applied to the weak derivatives of [F1] and no smoothness of $\Omega$ being used. This proves all the claims of the Statement, and no choice beyond the completeness interface [F3]/[A1] has been used. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 4.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ in the graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]; connectedness is unnecessary. Write $H^m(\Omega)=W^{m,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the multi-index integral norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ for the $H^1$ closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). For every real $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ there is a unique $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)$ satisfying

$$\int_\Omega(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+uv)=\int_\Omega fv\qquad(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

It satisfies $(1-\Delta)u=f$ distributionally and almost everywhere as an $L^2$ identity, and

$$\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad\|u\|_{H^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$

Moreover $D=\{\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega):\varphi|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$ is dense in $H^2(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$ in the $H^2$ norm: every such $w$ has $\varphi_j\in D$ with $\varphi_j\to w$ in $H^2$. Here smoothness on the closure means restriction of a smooth function on a neighbourhood of the closure, equivalently the smooth chart representatives used below. In particular $\nabla\varphi_j\to\nabla w$ in the graph norm of $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$, with zero curl and $\operatorname{div}\nabla w=\Delta w$; every $\nabla\varphi_j$ is smooth and PEC since its tangential derivatives vanish at the boundary. For precision, let $X_\Omega$ be the graph-norm closure of smooth vector fields on a neighbourhood of the closure with $\nu\times v=0$ on the boundary, where $\nu$ is the outward Euclidean unit normal. The ambient graph space consists of real $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_i\partial_iv_i$ and $\operatorname{curl}v=(\partial_2v_3-\partial_3v_2,\partial_3v_1-\partial_1v_3,\partial_1v_2-\partial_2v_1)$ lie in $L^2$; its norm squared is $\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2$. Thus $\nabla w$ belongs to this explicitly defined $X_\Omega$, the same completion used by the later cavity item. No equality with every maximal trace realisation is asserted.

No smoothness of $f$, no classical boundary value for general $u$, and no general nonsmooth-domain, Neumann, interface, or variable-coefficient claim is included. Zero boundary condition means membership in $H_0^1$; the published trace theorem identifies its trace as zero.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; a bounded $C^\infty$ graph domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$; $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$; the spaces $H^m(\Omega)$, $H_0^1(\Omega)$, the graph space and its closure $X_\Omega$ of the Statement; the variational form $a(w,v)=\int_\Omega(\nabla w\cdot\nabla v+wv)$ and $\ell(v)=\int_\Omega fv$.

[F1] **Zero-boundary coercivity.** Under AC, $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is complete, $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is a closed complete subspace, the $W^{1,2}$ norm is a Hilbert norm, and $\|v\|_2\le2L\|\nabla v\|_2$ whenever $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ ([[lem-em-zero-boundary-coercivity]]).

[F2] **Symmetric coercive solver.** With Countable Choice, a symmetric bounded bilinear form on a real Hilbert space with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ and a bounded linear functional $\ell$ admit a unique $u$ with $a(u,v)=\ell(v)$ for all $v$, and $\|u\|\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$ ([[lem-em-symmetric-coercive-variational-solver]]).

[F3] **Domain charts.** A bounded $C^k$ graph domain carries a finite atlas of interior patches and boundary graph charts, with the boundary presented as graphs over coordinate hyperplanes ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]); finite ambient partitions subordinate to the chart cover exist ([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]), and smooth cutoffs equal to one on prescribed compact subsets exist ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F4] **Flattening.** A $C^k$ diffeomorphism $\Phi:U\to V$ with bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the relevant compact patches maps $W^{k,p}$ locally into $W^{k,p}$, with the chain rule for weak derivatives and a norm bound $\|u\circ\Phi\|_{W^{k,p}(U_0)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(V_0)}$ ([[lem-c-k-boundary-flattening-preserves-wkp-locally]]). Change of variables for Lebesgue integrals is available for the $C^1$ charts ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]), and the weak Leibniz rule for products with a smooth factor holds ([[lem-weak-leibniz-rule-with-a-smooth-factor]]).

[F5] **Difference quotients.** $\delta_h^iu(x)=(u(x+he_i)-u(x))/h$ on $\Omega_{i,h}$ ([[def-first-difference-quotient]]). Discrete integration by parts holds ([[lem-difference-quotient-integration-by-parts]]); for $u\in H^1$ and a cutoff $\eta$, the class $v=-\delta_{-h}^i(\eta^2\delta_h^iu)$ is an admissible compactly supported $H_0^1$ test, and on the half-space with a tangential index $j<n$ it lies in $H_0^1(H)$ and is admissible for an $L^2$ datum ([[lem-tangential-difference-quotient-test-function]]). For $u\in W^{1,2}$ the increment bound $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^2(\Omega')}\le\|D_iu\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ holds on $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and the converse characterizes $W^{1,p}$ by uniform increment bounds ([[thm-difference-quotient-characterisation-of-w-one-p-for-p-greater-than-one]]).

[F6] **Riesz representation and $L^2$ completeness.** For a closed subspace of a real Hilbert space, every bounded linear functional is represented by a unique element of the subspace ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]); $L^2$ is complete ([[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]]).

[F7] **Extensions, traces, kernels.** The half-space admits bounded linear $W^{2,2}$ extension operators to $\mathbb R^3$ ([[thm-wkp-extension-from-a-half-space]]); the flat trace satisfies the $W^{1,p}$ boundary estimate ([[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]]); a bounded $C^1$ domain has a bounded trace operator into $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ ([[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]), traces commute with smooth boundary cutoffs and match across a smooth interface ([[lem-trace-commutes-with-smooth-boundary-cutoffs-and-charts]]), and $\{u:Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ ([[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero]]).

[F8] **Extension and mollification in the interior.** Compactly supported $W^{k,p}$ functions admit zero extensions ([[lem-compact-support-zero-extension-in-wkp]]); whole-space mollification converges in $W^{k,p}$ and commutes with weak derivatives ([[lem-complex-translation-and-approximate-identity-interfaces]], [[lem-mollification-commutes-with-weak-derivatives-in-the-interior]]).

[F9] **Fubini and one-variable calculus.** Tonelli/Fubini hold for completed product measures ([[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]), and the Newton-Leibniz formula with interior derivative holds ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]); smooth mixed partials commute ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

[F10] **Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$.** $\int|fg|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 On $H_0^1$ with the full norm $\|v\|_{H^1}^2=\|v\|_2^2+\|\nabla v\|_2^2$ the form $a$ is symmetric and bounded, since $|a(w,v)|\le\|w\|_{H^1}\|v\|_{H^1}$ by [F10] applied to the four-component $L^2$ tuple; it is coercive with $a(v,v)=\|v\|_{H^1}^2$, and $\ell$ is bounded with $\|\ell\|\le\|f\|_2$ because $|\ell(v)|\le\|f\|_2\|v\|_2\le\|f\|_2\|v\|_{H^1}$; [F1] makes $H_0^1$ a complete real Hilbert space, so [F2] with $\alpha=1$ (Countable Choice covered by the assumed AC) gives a unique $u\in H_0^1$ with $a(u,v)=\ell(v)$ for all $v\in H_0^1$ and $\|u\|_{H^1}\le\|\ell\|\le\|f\|_2$; testing with $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subseteq H_0^1$ gives $\int(\nabla u\cdot\nabla\varphi+u\varphi)=\int f\varphi$, that is $(1-\Delta)u=f$ distributionally. [given, F1, F2, F10, algebra]

1.2 Cover the compact closure by finitely many interior patches and boundary graph patches, shrink each twice and choose cutoffs equal to one on the inner patches by [F3]; flattening the boundary charts and possibly reversing the last coordinate sends the domain side to $t>0$ and, by [F4], maps the local $H^1$ and $H^2$ classes with bounded norms. Writing $y=\Phi(x)$, $U=u\circ\Phi^{-1}$, $J=|\det D(\Phi^{-1})|$, the local weak equation becomes $\int A_{ij}\partial_jU\partial_iV+cUV=\int FV$ with $A=J(D\Phi)(D\Phi)^{\mathsf T}$, $c=J$ and $F=J(f\circ\Phi^{-1})$, where $A$ is symmetric and uniformly positive, the coefficients and their first derivatives are bounded on the patch, and $\|F\|_2\le C\|f\|_2$ locally; all identities are justified by the change-of-variables formula and the weak chain rule of [F4]. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 A localized flattened $U$ lies in $H_0^1$ of the half-space: multiplying the test functions approximating $u$ in $H_0^1(\Omega)$ by the patch cutoff and pulling back through the flattening gives smooth compactly supported functions on the open half-space converging in $H^1$ by [F4], so that the closure characterization of [F1] applies; their supports need not have a uniform distance from the boundary. Consequently tangential difference quotients and smooth cutoffs preserve this closure by [F5]. [given, F3, F4, F5]

2.1 For $k=1,2$ (tangential directions) put $w_h=\delta_h^kU$ and $V=-\delta_{-h}^k(\eta^2w_h)$, pulled back and extended by zero outside the chart; by the half-space part of [F5] each $V$ is an admissible $H_0^1$ test for the localized flattened equation whenever $0<|h|$ is small, and a larger preliminary localization equal to one on the quotient neighbourhood ensures that the cutoff does not change the equation on the test support; interior patches allow all three quotient directions, while no normal quotient crosses the boundary. [step 1.3, F5, algebra]

2.2 For arbitrary $w\in H^2(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$ choose a finite smooth ambient partition with one interior part and boundary parts compactly contained in graph charts by [F3]; multiplication by the partition and flattening preserve $H^2$ by [F4], and each boundary part becomes a compactly supported $W\in H^2(H)$ on the half-space whose flat trace is zero, either by chart compatibility and bounded trace continuity [F7] or by transporting the $H_0^1$ approximating sequence of step 1.3; its support is separated from the artificial edges of the chart. [given, F3, F4, F7]

3.1 Substituting $V$ into the local equation of step 1.2 and using the discrete integration by parts and the quotient product rule of [F5], with $S=F-cU\in L^2$, the principal term satisfies $\int\eta^2A_{ij}(y+he_k)\partial_jw_h\partial_iw_h\ge\alpha\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2^2$ and the remaining principal terms are $\int\eta^2(\delta_hA_{ij})\partial_jU\partial_iw_h$ and $\int[A_{ij}(y+he_k)\partial_jw_h+(\delta_hA_{ij})\partial_jU](\partial_i\eta^2)w_h$, whose absolute sum is at most $C(\|U\|_{H^1}+\|w_h\|_2)\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2+C\|U\|_{H^1}\|w_h\|_2$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F4, F5, F10, algebra]

3.2 Unrestricted smooth $H^2$ approximants of $W$ are obtained from the half-space extension of [F7] followed by multiplication by a fixed compact cutoff equal to one on the support and by whole-space mollification [F8]; they converge in $H^2$, so the traces of the functions and of their first derivatives converge in $L^2$ by the flat trace estimate [F7]; for $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ and tangential $k$, the classical boundary integration by parts for the smooth approximants gives $\int T(\partial_kW)\zeta=-\int TW\,\partial_k\zeta=0$, hence $T(\partial_kW)=0$ as a distribution and almost everywhere. [step 2.2, F7, F8, F9, algebra]

4.1 Here $\|\delta_hA\|_\infty\le\|\partial_kA\|_\infty$ on the patch by [F5], and the increment bound of [F5] at $p=2$ gives $\|w_h\|_2\le C\|U\|_{H^1}$ on the required enlarged quotient neighbourhood; the undifferentiated right-hand side obeys $\bigl|\int S\,\delta_{-h}^k(\eta^2w_h)\bigr|\le C\|S\|_2(\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2+\|w_h\|_2)$ because the same increment bound applies to $\eta^2w_h$ in that direction. [step 3.1, F5, F10, algebra]

4.2 Define the odd reflection $W_o(y,t)=W(y,t)$ for $t>0$ and $-W(y,-t)$ for $t<0$; a piecewise $H^1$ function whose two traces agree is globally $H^1$, proved by testing each half against a compact smooth ambient test, using smooth half-space approximation, one-variable integration and Fubini [F8, F9], the sole interface contribution being the difference of the two traces, which cancels; applying the gluing calculation first to $W_o$ (both traces zero) and then to its first derivatives, whose tangential components are odd reflections of $\partial_kW$ with both traces zero by step 3.2 and whose normal component is the even reflection of $\partial_tW$ with identical traces, shows $W_o\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\|W_o\|_{H^2}=\sqrt2\|W\|_{H^2}$ and no delta layer. [step 2.2, step 3.2, F8, F9, algebra]

5.1 Cauchy-Schwarz and the elementary absorption $2ab\le\varepsilon a^2+b^2/\varepsilon$ with a fixed small $\varepsilon$ let the principal gradient square absorb the corresponding right-hand contributions, yielding $\|\eta\nabla\delta_h^kU\|_2\le C(\|F\|_2+\|U\|_{H^1})$ uniformly for all sufficiently small nonzero $h$; this estimates the actual $L^2$ datum, and no difference quotient of $F$ or derivative of $f$ appears. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 Choose a real compactly supported mass-one mollifier invariant under $t\mapsto-t$ and convolve $W_o$; the mollifications converge in $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ by [F8], remain odd and hence vanish at $t=0$, and multiplication by a fixed smooth cutoff in the flattened ambient chart equal to one near the support of $W_o$, with support separated from the artificial edges, preserves this boundary vanishing and the convergence. [step 4.2, F8, algebra]

6.1 On a smaller patch where $\eta=1$, for every compactly supported smooth test $\psi$ the discrete integration by parts [F5] gives $\int\delta_h^k(\partial_jU)\psi=-\int\partial_jU\,\delta_{-h}^k\psi$, whose limit as $h\to0$ is $-\int\partial_jU\,\partial_k\psi$; the uniform bound of step 5.1 makes this a bounded linear functional of $\psi$ in the $L^2$ norm, so it extends continuously to the closed $L^2$ subspace generated by those tests, which is Hilbert by [F6], and the Riesz representation theorem [F6] gives an $L^2$ function representing $\partial_k\partial_jU$ distributionally with the same bound. [step 2.1, step 5.1, F5, F6, algebra]

6.2 Pulling back through the smooth chart and extending by zero outside its artificial support gives globally smooth functions on a neighbourhood of the closure with zero physical boundary value; approximating the interior part by compactly supported smooth functions with radii smaller than its distance from the physical boundary by [F8], and adding the finitely many parts with radii tending to zero (the sequence of radii is chosen by AC), yields $\varphi_j\in D$ with $\varphi_j\to w$ in $H^2$ and hence also in $H^1$, so each $\varphi_j$ lies in $H_0^1$ by the zero-trace kernel theorem [F7]. [step 2.2, step 5.2, F7, F8, algebra]

7.1 Boundary patches thus have every second derivative with at least one tangential index, and weak derivatives commute because for smooth tests the defining pairings reduce to the commutation of smooth mixed partials [F9]; the interior patches already have all second derivatives by applying step 6.1 in all three directions. [step 6.1, F9, algebra]

8.1 The missing normal derivative is recovered from the divergence-form equation with the signs $A_{33}\partial_{33}U=cU-F-\sum_{(i,j)\ne(3,3)}A_{ij}\partial_{ij}U-\sum_{i,j}(\partial_iA_{ij})\partial_jU$; every term on the right is in $L^2$ and $A_{33}\ge\alpha>0$, so division yields $\partial_{33}U\in L^2$ with its bound, this being established distributionally before any almost-everywhere identification. [step 1.2, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 Returning through the bounded $H^2$ chart maps of [F4] and summing the finitely many patch estimates gives $\|u\|_{H^2}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|u\|_{H^1})\le C_\Omega\|f\|_2$, so the equation holds in $L^2$ and almost everywhere; uniqueness in $H_0^1\cap H^2$ is uniqueness in the larger variational space of step 1.1. [step 1.1, step 8.1, F1, F4, algebra]

10.1 Since $\varphi_j$ is smooth and vanishes on the boundary, $\operatorname{curl}\nabla\varphi_j=0$ and $\operatorname{div}\nabla\varphi_j=\Delta\varphi_j$, while $\nu\times\nabla\varphi_j=0$ follows by differentiating the identically zero smooth boundary restriction; the weak derivatives commute by [F9], so the curls vanish distributionally and $\|\nabla\varphi_j-\nabla w\|_2+\|\operatorname{curl}(\nabla\varphi_j-\nabla w)\|_2+\|\operatorname{div}(\nabla\varphi_j-\nabla w)\|_2\to0$, which is exactly convergence in the graph norm of the Statement; hence $\nabla w\in X_\Omega$ without any maximal-trace-density assumption, and all the claims of the Statement are proved with AC used only through the cited completeness, extension, trace and Riesz interfaces. [step 6.2, F7, F9, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $\omega_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\chi$ be holomorphic on the upper half-plane and continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on its real boundary away from $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfying $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set ([[def-complex-domain]]). Let $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)(z-\omega_0)^j/j!$ be the Taylor polynomial at $\omega_0$ and $f(z)=[\chi(z)-P(z)]/(z-\omega_0)^n$, with the removable value at $\omega_0$. Assume the boundary restriction of $f$ is class $C^1$ (the local holomorphy supplies this at $\omega_0$). Then for real $\omega$,

$$\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Re}P(\omega)+\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,$$

$$\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}P(\omega)-\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi.$$

At $\omega=\omega_0$ the formula is read as the stated Taylor value. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is also valid with $P=0$, $f=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and the factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ for all $\omega$; at $\omega_0$ use the same principal-value formula rather than a Taylor-value convention. For the separate constitutive polynomial branch assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]), let $A_0,\ldots,A_m$ be real scalar coefficients or real matrices, and let $K$ satisfy all hypotheses of [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]. On histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$, the response $\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ is causal, and its transfer function in the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z):=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared polynomial $Q$ leaves the proved entrywise dispersion formulas for $\chi_K$; this branch does not require holomorphic continuation through a real subtraction point. The Taylor-subtracted formulas above apply to the total response when its additional local-holomorphy, growth and boundary hypotheses are satisfied; $Q$ need not equal its Taylor polynomial $P$. General passivity and storage remain separate model conditions.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** An integer $n\ge0$, a real $\omega_0$, a function $\chi$ with the listed holomorphy, continuity, boundary regularity and growth, its Taylor polynomial $P$ of degree $n-1$ at $\omega_0$, and the divided function $f$; in the constitutive branch, coefficients $A_0,\ldots,A_m$ and a matrix kernel $K$ satisfying the hypotheses of [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]].

[F1] **Holomorphy, domains and Taylor expansion.** The upper half-plane $H=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ is an open subset of $\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-domain]]); if $g$ is holomorphic on an open disc about $a$, then $g(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}g^{(j)}(a)(z-a)^j/j!$ throughout the largest centred disc contained in its domain ([[thm-taylor-expansion-holomorphic-function]]).

[F2] **Cauchy theorem and contour limits.** A closed rectifiable contour in a star-shaped open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]] applied to $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$) integrates a holomorphic function to $0$ ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-star-shaped-domain]]); uniform convergence of continuous integrands on a fixed rectifiable contour passes through the contour integral ([[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]]); a continuous function is uniformly continuous on every compact subset ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]).

[F3] **Integrable causal dispersion.** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $\mathrm{DC}$ with the meanings of [[def-countable-choice]] and [[def-dependent-choice]]; for a locally absolutely continuous matrix kernel $K$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1$ and $sK\in L^1$, the response function $\chi_K(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}ds$ is holomorphic on $H$, continuous and $C^1$ on the real boundary, satisfies $|\chi_K(z)|\le(|K(0)|+\|K'\|_1)/|z|$ for $z\ne0$, $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and its entries satisfy the principal-value formulas $\operatorname{Re}\chi_K(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\int\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_K(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi$, $\operatorname{Im}\chi_K(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\int\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_K(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi$ ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]). The first branch of this item uses no choice beyond the ambient conventions of the cited complex-analysis suppliers.

[F4] **Derivatives are local and convolution is causal.** The derivative $E^{(j)}(t)$ depends only on the values of $E$ in an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of $t$ ([[def-derivative]]), and $(K*E)(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ depends only on the values of $E$ on $(-\infty,t]$.


## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1] applied in a disc contained in the neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ on which $\chi$ is holomorphic, $\chi(z)=P(z)+(z-\omega_0)^n\tilde g(z)$ for a holomorphic $\tilde g$ there; hence $f$ has the holomorphic removable continuation $\tilde g$ at $\omega_0$, and elsewhere $f=(\chi-P)/(z-\omega_0)^n$ is holomorphic on $H$ because the denominator does not vanish; the two definitions agree on the punctured intersection, so $f$ is holomorphic on $H$ and near $\omega_0$, continuous on the closure of $H$ (the removable continuation at $\omega_0$ together with the continuity of $\chi$ and polynomiality of $P$), of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R$ by hypothesis, and $|f(z)|\le C'(1+|z|^{n-1})/|z-\omega_0|^n=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Fix real $\omega$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$, and form the closed indented contour $\Gamma$ consisting of the real segments from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and from $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, the upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$ traversed from $\omega-\eta$ to $\omega+\eta$, and the large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$ traversed from $\omega+R$ to $\omega-R$. For $\delta>0$ the domain $D_\delta=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$ is open and star-shaped about $\omega+iA$ for every $A>0$, the contour $\Gamma$ lies in $D_\delta$, and $z\mapsto f(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic on $D_\delta$ because $\operatorname{Im}(z+i\delta)>\delta/2>0$ and the denominator avoids its slit zero; hence [F2] gives $\int_\Gamma f(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)\,dz=0$. [given, F2, algebra]

1.3 Constitutive branch: for histories $E_1,E_2$ with the stated bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$ that agree on $(-\infty,t]$, each derivative at $t$ agrees, $E_1^{(j)}(t)=E_2^{(j)}(t)$, by the locality of the derivative [F4], and the convolutions agree, $(K*E_1)(t)=(K*E_2)(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E_i(t-s)ds$, because $t-s\le t$ for $s\ge0$; hence the response $\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ evaluated at $t$ is the same for $E_1$ and $E_2$: the response is causal. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 On the fixed contour $\Gamma$ the functions $z\mapsto f(z+i\delta)$ converge uniformly to $z\mapsto f(z)$ as $\delta\downarrow0$ by the uniform continuity [F2] of the continuous $f$ on a compact neighbourhood of $\Gamma$ in the closed half-plane, so [F2] transfers the identity of step 1.2 to $\int_\Gamma f(z)/(z-\omega)dz=0$; the large arc contributes at most $\pi R\cdot C/(R(R-|\omega|))=O(1/R)\to0$ as $R\to\infty$ because $|f(z)|\le C/|z|$ holds for $|z|\ge1$ in the closed half-plane, while the small arc, parametrized by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$, contributes $-i\pi f(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\eta\downarrow0$ by continuity of $f$ at $\omega$; the two real segments, whose tails are absolutely integrable since $f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$, therefore satisfy $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi f(\omega)$, the principal value existing because the constant term $f(\omega)/(\xi-\omega)$ cancels under the symmetric truncation and the $C^1$ hypothesis bounds the divided difference. [step 1.2, F2, algebra]

2.2 Transfer function: for the monochromatic history $E(t)=E_0e^{-i\omega t}$ with constant $E_0$, one has $E^{(j)}(t)=(-i\omega)^jE_0e^{-i\omega t}$ and $(K*E)(t)=\chi_K(\omega)E_0e^{-i\omega t}$ by the defining formula of [F3] with $z=\omega$; hence the response is $(Q(\omega)+\chi_K(\omega))E_0e^{-i\omega t}$ with $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$, and repeating the computation with $e^{-izt}$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ identifies the transfer function as $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$, a polynomial plus the holomorphic function of [F3]. [step 1.3, F3, algebra]

3.1 Taking real and imaginary parts of the identity $i\pi f(\omega)=\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$ gives $\operatorname{Re}f(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi$ and $\operatorname{Im}f(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}d\xi$; multiplying by the real number $(\omega-\omega_0)^n$ and adding the complex polynomial $P$ yields the two displayed formulas for $\operatorname{Re}\chi$ and $\operatorname{Im}\chi$, since $\chi=P+(\cdot-\omega_0)^nf$ on the closed half-plane. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At $\omega=\omega_0$ the factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^n$ vanishes and $P(\omega_0)=\chi(\omega_0)$ by Taylor's formula at $\omega_0$, so the displayed formulas are read as that Taylor value; the imaginary numerator subtracts the full complex polynomial $P$, which therefore cannot be omitted. For $n=0$ one has $P=0$, $f=\chi$, factor $1$, and the growth hypothesis is exactly $O(1/|z|)$, so the same contour argument of steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1 applies with the principal-value convention at $\omega_0$ as well. [step 3.1, step 2.1, F1, algebra]

5.1 Subtracting the declared polynomial $Q$ from $Q+\chi_K$ leaves $\chi_K$, whose entrywise principal-value dispersion formulas are exactly those proved in [F3]; this branch therefore requires no holomorphic continuation through a real subtraction point and no growth hypothesis beyond those of [F3]; general passivity and storage remain separate model conditions, and the declared polynomial $Q$ of this branch need not coincide with the Taylor polynomial $P$ of the first branch. This proves both branches of the Statement, the first with no choice beyond the cited complex-analysis suppliers and the second with the declared Countable Choice and Dependent Choice inherited from [F3]. [step 2.2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open, let $\varepsilon$ be a measurable symmetric real $3\times3$ matrix field on $\Omega$ with $\alpha|\xi|^2\le\xi\cdot\varepsilon(x)\xi\le\beta|\xi|^2$ for a.e. $x$ and all $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, $0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty$, let $G\in H^1(\Omega)$ be a specified lift, and let $F\in(H_0^1(\Omega))^*$ be bounded. Then there is exactly one $u\in G+H_0^1(\Omega)$ with

$$\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega),$$

where $H_0^1=W_0^{1,2}(\Omega)$ carries the gradient norm. For $F(v)=\int_\Omega\rho v$ with $\rho\in L^2(\Omega)$ this is the weak Poisson solution $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon\nabla u)=\rho$, with the homogeneous boundary datum represented by membership of $H_0^1$ rather than by an unproved classical trace. No boundary datum outside the specified lift class is assumed attainable; classical boundary regularity, general Neumann lifts and transmission regularity remain later obligations.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A bounded open $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$, a uniformly elliptic symmetric measurable coefficient field $\varepsilon$ with constants $0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty$, a lift $G\in H^1(\Omega)$, a bounded functional $F$ on $H_0^1(\Omega)$ with the gradient norm, and on $H_0^1$ the forms $a(w,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla w$ and $\ell(v)=F(v)-a(G,v)$.

[F1] **Zero-boundary coercivity.** Under AC, $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is complete for the full $W^{1,2}$ norm, has the Hilbert structure of its coordinate $L^2$ pairings, and $\|\nabla v\|_2\le\|v\|_{W^{1,2}}\le\bigl(1+(2L)^2\bigr)^{1/2}\|\nabla v\|_2$ for $v\in H_0^1$; in particular the gradient norm is equivalent to the full norm and $\|v\|_2\le2L\|\nabla v\|_2$ ([[lem-em-zero-boundary-coercivity]]).

[F2] **Symmetric coercive solver.** With Countable Choice, a symmetric bounded bilinear form on a real Hilbert space with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ and a bounded linear functional admit a unique solution $u$ with $a(u,v)=\ell(v)$ for all $v$, and the solver uses no further choice ([[lem-em-symmetric-coercive-variational-solver]]).

[F3] **Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$.** $\int|fg|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]); real $L^2$ with the integral pairing is a real Hilbert space ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

[F4] **Distributional derivative.** For a distribution $u$, $\langle\partial_ju,\varphi\rangle=-\langle u,\partial_j\varphi\rangle$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]]); for an $L^2$ vector field $V$, the distributional divergence is the functional $\varphi\mapsto\sum_j\int V_j\partial_j\varphi$, so $\langle-\operatorname{div}V,\varphi\rangle=\int\nabla\varphi\cdot V$ for $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The gradient form $a_0(w,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla w\cdot\nabla v$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $H_0^1$ with $a_0(v,v)=\|\nabla v\|_2^2$; it is positive definite, because $a_0(v,v)=0$ forces $\nabla v=0$ and then $\|v\|_2\le2L\|\nabla v\|_2=0$ by [F1], so $v=0$ in $H_0^1$; the parallelogram law for $\|\nabla v\|_2$ follows from the linearity of $v\mapsto\nabla v$ and the inner-product structure of real $L^2$ [F3], and completeness of $H_0^1$ for the gradient norm follows from its equivalence with the complete full norm [F1]; thus $H_0^1$ with the gradient norm is a real Hilbert space. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 The coefficient bounds make $a$ symmetric and bounded on this Hilbert space: $|a(w,v)|\le\int|\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla w|\le\beta\int|\nabla v|\,|\nabla w|\le\beta\|\nabla v\|_2\|\nabla w\|_2$ by the operator bound $\xi\cdot\varepsilon(x)\xi\le\beta|\xi|^2$ and Cauchy-Schwarz [F3], while coercivity holds with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|\nabla v\|_2^2$; also $\ell$ is bounded, since $|F(v)|\le\|F\|\,\|\nabla v\|_2$ and $|a(G,v)|\le\beta\|\nabla G\|_2\|\nabla v\|_2$, so $\|\ell\|\le\|F\|+\beta\|\nabla G\|_2$. [step 1.1, given, F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 Applying the symmetric coercive solver [F2] (Countable Choice is available under the AC standing hypothesis of [F1]) with coercivity constant $\alpha$ gives a unique $w\in H_0^1$ with $a(w,v)=\ell(v)$ for every $v\in H_0^1$, that is $a(w,v)+a(G,v)=F(v)$; hence $u:=G+w$ satisfies $\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=F(v)$ for every $v\in H_0^1$. [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 Uniqueness in the affine class: if $u_1=G+w_1$ and $u_2=G+w_2$ both solve, then subtracting the equations gives $a(w_1-w_2,v)=0$ for all $v\in H_0^1$; testing with $v=w_1-w_2$ gives $\alpha\|\nabla(w_1-w_2)\|_2^2\le a(w_1-w_2,w_1-w_2)=0$, so $\nabla(w_1-w_2)=0$ and, by the Poincare bound of [F1], $w_1-w_2=0$ in $H_0^1$, hence $u_1=u_2$. [step 3.1, given, F1, algebra]

5.1 Distributional form: for $F(v)=\int_\Omega\rho v$ with $\rho\in L^2(\Omega)$ the functional is bounded because $|F(v)|\le\|\rho\|_2\|v\|_2\le2L\|\rho\|_2\|\nabla v\|_2$ by [F1] and [F3], so the existence conclusion applies; testing the solution identity with $v=\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subseteq H_0^1$ gives $\int_\Omega\nabla\varphi\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=\int_\Omega\rho\varphi$, and since $\varepsilon\nabla u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ the distributional divergence of [F4] satisfies $\langle-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon\nabla u),\varphi\rangle=\int\nabla\varphi\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=\int\rho\varphi$ for every test function, that is $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon\nabla u)=\rho$ distributionally. [step 3.1, F1, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

The homogeneous boundary datum is membership of $u-G$ in $H_0^1$, not a classical trace statement; across finitely many material interfaces the weak equation encodes flux continuity wherever one-sided classical traces exist, and classical boundary regularity, general Neumann lifts and transmission regularity remain later obligations.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}J\subset B_a(0)$, $a>0$, and put $m=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Then for $r=|x|\ge2a$ the vector potential and magnetic field

$$A(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad B=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

satisfy, uniformly in $n=x/r$,

$$A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^3}\Bigr),\qquad B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^4}\Bigr).$$

The constants in the $O$ terms are absolute (the second follows by differentiating the first, not by differentiating an unspecified remainder), and $\|J\|_1=\int|J|$.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** Countable Choice, constants $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$, a divergence-free compactly supported smooth field $J$ with $\operatorname{supp}J\subseteq B_a(0)$, the moment $m=\tfrac12\int y\times J$, the potential $A$, and $r=|x|\ge2a$.

[F1] **Divergence integrals vanish.** If $F\in C^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ has $|F|\in L^1$ and $\operatorname{div}F\in L^1$, then $\int\operatorname{div}F=0$ ([[lem-integral-of-a-divergence-of-an-l-one-c-one-field-vanishes]]).

[F2] **Coulomb dipole remainder.** Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for $\rho\in L^1$ supported in $B_a$ and $r\ge2a$, $\int\rho(y)/|x-y|\,dy=Q/r+\langle p,x\rangle/r^3+R(x)$ with $Q=\int\rho$, $p=\int y\rho(y)dy$ and $|R(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/r^3$ ([[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]]).

[F3] **Cross product.** $u\times v$ is the bilinear alternating product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and the pairing is that of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; for $C^1$ fields, $\operatorname{div}(F\times G)=\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle$ and $\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+(DF)G-(DG)F$ ([[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]]).

[F4] **FTC with interior derivative.** For $h$ continuous on $[0,1]$, differentiable on $(0,1)$ with integrable derivative, $\int_0^1h'=h(1)-h(0)$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]); applied twice to $t\mapsto|x-ty|^{-1}$ this gives the integral remainder formula used below.

[F5] **Differentiation under the integral sign and calculus.** Parameter differentiation under an integral with an integrable dominating function is available coordinatewise ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]); the divergence and curl are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and the ordinary derivative rules (product, chain, power) for the rational radial functions are available from [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]. The modulus of an integral is bounded by the integral of the modulus ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For each $i$ the field $y\mapsto y_iJ(y)$ is compactly supported and smooth, and $\operatorname{div}(y_iJ)=J_i+y_i\operatorname{div}J=J_i$; both $|y_iJ|$ and $J_i$ are integrable, so [F1] gives $\int J_i=0$, that is $\int J=0$; similarly $\operatorname{div}(y_iy_jJ)=y_jJ_i+y_iJ_j$ is integrable with compactly supported smooth field $y_iy_jJ$, so [F1] gives $\int(y_jJ_i+y_iJ_j)=0$, that is the antisymmetry of $M_{ij}:=\int y_jJ_i$. [given, F1, F5, algebra]

2.1 The moment $m=\tfrac12\int y\times J$ is finite and $M_{ij}=-\varepsilon_{ijk}m_k$: indeed $\varepsilon_{ijk}m_k=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ijk}\varepsilon_{kpq}M_{pq}=\tfrac12(\delta_{ip}\delta_{jq}-\delta_{iq}\delta_{jp})M_{pq}=\tfrac12(M_{ij}-M_{ji})=M_{ij}$ by the antisymmetry of step 1.1 and the $\varepsilon$-identity; consequently $(Mx)_i=\sum_jM_{ij}x_j=\sum_j(-\varepsilon_{ijk}m_k)x_j=-(x\times m)_i=(m\times x)_i$, so $Mx=m\times x$. [step 1.1, given, F3, algebra]

3.1 Apply the Coulomb dipole expansion [F2] to each component $\rho=J_i$: since $Q_i=\int J_i=0$ and $p_i=\int yJ_i(y)dy$ satisfies $\langle p_i,x\rangle=(Mx)_i=(m\times x)_i$ by step 2.1, and $|R_i(x)|\le16a^2\|J_i\|_1/r^3$, summing over the three components gives $A(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\bigl(\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+R(x)\bigr)$ with $\|R(x)\|_2\le48a^2\|J\|_1/r^3$, so $A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+O(\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1/r^3)$ uniformly for $r\ge2a$ with the absolute constant $12/\pi$. [step 2.1, given, F2, F5, algebra]

4.1 The explicit remainder is $h_2(x,y)=1/|x-y|-1/r-\langle x,y\rangle/r^3$ with $R(x)=\int J(y)h_2(x,y)dy$; applying [F4] twice to $t\mapsto|x-ty|^{-1}$ gives $h_2(x,y)=\int_0^1(1-s)y_jy_k\partial_j\partial_k|x-sy|^{-1}ds$ (derivatives in $x$), and since $|x-sy|\ge r-s|y|\ge r/2$ on the support, each third derivative $\partial_i\partial_j\partial_k|x-sy|^{-1}$ is bounded by an absolute constant $C_3$ times $|x-sy|^{-4}\le16/r^4$; hence $|\nabla_xh_2|\le8C_3a^2/r^4$ and, because $\operatorname{curl}_x(J(y)h_2)=\nabla_xh_2\times J(y)$, the modulus bound [F5] gives $\|\operatorname{curl}R(x)\|_2\le8C_3a^2\|J\|_1/r^4$. [step 3.1, F4, F5, algebra]

5.1 For the leading term compute with [F3] and the constant field $F=m$, $G=x/r^3$: $\operatorname{div}(x/r^3)=3/r^3-3r^2/r^5=0$ and the Jacobian of $x/r^3$ applied to $m$ is $m/r^3-3x\langle x,m\rangle/r^5$ by [F5]; hence $\operatorname{curl}(m\times x/r^3)=\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)m-(DG)m=0-m/r^3+3x\langle x,m\rangle/r^5=\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}$ with $n=x/r$, because $\langle x,m\rangle/r^5=(m\cdot n)/(r^3)$; combining with steps 3.1 and 4.1 and differentiating the explicit formula for $A$ under the integral sign [F5] on the region $r\ge2a>\operatorname{diam}(\operatorname{supp}J)$ gives $B=\operatorname{curl}A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}+O(\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1/r^4)$ uniformly in $n=x/r$ with an absolute constant. [step 3.1, step 4.1, given, F3, F5, algebra]

6.1 The two $O$ constants depend only on absolute numbers and $\pi$, not on $J$, $a$, $x$ or $r$, and the second was obtained by differentiating the explicit remainder of the first rather than an unspecified $O$ term; Countable Choice is inherited from the Coulomb dipole expansion [F2] and the integrability interfaces of [F1], and no stronger principle is used. This proves both estimates. [step 3.1, step 5.1, given, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. For $k>0$ define $G_k(x)=e^{ik|x|}/(4\pi|x|)$ off the origin, a locally integrable complex function. Then

$$(-\Delta-k^2)G_k=\delta_0$$

distributionally ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). For a finite complex measure $\alpha$ supported in $B_a(0)$, the field $u=G_k*\alpha$ is smooth outside the support, solves $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there and is outgoing: for $x=rn$, $r\ge2a$,

$$u(rn)=\frac{e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{r}\Bigl[\frac{a}{r}+\frac{ka^2}{r}\Bigr]\Bigr)$$

uniformly in direction, and $r(\partial_ru-iku)=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly. For a planar aperture $y=(y_1,y_2,0)$ with observation $x=(\xi_1,\xi_2,z)$, $z>0$, $|\xi|\le b$, $a+b\ll z$, the Fresnel approximation replaces $R=|x-y|$ by $z+|\xi-y|^2/(2z)$ and $1/R$ by $1/z$ with phase error $O(k(a+b)^4/z^3)$ and relative amplitude error $O((a+b)^2/z^2)$, hence absolute field error $O(\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}z^{-1}[(a+b)^2/z^2+k(a+b)^4/z^3])$. Aperture data are an explicitly specified scalar source, not asserted to be the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces, and no uniqueness or existence for arbitrary obstacle boundary data is claimed.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** Countable Choice, $k>0$, the kernel $G_k$, a finite complex measure $\alpha$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\alpha(\mathbb R^3\setminus B_a(0))=0$, and the field $u(x)=\int G_k(x-y)d\alpha(y)$.

[F1] **Radial Laplacian and derivative rules.** For a $C^2$ function $f$ of $r=|x|$ one has $\Delta f=f''(r)+2f'(r)/r$ for $x\ne0$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); the modulus $|G_k(x)|=1/(4\pi|x|)$ is the real fundamental kernel, which is locally integrable ([[lem-laplace-fundamental-kernel-is-locally-integrable]]).

[F2] **Second Green identity.** On a bounded $C^1$ domain, $\int_\Omega(v\Delta u-u\Delta v)=\int_{\partial\Omega}(v\partial_\nu u-u\partial_\nu v)$ with outward normal ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]).

[F3] **Measure integrals and total variation.** Integrals against a signed or complex measure are those of [[def-simple-integral-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]], the total variation $\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=|\alpha|(\mathbb R^3)$ is that of [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]], and $\bigl|\int h\,d\alpha\bigr|\le\int|h|\,d|\alpha|\le\sup|h|\,\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$ ([[thm-integrals-against-signed-or-complex-measures-are-bounded-by-total-variation]]), so bounded continuous kernels are integrable and the modulus bound of [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]] applies.

[F4] **FTC with interior derivative.** If $h$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with integrable derivative, then $\int_a^bh'=h(b)-h(a)$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]); applied to $|e^{i\theta}|$-type and square-root expressions this yields $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$ and the Taylor remainders used below. The Euclidean inner product and norm are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $x\ne0$ write $r=|x|$; then $\partial_ir=x_i/r$ and the chain and algebra rules [F1] give $\Delta(f\circ r)=f''(r)+2f'(r)/r$ for $C^2$ functions $f$ of one variable, and with $f(r)=e^{ikr}/(4\pi r)$ a direct computation gives $f''+2f'/r=-k^2f$, so $(\Delta+k^2)G_k=0$ off the origin; since $|G_k(x)|=1/(4\pi|x|)$ is locally integrable, $G_k$ defines a regular distribution. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 For fixed $x=rn$ with $r\ge2a$ and $y\in B_a(0)$ put $h(s)=|x-sy|$, $R=h(1)$; then $h$ is $C^2$ with $h(0)=r$, $h'(0)=-n\cdot y$, $h''(s)=|y|^2/|x-sy|-((x-sy)\cdot y)^2/|x-sy|^3$ and $|h''(s)|\le2a^2/(r-a)\le4a^2/r$ because $|x-sy|\ge r-s|y|\ge r-a\ge r/2$; hence two applications of the FTC [F4] give $|R-r+n\cdot y|\le\sup|h''|/2\le2a^2/r$ and, since $R\ge r-a\ge r/2$ and $|R-r|\le a+2a^2/r\le2a$, also $|r/R-1|\le4a/r$. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 For $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ choose $R$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subset B_R(0)$ and $0<\delta<R$, and apply the second Green identity [F2] on $\Omega_\delta=B_R(0)\setminus\overline B_\delta(0)$ to $u=G_k$, $v=\psi$: since $\Delta G_k=-k^2G_k$ there, $\int_{\Omega_\delta}G_k(\Delta+k^2)\psi=\int_{\partial\Omega_\delta}(G_k\partial_\nu\psi-\psi\partial_\nu G_k)$; the outer sphere term vanishes because $\psi$ vanishes there, and on the inner sphere, where the outward normal of $\Omega_\delta$ is $-x/\delta$, one has $G_k=1/(4\pi\delta)+O(1)$ and $\partial_rG_k=-1/(4\pi\delta^2)+O(1/\delta)$, so the term $\int\psi\partial_\nu G_k$ contributes $-\psi(0)+o(1)$ and the derivative-test term is $O(\delta)$; hence $\int_{\mathbb R^3}G_k(\Delta+k^2)\psi=-\psi(0)$, that is $\langle(-\Delta-k^2)T_{G_k},\psi\rangle=\psi(0)$, so $(-\Delta-k^2)G_k=\delta_0$ distributionally. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.2 The field $u(x)=\int G_k(x-y)d\alpha(y)$ is smooth outside $\operatorname{supp}\alpha$ and solves $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there: on a compact observation set $K$ with $d=\operatorname{dist}(K,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)>0$ the kernel and all its parameter derivatives are continuous and uniformly bounded on $K\times\operatorname{supp}\alpha$, so the difference-quotient limits pass through the measure integral by the total-variation bound [F3], giving all derivatives by differentiation under the integral sign, and the two spatial derivatives may be moved inside to apply step 1.1 at $x-y\ne0$. [step 1.1, F3, F1, algebra]

2.3 For $r\ge2a$ the kernel difference from the Fraunhofer product is bounded by $\bigl|G_k(x-y)-\frac{e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}e^{-ikn\cdot y}\bigr|\le\frac1{4\pi}\bigl[\frac{|e^{ikR}-e^{ik(r-n\cdot y)}|}{R}+\frac{|r-R|}{rR}\bigr]\le\frac1{4\pi}\bigl[\frac{k|R-r+n\cdot y|}{R}+\frac{|r-R|}{rR}\bigr]\le\frac{C}{r}\Bigl[\frac{a}{r}+\frac{ka^2}{r}\Bigr]$, using $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$ [F4] with the phase error of step 1.2 and $R\ge r/2$; integrating this difference against $\alpha$ with the total-variation bound [F3] gives the displayed Fraunhofer formula with the stated error, uniformly in the direction $n=x/r$. [step 1.2, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 For the outgoing relation compute $\partial_rG_k(x-y)-ikG_k(x-y)=\frac{e^{ikR}}{4\pi R}\bigl[ik(\partial_rR-1)-\partial_rR/R\bigr]$ with $\partial_rR=(rn-y)\cdot n/R=1+O(a^2/r^2)$ and $1/R\le2/r$ by step 1.2, so $|\partial_rG_k(x-y)-ikG_k(x-y)|\le C(ka^2/r^3+1/r^2)$; integrating against $\alpha$ [F3] and multiplying by $r$ gives $r(\partial_ru-iku)=O(\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}r^{-1}(1+ka^2/r))=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly, the term $ka^2/r$ being bounded because $r\ge2a$. [step 2.2, step 1.2, F3, algebra]

4.1 For the planar aperture write $x=(\xi,z)$, $y=(y_1,y_2,0)$ and $s=|\xi-y|^2/z^2$, so $R=z\sqrt{1+s}$; on the declared range $s\le s_0<1$ the FTC [F4] applied to $\sqrt{1+\sigma}$ and $(1+\sigma)^{-1/2}$ gives $|\sqrt{1+s}-1-s/2|\le s^2/8$ and $|(1+s)^{-1/2}-1|\le s/2$; hence the phase error is $kz|\sqrt{1+s}-1-s/2|\le kz s^2/8=k|\xi-y|^4/(8z^3)\le k(a+b)^4/(8z^3)$, the relative amplitude error is $|1/R-1/z|/(1/z)=|z/R-1|\le s/2\le(a+b)^2/(2z^2)$, and with $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$ [F4] the kernel error is at most $Cz^{-1}[(a+b)^2/z^2+k(a+b)^4/z^3]$; integrating against $\alpha$ with [F3] gives the stated absolute field error, while the aperture datum remains an explicitly specified scalar source and no uniqueness or existence statement for obstacle boundary data is made; Countable Choice is inherited from the cited Green, surface and measure interfaces and no stronger principle is used. [step 1.2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $P_l$ denote the real vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]], [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]), $H_l=\ker(\Delta:P_l\to P_{l-2})$ with $P_k=\{0\}$ for $k<0$, and let spherical harmonics of degree $l$ be the restrictions of $H_l$ to $S^2$, with unnormalised surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Then $P_l=H_l\oplus|x|^2P_{l-2}$, $\dim H_l=2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degree are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and the union over $l$ of the spaces of spherical harmonics admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). For any real orthonormal basis $Y_{lm}$, $m=1,\dots,2l+1$, of degree-$l$ harmonics the addition theorem holds:

$$\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n'),$$

where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of the convergent zonal kernel lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]). The Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). This supplies the harmonic decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact addition kernel; it does not assert higher boundary regularity. The purely polynomial decomposition and finite dimension identities use no Choice; the surface/$L^2$/completeness claims retain the stated Countable Choice.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** Countable Choice; the spaces $P_l$ and $H_l$ of the Statement; the unit sphere $S^2$ with its chart/polar surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$; the Legendre polynomials $P_l$ of [[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]].

[F1] **Homogeneous polynomials.** A polynomial on $\mathbb R^3$ is homogeneous of degree $d$ when every occurring monomial has total degree $d$; monomials are indexed by exponent multi-indices and their total degree is the sum of exponents ([[def-homogeneous-polynomial-and-homogeneous-ideal]], [[def-monomials-multidegree-and-total-degree]]).

[F2] **Radial calculus and Euler identity.** For a $C^2$ function $f$ of $r=|x|$, $\Delta f=f''+2f'/r$ away from the origin, and differentiability rules hold for polynomials and composites ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); for a homogeneous polynomial $Q$ of degree $d$, Euler's identity $x\cdot\nabla Q=dQ$ holds, obtained by differentiating $t\mapsto Q(tx)=t^dQ(x)$.

[F3] **Second Green identity and Euler on spheres.** For a bounded $C^1$ domain, $\int_\Omega(v\Delta u-u\Delta v)=\int_{\partial\Omega}(v\partial_\nu u-u\partial_\nu v)$ with outward normal ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]); consequently homogeneous harmonics $H_k$ satisfy $\partial_\nu H_k=kH_k/R$ on the sphere of radius $R$.

[F4] **Sphere measure and surface integrals.** The chart surface measure on $S^2$ agrees with the polar measure ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]), is rotation invariant, and surface integrals over compact hypersurfaces are those of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; finite ambient partitions and smooth cutoffs subordinate to the six coordinate graph charts of $S^2$ exist ([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F5] **$L^2$ structure and density tools.** Real $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ with the integral pairing is a real Hilbert space under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]); whole-space mollification converges in $L^2$ and the translation and approximate-identity interfaces apply ([[lem-complex-translation-and-approximate-identity-interfaces]]); the restricted real polynomial algebra on $S^2$ is unital and separates points, so it is uniformly dense in $C(S^2)$ by Stone-Weierstrass ([[thm-real-stone-weierstrass-general]]); finite Gram-Schmidt orthonormalises a finite linearly independent family ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]).

[F6] **Circle character orthogonality.** For the lattice $\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\int_0^1e^{2\pi ik\theta}d\theta=\delta_{k0}$ ([[lem-character-orthogonality-on-a-lattice-fundamental-domain]]); after rescaling this is the vanishing of all nonzero Fourier coefficients of trigonometric polynomials used below.

[F7] **Solid zonal coefficient.** In the exterior expansion of [[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]], the solid coefficient $c_l(x,y)=|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(x\cdot y/(|x||y|))$ of $|x-y|^{-1}$ is, for each fixed $x\ne0$, a homogeneous polynomial of degree $l$ in $y$ that is harmonic in $y$.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For a homogeneous $Q$ of degree $d$, differentiating $t\mapsto Q(tx)$ at $t=1$ gives Euler's identity $x\cdot\nabla Q=dQ$ by [F2]; consequently, for homogeneous $Q$ of degree $l-2j$, the product and chain rules and $\Delta(r^{2j})=2j(2j+1)r^{2j-2}$, $\nabla(r^{2j})\cdot\nabla Q=2j(l-2j)r^{2j-2}Q$ give $\Delta(r^{2j}Q)=2j(2l-2j+1)r^{2j-2}Q+r^{2j}\Delta Q$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Continuous functions are dense in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$: cover $S^2$ by its six coordinate graph charts, take a subordinate finite ambient partition and smooth cutoffs by [F4], pull a localised $L^2$ function back to the compact planar chart support (the surface density is bounded above and below there, so the pullback is $L^2$ for Lebesgue measure), extend by zero, mollify in the plane by [F5], multiply by the cutoff, pull back and sum the finitely many parts, obtaining continuous functions converging in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$. [given, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 For $P\in P_l$ take $H=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor}a_jr^{2j}\Delta^jP$ with $a_0=1$ and $a_j=-a_{j-1}/[2j(2l-2j+1)]$; applying step 1.1 to each term, the coefficient of $r^{2j}\Delta^jP$ in $\Delta H$ is $(2j+2)(2l-2j-1)a_{j+1}+2j(2l-2j+1)a_j=0$ for $0\le j<\lfloor l/2\rfloor$, and the remaining top term $\Delta^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor+1}P$ vanishes because $\Delta$ lowers degree by two and $P_{\lfloor l/2\rfloor\cdot 2+2}$ exceeds $l$ when $\lfloor l/2\rfloor\cdot2+2>l$; hence $H\in H_l$ and $P-H\in r^2P_{l-2}$, so $P_l=H_l+r^2P_{l-2}$. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 For homogeneous harmonic $H_l,H_m$ with $l\ne m$, the second Green identity [F3] on the ball $B_R$ with both Laplacians zero gives $0=\int_{S_R}(H_l\partial_\nu H_m-H_m\partial_\nu H_l)=\frac{m-l}{R}\int_{S_R}H_lH_m\,dS$, and $\int_{S_R}H_lH_m\,dS=R^{l+m+2}\int_{S^2}H_lH_m\,d\Omega$ by homogeneity and [F4]; since $m\ne l$, the spherical functions $H_l|_{S^2}$ and $H_m|_{S^2}$ are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and by Euler the same computation shows the radial derivative of any homogeneous harmonic of degree $k$ on $S_R$ is $kH_k/R$. [step 2.1, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 If a harmonic homogeneous $H_l$ of degree $l$ equalled $r^2Q$ with $Q\in P_{l-2}$, then repeatedly applying step 2.1 to $Q$ would write $Q=\sum_kQ_{l-2-2j}$ as a finite sum of homogeneous harmonics of degrees $k<l$, so $H_l|_{S^2}=\sum_kQ_k|_{S^2}$ and step 3.1 would give $\int_{S^2}H_l^2d\Omega=\sum_k\int_{S^2}H_lQ_k\,d\Omega=0$, hence $H_l=0$ on $S^2$ and, by homogeneity, $H_l=0$ as a polynomial; therefore $H_l\cap r^2P_{l-2}=\{0\}$, the sum in step 2.1 is direct, and $\dim H_l=\dim P_l-\dim P_{l-2}=\frac{(l+1)(l+2)}2-\frac{l(l-1)}2=2l+1$ by the monomial count [F1]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, algebra]

5.1 The restricted real polynomial algebra on $S^2$ is unital and separates points (the three coordinate functions separate distinct points of the sphere), so it is uniformly dense in $C(S^2)$ by Stone-Weierstrass [F5]; decomposing each polynomial into homogeneous parts and each homogeneous part by step 2.1 into harmonic pieces of degrees $\le$ its degree, every polynomial restriction lies in the finite union of the spaces of spherical harmonics, so the union is dense in $C(S^2)$ in the uniform norm and hence in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ together with step 1.2. [step 4.1, step 1.2, F5, algebra]

6.1 For each $l$ the restrictions of $H_l$ form a finite-dimensional inner-product space of dimension $2l+1$ by step 4.1, and finite Gram-Schmidt [F5] applied to a fixed ordered monomial-elimination basis of $H_l$ produces an orthonormal basis $Y_{l1},\dots,Y_{l,2l+1}$; by step 3.1 the spaces of different degrees are mutually orthogonal, so the union is an orthonormal family whose closed span contains all spherical harmonics and is dense by step 5.1, that is, it is a complete orthonormal system of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ in the sense of [F5]'s definition. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F5, algebra]

7.1 Fix $l$ and set $K_l(n,n')=\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')$; if $\tilde Y_{lm}=\sum_kO_{mk}Y_{lk}$ is another real orthonormal basis, then $\sum_m\tilde Y_{lm}(n)\tilde Y_{lm}(n')=\sum_{k,k'}\bigl(\sum_mO_{mk}O_{mk'}\bigr)Y_{lk}(n)Y_{lk'}(n')=K_l(n,n')$ because $O$ is orthogonal, so $K_l$ is basis independent. [step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 For a proper rotation $R$ of $\mathbb R^3$, the map $H\mapsto H\circ R$ permutes the harmonic polynomials of each degree and preserves the sphere measure [F4]; hence $K_l(Rn,Rn')=K_l(n,n')$. For fixed $n'$, the function $n\mapsto K_l(n,n')$ is the restriction of a homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree $l$ (a linear combination of the chosen representatives of the $Y_{lm}$) that is invariant under all rotations fixing $n'$; after rotating $n'$ to $e_3$, such an invariant homogeneous polynomial has the form $\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor}b_jx_3^{l-2j}(x_1^2+x_2^2)^j$, because in the complex coordinates $u=x_1+ix_2$, $v=x_1-ix_2$ the monomial $u^pv^qz^c$ acquires the factor $e^{i(p-q)\theta}$ under the rotation by $\theta$ and the vanishing of all nonzero Fourier coefficients [F6] forces $p=q$; harmonicity then gives the recursion $4(j+1)^2b_{j+1}=-(l-2j)(l-2j-1)b_j$, so all coefficients are determined by $b_0$ and the space of invariant harmonics of degree $l$ is at most one dimensional. [step 7.1, F2, F4, F6, algebra]

9.1 By [F7] the solid zonal coefficient $c_l(x,y)$ of the convergent kernel lemma, read for fixed $x\ne0$ as a function of $y$, is a homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree $l$, equal to $|y|^lP_l(x\cdot y/(|x||y|))$; for $n'=x/|x|$ and $y=rn$ it restricts to the nonzero invariant harmonic $r^lP_l(n\cdot n')$, so by the one-dimensionality of step 8.1 there is a scalar $\lambda(n')$ with $K_l(n,n')=\lambda(n')P_l(n\cdot n')$; since $K_l$ is symmetric in its arguments, $\lambda$ is independent of $n'$, and $K_l(n,n)=\lambda P_l(1)=\lambda$ by $P_l(1)=1$. [step 8.1, given, F7, algebra]

10.1 Integrate the diagonal identity $K_l(n,n)=\sum_mY_{lm}(n)^2=\lambda$ over $S^2$: orthonormality gives $\sum_m\|Y_{lm}\|_{L^2(S^2)}^2=2l+1$ while the constant $\lambda$ integrates to $4\pi\lambda$ by the total mass [F4], so $\lambda=(2l+1)/(4\pi)$ and $\sum_mY_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n')$; this proves the addition theorem and completes the decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact kernel assertions of the Statement, with Countable Choice used only through the cited surface, $L^2$ and mollification interfaces. [step 9.1, given, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $c>0$, let $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ (unbounded $f$ is allowed), and define the spherical mean

$$M_rf(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}f(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n),\qquad r\ge0,$$

with the outward sphere measure of total area $4\pi$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Then $r\mapsto M_rf(x)$ is smooth for $r\ge0$ and satisfies the Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity

$$\partial_r^2M_rf(x)+\frac2r\partial_rM_rf(x)=\Delta M_rf(x)\qquad(r>0),$$

and the function $H_f(x,t)=t\,M_{ct}f(x)$, $t\ge0$, satisfies

$$\partial_t^2H_f=c^2\Delta H_f,\qquad H_f(x,0)=0,\qquad\partial_tH_f(x,0)=f(x).$$

All identities are local and need no decay of $f$, since every integration set is compact. This is the pure spherical-mean identity; it makes no claim about finite-domain boundary data or about general rough data.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A constant $c>0$, a function $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, and the spherical mean $M_rf(x)$ over the unit sphere with chart/polar measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$.

[F1] **Parameter integrals over the sphere.** Differentiating a compact surface integral in a parameter is legitimate when the integrand is smooth and all derivatives are continuous on the compact parameter and surface sets; the parameter-integral lemma supplies the surface-measure form and the interchange of the parameter derivative with the integral ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[F2] **Divergence theorem and the Laplacian.** On a bounded piecewise $C^1$ domain with outward normal, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$ for $C^1$ fields ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]]); the Laplacian is $\Delta f=\sum_i\partial_i\partial_if$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]) and $\int_{B_r(x)}\Delta f\,dy=\int_{S_r(x)}\partial_\nu f\,dS$.

[F3] **Radial differentiation and polar coordinates.** The ball integral $J(r)=\int_{B_r(x)}g\,dy$ of a continuous $g$ has derivative $J'(r)=\int_{S_r(x)}g\,dS$, by polar integration and the one-variable fundamental theorem ([[thm-ftc-first-part]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]); on $S_r(x)$ the outward normal is $\nu=(y-x)/r$ and the substitution $y=x+rn$ gives $dS=r^2d\Omega(n)$ with the chart/polar measure ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).

[F4] **Calculus rules.** The product, chain and algebra rules for smooth functions ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For fixed $x$ the function $r\mapsto f(x+rn)$ is smooth on the compact sphere and the sphere measure is finite, so [F1] permits differentiation under the integral sign and gives $\partial_rM_rf(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}n\cdot\nabla f(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n)$, with all higher $r$-derivatives obtained by iteration. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 For $r>0$ apply the divergence theorem [F2] on $B_r(x)$ to the $C^1$ field $\nabla f$: $\int_{B_r(x)}\Delta f(y)dy=\int_{S_r(x)}\partial_\nu f\,dS$; substituting $y=x+rn$ with outward normal $n$ and $dS=r^2d\Omega$ by [F3] gives $\int_{B_r(x)}\Delta f=4\pi r^2\partial_rM_rf(x)$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 Differentiate the identity of step 2.1 in $r$: by [F3] the derivative of the left side is $\int_{S_r(x)}\Delta f\,dS=r^2\int_{S^2}\Delta f(x+rn)d\Omega(n)=4\pi r^2M_r(\Delta f)(x)$, while the derivative of the right side is $4\pi(2r\partial_rM_rf+r^2\partial_r^2M_rf)$; moving the Laplacian through the sphere integral by [F1] gives $M_r(\Delta f)=\Delta M_rf$, so dividing by $4\pi r^2$ yields $\partial_r^2M_rf+\frac2r\partial_rM_rf=\Delta M_rf$ for $r>0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 Set $H_f(x,t)=tM_{ct}f(x)$ for $t>0$; differentiating twice with [F4] and the chain rule gives $\partial_tH_f=M_{ct}f+ct\cdot c\,\partial_rM_{ct}f$ and $\partial_t^2H_f=2c\partial_rM_{ct}f+c^2t\partial_r^2M_{ct}f$; substituting step 3.1 at $r=ct$ cancels the terms with $\partial_rM_{ct}f$ and leaves $\partial_t^2H_f=c^2t\Delta M_{ct}f=c^2\Delta H_f$. [step 3.1, F4, algebra]

5.1 At $t=0$ one has $M_0f(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}f(x)d\Omega=f(x)$, and $\partial_rM_0f(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}n\cdot\nabla f(x)d\Omega=0$ because the chart/polar measure is invariant under $n\mapsto-n$ while $n\mapsto n\cdot\nabla f(x)$ is odd ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]); hence $H_f(x,0)=0$ and $\partial_tH_f(x,0)=f(x)$, while the displayed equation at $t=0$ reduces to $2c\,\partial_rM_0f=0=c^2\cdot0$. [step 4.1, F1, F3, algebra]

6.1 Every identity was proved on compact parameter and spatial sets with no decay of $f$ used, and the defining integral is smooth in signed $r$ as well, so the equation, the initial value and the initial velocity extend to $t=0$; this proves the stated spherical-mean identity. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, algebra] ∎
