## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $f\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ with harmonic coefficients $f_{lm}$ in an orthonormal basis of the spherical-harmonic lemma ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]), and for $0\le r<1$ set $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ (the $l=0$ term being the constant value at $r=0$). Then the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on every closed smaller ball, $u$ is harmonic there ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), $u(r\,\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$, and $u$ is the unique harmonic function on the unit ball with $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\,\cdot)\|_{L^2}<\infty$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$. For continuous $f$ the same function is

$$u(rn)=\int_{S^2}\frac{1-r^2}{4\pi|rn-n'|^3}f(n')\,d\Omega(n'),$$

it extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary value $f$, and the kernel is positive of total mass one. This is the stated ball boundary branch; generic smooth-domain classical regularity remains a separate obligation.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** Countable Choice, $f\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, the canonical orthonormal bases $\{Y_{lm}:m=1,\dots,2l+1\}$ of the harmonic lemma, the coefficients $f_{lm}=\int_{S^2}fY_{lm}\,d\Omega$, the partial sums $S_N=\sum_{l\le N,m}f_{lm}Y_{lm}$, and the series $u$.

[F1] **Spherical harmonics.** The $Y_{lm}$ are orthonormal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, each $Y_{lm}$ is the restriction of a homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree $l$, harmonics of distinct degrees are orthogonal, and the family is complete; the addition theorem gives $\sum_mY_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n')$ and, on the diagonal, $\sum_m|Y_{lm}(n)|^2=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}$ ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).

[F2] **$L^2$ Hilbert space and Cauchy-Schwarz.** $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ is a real Hilbert space with the integral pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]); finite and countable Cauchy-Schwarz and Bessel/Parseval bounds hold ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]).

[F3] **Harmonic estimates.** For harmonic $v$ near $x$, $|D^\alpha v(x)|\le C_{3,\alpha}r^{-3-|\alpha|}\int_{B_r(x)}|v|$ whenever $B_r(x)$ lies in the domain ([[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]).

[F4] **Ball Dirichlet theorem and Poisson kernel.** For continuous data on $\partial B_R(a)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ the Poisson integral $U_g(x)=\int P_{R,a}(x,y)g(y)dS_y$ with $P_{R,a}(x,y)=(R^2-|x-a|^2)/(4\pi R|x-y|^3)$ is smooth harmonic in the ball, extends continuously with trace $g$, and is the unique $C^2\cap C(\overline{B_R(a)})$ harmonic solution with that trace ([[thm-dirichlet-problem-on-a-ball-by-the-poisson-integral]]).

[F5] **Generating function and series calculus.** $\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)=(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}$ for $|q|<1$ ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]), and real power series are smooth inside their disc of convergence with termwise differentiation ([[cor-power-series-sums-are-smooth-with-coefficient-formula]]).

[F6] **Integration rules.** The sphere integral is that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], linear and monotone with the nonnegative-integral rules ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]), and dominated convergence applies to dominated pointwise-convergent families ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]); uniform derivative limits are identified along coordinate segments by the FTC ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Completeness of the basis [F1] and the Bessel/Parseval identity [F2] give $\|f-S_N\|_2^2=\sum_{l>N,m}|f_{lm}|^2\to0$, and $\sum_{l,m}|f_{lm}|^2=\|f\|_2^2<\infty$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For the general $L^2$ uniqueness, let $v$ be a smooth harmonic function on the unit ball with $\sup_{r<1}\|v(r\,\cdot)\|_2<\infty$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$. For $0<s<1$ the published Dirichlet theorem [F4] applied on $B_s(0)$ to the continuous data $v(s\,\cdot)$ gives, for $0<r<s$, $v(rn)=\int_{S^2}\frac{1-(r/s)^2}{4\pi|(r/s)n-n'|^3}v(sn')d\Omega(n')$, the scaled form of the radius-$s$ Poisson kernel; expanding this kernel with the addition theorem and integrating against $v(s\,\cdot)$ [F1, F6] gives $v(rn)=\sum_{l,m}(r/s)^lv_{lm}(s)Y_{lm}(n)$ with $v_{lm}(s)=\int_{S^2}v(sn')Y_{lm}(n')d\Omega(n')$. [given, F1, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 Each $r^lY_{lm}(n)$ is the homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree $l$ representing $Y_{lm}$, evaluated at $x=rn$ [F1], so the partial sums $P_N(x)=\sum_{l\le N,m}f_{lm}r^lY_{lm}(n)$ are harmonic polynomials; by the addition theorem [F1] and Cauchy-Schwarz over the multi-index $(l,m)$, the absolute tail on $|x|\le r_0<1$ is bounded by $\|f-S_N\|_2\bigl(\sum_{l>N}r_0^{2l}\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}\bigr)^{1/2}\le C(r_0)\|f-S_N\|_2r_0^{N+1}$, which tends to $0$ by step 1.1; hence the series converges uniformly on every closed smaller ball and defines a continuous function $u$ there. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.2 Orthonormality gives $\|u(r\,\cdot)\|_2^2=\sum_{l,m}r^{2l}|f_{lm}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$ and $\|u(r\,\cdot)-f\|_2^2=\sum_{l,m}(1-r^l)^2|f_{lm}|^2$; since $0\le(1-r^l)^2\le4$ and $(1-r^l)^2\to0$ for each $(l,m)$ as $r\uparrow1$, dominated convergence [F6] on the countable coefficient family with the summable bound $4\sum|f_{lm}|^2$ gives $u(r\,\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F6, algebra]

3.1 For $x\in B_{r_1}$ with $r_1<r_0<1$ and $0<\rho<r_0-r_1$, the harmonic estimate [F3] applied to the harmonic differences $P_N-P_M$ gives $|D^\alpha(P_N-P_M)(x)|\le C_{3,\alpha}\rho^{-3-|\alpha|}\int_{B_\rho(x)}|P_N-P_M|$, and the $L^2$ bound inherited from the uniform tail of step 2.1 makes this tend to $0$ uniformly on $B_{r_1}$; hence every derivative series converges uniformly on each closed smaller ball, and the FTC [F6] identifies the derivatives of the limit: $u\in C^\infty(B_1)$ and $\Delta u=\lim_N\Delta P_N=0$, so $u$ is harmonic on the unit ball. [step 2.1, F3, F6, algebra]

3.2 Inserting $f_{lm}=\int_{S^2}f(n')Y_{lm}(n')d\Omega(n')$ and the addition theorem [F1] into the partial sums gives $P_N(rn)=\int_{S^2}\bigl[\sum_{l\le N}\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}r^lP_l(n\cdot n')\bigr]f(n')d\Omega(n')$; for $r\le r_0<1$ the zonal series converges absolutely and uniformly by [F5], and letting $N\to\infty$ with the linearity and dominated-convergence rules [F6] identifies $u(rn)=\int_{S^2}K_r(n,n')f(n')d\Omega(n')$ with $K_r(n,n')=\frac1{4\pi}\sum_l(2l+1)r^lP_l(n\cdot n')$. [step 2.1, F1, F5, F6, algebra]

3.3 Completeness [F1] applied on the sphere of radius $r$ gives $v(rn)=\sum_{l,m}v_{lm}(r)Y_{lm}(n)$; comparing with step 1.2 and using orthonormality yields $v_{lm}(r)=(r/s)^lv_{lm}(s)$ for all $0<r<s<1$, and letting $s\uparrow1$ with Cauchy-Schwarz [F2], $|v_{lm}(s)-f_{lm}|=|\int(v(sn')-f(n'))Y_{lm}(n')d\Omega|\le\|v(s\,\cdot)-f\|_2\to0$, so $v_{lm}(r)=r^lf_{lm}$ for every degree and every $0<r<1$. [step 1.2, step 2.2, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 Applying the operator $1+2r\partial_r$ to the generating function of [F5] - legitimate inside $|r|<1$ by termwise differentiation [F5] - gives $\sum_l(2l+1)r^lP_l(z)=\frac{1-r^2}{(1-2rz+r^2)^{3/2}}$; since $1-2r(n\cdot n')+r^2=|rn-n'|^2$, the kernel is $K_r(n,n')=\frac{1-r^2}{4\pi|rn-n'|^3}$, positive with numerator $1-r^2>0$ and positive denominator; integrating over $n'$ leaves only the constant $l=0$ harmonic in the zonal expansion, so $\int_{S^2}K_r(n,n')d\Omega(n')=1$. [step 3.2, F1, F5, F6, algebra]

5.1 For continuous $f$, uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact sphere and the concentration of the normalised kernel [F4] give $\sup_{n}|u(rn)-f(n)|\le\int K_r(n,n')|f(n')-f(n)|d\Omega(n')\to0$ as $r\uparrow1$: near $n'=n$ the integrand is small by continuity and the kernel mass is one, while the complement carries vanishing kernel mass because $|rn-n'|\ge\sqrt{1-r^2}$ there. [step 4.1, F4, F6, algebra]

6.1 For continuous $f$ the Poisson integral of [F4] on the unit ball is exactly the integral representation of step 4.1, so the published ball Dirichlet theorem [F4] shows that $u$ extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary value $f$ and is the unique $C^2\cap C(\overline{B_1})$ harmonic function with that trace; the formula of the Statement is the kernel of step 4.1. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F4, algebra]

7.1 Hence $v(r\,\cdot)$ and $u(r\,\cdot)$ have the same complete orthonormal expansion on every sphere $r<1$, so they agree in $L^2$ there and, being continuous on each sphere, agree pointwise; equality at the centre follows by continuity, so $v=u$ on the unit ball. This proves the interior convergence and harmonicity, the $L^2$ boundary limit, the kernel formula for continuous data with its continuous extension, and $L^2$-boundary uniqueness, with Countable Choice used only through the cited harmonic, $L^2$ and Poisson interfaces. [step 3.1, step 2.2, step 6.1, step 3.3, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $k>0$ and $x\in\Omega$, and use the outgoing kernel $G_k$ of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]. A sufficient classical specialization is that $u$ and $f$ extend smoothly to an open neighbourhood of the closed domain and $(-\Delta-k^2)u=f$ there. More generally, retain the justified weaker classical-trace branch: $u$ is $C^2$ inside $\Omega$, $u$ and all first derivatives extend continuously to its closure, $f=(-\Delta-k^2)u$ belongs to $L^1(\Omega)$, and the equation holds inside. The boundary values and normal derivative in the formula below are these actual continuous traces. Then

$$u(x)=\int_\Omega G_k(x-y)f(y)\,dy+\int_{\partial\Omega}\bigl[G_k(x-y)\partial_nu(y)-u(y)\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)\bigr]dS_y,$$

with $n$ the outward domain normal; both integrals are absolutely convergent. Merely being smooth on the open domain without these trace/integrability data is insufficient.

For an exterior $D=\mathbb R^3$ minus the closure of a bounded smooth obstacle, retain the exterior counterpart with actual inner boundary traces: suppose $u$ is $C^2$ on $D$ with $u$ and first derivatives continuous to its compact boundary, solves $(-\Delta-k^2)u=f$ there, $f$ is locally continuous and $\int_D|G_k(x-y)f(y)|dy$ is finite at the observation $x$, and the prescribed outgoing condition gives, uniformly on spheres at infinity, $u(y)=O(|y|^{-1})$ and $\partial_ru(y)-iku(y)=o(|y|^{-1})$. Then the same formula holds with volume $D$ and its obstacle boundary, with $n$ outward from $D$. Compactly supported $L^1$ sources with the displayed local regularity are a sufficient source subclass. For the smooth-trace modal outgoing specialization beyond a source-containing sphere of radius $R_0>0$, retain the declared full Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for this sufficient branch. Write the smooth angular trace as $g(n)=u(R_0n)$, use the real unit-sphere harmonics of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], set $c_{lm}=\int_{S^2}g(n)Y_{lm}(n)d\Omega(n)$, and define the outgoing modal class outside that sphere by

$$u(rn)=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}c_{lm}\,\frac{h_l(kr)}{h_l(kR_0)}Y_{lm}(n),\qquad r\ge R_0,$$

where $h_l$ are exactly the earlier explicit functions of [[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]. The proof establishes smooth convergence, the homogeneous exterior equation, the actual trace $g$, the uniform bound $\sup_{r\ge R_0,n\in S^2}r|u(rn)|<\infty$ and the uniform Sommerfeld residual $\sup_{n\in S^2}r|\partial_ru(rn)-iku(rn)|\to0$. Thus this smooth modal branch satisfies the prescribed far conditions without a later same-page supplier. Its full-Choice premise is retained; the earlier prescribed-outgoing branch remains under Countable Choice.

The Green formula uses the consistent actual pair of traces. Assigning both aperture values independently does not establish an exact boundary problem; a declared scalar aperture-source model remains a separate approximation. No weak boundary trace or normal trace for arbitrary rough data is asserted by mere interior smoothness.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** Countable Choice; a bounded $C^\infty$ domain $\Omega$ with outward normal $n$ and compact boundary $S=\partial\Omega$; $k>0$; the outgoing kernel $G_k$ with $(-\Delta-k^2)G_k=\delta_0$ and $(\Delta+k^2)G_k=0$ off the pole ([[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]); and the data of the three branches.

[F1] **Second Green identity.** On a bounded $C^1$ domain, $\int_\Omega(v\Delta u-u\Delta v)=\int_{\partial\Omega}(v\partial_\nu u-u\partial_\nu v)$ with outward normal ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]), applied to the real and imaginary parts and combined complex-bilinearly.

[F2] **Normal tube and collar.** Under Countable Choice, a compact smooth boundary has a tubular neighbourhood and a positive smooth radius; the collar $S_t=\{p-tn(p)\}$ is a smooth surface inside the domain bounding the inner domain $\Omega_t$, and in normal graph charts the surface Jacobian and outward normals converge uniformly to those of $S$ as $t\downarrow0$ ([[thm-euclidean-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem]], [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).

[F3] **Dominated convergence and calculus.** Dominated convergence for a dominated pointwise-convergent family ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]); the product, chain and algebra rules and the coordinate FTC ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

[F4] **Spherical harmonics and Cauchy-Schwarz.** The complete orthonormal basis and addition theorem of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], with $\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty\le\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}$, and Cauchy-Schwarz in $L^2(S^2)$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]).

[F5] **Hankel functions.** The explicit $h_l$ of [[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]] solve the spherical radial Helmholtz equation, satisfy $F_l(z)=z^2|h_l(z)|^2=\sum_{j=0}^la_jz^{-2j}$ with $a_0=1$ and $a_j>0$ (hence $F_l$ is nonincreasing on $(0,\infty)$), and the logarithmic-derivative bounds give $|kh_l'(kr)/h_l(kr)|\le(l+1)/r+k$ for $r>0$; the cross product is that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

[F6] **Angular operator.** For a smooth function $w$ on $S^2$ and the elementary coordinate rotations $Q_j(t)$, the generator $L_jw=\frac{d}{dt}w(Q_j(t)n)|_{t=0}$ has tangent velocity $e_j\times n$; the surface measure is rotation invariant, and $\Lambda=\sum_jL_j^2$ satisfies $\int(L_jw)v=-\int w(L_jv)$ by differentiating the invariant integral with uniform difference quotients, and on ambient extensions $\sum_jL_j^2=|x|^2\Delta-(x\cdot\nabla)^2-x\cdot\nabla$ ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [F3]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Bounded smooth specialization: apply the second Green identity [F1] on $\Omega\setminus\overline B_\delta(x)$ to $u$ and $y\mapsto G_k(x-y)$; since $(-\Delta-k^2)u=f$ and $(\Delta+k^2)G_k=0$ off the pole, the $k^2$ terms cancel and $-\int_{\Omega\setminus B_\delta}G_k(x-y)f(y)dy=\int_{\partial\Omega}(G_k\partial_nu-u\partial_nG_k)+\int_{\partial B_\delta(x)}(G_k\partial_{n'}u-u\partial_{n'}G_k)$; the inner-sphere term tends to $-u(x)$ because $G_k=1/(4\pi\delta)+O(1)$, $\partial_{n'}G_k=1/(4\pi\delta^2)+O(1/\delta)$ with $n'=-(y-x)/\delta$, the derivative-test term is $O(\delta)$ and the sphere area is $4\pi\delta^2$; the volume integral tends to the absolutely convergent $\int_\Omega G_k(x-y)f(y)dy$ because $f$ is continuous near $x$ and $G_k$ is locally integrable. This gives the displayed interior formula. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Modal branch: for smooth $g$ set $c_{lm}=\int_{S^2}gY_{lm}d\Omega$; by [F6] the operator $\Lambda$ is symmetric for the integral pairing and annihilates nothing nontrivially on constants, and since each $Y_{lm}$ is the restriction of a degree-$l$ homogeneous harmonic polynomial, Euler's identity and the ambient formula for $\sum_jL_j^2$ give $\Lambda Y_{lm}=-l(l+1)Y_{lm}$; hence for every integer $p\ge1$ and $l\ge1$, $[l(l+1)]^pc_{lm}=\int_{S^2}(-\Lambda)^pg\,Y_{lm}d\Omega$ and Cauchy-Schwarz [F4] gives $|c_{lm}|\le\|\Lambda^pg\|_2[l(l+1)]^{-p}$. [given, F4, F6, algebra]

1.3 Radial majorants: with $\phi_l(r)=h_l(kr)/h_l(kR_0)$ and $F_l$ of [F5], $|h_l(kr)|/|h_l(kR_0)|=\sqrt{F_l(kr)/F_l(kR_0)}\le1$; more precisely the monotonicity of $F_l$ and $F_l(kR_0)=k^2R_0^2|h_l(kR_0)|^2$ give $|\phi_l(r)|\le R_0/r$ and $|\phi_l'(r)|=|kh_l'(kr)|/|h_l(kR_0)|\le[(l+1)/r+k]|\phi_l(r)|$, hence $r|\phi_l'(r)-ik\phi_l(r)|\le R_0[(l+1)/r+2k]\le l+1+2kR_0$ for $r\ge R_0$; for every fixed $l$ the explicit outgoing polynomial gives $r(\phi_l'(r)-ik\phi_l(r))\to0$ as $r\to\infty$. [given, F5, algebra]

2.1 Weaker trace branch: let $S_t$ be the inner collar surface of [F2] with inner domain $\Omega_t\ni x$; for small $t$ the punctured Green argument of step 1.1 applies on $\Omega_t$, so $u(x)=\int_{\Omega_t}G_k(x-y)f(y)dy+\int_{S_t}(G_k\partial_{n_t}u-u\partial_{n_t}G_k)dS$; as $t\downarrow0$ the traces $u|_{S_t}$ and $\partial_{n_t}u|_{S_t}$ converge uniformly to the actual continuous traces on $S$ and the surface Jacobians and normals converge uniformly by [F2], so the boundary integrals converge to the displayed ones with the compact chart formula; the volume integrals increase to $\Omega$ and converge by dominated convergence [F3] using the integrable majorant $\mathbf 1_\Omega|G_k(x-\cdot)||f|$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.2 Exterior branch: for a large ball $B_R$ containing $x$ and the obstacle, apply the same punctured identity on $D_R=(D\cap B_R)\setminus\overline B_\delta(x)$; the inner boundary term tends to $-u(x)$ as in step 1.1 and the obstacle boundary contributes the displayed trace integral, while the outer sphere term is $\int_{|y|=R}(v\partial_Ru-u\partial_Rv)dS$ with $v=G_k(x-y)$; writing it as $\int[v(\partial_Ru-iku)-u(\partial_Rv-ikv)]dS$, the kernel estimates $v=O(R^{-1})$ and $\partial_Rv-ikv=O(R^{-2})$ for fixed $x$ combine with the prescribed far conditions to bound the integrand by $o(R^{-2})$ uniformly, so the outer term tends to $0$ after multiplication by the area $4\pi R^2$; absolute convergence of the volume term follows from the stated integrability of $G_k(x-\cdot)f$ on $D$. [step 1.1, given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.3 With $p=2$ and the addition diagonal $\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty\le\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}$ [F4], the weighted sum $W=\sum_{l,m}(l+1+2kR_0)|c_{lm}|\,\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty$ is finite: the $l=0$ term is finite and for $l\ge1$ the degree-$l$ contribution is at most a constant times $(2l+1)(l+1+2kR_0)\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}[l(l+1)]^{-2}=O(l^{-3/2})$, which is summable. [step 1.2, F4, algebra]

3.1 By steps 2.3 and 1.3 the modal series and its first radial derivatives are dominated on $r\ge R_0$ by $W<\infty$, so they converge absolutely and uniformly there and on every closed exterior annulus; the coordinate FTC [F3] identifies the radial derivative of the sum with the summed derivative, and finite combinations of radial derivatives with the smooth angular derivatives identify all Cartesian derivatives by [F3], so the modal series defines a $C^\infty$ exterior field; at $r=R_0$ completeness of the harmonics [F4] and continuity give the actual trace $g$, and if the coefficients are recorded in the sphere-normalised basis $Y^{R_0}_{lm}(R_0n)=R_0^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ they become $R_0c_{lm}$, giving the same displayed expansion. [step 2.3, step 1.3, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 Each summand $\phi_l(r)Y_{lm}(n)$ is annihilated by $\Delta+k^2$: the angular eigenvalue and the radial Helmholtz equation of [F5] give the polar Laplacian identity, and finite combinations of two radial and angular derivatives with smooth coefficients identify $\Delta$; termwise second derivatives prove the equation for the uniformly convergent limit on each compact exterior set, and uniqueness of limits identifies it as the homogeneous exterior solution with the trace $g$. [step 3.1, F5, F6, F3, algebra]

5.1 Bounds: step 1.3 gives $r|u(rn)|\le R_0W$ uniformly; and $r|\partial_ru(rn)-iku(rn)|\le\sum_{l,m}|c_{lm}|\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty\,r|\phi_l'(r)-ik\phi_l(r)|\le W$ for all $r\ge R_0$, so the amplitude bound holds; for the Sommerfeld residual, given $\epsilon$ choose a finite degree cutoff with tail $<\epsilon/2$ by step 2.3 and then the finitely many remaining terms have fixed finite angular suprema and radial residuals tending to $0$ by step 1.3, giving $\sup_nr|\partial_ru(rn)-iku(rn)|\to0$. [step 2.3, step 1.3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

The full Axiom of Choice is retained only for the smooth modal branch, as declared; the bounded, weak-trace and exterior branches use Countable Choice through the cited Green, tubular and surface interfaces. Assigning boundary values and normal derivatives independently is not asserted to solve a boundary problem, and no rough weak-trace Green theorem is claimed.

## Statement

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) with $c>0$ the model's conversion constant, let $[a,b]$ be a nondegenerate compact interval, let $X:[a,b]\to A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), and let $A_\mu$ be a $C^2$ covector field on a neighbourhood of the image of $X$. All integrals in this particle lemma are finite-interval Riemann integrals. On $[a,b]$, $C^2$ means continuous components and continuous first and second derivatives with their one-sided endpoint values; equations at endpoints use those same one-sided derivatives. For fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations $h:[a,b]\to V$ with $h(a)=h(b)=0$ and for $m,c>0$ and real $q$ consider

$$S[X]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,ds+q\int_a^bA_\mu(X)\dot X^\mu\,ds .$$

Then for each such $h$ the curve $X+\varepsilon h$ remains future timelike for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$, and stationarity of $S$ under all such variations is equivalent to

$$m\frac{dU_\nu}{d\tau}=qF_{\nu\mu}U^\mu,\qquad\frac{d\tau}{ds}=\frac{\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}}c,\qquad F=dA,$$

where $U$ is the four-velocity and $\tau$ the proper-time parameter supplied by the observer-decomposition theorem ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). This is a calculation about the chosen functional; adopting it as a physical particle action is an additional model assumption, and it makes no existence claim for coupled singular particles and fields. The coefficient-localization proof below is one-dimensional and choice-free; it does not invoke an AC-qualified Lebesgue fundamental lemma.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with constant $c>0$; a nondegenerate compact interval $[a,b]$; a $C^2$ future timelike curve $X:[a,b]\to A$; a $C^2$ covector field $A_\mu$ on a neighbourhood of its image; constants $m>0$ and real $q$; and the functional $S$ of the Statement.

[F1] **Minkowski geometry and worldlines.** $\eta$ is a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of signature $(1,3)$ on $V$, $C^+$ is the future cone, and a $C^2$ future timelike curve has $\eta(\dot X,\dot X)<0$ and future-directed velocity ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

[F2] **Observer decomposition.** The four-velocity and proper time satisfy $U=\dot X/\tau'$ with $\tau'=\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}/c>0$, so $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,\dot X)=c\tau'$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]).

[F3] **Compact-interval calculus.** Continuous real functions on a nondegenerate compact interval attain extrema ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]) and are Riemann integrable ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]); differentiation under the integral sign holds on a compact parameter rectangle with continuous integrands and continuous parameter derivatives ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]]); the positive-base power derivative and its agreement with the square root, the product/chain rules and the FTC are available ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

[F4] **Integration and localization.** Integration by parts on $[a,b]$ for $C^1$ data, monotonicity and additivity of the integral, and the one-dimensional ZF cutoff construction ([[thm-integration-by-parts]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]], [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix an inertial coordinate frame; the continuous function $s\mapsto-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)$ is strictly positive on the compact $[a,b]$ and attains a positive minimum $-m_0<0$ by [F3], and $\dot X^0$ likewise has a positive minimum by future directedness [F1]; the variation $h$ and its derivative are bounded on $[a,b]$ with bounds $H_1,H_2$, and the compact image of $X$ lies in the open domain of $A_\mu$ with a positive Lebesgue number for a finite coordinate-ball cover. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 For $|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0$ sufficiently small, $-\eta(\dot X+\varepsilon\dot h,\dot X+\varepsilon\dot h)\ge m_0-2|\varepsilon|(\|\dot X\|_{2}\|\dot h\|_{2}+\varepsilon^2\|\dot h\|_2^2)$-type bound stays positive and the time component $\dot X^0+\varepsilon\dot h^0$ stays positive, so $X+\varepsilon h$ is again a $C^2$ future timelike curve with the same endpoints; shrinking $|\varepsilon|$ further by the boundedness of $h$ keeps every $X+\varepsilon h$ inside the potential's neighbourhood. [step 1.1, given, F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 With the parameter rectangle $[a,b]\times(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)$ the integrands of $S$ and their $\varepsilon$-derivatives are continuous and the square-root argument is bounded away from zero by step 2.1, so [F3] applies and the first variation is $\delta S=-mc\int_a^b\frac{-\eta(\dot h,\dot X)}{\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}}ds+q\int_a^b\bigl[(\partial_\nu A_\mu)(X)h^\nu\dot X^\mu+A_\nu(X)\dot h^\nu\bigr]ds$; by [F2] the first integrand is $mU_\nu\dot h^\nu$. [step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 Integration by parts [F4] with $h(a)=h(b)=0$ gives $\int_a^b mU_\nu\dot h^\nu ds=-\int_a^bm\frac{dU_\nu}{ds}h^\nu ds$ and $\int_a^bA_\nu(X)\dot h^\nu ds=-\int_a^b(\partial_\mu A_\nu)(X)\dot X^\mu h^\nu ds$, since all factors are $C^1$ on $[a,b]$; hence $\delta S=\int_a^bC_\nu(s)h^\nu(s)ds$ with $C_\nu=-m\frac{dU_\nu}{ds}+q(\partial_\nu A_\mu-\partial_\mu A_\nu)(X)\dot X^\mu=-m\frac{dU_\nu}{ds}+qF_{\nu\mu}\dot X^\mu$, a continuous coefficient on $[a,b]$. [step 3.1, F3, F4, algebra]

5.1 Choice-free coefficient vanishing: if $C_\nu(s_0)\ne0$ at some interior point, choose the sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ with $\sigma C_\nu(s_0)>0$ and a small open interval $J\subset(a,b)$ on which $\sigma C_\nu\ge d>0$, then a nondegenerate closed subinterval $K\subset J$; the one-dimensional ZF cutoff [F4] gives $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(J)$ with $0\le\zeta\le1$ and $\zeta=1$ near $K$, and $h^\nu:=\sigma\zeta$ (other components zero) is an admitted fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variation, for which monotonicity and additivity [F4] give $\delta S=\int\sigma C_\nu\zeta\,ds\ge d\,\mathrm{length}(K)>0$, contradicting stationarity. [step 4.1, F4, algebra]

6.1 Hence $C_\nu=0$ on $(a,b)$ and, by continuity, on $[a,b]$; conversely $C_\nu\equiv0$ makes the first variation $\delta S=\int C_\nu h^\nu ds$ vanish for every fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variation, so stationarity is indeed equivalent to $C_\nu\equiv0$. [step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Dividing $m\frac{dU_\nu}{ds}=qF_{\nu\mu}\dot X^\mu$ by the positive factor $\tau'=d\tau/ds=\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}/c$ of [F2] and using $\dot X^\mu=\tau'U^\mu$ gives $m\frac{dU_\nu}{d\tau}=qF_{\nu\mu}U^\mu$; raising the index with the constant metric gives the equivalent vector form. The proof uses only finite choices, finite-interval Riemann calculus and the explicit ZF cutoff, and asserts no existence or coupling theory for singular particles and fields; adopting $S$ as a physical action is an additional model assumption. [step 6.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the trace and Sobolev suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain, let $\varepsilon$ be a measurable symmetric uniformly elliptic coefficient as in the lift lemma ([[lem-em-lift-specified-dirichlet-existence]]), let $\rho\in L^2(\Omega)$, and prescribe $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$, the fractional Sobolev space of the boundary definition, defined by a finite graph atlas and partition with norm given by the finite sums of localised $L^2$ norms and Gagliardo seminorms ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]], [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]). Then there is exactly one $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with trace $Tu=g$ solving

$$\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=\int_\Omega\rho\,v\qquad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega),$$

and the solution depends continuously on $(\rho,g)$: $\|u\|_{H^1}\le C(\|\rho\|_{L^2}+\|g\|_{H^{1/2}})$. The prescribed trace is exact and no classical $C^2$ boundary regularity is inferred.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ with trace operator $T$, a uniformly elliptic coefficient $\varepsilon$ with constants $0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty$, data $\rho\in L^2(\Omega)$ and $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, and the weak equation of the Statement.

[F1] **Sharp trace and bounded right inverse.** Under the Axiom of Choice, $T:W^{1,2}(\Omega)\to W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ is bounded and onto ([[thm-sharp-trace-theorem-for-w-one-p]]), and there is a bounded linear right inverse $R:H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)\to H^1(\Omega)$ with $TRg=g$ and $\|Rg\|_{H^1}\le C\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$ ([[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace]]); the fractional space is defined by the finite chart/Gagliardo construction ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]).

[F2] **Trace kernel.** $\{u\in W^{1,2}(\Omega):Tu=0\}=H_0^1(\Omega)$ ([[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F3] **Lift existence and bounds.** For every specified lift $G\in H^1(\Omega)$ and bounded $F$ on $H_0^1$, there is a unique $u\in G+H_0^1$ with $\int\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=F(v)$ for all $v\in H_0^1$; writing $u=G+w$ the solution obeys $\|\nabla w\|_2\le\alpha^{-1}\|\ell\|$ with $\ell(v)=F(v)-\int\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla G$, and for $F(v)=\int\rho v$ one has $|F(v)|\le2L\|\rho\|_2\|\nabla v\|_2$ and $|a(G,v)|\le\beta\|\nabla G\|_2\|\nabla v\|_2$ ([[lem-em-lift-specified-dirichlet-existence]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1] choose the bounded right inverse $R$ and put $G=Rg\in H^1(\Omega)$; then $TG=T(Rg)=g$, so $G$ is an exact $H^1$ lift of the prescribed fractional datum. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 A function $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ satisfies $Tu=g$ exactly when $u-G\in H_0^1(\Omega)$: indeed $T(u-G)=g-g=0$ is equivalent to $u-G\in H_0^1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

3.1 Apply the lift existence theorem [F3] with the specified lift $G=Rg$ and the functional $F(v)=\int\rho v$: there is a unique $u=G+w$, $w\in H_0^1$, with $\int\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=F(v)$ for every $v\in H_0^1$; by step 2.1 its trace is exactly $g$, and uniqueness of $w$ gives uniqueness of $u$ among $H^1$ functions with trace $g$ solving the equation. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F3, algebra]

4.1 Continuous dependence: for two data sets $(\rho_i,g_i)$, $i=1,2$, put $G_i=Rg_i$ and $w_i=u_i-G_i$; subtracting the weak equations and testing with $v=w_1-w_2$ gives $\alpha\|\nabla(w_1-w_2)\|_2^2\le\bigl(2L\|\rho_1-\rho_2\|_2+\beta\|\nabla R(g_1-g_2)\|_2\bigr)\|\nabla(w_1-w_2)\|_2$ by [F3], hence $\|\nabla(w_1-w_2)\|_2\le\alpha^{-1}\bigl(2L\|\rho_1-\rho_2\|_2+\beta\|\nabla R(g_1-g_2)\|_2\bigr)$; adding $\|R(g_1-g_2)\|_{H^1}\le C\|g_1-g_2\|_{H^{1/2}}$ by [F1] and using the equivalence of the gradient and full norms on $H_0^1$ [F3] yields the stated bound $\|u\|_{H^1}\le C(\|\rho\|_2+\|g\|_{H^{1/2}})$ with the case $(\rho_2,g_2)=(0,0)$. [step 3.1, F1, F3, algebra]

5.1 The prescribed trace is membership in the affine class $G+H_0^1$ and its identification $Tu=g$ through the bounded trace operator [F1], not a classical $C^2$ boundary regularity statement; this proves existence, exactness of the trace, uniqueness and continuous dependence. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the explicitly used trace and weak Dirichlet-solvability suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k>0$ and $R>0$. Use the sphere-normalised basis $Y^R_{lm}(Rn):=R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ on $S_R$, where $Y_{lm}$ is the complete normalised unit-sphere basis of the spherical-harmonic lemma ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]) and the coefficients $t_l$ are those of the outgoing radial-function lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]). The map

$$T_Rf=\sum_{l,m}t_l\,f_{lm}Y^R_{lm},\qquad f\in H^{1/2}(S_R),$$

is a bounded linear operator $H^{1/2}(S_R)\to H^{-1/2}(S_R)$ with

$$\operatorname{Re}\langle T_Rf,f\rangle\le0,\qquad\operatorname{Im}\langle T_Rf,f\rangle=\sum_{l,m}(\operatorname{Im}t_l)|f_{lm}|^2>0\quad(f\ne0).$$

It is precisely the outgoing scalar Helmholtz normal derivative at $r=R$: for every $f\in H^{1/2}(S_R)$ the function $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}f_{lm}h_l(kr)/h_l(kR)\,R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ for $r\ge R$ is the unique outgoing finite-local-energy exterior solution with trace $f$ on $S_R$ and normal derivative $T_Rf$ in the weak trace sense; it is smooth away from the sphere, and for smooth $f$ it satisfies the ordinary Sommerfeld condition. No uniform pointwise outgoing condition is asserted for arbitrary rough traces; the outgoing condition there is its modal/weak version. Here finite-local-energy means membership in $H^1(\{R<|x|<R_1\})$ for every finite $R_1>R$, with the $H^{1/2}$ trace on $S_R$; no global $H^1$ or global $L^2$ condition at infinity is imposed. The outgoing modal class consists of the displayed outgoing $h_l$ radial factors with no incoming partners; for rough traces this modal class is the definition, rather than a pointwise Sommerfeld assertion. Here the boundary Sobolev spaces are their complex versions (or complexifications of the real trace spaces), $f_{lm}=\int_{S_R}f\overline{Y^R_{lm}}\,d\sigma_R$, and the DtN dual pairing is linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; $k>0$, $R>0$; the unit-sphere harmonics $Y_{lm}$ and their solid homogeneous harmonic extensions; the sphere-normalised basis $Y^R_{lm}(Rn)=R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ with $\sigma_R$ the surface measure on $S_R$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]); the coefficients $t_l$ of [[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]] with $-(l+1)/R\le\operatorname{Re}t_l\le-1/R$ and $0<\operatorname{Im}t_l\le k$; and the data $f\in H^{1/2}(S_R)$.

[F1] **Traces and weak solvability.** The trace operator on $W^{1,2}$ of a bounded $C^1$ domain is bounded and onto $H^{1/2}$ of the boundary, and for prescribed fractional data there is a unique harmonic $H^1$ extension whose trace is the data, with $\|u\|_{H^1}\le C\|f\|_{H^{1/2}}$ ([[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]], [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F2] **Spherical harmonics and ball expansion.** The $Y_{lm}$ form a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2)$, with solid homogeneous harmonic extensions; the ball Poisson series has interior convergence with all derivatives, $L^2$ boundary limits and uniqueness ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], [[lem-em-ball-poisson-series-boundary-convergence]]). Real $L^2$ (and its complexification) is a Hilbert space with the integral pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

[F3] **First Green identity and Dirichlet energy.** For $C^2$ functions, $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2=-\int_\Omega u\Delta u+\int_{\partial\Omega}u\partial_\nu u$ on a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]); the Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F4] **Hankel functions.** The $h_l$ solve the radial Helmholtz equation, $F_l(z)=z^2|h_l(z)|^2$ is nonincreasing with $a_0=1$, and the Wronskian pairing of $h_l$ with its incoming partner is nonzero ([[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]).

[F5] **Bounds.** Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]), dominated convergence ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]) and the algebra of derivatives ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For finite harmonic data the harmonic ball extension $v(rn)=\sum(r/R)^lf_{lm}R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ has, by [F3] and the orthonormality of the solid harmonics, Dirichlet energy $\int_{B_R}|\nabla v|^2=\sum_{l,m}(l/R)|f_{lm}|^2$ and $L^2$ norm $\sum_{l,m}R|f_{lm}|^2/(2l+3)$; hence its $H^1$ norm squared is $\sum_{l,m}|f_{lm}|^2(l/R+R/(2l+3))$, comparable to $\sum_{l,m}(l+1)|f_{lm}|^2$; the trace theorem and harmonic-solvability bounds [F1] extend this equivalence of the $H^{1/2}(S_R)$ norm with $\bigl(\sum(l+1)|f_{lm}|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$ to all $f\in H^{1/2}(S_R)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Define $T_Rf=\sum_{l,m}t_lf_{lm}Y^R_{lm}$ and pair it with $f'\in H^{1/2}(S_R)$ by $\langle T_Rf,f'\rangle=\sum_{l,m}t_lf_{lm}\overline{f'_{lm}}$; the bounds $|t_l|\le(l+1)/R+k$ of [F4] and Cauchy-Schwarz [F5] give $|\langle T_Rf,f'\rangle|\le C(R,k)\|f\|_{H^{1/2}}\|f'\|_{H^{1/2}}$ with the weight $(l+1)$ supplied by step 1.1, so $T_R$ is a bounded operator into $H^{-1/2}(S_R)$. [step 1.1, given, F4, F5, algebra]

2.2 Exterior realisation: define $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}f_{lm}h_l(kr)/h_l(kR)R^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$ for $r\ge R$; from the monotonicity of $F_l$ in [F4], $|h_l(kr)/h_l(kR)|\le R/r$, and the radial equation together with the logarithmic-derivative bounds gives, on every compact interval of $r>R$, geometric decay of the radial ratios in $l$; hence the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on closed annuli $R+\delta\le r\le R_1$; the terms are outgoing radial solutions of the Helmholtz equation, so the limit is a smooth solution of $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ away from the sphere and, by [F2], its trace on $S_R$ is $f$. [step 1.1, given, F4, F5, algebra]

3.1 Signs: $\operatorname{Re}\langle T_Rf,f\rangle=\sum\operatorname{Re}(t_l)|f_{lm}|^2\le0$ and $\operatorname{Im}\langle T_Rf,f\rangle=\sum(\operatorname{Im}t_l)|f_{lm}|^2>0$ for $f\ne0$, by $-(l+1)/R\le\operatorname{Re}t_l\le-1/R$ and $0<\operatorname{Im}t_l$ of [F4] together with the completeness of the basis (a nonzero $f$ has some nonzero coefficient). [step 2.1, given, F4, F2, algebra]

3.2 Finite local energy and the weak normal derivative: for each mode the annular Green identity [F3] on $\{R\le r\le R_1\}$ bounds $\int_{R<|x|<R_1}|\nabla u|^2$ by the boundary data and the radial-ratio bounds, so $u\in H^1$ of every finite exterior annulus; integrating the mode equation against the exterior trace pairing identifies the normal derivative of $u$ on $S_R$ with $\sum t_lf_{lm}Y^R_{lm}=T_Rf$ in the weak trace sense, since $\partial_rh_l(kR)/h_l(kR)=t_l$ by the definition of the DtN coefficients in [F4]. [step 2.2, given, F4, F1, algebra]

4.1 Uniqueness: the radial Helmholtz equation has the two-dimensional solution space spanned by $h_l$ and its incoming partner, whose Wronskian is nonzero by [F4]; the outgoing modal condition selects the $h_l$ multiples, harmonic completeness [F2] forces every finite-local-energy exterior solution with trace $f$ to have exactly the coefficients $f_{lm}$ on each sphere, and the l=0 mode $e^{ikr}/r$ shows why no global $L^2$ or $H^1$ condition at infinity is imposed (its global energy integrals diverge). [step 2.2, step 3.2, F4, F2, algebra]

5.1 For complex boundary data apply the real prescribed-trace and harmonic solver of [F1] to the real and imaginary parts and combine; the squared boundary norm is the sum of the two real energy norms and the pairing is linear-conjugate-linear as stated, completing the identification of $T_R$ with the outgoing DtN map and its properties. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, F1, F5, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the actually cited Sobolev trace, lift and mean-zero density interfaces, and its Countable Choice consequence for the measure and variational interfaces ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain, let $\varepsilon$ be measurable symmetric uniformly elliptic ([[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]]), let $\rho\in L^2(\Omega)$, and let $g\in H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, the bounded real dual of the boundary trace space ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]). Define $\ell(v)=\int_\Omega\rho v+\langle g,Tv\rangle$ on $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]). A weak Neumann solution is a $u\in H^1$ with

$$\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1(\Omega).$$

Such a solution exists if and only if $\ell(1)=0$, and is then unique up to an additive constant; normalising $\int_\Omega u=0$ makes it unique. On finitely many connected components the compatibility and normalisation are imposed separately on each component. For finitely many disjoint smooth stationary interfaces with piecewise smooth uniformly elliptic $\varepsilon$, bulk data $\rho\in L^2$ and prescribed sheet charge $\sigma$ on the interfaces defining a bounded trace functional on $H^1$ (for instance $\sigma\in L^2$ of each smooth compact interface), the same argument gives weak Dirichlet or compatible Neumann existence for the transmission problem, with the globally $H^1$ potential having identical one-sided trace; where the solution is classically smooth on each side, integration by parts gives the jump $n\cdot[\varepsilon\nabla u]=-\sigma$, equivalently $n\cdot[D]=\sigma$ for the explicitly defined mathematical flux $D:=-\varepsilon\nabla u$ on each side. General piecewise classical regularity remains a separate requirement.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A bounded connected $C^1$ domain $\Omega$ with outward normal $n$; a uniformly elliptic symmetric measurable $\varepsilon$ with constants $0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty$; data $\rho\in L^2(\Omega)$ and $g\in H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$; the functional $\ell$ and the weak Neumann problem of the Statement.

[F1] **Trace and lift interfaces.** The trace $T:W^{1,2}(\Omega)\to H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ is bounded and onto, with a bounded right inverse, and prescribed fractional data have a unique harmonic extension, under the declared Choice ([[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], [[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]], [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F2] **Mean-zero coercivity.** On a bounded connected $C^1$ domain, $\|v-v_\Omega\|_{L^2}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$, where $v_\Omega$ is the mean; hence the gradient norm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm on the closed mean-zero subspace ([[lem-em-mean-zero-coercivity-on-a-c-one-domain]]).

[F3] **Symmetric coercive solver.** A symmetric bounded coercive bilinear form on a real Hilbert space with a bounded functional has a unique solution, under Countable Choice ([[lem-em-symmetric-coercive-variational-solver]], [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F4] **Cauchy-Schwarz and calculus.** Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) and the product/chain rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Boundedness of $\ell$: $|\ell(v)|\le\|\rho\|_2\|v\|_2+\|g\|_{H^{-1/2}}\|Tv\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C(1+\|\rho\|_2+\|g\|_{H^{-1/2}})\|v\|_{H^1}$ by the trace bound [F1] and Cauchy-Schwarz [F4]. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 Necessity of compatibility: the constant function $1$ lies in $H^1(\Omega)$ with $\nabla 1=0$, so testing the equation with $v=1$ gives $0=\ell(1)$; hence $\ell(1)=0$ is necessary for existence. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.2 Let $H^1_*=\{v\in H^1(\Omega):\int_\Omega v=0\}$, a closed subspace, and restrict the symmetric form $a(w,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla w$ and the functional $\ell$ to it; $a$ is bounded by $\beta$ and coercive with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|\nabla v\|_2^2\ge c\|v\|_{H^1}^2$ by the equivalence of norms of [F2], and $\ell$ remains bounded by step 1.1, so the solver [F3] gives a unique $u_*\in H^1_*$ with $a(u_*,v)=\ell(v)$ for every $v\in H^1_*$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 Extension to all of $H^1$: every $v\in H^1$ decomposes as $v=v_*+c$ with $v_*\in H^1_*$ and constant $c=v_\Omega$; then $a(u_*,v)=a(u_*,v_*)+a(u_*,c)=a(u_*,v_*)=\ell(v_*)=\ell(v_*)+c\,\ell(1)=\ell(v)$ by step 2.1 and $\nabla c=0$, so $u_*$ solves the full weak Neumann problem; normalising $\int u_*=0$ selects this representative. [step 2.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Uniqueness: for two solutions $u_1,u_2$ the difference $w$ satisfies $\int\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla w=0$ for all $v\in H^1$; testing $v=w$ gives $\alpha\|\nabla w\|_2^2\le\int\nabla w\cdot\varepsilon\nabla w=0$, so $\nabla w=0$ and, by the mean-zero inequality [F2], $w-w_\Omega=0$, i.e. $w$ is constant; hence solutions are unique up to additive constants and the mean-zero normalisation makes the solution unique. [step 3.1, F2, algebra]

5.1 Finitely many connected components: on a bounded $C^1$ domain with components $\Omega_1,\dots,\Omega_N$, $H^1(\Omega)$ is the direct sum of the $H^1(\Omega_j)$ extended by zero, the gradient form and the functional $\ell$ split, and the trace space splits accordingly, so the argument of steps 1.1-4.1 applies on each component separately: compatibility $\ell(\mathbf 1_{\Omega_j})=0$ is required on each component and the solution is unique up to one constant per component, fixed by the per-component mean-zero normalisation. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

6.1 Transmission problems: let finitely many disjoint smooth compact stationary interfaces carry a prescribed sheet charge $\sigma$ defining a bounded trace functional $v\mapsto\langle\sigma,T_\Sigma v\rangle$ on $H^1$ (for instance $\sigma\in L^2$ of each interface), and let $\ell$ be the sum of the bulk term, the possible outer-boundary Neumann term and this interface term; step 1.1 makes $\ell$ bounded and the same mean-zero argument gives weak existence and uniqueness up to constants, with the globally $H^1$ potential having identical one-sided traces because the trace onto each smooth interface is continuous from $H^1$ in both chart directions and the same representative approaches from both sides. [step 5.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

7.1 Classical jump: where the transmission solution is classically smooth on each side of an interface $\Sigma$ with unit normal $n$, apply the divergence theorem to $\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u$ on each side and subtract the weak equation; the bulk terms cancel and the remaining boundary identity is $n\cdot[\varepsilon\nabla u]=-\sigma$, i.e. $n\cdot[D]=\sigma$ for the explicitly defined mathematical flux $D:=-\varepsilon\nabla u$, since $[D]=-[\varepsilon\nabla u]$; this is conditional on the one-sided classical smoothness, and general piecewise classical regularity remains a separate requirement. [step 6.1, F1, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a **bounded smooth graph domain**: a nonempty bounded open set such that for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and a function $h\in C^\infty(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,

$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\},$$

which is the $C^\infty$ case of the bounded $C^k$ graph domain of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open set with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$. Then there exists a real-linear operator $E_\Omega$, determined only by $\Omega$, a finite smooth atlas and fixed cutoffs, such that for every open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and every function $u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ that is of class $C^\infty$ on the open set $\Omega\times J$ and whose every mixed derivative $D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ has a continuous extension to $\overline\Omega\times J$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), the function $E_\Omega u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$, satisfies $E_\Omega u(x,\tau)=u(x,\tau)$ for all $(x,\tau)\in\overline\Omega\times J$ and

$$D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)\big|_{\overline\Omega\times J}=\text{the continuous extension of }D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j u$$

for all multi-indices $\alpha$ and all $j\ge0$, and is spatially supported in one fixed compact subset of $V$, in the sense that there is a compact $K_\Omega\subseteq V$ with $E_\Omega u(x,\tau)=0$ for all $x\notin K_\Omega$, $\tau\in J$. For every compact $K\subseteq J$, every integer $m\ge0$ and every $j\ge0$,

$$\sup_{\tau\in K}\|\partial_\tau^j E_\Omega u(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_m\sup_{\tau\in K}\|\partial_\tau^j u(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)},$$

where $\|w\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|D^\alpha w(x)|$ and $\|W\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}|D^\alpha W(x)|$, and the constant $C_m$ depends only on $m$, $\Omega$, the atlas and cutoffs. The extension commutes with every time derivative: $\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)=E_\Omega(\partial_\tau^j u)$ for all $j\ge0$. No bound uniform over an unbounded $J$ is asserted. Vector-valued inputs of finite dimension are extended componentwise. The construction adds no choice principle: the finite atlas is selected from the cover of all admissible smooth chart patches, finite cutoffs come from the published choice-free compact cutoff lemma, and the infinite coefficient sequence is defined by the explicit formula below. The consuming elliptic or Sobolev argument retains whatever choice principles its own suppliers declare.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A bounded smooth graph domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, an open set $V$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$, an open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, and a function $u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$ whose mixed derivatives all extend continuously to $\overline\Omega\times J$.

[L1] **Smooth graph charts and flattening** ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A bounded $C^k$ domain $\Omega$ has, at each boundary point, graph data $W,R,B,h$ with $R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{s<h(y)\}$; its flattening chart is $\Phi(p):=(y,s-h(y))$ on $W$, a $C^k$ diffeomorphism onto $\Phi(W)$ with $C^k$ inverse and $\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$; on compactly contained patches the derivatives of $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$ through order $k$ are bounded. Here $h\in C^\infty(B)$, so these charts and inverses are of class $C^\infty$.

[L2] **Compactness** ([[def-compact-space]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]). A space is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover. A subset of $\mathbb R^n$ ($n\ge1$) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded; closed boxes are compact. $\partial\Omega$ and $\overline\Omega$ are the set-theoretic boundary and closure, $\overline\Omega$ is closed and, being the closure of a bounded set, is bounded.

[L3] **Choice-free Euclidean cutoffs** ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]). In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $O$ open there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(O)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighbourhood of $K$.

[L4] **$C^k$ calculus** ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]). A map $f$ is $C^k$ on an open set when every word of at most $k$ coordinate partial derivatives exists and is continuous; $C^\infty$ means $C^k$ for all $k$. Sums, scalar multiples and products of $C^k$ functions are $C^k$; a composition of $C^k$ maps is $C^k$; a map with continuous first partial derivatives everywhere on an open set is totally differentiable there, with derivative the Jacobian. Continuous functions on compact intervals are Riemann integrable.

[L5] **Fundamental theorem of calculus** ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[thm-ftc-first-part]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-derivative]]). If $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ (one-sided at the endpoints) and $G'=f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^bf=G(b)-G(a)$; if $f$ is continuous at $c\in[a,b]$ and $F$ is its integral function, then $F'(c)=f(c)$.

[L6] **Powers, series and monotone limits** ([[def-integer-power]], [[lem-power-laws]], [[def-series]], [[thm-geometric-series]], [[thm-monotone-convergence]]). $2^k$ is the integer power with $2^{k+1}=2\cdot2^k$, and $2^m2^n=2^{m+n}$; the series $\sum_{k=0}^\infty2^{-k}$ converges to $2$, and its tails are $\sum_{k=M}^\infty2^{-k}=2^{1-M}$; a nondecreasing sequence of reals bounded above converges to its supremum.

[L7] **Real polynomials and their roots** ([[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[thm-nonzero-real-polynomial-has-at-most-degree-many-distinct-roots]], [[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]). A formal real polynomial is $0$ or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\dots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$, evaluated by $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^na_kx^k$, with $\deg p=n$; a nonzero polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. Finite sums and products of reals are defined by recursion and obey additivity, splitting, scaling, and distributivity laws.

## Proof

The construction is standard Seeley reflection; the proof defines the reflection coefficients from scratch (so that no external coefficient-existence assertion is assumed), proves the exact moment identities, performs the reflected extension on one flattened half-space with parameters, glues the two sides by the fundamental theorem of calculus, and assembles finitely many chart pieces with a partition of unity.

1.1 Since $\overline\Omega$ is bounded and closed [L2], it is compact by Heine-Borel [L2]. The family of all admissible smooth chart neighbourhoods of boundary points is an open cover of $\partial\Omega\subseteq\overline\Omega$, and $\Omega$ itself is open; hence the family formed by $\Omega$ and all admissible smooth chart neighbourhoods covers the compact set $\overline\Omega$, so it contains a finite subcover, say $W_1,\dots,W_p$ together with $\Omega$, where each $W_i$ carries chart data $(R_i,B_i,h_i,\Phi_i)$ with $h_i\in C^\infty$ and rigid motion $R_i$ [L1, L2]. Extracting the finitely many chart data is a finite choice, available in ZF; replace each $W_i$ by the still admissible chart neighbourhood $W_i\cap V$, so that $W_i\subseteq V$, and fix these finitely many maps and data for the rest of the proof. [L1, L2, choose]

1.2 Put $b_k:=-2^k$ for $k\ge0$, the integer powers of [L6]. For $N\ge k\ge0$ define $a_k^{(N)}:=\prod_{\substack{0\le j\le N\\j\ne k}}\frac{1-b_j}{b_k-b_j}.$ Here $1-b_j=1+2^j>0$; for $j<k$ one has $b_k-b_j=-(2^k-2^j)<0$, and for $j>k$ one has $b_k-b_j=2^j-2^k>0$. Hence $a_k^{(N)}\ne0$ and its sign is $(-1)^k$ for every $N\ge k$. [L6, algebra]

1.3 For reals $x_0,\dots,x_M\in[0,1)$ with $\sum_{j=0}^Mx_j<1$ one has, by induction on $M$ using the field axioms, $\prod_{j=0}^M(1+x_j)\le\bigl(1-\sum_{j=0}^Mx_j\bigr)^{-1}$ and $\prod_{j=0}^M(1-x_j)\ge1-\sum_{j=0}^Mx_j$. Applying this with $x_j=2^{-j}$ and the geometric sums $\sum_{j\ge2}2^{-j}=\tfrac12$ and $\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}=1$ [L6] gives for every finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb N$ and every $M\ge0$ the two bounds $\prod_{j\in F}(1+2^{-j})\le6$ and $\prod_{l=1}^{M}(1-2^{-l})\ge\tfrac14$: the first because the product over $\{0,1\}$ equals $2\cdot\tfrac32=3$ and the product over $j\ge2$ is at most $\bigl(1-\tfrac12\bigr)^{-1}=2$, the second because the factor $l=1$ is $\tfrac12$ and the remaining product is at least $1-\sum_{l\ge2}2^{-l}=\tfrac12$. [L6, induction, algebra]

1.4 Let $f$ be continuous on the strip $B\times(-\delta,\delta)\times J$ (with $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ open, $\delta>0$) and suppose that every first partial derivative of $f$ exists and is continuous on each open half-strip $\{s>0\}$ and $\{s<0\}$ and extends continuously to the corresponding closed half-strip, the two extensions agreeing on $\{s=0\}$; let $E_i$ denote the resulting common continuous function on the whole strip, the index $i$ running over the four coordinates. Fix a point $p$ in the strip. If a segment $\beta\mapsto p+\beta e_i$, $\beta\in[0,h]$, stays inside one open half-strip, then $\beta\mapsto f(p+\beta e_i)$ is differentiable at every point of $[0,h]$ with derivative $E_i(p+\beta e_i)$ on $(0,h)$ and one-sided derivatives at the endpoints, and $E_i$ is continuous, hence integrable, on $[0,h]$ [L4, L5]; the second fundamental theorem gives $f(p+he_i)-f(p)=\int_0^hE_i(p+\beta e_i)\,d\beta$. If the segment crosses $\{s=0\}$ at a parameter $\beta_0$, split the integral at $\beta_0$ and apply the same argument on the two closed subintervals, where the endpoint derivative at $\beta_0$ is the common one-sided value supplied by the continuous extension; additivity of the integral gives the same identity. Dividing by $h$ and letting $h\to0$, continuity of $E_i$ at $p$ gives $(f(p+he_i)-f(p))/h=\tfrac1h\int_0^hE_i(p+\beta e_i)d\beta\to E_i(p)$; thus every first partial derivative of $f$ exists on the whole strip and equals the continuous function $E_i$. By [L4] $f$ is totally differentiable at every point with that Jacobian, and in particular all first partial derivatives are continuous, so $f$ is $C^1$ on the strip. [L4, L5, cases, algebra]

2.1 For $N\ge k$, rewriting each factor defined in step 1.2 as $1-b_j=2^j(1+2^{-j})$ and $b_k-b_j=\pm2^{\max(j,k)}(1-2^{-|j-k|})$ gives $\bigl|a_k^{(N)}\bigr|=2^{-k(k+1)/2}\,\frac{\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1+2^{-j})\prod_{j=k+1}^{N}(1+2^{-j})}{\prod_{l=1}^{k}(1-2^{-l})\prod_{m=1}^{N-k}(1-2^{-m})},$ where empty products are $1$; indeed the powers of $2$ contribute $\sum_{j<k}(j-k)=-k(k+1)/2$, and the two denominator products collect the factors $1-2^{j-k}$ for $j<k$ and $1-2^{k-j}$ for $j>k$. By step 1.3 the numerator is at most $36$ and each denominator product is at least $\tfrac14$, so $\bigl|a_k^{(N)}\bigr|\le576\cdot2^{-k(k+1)/2}$ for all $N\ge k$. For fixed $k$ the ratio $\bigl|a_k^{(N+1)}\bigr|/\bigl|a_k^{(N)}\bigr|=(1+2^{-(N+1)})/(1-2^{-(N+1-k)})$ exceeds $1$ whenever $N+1>k$, because its numerator exceeds $1$ and its denominator lies in $(0,1)$; hence $N\mapsto\bigl|a_k^{(N)}\bigr|$ is nondecreasing and bounded above by $576\cdot2^{-k(k+1)/2}$, so the monotone convergence theorem [L6] gives a limit $a_k:=\lim_{N\to\infty}a_k^{(N)}$ with sign $(-1)^k$ and $\bigl|a_k\bigr|\le576\cdot2^{-k(k+1)/2}$. Consequently, for every integer $r\ge0$ and every $k\ge2r+1$ one has $-\tfrac{k(k+1)}2+kr\le-k$, so $\bigl|a_k\bigr|\,\bigl|b_k\bigr|^r\le576\cdot2^{-k}$ for such $k$ and the series $\sum_{k=0}^\infty\bigl|a_k\bigr|\,\bigl|b_k\bigr|^r$ converges, with tails bounded by $\sum_{k>M}\bigl|a_k\bigr|\,\bigl|b_k\bigr|^r\le576\cdot2^{-M}$ whenever $M\ge2r+1$. [step 1.2, step 1.3, L6, algebra]

2.2 For every $N\ge0$ and every integer $r$ with $0\le r\le N$ one has $\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k^{(N)}b_k^r=1.$ Indeed, expanding the $N$ linear factors of each $\prod_{j\ne k}(z-b_j)$ by distributivity gives each function $z\mapsto\prod_{j\ne k}(z-b_j)/(b_k-b_j)$ the structure of a real polynomial of degree at most $N$ with explicit finite coefficient sums [L7], so $q(z):=z^r-\sum_{k=0}^{N}b_k^r\prod_{j\ne k}(z-b_j)/(b_k-b_j)$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $N$. At a node $z=b_i$ every product $\prod_{j\ne k}(b_i-b_j)$ vanishes for $k\ne i$ and equals $\prod_{j\ne i}(b_i-b_j)$ for $k=i$, so $q(b_i)=b_i^r-b_i^r=0$ for all $i=0,\dots,N$. Thus $q$ has $N+1$ distinct roots; were $q$ nonzero, its degree would be defined and at most $N$, contradicting the root bound [L7]. Hence $q$ is the zero polynomial, and evaluating at $z=1$, where $\prod_{j\ne k}(1-b_j)/(b_k-b_j)=a_k^{(N)}$, gives $0=q(1)=1-\sum_{k=0}^Na_k^{(N)}b_k^r$. [step 1.2, L7, algebra]

2.3 Let $f$ be continuous on the strip and suppose that for every word $(i_1,\dots,i_m)$ of coordinate indices with $m\ge1$ the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_m}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on each open half-strip and extends continuously to the closed half-strips, the two extensions agreeing on $\{s=0\}$; let $F_{i_1\dots i_m}$ be the common extension. Then $f$ is of class $C^\infty$ on the strip, and every iterated derivative of $f$ on the strip equals the corresponding common extension. Indeed, induct on $m$: for $m=0$ this is the assumed continuity, and for $m\ge1$ the iterated derivative $g:=\partial_{i_{m-1}}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ has, by the induction hypothesis, the continuous extension $F_{i_1\dots i_{m-1}}$ to the strip, whose first partial derivatives on each open half-strip exist and are continuous and extend continuously to the closed half-strips with the extensions $F_{i_1\dots i_{m-1}i}$ agreeing on $\{s=0\}$; step 1.4 applied to $g$ shows that $g$ is $C^1$ on the strip with $\partial_ig=F_{i_1\dots i_{m-1}i}$. Hence every iterated derivative of $f$ of every order exists and is continuous on the strip, that is, $f$ is $C^\infty$ there, and each iterated derivative equals the corresponding common extension. [step 1.4, induction]

2.4 Let $\mathcal U$ be the finite family consisting of the members $W_1,\dots,W_p$ of step 1.1 and the member $\Omega$. For each $x\in\overline\Omega$ choose a member of $\mathcal U$ containing $x$ and then an open Euclidean ball with rational centre and rational radius containing $x$ and contained in that member; the countable, explicitly defined family $\mathcal B$ of all open balls with rational centre and rational radius contained in at least one member of $\mathcal U$ covers the compact set $\overline\Omega$, so compactness [L2] yields finitely many balls $B_1,\dots,B_q\in\mathcal B$ covering $\overline\Omega$. For each $l\le q$ choose a member $U_{\sigma(l)}$ of $\mathcal U$ containing $B_l$; this is a finite choice in ZF. By [L3] applied to the compact sets $\overline{B_l}\subseteq U_{\sigma(l)}$ there are $\psi_l\in C_c^\infty(U_{\sigma(l)})$ with $0\le\psi_l\le1$ and $\psi_l=1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline{B_l}$. Then $S:=\sum_{l=1}^q\psi_l$ is smooth and positive on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$ because each $\overline{B_l}$ carries such a neighbourhood; apply [L3] again, with compact $K=\overline\Omega$ and open $O=\{S>0\}$, to obtain $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\{S>0\})$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. Since the support of $\chi$ is compact and contained in $\{S>0\}$, the function $\chi/S$, defined to be $\chi\cdot(1/S)$ on $\{S>0\}$ and $0$ elsewhere, is smooth with compact support in $\{S>0\}$. For $j=1,\dots,p$ put $\chi_j:=\frac{\chi}{S}\sum_{\substack{1\le l\le q\\\sigma(l)=j}}\psi_l$ and put $\chi_0:=\frac{\chi}{S}\sum_{\substack{1\le l\le q\\\sigma(l)=0}}\psi_l$, assigning index $0$ to the member $\Omega$. Each $\chi_j$ is smooth, compactly supported and nonnegative, with $\operatorname{supp}\chi_j\subseteq W_j$ for $j\ge1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\chi_0\subseteq\Omega$, and $\sum_{j=0}^p\chi_j=\chi=1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, in particular on $\Omega$. [step 1.1, L2, L3, choose, algebra]

3.1 For every integer $r\ge0$ the series $\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_kb_k^r$ converges absolutely with sum $1$. Indeed, fix $M$ and $N\ge\max(r,M)$; by step 2.2, $1=\sum_{k=0}^{N}a_k^{(N)}b_k^r$, so $1-\sum_{k=0}^{M}a_kb_k^r=\sum_{k=0}^{M}(a_k^{(N)}-a_k)b_k^r+\sum_{k=M+1}^{N}a_k^{(N)}b_k^r$; the first sum tends to $0$ as $N\to\infty$ because there are finitely many coefficients and each converges to $a_k$ by step 2.1, and the second sum is bounded in absolute value by $576\cdot2^{-M}$ uniformly in $N$ by step 2.1. Letting first $N\to\infty$ and then $M\to\infty$ gives $\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_kb_k^r=1$, the absolute convergence being part of step 2.1. [step 2.1, step 2.2, L6, algebra]

4.1 Fix $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ open, $\delta>0$ and an interval $J$, and let $w:(B\times(-\delta,0])\times J\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, of class $C^\infty$ on $B\times(-\delta,0)\times J$, with every mixed derivative $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw$ extending continuously to $B\times(-\delta,0]\times J$, and suppose $w$ vanishes outside a compact subset of $B\times(-\delta,0]$. Choosing a cutoff $\rho\in C_c^\infty((-\delta/2,\delta/2))$ with $0\le\rho\le1$ and $\rho=1$ near $0$ [L3], define $(\mathcal Ew)(y,s,\tau):=w(y,s,\tau)$ for $s\le0$ and $(\mathcal Ew)(y,s,\tau):=\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k\rho(b_ks)w(y,b_ks,\tau)$ for $s>0$, with the coefficients $a_k$ of step 1.2. For fixed $s>0$ the series is finite: $|b_ks|=2^ks\ge\delta/2$ for all large $k$, where $\rho$ vanishes, so only finitely many terms are nonzero; hence $\mathcal Ew$ is well defined on $B\times(-\delta,\delta)\times J$. As $s\downarrow0$ each term tends to $a_kw(y,0,\tau)$ by continuity of $w$ and $\rho(0)=1$, and the tail is bounded by $(\sup|w|)\sum_{k>M}|a_k|$, which tends to $0$ uniformly on compact sets by step 2.1; by step 3.1 with $r=0$ the lower and upper limits both equal $w(y,0,\tau)$, so $\mathcal Ew$ is continuous on the strip. Moreover $\mathcal Ew$ vanishes on the complement of the projection of the support of $w$ in the $y$-variable times $(-\delta/2,\delta/2)\times J$, so it is spatially supported in a fixed compact subset of $B\times(-\delta,\delta)$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, L3, L6, algebra]

5.1 $\mathcal Ew$ is of class $C^\infty$ on each of the two open half-strips, with the following derivative formula on $s>0$, valid for every multi-index $\alpha$ and all $r,j\ge0$: $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^j(\mathcal Ew)(y,s,\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_kb_k^r\,\bigl[D_z^rD_y^\alpha\partial_\tau^j\bigl(\rho(z)w(y,z,\tau)\bigr)\bigr]_{z=b_ks},$ a finite sum for each fixed $(y,s,\tau)$ because only the finitely many $k$ with $|b_ks|<\delta/2$ contribute. On $s<0$ the function $\mathcal Ew$ equals $w$, which is smooth there. Both assertions follow by applying the product and chain rules [L4] termwise to a finite sum: on each set $\{s>\varepsilon\}$ with $\varepsilon>0$ the constraint $2^ks<\delta/2$ admits only finitely many $k$, so $\mathcal Ew$ is a finite sum of smooth functions there, and every point of $\{s>0\}$ has a neighbourhood with such an $\varepsilon>0$. Moreover, for every compact $Y'\times K\subseteq B\times J$ and all $\alpha,r,j$ there is a finite constant $C_{\alpha,r,j}$, independent of $w$, with $\sup\{|D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^j(\mathcal Ew)|:y\in Y',\,|s|<\delta/2,\,\tau\in K\}\le C_{\alpha,r,j}\sum_{|\beta|\le|\alpha|}\sum_{q\le r}\sup\{|D_y^\beta\partial_z^q\partial_\tau^jw(y,z,\tau)|:y\in Y'',\,-\delta/2\le z\le0,\,\tau\in K\}$ for some open $Y''$ with $Y'\subseteq\overline{Y''}\subseteq B$: each term contributes a factor $|a_k||b_k|^r$ times a fixed bound for the derivatives of $\rho$ of order at most $r$, and $\sum_k|a_k||b_k|^r<\infty$ by step 2.1. [step 2.1, step 4.1, L4, algebra]

6.1 For every multi-index $\alpha$, all $r,j\ge0$ and every compact $Y'\times K\subseteq B\times J$, the derivatives in step 5.1 converge uniformly as $s\downarrow0$ to $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,0,\tau)$, and from the other side $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^j(\mathcal Ew)(y,s,\tau)=D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,s,\tau)\to D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,0,\tau)$. Indeed, choose an open $Y''$ with $Y'\subseteq\overline{Y''}\subseteq B$; all derivatives of $\rho w$ through order $r+|\alpha|+j$ appearing in step 5.1 are continuous on the compact set $\overline{Y''}\times[-\delta/2,0]\times K$, hence bounded by a finite constant $C$; the tail is bounded by $C\sum_{k>M}|a_k||b_k|^r\le576C\cdot2^{-M}$ by step 2.1, uniformly in $(y,s,\tau)$, while the finitely many head terms converge as $s\downarrow0$ because $\rho=1$ near $0$ and all positive-order derivatives of $\rho$ vanish at $0$, so each head term tends to $a_kb_k^rD_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,0,\tau)$; the moment identity of step 3.1 makes the total limit equal to $D_y^\alpha\partial_s^r\partial_\tau^jw(y,0,\tau)$, uniformly on $Y'\times K$. Consequently every mixed derivative of $\mathcal Ew$ on either side extends continuously to $s=0$, and the two one-sided continuous extensions agree there. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, L4, algebra]

7.1 Applying step 2.3 to the function $\mathcal Ew$ on the strip $B\times(-\delta,\delta)\times J$: it is continuous by step 4.1, and by step 6.1 every word of iterated derivatives of $\mathcal Ew$ has matching continuous one-sided extensions; hence $\mathcal Ew$ is of class $C^\infty$ on the strip, agrees with $w$ on $\{s\le0\}$, and every mixed derivative of $\mathcal Ew$ at a point with $s=0$ equals the corresponding boundary value of the mixed derivative of $w$. [step 2.3, step 4.1, step 6.1]

8.1 For $j\ge1$ put $w_j:=\chi_j\,u$ restricted to $\Omega\times J$; its support is compactly contained in $W_j\cap\overline\Omega$. Pulling back by the smooth diffeomorphism $\Phi_j$ [L1] gives a function, again written $w_j$, on the open half-strip $\Phi_j(W_j)\cap\{t<0\}$ times $J$ that is smooth up to $t=0$ with all mixed derivatives extending continuously, and whose support is compact in $\Phi_j(W_j)\cap\{t\le0\}$. Choose open boxes $B_j\times(-\delta_j,\delta_j)\subseteq\Phi_j(W_j)$ containing that compact support and extend $w_j$ by zero where needed on the half-strip $B_j\times(-\delta_j,0]\times J$, and let $\mathcal E_j$ be the construction of steps 4.1, 5.1 and 7.1 for these data. Then $\mathcal E_jw_j$ is $C^\infty$ on $B_j\times(-\delta_j,\delta_j)\times J$ by step 7.1, is supported in a compact subset of that box, and agrees with $w_j$ wherever $t\le0$. Pulling back by $\Phi_j^{-1}$ and extending by zero outside the box gives a function $g_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times J)$ supported in a compact subset of $W_j\subseteq V$. For $j=0$ extend $\chi_0u$ by zero on $(\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega)\times J$; since $\operatorname{supp}\chi_0$ is compact and contained in $\Omega$, the result $g_0$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ with compact spatial support in $\Omega$. Define $E_\Omega u:=\sum_{j=0}^{p}g_j.$ Each step is linear in $u$ (pullback, multiplication by the fixed cutoffs $\chi_j$ and the fixed coefficient series are linear), and the data $\Phi_j,\chi_j,\rho_j,B_j,\delta_j,a_k$ depend only on $\Omega$ and its fixed atlas and cutoffs, not on $J$, on $u$, or on $\tau$; hence $E_\Omega$ is a real-linear operator determined only by these fixed data, and it commutes with $\partial_\tau$ because no piece depends on $\tau$. Its values are spatially supported in the fixed compact set $\bigcup_{j=0}^p\operatorname{supp}g_j\subseteq V$. [step 2.4, step 5.1, step 7.1, construct]

9.1 By step 7.1 each $g_j$ with $j\ge1$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$, and $g_0$ is $C^\infty$ by construction, so the finite sum $E_\Omega u$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ [L4]. Its derivatives on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ are the corresponding sums of the derivatives of the $g_j$, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ and $j\ge0$ the boundary values on $\partial\Omega$ from the exterior side of the piece $g_i$ equal the corresponding boundary values of $\chi_iu$ by steps 6.1 and 7.1. [step 5.1, step 8.1, L4]

9.2 **Seminorm bound.** Let $m\ge0$, $j\ge0$ and compact $K\subseteq J$ be given. For $|\alpha|\le m$ and $\tau\in K$, step 5.1 bounds each $|D^\alpha\partial_\tau^jg_i(x,\tau)|$ by a finite constant times $\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta\partial_\tau^ju(\cdot,\tau)|$: for $i=0$ this is immediate from the Leibniz rule and compact support, and for $i\ge1$ the pullback introduces the bounded derivatives of $\Phi_i^{-1}$ on the compact piece, the local cutoff contributes finitely many bounded terms, and step 5.1 supplies the coefficient sum $\sum_k|a_k||b_k|^m<\infty$; the spatial derivatives of order at most $m$ and the fixed time order $j$ enter only through $D^\beta\partial_\tau^ju$ with $|\beta|\le m$, because the normal argument is sampled at $b_kt$ and differentiated at most $r\le m$ times. Summing over the finitely many pieces and over $|\alpha|\le m$ gives a constant $C_m$, independent of $u$, $j$, $K$ and $\tau$, with $\|\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_m\|\partial_\tau^ju(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)}$; taking the supremum over $\tau\in K$ gives the displayed estimate. Since each piece commutes with $\partial_\tau$, $\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)=E_\Omega(\partial_\tau^ju)$. [step 5.1, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 On $\Omega\times J$ one has $E_\Omega u=\sum_{j=0}^{p}\chi_ju=u$ because $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ there and each piece agrees with $\chi_ju$ on the physical side; by continuity this identity extends to $\overline\Omega\times J$. More generally, for every multi-index $\alpha$ and every $j\ge0$, the continuous extension of $D^\alpha\partial_\tau^ju$ to $\overline\Omega\times J$ equals $D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)$ on $\overline\Omega\times J$: on the open set $\Omega\times J$ this is the Leibniz rule for the finite sum $\sum_i\chi_iu$ [L4], and on $\partial\Omega$ it follows from step 9.1 because the exterior boundary values of the pieces add up to the boundary values of $u$, the partition identity $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ holding on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. [step 8.1, step 9.1, L4, algebra]

11.1 For a finite-dimensional vector-valued input $u=(u_1,\dots,u_N)$ the construction applied componentwise produces $E_\Omega u:=(E_\Omega u_1,\dots,E_\Omega u_N)$, and all bounds and agreement statements hold in each component. As to choice: the finite atlas is extracted by compactness from the definable family of all admissible smooth chart patches, the finitely many cutoffs and indices are finite choices in ZF, and the coefficients $a_k$ are fixed by the explicit formula of step 1.2 and the limits of step 2.1; no infinite selection is made, so the construction adds no choice principle beyond those carried by the cited suppliers. This completes the construction and proves every assertion of the statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, step 9.2, step 10.1] ∎
