## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the cited published suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0\in\mathbb R$, $T>t_0$, let $a,b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and let $h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ in the extension sense that $h$ is the restriction of a $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$, so that $c^2W=\Box_c$ is the wave operator of speed $c$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]). For $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and $s\ge0$ let $H_\varphi(x,s):=s\,M_{cs}\varphi(x)$, where $M_r\varphi(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}\varphi(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n)$ is the spherical mean of [[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]. Define, with $s=t-t_0$, $$u(x,t):=\partial_sH_a(x,s)+H_b(x,s)+c^2\int_{t_0}^{t}H_{h(\cdot,v)}(x,t-v)\,dv,\qquad (x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T],$$ where $h(\cdot,v)$ denotes the map $x\mapsto h(x,v)$ and $\partial_sH_a$ is the partial derivative of $H_a$ in its second argument, evaluated at $s=t-t_0$. Then:

(a) $u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, $Wu=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$ (indeed on the open neighbourhood of the closed time interval on which the extension of $h$ is defined), $u(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=b$.

(b) Uniqueness: every $v\in C^2(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ in the extension sense with $Wv=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, $v(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tv(\cdot,t_0)=b$ equals $u$.

(c) Domain of dependence: let $\tilde a,\tilde b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $\tilde h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ and let $\tilde u$ be the corresponding solution. If $\tilde a=a$ and $\tilde b=b$ on the closed ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ and $\tilde h=h$ on the closed backward cone $K(x_*,t_*):=\{(y,v)\in\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,t_*]:|y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v)\}$ ([[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]), then $\tilde u(x_*,t_*)=u(x_*,t_*)$ for every $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t_*\in[t_0,T]$.

(d) Compact support: if $a$ vanishes off a compact $K_a\subset\mathbb R^3$, $b$ vanishes off a compact $K_b$, and $h(\cdot,v)$ vanishes off a fixed compact $K_h$ for every $v\in[t_0,T]$, then for every $t\in[t_0,T]$ the function $u(\cdot,t)$ has compact spatial support: if $K_a\cup K_b\cup K_h\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$ for some $\rho>0$ (which exists, [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), then $u(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$.

No boundary condition on a finite spatial domain, no finite-total-energy hypothesis, and no decay of $a,b,h$ at infinity is assumed or asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; a speed $c>0$; times $t_0<T$; data $a,b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$; a function $h$ of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, that is, the restriction of a $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$; the operators $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ and $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$; and the surface measure $d\Omega$ on the unit sphere $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ of total mass $4\pi$.

[F1] A map is of class $C^k$ when every word iterated coordinate partial derivative of order at most $k$ exists and is continuous, and of class $C^\infty$ when it is $C^k$ for every $k$; the Laplacian is $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<3}\partial_i\partial_if$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F2] Finite sums, scalar multiples and products of $C^k$ maps are $C^k$ and composites of composable $C^k$ maps are $C^k$ ([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]); the chain rule holds for total derivatives and continuous first partial derivatives imply total differentiability ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]); mixed second partials of a $C^2$ function commute ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]); and sums, scalar multiples and products of differentiable real functions differentiate by the usual rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F3] Spherical-mean family of a smooth spacetime function: with $h$ as given and $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$, the family $m(x,s,v):=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h(x+sn,v)\,d\Omega(n)$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, and every word iterated partial derivative is obtained by differentiating the composed integrand under the sphere integral; the statement is local, assumes no decay, compact support or boundedness of $h$, and uses uniform bounds only on compact parameter sets ([[lem-em-spherical-mean-family-smoothness]]).

[F4] Spherical means of a fixed smooth datum: for $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and $M_rf(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}f(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n)$, $r\ge0$, the map $r\mapsto M_rf(x)$ is smooth for $r\ge0$ and satisfies the Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity $\partial_r^2M_rf+\frac{2}{r}\partial_rM_rf=\Delta M_rf$ for $r>0$, and $H_f(x,t):=t\,M_{ct}f(x)$, $t\ge0$, satisfies $\partial_t^2H_f=c^2\Delta H_f$, $H_f(\cdot,0)=0$ and $\partial_tH_f(\cdot,0)=f$; all identities are local and assume no decay of $f$ ([[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]).

[F5] Parameter integrals: if $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is compact, measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure, $a<b$, and $f,\partial_tf$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$, then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ with derivative $\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx$; the same holds, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], with surface measure on a fixed compact $C^1$ hypersurface in place of $K$; moving parameter sets and singularities crossing the integration set are excluded ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]).

[F6] Differentiating an integral with moving endpoints: if $I$ is an open interval, $\alpha,\beta\in C^1(I)$ with $\alpha<\beta$, $J$ is an open interval containing the closures of the intervals $[\alpha(t),\beta(t)]$ and $F:I\times J\to\mathbb R$ is continuous with continuous $\partial_tF$, then $G(t)=\int_{\alpha(t)}^{\beta(t)}F(t,y)\,dy$ is $C^1$ on $I$ with $G'(t)=F(t,\beta(t))\beta'(t)-F(t,\alpha(t))\alpha'(t)+\int_{\alpha(t)}^{\beta(t)}\partial_tF(t,y)\,dy$ ([[lem-derivative-of-an-integral-with-moving-endpoints]]).

[F7] Continuity under the integral sign: if $f:X\times I\to\mathbb R$ is such that $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable for every $t$, $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is continuous for almost every $x$, and $|f(x,t)|\le g(x)$ with $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, then $t\mapsto\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$ is continuous on the interval $I$ ([[thm-continuity-under-the-integral-sign]]).

[F8] Closed boxes in $\mathbb R^m$ are compact in the Euclidean metric ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and a continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space attains a maximum and a minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F9] The reflection $n\mapsto-n$ of $S^2$ preserves the surface measure $d\Omega$ and $\int_{S^2}n\,d\Omega(n)=0$; orthogonal transformations of $\mathbb R^3$ preserve the surface measure ([[lem-first-moment-of-the-unit-sphere-vanishes]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).

[F10] For the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^m$, $\lVert u+v\rVert_2\le\lVert u\rVert_2+\lVert v\rVert_2$ and $\lVert\lambda u\rVert_2=|\lambda|\,\lVert u\rVert_2$, so also $\lVert u\rVert_2\ge\lVert u+v\rVert_2-\lVert v\rVert_2$; and $B_r(x_0)=\{x:|x-x_0|<r\}$, $\overline B_r(x_0)=\{x:|x-x_0|\le r\}$ are the open and closed Euclidean balls ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F11] Wave operator and Cauchy data: $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ and $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$, so $\Box_c=c^2W$; a classical solution on a time slab is $C^2$ on the open slab and satisfies the equation there, and Cauchy data are the limits as $t\downarrow t_0$; the closed backward cone with vertex $(x_*,t_*)$ and speed $c$ is $K(x_*,t_*)=\{(y,v):t_0\le v\le t_*,\ |y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v)\}$ with base ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ ([[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]], [[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]).

[F12] Local uniqueness and domain of dependence: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $u,v\in C^2$ solve $\Box_cu=f$ and $\Box_cv=g$ on a neighbourhood of the closed backward cone $K^-(x_0,t_0)$ with $t_0>0$, if $f=g$ on the cone and $u(\cdot,0)=v(\cdot,0)$, $u_t(\cdot,0)=v_t(\cdot,0)$ on the base ball $B_{ct_0}(x_0)$, then $u=v$ on $K^-(x_0,t_0)$ ([[thm-domain-of-dependence-and-local-uniqueness]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The setting. Let $h$ also denote its $C^\infty$ extension to $\mathbb R^3\times J$, put $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\times J$, and let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:\langle n,n\rangle=1\}$ carry the surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$ with normalised probability $\nu:=d\Omega/4\pi$ of [F9]. For a fixed datum $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ put $m_\varphi(x,s,v):=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}\varphi(x+sn)\,d\Omega(n)$ (independent of $v$), so that $H_\varphi(x,t):=t\,m_\varphi(x,ct,v_0)$ for any fixed $v_0\in J$ is the $H_\varphi$ of the statement; for the datum $h$ put $m(x,s,v):=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h(x+sn,v)\,d\Omega(n)$ on $\Omega$, so that $m_\varphi=m_{h_\varphi}$ for the spacetime datum $h_\varphi(x,v):=\varphi(x)$. Define, for $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $s:=t-t_0$, $$u_h(x,t):=\partial_sH_a(x,s)+H_b(x,s),\qquad H(x,\sigma;v):=\sigma\,m(x,c\sigma,v),$$ and, for $t\in[t_0,T]$, $u_s(x,t):=c^2\int_{t_0}^{t}H(x,t-v;v)\,dv$ and $u:=u_h+u_s$; here $\partial_sH_a(x,s)$ is the derivative of $H_a$ in its second argument at $(x,s)$. All surface integrals are read under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention carried by [F3] and [F5]. [given, A1, F3, F4, F5, F9, F11]

1.2 Properties of the family. By [F3] applied to $h$ and to each $h_\varphi$, the families $m$ and $m_\varphi$ are of class $C^\infty$ on their domains in the extension sense, and every word iterated partial derivative equals the sphere integral of the corresponding derivative of the composed integrand. In particular $m(x,0,v)=h(x,v)$ and $m_\varphi(x,0,v)=\varphi(x)$, because the sphere integral of the constant $\varphi(x)$ is $\varphi(x)\cdot4\pi/4\pi$; consequently $H_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$ and $\partial_tH_\varphi(\cdot,0)=\varphi$ by the product rule [F2]. The reflection substitution $n\mapsto-n$ with [F9] gives $m(x,-s,v)=m(x,s,v)$ and $m_\varphi(x,-s,v)=m_\varphi(x,s,v)$: both families are even in $s$. Hence the Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity $$\partial_s^2m+\frac{2}{s}\partial_sm=\Delta m\qquad(s\ne0)$$ holds on $\Omega\setminus\{s=0\}$ and likewise with $m_\varphi$ in place of $m$: for $s>0$ it is [F4] applied to the fixed smooth datum $x\mapsto h(x,v)$ (respectively $x\mapsto\varphi(x)$), and for $s<0$ it follows from the evenness just proved, since for an even $C^\infty$ function of $s$ the derivative $\partial_s$ is odd and $\partial_s^2$ is even while $\Delta$ differentiates only the $x$-variable. [given, F2, F3, F4, F9]

2.1 The homogeneous blocks solve the wave equation with the prescribed data. Fix $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$. By [F2] the function $H_\varphi(x,t)=t\,m_\varphi(x,ct,v_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Differentiating in $t$ and using the identity of step 1.2 at $s=ct$, one has $\partial_t^2H_\varphi=2c\,\partial_sm_\varphi+c^2t\,\partial_s^2m_\varphi$ and $c^2\Delta H_\varphi=c^2t\,\Delta m_\varphi=c^2t\,\partial_s^2m_\varphi+2c\,\partial_sm_\varphi$ for $t\ne0$; at $t=0$ both sides vanish, since $H_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$ gives $\Delta H_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$ and $\partial_sm_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$ by evenness. Hence $\partial_t^2H_\varphi=c^2\Delta H_\varphi$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, and together with $H_\varphi(\cdot,0)=0$ and $\partial_tH_\varphi(\cdot,0)=\varphi$ from step 1.2 the same identities hold for $\partial_sH_\varphi$ after differentiating in $t$ and commuting $\partial_t$ with $\Delta$ through [F2] in the form $\partial_t\partial_i\partial_iH_\varphi=\partial_i\partial_i\partial_tH_\varphi$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, F4]

2.2 The Duhamel identity for a smooth datum. Let $g$ be of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, with family $m_g$, and for $\tau>0$ with $t_0+\tau\in J$ put $J_g(\tau):=\int_0^\tau\sigma\,m_g(x,c\sigma,t_0+\tau-\sigma)\,d\sigma$ at a fixed $x$. Then $$\partial_\tau^2J_g-c^2\Delta J_g=m_g(x,0,t_0+\tau).$$ Indeed two applications of [F6] (with $\alpha\equiv0<\beta(\tau)=\tau$, the integrand $F(\tau,\sigma):=\sigma\,m_g(x,c\sigma,t_0+\tau-\sigma)$ being continuous with continuous $\tau$-derivative since $m_g$ is $C^\infty$ by [F3] and [F2]) give $\partial_\tau J_g=\tau\,m_g(x,c\tau,t_0)+\int_0^\tau\sigma\,\partial_vm_g(x,c\sigma,t_0+\tau-\sigma)\,d\sigma$ and $\partial_\tau^2J_g=\partial_\tau[\tau\,m_g(x,c\tau,t_0)]+\tau\,\partial_vm_g(x,c\tau,t_0)+\int_0^\tau\sigma\,\partial_v^2m_g\,d\sigma$, where $\partial_v$ denotes the derivative in the third argument, while [F5] in the $x$-variables gives $\Delta J_g=\int_0^\tau\sigma\,\Delta m_g\,d\sigma$; substituting $r=\tau-\sigma$ in these three integrals and inserting the identity of step 1.2 for the bracket $\partial_v^2m_g-c^2\Delta m_g$ at $s=c(\tau-r)>0$, the computation telescopes: with $q(r):=m_g(x,c(\tau-r),t_0+r)$ one has $q(0)=m_g(x,c\tau,t_0)$, $q(\tau)=m_g(x,0,t_0+\tau)$, $q'(r)=-c\,\partial_sm_g+\partial_vm_g$ and $q''=c^2\partial_s^2m_g-2c\,\partial_s\partial_vm_g+\partial_v^2m_g$, all evaluated at $(x,c(\tau-r),t_0+r)$, so $\partial_v^2m_g-c^2\Delta m_g=q''+2c\,A'-\frac{2c}{\tau-r}A$ with $A(r):=\partial_sm_g(x,c(\tau-r),t_0+r)$; multiplying by $\tau-r$, integrating over $[0,\tau]$ and using $\int_0^\tau(\tau-r)q''(r)\,dr=-\tau q'(0)+q(\tau)-q(0)$ and $\int_0^\tau(\tau-r)A'(r)\,dr=-\tau A(0)+\int_0^\tau A\,dr$ leaves exactly $q(\tau)=m_g(x,0,t_0+\tau)$. [step 1.2, F2, F3, F5, F6, algebra]

2.3 Smoothness of the source term and its extension to a neighbourhood. Put $\theta:=t-t_0$ and, for $\theta$ in an open interval $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ containing $[0,T-t_0]$ and small enough that $t_0+\theta(1-z)\in J$ for all $z\in[0,1]$, define $$\tilde u_s(x,t):=c^2\theta^2\int_0^1z\,m(x,c\theta z,t_0+\theta(1-z))\,dz.$$ By step 1.2 and [F2] the integrand $A(x,\theta,z):=c^2z\,m(x,c\theta z,t_0+\theta(1-z))$ extends to a $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R^3\times(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times[0,1]$ whose word derivatives are continuous there. Iterating [F5] in the parameter directions $x_j$ and $\theta$ over the fixed compact set $[0,1]$ shows that every word derivative in $(x,\theta)$ of $\int_0^1A(x,\theta,z)\,dz$ exists and equals $\int_0^1D^wA(x,\theta,z)\,dz$; each of these integrals is continuous in $(x,\theta)$ by [F7], since for fixed $(x,\theta)$ the integrand $z\mapsto D^wA(x,\theta,z)$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ hence integrable, for fixed $z$ it is continuous in $(x,\theta)$, and it is dominated on a small parameter interval by the finite maximum of $|D^wA|$ over the nonempty closed box $\{x\}\times[\theta_1,\theta_2]\times[0,1]$, which is compact by [F8]. Hence $\int_0^1A\,dz$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(\theta_1,\theta_2)$, and so is $\tilde u_s=c^2\theta^2\int_0^1A\,dz$ by [F2]. For $\theta>0$ the substitution $v=t_0+\theta(1-z)$, $dv=-\theta\,dz$, in the defining integral of $u_s$ gives $\tilde u_s=u_s$, while $\tilde u_s(x,t_0)=0=u_s(x,t_0)$; hence $\tilde u:=u_h+\tilde u_s$ is a $C^\infty$ extension of $u$ to the open neighbourhood $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0-\delta,T+\delta)$ of the closed slab, and $u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense. [step 1.2, F2, F5, F7, F8, algebra, choose]

3.1 The wave equation on the whole neighbourhood. Let $\tilde H$ denote the $C^\infty$ extension of $h$ to $\mathbb R^3\times J$ and let $\tilde u=u_h+\tilde u_s$ be the extension of step 2.3, and put $R(x,t):=\partial_t^2\tilde u-c^2\Delta\tilde u-c^2\tilde H(x,t)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0-\delta,T+\delta)$; $R$ is continuous there by step 2.3 and [F2]. For $\theta>0$, [F5] gives $\Delta u_s=c^2\int_{t_0}^t\Delta_xH(x,t-v;v)\,dv$ and step 2.2 with $g=h$ gives $\partial_t^2u_s=c^2h+c^2\Delta u_s$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T+\delta)$; the homogeneous part satisfies $\partial_t^2u_h=c^2\Delta u_h$ on all of $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ by step 2.1 and [F2], so $R=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T+\delta)$. For $\theta<0$ put $\mu:=-\theta>0$ and $\hat h(x,v):=h(x,2t_0-v)$, an extension-sense smooth datum on an interval around $t_0$, with family $\hat m(x,s,v):=m(x,s,2t_0-v)$; the substitution $\sigma=\mu z$, $z\in[0,1]$, together with the evenness of step 1.2 gives $\tilde u_s(x,t_0-\mu)=c^2\int_0^\mu\sigma\,\hat m(x,c\sigma,t_0+\mu-\sigma)\,d\sigma$, so step 2.2 applied to $\hat h$ gives $\partial_t^2\tilde u_s-c^2\Delta\tilde u_s=c^2\hat m(x,0,t_0+\mu)=c^2h(x,t_0-\mu)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0-\delta,t_0)$, while the homogeneous part satisfies the homogeneous equation there by step 2.1; hence $R=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0-\delta,t_0)$. A continuous function vanishing on both open pieces vanishes on their union, so $\partial_t^2\tilde u=c^2\Delta\tilde u+c^2\tilde H$, that is $W\tilde u=\tilde H$, on the open neighbourhood $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0-\delta,T+\delta)$; restricting gives $Wu=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$ and indeed on the open neighbourhood of the closed time interval on which the extension of $h$ is defined. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, F2, F5, F11, algebra]

3.2 The initial data. At $t=t_0$ one has $\tilde u(x,t_0)=\partial_sH_a(x,0)+H_b(x,0)+0=a(x)+0+0$, since $\partial_sH_a(x,0)=m_a(x,0,v_0)=a(x)$ and $H_b(x,0)=0$ by step 2.1, while $\tilde u_s(x,t_0)=0$ by step 2.3. Likewise $\partial_t\tilde u(x,t_0)=\partial_s^2H_a(x,0)+\partial_sH_b(x,0)+\partial_t\tilde u_s(x,t_0)=0+b(x)+0$: here $\partial_s^2H_a(x,0)=c^2\Delta H_a(x,0)=0$ and $\partial_sH_b(x,0)=b(x)$ by step 2.1, and $\partial_t\tilde u_s(x,t_0)=0$ by the product rule [F2] applied to $\theta^2\int_0^1A(x,\theta,z)\,dz$ at $\theta=0$ in step 2.3. This proves the initial-data clause of (a). [step 2.1, step 2.3, F2, algebra]

4.1 Uniqueness. Let $v$ be of class $C^2$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense with $Wv=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, $v(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tv(\cdot,t_0)=b$, and form the function $\tilde v$ equal to $v$ for $t\ge t_0$ and to $u$ for $t\le t_0$: the pieces agree in value, in first partial derivatives and in second partial derivatives at $t=t_0$, the second time derivative there being $\partial_t^2v(\cdot,t_0)=\partial_t^2u(\cdot,t_0)=c^2\Delta a+c^2h(\cdot,t_0)$ by the equation of step 3.1 and the data, and each second partial derivative is continuous on its side and has the stated common value, so $\tilde v$ is $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of the closed slab; then $w:=u-\tilde v$ is $C^2$ on that neighbourhood, satisfies $\Box_cw=0$ on each of the open half-slabs $t>t_0$ (where both $u$ and $\tilde v$ solve $Wu=h$) and $t<t_0$ (where the two pieces coincide), and since $\Box_cw$ is continuous it vanishes at $t=t_0$ as well, so $\Box_cw=0$ on the whole neighbourhood; also $w(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $\partial_tw(\cdot,t_0)=0$ on all of $\mathbb R^3$. Fix $(x_*,t_*)$ with $t_0<t_*\le T$ and apply [F12] in the translated time coordinates $\tau:=t-t_0$ to the pair $(w,0)$ on the closed backward cone with vertex $(x_*,t_*)$: the vertex time is $t_*-t_0>0$, both functions are $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of the closed cone (contained in the neighbourhood of the closed slab on which $w$ is defined), the sources agree on the cone, and the Cauchy data agree on the base ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$; hence $w=0$ on the cone, so $u(x_*,t_*)=\tilde v(x_*,t_*)=v(x_*,t_*)$. Since $(x_*,t_*)$ is arbitrary in $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T]$, this gives $u=v$, which is clause (b). [step 3.1, step 3.2, F2, F11, F12]

4.2 Domain of dependence. Let $\tilde a,\tilde b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, let $\tilde h$ be of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, and let $\tilde u$ be the solution produced by the construction of steps 2.3 and 3.1 applied to $(\tilde a,\tilde b,\tilde h)$; by those steps $\tilde u$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, satisfies $W\tilde u=\tilde h$ on an open neighbourhood of the closed slab and has data $\tilde a,\tilde b$ at $t_0$. Suppose $\tilde a=a$ and $\tilde b=b$ on the closed ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ and $\tilde h=h$ on the closed cone $K(x_*,t_*)$ of [F11]. Then $w:=u-\tilde u$ is $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of the closed slab with $\Box_cw=c^2(h-\tilde h)$ on each open half-slab, hence on the whole neighbourhood because both sides are continuous, it vanishes together with its time derivative at $t_0$ on the base ball, and $h-\tilde h=0$ on the cone; applying [F12] in translated time coordinates to the pair $(w,0)$ therefore gives $w=0$ on the closed backward cone, and in particular $u(x_*,t_*)=\tilde u(x_*,t_*)$. This is clause (c). [step 3.1, F11, F12]

5.1 Compact support. Assume that $a$ vanishes off a compact $K_a\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, that $b$ vanishes off a compact $K_b$, that $h(\cdot,v)$ vanishes off a fixed compact $K_h$ for every $v\in[t_0,T]$, and that $K_a\cup K_b\cup K_h\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$ for some $\rho>0$, which exists because every compact subset of $\mathbb R^3$ is bounded by [F8]. Fix $t\in[t_0,T]$ and $x$ with $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$ and compare $u$ with the solution $\tilde u$ of the construction for the data $\tilde a=\tilde b=0$, $\tilde h=0$, namely $\tilde u=0$. Every $y\in\overline B_{c(t-t_0)}(x)$ satisfies $|y|\ge|x|-|y-x|\ge|x|-c(t-t_0)>\rho$ by the reverse triangle inequality [F10], so $y\notin K_a\cup K_b$ and $a(y)=b(y)=0=\tilde a(y)=\tilde b(y)$; similarly every $(y,v)\in K(x,t)$ satisfies $|y|\ge|x|-|y-x|\ge|x|-c(t-v)\ge|x|-c(t-t_0)>\rho$, so $y\notin K_h$ and $h(y,v)=0=\tilde h(y,v)$. The hypotheses of clause (c), proved in step 4.2, are therefore met at the vertex $(x,t)$ and give $u(x,t)=\tilde u(x,t)=0$. This is clause (d). [step 4.2, F8, F10, F11, algebra]

6.1 Conclusion. Steps 2.3 and 3.1 show that $u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense and that $Wu=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, indeed on the open neighbourhood of the closed time interval on which the extension of $h$ is defined; step 3.2 gives $u(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=b$, completing clause (a); clause (b) is step 4.1, clause (c) is step 4.2 and clause (d) is step 5.1. The argument assumed no boundary condition on a finite spatial domain, no finite-total-energy hypothesis and no spatial decay or compact support of the data; only local bounds on compact parameter sets were used. [step 2.3, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, F1] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] and its suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]]). All three computations use the notation of that theorem: $c>0$, $H_\varphi(x,s)=s\,M_{cs}\varphi(x)$ with the spherical mean $M$ of [[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]], $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ and $u$ the solution displayed there.

(i) (The compact-support clause needs its hypothesis.) Take $t_0=0$, $a=b=0$ and the spatially constant source $h(x,t)=1$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[0,T]$. Then the theorem's solution is $u(x,t)=c^2t^2/2$, which is independent of $x$; it satisfies $\partial_t^2u=c^2=c^2h$ and $\Delta u=0$, hence $Wu=h$, with $u(\cdot,0)=\partial_tu(\cdot,0)=0$. For every $t>0$ the function $u(\cdot,t)=c^2t^2/2$ is a nonzero constant on $\mathbb R^3$, so it is not compactly supported: the hypothesis in clause (d) that $h(\cdot,v)$ vanish off one fixed compact set cannot be dropped, and the corresponding hypothesis of [[thm-wave-duhamel-principle]] (source compactly supported in $x$ for each fixed $s$) is genuinely used by that item.

(ii) (Support propagation made explicit.) Take $a=b=0$, $t_0=0$ and $h(x,t)=h_0(x)$ with $h_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ vanishing off $\overline B_1(0)$. Then $u(x,t)=c^2\int_0^t(t-v)M_{c(t-v)}h_0(x)\,dv$, and $M_rh_0(x)=0$ for every $r>0$ with $S_r(x)\cap\overline B_1(0)=\emptyset$; hence $u(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>1+ct$. This is clause (d) with $K_h=\overline B_1(0)$ and $\rho=1$, exhibited from the explicit formula.

(iii) (The class contains non-decaying data with divergent total energy.) Take $a=0$, $b(x)=x_1$ and $h=0$. Since the first moment of the unit-sphere measure vanishes, $M_{cs}b(x)=x_1$ ([[lem-first-moment-of-the-unit-sphere-vanishes]], with the surface measure identified with the polar measure of [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]), so the theorem's solution is $u(x,t)=(t-t_0)x_1$: it satisfies $\partial_t^2u=0=\Delta u$, hence $Wu=0$, with $u(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=x_1$. The solution is unbounded on every time slice $t>t_0$. Moreover its total energy at time $t$ in the sense of [[def-wave-energy-and-energy-flux]] is $+\infty$ whenever $t\ne t_0$: the energy density is $\tfrac12(x_1^2+c^2(t-t_0)^2)$, and for every $R>0$ the box $[-R,R]^3$ gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\tfrac12\bigl(x_1^2+c^2(t-t_0)^2\bigr)\,d\lambda\;\ge\;\frac12\int_{[-R,R]^3}x_1^2\,d\lambda\;=\;\frac12\Bigl(\frac{2R^3}{3}\Bigr)(4R^2)\;=\;\frac{4}{3}R^5\longrightarrow+\infty$$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Hence the finite-initial-energy hypothesis of [[cor-energy-uniqueness-for-the-wave-cauchy-problem]] fails for this smooth datum while the theorem's local uniqueness (b) still applies; the theorem asserts no decay at spatial infinity and no finite-energy property, and needs none.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; a speed $c>0$; the data of clause (i) $t_0=0$, $a=b=0$, $h\equiv1$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[0,T]$; of clause (ii) $a=b=0$, $t_0=0$, $h(x,t)=h_0(x)$ with $h_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ vanishing off $\overline B_1(0)$; and of clause (iii) $a=0$, $b(x)=x_1$, $h=0$, with $t_0<T$ arbitrary.

[F1] Wave Cauchy problem: for $c>0$, $t_0<T$, $a,b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and $h$ of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, the function $$u(x,t)=\partial_sH_a(x,s)+H_b(x,s)+c^2\int_{t_0}^tH_{h(\cdot,v)}(x,t-v)\,dv,\qquad s=t-t_0,$$ where $H_\varphi(x,\sigma)=\sigma M_{c\sigma}\varphi(x)$ and $M_r\varphi(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}\varphi(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n)$, is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense and satisfies $Wu=h$, $u(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=b$ with $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$; every $C^2$ extension-sense solution with the same data equals it (clause (b)); and if $a$ vanishes off a compact $K_a$, $b$ off a compact $K_b$ and every $h(\cdot,v)$ off one fixed compact $K_h\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$, then $u(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$ (clause (d)) ([[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]).

[F2] For $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $r\mapsto M_rf(x)$ is smooth for $r\ge0$ with the normalisation of [F1] and no decay hypotheses; for each fixed $f$ the function $H_f(x,t)=tM_{ct}f(x)$ is the one used in [F1] ([[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]).

[F3] The reflection $n\mapsto-n$ preserves the surface measure $d\Omega$, $\int_{S^2}1\,d\Omega=4\pi$, $\int_{S^2}n\,d\Omega(n)=0$, and the chart surface measure on $S^2$ is the polar surface measure ([[lem-first-moment-of-the-unit-sphere-vanishes]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Consequently $M_r1(x)=1$ and $M_r(x\mapsto x_1)(x)=x_1$ for every $r\ge0$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^3$, since the sphere integral of the constant $1$ is $4\pi$ and the sphere integral of $n\mapsto x_1+rn_1$ is $4\pi x_1$.

[F4] Energy: for a $C^2$ function $u$ the energy density is $e=\frac12(u_t^2+c^2|Du|^2)$ with $u_t=\partial_tu$ and $Du$ the spatial gradient; for measurable $\Omega$ with $\int_\Omega e<\infty$ the total energy is $E_\Omega(t)=\int_\Omega e(x,t)\,dx$, and when the integral is infinite the total energy is $+\infty$ ([[def-wave-energy-and-energy-flux]]).

[F5] Energy uniqueness for the wave Cauchy problem: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if a classical solution of $\Box_cu=0$ has Cauchy data $(u_0,u_1)$ with differentiable $u_0$ and the total energy has a finite initial value $E_{\mathbb R^3}(0)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}(u_1^2+c^2|Du_0|^2)$ and is conserved in the sharp form $E_{\mathbb R^3}(t)=E_{\mathbb R^3}(0)$, then vanishing data force $u\equiv0$ ([[cor-energy-uniqueness-for-the-wave-cauchy-problem]]).

[F6] For nonnegative measurable $f\le g$ one has $\int f\le\int g$; Tonelli's theorem permits the iterated integral of a nonnegative measurable function on a product of $\sigma$-finite spaces to be computed in either order; the box $[-R,R]^3$ has Lebesgue measure $(2R)^3$ with $\int_{-R}^Rx_1^2\,dx_1=2R^3/3$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

[F7] The published Duhamel principle for the forced wave equation assumes a source continuous and compactly supported in $x$ for each fixed $s$, with all spatial derivatives through order $\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1$ jointly continuous; its launched-solution construction applies to the admissible slices of the source ([[thm-wave-duhamel-principle]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Setting and clause (i). With $a=b=0$, $t_0=0$ and $h\equiv1$, [F1] gives $u(x,t)=c^2\int_0^tH_1(x,t-v)\,dv$ with $H_1(x,\sigma)=\sigma M_{c\sigma}1(x)=\sigma$ by [F3]; hence $u(x,t)=c^2\int_0^t(t-v)\,dv=c^2t^2/2$ for $0\le t\le T$. Then $\partial_t^2u=c^2$, $\Delta u=0$ by [F1], so $Wu=c^{-2}c^2-0=1=h$, and $u(\cdot,0)=0$, $\partial_tu(\cdot,0)=0$ by the same formula. For every $t>0$ the function $u(\cdot,t)=c^2t^2/2$ is a nonzero constant on $\mathbb R^3$, so it does not vanish off any compact subset of $\mathbb R^3$: the hypothesis of clause (d) that the source vanish off one fixed compact set cannot be dropped. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Clause (ii). With $a=b=0$, $t_0=0$ and $h(x,t)=h_0(x)$, [F1] gives $u(x,t)=c^2\int_0^t(t-v)M_{c(t-v)}h_0(x)\,dv$. Fix $t\in[0,T]$ and $x$ with $|x|>1+ct$; for every $v\in[0,t]$ and every $y$ with $|y-x|=c(t-v)$ one has $|y|\ge|x|-|y-x|>1+ct-c(t-v)\ge1$ by the reverse triangle inequality [F3], so $y\notin\overline B_1(0)$ and the integrand $h_0(y)$ vanishes identically on the sphere $S_{c(t-v)}(x)$; hence $M_{c(t-v)}h_0(x)=0$ and $u(x,t)=0$. This exhibits clause (d) with $K_h=\overline B_1(0)$ and $\rho=1$ from the displayed formula of the theorem. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3]

2.2 Clause (iii). With $a=0$, $b(x)=x_1$ and $h=0$, [F1] gives $u(x,t)=H_b(x,s)=sM_{cs}b(x)=(t-t_0)x_1$ by [F3]; then $\partial_t^2u=0$ and $\Delta u=0$, so $Wu=0$, while $u(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=x_1=b$. The solution is unbounded on every time slice $t>t_0$. Its energy density is $e(x,t)=\frac12x_1^2+\frac12c^2(t-t_0)^2$ by [F4] and [F1]; for every $R>0$ the box integral is $\int_{[-R,R]^3}e\,d\lambda=\frac12\bigl(\frac{2R^3}{3}\bigr)(2R)^2+\frac12c^2(t-t_0)^2(2R)^3=\frac{4}{3}R^5+4c^2(t-t_0)^2R^3\ge\frac43R^5$ by [F6], which tends to $+\infty$; monotonicity of the nonnegative integral over $\mathbb R^3$ therefore gives total energy $+\infty$ for every $t\ne t_0$, and in particular the initial energy $E_{\mathbb R^3}(t_0)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}x_1^2\,d\lambda=+\infty$. So the finite-initial-energy hypothesis of the energy-uniqueness corollary [F5] fails for this smooth datum, while clause (b) of [F1] still supplies uniqueness, since it assumes no finite-energy or decay hypothesis. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6]

3.1 The two hypothesis boundaries and the published Duhamel principle. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show that in the wave Cauchy theorem the compact-support hypothesis of clause (d) is a genuine hypothesis and that it yields the sharp propagation bound $|x|>1+ct$ for a source supported in $\overline B_1(0)$; step 2.2 shows that smooth data of unbounded energy are admitted by the theorem's existence, uniqueness and representation clauses, although they are outside the energy-uniqueness corollary. The published Duhamel principle [F7] carries the per-slice compact-support hypothesis by which its own statement places each source slice in the admissible velocity-data class, so that hypothesis does real work in the item; the constant source of step 1.1 has no compact spatial support on any slice, so [F7] is not applicable to that witness, while the theorem of this pair is defined for it and yields the non-compactly-supported solution displayed in step 1.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, F7] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), in the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $s\ge1$ be an integer and put $\tau=s+1$. Write $r(x)=|x|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $\Delta$ be the Euclidean Laplacian ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). Then for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, $$\|r^{-\tau}u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}\le\frac{2}{s}\,\|r^{-\tau+2}\Delta u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}.$$ Moreover, if $u\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ is compactly supported in an annulus $\{0<a\le|x|\le b\}$, then the weak second derivatives of $u$ exist as locally square integrable functions, $\Delta u$ denotes their sum in the weak sense ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]), and the same inequality holds for $u$. The weights $r^{-\tau}$ and $r^{-\tau+2}$ are bounded on every fixed compact annulus $\{a_0\le|x|\le b_0\}$ with $0<a_0\le b_0$, and this boundedness on the support of the function is the only property of the weights used in the density extension below; the weight $r^{-\tau}$ is unbounded at the origin for every $s\ge1$, and the weight $r^{-\tau+2}$ is unbounded at the origin for every $s\ge2$ and equals the constant $1$ for $s=1$. That is why the extension is stated for functions whose support stays away from $r=0$. The constant $2/s$ is explicit and is not claimed to be sharp.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]); an integer $s\ge1$ with $\tau=s+1$; first a function $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$, later a class $u\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ compactly supported in $\{0<a\le|x|\le b\}$.

[L1] Polar coordinates: for every Borel measurable $f:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\,d\lambda_3=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^2}f(r\omega)r^{2}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$, where $\sigma$ is the polar surface measure on $S^2$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

[L2] One-dimensional substitution with the absolute derivative: if $\varphi$ is $C^1$ and injective with nonvanishing derivative on a neighbourhood of $[a,b]$ and $f$ is continuous on an interval containing $\varphi([a,b])$, then $\int_{\min\{\varphi(a),\varphi(b)\}}^{\max\{\varphi(a),\varphi(b)\}}f(y)\,dy=\int_a^bf(\varphi(x))|\varphi'(x)|\,dx$ ([[cor-one-dimensional-change-of-variables-with-absolute-derivative]]).

[L3] The Laplacian is $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_i\partial_i\partial_if$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), the divergence and gradient are the coordinate operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F$ for $C^1$ data ([[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]).

[L4] Coordinate differentiation of the composites below uses the chain rule for total derivatives and the sum, scalar and product rules ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[L5] Spherical harmonics: the space $H_l$ of homogeneous harmonic polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$ has dimension $2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degrees are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ for the unnormalised surface measure of total mass $4\pi$, and the union over $l$ of their restrictions to $S^2$ admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]).

[L6] Parseval for a complete orthonormal family: a family is complete if and only if $\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$ for every $x$, the sum being the supremum of finite subsums ([[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]).

[L7] Fourier calculus in the $2\pi$ convention: Plancherel's theorem makes the Fourier transform a unitary isometry of $L^2$, and $\mathcal F(\partial_tu)(\xi)=2\pi i\xi\,\mathcal Fu(\xi)$ ([[thm-plancherel]], [[thm-fourier-differentiation-and-multiplication-identities-on-tempered-distributions]]).

[L8] Tonelli's theorem: for a nonnegative measurable function on a $\sigma$-finite product space the iterated integrals agree; the counting measure on $\mathbb N_0^2$ is $\sigma$-finite ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[L9] Between concentric balls $0<\rho<R$ there is a smooth bump equal to $1$ on $\overline B_\rho(0)$ with support in $B_R(0)$ ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]).

[L10] Under Countable Choice, $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ is dense in $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ in the Sobolev norm ([[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]]).

[L11] Weak Leibniz rule with a smooth factor: for $\eta\in C_c^\infty$ and $u\in W^{k,2}$, the product $\eta u$ belongs to $W^{k,2}$ with $D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$, and the weak derivatives are the almost-everywhere classes of these sums ([[lem-weak-leibniz-rule-with-a-smooth-factor]]).

[L12] Weak derivatives and Sobolev spaces: the weak derivative is defined by the signed test identity, and $W^{k,p}$ consists of $L^p$ classes whose weak derivatives of every order at most $k$ are $L^p$ classes ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

**Choice accounting.** Countable Choice is used through [L10] (whose density statement carries it) and through [L6] and [L7] (the Parseval and Plancherel suppliers carry it); the coordinate computations, the polar-coordinate identity and the modal summation consume nothing beyond those suppliers.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, an integer $s\ge1$ with $\tau=s+1$, and first a smooth compactly supported $u$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$.

1.1 **Change of variables.** Assume first $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$. The map $(t,n)\mapsto e^{-t}n$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R\times S^2$ onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$; since $u$ is smooth and compactly supported away from the origin, the functions $v(t,n):=e^{-t/2}u(e^{-t}n)$ and $w(t,n):=e^{st}v(t,n)$ are smooth and $w$ is compactly supported in $t$ uniformly in $n$. By [L1] with the substitution $r=e^{-t}$, whose derivative $|\mathrm dr/\mathrm dt|=e^{-t}=r$ is supplied by [L2], the measure becomes $dx=e^{-3t}\,dt\,d\sigma(n)$; writing $u(x)=e^{(1/2-s)t}w(t,n)$ gives $$r^{-2\tau}u^2\,dx=e^{2\tau t}e^{(1-2s)t}w^2e^{-3t}\,dt\,d\sigma=w^2\,dt\,d\sigma,$$ because $2\tau-2s-2=0$. Hence $\int_{\mathbb R^3}r^{-2\tau}u^2\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{S^2}w^2\,d\sigma\,dt$. [L2, L1, L4]

1.2 **Spherical Laplacian and the polar form of $\Delta$.** For $g\in C^2(S^2)$ let $G(x):=g(x/|x|)$ be its degree-zero homogeneous extension to $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and define $\Delta_{S^2}g(n):=\Delta G(n)$ for $n\in S^2$. This is well defined: by the chain rule, $\Delta(G\circ m_t)=t^2(\Delta G)\circ m_t$ for every $t>0$ and every $C^2$ function on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, while $G\circ m_t=G$; hence $(\Delta G)(tn)=t^{-2}\Delta G(n)$, and $r^2\Delta G(rn)=\Delta G(n)$ does not depend on $r$, so the value at $r=1$ defines a function of $n$ alone. For $\psi\in C^2((0,\infty))$ the product rule gives $\nabla(\psi(r)G(x))=\psi'(r)G(x)\,x/r+\psi(r)\nabla G(x)$, and $\langle\nabla G(x),x\rangle/r=\partial_rG=0$; using [L3] twice and the direct computation $\operatorname{div}(x/r)=\sum_i\partial_i(x_i/r)=3/r-r^2/r^3=2/r$, $$\operatorname{div}\bigl(\psi'G\tfrac xr\bigr)=\psi''G+\psi'G\tfrac2r,\qquad \operatorname{div}(\psi\nabla G)=\psi'\langle\tfrac xr,\nabla G\rangle+\psi\Delta G=\psi\,\Delta G,$$ so that $\Delta(\psi(r)G)=\bigl(\psi''(r)+\tfrac2r\psi'(r)\bigr)G+r^{-2}\psi(r)\Delta_{S^2}g(n)$, the last step using $\Delta G(rn)=r^{-2}\Delta_{S^2}g(n)$. In particular, for a harmonic homogeneous polynomial $H_l$ of degree $l$ and $h:=H_l|_{S^2}$, the identity with $\psi(r)=r^l$ and $G=H_l$ gives $0=\Delta H_l=r^{l-2}\bigl(l^2+l+\Delta_{S^2}h\bigr)$, hence $\Delta_{S^2}h=-l(l+1)h$. The same computation applied to a general $F\in C^2(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$ with $f(r,n):=F(rn)$, whose gradient splits as $\nabla F=(\partial_rf)\,n+r^{-1}\nabla_{S^2,n}f$ into radial and tangential parts, gives the general polar form $\Delta F(rn)=\partial_r^2f+\tfrac2r\partial_rf+r^{-2}\Delta_{S^2,n}f$; the divergence of a tangential field $Y$ with $Y(x)=\tilde Y(x/|x|)$ is $r^{-1}\operatorname{div}_{S^2}\tilde Y$ in these coordinates, and $\operatorname{div}_{S^2}\nabla_{S^2}=\Delta_{S^2}$. [L3, L4]

2.1 **The conjugated operator.** Apply the polar form of step 1.2 to $u(x)=r^{-1/2}v(t,n)$, $t=-\ln r$, whose radial part is $f(r,n)=r^{-1/2}v(-\ln r,n)$. Coordinate differentiation by [L4] gives $\partial_ru=-\tfrac12r^{-3/2}v-r^{-3/2}v_t$ and $\partial_r^2u=r^{-5/2}\bigl(v_{tt}+2v_t+\tfrac34v\bigr)$, so $$\partial_r^2u+\frac2r\partial_ru=r^{-5/2}\bigl(v_{tt}-\tfrac14v\bigr),$$ while $r^{-2}\Delta_{S^2,n}u=r^{-5/2}\Delta_{S^2}v$. Hence $$\Delta u=r^{-5/2}\bigl(v_{tt}+\Delta_{S^2}v-\tfrac14v\bigr).$$ Substituting $v=e^{-st}w$ gives $v_{tt}=e^{-st}(\partial_t-s)^2w$ and $\Delta_{S^2}v=e^{-st}\Delta_{S^2}w$, so with $L:=(\partial_t-s)^2+\Delta_{S^2}-\tfrac14$ one has $$\Delta u=r^{-5/2}e^{-st}\,Lw.$$ [step 1.2, L4]

2.2 **Modal decomposition.** For almost every $t$ the function $w(t,\cdot)$ is smooth on $S^2$, hence in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$, and by [L5] it expands as $w(t,\cdot)=\sum_{l,m}w_{lm}(t)Y_{lm}$ in a complete orthonormal basis $\{Y_{lm}\}$ of degree-$l$ spherical harmonics, the coefficients $w_{lm}(t)=\langle w(t,\cdot),Y_{lm}\rangle$ being smooth in $t$. By step 1.2, each $Y_{lm}$ satisfies $\Delta_{S^2}Y_{lm}=-l(l+1)Y_{lm}$, and $\Delta_{S^2}$ is symmetric for the surface pairing: in the spherical charts its explicit form $(1/\sin\theta)\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta\,\cdot)+\sin^{-2}\theta\,\partial_\varphi^2$ makes the surface divergence theorem on the closed sphere give $\int_{S^2}(\Delta_{S^2}w)h\,d\sigma=\int_{S^2}w(\Delta_{S^2}h)\,d\sigma$ with no boundary term, so the coefficients of $Lw$ against $Y_{lm}$ are exactly $(L_lw_{lm})(t)$; hence $$Lw(t,\cdot)=\sum_{l,m}(L_lw_{lm})(t)\,Y_{lm},\qquad L_l:=(\partial_t-s)^2-(l+\tfrac12)^2,$$ since $-l(l+1)-\tfrac14=-(l+\tfrac12)^2$. Parseval for the complete family at each $t$ [L6] and Tonelli's theorem against the counting measure on the index set [L8] give $$\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{S^2}w^2\,d\sigma\,dt=\sum_{l,m}\int_{\mathbb R}w_{lm}^2\,dt,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\int_{S^2}(Lw)^2\,d\sigma\,dt=\sum_{l,m}\int_{\mathbb R}(L_lw_{lm})^2\,dt,$$ all terms being nonnegative; each $w_{lm}$ is smooth and compactly supported on $\mathbb R$, and $L_lw_{lm}$ is its second derivative combination, again compactly supported and square integrable. [L5, L6, L8, step 1.2]

2.3 **Fourier multiplier bound, mode by mode.** Fix $(l,m)$. In the $2\pi$ convention of [L7], the distributional Fourier transform of $L_lw_{lm}$ is the bounded continuous function $m_l\hat w_{lm}$ with symbol $m_l(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi-s)^2-(l+\tfrac12)^2$, and Plancherel gives $\|L_lw_{lm}\|_2^2=\int_{\mathbb R}|m_l(\xi)|^2|\hat w_{lm}(\xi)|^2\,d\xi$. Put $x=4\pi^2\xi^2\ge0$, $A=s-l-\tfrac12$ and $B=s+l+\tfrac12$. Then $s^2-(l+\tfrac12)^2=AB$ and $A^2+B^2+2AB=(A+B)^2=4s^2$, so $$|m_l(\xi)|^2=\bigl(AB-x\bigr)^2+4s^2x=\bigl(x+A^2\bigr)\bigl(x+B^2\bigr)\ge A^2B^2.$$ For integers $l\ge0$ and $s\ge1$ one has $|AB|=|s^2-(l+\tfrac12)^2|\ge s-\tfrac14$: on the range $l\le s-2$, nonempty only for $s\ge2$, the function $l\mapsto s^2-(l+\tfrac12)^2$ is decreasing, so $AB\ge s^2-(s-\tfrac32)^2=3s-\tfrac94\ge s-\tfrac14$; at $l=s-1$ and $l=s$ the values are $s-\tfrac14$ and $s+\tfrac14$; and on the range $l\ge s+1$ one has $|AB|=(l+\tfrac12)^2-s^2\ge(s+\tfrac32)^2-s^2=3s+\tfrac94\ge s-\tfrac14$. Since $s-\tfrac14\ge\tfrac s2$ for every $s\ge1$, conclude $|m_l(\xi)|^2\ge s^2/4$ for all $\xi$, and therefore $$\|w_{lm}\|_2\le\tfrac2s\|L_lw_{lm}\|_2 .$$ [L7, step 1.2]

3.1 **The weighted right-hand side.** Combining step 2.1 with the measure identity of step 1.1 gives $$r^{-2\tau+4}(\Delta u)^2\,dx=r^{-2\tau+4}\cdot r^{-5}e^{-2st}(Lw)^2\cdot r^{3}\,dt\,d\sigma =r^{2-2\tau}e^{-2st}(Lw)^2\,dt\,d\sigma=(Lw)^2\,dt\,d\sigma,$$ because $r^{2-2\tau}=e^{(2\tau-2)t}=e^{2st}$; hence $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}r^{-2\tau+4}(\Delta u)^2\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{S^2}(Lw)^2\,d\sigma\,dt.$$ [step 2.1, step 1.1]

4.1 **Summation.** Squaring the mode-wise inequality of step 2.3, summing over all $(l,m)$ and inserting the two identities of step 2.2 and step 3.1 yields $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}r^{-2\tau}u^2\,dx=\sum_{l,m}\int w_{lm}^2\le\frac{4}{s^2}\sum_{l,m}\int (L_lw_{lm})^2=\frac{4}{s^2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}r^{-2\tau+4}(\Delta u)^2\,dx,$$ which is the asserted inequality after taking square roots. Both sides are finite because $u$ is compactly supported in an annulus on which the two weights are bounded. [step 2.3, step 2.2, step 3.1]

5.1 **Density extension to $H^2$ functions supported in an annulus.** Now let $u\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ be compactly supported in $\{0<a\le|x|\le b\}$, so its weak derivatives through order two exist as locally square integrable functions and $\Delta u$ is their weak sum [L12]. By [L9] fix $\chi_0\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;[0,1])$ with $\chi_0=1$ on $\overline B_{a/4}(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}\chi_0\subseteq B_{a/2}(0)$, and put $\chi:=1-\chi_0$; then $\chi$ is smooth, $\chi=0$ on $\overline B_{a/4}(0)$, $\chi=1$ outside $B_{a/2}(0)$, and $\chi u=u$ because $\chi=1$ on a neighbourhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$. By [L10] choose $u_k\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $u_k\to u$ in $W^{2,2}$; then $\chi u_k\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$ with $\chi u_k\to\chi u=u$ in $W^{2,2}$, because the weak Leibniz expansion of [L11] through order two bounds $\|\chi(u_k-u)\|_{W^{2,2}}$ by a constant times $\|u_k-u\|_{W^{2,2}}$, and likewise $\Delta(\chi u_k)\to\Delta(\chi u)=\Delta u$ in $L^2$. Every $\chi u_k$ and every $\Delta(\chi u_k)=\chi\Delta u_k+2\langle\nabla\chi,\nabla u_k\rangle+(\Delta\chi)u_k$ is supported in $\{|x|\ge a/4\}$, as is $\Delta u$ because weak derivatives of a class supported in $\{a\le|x|\le b\}$ are supported there, and on $\{|x|\ge a/4\}$ the weights $r^{-\tau}$ and $r^{-\tau+2}$ are bounded by $(a/4)^{-\tau}$ and by $(a/4)^{-\tau+2}$ (the exponent $2-\tau\le0$). Applying step 4.1 to each $\chi u_k$ and passing to the limit in $$\|r^{-\tau}\chi u_k\|_2\le\tfrac2s\|r^{-\tau+2}\Delta(\chi u_k)\|_2$$ gives $\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2\le\tfrac2s\|r^{-\tau+2}\Delta u\|_2$, and the weak derivatives and weak Laplacian of $u$ are those named in the statement. [L9, L10, L11, L12, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be nonempty, open and connected, let
$V\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\psi\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ satisfy $\Delta\psi=V\psi$ in the
distributional sense: $\int_\Omega\psi\,\Delta\varphi\,dx=\int_\Omega V\psi\,\varphi\,dx$
for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, with $\Delta\varphi$ the classical
Laplacian. Here $H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ denotes the locally integrable
classes on $\Omega$ whose weak derivatives of every order at most two exist
and are locally square integrable
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]); $V\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$
means that $V$ is measurable and that $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ on every compact
subset, with the essential supremum of
[[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]] and the space of
[[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]]. If $\psi=0$ on a nonempty open subset
of $\Omega$, then $\psi=0$ on $\Omega$. No smoothness, sign, symmetry or decay
hypothesis on $V$ beyond local essential boundedness is used, and no
analyticity is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]); a
nonempty open connected $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$; $V\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$;
$\psi\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ with $\Delta\psi=V\psi$ in the
distributional sense; and a nonempty open $U_0\subseteq\Omega$ on which $\psi$
vanishes.

[L1] Radial Carleman lemma: for every integer $s\ge1$ with $\tau=s+1$ and
every $u\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ compactly supported in an annulus
$\{0<a\le|x|\le b\}$, the weak Laplacian exists as a locally square integrable
function and $\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2\le\frac2s\|r^{-\tau+2}\Delta u\|_2$
([[lem-three-dimensional-radial-carleman-integer-weight]]).

[L2] Bumps: for $0<\rho<R$ there is a smooth $\chi_0:\mathbb R^3\to[0,1]$
equal to $1$ on $\overline B_\rho(0)$ with support in $B_R(0)$
([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]).

[L3] Weak Leibniz rule: for $\eta\in C_c^\infty$ and $u\in W^{k,2}$, the
product $\eta u$ is in $W^{k,2}$ and
$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u$
for every $|\alpha|\le k$, the derivatives being the locally integrable weak
derivatives ([[lem-weak-leibniz-rule-with-a-smooth-factor]]).

[L4] Weak derivatives are defined by the signed test identity and
$W^{2,2}$ consists of $L^2$ classes with weak derivatives of order at most two
in $L^2$; $W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ is the corresponding local class
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

[L5] Essential supremum and $L^\infty$: $\|f\|_\infty=\inf\{M\ge0:|f|\le M\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}$,
$L^\infty(\mu)$ is the set of measurable $f$ with $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$, and if
$\|f\|_\infty<\infty$ then $|f|\le\|f\|_\infty$ almost everywhere
([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]],
[[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]],
[[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound]]).

[L6] Connectedness: a separation of a topological space is an ordered pair of
nonempty disjoint open sets with union the whole space, and the space is
connected when no separation exists; equivalently a connected space has no
nonempty proper clopen subset ([[def-connected-space]]).

[L7] $\mathbb Q^3$ is countable and dense in $\mathbb R^3$, and the open boxes
$\prod_{i<3}(a_i,b_i)$ with rational $a_i<b_i$ form a countable basis for the
topology of $\mathbb R^3$, which coincides with the Euclidean metric topology
([[thm-rational-points-and-boxes-in-rn]],
[[lem-product-topology-on-rn]], [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]]).

[L8] Null sets and almost everywhere: a measurable set is null if its measure
is zero, and a property holds almost everywhere if its exceptional set is
contained in a null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

[L9] Countable subadditivity: for a sequence of measurable sets,
$\mu(\bigcup_k E_k)\le\sum_k\mu(E_k)$
([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[L10] Smoothness: $C^k$ mean continuous partial derivatives through order $k$
and $C^\infty$ means $C^k$ for every $k$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); in particular a
$C_c^\infty$ cutoff is $C^2$, so its classical Laplacian is defined.

[L11] Metric topology: $U$ is open in a metric space exactly when every
$x\in U$ has some $r>0$ with the metric ball $B(x,r)$ contained in $U$, and
closed means open complement ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

**Choice accounting.** Countable Choice is inherited through [L1], which is
the only supplier carrying a choice assumption; the localization, absorption,
zero-set and counting arguments below use no further choice principle.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, a nonempty open connected
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, $V\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, an
$H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ solution $\psi$ of $\Delta\psi=V\psi$ distributionally,
and $\psi=0$ on a nonempty open $U_0\subseteq\Omega$.

1.1 **Localization at a zero point.** Fix $z_0\in U_0$ and choose $r_0>0$ with $B_{r_0}(z_0)\subseteq U_0$ and $R>0$ with $\overline B_R(z_0)\subseteq\Omega$ (both possible by [L11]); translate so that $z_0=0$. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B_R(0);[0,1])$ with $\chi=1$ on $B_{R/2}(0)$ [L2] and set $u:=\chi\psi$. Since $\psi\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and $\chi$ is smooth with compact support in $\Omega$, the weak Leibniz rule [L3] through order two shows that $u$, extended by zero, lies in $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$ with weak Laplacian the square integrable function $\Delta u=\chi\Delta\psi+2\langle\nabla\chi,\nabla\psi\rangle+(\Delta\chi)\psi$; the hypothesis that $\Delta\psi=V\psi$ holds distributionally says exactly that the distribution $\Delta\psi$ is the regular distribution of the locally integrable function $V\psi$, so testing this identity against $\chi\varphi$ for arbitrary $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ gives $\chi\Delta\psi=\chi V\psi$, and $\chi\in C_c^\infty$ is $C^2$ so its classical Laplacian is defined [L10]. Thus $\Delta u=Vu+e$ as $L^2$ classes with $e:=2\langle\nabla\chi,\nabla\psi\rangle+(\Delta\chi)\psi$, and $e$ is supported in the annulus $\{R/2\le|x|\le R\}$ because $\chi=1$, hence $\nabla\chi=\Delta\chi=0$, on $B_{R/2}(0)$. Finally $u=0$ almost everywhere on $B_{r_0}(0)\subseteq U_0$, so $u$ is compactly supported in the annulus $\{0<r_0\le|x|\le R\}$. [L2, L3, L4, L10, L11]

2.1 **Carleman estimate with the potential split.** Let $M$ be the essential supremum of $|V|$ over $B_R(0)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure [L5]; it is finite because $B_R(0)$ is compactly contained in $\Omega$ and $V\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and by [L5] one has $|V|\le M$ almost everywhere on $B_R(0)$. Applying [L1] to $u$ with parameter $s\ge1$, $\tau=s+1$, and using $|V|\le M$ together with $r\le R$ on the support of $u$, one has $\|r^{-\tau+2}Vu\|_2\le MR^2\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2$ and therefore $\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2\le\frac2s\bigl(MR^2\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2+\|r^{-\tau+2}e\|_2\bigr)$. [L1, L5, step 1.1]

3.1 **Absorption and the inner-ball bound.** For every integer $s\ge\max\{1,4MR^2\}$ the factor satisfies $2MR^2/s\le1/2$, so absorbing the first term in the estimate of step 2.1 gives $\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2\le\frac4s\|r^{-\tau+2}e\|_2$; since $e$ is supported in $\{R/2\le|x|\le R\}$ where $r^{2-\tau}\le(R/2)^{2-\tau}$ (the exponent $2-\tau\le0$), this yields $\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2\le\frac4s(R/2)^{2-\tau}\|e\|_2$. For every $0<\sigma\le R/2$ one has $u=\psi$ almost everywhere on $B_\sigma(0)$ (because $\chi=1$ on $B_{R/2}(0)$) and $r\le\sigma$ there, so $\|\psi\|_{L^2(B_\sigma(0))}=\|u\|_{L^2(B_\sigma(0))}\le\sigma^\tau\|r^{-\tau}u\|_2\le\frac{4(R/2)^2}{s}\bigl(\frac{2\sigma}{R}\bigr)^{\tau}\|e\|_2$. [step 2.1]

4.1 **Limit and local propagation.** For fixed $\sigma<R/2$ the bound of step 3.1 tends to $0$ as the integer $s\to\infty$, because $\|e\|_2$ is fixed by the localization of step 1.1, $2\sigma/R<1$ and $\tau=s+1$; hence $\psi=0$ almost everywhere on $B_\sigma(0)$ for every $\sigma<R/2$. Since $B_{R/2}(0)$ is the countable union of the balls $B_{R/2-1/n}(0)$, $n\ge1$, and a countable union of null sets is null by [L8] and [L9], it follows that $\psi=0$ almost everywhere on $B_{R/2}(0)$. Restated without the translation: if $z\in\Omega$ has a neighbourhood on which $\psi$ vanishes almost everywhere and $R>0$ satisfies $\overline B_R(z)\subseteq\Omega$, then $\psi=0$ almost everywhere on $B_{R/2}(z)$. [L8, L9, step 3.1]

5.1 **The zero set is open in $\Omega$ and carries no mass.** Let $Z:=\bigcup\{U\subseteq\Omega:U\text{ open},\ \psi=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}$. Then $Z$ is open and nonempty (it contains $U_0$), and $\psi=0$ almost everywhere on $Z$: for $y\in Z$ choose $\varepsilon_y>0$ with $B(y,\varepsilon_y)\subseteq\Omega$ [L11]; step 4.1 with $R=\varepsilon_y/2$ gives that $\psi=0$ almost everywhere on the open ball $B_{\varepsilon_y/4}(y)\subseteq Z$, so these balls cover $Z$; by [L7] each $y\in B_{\varepsilon_y/4}(y)$ is contained in a rational box $Q_y$ with $Q_y\subseteq B_{\varepsilon_y/4}(y)$, the family of all rational boxes obtained this way is countable, and each is a null set for $\psi$ because its exceptional set $\{x:\psi(x)\ne0\}\cap Q_y$ is measurable and contained in the exceptional set of the enclosing ball, which is null by [L8]; since $Z$ is covered by countably many of these boxes, [L9] makes $\{x\in Z:\psi(x)\ne0\}$ null, that is, $\psi=0$ almost everywhere on $Z$. [L7, L8, L9, L11, step 4.1]

5.2 **$\Omega\setminus Z$ is open.** Let $x\in\Omega\setminus Z$ and choose $\varepsilon>0$ with $\overline B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq\Omega$: [L11] gives $\delta>0$ with $B(x,2\delta)\subseteq\Omega$, and $\overline B(x,\delta)\subseteq B(x,2\delta)\subseteq\Omega$, so $\varepsilon:=\delta$ qualifies. If some $y\in Z\cap B(x,\varepsilon/3)$ existed, then $R:=\varepsilon-|x-y|>2\varepsilon/3$; every $z\in\overline B_R(y)$ satisfies $|z-x|\le|z-y|+|y-x|\le R+|x-y|=\varepsilon$, so $\overline B_R(y)\subseteq\overline B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq\Omega$, and step 4.1 would give $\psi=0$ almost everywhere on $B_{R/2}(y)$; since $|x-y|<\varepsilon/3<R/2$, the point $x$ lies in that ball, so $x$ would have a neighbourhood on which $\psi$ vanishes almost everywhere, contradicting $x\notin Z$. Hence $B(x,\varepsilon/3)\cap Z=\varnothing$, and $\Omega\setminus Z$ is open. [L11, step 4.1]

6.1 **Conclusion.** The sets $Z$ and $\Omega\setminus Z$ are disjoint, open, and their union is $\Omega$, and $Z$ is nonempty; since $\Omega$ is connected [L6], no separation of $\Omega$ exists, so $\Omega\setminus Z=\varnothing$ and $Z=\Omega$. By step 5.1, $\psi=0$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$, which is the class statement $\psi=0$ on $\Omega$. [L6, step 5.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ vanish outside $\overline B_a(0)$. Use the complete orthonormal basis $\{Y_{lm}\}$ of real spherical harmonics on $S^2$ with unnormalised surface measure $d\sigma$ of total mass $4\pi$ and the addition theorem of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], and the Legendre generating kernel and its compact remainder bound from [[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]. Write $x=rn$, $r=|x|$, $n\in S^2$. Then:

(a) **Exterior multipole expansion.** For every $x$ with $|x|>a$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\frac{Y_{lm}(n)}{r^{l+1}}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy,$$ the series converging absolutely and uniformly on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ for every $r_0>a$, with tail after degree $N$ bounded by $\|\rho\|_1\,a^{N+1}/(r_0^{N+2}(1-a/r_0))$; for every fixed $r>a$, the degree-$l$ term is the $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ angular projection of $n\mapsto F_r(n):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|rn-y|^{-1}\rho(y)\,dy$ onto the degree-$l$ harmonics. This function is continuous and bounded by $\|\rho\|_1/(r-a)$, so it is in $L^2(S^2)$; no sphere trace or $L^2$ property of the volume density $\rho$ is asserted. The degree-zero and degree-one terms are the Coulomb and dipole terms with the explicit remainder bound of [[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]] ($Q=\int\rho$, $p=\int y\rho(y)\,dy$, $|R(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/|x|^3$ for $|x|\ge2a$).

(b) **Termwise differentiation.** On every compact $K$ with $\inf_K|x|>a$ the series may be differentiated termwise to every order, the differentiated series converging uniformly on $K$; in particular the potential is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$.

(c) **Ball boundary branch.** For $f\in L^2(S^2)$ with coefficients $f_{lm}$ the series $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ converges in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$ and, with all derivatives, uniformly on each closed ball of radius $<1$, is harmonic on the open unit ball, and is the unique harmonic function there with a finite $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\cdot)\|_2$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$; for continuous $f$ it equals the Poisson integral $(1-r^2)/(4\pi|rn-n'|^3)$ of $f$ and extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary values $f$.

This is a statement about the Newtonian integral of a compactly supported $L^1$ density and about harmonic functions; no physical charge distribution or electrostatic interpretation is asserted. In every coefficient integral the factor $|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)$ is defined at $y=0$ by its homogeneous polynomial extension: zero for $l\ge1$ and the constant degree-zero harmonic for $l=0$. This is a finite assignment, and changing its value at that null singleton changes no integral.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $a>0$; a density $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ vanishing outside $\overline B_a(0)$; the complete orthonormal basis $\{Y_{lm}\}$ of real spherical harmonics with unnormalised surface measure $d\sigma$ of total mass $4\pi$; and the notation $x=rn$, $r=|x|$, $n\in S^2$, with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

[L1] Legendre kernel and its consequences: $P_l(z)=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\pi[z+i\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\theta]^l\,d\theta$ is a real polynomial with $|P_l(z)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_0=1$, $P_1(z)=z$; $(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\sum_{l\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ for $|q|<1$; for $r>|y|$, $|x-y|^{-1}=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)$ with the remainder after degree $N$ bounded by $|y|^{N+1}|x|^{-N-2}(1-|y|/|x|)^{-1}$ uniformly on $|y|\le a<r$; the coefficient terms $x\mapsto|x|^{-l-1}P_l(x\cdot y/(|x||y|))$ are harmonic on $\{|x|>|y|\}$, and on an observation compact set disjoint from $\overline B_a(0)$ every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]).

[L2] Spherical harmonics and addition: the real harmonic polynomials of degree $l$ restricted to $S^2$ form a $(2l+1)$-dimensional space, distinct degrees are orthogonal for $d\sigma$, the union admits the complete orthonormal basis $\{Y_{lm}\}$, and $\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n')$; in particular $\sum_m|Y_{lm}(n)|^2=(2l+1)/(4\pi)$ ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]).

[L3] The ball boundary branch: for $f\in L^2(S^2)$ with coefficients $f_{lm}$, the series $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$, $0\le r<1$, and all its derivatives converge uniformly on every closed smaller ball, $u$ is harmonic, $u(r\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$, $u$ is the unique harmonic function with $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\cdot)\|_2<\infty$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$, and for continuous $f$ it equals $\int_{S^2}\frac{1-r^2}{4\pi|rn-n'|^3}f(n')\,d\sigma(n')$ with continuous extension to the closed ball ([[lem-em-ball-poisson-series-boundary-convergence]]).

[L4] Coulomb–dipole splitting: with $Q=\int\rho$ and $p=\int y\rho(y)\,dy$, for $r\ge2a$, $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{|x-y|}dy=\frac Qr+\frac{p\cdot x}{r^3}+R(x)$ with $|R(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/r^3$ ([[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]]).

[L5] $L^2$ Cauchy–Schwarz: $\int|fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]).

[L6] Monotonicity and scalar rules for nonnegative integrals: $f\le g$ pointwise implies $\int f\le\int g$, and $\int cf=c\int f$ for $c\ge0$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[L7] Orthonormal families and orthonormal bases: an orthonormal family has $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$, and a complete orthonormal system has closed linear span the whole Hilbert space ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).

[L8] Interior derivative estimates for harmonic functions: on a ball of radius $R$ contained in the harmonicity domain, $|D^\alpha v(x)|\le C_\alpha R^{-3-|\alpha|}\int_{B_R}|v|$, so derivatives on a compact set are controlled by the supremum on a slightly larger compact set ([[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]).

[L9] Newton–Leibniz with interior derivative: a continuous function with continuous coordinate derivative $g$ on an interval differs from a primitive of $g$ by a constant; applied along coordinate segments this identifies uniform derivative limits with derivatives of the limit ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

[L10] Smoothness: $C^k$ maps have continuous partial derivatives through order $k$, and $C^\infty$ means $C^k$ for every $k$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

**Choice accounting.** Countable Choice is assumed in the Statement and is carried by the spherical-harmonic and ball-series suppliers [L2]–[L3]; the measure-theoretic integrations and the differentiation argument introduce no further choice.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** Countable Choice, $a>0$, $\rho\in L^1$ supported in $\overline B_a(0)$, the orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis and the Legendre kernel.

1.1 **Zonal expansion with uniform tail.** Fix $x=rn$ with $r>a$ and let $N\ge0$. By [L1] the kernel expansion $|x-y|^{-1}=\sum_{l\ge0}|y|^l r^{-l-1}P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)$ converges absolutely and uniformly for $y\in\overline B_a(0)$ (the term at $y=0$ being read by the stated homogeneous extension), and its remainder after degree $N$ is bounded by $|y|^{N+1}r^{-N-2}(1-|y|/r)^{-1}$; multiplying by the $L^1$ density $\rho$ and integrating, the uniform bound gives $\bigl|\int\rho(y)/|x-y|\,dy-\sum_{l\le N}r^{-l-1}\int|y|^lP_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy\bigr|\le\|\rho\|_1 a^{N+1}r^{-N-2}(1-a/r)^{-1}$, so $F(x):=\int\rho(y)/|x-y|\,dy=\sum_{l=0}^\infty r^{-l-1}\int|y|^lP_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy$, the zonal series converging absolutely and, for every $r_0>a$, uniformly on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$ with the stated tail bound $\|\rho\|_1a^{N+1}/(r_0^{N+2}(1-a/r_0))$. [L1]

1.2 **Ball boundary branch.** Part (c) of the Statement is exactly [L3]: the series $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ and all its derivatives converge uniformly on each closed smaller ball, $u$ is harmonic, $u(r\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$, uniqueness holds in the class with finite radial $L^2$ supremum, and for continuous $f$ the Poisson representation and the continuous extension to the closed ball hold. [L3]

2.1 **Spherical form, absolute convergence and the degree tail.** For $y\ne0$ the addition theorem [L2] gives $P_l(n\cdot y/|y|)=\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(y/|y|)$. For each $l$ put $q_{lm}:=\int|y|^lY_{lm}(y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy$, a finite integral because $|Y_{lm}|$ is bounded on $S^2$ and $\rho\in L^1$; then by [L2] and [L5], and by the monotonicity rule [L6] applied to the absolute values, $$\sum_m|Y_{lm}(n)q_{lm}|\le\int|y|^l|\rho(y)|\sum_m|Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(y/|y|)|\,dy\le a^l\|\rho\|_1\Bigl(\sum_m|Y_{lm}(n)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_m|Y_{lm}(y/|y|)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}a^l\|\rho\|_1,$$ so the degree-$l$ contribution of the spherical series is bounded in modulus by $(a/r)^l\|\rho\|_1/r$ and the series $\sum_l\sum_m\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)r^{-l-1}q_{lm}$ converges absolutely, with degree tail after $N$ bounded by $\|\rho\|_1r_0^{-1}\sum_{l>N}(a/r_0)^l=\|\rho\|_1a^{N+1}/(r_0^{N+2}(1-a/r_0))$. Substituting the addition theorem degree by degree into step 1.1 gives, for every $N$, the equality of the truncated zonal and spherical sums, and both truncations converge to the same limit by step 1.1 and this bound; this proves the expansion of part (a) and its uniform convergence on $\{|x|\ge r_0\}$. [L1, L2, L5, L6, step 1.1]

3.1 **The degree-$l$ term is the angular projection.** Fix $r>a$ and put $F_r(n):=\int|rn-y|^{-1}\rho(y)\,dy$. Then $|F_r(n)|\le\|\rho\|_1/(r-a)$ for every $n$, and $F_r$ is continuous: for $n_k\to n$ the integrands $|rn_k-y|^{-1}\rho(y)$ converge pointwise and are dominated by the integrable $|r\min_k|n_k|-a|^{-1}\rho$ (or by the bounded kernel times $|\rho|$), so dominated convergence applies. Hence $F_r\in L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ with $\|F_r\|_2^2\le4\pi\|\rho\|_1^2/(r-a)^2$. By step 2.1 the spherical series for $F_r$ converges uniformly on the compact sphere $S^2$, so the pairing with each basis element may be taken termwise and $$\langle F_r,Y_{km}\rangle=\sum_{l,m'}\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}r^{-l-1}q_{lm'}\langle Y_{lm'},Y_{km}\rangle=\frac{4\pi}{2k+1}r^{-k-1}q_{km}$$ by the orthonormality of the basis [L7]; this is precisely the stated $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ angular projection. [L2, L7, step 2.1]

3.2 **Coulomb and dipole identification.** Summing the degree-$l$ spherical term over $m$ and using the addition theorem in reverse gives $\sum_m\frac{4\pi}{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)q_{lm}=r^{-l-1}\int|y|^lP_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy$, the zonal degree term computed in step 1.1, and it is the degree-$l$ term of the spherical series of step 2.1. Since $P_0=1$ and $P_1(z)=z$ [L1], the degrees $l=0$ and $l=1$ contribute $r^{-1}\int\rho=Q/r$ and $r^{-2}\int(n\cdot y)\rho(y)\,dy=p\cdot x/r^3$; the remaining tail is $F(x)-Q/r-p\cdot x/r^3$, and for $r\ge2a$ the explicit remainder bound $|R(x)|\le16a^2\|\rho\|_1/r^3$ of [L4] applies to it, so the degree-zero and degree-one terms are the Coulomb and dipole terms of the Statement. [L1, L2, L4, step 2.1]

3.3 **Termwise differentiation.** Each degree term $x\mapsto r^{-l-1}\int|y|^lP_l(n\cdot y/|y|)\rho(y)\,dy=\int\rho(y)|x|^{-l-1}P_l(x\cdot y/(|x||y|))\,dy$ is harmonic on $\{|x|>a\}$ as an integral over $y\in\overline B_a(0)$ of the harmonic coefficient functions of [L1] (finite sums of harmonic functions are harmonic, and the partial sums are exactly these integrals by linearity). Let $K$ be compact with $\inf_K|x|=r_1>a$, choose $a<r_2<r_1$ and a compact neighbourhood $K'$ of $K$ contained in $\{|x|>r_2\}$. The partial sums $S_N(x)=\sum_{l\le N}(\text{degree-}l\text{ term})$ are harmonic on $\{|x|>a\}$, and by step 2.1 they converge uniformly on $K'$; applying the interior derivative estimates [L8] to $S_M-S_N$ on $K'$ for each multi-index $\alpha$ gives $\sup_K|D^\alpha(S_M-S_N)|\to0$, so the differentiated series converges uniformly on $K$ for every $\alpha$. Since $S_N\to F$ pointwise and the first derivatives converge uniformly on $K$, the Newton–Leibniz theorem [L9] applied along coordinate segments identifies the limit of $\partial_iS_N$ with $\partial_iF$ on $K$; inductively the same identification holds for every order, so the series may be differentiated termwise to every order on $K$ and $F$ is $C^\infty$ on $\{|x|>a\}$ in the sense of [L10]. [L1, L8, L9, L10, step 2.1]

4.1 **Assembly.** Part (a) is steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 3.2 (expansion, uniform tail, angular projection and Coulomb–dipole identification); part (b) is step 3.3; part (c) is step 1.2; the statement about the value at $y=0$ is the finite-assignment convention recorded in the Statement, which leaves every integral unchanged because a singleton is null. This proves all three parts. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3] ∎
