## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the smooth Riemann/Lebesgue comparison route below; in clause (c), also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) inherited from the AC supplier. Let $d\ge1$. All kernels below are real $d\times d$ matrix kernels and all histories are $\mathbb R^d$-valued; conditions on matrices are read entrywise, every matrix- or vector-valued integral below is read entrywise as a scalar Lebesgue integral, and $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ means entrywise Lebesgue integrability on $(0,\infty)$ with Lebesgue measure.

For a real-variable scalar function $F$ and real $\omega$, the **principal value** is defined by $$\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{F(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\Bigl(\int_{\omega-R}^{\omega-\eta}+\int_{\omega+\eta}^{\omega+R}\Bigr)\frac{F(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,$$ read entrywise when applied to matrix entries; under the bounds proved in (b) and (c) the tails converge absolutely, so this limit exists and the centering at infinity does not affect it.

(a) (Causal convolution.) Let $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and continuous. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the integral $P(t):=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely, read componentwise as $$P_j(t)=\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^dK_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)\Bigr)ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d),$$ and satisfies $$|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d\Bigl(\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|E_k(s)|\Bigr)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d);$$ the response $P$ is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$, then their responses coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

(b) (Compact branch.) If $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (smooth, with compact support contained in the open half-line), then the transfer function $$\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and for any $b>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$ the full entire-plane bound is $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}\|K_{jk}''\|_1|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$. Its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi$$ for every real $\omega$.

(c) (Integrable branch.) If instead $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is locally absolutely continuous entrywise in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]] on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$, with $K'$ its almost-everywhere derivative with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $s\mapsto sK(s)$ in $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, then $\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on the open upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the same pair of dispersion relations for every real $\omega$, and is bounded on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ by $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}$ for $|z|\ge1$; for an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$ and apply the relations to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$.

(d) (Monochromatic work and passivity.) Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be a real parameter (a response normalization; the equivalence below is independent of its value). Put $E(t):=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t):=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, real parts taken componentwise and $\chi(\omega)$ acting by matrix multiplication. Then, with $T:=2\pi/\omega$ and the Euclidean dot product on $\mathbb R^d$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T E(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),\qquad e^*\chi(\omega)e:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\overline{e_j}\,\chi_{jk}(\omega)\,e_k,$$ where $\chi(\omega)^*$ denotes the conjugate transpose, $(\chi(\omega)^*)_{jk}:=\overline{\chi_{kj}(\omega)}$, and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$ if and only if the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega):=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), and in clause (c) additionally Dependent Choice $\mathrm{DC}$ ([[def-dependent-choice]]); a fixed dimension $d\ge1$; a real $d\times d$ matrix kernel $K=(K_{jk})$ and an $\mathbb R^d$-valued history $E=(E_k)$; all matrix- and vector-valued integrals are read entrywise as scalar Lebesgue integrals on $(0,\infty)$. In clause (b), $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ with $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$ for some real $b>0$; in clause (c) the kernel satisfies the integrable-branch hypotheses of [F14]; in clause (d), $\omega>0$, $T=2\pi/\omega$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and $a:=\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\in\mathbb C^d$.

[F1] A measurable $h=u+iv:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable exactly when $\int|h|\,d\mu<+\infty$, and then $\int h\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu$; $L^1(\mu)$ is the class of integrable complex functions. ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]])

[F2] For integrable functions $|\int f\,d\mu|\le\int|f|\,d\mu$; for measurable $0\le f\le g$ one has $\int f\le\int g$ and $\int cf=c\int f$ for $c\ge0$; the integral over a measurable set is $\int_E f=\int f\chi_E$; and the integral is complex-linear, $\int(\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu$. ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]])

[F3] Every continuous map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is Borel measurable (under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), and sums, scalar multiples, absolute values and pointwise products of measurable functions are measurable. ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]])

[F4] Dominated convergence: if $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single integrable $g$, then $\int f_n\to\int f$. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]])

[F5] Continuity under the integral sign: if $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable for every $t$ in an interval $I$, if $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is continuous for almost every $x$, and if $|f(x,t)|\le g(x)$ for a single integrable $g$, then $t\mapsto\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$ is continuous on $I$. ([[thm-continuity-under-the-integral-sign]])

[F6] Differentiation under the integral sign in a real parameter: under the hypotheses stated there (integrability for every parameter, almost-everywhere differentiability, measurability of the derivative and a single integrable dominating function for the derivative), $F(t)=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$ is differentiable with $F'(t)=\int\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$. ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]])

[F7] The complex exponential is defined by $\exp z=\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, that series converges absolutely for every $z$, $\exp$ is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ and hence continuous, and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$ for real $x,y$; conjugation is a real-field automorphism with $z\overline z=|z|^2$, hence $|\overline z|=|z|$ and conjugation is continuous, while $\operatorname{Re}$, $\operatorname{Im}$ and $\overline{\phantom{z}}$ are the coordinate maps of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. In particular $\operatorname{Re}(e^{i\theta})=\cos\theta$ and $\operatorname{Im}(e^{i\theta})=\sin\theta$ for real $\theta$, and $\operatorname{Re}(\overline w)=\operatorname{Re}w$. ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[cor-complex-differentiability-implies-continuity]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]])

[F8] If the four first partial derivatives of $u,v$ exist on a neighbourhood of $a$ and are continuous at $a$ with $u_x(a)=v_y(a)$ and $u_y(a)=-v_x(a)$, then $f=u+iv$ is complex differentiable at $a$; holomorphic means complex differentiable on an open set and entire means holomorphic on $\mathbb C$. ([[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]], [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]])

[F9] If $f$ is holomorphic on an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ and the closed rectifiable contour $\gamma$ is path-homotopic relative to endpoints to a constant loop in $\Omega$, then $\int_\gamma f\,dz=0$. ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]])

[F10] Integration by parts: if $u,v$ are differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ with integrable derivatives, then $\int_a^bu\,v'=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^bu'v$; the bounded Riemann integrable case has the same Lebesgue integral; and integrable functions that agree almost everywhere have the same integral. ([[thm-integration-by-parts]], [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])

[F11] The real sine and cosine are differentiable with $(\sin)'=\cos$ and $(\cos)'=-\sin$; the chain rule for total derivatives and the algebra of derivatives give the derivative of every finite combination $t\mapsto c_0+c_1\cos(\omega t)+c_2\sin(\omega t)$. ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]])

[F12] On $\mathbb R^d$ and $\mathbb C^d$ the dot product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_kx_ky_k$, $x\cdot\overline y=\sum_kx_k\overline{y_k}$, and the Euclidean norm is induced by the inner product. ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]])

[F13] Absolute continuity on a compact interval is the finite disjoint-interval condition of the cited definition; it is the exact hypothesis by which clause (c) reads its kernel, and no differentiability of the kernel beyond the stated almost-everywhere derivative is assumed. ([[def-absolutely-continuous-function]])

[F14] Integrable-branch supplier, consumed verbatim in clause (c): assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $\mathrm{DC}$; for a locally absolutely continuous real matrix kernel $K$ with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, the transform $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}ds$ has holomorphic entries on the upper half-plane, continuous and $C^1$ on the real boundary, is bounded on the closed upper half-plane with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$ (indeed $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le(|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_1)/|z|$ for every nonzero $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$), satisfies the two displayed principal-value formulas for every real $\omega$, and carries the instantaneous-response subtraction for a real matrix $\chi_\infty$; causality alone supplies neither further growth hypotheses nor the passivity quadratic-form condition. ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]])

[F15] Period-average supplier, consumed in clause (d) in its scalar form applied componentwise: for $\omega>0$, $T=2\pi/\omega$ and all $a,d\in\mathbb C$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr);$$ the vector form follows by summing this over the coordinate pairs of $a,d\in\mathbb C^d$. ([[lem-em-period-average]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; the steps are ordered in dependency layers, so the four clauses of the Statement are interleaved, and every step cites only earlier steps.

1.1 Fix $t\in\mathbb R$, $j\le d$ and set $g_j(s):=\sum_{k=1}^dK_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$ for $s>0$. Each summand is a product of the measurable function $K_{jk}$ with the continuous, hence Borel measurable, function $s\mapsto E_k(t-s)$; so $g_j$ is measurable. With $M:=\max_k\sup_{\mathbb R}|E_k|<+\infty$ one has $|g_j(s)|\le M\sum_{k=1}^d|K_{jk}(s)|$ for every $s>0$, and $\sum_{k=1}^d|K_{jk}|$ lies in $L^1(0,\infty)$; hence $g_j\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $P_j(t):=\int_0^\infty g_j(s)\,ds$ converges absolutely with $|P_j(t)|\le M\sum_{k=1}^d\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Fix $z=x+iy\in\mathbb C$. The map $s\mapsto e^{izs}$ is continuous, since it is the composition of the continuous linear map $s\mapsto izs$ with the continuous exponential, and $K_{jk}$ is measurable; hence $s\mapsto K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}$ is measurable as a product of measurable functions. On $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$ one has $|e^{izs}|=|e^{ixs}|e^{-ys}=e^{-ys}\le e^{b|y|}$, so $|K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}|\le e^{b|y|}|K_{jk}(s)|$; the right-hand side is integrable, so the integrand is integrable and $\chi_{jk}(z):=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined with $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le e^{b|y|}\|K_{jk}\|_1$. [F1, F3, F7]

1.3 Clause (c) is exactly the supplied integrable-branch theorem [F14]: its hypotheses on $K$ are those stated in clause (c) (local absolute continuity entrywise in the sense of [F13], $K,K',sK\in L^1$), and it concludes the well-definedness and holomorphy of $\chi$ on the open upper half-plane, continuity on the closed upper half-plane and continuous first derivative on the real boundary, the entrywise principal-value formulas for every real $\omega$, and the bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_1$ for $|z|\ge1$ (which follows from its sharper $|z|^{-1}$ bound), together with the instantaneous-response subtraction for a real matrix $\chi_\infty$ and the scalar case $d=1$. Continuity on the closed upper half-plane combines the lemma's holomorphy on the open half-plane, hence continuity there, with its continuity at every real boundary point. [F14, F13, F8]

1.4 Write $a_j=\alpha_j+i\beta_j$ and $e_j=p_j+iq_j$ for the components of $a=\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ and $e$. By [F7], $e^{i\omega t}=\cos(\omega t)+i\sin(\omega t)$, and $\operatorname{Re}(w)=\operatorname{Re}(\overline w)$ for every $w\in\mathbb C$; therefore $E_j(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e_je^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{Re}(\overline{e_j}e^{i\omega t})=p_j\cos(\omega t)+q_j\sin(\omega t)$ and $P_j(t)=\operatorname{Re}(a_je^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{Re}(\overline{a_j}e^{i\omega t})=\alpha_j\cos(\omega t)+\beta_j\sin(\omega t)$, using the component computation $\operatorname{Re}((u+iv)(\cos+i\sin))=u\cos-v\sin$. [F7, F12]

2.1 The estimate of step 1.1 is uniform in $t$, so $\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|P_j(t)|\le M\sum_{k=1}^d\|K_{jk}\|_1$ and $P=(P_1,\dots,P_d)$ is bounded. The map $E\mapsto P$ is linear: for $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$ and bounded continuous $E,F$ the integrand defining $P_{\alpha E+\beta F}$ equals $\alpha$ times that of $P_E$ plus $\beta$ times that of $P_F$ pointwise, so the linearity of the scalar integral gives $P_{\alpha E+\beta F}=\alpha P_E+\beta P_F$. [step 1.1, F2, F1]

2.2 Fix $j$ and apply [F5] with $X=(0,\infty)$ carrying Lebesgue measure, $I=\mathbb R$ and $f(s,t):=\sum_{k=1}^dK_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$: for every $t$ the function $f(\cdot,t)$ is integrable by step 1.1; for every $s$ the map $t\mapsto f(s,t)$ is continuous, being a finite sum of products of constants with the continuous functions $t\mapsto E_k(t-s)$; and $|f(s,t)|\le M\sum_{k=1}^d|K_{jk}(s)|$ for the single integrable function named in step 1.1. Therefore $t\mapsto P_j(t)$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, and $P$ is continuous componentwise. [step 1.1, F5, F3]

2.3 Causality: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and agree on $(-\infty,t_0]$, and if $t\le t_0$, then for every $s>0$ the argument $t-s$ lies in $(-\infty,t_0]$, so the integrands of step 1.1 agree pointwise and hence $P_{E_1}(t)=P_{E_2}(t)$; thus the response at time $t$ depends only on the history up to time $t$. [step 1.1, F1]

2.4 Fix $y$ and apply [F6] in the parameter $x$ to $f(s,x):=K_{jk}(s)e^{i(x+iy)s}$ on a bounded interval of $x$-values: for each $x$ the function $f(\cdot,x)$ is integrable by step 1.2, the map $x\mapsto K_{jk}(s)e^{i(x+iy)s}$ is differentiable for every $s$ with derivative $isK_{jk}(s)e^{i(x+iy)s}$, and on the bounded parameter set this derivative is dominated by $(1+b)e^{b|y|}|K_{jk}(s)|$, an integrable function. Hence $x\mapsto\chi_{jk}(x+iy)$ is differentiable with $\partial_x\chi_{jk}(z)=\int_0^\infty isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$; exchanging the roles of $x$ and $y$ and repeating the same argument gives $\partial_y\chi_{jk}(z)=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$. Both partials are continuous in $(x,y)$: if $(x_n,y_n)\to(x,y)$, the integrands $isK_{jk}(s)e^{i(x_n+iy_n)s}$ converge pointwise to $isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}$ and are dominated on a bounded parameter neighbourhood by $(1+b)e^{bY}|K_{jk}(s)|$ for a suitable $Y$, so [F4] gives convergence of the integrals. [step 1.2, F6, F4, F3]

2.5 Reality identity: for real $\omega$, conjugating the partial sums of the absolutely convergent series defining $e^{i\omega s}$ term by term gives $\sum_{n\le m}\overline{(i\omega s)^n/n!}=\sum_{n\le m}(-i\omega s)^n/n!$, because conjugation is a continuous real-field automorphism with $\overline i=-i$ and fixes the real numbers $1/n!$; passing to the limit with continuity of conjugation gives $\overline{e^{i\omega s}}=e^{-i\omega s}$. Since $K_{jk}$ is real, $\overline{K_{jk}(s)e^{i\omega s}}=K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}$. For $h:=K_{jk}(\cdot)e^{i\omega\cdot}\in L^1(0,\infty)$ one has $\overline{\int h}=(\int\operatorname{Re}h)-i(\int\operatorname{Im}h)=\int(\operatorname{Re}h-i\operatorname{Im}h)=\int\overline h$ by [F1] and the complex linearity of the integral; hence $\chi_{jk}(-\omega)=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}ds=\int\overline h=\overline{\int h}=\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, F7]

2.6 By-parts identity: fix $z\ne0$. On $[0,b]$ the real and imaginary parts of $s\mapsto K_{jk}(s)$ and of $v(s):=e^{izs}/(iz)$ are differentiable with continuous derivatives, and $K_{jk}(0)=K_{jk}(b)=K_{jk}'(0)=K_{jk}'(b)=0$ because $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$; applying [F10] first with $u=K_{jk}$ and then with $u=K_{jk}'$ gives $\int_0^bK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}ds=-\frac1{iz}\int_0^bK_{jk}'(s)e^{izs}ds=\frac1{(iz)^2}\int_0^bK_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}ds=-z^{-2}\int_0^bK_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}ds$, the boundary terms vanishing at both steps. All three integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable on $[0,b]$, so [F10] transfers the identity to Lebesgue integrals; and since $K_{jk}$, $K_{jk}'$ and $K_{jk}''$ all vanish off $(0,b)$, the a.e.-equality clause of [F10] replaces each integral over $[0,b]$ by the integral over $(0,\infty)$. Hence $\chi_{jk}(z)=-z^{-2}\int_0^\infty K_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}ds$ for every $z\ne0$. [step 1.2, F10, F2, F7]

2.7 Differentiating the expressions of step 1.4 and using [F11] together with the algebra of derivatives gives $P_j'(t)=\omega(-\alpha_j\sin(\omega t)+\beta_j\cos(\omega t))$; on the other hand, expanding $(-i\omega)(\alpha_j+i\beta_j)= \omega\beta_j-i\omega\alpha_j$ and multiplying by $e^{-i\omega t}=\cos(\omega t)-i\sin(\omega t)$ shows that the real part of $(-i\omega)a_je^{-i\omega t}$ equals $\omega\beta_j\cos(\omega t)-\omega\alpha_j\sin(\omega t)$, the same number. Hence $P'(t)=\operatorname{Re}((-i\omega)a\,e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{Re}((-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise, and $P'$ is the real part of a monochromatic complex expression with vector amplitude $d:=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$. [step 1.4, F11, F7, F12]

3.1 By step 2.4 and the linearity of the integral, $\partial_y\chi_{jk}(z)=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds=\int_0^\infty i\bigl(isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\bigr)ds=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}(z)$ for every $z$. Writing $\chi_{jk}=u+iv$, this says $u_y+iv_y=i(u_x+iv_x)=-v_x+iu_x$, that is $u_y=-v_x$ and $v_y=u_x$; the four partials exist everywhere and are continuous by step 2.4, so [F8] makes $\chi_{jk}$ complex differentiable at every point of $\mathbb C$, that is, entire. [step 2.4, F2, F8]

3.2 Bounds and boundary continuity: for $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, step 2.6 and $|e^{izs}|\le1$ for $s\ge0$ give $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|z|^{-2}\|K_{jk}''\|_1$; for arbitrary $z\ne0$ one has $|e^{izs}|=e^{-s\operatorname{Im}z}\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ on $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$, whence $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}\|K_{jk}''\|_1|z|^{-2}$. Also $\chi_{jk}$ is continuous on the closed upper half-plane: if $z_n\to z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z_n\ge0$, the integrands of step 1.2 converge pointwise and are dominated by $e^{bY}|K_{jk}|$ once all $\operatorname{Im}z_n$ lie below a bound $Y$, so [F4] gives $\chi_{jk}(z_n)\to\chi_{jk}(z)$. [step 2.6, step 1.2, F4, F2, F7]

3.3 Applying the period-average identity of [F15] with amplitude vectors $a=e$ and $d=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ componentwise, and using step 2.7, $\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(e_je^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(d_je^{-i\omega t})\,dt=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\overline{d_j}\bigr)=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\cdot\overline d\bigr)$. Since $\overline d=i\omega\varepsilon_0\overline{\chi(\omega)e}$ and $e\cdot\overline{\chi(\omega)e}=\sum_{j,k}e_j\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}\overline{e_k}=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$, this equals $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(i\,\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}\bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr)$. [step 2.7, F15, F7, F2, F12]

4.1 Dispersion relations: fix real $\omega$ and $j,k$, and put $\varphi(z):=\chi_{jk}(z)/(z-\omega)$ for $z\ne\omega$. For $R>|\omega|+1$ and $0<\delta<1$ let $\gamma$ be the closed piecewise $C^1$ contour running along $[\omega-R,\omega-\delta]$, then along the clockwise semicircle $z=\omega+\delta e^{i\theta}$, $\pi\ge\theta\ge0$, then along $[\omega+\delta,\omega+R]$, and then back along the counterclockwise large semicircle $z=\omega+Re^{i\theta}$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$. The interior of $\gamma$ is a simply connected upper half-disk with a semicircular notch removed at $\omega$, on a neighbourhood of which $\varphi$ is holomorphic because $\chi_{jk}$ is entire and $z\mapsto(z-\omega)^{-1}$ is holomorphic off $\omega$; hence [F9] gives $\int_\gamma\varphi\,dz=0$. The large arc contributes at most $\pi R\|K_{jk}''\|_1R^{-2}/(R-|\omega|)\to0$ by step 3.2; the small arc contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\delta\downarrow0$ because $\varphi(\omega+\delta e^{i\theta})\to\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ uniformly in $\theta$; and the two real segments converge to the principal value of $\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi$ as first $\delta\downarrow0$ and then $R\to\infty$: near $\omega$ the term $\chi_{jk}(\omega)/(\xi-\omega)$ cancels between the symmetric punctured intervals while $(\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega))/(\xi-\omega)$ stays bounded, and for $|\xi|\ge2|\omega|$ the estimate $|\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)|\le2\|K_{jk}''\|_1|\xi|^{-2}$ makes the tails absolutely integrable. Passing to the limits in the identity $0=\int_\gamma\varphi\,dz$ therefore yields $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; taking real and imaginary parts gives the two displayed relations, since $i\pi\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)-\pi\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ and $-\pi\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ are the real and imaginary parts of $i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F9, F4, F2]

5.1 Finally $M(\omega)=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ has quadratic form $e^*M(\omega)e=\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e-e^*\chi(\omega)^*e\bigr)/(2i)$, and $e^*\chi(\omega)^*e=\sum_{j,k}\overline{e_j}\overline{\chi_{kj}(\omega)}e_k=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$ because $\chi(\omega)^*$ is the conjugate transpose; hence $e^*M(\omega)e=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$. By step 3.3 the period-averaged work equals $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}e^*M(\omega)e$ with $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}>0$, so it is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e$; clause (a) shows the response is causal throughout, so this positivity is an additional passivity condition on the model and not a consequence of causality. [step 3.3, F2, F7, F12] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the declared polar/surface and change-of-variables suppliers. Let $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$ and $t_0<T$ be constants, let $\rho\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ and $\mathbf J\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy (H1) $\rho(y,v)=\mathbf J(y,v)=0$ whenever $|y|>a$ or $v\notin[t_0,T]$, and (H2) $\partial_v\rho+\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Here and below $B_a:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:|y|<a\}$ and $\overline B_a:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:|y|\le a\}$ are the open and closed Euclidean balls of radius $a$ about the origin, and $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$ is the unit sphere. For $x$ with $r:=|x|\ge2a$ define the retarded scalar and vector potentials $$\varphi(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0c^2}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad \mathbf A(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\mathbf J(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$ and the fields $\mathbf E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$, $\mathbf B:=\nabla\times\mathbf A$, where the derivatives are taken in $x$ and all objects are read on $\{|x|\ge2a\}$; all vector-valued integrals are read componentwise as scalar Lebesgue integrals.

(a) (Fields as retarded integrals.) On the open set $\{|x|>2a\}$ the potentials $\varphi,\mathbf A$ are of class $C^\infty$ in $(x,t)$, and there $$\mathbf E(x,t)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf N}{R^2}c^2\rho\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)+\frac{c\,\mathbf N}{R}\rho_t\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)-\frac{\mathbf J_t\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)}{R}\Bigr]dy,\qquad \mathbf B(x,t)=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf N\times\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf J(y,t-\frac Rc)}{R^2}+\frac{\mathbf J_t(y,t-\frac Rc)}{cR}\Bigr]dy,$$ where $R:=|x-y|$, $\mathbf N:=(x-y)/R$, and $\rho_t,\mathbf J_t$ are the partial derivatives in the second variable. Moreover, on $\{|x|\ge2a\}\times[t_0,T]$, $\varphi$ and each component of $\mathbf A$ coincide with the corresponding solution constructed in the wave Cauchy problem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] for zero Cauchy data at $t_0$ and scalar source $h=\mu_0c^2\rho$, respectively $h=\mu_0 J_k$.

(b) (Uniform far-zone expansion.) For $n\in S^2$ and $u\in[t_0,T]$ put $\mathbf I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and $\mathbf V(n,u):=\partial_u\mathbf I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$. Then $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy=\frac1c\,n\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$, and there are constants $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$, depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and on the suprema of $|\rho|,|\rho_t|,|\rho_{tt}|,|\mathbf J|,|\mathbf J_t|,|\mathbf J_{tt}|$ on $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$, such that for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$ and $r\ge2a$, with $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathbf V(n,u))$, $$\Bigl|\mathbf E(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2},\qquad \Bigl|\mathbf B(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-\frac{n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)}{c}\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}.$$

(c) (Retarded-time flux limit.) Let $\mathbf S:=\mu_0^{-1}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ and let $d\Omega$ be the surface measure on $S^2$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]). Then for every $u\in[t_0,T]$, $$\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}\bigl|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)\bigr|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$ This is a limit at fixed retarded time $u$, not at fixed observation time $t$; no decay or boundary condition at spatial infinity is assumed beyond the compact spatial support in (H1).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); constants $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$, $t_0<T$; sources $\rho\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$, $\mathbf J\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying (H1) and (H2) of the Statement; the retarded potentials and fields of the Statement, with all vector integrals read componentwise. For $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$, $r\ge2a$ we write $x:=rn$, $t:=u+r/c$, $R:=|x-y|=\bigl((r-n\cdot y)^2+|y|^2-(n\cdot y)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$, $\mathbf N:=(x-y)/R$, $\sigma:=n\cdot y$, $v_y:=u+\sigma/c$ and $\delta_y:=(r-\sigma-R)/c$, so that $t-R/c=v_y+\delta_y$; $\Gamma_\rho,\Gamma_{\rho t},\Gamma_{\rho tt},\Gamma_J,\Gamma_{Jt},\Gamma_{Jtt}$ denote the suprema of $|\rho|,|\rho_t|,|\rho_{tt}|,|\mathbf J|,|\mathbf J_t|,|\mathbf J_{tt}|$ on $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$, and $\lambda(B_a)$ the Lebesgue measure of the ball.

[F1] A measurable $h$ is integrable exactly when $\int|h|<+\infty$, and then the integral is computed from the positive and negative parts or, for complex $h=u+iv$, as $\int u+i\int v$; $L^1$ denotes the integrable class and $\int_E f=\int f\chi_E$ is the integral over a measurable set. ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]])

[F2] The integral is linear, $|\int f|\le\int|f|$, $0\le f\le g$ measurable implies $\int f\le\int g$, $\int cf=c\int f$ for $c\ge0$, and integrable functions that agree almost everywhere have the same integral. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]])

[F3] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ the ball $B_a$ is Lebesgue measurable with $0<\lambda(B_a)<+\infty$; every continuous map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is Borel measurable; and sums, scalar multiples and pointwise products of measurable functions are measurable. ([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]])

[F4] Mean value theorem: if $\phi$ is continuous on $[p,q]$ and differentiable on $(p,q)$ then $\phi(q)-\phi(p)=\phi'(\xi)(q-p)$ for some $\xi\in(p,q)$. ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]])

[F5] Parameter integrals over a fixed compact measurable set of finite measure: if $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is compact, measurable and of finite measure, if $a<b$, and if the real-valued $f$ and $\partial_tf$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$, then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with derivative $\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx$ and has the corresponding one-sided relative derivatives at the endpoints of $[a,b]$; the lemma is stated pointwise in its one real parameter and explicitly asserts nothing for moving parameter sets or for singularities crossing $K$. Applying it once per parameter direction with its parameter renamed to $x_1,x_2,x_3$ or $t$ (all other variables held fixed), and iterating on the resulting integrals, yields the corresponding partial derivatives of a parameter integral whose integrand is smooth in all variables on a neighbourhood of the fixed $K$. ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]])

[F6] Chain rule and algebra of derivatives for the composite maps appearing below, such as $y\mapsto(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ and $(x,t)\mapsto(y,t-|x-y|/c)$. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]])

[F7] A map is of class $C^k$ (respectively $C^\infty$) when all its scalar components are, in the standard several-variable sense with continuous partial derivatives of all orders up to $k$. ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])

[F8] Zero-data wave Cauchy problem of speed $c$ from time $t_0$ with source $h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ in the extension sense: its solution is $u(x,t)=c^2\int_{t_0}^t(t-v)M_{c(t-v)}h(\cdot,v)(x)\,dv$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$, it is $C^\infty$ there, and it satisfies $c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u=h$; here $M_rh(x,v)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h(x+rn,v)\,d\Omega(n)$. ([[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]])

[F9] Polar-coordinates formula: for every nonnegative Borel $f:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(y)\,dy=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^2}f(r\omega)r^2\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$; here $\sigma$ is the polar surface measure of the cited formula, which equals the chart surface measure $d\Omega$ of [F13] ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]), so the two symbols are used interchangeably; a signed or complex $f$ is handled by applying the formula to positive and negative parts and subtracting. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]])

[F10] One-dimensional $L^1$ change of variables: for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ of open subsets of $\mathbb R$ and $f\in L^1(V)$, $\int_Vf=\int_Uf\circ T\,|T'|$. ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]])

[F11] Divergence theorem for a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain $\Omega$ and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$: $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$, with the outward normal. ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]])

[F12] Cross product and inner product on $\mathbb R^3$: $u\times v$ is bilinear and antisymmetric, $n\cdot(u\times v)=\det(n,u,v)$, and for $|n|=1$ the identities $n\cdot(n\times w)=0$ and $n\times(n\times w)=n(n\cdot w)-w$ hold, so $|n\times(n\times w)|=|n\times w|$. ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]])

[F13] Surface integral on the compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface $S^2$: for a nonnegative Borel $f$ the integral $\int_{S^2}f\,d\Omega$ is defined by finitely many regular parametrizations and an ambient partition of unity, the empty surface integrates to $0$, the definition is independent of the chosen presentation, the total surface measure $\int_{S^2}1\,d\Omega$ is finite, and the integral is monotone in $f$; the definition carries the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention already declared. ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]])

[F14] $C^1$ change of variables for nonnegative Borel functions: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ of open subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ and every nonnegative Borel $h:V\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_Vh(y)\,dy=\int_Uh(T(z))|\det DT(z)|\,dz$ with equality in $[0,\infty]$; in particular the translation $T(z)=x+z$ of $\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with $\det DT=1$, and a signed integrand is handled through its positive and negative parts by linearity. ([[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; part (a) differentiates the retarded integrals and identifies them with the wave Cauchy solution, part (b) expands the field integrals uniformly in the far zone and derives the continuity identity, part (c) passes to the surface integral.

1.1 Smoothness of the potentials: for $|x|>2a$ and $y\in\overline B_a$ one has $R=|x-y|\ge|x|-a>a$, so the maps $(x,t,y)\mapsto\rho(y,t-R/c)/R$ and $(x,t,y)\mapsto\mathbf J(y,t-R/c)/R$ are $C^\infty$ on a neighbourhood of $\{|x|>2a\}\times\mathbb R\times\overline B_a$ by [F6] and [F7]. Apply [F5] to the fixed compact set $K=\overline B_a$ once for each parameter direction with its one real parameter renamed to $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$ and $t$ (the remaining variables held fixed) and iterate on the resulting integrals: every differentiated integrand is again continuous on a neighbourhood of $K$, so each application is covered by the lemma and $\varphi$ and each component of $\mathbf A$ have continuous partial derivatives of every order on $\{|x|>2a\}\times\mathbb R$, hence are $C^\infty$ there by [F7]. [F5, F6, F7, F3]

1.2 Elementary estimates in the far zone: for $y\in B_a$, $r\ge2a$ and $n\in S^2$, expanding $R^2=(r-\sigma)^2+|y|^2-\sigma^2$ with $\sigma=n\cdot y$ gives $|R-(r-\sigma)|=\bigl||y|^2-\sigma^2\bigr|/(R+r-\sigma)\le a^2/r$ because $R+r-\sigma\ge r-\sigma+|r-\sigma|\ge r$; consequently $r-R\le a+a^2/r$, $|\mathbf N-n|=|(r-R)n-y|/R\le(a+a^2/r+a)/(r-a)\le5a/r$, $|1/R-1/r|\le(a+a^2/r)/(r(r-a))\le3a/r^2$, and $|\delta_y|\le a^2/(rc)$, all uniformly in $y,n$. [F12, F1]

2.1 Field formulas: by [F6], $\nabla_xR=\mathbf N$, $\nabla_x(t-R/c)=-\mathbf N/c$ and $\nabla_x\times[\mathbf J(y,t-R/c)]=-\mathbf N\times\mathbf J_t(y,t-R/c)/c$, while $\nabla_x(1/R)=-\mathbf N/R^2$; hence $\nabla_x[\rho(y,t-R/c)/R]=-\mathbf N[\rho/R^2+\rho_t/(cR)]$ and $\nabla_x\times[\mathbf J(y,t-R/c)/R]=-\mathbf N\times[\mathbf J/R^2+\mathbf J_t/(cR)]$. Each of these first derivatives of the integrands is continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline B_a$, so by [F5] the derivatives may be taken under the integral: $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf A$ are given on $\{|x|>2a\}$ by the two displayed integrals of the statement, since $\mathbf E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$. [step 1.1, F5, F6, F12]

2.2 Polar-coordinates identity: fix $|x|>2a$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, and let $h$ be either $\rho$ or one component $J_k$; then $y\mapsto h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/|x-y|$ vanishes off $\overline B_a$ and $|x-y|\ge a$ there, so $f(y):=h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/|x-y|$ is a bounded Borel function. The translation $T(z):=x+z$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\det DT=1$, so [F14] applied to the positive and negative parts of $f$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(x+z)\,dz$; applying [F9] to the positive and negative parts of $z\mapsto f(x+z)$, which at $z=\rho\omega$ equals $h(x+\rho\omega,t-\rho/c)/\rho$ and therefore has inner angular integral $\frac1\rho\int_{S^2}h(x+\rho n,t-\rho/c)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{4\pi}{\rho}M_\rho h(x,t-\rho/c)$, gives $\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}dy=\int_0^\infty r\,M_rh(x,t-r/c)\,dr$ with $M_rh(x,v)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h(x+rn,v)\,d\Omega(n)$, because the inner angular integral is $4\pi M_rh$ and the radial factor is $r^2/r=r$. [step 1.1, F9, F14, F1, F3]

2.3 Continuity identity: fix $n,u$ and let $\rho_0>a$; the map $F(y):=\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ is $C^1$ on $\overline B_{\rho_0}$, and [F6] gives $\operatorname{div}F(y)=\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J(y,v_y)+\frac nc\cdot\mathbf J_t(y,v_y)$ with $v_y=u+n\cdot y/c$. By [F11] on $B_{\rho_0}$, whose boundary flux vanishes because $\mathbf J=0$ for $|y|>a$, $\int_{B_{\rho_0}}\operatorname{div}F\,dy=0$; substituting the chain-rule expression and using (H2), $0=\int_{B_{\rho_0}}\bigl[-\rho_t(y,v_y)+\frac1cn\cdot\mathbf J_t(y,v_y)\bigr]dy$. The integrands vanish for $|y|>a$ by (H1), so [F2] lets the integrals be taken over $B_a$; the second is $\frac1cn\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$ by the definition of $\mathbf V$, whence $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,v_y)\,dy=\frac1cn\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$. [step 1.2, F11, F6, F2]

3.1 Identification with the Cauchy solution: for $t\in[t_0,T]$ substitute $r=c(t-v)$ in the identity of step 2.2; the integrand $r\,M_rh(x,t-r/c)$ is continuous and compactly supported in the variable $v$ on $[t_0,t]$, so [F10] applied on that compact interval gives $\int_0^\infty r\,M_rh(x,t-r/c)\,dr=c^2\int_{t_0}^t(t-v)M_{c(t-v)}h(x,v)\,dv$. For $h=\mu_0c^2\rho$ this last expression is exactly the zero-data solution of [F8], and therefore $\varphi(x,t)=\frac{\mu_0c^2}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y,t-R/c)/R\,dy=\mu_0c^2\int_0^\infty rM_r\rho\,dr=c^2\int_{t_0}^t(t-v)M_{c(t-v)}(\mu_0c^2\rho)(x,v)\,dv$ coincides with it on $\{|x|\ge2a\}\times[t_0,T]$; the same computation with $h=\mu_0J_k$ identifies $A_k$ with the zero-data solution for source $\mu_0J_k$. [step 2.2, F10, F8]

3.2 Uniform error estimates: fix $n,u,r$, let $\mathrm{ret}$ denote the argument $v_y+\delta_y$ and $0$ the argument $v_y$, and write $F_{\mathrm{tot}}:=c^2\mathbf N\rho_{\mathrm{ret}}/R^2+c\mathbf N\rho_{t,\mathrm{ret}}/R-\mathbf J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}/R$ and $F_{\mathrm{lead}}:=\frac1r\bigl(c\,n\,\rho_{t,0}-\mathbf J_{t,0}\bigr)$, so that the field formula of step 2.1 and the definition of $\mathbf V$ give $\mathbf E(rn,u+r/c)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{B_a}(F_{\mathrm{tot}}-F_{\mathrm{lead}})\,dy$ by the linearity of the integral. Every source factor is bounded by its supremum on $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$, and (H1) makes $\rho$ and $\mathbf J$ vanish on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times((-\infty,t_0)\cup(T,\infty))$, hence makes all their partial derivatives vanish there too, so these suprema also dominate the retarded arguments $v_y+\delta_y$; the mean value theorem [F4] gives $|\rho_{t,\mathrm{ret}}-\rho_{t,0}|\le\Gamma_{\rho tt}|\delta_y|$ and similarly for $\mathbf J_t$, and combining these with the estimates of step 1.2 term by term yields $|F_{\mathrm{tot}}-F_{\mathrm{lead}}|\le\Gamma_E'/r^2$ for all $r\ge2a$; hence, by the triangle inequality for the integral and the finiteness of $\lambda(B_a)$, $\bigl|\mathbf E(rn,u+r/c)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\bigr|\le\Gamma_E/r^2$ with $\Gamma_E:=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\Gamma_E'\lambda(B_a)$. The same computation applied to $\mathbf B(rn,u+r/c)=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{B_a}\mathbf N\times[\mathbf J_{\mathrm{ret}}/R^2+\mathbf J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}/(cR)]dy$ and to $n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}/c=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{B_a}\frac1{cr}n\times\mathbf J_{t,0}\,dy$ gives $\bigl|\mathbf B(rn,u+r/c)-n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)/c\bigr|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$. [step 1.2, step 2.3, F2, F3, F4, F12]

4.1 Smoothness of the far-zone moments: the map $(n,u)\mapsto\mathbf I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and its partial derivative $\partial_u\mathbf I=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy=\mathbf V(n,u)$ are $C^\infty$ in $(n,u)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: apply [F5] repeatedly in the directions $n_1,n_2,n_3,u$ with the fixed compact set $B_a$, each differentiated integrand again being continuous on a neighbourhood of $B_a$. In particular $n\mapsto|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2$ is continuous for each fixed $u$. [step 3.2, F5, F6, F7, F12]

4.2 Pointwise flux asymptotics: by step 3.2 write $\mathbf E=\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}+\boldsymbol\rho_E$ and $\mathbf B=n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}/c+\boldsymbol\rho_B$ at $(rn,u+r/c)$ with $|\boldsymbol\rho_E|\le\Gamma_E/r^2$, $|\boldsymbol\rho_B|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$; then $n\cdot\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}=0$ and $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}\times(n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})=|\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}|^2n$ by [F12], while $|\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|$ because $|n\times(n\times\mathbf V)|=|n\times\mathbf V|$. Expanding the cross product bilinearly, the error terms are $O(r^{-3})$, so $r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,u+r/c)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2+R(n,u,r)$ with $|R(n,u,r)|\le C/r$ for a constant $C$ depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and the source suprema, uniformly in $n\in S^2$ and $u\in[t_0,T]$. [step 3.2, F12, F2]

5.1 Flux limit: by [F13] the surface integral over the compact sphere of a bounded Borel function is finite and monotone, so for every $u\in[t_0,T]$ and $r\ge2a$ the difference $\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,u+r/c)\,d\Omega(n)-\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2\,d\Omega(n)=\int_{S^2}R(n,u,r)\,d\Omega(n)$ has absolute value at most $\frac{C}{r}\int_{S^2}1\,d\Omega$, which tends to $0$; the function $n\mapsto|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2$ is continuous by step 4.1, so its surface integral is the displayed finite constant. Hence the stated limit at fixed retarded time $u$ follows; no step compares different values of $u$, so the limit is asserted only at fixed retarded time. [step 4.2, step 4.1, F13, F2] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the surface-integral conventions used by [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]].

(i) (Causality without passivity.) In this clause also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]), inherited from the exact AC supplier. Let $K(s):=-e^{-s}$ for $s\ge0$. Then $K$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ (indeed $K'=e^{-s}=-K$, $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=1$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$), so the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] applies: $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ is a bounded causal linear response on bounded continuous histories, its transfer function is $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and its boundary value $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ for every $\omega>0$. Hence the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$ is strictly negative, not positive semidefinite, and the monochromatic period-averaged work of clause (d) of that theorem is strictly negative for $d=1$, every $e\ne0$ and every $\omega>0$ (with any response normalization $\varepsilon_0>0$), although the response is causal and its entry satisfies the dispersion relations of clause (c). Nonnegative period-averaged work (passivity) is therefore an additional condition on the model, not a consequence of temporal causality.

(ii) (The flux limit needs fixed retarded time.) In the setting of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]], fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in S^2$, and let $r>\max\{2a,\;a+c(t-t_0)\}$. Then for every $y\in B_a$ one has $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$, so $t-R/c<t_0$; by hypothesis (H1) of that theorem the functions $\rho,\rho_t,\mathbf J,\mathbf J_t$ all vanish at $(y,t-R/c)$, so every integrand in the field formulas of clause (a) of that theorem vanishes and $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$, hence $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. Therefore $\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)\,d\Omega(n)=0$ for all such $r$: at fixed observation time the far-zone flux integral is identically zero beyond the light cone of the compact spacetime support, whereas clause (c) of that theorem is a limit at fixed retarded time. The retarded-time formulation cannot be replaced by a fixed-observation-time one.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and, in clause (i), also Dependent Choice $\mathrm{DC}$ ([[def-dependent-choice]]); the kernel $K(s)=-e^{-s}$ on $[0,\infty)$; in clause (i) the causal-response theorem [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] with its clauses (a), (c) and (d); in clause (ii) the radiation theorem [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] with its hypotheses (H1), (H2) and its clauses (a), (b), (c), together with its constants $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$, $t_0<T$, sources $\rho,\mathbf J$ and fields $\mathbf E,\mathbf B$, $\mathbf S=\mu_0^{-1}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$.

[F1] The real exponential satisfies $\exp(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!$ with $e=\exp(1)$, is $C^\infty$ with $\exp^{(m)}=\exp$ for every $m$, and satisfies $\exp(x)>0$ and $\exp(-x)=1/\exp(x)$ for every real $x$. ([[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]])

[F2] Newton–Leibniz on $[a,b]$ for a function differentiable on $(a,b)$ with Riemann integrable derivative, and integration by parts on $[a,b]$ for differentiable functions with integrable derivatives; a bounded Riemann integrable function on $[a,b]$ has the same Lebesgue integral. ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], [[thm-integration-by-parts]], [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]])

[F3] Monotone convergence for a nondecreasing sequence of nonnegative measurable functions. ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]])

[F4] Dominated convergence; the integral over a measurable set; the $L^1$ conventions; linearity of the integral, including $\int-cf=-c\int f$; and equality of integrals of integrable functions that agree almost everywhere. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]])

[F5] A function that is continuous on a compact interval, differentiable in the interior, and whose derivative extends continuously is Lipschitz, hence absolutely continuous; absolute continuity is the finite disjoint-interval condition; and $C^k$ is the usual several-variable class. ([[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]], [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])

[F6] Chain rule and algebra of derivatives for the real composites used below, including the derivative of $s\mapsto e^{-s}$. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]])

[F7] The complex exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$; for every nonzero $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ the function $F(s)=e^{\lambda s}/\lambda$ is a primitive of $s\mapsto e^{\lambda s}$ on $\mathbb C$, so for the interval path $[0,N]$ the complex line integral equals $F(N)-F(0)$; the Riemann–Stieltjes and parametric contour integrals agree for piecewise $C^1$ contours. ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]], [[def-complex-primitive]], [[thm-fundamental-theorem-for-complex-line-integrals]], [[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]], [[thm-riemann-stieltjes-and-parametric-contour-integrals-agree]])

[F8] $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$ for real $x,y$, and $\operatorname{Re},\operatorname{Im},\overline{\phantom{z}}$ are the coordinate maps of the cited definition. ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]])

[F9] The causal-response theorem, consumed in clause (i): clause (a) gives the bounded causal linear response of an $L^1$ kernel together with its transfer function; clause (c) gives the transform of an integrable kernel as a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane with its boundary values, dispersion relations and the sharper bound; clause (d) gives the monochromatic period-averaged work $(\varepsilon_0\omega/2)\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ and its equivalence with positive semidefiniteness of $M(\omega)=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$. ([[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]])

[F10] The radiation theorem, consumed in clauses (i) and (ii): under (H1) and (H2), its clause (a) gives the retarded field integrals on $\{|x|>2a\}$ for all times, its clause (b) gives the uniform far-zone errors and the identity $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy=\frac1cn\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$, and its clause (c) is the flux limit at fixed retarded time. ([[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]])

[F11] The Euclidean norm obeys the triangle inequality, hence $|rn-y|\ge\bigl||rn|-|y|\bigr|=r-|y|$ for $y\in B_a$, and the dot product and cross product are those of the cited definitions. ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]])

[F12] On a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface the surface integral is defined by finitely many regular parametrizations, and the identically zero nonnegative function has integral $0$. ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]])

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct computation for clause (i); direct substitution into the cited theorem and the triangle inequality for clause (ii).

1.1 The kernel $K(s)=-e^{-s}$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K'=e^{-s}=-K$ by [F1] and [F6]; $K(s)<0$ for every $s$, and $|K(s)|=e^{-s}$, $|K'(s)|=e^{-s}$, $|sK(s)|=se^{-s}$. Newton–Leibniz gives $\int_0^Ne^{-s}ds=1-e^{-N}$ and integration by parts gives $\int_0^Nse^{-s}ds=1-(1+N)e^{-N}$ for every $N$, and [F2] converts these to Lebesgue integrals; since the integrands are nonnegative, [F3] lets $N\to\infty$, giving $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=1$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$. Hence $K,K',sK\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and, by [F5], $K$ is locally absolutely continuous on $[0,\infty)$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6]

2.1 Therefore the integrable branch of clause (c) of [F9] applies to $K$: $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ is a bounded causal linear response on bounded continuous histories by clause (a), $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane, and its boundary values satisfy the dispersion relations of clause (c). [step 1.1, F9, F4]

3.1 Computation of the transfer function: fix $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ and put $\lambda:=iz-1$, so $\lambda\ne0$ and $|e^{\lambda N}|=e^{-N}e^{-N\operatorname{Im}z}\le e^{-N}\to0$ by [F8]. For every $N>0$ the function $s\mapsto e^{\lambda s}$ is continuous, so its Lebesgue integral over $(0,N)$ agrees with its Riemann and parametric line integral over $[0,N]$ by [F2] and [F7], and the first fundamental theorem of [F7] applied to the primitive $F(s)=e^{\lambda s}/\lambda$ gives $\int_0^Ne^{\lambda s}ds=(e^{\lambda N}-1)/\lambda$; the truncated integrands $s\mapsto-e^{\lambda s}\mathbf 1_{(0,N)}(s)$ converge pointwise to $s\mapsto-e^{\lambda s}$ and are dominated by $e^{-s}\in L^1(0,\infty)$, so [F4] gives $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty(-e^{\lambda s})ds=-\lim_{N\to\infty}(e^{\lambda N}-1)/\lambda=1/\lambda=-1/(1-iz)$, where for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ the first equality is the defining integral of clause (c) of [F9] and for real $z$ it is its continuous boundary value. [step 2.1, F7, F8, F4, F2]

4.1 Boundary values and the dissipative part: for real $\omega$, step 3.1 gives $\chi(\omega)=-1/(1-i\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ by multiplication with the conjugate denominator, so $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ for every $\omega>0$; for $d=1$ and $e\ne0$, $e^*\chi(\omega)e=|e|^2\chi(\omega)$ and $e^*M(\omega)e=|e|^2\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)<0$, so the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$ is strictly negative and in particular not positive semidefinite. By clause (d) of [F9] the monochromatic period-averaged work equals $(\varepsilon_0\omega/2)|e|^2\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$, which is strictly negative for every $e\ne0$ and every $\varepsilon_0>0$, while steps 2.1 and 3.1 exhibit the response as causal with dispersion relations. Passivity is therefore an additional condition and not a consequence of causality. [step 3.1, F9, F8, F4]

5.1 Clause (ii): fix $t\in\mathbb R$, $n\in S^2$ and $r>\max\{2a,a+c(t-t_0)\}$, so $r>2a$ and $r-a>c(t-t_0)$. For every $y\in B_a$ the triangle inequality of [F11] gives $R=|rn-y|\ge r-|y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$, hence $t-R/c<t_0$; since (H1) makes $\rho$ and $\mathbf J$ vanish on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times((-\infty,t_0)\cup(T,\infty))$, all their partial derivatives vanish there too, so $\rho,\rho_t,\mathbf J,\mathbf J_t$ all vanish at $(y,t-R/c)$ for every $y\in B_a$, and the integrands of the field formulas of clause (a) of [F10] vanish pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$. Hence $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$, so $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=\mu_0^{-1}n\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$, and [F12] gives $\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)\,d\Omega(n)=0$ for all such $r$. [step 4.1, F10, F11, F12]

6.1 The two formulations differ: clause (c) of [F10] is the limit along $t=u+r/c$ with $u$ fixed, that is, at fixed retarded time, whereas step 5.1 shows that the flux integral at fixed observation time $t$ is identically zero for every $r>\max\{2a,a+c(t-t_0)\}$. The retarded-time formulation therefore cannot be replaced by a fixed-observation-time one, and no decay assumption beyond (H1) was used. [step 5.1, F10] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\theta_0\in U$, and let $u\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfy $\lVert u\rVert_2=1$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval with $0\in I$ and such that $\gamma(\theta):=\theta_0+\theta u\in U$ for every $\theta\in I$. Let $F:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $F(\theta_0)=0$, and suppose that for every $\theta\in I$ the directional derivative of $F$ along $u$ satisfies

$$D_uF(\theta_0+\theta u)=\langle\nabla F(\theta_0+\theta u),u\rangle\ge m>0$$

([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). Let a recorded scalar $\hat y\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\hat y|\le s$ with $s\ge0$, and let a calibration-error bound $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$ with $\delta\ge0$ hold for $y:=F(\theta_0+\theta u)$ at a candidate $\theta\in I$. Then

$$|\theta|\le\frac{s+\delta}{m},$$

and the corresponding configuration displacement $\gamma(\theta)-\theta_0=\theta u$ has Euclidean length $\lVert\theta u\rVert_2=|\theta|$. The conclusion is a deterministic conditional statement about the stated bounds; it is not a sampling law, a statistical inference, or a claim about any historical report, and the parameters $s,\delta,m$ are supplied by the user of the statement rather than estimated from data here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** a natural $n\ge1$; an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$; a point $\theta_0\in U$; a vector $u\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\lVert u\rVert_2=1$; an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with $0\in I$ and $\gamma(\theta):=\theta_0+\theta u\in U$ for every $\theta\in I$; a function $F:U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^1$ with $F(\theta_0)=0$ and $D_uF(\theta_0+\theta u)=\langle\nabla F(\theta_0+\theta u),u\rangle\ge m>0$ for every $\theta\in I$; a recorded scalar $\hat y\in\mathbb R$ with $|\hat y|\le s$, $s\ge0$; a calibration bound $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$, $\delta\ge0$, for $y=F(\theta_0+\theta u)$ at a candidate $\theta\in I$.

[F1] The intervals that are open in the sense of [[def-interval]] are the four forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)=\mathbb R$, and a set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ is open when every $x\in A$ has a real $\varepsilon>0$ with $N_\varepsilon(x)\subseteq A$, where $N_\varepsilon(x)$ is the neighbourhood of [[def-open-and-closed-in-r]].

[F2] The punctured neighbourhood $N^{*}_\varepsilon(x)=\{\,y:0<|y-x|<\varepsilon\,\}$ is never empty: the element $x+\varepsilon/2$ satisfies $|(x+\varepsilon/2)-x|=\varepsilon/2$, which is $>0$ and $<\varepsilon$ ([[def-neighbourhood-r]]).

[F3] Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it ([[def-derivative]]).

[F4] A limit point of $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a point $p$ with $N^{*}_\eta(p)\cap A\ne\varnothing$ for every real $\eta>0$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]).

[F5] The derivative of $h:A\to\mathbb R$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ is $h'(c)=\lim_{x\to c}\bigl(h(x)-h(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, the limit of the difference quotient, and $h$ is differentiable at $c$ when that limit exists ([[def-derivative]]).

[F6] If $B\subseteq A$, if $c\in B$ is a limit point of $B$ and if $h:A\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at $c$, then the restriction $h|_B:B\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at $c$ with $(h|_B)'(c)=h'(c)$ ([[def-derivative]]).

[F7] For a natural number $n\ge1$ the function $p_n(x)=x^{n}$ is differentiable at every real, with derivative $n\,c^{\,n-1}$ at $c$ when the natural number $n$ is read as a real number, and the constant function $p_0\equiv1$ is differentiable at every real with derivative $0$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]]).

[F8] If $f,g:A\to\mathbb R$ are differentiable at a limit point $c$ of $A$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$ and $\alpha f$ are differentiable at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\alpha f)'(c)=\alpha f'(c)$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], claims 1 and 2).

[F9] For $U'\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U'$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$ and $f:U'\to\mathbb R^n$, if the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the directional derivative $D_vf(a)=\lim_{t\to0}\bigl(f(a+tv)-f(a)\bigr)/t$, and for a standard basis vector $e_j$ one writes $\partial_jf(a)=D_{e_j}f(a)$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); in $\mathbb R^1$ the only standard basis vector is $e_0=1$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

[F10] For $h:A\to\mathbb R$ with $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $c$ a limit point of $A$, the statement $\lim_{x\to c}h(x)=L$ means: for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is a real $\delta>0$ such that every $x\in A$ with $0<|x-c|<\delta$ satisfies $|h(x)-L|<\varepsilon$ ([[def-function-limit]]).

[F11] For $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, $c$ a limit point of $A$, $f:A\to\mathbb R^m$ and $L\in\mathbb R^m$, one has $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L$ if and only if $\lim_{x\to c}f_i(x)=L_i$ for every $i<m$ ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]], clause 2).

[F12] A vector-valued $f:A\to\mathbb R^m$ on $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ is continuous at $a\in A$ when for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is a real $\delta>0$ such that every $x\in A$ with $|x-a|<\delta$ satisfies $\lVert f(x)-f(a)\rVert_2<\varepsilon$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]).

[F13] A map $f:U'\to\mathbb R^n$ on an open $U'\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is totally differentiable at $a\in U'$ when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ with $\lVert f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\rVert_2/\lVert h\rVert_2\to0$ as $h\to0$, and then $L$ is written $Df(a)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

[F14] If every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ of $f:U'\to\mathbb R^n$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U'$ and is continuous at $a$, then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]).

[F15] If $f:U'\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)$ exists for every $v$ and equals $Df(a)v$; in particular $\partial_jf(a)=Df(a)e_j$ ([[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F16] A map is of class $C^1$ when each component is; for a scalar function on an open set this means that the function and each of its first coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous on the domain ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

[F17] If a scalar-valued $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, then $D_vf(a)=\langle\nabla f(a),v\rangle$ for every $v$ ([[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]).

[F18] For scalar $f$ whose partial derivatives exist at $a$, the gradient is $\nabla f(a)=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

[F19] The Euclidean inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$ with norm $\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$; for $n\ge1$ one has $\lVert x-y\rVert_2=d_2(x,y)$; and two elements of $\mathbb R^n$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k<n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F20] If $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $g$ is totally differentiable at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ with $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F21] Real continuity ([[def-continuity-real]]), metric continuity ([[def-metric-continuity]]), the choice-free equivalence of continuity with openness of preimages ([[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]], conditions (a) and (b)), the agreement of the real and metric notions on subsets of $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]]), and continuity of sums and scalar multiples at a point of a common domain $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], claim 1).

[F22] For every norm $N$ on a real vector space and all $\lambda$ in $\mathbb R$ one has $N(\lambda v)=|\lambda|N(v)$ (axiom (N2) of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb R^n$ for every natural number $n$, inducing the metric $d_2$ whenever $n\ge1$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], clause 2).

[F23] Images and preimages of sets under a function are those of the induced relation, and $f^{-1}[V]$ denotes the preimage of $V$ under $f$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

[F24] The bounded-error model comparison: for an interval $I$ with at least two elements, $\theta_0\in I$ and $f:I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^1$ with $f(\theta_0)=0$ and $f'\ge m>0$ on $I$, every candidate $\theta\in I$ for which a recorded scalar $\hat y$ satisfies $|\hat y|\le s$, $s\ge0$, and $y=f(\theta)$ satisfies $|y-\hat y|\le\delta$, $\delta\ge0$, obeys $|\theta-\theta_0|\le(s+\delta)/m$ ([[lem-em-bounded-error-model-comparison]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The interval $I$ is one of the four open forms of [F1], hence an open subset of $\mathbb R$; fix a real $\varepsilon>0$ with $N_\varepsilon(0)\subseteq I$. By [F2] the punctured neighbourhood $N^{*}_\varepsilon(0)$ is a nonempty subset of $N_\varepsilon(0)\subseteq I$, so $I$ contains $0$ and at least one further point and is therefore nondegenerate; by [F3] every point of $I$ is a limit point of $I$, that is, by [F4], $N^{*}_\eta(\theta)\cap I\ne\varnothing$ for every $\theta\in I$ and every real $\eta>0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4]

1.2 The function $F$ is totally differentiable at $p:=\gamma(\theta)=\theta_0+\theta u$, and $D_uF(p)=\langle\nabla F(p),u\rangle$: as $F$ is of class $C^1$, each first partial derivative $\partial_jF$ exists and is continuous on the open set $U$ by [F16], so [F14] gives total differentiability of $F$ at $p\in U$, and [F17] gives $D_uF(p)=\langle\nabla F(p),u\rangle$. [given, F16, F14, F17]

1.3 The path $\gamma:I\to U$ is continuous at every $\theta'\in I$: given a real $\varepsilon>0$ take $\delta:=\varepsilon$; for $\theta''\in I$ with $|\theta''-\theta'|<\delta$ one has $d_2\bigl(\gamma(\theta''),\gamma(\theta')\bigr)=\lVert\gamma(\theta'')-\gamma(\theta')\rVert_2=\lVert(\theta''-\theta')u\rVert_2=|\theta''-\theta'|\,\lVert u\rVert_2=|\theta''-\theta'|<\varepsilon$, by [F19], the homogeneity axiom (N2) of [F22] and $\lVert u\rVert_2=1$; this is continuity in the metric sense of [F21]. [given, F19, F22, F21]

1.4 The configuration displacement has Euclidean length $\lVert\gamma(\theta)-\theta_0\rVert_2=\lVert\theta u\rVert_2=|\theta|\,\lVert u\rVert_2=|\theta|$, by the Euclidean norm of [F19], the homogeneity axiom (N2) of [F22] and $\lVert u\rVert_2=1$. [F19, F22, given]

2.1 For every $\theta\in I$ the components of the path satisfy $\gamma_j(\theta+t)=\gamma_j(\theta)+tu_j$ for every real $t$ with $\theta+t\in I$, since $\gamma_j(\theta+t)=(\theta_0)_j+(\theta+t)u_j=(\theta_0)_j+\theta u_j+tu_j=\gamma_j(\theta)+tu_j$ by field arithmetic; on $I$ the functions $1_I:=p_0|_I$, constantly $1$, and $\mathrm{id}_I:=p_1|_I$, the identity, are differentiable at $\theta$ with derivatives $0$ and $1$, because the power functions $p_0$ and $p_1$ have those derivatives at every real by [F7] and $\theta$ is a limit point of $I$ by step 1.1, so [F6] restricts; since $\gamma_j=(\theta_0)_j\cdot1_I+u_j\cdot\mathrm{id}_I$ on $I$, the sum and scalar rules of [F8] give that $\gamma_j$ is differentiable at $\theta$ with $\gamma_j'(\theta)=(\theta_0)_j\cdot0+u_j\cdot1=u_j$. [step 1.1, F7, F6, F8, algebra]

2.2 Each composite $\partial_jF\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R$ is continuous: for open $V\subseteq\mathbb R$ the preimage $(\partial_jF\circ\gamma)^{-1}[V]$ is, by [F23], the preimage $\gamma^{-1}\bigl[\partial_jF^{-1}[V]\bigr]$; the set $\partial_jF^{-1}[V]$ is open in the domain $U$ of the continuous $\partial_jF$ by the choice-free equivalence (a)$\Leftrightarrow$(b) of [F21], and its preimage under the continuous $\gamma$ is therefore open in $I$; the same equivalence then gives continuity of $\partial_jF\circ\gamma$ on $I$. [step 1.3, F16, F23, F21]

3.1 For every $\theta\in I$ the partial derivative of $\gamma_j$ in the direction $e_0=1$ equals its ordinary derivative, so $\partial_0\gamma_j(\theta)=u_j$: by [F9] the directional derivative $D_{e_0}\gamma_j(\theta)$ is the limit at $0$ of $t\mapsto\bigl(\gamma_j(\theta+t)-\gamma_j(\theta)\bigr)/t$, while by [F5] the derivative $\gamma_j'(\theta)=u_j$ of step 2.1 is the limit at $\theta$ of $x\mapsto\bigl(\gamma_j(x)-\gamma_j(\theta)\bigr)/(x-\theta)$; the substitution $x=\theta+t$ carries one punctured domain bijectively onto the other and the two $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ conditions of [F10] are the same condition, so $D_{e_0}\gamma_j(\theta)=\gamma_j'(\theta)=u_j$. [step 2.1, F9, F5, F10, algebra]

4.1 For every $\theta\in I$ the partial derivative of the path is the vector $\partial_0\gamma(\theta)=u$: the quotient $q_\theta(t):=\bigl(\gamma(\theta+t)-\gamma(\theta)\bigr)/t$ on its domain $\{\,t:t\ne0,\ \theta+t\in I\,\}$ has limit $\partial_0\gamma(\theta)$ by [F9], the $j$-th component of $q_\theta$ is $t\mapsto\bigl(\gamma_j(\theta+t)-\gamma_j(\theta)\bigr)/t$ with limit $\partial_0\gamma_j(\theta)$, and step 3.1 gives $\partial_0\gamma_j(\theta)=u_j$; by the componentwise limit criterion [F11] the $j$-th coordinate of $\partial_0\gamma(\theta)$ equals $u_j$ for every $j<n$, and two vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ with equal coordinates are equal by [F19], so $\partial_0\gamma(\theta)=u$. [step 3.1, F9, F11, F19]

5.1 The only partial derivative of $\gamma$ is the constant $\partial_0\gamma\equiv u$ on $I$ by step 4.1 applied at every $\theta\in I$, and it is continuous at $\theta$: given a real $\varepsilon>0$, every $\delta>0$ serves for the continuity condition of [F12], because $\lVert\partial_0\gamma(\theta')-\partial_0\gamma(\theta)\rVert_2=\lVert u-u\rVert_2=0<\varepsilon$ for every $\theta'\in I$. [step 4.1, F12]

6.1 The path $\gamma$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$ with $D\gamma(\theta)(1)=u$: the partial derivative $\partial_0\gamma$ exists on the neighbourhood $I$ of $\theta$ in the open domain $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and is continuous at $\theta$ by step 5.1, so $D\gamma(\theta)$ exists by [F14]; moreover $D\gamma(\theta)(1)=D\gamma(\theta)(e_0)=\partial_0\gamma(\theta)=u$ by [F15] and step 4.1. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F13, F14, F15]

7.1 The composite $g:=F\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at every $\theta\in I$ with $Dg(\theta)=DF(\gamma(\theta))\circ D\gamma(\theta)$ by the chain rule [F20], applied to the totally differentiable $\gamma$ of step 6.1 and $F$ of step 1.2; consequently $g'(\theta)=Dg(\theta)(1)=DF(\gamma(\theta))\bigl(D\gamma(\theta)(1)\bigr)=DF(\gamma(\theta))(u)=D_uF(\gamma(\theta))=\langle\nabla F(\gamma(\theta)),u\rangle\ge m$ for every $\theta\in I$, where the first equality identifies the ordinary derivative with the total derivative applied to $1$ (the limits of [F9] and [F5] coincide as in step 3.1) and the remaining equalities are step 6.1, [F15] and step 1.2. [step 1.2, step 3.1, step 6.1, F20, F15, F9, F5]

8.1 The derivative $g'$ is continuous on $I$: on $I$ one has $g'(\theta)=\sum_{j<n}u_j\,(\partial_jF\circ\gamma)(\theta)$ by step 7.1, the gradient definition [F18] and the inner product of [F19]; the composites are continuous by step 2.2, the dictionary of [F21] transfers this to the real reading, and finite sums and scalar multiples of functions continuous at each point of $I$ are continuous there by the algebra clause of [F21]; in particular $g'$ is continuous on $I$ in the sense required by [F24]. [step 2.2, step 7.1, F18, F19, F21, F24]

9.1 The value of $g$ at the centre is $g(0)=F(\theta_0+0\cdot u)=F(\theta_0)=0$, and $I$ has at least two elements with $0\in I$ by step 1.1; the function $g:I\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ with continuous derivative by steps 7.1 and 8.1, and $g'\ge m>0$ on $I$ by step 7.1. [step 1.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, given]

10.1 The bounded-error model comparison [F24] now applies to $g$ on $I$ with centre $\theta_0:=0$ and the recorded scalar $\hat y$, $s$, $\delta$ of the statement, because a model value $y=g(\theta)=F(\theta_0+\theta u)$ at the candidate $\theta\in I$ is exactly the quantity the calibration bound constrains; its conclusion is $|\theta-0|\le(s+\delta)/m$, that is $|\theta|\le(s+\delta)/m$, and the equivalent contrapositive form says that a proposed $\theta$ violating this bound is incompatible with the two stated bounds; with the displacement identity of step 1.4 the statement is proved. [step 1.4, step 9.1, F24, given] ∎

## Remarks

- **What the statement does not assert.** The bounds $s,\delta,m$ are parameters of the *statement*, not estimates: no sampling distribution, likelihood, confidence level or measurement precision is introduced or claimed, and the conclusion is the deterministic conditional inequality alone. The consumer on the empirical-testing page must supply and qualify $s$, $\delta$ and $m$ from an explicit detector and calibration model before any physical reading.

- **Where the hypotheses are used.** The unit length of $u$ enters only in the final length identity; the lower bound $D_uF\ge m$ enters through the interpolating lemma and is exactly the hypothesis the companion example shows cannot be dropped; the openness of $I$ and $0\in I$ make every point of $I$ a limit point of $I$ and $I$ nondegenerate, which is what lets the one-variable and total-differential machinery apply on $I$.

- **No choice principle is used.** The proof invokes only the choice-free parts of [[thm-metric-continuity-characterisations]], namely the equivalence of continuity with openness of preimages, and nothing is selected from a family of nonempty sets. The single application of the bounded-error lemma inherits no choice assumption.

## Example

(i) Specialise [[thm-em-uncertainty-analysis]] to $n=1$, $U=\mathbb R$, $\theta_0=0$, $u=1$, $I=\mathbb R$ and $F(\theta)=m\theta$ with $m>0$. Then $F$ is $C^1$, $F(0)=0$, $\nabla F(\theta)=m$ and $\langle\nabla F(\theta),1\rangle=m\ge m$, so the theorem's hypothesis holds with equality. Fix the recorded value $\hat y=0$ (so $s=0$) and any $\delta\ge0$. A candidate $\theta\in\mathbb R$ is compatible with the calibration bound exactly when $|F(\theta)-\hat y|=|m\theta|\le\delta$, that is, exactly when $|\theta|\le\delta/m$; this is precisely the theorem's bound $(s+\delta)/m=\delta/m$, and the bound is attained (equality) at $\theta=\pm\delta/m$. Hence the constant $(s+\delta)/m$ cannot be improved for this instance, and the special case $\delta=0$ leaves $\theta=0$ as the only compatible candidate. (ii) The positive lower bound on the response is not removable. If it is dropped, take $m=0$ and $F\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R$: the hypothesis $\langle\nabla F(\theta),u\rangle\ge m>0$ fails, and with the same data $\hat y=0$, $s=0$, $\delta\ge0$ every $\theta\in\mathbb R$ is compatible, because $y=0$ and $|y-\hat y|=0\le\delta$; no finite parameter bound then follows from the indicator and the two bounds alone. (iii) These are mathematical observations about a hypothetical bounded-error model: no experimental data, sampling law or statistical inference is used or asserted, and the displayed numbers are stipulated parameters, not measurements.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** a real $m>0$; a real $\delta\ge0$; the linear function $F(\theta)=m\theta$ on $\mathbb R$; the recorded value $\hat y=0$ with $s=0$; and the alternative function $F\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R$ read with $m=0$.

[F1] The uncertainty theorem: for open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, unit $u$, an open interval $I\ni0$ with $\gamma(\theta)=\theta_0+\theta u\in U$, a $C^1$ function $F$ with $F(\theta_0)=0$ and $D_uF(\theta_0+\theta u)=\langle\nabla F(\theta_0+\theta u),u\rangle\ge m>0$ on $I$, and recorded $\hat y$, $s\ge0$, $\delta\ge0$ with $|\hat y|\le s$ and $|F(\theta_0+\theta u)-\hat y|\le\delta$ at a candidate $\theta\in I$, one has $|\theta|\le(s+\delta)/m$, and then $\lVert\theta u\rVert_2=|\theta|$ ([[thm-em-uncertainty-analysis]]).

[F2] $\mathbb R=(-\infty,\infty)$ is the open interval of [[def-interval]] containing $0$, and $\mathbb R$ is an open subset of itself ([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]).

[F3] Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it, and a limit point of $A$ is a point every punctured neighbourhood of which meets $A$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-limit-point-r]]).

[F4] The identity $p_1(x)=x$ is differentiable at every real with $p_1'(c)=1$, and the constant $p_0\equiv1$ is differentiable at every real with derivative $0$ ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]]).

[F5] At a limit point $c$ of a common domain $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, sums and scalar multiples of functions differentiable at $c$ are differentiable at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\alpha f)'(c)=\alpha f'(c)$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F6] For $f$ on a subset of $\mathbb R$, the derivative at a limit point $c$ is the limit of the difference quotient ([[def-derivative]]), and the directional derivative in the direction $e_0=1$ is the limit of $t\mapsto(f(c+t)-f(c))/t$, the two limits coinciding under the substitution $x=c+t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); in $\mathbb R^1$ the only standard basis vector is $e_0=1$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

[F7] The gradient of a scalar function is the vector of its partial derivatives, $\nabla f(a)=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

[F8] The Euclidean inner product on $\mathbb R^n$ is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$ with norm $\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$, and a nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root, so $\lVert(1)\rVert_2=\sqrt{1}=1$ in $\mathbb R^1$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F9] Absolute value: $|x|\ge0$, $|x|=0$ if and only if $x=0$, and $|xy|=|x|\,|y|$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), with the case definition $|x|=x$ for $x\ge0$ and $|x|=-x$ for $x<0$ ([[def-abs-value]]).
