## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\mu_0=(\varepsilon_0c^2)^{-1}$, and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for all $s$. These are mathematical parameters. On $Q=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ let $\rho,J$ and $\Phi,\Upsilon$ be exactly the proper point-current and retarded-history distributions of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] and [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]], with the kernel $K$ of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] and no independent free addition. Put $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Then:

(a) $W\Phi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $W\Upsilon=\mu_0J$ and $\operatorname{div}\Upsilon+c^{-2}\partial_t\Phi=0$ in $\mathcal D'(Q)$.

(b) Define the vector distributions $\mathcal E=-\nabla\Phi-\partial_t\Upsilon$ and $\mathcal B=\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon$ using componentwise [[def-distributional-derivative]] and the finite-coordinate cross and curl conventions. They satisfy

$$\operatorname{div}\mathcal E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathcal B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathcal E=-\partial_t\mathcal B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\mathcal B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_t\mathcal E.$$

(c) On the complement of $\Gamma=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$, the distributions $\mathcal E,\mathcal B$ restrict to the exact $C^1$ fields of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]], with all its higher-regularity branches retained. The zero extensions of those field formulas on $\Gamma$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(Q)$, and their regular distributions are precisely $\mathcal E,\mathcal B$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). The off-worldline $C^1$ fields also satisfy the source-free classical Maxwell equations there, because the point pair restricts to zero and each continuous regular residual is zero. Thus the equations in (b) are equations for locally integrable fields with the exact point source, not merely arbitrary field distributions. No field value on $\Gamma$ is physically assigned; zero extension is a representative convention on a null set. No physical adoption, nonlinear distribution product, finite self-energy, self-force, global acceleration bound, or incoming-field uniqueness theorem is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The mathematical parameters $c,\varepsilon_0,q,\mu_0$, the all-time uniformly subluminal $C^3$ trajectory $z$, the distributions $\rho,J,\Phi,\Upsilon$ and the kernel $K$ of the cited items, and a test function $\psi\in\mathcal D(Q)$ in the arguments below.

[F1] On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, with $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$ and $\kappa,r,\beta,D$ as in that item: the retarded-history pairings $\Phi,\Upsilon$ are distributions given by explicit history integrals, satisfy $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}C\psi/(\kappa r)dxdt$ and $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}(\beta/c)C\psi/(\kappa r)dxdt$, are finite for every test, and the potentials $\varphi=C/(\kappa r)$, $A=\beta\varphi/c$ are $C^2$ off the worldline with zero extensions in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; the classical fields $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $\operatorname{curl}A$ are $C^1$ off the worldline and their higher-regularity branches hold ([[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]).

[F2] For the retarded kernel $K$, $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau)=(4\pi)^{-1}\int\psi(y+w,\tau+|w|/c)|w|^{-1}dw$, and $WK=\delta_{(0,0)}$ distributionally, that is, $\langle K,W\chi\rangle=\chi(0,0)$ for every test $\chi$; no smoothness of $K$ on the cone is asserted ([[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]]).

[F3] The functionals $\rho,\psi\mapsto q\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)ds$ and $J,\psi\mapsto q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)\psi(z(s),s)ds$ are distributions on $\Omega$ with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ ([[lem-em-point-current-continuity]]).

[F4] Distributional derivatives satisfy $\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$, are continuous linear on $\mathcal D'$ for the weak and strong topologies, and satisfy $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$ for $f\in C^k$ with $|\alpha|\le k$ under Countable Choice ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]).

[F5] A locally integrable function defines the regular functional $u_f(\varphi)=\int f\varphi$, the map $f\mapsto u_f$ is injective modulo almost-everywhere equality, and the regular functional is linear in $f$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

[F6] For smooth fields: $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}Z=0$; $\operatorname{curl}\nabla f=0$; $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}Z=\nabla\operatorname{div}Z-\Delta Z$ ([[thm-the-divergence-of-a-curl-vanishes]], [[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]], [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]]).

[F7] Dominated convergence: pointwise convergence with one integrable majorant gives convergence of integrals ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F8] The mean value inequality bounds $\|f(b)-f(a)\|$ by $\sup|f'|\,(b-a)$ for a continuous function differentiable on the open interval; partial derivatives are one-variable derivatives along coordinate lines; the chain rule holds for composed differentiable maps; and $C^k$ is the componentwise regularity class ([[thm-mean-value-inequality]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F9] Under Countable Choice: the polar formula $\int_{\mathbb R^n}f\,d\lambda_n=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}f(r\omega)r^{n-1}d\sigma dr$ for nonnegative Borel $f$, and change of variables $\int_Vg=\int_Ug(T)|\det DT|$ for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism and nonnegative Borel $g$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]]).

[F10] Nonnegative integrals are monotone and scale; the integral is linear on $L^1$ and obeys the triangle inequality; a nonnegative measurable function has zero integral exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere; Euclidean balls have positive finite measure ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]).

[F11] Tonelli and Fubini hold on sigma-finite products; Euclidean Borel sets and Lebesgue measure agree with the product Borel structure and product measure ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]).

[F12] Newton-Leibniz with an interior derivative, one-dimensional integration by parts, rectangle Riemann-Fubini, Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison for compact test integrands, translations preserve Lebesgue measure, and smooth compact cutoffs exist in ZF ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], [[thm-integration-by-parts]], [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]], [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]], [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F13] The Euclidean inner product and the cross product are the cited bilinear operations on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $\psi\in\mathcal D(Q)$ and put $F:=K\circledast\psi$, so that $F(y,s)=(4\pi)^{-1}\int\psi(y+w,s+|w|/c)|w|^{-1}dw$. Then $F$ is of class $C^1$ on $Q$ and $\partial_{y_i}F=K\circledast(\partial_{x_i}\psi)$, $\partial_sF=K\circledast(\partial_t\psi)$. Indeed, fix a bounded parameter neighbourhood $|y|\le R$, $|s|\le R$ and choose $M$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq\overline B_M(0)\times[-M,M]$; every nonzero contribution then has $w\in B_{M+R}$, on which $|w|^{-1}$ is integrable by the polar formula. For fixed $(y,s)$ the difference quotients $[\psi(y+he_i+w,s+|w|/c)-\psi(y+w,s+|w|/c)]/h$ converge as $h\to0$ to the partial derivative $\partial_{x_i}\psi(y+w,s+|w|/c)$ by definition of the partial derivative, and the mean value inequality bounds them by $\sup|\partial_{x_i}\psi|\,\mathbf 1_{B_{M+R}}|w|^{-1}$, an integrable majorant; dominated convergence gives $\partial_{y_i}F=K\circledast(\partial_{x_i}\psi)$ on the parameter neighbourhood, and the same argument with the $s$-difference quotients and the $t$-partial derivatives gives $\partial_sF=K\circledast(\partial_t\psi)$; the resulting integrals are continuous in $(y,s)$ by the same dominated convergence, so $F$ is $C^1$. [given, F2, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11]

1.2 For every test $\psi$ and every $(y,s)\in Q$, $(K\circledast W\psi)(y,s)=\psi(y,s)$. Indeed, with the translated test $\chi(z,\tau):=\psi(y+z,s+\tau)$ one has $(W\psi)(y+\cdot,s+\cdot)=W\chi$ by the chain rule and the constant coefficients of $W$, so $(K\circledast W\psi)(y,s)=\langle K,W\chi\rangle=\langle WK,\chi\rangle=\langle\delta_{(0,0)},\chi\rangle=\chi(0,0)=\psi(y,s)$, where the second equality is the definition of the distributional operator $W$ applied to $K$ and the third is $WK=\delta_{(0,0)}$. [given, F2, F4, F8]

1.3 Local integrability of the classical fields. On $V:=Q\setminus\Gamma$ the map $g(s,w):=(z(s)+w,s+|w|/c)$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism from $U:=\mathbb R\times(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})$ onto $V$ with $|\det Dg(s,w)|=\kappa(s,w)\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c]$: the inverse is $(x,t)\mapsto(s(x,t),x-z(s(x,t)))$ by the root of [F1], injectivity follows from $|s-s'|=||w'|-|w||/c\le(v_*/c)|s-s'|$, and the determinant expansion along the last row gives $-1+z'(s)\cdot w/(c|w|)=-\kappa$. For a compact observation window $Q_0\subseteq Q$ contained in $\{|x|\le M,\ t_0\le t\le t_1\}$ put $Z:=|z(0)|$, $S:=\max\{0,(M+Z-ct_0)/(c-v_*)\}$, $L:=1+M+Z+v_*\max\{S,|t_1|\}$ and $T:=\max\{0,t_1+S\}$; then every $(s,w)$ with $g(s,w)\in Q_0$ has $s\in[-S,t_1]$ and $|w|<L$, so by [F9] $\int_{Q_0}r^{-p}\,dx\,dt=\int_U\mathbf 1_{Q_0}(g(s,w))|w|^{-p}\,ds\,dw\le T\int_{B_L}|w|^{-p}dw$, which is finite for $p=1,2$ by the polar formula ($\sigma(S^2)L^2/2$ and $\sigma(S^2)L$ respectively). On the other hand the explicit formulas of [F1] show $|\varphi|+|\nabla\varphi|+|\partial_tA|+|\operatorname{curl}A|\le C_0(r^{-2}+r^{-1})$ on $Q_0$ with $C_0$ depending on $q,\varepsilon_0,c,v_*$ and the supremum of $|\dot\beta|$ over the compact history interval. Hence the zero extensions of $\varphi,A$ and of the classical fields $E_0:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B_0:=\operatorname{curl}A$, and of all their first partial derivatives, are locally integrable on $Q$. [given, F1, F9, F10, F13, A1]

2.1 The history function $s\mapsto F(z(s),s)$ is $C^1$ with compact support contained in a finite interval, and its derivative is $\nabla_yF(z(s),s)\cdot z'(s)+\partial_sF(z(s),s)$. Indeed $F$ is $C^1$ by step 1.1, $z$ is $C^1$, and the chain rule gives the derivative; the support bound $\{s:g(s,w)\in\operatorname{supp}\psi\ \text{for some }w\}\subseteq[-S,t_1]$ of the same cylinder estimate shows compact support, so the total derivative integrates to zero over $\mathbb R$. [step 1.1, given, F8, F12]

2.2 Zero-extension representatives of the first derivatives. Let $f$ be one of the components of $\varphi$ and $A$ on $V$, with zero extension $\widetilde f$, and let $D\in\{\partial_t,\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3\}$. Since $\widetilde f$ and $Df$ (zero extended) are locally integrable by step 1.3, both $u_{\widetilde f}$ and $u_{(Df)^{\sim}}$ are distributions. Then $Du_{\widetilde f}=u_{(Df)^{\sim}}$: choose the spatial cutoff $\chi_\varepsilon(x,t):=\chi((x-z(t))/\varepsilon)$ built from a smooth cutoff $\chi$ that is $0$ on $\overline B_1(0)$ and $1$ outside $B_2(0)$; it is $C^3$ and its first derivatives satisfy $|D\chi_\varepsilon|\le C'/\varepsilon$ with support in the shell $\varepsilon\le d\le2\varepsilon$, where $d:=|x-z(t)|$ and $(1-v_*/c)r\le d\le(1+v_*/c)r$; the product $\chi_\varepsilon\widetilde f$ is $C^1$ on $Q$ because it vanishes on a neighbourhood of the singular set. Classical integration by parts in each coordinate over a large box containing $\operatorname{supp}\psi$ (boundary terms vanish, Riemann-Fubini iterates the one-dimensional identities, and the Riemann-Lebesgue comparison converts to Lebesgue integrals) gives $\int_Q\chi_\varepsilon\widetilde f\,D\psi=-\int_Q\chi_\varepsilon(Df)^{\sim}\psi-\int_Q\widetilde f(D\chi_\varepsilon)\psi$, and dominated convergence with the locally integrable bounds of step 1.3 lets $\varepsilon\to0$ in the first two integrals; the third is $O(\varepsilon)$ because $|\widetilde f|\le C_0'/\varepsilon$ on the shell of volume $O(\varepsilon^3)$ in space and $O(1)$ in time. Hence $-\int_Q\widetilde fD\psi=\int_Q(Df)^{\sim}\psi$, that is, $\langle Du_{\widetilde f},\psi\rangle=\langle u_{(Df)^{\sim}},\psi\rangle$ for every test, proving the claim. Consequently $\mathcal E=-\nabla\Phi-\partial_t\Upsilon=u_{E_0^{\sim}}$ and $\mathcal B=\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon=u_{B_0^{\sim}}$ by linearity of the regular functional, with $E_0,B_0$ the classical fields of step 1.3. [step 1.3, given, F1, F4, F5, F10, F12]

3.1 The wave equations. For every test $\psi$, $\langle\Phi,W\psi\rangle=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast W\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(z(s),s)\,ds=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\langle\rho,\psi\rangle$, the first equality by the definition of $\Phi$ in [F1], the second by the pointwise identity of step 1.2 applied under the history integral (whose integrand is bounded by the cylinder estimate of step 2.1, so the interchange is legitimate), and the last by [F3]. Since $\langle W\Phi,\psi\rangle=\langle\Phi,W\psi\rangle$ for the even-order constant-coefficient operator $W$, this gives $W\Phi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$. The same computation componentwise with the prefactor $\mu_0q$ and the weight $z_j'$ gives $\langle\Upsilon_j,W\psi\rangle=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z_j'(s)\psi(z(s),s)ds=\mu_0\langle J_j,\psi\rangle$, hence $W\Upsilon=\mu_0J$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, given, F1, F3, F4, F7]

3.2 The Lorenz identity. For every test $\psi$, using the definitions of the distributional derivatives and the identities of step 1.1, $\langle\operatorname{div}\Upsilon+c^{-2}\partial_t\Phi,\psi\rangle=-\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl[z'(s)\cdot(K\circledast\nabla\psi)(z(s),s)+(K\circledast\partial_t\psi)(z(s),s)\bigr]ds=-\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl[z'(s)\cdot\nabla_yF(z(s),s)+\partial_sF(z(s),s)\bigr]ds$, that is, $-\mu_0q$ times the integral of the total derivative of $s\mapsto F(z(s),s)$, where $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$; by step 2.1 that total derivative is $C^1$ with compact support, so Newton-Leibniz gives $\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{d}{ds}[F(z(s),s)]ds=0$ and the pairing vanishes for every test. Hence $\operatorname{div}\Upsilon+c^{-2}\partial_t\Phi=0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, F1, F4, F12]

4.1 The four Maxwell equations. Using the distributional algebra for finite combinations of coordinate derivatives (which commutes in the sense $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}$ and is linear) together with the classical identities [F6] applied to smooth tests, one computes, with $G:=\operatorname{div}\Upsilon+c^{-2}\partial_t\Phi=0$ from step 3.2: $\operatorname{div}\mathcal E=-\Delta\Phi-\partial_t\operatorname{div}\Upsilon=W\Phi-c^{-2}\partial_t^2\Phi-\partial_t\operatorname{div}\Upsilon=\rho/\varepsilon_0-\partial_tG=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ by step 3.1; $\operatorname{div}\mathcal B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon=0$; $\operatorname{curl}\mathcal E=-\operatorname{curl}\nabla\Phi-\partial_t\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon=-\partial_t\mathcal B$; and $\operatorname{curl}\mathcal B=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon=\nabla\operatorname{div}\Upsilon-\Delta\Upsilon=\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_t^2\Upsilon+\nabla\operatorname{div}\Upsilon=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_t\mathcal E+\nabla G=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_t\mathcal E$, where the fourth step uses $-\Delta\Upsilon=W\Upsilon-c^{-2}\partial_t^2\Upsilon$ and $\partial_t\mathcal E=-\nabla\partial_t\Phi-\partial_t^2\Upsilon$. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F4, F6]

5.1 Off the worldline. For a test $\psi$ supported in $V$ one has $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int\psi(z(s),s)ds=0$ and likewise $\langle J,\psi\rangle=0$, since $\psi$ vanishes on $\Gamma$. By step 2.2 the restrictions of $\mathcal E,\mathcal B$ and of their first distributional derivatives to $V$ are the regular distributions of the continuous fields $E_0,B_0$ and of their classical first derivatives; hence the four equations of step 4.1, restricted to $V$, read $\operatorname{div}E_0=0$, $\operatorname{div}B_0=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E_0=-\partial_tB_0$, $\operatorname{curl}B_0=c^{-2}\partial_tE_0$ as identities of continuous regular distributions. If a continuous function on $V$ has zero regular distribution, then it vanishes almost everywhere and hence, by continuity and the positivity of ball measure, at every point; applying this to each component of the classical residuals gives the source-free Maxwell equations pointwise on $V$. ∎ [step 2.2, step 4.1, given, F5, F10]

## Remarks

- **Choice accounting.** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used through the polar formula and change of variables in step 1.3, the Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison in step 2.2, and the regular-distribution injectivity in step 5.1; the root, the point-current pair and the algebraic identities are choice-free as stated in their own items.

- **What "the equations hold" means here.** The identities of (a) and (b) are distributional identities tested against $\mathcal D(Q)$; the point source is the functional of [F3], and no product of singular distributions, no field value on $\Gamma$ and no finite self-energy is asserted. The identification in (c) is with the zero extensions of locally integrable classical fields; the value on the null graph is a representative convention only.

- **Not asserted.** No physical adoption of these equations, no radiation-reaction law, no global bound on the acceleration and no uniqueness theorem for incoming fields beyond the retarded construction are claimed.

## Example

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). The following are explicit mathematical checks of the conventions and hypotheses of the items on this page; no measurement, physical field identification or empirical claim is made.

(i) Static specialization. Take $z\equiv0$ (so $v_*=0$), $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$ in the setting of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]. Then for $x\ne0$ the root is $s=t-|x|/c$, $r=|x|$, $n=x/|x|$, $\beta=0$, $\kappa=1$, $\dot\beta=0$, so the potentials and fields are $\varphi=C/|x|$, $A=0$, $E=C\,x/|x|^3$, $B=0$. Thus the retarded formulas reduce exactly to the Coulomb field with the convention $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and the kernel's explicit retarded-history integral reproduces the time-independent Poisson kernel $1/(4\pi|x-y|)$: for a static spatial source $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ define $u(x,t):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy$. Indeed the retarded time is $t-|x-y|/c$ and evaluating the static source there leaves $h(y)$ unchanged. This finite integral is the extension of the compact spacetime-source formula by source-time cutoffs on each compact observation region; a time-independent nonzero source is not itself compactly supported in spacetime.

(ii) Explicit Lorenz-gauge transformation. On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ take $\varphi\equiv0$ and $A(x,t)=(x_1,0,0)$. Then $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A=1$ and $E=-\partial_tA=0$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A=0$. The quadratic function $\chi(x,t):=-|x|^2/6$ satisfies $W\chi=G$: indeed $\partial_t^2\chi=0$ and $\Delta\chi=-1$, so $W\chi=c^{-2}\cdot0-(-1)=1=G$. Its gauge transform is $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(0,\ ((2/3)x_1,-x_2/3,-x_3/3))$, which satisfies $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=\frac23-\frac13-\frac13=0$ and has the same fields: $E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=0=E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=0=B(\varphi,A)$. This checks clauses (b) and (c) of [[lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability]] in an instance where $G$ is a nonzero constant and where the gauge function does not have the zero Cauchy data used in the existence construction of that lemma; by its clause (d), the difference of this $\chi$ and the zero-data solution of $W\chi=G$ solves the homogeneous wave equation, which is why both may be used.

(iii) Sharpness of the kernel support at the apex. For a nonnegative $\psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ with $\psi(0,0)>0$ one has $\langle K,\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\psi(y,|y|/c)|y|^{-1}dy>0$, so $(0,0)\in\operatorname{supp}K$ and the apex is not an artefact of the definition; the same computation with a bump near $(y_0,|y_0|/c)$, $y_0\ne0$, shows that every point of the cone is in the support.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The countable-choice hypothesis, the constants $c,q,\varepsilon_0,C$, the static trajectory $z\equiv0$, the pair $\varphi\equiv0$, $A(x,t)=(x_1,0,0)$, the gauge function $\chi=-|x|^2/6$, the kernel $K$ of the retarded-wave-kernel item, and a static source $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$.

[F1] For $c>0$ and $C^1$ $z$ with $|z'|\le v_*<c$ there is exactly one retarded root $s$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, with $s\le t$ and equality exactly on the worldline; a $C^k$ trajectory gives a $C^k$ root off the worldline ([[lem-em-global-retarded-root]]).

[F2] In the setting of that item, $\varphi=C/(\kappa r)$, $A=\beta\varphi/c$, and the fields $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ obey the displayed Lienard-Wiechert formulas; the pairings against the kernel satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities ([[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]).

[F3] For the kernel $K$ and $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$, $(K*h)(x,t)=\int h(y,t-|x-y|/c)(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}dy$ is well defined and for a nonnegative test $\psi$ the pairing $\langle K,\psi\rangle$ is the displayed integral; $\operatorname{supp}K=C$ ([[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]]).

[F4] For a potential pair, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, $G=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$, $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$, and the gauge transform is $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,A+\nabla\chi)$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]).

[F5] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $(\varphi,A)$ is a $C^\infty$ potential pair on a slab, then there is a $C^\infty$ gauge function $\chi$ with zero Cauchy data and $W\chi=G(\varphi,A)$, the gauge transform preserves $E$ and $B$ and is in Lorenz gauge, and differences of functions with the same $W$-image satisfy $W(\chi_1-\chi_2)=0$ ([[lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability]]).

[F6] $\Delta|x|^2=6$, $\partial_1x_1=1$ and $\operatorname{curl}\nabla f=0$ for $C^2$ $f$; divergence and curl are linear and computed from the first partial derivatives ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]], [[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]).

[F7] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ the polar formula holds for nonnegative Borel functions, a nonnegative measurable function has zero integral exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere, Euclidean balls have positive finite measure, and nonnegative integrals are monotone and scale ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F8] Compact subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ are bounded and closed ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and for a compact set inside an open set there is a smooth compact cutoff equal to one near it ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F9] The Euclidean norm and inner product are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and $C^k$ regularity is componentwise ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Static specialization (i). With $z\equiv0$ the root equation reads $t-s=|x|/c$, whose unique solution is $s=t-|x|/c$; then $R=x$, $r=|x|$, $n=x/|x|$, $\beta=0$, $N=0$, $\kappa=1$, $D=|x|$ and $\dot\beta=0$. By [F2] the potentials are $\varphi=C/|x|$ and $A=0$ (since $\beta=0$), and the field formulas give $E=C(1-0)(n-0)/(1\cdot|x|^2)=Cx/|x|^3$ and $B=n\times E/c=(C/c)(n\times n)/|x|^2=0$, using $n\times n=0$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F6, F9]

1.2 Static Poisson kernel (i). Let $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, fix a compact observation region $Q_0\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and note that for $(x,t)\in Q_0$ and $y$ in the support of $h$ the retarded time $s=t-|x-y|/c$ stays in a bounded interval; choose a smooth nonnegative time cutoff $\sigma$ equal to one on that interval with compact support, and put $h_\#(x,t):=\sigma(t)h(x)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$, which agrees with the time-independent extension of $h$ on the contributing region. By [F3], $(K*h_\#)(x,t)=\int h_\#(y,t-|x-y|/c)(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}dy=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int h(y)/|x-y|\,dy$ on $Q_0$, since $\sigma$ equals one at the retarded times and the static source does not depend on time; the remaining integral is finite because $y\mapsto h(y)/|x-y|$ is bounded and compactly supported away from the single point $y=x$, where the polar formula gives integrability of $|x-y|^{-1}$ over bounded regions. This is the stated extension of the compact spacetime-source formula by source-time cutoffs; the uncut static source is not compactly supported in spacetime. [given, F3, F7, F8, A1]

1.3 The gauge transformation (ii). For $\varphi\equiv0$ and $A=(x_1,0,0)$: $\operatorname{div}A=\partial_1x_1=1$, so $G=1$; $\operatorname{curl}A=0$; $E=-\partial_tA=0$. For $\chi=-|x|^2/6$: $\partial_t^2\chi=0$, and $\Delta\chi=-\frac16\Delta|x|^2=-1$ with $\Delta|x|^2=6$, so $W\chi=c^{-2}\cdot0-(-1)=1=G$. Since $\nabla\chi=(-x_1/3,-x_2/3,-x_3/3)$, the gauge transform is $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(0-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi)=(0,((2/3)x_1,-x_2/3,-x_3/3))$, whose divergence is $\frac23-\frac13-\frac13=0$ and whose curl vanishes because it is the gradient of $\frac13x_1^2-\frac16x_2^2-\frac16x_3^2$ by the curl-of-gradient theorem; hence $E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=-\nabla0-\partial_t(0,\ldots)=0=E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=0=B(\varphi,A)$, and the transformed pair is in Lorenz gauge. This instantiates clauses (b) and (c) of [F5] with a nonzero constant $G$ and a gauge function that does not have the zero Cauchy data of the existence construction; by clause (d) of [F5], $W(\chi-\chi_0)=1-1=0$ for the zero-data solution $\chi_0$ of $W\chi_0=1$, so the two are compatible. [given, F4, F5, F6, F9]

2.1 Sharpness at the apex (iii). Let $0\le\psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ with $\psi(0,0)>0$. By continuity and $\psi(0,0)>0$ there are $a>0$ and $\delta>0$ with $\psi(y,|y|/c)\ge a$ whenever $|y|<\delta$. On that ball $y\mapsto\psi(y,|y|/c)/|y|$ is nonnegative and bounded below by $a/|y|$, so by the polar formula and the positivity of the integral of a nonnegative measurable function that is positive on a set of positive measure, $\langle K,\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\psi(y,|y|/c)|y|^{-1}dy\ge\frac{a}{4\pi}\int_{B_\delta}|y|^{-1}dy=\frac{a}{4\pi}\cdot\frac{\sigma(S^2)\delta^2}{2}>0$; hence $(0,0)$ lies in $\operatorname{supp}K$. For $y_0\ne0$ and a nonnegative bump $\psi$ positive at $(y_0,|y_0|/c)$ with support in a small ball, continuity gives $\psi(y,|y|/c)\ge a>0$ on a neighbourhood of $y_0$, while $|y|^{-1}\ge 1/(2|y_0|)$ there, and the same computation gives $\langle K,\psi\rangle>0$, so every such cone point lies in the support in accordance with the support computation of [F3]. Both computations use only nonnegative tests, and no factorization of an arbitrary test into radial and time factors is assumed. ∎ [given, F3, F7, F8, A1]

## Remarks

- **Consistency, not evidence.** These are internal consistency checks of conventions and hypotheses; they neither prove any physical field identification nor test any model against observation.

- **Choice accounting.** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ enters only through the polar formula and the positivity criteria of [F7] and through the kernel item [F3]; the algebraic computations are choice-free.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the change-of-variables corollaries inside the proof of the retarded-convolution identity cited in clause (b) ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, let $v_*<c$, let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, put $\mu_0:=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$ and $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and write $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$.

(a) [Root and emission-time Jacobian] For every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ (equivalently $x\ne z(t)$) there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. The map $s:\Omega\setminus\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with $R:=x-z(s)$, $r:=|R|$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) one has $$\partial_ts(x,t)=\kappa^{-1},\qquad \nabla_xs(x,t)=-\frac{n}{c\,\kappa},\qquad \kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c],$$ so $\kappa\ge 1-v_*/c>0$ uniformly on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. Moreover, for the fixed $x$ and near the root, the function $s'\mapsto s'+|x-z(s')|/c$ is differentiable at $s'=s$ with derivative $\kappa(x,t)$: this emission-time Jacobian $1-n\cdot\beta$ is the denominator produced by the delta substitution of clause (b).

(b) [Delta substitution and Liénard-Wiechert potentials] Let $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the point-source distributions of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]] attached to $q$ and the worldline $z$, let $K$ be the retarded wave kernel of [[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]], and for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ put $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$ and define the retarded-history pairings by the explicit integrals $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle:=(q/\varepsilon_0)\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds$, $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle:=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)\,ds$, componentwise in the second case. These are the history-integral interpretation supplied by clause (b) of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]], not ordinary distribution action on a noncompact test. Then these pairings are finite for every $\psi$ and their exact retarded-convolution values are $$\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt,\qquad \langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta}{c}\,\frac{C\,\psi}{\kappa\,r}\,dx\,dt$$ (the second identity componentwise); equivalently, $\Phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are the regular distributions of the locally integrable zero extensions to $\Gamma$ of the $C^2$ functions $\varphi:=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A:=\beta\varphi/c$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. The weight $(\kappa r)^{-1}$ with $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ is the exact form of the substitution with denominator $1-n\cdot\beta$ (the rigorous statement is the displayed pairing identity; composition of $\delta$ with a function is not part of the distribution calculus used here).

(c) [Fields and the velocity/acceleration split] With $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]), and writing $\dot\beta:=z''(s)/c$ at the root, $$E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{vel}}=\frac{C(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2},\qquad E_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r},\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}$$ at every event of $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). Both $E$ and $B$ are $C^1$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, and the velocity field obeys the bound $$|E_{\mathrm{vel}}(x,t)|\le |C|\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r(x,t)^{-2}$$ at every event.

(d) [Uniform far-zone remainder] For every $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and every $n\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|n|=1$, put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$ and $t_r:=s_0+r/c$ for $r>0$, and set $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $\dot\beta_0:=z''(s_0)/c$, $\kappa_0:=1-n\cdot\beta_0$. Then $(x_r,t_r)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$ for every $r>0$, and $$E(x_r,t_r)=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0\bigr)}{c\,\kappa_0^3\,r}+\rho_E(s_0,n,r),\qquad B(x_r,t_r)=\frac{n\times E(x_r,t_r)}{c},$$ where the remainder is bounded uniformly in the direction, $$|\rho_E(s_0,n,r)|\le |C|\,\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\,r^{-2}\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2\text{ and every }r>0.$$ Equivalently, $rE(x_r,t_r)\to C\,n\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)/(c\,\kappa_0^3)$ as $r\to\infty$, uniformly over $n\in S^2$ at the explicit rate $O(r^{-1})$ given by the same bound multiplied by $r$. The uniformity is in the direction $n$ at a fixed emission event $s_0$; no uniformity in $s_0$ is asserted ($z''$ is not assumed bounded), and no finite-energy, decay or radiation-flux conclusion is drawn.

This is a mathematical model computation for the stipulated $C^3$ uniformly subluminal worldline and the retarded choice; no self-force law, no radiation-reaction postulate and no physical Maxwell coupling is asserted or proved, and the uniform speed bound and the exclusion of $\Gamma$ are essential hypotheses (see the companion example page).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A speed $c>0$, a real bound $v_*<c$, a worldline $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$, a real $q$ and a positive $\varepsilon_0$, together with the constants $\mu_0=(c^2\varepsilon_0)^{-1}$, $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$ and the sets $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, $\Gamma=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$.

[F1] Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$ and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s$. Then for every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$ with equality exactly when $x=z(t)$; on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\{(x,t):x\ne z(t)\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, the root is $C^1$, and with $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ its derivatives are $\partial_ts=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$ for an integer $k\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root ([[lem-em-global-retarded-root]]).

[F2] For $f:A\to\mathbb R^m$ with $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ and a limit point $c\in A$, $f$ is differentiable at $c$ when the difference quotients $q_{f,c}(x)=\frac{1}{x-c}(f(x)-f(c))$ converge as $x\to c$, and then the derivative is the limit $f'(c):=\lim_{x\to c}q_{f,c}(x)\in\mathbb R^m$; the notion is intrinsic and is computed componentwise ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]).

[F3] A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$ in the multi-index sense; it is smooth when it is $C^k$ for every $k$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F4] On $\mathbb R^n$ the Euclidean inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$, it is bilinear and symmetric, $\langle z,z\rangle\ge0$ with $\langle z,z\rangle=0$ only for $z=0$, and the Euclidean norm is $\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F5] For all $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ one has $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert\le\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$; $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm, so $\lVert u+v\rVert_2\le\lVert u\rVert_2+\lVert v\rVert_2$ and $\lVert\lambda u\rVert_2=\lvert\lambda\rvert\lVert u\rVert_2$, and consequently the reverse triangle inequality $\lvert\lVert u\rVert_2-\lVert v\rVert_2\rvert\le\lVert u-v\rVert_2$ holds ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F6] Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory, $q\in\mathbb R$, and $\Omega\supseteq\Gamma$ open on which the graph map is proper. Then $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)dt$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_Iz'(t)\psi(z(t),t)dt$ define distributions with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; properness is automatic for $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, in particular for the all-time history $I=\mathbb R$ ([[lem-em-point-current-continuity]]).

[F7] The retarded wave kernel is the distribution $K$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ given by $\langle K,\psi\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\psi(y,\lvert y\rvert/c)}{\lvert y\rvert}dy$, and for $(y,\tau)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the shifted pairing $(K\circledast\psi)(y,\tau):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,\tau+\cdot)\rangle$ equals the absolutely convergent integral $\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\psi(y+z,\tau+\lvert z\rvert/c)}{\lvert z\rvert}dz$ ([[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]]).

[F8] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $c>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$ and let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$ for all $s$. With $K$ the retarded kernel of [F7] and, for tests $\psi$, $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=(q/\varepsilon_0)\int_{\mathbb R}(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)ds$, $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\mu_0q\int_{\mathbb R}z'(s)(K\circledast\psi)(z(s),s)ds$ componentwise, these pairings are finite for every $\psi$ and satisfy the exact retarded-convolution identities $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{C\psi}{\kappa r}dxdt$ and $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}\frac{\beta}{c}\frac{C\psi}{\kappa r}dxdt$; consequently $\Phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are the regular distributions of the locally integrable zero extensions of the $C^2$ functions $\varphi=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A=\beta\varphi/c$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]).

[F9] In the situation of [F8], the fields $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ satisfy $$E=C\Bigl[\frac{(1-\lvert\beta\rvert^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2}+\frac{n\times((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta)}{c\kappa^3r}\Bigr],\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c}$$ and are of class $C^1$ there, where $\dot\beta=z''(s)/c$ is evaluated at the retarded root ([[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]]).

[F10] For $c>0$ and an open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, a $C^k$ scalar-vector potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ on $\Omega$ with $k\ge1$ has fields $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, both of class $C^{k-1}$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]).

[F11] The right-handed cross product on $\mathbb R^3$ is $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); it is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$ ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]).

[F12] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every family $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement: $c>0$, $v_*<c$, a $C^3$ worldline $z$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s$, $q\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, and the derived data $\mu_0$, $C$, $\Omega$, $\Gamma$.

**Proof technique:** direct: clause (a) is the root lemma together with the one-variable computation of the emission-time Jacobian; clause (b) is the supplier's pairing identity read in the stated history-integral interpretation; clause (c) is the supplier's field formula with an elementary uniform bound; clause (d) evaluates the field on the ray family and reads off the uniform limit.

1.1 Hypothesis audit and the root. The hypothesis gives $0\le|z'(0)|\le v_*$, so $0\le v_*<c$, and $z$ is of class $C^3$, hence $C^1$; the root lemma [F1] therefore applies with these $c$, $v_*$, $z$, and since $z$ is $C^3$ its $C^k$ branch with $k=3$ applies. Hence for every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, the root map is of class $C^3$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, and with $R=x-z(s)$, $r=|R|>0$, $n=R/r$, $\beta=z'(s)/c$, $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ one has $\partial_ts=\kappa^{-1}$, $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$ and $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$, so $\kappa\ge1-v_*/c>0$. The differentiability vocabulary and the $C^k$ vocabulary used throughout are [F2] and [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, given]

1.2 The norm term. Fix $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ with root $s$ and put $R=x-z(s)$, $r=\lVert R\rVert_2>0$, $n=R/r$; I show that $\psi(s'):=\lVert x-z(s')\rVert_2$ is differentiable at $s'=s$ with $\psi'(s)=-\langle z'(s),R\rangle/r$. For $h\ne0$ put $V_h:=\frac{z(s+h)-z(s)}{h}$; by [F2] one has $V_h\to z'(s)$ as $h\to0$, so with $M:=\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2+1$ there is $\delta>0$ with $\lVert V_h\rVert_2\le M$ for $0<\lvert h\rvert<\delta$; shrinking $\delta$ if necessary so that $M\delta<r/2$, the vector $w_2:=x-z(s+h)$ satisfies $\lVert w_2-R\rVert_2=\lVert z(s+h)-z(s)\rVert_2=\lvert h\rvert\lVert V_h\rVert_2\le M\lvert h\rvert$ and $\lVert w_2\rVert_2\ge r-M\lvert h\rvert>r/2$. Writing $w_1:=R$, the identity $\lVert w_2\rVert_2-\lVert w_1\rVert_2=\frac{\langle w_2-w_1,\,w_2+w_1\rangle}{\lVert w_2\rVert_2+\lVert w_1\rVert_2}$ holds, because $\lVert w_2\rVert_2^2-\lVert w_1\rVert_2^2=\langle w_2+w_1,w_2-w_1\rangle$ by bilinearity and symmetry and the denominator is positive [F4]; since $w_2-w_1=-hV_h$, dividing by $h$ gives $\frac{\psi(s+h)-\psi(s)}{h}=-\langle V_h,U_h\rangle$ with $U_h:=\frac{w_1+w_2}{\lVert w_1\rVert_2+\lVert w_2\rVert_2}$. The triangle inequality gives $\lVert U_h\rVert_2\le1$, and $\lVert U_h-n\rVert_2=\frac{\lVert rw_2-\lVert w_2\rVert_2w_1\rVert_2}{r(r+\lVert w_2\rVert_2)}\le\frac{2\lVert w_2-w_1\rVert_2}{r+\lVert w_2\rVert_2}\le\frac{2M\lvert h\rvert}{r}$, where the middle step is the reverse triangle inequality [F5]. Cauchy-Schwarz then gives $\lvert\langle V_h,U_h\rangle-\langle z'(s),n\rangle\rvert\le\lVert V_h-z'(s)\rVert_2\lVert U_h\rVert_2+\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2\lVert U_h-n\rVert_2\le\lVert V_h-z'(s)\rVert_2+\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2\frac{2M\lvert h\rvert}{r}$, which tends to $0$ as $h\to0$; hence the difference quotients converge and $\psi'(s)=-\langle z'(s),n\rangle=-n\cdot z'(s)$ [F5]. [F2, F4, F5, algebra]

1.3 The ray family. Fix $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in\mathbb R^3$ with $\lVert n\rVert_2=1$, and let $r>0$; put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$ and $t_r:=s_0+r/c$. Then $t_r-s_0=r/c=\lVert x_r-z(s_0)\rVert_2/c$, so $s_0$ solves the retarded equation at the event $(x_r,t_r)$; by the uniqueness in [F1] applied at that event the root is $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$, and since $s_0<t_r$, the equality clause of [F1], which says that the root equals $t$ exactly when the observation point is $z(t)$, gives $x_r\ne z(t_r)$, that is $(x_r,t_r)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Emission-time Jacobian. With the fixed $x$ of step 1.2, the function $g_x(s'):=s'+\frac{1}{c}\lVert x-z(s')\rVert_2$ is differentiable at $s'=s$, as the sum of the identity map, whose derivative is $1$, and the constant multiple $\frac1c\psi$ of the differentiable map $\psi$ of step 1.2, and its derivative is $g_x'(s)=1-\frac{1}{c}n\cdot z'(s)=1-n\cdot\beta=\kappa(x,t)$, using $\beta=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ from step 1.1; this is exactly the emission-time Jacobian $1-n\cdot\beta$ asserted in clause (a). [step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra]

2.2 Clause (b). The definitions of the retarded-history pairings in clause (b) coincide with [F8], with the same signed constant $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, the same $\beta=z'(s)/c$ and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta$ of step 1.1, and the same shifted-kernel pairing $(K\circledast\psi)$ of [F7]; the point-source distributions and their continuity equation are [F6], whose proper-graph hypothesis is automatic for the all-time history $I=\mathbb R$. The supplier [F8] proves, under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [F12], that the pairings are finite for every test, that the displayed exact identities hold, and that $\Phi$ and $\Upsilon$ are the regular distributions of the locally integrable zero extensions of $\varphi=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A=\beta\varphi/c$, which are $C^2$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ by the supplier's regularity branch fed by the $C^3$ root of step 1.1; this is the whole content of clause (b). [F6, F7, F8, F12, step 1.1, given]

2.3 Clause (c). By step 1.1 and [F8] the pair $(\varphi,A)$ is a $C^2$ potential pair on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, so [F10] identifies its fields as $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, both $C^1$; the supplier's formula [F9] gives the displayed $E$ and $B$, whose acceleration numerator is the cross product of [F11], and splitting the bracket defines $E_{\mathrm{vel}}$ and $E_{\mathrm{acc}}$ as in the Statement. For the bound, at every event $\lVert n\rVert_2=1$ and $\lVert\beta\rVert_2=\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2/c\le v_*/c$, so $\lvert1-\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2\rvert\le1$ and the triangle inequality [F5] gives $\lVert n-\beta\rVert_2\le1+\lVert\beta\rVert_2\le1+v_*/c$; with $\kappa\ge1-v_*/c>0$ from step 1.1 this yields $\kappa^3\ge(1-v_*/c)^3$ and hence $\lVert E_{\mathrm{vel}}(x,t)\rVert_2\le\lvert C\rvert\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}r^{-2}$, the signed constant $C$ being kept in the formula and $\lvert C\rvert$ used in the bound. [step 1.1, F5, F8, F9, F10, F11, algebra]

3.1 The far-zone expansion. At the event $(x_r,t_r)$ of step 1.3 the retarded data are the root $s_0$, the separation $x_r-z(s_0)=rn$, the retarded distance $\lVert x_r-z(s_0)\rVert_2=r$, which is the ray parameter, the unit vector $n$, and $\beta=\beta_0=z'(s_0)/c$, $\dot\beta=\dot\beta_0=z''(s_0)/c$, $\kappa=\kappa_0=1-n\cdot\beta_0$; hence step 2.3 gives $E(x_r,t_r)=\frac{Cn\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)}{c\kappa_0^3r}+\rho_E(s_0,n,r)$ with $\rho_E(s_0,n,r):=E_{\mathrm{vel}}(x_r,t_r)$ and $B(x_r,t_r)=\frac{n\times E(x_r,t_r)}{c}$, while the uniform bound of step 2.3 gives $\lvert\rho_E(s_0,n,r)\rvert\le\lvert C\rvert\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}r^{-2}$ for every unit $n$ and every $r>0$. Multiplying by $r$ yields $\bigl\lVert rE(x_r,t_r)-\frac{Cn\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)}{c\kappa_0^3}\bigr\rVert_2\le\lvert C\rvert\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}\frac1r$, which tends to $0$ as $r\to\infty$ with a constant depending only on $C$, $v_*$ and $c$; hence $rE(x_r,t_r)\to\frac{Cn\times((n-\beta_0)\times\dot\beta_0)}{c\kappa_0^3}$ uniformly over the unit directions $n$ at the fixed emission event $s_0$, at the explicit rate $O(r^{-1})$, and no bound on $z''$ enters the remainder. [F5, F11, step 1.3, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 Assembly. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 give clause (a): at every event off the worldline there is a unique retarded root strictly below the observation time, the root map is $C^3$, $\partial_ts=\kappa^{-1}$, $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$ and $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$, and the emission-time Jacobian is $1-n\cdot\beta=\kappa$; step 2.2 gives clause (b) with the finiteness of the history pairings, the exact pairing identities and the identification of $\Phi,\Upsilon$ as the regular distributions of the zero extensions of the $C^2$ potentials $\varphi=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A=\beta\varphi/c$; step 2.3 gives clause (c) with the velocity/acceleration split, the $C^1$ regularity and the uniform velocity-field bound; and steps 1.3 and 3.1 give clause (d) with $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$, the expansion, the direction-uniform remainder bound and the equivalent $O(r^{-1})$ limit of $rE$. All hypotheses are those of the Statement, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is assumed and used only through clause (b), the signed constant $C$ is retained in the field formulas while the bounds use $\lvert C\rvert$, and no self-force, radiation-reaction, Maxwell-coupling, finite-energy, decay or flux conclusion is asserted. [given, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1] ∎

## Example

For clause (i) assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Euclidean box-measure interface; the direct root counterexamples in (ii), (iii) are choice-free.

(i) [Plane-wave solutions with infinite spatial $L^2$ norm] Let $c>0$ and $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as in [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function $u:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $u(x,t):=f(x_1-ct)$, is of class $C^\infty$ and satisfies $Wu=0$ identically. If $f\ne0$, then for every $t$ the level set $\{x:u(x,t)\ne0\}=(ct+U)\times\mathbb R^2$, where $U:=\{s\in\mathbb R:f(s)\ne0\}$ is nonempty and open, is unbounded, and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(x,t)|^2\,dx=+\infty$. Consequently the smooth-data existence and smoothness clause (a) of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] carries no global finite-energy or decay conclusion: compact support of the data is a genuine hypothesis of its clause (d), not a consequence of smoothness.

(ii) [Failure of root existence without the uniform speed bound] Let $c>0$, $a>0$ and $z(s):=(\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2},0,0)$. Then $z$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with $|z'(s)|=\dfrac{c^2|s|}{\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2}}<c$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$, while $\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|z'(s)|=c$; so there is no $v_*<c$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for all $s$: the worldline is subluminal at every finite time but has no uniform subluminal bound. For the observation $(x,t)=(0,0)$ there is no root $s<t$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$: the equation would read $-s=\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2}/c$ with $s<0$, and squaring gives $s^2=s^2+a^2/c^2$, i.e. $a=0$, a contradiction. Thus the existence clause of [[thm-em-retarded-root-and-fields]] genuinely needs its hypothesis $|z'|\le v_*<c$; the substitution denominator degenerates along this curve in the same limit.

(iii) [The event must lie off the worldline] Let $z$ be of class $C^1$ with $|z'|\le v_*<c$, and let $x=z(t)$ for some $t\in\mathbb R$. Then $s=t$ solves $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$ trivially, and the strict decrease of $s\mapsto t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ shows that no root $s<t$ exists; hence the exclusion of the worldline $\Gamma$ in clause (a) of [[thm-em-retarded-root-and-fields]] is a genuine hypothesis.

These are explicit mathematical checks of hypotheses and conventions of the wave and retarded-root results; no measurement, physical field identification or empirical claim is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A speed $c>0$, a profile $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ (taken nonzero in part (i) of the Verification), a parameter $a>0$ for part (ii), and a $C^1$ worldline with a uniform bound $|z'|\le v_*<c$ for part (iii).

[F1] With the partial derivatives of [F7] and the Laplacian of [F2], the wave operator of speed $c$ is $\Box_c:=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ and the wave equation with source $g$ is $\Box_cu=g$; the operator used in this example is $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta=c^{-2}\Box_c$ ([[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]).

[F2] For open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $C^2$ $h:U\to\mathbb R$, the Laplacian is $\Delta h=\operatorname{div}\nabla h=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_ih$, with the gradient of [F8]; for a $C^2$ map it is taken componentwise ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F3] For $k\in\mathbb N$, a map is of class $C^k$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on its domain, the word of length $0$ denoting $f$ itself ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]); on open Euclidean domains this is read componentwise, with the same convention for the word of length $0$, and the map is smooth when it is $C^k$ for every $k$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F4] Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, scalar multiples are included, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$ ([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]).

[F5] If $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ with $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F6] Sums, scalar multiples, products and quotients (where defined) of differentiable functions are differentiable with the usual rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F7] For open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$, the directional derivative is $D_vF(a)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{F(a+tv)-F(a)}{t}$; for a standard basis vector $e_j$ the $j$th partial derivative is $\partial_jF(a)=D_{e_j}F(a)$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F8] For $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ with all partial derivatives existing, the Jacobian matrix is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))$; for scalar $f$ the gradient is $\nabla f(a)=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))$ in the standard basis ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

[F9] For $f:A\to\mathbb R^m$ with $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ and a limit point $c\in A$, differentiability at $c$ means that the difference quotients $\frac{1}{x-c}(f(x)-f(c))$ converge, and the derivative is their limit; the notion is computed componentwise ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]).

[F10] On $\mathbb R^n$ the Euclidean inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$, it is bilinear and symmetric with $\langle z,z\rangle\ge0$ and equality only for $z=0$, and the Euclidean norm is $\lVert x\rVert_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F11] Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable on a measure space. If $f\le g$ then $\int f\le\int g$; if $c>0$ then $\int cf=c\int f$, and the integral of the zero function is $0$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F12] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For reals $a_i\le b_i$, every box $R$ with $R^\circ\subseteq R\subseteq\overline R$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(R)=\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$; in particular a box of side lengths $L_1,\dots,L_n>0$ has measure $L_1\cdots L_n$, and one with some $a_i=b_i$ has measure $0$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F13] For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ with $(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}$; in particular the square root is smooth on $(0,\infty)$ with $(\sqrt x)'=1/(2\sqrt x)$, and $a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ for $a>0$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]).

[F14] If $f:A\to\mathbb R$, $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, is differentiable at a limit point $c\in A$, then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).

[F15] $f$ is continuous at $c\in A$ when for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $\lvert x-c\rvert<\delta$ and $x\in A$ implying $\lvert f(x)-f(c)\rvert<\varepsilon$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

[F16] Every continuous map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is Borel measurable ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]) in the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]; since every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), a continuous real-valued function on $\mathbb R^n$ is measurable for the Lebesgue measure space to which the nonnegative-integral rules [F11] and the box-measure theorem [F12] refer.

[F17] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every family $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F18] Let $c>0$, $0\le v_*<c$ and $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s$. Then for every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\le t$ with equality exactly when $x=z(t)$ ([[lem-em-global-retarded-root]]).

[F19] With $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, a $C^3$ worldline $z$ with $|z'|\le v_*<c$, $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ and $\Gamma=\{(z(s),s)\}$, the theorem of [[thm-em-retarded-root-and-fields]] asserts: for every $(x,t)\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, with the derivative formulas and uniform bounds of its clause (a); its clauses (b)-(d) give the retarded pairings, the Liénard-Wiechert fields and the far-zone remainder.

[F20] The Cauchy-Kirchhoff theorem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] solves $Wu=g$ on slabs from smooth data: clause (a) gives a $C^\infty$ solution for smooth data and source with no finite-energy or decay hypothesis, and clause (d) states the compact-support conclusion under the hypothesis that the data and the source vanish off fixed compact sets. No boundary condition on a finite spatial domain, no finite-total-energy hypothesis and no decay of the data at infinity is assumed or asserted.

## Verification

1.1 Smoothness and the wave equation. The map $\pi(x,t):=x_1-ct$ is affine, hence $C^\infty$ from [F3]; $f$ is $C^\infty$ and $u=f\circ\pi$ is therefore $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ by the composition clause of [F4]. Its partial derivatives are $\partial_tu=-c\,(f'\circ\pi)$, $\partial_t^2u=c^2(f''\circ\pi)$ and $\partial_1u=f'\circ\pi$ with $\partial_2u=\partial_3u=0$, by the chain rule [F5] together with the scalar-multiple and linearity rules [F6] and the definitions of the partial derivatives and the gradient [F7, F8]; hence $\nabla u=(f'\circ\pi,0,0)$ and $\Delta u=\partial_1\partial_1u=f''\circ\pi$ by [F2]. Consequently $Wu=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u=f''\circ\pi-f''\circ\pi=0$ identically, with $W$ as in [F1]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

1.2 The nonzero level set. Assume $f\ne0$. The profile $f$ is differentiable on $\mathbb R$ because it is $C^\infty$ [F3], so it is continuous at every point by [F14]; hence $U=\{s:f(s)\ne0\}$, the preimage of the open set $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, is open, and it is nonempty because $f$ is not the zero function. For every $t\in\mathbb R$ the equivalence $u(x,t)\ne0\Leftrightarrow f(x_1-ct)\ne0\Leftrightarrow x_1-ct\in U$ exhibits the level set as $\{x:u(x,t)\ne0\}=(ct+U)\times\mathbb R^2$; since $U\ne\varnothing$ and the last factor is all of $\mathbb R^2$, this set is nonempty and unbounded, so for every $t$ the function $u(\cdot,t)$ does not have compact spatial support. [F3, F14, algebra]

1.3 The spatial $L^2$ norm diverges. Assume $f\ne0$; pick $s_0$ with $f(s_0)\ne0$ and put $\eta:=\lvert f(s_0)\rvert^2/4>0$. Continuity of $f$ at $s_0$ [F14, F15] gives $\delta>0$ with $\lvert f(s)-f(s_0)\rvert<\lvert f(s_0)\rvert/2$ for $\lvert s-s_0\rvert<\delta$, whence $\lvert f(s)\rvert\ge\lvert f(s_0)\rvert/2$ and $\lvert f(s)\rvert^2\ge\eta$ on the interval $I:=[s_0-\delta,s_0+\delta]$. Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and $R>0$ and put $K:=(ct+I)\times(-R,R)^2$, so that for $x\in K$ one has $x_1-ct\in I$ and therefore $\lvert u(x,t)\rvert^2=\lvert f(x_1-ct)\rvert^2\ge\eta\,\mathbf 1_K(x)$. The map $x\mapsto\lvert u(x,t)\rvert^2$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3$ by the composition and product clauses of [F4] applied to the affine map $x\mapsto x_1-ct$ and the smooth profile, hence continuous [F3] and Borel measurable with $\mathbf 1_K$ Borel; by [F16] both functions are measurable for the Lebesgue measure space, so the monotonicity and scalar rules [F11] give $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\lvert u(x,t)\rvert^2dx\ge\eta\lambda_3(K)=\eta\cdot2\delta\cdot(2R)^2$ by the box-measure theorem [F12], and the right-hand side exceeds every prescribed real number for $R$ large. Hence $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\lvert u(x,t)\rvert^2dx=+\infty$ for every $t$. Finally, the Cauchy data of $u$ at $t=0$ are the smooth functions $x\mapsto f(x_1)$ and $x\mapsto-cf'(x_1)$, which do not have compact support as functions of $x\in\mathbb R^3$; by clauses (a) and (d) of [F20] the smooth-data clause carries no global finite-energy or decay conclusion, while the compact-support clause is stated for data vanishing off compact sets, so compact support is a genuine hypothesis of clause (d) and not a consequence of smoothness. Countable Choice is used in this step through the box-measure and measurability interfaces [F12, F16, F17]. [F3, F4, F11, F12, F14, F15, F16, F17, F20, algebra]

1.4 The curve of part (ii). Let $c>0$, $a>0$ and $z(s):=(g(s),0,0)$ with $g(s):=\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2}$. The polynomial $s\mapsto c^2s^2+a^2$ takes values in $(0,\infty)$ and is $C^\infty$ [F3], so $g$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ by the composition clause of [F4] and the differentiability of $x\mapsto x^{1/2}$ on $(0,\infty)$ [F13], and $z$ is $C^\infty$ [F3]. The chain rule [F5] with $(\sqrt x)'=1/(2\sqrt x)$ [F13] gives $g'(s)=c^2s/g(s)$, so $z'(s)=(c^2s/g(s),0,0)$ [F8, F9] and $\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2=c^2\lvert s\rvert/g(s)$ [F10]. One has $\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2<c$ for every $s$ because $c^2\lvert s\rvert<c\,g(s)$ is equivalent to $c^2s^2<c^2s^2+a^2$, true for $a>0$; and $c^2\lvert s\rvert/g(s)=c\cdot\frac{c\lvert s\rvert}{\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2}}\to c$ as $\lvert s\rvert\to\infty$, so $\sup_{s}\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2=c$ and there is no $v_*<c$ with $\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2\le v_*$ for all $s$. [F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, F10, F13, algebra]

1.5 Events on the worldline. Let $z$ be $C^1$ with $|z'|\le v_*<c$ and let $x=z(t)$ for some $t\in\mathbb R$; then $0=t-t=|x-z(t)|/c$, so $s=t$ solves $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$. Applying [F18] at the event $(x,t)=(z(t),t)$: its unique root $s(x,t)$ satisfies $s(x,t)\le t$ with equality exactly when the observation point equals $z(t)$, which is exactly the present case, so $s(x,t)=t$ and there is no root strictly below $t$. Hence, for the model of [F19], which is defined on the complement of the worldline $\Gamma=\{(z(s),s)\}$, the domain restriction $x\ne z(t)$ in clause (a) is not redundant: at an event with $x=z(t)$ the retarded root below $t$ does not exist. [F10, F18, F19, algebra]

2.1 No root at the origin for the curve of part (ii). With $z$ as in step 1.4, suppose a root $s<0$ existed for the observation $(x,t)=(0,0)$: then $-s=\lvert x-z(s)\rvert/c=\lVert z(s)\rVert_2/c=\sqrt{c^2s^2+a^2}/c$. Since $s<0$ the left side is positive, so squaring is legitimate and gives $s^2=(c^2s^2+a^2)/c^2=s^2+a^2/c^2$, hence $a^2=0$ and $a=0$, contradicting $a>0$. So no root $s<0$ exists at $(0,0)$ even though $z$ is $C^\infty$ with $\lVert z'(s)\rVert_2<c$ at every $s$; therefore the existence clause of the theorem [F19], whose hypothesis $|z'|\le v_*<c$ fails for this curve, cannot be applied here, and the uniform speed bound is a genuine hypothesis. The substitution denominator degenerates in the same limit: with $x=0$ one has $n(s)=(0-z(s))/\lVert z(s)\rVert_2=-e_1$ and $\beta(s)=z'(s)/c\to(-1,0,0)=-e_1$ as $s\to-\infty$, so $n(s)\cdot\beta(s)\to1$ and $\kappa(s)=1-n(s)\cdot\beta(s)\to0$ [F6, F10]. [F6, F10, F19, step 1.4, algebra]

3.1 Audit. Step 1.1 proves the smoothness and $Wu=0$ claims of (i), step 1.2 the structure, nonemptiness and unboundedness of the nonzero level set, and step 1.3 the divergence of the spatial $L^2$ norm together with the stated consequence for clauses (a) and (d) of the wave theorem; steps 1.4 and 2.1 prove that the pointwise subluminal curve without a uniform bound fails the root-existence conclusion and degenerates the denominator $1-n\cdot\beta$; and step 1.5 proves that events on the worldline have no retarded root below the observation time, so the exclusion of $\Gamma$ is needed. The counterexamples (ii) and (iii) are choice-free: they use only the explicit algebraic curve, the strict inequalities and the root lemma [F18]; Countable Choice is assumed only in part (i), where it enters through the box-measure and measurability interfaces [F12, F16, F17]. No measurement, physical field identification or empirical claim is made, and no quantitative physical precision is asserted. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

## Definition

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

## Definition

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

## Definition

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) $E$ is a **polar vector** and $B$ an **axial vector** relative to the
orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted
for this framework are proper and orientation preserving, so
orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.
