## Postulate

Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework:

(i) The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of the
mathematical model [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], together with the
conversion constant $c>0$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]], is the spacetime of the
framework: its points represent idealized physical events, displacements
represent idealized spacetime separations, and the causal classification of the
model is the framework's causal structure.

(ii) The inertial frames and charts of
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] are the inertial descriptions of the
framework, and changes of description are the proper orthochronous isometries
adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]].

(iii) The ideal clock reading rule along future timelike curves and the
identification of ideal vacuum light rays with future null straight lines, both
with the same constant $c$, are those adopted in
[[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]].

(iv) The laboratory description of fields and sources is the restricted
inertial chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the spatial Euclidean structure
and the SI conventions of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

Status and scope: the mathematical model defines the geometry and its theorems
prove geometric facts only; that physical events are described by the model,
that ideal clocks read the stated proper time and that ideal vacuum light
follows null straight lines are adopted assumptions, not deductions from
experiment or from the mathematical axioms. The special-relativity postulates
adopted here do not by themselves select the Maxwell equations, a force law or
any matter model: the electromagnetic equations and couplings of this framework
are further postulates of it. The framework is classical, flat and non-quantum;
gravitational curvature, quantum fields and measurement postulates are outside
its scope.

## Definition

The particle and light objects of the framework are the following curves and
vector fields of the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]],
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with the physical interpretation of
[[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and the units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Worldlines] A **worldline** is a regular causal curve $x:J\to A$ in one of
the regularity classes of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] ($J$ an
order-convex subset of $\mathbb R$ with at least two elements). A **massive
worldline** is a $C^k$ future timelike worldline, $k\ge1$, with everywhere
nonzero future timelike tangent; a **light ray** is a $C^1$ future null curve
with everywhere nonzero future null tangent. Along a null curve the integrand
$-\eta(x',x')$ of the proper-time construction
([[def-sr-proper-time]]) vanishes identically, so that construction yields no
proper-time parametrization of it, and a light ray is never treated as a
massive worldline. A worldline is a curve in spacetime; its reading $r\circ x$
in a named laboratory chart is a coordinate description of it, not an object of
another observer.

(b) [Four-velocity and four-acceleration] For a massive worldline the
four-velocity $U$ and, when it is $C^2$, the four-acceleration $A$ are those of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]; wherever defined they satisfy
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$, by
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(c) [Chart reading] If a massive $C^2$ worldline is described in a laboratory
chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] by $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ on an open interval of
laboratory times, then $|r'(t)|<c$ for every $t$, with four-velocity
$U=\gamma(c,r')$ and Lorentz factor
$\gamma=(1-|r'|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, by clause (e) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]].

(d) [Frames and observers] An inertial frame in this framework is the
origin-with-basis object of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]; a point
observer is a future unit timelike vector $n\in V$ with rest space $n^\perp$ and
rest projection $h$, as in clauses (c)-(d) of
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. An observer congruence and a
noninertial tetrad field are further objects, not defined by this item; the
words 'frame', 'chart', 'observer' and 'tetrad' denote distinct notions and are
not interchangeable.

(e) [Scope] No force law, no self-field and no extended-body structure is
supplied here; an accelerating massive worldline requires a force model stated
separately, and an ideal light ray carries no dispersive, quantum or
polarisation structure in this definition.

## Postulate

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

## Definition

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

---

## Statement

Assume the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory
region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the fields of
[[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]], and fix the constants
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $n\ge1$, let
$(E_1,B_1,\rho_1,J_1),\dots,(E_n,B_n,\rho_n,J_n)$ be $n$ field-source pairs
each satisfying one and the same branch of the postulate on the same region
(all in the smooth branch, or all in the weak branch), and let
$a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R$. Put $E:=\sum_{j=1}^na_jE_j$,
$B:=\sum_{j=1}^na_jB_j$, $\rho:=\sum_{j=1}^na_j\rho_j$ and
$J:=\sum_{j=1}^na_jJ_j$. Then:

(a) $(E,B,\rho,J)$ satisfies the same branch of the postulate on the same
region with the same constants: pointwise in the smooth branch and in the sense
of the pairings of clause (b) of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] in the weak branch.

(b) Nothing beyond this linearity is asserted: the result does not apply to a
source whose density depends nonlinearly on the fields (a nonlinear
constitutive law), and no convergence statement is made for infinite series or
integrals of solutions or for infinite linear combinations.

(c) The theorem is conditional on the adopted postulate and is not an empirical
claim about nature.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on
$U\cong I\times\Omega$; an integer $n\ge1$; field-source pairs
$(E_j,B_j,\rho_j,J_j)$, $j=1,\dots,n$, each satisfying one and the same branch
of the postulate on $U$; coefficients $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R$; and the
combinations $E,B,\rho,J$ of the statement.

[F1] In the smooth branch the four equations
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ hold pointwise for jointly
$C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation, and
continuous sources. ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]])

[F2] In the weak branch, for locally integrable fields and sources the four
pairings $\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle$,
$\langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle$,
$\langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle$ and
$\langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$ vanish for
every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$, all derivatives being
distributional. ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]])

[F3] The divergence is the sum of the three coordinate partial derivatives of
the components, and each component of the curl is the difference of two such
partial derivatives; only first partial derivatives occur.
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]])

[F4] The partial derivative $\partial_\mu F(a)$ is the derivative at $0$ of
the line map $t\mapsto F(a+te_\mu)$.
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]])

[F5] Derivatives of sums and scalar multiples in one variable are the sums and
scalar multiples of the derivatives.
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]])

[F6] For a metric space $X$ and $A\subseteq X$, sums $f+g$ and scalar multiples
$\lambda f$ of maps $A\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous at a point are continuous at
that point; for $m=1$ this yields continuity of finite sums of continuous real
functions. ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]])

[F7] For a measure space, $L^1$ is a vector space, so a finite linear
combination of $L^1$ functions is $L^1$; applied on each compact subset of
$I\times\Omega$ this gives local integrability of finite combinations of
locally integrable functions. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]])

[F8] The regular functional $u_f(\varphi)=\int f\varphi$ is complex-linear in
$f$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$.
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]])

[F9] The distribution pairing is bilinear, and the distributional derivative
is defined by
$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$,
so it is linear in $u$. ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; the smooth branch and the weak branch are computed separately.

1.1 Assume first that all pairs lie in the smooth branch. For jointly $C^1$ maps $F_1,\dots,F_n$ from the open set $\Omega\times I$ to $\mathbb R^q$ and scalars $a_1,\dots,a_n$, the combination $F:=\sum_ja_jF_j$ is jointly $C^1$ and $\partial_\mu F=\sum_ja_j\partial_\mu F_j$ for every coordinate index $\mu$: componentwise, at a point $a$ the line map $t\mapsto F^i(a+te_\mu)=\sum_ja_jF^i_j(a+te_\mu)$ is a finite sum of one-variable functions differentiable at $0$, so its derivative at $0$ exists and equals the combination $\sum_ja_j\partial_\mu F^i_j(a)$ of derivatives by [F5] through the line-map definition [F4], and each partial $\partial_\mu F^i=\sum_ja_j\partial_\mu F^i_j$ is continuous by the finite-sum clause [F6]; hence $E$, $B$, $\rho$ and $J$ meet the regularity hypotheses of the smooth branch. [F4, F5, F6]

1.2 Assume instead that all pairs lie in the weak branch. For locally integrable scalar fields $f_1,\dots,f_n$ on $I\times\Omega$ the combination $f:=\sum_ja_jf_j$ is locally integrable: on each compact $K\subseteq I\times\Omega$ the restrictions of the $f_j$ are $L^1$ functions on $K$, so their finite linear combination is $L^1$ on $K$ by [F7] and $\int_K|f|<\infty$. By the linearity in $f$ of the regular functional [F8] one has $u_f=\sum_ja_ju_{f_j}$, and by the defining formula and the bilinearity of the pairing [F9] the distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha u_f=\sum_ja_j\partial^\alpha u_{f_j}$, so that $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ of the combination are the corresponding combinations of the summands' distributional derivatives; componentwise the same holds for the vector fields $E_j$, $B_j$, $J_j$ and the scalar fields $\rho_j$. [F7, F8, F9]

2.1 The operators $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are linear on jointly $C^1$ vector fields: by the component formulas [F3] together with step 1.1, $\operatorname{div}(\sum_ja_jF_j)=\sum_i\partial_i(\sum_ja_jF^i_j)=\sum_ja_j\sum_i\partial_iF^i_j=\sum_ja_j\operatorname{div}F_j$, and the same finite rearrangement applied to the two-term difference in each curl component gives $\operatorname{curl}(\sum_ja_jF_j)=\sum_ja_j\operatorname{curl}F_j$; the same argument gives $\partial_t(\sum_ja_jF_j)=\sum_ja_j\partial_tF_j$. [step 1.1, F3]

2.2 In the weak branch, for each $\psi\in C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$, step 1.2 expands every pairing of the combination into the finite sum of the corresponding pairings of the summands, for instance $\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle=\sum_ja_j\langle\operatorname{div}E_j-\rho_j/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle$, and likewise for $\langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle$ and $\langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$; since each summand pairing vanishes by [F2], all four pairings of the combination vanish, so the combination satisfies the branch in the distributional sense, which is clause (a) in that branch. [step 1.2, F2]

3.1 In the smooth branch, applying step 2.1 to the combinations $E=\sum_ja_jE_j$, $B=\sum_ja_jB_j$, $\rho=\sum_ja_j\rho_j$ and $J=\sum_ja_jJ_j$, and using [F1] for each summand, gives $\operatorname{div}E=\sum_ja_j\rho_j/\varepsilon_0=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=\sum_ja_j\cdot0=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\sum_ja_j\partial_tB_j=-\partial_tB$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\sum_ja_j(\mu_0J_j+c^{-2}\partial_tE_j)=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, while step 1.1 supplies the regularity hypotheses; thus the combination satisfies the branch pointwise, which is clause (a) in that branch. [step 2.1, F1]

4.1 The two branches are exactly those the hypothesis permits, so clause (a) holds in every case; clause (b) records that only the finite linearity actually computed is asserted, with no nonlinear constitutive law and no infinite superposition, and clause (c) records that the result is a conditional consequence of the adopted postulate, which completes the proof. [step 3.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Postulate

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where $\Phi$ is the raised-index operator of the field at the event $x(\tau)$,
defined by $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to proper time, that is, the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

## Example

This example is conditional on the definitions [[def-em-sources]],
[[def-em-fields]] and the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], and
assumes Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ both for the Lebesgue-volume
source branch and for the injectivity of the regular-distribution embedding
used below ([[def-countable-choice]]).

(a) [Smooth source] Let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ be nonnegative with
Lebesgue normalization $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\,d\lambda_3=1$ (the Riemann
integral over any compact box containing $\operatorname{supp}f$ has the same
value by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]])
(for instance any nonzero nonnegative smooth compactly supported bump divided
by its finite nonzero integral), let $q\in\mathbb R$, and let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set containing
$\operatorname{supp}f$. Then $\rho:=qf$ and $J:=0$ is a smooth source field of
[[def-em-sources]]: $\rho$ is compactly supported and of class $C^\infty$,
hence continuous, and for every bounded Lebesgue-measurable $V$ with compact
closure inside $\Omega$ and containing $\operatorname{supp}f$, the charge is
$Q(V,t)=q\int f=q$; the same value holds for the retained compact
Jordan/Riemann branch at every time $t$, so the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] applies to this source.

(b) [Point source] Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and
$z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map
$t\mapsto(z(t),t)$ is proper into $\Omega\times I$
([[lem-em-point-current-continuity]]; properness is automatic when
$\Omega\times I$ is the whole ambient domain or when $I=\mathbb R$). For
$q\in\mathbb R$, the pairings
$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and
$\langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_Iz'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$, for
$\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega\times I)$, are the point-source distributions of
[[lem-em-point-current-continuity]]: they are distributions
([[def-distribution]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]])
satisfying $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ in the distributional sense.
At each fixed time $t$ this model assigns the charge
$q\cdot\mathbf 1_{z(t)\in V}$ to a Jordan-measurable $V\subseteq\Omega$, and its
instantaneous spatial density is the evaluation functional $q\delta_{z(t)}$
([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]),
$\varphi\mapsto q\,\varphi(z(t))$; a source field of the smooth branch instead
gives the integrals $\varphi\mapsto\int_\Omega\rho(y,t)\varphi(y)\,dy$ of its
continuous density.

(c) [The two classes differ] Fix $t\in I$, put $z_0:=z(t)\in\Omega$ and
suppose $q\ne0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice AC_omega only as it is
carried by [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] in the
argument below, through the injectivity of the regular-distribution map
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then no locally integrable
$\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ represents the point charge: there is no
such $\rho$ whose regular distribution
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]) satisfies
$\langle\rho,\varphi\rangle=q\,\varphi(z_0)$ for every
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Indeed, if $\rho$ did, then on the open set
$\Omega\setminus\{z_0\}$ every test vanishes at $z_0$, so the regular
distribution of the restriction of $\rho$ is zero, and injectivity gives
$\rho=0$ almost everywhere there
([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]); since $\{z_0\}$ is
Lebesgue-null ([[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]) and a union
of two null sets is null
([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]), $\rho=0$ almost
everywhere on $\Omega$. The regular distribution depends only on the
almost-everywhere class, so $\langle\rho,\varphi_0\rangle=0$ for a cutoff
$\varphi_0\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\varphi_0=1$ near $z_0$
([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]), while the assumed
identity gives $\langle\rho,\varphi_0\rangle=q\varphi_0(z_0)=q\ne0$: a
contradiction. Hence the point source is not a source field of the smooth
branch of [[def-em-sources]] (whose densities are continuous functions), and
the smooth-branch equations are not applied to it pointwise; the point source
enters the framework only through its distributional pairings.

(d) [Conclusion] The two source classes carry the same parameter $q$ and the
same total charge $q$ (the smooth density integrates to $q$; the point model
assigns charge $q$ to regions containing the particle), but they are different
mathematical objects with different regularity, and they enter the framework
through different branches. This example asserts no field value at $z(t)$ and
contains no measurement or empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** a nonnegative $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with
$\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\,d\lambda_3=1$; $q\in\mathbb R$; a nonempty open
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq\Omega$; an
open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ and a $C^1$ trajectory $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$
whose graph map is proper into $\Omega\times I$; a time $t\in I$ with
$z_0:=z(t)$; and Countable Choice where the cited measure and embedding
suppliers carry it.

[F1] A smooth source field is a pair $(\rho,J)$, continuous and $C^1$ wherever
differentiated, with frame charge $Q(V,t)=\int_V\rho(y,t)\,d\lambda_3$ for
bounded Lebesgue-measurable $V$ with compact closure in $\Omega$, and compact
Jordan charge $Q_R(V,t)=\int_V\rho(y,t)\,dy$; the empty region has charge zero.
([[def-em-sources]])

[F2] The smooth branch of the Maxwell postulate refers to jointly $C^1$ fields
and continuous sources. ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]])

[F3] The point-source pairings
$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$,
$\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_Iz'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ over an open interval
$I$ with proper graph map define distributions satisfying
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. ([[lem-em-point-current-continuity]])

[F4] The Dirac distribution at $a$ is the evaluation functional
$\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on the test space. ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]])

[F5] The regular functional
$u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$ is complex-linear in $f$ and depends only
on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]])

[F6] Under Countable Choice, the map $f\mapsto u_f$ from
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into
distributions is injective. ([[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]])

[F7] Under Countable Choice, every at most countable subset of
$\mathbb R^n$ is Lebesgue-null; in particular singletons are null.
([[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]])

[F8] A union of finitely many ($\mu$-null) measurable sets is null, and
almost-everywhere statements refer to a measurable null exceptional set.
([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]],
[[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]])

[F9] For compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ with $\Omega$ open there is
$\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a
neighborhood of $K$. ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]])

[F10] On a compact Jordan region the bounded Borel zero extension of a
continuous function is Riemann integrable and its Riemann and Lebesgue
integrals agree; the Riemann integral over a Jordan set is defined by that zero
extension. ([[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]],
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]])

[F11] The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1$; in particular
$\int_Vqg\,d\lambda_3=q\int_Vg\,d\lambda_3$ for a real constant $q$.
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]],
[[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]])

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct computations for the two source classes and a short
contradiction for their difference.

1.1 For the smooth source $\rho=qf$, $J=0$: $\rho$ is $C^\infty$ with compact support and $J=0$ is smooth, so $(\rho,J)$ is a smooth source field in the sense of [F1]; for every bounded Lebesgue-measurable $V$ with compact closure in $\Omega$ containing $\operatorname{supp}f$ one has $f\mathbf 1_V=f$ pointwise, hence $Q(V,t)=\int_Vqf\,d\lambda_3=q\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\,d\lambda_3=q$ by [F11], and the same pair is therefore a source to which the smooth branch [F2] refers. [F1, F2, F11]

1.2 For the same $V$ required to be compact and Jordan measurable, the zero extension of $qf$ to a bounding rectangle is the bounded zero extension of a continuous function on a compact Jordan region, so it is Riemann integrable with $Q_R(V,t)=\int_Vqf=q$ by [F10]; thus both charge branches of [F1] give the same value $q$ on this source, as the definition of $\rho=qf$ predicts. [F10, F1]

1.3 For the point source, the pairings of [F3] applied to the given proper trajectory define distributions on $\Omega\times I$ satisfying $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; its fixed-time reading is the evaluation functional $q\delta_{z(t)}$ of [F4], in contrast with the fixed-time reading $\varphi\mapsto\int_\Omega\rho(y,t)\varphi(y)\,dy$ of a smooth-branch density. [F3, F4]

2.1 Suppose a locally integrable $\rho\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ satisfied $\langle\rho,\varphi\rangle=q\varphi(z_0)$ for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Every test supported in the open set $\Omega\setminus\{z_0\}$ vanishes at $z_0$, so the regular distribution of $\rho|_{\Omega\setminus\{z_0\}}$ is zero; by injectivity [F6] this gives $\rho=0$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus\{z_0\}$. The singleton $\{z_0\}$ is null by [F7], so their union is null by [F8] and $\rho=0$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$; since the regular distribution depends only on the almost-everywhere class [F5], $\langle\rho,\varphi_0\rangle=0$ for the cutoff $\varphi_0$ of [F9] with $\varphi_0=1$ on a neighborhood of the compact $\{z_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. But the assumed identity gives $\langle\rho,\varphi_0\rangle=q\varphi_0(z_0)=q\ne0$, a contradiction. [step 1.3, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9]

3.1 Consequently no locally integrable density represents the point charge, so the smooth-branch equations, whose densities are continuous functions [F1], are not applied to it pointwise; both classes carry the parameter $q$ and total charge $q$ (step 1.1 for the smooth density and the fixed-time reading of step 1.3 for the point model), but they are different objects in different branches, and the example asserts no field value at $z(t)$ and no measurement. [step 2.1, step 1.1, step 1.2, F1] ∎

## Example

This example is conditional on the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], the
definitions of divergence and curl in
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the equations of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and the coupling of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]];
all equalities below are equalities of units, using
$1\ \mathrm{C}=1\ \mathrm{A\,s}$, $1\ \mathrm{V}=1\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$,
$1\ \mathrm{J}=1\ \mathrm{N\,m}$,
$1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$,
$1\ \mathrm{F}=1\ \mathrm{C\,V^{-1}}$ and
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$.

(a) $\operatorname{div}E$ has unit $\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}}$ and
$\rho/\varepsilon_0$ has unit
$\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}/(F\,m^{-1})}=\mathrm{C\,V\,m^{-2}\,C^{-1}}
=\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}}$, so the two sides of
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ agree.

(b) $\operatorname{curl}B$ has unit $\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}}$; $\mu_0J$ has unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}\cdot A\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-2}}
=\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}}$; $c^{-2}\partial_tE$ has unit
$\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{2}\cdot V\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{V\,s\,m^{-3}}
=\mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}}$, so both source terms of
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ have the unit of
$\operatorname{curl}B$.

(c) $\operatorname{curl}E$ has unit
$\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{T\,s^{-1}}$ and $\partial_tB$ has unit
$\mathrm{T\,s^{-1}}$, so $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ is homogeneous;
$\operatorname{div}B=0$ is a homogeneous equation.

(d) In the coupling of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], the adopted right-hand
side $q\,\Phi(U)$ has unit
$\mathrm{C\cdot T\cdot m\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{C\,N\,A^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{N}$
(using $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$ and
$1\ \mathrm{C}=1\ \mathrm{A\,s}$) and the left-hand side $m\,dU/d\tau$ has unit
$\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}=\mathrm{N}$, so the two sides of
$m\,dU/d\tau=q\,\Phi(U)$ agree; in the coordinate expression
$q(E+r'\times B)$ that the postulate displays and explicitly does not adopt as
exact, $qE$ has unit
$\mathrm{C\cdot V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{J\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{N}$ and
$q\,(r'\times B)$ has unit
$\mathrm{C\,m\,s^{-1}\,T}=\mathrm{C\,N\,A^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{N}$, so its
two terms add with the unit of a force; and $\rho E+J\times B$ has unit
$\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}\,V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$, the unit of a force
density, while $J\cdot E$ has unit
$\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}\cdot V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$, the unit of a power
density.

(e) The energy density $\tfrac12(\varepsilon_0E^2+B^2/\mu_0)$ has unit
$\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ and the flux $E\times B/\mu_0$ has unit
$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, consistent with
$\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\cdot m\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

(f) The check is exact arithmetic of the adopted units; it is not a
measurement, it does not prove the equations, and no numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is used or asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the unit conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], the component
definitions of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and the
adopted equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]].

[F1] The SI unit table: $c$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $E$ in
$\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $B$ in T with
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$, $\rho$ in
$\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$, $J$ in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, force in N,
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ with $\mu_0$ in
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$, energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ and energy flux
in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. ([[def-em-si-conventions]])

[F2] The divergence is $\sum_i\partial_iF_i$ and each curl component is a
difference of two first partial derivatives, so divergence and curl divide the
field unit by a length. ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]])

[F3] The four Maxwell equations are
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]])

[F4] The adopted coupling is $m\,dU/d\tau=q\,\Phi(U)$, with the coordinate
expression $q(E+r'\times B)$ displayed and explicitly not adopted as exact, and
with the force density $\rho E+J\times B$ and the power density $J\cdot E$.
([[post-em-lorentz-coupling]])

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct unit arithmetic for each displayed term.

1.1 Reading the units of $E$, $\rho$ and $\varepsilon_0$ from [F1] and the component formula for the divergence from [F2]: $\operatorname{div}E$ has unit $\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}}$, while $\rho/\varepsilon_0$ has unit $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}/(F\,m^{-1})}=\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}\cdot m\,F^{-1}}=\mathrm{C\,V\,m^{-2}\,C^{-1}}=\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}}$, using $1\ \mathrm{F}=1\ \mathrm{C\,V^{-1}}$; the two sides of the first equation of [F3] therefore carry the same unit. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Again by [F1] and [F2], $\operatorname{curl}B$ has unit $\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}}$; $\mu_0J$ has unit $\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}\cdot A\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}}$; and $c^{-2}\partial_tE$ has unit $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{2}\cdot V\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{V\,s\,m^{-3}}$, which equals $\mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}}$ because $1\ \mathrm{V}=1\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$, $1\ \mathrm{J}=1\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ and $1\ \mathrm{C}=1\ \mathrm{A\,s}$; hence all three terms of the fourth equation of [F3] carry the unit $\mathrm{T\,m^{-1}}$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.3 By [F1] and [F2], $\operatorname{curl}E$ has unit $\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}}$ and $\partial_tB$ has unit $\mathrm{T\,s^{-1}}$; since $\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{N\,m\,C^{-1}\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,s^{-1}\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{T\,s^{-1}}$ by the conversion identities, the third equation of [F3] is homogeneous, and the second equation of [F3] is homogeneous because both sides are zero. [F1, F2, F3]

1.4 By [F1] and [F4]: the adopted term $q\,\Phi(U)$ has unit $\mathrm{C\cdot T\cdot m\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{C\,N\,A^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{N}$ and $m\,dU/d\tau$ has unit $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}=\mathrm{N}$; in the displayed coordinate expression, $qE$ has unit $\mathrm{C\cdot V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{C\cdot J\,C^{-1}\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{N}$ and $q(r'\times B)$ has unit $\mathrm{C\cdot m\,s^{-1}\cdot N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{C\,N\,A^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{N}$; $\rho E$ has unit $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}\cdot V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{C\,V\,m^{-4}}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$ and $J\times B$ has unit $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}\cdot N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$, so the force density $\rho E+J\times B$ has unit $\mathrm{N\,m^{-3}}$; and $J\cdot E$ has unit $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}\cdot V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ because $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. [F1, F4]

1.5 By [F1]: $\varepsilon_0E^2$ has unit $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}\cdot V^2\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{F\,V^2\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{C\,V\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ and $B^2/\mu_0$ has unit $\mathrm{N^2\,A^{-2}\,m^{-2}\cdot A^2\,N^{-1}}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, so the energy density $\tfrac12(\varepsilon_0E^2+B^2/\mu_0)$ has unit $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$; the flux $E\times B/\mu_0$ has unit $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}\cdot N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}\cdot A^2\,N^{-1}}=\mathrm{V\,A\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. [F1]

2.1 Every term listed in (a)-(e) of the example has been assigned the same unit as the term it is compared with, so each displayed Maxwell equation and coupling expression is dimensionally homogeneous in the adopted SI conventions; the computation used only the unit table and the component definitions, and no numerical value of $\mu_0$, no measurement and no claim that the equations hold was used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5, F1, F3, F4] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the ambient
convention under which the Lebesgue measure and integration interface used
below is stated ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$, let
$U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R$ be continuous.

For a closed axis-parallel cube $Q=\prod_{i<n}[a_i,a_i+\ell]\subseteq U$ with
$\ell>0$, the restriction $g|_Q$ is continuous on the compact nondegenerate
rectangle $Q$, hence bounded and Borel and Riemann integrable; denote by
$\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n$ the Lebesgue integral of $g$ over $Q$ with respect to
the restriction of Lebesgue measure, which by the comparison of the Riemann
and Lebesgue integrals equals the Riemann integral of $g$ over $Q$. Suppose
that

$$\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n=0$$

for every closed axis-parallel cube $Q\subseteq U$ with side $\ell>0$. Then
$g=0$ on $U$.

In particular, for $n=2$, a continuous function on an open subset of the
plane whose integral over every closed axis-parallel square contained in its
domain vanishes is identically zero.

The hypothesis requires every closed axis-parallel cube, with every centre and
every positive side length. A single cube does not suffice, and neither do the
cubes centred at one fixed point: on $U=\mathbb R^n$ the nonzero continuous
function $g(x)=x_1-p_1$ has $\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every closed cube $Q$
centred at $p$, by cancellation in its first coordinate. This family also
differs from the family of closed cubes that merely contain $p$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A natural number $n\ge1$, an open set
$U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a continuous $g:U\to\mathbb R$, and the hypothesis
that $\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every closed axis-parallel cube $Q\subseteq U$
of positive side length, the integral being interpreted as in the Statement.
Throughout, $\mathbb R^n$ carries the Euclidean metric $d_2$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and subsets carry the subspace metric
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

[F1] $U$ is open: for every $x\in U$ there is a real $r>0$ with
$B(x,r)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-ball]]). The map
$g$ is continuous, that is, continuous at every point of $U$: for every $a\in U$
and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a real $\delta>0$ such that
$|g(x)-g(a)|<\varepsilon$ for every $x\in U$ with $d_2(x,a)<\delta$
([[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F2] For $n\ge1$ the Euclidean metric is
$d_2(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_{i<n}(x_i-y_i)^2}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F3] For reals $a_i\le b_i$ the box
$\{\,x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i\le x_i\le b_i\text{ for every }i<n\,\}$ is a compact
subset of $(\mathbb R^n,d_2)$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F4] A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space is
bounded and attains a greatest and a least value
([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F5] Every set $R$ with $R^\circ\subseteq R\subseteq\overline R$ determined by
reals $a_i\le b_i$ is Lebesgue measurable with
$\lambda_n(R)=\prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i)$; in particular a closed cube of side
$\ell>0$ has measure $\ell^n>0$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F6] A continuous map between topological spaces has Borel preimages of Borel
sets ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]).

[F7] Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable
([[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]).

[F8] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $m\ge1$ and reals $a_i<b_i$, if a
bounded Borel real function $f$ on the box $Q=\prod_{i<m}[a_i,b_i]$ is Riemann
integrable, then $f$ is Lebesgue integrable on $Q$ and its Lebesgue and
Riemann integrals agree ([[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F9] For integrable $f\le h$ on a nondegenerate rectangle the Riemann
integrals satisfy $\int_Qf\le\int_Qh$, and Riemann integrals are linear in the
integrand ([[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]]).

[F10] Lower and upper Darboux sums of a bounded $f$ over a grid $P$ are
$L(f,P)=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)$ and
$U(f,P)=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)$, with $m_i=\inf f[Q_i]$ and
$M_i=\sup f[Q_i]$; the cells $Q_i$ of a grid partition have
$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q)$; and the Darboux
integrals are the suprema and infima of these sums, the function being Riemann
integrable when they agree ([[def-multidimensional-darboux-sums]],
[[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]], [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]).

[F11] If a grid $P'$ refines a grid $P$, then
$L(f,P)\le L(f,P')\le U(f,P')\le U(f,P)$
([[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]]).

[F12] For every real $\eta>0$ there is a natural number $k\ge1$ with
$1/k<\eta$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

## Proof

1.1 Suppose that $g(p)\ne0$ for some $p\in U$. Replacing $g$ by $-g$ if necessary, assume $g(p)>0$: the replacement preserves the hypothesis, because for every admissible cube the two Riemann integrals satisfy $\int_Q(-g)=-\int_Qg$ and the Lebesgue integrals equal them by [F8], so $\int_Q(-g)\,d\lambda_n=-\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n=0$, and it preserves the conclusion $g=0$; both $g$ and $-g$ are continuous. [given, F8, F9, algebra]

1.2 By continuity of $g$ at $p$ with $\varepsilon=g(p)/2>0$ there is $\delta_1>0$ with $|g(x)-g(p)|<g(p)/2$ for every $x\in U$ with $d_2(x,p)<\delta_1$; by openness of $U$ there is $\delta_2>0$ with $B(p,\delta_2)\subseteq U$. Put $\delta:=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\}>0$ and $\ell:=\delta/\sqrt n>0$, and consider the closed axis-parallel cube $Q:=\prod_{i<n}[p_i-\ell/2,\,p_i+\ell/2]$. For $x\in Q$ we have $d_2(x,p)^2=\sum_{i<n}(x_i-p_i)^2\le n(\ell/2)^2=\delta^2/4$, so $d_2(x,p)\le\delta/2<\delta\le\delta_1$ and $x\in B(p,\delta_2)\subseteq U$; thus $Q\subseteq U$ and $g(x)>g(p)-g(p)/2=g(p)/2$ for every $x\in Q$. [F1, F2, choose, algebra]

1.3 It remains to verify the sharpness clause. Fix $p\in\mathbb R^n$, put $a=\ell/2>0$ and $Q=\prod_{i<n}[p_i-a,p_i+a]$, and let $h(x)=x_1-p_1$ on $\mathbb R^n$. Let $\Phi(x):=(2p_1-x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)$; then $\Phi$ maps $Q$ onto $Q$, $\Phi\circ\Phi$ is the identity, and for each cell $A$ of a grid whose first-coordinate partition is symmetric about $p_1$ the mirror cell $\Phi(A)$ has $\operatorname{vol}(\Phi(A))=\operatorname{vol}(A)$, $\inf h[\Phi(A)]=-\sup h[A]$ and $\sup h[\Phi(A)]=-\inf h[A]$. [F2, F10, construct, algebra]

2.1 The set $Q$ is a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$ and the restriction $g|_Q$ is continuous for the subspace metric, so it is bounded and attains its extrema; its Borel measurability is [F6] applied to the continuous map $g|_Q$, and continuity on the closed nondegenerate rectangle gives Riemann integrability. By [F8] the Lebesgue integral $\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n$ exists and equals the Riemann integral of $g|_Q$, and by [F5] $\lambda_n(Q)=\ell^n>0$. [F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.2]

2.2 The constant $c:=g(p)/2>0$ has Riemann integral $c\,\ell^n$ over $Q$: for every grid $P$ of $Q$ every cell satisfies $m_i=M_i=c$, so $L(c,P)=U(c,P)=c\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=c\operatorname{vol}(Q)=c\,\ell^n$ by [F10]; hence the Darboux integrals of $c$ equal $c\,\ell^n$, the function is Riemann integrable, and by [F8] its Lebesgue integral over $Q$ is $c\,\ell^n>0$. [F5, F8, F10, step 1.2, algebra]

2.3 Let $P$ be any grid of $Q$ and let $P''$ be the grid with first-coordinate partition the union of the first-coordinate breakpoints of $P$ with their reflections $t\mapsto2p_1-t$, and with the remaining coordinate partitions those of $P$; then $P''$ refines $P$ and its first-coordinate partition is symmetric about $p_1$, so its cells fall into mirror pairs and self-mirrored cells, and summing the identities of step 1.3 over those classes gives $L(h,P'')=-U(h,P'')$, whence $L(h,P'')\le0\le U(h,P'')$; by [F11], $L(h,P)\le L(h,P'')\le0$ and $U(h,P)\ge U(h,P'')\ge0$ for every grid $P$. [F10, F11, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Since $g(x)>c$ for every $x\in Q$ by step 1.2 and both $g|_Q$ and the constant $c$ are Riemann integrable on $Q$, monotonicity [F9] gives $\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n\ge c\,\ell^n>0$, where step 2.1 identifies the Lebesgue integral of $g$ with its Riemann integral and step 2.2 evaluates the constant. This contradicts the hypothesis $\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for the admissible cube $Q\subseteq U$ constructed in step 1.2. Hence $g(p)=0$ for every $p\in U$, and the planar clause is the case $n=2$. [step 2.2, step 1.2, step 2.1, F9, given, contradiction]

3.2 For each integer $m\ge1$ let $P_m$ be the grid with first-coordinate breakpoints $p_1+ka/m$ for $-m\le k\le m$ and single intervals of length $2a$ in the remaining coordinates. Its first-coordinate partition is symmetric about $p_1$, so $L(h,P_m)=-U(h,P_m)$ by step 2.3, and direct summation over the $2m$ cells of first-coordinate length $a/m$ gives $L(h,P_m)=-U(h,P_m)=-a^2(2a)^{n-1}/m$, a quantity tending to $0$; hence $\sup_PL(h,P)\ge L(h,P_m)$ for every $m$ forces $\sup_PL(h,P)\ge0$, and together with step 2.3 this gives $\sup_PL(h,P)=0$, while $\inf_PU(h,P)=0$ likewise. Therefore $h$ is Riemann integrable over $Q$ with $\int_Qh=0$, and by [F8], using that $h|_Q$ is continuous hence bounded and Borel, the Lebesgue integral is $\int_Qh\,d\lambda_n=0$. [F7, F8, F12, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 The function $g(x)=x_1-p_1$ is continuous and nonzero on $\mathbb R^n$, and step 3.2 shows $\int_Qg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for the cube $Q$ of step 1.3 centred at $p$; every closed cube centred at $p$ is of that form, so the family of cubes with the single centre $p$ does not satisfy the localizing hypothesis although $g\ne0$, and a single cube plainly cannot either. Thus the all-cubes hypothesis of the Statement is exactly what the argument of steps 1.1-3.2 uses. [given, step 3.2, step 3.1] ∎



## Source notes

The localization statement is standard: a continuous function that is
orthogonal to every axis-parallel cube integral vanishes. The proof above is
written in the library's own measure and Darboux interfaces, using the
multidimensional Darboux integral of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]
and the comparison with the Lebesgue integral of
[[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]];
the sharpness witness is the coordinate-cancellation computation, proved
directly by mirror-symmetric grid refinements rather than by a separate
symmetry or change-of-variables theorem.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the surface-measure interface cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact
embedded $C^2$ hypersurface whose surface measure is that of the compact
embedded $C^1$ class of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] (the $C^2$ data are
special cases of the $C^1$ data), and let $a:S\to\mathbb R$ be continuous.
Suppose that

$$\int_Sa\psi\,dS=0$$

for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]),
the pairing being the signed surface integral of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] of the continuous
function $a\,(\psi|_S)$. Then $a=0$ on $S$. Equivalently, if two continuous
densities on $S$ pair equally against every test function, then they are equal
pointwise on $S$. The conclusion is pointwise and uses the continuity of $a$;
a merely locally integrable density would satisfy only an almost-everywhere
conclusion, which this statement does not claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. An open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb
R^3$, a compact embedded hypersurface $S\subset\Omega$ of the stated class
with its surface measure $dS$, a continuous $a:S\to\mathbb R$, and the
hypothesis that $\int_Sa\psi\,dS=0$ for every
$\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ carry the subspace
metric and the Euclidean distance $d_2$ ([[def-metric-continuity]],
[[def-metric-ball]]).

[F1] $\Omega$ is open: every $x_0\in\Omega$ has a ball $B(x_0,\rho)\subseteq
\Omega$ ([[def-metric-topology]]). A map is continuous at a point when the
usual $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition holds for the subspace metric
([[def-metric-continuity]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[F2] The class of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]
consists of finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations
$X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$, $O_j$ open in $\mathbb R^3$ and $V_j$ open in
$\mathbb R^2$, whose images cover $S$ and whose coordinate transitions are
$C^1$; a $C^1$ map is continuous
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). For a nonnegative Borel $f$
the integral is the finite chart sum
$\int_Sf\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_jf)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$ against a
subordinate ambient partition, the chart formula restricts to a compact Borel
face contained in a regular patch, and a signed $f$ with
$\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ is integrated through the difference of its positive
and negative parts.

[F3] The chart integral defines a finite Borel measure on $S$, independent of
the finite charts and the subordinate partitions, and every regular chart
density $J_{X_j}$ is continuous and strictly positive
([[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]).

[F4] For every $0<r<R$ and centre $x_0$ there is a smooth
$\psi:\mathbb R^3\to[0,1]$ equal to one on $\overline B_r(x_0)$ with support
strictly inside $B_R(x_0)$ ([[lem-scaled-euclidean-bumps-with-compact-support-and-gradient-bound]]);
a smooth function whose support is a compact subset of $\Omega$ belongs to
$\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).

[F5] The nonnegative Lebesgue integral of a measurable function is monotone and
homogeneous for nonnegative scalars, and the integral of the constant multiple
$\beta\mathbf 1_C$ of the indicator of a measurable set $C$ of finite measure
is $\beta\,\lambda_2(C)$ ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]],
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]],
[[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F6] Every closed axis-parallel square $C\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ of side
$\ell>0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_2(C)=\ell^2>0$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F7] The signed Lebesgue integral is defined through the positive and negative
parts and is real-linear on integrable functions
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

## Proof

1.1 Assume that $a(x_0)\ne0$ for some $x_0\in S$ and put $m:=|a(x_0)|/2>0$; let $\sigma:=\operatorname{sgn}(a(x_0))$, so that $\sigma a(x_0)=2m>0$. [given, choose, algebra]

1.2 Continuity of $a$ at $x_0$ gives $\delta_1>0$ with $|a(x)-a(x_0)|<m$ for every $x\in S$ with $d_2(x,x_0)<\delta_1$, hence $\sigma a(x)>m$; openness of $\Omega$ gives $\delta_2>0$ with $B(x_0,\delta_2)\subseteq\Omega$. With $N:=B(x_0,\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\})$ we have $N\subseteq\Omega$ open and $\sigma a>m$ on $S\cap N$. [F1, choose, algebra]

1.3 The function $a\psi$ is bounded on the compact $S$, so $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le C\,S(S)<\infty$ by monotonicity of the nonnegative surface integral and finiteness of the surface measure, and the signed integral $\int_Sa\psi\,dS$ is defined; it equals $\int_S(a\psi)^+\,dS-\int_S(a\psi)^-\,dS$, and on $S$ we have $(a\psi)^+=a^+\psi$ and $(a\psi)^-=a^-\psi$ because $\psi\ge0$. [F2, F3, F5, given]

2.1 The chart family of the class covers $S$, so $x_0\in S\cap O$ for one of its charts $X:V\to S\cap O$ with $V\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ open and $X$ regular, injective and $C^1$; write $u_0:=X^{-1}(x_0)$. Replacing $O$ by $O\cap N$ and $V$ by $X^{-1}(S\cap(O\cap N))$, the restricted parametrization is again a regular injective $C^1$ chart of the class with $X(V)=S\cap O$ and $O\subseteq N$, so $\sigma a>m$ on $X(V)$. [F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Choose $R>0$ with $\overline B_R(x_0)\subseteq O$ and put $r:=R/2$; the scaled Euclidean bump yields $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $0\le\psi\le1$, $\psi=1$ on $\overline B_r(x_0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq B_R(x_0)\subseteq O\subseteq\Omega$, so $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$. [F4, step 2.1, choose]

4.1 By continuity of $X$ at $u_0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $X[B(u_0,\delta)]\subseteq B_r(x_0)$, so choosing $\ell>0$ with $\ell/\sqrt2<\delta$ and $\ell$ small enough that the closed axis-parallel square $C:=u_0+[-\ell/2,\ell/2]^2$ lies in $V$ gives $C\subseteq B(u_0,\delta)$ and $X(C)\subseteq B_r(x_0)$; then $X(C)\subseteq B_r(x_0)\subseteq\overline B_R(x_0)\subseteq O$ and $\lambda_2(C)=\ell^2>0$, and $X(C)$ is a compact Borel face contained in the regular patch $X$. [F1, F2, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, choose, algebra]

5.1 The chart density $J=J_X$ is continuous and strictly positive on $V$, so by continuity at $u_0$ there is $\beta>0$ with $J\ge\beta$ on $C$; since $X$ is injective with $X(V)=S\cap O$, the restricted chart formula gives $S(X(C))=\int_V\mathbf 1_{X(C)}(X(y))J(y)\,dy=\int_V\mathbf 1_C(y)J(y)\,dy \ge\int_V\beta\mathbf 1_C(y)\,dy=\beta\lambda_2(C)=\beta\ell^2>0$. [F2, F3, F5, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 On the support of $\psi$ intersected with $S$ the sign $\sigma$ is constant and $|\sigma a|>m$; where $\psi$ vanishes the product $a\psi$ also vanishes. Consequently $\sigma a\psi\ge m\,\mathbf 1_{X(C)}$ pointwise on $S$: on $X(C)$ we have $\psi=1$ and $\sigma a>m$, and off $X(C)$ the left side is nonnegative on $S\cap\operatorname{supp}\psi$ and zero elsewhere. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Monotonicity of the nonnegative surface integral, applied through the chart formula, and the evaluation of step 5.1 give $\sigma\int_Sa\psi\,dS=\int_S\sigma a\psi\,dS\ge m\,S(X(C))\ge m\beta\ell^2>0$, so $\int_Sa\psi\,dS\ne0$; this contradicts the hypothesis for the test function $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$. Hence $a(x_0)=0$ for every $x_0\in S$. [step 5.1, step 1.3, step 5.2, F2, F5, given, contradiction]

7.1 For the equal-density clause let $a,b:S\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $\int_Sa\psi\,dS=\int_Sb\psi\,dS$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; both $a\psi$ and $b\psi$ are bounded on $S$, so both signed integrals are defined, and the chartwise representation of the signed integral as a finite sum of signed Lebesgue integrals, together with linearity of the Lebesgue integral, gives $\int_S(a-b)\psi\,dS=\int_Sa\psi\,dS-\int_Sb\psi\,dS=0$ for every $\psi$. The continuous density $c:=a-b$ therefore satisfies the hypothesis of the Statement, and step 6.1 gives $c=0$, that is $a=b$ on $S$. [step 6.1, F2, F3, F7, given, algebra] ∎



## Source notes

The pointwise conclusion is the standard reduction of a vanishing pairing
against every ambient smooth test function to a local positivity argument on
the hypersurface. The proof above keeps the library's own chart-measure
interface: the graph density of the published treatments appears here only
through the strict positivity and continuity of the regular chart density of
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], so no
product-extension assertion for arbitrary planar tests is used.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention
already carried by the imported finite piecewise $C^1$ boundary presentations
and by the compact $C^1$ surface measure cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ open and
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval. This definition fixes the
time-independent spatial test geometries of the integral form of the Maxwell
equations.

(a) [Volume test geometry] A **volume test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a pair
$(V,\nu_V)$ where $V\subseteq\Omega$ is a nonempty bounded open set with
$\overline V\subseteq\Omega$ and a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation
of its boundary ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), and
$\nu_V$ is the outward unit normal of that presentation off its edge set
([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]). The
**closed-surface flux** of a field $F$ continuous on a neighbourhood of
$\overline V$ is the finite face sum

$$\oint_{\partial V}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS:=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_V\,dS,$$

with the face surface integrals of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. For every closed
axis-parallel box $K=\prod_{i<3}[a_i,b_i]\subseteq\Omega$ with $a_i<b_i$, its
open interior $V=\prod_{i<3}(a_i,b_i)$ is a volume test geometry and
$\overline V=K$; its natural six-face presentation is the boundary of $K$, with
outward normals $\pm e_i$. The volume variable is $V$, while $K$ denotes its
compact closure. Each face is a degenerate three-dimensional box and hence has
$\lambda_3$-measure zero by
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]; their finite union
$K\setminus V$ is null. Thus for continuous $h$ on a neighbourhood of $K$,
$\int_Vh\,d\lambda_3=\int_Kh\,d\lambda_3$: the positive and negative integrals
over the null difference vanish by
[[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]] and
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

(b) [Patch test geometry] A **patch test geometry** in $\Omega$ is a regular
$C^2$ surface patch $(D,r)$ over a finite elementary Green region in the sense
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]],
[[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]): $D\subseteq\mathbb
R^2$ is a finite elementary Green region, $r$ is of class $C^2$ on an open
neighbourhood of $D$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]),
$r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]) and
no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$. Its
**induced boundary chain** $\partial S=r(\partial D)$ and its **circulation**
$\oint_{\partial S}F\cdot d\mathbf r$ for a field continuous on the image are
those of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]); its
**oriented flux** of a field $F$ continuous on the image is

$$\int_SF\cdot n_S\,dS:=\int_D(F\circ r)\cdot(r_u\times r_v)\,dudv,$$

the scalar Riemann integral of the continuous integrand on the compact Jordan
parameter region, in the orientation induced by $r$
([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]). The pair $(D,r)$
is part of the data. Every affine graph patch $r(u,v)=(u,v,\varphi(u,v))$ over
an axis-parallel square $D=[c_1,c_1+\ell]\times[c_2,c_2+\ell]$ with $\ell>0$,
whose graph lies in $\Omega$ with $\varphi$ affine (for instance constant), and
more generally every affine regular patch over such a square, is a patch test
geometry: the square is a finite elementary Green region, and $r$ is smooth and
regular with $\varphi_u,\varphi_v$ constant.

(c) [Regularity convention] When an integral identity of this framework is
asserted for a volume test geometry $V$, respectively for a patch test geometry
$S$, with respect to a field $F$ of stated class $C^k$, it concerns fields
defined and of class $C^k$ on an open neighbourhood of $\overline V$ in
$\Omega$, respectively of the image $r[D]$ in $\Omega$; when the identity
involves a time derivative of a flux, the field is defined with the stated
regularity on a neighbourhood of that compact set times the compact time
interval of the assertion. No regularity away from these neighbourhoods is
asserted.

(d) [Conventions and scope] Test geometries are fixed spatial subsets of
$\Omega$ and carry no motion. A patch's orientation is the one induced by its
parametrization, and its induced boundary chain has the compatible orientation
of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]], so that the
classical Stokes theorem applies with a plus sign. The definition retains the
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the imported boundary and surface-measure
definitions; it asserts no differential equation, no physical law and no
existence of fields.

## Source notes

The conventions recorded here are the classical textbook conventions for the
divergence and Stokes test geometries: outward normals on closed volume
boundaries, induced right-handed orientation on patch boundaries, and flux and
circulation signs tied to those orientations. The mathematical content of
every clause is carried by the imported items cited in place; the textbooks
supply orientation and notation only.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the surface-measure interface inherited from [[def-em-surface-distribution]]
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\mathcal D'(U)$ be the space of
distributions on $U$ ([[def-distribution]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]); recall that the pairing
$\langle T,\psi\rangle$ is bilinear with no conjugation and that the
distributional partial derivatives are
$\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$
([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(a) [Fields as distributions] Locally integrable fields and source densities on
$U$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

(b) [Point sources] Let $I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval,
let $z:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map
$\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is proper into the open set $U$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$
(coulombs). By [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],

$$\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$ with
$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$. If instead
$I_0=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the
absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite and both endpoint
events lie in $U$, the same formulas define distributions with

$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$$

([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); a finite-history point source
therefore contributes an endpoint term unless that term is included
explicitly, and the pairings above exclude it only by the stated properness or
endpoint hypotheses.

(c) [Stationary-sheet sources] Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded
$C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side
$\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]],
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a tangential surface current
density; the sheet is stationary). Then

$$\langle\rho_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_S\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_SK(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$: for $\psi$ with compact support the inner
integrals are continuous in $t$ on a compact parameter interval and the
functionals are bounded by
$(\sup|\sigma\psi|)\,\mathrm{area}(S)\,\mathrm{length}$ of the time projection
of the support, and likewise in the vector case. A normal sheet current (one
with $K\cdot n\ne0$), a line current and a moving sheet are not source types of
this definition.

(d) [Unrestricted weak fields and optional interface branches] The general
field class for the solution predicate (e) consists of all locally integrable
pairs $(E,B)$ on $U$, also when the source has a stationary-sheet part. No
classical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define
those four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional
hypotheses of interface and jump results, not admission requirements of the
general weak model.

For a pointwise classical jump branch, one may additionally assume that $E,B$
are $C^1$ off $S\times I$ and, around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side
is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of
the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. These
joint one-sided extensions make the field traces and first spatial and
temporal derivatives continuous up to that side, locally uniformly on compact
cylinders.

For the broader weak-trace branch, one may instead assume the original
one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional
conditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally
integrable on $S\times I$ for $dS\,dt$. This branch supports sheet-distribution
and almost-everywhere jump identities; spatial continuity at each time gives
pointwise spatial identities for almost every time, and joint continuity of
the jump densities gives the further all-time upgrade. Separate spatial $C^1$
traces at each time alone do not imply that joint regularity or upgrade.
Whenever such traces exist, $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ denotes their jump in the chosen
normal convention.

(e) [Weak Maxwell equations with a distributional source pair] Let $E,B$ be a
field pair of class (d), let $\rho=\rho_v+\rho_s$ and $J=J_v+J_s$ be source
distributions on $U$ whose volume parts $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable
volume densities with the charge and current quantity types of
[[def-em-sources]] (the weak predicate requires this stated
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity, not the classical continuous-source
regularity) and whose singular parts $(\rho_s,J_s)$ are point sources as in (b)
or stationary-sheet sources as in (c), and let
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. Say that $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations
with the source pair $(\rho,J)$ when, for every
$\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, the four pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish, all derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular
distributions of the fields and the source pairings being those of (b) and (c).
This clause defines a solution predicate. When the singular parts vanish, its
four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point
and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here;
adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after
this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining
this predicate.

(f) [Scope] No product of two distributions is formed anywhere: the fields
occur only through their distributional derivatives paired with a test
function, and the source densities $\sigma,K$ occur only inside the ordinary
surface and time integrals of (b) and (c); products such as $\rho_sE$ or
$J_s\times B$ are not defined by this item. The definition asserts no existence
theorem for fields with singular sources, no conservation law (continuity for
these sources is proved separately where used) and no regularisation. Sources
that are not locally integrable and are not point or stationary-sheet sources,
moving sheets, line currents, and arbitrary products of distributions are
outside the definition.

## Source notes

The distributional treatment of point charges and surface sources follows the
standard classical presentations cited in the frontmatter; the pairings are
defined with the library's own distribution and surface-measure conventions,
and the continuity statements quoted in (b) are the conclusions of
[[lem-em-point-current-continuity]], consumed here as the exact interface of
the point-source pairings.

## Postulate

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) as carried by the declared
distributional and surface source objects of [[def-em-weak-sources]]. In the
flat classical laboratory model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the positive
constants and SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], adopt the following
additional physical assumption for models using the declared point or
stationary-sheet sources: the locally integrable field pair and the
volume-plus-singular source pair of [[def-em-weak-sources]](a)-(d) must satisfy
its solution predicate (e). Explicitly,

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

are required in $\mathcal D'(U)$, meaning that all four residual pairings
defined there vanish for every compact smooth test. This is a physical adoption
of the classical vacuum idealisation in that source class, not a theorem about
sources and not a consequence of the original locally integrable source branch
of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. When the singular part vanishes, the adopted
identities coincide with that earlier weak branch.

Only source and field tuples satisfying these identities are models of this
postulate; the postulate does not assert existence for every prescribed source
pair, and compatibility conditions remain consequences to be checked. Sources
are the exact point and stationary-sheet types defined earlier, including their
properness or endpoint and tangential-current qualifications. No moving sheet,
line current, magnetic source, product of distributions, self-force,
regularisation, matter dynamics or material constitutive law is introduced.
This postulate reports no experiment or measurement and does not infer
empirical certainty from its mathematical formulation.

## Source notes

The adoption of the vacuum field equations for idealised point and stationary
sheet sources is the standard classical idealisation of the cited treatments:
the point-particle delta current and the surface charge and current
dictionaries are presented there as modelling assumptions of the same type.
The formulation, the field and source types, the units and the distributional
scope are the framework's own, as recorded in the cited definitions.
