## Statement

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E,B$ be the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and
$\rho,J$ the source fields of [[def-em-sources]], with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ on $\Omega\times I$ and
$\rho,J$ of class $C^1$, and suppose the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds with these fields and sources, in particular
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. Then the continuity equation

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$$

holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, where $\operatorname{div}$ is the
divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and
$\partial_t$ the partial time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(b) [Distributional branch] Let $E,B,\rho,J$ be distributions on
$\Omega\times I$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]); in
particular they may be locally integrable fields and sources identified with
their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Suppose the four
equations

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$ with distributional derivatives. This
includes the original locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and the separately adopted declared singular-source
models of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], when their source and
field hypotheses hold. More generally the formal compatibility implication
applies to every distributional source pair for which the four identities
hold, without asserting physical adoption of arbitrary distributions. Then
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$.

The conclusion is a compatibility condition: it does not assert that every
source pair is compatible with the Maxwell equations, and by itself it proves
no conservation of physical charge. The derivative compatibility argument is
choice-free. An application to the declared singular-source model retains the
Countable Choice assumption of its defining source and surface-measure
formulation ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The laboratory region, fields, sources and constants of the
Statement; in clause (a) the joint $C^2$ and $C^1$ regularity and the smooth
branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]; in clause (b) the four distributional
identities.

[F1] The smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds pointwise, in
particular $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0>0$
([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F2] The separately adopted distributional postulate requires the four
identities in $\mathcal D'(U)$ for the declared singular-source models
([[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]]).

[F3] For a $C^2$ vector field on an open set the divergence of its curl
vanishes pointwise ([[thm-the-divergence-of-a-curl-vanishes]]), and mixed
partial derivatives commute ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]);
derivatives of sums and scalar multiples are computed termwise
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]],
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F4] Distributional derivatives are defined by
$\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$ on
tests $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, are linear in $T$ and commute with one another
([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]],
[[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]).

[F5] Locally integrable functions and fields embed in the distributions as
their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

## Proof

1.1 In the smooth branch, the identity $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B)=0$ holds pointwise. Taking the divergence of the Ampere equation and using linearity of the coordinate derivatives gives $0=\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B)=\mu_0\operatorname{div}J+c^{-2}\operatorname{div}(\partial_tE)$, and the mixed partials commute, so $\operatorname{div}(\partial_tE)=\partial_t(\operatorname{div}E)$; the Gauss law gives $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and, $\rho$ being $C^1$, $\partial_t(\operatorname{div}E)=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho$. Substituting gives $0=\mu_0\operatorname{div}J+c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho=\mu_0(\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho)$, because $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ by the definition of $\varepsilon_0$, and division by $\mu_0>0$ gives $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 In the distributional branch, fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega\times I)$. The distributional curl is built from the components $\partial_jB_k-\partial_kB_j$, so $\langle\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B),\psi\rangle=\sum_{i,j,k}\varepsilon_{ijk}\langle\partial_i\partial_jB_k,\psi\rangle$, a finite sum over three indices; the distributional derivatives commute and $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is antisymmetric, so exchanging the summation indices $i$ and $j$ presents this number as its own negative, and hence it is zero. The Ampere identity in $\mathcal D'$, linearity of the pairing and commutativity with $\partial_t$ give $0=\mu_0\langle\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle+c^{-2}\langle\partial_t\operatorname{div}E,\psi\rangle$; the Gauss identity in $\mathcal D'$ reads $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, so $\partial_t\operatorname{div}E=\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho$ as distributions, and substitution with $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\mu_0>0$ gives $\langle\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle=0$. As $\psi$ was arbitrary, $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Omega\times I)$; every ingredient is either a distributional identity or a constant multiple, so no choice principle is used. [F2, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 The locally integrable case of the Statement is clause (a) of the embedding of [F5]: locally integrable fields and sources have well-defined regular distributions, and the argument of step 1.2 applies unchanged. The physical adoption of the singular-source models remains the separate postulate [F2], and the Countable Choice assumption is carried only by their defining source and surface-measure formulation. [F4, F5, given] ∎

## Source notes



Continuity as a compatibility condition of the Maxwell equations, obtained by
the divergence-of-curl cancellation, is the standard textbook derivation cited
in the frontmatter. The distributional form uses the library's own
distribution interface; the singularity of point and sheet sources is handled
only through the separate adopted postulate, never through an undefined
product of distributions.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of the
imported piecewise $C^1$ boundary and surface-measure definitions
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let
$E,B$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$; and let $(V,\nu_V)$ and $(D,r)$ be the
volume and patch test geometries of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]. Assume the
fields are jointly $C^1$ on $\Omega\times I$ and that the additional
derivatives appearing below exist and are continuous there; for instance $E,B$
jointly of class $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ is sufficient.

(a) [Differential implies integral] If the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, then for every
volume test geometry $(V,\nu_V)$ and every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \oint_{\partial V}B(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=0,$$

and for every patch test geometry $(D,r)$ the flux functions
$t\mapsto\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and
$t\mapsto\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ are differentiable on $I$ and, for
every $t\in I$,

$$\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS,\qquad \oint_{\partial S}B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS+c^{-2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS.$$

(b) [Integral implies differential] Conversely, suppose the two volume
identities of (a) hold for every volume test geometry and every $t\in I$, and
that for every patch test geometry the two flux functions are differentiable
on $I$ and the two patch identities of (a) hold for every $t\in I$. Then the
four smooth-branch equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold pointwise on
$\Omega\times I$:

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

The equivalence is asserted for the exact class of test geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], which contains the open interiors of all closed
axis-parallel boxes compactly contained in $\Omega$ and the affine square
patches; it is not a recovery from one selected volume or one selected patch,
and the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the time derivative of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] are the operators used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The laboratory region $U\cong
I\times\Omega$, the fields $E,B$ of the stated class, the source fields
$\rho,J$, the volume and patch test geometries of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], and the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. In clause (b) also the integral identities of (a)
for every test geometry of the class and the differentiability of the two flux
functions.

[F1] The smooth branch of the postulate holds pointwise:
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$,
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ on $\Omega\times I$, with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$ ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]],
[[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F2] Volume test geometries are nonempty bounded open $V$ with
$\overline V\subseteq\Omega$ and a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ boundary
presentation with outward normal $\nu_V$ and the face-sum closed-surface flux;
the open interior of every closed axis-parallel box
$K=\prod_{i<3}[a_i,b_i]\subseteq\Omega$ with $a_i<b_i$ is a volume test
geometry with $\overline V=K$, and $\int_Vh\,d\lambda_3=\int_Kh\,d\lambda_3$
for continuous $h$ on a neighbourhood of $K$ because the six faces are
$\lambda_3$-null. Patch test geometries are regular $C^2$ patches over finite
elementary Green regions with induced boundary chain, circulation and induced
orientation, and every affine patch $r(u,v)=p+ue_j+ve_k$ over an axis-parallel
square whose image lies in $\Omega$ is a patch test geometry with
$r_u\times r_v=e_j\times e_k$ ([[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]],
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]],
[[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).

[F3] The divergence, curl and the partial derivatives are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]; they are linear in the field and
continuous when the field is $C^1$.

[F4] If $\Omega_0$ has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and
$F\in C^1(\overline{\Omega_0};\mathbb R^3)$, then
$\int_{\Omega_0}\operatorname{div}F\,d\lambda_3=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$,
all integrals finite, the faces carrying their actual outward normals
([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]]).

[F5] For a $C^2$ patch $(D,\varphi)$ over a finite elementary Green region and
a $C^1$ vector field $F$ on an open set containing $\varphi[D]$,
$\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_D\langle(\operatorname{curl}F)\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\rangle$,
the induced orientation being that of the patch
([[thm-the-classical-stokes-theorem-for-a-c2-surface-patch]]).

[F6] A Riemann integral of a continuous integrand over a compact Jordan region
equals the corresponding Lebesgue integral, and continuous integrands on
compact Jordan regions are Riemann integrable
([[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F7] If a parameter family of integrals has a continuous integrand with
continuous parameter derivative on a neighbourhood of a compact parameter set,
the integral is differentiable in the parameter with the derivative obtained
by differentiating under the integral ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]).

[F8] A continuous function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ whose integral
over every closed axis-parallel cube of positive side length contained in its
domain vanishes is identically zero; for $n=2$ the same holds with closed
axis-parallel squares ([[lem-em-coordinate-cell-localization]]).

[F9] The Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F10] The laboratory fields, sources and constants are those of
[[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]] on the
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$, $B$ carries T,
$\rho$ carries C m$^{-3}$, $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$.

## Proof

1.1 For the volume identities of (a), fix $t\in I$ and a volume test geometry $(V,\nu_V)$; the fixed-time fields $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t)$ are $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline V$ by the said regularity, and the divergence theorem [F4] applies to that presentation: $\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=\int_V\operatorname{div}E(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3$ and likewise for $B$. Substituting the Gauss laws of [F1] gives $\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=(1/\varepsilon_0)\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3$ and $\oint_{\partial V}B(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS=0$. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 For the patch identities of (a), fix a patch test geometry $(D,r)$ and put $S=r[D]$, with parameter derivatives $r_u,r_v$ and oriented area vector $r_u\times r_v$. The flux functions $\Phi_B(t):=\int_D\langle B(r(u,v),t),r_u(u,v)\times r_v(u,v)\rangle\,dudv$ and $\Phi_E$ are differentiable on $I$ with $\Phi_B'(t)=\int_S\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and $\Phi_E'(t)=\int_S\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$: the integrands are the continuous functions $\langle B(r(u,v),t),r_u\times r_v\rangle$ with continuous $t$-derivative $\langle\partial_tB(r(u,v),t),r_u\times r_v\rangle$ on a neighbourhood of the compact Jordan region $D$ times a compact interval around $t$, [F6] identifies the Riemann integral with the Lebesgue integral, and [F7] differentiates under the integral. Stokes' theorem [F5] applied to the $C^1$ fields gives $\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_S\operatorname{curl}E(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and the corresponding identity for $B$, in the induced orientation of the patch; substituting the Faraday law $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ of [F1] gives $\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\int_S\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS=-\Phi_B'(t)$, and substituting the Ampere law gives $\oint_{\partial S}B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS+c^{-2}\Phi_E'(t)$. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, given, algebra]

1.3 For clause (b), fix a closed axis-parallel box $K=\prod_{i<3}[a_i,b_i]\subseteq\Omega$ with $a_i<b_i$ and let $V$ be its open interior, a volume test geometry with $\overline V=K$ by [F2]. The volume identity hypothesis and the divergence theorem give $0=\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS-(1/\varepsilon_0)\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3=\int_Vh\,d\lambda_3$ for the continuous function $h:=\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0$, where linearity [F9] combines the two finite integrals and [F4] identifies the flux with $\int_V\operatorname{div}E$; by [F2] and [F9] this equals $\int_Kh\,d\lambda_3$, because $K\setminus V$ is $\lambda_3$-null. Since every closed axis-parallel box $K\subseteq\Omega$ with positive sides arises this way, [F8] with $n=3$ gives $h=0$ on $\Omega$, that is $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$. The same computation with the second volume identity and $\int_V\operatorname{div}B=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}B=0$. [F1, F2, F4, F8, F9, given, algebra]

1.4 For the curl equations fix a point $p\in\Omega$ and let $(j,k)$ be the cyclic pair with $e_j\times e_k=e_i$ for a coordinate index $i$. Put $W:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:p+ue_j+ve_k\in\Omega\}$, an open set, and $\varphi_i(u,v):=\bigl(\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB\bigr)(p+ue_j+ve_k)\cdot e_i$ on $W$, a continuous function. For every closed axis-parallel square $Q\subseteq W$ with side $\ell>0$ the affine patch $r(u,v):=p+ue_j+ve_k$ over $Q$ is a patch test geometry with $r_u\times r_v=e_i$ and image in $\Omega$; Stokes [F5], the differentiability of its flux function and the Faraday identity of the hypothesis give $\int_Q\varphi_i\,dudv=\int_Q\langle(\operatorname{curl}E)\circ r,r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dudv+\frac{d}{dt}\int_Q\langle B\circ r,r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dudv=\oint_{\partial S}E\cdot d\mathbf r+\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB\cdot n_S\,dS=0$. Hence the continuous function $\varphi_i$ has vanishing integral over every closed axis-parallel square contained in $W$, so the planar clause of [F8] gives $\varphi_i=0$ on $W$. The point $p\in\Omega$ was chosen arbitrarily, and $(0,0)\in W$ because $p\in\Omega$, so evaluating at $(0,0)$ gives $(\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB)(p)\cdot e_i=0$ for every $p\in\Omega$; letting $i$ run over the three coordinate indices, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ on $\Omega$. The same argument with the Ampere identity in place of Faraday gives $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, the flux derivative producing $c^{-2}\Phi_E'$. [F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove that the smooth-branch equations imply all the integral identities of (a) for every volume and patch test geometry, and steps 1.3 and 1.4 prove the converse for the same exact class; the recovery uses the open interiors of all closed axis-parallel boxes and all affine square patches, so no single selected volume or patch suffices, the marked $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is exactly the convention of the divergence theorem and of the surface-measure interface used in [F4], [F2] and [F5], and the fields, sources and constants throughout are those of the framework definitions recorded in [F10]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, F10, given] ∎

## Source notes

The passage between the differential and integral forms over the declared test
geometries is the standard localization argument of the cited treatments,
written here with the library's own divergence theorem, patch Stokes theorem,
parameter-integral and cube-localization interfaces. The textbooks supply the
formulation and the physical reading; the deductions use only the imported
mathematical items and the adopted smooth-branch postulate.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the interface and surface-measure definitions cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]] and the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and source
fields of [[def-em-sources]].

Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a
chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side
$\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a tangential surface current
density). Let $E,B$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and $C^1$ on
$(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ with the following explicit joint one-sided
regularity: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side is the restriction
of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding
closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. Thus the fields and their
first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side of
$S\times I$, locally uniformly on compact cylinders, and let $\rho_v,J_v$ be
continuous on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ and locally integrable on
$\Omega\times I$. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces of
such a field $F$.

Under the separate singular-source physical adoption
[[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], suppose that $E,B$ satisfy the weak
Maxwell equations with the source pair

$$\rho=\rho_v+\rho_S,\qquad J=J_v+J_S,$$

where $(\rho_S,J_S)$ is the stationary-sheet source of
[[def-em-weak-sources]](c) with densities $\sigma,K$ and the pairings there, in
the sense of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e), and where the volume parts
$\rho_v,J_v$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Then, pointwise
on $S\times I$,

$$n\cdot[E]=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad n\times[B]=\mu_0K,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,$$

with the ordinary Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces
([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Equivalently, the surface current density is
$K=(\mu_0)^{-1}\,n\times[B]$ and the surface charge density is
$\sigma=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot[E]$.

The theorem assumes a stationary interface: the hypersurface $S$ and its
normal do not depend on $t$, so the one-sided $C^1$ traces also make
$\partial_tE$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally
integrable, contributing no delta terms. No magnetic surface charge or
magnetic surface current is present in the sources, and correspondingly the
last two identities assert the absence of magnetic sheet delta terms. A moving
interface, a normal sheet current, or a sheet whose support changes with time
is outside this statement and would require additional terms.

[General weak-trace branch] The weak Maxwell framework continues to allow the
full locally integrable field and source class, without asserting undefined
classical trace values. If instead of the joint extension condition the fields
have the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time, assume in
addition that their piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega\times I)$ and that their one-sided field traces are
measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$.
The one-sided traces are then locally integrable densities on the sheet, so
the four pairings
$$\int_I\int_S\bigl(n\cdot[E]-\sigma/\varepsilon_0\bigr)\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S(n\cdot[B])\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S(n\times[E])\cdot\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S\bigl(n\times[B]-\mu_0K\bigr)\cdot\psi\,dS\,dt$$
against every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$ are well defined by the ordinary
surface-and-time integrals, with no product of distributions formed; these
vanishing pairings are the precise weak form of the four jump identities, and
they do vanish. The identities then hold for $dS\,dt$-almost every $(x,t)$;
since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for
every $x\in S$ for almost every $t\in I$. They hold at every $(x,t)$ whenever
the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous. Merely having
one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify this
last upgrade.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The laboratory region, the stationary
interface $S$ with normal $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, the fields and
sources with the stated regularity (joint one-sided in the main branch),
continuous $\sigma$ and tangential continuous $K$, and the weak Maxwell
equations for the source pair $(\rho_v+\rho_S,J_v+J_S)$ under the separate
adoption.

[F1] The interface conventions: $\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S\psi\,dS$ defines a
finite Borel measure ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), the jump is
$[F]=F_+-F_-$ with $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, and the surface measures
and chart formulas are those of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; the cross and inner
products are those of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and the Euclidean structure
of the frame ([[def-em-lab-geometry]]).

[F2] The separately adopted postulate requires the four identities in
$\mathcal D'(U)$ for the declared singular-source models, with the source
pairings of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b)-(e)
([[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], [[def-em-weak-sources]],
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]).

[F3] The interface-derivative lemma: for a $C^1$ field off a two-sided compact
embedded $C^2$ interface with one-sided $C^1$ traces,
$\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}+n\cdot[F]\delta_S$ and
$\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}+n\times[F]\delta_S$ in the
distributional sense, the bracket terms being the locally integrable
piecewise classical fields ([[lem-em-interface-derivatives]]).

[F4] The surface-density localization lemma: a continuous density on $S$
whose surface integral against every ambient compact smooth test vanishes is
identically zero ([[lem-em-surface-density-localization]]).

[F5] Partition and cutoff machinery: compact supports admit finite ambient
partitions of unity subordinate to a cover
([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]),
cutoffs equal to one near a compact set exist inside an open set
([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]), and for every
$0<r<R$ there are smooth bumps equal to one on $\overline B_r$ and supported
inside $B_R$ ([[lem-scaled-euclidean-bumps-with-compact-support-and-gradient-bound]]).

[F6] Integration tools: the Fubini theorem for $L^1$ functions on sigma-finite
product spaces ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]),
integration by parts on a compact interval
([[thm-integration-by-parts]]), and the Riemann-Lebesgue comparison
([[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F7] Nullity and its calculus: $S$ is a Lebesgue-null subset of $\mathbb R^3$
(its slice charts give singleton sections; [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]],
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]), $\lambda_3$ is complete
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]), a locally integrable
function vanishing off a null set represents the zero distribution
([[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]), and countable unions of null sets
are null ([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]).

[F8] Integral comparisons used by the sign-and-bump argument: the nonnegative
integral is monotone and homogeneous
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]), agrees with
the simple integral, and the integral of an indicator is the measure
([[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]],
[[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]],
[[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]); continuous functions are Borel
measurable ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]); the rationals
are dense ([[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]]); and the distributions and their
derivatives are those of [[def-distribution]],
[[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]],
[[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]].

## Proof

1.1 Under the joint one-sided regularity, each side of $S\times I$ carries a $C^1$ extension to a closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder; on each compact closed half-cylinder the extensions and their first spatial and temporal derivatives are bounded, so the piecewise first derivatives of $E,B$ and the volume sources are locally bounded and locally integrable on $U$, their one-sided traces and jumps are jointly continuous, and the jump densities are bounded on compact subsets of $S\times I$. [F1, F2, given]

1.2 The interface $S$ is Lebesgue-null in $\mathbb R^3$: in the finite graph charts of [F1] every normal section of the graph over the parameter plane is a singleton, so Fubini and the nullity of singletons give $\lambda_3(S)=0$, and the finitely many charts cover $S$; hence $S\times I$ has four-dimensional measure zero locally and every locally integrable function vanishing off $S\times I$ represents the zero distribution. [F7, given]

1.3 Spacetime interface formula for a component: for each fixed $t$ the spatial restriction of the hypothesis satisfies the interface-derivative lemma on the spatial slice, so for a compactly supported spacetime test $\psi$ the identity $\partial_iF_j=\{\partial_iF_j\}+n_i[F_j]\,\delta_S$ may be applied slicewise and integrated in $t$; a time-independent finite partition of unity subordinate to stationary graph neighbourhoods of the spatial support of $\psi$, with cutoffs as in [F5], makes the terms $F_j\partial_i\psi$, $(\partial_iF_j)\psi$ and $n_i[F_j]\psi$ absolutely integrable on the compact support, because the piecewise derivatives and the continuous jumps are bounded there and the surface measure of the compact sheet is finite by [F1]; Fubini [F6] then justifies integrating the slicewise identity, giving $\partial_iF_j=\{\partial_iF_j\}+n_i[F_j]\otimes\delta_{S\times I}$ for the spacetime distribution, where the sheet term acts as $\int_I\int_Sn_i[F_j]\psi\,dS\,dt$. For the time derivative, on each spatial side the field is $C^1$, and compact-support integration by parts on a compact interval containing the time support of each spatially localized piece, followed by the Riemann-Lebesgue comparison and Fubini, gives $-\int F_j\partial_t\psi=\int(\partial_tF_j)\psi$ with no endpoint contribution, so $\partial_tF_j=\{\partial_tF_j\}$ carries no sheet term: the interface is stationary. [F1, F3, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply the formula of step 1.3 to each of the four weak Maxwell identities. Off the sheet the fields and sources are $C^1$ and continuous, so the classical residuals $h_1=\operatorname{div}E-\rho_v/\varepsilon_0$, $h_2=\operatorname{div}B$, $h_3=\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB$, $h_4=\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J_v-c^{-2}\partial_tE$ are continuous on the open set $U\setminus(S\times I)$; against every test supported in that open set the four weak identities reduce to $\int h_\ell\psi=0$, and the sign-and-bump argument of [F8] (a positive value of a continuous $h_\ell$ at a point persists with a fixed sign on a small axis-parallel cube of positive measure, on which a bump equal to one on a smaller cube, supplied by [F5], makes $\int h_\ell\psi$ strictly nonzero) forces $h_\ell=0$ on $U\setminus(S\times I)$. Each residual is locally integrable on $U$ and vanishes off the null set $S\times I$ by step 1.2, hence represents the zero regular distribution; subtracting the off-sheet parts from the four identities leaves four sheet identities whose densities are $n\cdot[E]-\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, $n\cdot[B]$, $n\times[E]$ and $n\times[B]-\mu_0K$, each multiplied by the sheet distribution $\delta_{S\times I}$. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.2, step 1.3, given, algebra]

3.1 Write $a_1=n\cdot[E]-\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, $a_2=n\cdot[B]$, $a_3\in\mathbb R^3$ with components of $n\times[E]$, and $a_4=n\times[B]-\mu_0K$ for the continuous sheet densities of step 2.1. For a fixed spatial test $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ and each component density $a$ of these four, the function $H_\varphi(t):=\int_Sa(x,t)\varphi(x)\,dS$ is continuous on $I$: on a compact time interval the joint continuity of $a$ on the compact sheet gives uniform convergence as $t\to t_0$, and $|H_\varphi(t)-H_\varphi(t_0)|\le S(S)\|\varphi\|_\infty\sup_{x\in S}|a(x,t)-a(x,t_0)|$ tends to $0$. Testing the sheet identity with $\varphi(x)\eta(t)$ for $\eta\in C_c^\infty(I)$ gives $\int_IH_\varphi(t)\eta(t)\,dt=0$ for every such $\eta$; the one-dimensional sign-and-bump argument of [F8] then gives $H_\varphi(t)=0$ for every $t\in I$. Since $\varphi$ was an arbitrary ambient test, the surface-density localization lemma [F4] applied at each fixed $t$ to the continuous density $a(\cdot,t)$ gives $a(\cdot,t)=0$ on $S$; hence all four pointwise jump identities $n\cdot[E]=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, $n\cdot[B]=0$, $n\times[E]=0$, $n\times[B]=\mu_0K$ hold on $S\times I$, and the equivalent solved forms for $\sigma$ and $K$ follow by dividing by $\varepsilon_0>0$ and $\mu_0>0$. [F1, F4, F5, F8, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 For the general weak-trace branch the same interface formula of step 1.3 is available with the weaker justification: the one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions give the slicewise lemma at every time, the additional local $L^1$ hypotheses on the piecewise first derivatives make the localized terms of step 1.3 integrable, the measurable locally integrable traces make the sheet pairings $\int_I\int_Sa\psi\,dS\,dt$ well defined by the ordinary integrals for every test $\psi$, and Fubini still applies; the temporal identity holds because each fixed off-sheet point has a $C^1$ dependence in $t$ and integration by parts against a compactly supported test is justified by the integrable derivative. Consequently each of the four sheet pairings of the Statement vanishes for every test; no product of distributions is formed, only the pairing of a locally integrable sheet density with a compact smooth test. For the almost-everywhere conclusion, use the countable family of ambient bumps with rational centres and rational radii $0<r<R$ with $\overline B_R(q)\subseteq\Omega$, each fixed by the scaled-bump construction of [F5] rather than chosen per instance; by the preceding paragraph each such test gives a null set of exceptional times, and the countable union of these null sets is null by [F7]. At each remaining time $t$, if some continuous-in-$x$ density $a(\cdot,t)$ were nonzero at a point $x_0\in S$, its fixed sign would persist on a small graph neighbourhood of $x_0$; density of the rationals [F8] provides one of the rational balls inside that neighbourhood whose inner ball contains $x_0$, and a positive-area graph cell inside that inner ball, as in [F4], makes the pairing nonzero against the corresponding bump, a contradiction. Hence all four identities hold at every $x\in S$ for almost every $t\in I$; if the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous, the same positive-area-cell argument applied on nondegenerate time intervals upgrades the identities to all $(x,t)$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.3, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 Steps 1.1-3.1 prove the four pointwise jump identities under the joint one-sided regularity, and step 4.1 proves the weak-trace branch with its almost-everywhere and continuity upgrades; the sources used are exactly the stationary tangential sheet and volume parts, so no normal sheet current, magnetic sheet source, moving interface or product of distributions enters, and the normal $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$ with $[F]=F_+-F_-$ throughout. The separate adoption [F2] is what makes the starting identities physical for the singular-source model; no empirical claim or measurement enters the deduction. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, given] ∎

## Source notes

The jump identities are the standard pillbox and loop boundary conditions of
the cited treatments, here derived distributionally from the adopted weak
identities with the library's interface convention. The treatments motivate the
identities but do not supply the distributional deduction; that deduction uses
the imported interface-derivative, Fubini, integration-by-parts and
localization interfaces, and the separate singular-source adoption.

## Statement

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], with nonempty open time interval $I$
([[def-interval]]), positive constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. Define the **Gauss defects**

$$D_B:=\operatorname{div}B,\qquad D_E:=\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0.$$

(a) [Smooth evolution branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^2$ fields and $\rho,J$
$C^1$ source fields of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]]. Assume only
the two evolution equations

$$\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E,\qquad\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B-c^2\mu_0J,$$

and, separately, source continuity $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. No
Gauss constraint is assumed. Then $\partial_tD_B=\partial_tD_E=0$ pointwise.
For each fixed $x$, both defects are constant on $I$. Initial zero constraints
at any $t_0\in I$ persist at every time; a nonzero defect at a point persists
with the same value. Thus evolution and continuity cannot repair a nonzero
initial Gauss defect.

(b) [Distributional evolution branch] The same derivative conclusion holds for
arbitrary scalar and vector distributions $E,B,\rho,J$ on $U$ satisfying the
two evolution identities and, independently, continuity in
$\mathcal D'(U)$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]).
This includes the original locally integrable field and source branch
identified with regular distributions and the declared singular-source class
when its equations hold. Thus $\partial_tD_B=\partial_tD_E=0$
distributionally. If a defect has a continuous representative $h$ on $U$,
assume Countable Choice for the indicated Lebesgue integral and localization
interface ([[def-countable-choice]]); then $h(x,t)$ is independent of $t$. In
this continuous-representative case its zero or nonzero value at a time
persists. No restriction of an arbitrary distribution to a time slice is
assumed.

(c) [Full-Maxwell corollaries] Smooth solutions of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] satisfy the evolution and source-continuity
hypotheses by [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](a), and their Gauss defects are
identically zero by the two Gauss equations. Its original locally integrable
weak branch has the same distributional conclusion. For admitted point and
stationary-sheet models under [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]],
[[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](b) supplies compatibility and the four
identities again give zero defects. Conversely, in (a), or in (b) when both
defects have continuous representatives, evolution plus continuity and zero
Gauss defects at one time give all four Maxwell identities on $U$, pointwise
in (a) and distributionally in (b).

This theorem is conditional on the stated equations and regularity. It proves
no existence, matter dynamics, observation or empirical fact. The derivative
algebra is choice-free; Countable Choice is confined to the
continuous-representative localization and the inherited declared
singular-source formulation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The laboratory region and its time interval, the fields and sources
with the stated regularity, the two evolution equations and source continuity
(or their distributional versions), and $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$,
$c^2\mu_0=\varepsilon_0^{-1}$.

[F1] The operators are the divergence, curl and partial derivatives of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and are linear in the fields
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); the smooth fields and sources have the
regularity of the Statement ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]],
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F2] In the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] the four equations hold
with the Gauss constraints among them; the two evolution equations used here
are $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and
$\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B-c^2\mu_0J$
([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]). The distributional adoption
[[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]] asserts the four identities in
$\mathcal D'(U)$ for the declared singular-source models
([[def-em-weak-sources]]).

[F3] The divergence of a curl vanishes for $C^2$ fields, and mixed partial
derivatives commute ([[thm-the-divergence-of-a-curl-vanishes]],
[[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]); a differentiable function on an open
interval with identically zero derivative is constant
([[cor-mean-value-theorem]], [[def-interval]]).

[F4] Distributional derivatives are linear, commute with one another, and are
computed by the adjoint action on tests ([[def-distribution]],
[[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]],
[[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]); locally
integrable fields and sources embed as regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

[F5] The charge-continuity theorem supplies, in both branches, the compatibility
identity used in (c) ([[pthm-em-charge-continuity]]).

[F6] Continuous-representative machinery: a continuous function on a compact set
is bounded ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]), bounded sets have finite Lebesgue
measure ([[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]),
dominated convergence passes limits through integrals
([[thm-dominated-convergence]]), the Euclidean Borel structure and product
measure identify multiple integrals with iterated ones
([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]],
[[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]],
[[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]), Riemann and
Lebesgue integrals of continuous compactly supported integrands agree
([[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]), the
FTC gives primitives with the stated derivative ([[thm-ftc-first-part]]), balls
have positive finite measure
([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]), bumps exist
([[lem-scaled-euclidean-bumps-with-compact-support-and-gradient-bound]]), and
monotonicity and the simple-integral value evaluate the pairing against a bump
([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]],
[[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]],
[[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

## Proof

1.1 In the smooth branch, mixed partials commute and the divergence of a curl vanishes, so $\partial_tD_B=\operatorname{div}(\partial_tB)=-\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}E)=0$ pointwise, and $\partial_tD_E=\operatorname{div}(\partial_tE)-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho=c^2\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}B)-c^2\mu_0\operatorname{div}J-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}(\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho)=0$ pointwise, using $c^2\mu_0=\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ and the separately assumed continuity in the last equality. For each fixed $x$ the two functions $t\mapsto D_B(x,t)$ and $t\mapsto D_E(x,t)$ are differentiable on the interval $I$ with zero derivative, hence constant; therefore zero constraints at any $t_0$ persist at every time and a nonzero value at a point persists unchanged. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 In the distributional branch the identical componentwise cancellation holds: for every test, the distributional divergence of the distributional curl of $B$ pairs to $\sum_{i,j,k}\varepsilon_{ijk}\langle\partial_i\partial_jB_k,\psi\rangle$, which the commuting derivatives and the antisymmetry of $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ present as its own negative, hence zero; applying the two evolution identities and the independent continuity identity, all derivatives being distributional, gives $\partial_tD_B=\partial_tD_E=0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$, without forming any product of distributions, since $D_B,D_E$ themselves are distributions only through their derivatives acting on tests. [F2, F4, given, algebra]

1.3 For the continuous-representative statement assume $\partial_th=0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ for a continuous $h$, and let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. The function $F(t):=\int_\Omega h(x,t)\varphi(x)\,d\lambda_3(x)$ is continuous on $I$: on a compact time interval the integrands have the fixed compact spatial support of $\varphi$ and a uniform bound coming from continuity of $h$ on the compact set $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\times$ that interval, so dominated convergence applies. For $\eta\in C_c^\infty(I)$ with $\int_I\eta=0$, extend $\eta$ by zero and put $H(t):=\int_{-\infty}^t\eta(v)\,dv$; the FTC makes $H$ smooth with $H'=\eta$, and $H$ vanishes off the support of $\eta$, so $\Psi(x,t):=\varphi(x)H(t)$ is a compact smooth test with $\partial_t\Psi=\varphi\eta$; applying the derivative equation to this primitive test gives $0=\langle\partial_th,\Psi\rangle=-\langle h,\partial_t\Psi\rangle=-\int_IF(t)\eta(t)\,dt$, the multiple integral being identified with the iterated one by the Borel product structure and Fubini and its Riemann-Lebesgue value by the comparison lemma. Choosing a nonnegative compact bump $\beta$ of integral one and writing an arbitrary temporal test as $\eta=\eta_0+(\int_I\eta)\beta$ with $\int_I\eta_0=0$ gives $\int_I(F-C)\eta_0=0$ for all $\eta_0$ with zero integral and $C:=\int_IF\beta$; since also $\int_I(F-C)\beta=\int_IF\beta-C\int_I\beta=0$, every $\eta\in C_c^\infty(I)$ satisfies $\int_I(F-C)\eta=0$, and the sign-and-bump argument (a nonzero value of the continuous $F-C$ at a point persists with one sign on a subinterval of positive measure, and a nonnegative bump equal to one on a smaller subinterval has strictly nonzero pairing by monotonicity and the positive finite measure of that subinterval) then forces $F-C=0$, that is, $F=C$ constant on $I$. Since $\varphi$ is arbitrary, $h(\cdot,t_1)-h(\cdot,t_2)$ is a continuous function on $\Omega$ whose pairing against every spatial test vanishes, so the same sign-and-bump argument in $\mathbb R^3$ gives $h(\cdot,t_1)=h(\cdot,t_2)$; hence $h$ is independent of $t$. [F4, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 In clause (c), a smooth solution of the full postulate satisfies the two evolution equations and, by the smooth branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]], source continuity; its Gauss defects vanish identically by the two Gauss equations, and step 1.1 applies to its evolution and continuity hypotheses with the conclusion that the already vanishing defects persist. The original locally integrable weak branch has the four identities in $\mathcal D'$, hence zero defects and the statement of step 1.2. For the admitted point and stationary-sheet models, the separate adoption supplies the four identities and the distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] supplies the compatibility identity, so the defects vanish and step 1.2 applies. Conversely, if in (a) or in the continuous-representative case of (b) the defects vanish at one time, then by constancy they vanish at all times, which is exactly the pair of Gauss equations; adding them to the two evolution equations and the independently assumed continuity yields all four Maxwell identities on $U$, pointwise in (a) and distributionally in (b). [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Steps 1.1-2.1 prove the smooth and distributional propagation statements, the persistence and nonzero-persistence readings for the smooth branch, the time independence of a continuous representative of a defect under Countable Choice, and the full-Maxwell corollaries and their converse; the nonzero-defect persistence is exactly the statement that evolution plus continuity cannot repair an initial Gauss defect, and no existence, matter dynamics or empirical claim enters the argument. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Source notes



The constraint structure of the Maxwell system is the standard content of the
cited treatments: the two evolution equations propagate the two Gauss
constraints, and source continuity is required for the electric constraint.
The textbooks motivate the statement; the deductions use the imported
divergence-of-curl, mean-value, distributional-calculus, Fubini and
integration interfaces, and the singular-source class enters only through the
separate adoption.

## Example

Let $q\ne0$ be a real charge parameter (coulombs) and let
$U:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with the laboratory conventions of
[[def-em-weak-sources]]. Define a distribution $\rho$ on $U$ by

$$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_0^\infty\psi(0,t)\,dt,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$$

— an explicit switched-history distribution for $z(t)=0$ on $(0,\infty)$, with
no compensating current or source contribution at the appearance event; it does
not satisfy the proper-graph hypothesis of the zero-endpoint continuity branch
of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) — and let $J:=0$ be the zero distribution. Then:

(a) $\partial_t\rho=q\,\delta_{(0,0)}$ and $\operatorname{div}J=0$
([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]), hence
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{(0,0)}\ne0$ in
$\mathcal D'(U)$: for every test function $\psi$,
$\langle\partial_t\rho,\psi\rangle=-q\int_0^\infty\partial_t\psi(0,t)\,dt=q\,\psi(0,0)$,
because $t\mapsto\psi(0,t)$ is smooth with compact support. In particular the
continuity identity fails at the appearance event $(0,0)$.

(b) Consequently there are no locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $U$
satisfying the four weak residual identities of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e)
with the source pair $(\rho,0)$, the $\rho$-pairing being the explicit pairing
displayed above and $J=0$: such fields would satisfy the distributional
continuity identity of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](b), which applies to
every distributional source pair for which the four identities hold, and (a)
contradicts it. The source pair $(\rho,0)$ is therefore incompatible with the
formal four residual identities themselves; it is not one of the declared
point sources of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b), because the properness hypothesis
fails here as recorded, and no fields turn it into an admitted singular-source
model under [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]].

(c) The failure is exactly the omitted endpoint term of the point-source
construction: by the endpoint clause of [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],
the same trajectory on a bounded interval $I_0=(a,b)$ has
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$
with $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$. A switched point charge with $J=0$ and no endpoint
or current term is thus inadmissible; a switched charge must be accompanied by
an explicit current or endpoint source term, which the weak equations of
[[def-em-weak-sources]] then require to satisfy continuity.

This is a mathematical incompatibility statement about a declared source
model, not a report of a measurement: no apparatus, sampling model,
uncertainty or empirical claim is involved.

## Verification

**Given:** A real $q\ne0$, the distribution $\rho$ with $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_0^\infty\psi(0,t)\,dt$ on $U=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, and the zero distribution $J$. The ambient $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention is that of [[def-em-weak-sources]].

[F1] Distributional derivatives act on tests by $\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$, and a test function is smooth with compact support ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).

[F2] The point evaluation $\delta_{(0,0)}(\psi)=\psi(0,0)$ defines the Dirac distribution at the origin, and it is nonzero ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); some compactly supported smooth test equals one at the origin ([[lem-scaled-euclidean-bumps-with-compact-support-and-gradient-bound]]).

[F3] The charge-continuity theorem states that any distributional source pair satisfying the four distributional Maxwell equations satisfies $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ ([[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](b)); the weak solution predicate and the source pairings are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b)-(e), and the singular-source adoption is [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]]; the excluded original locally integrable branch is [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]].

[F4] The endpoint clause of the point-current supplier gives, for a finite-endpoint $C^1$ history with finite absolute derivative integral, $\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\delta_{\gamma(b)}$ ([[lem-em-point-current-continuity]]).

1.1 For every test $\psi$, the map $t\mapsto\psi(0,t)$ is smooth and compactly supported, so $\langle\partial_t\rho,\psi\rangle=-q\int_0^\infty\partial_t\psi(0,t)\,dt=q\,\psi(0,0)$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus, the integration being over an interval containing the support of that map; hence $\partial_t\rho=q\,\delta_{(0,0)}$ as distributions, and this is nonzero because $q\ne0$ and a compactly supported smooth test equals one at the origin. The divergence of the zero distribution is zero, so $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\,\delta_{(0,0)}\ne0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Suppose locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $U$ satisfied the four weak residual identities with the source pair $(\rho,0)$ in the formal residual reading of the solution predicate. The fields' regular distributions and the pair $(\rho,0)$ are then a distributional source pair satisfying the four identities, so the distributional branch of the charge-continuity theorem, which applies to every distributional source pair for which the four identities hold, would give $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$. This contradicts step 1.1, so no such fields exist; moreover the pair is not among the declared point sources of the framework, so it cannot be admitted through the singular-source adoption either. [F3, step 1.1, given]

2.2 The failure is exactly the omitted endpoint term: the endpoint clause of the point-current supplier evaluates the same trajectory over a bounded history $I_0=(a,b)$ as $\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\delta_{\gamma(b)}$, so a switched charge with $J=0$ and no endpoint term is precisely the case in which that endpoint contribution has been dropped; retaining continuity therefore requires an explicit current or endpoint source term, which the weak identities then force to be the continuity-compatible one. [F4, step 1.1, given]

3.1 Steps 1.1-2.2 establish: the switched-history pair has $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(0,0)}\ne0$; no locally integrable field pair satisfies the four weak identities with it; and the failing term is exactly the endpoint contribution of the declared point-source construction. The argument is a conditional computation inside the declared distributional source model and makes no empirical claim. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the test-geometry and divergence-theorem items cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $E,B$ be jointly of class $C^2$ fields of
[[def-em-fields]] and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ source fields of
[[def-em-sources]] satisfying the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on a neighbourhood of the data below.

Suppose given two patch test geometries $(D,r_1)$, $(D,r_2)$ of
[[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]] over the same finite elementary Green region
$D$ whose induced boundary chains coincide as oriented paths (so both patches
span the same closed loop $\gamma$), and suppose there is a bounded open
region $V\subseteq\Omega$ with a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation
whose boundary faces are exactly the two images $r_1[D]$, $r_2[D]$ with
outward normals $-n_1$ and $+n_2$ respectively, where $n_i$ is the normal
induced by $r_i$ (that is, $V$ is the region enclosed between the two patches;
this is a hypothesis on the pair, part of its data). Then, for every $t\in I$:

(a) [Total current flux is surface independent]

$$\int_{S_1}\bigl(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE\bigr)(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS=\int_{S_2}\bigl(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE\bigr)(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\oint_\gamma B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

where $S_i=r_i[D]$ and the flux is that of
[[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

(b) [Conduction-only flux need not be] For every $t\in I$ the difference of
the conduction fluxes equals the negative of the difference of the
displacement fluxes:

$$\int_{S_1}J(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS-\int_{S_2}J(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS=-\varepsilon_0\left(\int_{S_1}\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_1\,dS-\int_{S_2}\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_2\,dS\right).$$

Hence the conduction-only fluxes are equal exactly when the displacement
fluxes are equal, and neither conclusion is forced by the Maxwell equations
alone.

(c) [Explicit realisation] The following declared smooth data satisfies all
the hypotheses above and has different conduction fluxes through the two
surfaces. On $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, fix $\chi\in C^\infty(\mathbb
R)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi(z)=1$ for $z\le-1$ and $\chi(z)=0$ for
$z\ge0$, and set

$$E(x,t):=\frac{t}{\varepsilon_0}\chi(z)\,e_z,\qquad B:=0,\qquad \rho(x,t):=t\,\chi'(z),\qquad J(x,t):=-\chi(z)\,e_z.$$

Then $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=0=-\partial_tB$,
$\operatorname{curl}B=0=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ (the last identity because
$c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$), and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$.
Take $D=[-1,1]^2$ and its interior $D^\circ=(-1,1)^2$. Let $\sigma$ be the
standard smooth step of [[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]] and define
$h(s):=\sigma(2(1-s^2))$, $\eta(u,v):=h(u)h(v)$. Then
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, $0\le\eta\le1$, $\eta=1$ in a
neighbourhood of the origin, $\eta>0$ at every point of $D^\circ$, and $\eta=0$
on $\partial D$ and outside $D$. Take the graphs

$$r_1(u,v):=(u,v,-2\eta(u,v)),\qquad r_2(u,v):=(u,v,0).$$

Both induced boundary chains are the square
$\{(u,v,0):(u,v)\in\partial D\}$, the region
$V=\{(u,v,w):(u,v)\in D^\circ,\ -2\eta(u,v)<w<0\}$ is enclosed between the
patches, and

$$\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS=-\int_D\chi(-2\eta(u,v))\,dudv<0,\qquad \int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS=-\int_D\chi(0)\,dudv=0,$$

the first inequality because $\eta=1$ in a neighbourhood of the origin, so
$\chi(-2\eta)=1$ on a nonempty open subset of $D$, whose area is positive,
while both total current fluxes in (a) vanish, consistently with the loop
integral $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=0$. In the standard
charging-capacitor discussion the two spanning surfaces cut the conduction
current in different ways and the difference is carried by the displacement
term; the realisation above exhibits exactly this phenomenon in a
self-contained smooth model. An idealised thin-wire current is not a source
type of this framework and the capacitor interpretation is explanatory, not
an additional empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The fields $E,B$ jointly of class $C^2$
and sources $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ satisfying the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on a neighbourhood of the data; two patch test
geometries $(D,r_1),(D,r_2)$ with coincident induced boundary chains, and a
bounded open region $V$ of the stated finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation with
faces $S_1,S_2$ and outward normals $-n_1,+n_2$.

[F1] The smooth branch gives
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]],
[[def-em-si-conventions]]), and the smooth branch of
[[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives
$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; the operators are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], with mixed partials commuting
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]) and derivatives acting termwise
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F2] For the declared finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of $V$ and a $C^1$
field $G$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline V$, the divergence theorem gives
$\int_V\operatorname{div}G=\sum_j\int_{S_j}G\cdot\nu_j\,dS$ with the actual
outward normals ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]],
[[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]).

[F3] The integral Maxwell identities of [[pthm-em-integral-maxwell]](a) hold
for the smooth branch: for every patch test geometry with induced boundary
chain $\gamma$ and induced normal $n$,
$\oint_\gamma B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS+c^{-2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS$,
the flux being that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]
and the circulation that of [[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]
and [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]].

[F4] Patch test geometries are regular $C^2$ patches over finite elementary
Green regions with induced orientation, and affine and graph patches over
axis-parallel squares are instances ([[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]],
[[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]],
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F5] The standard smooth step is smooth, vanishes for arguments at most zero,
equals one from one onward and is strictly positive on $(0,1)$
([[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]]); scaled bumps and their positive
area cells supply the strict-positivity argument
([[lem-scaled-euclidean-bumps-with-compact-support-and-gradient-bound]],
[[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]],
[[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]],
[[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]).

[F6] The laboratory region, fields, sources and constants are those of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

## Proof

1.1 Put $G:=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$, a $C^1$ field on a neighbourhood of $\overline V$ by the regularity of the data. The Gauss law, commutation of mixed partials and the smooth continuity identity give $\operatorname{div}G=\operatorname{div}J+\varepsilon_0\partial_t\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho=0$ there; applying the divergence theorem to $G$ on the specified presentation of $V$, whose faces are $S_1,S_2$ with outward normals $-n_1,+n_2$, gives $0=\int_V\operatorname{div}G=\int_{S_2}G\cdot n_2\,dS-\int_{S_1}G\cdot n_1\,dS$, which is the first asserted equality of (a). For the second equality, the integral Ampere identity applies to either patch; since both induced boundary chains are the same oriented loop $\gamma$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\int_SE\cdot n\,dS=\int_S\partial_tE\cdot n\,dS$ on a fixed patch, the identity reads $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_{S_i}(J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE)\cdot n_i\,dS$ for $i=1,2$, because $c^{-2}/\mu_0=\varepsilon_0$; dividing by $\mu_0>0$ gives the stated value. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 For (c), verify the smooth equations by direct substitution: $\operatorname{div}E=(t/\varepsilon_0)\chi'(z)$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$; $\operatorname{curl}(E_z(z,t)e_z)=0$ because $E_z$ is independent of the first two coordinates, so $\operatorname{curl}E=0=-\partial_tB$; $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ and $\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE=-\mu_0\chi(z)e_z+c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}\chi(z)e_z=0$ because $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$; and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=\chi'(z)-\chi'(z)=0$. For the standard smooth step the function $h(s)=\sigma(2(1-s^2))$ is smooth, equals one for $|s|\le1/\sqrt2$, is strictly positive for $|s|<1$ and vanishes for $|s|\ge1$; hence $\eta(u,v)=h(u)h(v)$ is a smooth compactly supported function with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one near the origin, strictly positive on the open square $D^\circ=(-1,1)^2$ and zero on and outside $\partial D$. [F1, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Splitting $G=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$ in the equality of step 1.1 and using linearity of the surface integrals in the integrand gives $\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1-\int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2=-\varepsilon_0(\int_{S_1}\partial_tE\cdot n_1-\int_{S_2}\partial_tE\cdot n_2)$, which is (b); in particular the two conduction fluxes are equal exactly when the two displacement fluxes are, and the Maxwell equations alone force neither equality. [F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.2 For (c), the graphs $r_1(u,v)=(u,v,-2\eta(u,v))$ and $r_2(u,v)=(u,v,0)$ have parameter derivatives with cross products $r_{1,u}\times r_{1,v}=(2\eta_u,2\eta_v,1)$ and $r_{2,u}\times r_{2,v}=e_z$, both nonzero on the interior of $D$; the boundary chains take values $(u,v,0)$ on $\partial D$ for both, so they coincide, and the region $V=\{(u,v,w):(u,v)\in D^\circ,-2\eta(u,v)<w<0\}$ is bounded, open, nonempty, and has exactly the two graph faces with outward normals $-n_1$ and $+n_2$ off the square seam, which is a finite union of line segments of surface measure zero; thus the presentation hypotheses of [F2] are met. The oriented flux formula gives $\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS=\int_D(J\circ r_1)\cdot(r_{1,u}\times r_{1,v})\,dudv=-\int_D\chi(-2\eta(u,v))\,dudv$ and $\int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS=-\int_D\chi(0)\,dudv=0$. Since $\eta=1$ on a neighbourhood of the origin, $\chi(-2\eta)=1$ there, so the first integrand is strictly positive on a nonempty open subset of the square of positive area and the first flux is strictly negative, while the second vanishes; the total fluxes vanish because $G=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE=-\chi(z)e_z+\chi(z)e_z=0$, consistently with $\oint_\gamma B\cdot d\mathbf r=0$. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove (a) and (b) under the stated hypotheses, and steps 1.2 and 2.2 verify that the declared smooth slab data satisfy every hypothesis of (a) and (b) with $\int_{S_1}J\cdot n_1\,dS<0=\int_{S_2}J\cdot n_2\,dS$, so the conduction-only flux genuinely depends on the spanning surface while the total current flux does not; the construction is a conditional model computation, the capacitor reading is explanatory, and no measurement or thin-wire source is claimed. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, given] ∎

## Source notes

The surface-choice phenomenon in the integral Ampere law is the standard
motivation of the displacement current in the cited treatments; the
realisation is the framework's own smooth slab model, chosen because idealised
thin-wire currents are not among the declared source types. The mathematical
content uses the imported divergence theorem, patch flux and step-function
interfaces, not textbook authority.

        "strategy": "The continuous norm makes $B_R$ and $A_{\\varepsilon,R}$ nonempty bounded open sets, and radial perturbations show their boundaries are respectively $S_R$ and $S_\\varepsilon\\cup S_R$ ([[thm-continuity-preimage-characterisation]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]). Here is an explicit finite graph cover of a sphere $S_r$. For $k=1,2,3$ and $\\sigma\\in\\{+1,-1\\}$ use the relatively open patch $\\sigma x_k>r/(2\\sqrt3)$; these six patches cover because some $|x_k|\\ge r/\\sqrt3$. In rigid coordinates $(y,z)$ with $z=\\sigma x_k$, each patch lies on the positive graph $z=h(y)=\\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$.         "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\\Omega:=\\mathbb R^3\\setminus\\{x:x_1=x_2=0\\}$ (the complement of the $z$-axis), let $\\rho(x):=\\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$ and $\\hat e_r(x):=(x_1,x_2,0)/\\rho(x)$ for $x\\in\\Omega$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]), let $\\lambda\\in\\mathbb R$ be a line charge density in $\\mathrm{C\\,m^{-1}}$, let $r_0>0$, and define, with the constants and units of [[def-em-si-conventions]] ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]]),\n$$E(x):=\\frac{\\lambda\\,\\hat e_r(x)}{2\\pi\\varepsilon_0\\,\\rho(x)},\\qquad \\varphi(x):=-\\frac{\\lambda}{2\\pi\\varepsilon_0}\\log\\frac{\\rho(x)}{r_0}\\qquad(x\\in\\Omega).$$\nThen:\n(a) [Gradient] $E=-\\nabla\\varphi$ on $\\Omega$ ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]);\n(b) [Classical equations] $\\operatorname{div}E=0$ and $\\operatorname{curl}E=0$ pointwise on $\\Omega$; hence the fixed-time pair $(E,0)$ satisfies the reduced smooth-branch electrostatic equations with zero volume source on $\\Omega$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (c), [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]);\n(c) [Flux per length] for every $r>0$ and $L>0$ the flux of $E$ through the lateral cylinder surface $\\{x:\\rho(x)=r,\\ |x_3|\\le L/2\\}$ in the outward orientation is $\\Phi_r=\\lambda L/\\varepsilon_0$;           "quote": "Let $(A,V,\\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space\n([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial\nframe with inertial chart $x:A\\to\\mathbb R^4$\n([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's\nconversion constant, and let $\\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that\nframe on $n^\\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\\cdot|$ and positive spatial\norientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a\nnonempty open interval $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty\nopen set $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$, and put\n\n$$U:=\\{p\\in A:\\ \\text{there are }t\\in I,\\ y\\in\\Omega\\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\\}.$$\n\nThen:\n\n(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\\{(ct,y):t\\in I,\\ y\\in\\Omega\\}$ and\n$\\Phi:U\\to I\\times\\Omega$, $\\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a\nbijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\\to\\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and\n$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**\n$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**\n$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair\n$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing\n$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\\in\\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of\n$\\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate\ndirections, and the identification $\\mathbb R^3\\cong n^\\perp$ is the linear\nmap $\\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space\n$n^\\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).\n\n(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\\in I$ the slice\n$U_t:=\\{p\\in U:t(p)=t\\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\\Omega$ by $r$; the\nconstant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the\n$\\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\\perp$ in which the\ncoordinates of $r$ are expressed.\n\n(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map\n$F:\\Omega\\times I\\to\\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\\to\\mathbb R^m$,\n$p\\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\\cdot,t))_{t\\in I}$ of maps\n$\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class\n$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of\n[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed\n$t$) and $\\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of\n[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is\nasserted beyond the class stated for it.\n\n(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification\ninside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean\ntransformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not\nassert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\\Omega,t,r,\\delta$ and the\nidentification $\\mathbb R^3\\cong n^\\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes\nof inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in\n[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an\nordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer\nfield is defined here.",

The SI brochure\nquotes the nominal $\\mu_{0,\\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption\nwith relative standard uncertainty $2.3\\times10^{-10}$; this is historical\nestimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\\mu_0$\nor a current measured value. No\nclassical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define\nthose four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional\nhypotheses of interface and jump results, not admission requirements of the\ngeneral weak model.\n\nFor a pointwise classical jump branch, one may additionally assume that $E,B$\nare $C^1$ off $S\\times I$ and, around every $(x_0,t_0)\\in S\\times I$, each side\nis the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of\nthe corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. These\njoint one-sided extensions make the field traces and first spatial and\ntemporal derivatives continuous up to that side, locally uniformly on compact\ncylinders.\n\nFor the broader weak-trace branch, one may instead assume the original\none-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional\nconditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in\n$L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally\nintegrable on $S\\times I$ for $dS\\,dt$. Separate spatial $C^1$\ntraces at each time alone do not imply that joint regularity or upgrade.\nWhenever such traces exist, $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ denotes their jump in the chosen\nnormal convention.\n\n(e) [Weak Maxwell equations with a distributional source pair] Let $E,B$ be a\nfield pair of class (d), let $\\rho=\\rho_v+\\rho_s$ and $J=J_v+J_s$ be source\ndistributions on $U$ whose volume parts $\\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable\nvolume densities with the charge and current quantity types of\n[[def-em-sources]] (the weak predicate requires this stated\n$L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity, not the classical continuous-source\nregularity) and whose singular parts $(\\rho_s,J_s)$ are point sources as in (b)\nor stationary-sheet sources as in (c), and let\n$\\varepsilon_0=(\\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the constants of\n[[def-em-si-conventions]].           "quote": "Let $U\\cong I\\times\\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\\Omega\\times I\\to\\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\\Omega\\times I\\to\\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\\Omega\\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].\n\n(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\\Omega\\times I$ is the requirement\n$$\\partial_tE=0,\\qquad\\partial_tB=0,\\qquad\\partial_t\\rho=0,\\qquad\\partial_tJ=0\\qquad\\text{on }\\Omega\\times I.$$\n\n(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\\Omega\\times I$.\n\n(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to\n$$\\operatorname{div}E=\\rho/\\varepsilon_0,\\qquad\\operatorname{curl}E=0,\\qquad\\operatorname{div}B=0,\\qquad\\operatorname{curl}B=\\mu_0J$$\npointwise on $\\Omega\\times I$, with $\\operatorname{div}$ and $\\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\\operatorname{div}E=\\rho/\\varepsilon_0$, $\\operatorname{curl}E=0$.\n\n(d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced.           "quote": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$) as carried by the Lebesgue, polar and surface interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]).\nLet $\\rho\\in C^1_c(\\mathbb R^3;\\mathbb R)$ with support in $\\overline B_R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), let $\\varphi=\\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\\rho$ and $E=-\\nabla\\varphi$ be the smooth-branch Coulomb solution of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](a) with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], and let $\\Phi$ be the $n=3$ kernel, $\\Phi(z)=1/(4\\pi|z|)$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).\nThen:\n\n(a) [Finiteness] the three quantities\n$$\\frac{\\varepsilon_0}{2}\\int_{\\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\\,d\\lambda_3,\\qquad \\frac12\\int_{\\mathbb R^3}\\rho\\varphi\\,d\\lambda_3,\\qquad +\\frac{1}{2\\varepsilon_0}\\iint_{\\mathbb R^3\\times\\mathbb R^3}\\Phi(x-y)\\rho(x)\\rho(y)\\,d(\\lambda_3\\times\\lambda_3)(x,y)$$\nare finite real numbers;\n\n(b) [Identity] they are equal:\n$$\\frac{\\varepsilon_0}{2}\\int_{\\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\\,d\\lambda_3=\\frac12\\int_{\\mathbb R^3}\\rho\\varphi\\,d\\lambda_3=\\frac{1}{2\\varepsilon_0}\\iint_{\\mathbb R^3\\times\\mathbb R^3}\\Phi(x-y)\\rho(x)\\rho(y)\\,d(\\lambda_3\\times\\lambda_3)(x,y).$$\nThe last expression is the **external assembly work** of the ideal quasistatic bookkeeping family $\\rho_s=s\\rho$, $\\varphi_s=s\\varphi$ for $0\\le s\\le1$. An added test charge brought from infinity, where the potential is zero, has electric-force work $-dq\\,\\varphi_s$ by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-work]]; the balancing external work is $+dq\\,\\varphi_s$. Therefore $W_{\\rm ext}=\\int_0^1s\\,ds\\int\\rho\\varphi=\\tfrac12\\int\\rho\\varphi$. Both signs of $\\rho$ are allowed. The symmetric double kernel gives the equivalent ordered-pair interpretation of the factor $1/2$.\n\n(c) [Scope] the identity is a statement about the ideal quasi-static assembly of a compactly supported $C^1$ charge distribution in vacuum, all sources being held in place by external support ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]]).
