          "quote": "Let $(A,V,\\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space\n([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial\nframe with inertial chart $x:A\\to\\mathbb R^4$\n([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's\nconversion constant, and let $\\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that\nframe on $n^\\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\\cdot|$ and positive spatial\norientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a\nnonempty open interval $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty\nopen set $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$, and put\n\n$$U:=\\{p\\in A:\\ \\text{there are }t\\in I,\\ y\\in\\Omega\\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\\}.$$\n\nThen:\n\n(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\\{(ct,y):t\\in I,\\ y\\in\\Omega\\}$ and\n$\\Phi:U\\to I\\times\\Omega$, $\\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a\nbijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\\to\\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and\n$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**\n$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**\n$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair\n$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing\n$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\\in\\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of\n$\\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate\ndirections, and the identification $\\mathbb R^3\\cong n^\\perp$ is the linear\nmap $\\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space\n$n^\\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).\n\n(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\\in I$ the slice\n$U_t:=\\{p\\in U:t(p)=t\\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\\Omega$ by $r$; the\nconstant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the\n$\\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\\perp$ in which the\ncoordinates of $r$ are expressed.\n\n(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map\n$F:\\Omega\\times I\\to\\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\\to\\mathbb R^m$,\n$p\\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\\cdot,t))_{t\\in I}$ of maps\n$\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class\n$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of\n[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed\n$t$) and $\\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of\n[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is\nasserted beyond the class stated for it.\n\n(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification\ninside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean\ntransformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not\nassert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\\Omega,t,r,\\delta$ and the\nidentification $\\mathbb R^3\\cong n^\\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes\nof inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in\n[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an\nordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer\nfield is defined here.",

          "fact": "F4",
          "source": "def-distributional-derivative",
          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "For a distribution $u\\in\\mathcal D'(\\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\\alpha\\in\\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is\n$$\\langle\\partial^\\alpha u,\\varphi\\rangle=(-1)^{|\\alpha|}\\langle u,\\partial^\\alpha\\varphi\\rangle\\qquad(\\varphi\\in\\mathcal D(\\Omega)).$$\nThe test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.",

          "source": "def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function",
          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "For open $\\Omega\\subseteq\\mathbb R^n$, write $f\\in L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}(\\Omega)$ when $f:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\\int_K|f|<\\infty$ for every compact $K\\subseteq\\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.\n\nFor a test $\\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**\n\n$$\\langle u_f,\\varphi\\rangle=\\int_\\Omega f(x)\\varphi(x)\\,dx.$$\n\nThis is well-defined since $|\\int f\\varphi|\\le\\sup_K|\\varphi|\\int_K|f|$ for $K=\\operatorname{supp}\\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. Then:\n(a) [Compactness and finiteness] $\\partial D$ is nonempty and compact; the complement $\\mathbb R^3\\setminus\\partial D$ need not be connected here. Moreover $\\partial D$ has finitely many connected components, and each connected component of $\\partial D$ is compact.\n(b) [Finite embedded presentation] the local boundary charts give finitely many regular injective $C^k$ parametrisations of $\\partial D$ with $C^k$ coordinate transitions, of the graph type required by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]: writing a chart as $R(p)=(y,s)$, the graph map $y\\mapsto R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ is injective, of class $C^k$, with $C^k$ inverse (the inverse is $p\\mapsto\\pi(R(p))$ restricted to the graph, where $\\pi(y,s)=y$); consequently $\\partial D$ is a compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurface, and for $k\\ge1$ it carries the finite surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]].\n(c) [Normal field] the outward unit normal $\\nu$ of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a continuous unit normal field on $\\partial D$, with $\\nu(x)$ orthogonal to the tangent plane of the graph chart at each $x$; it is the field used by the Green and divergence items cited by this page's consumers.\nThe statement is geometric: it asserts no differentiability of $D$ beyond $C^k$, no boundedness of chart derivatives beyond the compact patches, and no connectedness of either $D$ or $\\partial D$.",
        "strategy": "The boundary is nonempty: otherwise the nonempty open bounded $D$ would also be closed and disconnect connected $\\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[cor-rn-is-polygonally-connected-and-locally-path-connected]], [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]). It is closed and bounded, hence compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. At every boundary point first shrink its graph chart to the inverse image of a small flattening cylinder $B'\\times(-b,b)$ with $\\overline{B'}$ compactly contained in the original parameter ball. Its boundary patch is exactly the graph $X(y)=R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ over the connected ball $B'$. The graph is homeomorphic to $B'$ by the coordinate projection, so is a connected relatively open neighbourhood in $\\partial D$. Arbitrarily small such graph neighbourhoods prove local connectedness of $\\partial D$ directly; local connectedness is not inherited by arbitrary Euclidean subspaces. A component is open because each of these connected neighbourhoods meeting it lies in it by maximality; it is closed because the closure of a connected set is connected (if separated, the two relative open separating sets would also separate the dense original connected set).         "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$) as carried by the boundary interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $k\\ge1$, let $\\Omega\\subset\\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain, and let $D_1,\\dots,D_m$ ($m\\ge0$) be bounded $C^k$ domains with pairwise disjoint closures whose closures satisfy $\\overline{D_1}\\cup\\cdots\\cup\\overline{D_m}\\subset\\Omega$ strictly inside $\\Omega$. Each component $U$ is an open bounded $C^k$ domain; its boundary is the compact restricted subset $\\partial U\\subseteq\\partial\\Omega_v$, a union of the boundary components incident to $U$. The normal formulas in (c) restrict to those boundary pieces. It need not have every boundary piece of $\\Omega_v$, and connectedness of $\\Omega_v$ is not asserted.\nNo regularity beyond $C^k$, no convexity and no topological simplicity is claimed.",
        "strategy": "Let $K=\\bigcup_j\\overline D_j$. It is compact, contained in open $\\Omega$, and its constituent closures are pairwise disjoint. For $m=0$, $K=\\varnothing$. Thus $\\Omega_v=\\Omega\\setminus K$ is open and bounded. It is nonempty: choose a boundary point of nonempty bounded $\\Omega$ by [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]; a small neighbourhood of that point avoids compact $K$ and contains interior points of $\\Omega$. At an outer boundary point shrink the $\\Omega$ graph cylinder to avoid $K$; locally the vacuum is the same subgraph as $\\Omega$. At a point of $\\partial D_j$ shrink the $D_j$ chart cylinder to lie inside $\\Omega$ and avoid every other closed body. Precisely $\\Omega_v\\cap W=W\\setminus\\overline D_j$, not $W\\setminus D_j$: in graph coordinates its inequality is strictly $s>h(y)$. Reflection $w=-s$ makes this the subgraph $w<-h(y)$ with $C^k$ graph. These local charts also show $\\partial\\Omega_v=\\partial\\Omega\\sqcup\\bigsqcup_j\\partial D_j$, since the disjoint compact closures prevent other bodies from hiding or touching any boundary piece. The outward normal is the outer-domain normal on $\\partial\\Omega$, and its negative on $\\partial D_j$, because the latter vacuum chart is the exterior of the body. The graph-normal formula in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] verifies this sign. All boundary pieces are compact smooth hypersurfaces by [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]. For components, every point of the open vacuum has a connected open ball inside it; hence its connected component is open. Every boundary point of a component lies on $\\partial\\Omega_v$: a connected ball inside $\\Omega_v$ cannot meet two components. Choose a small flattened cylinder at such a boundary point whose vacuum half-cylinder is connected. Because that half-cylinder meets the component, all of it lies in the component; its graph is therefore the component's local boundary. Thus the component is a bounded $C^k$ domain with the inherited normal on the restricted boundary. A finite cover of compact $\\partial\\Omega_v$ by such connected one-sided graph cylinders meets only finitely many vacuum components. Every nonempty bounded open component has a boundary point, so there are only finitely many components. A boundary component of $\\Omega_v$ is incident to a single vacuum component: the incident component is locally constant along each connected graph boundary patch, hence constant along that boundary component. Consequently each $\\partial U$ is a union of the incident compact boundary components, not necessarily the entire displayed disjoint union. None of these conclusions asserts vacuum connectedness.         "statement": "Under the Countable Choice convention of the stated boundary and sheet-distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), Adopt as a physical model of ideal electrostatic conductors, for the classical laboratory framework of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]: a **conductor configuration** consists of the following data, and every model of this postulate is required to satisfy the clauses below.           "quote": "Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this

the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative

          "quote": "Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ and let

- $x$ is an **interior point** of $A$ if $B(x,r) \subseteq A$ for some $r$. The
  set of interior points is the **interior** $\operatorname{int}(A)$.
- $x$ is an **adherent point** of $A$ if $B(x,r) \cap A \ne \emptyset$ for every
  $r$. The set of adherent points is the **closure** $\overline{A}$.
- $x$ is a **limit point** (accumulation point) of $A$ if
  $B(x,r) \cap (A \setminus \{x\}) \ne \emptyset$ for every $r$. The set of limit
  points is the **derived set** $A'$.
- $x$ is an **isolated point** of $A$ if $x \in A$ and $B(x,r) \cap A = \{x\}$
  for some $r$.
- The **boundary** of $A$ is $\partial A := \overline{A} \setminus \operatorname{int}(A)$.
- $A$ is **dense** in $X$ if $\overline{A} = X$.

**The interior is open, and it is the largest open subset of $A$.** If
$x \in \operatorname{int}(A)$, fix $r$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq A$; the ball
$B(x,r)$ is itself open ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]), so every
$y \in B(x,r)$ has some $s$ with $B(y,s) \subseteq B(x,r) \subseteq A$, which
puts $y$ in $\operatorname{int}(A)$. Hence $B(x,r) \subseteq \operatorname{int}(A)$
and $\operatorname{int}(A)$ is open. It is contained in $A$, since
$x \in B(x,r) \subseteq A$ for an interior point $x$; and if $V \subseteq A$ is
open then every $v \in V$ has a ball inside $V \subseteq A$, so
$V \subseteq \operatorname{int}(A)$.

**Two descriptions of the boundary agree.** $x \in \partial A$ says that every
ball around $x$ meets $A$ and that no ball around $x$ is contained in $A$; the
second half says exactly that every ball around $x$ meets $X \setminus A$. So

$$\partial A = \{\, x \in X : B(x,r) \cap A \ne \emptyset \text{ and } B(x,r) \cap (X \setminus A) \ne \emptyset \text{ for every } r \,\},$$

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

          "quote": "Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

least index instead.",

([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. This is the same convention [[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]]
records for metrics.

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with

strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.",

          "quote": "Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]), let

$f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that

$$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$

$f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of
$X$.

**The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$
and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$
([[def-metric-ball]]), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there
is $\delta > 0$ with

$$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$

Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice.

**Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the
triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same
underlying sets are in play, as in [[def-equivalent-metrics]], the metrics are
always written out.

the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is
a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page
of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full

**Diameter, for nonempty bounded $A$ only.** Suppose $A$ is nonempty and
bounded, and put

$$D(A) := \{\, d(a,b) : a, b \in A \,\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}.$$

Then $D(A)$ is nonempty, since $A$ is, and it is bounded above: fixing $x_0$ and

  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

          "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. This is the same convention [[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]]
records for metrics.

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.",

- The **connected component of $x$** is
  $$C(x) \;:=\; \bigcup \{\, A \subseteq X : x \in A \text{ and } A \text{ is connected} \,\} .$$
  A **component of $X$** is a set of the form $C(x)$ for some $x \in X$.
- The **quasicomponent of $x$** is
  $$Q(x) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, K \subseteq X : x \in K \text{ and } K \text{ is clopen in } X \,\} .$$
  A **quasicomponent of $X$** is a set of the form $Q(x)$.
- $X$ is **totally disconnected** when $C(x) = \{x\}$ for every $x \in X$.

**Both are well posed, and the obligations are discharged here.** The family
united in the definition of $C(x)$ is nonempty, since the singleton $\{x\}$ is

intersected in the definition of $Q(x)$ is nonempty as well, since $X$ itself is
clopen ([[def-topological-space]]), so the intersection is a set; it contains
$x$, every member doing so.

component of a subspace $S \subseteq X$ means a component of the space $S$, and
is written $C_S(y)$ when the space needs naming. The same holds for

- $X$ is **disconnected** when a separation of $X$ exists, and **connected** when

  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). "Disconnected subset" is read the same way.

clopen pieces ([[def-topological-space]]). The **clopen** subsets of $X$ are
those that are both open and closed, and $\varnothing$ and $X$ are always among
them.

Neither admits a separation: a separation requires two nonempty disjoint sets
whose union is the whole space, and neither $\varnothing$ nor a singleton can be
written as such a union. So both are connected under the definition above,
without any special clause. **This is a live convention fork** and the competing
choice is recorded in [[rem-connectedness-conventions]]; nothing on this page
depends on which is taken except the reading of the word "connected" applied to
those two spaces.

**Connectedness is a property of a space, not of an ambient pair.** The condition
above mentions only $(X,\mathcal{T})$. When it is applied to $A \subseteq X$ it
is applied to the space $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$, so it does not change if $A$ is

particular a subset of $A$ is connected as a subset of $A$ exactly when it is
connected as a subset of $X$, by transitivity of the subspace topology

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. $$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le\sup_{K\setminus S}\lVert F\rVert_2\cdot\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. $$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. $$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. $$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le\sup_{K\setminus S}\lVert F\rVert_2\cdot\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

          "quote": "Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.",

$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. $$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le\sup_{K\setminus S}\lVert F\rVert_2\cdot\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\\varepsilon_0=(\\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.\n\n(a) [Steady-current regime] A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\\Omega\\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\\Omega\\times I\\to\\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\\rho:\\Omega\\times I\\to\\mathbb R$, $J:\\Omega\\times I\\to\\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair\n\n$$\\operatorname{div}E=\\rho/\\varepsilon_0,\\qquad \\operatorname{curl}E=0,\\qquad \\operatorname{div}B=0,\\qquad \\operatorname{curl}B=\\mu_0J .$$\n\n(b) [Compact smooth current class] The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\\in C_c^\\infty(\\Omega;\\mathbb R^3)$ with $\\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\\mathbb R^3$. For $B$ of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the magnetic flux of the circuit at time $t$ is the parametrized flux\n$$\\Phi_B(t):=\\int_D\\bigl\\langle B(r(u,w,t),t),\\,r_u(u,w,t)\\times r_v(u,w,t)\\bigr\\rangle\\,du\\,dw$$\nof [[def-em-moving-patch]]; its unit is the weber, $\\mathrm{Wb}=\\mathrm T\\,\\mathrm m^2$.\n\n(c) [Electromotive force] For $E,B$ continuous on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the electromotive force (emf) of the circuit at time $t$ is the vector line integral over the oriented closed path $C(t)$\n$$\\mathrm{emf}(t):=\\oint_{C(t)}\\bigl\\langle E(\\cdot,t)+v(\\cdot,t)\\times B(\\cdot,t),\\,d\\mathbf r\\bigr\\rangle$$\nin the convention of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]], with the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; its unit is the volt, $1\\,\\mathrm V=1\\,\\mathrm{kg}\\,\\mathrm m^2\\,\\mathrm s^{-3}\\mathrm A^{-1}$. Under the framework's Lorentz coupling the integrand is the force per unit charge on a charge moving with the conductor material; the definition itself only names the line integral.\n\n(d) [Scope and exclusions] The fields are assumed of the stated regularity on a neighbourhood of the swept set: circuits passing through a point charge, a curve or surface singularity, or any place where the fields fail to be of that regularity are excluded (no singularity crossings). ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the Lebesgue interface used below ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Let $n\ge3$, let $\Phi$ be the fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ on $\mathbb R^n$ normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]), so that for $z\ne0$
$$\Phi(z)=\frac{|z|^{2-n}}{(n-2)\omega_{n-1}},\qquad \nabla\Phi(z)=-\frac{z}{\omega_{n-1}|z|^n},\qquad |\nabla\Phi(z)|=\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}|z|^{n-1}},$$
let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ be real, measurable and zero $\lambda_n$-almost everywhere outside a closed ball $\overline B_R(0)=\{x:|x|\le R\}$ of finite radius $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$$
be the Newtonian potential ([[def-newtonian-potential]]). Then:

(a) [Representation and differentiability off the far field] for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $|x|>2R$ the integral $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$ is absolutely convergent, the function $Nf$ is differentiable at $x$ with
$$\nabla(Nf)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y),$$
and $x\mapsto\nabla(Nf)(x)$ is continuous on the open set $\{x:|x|>2R\}$;

(b) [Decay bound] for every $x$ with $|x|>2R$,
$$|\nabla(Nf)(x)|\le\frac{2^{n-1}\|f\|_1}{\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1}},\qquad \|f\|_1:=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|f|\,d\lambda_n;$$

(c) [Scope] the hypothesis is compact support together with $L^1$-integrability; no boundedness of $f$ is assumed, and nothing is asserted at points with $|x|\le2R$ (where the kernel singularity may meet the support of $f$).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, $n\ge3$, the fundamental solution $\Phi$ of $-\Delta$ with the displayed form off the origin, and a real $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ vanishing $\lambda_n$-almost everywhere outside $\overline B_R(0)$, $R>0$.

[F1] The fundamental solution is $\Phi(z)=|z|^{2-n}/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ for $z\ne0$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]), and the Newtonian potential is $Nf(x)=\int\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$, defined where the integral is absolutely finite and agreeing with its almost-everywhere class wherever that holds ([[def-newtonian-potential]]).

[F2] Real powers are smooth where defined; the chain, product and algebra rules hold for derivatives, and a map with continuous partial derivatives is totally differentiable with the gradient as derivative ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F3] The Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality and the reverse triangle inequality, and is continuous and nonnegative ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[F4] Differentiation under the integral sign: if $f(x,t)$ is integrable in $x$ for every $t$, differentiable in $t$ for almost every $x$, with measurable $t$-derivative dominated by one integrable $g$ uniformly in $t$, then $t\mapsto\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$ is differentiable with the derivative integrated ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]).

[F5] Dominated convergence: pointwise almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant passes to the integrals ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F6] Continuous functions are Borel measurable, and measurability is preserved by products with measurable functions and by composition with continuous maps; integrals are unchanged by modification on a null set, $|\int h|\le\int|h|$, and the nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $x_0$ with $|x_0|>2R$, choose $0<\delta<|x_0|-2R$, put $U:=B_\delta(x_0)$ and $c:=|x_0|-\delta-R>0$. Since $f$ vanishes almost everywhere on the complement of $\overline B_R$, the function $f_0:=f\,\mathbf 1_{\overline B_R}$ is measurable, integrable, agrees with $f$ almost everywhere and is pointwise zero outside $\overline B_R$; replacing $f$ by $f_0$ changes no integral of the form $\int\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ or $\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ ([F6]), so we may assume $f$ vanishes pointwise off $\overline B_R$. Differentiating the displayed formula of [F1] with the chain and algebra rules gives, for every $z\ne0$, $\nabla\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{(n-2)\omega_{n-1}}(2-n)|z|^{-n}z=-\frac{z}{\omega_{n-1}|z|^n}$ and hence $|\nabla\Phi(z)|=\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}|z|^{n-1}}$ ([F2]). [given, F1, F2, F6]

2.1 For $x\in U$ and $y\in\overline B_R$ the triangle inequality of [F3] gives $$|x-y|\ge|x_0-y|-|x-x_0|\ge|x_0|-R-\delta=c,$$ so with $f$ vanishing off $\overline B_R$ the bounds $$|\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\le\frac{c^{2-n}|f(y)|}{(n-2)\omega_{n-1}},\qquad|\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\le\frac{c^{1-n}|f(y)|}{\omega_{n-1}}$$ hold for all $x\in U$ and $y\in\mathbb R^n$, the exponents being nonpositive because $n\ge3$ and $c>0$ ([F3]). Both majorants are integrable: $f\in L^1$ and the constants are finite. Hence $Nf(x)$ and each integral $\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$ exist absolutely for every $x\in U$, and $g:=c^{1-n}|f|/\omega_{n-1}$ is a single integrable majorant for all partial-derivative integrands on $U$. Moreover each integrand $y\mapsto\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)$ is measurable, being the product of the continuous (off the singularity, which is avoided since $|x-y|\ge c$) kernel with $f$ ([F6]). [step 1.1, F3, F6]

3.1 Fix $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $x\in U$; since $U$ is open there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $x+te_i\in U$ for $|t|<\varepsilon$. Put $J:=(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ and $h(y,t):=\Phi(x+te_i-y)f(y)$ on $\mathbb R^n\times J$. For every $t\in J$ the section $y\mapsto h(y,t)$ is integrable by step 2.1; for every $y$ the map $t\mapsto h(y,t)$ is differentiable on $J$ because $x+te_i-y\ne0$ there, with derivative $\partial_i\Phi(x+te_i-y)f(y)$; this derivative is measurable in $y$ by step 2.1; and it is dominated uniformly on $J$ by the integrable $g$ of step 2.1. The differentiation-under-the-integral-sign theorem [F4] therefore gives that $t\mapsto Nf(x+te_i)$ is differentiable at $t=0$ with derivative $\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)$; by the definition of the partial derivative [F2] this says that $\partial_iNf(x)$ exists and equals that integral. [step 2.1, F2, F4]

4.1 Let $x_m\to x$ be a sequence in $U$. For every $y$ with $f(y)\ne0$ (so $y\in\overline B_R$) the points $x_m-y$ stay at distance at least $c$ from the origin by step 2.1, so $\partial_i\Phi(x_m-y)f(y)\to\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)$ by continuity of the kernel off the origin ([F1], [F2]); the convergence also holds where $f(y)=0$, both sides being $0$. All these integrands are dominated by the integrable $g$ of step 2.1, so dominated convergence [F5] gives $$\int\partial_i\Phi(x_m-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)\to\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y).$$ By step 3.1 the left-hand side is $\partial_iNf(x_m)$, so each partial derivative of $Nf$ is continuous on $U$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, F5]

5.1 By steps 3.1 and 4.1 the function $Nf$ has all first partial derivatives at every point of $U$ and each of them is continuous on $U$; the characterization of total differentiability by continuous partial derivatives [F2] therefore makes $Nf$ differentiable at every $x\in U$, with $\nabla(Nf)(x)$ the vector of the partial derivatives, namely $$\nabla(Nf)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y),$$ the vector integral being absolutely convergent by step 2.1. As $x_0$ with $|x_0|>2R$ was arbitrary, this proves (a) throughout the open far field $\{|x|>2R\}$. [step 4.1, F2]

6.1 For (b), let $|x|>2R$ and let $y$ satisfy $f(y)\ne0$, so $|y|\le R$; the reverse triangle inequality gives $|x-y|\ge|x|-R>|x|/2$ ([F3]), hence by step 1.1 $$|\nabla\Phi(x-y)|=\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}|x-y|^{n-1}}\le\frac{2^{n-1}}{\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1}}.$$ Integrating against $|f|$ and using the estimate of step 5.1 gives $|\nabla(Nf)(x)|\le\int|\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\,d\lambda_n(y)\le\frac{2^{n-1}\|f\|_1}{\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1}}$, which is (b). The argument used only the $L^1$ hypothesis and the a.e. compact support, never boundedness of $f$, and it makes no assertion at points with $|x|\le2R$, where the singularity of $\Phi$ can meet the support of $f$; this is exactly the scope recorded in (c). [step 1.1, step 5.1, F3, F6] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) for the Lebesgue and product-measure interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Let $n\ge2$, let $p\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$ be continuous on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{p\}$ and of class $C^1$ there, with each classical partial derivative $\partial_iu:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{p\}\to\mathbb R$ (extended by $0$ at $p$) again in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$ ([[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]).
Then for every $i=1,\dots,n$, with $T_u\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ the regular distribution of $u$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\partial_i$ the distributional derivative ([[def-distributional-derivative]]),
$$\partial_iT_u=T_{\partial_iu}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n),$$
that is, $\langle\partial_iT_u,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_iu\,\psi\,d\lambda_n$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
The value assigned to $\partial_iu$ at the single point $p$ is immaterial, because a singleton is Lebesgue null ([[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]).
Both hypotheses are used: $u$ must be locally integrable and continuous away from $p$, and each classical partial must be locally integrable; the lemma is asserted for one exceptional point, not for an exceptional set of positive surface measure.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, $n\ge2$, $p\in\mathbb R^n$, and a function $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$ that is continuous on $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{p\}$ and $C^1$ there, with every classical partial $\partial_iu$ (extended by $0$ at $p$) in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$. Fix an index $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a test function $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$.

[F1] For $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$ the regular distribution is $\langle T_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f\varphi\,d\lambda_n$, and the embedding $f\mapsto T_f$ is complex-linear and injective modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

[F2] The distributional derivative is defined by $\langle\partial_iT,\varphi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_i\varphi\rangle$, and the pairing is bilinear with no conjugation ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

[F3] The test space $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ consists of smooth compactly supported functions; each such $\psi$ is bounded and its support is a compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F4] A singleton $\{p\}$ is Lebesgue null, the integral over a measurable null set vanishes, and changing an integrand on a null set does not change its integral or its $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ class ([[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

[F5] Measurability is preserved by sums, scalar multiples, absolute values, pointwise limits, and composition with continuous functions; for bounded measurable multipliers the product is measurable, and $|\int f|\le\int|f|$ with monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F6] $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$ means that $f$ is measurable and $\int_{B(x,r)}|f|\,d\lambda_n<\infty$ for every Euclidean ball ([[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]], [[def-metric-ball]]); the Lebesgue and product-measure interfaces used below carry the declared Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F7] Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^n=\mathbb R^{n-1}\times\mathbb R$, the Borel sigma-algebras satisfy $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{n-1})\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)=\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$, and $\lambda_n$ is the completion of the product measure $\lambda_{n-1}\times\lambda_1$ ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], [[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]).

[F8] Fubini and Tonelli hold for the completed product of two sigma-finite measure spaces: for $G\in L^1(\lambda_n)$ the sections are integrable almost everywhere and the repeated integrals agree with the integral against $\lambda_n$ ([[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]).

[F9] A coordinate permutation of $\mathbb R^n$ is a linear isometry for the Euclidean norm, hence an orthogonal operator, and every orthogonal operator has $|\det T|=1$; for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T$ and $F\in L^1(\lambda_n)$, $\int F\,d\lambda_n=\int F\circ T\,|\det DT|\,d\lambda_n$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], [[cor-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators-form-groups-and-have-unit-determinant-modulus]], [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]).

[F10] Integration by parts holds on a compact interval for functions differentiable at every point whose derivatives are integrable, continuous functions on a compact interval are Darboux integrable, and a bounded Borel Riemann integrable function on a box has equal Riemann and Lebesgue integrals ([[thm-integration-by-parts]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F11] The classical partial derivative $\partial_iu$ is the derivative of the one-variable function obtained by freezing all other coordinates ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Set $F:=\partial_iu\cdot\psi$ and $H:=u\cdot\partial_i\psi$ on $\mathbb R^n$. By [F4] we may replace $u$ and each $\partial_iu$ at the single point $p$ by $0$ without changing any $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ class or integral; with those values, $u$ and $\partial_iu$ are Borel on $\mathbb R^n$, being continuous on the open set $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{p\}$ with one point added ([F5]). Hence $F$ and $H$ are Borel, and since $\psi$ is bounded and compactly supported ([F3]), $|F|\le\|\psi\|_\infty|\partial_iu|$ and $|H|\le\|\partial_i\psi\|_\infty|u|$ show $F,H\in L^1(\lambda_n)$ ([F5], [F6]). [given, F3, F4, F5, F6]

2.1 Let $\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be the coordinate permutation moving the $i$-th coordinate to the last position, $\pi(x)=(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\dots,x_n,x_i)$. Then $\|\pi(x)\|^2=\sum_jx_j^2=\|x\|^2$, so $\pi$ is a linear isometry, hence an orthogonal operator with $|\det D\pi|=|\det\pi|=1$ ([F9]); $\pi$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ onto itself. Applying the change-of-variables identity of [F9] to $F$ and to $H$, and using $|\det D\pi|=1$, gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^n}F\,d\lambda_n=\int_{\mathbb R^n}F\circ\pi\,d\lambda_n,\qquad\int_{\mathbb R^n}H\,d\lambda_n=\int_{\mathbb R^n}H\circ\pi\,d\lambda_n.$$ The compositions $F\circ\pi$ and $H\circ\pi$ are Borel and in $L^1(\lambda_n)$ because $\int|F\circ\pi|\,d\lambda_n=\int|F|\,d\lambda_n<\infty$ and likewise for $H$. [step 1.1, F5, F9]

3.1 Identify $\mathbb R^n$ with $\mathbb R^{n-1}\times\mathbb R$ by the standard ordering, so that a point with last coordinate $t$ and remaining coordinates $y$ is written $(y,t)$; the permutation of step 2.1 then satisfies $\pi(x)=(y(x),x_i)$ where $y(x)$ lists the coordinates other than the $i$-th. Define $G(y,t):=F(x(y,t))$ and $K(y,t):=H(x(y,t))$, where $x(y,t)\in\mathbb R^n$ is the point with $i$-th coordinate $t$ and remaining coordinates $y$. Then $G=F\circ\pi$ and $K=H\circ\pi$ under the identification, so step 2.1 reads $\int F\,d\lambda_n=\int G\,d\lambda_n$ and $\int H\,d\lambda_n=\int K\,d\lambda_n$; by [F7] and [F8] these equal the repeated integrals $\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\bigl(\int_{\mathbb R}G(y,t)\,dt\bigr)dy$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\bigl(\int_{\mathbb R}K(y,t)\,dt\bigr)dy$, the inner sections being integrable for almost every $y$. [step 2.1, F7, F8]

4.1 Fix $y\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ such that the line $L_y=\{x(y,t):t\in\mathbb R\}$ does not pass through $p$; the exceptional set of such $y$ is the single point $y^\ast$ listing the coordinates of $p$ other than $p_i$, which is a degenerate box and hence $\lambda_{n-1}$-null ([F4]). For such $y$, the map $t\mapsto u(x(y,t))$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R$ with derivative $t\mapsto\partial_iu(x(y,t))$ ([F11]), and $t\mapsto\psi(x(y,t))$ is smooth with compact support ([F3]). Choose $a<b$ with the support of $t\mapsto\psi(x(y,t))$ contained in $(a,b)$. Then $v(t):=u(x(y,t))\,\psi(x(y,t))$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ with continuous derivative $v'=\partial_iu\,\psi+u\,\partial_i\psi$ there, so $v'$ is integrable in the Darboux sense ([F10]); applying integration by parts of [F10] to $u(x(\cdot,y))$ and $\psi(x(\cdot,y))$ on $[a,b]$ and using that both boundary terms vanish gives $$\int_{\mathbb R}G(y,t)\,dt=-\int_{\mathbb R}K(y,t)\,dt,$$ where the Darboux integrals have been replaced by the equal Lebesgue integrals of the continuous compactly supported integrands ([F10]). [step 3.1, F3, F4, F10, F11]

5.1 The equality of step 4.1 holds for every $y$ outside the null set $\{y^\ast\}$ ([F4]), hence almost everywhere, and the section functions are integrable there by step 3.1. Integrating the identity over $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and using the linearity of the integral gives $\int F\,d\lambda_n=\int G\,d\lambda_n=-\int K\,d\lambda_n=-\int H\,d\lambda_n$. Therefore, by [F1] and [F2], $$\langle\partial_iT_u,\psi\rangle=-\langle T_u,\partial_i\psi\rangle=-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\partial_i\psi\,d\lambda_n=-\int_{\mathbb R^n}H\,d\lambda_n=\int_{\mathbb R^n}F\,d\lambda_n=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_iu\,\psi\,d\lambda_n=\langle T_{\partial_iu},\psi\rangle.$$ Since $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ was arbitrary, $\partial_iT_u=T_{\partial_iu}$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$, as claimed. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, F5] ∎
