## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces used below ([[def-countable-choice]]).
On $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) let $0<\varepsilon<R$ and put
$$B_R:=\{x:|x|<R\},\qquad \overline B_R:=\{x:|x|\le R\},\qquad A_{\varepsilon,R}:=\{x:\varepsilon<|x|<R\},\qquad S_r:=\{x:|x|=r\}.$$
Then:

(a) [Domains] $B_R$ and $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ are bounded $C^1$ domains in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; their boundaries are $S_R$, respectively $S_\varepsilon\cup S_R$, and the corresponding outward unit normals are
$$\nu(x)=\frac{x}{|x|}\ \ (x\in S_R),\qquad \nu(x)=-\frac{x}{|x|}\ \ (x\in S_\varepsilon,\ \text{boundary of }A_{\varepsilon,R});$$

(b) [Spheres] each $S_r$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ (indeed $C^\infty$) hypersurface in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] with two-sided unit normals $\pm x/|x|$, and the boundary components $S_\varepsilon,S_R$, each subdivided into six compact signed-maximal-coordinate graph faces $F_{r,k,\sigma}:=\{x\in S_r:\sigma x_k\ge |x_j|\text{ for all }j\}$ ($k=1,2,3$, $\sigma=\pm1$), with the compact edge set consisting of their seams $\sigma x_k=|x_j|$ for $j\ne k$, give a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ in the sense of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]];

(c) [Consequences used downstream] the divergence theorem and Green's first identity of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] and [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] apply on $B_R$ and on $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ with the outward normals of (a), and $S_r$ carries a finite Borel surface measure with the standard graph charts.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, reals $0<\varepsilon<R$, the sets $B_R,\overline B_R,A_{\varepsilon,R},S_r$ above, and the Euclidean norm $N(x)=|x|$ on $\mathbb R^3$.

[F1] The Euclidean norm is continuous, and a map between metric spaces is continuous exactly when preimages of open sets are open ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[thm-continuity-preimage-characterisation]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F2] The interior, closure, and boundary of a subset of a metric space are the sets determined by its open balls; $B_R$ is the open ball of radius $R$ and $\overline B_R$ its closed ball ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[F3] Real powers are smooth where defined, with the chain, product and algebra rules for derivatives and the converse characterization of differentiable maps by continuous partial derivatives ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F4] A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function with the set locally the subgraph; the outward normal in these coordinates is $\nu=(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, transported by the orthogonal coordinate map, and $|\cdot|$ enters through the Euclidean inner product ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F5] A subset of $\mathbb R^3$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[F6] The chart surface integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface is a finite Borel measure independent of charts and partitions; in graph coordinates its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, and outward unit normals agree on chart overlaps ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]).

[F7] A finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a bounded open set consists of compact faces covering its boundary, each inside a regular $C^1$ patch and carrying the actual outward normal off the compact edge set $E$, with $S_j\cap E$ of surface measure zero, and $E$ containing the relative face boundaries and all overlaps ([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]).

[F8] For a bounded Borel function on a compact parameter rectangle the iterated planar integral of its indicator vanishes when almost every section is a null set, and coordinate hyperplanes and degenerate boxes are Lebesgue null; the Borel product sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^2$ is the Euclidean one and the product measure agrees with $\lambda_2$ there ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]], [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]).

[F9] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous and the integral of an indicator is the measure of the set ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F10] On a bounded $C^1$ domain the divergence theorem holds for $C^1$ fields up to the closure and Green's first identity holds for real $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, $v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, both with the outward normal on each boundary component ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]], [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Because $N$ is continuous and $(0,R)$ and $(\varepsilon,R)$ are open, $B_R=N^{-1}\bigl((-\infty,R)\bigr)$ and $A_{\varepsilon,R}=N^{-1}\bigl((\varepsilon,R)\bigr)$ are open, nonempty (they contain the origin, respectively a point of norm $(\varepsilon+R)/2$) and bounded, being contained in the closed ball of radius $R$ ([F1], [F2]). If $|x|>R$, continuity of $N$ gives a ball about $x$ on which $|y|>R$, so no point outside $\overline B_R$ is a limit of points of $B_R$; if $|x|=R$, the points $\bigl(1-1/n\bigr)x$ lie in $B_R$ and converge to $x$; hence the closure of $B_R$ is $\overline B_R$ and, since $B_R$ is open, its boundary is $S_R$ ([F1], [F2]). The same argument with $N^{-1}\bigl((\varepsilon,R)\bigr)$, together with the identification of its closure with $\{x:\varepsilon\le|x|\le R\}$, gives that the boundary of $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ is $S_\varepsilon\cup S_R$, and both sets have nonempty interior equal to themselves because they are open. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Fix $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $\sigma\in\{\pm1\}$, let $z=\sigma x_k$ and let $y$ collect the two remaining coordinates in a fixed order; the map $x\mapsto(y,z)$ is a rigid change of coordinates (a permutation with one sign change). Put $U_{k,\sigma}:=\{x:\sigma x_k>R/(2\sqrt 3)\}$ and $h(y):=\sqrt{R^2-|y|^2}$, which is $C^\infty$ on the open set $|y|<R$ with $Dh(y)=-y/h(y)$ ([F3]). On $U_{k,\sigma}\cap\{|y|<R\}$ one has $z>0$ and $$|x|^2<R^2\iff z^2<R^2-|y|^2\iff z<h(y),$$ so $S_R\cap U_{k,\sigma}$ is the graph $z=h(y)$ over the open parameter set $|y|<R$ and $B_R\cap U_{k,\sigma}\cap\{|y|<R\}$ is its subgraph; this is the local presentation required of a bounded $C^1$ domain ([F4]). The graph normal of [F4] is $$\frac{(-Dh(y),1)}{\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}}=\frac{(y,h(y))}{R},$$ because $-Dh=y/h$ and $1+|Dh|^2=R^2/h^2$; transporting back through the rigid coordinate map gives $\nu(x)=x/R=x/|x|$ on $S_R$. The six patches cover the exterior $\{|x|\ge R\}$: for $x\ne0$ some coordinate satisfies $|x_k|\ge|x|/\sqrt3$, so with $\sigma:=\operatorname{sign}(x_k)$ one has $\sigma x_k=|x_k|\ge R/\sqrt3>R/(2\sqrt3)$ whenever $|x|\ge R$, and in particular the sphere $S_R$ is covered by the six graph patches. [step 1.1, F3, F4]

3.1 Fix again $k,\sigma$ and put $h_\varepsilon(y)=\sqrt{\varepsilon^2-|y|^2}$ on $|y|<\varepsilon$. In the coordinates $(y,z)$ of step 2.1 the complement of the closed ball satisfies $z>h_\varepsilon(y)$ inside the patch $\sigma x_k>\varepsilon/(2\sqrt3)$ with $|y|<\varepsilon$, and the second rigid change $w=-z$ turns this into the subgraph $w<-h_\varepsilon(y)$ of the smooth function $g(y):=-h_\varepsilon(y)$ with $Dg(y)=y/h_\varepsilon(y)$ ([F3]). The graph normal of [F4] in the $(y,w)$ coordinates is $$\frac{(-Dg(y),1)}{\sqrt{1+|Dg(y)|^2}}=\frac{(-y,h_\varepsilon(y))}{\varepsilon},$$ and transporting back through $w=-\sigma x_k$ gives $\nu(x)=-x/\varepsilon=-x/|x|$ on $S_\varepsilon$. Near a point of $S_\varepsilon$ the ball $B_R$ occupies a full neighborhood because $|x|=\varepsilon<R$, so $A_{\varepsilon,R}=B_R\setminus\overline B_\varepsilon$ is locally exactly the subgraph just described, while near a point of $S_R$ it is locally the subgraph of $h$ from step 2.1 with normal $x/|x|$. Hence $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain with boundary $S_\varepsilon\cup S_R$ and the stated outward normals ([F4]). [step 2.1, F3, F4]

4.1 Each $S_r$ is closed, being the preimage of the closed set $\{r\}$ under the continuous norm, and bounded, hence compact ([F1], [F5]). The restrictions of the six maps $y\mapsto(y,h_r(y))$ from steps 2.1 and 3.1, composed with the inverse rigid coordinate maps, are regular injective $C^\infty$ parametrizations of the open patches $S_r\cap U_{k,\sigma}$ with $C^\infty$ transitions (every transition is the identity in the shared $y$-coordinates, or a smooth composition of two such graph maps) ([F3]). Therefore each $S_r$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in the sense of [F6], and the two graph normal computations of steps 2.1 and 3.1 exhibit both unit normals $\pm x/|x|$: the positive sign from the ball chart and the negative sign from the complement chart, continuously across overlaps. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F3, F5, F6]

5.1 For $r=\varepsilon,R$ define the twelve compact faces $F_{r,k,\sigma}=\{x\in S_r:\sigma x_k\ge|x_j|\ \text{for all }j\}$, $k=1,2,3$, $\sigma=\pm1$. They cover $S_r$: choose $k$ with $|x_k|=\max_j|x_j|$; then $x_k\ne0$ and $\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(x_k)$ gives $\sigma x_k\ge|x_j|$ for all $j$. Each $F_{r,k,\sigma}$ is closed in the compact $S_r$, hence compact, and on it $\sigma x_k\ge r/\sqrt3>r/(2\sqrt3)$, so it is contained in the single regular patch $U_{k,\sigma}$ of steps 2.1-3.1 with parameter set contained in the compact set $\{|y|\le r\sqrt{2/3}\}\subset\{|y|<r\}$ ([F5]). [step 4.1, F5]

6.1 Let $E$ be the union over $r=\varepsilon,R$ of the seams $\{x\in S_r:\ \sigma x_k=|x_j|\ \text{for some }j\ne k,\ \sigma=\pm1\}$, a finite union of closed subsets of the compact spheres, hence compact. Every relative boundary point of a face $F_{r,k,\sigma}$ has $\sigma x_k=|x_j|$ for some $j$, and every overlap $F_{r,k,\sigma}\cap F_{r,k',\sigma'}$ with $(k,\sigma)\ne(k',\sigma')$ lies in such a seam, so $E$ contains all relative face boundaries and all overlaps ([F7]). To see that $S_r\cap E$ has zero surface measure in each face, work in the chart $z=\sigma x_k=h_r(y)$ of $F_{r,k,\sigma}$: a seam condition $|x_j|=\sigma x_k$ reads $|y_j|=h_r(y)$, that is $y_j^2=\bigl(r^2-y_\ell^2\bigr)/2$ for the remaining coordinate $y_\ell$, so the parameter set of the seam inside the face is contained in the union of the two graphs $y_j=\pm\sqrt{(r^2-y_\ell^2)/2}$ over the interval where the radicand is nonnegative. For each fixed $y_\ell$ such a graph meets the vertical line in at most two points, a planar degenerate box and hence a $\lambda_1$-null set ([F8]); Tonelli's theorem therefore gives the planar Lebesgue measure of the seam parameter set as the integral of zero section measures, namely zero ([F8]). The graph density $\sqrt{1+|Dh_r|^2}=r/h_r$ is continuous and bounded on the compact parameter set $\{|y|\le r\sqrt{2/3}\}$, so integrating it against the indicator of a planar null set gives zero ([F9]); by the chart-independence of the surface measure this says exactly that $S_j\cap E$ has zero surface measure in each face, as required by [F7]. [step 5.1, F6, F7, F8, F9]

7.1 Statement (a) is steps 2.1 and 3.1; statement (b) is steps 4.1, 5.1 and 6.1, the twelve compact faces with their null compact seam set satisfying exactly the requirements of [F7] for the annulus $A_{\varepsilon,R}$, whose exposed faces carry the outward normals computed in steps 2.1 and 3.1 off $E$. Finally, (c): the divergence theorem and Green's first identity of [F10] apply on $B_R$ and on $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ because both are bounded $C^1$ domains with the outward normals of (a), and $S_r$ carries a finite Borel surface measure with the standard graph charts by [F6]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, F6, F7, F10] ∎

## Definition

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement
$$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$
pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$.

(d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps.

(e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

(f) [Conventions and scope] The regime is imposed in the one inertial frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; no claim is made that time independence survives a change of inertial description, and where a frame change is used the transformed fields must be rechecked. The static regime is an adopted idealization, not a dynamical stability theorem: static charged matter requires external support or an adopted equilibrium model. No equation is asserted here for singular sources beyond the dictionary of (e), and no empirical claim is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ with $I$ a nonempty open interval and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ nonempty open, jointly $C^1$ fields $E,B$ and $C^1$ sources $(\rho,J)$ as in [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell equations, and for clause (e) locally integrable time-independent fields and densities on $\Omega\times I$ together with $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$.

[F1] The laboratory region, its fixed-time slices, its fields and its units are those of the primitives: the chart restriction $x(U)=\{(ct,y)\}$, the fixed-time readings, and the identification $U\cong I\times\Omega$ ([[def-em-lab-geometry]]); the SI constants with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$ and the units of $E,B,\rho,J$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]]); a $C^k$ field on $\Omega\times I$ with its polar/axial conventions and no asserted values at singular support ([[def-em-fields]]); smooth source fields $(\rho,J)$ and their branches ([[def-em-sources]]).

[F2] The smooth Maxwell branch asserts $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ pointwise for jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives continuous, and the weak branch asserts the same four pairings against $C_c^\infty(U)$ tests for locally integrable fields ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]).

[F3] The weak solution predicate of the singular-source formulation is: for locally integrable $E,B$ and a source pair with volume part $(\rho_v,J_v)$ and singular part of point or stationary-sheet type, $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations when the four distributional pairings $\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$ vanish for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$; point sources with $C^1$ trajectory $z$ proper into $U$ have $\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle=q\int\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle=q\int z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ ([[def-em-weak-sources]](b),(e)).

[F4] Divergence and curl are the coordinate expressions of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] evaluated at fixed time, and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F5] A real function on an interval with everywhere-vanishing derivative is constant ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]), and for a differentiable function with integrable derivative on $[a,b]$, $\int_a^bG'=G(b)-G(a)$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

[F6] Locally integrable functions are identified with their regular distributions, $\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$, and test functions are smooth with compact support in $U$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).

[F7] Under Countable Choice every measurable function has a Borel representative modulo null sets, the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^4$ is the product of those of $\mathbb R^3$ and $\mathbb R$, and the corresponding product measure agrees with Lebesgue measure on Borel sets; Fubini applies to integrable functions on such products, and a continuous compactly supported one-variable integrand has equal Riemann and Lebesgue integrals ([[thm-completion-measurable-functions-have-base-measurable-representatives]], [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]], [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F8] The spatial point source $\delta_{x_0}$ pairs a compactly supported smooth test $\eta$ as $\eta\mapsto\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Clause (c): in the static regime $\partial_tE=\partial_tB=0$; substituting into the two curl equations of the smooth branch of [F2] leaves $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ at every point and every fixed time, while the two divergence equations are unchanged, giving exactly the displayed four equations; the operators are those of [F4] applied to the fixed-time fields of [F1]. In the pure electrostatic regime $B=0$ and $J=0$, so $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ are identities and the reduction is the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$. [given, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 Clause (d): in the static regime each of $E,B,\rho,J$ has vanishing partial $t$-derivative at every point of $\Omega\times I$. For fixed $y$ and two times $t_1<t_2$ in $I$, the mean value theorem [F5] applied to $t\mapsto F(y,t)$ on $[t_1,t_2]$ gives $F(y,t_2)-F(y,t_1)=0$, so $F(y,t)$ depends only on $y$; writing $F_0(y):=F(y,t_0)$ for a fixed $t_0\in I$ we get $F=F_0\circ\pi$ with $\pi(y,t):=y$, and the four reduced equations of clause (c), which are pointwise conditions at each fixed time [F4], are therefore equations between the spatial maps $E_0,B_0,\rho_0,J_0$. The same reading is available for the locally integrable time-independent objects of clause (e), for which time independence is an explicit hypothesis rather than a consequence of differentiability. [step 1.1, F4, F5]

3.1 Clause (e), spatial pairings as time integrals: let the time-independent locally integrable data be read as spatial maps $E_0,B_0,\rho_0,J_0$ by the fixed-time reading of step 2.1, and fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$. For a spatial operator expression $S$ that is linear in the data (for instance $S=\operatorname{div}E_0-\rho_0/\varepsilon_0$), choosing Borel representatives of the coefficients [F7] and moving every distributional spatial derivative onto the test gives the pairing identity $$\langle S_U,\psi\rangle=\int_I\langle S_\Omega,\psi(\cdot,t)\rangle_\Omega\,dt,$$ where $S_U$ denotes the distributional expression on $U$ evaluated with distributional derivatives on $U$ and $S_\Omega$ the same expression on $\Omega$ evaluated with distributional spatial derivatives; in the displayed instance both sides equal the same absolutely convergent iterated integrals, computed for $S_\Omega$ by moving the spatial derivative onto the test, $$-\int_I\int_\Omega E_0\cdot\nabla_y\psi\,d\lambda_3\,dt-\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_I\int_\Omega\rho_0\psi\,d\lambda_3\,dt,$$ products of locally integrable coefficients with derivatives of the compactly supported test being integrable by Fubini [F7], and for data that are additionally $C^1$ the inner pairing agrees with the classical integral $\int_\Omega(\operatorname{div}E_0-\rho_0/\varepsilon_0)\psi(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3$ ([F4]); each $t$-slice $\psi(\cdot,t)$ is smooth with compact support in $\Omega$ because the section at $t$ of the compact support of $\psi$ is compact and lies in $\Omega$ ([F6]). The same computation applies to $\operatorname{div}B$, $\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J$. [step 2.1, F4, F6, F7]

4.1 Clause (e), vanishing of the time derivatives: let $F$ be a time-independent locally integrable function on $U$ (one component of $E$ or $B$, or $\rho$). Choosing a Borel representative of $F$ [F7] and using the product structure and the fixed-time reading of step 3.1, $$-\langle T_F,\partial_t\psi\rangle=\int_U F(y)\,\partial_t\psi(y,t)\,d\lambda_4=\int_\Omega F(y)\Bigl(\int_I\partial_t\psi(y,t)\,dt\Bigr)d\lambda_3(y)=0,$$ because for each $y$ the function $t\mapsto\psi(y,t)$ is smooth with compact support in $I$, so its integral of derivative vanishes by the fundamental theorem [F5] (the inner integral is a Lebesgue integral of a continuous compactly supported integrand, equal to its Riemann value [F7]); the iterated integral is absolutely convergent since $\psi$ has compact support and $F$ is locally integrable on the bounded region of the support. By [F6] this says $\partial_tT_F=0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$, so the two time-dependent terms of the weak predicate [F3] vanish identically for time-independent fields. [step 3.1, F5, F6, F7]

5.1 Clause (e), the equivalence: if the four spatial equations hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, then for every $t\in I$ the test $\psi(\cdot,t)$ of step 3.1 gives $\langle S_\Omega,\psi(\cdot,t)\rangle_\Omega=0$, hence the integral of step 3.1 vanishes; together with the vanishing time-derivative pairings of step 4.1 this makes all four weak pairings of [F3] vanish, so the weak equations hold. Conversely, if the four weak pairings of [F3] vanish, choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, $\chi\in C_c^\infty(I)$ with $\int_I\chi=1$ and test with $\psi(y,t)=\eta(y)\chi(t)$, which lies in $C_c^\infty(U)$; by steps 3.1 and 4.1, $0=\int_I\chi(t)\langle S_\Omega,\eta\rangle_\Omega\,dt=\langle S_\Omega,\eta\rangle_\Omega$, so each spatial equation holds in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ since $\eta$ was arbitrary. This is the asserted if-and-only-if, and it uses no product of distributions: all pairings are against a single test function. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F3, F5, F6]

6.1 Clause (e), stationary point charge: take $I_0:=I$, the constant $C^1$ trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$ with $x_0\in\Omega$, and $q\in\mathbb R$. Its graph is $\{x_0\}\times I$, and the graph map is proper into $U=I\times\Omega$ because the preimage of a compact subset of $U$ is the corresponding compact closed subset of $I$; the source of [F3] is then $\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and $\langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle=q\int_Iz'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt=0$. For each fixed time the spatial reading is the point source pairing a compactly supported smooth spatial test $\eta$ as $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$, which is exactly the spatial point source of [F8]; the time integral above is the pairing of $q\,\delta_{x_0}$ against the compactly supported function $t\mapsto\psi(x_0,t)$ under the identification of [F6]. [step 5.1, F3, F6, F8]

7.1 Clauses (a) and (b) are the definitions of the static and pure electrostatic regimes; clause (c) is step 1.1, clause (d) is step 2.1, clause (e) is steps 3.1-6.1, and clause (f) records that the conditions were imposed in the one frame, that no stability, support, boost or singular-source equation beyond the dictionary of (e), and no empirical claim, is asserted. The verification used only the cited smooth branch, the definitions of the primitives, and the measure/distribution interfaces; no equation of motion and no empirical premise entered. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎

      locator: Sections 3.3.2-3.3.3 printed pp. 35-36 (Poisson's equation (3.3.9) and the static Green's function). Read in the stamped full text.
---

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set that is star-shaped with respect to some $a\in\Omega$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $E:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ in the spatial vector-field sense of [[def-em-fields]] ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and let $\rho:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous — the fixed-time reading, in the sense of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], of a pure electrostatic regime with the units and constant $\varepsilon_0>0$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]] ([[def-em-sources]]).
Suppose the reduced smooth-branch equations hold pointwise on $\Omega$:
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$
with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]].
Then:

(a) [Closed field and potential] $-E$ is closed in the sense of [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]] — equivalently $\operatorname{curl}(-E)=0$ ([[cor-curl-vanishes-exactly-when-a-field-is-closed]]) — and the function
$$\varphi(x):=-\int_0^1E\bigl(a+s(x-a)\bigr)\cdot(x-a)\,ds$$
(the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is a $C^2$ function on $\Omega$ with
$$\nabla\varphi=-E\qquad\text{on }\Omega$$
([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]] applied to the closed $C^1$ field $-E$); continuity of the integrand and its first parameter derivatives and the proved identity $\nabla\varphi=-E$ with $E\in C^1$ give the stated regularity.

(b) [Poisson equation] with $\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}\nabla\varphi$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]],
$$-\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{pointwise on }\Omega.$$

(c) [Uniqueness up to constants] if $\psi\in C^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $\nabla\psi=-E$ on $\Omega$, then $\psi-\varphi$ is constant on $\Omega$; in particular $\varphi$ is uniquely determined by $\nabla\varphi=-E$ and one prescribed value. Star-shapedness gives path-connectedness through the centre $a$, so the constant is the same on all of $\Omega$ ([[cor-potentials-differ-by-a-componentwise-constant]], [[def-piecewise-c1-path-connected-conservative-and-path-independent]]).

No normalisation of $\varphi$ at infinity, and no boundary condition, is asserted on a general star-shaped $\Omega$; the additive constant remains free.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A star-shaped open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with centre $a\in\Omega$, a $C^1$ field $E:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, a continuous $\rho:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$, the fixed-time reading of a pure electrostatic regime in which $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ hold pointwise.

[F1] The fixed-time reading of a pure electrostatic regime, the field conventions and the source conventions are those of the primitives: in particular $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ and $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ are the reduced smooth-branch equations, and the objects carry no time dependence ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F2] A field is closed exactly when its curl vanishes identically on $\mathbb R^3$; closedness is the symmetry system $\partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j$ ([[cor-curl-vanishes-exactly-when-a-field-is-closed]], [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]]).

[F3] Every closed $C^1$ field on an open star-shaped $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is exact, with the $C^2$ potential $\phi(x)=\int_0^1\langle F(a+t(x-a)),x-a\rangle\,dt$ satisfying $\nabla\phi=F$ ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]]).

[F4] The Laplacian is $\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}\nabla\varphi$, and divergence and curl are linear in the field with the partial-derivative convention of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F5] If two $C^1$ functions have the same gradient, their difference is constant on each piecewise-$C^1$ path component; a star-shaped set is connected through its centre by the $C^1$ segments $s\mapsto a+s(x-a)$, $s\in[0,1]$ ([[cor-potentials-differ-by-a-componentwise-constant]], [[def-piecewise-c1-path-connected-conservative-and-path-independent]], [[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The field $F:=-E$ is $C^1$ on the open set $\Omega$, being the componentwise negative of the $C^1$ field $E$ ([F1], [F4]), and it is closed: by [F2] closedness is equivalent to the vanishing of the curl, and $\operatorname{curl}F=-\operatorname{curl}E=0$ by linearity of the curl in the field and the reduced equation $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ ([F2], [F4]). [given, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 The Poincaré lemma [F3] applies to the closed $C^1$ field $F=-E$ on the star-shaped open set $\Omega$ with centre $a$, and yields the $C^2$ function $$\varphi(x)=\int_0^1\bigl\langle F(a+s(x-a)),x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds=-\int_0^1E\bigl(a+s(x-a)\bigr)\cdot(x-a)\,ds$$ with $\nabla\varphi=F=-E$ on $\Omega$, the inner product being the Euclidean one; this is clause (a). [step 1.1, F3]

3.1 For clause (b), the Laplacian of the $C^2$ potential is $\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}\nabla\varphi$ ([F4]); substituting $\nabla\varphi=-E$ from step 2.1 and using the linearity of the divergence in the field gives $\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}(-E)=-\operatorname{div}E$, so $-\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ by the reduced divergence equation ([F1], [F4]). [step 2.1, F1, F4]

3.2 For clause (c), let $\psi\in C^2(\Omega)$ satisfy $\nabla\psi=-E$. Then $\nabla(\psi-\varphi)=\nabla\psi-\nabla\varphi=0$ on $\Omega$, because both gradients equal $-E$ and differentiation is linear ([F4]); by [F5] the difference $\psi-\varphi$ is constant on every piecewise-$C^1$ path component of $\Omega$. Every $x\in\Omega$ is joined to the centre $a$ by the segment $s\mapsto a+s(x-a)$, $s\in[0,1]$, which is $C^1$, lies in $\Omega$ by star-shapedness and has constant value $a$ at $s=0$; hence all points lie in the single path component containing $a$ ([F5]), and $\psi-\varphi$ is constant on $\Omega$. Fixing the value of $\varphi$ at one point therefore determines $\varphi$ uniquely. [step 2.1, F4, F5]

4.1 Clauses (a), (b) and (c) are steps 2.1, 3.1 and 3.2. The argument used only the pointwise reduced equations, the $C^1$ regularity of the field, continuity of $\rho$, star-shapedness of $\Omega$ and the cited mathematical suppliers; no boundary condition, no normalisation at infinity, no uniqueness of the field equations, no existence of a physical equilibrium and no empirical assertion entered, which is exactly the scope stated. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, F1, F5] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$.
Let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$; then $\omega_2=4\pi$ and
$$\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi|z|}\qquad(z\ne0)$$
([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).
Let $Nf$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-newtonian-potential]].

(a) [Smooth compact sources] Let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ with compact support contained in $\overline B_R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), put $\varphi:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E:=-\nabla\varphi$.
Then $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]]), and pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$
$$-\Delta\varphi=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0$$
with the operators of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]].
Moreover, with $Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Coulomb integral representation holds, and its far-field bound holds for $|x|>2R$,
$$E(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^3}\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad |E(x)|\le\frac{\| \rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}\quad(|x|>2R),$$
and for $|x|>\max(2R,1)$ the potential obeys the decay bound $|\varphi(x)|\le\bigl(|Q|/(4\pi)+R\|\rho\|_1/\pi\bigr)/(\varepsilon_0|x|)$ ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]).
The pair $(E,0,\rho,0)$ therefore realises the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with source $\rho$, and $E$ is the field of the localised Newtonian potential.

(b) [Uniqueness with vanishing at infinity] If $\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $-\Delta\psi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lim_{|x|\to\infty}\psi(x)=0$, then $\psi=\varphi$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]).
In particular, among $C^2$ solutions of the Poisson equation of a compactly supported $C^1$ source decaying at infinity, the localised Newtonian potential is the unique one.

(c) [Compactly supported $L^1$ sources] If instead $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is real, measurable and compactly supported, then $N\rho$ is finite $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere, belongs to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, is $C^\infty$ and harmonic off the support of $\rho$, and its regular distribution satisfies
$$-\Delta T_{\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho}=T_{\rho/\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]], scaled by $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$; [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(d) [Point charge] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and define, with arbitrary values at $x_0$,
$$\varphi_q(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|},\qquad E_q(x):=\frac{q\,(x-x_0)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^3}\qquad(x\ne x_0).$$
Then $\varphi_q\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $E_q$ is locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off $x_0$, $E_q=-\nabla\varphi_q$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{x_0\}$, and, with $T_{\varphi_q}$ the regular distribution of $\varphi_q$ and $\operatorname{div}E_q:=\sum_i\partial_iT_{E_{q,i}}$, $\operatorname{curl}E_q:=(\partial_2T_{E_{q,3}}-\partial_3T_{E_{q,2}},\ \partial_3T_{E_{q,1}}-\partial_1T_{E_{q,3}},\ \partial_1T_{E_{q,2}}-\partial_2T_{E_{q,1}})$,
$$-\Delta T_{\varphi_q}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E_q=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E_q=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]] for the first identity, [[lem-em-distributional-gradient-smooth-off-a-point]] for the passage from the potential to the field, [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).
The distribution $q\delta_{x_0}$ is the fixed-time reading of the stationary point charge of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with charge parameter $q$ and constant trajectory $z\equiv x_0$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); so the pair $(E_q,0)$ satisfies the distributional pure electrostatic equations with that point source.
This is an idealised point-source model: no claim of uniqueness for the point source, no self-force and no statement about the field at $x_0$ itself is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, the $n=3$ kernel $\Phi$ with $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ off the origin and $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$, the SI constant $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$, and the compactly supported data and point data of clauses (a)-(d).

[F1] The $n=3$ kernel is $\Phi(z)=|z|^{-1}/\omega_2$ with $\omega_2=4\pi$, since the chart/polar sphere measure satisfies $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$ and the unit ball in dimension three has volume $4\pi/3$; the kernel is locally integrable, smooth off the pole and harmonic there, and $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$, with the same identity for every translate ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]], [[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]]).

[F2] The Newtonian potential is $Nf(x)=\int\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$, defined where the integral is absolutely finite; for continuous compactly supported $f$ with finite global Hölder seminorm of exponent $\alpha\in(0,1)$ it is $C^2$ on all of $\mathbb R^3$ with $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise; for compactly supported $f\in L^1$ it is finite almost everywhere, locally integrable, $C^\infty$ and harmonic off the support, and satisfies $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ in $\mathcal D'$ ([[def-newtonian-potential]], [[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]], [[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]).

[F3] On the far field the gradient representation and the decay of the potential hold: for compactly supported $L^1$ data $f$ and $|x|>2R$ one has $\nabla(Nf)(x)=\int\nabla\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$, $|\nabla(Nf)(x)|\le2^{n-1}\|f\|_1/(\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1})$, and for $n=3$, $|Nf(x)-Q/(4\pi|x|)|\le R\|f\|_1/(\pi|x|^2)$ whenever $f$ vanishes off the open ball $B_R$, with $Q=\int f$ and $f$ real ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]).

[F4] The Laplacian and the divergence and curl are the classical operators of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]; the curl of a gradient of a $C^2$ function vanishes, divergence is linear in the field with coordinate partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the algebra and chain rules for derivatives apply to real powers ([[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F5] A $C^1$ compactly supported function on $\mathbb R^3$ is bounded and Lipschitz: the continuous gradient attains its maximum on the compact support, and the mean value theorem bounds increments; consequently it has finite global $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm for every $\alpha\in(0,1]$ ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F6] Differentiation under the integral sign and $C^1$ change of variables for $L^1$ functions are available: a continuously differentiable family of integrable sections with one integrable majorant may be differentiated under the integral, and integrals are invariant under translations and reflections of bounded measurable sets ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]], [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]).

[F7] Locally integrable functions are identified with their regular distributions; distributional derivatives satisfy $\langle\partial^\alpha T,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle T,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$, commute with one another and with constant multiples, and agree with classical derivatives for $C^k$ functions; the regular pairing depends only on the almost-everywhere class, and a singleton is Lebesgue null ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]], [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]], [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

[F8] The Dirac distribution is $\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)=\varphi(x_0)$; test functions are smooth with compact support, and the polar formula computes radial integrals: $\int_{|z|<b}|z|^{-1}\,d\lambda_3=2\pi b^2$ and $\int_{|z|<b}|z|^{-2}\,d\lambda_3=4\pi b$ for $b>0$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F9] The pure electrostatic regime and its fixed-time reading are those of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], the field and source conventions are those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], the laboratory region is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the units are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and the weak solution predicate and stationary point source are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b),(e).

[F10] The weak maximum principle: for nonempty bounded open $\Omega$ and $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ with $\Delta u\ge0$, $\max_{\overline\Omega}u=\max_{\partial\Omega}u$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], $\omega_2=|S^2|=4\pi$ and $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$, so $\nabla\Phi(z)=-z/(4\pi|z|^3)$ and $|\nabla\Phi(z)|=1/(4\pi|z|^2)$ by the chain and power rules ([F4]); $\Phi$ and $\nabla\Phi$ are locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$, since $\int_{|z|<b}|z|^{-k}d\lambda_3=4\pi b^{3-k}/(3-k)$ is finite for $k=1,2$, while away from the pole the kernels are continuous and hence bounded on compacta ([F8]). Let $\rho\in C^1_c$ with support in $\overline B_R$; by [F5] it is bounded, Lipschitz and has finite global $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm for $\alpha=1/2$, and it vanishes off the open ball $B_R$ because it is continuous and zero on and beyond $S_R$. [given, F1, F4, F5, F8]

2.1 The Hölder theorem [F2] applied with $\alpha=1/2$ gives $N\rho\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ with $-\Delta (N\rho)=\rho$ pointwise; scaling $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and using linearity of the second coordinate derivatives gives $-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise, because $\varepsilon_0>0$ is a constant ([F4]). With $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ one has $\operatorname{div}E=-\operatorname{div}\nabla\varphi=-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\operatorname{curl}\nabla\varphi=0$ by [F4], since $\varphi$ is $C^2$. [step 1.1, F2, F4, F9]

3.1 Coulomb representation: since Lebesgue measure is translation invariant, $N\rho(x)=\int\Phi(x-y)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)=\int\Phi(z)\rho(x-z)\,d\lambda_3(z)$ ([F6]); fix $x_0$ and a bounded open interval $J$ of $x_i$-values with $x_0+se_i$ ranging in a bounded ball $B(x_0,\delta)$. For such $x$ the integrand $\Phi(z)\rho(x-z)$ is supported in the bounded set $K:=\{z:x-z\in\overline B_R\ \text{for some }x\in B(x_0,\delta)\}$, and its $s$-derivative $\Phi(z)\partial_i\rho(x-z)$ is dominated on $J$ by $\|\nabla\rho\|_\infty|\Phi(z)|\mathbf 1_K(z)$, which is integrable ([F5], [F8]); differentiation under the integral sign [F6] therefore gives $\partial_iN\rho(x)=\int\Phi(z)\partial_i\rho(x-z)\,d\lambda_3(z)$. For fixed $x$ put $h(z):=\rho(x-z)$, a $C^1$ compactly supported function; then $\partial_i\rho(x-z)=-\partial_{z_i}h(z)$, so $$\partial_iN\rho(x)=-\int\Phi(z)\partial_{z_i}h(z)\,d\lambda_3(z)=-\langle T_\Phi,\partial_ih\rangle.$$ The kernel $\Phi$ is locally integrable, continuous and smooth off the single point $0$, its classical partials are locally integrable, so [[lem-em-distributional-gradient-smooth-off-a-point]] applies with $u=\Phi$ and gives $\partial_iT_\Phi=T_{\partial_i\Phi}$; hence $\langle T_\Phi,\partial_ih\rangle=-\langle\partial_iT_\Phi,h\rangle=-\int\partial_i\Phi(z)h(z)\,d\lambda_3(z)$ ([F7]). Substituting back and translating gives $$\partial_iN\rho(x)=\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{x_i-y_i}{|x-y|^3}\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$, the integral being absolutely convergent because $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_R$ lies in the ball $B(x,|x|+R)$ and $\int_{B(x,|x|+R)}|x-y|^{-2}d\lambda_3(y)=4\pi(|x|+R)<\infty$, while $|\rho|\le\|\rho\|_\infty$ on the support ([F1], [F5], [F8]). Multiplying by $-\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ gives exactly the displayed Coulomb representation of $E=-\nabla\varphi$. [step 2.1, F1, F5, F6, F7, F8]

4.1 Bounds and regime reading: for $|x|>2R$ the far-field lemma [F3] with $n=3$, $\omega_2=4\pi$ gives $|\nabla N\rho(x)|\le4\|\rho\|_1/(4\pi|x|^2)=\|\rho\|_1/(\pi|x|^2)$, hence $|E(x)|=\varepsilon_0^{-1}|\nabla N\rho(x)|\le\|\rho\|_1/(\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2)$. Since $\rho$ is continuous, compactly supported in $\overline B_R$ and zero off $B_R$, the decay theorem [F3] gives $|N\rho(x)-Q/(4\pi|x|)|\le R\|\rho\|_1/(\pi|x|^2)$ for $|x|>2R$, so for $|x|>\max(2R,1)$ we get $|\varphi(x)|\le\bigl(|Q|/(4\pi)+R\|\rho\|_1/\pi\bigr)/(\varepsilon_0|x|)$, as claimed. Finally the fields and density are time independent, and the pointwise identities of step 2.1 are exactly the reduced equations of the pure electrostatic regime, so $(E,0,\rho,0)$ realises that regime with source $\rho$ in the sense of the fixed-time reading ([F9]). [step 3.1, F3, F9]

5.1 Uniqueness (b): let $\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ with $-\Delta\psi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise and $\psi(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$, and put $h:=\psi-\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the potential of clause (a). Then $h\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$, $\Delta h=\Delta\psi-\Delta\varphi=-\rho/\varepsilon_0+\rho/\varepsilon_0=0$ and $h(x)\to0$ ([F4]). Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $R_\varepsilon$ with $|h(x)|\le\varepsilon$ for $|x|\ge R_\varepsilon$; for $R>R_\varepsilon$ the weak maximum principle [F10] applied on the bounded open ball $B_R$ to the harmonic $h$ gives $\max_{\overline B_R}h=\max_{\partial B_R}h\le\varepsilon$, and applied to the harmonic $-h$ gives $\min_{\overline B_R}h\ge-\varepsilon$; hence $|h|\le\varepsilon$ on $\overline B_R$. Every point of $\mathbb R^3$ lies in $B_R$ for large $R$, so $|h(x)|\le\varepsilon$ for all $x$ and all $\varepsilon>0$, whence $h=0$ and $\psi=\varphi$ ([F4]). [step 4.1, F4, F10]

6.1 Clause (c): let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be real, measurable and compactly supported. The distributional Poisson theorem [F2] gives that $N\rho$ is finite almost everywhere, belongs to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, is $C^\infty$ and harmonic off the support of $\rho$, and satisfies $-\Delta T_{N\rho}=T_\rho$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$. Multiplying the regular distribution by the positive constant $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ and using linearity of distributional differentiation, $-\Delta T_{\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho}=\varepsilon_0^{-1}(-\Delta T_{N\rho})=T_{\rho/\varepsilon_0}$ ([F7]); this is the displayed identity, with the same smoothness and harmonicity assertions carried over. [step 5.1, F2, F7]

7.1 Clause (d), first part: $\varphi_q=(q/\varepsilon_0)\Phi(\cdot-x_0)$, so $\varphi_q\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and its classical partials $\partial_i\varphi_q$ are locally integrable, by the local integrability of $|z|^{-1}$ and $|z|^{-2}$ in dimension three ([F1], [F8]); the value at $x_0$ is arbitrary and immaterial ([F7]). By [F1] the translated kernel satisfies $-\Delta_xT_{\Phi(\cdot-x_0)}=\delta_{x_0}$; multiplying by $q/\varepsilon_0$ and using linearity of distributional differentiation gives $-\Delta T_{\varphi_q}=(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta_{x_0}$ ([F7]). Moreover $E_q=-\nabla\varphi_q$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{x_0\}$: differentiating $\varphi_q(x)=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|)$ by the chain and power rules gives $\nabla\varphi_q(x)=-\frac{q(x-x_0)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^3}$ for $x\ne x_0$ ([F4]). [step 6.1, F1, F4, F7, F8]

8.1 Clause (d), field identities and reading: by [[lem-em-distributional-gradient-smooth-off-a-point]] applied to $u=\varphi_q$ (locally integrable, continuous and smooth off the single point $x_0$, classical partials locally integrable), $\partial_iT_{\varphi_q}=T_{\partial_i\varphi_q}$ ([F7]). Since $E_{q,i}=-\partial_i\varphi_q$ off $x_0$ and a singleton is null, the two functions agree almost everywhere, hence $T_{E_{q,i}}=-T_{\partial_i\varphi_q}=-\partial_iT_{\varphi_q}$ ([F7]); taking one more distributional derivative and summing over $i$ gives $$\operatorname{div}E_q=\sum_i\partial_iT_{E_{q,i}}=-\sum_i\partial_i\partial_iT_{\varphi_q}=-\Delta T_{\varphi_q}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},$$ and the curl components vanish because distributional partial derivatives commute: $$\partial_2T_{E_{q,3}}-\partial_3T_{E_{q,2}}=-(\partial_2\partial_3-\partial_3\partial_2)T_{\varphi_q}=0,$$ and likewise for the other two components ([F7]). By [F9] the distribution $q\delta_{x_0}$ is the fixed-time reading of the stationary point source with charge $q$ at $x_0$, so $(E_q,0)$ satisfies the distributional pure electrostatic equations with that source. No product of distributions was formed, no value of the field at $x_0$ was used, and no uniqueness, self-force, reaction or empirical claim is made; this is exactly the scope stated. [step 7.1, F7, F8, F9] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, star-shaped ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and the spatial region of a pure electrostatic regime as in [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]], with fields of [[def-em-fields]], charge parameters of [[def-em-sources]] and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; thus $E:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is $C^1$, $B=0$ and $J=0$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]]), and by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]] there is $\varphi\in C^2(\Omega)$ with $E=-\nabla\varphi$.
Let $q\in\mathbb R$ (coulombs) be the charge of a test particle and let $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to\Omega$ be a piecewise $C^1$ path ([[def-interval]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
Define the **work of the electric force** along the prescribed path by the vector line integral
$$W(\gamma):=\int_\gamma qE\cdot d\mathbf r$$
of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]; $qE$ is the electric term of the external force adopted for a test charge in [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](i), and this identification of the electric term is a physical reading adopted with the coupling, not a decomposition derived in this item.
Then:

(a) [Value] $W(\gamma)=q\,(\varphi(\gamma(t_0))-\varphi(\gamma(t_1)))$;

(b) [Path independence] if $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ are piecewise $C^1$ paths in $\Omega$ with the same initial and the same terminal point, then $W(\gamma_1)=W(\gamma_2)$; in particular $W(\gamma)=0$ for every closed piecewise $C^1$ path;

(c) [Potential energy] with the potential energy $U:=q\varphi$ (joules) the identity reads $W(\gamma)=-(U(\gamma(t_1))-U(\gamma(t_0)))$;

(d) [Gauge invariance of the work] if $\varphi' \in C^2(\Omega)$ is any other potential with $\nabla\varphi'=-E$, then $\varphi'=\varphi+c$ with a constant $c\in\mathbb R$ and the formula of (a) is unchanged ([[cor-potentials-differ-by-a-componentwise-constant]]).

The statement is a line-integral identity for a prescribed path in a prescribed static external field. It asserts no equation of motion, no radiation, no work done on the sources and no claim that the test particle actually follows $\gamma$; the interpretation of $W$ as work done by the adopted external coupling is the physical reading supplied by [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], not a dynamical theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A star-shaped open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ carrying a pure electrostatic regime with $C^1$ field $E$ and $B=J=0$, a charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$, and a piecewise $C^1$ path $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to\Omega$.

[F1] The pure electrostatic regime has $B=0$, $J=0$, time-independent fields and the reduced equations; on a star-shaped region the potential theorem provides $\varphi\in C^2(\Omega)$ with $\nabla\varphi=-E$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]).

[F2] The vector line integral is $\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r=\sum_i\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt$ over an admissible partition, the inner product is the Euclidean one and the integral is linear in the field ([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-interval]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F3] The gradient theorem evaluates the line integral of a gradient of a $C^1$ function along a piecewise $C^1$ path as the endpoint increment ([[thm-gradient-theorem-for-line-integrals]]).

[F4] Two $C^1$ potentials with the same gradient differ by a constant on each piecewise-$C^1$ path component, and a star-shaped set has a single such component through its centre ([[cor-potentials-differ-by-a-componentwise-constant]], [[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F5] The adopted external coupling is read in the laboratory frame through the electric term $qE$ on a test charge of parameter $q$ in a prescribed external field; this identification is an adopted physical reading, not a derived decomposition ([[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](i)).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1] the potential $\varphi\in C^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $\nabla\varphi=-E$; the field $qE$ is $C^1$ on $\Omega$ for the constant $q$, and the work $W(\gamma)=\int_\gamma qE\cdot d\mathbf r$ is defined by the vector line integral of [F2], which is finite because the integrand is continuous on each smooth piece of the compact parameter interval. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Clause (a): by the linearity of the line integral in the field and the constancy of $q$, $W(\gamma)=q\int_\gamma E\cdot d\mathbf r$ ([F2]); substituting $E=-\nabla\varphi$ and applying the gradient theorem [F3] gives $$W(\gamma)=-q\int_\gamma\nabla\varphi\cdot d\mathbf r=-q\bigl(\varphi(\gamma(t_1))-\varphi(\gamma(t_0))\bigr)=q\bigl(\varphi(\gamma(t_0))-\varphi(\gamma(t_1))\bigr),$$ which is the displayed formula, including the degenerate case $t_0=t_1$ where the line integral is $0$ and the right side vanishes too. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3]

3.1 Clause (b): if $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ are piecewise $C^1$ paths in $\Omega$ with the same initial point $x$ and the same terminal point $y$, then by step 2.1 applied to each path $W(\gamma_1)=q(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y))=W(\gamma_2)$; for a closed path, where $x=y$, both formulas give $W(\gamma)=0$. [step 2.1]

4.1 Clause (c): with $U:=q\varphi$, the identity of step 2.1 reads $W(\gamma)=U(\gamma(t_0))-U(\gamma(t_1))=-\bigl(U(\gamma(t_1))-U(\gamma(t_0))\bigr)$, the potential energy being the constant multiple $q\varphi$ of the potential. [step 3.1]

5.1 Clause (d): let $\varphi'\in C^2(\Omega)$ satisfy $\nabla\varphi'=-E=\nabla\varphi$. Then $\nabla(\varphi'-\varphi)=0$ on $\Omega$, and by [F4] the difference is constant on every piecewise-$C^1$ path component of $\Omega$; since $\Omega$ is star-shaped, every point is joined to the centre by a $C^1$ segment, so all of $\Omega$ is one path component ([F4]) and $\varphi'=\varphi+c$ for a constant $c\in\mathbb R$. Substituting into the formula of step 2.1 replaces $\varphi$ by $\varphi+c$ and leaves the right side unchanged, so the work is independent of the additive normalisation of the potential. [step 4.1, F4]

6.1 Clauses (a)-(d) are steps 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1. The force whose work was computed is the electric term $qE$ of the adopted external coupling [F5] along the prescribed path; the computation used only the potential representation, the gradient theorem and the constancy of the potential up to an additive constant, and asserted no equation of motion, no radiation, no work done on the sources and no claim that the particle follows $\gamma$, which is exactly the scope stated. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F5] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the Lebesgue, polar and surface interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Let $\rho\in C^1_c(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ with support in $\overline B_R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), let $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E=-\nabla\varphi$ be the smooth-branch Coulomb solution of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](a) with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], and let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ kernel, $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).
Then:

(a) [Finiteness] the three quantities
$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3,\qquad +\frac{1}{2\varepsilon_0}\iint_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3}\Phi(x-y)\rho(x)\rho(y)\,d(\lambda_3\times\lambda_3)(x,y)$$
are finite real numbers;

(b) [Identity] they are equal:
$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon_0}\iint_{\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3}\Phi(x-y)\rho(x)\rho(y)\,d(\lambda_3\times\lambda_3)(x,y).$$
The last expression is the **external assembly work** of the ideal quasistatic bookkeeping family $\rho_s=s\rho$, $\varphi_s=s\varphi$ for $0\le s\le1$. An added test charge brought from infinity, where the potential is zero, has electric-force work $-dq\,\varphi_s$ by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-work]]; the balancing external work is $+dq\,\varphi_s$. Therefore $W_{\rm ext}=\int_0^1s\,ds\int\rho\varphi=\tfrac12\int\rho\varphi$. Both signs of $\rho$ are allowed. The symmetric double kernel gives the equivalent ordered-pair interpretation of the factor $1/2$.

(c) [Scope] the identity is a statement about the ideal quasi-static assembly of a compactly supported $C^1$ charge distribution in vacuum, all sources being held in place by external support ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]]). It asserts no time-dependent work, no radiation, no material or stability model, and it does not identify the field energy with the rest mass of any particle; the point-source limit is treated separately below and is divergent.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, a real $C^1$ function $\rho$ compactly supported in $\overline B_R$, the potential $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and field $E=-\nabla\varphi$ of the smooth Coulomb branch, and the kernel $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ off the origin.

[F1] The Coulomb solution gives $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$, $E=-\nabla\varphi\in C^1$, $-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, the far-field bound $|E(x)|\le\|\rho\|_1/(\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2)$ for $|x|>2R$, and the potential decay used below; the kernel is $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ with $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]], [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], [[def-newtonian-potential]], [[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]).

[F2] Green's first identity holds on a bounded $C^1$ domain for real $u=v\in C^2$ up to the closure, with the outward normal; the Euclidean balls are bounded $C^1$ domains with outward normal $x/|x|$ on their bounding spheres, and $|S_{R'}|=4\pi R'^2$ ([[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], [[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]).

[F3] The Laplacian, divergence and gradient are the classical operators of the cited definitions, with the partial derivative convention of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and the algebra rules for derivatives; the regime, field and unit conventions are those of the primitives ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F4] The polar formula, translation invariance of Lebesgue measure, the product-measure identification for Euclidean spaces, Fubini and Tonelli, monotone and dominated convergence, and the order and scalar rules for the nonnegative integral are available; continuous functions on compact sets are bounded and attain extrema, and are Borel ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]], [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]], [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F5] The work of the electric force along a prescribed path is $q$ times the potential drop and is additive in the added charge; the potential is linear in the source ([[pthm-em-electrostatic-work]], [[def-newtonian-potential]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Finiteness of the field energy: on the bounded ball $\overline B_{2R}$ the continuous function $|E|^2$ is bounded by [F4] and $\lambda_3(\overline B_{2R})<\infty$, so $\int_{|x|\le2R}|E|^2<\infty$; on the far field the bound of [F1] gives $\int_{|x|>2R}|E|^2\le\frac{\|\rho\|_1^2}{\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}\int_{|x|>2R}|x|^{-4}\,d\lambda_3$, and the polar formula computes $\int_{2R}^{\infty}r^{-4}\cdot4\pi r^2dr=4\pi/(2R)<\infty$ ([F1], [F4]). [given, F1, F4]

2.1 Finiteness of the other two quantities: $\rho$ is bounded and supported in $\overline B_R$ and $\varphi$ is continuous, so $|\rho\varphi|$ is bounded with compact support and $\int|\rho\varphi|<\infty$ ([F1], [F4]). For the double integral, put $M:=\sup|\rho|$ and bound, uniformly in $x$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi(x-y)|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)\le M\int_{|x-y|<1}\Phi(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{|x-y|\ge1}|\rho(y)|\,d\lambda_3(y)\le\frac{M}{2}+\frac{\|\rho\|_1}{4\pi},$$ using $\int_{|z|<1}|z|^{-1}d\lambda_3=2\pi$ from the polar formula, so that the first term is $M\int_{|z|<1}\Phi(z)\,d\lambda_3=M/2$, and translation invariance of Lebesgue measure ([F4]); Tonelli's theorem then makes the absolute double integral at most $\|\rho\|_1\bigl(M/2+\|\rho\|_1/(4\pi)\bigr)<\infty$, so the double integral of the statement is absolutely convergent and the three quantities of (a) are finite real numbers. [step 1.1, F4]

3.1 Green's identity on the ball: fix $R'>R$. By [F2] the ball $B_{R'}$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain with outward normal $\nu(x)=x/|x|$ on $S_{R'}$, and $\varphi\in C^2(\overline B_{R'})$; Green's first identity with $u=v=\varphi$ gives $$\int_{B_{R'}}\bigl(\varphi\Delta\varphi+|D\varphi|^2\bigr)d\lambda_3=\int_{S_{R'}}\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi\,dS.$$ Substituting $\Delta\varphi=-\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $|D\varphi|^2=|E|^2$ from [F1], [F3] and rearranging gives $$\int_{B_{R'}}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{B_{R'}}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3+\int_{S_{R'}}\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi\,dS.$$ [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3]

4.1 Boundary estimate: on $S_{R'}$ the decay bound of [F1] gives $|\varphi(x)|\le C/R'$ with $C$ depending on $\rho$ and $\varepsilon_0$, the far-field bound gives $|\nabla\varphi(x)|\le\|\rho\|_1/(\pi\varepsilon_0R'^2)$, and $\partial_\nu\varphi=\nabla\varphi\cdot x/|x|$ has the same bound; with $|S_{R'}|=4\pi R'^2$ from [F2] this yields $$\Bigl|\int_{S_{R'}}\varphi\,\partial_\nu\varphi\,dS\Bigr|\le\frac{C}{R'}\cdot\frac{\|\rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0R'^2}\cdot4\pi R'^2=\frac{4C\|\rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0R'},$$ which tends to $0$ as $R'\to\infty$ ([F1], [F2], [F4]). [step 3.1, F1, F2, F4]

5.1 First equality: the sets $B_{R'}$ increase to $\mathbb R^3$ as $R'\to\infty$ along any sequence, and $|E|^2\ge0$, so monotone convergence gives $\int_{B_{R'}}|E|^2\to\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2$; since $\rho$ is supported in $\overline B_R\subset B_{R'}$, the integrals $\int_{B_{R'}}\rho\varphi$ are eventually constant equal to $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi$, which is finite by step 2.1; the boundary term vanishes by step 4.1. Passing to the limit in the identity of step 3.1 therefore gives $\int|E|^2=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int\rho\varphi$, that is $\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int|E|^2=\frac12\int\rho\varphi$ ([F4]). [step 3.1, step 4.1, F4]

6.1 Second equality: by [F1] the potential is $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$, and the product $\rho(x)\Phi(x-y)\rho(y)$ is absolutely integrable over $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$ by step 2.1, so Fubini applies: $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(x)\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi(x-y)\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\Bigr)d\lambda_3(x)=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\iint\Phi(x-y)\rho(x)\rho(y)\,d(\lambda_3\times\lambda_3).$$ Since $\Phi(x-y)=\Phi(y-x)$ and $\rho(x)\rho(y)=\rho(y)\rho(x)$, the double integral is unchanged by exchanging $x$ and $y$, which is the ordered-pair reading of the factor; multiplying the identity by $\frac12$ gives $\frac12\int\rho\varphi=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon_0}\iint\Phi(x-y)\rho(x)\rho(y)\,d(\lambda_3\times\lambda_3)$, the second equality of (b) ([F1], [F4]). [step 5.1, F1, F4]

7.1 Assembly reading: for $0\le s\le1$ put $\rho_s:=s\rho$ and $\varphi_s:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho_s=s\varphi$, so that $E_s=sE$ and all the above estimates hold with $\rho_s$ in place of $\rho$ ([F1], [F5]). An increment of charge $d\rho_s=\rho\,ds$ added at $x$ to a configuration whose potential is $\varphi_s$ has electric-force work $-d\rho_s\,\varphi_s(x)$ when the charge is brought from infinity, by the work formula of [F5] together with the decay $\varphi_s(x)\to0$ at infinity; the balancing external work is $+d\rho_s\,\varphi_s(x)$, so the total external assembly work is $$W_{\rm ext}=\int_0^1\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(x)\varphi_s(x)\,d\lambda_3(x)\Bigr)ds=\int_0^1s\,ds\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3,$$ the interchange being justified by the absolute finiteness of step 2.1 applied to $\rho_s$; both signs of $\rho$ are allowed because all integrals involved are absolutely convergent ([F4], [F5]). [step 6.1, F1, F4, F5]

8.1 Clauses (a), (b) and (c): finiteness is steps 1.1-2.1, the two equalities are steps 5.1 and 6.1, the assembly reading is step 7.1, and the scope clause records that the construction is an ideal quasi-static bookkeeping with external support, uses the pure electrostatic regime, and neither models radiation or material dynamics nor identifies the field energy with a particle rest mass; the divergent point-source limit is treated separately below and is not asserted here. [step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, F1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the Lebesgue and polar interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Let $q\in\mathbb R$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, and let $E_q$ be the ideal point-charge field of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d) ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]).
For $0<\delta<R$ put
$$U_q(\delta,R):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R\}}|E_q(x)|^2\,d\lambda_3(x)$$
(the truncated field energy of the shell between the two spheres, [[def-metric-ball]]).
Then:

(a) [Exact truncated energy] for all $0<\delta<R$,
$$U_q(\delta,R)=\frac{q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0}\Bigl(\frac1\delta-\frac1R\Bigr);$$

(b) [Divergence] $\lim_{R\to\infty}U_q(\delta,R)=q^2/(8\pi\varepsilon_0\delta)$ for every $\delta>0$, and for $q\ne0$
$$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}U_q(\delta,R)=+\infty\qquad\text{for every }R>0;$$
so the field energy of the ideal point charge is locally infinite at its own location, and any finite-energy treatment of a point-like charge must modify the source/field near the singularity or introduce an explicit cutoff;

(c) [Limits of the mass inference] the identity is a divergence of the *field energy of the idealised point source* in the framework's SI conventions. It does not assert that a physical particle has infinite rest mass, does not identify field energy with rest mass, contains no measurement, and involves neither a self-force nor a contradiction claim for classical electrodynamics: the framework supplies no mass-energy identification for a charged particle, and the smooth compact-source field/assembly energy of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] remains finite. The compact $L^1$ branch of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] retains its locally integrable potential and distributional Poisson equation; it does not guarantee finite field energy for arbitrary $L^1$ densities. The point source itself is the idealisation of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); its energy divergence is a mathematical property of that idealisation, not an empirical result.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, $q\in\mathbb R$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, the point-charge field $E_q(z)=q z/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|z|^3)$ off $z=0$ of the Coulomb solution, and $0<\delta<R$.

[F1] The ideal point-charge field satisfies $|E_q(z)|=|q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|z|^2)$ for $z\ne0$; its value at the pole is arbitrary and immaterial; the compact-source field/assembly energy of a $C^1$ compactly supported density is finite and equal to $\frac12\int\rho\varphi$, and the compact $L^1$ branch keeps a locally integrable potential with distributional Poisson equation but asserts no finite field energy ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]], [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F2] The polar formula computes radial integrals, the sphere area is $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ from $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$ and $|B_1|=4\pi/3$, and the fundamental theorem evaluates $\int_\delta^Rr^{-2}dr$ as the increment of the primitive $-1/r$ on compact subintervals, the Riemann and Lebesgue values agreeing for the continuous integrand; a singleton or the pole sphere set $\{x_0\}$ is null and does not affect the integral ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).

[F3] The nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous, the integral of a radial density is the polar integral, and monotone convergence passes increasing limits; the point source is the idealisation of the weak point-source definition and of the static-to-distributional reading ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-em-weak-sources]], [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $z\ne0$ the field satisfies $|E_q(z)|^2=q^2/(16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2|z|^4)$ by [F1]; the shell $\{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R\}$ excludes $x_0$ because $\delta>0$, and the integrand is continuous on the shell, hence Borel and locally bounded there; the value assigned to $E_q$ at $x_0$ does not affect the integral since $\{x_0\}$ is null ([F1], [F2], [F3]). [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Polar integration about $x_0$: substituting $x=x_0+z$ and using the polar formula in $z$ with the radial density $q^2/(16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2r^4)$ gives $$\int_{\{\delta\le|x-x_0|\le R\}}|E_q(x)|^2\,d\lambda_3(x)=\frac{q^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}\int_\delta^R r^{-4}\cdot 4\pi r^2\,dr=\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0^2}\int_\delta^R r^{-2}\,dr,$$ where $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ and the radial integrals are taken over the compact interval $[\delta,R]$ ([F2], [F3]). [step 1.1, F2, F3]

3.1 The fundamental theorem with the primitive $r\mapsto-r^{-1}$ of $r\mapsto r^{-2}$ gives $\int_\delta^Rr^{-2}dr=1/\delta-1/R$ ([F2]); substituting into step 2.1 and multiplying by $\varepsilon_0/2$ yields $$U_q(\delta,R)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\cdot\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0^2}\Bigl(\frac1\delta-\frac1R\Bigr)=\frac{q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0}\Bigl(\frac1\delta-\frac1R\Bigr),$$ which is clause (a); the quantity is finite for $0<\delta<R$ and of the sign of $q^2$ ([F3]). [step 2.1, F2, F3]

4.1 Clause (b): letting $R\to\infty$ in the exact formula gives $\lim_{R\to\infty}U_q(\delta,R)=q^2/(8\pi\varepsilon_0\delta)$ for every $\delta>0$, and letting $\delta\downarrow0$ gives $\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}U_q(\delta,R)=+\infty$ whenever $q\ne0$, while for $q=0$ both expressions vanish identically; the limits are read off the continuous elementary functions $R\mapsto1/R$ and $\delta\mapsto1/\delta$ on $(0,\infty)$ ([F2], [F3]). [step 3.1, F2, F3]

5.1 Clause (c): the computation used only the idealised point field of [F1] and the radial integration of [F2]; it yields a divergence of the truncated field energy of that idealisation. No identification of field energy with rest mass, no self-force, no measurement and no inconsistency claim is made; the smooth compact-source energy of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] remains finite by [F1], the compact $L^1$ branch keeps only its locally integrable potential and distributional Poisson equation, and the point source is the idealisation of the weak point-source definition together with the static-to-distributional reading [F3]. [step 4.1, F1, F3] ∎
