## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Let $\Omega:=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{x:x_1=x_2=0\}$ (the complement of the $z$-axis), let $\rho(x):=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$ and $\hat e_r(x):=(x_1,x_2,0)/\rho(x)$ for $x\in\Omega$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]), let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a line charge density in $\mathrm{C\,m^{-1}}$, let $r_0>0$, and define, with the constants and units of [[def-em-si-conventions]] ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]]),
$$E(x):=\frac{\lambda\,\hat e_r(x)}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\,\rho(x)},\qquad \varphi(x):=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\log\frac{\rho(x)}{r_0}\qquad(x\in\Omega).$$
Then:

(a) [Gradient] $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega$ ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]);

(b) [Classical equations] $\operatorname{div}E=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ pointwise on $\Omega$; hence the fixed-time pair $(E,0)$ satisfies the reduced smooth-branch electrostatic equations with zero volume source on $\Omega$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (c), [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]);

(c) [Flux per length] for every $r>0$ and $L>0$ the flux of $E$ through the lateral cylinder surface $\{x:\rho(x)=r,\ |x_3|\le L/2\}$ in the outward orientation is $\Phi_r=\lambda L/\varepsilon_0$; the parametrization $(\theta,z)\mapsto(r\operatorname{Re}e^{i\theta},r\operatorname{Im}e^{i\theta},z)$ over the rectangle $[0,2\pi]\times[-L/2,L/2]$ is an admissible regular surface patch ([[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]], [[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]]);

(d) [Distributional line source] extend $E$ by $0$ on the axis and let $\rho_\lambda(\psi):=\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(0,0,z)\,dz$ be the line-charge distribution on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). Then, with distributional derivatives and the regular distribution of $E$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]),
$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\rho_\lambda,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3),$$
by superposition of the point-charge identities of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (d) along the axis ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the line density fixed by the field in this weak sense is exactly $\lambda$;

(e) [Normalization] for fixed $r_0$, $\varphi(\rho)\to-\infty$ as $\rho\to\infty$ if $\lambda>0$ and $\to+\infty$ if $\lambda<0$, while changing $r_0$ to $r_0'$ shifts $\varphi$ by $\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\log(r_0'/r_0)$ and leaves $E$ unchanged. For $\lambda\ne0$ the infinity normalization of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (b) is therefore unavailable; for $\lambda=0$ the field, potential and line source are zero and all cutoff energies and fluxes vanish; and $\Omega$ is not star-shaped (for every $a\in\Omega$ the segment from $a$ to $-a$ passes through the axis, which is not in $\Omega$), so [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]] does not apply to $\Omega$, although the displayed $\varphi$ still satisfies $E=-\nabla\varphi$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]);

(f) [Energy per length] for $0<\delta<r<R$ and $L>0$,
$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\{\delta<\rho<R,\ |x_3|<L/2\}}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac{\lambda^2L}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\log\frac{R}{\delta},$$
which for $\lambda\ne0$ diverges both as $\delta\downarrow0$ and as $R\to\infty$; there is no finite energy per unit length ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]);

(g) [Scope and idealization] the line charge $\rho_\lambda$ is *not* a source type of [[def-em-weak-sources]]: only point sources and stationary sheets are declared there, and no line current, moving sheet or other distribution is included. The item therefore verifies classical, flux and distributional identities for an explicitly specified distribution $\rho_\lambda$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with a noncompact singularity; it is not a framework postulate covering infinite line charges, asserts no physical realisation, equilibrium or empirical content, and is not a compact-source Coulomb corollary. Real line-like distributions have finite length and transverse size, and their far fields and energies require their own hypotheses.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, the open set $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{\text{axis}\}$, the transverse radius $\rho(x)=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, the radial unit vector $\hat e_r(x)=(x_1,x_2,0)/\rho(x)$, real $\lambda$ and $r_0>0$, and the fields $E,\varphi$ displayed above.

[F1] The transverse radius is continuous and positive exactly on $\Omega$, so $\Omega$ is open; on it $\rho$ is smooth with $\partial_i\rho=x_i/\rho$ for $i=1,2$ and $\partial_3\rho=0$ ([[def-metric-topology]], [[thm-continuity-preimage-characterisation]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F2] The logarithm is smooth on $(0,\infty)$ with derivative $1/t$; the divergence and curl are the classical operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and the regime conventions are those of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]).

[F3] The complex exponential is entire with derivative $ie^{i\theta}$; its real and imaginary parts and modulus satisfy $|e^{i\theta}|=1$ and Euler's identity ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

[F4] For a regular patch the outward-oriented flux is the integral of $F\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$ over the parameter region; the cross product and its norm are those of the Euclidean structure, and a compact Jordan parameter region is admissible when the parametrization is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood, the cross product is nonzero on the interior and the interior map is injective ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]], [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F5] The polar formula computes integrals in every dimension; the transverse plane is $\mathbb R^2$ with $\sigma(S^1)=2\pi$ from $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$ and $|B_1|=\pi$ in dimension two ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).

[F6] Fubini and Tonelli apply on sigma-finite products; the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^3$ is that of $\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R$ and the product measure agrees with $\lambda_3$ on Borel sets ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]).

[F7] Distributions, their derivatives, test functions and the embedding of locally integrable functions are as in the cited interfaces, and the ideal point charge with charge parameter $q$ at $x_0$ has $\operatorname{div}E_q=(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta_{x_0}$ and $\operatorname{curl}E_q=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]]).

[F8] The fundamental theorem and its integrable-derivative form evaluate one-variable integrals of continuous integrands on compact intervals, and the Riemann and Lebesgue integrals of a continuous compactly supported integrand agree ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F9] Monotone and dominated convergence pass limits through integrals under the stated majorants, and continuous functions are Borel with the usual monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[F10] The $z$-axis is Lebesgue null: it lies in the coordinate hyperplane $x_1=0$ ([[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]).

[F11] Star-shapedness is defined through segments to a centre, and the compact-source uniqueness of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]] requires a star-shaped region; the framework's declared source types are point and stationary-sheet sources of [[def-em-weak-sources]] ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]], [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]], [[def-em-weak-sources]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1] $\Omega$ is open and $\rho$ is smooth and positive on it with $\partial_i\rho=x_i/\rho$ for $i=1,2$ and $\partial_3\rho=0$; consequently $E$ is $C^\infty$ on $\Omega$ and $E\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ with $|E|=\frac{|\lambda|}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\rho}$, since on every bounded set the transverse polar formula gives $\int_{\rho<A}\rho^{-1}\,d\lambda_2=2\pi A$ and multiplication by the finite longitudinal length of the containing cylinder yields a finite integral ([F1], [F5]). Extending $E$ by $0$ on the axis does not change its $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ class or any regular distribution, because the axis is null ([F10]), and the functional $\rho_\lambda(\psi)=\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(0,0,z)\,dz$ is a distribution: on a compact test support contained in a cylinder $\rho\le A$, $|z|\le H$ its absolute pairing is at most $|\lambda|\,2H\|\psi\|_\infty$ ([F7], [F9], [F10]). [given, F1, F5, F7, F9, F10]

2.1 Clause (a): the chain rule and the derivative of the logarithm [F1], [F2] give $\nabla\varphi=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla\rho=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\rho}\hat e_r=-E$ on $\Omega$, since $\nabla\rho=(x_1,x_2,0)/\rho=\hat e_r$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 Clause (b): writing $E=(E_1,E_2,0)$ with $E_i=\frac{\lambda x_i}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\rho^2}$, the quotient rule and $\partial_i\rho=x_i/\rho$ give $\partial_iE_i=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\rho^2-2x_i^2}{\rho^4}$ for $i=1,2$, so $\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2\rho^2-2x_1^2-2x_2^2}{\rho^4}=0$; and $\operatorname{curl}E$ has components $\partial_2E_3-\partial_3E_2=0$, $\partial_3E_1-\partial_1E_3=0$ and $\partial_1E_2-\partial_2E_1=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{-2x_1x_2+2x_1x_2}{\rho^4}=0$, because $E_3=0$ and $E$ does not depend on $x_3$ ([F1], [F2]). Hence $(E,0)$ satisfies the reduced equations with zero volume source on $\Omega$: the pair is time independent and the reduced smooth-branch equations are exactly $\operatorname{div}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ [F2]. [step 2.1, F1, F2]

4.1 Clause (c): let $u(\theta)=\operatorname{Re}e^{i\theta}$, $v(\theta)=\operatorname{Im}e^{i\theta}$, and let $\Phi(\theta,z)=(ru(\theta),rv(\theta),z)$ on $D=[0,2\pi]\times[-L/2,L/2]$. By [F3], $\Phi$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $D$ with $\partial_\theta\Phi=r(u',v',0)=r(-v,u,0)$ and $\partial_z\Phi=(0,0,1)$, so $\partial_\theta\Phi\times\partial_z\Phi=r(u,v,0)$ is nonzero on the interior because $r>0$ and $u^2+v^2=|e^{i\theta}|^2=1$; the interior map is injective since $\theta\mapsto(u,v)$ is injective on $(0,2\pi)$, and the seam $\theta=0\leftrightarrow2\pi$ lies on the boundary. Hence $(D,\Phi)$ is an admissible regular patch for the lateral surface [F4]. Since $E(\Phi(\theta,z))=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}(u,v,0)$, the flux integrand is $E\cdot(\partial_\theta\Phi\times\partial_z\Phi)=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}\cdot r=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}$, and the flux equals $\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\lambda_2(D)=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot2\pi L=\frac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0}$ by the box measure and the Riemann/Lebesgue agreement for the constant integrand ([F4], [F8]). [step 3.1, F3, F4, F8]

5.1 Clause (d), superposition representation: for $x\in\Omega$ and $t\in\mathbb R$ put $z_t:=te_3$ and $E_{1,t}(x):=\frac{x-z_t}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-z_t|^3}$ (the unit point-charge field of [F7] at $z_t$). Direct computation with the primitive $t\mapsto\frac{t}{\rho^2\sqrt{\rho^2+t^2}}$ of $(\rho^2+t^2)^{-3/2}$ shows $\int_{-T}^{T}\frac{dt}{(\rho^2+t^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{2T}{\rho^2\sqrt{\rho^2+T^2}}\to\frac{2}{\rho^2}$ as $T\to\infty$ and $\int_{-T}^{T}\frac{x_3-t}{(\rho^2+(x_3-t)^2)^{3/2}}dt=0$ by oddness for every $T$ ([F8]); hence, for every $x\in\Omega$, $$\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}E_{1,t}(x)\,dt=\lambda\Bigl(\frac{x_1}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\rho^2},\frac{x_2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0\rho^2},0\Bigr)=E(x),$$ the first two components because $\int_{\mathbb R}(\rho^2+t^2)^{-3/2}dt=2/\rho^2$ and the third by oddness. Moreover $|E_{1,t}(x)|=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(\rho^2+(x_3-t)^2)}\le\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\bigl(\frac{\mathbf 1_{|x_3-t|\le\rho}}{\rho^2}+\frac{\mathbf 1_{|x_3-t|>\rho}}{(x_3-t)^2}\bigr)$, whose $t$-integral is at most $\frac{4}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\rho}=\frac{1}{\pi\varepsilon_0\rho}$, and $x\mapsto\frac{|D\psi(x)|}{\rho(x)}$ is integrable for every compactly supported test ([F5], [F9]). [step 4.1, F5, F7, F8, F9]

6.1 Clause (d), the distributional identities: let $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and let $\Psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. By step 5.1 and absolute Fubini integrability of $\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E_{1,t}(x)||D\psi(x)|\,dx\,dt\le\frac{1}{\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|D\psi(x)|}{\rho(x)}dx<\infty$ ([F6], [F9]), $$\langle\operatorname{div}E,\psi\rangle=-\int_{\mathbb R^3}E\cdot\nabla\psi\,d\lambda_3=-\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^3}E_{1,t}\cdot\nabla\psi\,d\lambda_3\Bigr)dt=\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}\langle\operatorname{div}E_{1,t},\psi\rangle\,dt,$$ and [F7] gives $\operatorname{div}E_{1,t}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{z_t}$, so the last expression is $\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(0,0,t)\,dt=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\rho_\lambda(\psi)$ for every test function, which is the first identity. The same interchange with $\int_{\mathbb R}\int|E_{1,t}||\operatorname{curl}\Psi|$ finite gives $\langle\operatorname{curl}E,\Psi\rangle=\int E\cdot\operatorname{curl}\Psi=\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}\langle\operatorname{curl}E_{1,t},\Psi\rangle dt=0$, since each translated unit-charge field has vanishing distributional curl by [F7]; hence $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$. [step 5.1, F6, F7, F9]

7.1 Clause (e): with $\varphi=-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\log(\rho/r_0)$, the limits $\rho\to\infty$ and the $r_0$-shift are the elementary properties of the logarithm [F2]: replacing $r_0$ by $r_0'$ adds $-\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\log(r_0/r_0')=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\log(r_0'/r_0)$ to $\varphi$, which cancels in $\nabla\varphi$, and as $\rho\to\infty$ the logarithm diverges to $-\infty$ for $\lambda>0$ and to $+\infty$ for $\lambda<0$, so for $\lambda\ne0$ no normalisation at infinity is available ([F11]). If $\lambda=0$ then $E=0$, $\varphi=0$, $\rho_\lambda=0$, and every flux and cutoff energy vanishes by the identities above. For non-star-shapedness, let $a\in\Omega$; then $-a$ lies in $\Omega$ and the segment $s\mapsto(1-2s)a$ at $s=1/2$ is $0$, which is not in $\Omega$, so no point of $\Omega$ is a star centre for the whole set ([F1], [F11]). [step 6.1, F1, F2, F11]

8.1 Clause (f): $|E|^2=\frac{\lambda^2}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2\rho^2}$, and the two-dimensional polar formula of [F5], applied in the transverse variables and combined with Fubini in the $x_3$-variable [F6], gives $\int_{\{\delta<\rho<R,|x_3|<L/2\}}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=L\cdot\frac{\lambda^2}{4\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}\cdot2\pi\log\frac{R}{\delta}=\frac{\lambda^2L}{2\pi\varepsilon_0^2}\log\frac{R}{\delta}$; multiplying by $\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}$ gives the displayed identity. For $\lambda\ne0$ the factor $\log(R/\delta)$ tends to $+\infty$ as $\delta\downarrow0$ and as $R\to\infty$, so no finite energy per unit length exists ([F5], [F9]). [step 7.1, F5, F6, F9]

9.1 Clause (g) records the scope: [F11] declares only point and stationary-sheet sources, so the line distribution $\rho_\lambda$ is outside the framework's source types; the construction used the ideal point-charge identity of [F7] superimposed along the axis with the absolute majorant of step 5.1, the classical computations of steps 2.1-4.1 on the open set $\Omega$, and the polar/Fubini computations of steps 6.1-8.1. No physical realisation, equilibrium, material model, self-force or empirical claim is made, and no compact-source corollary is asserted; this is exactly the scope stated. [step 8.1, F7, F11] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Let $a>0$, $Q\in\mathbb R$, let $\overline B_a=\{x:|x|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and define, with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]]),
$$\rho(x):=\frac{3Q}{4\pi a^3}\,\mathbf 1_{\{|x|<a\}}(x),\qquad E(x):=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\begin{cases}x/a^3,&|x|<a,\\ x/|x|^3,&|x|\ge a,\end{cases}\qquad \varphi(x):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{Q(3a^2-|x|^2)}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a^3},&|x|\le a,\\ \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|},&|x|\ge a.\end{cases}$$
(The value of $\rho$ on the sphere $\{|x|=a\}$ is immaterial: it is a Lebesgue-null set by the polar calculation $\lambda_3(S_a)=4\pi\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{a\}}(r)r^2dr=0$, since the one-dimensional singleton has measure zero ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).) Then:

(a) [Regularity and gradient] $E$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$, of class $C^\infty$ on each of the open regions $\{|x|<a\}$, $\{|x|>a\}$; $\varphi\in C^1(\mathbb R^3)$, its displayed branch derivatives agree on $\{|x|=a\}$, and $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]);

(b) [Classical equations] for every $x$ with $|x|\ne a$,
$$\operatorname{div}E(x)=\rho(x)/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E(x)=0$$
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]);

(c) [Weak equations] the pair $(E,(\rho,0))$ satisfies the spatial distributional equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$: $E$ is $C^1$ on each side of the sphere $S_a=\{|x|=a\}$ with one-sided continuous traces that agree, $[E]=0$, so [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] gives
$$\operatorname{div}E=\{\operatorname{div}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[E]\,\delta_{S_a}=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[E]\,\delta_{S_a}=0,$$
with $\rho$ the displayed locally integrable density and no surface-charge term ([[def-em-weak-sources]], [[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]] for the sphere as a compact embedded smooth hypersurface); by the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e) these are the weak equations of the static model for this source, with zero singular part;

(d) [Energy] the field energy is finite and equals the assembly integral,
$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a},$$
computed with the polar formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]); the value agrees with the smooth-source identity of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] although the density here is only piecewise continuous;

(e) [Consistency and contrast] for $|x|>a$ the field is exactly the point-charge Coulomb field of total charge $Q$ centred at the origin ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (d) with $x_0=0$) although the source is the extended ball, and for $|x|<a$ it is the affine field $Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)$; $\varphi$ is continuous at $|x|=a$ and decays at infinity; the field is bounded on $\mathbb R^3$, so no divergence of field energy occurs for the extended source;

(f) [Scope] the example verifies the displayed candidate and its energy; it does not claim uniqueness of the solution (this would require boundary data and an infinity condition, and the density is not continuous), it asserts no empirical content, and the density $\rho$ is treated as a bounded $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ density with the sphere carrying no surface charge ($[E]=0$).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, $a>0$, $Q\in\mathbb R$, the density $\rho$, field $E$ and potential $\varphi$ displayed above, and the sphere $S_a=\{x:|x|=a\}$.

[F1] The polar formula and the sphere area $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, together with $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$ and $|B_1|=4\pi/3$, compute radial integrals; the one-dimensional singleton is null, so the sphere $\{|x|=a\}$ is Lebesgue null and integrals are unchanged by modifying the integrand there ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F2] Real powers, the chain rule and the algebra rules for derivatives compute the gradients and divergences below, and continuous partial derivatives give total differentiability with the gradient as derivative ([[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

[F3] Across a stationary interface the distributional divergence and curl of a field that is $C^1$ on each side with one-sided $C^1$ traces are the piecewise classical expressions plus the jump terms $n\cdot[F]\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\delta_S$, with $[F]=F_+-F_-$; the surface distribution $\delta_S$ is the surface integral functional, and the sphere is a compact embedded smooth hypersurface with two-sided normal ([[lem-em-interface-derivatives]], [[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]], [[def-distribution]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).

[F4] The smooth-branch Coulomb solution provides the exterior point-charge field $Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3)$ with its distributional identities, and the compact-source energy identity states that for smooth compactly supported densities the field energy $(\\varepsilon_0/2)\\int|E|^2$ equals the assembly integral $\\frac12\\int\\rho\\varphi$; the weak-solution predicate and the static-to-distributional reading are those of the framework ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]], [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]], [[def-em-weak-sources]], [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Setup: the density is bounded and supported in $\overline B_a$, hence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and locally integrable on $\Omega$; the sphere is null, so the value of $\rho$ there is immaterial ([F1]). Writing $r=|x|$ and $h(r):=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}$ for $r<a$ and $h(r):=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^3}$ for $r\ge a$, the field is $E(x)=h(r)x$ and the potential is the radial function $\varphi(x)=f(r)$ with $f(r)=\frac{Q(3a^2-r^2)}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}$ for $r\le a$ and $f(r)=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$ for $r\ge a$. Both branches are smooth on their open regions, $h$ is continuous at $r=a$ with common value $\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}$, and $f$ is continuous with $f(a)=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}$ from both branches; moreover $f'(r)=-rh(r)$ on each side, with common value $f'(a)=-\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}$, so the one-sided limits of $\nabla\varphi=f'(r)x/r$ agree on $S_a$ ([F2]). [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Clause (a): since $\varphi$ is continuous, smooth off the sphere, and its gradient has the common continuous extension $-E$ across the sphere, the continuous-partial-derivatives characterization gives differentiability at every point with $\nabla\varphi=-E$; $E$ is continuous because $h$ is, and both $E$ and $\varphi$ are smooth on each open side ([F2]). [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Clause (b): for $|x|<a$, $E(x)=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}x$ is affine, so $\operatorname{div}E=\frac{3Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}=\rho(x)/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$; for $|x|>a$, $E(x)=\frac{Qx}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3}$ is radial of the Coulomb shape, and the quotient rule with $\partial_i|x|=x_i/|x|$ gives $\operatorname{div}E=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_i(\frac{1}{|x|^3}-\frac{3x_i^2}{|x|^5})=0=\rho(x)/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ componentwise, the third components vanishing because $E$ has no dependence on $x_3$ beyond the radial one and all mixed terms cancel as in the radial computation ([F2]). [step 2.1, F1, F2]

4.1 Clause (c): the sphere $S_a$ is a compact embedded smooth two-sided hypersurface with outward normal $n(x)=x/|x|$; the field $E$ is $C^1$ on $\{|x|<a\}$ and on $\{|x|>a\}$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces on $S_a$, and by step 2.1 both traces are the continuous field $E$, so $[E]=E_+-E_-=0$ on $S_a$ ([F3]). The interface lemma [F3] therefore gives $\operatorname{div}E=\{\operatorname{div}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[E]\delta_{S_a}$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[E]\delta_{S_a}$; the jump terms vanish, and the piecewise expressions equal $\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $0$ respectively as locally integrable functions by step 3.1 and the nullity of the sphere ([F1], [F3]). Hence $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$; by the static-to-distributional reading these are the weak equations for the source $(\rho,0)$ with zero singular part ([F4]). [step 3.1, F1, F3, F4]

5.1 Clause (d), field energy: $|E|^2=h(r)^2r^2$, so the polar formula gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=4\pi\Bigl(\int_0^a\frac{Q^2r^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2a^6}r^2\,dr+\int_a^\infty\frac{Q^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2r^4}r^2\,dr\Bigr)=\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0^2}\Bigl(\frac{a^5}{5a^6}+\frac1a\Bigr)=\frac{3Q^2}{10\pi\varepsilon_0^2a},$$ using $\int_0^ar^4dr=a^5/5$ and $\int_a^\infty r^{-2}dr=1/a$ ([F1], [F2]); multiplying by $\varepsilon_0/2$ gives $\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int|E|^2=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a}$, which is finite. [step 4.1, F1, F2]

6.1 Clause (d), assembly integral: since $\rho$ vanishes off $\{|x|<a\}$, $$\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac12\cdot\frac{3Q}{4\pi a^3}\cdot\frac{Q}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}\int_{|x|<a}\bigl(3a^2-|x|^2\bigr)d\lambda_3,$$ and the polar formula gives $\int_{|x|<a}(3a^2-|x|^2)d\lambda_3=4\pi\int_0^a(3a^2r^2-r^4)dr=4\pi\bigl(a^5-\frac{a^5}{5}\bigr)=\frac{16\pi a^5}{5}$ ([F1]); hence $\frac12\int\rho\varphi=\frac12\cdot\frac{3Q^2}{32\pi^2\varepsilon_0a^6}\cdot\frac{16\pi a^5}{5}=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a}$, which equals the field energy of step 5.1; the same value as the smooth-source identity of [F4] is thus obtained although $\rho$ is only piecewise continuous, the computation being valid because the finiteness and equalities were verified directly for this density with a null interface ([F1]). [step 5.1, F1, F4]

7.1 Clause (e): for $|x|>a$ the second branch of $E$ is exactly the point-charge field $\frac{Qx}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3}$ of [F4] with $x_0=0$, so the exterior field is the Coulomb field of the total charge $Q$ even though the source is extended; for $|x|<a$ the field is the affine field $\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}x$; the potential is continuous at $|x|=a$ and decays as $|x|\to\infty$ by its exterior branch; and $|E(x)|\le\frac{|Q|}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}$ on all of $\mathbb R^3$, the maximum being attained at $|x|=a$, so the field energy is finite and no divergence occurs ([F1], [F2], [F4]). [step 6.1, F1, F2, F4]

8.1 Clause (f): the verification produced the displayed candidate, its pointwise equations off the sphere, its distributional equations with zero surface-charge jump, and its exact finite energy; no uniqueness is claimed, since uniqueness would require boundary data and an infinity condition and the density is not continuous, and the pair $(E,(\rho,0))$ is read through the weak predicate and the static-to-distributional dictionary only. No empirical content is asserted, and the sphere carries no surface charge because $[E]=0$; this is exactly the scope stated. [step 4.1, step 7.1, F3, F4] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no other choice principle is used. Let $k\ge1$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] (nonempty, bounded, open, and locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ graph function over a hyperplane). Then:

(a) [Compactness and finiteness] $\partial D$ is nonempty and compact; the complement $\mathbb R^3\setminus\partial D$ need not be connected here. Moreover $\partial D$ has finitely many connected components, and each connected component of $\partial D$ is compact.

(b) [Finite embedded presentation] the local boundary charts give finitely many regular injective $C^k$ parametrisations of $\partial D$ with $C^k$ coordinate transitions, of the graph type required by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]: writing a chart as $R(p)=(y,s)$, the graph map $y\mapsto R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ is injective, of class $C^k$, with $C^k$ inverse (the inverse is $p\mapsto\pi(R(p))$ restricted to the graph, where $\pi(y,s)=y$); consequently $\partial D$ is a compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurface, and for $k\ge1$ it carries the finite surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]].

(c) [Normal field] the outward unit normal $\nu$ of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a continuous unit normal field on $\partial D$, with $\nu(x)$ orthogonal to the tangent plane of the graph chart at each $x$; it is the field used by the Green and divergence items cited by this page's consumers.

The statement is geometric: it asserts no differentiability of $D$ beyond $C^k$, no boundedness of chart derivatives beyond the compact patches, and no connectedness of either $D$ or $\partial D$.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $k\ge1$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain; write $\partial D$ for its metric boundary ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]) and use the Euclidean metric $d_2$ with induced norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F1] The chart property: for every $x\in\partial D$ there are an open $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $x\in W$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ with $R(D\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s):s<h(y)\}$; in particular $\partial D\cap W=R^{-1}(\{(y,s):s=h(y)\}\cap R(W))$ ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]). Shrinking $W$ preserves this identity.

[F2] In such coordinates the outward normal is $\nu=(-Dh(y),1)/\sqrt{1+\lvert Dh(y)\rvert^2}$ transported by the orthogonal map $Q$, and it agrees on chart overlaps ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]).

[F3] Surface integration on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface is built from finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrisations with $C^1$ transitions and an ambient partition subordinate to the chart neighbourhoods ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[F4] For any compact Euclidean set covered by finitely many open sets $U_j$ there are smooth nonnegative $\chi_j$ with compact support in $U_j$ and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighbourhood of the set ([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).

[F5] The chart integral of [F3] defines a finite Borel measure independent of charts and partitions; in graph coordinates its density is $\sqrt{1+\lvert Dh\rvert^2}$; on a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal of [F2] is continuous ([[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]).

[F6] Metric boundary, interior and closure: $\partial A=\overline A\setminus\operatorname{int}(A)$, $\operatorname{int}(A)\subseteq A\subseteq\overline A$, every ball about an adherent point meets $A$, and $\operatorname{int}(A)$ is open ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

[F7] Open and closed sets; a set is closed exactly when its complement is open, and open/closed are preserved by finite unions, arbitrary intersections and complements ([[def-metric-topology]]).

[F8] $\overline A$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed superset of $A$; $A$ is closed if and only if $A=\overline A$ ([[thm-metric-closure-characterisation]]).

[F9] A subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F10] $A$ is bounded when $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0$ and $r>0$, where $B(x_0,r)=\{y:d_2(y,x_0)<r\}$; distances satisfy the triangle inequality ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-space]]).

[F11] $\mathbb R^3$ is polygonally connected and connected, and every path-connected space is connected ([[cor-rn-is-polygonally-connected-and-locally-path-connected]], [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]).

[F12] A continuous image of a connected space is connected ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-connected-space]]).

[F13] The only clopen subsets of a connected space are the empty set and the whole space ([[thm-connectedness-characterisations]]).

[F14] Components are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, cover the space, are maximal connected sets, and are closed ([[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]], [[thm-components-partition-and-are-closed]]).

[F15] A union of connected sets with a common point is connected ([[thm-unions-of-connected-sets]]).

[F16] Local connectedness at $x$ means that every open neighbourhood of $x$ contains an open connected neighbourhood of $x$; a set that is locally connected at each of its points is locally connected ([[def-locally-connected]]).

[F17] $C^k$ maps between open Euclidean sets, their composition rule, the chain rule, and the algebra of derivatives; $C^k$ means all partial derivatives through order $k$ exist and are continuous, and total differentiability implies continuity ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]]).

[F18] The Euclidean norm is a norm inducing $d_2$, so it is homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality; orthogonal maps are invertible linear isometries and preserve norms and distances, hence are continuous in both directions ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], [[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F19] Every norm on $\mathbb R^n$ is continuous for $d_2$, and $e_1$ denotes the first standard basis vector, with $\lVert e_1\rVert_2=1$ ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

[F20] The open ball $B_R(a)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, is a bounded $C^1$ domain with boundary the Euclidean sphere $S_R(a)$; the local graph function $h(w)=\sqrt{R^2-\lvert w\rvert^2}-R$ is $C^\infty$ on $\lvert w\rvert<R$, by iterated differentiation of the real power $s\mapsto s^{1/2}$ on $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]) composed with the polynomial $R^2-\lvert w\rvert^2$ ([[lem-euclidean-balls-are-bounded-c-one-domains]], [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $\partial D$ is closed. By [F6], $\partial D=\overline D\setminus\operatorname{int}(D)=\overline D\cap(\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}(D))$, an intersection of the closed set $\overline D$ [F8] with the complement of the open set $\operatorname{int}(D)$ [F6], hence closed [F7]. [F6, F7, F8]

1.2 $\partial D$ is bounded. Since $D$ is bounded, fix $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and $r>0$ with $D\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ [F10]. Let $x\in\overline D$. By [F6] the ball $B(x,1)$ meets $D$, so there is $y\in D$ with $d_2(x,y)<1$; then $d_2(y,x_0)<r$ and the triangle inequality gives $d_2(x,x_0)\le d_2(x,y)+d_2(y,x_0)<1+r$ [F10]. Hence $\overline D\subseteq B(x_0,1+r)$ is bounded, and $\partial D\subseteq\overline D$ is bounded [F10, F6]. [F6, F10]

1.3 Chart patches. Let $x\in\partial D$ and let $G$ be an open neighbourhood of $x$ in $\mathbb R^3$. Apply [F1] to get $W$, $R$, $B$, $h$ with the chart identity; replacing $W$ by the open set $W\cap G$ preserves it [F1], so assume $W\subseteq G$. Write $R(p)=(y,s)$, $\pi(y,s)=y$, put $y_x:=\pi(R(x))$, and set $B'':=\pi\bigl(R(W)\cap\{(y,s):s=h(y)\}\bigr)$. This is an open subset of $B$ containing $y_x$: the set $R(W)\cap\{s=h(y)\}$ is relatively open in the graph $\Gamma=\{(y,h(y)):y\in B\}$, and $\pi|_\Gamma:\Gamma\to B$ is a homeomorphism [F16], so its image is open; and $y_x\in B''$ because $x\in\partial D\cap W$ maps to a point of the graph [F1]. Define $X:B''\to\mathbb R^3$, $X(y):=R^{-1}(y,h(y))$. Then $X(B'')=\partial D\cap W$: every $X(y)$ lies in $\partial D\cap W$ by [F1], and conversely for $p\in\partial D\cap W$ the point $R(p)\in R(W)$ has $s=h(y)$ [F1], so $\pi(R(p))\in B''$ and $X(\pi(R(p)))=R^{-1}(y,h(y))=R^{-1}(R(p))=p$. Moreover $X$ is injective with inverse $\pi\circ R$ restricted to $X(B'')$, because $\pi(R(X(y)))=y$ and $X(\pi(R(p)))=p$ for $p=X(y)$. [F1, F16, given]

2.1 $\partial D\ne\varnothing$. Suppose $\partial D=\varnothing$. Then $\overline D\subseteq\operatorname{int}(D)$ by [F6], and since $\operatorname{int}(D)\subseteq D\subseteq\overline D$ [F6] we get $D=\overline D$, so $D$ is closed [F8] as well as open; that is, $D$ is clopen, and $D\ne\varnothing$ by hypothesis. Moreover $D\ne\mathbb R^3$: if $D=\mathbb R^3$ then $\mathbb R^3=D\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for the ball of step 1.2, but the point $w:=x_0+(r+1)e_1$ satisfies $d_2(w,x_0)=\lVert (r+1)e_1\rVert_2=(r+1)\lVert e_1\rVert_2=r+1>r$, so $w\in\mathbb R^3\setminus B(x_0,r)$ [F18, F19]. Thus $D$ is a proper nonempty clopen subset of the connected space $\mathbb R^3$ [F11], contradicting [F13]. Hence $\partial D\ne\varnothing$. [F6, F8, F10, F11, F13, F18, F19, step 1.2]

2.2 $\partial D$ is compact by [F9], being closed [step 1.1] and bounded [step 1.2]. [F9, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.3 $X$ is of class $C^k$, regular, and its inverse is $C^k$. The map $g(y):=(y,h(y))$ has components the coordinate functions and $h$, all $C^k$, so $g$ is $C^k$ with all partial derivatives continuous [F17]; $R^{-1}(z)=Q^{\mathsf T}(z-b)$ is affine with orthogonal linear part, hence $C^\infty$, continuous, with continuous inverse [F18]. By the chain rule $X=R^{-1}\circ g$ is $C^k$, hence continuous, with $DX(y)=Q^{\mathsf T}\circ Dg(y)$ [F17]. The differential $Dg(y)$ has first two rows the identity, hence is injective, and $Q^{\mathsf T}$ is invertible, so $DX(y)$ is injective at every $y$; thus $X$ is a regular injective parametrisation, regularity being exactly the injectivity of $DX(y)$ just proved. The inverse $\pi\circ R|_{X(B'')}$ is the restriction of the continuous map $\pi\circ R$ [F18] and is continuous at every point of $X(B'')$; so $X$ is a homeomorphism onto $X(B'')$. [F17, F18, step 1.3]

3.1 Connected sub-patches. Let $B_1$ be an open ball with $y_x\in B_1$ and $\overline{B_1}\subseteq B''$, and put $O_1:=W\cap R^{-1}(B_1\times\mathbb R)$, an open neighbourhood of $x$. Then $X(B_1)=\partial D\cap O_1$: the inclusion $\subseteq$ is [step 1.3] with $y\in B_1\subseteq B''$; conversely $p\in\partial D\cap O_1$ has $\pi(R(p))\in B''\cap B_1=B_1$ [step 1.3]; this set is relatively open in $\partial D$ because $O_1$ is open in $\mathbb R^3$ [F7]. The ball $B_1$ is path-connected: for $u,v\in B_1$ and $t\in[0,1]$ the triangle inequality and homogeneity of the norm give $\lVert(1-t)u+tv-y_x\rVert_2\le(1-t)\lVert u-y_x\rVert_2+t\lVert v-y_x\rVert_2<(1-t)\rho+t\rho=\rho$ when $B_1=B(y_x,\rho)$, so the segment $t\mapsto(1-t)u+tv$ stays in $B_1$ [F18]; thus $B_1$ is path-connected, hence connected [F11]. As the continuous image of $B_1$ under $X$ [step 2.3] the set $X(B_1)$ is connected [F12]. Since $B_1$ can be chosen with arbitrarily small radius, $\partial D$ is locally connected [F16]. [F7, F11, F12, F16, F18, step 1.3, step 2.3]

3.2 The normal field. In the coordinates of [step 1.3] the vector $(-Dh_j(y),1)$ is orthogonal to every tangent column $(e_i,\partial_i h_j(y))$ of [step 2.3] because $- (\partial_i h_j)(y)+(\partial_i h_j)(y)=0$, and it is nonzero, so $(-Dh_j,1)/\sqrt{1+\lvert Dh_j\rvert^2}$ is a unit normal field of the graph; by [F2] it is the prescribed outward normal $\nu$, transported by $Q_j$. Since $h_j$ is $C^k$ with $k\ge1$, $Dh_j$ is continuous, and the norm of $(-Dh_j(y),1)$ is $\sqrt{1+\lvert Dh_j(y)\rvert^2}\ge1$, so $y\mapsto\nu(X_j(y))$ is continuous as a composition of continuous maps on each patch [F17, F19]; by [F5] the field $\nu$ is defined consistently on overlaps and is continuous on all of $\partial D$. This proves (c). [F2, F5, F17, F19, step 1.3, step 2.3]

4.1 Components are open. Let $C$ be a connected component of $\partial D$ [F14] and let $x\in C$. By [step 3.1] and [F16] applied to the open set $\partial D$ itself, there is a connected open-in-$\partial D$ set $V$ with $x\in V$. Then $V\cup C$ is connected [F15], contains $x$, and contains the maximal connected set $C$ [F14], so $V\cup C=C$, i.e. $V\subseteq C$. Hence every point of $C$ has a neighbourhood contained in $C$, so $C$ is open in $\partial D$ [F7]. [F7, F14, F15, step 3.1]

4.2 Finite embedded presentation. The family of all open balls $B_1$ with $\overline{B_1}\subseteq B''$ for charts of [step 1.3] over all $x\in\partial D$ produces open sets $O_1=W\cap R^{-1}(B_1\times\mathbb R)$ whose patches $X(B_1)=\partial D\cap O_1$ [step 3.1] cover $\partial D$; compactness [step 2.2] gives a finite subcover $O_1,\dots,O_N$ with parametrisations $X_j:B_{1,j}\to\partial D\cap O_j$, each regular, injective and $C^k$ [step 2.3] with connected open parameter balls. Let $T:=X_\ell^{-1}\circ X_j$ be a transition, defined on the open set $X_j^{-1}(\partial D\cap O_j\cap O_\ell)\subseteq B_{1,j}$: it is a composition of the homeomorphisms of [step 1.3] and [step 2.3], hence a bijection onto its image, and it is given by $T(y)=\pi(R_\ell(R_j^{-1}(y,h_j(y))))$, a composition of affine $C^\infty$ maps with the $C^k$ map $g_j(y)=(y,h_j(y))$ and the linear projection $\pi$; so $T$ is $C^k$ with $C^k$ inverse $X_j^{-1}\circ X_\ell$ [F17]. With $K:=\partial D$ and the finitely many open sets $O_j$ covering it, [F4] supplies smooth $\chi_j$ with compact support in $O_j$ and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a neighbourhood of $\partial D$. This is exactly the finite presentation used by the surface integral [F3]; by [F5] the chart integral then defines the finite Borel surface measure of $\partial D$, independent of the charts and partition, with graph density $\sqrt{1+\lvert Dh_j\rvert^2}$, and $\partial D$ is a compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurface. This proves (b). [F3, F4, F5, F17, step 2.2, step 1.3, step 2.3, step 3.1]

5.1 Finitely many components. The components of $\partial D$ are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, cover $\partial D$ [F14], and are open [step 4.1]; being pairwise disjoint, every subfamily with the same union has the same members. Hence they form an open cover of the compact space $\partial D$ [step 2.2], which therefore has a finite subcover [F9]; any component meets that finite union and is therefore one of its finitely many members. So $\partial D$ has finitely many components; each is closed [F14] and bounded (being a subset of bounded $\partial D$), hence compact [F9]. This proves (a). [F9, F14, step 2.2, step 4.1]

6.1 The complement need not be connected. Let $c_1:=0$, $c_2:=4e_1$ and $D_0:=B_1(c_1)\cup B_1(c_2)$. Each ball is a bounded $C^1$ domain whose local graph function is $C^\infty$ [F20]; since $d_2(c_1,c_2)=4>2$, the closed balls are disjoint, and at a boundary point of $B_1(c_1)$ the chart of [F20] shrunk to the open complement of the closed ball around $c_2$ exhibits $D_0$ locally as the same subgraph, and symmetrically, so $D_0$ is a bounded $C^k$ domain for every $k\ge1$ [F1, F20]. Its boundary is $\partial D_0=S_1(c_1)\cup S_1(c_2)$: a point of either sphere lies in $\overline{D_0}$ but, every ball about it meeting the exterior of that ball, outside $\operatorname{int}(D_0)$ [F6, F20], while a point of $B_1(c_1)$ or $B_1(c_2)$ lies in the interior of $D_0$, and a point outside both closed balls has a ball avoiding $D_0$ entirely [F6, F7, F20]. Now put $U:=B_1(c_1)$ and $V:=B_1(c_2)\cup(\mathbb R^3\setminus(\overline B_1(c_1)\cup\overline B_1(c_2)))$. Both are open [F7, F20], nonempty, and disjoint, because $B_1(c_2)\subseteq\overline B_1(c_2)$ is disjoint from the exterior term; and $U\cup V=\mathbb R^3\setminus\partial D_0$, since the removed set $\partial D_0$ is exactly the union of the two spheres. Thus $U$ and $V$, open in the subspace $\mathbb R^3\setminus\partial D_0$, nonempty, disjoint and covering it, form a separation of the complement [F6, F7]. This witnesses the asserted non-claim for every $k\ge1$. [F1, F6, F7, F20] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the boundary interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $k\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain, and let $D_1,\dots,D_m$ ($m\ge0$) be bounded $C^k$ domains with pairwise disjoint closures whose closures satisfy $\overline{D_1}\cup\cdots\cup\overline{D_m}\subset\Omega$ strictly inside $\Omega$. Put

$$\Omega_v:=\Omega\setminus\bigl(\overline{D_1}\cup\cdots\cup\overline{D_m}\bigr).$$

Then:

(a) [Domain] $\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^k$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] (in particular nonempty, bounded and open);

(b) [Boundary] $\partial\Omega_v=\partial\Omega\cup\partial D_1\cup\cdots\cup\partial D_m$, a disjoint union of nonempty compact sets; the compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurfaces $\partial\Omega,\partial D_1,\dots,\partial D_m$ are pairwise disjoint ([[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]);

(c) [Normals and sign] the outward unit normal of $\Omega_v$ at a point of $\partial\Omega$ equals the outward unit normal of $\Omega$, and at a point of $\partial D_j$ it equals the negative of the outward unit normal of $D_j$ defined by [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] and [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; so the outward normal of $\Omega_v$ on $\partial D_j$ points from the vacuum into the conductor;

(d) [Componentwise statement] $\Omega_v$ has finitely many connected components. Each component $U$ is an open bounded $C^k$ domain; its boundary is the compact restricted subset $\partial U\subseteq\partial\Omega_v$, a union of the boundary components incident to $U$. The normal formulas in (c) restrict to those boundary pieces. It need not have every boundary piece of $\Omega_v$, and connectedness of $\Omega_v$ is not asserted.

No regularity beyond $C^k$, no convexity and no topological simplicity is claimed.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in [[def-countable-choice]]; a bounded $C^k$ domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, $k\ge1$; bounded $C^k$ domains $D_1,\dots,D_m$ ($m\ge0$) with pairwise disjoint closures all strictly contained in $\Omega$. All metric notions use the Euclidean metric $d_2$ and norm on $\mathbb R^3$; write $B(x,r)$ for open balls, $\overline A$ for closure and $\partial A$ for the metric boundary.

[F1] A bounded set lies in some ball; closures of bounded sets are bounded; a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded; a finite union of compact or of closed sets is closed, and a finite union of bounded sets is bounded ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[def-metric-compactness]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

[F2] Closure is the smallest closed superset: $A\subseteq F$ with $F$ closed implies $\overline A\subseteq F$, and $A$ is closed iff $A=\overline A$. The boundary is $\partial A=\overline A\setminus\operatorname{int}(A)$, and for open $A$ the interior is $A$ itself; boundaries are closed; every ball about a point of $\overline A$ meets $A$ ([[thm-metric-closure-characterisation]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

[F3] Distances: $d(x,A)$ is the infimum of $\{d(x,a):a\in A\}$ for nonempty $A$; a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum; $|d(x,a)-d(x,a')|\le d(a,a')$, so $q\mapsto d(x,q)$ is continuous, and if $K$ is compact with $x\notin K$ then $d(x,K)>0$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[def-metric-space]], [[def-metric-continuity]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]).

[F4] The chart property and the outward normal: at every boundary point $x$ of a bounded $C^k$ domain $D$ there are an open $W\ni x$, a rigid motion $R=Q\cdot+b$ with orthogonal $Q$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, $h\in C^k(B)$ with $R(D\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s):s<h(y)\}$, and the prescribed outward normal in the chart is $Q(-Dh(y),1)/\sqrt{1+\lvert Dh(y)\rvert^2}$, agreeing on overlaps; shrinking $W$ preserves the identity ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]).

[F5] For a bounded $C^k$ domain the boundary is nonempty, compact, and a compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurface with finitely many connected components; hence also $\partial D\cap W=R^{-1}(\{(y,h(y)):y\in B\}\cap R(W))$ and points of $R(W)$ with $s>h(y)$ lie outside $\overline D$ ([[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]).

[F6] Let $B_1\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a ball, $h\in C(B_1;\mathbb R)$, $c\in\mathbb R$ and $\delta>0$, and suppose $|h(y)-c|\le\delta/4$ for all $y\in B_1$. With $H:=c+\delta/2$ one then has $h(y)<H<h(y)+\delta$ for every $y\in B_1$. Consequently each of the regions $S_+:=\{(y,s):y\in B_1,\ h(y)<s<h(y)+\delta\}$ and $S_-:=\{(y,s):y\in B_1,\ h(y)-\delta<s<h(y)\}$ is polygonally connected: for $u=(y_1,s_1)$ and $v=(y_2,s_2)$ in $S_+$ the segment $[y_1,y_2]$ lies in the convex ball $B_1$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]), every point $(y,H)$ of the middle segment satisfies $h(y)<H<h(y)+\delta$ by the displayed inequality, and the vertical segments from $s_1$ up to $H$ at $y_1$ and from $H$ down to $s_2$ at $y_2$ have all their intermediate heights between the endpoint heights, hence also lie in $S_+$; the same with $H_-:=c-\delta/2$ and the reversed inequalities applies to $S_-$. These three-segment paths are polygonal paths ([[def-polygonal-path-and-polygonal-connectedness]], [[lem-euclidean-polygonal-paths-are-continuous]]), so a polygonally connected set is path-connected and hence connected ([[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]).

[F7] Rigid motions and reflections: $R=Q\cdot+b$ and $\rho(y,s)=(y,-s)$ are continuous bijections with continuous inverses and preserve distances; images of connected sets under them are connected ([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]], [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-connected-space]]).

[F8] $C^k$ maps and their algebra: $h\in C^k$ remains $C^k$ under negation; the coordinate functions $(y,s)\mapsto y$ and $(y,s)\mapsto s$ and affine maps are $C^\infty$; the set $\{s>h(y)\}$ is open as the preimage of the open set $(0,\infty)$ under the continuous map $s-h(y)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-continuity-preimage-characterisation]], [[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]]).

[F9] Every connected component of an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is open in $\mathbb R^n$ and polygonally connected; components are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, cover the space, are the maximal connected subsets, and are closed; a union of connected sets with a common point is connected ([[cor-components-of-open-subsets-of-rn-are-polygonally-connected]], [[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]], [[thm-components-partition-and-are-closed]], [[thm-unions-of-connected-sets]]).

[F10] A nonempty space is connected exactly when its only clopen subsets are the empty set and the whole space; a connected space is not the disjoint union of two nonempty open subsets; $\mathbb R^3$ is connected ([[thm-connectedness-characterisations]], [[def-connected-space]], [[cor-rn-is-polygonally-connected-and-locally-path-connected]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Put $K:=\overline{D_1}\cup\cdots\cup\overline{D_m}$ (so $K=\varnothing$ when $m=0$). Each $\overline{D_j}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact [F1, F2]; $K$ is a finite union of compact sets, hence closed and bounded and therefore compact [F1]. By hypothesis $K\subseteq\Omega$, so $\partial\Omega\cap K=\varnothing$, and the sets $\overline{D_1},\dots,\overline{D_m}$ are pairwise disjoint. Put $\Omega_v:=\Omega\setminus K$; it is open, since $\Omega$ is open and $K$ is closed, and bounded, since $\Omega$ is; and for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ we have $d(x,K)>0$ by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 $\Omega_v\ne\varnothing$. Since $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^k$ domain, $\partial\Omega\ne\varnothing$ [F5]; fix $x\in\partial\Omega$ and put $\rho:=d(x,K)>0$ [F3, step 1.1]. Every ball about $x$ meets $\Omega$ while $x\notin\Omega$ [F2], so there is $y\in B(x,\rho/2)\cap\Omega$. Then $d(y,q)\ge d(x,q)-d(x,y)>\rho-\rho/2>0$ for every $q\in K$, so $y\notin K$; hence $y\in\Omega_v$. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

2.2 $\partial\Omega_v=\partial\Omega\cup\partial D_1\cup\cdots\cup\partial D_m$ as a disjoint union. For $x\in\partial D_j$: $x\in\overline{D_j}\subseteq\Omega$, so $x\notin\Omega_v$; every ball about $x$ meets $D_j\subseteq K$ [F2], and for a sufficiently small ball it lies in $\Omega$ and misses $\bigcup_{i\ne j}\overline{D_i}$ (positive distances between the pairwise disjoint compact sets [F3]) and meets $\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline{D_j}$ [F4, F5], hence meets $\Omega_v$; so $x\in\partial\Omega_v$. For $x\in\partial\Omega$: every ball about $x$ meets $\Omega$ while $x\notin K$ with $d(x,K)>0$ [step 1.1, F3], so small balls meet $\Omega_v$; and $x\notin\Omega_v$; so $x\in\partial\Omega_v$. Conversely let $x\in\partial\Omega_v$; then $x\in\overline{\Omega_v}\subseteq\overline\Omega$ and $x\notin\Omega_v$ [F2]. If $x\notin\Omega$ then $x\in\partial\Omega$. If $x\in\Omega$, then $x\in K$, say $x\in\overline{D_j}$; if $x\in D_j$ then $D_j$ is open and a small ball about $x$ lies in $D_j\subseteq K$, so it misses $\Omega_v$, contradicting $x\in\overline{\Omega_v}$; hence $x\in\overline{D_j}\setminus D_j=\partial D_j$. The displayed pieces are pairwise disjoint because $K\subseteq\Omega$ and the $\overline{D_j}$ are pairwise disjoint, and each is nonempty and compact [F5]. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 At every point of $\partial\Omega_v$ the vacuum region $\Omega_v$ is locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ graph. Let $x\in\partial\Omega$. Use the chart of [F4] for $\Omega$ at $x$ and let $\rho:=d(x,K)>0$ [step 1.1, F3]; replacing $W$ by the open set $W\cap B(x,\rho/2)$ preserves the chart identity [F4] and makes $W\cap K=\varnothing$, so $\Omega_v\cap W=\Omega\cap W$ and $R(\Omega_v\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{s<h(y)\}$. Let $x\in\partial D_j$. Use the chart of [F4] for $D_j$ at $x$, and replace $W$ by an open ball about $x$ contained in $\Omega$ and avoiding $\bigcup_{i\ne j}\overline{D_i}$; this keeps the chart identity [F4] and gives $\Omega_v\cap W=W\setminus\overline{D_j}$, whose image is $R(W)\cap\{s>h(y)\}$: points with $s<h(y)$ lie in $D_j$, points with $s=h(y)$ lie on $\partial D_j$ [F4, F5]. Put $\rho_0(y,s):=(y,-s)$ and $R_0:=\rho_0\circ R$, $h_0:=-h$; then $R_0$ is a rigid motion, $h_0\in C^k$, and $R_0(\Omega_v\cap W)=R_0(W)\cap\{s<h_0(y)\}$ [F7, F8]. [F4, F5, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 2.2]

3.2 The boundary pieces of [step 2.2] are the compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurfaces of the boundary lemma, and they are pairwise disjoint with nonempty compact pieces; this is (b). [F5, step 2.2]

4.1 $\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^k$ domain: it is nonempty [step 2.1], bounded and open [step 1.1], and by [step 2.2] every boundary point is treated by one of the two local charts of [step 3.1], each exhibiting $\Omega_v$ locally as the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ function over an open ball after a rigid motion [F4, F8]. This is (a). [F4, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1]

4.2 The normals. In the $\partial\Omega$ case of [step 3.1] the chart data for $\Omega_v$ and for $\Omega$ are identical, so the prescribed outward normal of $\Omega_v$, computed by the formula of [F4], equals that of $\Omega$ at every point of $\partial\Omega$. In the $\partial D_j$ case, the chart of $\Omega_v$ is $R_0=\rho_0\circ R$ with graph $h_0=-h$; the formula of [F4] gives the vacuum normal $(Q\rho_0)(-Dh_0(y),1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh_0(y)|^2}=(Q\rho_0)(Dh(y),1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}$, and since $\rho_0(Dh,1)=(Dh,-1)=-(-Dh,1)$ this equals $-Q(-Dh(y),1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}$, the negative of the prescribed outward normal of $D_j$ [F4, F8]. This is (c). [F4, F7, F8, step 3.1]

4.3 Connected collars and patches. Fix one of the charts of [step 3.1]. Write $R$ for its rigid motion, $W$ for its domain, $h$ for its graph function and $B''$ for the set of parameters $y$ with $(y,h(y))\in R(W)$, an open subset of $B$ containing the parameter of the distinguished boundary point. Choose a ball $B_1$ with $\overline{B_1}\subseteq B''$; the compact graph set $G:=\{(y,h(y)):y\in\overline{B_1}\}\subseteq R(W)$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]) is disjoint from the closed set $\mathbb R^3\setminus R(W)$, so $\delta:=d(G,\mathbb R^3\setminus R(W))>0$ [F3]. By continuity of $h$ at the parameter $y_x$ of the distinguished point choose a ball $B_1'\subseteq B_1$ around $y_x$ with $|h(y)-h(y_x)|\le\delta/4$ for $y\in B_1'$ [F8]. In the inner case the region $T:=\{(y,s):y\in B_1',\ h(y)<s<h(y)+\delta\}$ is contained in $R(W)$ (every point of $T$ is within $\delta$ of its graph point, which lies in $G$) and in $\{s>h(y)\}$, so $R^{-1}(T)\subseteq\Omega_v\cap W$; in the outer case the same holds for $T:=\{(y,s):y\in B_1',\ h(y)-\delta<s<h(y)\}$ and $\{s<h(y)\}$, by the descriptions of [step 3.1]. The set $T$ is polygonally connected by [F6], hence connected, so $N:=R^{-1}(T)$ is connected as its continuous image [F7]; moreover $N$ accumulates at every point $X(y)$ of the patch $P:=X(B_1')\subseteq\partial\Omega_v$, since the points $(y,h(y)\pm\varepsilon)$ with $0<\varepsilon<\delta$ lie in $T$ and converge to $(y,h(y))$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. [F3, F6, F7, F8, step 3.1]

5.1 Each connected component of the open set $\Omega_v$ is open in $\mathbb R^3$ and polygonally connected [F9]; in particular every component is open. [F9, step 4.1]

5.2 Each patch is incident to exactly one component. With $N$ and $P$ as in [step 4.3], $N\subseteq\Omega_v$ is connected and nonempty, so it lies in a unique component $U$ of $\Omega_v$ [F9]. If a component $U_1$ of $\Omega_v$ has a boundary point in $P$, then $U_1$ meets $N$: every neighbourhood of a boundary point of $U_1$ meets $U_1$, and $N$ contains points of $\Omega_v$ arbitrarily close to each point of $P$ [step 4.3]; hence $N\cup U_1$ is connected [F9] and maximality of the component $U_1$ gives $N\subseteq U_1$, so $U_1=U$. Thus every patch is incident to exactly one component, namely the component containing its collar $N$. [F9, step 4.3]

6.1 Every component is incident to a patch. Let $U$ be a component of $\Omega_v$. It is nonempty, open and bounded, so $\partial U\ne\varnothing$: otherwise $\overline U=U$, making $U$ a nonempty clopen proper subset of the connected space $\mathbb R^3$ (proper since $U$ is bounded), contradicting [F10]. Also $\partial U\subseteq\partial\Omega_v$: if $x\in\partial U$ then $x\in\overline U\subseteq\overline{\Omega_v}$ and $x\notin\Omega_v$, because $\Omega_v$ is open and $x$ lies neither in the open set $U$ nor in its open complement in $\Omega_v$ [F2, F9]. By [step 2.2] and [step 3.2] every point of $\partial\Omega_v$ lies on one of the finitely many boundary pieces, and the patches of the kind constructed in [step 4.3] cover each piece; so some such patch $P$ meets $\partial U$, and [step 5.2] identifies $U$ as the unique component incident to $P$. [F2, F9, F10, step 2.2, step 3.2, step 5.2]

7.1 Finitely many components. The patches of the kind constructed in [step 4.3], for all boundary points, cover $\partial\Omega_v$ [step 6.1], and $\partial\Omega_v$ is compact [step 3.2]; hence finitely many of them already cover $\partial\Omega_v$. Each determines exactly one component [step 5.2], and every component is determined by one of them [step 6.1]; therefore the components of $\Omega_v$ are among these finitely many, so $\Omega_v$ has finitely many connected components. [step 3.2, step 5.2, step 6.1]

8.1 Each component is a bounded $C^k$ domain with the stated boundary. Let $U$ be a component of $\Omega_v$ and let $P$ be a patch incident to $U$ [step 6.1]. The local description of [step 3.1] shows that, in the chart of $P$, $U$ coincides with the one-sided region described there, hence is locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of the $C^k$ function $h$ (outer case) or of the reflected $C^k$ function $h_0=-h$ (inner case) over a ball [F4, F8, step 3.1, step 5.2]. So $U$ is a bounded $C^k$ domain: it is open [step 5.1], bounded (a subset of bounded $\Omega_v$) and nonempty [F9]. Every point of a patch incident to $U$ is a boundary point of $U$ (it lies in $\partial\Omega_v$ and in the closure of the collar $N\subseteq U$ [step 4.3, step 5.2]), and conversely every boundary point of $U$ lies in a patch incident to $U$ [step 6.1]; hence $\partial U$ equals the union of the finitely many patches incident to $U$, a compact subset of $\partial\Omega_v$ [step 3.2]. Finally, let $C$ be a connected component of $\partial\Omega_v$; the assignment to $x\in C$ of the component of $\Omega_v$ incident to a patch containing $x$ takes values in a finite set and is locally constant on $C$ (near a point of a patch it is given by the single component of that patch [step 5.2]), so it is constant on the connected set $C$ [F10]; hence each boundary component of $\partial\Omega_v$ is incident to exactly one component of $\Omega_v$, and $\partial U$ is a union of such boundary components. The normal formulas of [step 4.2] apply verbatim to each piece of $\partial U$, since they are the same local charts. This is (d); connectedness of $\Omega_v$ itself is neither assumed nor asserted. [F4, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, step 3.2, step 4.3, step 5.2, step 6.1, step 7.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $H:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_3>0\}$ be the open upper half-space, let $a>0$ and $p:=a e_3\in H$. Let $w:\overline H\setminus\{p\}\to\mathbb R$ be a function (closure as in [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]) with:

(i) $w$ is continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]) on $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$ and of class $C^2$ with $\Delta w=0$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]);

(ii) $w=0$ on $\partial H=\{x_3=0\}$;

(iii) $|x-p|w(x)\to0$ as $x\to p$, $x\ne p$;

(iv) $w(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ within $H$: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $R>0$ with $|w(x)|\le\varepsilon$ for all $x\in H\setminus\overline B_R(0)$.

Then $w=0$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$.

The conclusion is a uniqueness statement for the stated class only: no removable-singularity theorem, no pole condition beyond the sub-Coulomb growth (iii), no boundary regularity of $\partial H$ beyond the flat graph, and no claim about $w$ outside $H$ are asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions


**Given:** The open upper half-space $H=\{x_3>0\}$, the point $p=ae_3$ with $a>0$, and a function $w:\overline H\setminus\{p\}\to\mathbb R$ satisfying (i)-(iv) of the statement. Write $B_r(q)$ for the open ball and use the Euclidean norm and metric on $\mathbb R^3$.

[F1] The weak maximum principle: if $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, is bounded, nonempty and open and $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ satisfies $\Delta u\ge0$ on $\Omega$, then $\max_{\overline\Omega}u=\max_{\partial\Omega}u$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]).

[F2] A $C^2$ function is harmonic where $\Delta u=0$; $\Delta$ is defined as the sum of the pure second partial derivatives, is linear on $C^2$ functions and annihilates constants ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F3] For $n=3$ the fundamental solution is $\Phi(x)=|x|^{-1}/\omega_2$ with $\omega_2>0$, and for every pole $q$ the function $x\mapsto\Phi(x-q)$ is smooth and harmonic on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{q\}$; the function $b_q(x):=|x-q|^{-1}=\omega_2\,\Phi(x-q)$ is therefore a positive constant multiple of a harmonic function, hence $C^\infty$ and harmonic off $q$, and it is continuous wherever it is defined ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], [[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F4] An open ball is open, its closure is the corresponding closed ball, and $x\mapsto|x-q|$ is continuous for the Euclidean metric; the reciprocal $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous on $t>0$; a function with $|x-q|\ge\delta>0$ on its domain has $|b_q(x)-b_q(y)|\le|x-y|/\delta^2$ there, by the reverse triangle inequality ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-topology]], [[def-metric-space]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-metric-continuity]], [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]).

[F5] Closure is the smallest closed superset: if $A\subseteq F$ and $F$ is closed then $\overline A\subseteq F$; closed balls and spheres in $\mathbb R^3$ are compact, hence closed ([[thm-metric-closure-characterisation]], [[cor-euclidean-closed-balls-and-spheres-are-compact]]).

[F6] The boundary of the open set $U$ is $\partial U=\overline U\setminus U$; for an open set the interior is the set itself ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

[F7] Unwinding hypothesis (iii): for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $|w(x)|\le\varepsilon/|x-p|$ for all $x$ in $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$ with $0<|x-p|<\delta$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F8] Hypothesis (iv) says exactly that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\rho>0$ with $|w(x)|\le\varepsilon$ for all $x\in H$ with $|x|>\rho$ ([[def-metric-ball]]).

[F9] Countable Choice holds in the ambient measure conventions inherited from the kernel supplier; the argument below is pointwise and uses no choice principle ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $y\in H\setminus\{p\}$ and $\eta>0$. By [F8] there is $\rho>0$ with $|w|\le\eta$ on $H\cap\{|x|>\rho\}$; put $R:=\max\{\rho,2a,|y|\}+1$, so that $R>|p|+a$, $R>|y|$ and $|w|\le\eta$ on $H\cap\{|x|\ge R\}$. By [F7] there is $\delta_0>0$ with $|w(x)|\le\eta/|x-p|$ whenever $0<|x-p|<\delta_0$; put $\delta:=\tfrac12\min\{\delta_0,a/2,|y-p|,R-|p|\}$, so $0<\delta<a/2$, $\delta<|y-p|$, $\delta<R-|p|$ and $\delta<\delta_0$. Define the open set $U:=H\cap B_R(0)\cap\{x:|x-p|>\delta\}$, the barrier $b(x):=|x-p|^{-1}$, and $v_\pm:=\pm w-\eta(1+b)$ on $U$. [given, F3, F7, F8]

2.1 $U$ is bounded, nonempty and open, and $y\in U$; explicitly, $R>|y|$ and $\delta<|y-p|$ put $y$ in $U$. The closure satisfies $\overline U\subseteq\overline H\cap\overline{B_R(0)}\cap\{x:|x-p|\ge\delta\}$: each of $\overline H$, $\overline{B_R(0)}$ and $\{x:|x-p|\ge\delta\}$ is closed (the last is the complement of the open ball $B_\delta(p)$) and contains $U$, so [F5] applies factor by factor. In particular $|x-p|\ge\delta>0$ on $\overline U$, so $p\notin\overline U$ and $\overline U\subseteq\overline H\setminus\{p\}$. [F4, F5, F8, step 1.1]

3.1 Each $v_\pm$ lies in $C^2(U)\cap C(\overline U)$ and satisfies $\Delta v_\pm=0$ on $U$. Indeed $U\subseteq H\setminus\{p\}$ by construction, where $w$ is $C^2$ and $\Delta w=0$, while $b=\omega_2\Phi(\cdot-p)$ is $C^\infty$ and harmonic off $p$ [F3]; constants are $C^\infty$; $\Delta$ is linear and annihilates constants [F2], so $\Delta v_\pm=\pm\Delta w-\eta(0+\Delta b)=0$. Continuity on $\overline U$ holds because $w$ is continuous there by (i) and step 2.1, and $b$ is continuous on $\overline U$ by [F3] and [F4], the bound $|x-p|\ge\delta$ giving $|b(x)-b(y)|\le|x-y|/\delta^2$; sums and scalar multiples of continuous functions are continuous [F4]. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Each $v_\pm$ is nonpositive on $\partial U$. Let $x\in\partial U=\overline U\setminus U$ [F6]. Since $x\in\overline U$ and $x\notin U$, at least one of $x_3=0$, $|x|=R$, $|x-p|=\delta$ holds, by the description of $\overline U$ in step 2.1 and the definition of $U$. If $x_3=0$ then $w(x)=0$ by (ii), so $v_\pm(x)=-\eta(1+b(x))<0$. Otherwise $x_3>0$, and since at least one of the three conditions holds, $|x|=R$ or $|x-p|=\delta$ (or both); if $|x|=R$ then $|w(x)|\le\eta$ by the choice of $R$ in step 1.1, so $v_\pm(x)\le\eta-\eta(1+b(x))=-\eta b(x)<0$, and if $|x-p|=\delta$ then $|w(x)|\le\eta/\delta=\eta/|x-p|$ by the choice of $\delta$ in step 1.1 (and $x\in\overline H\setminus\{p\}$ by step 2.1), so $v_\pm(x)\le\eta b(x)-\eta(1+b(x))=-\eta<0$. [F6, given, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The weak maximum principle applies to each $v_\pm$ on the bounded nonempty open set $U$ [step 2.1, step 3.1] and gives $\max_{\overline U}v_\pm=\max_{\partial U}v_\pm\le0$ by step 3.2, so $v_\pm\le0$ on $\overline U$. In particular at $y\in U\subseteq\overline U$, $\pm w(y)\le\eta(1+|y-p|^{-1})$. [F1, step 3.1, step 3.2]

5.1 Since $\eta>0$ was arbitrary in step 1.1 and the bound of step 4.1 holds for every $\eta>0$, the real number $t:=|w(y)|$ satisfies $t\le\eta(1+|y-p|^{-1})$ for every $\eta>0$; if $t>0$ then $\eta:=t/\bigl(2(1+|y-p|^{-1})\bigr)>0$ gives $t\le t/2<t$, a contradiction, so $t=0$, that is $w(y)=0$. As $y\in H\setminus\{p\}$ was arbitrary, $w=0$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$. This proves uniqueness in the stated sub-Coulomb class; no removable-singularity theorem, no boundedness or growth assumption beyond (iii)-(iv), and no boundary regularity beyond the flat trace (ii) was used, and the only ambient choice convention is the one inherited from the kernel interfaces [F9]. [given, F9, step 1.1, step 4.1] ∎
