## Postulate

Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following coarse-graining convention for matter. Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its units, its fields and its sources be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis of the smoothing theorem cited in clause (b).

**(a) [Averaging length, kernel and footprint]** Fix $\ell>0$ and nonnegative $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\int\eta=1$, in the Euclidean test-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Put $\eta_\ell(x)=\ell^{-3}\eta(x/\ell)$, $K=\operatorname{supp}\eta$ and choose a declared finite bound $R_\eta>0$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_{R_\eta}(0)$. The kernel and length are fixed data; the imported mass-one mollifier definition [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]] does not require $K\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$. At $x$ the exact averaging footprint is $x-\ell K$. Define the open interior averaging domain

$$\Omega_{\ell,\eta}:=\{x\in\Omega:x-\ell K\subseteq\Omega\}.$$

The sufficient condition $\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega)>\ell R_\eta$ implies membership. If the additional unit-support condition $K\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$ is declared, the original sufficient region $\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega)>\ell$ and the ball $B_\ell(x)$ are valid special cases; unit support is not inferred from mass one.

**(b) [Averaged fields and input regularity]** For an open spatial domain $V$, locally integrable means measurable and absolutely integrable on every compact subset of $V$, componentwise for maps to $\mathbb R^m$, $m=1$ or $3$ ([[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]). First suppose $F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$ has a locally integrable spatial slice $F(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$ under consideration. No integrability across the boundary of $\Omega$ is required for the interior branch. Define, for $x\in\Omega_{\ell,\eta}$,

$$F_\ell(x,t)=\int_\Omega\eta_\ell(x-y)F(y,t)\,dy.$$

The compact footprint lies in $\Omega$, so this integral exists absolutely, and for each such $t$ it is smooth in $x$ on $\Omega_{\ell,\eta}$ with

$$\partial_x^\alpha F_\ell(x,t)=\int_\Omega(\partial^\alpha\eta_\ell)(x-y)F(y,t)\,dy$$

for every multi-index; these are applications of the pinned mollifier smoothing supplier [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]] after a local compact cutoff ([[lem-complex-translation-and-approximate-identity-interfaces]]), not an assumption that zero extension across the original boundary is locally integrable. For each admissible fixed $t$ the spatial convolution is measurable in $x$ and independent of a.e.-equal spatial representatives ([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]); no joint $(x,t)$ measurability follows from the every-slice hypothesis alone. Joint $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega\times I)$ input alone instead gives these slice statements for almost every $t$, by local Fubini on compact spatial/time exhaustions ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-countable-union-of-null-is-null]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]); it gives no every-time slice claim. A claim for every $t$ must explicitly supply locally integrable slices for every $t$ (for example jointly continuous fields supply that condition). A spacetime a.e. class alone determines the resulting averages only for almost every $t$; changing an exceptional time slice may change its pointwise-time assignment. Spatial smoothing asserts no time differentiability or joint smoothness without separately stated time hypotheses.

**[Compatible extension branch]** If a declared extension $\widehat F(\cdot,t)$ agrees with $F$ a.e. on $\Omega$ and is locally integrable on an open larger spatial domain $V$, use the same formula there for all $x$ whose compact footprint lies in $V$. If $V=\mathbb R^3$ and every declared slice is globally locally integrable, the average is defined and spatially smooth on all $\mathbb R^3\times I$. If only joint local integrability of the extension is supplied, the global spatial conclusion is for almost every $t$ unless the every-slice hypothesis is added. The zero extension is an allowed choice only when it meets this local-integrability condition: equivalently, at each declared $t$, $\int_{Q\cap\Omega}|F(y,t)|\,dy<\infty$ for every compact $Q\subset\mathbb R^3$. Mere local integrability inside $\Omega$ does not imply that boundary condition. All these extension and per-time conditions are part of the declared configuration, with the original interior branch retaining every locally integrable spatial input.

**(c) [Macroscopic reading and scale separation]** The framework reads its macroscopic fields and source densities as such averages only in situations where a separation of microscopic and observation scales is stated for the problem at hand; the averaging length and the actual kernel footprint (or its radius bound $\ell R_\eta$) are part of that statement, and no canonical value of $\ell$ is asserted. This is a formulation choice for the macroscopic description, not a consequence of the vacuum equations.

**(d) [Boundary handling]** For requested averages at $x\in\Omega$, boundary handling concerns the locations where $x-\ell K$ is not contained in the original spatial domain. The region $\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\le\ell R_\eta\}$ is a sufficient enclosing boundary layer, with $\ell$ in place of $\ell R_\eta$ only in the declared unit-support special case. Every requested average at an exterior location $x\notin\Omega$ must separately satisfy the extension/domain conditions of (b); the interior boundary-layer statement makes no claim to enclose exterior locations. In the interior layer a zero-extension average is used only under the compatible-extension hypothesis of (b). Otherwise one must declare another locally integrable extension, a boundary-layer model with its own well-definedness hypotheses, or restrict the averaging domain to the exact interior footprint domain. No boundary model is supplied by local integrability alone. An extension does not automatically extend a microscopic field equation across the original boundary; any averaging of such equations must either declare their validity on all used extended footprints or retain the resulting boundary distribution terms. These boundary qualifications do not impose a constitutive law.

**(e) [No constitutive content]** Coarse graining reorganises the description; it does not by itself produce a constitutive relation between averaged fields and averaged sources, and no linear, local or instantaneous response is asserted by this postulate. Such a response is the separate assumption `post-em-material-closure`, and the derivation of macroscopic field equations from the vacuum equations is the separate result `pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell`.

## Status and conventions

This is an adopted modelling assumption, not a theorem of the framework and not an empirical law: it fixes the kernel, the averaging length and the boundary/scale conventions with which this framework reads macroscopic matter. The mathematical content used in clauses (a)-(b) is discharged by the named published suppliers under the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention; the averaging, scale-separation and boundary conventions themselves are not deduced from the vacuum equations. Clauses (c)-(e) record scope: a scale separation must be declared for each problem, the footprint (not merely a radius bound) enters the boundary layer, and the postulate supplies neither a constitutive law nor a field equation. The item `pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell` uses this convention to formulate macroscopic fields and sources, and `post-em-material-closure` adds the material response; neither is proved or assumed here.

## Definition

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its units, its fields $E,B$ and its source densities $\rho,J$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], and let the averaging convention be that of [[post-em-coarse-graining]], in whose sense the objects below are macroscopic. Any convolution used to instantiate that reading is taken on its declared exact interior-footprint domain, or under a declared locally integrable compatible extension covering every used footprint. Its every-time use requires every-time locally integrable spatial slices; joint spacetime local integrability alone supplies only the almost-every-time branch. The joint $C^2$ regularity specified below is a separate model hypothesis, not a consequence of spatial smoothing.

**(a) [Polarization and magnetization]** The material model specifies two maps $P,M:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] on the open set $\Omega\times I$: $P$ is the electric dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $M$ the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, both read in the frame basis. They are data of the chosen material model: this definition does not compute them from $E$ and $B$, and no relation between $(P,M)$ and the fields is asserted here.

**(b) [Bound sources]** Write $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ for the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] taken at fixed $t$, and $\partial_t$ for the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] at fixed position, and define the bound charge density and bound current density by

$$\rho_b:=-\operatorname{div}P,\qquad J_b:=\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M.$$

Since $P,M$ are jointly $C^2$, $\rho_b$ and $J_b$ are continuous, indeed $C^1$, by the componentwise sum and product rules of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]; $\rho_b$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $J_b$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$.

**(c) [Free sources]** Define $\rho_f:=\rho-\rho_b$ and $J_f:=J-J_b$, in the same units as $\rho$ and $J$; these are the free charge and free current densities of the model. The decomposition $\rho=\rho_f+\rho_b$, $J=J_f+J_b$ is part of the chosen material model: the same total pair $(\rho,J)$ with a different pair $(P,M)$ is a different model.

**(d) [Displacement and magnetic intensity]** Define the electric displacement and the magnetic intensity by

$$D:=\varepsilon_0E+P,\qquad H:=\mu_0^{-1}B-M,$$

where $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0,c>0$ are the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; $D$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $H$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

**(e) [Status]** This item fixes objects and the bound/free convention only. No field equation (the item `pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell`), no constitutive relation (the item `post-em-material-closure`), no conservation of the bound pair (the item `pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell`, clause (a)) and no identification of $P,M$ with microscopic dipole sums is asserted here.

## Statement

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

**(a) [Bound-source conservation]** $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then

$$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$

as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.

**(b) [Macroscopic equations]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$

**(c) [Interpretation and scope]** Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). The distributional conservation conclusion embeds the adopted smooth solution only; no macroscopic field-equation claim is made for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular or sheet sources or for discontinuous $(P,M)$; no constitutive relation and no empirical statement is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smooth-branch data of the Statement: $E,B$ jointly $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by the adopted equations existing and continuous, continuous $\rho,J$, and jointly $C^2$ model maps $P,M$ with the derived objects $\rho_b=- \operatorname{div}P$, $J_b=\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M$, $\rho_f=\rho-\rho_b$, $J_f=J-J_b$, $D=\varepsilon_0E+P$, $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M$ of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], on the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[A1] The adopted smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations: $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, with the divergence and curl of the named vector-calculus definition and the partial derivative of the named partial-derivative definition, as fixed in the Statement ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], clause (a)).

[L1] The definition of the derived objects gives $\rho_b=-\operatorname{div}P$, $J_b=\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M$, $\rho=\rho_f+\rho_b$, $J=J_f+J_b$, $D=\varepsilon_0E+P$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M$ ([[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], clauses (b)-(d)).

[L2] If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_jf=\partial_j\partial_if$ there ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

[L3] The one-variable sum and scalar-multiple rules, $f+g$ and $\alpha f$ differentiable with $(f+g)'=f'+g'$ and $(\alpha f)'=\alpha f'$, and the product rule, hold for differentiable real maps ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); partial derivatives are the one-variable derivatives of the line maps ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), so these rules apply componentwise to the partial derivatives used below.

[L4] Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$ for $f\in C^k$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, under Countable Choice ([[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]); derivatives act by $\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]]), and the pairing is bilinear ([[def-distribution]]).

[L5] Locally integrable functions embed as regular distributions, $u_f(\psi)=\int f\psi$, and this identification is injective on continuous functions: a continuous function whose regular distribution vanishes is identically zero ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

[L6] $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, so $1/(c^2\varepsilon_0)=\mu_0$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]], clause (a)).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct substitution, distributional for the free/total identity and classical for the bound pair and the macroscopic equations.

1.1 Compute $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=-\partial_t\operatorname{div}P+\operatorname{div}\partial_tP+\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}M$ by [L1], where the operators are those of [A1]'s conventions; the first two terms cancel because $\partial_t\operatorname{div}P=\operatorname{div}\partial_tP$, and the last vanishes because $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}M=\sum_{i,j,k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}\partial_i\partial_jM_k$ is an antisymmetrisation of the equal mixed partials $\partial_i\partial_jM_k=\partial_j\partial_iM_k$; both identities are [L2] applied to the $C^2$ components of $P$ and $M$, and the algebra is [L3]. [A1, L1, L2, L3]

1.2 Identify the continuous fields and sources with their regular distributions by [L5] and apply the distributional divergence of [L4] to the adopted Ampere-Maxwell identity $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ of [A1]: the left side gives $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}B=\sum_{i,j,k}\varepsilon_{ijk}\partial_i\partial_jB_k=0$ by the commutation of distributional derivatives [L4], while the right side gives $\mu_0\operatorname{div}J+c^{-2}\partial_t\operatorname{div}E$ with $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ transferred by the classical-compatibility clause of [L4]; hence $0=\mu_0\operatorname{div}J+c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}\partial_t\rho=\mu_0(\operatorname{div}J+\partial_t\rho)$ by [L6], so $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ as distributions, where $\partial_t\rho$ and $\operatorname{div}J$ denote the distributional derivatives of the regular distributions. [A1, L4, L5, L6]

1.3 Compute the macroscopic equations: $\operatorname{div}D=\varepsilon_0\operatorname{div}E+\operatorname{div}P=\rho-\operatorname{div}P=\rho_f$ because $\varepsilon_0\operatorname{div}E=\rho_f+\rho_b$ and $\rho_b=-\operatorname{div}P$ by [L1] and $\rho=\rho_f+\rho_b$ by [L1]; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ are the corresponding adopted equations of [A1] unchanged; and $\operatorname{curl}H=\mu_0^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B-\operatorname{curl}M=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE-\operatorname{curl}M=J_f+\partial_t(\varepsilon_0E+P)=J_f+\partial_tD$, using [L1], $\mu_0^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0^{-1}(\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE)=J+(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}\partial_tE=J+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$ by [L6], and the decomposition $J=J_f+\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M$ of [L1]; all identities are the componentwise algebra of [L3]. [A1, L1, L3, L6]

2.1 Subtract the distributional bound identity from the distributional total identity: by the decompositions of [L1] and the linearity of distributional differentiation [L4], $\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=(\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J)-(\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b)$, the second summand is the regular distribution of the continuous function shown to vanish in step 1.1, and the first is the zero distribution by step 1.2; hence $\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ as distributions on $U$, and the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L4]

3.1 If in addition $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist and are continuous on $U$, the distribution $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$ of steps 1.2 and 2.1 is the regular distribution of the continuous function $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$ by the classical-compatibility clause of [L4], so that function vanishes pointwise by the injectivity in [L5]; the same identification applied to the continuity equation of the free pair, whose derivatives exist and are continuous because $\rho_f=\rho-\rho_b$, $J_f=J-J_b$ and $P,M\in C^2$, gives the classical pointwise continuity equations for both pairs. Combining steps 1.1, 1.3 and 2.1, the bound pair is classically conserved, the four macroscopic equations (b) hold on $\Omega\times I$, and the scope stated in (c) holds: all identities are conditional on the adopted postulates and on the declared regularity, no weak-branch, singular-source or discontinuous-dipole claim is made, and no constitutive or empirical content is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, L4, L5] ∎

## Postulate

Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following constitutive branches for the material described by the macroscopic fields of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]].

**(a) [Material rest frame]** The relations below are stated in a material rest frame: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the Minkowski model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) in which the material element under consideration is at rest, with spatial basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; when the material is at rest in the laboratory frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the components below are the laboratory components. Boosting the material changes both the fields and the rest observer; this postulate does not assert that the relations below hold with the same constants in every frame.

**(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch]** In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes

$$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$

where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$; local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.

**(c) [Causal memory branch]** Alternatively, and again in the rest frame, the polarisation response to the electric history is the causal convolution

$$P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)\,E(t-s)\,ds$$

for a declared real matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ in $L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]); the integral then converges absolutely for bounded continuous histories $E$ because $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$. The kernel class actually used, together with causality and passivity, is part of the model and is analysed in the item `pthm-em-causal-dispersive-response`; neither causality nor passivity is automatic. A finitely-subtracted analytic response may instead be declared by a scalar transfer function $\chi$ that is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, of class $C^1$ on the real boundary away from a real subtraction point $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfies $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ outside a compact set for some integer $n\ge1$ and constant $C>0$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

**(d) [Status]** These are adopted model assumptions, one branch at a time; the framework does not derive them from the vacuum equations or from coarse graining, and no microscopic mechanism, material data or empirical validity is claimed. Ferroelectric and ferromagnetic response, hysteresis, nonlinear response and general nonlocal response lie outside the branches declared here.

## Status and conventions

The equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] are formulated for arbitrary declared $C^2$ maps $P,M$; the branches above are the additional modelling assumptions by which a given medium is closed. Clause (a) fixes the frame in which the constant coefficients and kernels are declared, clause (b) is a restricted instantaneous branch with explicit positivity and the separate isotropic broadband condition, and clause (c) retains a causal memory response whose analysis is the separate result `pthm-em-causal-dispersive-response`. No branch is deduced from the vacuum equations, from the averaging convention of the item `post-em-coarse-graining` or from material data, and none is asserted to hold for any actual substance; the exclusions in (d) delimit the model.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] and the surface conventions of [[def-em-weak-sources]] are stated, and let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]].

Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), let $\sigma_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K_f(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a free surface charge density and a tangential free surface current density, both stationary in $t$), and let $\rho_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$. Let $E,B,D,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$, with the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension property: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side of each field is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder, so that the fields and their first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces.

**[Thin-interface hypothesis]** Suppose that $E,B,D,H$ satisfy the four macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the distributional sense on $U$ with the source pair $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $J_f=J_v+K_f\delta_S$, where the stationary-sheet pairings are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) and the equations are $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ as identities in the sense of [[def-distribution]], the fields being identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\psi$ ranging over $C_c^\infty(U)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). This thin-interface solution hypothesis is a modelling assumption of the statement: it is the natural weakening of the smooth macroscopic equations to fields with a common stationary discontinuity, and it is not deduced from the smooth-region equations alone.

Then, pointwise on $S\times I$,

$$n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,\qquad n\times[H]=K_f,$$

with the Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$ recover the free sheet densities from the field jumps.

**[Weak-trace branch]** If instead of the joint extension hypothesis the fields have the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time and, in addition, the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the one-sided field traces are measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$, then the same four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions and for $dS\,dt$-almost every $(x,t)$; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and at every $(x,t)$ whenever the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous. Merely having one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify the last upgrade.

**[Scope]** In the joint one-sided spacetime $C^1$ extension branch, stationarity and the joint extensions make $\partial_tD$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally integrable, contributing no delta terms. In the weak-trace branch the explicitly assumed locally integrable temporal derivatives provide this conclusion instead. No magnetic charge and no magnetic surface current are present in the sources; no dipolar sheet layer (a concentrated dipole distribution in $P$ or $M$, which would make the fields non-integrable) is included. No existence theorem for fields with singular sources is asserted, no constitutive law is used, and no empirical claim is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses of the Statement, with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the operators and constant conventions of the Statement; and the thin-interface hypothesis [A1]. The fields $E,B,D,H$ are identified with their regular distributions, and the source pair with the stationary-sheet pairings of [A1].

[A1] The thin-interface hypothesis: the four identities $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_v+K_f\delta_S+\partial_tD$ hold as distributions on $U$, with the source pair of the stationary-sheet pairings and the equation forms of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]. This solution hypothesis is assumed, not deduced.

[L1] For a two-sided compact embedded $C^2$ interface $S$ with unit normal $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$ and a field $F$ that is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces, $\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}+n\cdot[F]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}+n\times[F]\delta_S$, where $\{\cdot\}$ denotes the piecewise classical field and $[F]=F_+-F_-$ ([[lem-em-interface-derivatives]]).

[L2] The surface convention: $\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S\psi\,dS$ for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with $dS$ the surface measure of the compact embedded hypersurface; a continuous density $a$ on $S$ defines $a\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S a\psi\,dS$, both functionals of finite order ([[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[L3] The chart integral defines a finite Borel measure on the compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, independent of the finite regular charts; every regular chart density $J_X$ is continuous and strictly positive ([[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[L4] Locally integrable fields embed as regular distributions by $u_f(\psi)=\int_U f\psi$, and the embedding is injective modulo almost-everywhere equality under Countable Choice ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

[L5] The image of a $C^1$ map from a lower-dimensional smooth manifold into a higher-dimensional one is a null subset ([[prop-the-image-of-a-lower-dimensional-c1-manifold-is-null]]), and a countable union of null sets is null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]).

[L6] For compact $K$ in an open set there are smooth compactly supported cutoffs equal to one near $K$ ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]); if $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere with $|f_n|\le g$ for a single integrable $g$, then $\int f_n\to\int f$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]); the coordinate hyperplane $\{x_3=0\}$ in $\mathbb R^4$ is Lebesgue-null as the graph of a measurable function ([[cor-graph-of-a-measurable-function-is-lebesgue-null]]).

[L7] If $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega')$ on an open $\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ satisfies $\int g\varphi=0$ for every test function $\varphi$, then $g=0$ almost everywhere ([[lem-fundamental-lemma-of-the-calculus-of-variations]]); locally a $C^1$ domain boundary is, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with the domain on one side ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]).

[L8] For $C^1$ functions on a closed interval, one-dimensional integration by parts holds ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]); for $L^1$ functions on sigma-finite product spaces the iterated and multiple integrals agree ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** split the distributional equations into a volume part and a surface coefficient by testing with rescaled cutoff functions, then extract the continuous coefficient with the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations in surface charts.

1.1 The surface $S$ is Lebesgue-null in $\Omega$: by [L3] the finitely many regular charts $X_j:V_j\to S$ cover $S$, each image $X_j(V_j)$ is null in $\mathbb R^3$ by [L5] because $X_j$ is a $C^1$ map from the lower-dimensional open set $V_j\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, and a finite union of null sets is null by [L5]. Consequently, for $F\in\{B,D\}$ the distributional time derivative of the regular distribution of $F$ is the regular distribution of the piecewise classical time derivative: fix a test $\psi$ with support in a compact cylinder $\overline Q\times J\subseteq U$, so that $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=-\int_U F\partial_t\psi$; by [L8] applied after Fubini, this iterated integral equals $-\int_Q\int_JF(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt\,dx$, and for every $x\in\Omega\setminus S$ the inner integrand is $C^1$ in $t$ with $\psi(x,\cdot)$ compactly supported in $J$, so [L8] gives $\int_JF(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt=-\int_J\partial_tF(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dt$; since $S$ is null, replacing the outer integral over $\Omega\setminus S$ by one over $\Omega$ changes nothing, so $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_tF\}\psi$ for every test $\psi$, where $\{\partial_tF\}$ is locally bounded by the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension hypothesis. [L3, L5, L8]

1.2 By [L1], applied to $D$, $B$, $E$, $H$ (each is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces under the joint extension hypothesis), the four spatial identities $\operatorname{div}D=\{\operatorname{div}D\}+n\cdot[D]\delta_S$, $\operatorname{div}B=\{\operatorname{div}B\}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S$, $\operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+n\times[E]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}H=\{\operatorname{curl}H\}+n\times[H]\delta_S$ hold as distributions on $U$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, with the piecewise fields locally bounded near $S$. [L1]

1.3 [Coefficient extraction] Let $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and let $a$ be measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$, and suppose $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ as distributions on $U$. Then $a=0$ $dS\,dt$-almost everywhere. Indeed, fix $b\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $b(0)=1$ and $0\le b\le1$ [L6], let $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$ and $\psi_h:=\psi\,b(x_3/h)\in C_c^\infty(U)$ for $h>0$; testing with $\psi_h$ gives $0=\int_Ug\psi_h\,dS\,dt+\int_{S\times I}a\psi_h\,dS\,dt$, whose second term tends to $\int_{S\times I}a\psi\,dS\,dt$ as $h\downarrow0$ because $b(x_3/h)\to b(0)=1$ everywhere on $S\times I$ and the integrands are dominated by $|a\psi|$, an integrable function on the compactly supported part of $S\times I$ by [L3]; the first term tends to $0$ because $|\int_Ug\psi_h|\le\int_U|g\psi|\mathbf 1_{\{|x_3|\le h\}}$ and the integrands converge to $0$ almost everywhere, being dominated by $|g\psi|\in L^1$, with the exceptional set $\{x_3=0\}$ Lebesgue-null [L6]; hence $\int_{S\times I}a\psi\,dS\,dt=0$ for every test $\psi$. In a chart $X:V\to S$ of the finite family [L3], with $J_X>0$ continuous, choose for $\eta\in C_c^\infty(V\times J)$ the test function $\psi(y,z,t):=\eta(y,t)\beta(z-h(y))\rho(y,t)$ built from the local graph $S=\{z=h(y)\}$ of [L7] and cutoffs $\beta$ with $\beta(0)=1$, $\rho$ [L6]; then $\psi\circ(X\times\mathrm{id})=\eta$ on $V\times J$, so the chart formula of [L3] gives $\int_{V\times J}(a\circ X)(y,t)\eta(y,t)J_X(y)\,dy\,dt=0$ for every such $\eta$, and [L7] yields $(a\circ X)J_X=0$ almost everywhere; since $J_X>0$ is continuous and $a\circ X$ is continuous in the joint branch, $a\circ X=0$ on $V\times J$. The finitely many charts cover $S\times I$, so $a=0$; in the weak-trace branch, where $a$ is only locally integrable, the same computation gives $(a\circ X)J_X=0$ and hence $a\circ X=0$ $dS\,dt$-almost everywhere. [L2, L3, L6, L7]

2.1 Substituting the spatial identities of step 1.2 and the temporal identity of step 1.1 into the assumed identities [A1] gives four distributional identities of the form $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ with locally integrable volume parts: $u_{\{\operatorname{div}D\}-\rho_v}+(n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f)\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{div}B\}}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+\{\partial_tB\}}+n\times[E]\delta_S=0$ and $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}H\}-J_v-\{\partial_tD\}}+(n\times[H]-K_f)\delta_S=0$; the sums are locally integrable because the piecewise fields and $J_v,\rho_v$ are locally integrable and the piecewise derivatives are locally bounded near $S$ (joint branch) or assumed locally integrable (weak-trace branch), and the sheet coefficients are the stated one-sided jump densities, continuous in the joint branch. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, L2, L4]

3.1 Apply step 1.3 to each of the four identities of step 2.1: the four coefficients $n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f$, $n\cdot[B]$, $n\times[E]$ and $n\times[H]-K_f$ vanish $dS\,dt$-almost everywhere, and in the joint branch they are continuous on $S\times I$ (one-sided traces of locally uniformly continuous extensions), hence vanish pointwise on $S\times I$; this proves $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$, $n\cdot[B]=0$, $n\times[E]=0$ and $n\times[H]=K_f$ pointwise, equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$, and the inner and cross products are those of the one-sided traces written in the frame basis of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. In the weak-trace branch the four coefficients vanish $dS\,dt$-almost everywhere; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, vanishing on a set of full $dS$-measure for almost every $t$ upgrades to every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and if the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous, to every $(x,t)\in S\times I$; the four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions in both branches, and all statements are conditional on the assumed distributional equations [A1] with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ carried from step 1.2. [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, A1, L1, L2, L5] ∎

## Statement

Assume the memory branch of the material-closure postulate [[post-em-material-closure]] in a material rest frame, and assume the hypotheses of the mathematical suppliers [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] and [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]]: Countable Choice for the smooth comparison route and, in the integrable branches, Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric-field history in the material rest frame, read componentwise in its spatial basis ([[def-em-fields]]), and let $P$ be the polarisation response declared by the model.

**(a) [Causal response]** If the kernel of [[post-em-material-closure]](c) satisfies $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$, then for every bounded continuous history $E$ the response $P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ is well defined for every $t$, bounded and continuous, linear in $E$, and causal: histories equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$ produce responses equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

**(b) [Transfer function and dispersion relations]** If $K$ is smooth with compact support in $(0,\infty)$, the transfer function $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1}|z|^{-2}$ for $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ (with the whole-plane bound carrying the exponential factor $e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ when $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$), and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](b). If $K$ is locally absolutely continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1$ and $sK\in L^1$, then $\chi$ is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, obeys the stated growth bound, and satisfies the same pair of relations; an instantaneous real part $\chi_\infty$ may be added to the model, and the relations apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty$ for $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$.

**(c) [Finitely-subtracted and polynomial branches]** For each specified integer $n\ge1$ for which the full hypotheses of [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]] hold for the declared response transfer function, its $n$-subtracted relations apply entrywise. These hypotheses include upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closed upper half-plane, the stated boundary $C^1$ regularity, holomorphy near the real subtraction point $\omega_0$, and the order-specific growth bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le C_{jk}(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set. The Taylor polynomial and residual are

$$P_n(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)}{j!}(z-\omega_0)^j,\qquad f_n(z)=\frac{\chi(z)-P_n(z)}{(z-\omega_0)^n},$$

with removable values and the boundary $C^1$ hypothesis read entrywise as in the supplier. A growth bound for one order $n_0$ permits every order $n\ge n_0$ under the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses; it does not justify lower orders for which the required growth fails. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is included only under its own decay and boundary hypotheses: $P_0=0$, $f_0=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ with the supplier's principal-value convention. The separate constitutive-polynomial branch $\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$, with real coefficients or matrices $A_j$ and $K$ satisfying the supplier's integrable causal hypotheses, is causal on histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$. Its transfer is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared $Q$ leaves the proved relations for $\chi_K$, without assuming that $Q$ is the Taylor polynomial $P_n$.

**(d) [Monochromatic work, instantaneous work and passivity]** Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^3$ and $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$. Write $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)$ for the full transfer matrix used in the response: it is $\chi(\omega)$ without an instantaneous term and $\chi_\infty+\chi(\omega)$ when the arbitrary real instantaneous matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is present. The period-averaged work per unit volume is

$$\langle E\cdot\partial_tP\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e).$$

It is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if the full Hermitian dissipative part

$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)-\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)^*}{2i}$$

is positive semidefinite. This frequencywise monochromatic passivity is an additional model condition, not a consequence of causality or dispersion.

For the instantaneous part set $S=(\chi_\infty+\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $A=(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$, so $S^{\mathsf T}=S$ and $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$. For any real $C^1$ history its exact instantaneous work split is

$$E\cdot\partial_t(\varepsilon_0\chi_\infty E)=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E\cdot S E\right)+\varepsilon_0 E\cdot A\partial_tE.$$

The symmetric part therefore supplies the quadratic storage term; no positivity of that term is asserted unless $S$ is additionally positive semidefinite. The antisymmetric part has $E\cdot A E=0$ but can supply nonzero work over a cycle. Its monochromatic contribution is $\varepsilon_0\omega\operatorname{Im}(e^*A e)/2$, and

$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=M_K(\omega)+A/i,\qquad M_K(\omega)=\frac{\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*}{2i}.$$

Thus only a symmetric real instantaneous matrix contributes purely this storage term for all histories; for an arbitrary real instantaneous matrix the passivity test must include its antisymmetric contribution. For example, $\chi_\infty=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $K=0$ and $e=(1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ give $E=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t,0)$, zero quadratic storage and averaged work $\varepsilon_0\omega>0$. The opposite circular amplitude $(1,-i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ gives averaged work $-\varepsilon_0\omega$, so this instantaneous response is causal but fails the all-amplitude passivity condition.

**(e) [Scope]** The response is declared in the material rest frame of [[post-em-material-closure]](a); boosting the material changes the fields and the rest observer, and no frame-independent instantaneous response law is asserted. The framework does not claim that any particular material realises these branches, no microscopic mechanism is derived, and no empirical statement is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The memory-branch model data of the Statement in the material rest frame: either a kernel $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$ or one of the declared transfer-function branches of the Statement, together with the temporal Fourier convention $e^{-i\omega t}$ of the suppliers and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice in the integrable branches.

[A1] The memory branch of the material closure declares the rest-frame polarisation response $P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ with a real matrix kernel in $L^1(0,\infty)$, or a finitely-subtracted analytic transfer function with the holomorphy, boundary and growth hypotheses listed in the Statement; the kernel or transfer data are model data, and causality and passivity are not automatic ([[post-em-material-closure]], clauses (c)-(d)).

[L1] Clause (a) of the response theorem: for $d\ge1$, $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and bounded continuous $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$, the convolution $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely for every $t$, read componentwise, with the componentwise bound $|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d(\sup_s|E_k(s)|)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds$; the response is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal ([[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]], clause (a)).

[L5] Clauses (b)-(d) of the response theorem: in the compact smooth-kernel branch the transfer function $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is entire with $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_1|z|^{-2}$ for $z\ne0$, $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and the whole-plane bound with the factor $e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ for $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$, and satisfies the principal-value dispersion relations; in the locally-absolutely-continuous integrable branch $\chi$ is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the stated growth bound and the same relations, and an instantaneous real matrix $\chi_\infty$ is subtracted before applying them, $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$; in the monochromatic clause, with $T=2\pi/\omega$, $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$, $P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$, $\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$, and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if $M(\omega)=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e$ ([[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]], clauses (b)-(d)).

[L2] The finitely-subtracted supplier: under upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closure, boundary $C^1$ regularity away from the real subtraction point, holomorphy near it and the order-specific growth $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set, the Taylor polynomial $P$ and residual $f=(\chi-P)/(z-\omega_0)^n$ with removable value satisfy the two $n$-subtracted principal-value relations; the unsubtracted $n=0$ case holds with $P=0$, $f=\chi$ and growth $O(1/|z|)$; and for real coefficients $A_0,\dots,A_m$ or matrices and $K$ satisfying the integrable causal hypotheses, the response $\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ is causal with transfer $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$, $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$, the polynomial subtraction leaving the proved relations for $\chi_K$ ([[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]]).

[L3] $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$ is the framework's positive constant; multiplying a response by the positive scalar $\varepsilon_0$ preserves the existence, boundedness, continuity, linearity and causality conclusions and rescales the monochromatic work exactly as displayed ([[def-em-si-conventions]], clause (a)).

[L4] The one-variable sum, scalar-multiple and product rules hold for differentiable maps ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]), and the Euclidean dot product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] is the symmetric positive-definite bilinear form used for the quadratic form $E\mapsto E\cdot SE$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** supplier identification for the analytic and causal branches, followed by finite-dimensional algebra for the instantaneous work split.

1.1 Since $\varepsilon_0>0$ by [L3] and $\varepsilon_0K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$ whenever $K$ is, clause (a) of the Statement is clause (a) of [L1] with $d=3$ and kernel $\varepsilon_0K$: for every bounded continuous $E$ the convolution $\int_0^\infty\varepsilon_0K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely for every $t$, obeys the componentwise bound with $\sup|E_k|$ and $\int|\varepsilon_0K_{jk}|$, is bounded, continuous and linear in $E$, and is causal. [A1, L1, L3]

1.2 Clause (b) is the compact smooth-kernel and integrable branches of [L5] applied to the same kernel: entireness, the reality identity $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$, the decay and whole-plane bounds and the dispersion relations in the compact branch; holomorphy on the open upper half-plane, boundary $C^1$ regularity, the growth bound and the same relations in the integrable branch. Adding the real instantaneous matrix changes the total transfer to $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$ and leaves $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$, to which the relations apply; no work or storage property is asserted by this analytic subtraction. [A1, L5]

1.3 Clause (c) instantiates [L2] at each declared order $n$ whose hypotheses hold; the removable values and entrywise boundary hypotheses are those of the supplier, so the $n$-subtracted pair of relations holds entrywise for $n\ge1$, and the $n=0$ case requires its own $O(1/|z|)$ decay. If the growth bound holds at $n_0$, then for $n\ge n_0$ and $|z|\ge1$ one has $1+|z|^{n_0-1}\le2(1+|z|^{n-1})$, while on $|z|\le1$ both sides are bounded by a constant, so the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses give the bound at every larger order; no lower order is thereby justified. The constitutive-polynomial branch is the last clause of [L2]: the derivative of $e^{-i\omega t}$ contributes the multiplier $(-i\omega)^j$, so the declared transfer polynomial is exactly $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$, the response is causal, and subtracting $Q$ leaves the proved relations for $\chi_K$, with no identification of $Q$ with the Taylor polynomial $P_n$. [L2]

1.4 Clause (d) is clause (d) of [L5] applied to the matrix $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)$, which is a fixed complex matrix in the monochromatic calculation and therefore enters its finite period-average identity without any analytic, decay, symmetry or memory-kernel hypothesis: with $T=2\pi/\omega$, $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$, the period-averaged work is $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e)$, and it is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if $M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)$ is positive semidefinite, exactly as displayed. [L5, L3]

1.5 For the instantaneous part write $\chi_\infty=S+A$ with $S$ symmetric and $A$ antisymmetric, as in the Statement. For any real $C^1$ history, the product rule of [L4] gives $\frac{d}{dt}(E\cdot SE)=2\,E\cdot S\partial_tE$, while $E\cdot AE=0$ because $(E\cdot AE)^{\mathsf T}=E\cdot A^{\mathsf T}E=-E\cdot AE$; hence $E\cdot\partial_t(\varepsilon_0\chi_\infty E)=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E\cdot SE)+\varepsilon_0E\cdot A\partial_tE$, the exact split displayed. For a periodic history the storage derivative has zero period average, and with $E=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$ the remaining average is $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*Ae)$; since $\chi_\infty$ is real, $\chi_\infty^*=\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T}$ and $(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^*)/(2i)=A/i$, so $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=M_K+A/i$. In the explicit example $\chi_\infty=A$ has $\chi_\infty e=(i,-1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $e^*\chi_\infty e=2i$ for $e=(1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}$; directly $E=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t,0)$ and $\chi_\infty\partial_tE=\omega E$, so the work is $\varepsilon_0\omega$ at every time, while $e=(1,-i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ gives $E=(\cos\omega t,-\sin\omega t,0)$, $\chi_\infty\partial_tE=-\omega E$ and averaged work $-\varepsilon_0\omega$. More generally a real antisymmetric $A$ with $A_{jk}=a\ne0$ gives $e^*Ae=2ia\ne0$ for $e=e_j+ie_k$, so an antisymmetric instantaneous part that is nonzero fails all-amplitude passivity, and pure storage for every history requires $A=0$. [L5, L4]

2.1 Clauses (a)-(d) of the Statement now follow: (a) from step 1.1, (b) from step 1.2, (c) from step 1.3, and (d) from steps 1.4 and 1.5, with the passivity criterion holding for the full transfer matrix and the storage term assigned only to the symmetric part of an arbitrary real instantaneous matrix. Clause (e) fixes the scope: all statements are conditional on the declared model data of [A1] and on the Choice hypotheses of the suppliers, no material realization, microscopic mechanism or empirical claim is made, and the growth, boundary and decay hypotheses are required per branch and per subtraction order. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5] ∎

## Statement

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (isotropic scalar case included) with $D=\varepsilon E$ and $B=\mu H$, and the conduction relation $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite and a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the regularity hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], so that its macroscopic equations hold on $\Omega\times I$. Define the stored-energy density and the energy-flux vector

$$u:=\tfrac12\bigl(E\cdot D+B\cdot H\bigr),\qquad S:=E\times H,$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; $u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Then:

**(a) [Local balance and positivity]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E.$$

Moreover $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)\ge0$, with $u(x,t)>0$ whenever $(E(x,t),H(x,t))\ne(0,0)$.

**(b) [Dissipation reading]** With $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite, $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ and the balance reads

$$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S+E\cdot\sigma E=-J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E;$$

the nonnegative term $E\cdot\sigma E$ is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model.

**(c) [Fixed-volume balance]** Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with $\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let $t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in that divergence theorem, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega'$. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS.$$

**(d) [Scope]** The density $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ is a stored-energy density only for this constant symmetric nondispersive model; for general dispersive, nonlocal, nonlinear or hysteretic response no instantaneous stored-energy density is defined or claimed by this item, and the general dispersive work balance is not supplied. The identities hold only where the fields and sources have the stated regularity, the fixed-volume form keeps its boundary term, and no conservation of $\int_{\Omega'}u$ is asserted unless that term vanishes. No empirical claim is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The laboratory region and units of the Statement, the smooth-branch data of the declared constant model with symmetric positive-definite $\varepsilon,\mu$ and symmetric positive-semidefinite $\sigma$ of [A2], and the regularity of [A1]; the operators are the divergence, curl and partial derivatives of the named definitions, with the Euclidean inner and cross products of the Statement.

[A1] Under the smooth branch of the vacuum postulate with the regularity hypotheses of the macroscopic theorem, the macroscopic equations hold on $\Omega\times I$: $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ ([[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], clauses (a)-(b); [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], smooth branch).

[A2] The elementary inertial-rest branch: $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu$, and $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite ([[post-em-material-closure]], clause (b)).

[L1] $\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E-E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H$ for $C^1$ fields ([[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]]).

[L2] For a symmetric real matrix $\varepsilon$, $E\cdot\varepsilon E$ is differentiable in $t$ with $\frac{d}{dt}(E\cdot\varepsilon E)=2\,\partial_tE\cdot\varepsilon E$ when $E$ is $C^1$, by the product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); and $E\cdot\varepsilon E\ge0$ with equality only for $E=0$ when $\varepsilon$ is positive definite, and likewise for $\mu$ and $H$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[L3] If $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is compact, measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure, $f$ and $\partial_tf$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$, then $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf=\int_K\partial_tf$ on $[a,b]$ ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]).

[L4] For a bounded piecewise $C^1$ domain, the divergence theorem holds: $\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}F\cdot n\,dS$ for the outward unit normal, under the stated finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and Countable Choice ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** dot the macroscopic curl equations with the complementary fields and use the cross-product divergence identity, then integrate over a fixed volume.

1.1 By [A1] the two curl equations $E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H=E\cdot J_f+E\cdot\partial_tD$ and $H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E=-H\cdot\partial_tB$ hold on $\Omega\times I$ after taking the Euclidean inner product with the complementary field. [A1, given]

1.2 The identity $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)$ follows from [A2], and both quadratic forms are nonnegative by [L2], with equality in both simultaneously only when $E=H=0$; hence $u\ge0$, and $u(x,t)>0$ whenever $(E(x,t),H(x,t))\ne(0,0)$. [A2, L2]

1.3 By [A2], $J_f\cdot E=E\cdot\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E$, and $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ because $\sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite; the term is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model. [A2, L2]

2.1 By [L1], $\operatorname{div}S=\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E-E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H$, so the two scalar identities of step 1.1 give $\operatorname{div}S=-(E\cdot J_f+E\cdot\partial_tD+H\cdot\partial_tB)$; differentiating $u$ in time and using the symmetry of $\varepsilon$ and $\mu$ with the product rule of [L2] gives $\partial_tu=\tfrac12\partial_t(E\cdot\varepsilon E)+\tfrac12\partial_t(H\cdot\mu H)=\partial_tE\cdot\varepsilon E+\partial_tH\cdot\mu H=E\cdot\partial_tD+H\cdot\partial_tB$ by [A2]; adding the two identities yields $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E$ on $\Omega\times I$, proving (a). [step 1.1, A2, L1, L2]

3.1 For (c), fix $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and apply [L3] to $K=\overline{\Omega'}$ and $f=u$: $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u\,dx=\int_{\Omega'}\partial_tu\,dx$, where the regularity hypotheses on the fields supply the continuous $\partial_tu$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}\times[t_0,t_1]$; substituting the local balance of step 2.1 and applying the divergence theorem [L4] to $F=S$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E-\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}S=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS$, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis carried by [L4]. Thus (a)-(c) hold; the reading (b) is step 1.3 substituted into the balance, and (d) is the scope: $u$ is a stored-energy density only for this constant symmetric nondispersive model, no instantaneous stored energy is claimed for dispersive, nonlocal, nonlinear or hysteretic response, the boundary term is retained, and no conservation of $\int_{\Omega'}u$ or empirical statement is asserted. [step 1.3, step 2.1, L3, L4] ∎

## Example

**(a) [Dimensional exclusion of $E=\varepsilon_0D$]** In the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]]: the electric constant $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ carries $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}=\mathrm C^2\mathrm s^2\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\mathrm m^{-3}$, the displacement $D$ of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]] carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, and the electric field $E$ of [[def-em-fields]] carries $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}\mathrm C^{-1}$. The product $\varepsilon_0D$ therefore carries $\mathrm F\,\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm C^3\mathrm s^2\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\mathrm m^{-5}$, which is not the dimension of $E$: the proposed identification $E=\varepsilon_0D$ fails dimensionally in SI and cannot be a field relation of the framework.

**(b) [Units do not determine the law]** Solving the definition $D=\varepsilon_0E+P$ of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]] gives $E=(D-P)/\varepsilon_0$, which in vacuum ($P=0$) reads $E=\varepsilon_0^{-1}D$. Any proposed law $E=\eta D$ with a constant $\eta>0$ of dimension $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm C^{-1}$ is dimensionally admissible; dimensional consistency therefore does not identify $\eta$, and it does not determine whether the response is local, linear or instantaneous. In the model of [[post-em-material-closure]] the scalar relation is $D=\varepsilon E$, i.e. $\eta=\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $\varepsilon$ (or $\chi_e=\varepsilon/\varepsilon_0-1$) is fixed by the declared material model, not by units.

**(c) [Frequency-domain symbols are not instantaneous coefficients]** In the memory branch of [[post-em-material-closure]](c) the response is a causal convolution in time; a scalar $\varepsilon(\omega)$ introduced in the harmonic description acts on the Fourier components of the field history in the material rest frame. The framework therefore does not read $\varepsilon(\omega)$ as an instantaneous multiplicative coefficient in the time domain: doing so silently replaces the convolution by an instantaneous law and is a model-identification error of the same kind as (a).

**(d) [Scope]** A dimensional and model-identification statement about the framework's own conventions; it asserts no measurement, no material property and no empirical claim.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct dimensional computation and immediate consequences of the definitions.

**Given:** The SI unit conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], the coefficient types of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], and the declared material branches of [[post-em-material-closure]], on the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

[L1] The electric constant is $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, carrying $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}$; the farad is $\mathrm F=\mathrm C\,\mathrm V^{-1}$ and the volt is $\mathrm V=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^2\mathrm s^{-2}\mathrm C^{-1}$, so $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}=\mathrm C^2\mathrm s^2\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\mathrm m^{-3}$; the electric field carries $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}\mathrm C^{-1}$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]], clause (a)).

[L2] The displacement is defined by $D=\varepsilon_0E+P$ and carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ ([[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], clause (d)); the linear branch declares $D=\varepsilon E$ with constant positive matrix $\varepsilon$, and the memory branch declares the causal convolution $P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ with $K\in L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[post-em-material-closure]], clauses (b)-(c)).

1.1 Multiplying the dimension of $\varepsilon_0$ from [L1] by the dimension $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ of $D$ from [L2] gives $\mathrm C^3\mathrm s^2\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\mathrm m^{-5}$, which differs from the dimension $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}\mathrm C^{-1}$ of $E$ in the exponent of $\mathrm C$ and of $\mathrm m$; the proposed law $E=\varepsilon_0D$ is therefore excluded. [L1, L2]

1.2 Solving $D=\varepsilon_0E+P$ for $E$ gives $E=(D-P)/\varepsilon_0$, so in vacuum $E=\varepsilon_0^{-1}D$; a law $E=\eta D$ with constant $\eta>0$ of dimension $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm C^{-1}$ has the correct dimension for every such $\eta$, so the unit check alone leaves $\eta$ free and says nothing about locality, linearity or instantaneity. [L2]

1.3 In the memory branch the response is the convolution of [L2], not a multiplication by a constant: for the bounded continuous history $E(t)=\min(1,\max(0,-t))$ (zero for $t\ge0$, equal to $s$ at $t=-s$ for $0\le s\le1$, equal to $1$ for $t\le-1$, so that $0\le E\le1$ and $E$ is continuous) and the nonnegative kernel $K=\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$, the causal response at $t=0$ is $P(0)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^1s\,ds=\varepsilon_0/2>0$, while any instantaneous multiplicative law $P=cE$ gives $P(0)=cE(0)=0$; hence the convolution is not an instantaneous coefficient law, and substituting a harmonic symbol $\varepsilon(\omega)$ as a time-domain factor changes the declared model. [L2]

2.1 Steps 1.1-1.3 verify (a)-(c): the identification $E=\varepsilon_0D$ fails dimensionally, dimensionally admissible laws do not determine $\eta$ or the response type, and the frequency-domain symbol is defined by its action on Fourier components rather than as an instantaneous coefficient, as the explicit history shows. The scope (d) holds: the example uses only the framework's unit and definition conventions, asserts no measurement, no material property and no empirical claim, and the material constant $\varepsilon$ or susceptibility $\chi_e$ remains fixed by the declared model. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Example

Let the laboratory frame, coordinates $(x,y,z)$ and units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $S=\{z=0\}\cap\Omega$ be a stationary planar interface with unit normal $n=e_z$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-=\{z<0\}$ to the side $\Omega_+=\{z>0\}$. Suppose each half-space carries a homogeneous linear dielectric at rest in the laboratory frame in the elementary branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constants $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in(0,\infty)$ with $D=\varepsilon_1E$ on $\Omega_-$ and $D=\varepsilon_2E$ on $\Omega_+$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $E,B,D,H$ be locally integrable, $C^1$ off the plane and jointly one-sided $C^1$ up to it on every compact test cylinder, as in the joint branch of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]. Assume locally the four distributional macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], with volume sources $\rho_v,J_v$ continuous off the plane and locally integrable across it, free charge $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$ for a constant $\sigma_f\in\mathbb R$, and free current $J_f=J_v$ (no free sheet current). Here the plane distribution is defined locally by $\langle\delta_S,\psi\rangle=\int\psi(x,y,0,t)\,dx\,dy\,dt$ for compactly supported tests on the laboratory region; no global compactness of this plane is asserted. These are the local planar counterparts of the compact-interface hypotheses in [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]. Write $E_{j\,t}$, $E_{j\,n}$ for the tangential and normal parts of the one-sided trace $E_j$ and $D_j$ ($j=1$ on $\Omega_-$, $j=2$ on $\Omega_+$), defined by the Euclidean decomposition against $n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

**(a) [Tangential field]** $n\times[E]=0$, i.e. $E_{2t}=E_{1t}$: the tangential electric field is continuous across the interface.

**(b) [Normal displacement]** $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$, i.e. $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}-\varepsilon_1E_{1n}=\sigma_f$, hence $E_{2n}=\frac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2}E_{1n}+\frac{\sigma_f}{\varepsilon_2}$.

**(c) [No free sheet charge]** If $\sigma_f=0$, then $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}=\varepsilon_1E_{1n}$ and $E_{2n}=\frac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2}E_{1n}$: the normal component is scaled by the positive ratio $\varepsilon_1/\varepsilon_2$, so $E_{2n}$ and $E_{1n}$ have the same sign (and vanish together). Precisely, $E_{2n}=E_{1n}$ if and only if $(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}=0$: equality holds when the normal field is zero even for unequal permittivities; if $E_{1n}\ne0$, it holds exactly when $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$. A free surface charge $\sigma_f\ne0$ modifies the normal condition as displayed and is not silently set to zero.

**(d) [Magnetic companions]** $n\cdot[B]=0$ and, with $K_f=0$, $n\times[H]=0$; for nonmagnetic media with $H=\mu_0^{-1}B$ on both sides this gives $B_{2n}=B_{1n}$ and $B_{2t}=B_{1t}$.

**(e) [Scope]** A local interface computation under the stated model hypotheses: it solves the electric jump relations against the linear constitutive relations on the two sides and asserts no global field configuration, no existence of the fields, no constitutive law beyond the declared branch and no empirical claim.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** local compact-test interface integration by parts on the plane followed by substitution of the constitutive relations.

**Given:** The planar configuration, regularity, sources and assumed local distributional equations of the Example, with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the fields are identified with their regular distributions and the plane functional is $\langle\delta_S,\psi\rangle=\int\psi(x,y,0,t)\,dx\,dy\,dt$ ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).

[A1] The constitutive relations: $D=\varepsilon_1E$ on $\Omega_-$ and $D=\varepsilon_2E$ on $\Omega_+$ with constants $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2>0$, the elementary branch of [[post-em-material-closure]].

[A2] The assumed local distributional macroscopic equations with $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$ and $J_f=J_v$, in the equation forms of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]; this is a hypothesis of the Example, not a conclusion of the item.

[L1] One-dimensional integration by parts: for differentiable $u,v$ on $[a,b]$ with integrable derivatives, $\int_a^bu\,v'=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^bu'\,v$ ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]); the integral of a derivative is the difference of endpoint values ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

[L2] For $L^1$ functions on sigma-finite product spaces the iterated and multiple integrals agree ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[L3] There are smooth compactly supported cutoffs equal to one on a neighbourhood of a compact set ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]), and if $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere with $|f_n|\le g$ for a single integrable $g$, then $\int f_n\to\int f$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[L4] The coordinate hyperplane $\{z=0\}$ in $\mathbb R^4$ is Lebesgue-null, being the graph of a measurable function ([[cor-graph-of-a-measurable-function-is-lebesgue-null]]).

[L5] If $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ on an open set satisfies $\int g\varphi=0$ for every test function $\varphi$, then $g=0$ almost everywhere ([[lem-fundamental-lemma-of-the-calculus-of-variations]]).

[L6] The Euclidean dot and cross products on $\mathbb R^3$: $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_kx_ky_k$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and the antisymmetric cross product with $e_z\times(F_1,F_2,F_3)=(-F_2,F_1,0)$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

1.1 Let $F\in\{E,B,D,H\}$ and let $\psi$ be a test function supported in a compact cylinder of $U$. For fixed $(x,y,t)$ with $z\ne0$ the map $z\mapsto F(x,y,z,t)$ is $C^1$ on each open half-line and $\psi$ has compact support in $z$; applying [L1] on $(-\infty,0)$ and on $(0,\infty)$ and summing gives $\int_{\mathbb R}F\,\partial_z\psi\,dz=-[F](x,y,0,t)\,\psi(x,y,0,t)-\int_{\mathbb R}\{\partial_zF\}\psi\,dz$, because the outer boundary terms vanish by compact support; integrating over $x,y,t$ by [L2], with the plane $\{z=0\}$ null by [L4] so that the split into the two half-spaces is exact, gives $\langle\partial_zF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_zF\}\psi+\langle[F_3]\delta_S,\psi\rangle$ componentwise, i.e. $\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}+e_z\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}+e_z\times[F]\,\delta_S$ by [L6], the tangential derivatives contributing no sheet term. [L1, L2, L4, L6]

1.2 The same per-line integration by parts in $t$, with $\psi$ of compact $t$-support and the plane stationary and null by [L4], gives $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_tF\}\psi$ for every test $\psi$: time differentiation at the fixed plane contributes no sheet term, and the piecewise derivatives are locally bounded by the joint one-sided $C^1$ hypothesis. [L1, L2, L4]

2.1 Substituting the spatial identities of step 1.1 and the temporal identity of step 1.2 into the assumed equations [A2] gives four distributional identities of the form $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ on the local region, with locally bounded volume parts $g$: $u_{\{\operatorname{div}D\}-\rho_v}+(n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f)\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{div}B\}}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+\{\partial_tB\}}+n\times[E]\delta_S=0$ and $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}H\}-J_v-\{\partial_tD\}}+n\times[H]\delta_S=0$, where the two half-space fields are $C^1$ with locally bounded derivatives and $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable. [A2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 [Coefficient extraction] Let $b\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $b(0)=1$, $0\le b\le1$ [L3] and put $\psi_h:=\psi\,b(z/h)$ for a test $\psi$; testing an identity $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ of step 2.1 with $\psi_h$ gives $0=\int_Ug\psi_h+\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi_h$, whose second term tends to $\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi$ because $b(z/h)\to b(0)=1$ everywhere on the plane and the integrands are dominated by $|a\psi|$ on the compactly supported part of the plane, while the first term tends to $0$ because $|\int_Ug\psi_h|\le\int_U|g\psi|\mathbf 1_{\{|z|\le h\}}$ with integrands converging to $0$ almost everywhere, dominated by the integrable $|g\psi|$, the exceptional set $\{z=0\}$ being null [L4]. Hence $\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi=0$ for every test $\psi$; taking $\psi(x,y,z,t)=\eta(x,y,t)\beta(z)$ with $\eta$ a test function in the tangential/time variables and $\beta$ a cutoff with $\beta(0)=1$ reduces this to $\int a(x,y,0,t)\eta(x,y,t)\,dx\,dy\,dt=0$ for every $\eta$, so the continuous function $(x,y,t)\mapsto a(x,y,0,t)$ vanishes identically by [L5]. All four coefficients of step 2.1 therefore vanish pointwise on the plane. [step 2.1, L3, L4, L5]

4.1 Applying step 3.1 and the constitutive relations [A1]: (a) $n\times[E]=0$, so the tangential parts agree, $E_{2t}=E_{1t}$; (b) $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$ with $D_j=\varepsilon_jE_j$ on the two sides gives $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}-\varepsilon_1E_{1n}=\sigma_f$ and, since $\varepsilon_2>0$, $E_{2n}=(\varepsilon_1/\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}+\sigma_f/\varepsilon_2$; (c) if $\sigma_f=0$ the previous identity reads $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}=\varepsilon_1E_{1n}$, so $E_{2n}=(\varepsilon_1/\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}$ has the same sign as $E_{1n}$ and vanishes with it, and $E_{2n}=E_{1n}$ holds if and only if $(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}=0$, i.e. when $E_{1n}=0$ or $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$; (d) $n\cdot[B]=0$ and $n\times[H]=0$, and in the nonmagnetic case $H=\mu_0^{-1}B$ on both sides the two identities give $[B_n]=0$ and $[B_t]=0$, hence $B_{2n}=B_{1n}$ and $B_{2t}=B_{1t}$ by the decomposition of [L6]. The scope (e) holds: the computation uses only the assumed local equations and the declared linear branch, asserts no global configuration, no existence, no further constitutive law and no empirical claim. [step 3.1, A1, L6] ∎
