## Example

Let the laboratory frame and units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], with spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, $z=x_3$, $r=|x|$ and the applied field along $e_3$. Fix $a>0$ with $\overline B_a\subseteq\Omega$, so that the interface $S=\{r=a\}$ below lies in the laboratory region, a field magnitude $E_0>0$ and constants $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\in(0,\infty)$ (the interior and exterior permittivities of the elementary branch of [[post-em-material-closure]], the material being at rest in the laboratory frame), and put

$$C:=\frac{3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}},\qquad d:=\frac{E_0a^3(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}})}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}}.$$

Consider the time-independent potentials

$$\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}(x):=-C\,E_0\,z\quad(r<a),\qquad \varphi_{\mathrm{out}}(x):=-E_0\,z+\frac{d\,z}{r^3}\quad(r>a),$$

with fields $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ and $D:=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}E$ inside, $D:=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}E$ outside ($E$ being of the class of [[def-em-fields]] restricted to this time-independent configuration). Write $S=\{r=a\}$ and $n=e_r$ for the outward normal. Then:

**(a) [Harmonicity]** $\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ on $r<a$ and $\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ on $r>a$ in the classical sense of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], and the potentials and their first derivatives extend continuously to the closed sides of $S$.

**(b) [Interface conditions]** With one-sided traces at $r=a$, $\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}\,\partial_r\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\,\partial_r\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$ on $S$; equivalently the tangential electric field and the normal component of $D$ are continuous. These electric matching identities hold independently of any magnetic completion. In addition, declare the static completion $B=H=0$, $\rho_f=J_f=0$, with any constant symmetric positive-definite permeability and the zero-conductivity branch $\sigma=0$, $J_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$ of [[post-em-material-closure]]. The four fields then satisfy all four thin-interface macroscopic equations distributionally with $\sigma_f=K_f=0$, and the joint one-sided regularity at the compact sphere verifies the hypotheses of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]. Assume its inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention ([[def-countable-choice]]) for this distribution/surface reading.

**(c) [Asymptotics]** $\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}(x)+E_0z=dz/r^3$ and $\nabla(\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}+E_0z)=O(r^{-3})$ as $r\to\infty$: the difference from the applied uniform potential decays like $r^{-2}$ and its gradient like $r^{-3}$.

**(d) [Uniqueness in the declared class]** Let $(\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{in}},\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{out}})$ be $C^2$ on the closed ball $\overline{B_a}$ respectively on every closed exterior region $\{a\le r\le R\}$, harmonic on $r<a$ and $r>a$, satisfying the same interface conditions (b), and satisfying $|\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}+E_0z|\le M/r$ for some $M$ and all sufficiently large $r$. Then $\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}=\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$. Hence the displayed pair is the unique solution of the dielectric-sphere transmission problem in that class, existence being exhibited explicitly; the uniqueness proof uses only the Green identity, the matching conditions and the decay, with no maximum principle.

**(e) [Fields, polarisation and induced dipole]** On $r<a$ the field is uniform, $E=C E_0e_3$ with $D=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}CE_0e_3$; outside, the field is that of the applied uniform field plus the field of a point dipole at the origin with moment $p=4\pi\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\,d\,e_3$; the interior polarisation is $P_{\mathrm{in}}=(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}-\varepsilon_0)CE_0e_3$ and the bound surface charge density on $S$ is $\sigma_b=n\cdot(P_{\mathrm{in}}-P_{\mathrm{out}})$, the singular coefficient of $\rho_b=-\operatorname{div}P$ at $S$ (with the exterior polarisation $P_{\mathrm{out}}=(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}-\varepsilon_0)E_{\mathrm{out}}$).

**(f) [Regime and scope]** The computation is a quasistatic result of the declared linear branch at $\sigma_f=0$; using $p$ as a dynamic wave polarisability of the sphere requires a separate quasistatic/dipole approximation and is not asserted here. The example asserts no material data and no empirical claim.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** explicit substitution plus a Green-identity uniqueness argument.

**Given:** The potentials, constants $C,d$, interface $S=\{r=a\}$ and spatial data of the Example, with $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}>0$ and the static completion of (b); assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the distributional interface reading.

[A1] The elementary branch: $D=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}E$ inside and $D=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}E$ outside with positive constants, with the declared static completion $B=H=0$, $\rho_f=J_f=0$, permeability constant symmetric positive definite, $\sigma=0$ and $J_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$ ([[post-em-material-closure]], clause (b)); the macroscopic equation forms are those of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]].

[L1] The calculus of the displayed potentials: for smooth functions and total derivatives, sums, scalar multiples and compositions obey the sum, product and chain rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]), the Euclidean radius powers $r\mapsto r^{-3}$ are smooth away from the origin with the stated derivatives ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and the Laplacian is $\Delta f=\sum_i\partial_i^2f$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[L2] The first Green identity on a bounded $C^1$ domain: for $C^2$ functions $u,v$ up to the boundary, $\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=\oint_{\partial\Omega}u\,\partial_\nu v-\int_\Omega u\,\Delta v$ ([[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]); harmonic functions obey the interior Cauchy estimates in supremum norm, so $|\nabla w(x)|\le C R^{-1}\sup_{B_{R}}|w|$ on compact subballs ([[cor-harmonic-cauchy-estimates-in-supremum-norm]]); and the classical Dirichlet problem on a ball has at most one solution ([[cor-classical-dirichlet-and-poisson-problems-are-unique]]).

[L3] For a two-sided compact embedded $C^2$ interface with one-sided $C^1$ traces, $\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}+n\cdot[F]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}+n\times[F]\delta_S$, under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[lem-em-interface-derivatives]]), the derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular distributions of the fields.

[L4] The Euclidean inner and cross products of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), and the jump and free/bound conventions of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: $\rho_b=-\operatorname{div}P$, $D=\varepsilon_0E+P$.

1.1 On $r\ne0$ the functions $z$ and $z\,r^{-3}$ are smooth and $r^{-3}$ is smooth away from the origin; the sum and scalar rules of [L1] give $\Delta z=0$ and $\Delta(z\,r^{-3})=z\,\Delta(r^{-3})+2\,\nabla z\cdot\nabla(r^{-3})$, with $\partial_ir^{-3}=-3x_ir^{-5}$ and $\Delta(r^{-3})=\sum_i\partial_i(-3x_ir^{-5})=-9r^{-5}+15r^{-5}=6r^{-5}$; hence $\Delta(zr^{-3})=6zr^{-5}+2\cdot(-3zr^{-5})=0$, so $\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ on $r<a$ and $\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ on $r>a$; the displayed functions and their gradients are continuous on each closed side of $S$ because $r\ge a>0$ there. [L1]

1.2 At $r=a$: $\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}(a)=-CE_0a\cos\theta$ and $\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}(a)=(-E_0a+d/a^2)\cos\theta$, whose equality for every angle is the scalar equation $C=1-d/(E_0a^3)$; the radial derivatives are $\partial_r\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=-CE_0\cos\theta$ and $\partial_r\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}=(-E_0-2d/a^3)\cos\theta$, whose equality after the weights $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}$ is $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}C=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}(1+2d/(E_0a^3))$. Substituting the displayed $C$ and $d$ satisfies both equations (the determinant of the pair is $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}>0$), so the two matching identities hold; because the traces of $\varphi$ agree as functions on $S$, their tangential derivatives agree, and the equivalence with the continuity of the tangential electric field and of the normal component of $D$ is the direct evaluation $E=-\nabla\varphi$, $D=\varepsilon E$. The asymptotics (c) follow from $|z|\le r$: $|\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}+E_0z|=|d||z|r^{-3}\le|d|r^{-2}$ and $\partial_i(dzr^{-3})=d(\delta_{i3}r^{-3}-3zx_ir^{-5})$ has norm at most $4|d|r^{-3}$. [L1]

2.1 For the declared static completion, [L3] gives $\operatorname{div}D=\{\operatorname{div}D\}+n\cdot[D]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+n\times[E]\delta_S$, with analogous formulas for $B$ and $H$; by step 1.1 the piecewise classical divergences and curls of $D$ and $E$ vanish (each side is a constant multiple of the gradient of a harmonic function, so $\operatorname{div}E=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ there), and by step 1.2 the normal jump $n\cdot[D]$ and tangential jump $n\times[E]$ vanish; since $B=H=0$ and $\rho_f=J_f=0$ with $\sigma_f=K_f=0$, all four distributional macroscopic equations hold on the local region and the hypotheses of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]] ($S=\{r=a\}$ a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface in $\Omega$ because $\overline B_a\subseteq\Omega$, locally integrable fields, $C^1$ off $S$, joint one-sided $C^1$ extensions, stationary free sheet data) are verified. [step 1.1, step 1.2, A1, L3]

2.2 For uniqueness, let $w_{\mathrm{in}}=\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}-\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}$ on $\overline{B_a}$ and $w_{\mathrm{out}}=\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}-\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$ on $\{r\ge a\}$; both are harmonic with $C^2$ regularity on the closed regions, their traces and weighted radial derivatives agree on $S$ by the shared interface conditions, and $|w_{\mathrm{out}}|\le(M+|d|)r^{-1}$. Apply the first Green identity of [L2] with $u=v=w_{\mathrm{in}}$ on the ball $B_a$ and with $u=v=w_{\mathrm{out}}$ on the annulus $\{a<r<R\}$: since the Laplacians vanish, $\int_{B_a}|\nabla w_{\mathrm{in}}|^2=\oint_Sw_{\mathrm{in}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\int_{a<r<R}|\nabla w_{\mathrm{out}}|^2=\oint_{\{r=R\}}w_{\mathrm{out}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{out}}-\oint_Sw_{\mathrm{out}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{out}}$; multiplying by $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}$ and adding, the two surface terms on $S$ cancel by $w_{\mathrm{in}}=w_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{in}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{out}}$, while the term on $\{r=R\}$ is bounded by $(4\pi R^2)\cdot(M+|d|)R^{-1}\cdot C R^{-2}$ using [L2]'s Cauchy estimate for $\nabla w_{\mathrm{out}}$, hence tends to $0$; since $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}>0$, both gradients vanish, so $w_{\mathrm{in}}$ is constant on the ball and $w_{\mathrm{out}}$ is constant on $r>a$; the decay forces that constant to be $0$, hence the common trace is $0$, and then $w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ by the Dirichlet uniqueness of [L2] applied on the ball to $w_{\mathrm{in}}$ and the zero function. [step 1.2, A1, L4]

3.1 Steps 1.1-1.2 verify (a)-(c), step 2.1 verifies (b) and the distributional thin-interface reading, step 2.2 gives the uniqueness statement (d) with existence exhibited by the displayed pair, and step 2.3 gives the fields, polarisation, exterior dipole moment and bound surface charge of (e). The scope (f) holds: the computation is quasistatic, of the declared linear branch at $\sigma_f=0$, conditional on the stated constants and regularity; the identification of $p$ with a dynamic wave polarisability requires a separate quasistatic/dipole approximation, and no material data, empirical claim or global existence statement is made. ## Definition

Let the laboratory region $\Omega\times I$ and its inertial chart, the field objects $E,B$ and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], with $c>0$; here $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ is a nonempty open set and $I$ is a nonempty open interval.

(a) [Moving material circuit] A **moving material circuit** on the laboratory region is the data $(D,r,v)$ specified as follows. $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a compact finite elementary Green region with its positive boundary chain ([[def-em-moving-patch]]); $r:D\times I\to\Omega$ extends to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ and $r(\cdot,t)$ injective on $D$ for every $t\in I$ (embedded material sheet); and $v$ is a $C^1$ vector field on a neighbourhood of the swept set $S=\bigcup_{t\in I}r(D\times\{t\})$ in $\Omega\times I$ satisfying the single-valued condition $v(r(u,w,t),t)=\partial_tr(u,w,t)$ for all $(u,w)\in D$ and all $t\in I$. In the notation of [[def-em-moving-patch]] the map $r$ is the swept moving patch and $v$ is its single-valued velocity; material points of the circuit are the images of the parameter points $(u,w)$.

(b) [Surface, boundary and flux] For $t\in I$ put $S(t):=r(D,t)$ and let
$$\gamma_t:=r(\cdot,t)|_{\partial D}$$
be the positive boundary chain of $D$ composed with $r(\cdot,t)$; its trace is the set $C(t):=r(\partial D,t)$, and $C(t)$ carries the boundary orientation induced by the positive orientation of $D$. For $B$ of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the **magnetic flux** of the circuit at time $t$ is the parametrized flux
$$\Phi_B(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(u,w,t),t),\,r_u(u,w,t)\times r_v(u,w,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dw$$
of [[def-em-moving-patch]]; its unit is the weber, $\mathrm{Wb}=\mathrm{T}\,\mathrm{m}^2$.

(c) [Electromotive force] For $E,B$ continuous on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the **electromotive force** (emf) of the circuit at time $t$ is the vector line integral over the oriented closed path $\gamma_t$
$$\mathrm{emf}(t):=\oint_{\gamma_t}\bigl\langle E(\cdot,t)+v(\cdot,t)\times B(\cdot,t),\,d\mathbf r\bigr\rangle$$
in the convention of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]], with the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; its unit is the volt, $1\,\mathrm V=1\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^2\,\mathrm s^{-3}\mathrm A^{-1}$. Under the framework's Lorentz coupling the integrand is the force per unit charge on a charge moving with the conductor material; the definition itself only names the line integral.

(d) [Scope and exclusions] The fields are assumed of the stated regularity on a neighbourhood of the swept set: circuits passing through a point charge, a curve or surface singularity, or any place where the fields fail to be of that regularity are excluded (no singularity crossings). When the emf is interpreted through the framework's relativistic Lorentz coupling, material speeds are required to be subluminal, $|v|<c$. The definition asserts no conservation law and no relation between $\mathrm{emf}$ and $\Phi_B'$; in particular the flux concerns the single field $B$ and the emf the pair $(E,B)$, and neither object is claimed independent of the chosen parametrization.

### Well-definedness and conventions

*The flux is well defined.* With $B$ and $r$ of the stated regularity, the integrand of (b) is continuous on the compact Jordan measurable set $D$, so the Riemann integral exists and coincides with the flux of the moving patch $(D,r,v)$ in [[def-em-moving-patch]]; the value is independent of any $C^2$ extension of $r$ by the conventions recorded there.

*The boundary path is a closed piecewise $C^1$ path.* The positive boundary chain of a finite elementary Green region is a finite concatenation of $C^1$ arcs ([[def-em-moving-patch]] and the boundary-orientation conventions cited there); composing each arc with the $C^2$ map $r(\cdot,t)$ gives a finite concatenation of $C^1$ arcs with matching one-sided endpoints and equal initial and terminal points, that is, a closed piecewise $C^1$ path in the sense of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. Its trace is $C(t)\subseteq S$, and $E+v\times B$ is continuous on a neighbourhood of $S$, hence on the trace; the line integral of (c) is therefore defined and independent of the admissible partition of the path. The integral is unchanged by the chosen $C^2$ extension of $r$, because the path and the integrand depend only on the values of $r$ and $v$ on $D\times I$ and on the neighbourhood of $S$ recorded in the data; it depends on the orientation of $D$, as recorded in (b).

*The embedded sheet and its boundary.* Because $r(\cdot,t)$ is injective and continuous on the compact set $D$, each slice $S(t)=r(D,t)$ is an embedded sheet homeomorphic to $D$, and $r(\partial D,t)=\partial S(t)$ is its topological boundary; the parametrized path $\gamma_t$ therefore parametrizes the positively oriented boundary of $S(t)$ induced by the positive orientation of $D$, with the orientation fixed by the boundary chain as in (b). Rank failures on the boundary of the parameter region (seams) remain permitted, since $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ is required only on the interior.

*No physical assertion.* The definition introduces geometric data, a flux integral and an emf line integral, with the stated regularity, orientation and unit conventions. It asserts no field equations, no relation between $\mathrm{emf}$ and $\Phi_B'$, no conservation law, and no statement about singular sources; the transport identity is proved separately under its own hypotheses.

## Source notes

Tong §4.1 and §4.1.1, printed pp. 67-71, defines the emf as the line integral of the force per unit charge around a moving loop and derives the moving-wire expression from the swept surface; Griffiths §7.1.2-7.1.3, printed pp. 292-296, uses the same line-integral reading and the moving-loop construction. The present item extracts exactly the geometric data, the flux and the emf integral, with explicit regularity, injectivity, orientation and unit conventions; no conservation law or flux-derivative identity is included here, and the $C^2$ sheet with single-valued $C^1$ velocity is the strict branch that the companion transport theorem requires.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $N$ be the Newtonian potential transform of [[def-newtonian-potential]] in dimension $n=3$: for a finite-valued function $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}f=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^3:f(x)\ne0\}}$ is compact ([[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]),
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$$
at each $x\in\mathbb R^3$ where this integral is absolutely finite, where $\Phi$ is the normalized kernel of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]] with its value at the pole assigned $0$, so that $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$; write also $g(0):=0$ and $g(z):=|z|^{-1}$ for $z\ne0$, so that $\Phi=g/(4\pi)$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$. Let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ be the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ be the set of maps each of whose three components is smooth ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with compact support in the above sense. For $u,v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ write $Nu:=(Nu_1,Nu_2,Nu_3)$ componentwise, so that the linkage pairing is the map
$$B(u,v):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle u(x),Nv(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x).$$
Then all three integrals
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle u(x),Nv(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle Nu(x),v(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)$$
converge absolutely ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]) and have the same value; therefore $B$ is well defined, real-valued, symmetric, $B(u,v)=B(v,u)$, and bilinear over $\mathbb R$ in each argument. In particular the common value of the three integrals is unchanged by exchanging the two density fields $u$ and $v$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and let $u,v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth with compact supports, with $N$, $B$ and $g$ as in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, says every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] For a measurable compactly supported $f$, the Newtonian potential is $Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. ([[def-newtonian-potential]]).

[F2] The normalized Laplace kernel is $\Phi_n(x)=|x|^{2-n}/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ for $n\ge3$ and $x\ne0$; its value at $0$ may be assigned arbitrarily, and $\omega_{n-1}$ is the chart surface measure, which agrees with the polar measure $\sigma$. ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]).

[F3] The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$. ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).

[F4] For every $n\ge1$, the unit ball has $V_n(1)=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$. ([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]).

[F5] For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$. ([[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]]).

[F6] $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$. ([[cor-real-gamma-one-half-is-root-pi]]).

[F7] The normalized Laplace kernel $\Phi$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^n$ for $n\ge2$. ([[lem-laplace-fundamental-kernel-is-locally-integrable]]).

[F8] For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ the support is $\operatorname{supp}f:=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\ne0\}}$, and $f$ is compactly supported when $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compact. ([[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]).

[F9] Let $k\in\mathbb N$, $m,q\ge1$ and $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open; a map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$, and it is smooth, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, in particular for every $k\ge1$. ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F10] A scalar function of class $C^k$ on $U$ has every iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ for words of length $0\le r\le k$ existing and continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$ itself. ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

[F11] For $n\ge1$ the Euclidean distance $d_2$ is a metric on $\mathbb R^n$. ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F12] In a metric space, closed balls $\bar B(x,r)$ are closed. ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]).

[F13] A subset $K$ of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded for the Euclidean metric. ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F14] A nonempty compact $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ has the property that every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb R$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$. ([[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]).

[F15] Every compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded. ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]).

[F16] A subset $A$ of a metric space is bounded if $A=\emptyset$ or there are $x_0$ and $r>0$ with $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$. ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

[F17] For a measurable $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ and $E\in\mathcal A$, the integral over $E$ is $\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu$. ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

[F18] For measurable $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with $f\le g$, the integrals satisfy $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$. ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F19] If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then $\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu$. ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]).

[F20] The Lebesgue integral is complex-linear on $L^1(\mu)$. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F21] For $n\ge1$, $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $r>0$, the Euclidean ball satisfies $0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty$. ([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]).

[F22] Assume Countable Choice. Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and $T:U\to V$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. Then for every $f\in L^1(\lambda_n)$, $\int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y)=\int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x)$. ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]).

[F23] For nonnegative product-measurable $f$ on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces, the iterated integrals and the product integral agree. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F24] For $f\in L^1(\mu\times\nu)$ on a product of sigma-finite measure spaces, the section integrals are integrable after the stated exceptional-set convention and the three integrals agree. ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F25] Under the identification $\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n$, the Lebesgue measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ is the completion of the product measure $\lambda_m\times\lambda_n$. ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]).

[F26] The Euclidean inner product satisfies $\langle x,y\rangle=\langle y,x\rangle$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$. ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F27] Under Countable Choice, every continuous map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is Borel measurable. ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]).

[F28] If $\tilde f,\tilde g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ are Borel measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto\tilde f(x-y)\tilde g(y)$ is Borel measurable on $\mathbb R^{2n}$. ([[lem-borel-representatives-make-the-convolution-integrand-borel-measurable]]).

[F29] For positive Euclidean dimensions the Borel product sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n$ is the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$. ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]]).

[F30] Composition of Borel measurable maps preserves Borel measurability. ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The supports $K_u:=\operatorname{supp}u$ and $K_v:=\operatorname{supp}v$ are compact by [F8], hence closed and bounded in $(\mathbb R^3,d_2)$ by [F11] and [F15]; by [F16] there are $x_u,\rho_u$ and $x_v,\rho_v$ with $K_u\subseteq B(x_u,\rho_u)$ and $K_v\subseteq B(x_v,\rho_v)$ (for an empty support any pair works, since the empty set is bounded). Put $R:=\max\{|x_u|+\rho_u,\,|x_v|+\rho_v\}>0$. For $x\in K_u$ the triangle inequality gives $|x|\le|x_u|+|x-x_u|<|x_u|+\rho_u\le R$, and likewise on $K_v$, so $K_u\cup K_v\subseteq B_R(0)=B(0,R)$; moreover $u(x)=0$ for $x\notin K_u$ and $v(y)=0$ for $y\notin K_v$ by [F8]. [F8, F11, F15, F16, algebra]

1.2 For $z\ne0$, [F2] gives $\Phi(z)=|z|^{2-3}/((3-2)\omega_2)=|z|^{-1}/\omega_2$, and [F3] gives $\omega_2=|S^2|=3|B_1|$ with $|B_1|=V_3(1)$. By [F4], $V_3(1)=\pi^{3/2}/\Gamma(5/2)$; by [F5] applied twice and [F6], $\Gamma(5/2)=\frac32\cdot\frac12\cdot\Gamma(1/2)=\frac34\sqrt\pi$, hence $V_3(1)=\pi^{3/2}/(\frac34\sqrt\pi)=\frac43\pi$ and $\omega_2=4\pi$. Therefore $4\pi\Phi(z)=|z|^{-1}=g(z)$ for $z\ne0$; assigning the permitted pole value $\Phi(0)=0$ by [F2] gives $\Phi=g/(4\pi)$ on all of $\mathbb R^3$, so by [F1] the transform of the Statement is $Nf(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(y)g(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$ at each $x$ where this integral is absolutely finite. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

1.3 By [F9] the components $u_i,v_j$ are smooth, so by [F10] they are continuous, and by [F27] they are Borel measurable; likewise $g$ is Borel measurable because assigning the value $0$ at the pole of the continuous function $z\mapsto|z|^{-1}$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ gives the function whose superlevel sets $\{g>t\}$ are $B_{1/t}(0)\setminus\{0\}$ for $t>0$, $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ for $t=0$ and $\mathbb R^3$ for $t<0$, all open and hence Borel. Applying [F28] to $g$ and $v_j$ shows $(x,y)\mapsto g(x-y)v_j(y)$ is Borel on $\mathbb R^6$; the maps $(x,y)\mapsto u_i(x)$ are Borel as compositions with the continuous projection, and for each pair $(i,j)$ the map $\Phi_{ij}(x,y):=(u_i(x),\,g(x-y)v_j(y))$ has Borel preimages of open rectangles by [F29]; multiplication $\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, so [F30] makes $(x,y)\mapsto u_i(x)v_j(y)g(x-y)$ Borel, and the finite sum $H(x,y):=\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle g(x-y)$ is Borel as well. [F9, F10, F26, F27, F28, F29, F30]

2.1 The closed ball $\bar B_{2R}(0)$ is closed by [F12] and bounded by [F16], hence compact in $(\mathbb R^3,d_2)$ by [F13]. Since $\Phi\ge0$ in dimension three and $\Phi=g/(4\pi)$ by step 1.2, [F7] and [F18] give $$K_R:=\int_{B_{2R}(0)}g\,d\lambda_3=\int_{B_{2R}(0)}4\pi\Phi\,d\lambda_3\le4\pi\int_{\bar B_{2R}(0)}\Phi\,d\lambda_3<\infty.$$ [F7, F12, F13, F16, F18, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Fix $x\in B_R(0)$. The translation-dilation map $T_x:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, $T_x(y):=x-y$, is smooth with $T_x^{-1}=T_x$ and $|\det DT_x(y)|=1$ for every $y$, so it is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism; and $T_x(B_R(0))=x-B_R(0)\subseteq B_{2R}(0)$, since $|x-y|\le|x|+|y|<2R$ for $|y|<R$. The function $g$ is nonnegative and $\lambda_3$-measurable, and $\int_{B_{2R}(0)}g<\infty$ by step 2.1, so $g\mathbf 1_{B_{2R}(0)}\in L^1(\lambda_3)$; applying [F22] to it and using [F18] and $T_x(B_R(0))\subseteq B_{2R}(0)$ yields $$\int_{B_R(0)}g(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{T_x(B_R(0))}g(z)\,d\lambda_3(z)\le\int_{B_{2R}(0)}g\,d\lambda_3=K_R .$$ [F18, F22, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 By step 1.1, $|u_i|\le M_u$ and $|v_j|\le M_v$ on all of $\mathbb R^3$ for the finite constants $M_u:=\max_{\bar B_R(0)}|u|$ and $M_v:=\max_{\bar B_R(0)}|v|$, which exist by [F14] applied to the continuous functions $|u|,|v|$ on the nonempty compact set $\bar B_R(0)$ of steps 1.1 and 2.1 (a vanishing field has $M=0$). Hence, using [F17] and [F23] for the nonnegative Borel function $|u_i(x)||v_j(y)|g(x-y)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3$, [F18] and step 3.1 give $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u_i(x)||v_j(y)|g(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)=\int_{B_R(0)}\int_{B_R(0)}|u_i(x)||v_j(y)|g(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)\le M_uM_v\lambda_3(B_R(0))K_R<\infty,$$ with $\lambda_3(B_R(0))<\infty$ by [F21] and $K_R<\infty$ by step 2.1. Summing over the three pairs $(i,j)=(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)$ and using $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\sum_i|u_i||v_i|$, the double integral of $\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle g(x-y)/(4\pi)$ converges absolutely; by [F25] and [F29] the Euclidean and product-measure structures on $\mathbb R^6$ agree on Borel sets, so [F24] applies to this $L^1$ function and permits either order of integration. [F17, F18, F21, F23, F24, F25, F29, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.3, step 1.1, algebra]

5.1 Fix $x\in B_R(0)$. Since $v$ vanishes off $K_v\subseteq B_R(0)$ by step 1.1, the estimate of step 3.1 gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|v_j(y)|\,\Phi(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\le M_vK_R/(4\pi)<\infty$, so $Nv_j(x)$ is absolutely finite, and [F20] applied componentwise to the integrable functions $y\mapsto v_j(y)\Phi(x-y)$ gives $\langle u(x),Nv(x)\rangle=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle g(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$. Integrating this identity over $x\in B_R(0)$, using [F17], the everywhere-vanishing of $u$ off $B_R(0)$, and the identification of the iterated integral with the double integral already proved absolutely convergent in step 4.1, yields $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle u(x),Nv(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x),$$ the left-hand integral being absolutely finite because its absolute value is bounded by the finite quantity of step 4.1 divided by $4\pi$ by [F19]. [F17, F19, F20, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 1.1, algebra]

6.1 The same computation with the roles of $u$ and $v$ exchanged, using [F24] to interchange the two orders of integration of the common absolutely convergent double integral of step 4.1, gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle Nu(x),v(x)\rangle\,d\lambda_3(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x).$$ [F24, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

6.2 For bilinearity let $u^{(1)},u^{(2)},v,\alpha,\beta$ be given as in the Statement, with $w:=\alpha u^{(1)}+\beta u^{(2)}$. The componentwise linearity of the Newtonian integral [F20] and step 1.1's support bound for the union of the supports show $Nw=\alpha Nu^{(1)}+\beta Nu^{(2)}$ at every point, hence $B(w,v)=\alpha B(u^{(1)},v)+\beta B(u^{(2)},v)$ by [F20] and the absolute finiteness of step 4.1 (the argument of steps 1.1-6.1 applies verbatim to $w$, whose support is contained in the sum of the two supports and hence bounded). The second-slot computation is the same with the roles exchanged. [F20, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Steps 5.1, 6.1 and the definition of $B$ show that $B(u,v)$ is well defined and real-valued, that all three integrals of the Statement are absolutely convergent with that common value, and that the exchanged pairing satisfies $B(v,u)=\frac1{4\pi}\int\int\frac{\langle v(y),u(x)\rangle}{|y-x|}\,d\lambda_3(x)\,d\lambda_3(y)$; since $|x-y|=|y-x|$ and $\langle v(y),u(x)\rangle=\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle$ by [F26], [F24] identifies this with $B(u,v)$, giving symmetry. [F24, F26, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 If $u=0$ or $v=0$ then all integrands above vanish identically, all three integrals are $0$, and the symmetry and bilinearity identities hold trivially; the empty support case was already admitted in step 1.1. The proof uses Countable Choice exactly through [A1] in the cited change-of-variables, product-measure, ball-measure and Borel-measurability interfaces, and no full Axiom of Choice. [A1, F22, F24, F25, step 1.1, step 7.1, step 6.2, cases] ∎



## Source notes

Hunter §2.6.1 and §2.7, printed pp. 33-37, treat the Newtonian potential of compactly
supported data and its local kernel estimates; Teschl §5.3, equations (5.21)-(5.26),
printed pp. 117-118, records the fundamental solution and the local integrability of
the kernel. Neither text states the linkage pairing $B(u,v)$ or its symmetry; the
statement and its proof assemble the two cited representations with the
Tonelli/Fubini machinery of the measure-theory pages. The kernel normalization
$\omega_2=4\pi$ used for the $n=3$ specialization is computed here from the
chart-surface-measure convention, the unit-ball volume formula and the Gamma
functional equation rather than quoted as a numerical convention.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$ be a real scalar parameter, let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]), and define componentwise
$$A:=\mu_0N(J),\qquad A_i=\mu_0\,N(J_i),\qquad N f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y),$$
the Newtonian vector potential attached to [[def-newtonian-potential]] in dimension three. Then:

(a) $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}A=0$ and $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$, componentwise ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]);

(b) there is $C>0$ with $|\operatorname{curl}A(x)|\le C/(1+|x|^2)$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$; hence $\operatorname{curl}A\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\langle A,J\rangle\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$, both in the ordinary Lebesgue sense ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]);

(c) the curl-field energy identity
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3=\mu_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3$$
holds, and equivalently $\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3\ge0$.

The identity is stated for the explicit smooth compact currents and the Newtonian construction; no uniqueness, no decay of $A$ itself beyond the curl bound of (b), and no extension to singular currents is claimed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, let $\mu_0>0$ and let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}J=0$, with $A=\mu_0N(J)$ componentwise as in the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, says every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, let $\varepsilon_0>0$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ with $Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(y)/(4\pi|x-y|)\,dy$. Then $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ one has $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$. ([[lem-em-smooth-newtonian-upgrade]]).

[F2] For a measurable compactly supported $f$, the Newtonian potential is $Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. ([[def-newtonian-potential]]).

[F3] Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge3$, let $f$ be integrable and zero outside $B_R(0)$, and put $M=\int f$. For $r=|x|>2R$, $\left|Nf(x)-\frac{M r^{2-n}}{(n-2)\omega_{n-1}}\right|\le\frac{2^{n-1}R}{\omega_{n-1}}\|f\|_1r^{1-n}$. ([[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]).

[F4] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, let $n\ge3$, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ vanish outside a closed ball of radius $R$, and let $Nf$ be the Newtonian potential. Then for every $x$ with $|x|>2R$ the gradient is absolutely convergent and $|\nabla(Nf)(x)|\le\frac{2^{n-1}\|f\|_1}{\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1}}$. ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]]).

[F5] For $C^1$ fields on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, $\operatorname{div}(F\times G)=\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle$. ([[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]]).

[F6] For a $C^2$ field $F$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F$. ([[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]]).

[F7] The divergence and curl are defined pointwise from first partial derivatives; for $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ one has $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$. ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]).

[F8] For a $C^2$ function the Laplacian is $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}\nabla f$, and for a $C^2$ map $\Delta F$ is componentwise. ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F9] The cross product in coordinates is $(u\times v)_x=u_yv_z-u_zv_y$, with the cyclic permutations for the other two coordinates. ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[F10] The Euclidean inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$, and it is symmetric. ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F11] $B(x,r)=\{y:d(x,y)<r\}$ is the open ball of the metric space. ([[def-metric-ball]]).

[F12] Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable with $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$. ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]).

[F13] Let $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere with $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single integrable nonnegative $g$. Then $f\in L^1$ and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$. ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]).

[F14] For measurable $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ and $E\in\mathcal A$, $\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu$. ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

[F15] For measurable $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with $f\le g$ one has $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$. ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F16] For a nonnegative simple measurable function $s=\sum_jc_j\chi_{E_j}$ the simple integral is $\int s\,d\mu=\sum_jc_j\mu(E_j)$. ([[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]]).

[F17] The nonnegative integral of a nonnegative simple function equals its simple integral. ([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F18] Let $k\in\mathbb N$ and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open; a map on $U$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is, and it is smooth when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, in particular for every $k\ge1$. ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F19] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $0<\varepsilon<R$. Then $B_R=\{x:|x|<R\}$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain with boundary $S_R$ and outward normal $\nu(x)=x/|x|$, the divergence theorem applies on $B_R$, and each sphere $S_r$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface carrying a finite Borel surface measure with the standard graph charts. ([[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]]).

[F20] On a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain the divergence theorem holds with the outward normal, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,d\lambda=\int_{\partial\Omega}\langle F,\nu\rangle\,dS$. ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]).

[F21] On a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface the surface integral is defined by finitely many graph charts, and for a bounded continuous $g$ with finite area one has $\int_S|g|\,dS\le\sup_S|g|\int_S1\,dS$. ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[F22] The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$, scaling by $r$ multiplies surface measure by $r^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$. ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).

[F23] For every $n\ge1$, $V_n(1)=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$. ([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]).

[F24] For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$. ([[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]]).

[F25] $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$. ([[cor-real-gamma-one-half-is-root-pi]]).

[F26] A subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded for the Euclidean metric. ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F27] Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb R$ on a nonempty compact $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$. ([[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]]).

[F28] Closed balls $\bar B(x,r)$ in a metric space are closed. ([[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]).

[F29] A subset $A$ of a metric space is bounded if $A=\emptyset$ or there are $x_0$ and $r>0$ with $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$. ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

[F30] Every compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded. ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]).

[F31] For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ the support is $\operatorname{supp}f=\overline{\{x:f(x)\ne0\}}$, and $f$ is compactly supported when that support is compact. ([[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]).

[F32] The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1(\mu)$. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F33] For $n\ge1$ the Euclidean distance $d_2$ is a metric on $\mathbb R^n$. ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

[F34] Under Countable Choice every continuous map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is Borel measurable. ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]).

[F35] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, let $n\ge1$, $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $r>0$; then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is Lebesgue measurable with $0<\lambda_n(B(x,r))<\infty$. ([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The supports of the components $J_i$ are compact by [F31] and bounded by [F30], [F33] and [F29]. Fix $R>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}J\subseteq B_R(0)=B(0,R)$, an open ball in the sense of [F11] (for the empty case any $R$ works), and put $r_0:=\max\{2R,1\}$. [F11, F29, F30, F31, F33, algebra]

1.2 By [F1] applied to each component $J_i$ (with [F18] supplying the smoothness of the components of $J$), each $A_i=\mu_0N(J_i)$ lies in $C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and satisfies $-\Delta A_i=\mu_0J_i$ and $D^\alpha A_i=\mu_0N(D^\alpha J_i)$ for every multi-index $\alpha$; in particular $A$ is $C^\infty$, hence $C^2$ for [F6], and [F8] gives $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ componentwise. Moreover $\operatorname{div}A=\sum_i\partial_iA_i=\mu_0\sum_iN(\partial_iJ_i)=\mu_0N(\operatorname{div}J)=0$ pointwise, where the middle equality uses [F1] with $\alpha=e_i$ and the linearity [F32] (with [F2] supplying the integral representation). [F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, F18, F32, algebra]

1.3 For $r>r_0\ge2R$ and each $i$, [F3] with $n=3$ gives $\left|N J_i(x)-\frac{M_i}{4\pi r}\right|\le\frac{R\|J_i\|_1}{\pi r^2}$, where $M_i=\int J_i$ and $r=|x|$; hence $|A_i(x)|\le \mu_0\left(\frac{|M_i|}{4\pi}+\frac{R\|J_i\|_1}{\pi}\right)\frac1r$, and [F4] with $n=3$ gives $|\nabla A_i(x)|\le\frac{\mu_0\|J_i\|_1}{\pi r^2}$. By [F28], [F26], [F33] and [F27], the closed ball $\bar B_{r_0}(0)$ is compact and each of the continuous functions $A_i$ and $\partial_kA_i$ attains a finite maximum on it, so there are finite constants $c_1,c_2$ with $|A(x)|\le c_1$ and $|\partial_kA_i(x)|\le c_2$ for all $x$ and $i,k$; consequently $A$ and all its first partials are bounded on $\mathbb R^3$. [F3, F4, F26, F27, F28, F33, algebra]

2.1 By [F9] each coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}A$ is a difference of two entries of $\nabla A$, so [F7] yields $|\operatorname{curl}A(x)|\le 2\sum_{i,k}|\partial_kA_i(x)|\le 18c_2$ for $|x|\le r_0$, while for $|x|>r_0$ the gradient bound of step 1.3 gives $|\operatorname{curl}A(x)|\le 2\sum_{i,k}\frac{\mu_0\|J_i\|_1}{\pi|x|^2}\le\frac{36\mu_0\max_i\|J_i\|_1}{\pi|x|^2}$. Hence $|\operatorname{curl}A(x)|\le C/(1+|x|^2)$ on all of $\mathbb R^3$ with $C:=\max\{18c_2(1+r_0^2),\,72\mu_0\max_i\|J_i\|_1/\pi\}$. Moreover $\langle A,J\rangle$ is continuous because $A$ is $C^\infty$ by step 1.2 and $J$ is smooth, it is supported in the compact set $\operatorname{supp}J\subseteq B_R(0)$ with $R>0$, and it is bounded by $3c_1\max_i\|J_i\|_\infty$: by [F10], $|\langle A,J\rangle|\le\sum_i|A_i|\,|J_i|\le c_1\sum_i|J_i|\le 3c_1\max_i\|J_i\|_\infty$, since each $|A_i|\le|A|\le c_1$. Since $|\langle A,J\rangle|\mathbf 1_{B_R(0)}\le 3c_1\max_i\|J_i\|_\infty\,\mathbf 1_{B_R(0)}$ pointwise, [F14] and [F15] give $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\langle A,J\rangle|\,d\lambda_3=\int_{B_R(0)}|\langle A,J\rangle|\,d\lambda_3\le 3c_1\max_i\|J_i\|_\infty\int_{B_R(0)}1\,d\lambda_3=3c_1\max_i\|J_i\|_\infty\,\lambda_3\bigl(B_R(0)\bigr)<\infty,$$ the middle equality being the simple integral of the indicator by [F16] and [F17], and the finiteness of $\lambda_3(B_R(0))$ being [F35]. [F7, F9, F10, F14, F15, F16, F17, F35, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 On $\mathbb R^3$ one has, by [F5], [F6], [F10] and step 1.2, $$\operatorname{div}(A\times\operatorname{curl}A)=\langle\operatorname{curl}A,\operatorname{curl}A\rangle-\langle A,\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}A\rangle=|\operatorname{curl}A|^2-\mu_0\langle A,J\rangle,$$ because $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}A=\nabla\operatorname{div}A-\Delta A=-\Delta A=\mu_0J$. The fields $A$ and $\operatorname{curl}A$ are $C^1$ by step 1.2, so [F5] applies. [F5, F6, F10, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Fix $r>r_0$. By [F19] the ball $B_r(0)$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain with boundary $S_r$ and outward normal $\nu(x)=x/|x|$, and [F20] applied to $F=A\times\operatorname{curl}A$ together with step 2.2 gives $$\oint_{S_r}\langle A\times\operatorname{curl}A,\nu\rangle\,dS=\int_{B_r(0)}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3-\mu_0\int_{B_r(0)}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3 .$$ [F19, F20, step 2.2]

3.2 For $r>r_0$ the boundary term is bounded by the decay estimates: [F21] and the componentwise bound $|(u\times v)_x|\le2\max_k|u_k|\max_k|v_k|$ from [F9] give $$\left|\oint_{S_r}\langle A\times\operatorname{curl}A,\nu\rangle\,dS\right|\le\int_{S_r}|A\times\operatorname{curl}A|\,dS\le 4\sup_{S_r}|A|\sup_{S_r}|\operatorname{curl}A|\int_{S_r}1\,dS .$$ By [F22], [F23], [F24] and [F25] the sphere area is $\int_{S_r}1\,dS=|S^2|r^2=3V_3(1)r^2=4\pi r^2$, and by steps 1.3 and 2.1, $\sup_{S_r}|A|\le c_1'\,r^{-1}$ and $\sup_{S_r}|\operatorname{curl}A|\le c_2'\,r^{-2}$ for constants $c_1',c_2'$ independent of $r$. Hence the boundary term is at most $16\pi c_1'c_2'/r$, which tends to $0$ as $r\to\infty$. [F9, F21, F22, F23, F24, F25, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $r_n\uparrow\infty$ with $r_n>r_0$. The functions $|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\mathbf 1_{B_{r_n}(0)}$ are nonnegative and measurable by [F34], and increase to $|\operatorname{curl}A|^2$; [F12] therefore gives $$\int_{B_{r_n}(0)}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3\uparrow L:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\,d\lambda_3\in[0,+\infty].$$ The functions $\langle A,J\rangle\mathbf 1_{B_{r_n}(0)}$ converge pointwise to $\langle A,J\rangle$ and are dominated by the integrable function $|\langle A,J\rangle|$ of step 2.1, so [F13] gives $\int_{B_{r_n}(0)}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3\to\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle A,J\rangle\,d\lambda_3$, a finite real number. Passing to the limit in the identity of step 3.1 using the vanishing boundary term of step 3.2 yields $L=\mu_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle A,J\rangle$, so $\operatorname{curl}A\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and the identity of (c) holds; the equivalent form follows by dividing by $2\mu_0>0$, and $L\ge0$ gives the final inequality. [F12, F13, F34, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Clauses (a), (b), (c) are now established: (a) in step 1.2, the decay bound and the $L^1$ statement (b) in steps 2.1 and 4.1, and the identity with its equivalent form in step 4.1. The hypothesis $\operatorname{div}J=0$ was used only in step 1.2; smoothness and compact support only in steps 1.1 through 1.3; no uniqueness of $A$, no decay of $A$ beyond the curl bound, and no singular-current extension is asserted. Countable Choice enters only through the cited Newtonian, measure and surface interfaces, not through any selection. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F12, F13, F20, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎



## Source notes

Hunter §2.6.1 and §2.7, printed pp. 33-37, and Teschl §5.3, equations (5.21)-(5.26), printed pp. 117-118, supply the Newtonian potential, the local kernel estimates and the far-field behaviour behind the decay steps. Neither text states the curl-field energy identity in this exact form; the present proof assembles it from the supplied smoothness and decay of the Newtonian potential, the vector-calculus identity for $\operatorname{div}(F\times G)$, the divergence theorem on a ball and the monotone-convergence argument. The local identities $\operatorname{div}A=0$ and $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ are recorded pointwise for the explicit smooth compact currents; the fine behaviour of the fields at a singular current is not treated.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]], inherited from the Maxwell and transport suppliers below. Let $\Omega\times I$ be the laboratory region with $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0$, $\mu_0$ the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $E,B$ be fields and $\rho,J$ source fields of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], jointly of class $C^2$ and $C^1$ respectively on $\Omega\times I$, satisfying the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] pointwise on $\Omega\times I$. Let $(D,r,v)$ be a moving material circuit of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]] with time interval $I$, and fix a compact subinterval $J\subseteq I$ such that the swept set $r(D\times J)$ is compactly contained in $\Omega$ (no singularity crossing). Put $S(t)=r(D,t)$ and let $\gamma_t$ be the oriented closed boundary path of (b) of the definition, with trace $C(t)=\partial S(t)$.

Then the flux $\Phi_B:I\to\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]] is differentiable at every $t\in I$ with
$$\Phi_B'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{C(t)}(v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$
for every $t\in J$ the frozen patch $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t))$ is a test geometry of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]], the fixed-patch Faraday identity
$$\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS=-\oint_{C(t)}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$$
holds, and consequently the electromotive force of the circuit satisfies
$$\mathrm{emf}(t)=\oint_{C(t)}(E+v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\Phi_B'(t)\qquad\text{for every }t\in J.$$
The physical reading, under the adopted coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], is that the work per unit charge of the electromagnetic force on charges moving with the conductor material equals minus the rate of change of the magnetic flux. The result is conditional on the joint regularity, the smooth Maxwell branch and the no-singularity-crossing hypothesis; it asserts no fixed-loop formula for arbitrary moving loops, no field uniqueness, no statement about singular supports and no empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, constants $c>0,\varepsilon_0>0,\mu_0>0$, fields $E,B$ jointly $C^2$ and sources $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$ satisfying the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell equations pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, a moving material circuit $(D,r,v)$ with time interval $I$, and a compact subinterval $J\subseteq I$ with the swept set $r(D\times J)$ compactly contained in $\Omega$.

[A1] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, says every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] A moving material circuit is the data $(D,r,v)$: $D$ a compact finite elementary Green region with its positive boundary chain, $r:D\times I\to\Omega$ extending to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$ and $r(\cdot,t)$ injective on $D$ for every $t\in I$, and $v$ a $C^1$ single-valued velocity field with $v(r(u,w,t),t)=\partial_tr(u,w,t)$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set. ([[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]]).

[F2] The electromotive force of the circuit at $t$ is the vector line integral $\mathrm{emf}(t)=\oint_{\gamma_t}\langle E(\cdot,t)+v(\cdot,t)\times B(\cdot,t),d\mathbf r\rangle$ over the oriented closed path $\gamma_t$ with trace $C(t)=r(\partial D,t)$, in the piecewise $C^1$ convention, with unit V; the definition asserts no relation between emf and $\Phi_B'$. ([[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]]).

[F3] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, let $B$ be a $C^1$ field on a neighbourhood of the swept surface with $\operatorname{div}B=0$. Then the flux $\Phi$ of the moving patch is differentiable on $I$ and $\Phi'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$, the boundary integral using the induced orientation; the supplier states the differential identity at the times whose slice is regular on the interior of the parameter region, and the defining hypothesis of the moving material circuit below makes every slice regular at every $t\in I$. ([[lem-em-moving-flux]]).

[F4] A patch test geometry in $\Omega$ is a regular $C^2$ surface patch $(D,r)$ over a finite elementary Green region: $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ finite elementary Green region, $r$ of class $C^2$ on an open neighbourhood of $D$, $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior of $D$, and no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$; its induced boundary chain is $r(\partial D)$ with the circulation of the piecewise $C^1$ convention, and its oriented flux is $\int_SF\cdot n_S\,dS=\int_D(F\circ r)\cdot(r_u\times r_v)\,dudv$. ([[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]).

[F5] Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate holds pointwise with $E,B$ jointly $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ of class $C^1$. Then for every patch test geometry $(D,r)$ the flux functions $t\mapsto\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and $t\mapsto\int_SE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ are differentiable on $I$ and, for every $t\in I$, $\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$. ([[pthm-em-integral-maxwell]]).

[F6] A field of class $C^k$ is a map $\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$; $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T. ([[def-em-fields]]).

[F7] The framework adopts the SI constants $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, with time in seconds and the emf unit V; no numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted. ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F8] The source fields $\rho$ (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ (A m$^{-2}$) are maps on $\Omega\times I$. ([[def-em-sources]]).

[F9] In the smooth branch, jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous and continuous sources satisfy $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ pointwise. ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]).

[F10] The adopted coupling gives the continuum force density $\rho E+J\times B$ for matter interacting with the field through an explicitly stated matter model, and the covariant per-charge equation of motion for a test charge; the nonrelativistic coordinate statement is not adopted as exact. ([[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]).

[F11] The Euclidean inner product is additive in each argument: $\langle x+y,z\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle+\langle y,z\rangle$. ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F12] For $a<b$ and integrable $f,g$ on $[a,b]$, $f+g$ is integrable and $\int_a^b(f+g)=\int_a^bf+\int_a^bg$. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]).

[F13] For a piecewise $C^1$ path $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ with $a<b$ and a continuous vector field $F$ on a set containing the trace, $\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_i\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt$; the value is independent of the admissible partition. ([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The circuit data of [F1] satisfy the hypotheses of [F3]: $r$ extends $C^2$ to a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with the cross product nonzero on the interior, $v$ is single-valued of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, and $B$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set because it is jointly $C^2$ on $\Omega\times I$ and $r(D\times I)\subseteq\Omega$ (indeed $B$ is $C^2$ there); and $\operatorname{div}B=0$ pointwise by [F9]. Hence $\Phi_B$ is differentiable on $I$ and [F1, F3, F6, F9]
$$\Phi_B'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$$
for every $t\in I$, the boundary integral using the induced orientation of the patch boundary, which is the orientation of the path $\gamma_t$ of [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F6, F9]

1.2 Fix $t\in J$. The frozen data $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t))$ is a patch test geometry of [F4]: $D$ is a finite elementary Green region, $r(\cdot,\cdot,t)$ is $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $D$, its cross product is nonzero on the interior of $D$, and injectivity of $r(\cdot,t)$ on $D$ by [F1] implies that no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$; its image $S(t)=r(D,t)$ is compact and contained in the open set $\Omega$. Moreover $E,B$ are jointly $C^2$ and $\rho,J$ are $C^1$, so the smooth branch hypothesis of [F5] holds by [F9], [F6] and [F8]. Applying the patch clause of [F5] to the fixed patch $(D,r(\cdot,\cdot,t))$ gives that the frozen-patch flux function $s\mapsto\int_{S(t)}B(\cdot,s)\cdot n\,dS$ is differentiable on $I$ with derivative at $s=t$ equal to $\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS$, and that [F1, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9]
$$\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS=-\oint_{\partial S(t)}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$
the circulation being over the induced boundary chain of the patch, that is, over $\gamma_t$ with the orientation of [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9]

2.1 At every $t\in J$ the line integral of the sum splits: for the piecewise $C^1$ closed path $\gamma_t$, the identity $\langle E+v\times B,d\mathbf r\rangle=\langle E,d\mathbf r\rangle+\langle v\times B,d\mathbf r\rangle$ holds pointwise along the path by additivity of the inner product [F11], so the definition [F13] and the Riemann-integral linearity [F12] applied to the finitely many arcs give $\oint_{\gamma_t}(E+v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\oint_{\gamma_t}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r+\oint_{\gamma_t}(v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$, which is $\mathrm{emf}(t)$ by [F2]. Substituting the frozen-patch identity of step 1.2 into the first term, and then combining the two terms through the transport formula of step 1.1, yields [F2, F11, F12, F13, step 1.1, step 1.2]
$$\mathrm{emf}(t)=-\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n\,dS+\oint_{\gamma_t}(v\times B)(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\Phi_B'(t),$$
for every $t\in J$. [F2, F11, F12, F13, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 The frozen patch is a test geometry for every $t\in J$ (step 1.2), the fixed-patch Faraday identity holds (step 1.2), and the emf identity holds for every $t\in J$ (step 2.1); the flux formula of step 1.1 holds on all of $I$. The physical reading of the integrand as the force per unit charge on charges moving with the conductor material is the adopted coupling [F10], whose exact relativistic form is the covariant equation and whose nonrelativistic coordinate statement is not adopted as exact; the algebraic identity itself uses only [F1]-[F13]. The constants and units are those of [F6] and [F7]; the result asserts no fixed-loop formula for arbitrary moving loops, no field uniqueness and no statement about singular supports, and the no-singularity-crossing hypothesis is the containment of the swept set in the open region $\Omega$ on which the fields satisfy the stated regularity, where each image $S(t)$ is compact for $t\in I$ and the subinterval $J$ records the declared window. Countable Choice enters only through [A1] in the cited transport and integral-Maxwell suppliers. [A1, F6, F7, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎



## Source notes

Tong §4.1.1, printed pp. 69-71, derives the moving-loop statement $d\Phi/dt=-\oint(E+v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ from the swept surface; Griffiths §7.1.3, printed pp. 294-296, states the flux rule for motional emf and reads the emf as the line integral of the force per unit charge; Fitzpatrick §4.2, printed pp. 104-108, states the fixed-loop Faraday law from Stokes' theorem. The present theorem separates the two ingredients: the transport formula for the flux of the moving patch (supplied by the transport lemma on this page) and the frozen-patch Faraday identity (supplied by the integral-Maxwell theorem), both under explicitly stated regularity hypotheses, and combines them with the line-integral conventions. No source is cited for the strict regularity hypotheses, which are part of this framework's formulation rather than claims about any apparatus.

## Postulate

Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following reduced circuit description, to be used only within its declared regime. Let the laboratory region, its chart and units and the compact smooth current class be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-steady-current-regime]], and let the material response be one of the branches of [[post-em-material-closure]].

(a) [Circuit data] Fix a finite set of branches $\alpha=1,\dots,n$ (and capacitive branches $\beta=1,\dots,m$) and a time interval $J$. The model carries branch currents $I_\alpha:J\to\mathbb R$, branch charges $Q_\beta:J\to\mathbb R$, terminal potentials $V_\alpha:J\to\mathbb R$, and constant matrices $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ and $R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, with $L$ and $C$ symmetric, $C$ positive definite and $R$ symmetric positive semidefinite. The matrices, the terminal geometry and the choice of independent loops are fixed data of the model; they are declared, not derived here, and the smooth compact-current realization of the inductive couplings and its reciprocity are analysed separately on this page.

(b) [Branch relations and network laws] In the declared regime the inductive branches obey the Faraday branch relation $V(t)=L\dot I(t)$, i.e. each terminal potential is the rate of change of the branch flux linkage $LI$; the capacitive branches obey $V=C^{-1}Q$ (in the scalar case $V_\beta=Q_\beta/C_{\beta\beta}$); the resistive branches obey $V=RI$, the circuit form of the Ohmic relation of [[post-em-material-closure]]; and the network laws are Kirchhoff's current law at each node and loop voltage balance around each independent loop. The circuit-level bookkeeping quantities of the model are the flux linkage $LI$ and the stored energies $\tfrac12I^{\mathsf T}LI$ and $\tfrac12Q^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}Q$.

(c) [Quasistatic regime declaration] The description is confined to configurations whose largest geometric extent $\ell$ and shortest time scale $T$ of interest satisfy the quasistatic smallness condition $\ell/(cT)\ll1$, with negligible radiation and negligible leakage and with specified conductor geometry and ideal terminals. The inequality is a declared regime of validity of the model; no error bound for an arbitrary full Maxwell solution follows from it alone, and the model does not assert that every asymptotically small configuration is described to any particular accuracy.

(d) [Status, units and scope] This is an adopted reduced model, not a deduction from the vacuum Maxwell equations; the matrices $L,C,R$ are model data, no microscopic constitutive law beyond the adopted branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] is asserted, and no radiation, distributed-element, nonlinear, hysteretic, leakage or proximity effect is included. SI units consistent with [[def-em-si-conventions]] are used: $V$ in volts, $I$ in amperes, $Q$ in coulombs, $t$ in seconds, $L$ in henries ($\mathrm H=\mathrm V\,\mathrm s\,\mathrm A^{-1}$), $C$ in farads ($\mathrm F=\mathrm C\,\mathrm V^{-1}$) and $R$ in ohms ($\Omega=\mathrm V\,\mathrm A^{-1}$). Where conductor matter moves, material speeds are subluminal, $|v|<c$, when the relativistic force interpretation is used.

## Status and conventions

This is an explicitly adopted model assumption. Clause (a) fixes the branch and loop data together with the symmetry and positivity of $L,C,R$; clause (b) lists the terminal branch relations and the Kirchhoff network laws as model content; clause (c) states the quasistatic regime as a qualitative smallness declaration with the explicit warning that it does not by itself bound the error of any reduction and does not assert accuracy for every asymptotically small configuration; clause (d) records the status, the units and the exclusions.

The postulate is not derived from the vacuum Maxwell equations, from [[post-em-material-closure]] or from any measurement. The cited textbook treatments present the branch relations as part of the standard circuit model; the exact matrices, the terminal geometry and the loop choice remain model data. Consequences such as the energy bookkeeping, the RL and LC dynamics and the transformer idealisation on this page are conditional derivations from the adopted relations together with the smooth compact-current realization of the inductive couplings, and they inherit the regime declaration of clause (c).

## Source notes

Tong §4.1.2-4.1.3, printed pp. 71-77, defines the inductance through the flux linkage, introduces resistance as an additional material-dependent input and writes the coil equation; Griffiths §7.2.1-7.2.4, printed pp. 303-323, treats the flux-linkage definition, the coil equation $V=L\,\mathrm dI/\mathrm dt$, mutual inductance and the magnetic-energy bookkeeping; Fitzpatrick chapter 7, printed pp. 216-241, states the coil equation $V=L\,\mathrm dI/\mathrm dt+RI$ and the RL circuit. None of these texts derives the reduced branch relations from the vacuum field equations as a theorem with an error bound, and none is presented here as doing so; clause (c) records that limitation explicitly.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $j_1,\dots,j_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}j_\alpha=0$ be fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. Fix amplitudes $I\in\mathbb R^n$, put $J_I:=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nI_\alpha j_\alpha$, let $A_{J_I}$ be the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential of [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]] applied to the conserved current $J_I$, and let $B_{J_I}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}$. Define the linkage coefficients
$$L_{\alpha\beta}:=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\alpha,\beta=1,\dots,n .$$
Then:

(a) [Finiteness and self-energy] every $L_{\alpha\beta}$ is a finite real number: the defining double integral converges absolutely, and in particular every self-coefficient $L_{\alpha\alpha}$ is finite, so the compact smooth profiles carry a finite self-energy. This is a statement about the smooth profiles only; no finite value is assigned to a zero-radius thin-wire self-inductance.

(b) [Reciprocity and flux linkage] $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$ for all $\alpha,\beta$; $A_{J_I}=\sum_{\alpha}I_\alpha A_{j_\alpha}$ componentwise; and for every $\beta$ the linkage integral is
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle j_\beta,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nL_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha .$$
Thus the numbers $L_{\alpha\beta}$ are the linkage coefficients of the profiles: the linkage of profile $\beta$ with the field of the superposition is the linear combination $\sum_\alpha L_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha$.

(c) [Magnetic energy and positivity] with $U(I):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3$,
$$U(I)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^nL_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
all quantities finite; moreover $U(I)=0$ holds precisely when $J_I=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Consequently the symmetric matrix $L=(L_{\alpha\beta})$ is positive semidefinite, and it is positive definite exactly when the profiles are pointwise linearly independent, i.e. when $\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha\equiv0$ forces $I=0$.

(d) [Scope] the theorem concerns fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles and their Coulomb-gauge fields. It asserts no thin-wire, sheet or singular self-inductance; no time-dependent, moving, radiating or material configuration; and no uniqueness of the vector potential. The identification of these coefficients with the inductance matrix of the adopted lumped circuit model, and of the linkage derivatives with terminal voltages, is adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the strict material-loop theorem applies separately only to an actual moving sheet and compatible smooth Maxwell fields satisfying its hypotheses. No terminal-voltage law for arbitrary varying frozen profiles is inferred from the present magnetostatic computation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the constants $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, compact smooth divergence-free profiles $j_\alpha$, amplitudes $I\in\mathbb R^n$, the current $J_I=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha$, and the Coulomb-gauge field $A_{J_I}$ of the magnetostatic potential theorem.

[A1] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, says every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] For $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian potential $A=\mu_0N(J)$ is $C^\infty$ with $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ and $\operatorname{div}A=0$ pointwise, and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ is $C^\infty$ with $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ pointwise. ([[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]]).

[F2] For $u,v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ the three integrals $\int\langle u,Nv\rangle$, $\int\langle Nu,v\rangle$ and $\frac1{4\pi}\iint\frac{\langle u(x),v(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}$ converge absolutely and have a common value; the pairing is symmetric and bilinear. ([[lem-em-newtonian-linkage-symmetry]]).

[F3] For $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ and $A=\mu_0N(J)$: $\int|\operatorname{curl}A|^2=\mu_0\int\langle A,J\rangle$ and $\frac12\int\langle A,J\rangle=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|\operatorname{curl}A|^2\ge0$, the integrals finite, and $\operatorname{curl}A\in L^2$. ([[lem-em-newtonian-curl-field-energy]]).

[F4] The compact smooth current class consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. ([[def-em-steady-current-regime]]).

[F5] The framework constants are $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$ and $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F6] The lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] is an adopted reduced model: its matrix $L$ is declared model data, the flux linkage is $LI$, and its terminal law is a branch relation of the model, not a derivation from arbitrary time-dependent Maxwell fields. ([[post-em-circuit-approximation]]).

[F7] The Newtonian potential is $Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$ at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. ([[def-newtonian-potential]]).

[F8] The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1$. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F9] For a $C^2$ field $F$ on open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F$. ([[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]]).

[F10] For a $C^2$ map $\Delta F$ is componentwise and the Laplacian is $\operatorname{div}\nabla$. ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F11] The divergence and curl are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives. ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]).

[F12] The Euclidean inner product is symmetric and real bilinear. ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F13] A nonnegative measurable function has zero integral exactly when it vanishes almost everywhere. ([[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]]).

[F14] Under Countable Choice every continuous map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is Borel measurable. ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]).

[F15] For measurable $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with $f\le g$, $\int f\le\int g$. ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F16] For $n\ge1$, $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $r>0$ the ball satisfies $0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty$. ([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]).

[F17] For measurable $f$ and measurable $E$, $\int_Ef\,d\mu=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu$. ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For each $\alpha$ the profile $j_\alpha$ lies in the class of [F4], and so does $J_I$; by [F1] applied to $J_I$ the field $A_{J_I}$ is $C^\infty$ with $-\Delta A_{J_I}=\mu_0J_I$ and $\operatorname{div}A_{J_I}=0$ pointwise, and $B_{J_I}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}$ is $C^\infty$ with $\operatorname{curl}B_{J_I}=\mu_0J_I$, the Laplacian here being the componentwise operator of [F10]. Since each $A_{j_\alpha}=\mu_0N(j_\alpha)$ is the Newtonian potential of [F7] and $N$ is componentwise linear by [F8], $A_{J_I}=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha A_{j_\alpha}$ componentwise, and $B_{J_I}=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha B_{j_\alpha}$ by linearity of the pointwise curl [F11]. [F1, F4, F7, F8, F10, F11, algebra]

1.2 By [F2] applied to $(J_I,J_I)$ and the definitions of $U$ and the coefficients, $U(I)=\frac12\int\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle=\frac{\mu_0}{2}\frac1{4\pi}\iint\frac{\langle J_I(x),J_I(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta$, all finite. On the other hand [F3] applied to the divergence-free current $J_I$ with parameter $\mu_0$ gives $\int\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle=\frac1{\mu_0}\int|B_{J_I}|^2$, hence $U(I)=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|B_{J_I}|^2\ge0$; this is the energy identity of (c). [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the pair $(j_\alpha,j_\beta)$: the double integral defining $L_{\alpha\beta}$ (with the prefactor $\mu_0$) converges absolutely, so $L_{\alpha\beta}$ is a finite real number, and exchanging the two fields and the two integration variables leaves it unchanged, so $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$; this is (a) and the reciprocity of (b). Applying [F2] to $(j_\beta,J_I)$ and using the symmetry of the Euclidean pairing [F12] and the linearity of the integrals [F8] gives $\int\langle j_\beta,A_{J_I}\rangle=\mu_0\frac1{4\pi}\iint\frac{\langle j_\beta(x),J_I(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha L_{\beta\alpha}$; this is the linkage identity of (b). [F2, F8, F12, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 If $U(I)=0$ then $\int|B_{J_I}|^2=0$ by step 1.2. The function $|B_{J_I}|^2$ is nonnegative, continuous by step 1.1 and Borel by [F14], so [F13] gives $|B_{J_I}|=0$ almost everywhere; were $B_{J_I}(x_0)\ne0$ for some $x_0$, continuity would give $|B_{J_I}|^2\ge\varepsilon>0$ on a ball $B(x_0,r)$ of finite positive measure [F16], and [F15] with [F17] would give $\int|B_{J_I}|^2\ge\varepsilon\lambda_3(B(x_0,r))>0$, a contradiction; hence $B_{J_I}=0$ everywhere. Then $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}=\nabla\operatorname{div}A_{J_I}-\Delta A_{J_I}=\mu_0J_I$ by [F9] and step 1.1, while $\operatorname{curl}B_{J_I}=0$; so $\mu_0J_I=0$ and $J_I=0$. Conversely $J_I=0$ gives $A_{J_I}=0$ componentwise and $U(I)=0$. [F9, F13, F14, F15, F16, F17, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By step 1.2, $U$ is the quadratic form $I\mapsto\frac12I^{\mathsf T}LI$ of the symmetric matrix $L$ of step 2.1, and $U\ge0$; hence $L$ is positive semidefinite. By step 2.2, $U(I)=0$ exactly when $\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha\equiv0$; therefore $L$ is positive definite exactly when that vanishing forces $I=0$, that is, exactly when the profiles are pointwise linearly independent. [step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The theorem establishes (a)-(c) for the fixed compact smooth conserved profiles and their Coulomb-gauge fields, with no thin-wire, singular, moving, radiating or material configuration treated; the identification of $L$ with the lumped-model inductance matrix and of the linkage derivatives with terminal voltages is the adopted model content of [F6], not a consequence of this magnetostatic computation, and no terminal-voltage law for arbitrary varying frozen profiles is inferred. The constants used are those of [F5], and Countable Choice is inherited only through the named Newtonian, measure and vector-calculus interfaces. [A1, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎



## Source notes

Griffiths §7.2.3, printed pp. 310-317, derives $M_{21}=M_{12}$ and the Neumann formula; Fitzpatrick §7.2 and §7.5, printed pp. 222-231, treats two stationary loops, the flux proportional to the current and the mutual term $MI_1I_2$ in the magnetic energy; Tong §4.1.2, printed pp. 71-73, defines the inductance as flux per unit current and writes the magnetostatic energy $\frac12LI^2$. The present theorem replaces the thin-loop formulas by the explicitly defined smooth compact conserved profiles, makes the reciprocity an instance of the symmetry of the Newtonian linkage pairing, and identifies the energy with the frozen curl-field energy of the Newtonian construction; the thin-wire self-inductance and every singular limit remain outside the statement.
