## Statement

Assume the lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for clause (b), where it is inherited from the linkage suppliers.

(a) [Terminal-energy bookkeeping] Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]), let $t_0,t_1\in J$, let $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be constant and symmetric, let $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ in the following sense: $I$ extends to a $C^1$ map on an open interval containing $J$, so that the derivatives used below are those of the extension (one-sided at included endpoints of $J$, and not intrinsic to a value restriction when $J$ is a singleton), and let $V(t):=L\dot I(t)$ be the terminal-voltage vector of the inductive branches as adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] (the Faraday branch: the terminal voltage of a branch is the rate of change of its flux linkage $\Phi=LI$). Then
$$\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle ,$$
and for $n=1$ with $L>0$ this reads $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}V I\,dt=\frac12L\bigl(I(t_1)^2-I(t_0)^2\bigr)$: the accumulated terminal energy equals the change of the inductor bookkeeping energy $\frac12LI^2$. The identity is exact for every such $C^1$ current and fixed geometry; it uses only symmetry of $L$, the product rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus. For a changing geometry the mechanical work done on the circuit is an additional term and is not covered here.

(b) [Identification with the frozen field energy] Suppose in addition that the currents are realized by fixed compact smooth conserved profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$ of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), with instantaneous source $J(t):=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha(t)j_\alpha$, and that the inductance matrix is the linkage matrix of those profiles in the sense of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]: $L_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\iint\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)$. Then for every $t\in J$
$$\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J(t),A_{J(t)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J(t)}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
where $A_{J(t)}$ is the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential and $B_{J(t)}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J(t)}$ of that theorem: the right-hand side is the magnetic field energy of the frozen instantaneous configuration, and the accumulated terminal energy of (a) between $t_0$ and $t_1$ is the change of this field energy. The relation $V=L\dot I$ is the explicitly adopted terminal law of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the identification of the model's inductance matrix with the smooth-profile linkage matrix is part of the adopted model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]].

(c) [Scope] no radiation, distributed-element, material-loss, moving-geometry or thin-wire self-inductance claim is made; the frozen-configuration energy is not asserted to be the energy of a time-dependent full Maxwell solution.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume the lumped model data of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]], a constant symmetric $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, an interval $J$, points $t_0,t_1\in J$, a current $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ extending to a $C^1$ map on an open interval containing $J$, the terminal voltage $V=L\dot I$, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for clause (b).

[A1] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, says every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The adopted lumped circuit model carries branch currents $I_\alpha:J\to\mathbb R$ and constant matrices $L,C,R$ with $L$ symmetric, the Faraday branch relation $V(t)=L\dot I(t)$ (each terminal potential is the rate of change of the branch flux linkage $LI$), and the circuit-level bookkeeping quantities $LI$, $\tfrac12I^{\mathsf T}LI$; the matrices, terminal geometry and loop choice are declared model data, not derived from the vacuum Maxwell equations. ([[post-em-circuit-approximation]]).

[F2] A subset of $\mathbb R$ is an interval when it has one of the nine order-convex forms listed in the definition; in particular every interval is order-convex. ([[def-interval]]).

[F3] If $f,g$ are differentiable at a point $c$ of their common domain and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are differentiable at $c$, with $(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c)$, $(\alpha f)'(c)=\alpha f'(c)$ and $(fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c)$. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F4] If $a<b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, then $f$ is bounded and Riemann (Darboux) integrable on $[a,b]$. ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

[F5] If $a<b$, $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (one-sided at the endpoints), and $G'$ is integrable on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^bG'=G(b)-G(a)$. ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]).

[F6] The oriented integral is defined for all $u,v\in\mathbb R$ by: the Darboux integral over $[u,v]$ when $u<v$; $0$ when $u=v$; and $-\int_v^u f$ when $u>v$; on $u<v$ it is the published integral verbatim. ([[def-oriented-integral]]).

[F7] For fixed compact smooth conserved profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$ the linkage coefficients $L_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\iint\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle/|x-y|$ are finite real numbers with $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$, the linkage of the superposition is $\int\langle j_\beta,A_{J_I}\rangle=\sum_\alpha L_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha$, and with $U(I):=\frac12\int\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle$ one has $U(I)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|B_{J_I}|^2\ge0$, with $U(I)=0$ exactly when $J_I=0$. ([[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]).

[F8] The compact smooth current class consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. ([[def-em-steady-current-regime]]).

[F9] The framework uses SI units: $V$ in volts, $I$ in amperes, $t$ in seconds and $L$ in henries ($\mathrm H=\mathrm V\,\mathrm s\,\mathrm A^{-1}$). ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F10] The Euclidean inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_kx_ky_k$; it is symmetric and bilinear over $\mathbb R$, so $\langle Ly,x\rangle=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}y_\beta x_\alpha$ for every real matrix $L=(L_{\alpha\beta})$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$. ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix the $C^1$ extension of $I$ to an open interval $U\supseteq J$, and define $W(y):=\frac12\langle y,Ly\rangle=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}y_\alpha y_\beta$ for $y\in\mathbb R^n$, so that $t\mapsto G(t):=W(I(t))=\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle$ is the bookkeeping-energy function of the Statement. For each pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ the product $t\mapsto I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)$ is differentiable on $U$ with derivative $\dot I_\alpha I_\beta+I_\alpha\dot I_\beta$ by [F3], and $G$ is a finite linear combination of these products; applying the sum and scalar rules of [F3] repeatedly therefore gives, for every $t\in J$, $$G'(t)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}\bigl(\dot I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)+I_\alpha(t)\dot I_\beta(t)\bigr)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)=\langle L\dot I(t),I(t)\rangle=\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle ,$$ where the second equality relabels $\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta$ in one half of the sum and uses the symmetry $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$, and the last two use [F10] and $V=L\dot I$; the derivative $G'$ is continuous on $J$, being a finite sum of products of continuous functions. [F1, F3, F10, algebra]

1.2 Assume now the realization hypotheses of clause (b). For each fixed $t\in J$ put $J(t):=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha(t)j_\alpha$, a member of the compact smooth conserved class; applying [F7] to the amplitudes $I(t)=(I_1(t),\dots,I_n(t))$ (its coefficients are the linkage numbers of the profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$, which by hypothesis coincide with the entries of $L$) gives $$\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)=U(I(t))=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J(t),A_{J(t)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J(t)}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0 ,$$ the outer equalities by [F10] and the definition of $U$ in [F7]; this is clause (b)'s energy identity at each fixed $t$. [F7, F8, F10, algebra]

2.1 Let $u:=\min\{t_0,t_1\}$ and $v:=\max\{t_0,t_1\}$; then $[u,v]\subseteq J$, since $J$ is order-convex by [F2] and contains both $u$ and $v$. If $u<v$, then $G$ is differentiable at every point of $[u,v]$ as a function on $[u,v]$ (interior points lie in the open set $U$, and at $u,v$ the one-sided derivatives exist by restriction of the extension), while $G'$ is continuous on $[u,v]$ by step 1.1 and hence integrable there by [F4]; [F5] gives $\int_u^vG'=G(v)-G(u)$, that is $\int_u^v\langle V,I\rangle=G(v)-G(u)$ by step 1.1. If $u=v$ the same display is $0=G(v)-G(u)$, which holds identically and is the $u=v$ reading of [F6]. If $t_0>t_1$, applying the already-proved case to the pair $(t_1,t_0)$ and the sign clause of [F6] gives $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V,I\rangle=-\int_{t_1}^{t_0}\langle V,I\rangle=-(G(t_0)-G(t_1))=G(t_1)-G(t_0)$. In every case $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle$, which is the identity of (a); for $n=1$ the quadratic form is $\frac12LI^2$ by [F10]. [F2, F4, F5, F6, F10, step 1.1, algebra, cases]

3.1 Combining steps 2.1 and 1.2 gives, for all $t_0,t_1\in J$, $$\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J(t_1),A_{J(t_1)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J(t_0),A_{J(t_0)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J(t_1)}|^2\,d\lambda_3-\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J(t_0)}|^2\,d\lambda_3 ,$$ so that the accumulated terminal energy is the change of the frozen field energy, as asserted in (b). The terminal law $V=L\dot I$ is the adopted branch relation [F1], and the identification of the model's inductance matrix with the linkage matrix is the additional realization hypothesis of (b), not a consequence of the magnetostatic theorem alone. [step 2.1, step 1.2, F1, algebra]

4.1 Clause (c) holds as stated: the computation is fixed-geometry bookkeeping of the adopted model; changing geometry would add the mechanical work term, and the frozen realization is not asserted to solve any time-dependent Maxwell system. Units are those of [F9]; the singleton case of (a) was handled in step 2.1, where the extension supplies the derivative and no intrinsic derivative is inferred from the value restriction. Countable Choice enters only through clause (b), inherited from the linkage theorem [F7] and its Newtonian and measure interfaces; clause (a) is choice-free. [A1, F1, F9, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎



## Source notes

Fitzpatrick §7.5, printed pp. 225-231, writes the battery work for coupled coils as Ohmic terms plus the inductive energy and states that the energy of an inductor is stored in the magnetic field; Tong §4.1.2, printed pp. 71-73, integrates the work against the induced emf to $W=\frac12LI^2$ and rewrites it as the magnetostatic field energy under a decay assumption; Griffiths §7.2.4, printed pp. 317-320, records $\frac12LI^2$ and $U=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int B^2\,d\tau$. The present theorem replaces the decay assumption by the compact smooth conservative profiles of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]] and keeps the terminal law and the matrix identification as explicitly adopted model content; no error bound and no singular thin-wire self-inductance are claimed.

## Statement

Assume the lumped circuit model and its units as in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $t_0\in J$. For a nondegenerate $J$, derivatives are domain-relative, with one-sided values at included endpoints, in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; the functions constructed below also admit the stated $C^k$ open-neighbourhood extensions. If $J=\{t_0\}$, the formulas specify the initial values and the jets of the explicitly constructed extensions below, rather than an intrinsic derivative of a singleton restriction. The RL solution, the LC candidate and the bookkeeping-energy algebra use no choice principle. Only the optional geometric capacitor identification in (b) assumes full Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ consequence ([[def-countable-choice]]), exactly as [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] requires. The inductive energy is that of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]].

(a) [RL circuit] Let $L>0$ and $R\ge0$ be constants and let $V:J\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Then the initial value problem
$$L\dot I(t)+R\,I(t)=V(t),\qquad I(t_0)=I_0\in\mathbb R,$$
has exactly one $C^1$ solution on every nondegenerate $J$, namely
$$I(t)=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\Bigr)\Bigl[I_0+\frac1L\int_{t_0}^{t}\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{R(s-t_0)}{L}\Bigr)V(s)\,ds\Bigr],$$
and along it the inductive bookkeeping energy satisfies the power identity
$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\Bigl(\frac12LI(t)^2\Bigr)=L\dot I(t)I(t)=V(t)I(t)-R\,I(t)^2 ,$$
i.e. the terminal power splits into the rate of change of the inductive energy and the Ohmic term $RI^2$. (For $R=0$ the same formula reduces to $I=I_0+L^{-1}\int_{t_0}^tV$.) For $J=\{t_0\}$ its unique restriction is $I(t_0)=I_0$; the canonical extension obtained using the constant source $V(t_0)$ has jet $\dot I(t_0)=(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$ and satisfies the same power algebra. No uniqueness of arbitrary extension germs is asserted.

(b) [LC oscillation] Let $L>0$, $C>0$ and set $\Omega:=(LC)^{-1/2}>0$, $z_0:=Q_0-\mathrm i\,I_0/\Omega$, $w(t):=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))$ with the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]], and $Q(t):=\operatorname{Re}w(t)$. Then $Q$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, $Q(t_0)=Q_0$, $Q'(t_0)=I_0$, and
$$L\,Q''(t)+\frac{Q(t)}{C}=0\qquad\text{on }J ;$$
equivalently, with the real trigonometric functions of [[thm-eulers-formula]],
$$Q(t)=Q_0\cos\bigl(\Omega(t-t_0)\bigr)+\frac{I_0}{\Omega}\sin\bigl(\Omega(t-t_0)\bigr).$$
Moreover the total bookkeeping energy
$$E(t):=\frac12L\,Q'(t)^2+\frac{Q(t)^2}{2C}$$
satisfies $E'(t)=Q'(t)\bigl(LQ''(t)+Q(t)/C\bigr)=0$ on $J$, hence $E$ is constant with value $\frac12LI_0^2+\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}$: the two terms are the adopted capacitive and inductive bookkeeping energies, the latter as in [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]](a), so in the lossless loop their sum is conserved. For the additional geometric identification, explicitly choose the fixed compact separated conductor arrangement of [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] with bounded smooth ambient domain, connected vacuum, grounded outer boundary, zero volume source and its unit-Dirichlet solutions; drive only conductor 1 and ground the others, set the circuit parameter $C$ equal to that arrangement's $C_{11}>0$, and at each time set $V_1=Q/C_{11}$. Under full AC that supplier gives the frozen electrostatic field energy $Q^2/(2C_{11})$. An arbitrary declared $C>0$ is model data and is not automatically the capacitance of a particular arrangement. Any magnetic field-energy identification likewise requires the extra smooth-profile linkage realization of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]](b), under its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis. Neither frozen realization is an asserted time-dependent full Maxwell solution. At a singleton time the entire LC candidate supplies the jets $\dot Q=I_0$, $\ddot Q=-Q_0/(LC)$ and the same constant energy.

(c) [Scope] both statements are consequences of the expressly adopted circuit reduction, with the sign conventions and relations of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; they assert no general network completeness, no derivation from the full time-dependent Maxwell system, no radiation or distributed-element effect and no empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume the lumped circuit data of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], an interval $J$ with $t_0\in J$, constants $L>0$, $R\ge0$ in (a) and $C>0$ in (b), a continuous source $V:J\to\mathbb R$, and the initial data $I_0,Q_0\in\mathbb R$. For clause (b)'s geometric identification assume full $\mathrm{AC}$ with its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ consequence.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[A2] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, states that every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The adopted lumped model carries the Faraday branch relation $V=L\dot I$ for an inductive branch, the capacitive branch relation $V=C^{-1}Q$ (in the scalar case $V=Q/C$), the resistive branch relation $V=RI$ as the circuit form of the Ohmic branch of the material model, and Kirchhoff's loop voltage balance around each independent loop; the matrices and terminal data are declared model data, not derived from the vacuum Maxwell equations. ([[post-em-circuit-approximation]]).

[F2] A subset of $\mathbb R$ is an interval when it has one of the nine order-convex forms of the definition; in particular intervals are order-convex, nondegenerate intervals have at least two elements, and a nondegenerate interval contains the two-point set $\{u,v\}$ for suitable $u<v$. ([[def-interval]]).

[F3] Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, let $x_0\in I$ and let $p,q:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The initial value problem $y'+py=q$, $y(x_0)=y_0$, has exactly one solution on $I$, namely $y(x)=\exp(-P(x))\left(y_0+\int_{x_0}^x\exp(P(t))q(t)\,dt\right)$ with $P(x)=\int_{x_0}^xp(t)\,dt$. ([[thm-first-order-linear-ode-integrating-factor]]).

[F4] A solution of the first-order system $x'=F(t,x(t))$ with $x(t_0)=x_0$ on an interval $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ with $t_0\in I$, differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense, endpoints of $I$ using one-sided, domain-relative derivatives, and satisfying the equation and initial condition. ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]).

[F5] If $f,g$ are differentiable at a point of their common domain and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are differentiable there with the sum, scalar and product rules; in particular $\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\frac12Lf(t)^2=Lf(t)f'(t)$. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F6] Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values and (where defined) quotients of continuous functions are continuous, and every constant function and the identity are continuous. ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]).

[F7] The complex exponential is $\exp z=\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$. ([[def-complex-exponential]]).

[F8] The complex exponential is entire and $\exp'(z)=\exp z$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$. ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]).

[F9] For $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ open and $f:U\to\mathbb C$, the following are equivalent: $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$; under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$ the map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number; and the Cauchy--Riemann equations hold at $a$ with real total differentiability. When these hold, $f'(a)=\partial_zf(a)$. ([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]).

[F10] Complex derivatives obey the sum, scalar, product and quotient rules, the derivative of a constant is $0$, and the derivative of the identity is $1$. ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]).

[F11] If $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is complex differentiable at $a$ with $(g\circ f)'(a)=g'(f(a))f'(a)$. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]]).

[F12] If $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ with $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F13] For every real $\theta$, $\exp(\mathrm i\theta)=\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta$ with the real cosine and sine. ([[thm-eulers-formula]]).

[F14] The complex trigonometric functions restrict to their real power-series counterparts on the real axis. ([[thm-complex-trigonometric-hyperbolic-dictionary]]).

[F15] If $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is order-convex, $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $I$ and differentiable at every interior point of $I$ with $f'(x)=0$ there, then $f$ is constant on $I$. ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]).

[F16] For clause (b) of the Statement, the inductive bookkeeping energy and its smooth-profile realization are those of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]]: the terminal energy $\int\langle V,I\rangle$ is the change of $\frac12LI^2$ for constant symmetric $L$, and for a smooth compact conserved-profile realization it is the change of the frozen field energy $\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|B|^2$. ([[pthm-em-inductor-energy]]).

[F17] The SI units are those of the framework: $V$ in volts, $I$ in amperes, $Q$ in coulombs, $t$ in seconds, $L$ in henries and $C$ in farads. ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[L1] The optional geometric identification clause uses [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]]: for the fixed compact separated conductor arrangement with bounded smooth ambient domain of its clause (f), its clause (c) gives the field-energy identity $U(V)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\Omega_v}|\nabla\varphi^V|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12V^{\mathsf T}CV=\frac12\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)$, valid under full AC and its stated Dirichlet solvability hypotheses, and its clause (d) gives, with only conductor $1$ driven and the others grounded, $C_{11}>0$, $Q_1=C_{11}V_1$ and the frozen electrostatic field energy $U=\frac12C_{11}V_1^2=Q_1^2/(2C_{11})$. This consumer relies on exactly that clause with $C=C_{11}$ and no independent derivation of the electrostatic energy is substituted.



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 (a) Assume first that $J$ has at least two elements. Put $p:=R/L$, a constant of class $C^1$, and $q:=V/L$, continuous on $J$ by [F6]; $J$ is order-convex with at least two elements by [F2]. With $P(x):=\int_{t_0}^x p=\frac RL(x-t_0)$ one has $\exp(-P(x))=\exp\left(-\frac{R(x-t_0)}{L}\right)$ and $\exp(P(s))=\exp\left(\frac{R(s-t_0)}{L}\right)$, so the unique solution supplied by [F3] is exactly the displayed $I$. Its derivative is the domain-relative derivative of [F4] (one-sided at included endpoints), and the uniqueness is the uniqueness assertion of [F3], which is the uniqueness of the $C^1$ solution in the sense of [F4]. If $J=\{t_0\}$, the restriction of any solution is $I_0$ by [F4]; choosing the constant extension $V\equiv V(t_0)$ on an open interval and applying the already-proved nondegenerate case there produces a $C^1$ extension of the candidate whose jet at $t_0$ is obtained by substituting $t=t_0$ into the differential equation, $\dot I(t_0)=(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$, and no other extension is distinguished. [F2, F3, F4, F6, algebra, cases]

1.2 (b) Define the entire function $G(z):=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(z-t_0))$ on $\mathbb C$. By [F10] and [F11], applied to the affine map $z\mapsto \mathrm i\Omega(z-t_0)$ (derivative $\mathrm i\Omega$) and to [F8], $G$ is complex differentiable with $G'(z)=\mathrm i\Omega\,G(z)$ for every $z$; differentiating once more gives $G''=(\mathrm i\Omega)^2G=-\Omega^2G$. The function $w$ of the Statement is the restriction of $G$ to the real interval $J$, so by [F9] and the real chain rule [F12] it is real differentiable with $w'(t)=\mathrm i\Omega\,w(t)$ and $w''(t)=-\Omega^2w(t)$ for every $t\in J$; taking real parts, $Q=\operatorname{Re}w$ is of class $C^2$ with $Q'(t)=\operatorname{Re}w'(t)$ and $Q''(t)=\operatorname{Re}w''(t)$, because the real part is real-linear. Hence $Q''=-\Omega^2Q$, which is $LQ''+Q/C=0$ since $\Omega^2=1/(LC)$ by definition. At $t_0$: $w(t_0)=z_0$ gives $Q(t_0)=\operatorname{Re}z_0=Q_0$, and $w'(t_0)=\mathrm i\Omega z_0=\mathrm i\Omega Q_0+I_0$ gives $Q'(t_0)=I_0$. Euler's formula [F13] expands $\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))=\cos\Omega(t-t_0)+\mathrm i\sin\Omega(t-t_0)$, and multiplying out $w=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=Q_0\cos\Omega(t-t_0)+(I_0/\Omega)\sin\Omega(t-t_0)$, with the real trigonometric functions of [F13] and the real restriction recorded in [F14]. For $J=\{t_0\}$ the same formulas are evaluated at $t_0$, the entire function supplying the jets $\dot Q(t_0)=I_0$ and $\ddot Q(t_0)=-\Omega^2Q_0=-Q_0/(LC)$ by the same computation, so the LC candidate needs no separate singleton convention. [F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, F14, algebra, cases]

2.1 (a) Along the solution of step 1.1 the function $t\mapsto\frac12LI(t)^2$ is differentiable at every interior point of $J$ (and one-sidedly at included endpoints) by [F5], with derivative $LI\dot I$; substituting the circuit equation $L\dot I=V-RI$ gives $LI\dot I=VI-RI^2$, which is the power identity. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 (b) Define $E(t):=\frac12LQ'(t)^2+\frac{Q(t)^2}{2C}$; by [F6] and step 1.2 the functions $Q$ and $Q'$ are continuous, so $E$ is continuous on $J$, and at every interior point of $J$ the product and scalar rules of [F5] give $E'=LQ'Q''+QQ'/C=Q'(LQ''+Q/C)=0$ by the equation of step 1.2. By [F15], $E$ is constant on $J$, and its value is $E(t_0)=\frac12LI_0^2+\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}$ by the initial values of step 1.2. The first summand is the inductive bookkeeping energy of [F16], and for the optional geometric identification of the Statement the second summand is the frozen electrostatic field energy supplied by the declared clause of [L1] under full AC and the stated conductor arrangement, with $C=C_{11}$ and $V_1=Q/C_{11}$; the magnetic realization of the inductive term is the separate smooth-profile clause of [F16], under its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ premise. For $J=\{t_0\}$ the constant-energy display is the value at $t_0$ supplied by step 1.2, so no derivative of a singleton restriction is used. [A1, A2, F16, L1, F5, F6, F15, step 1.2, algebra, cases]

3.1 The full choice hypothesis of the geometric identification is [A1], and the inductive realization of [F16] carries the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [A2]; full AC yields it, because for a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets the family $\{X_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ of its values consists of nonempty sets, so [A1] provides a choice function $g$ on that family and $n\mapsto g(X_n)$ is a choice function for the sequence, as [A2] requires. Hence clause (b) is available under its stated hypotheses, and the RL and LC algebra of steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 is choice-free and uses neither [A1] nor [A2]. [A1, A2, F16, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Clauses (a)-(c) are established: step 1.1 and step 2.1 give the existence, uniqueness, formula and power identity of (a); step 1.2 and step 2.2 give the solution, initial values, cosine-sine form, energy identity and conservation of (b), with the geometric identification delegated to [L1]; step 3.1 accounts for the choice use. The units are [F17]; no general network completeness, no full time-dependent Maxwell solution, no radiation or distributed-element effect and no empirical claim is asserted, and both statements are consequences of the expressly adopted relations of [F1]. [F1, F17, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎



## Source notes

Fitzpatrick §7.5-7.6, printed pp. 225-234, writes the RL equation and the LCR circuit equation with the ideal element relations; Griffiths §7.2.3, printed pp. 310-317, records the battery-plus-RL exponential approach with time constant $L/R$; Tong §4.1.3, printed pp. 74-77, presents resistance as an additional material input in the circuit treatment. The RL solution is proved from the published integrating-factor theorem; the lossless LC candidate is verified by explicit complex-exponential differentiation with the real cosine-sine form displayed through Euler's formula, rather than through a real-trigonometric derivative supplier outside this page's declared prerequisite closure; and the optional capacitive identification is referred to its own supplier with the open obligation recorded. No numerical value, measurement or error bound is asserted.

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the explicitly used Lebesgue bar-volume interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Work in the laboratory frame and units of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix $l>0$, $B_0\ge0$, a nonempty interval $J$ with a specified $C^1$ neighbourhood extension for motion and its velocity jets when $J$ is not open (in particular singleton data are read through that supplied extension), and a prescribed $C^1$ motion $x:J\to(a_0,a_1)$ with $a_0<a_1$ and $|x'(t)|<c$. The fixed rails have centerlines $(s,\pm l/2,0)$, $a_0\le s\le a_1$, and the left closing side is $(a_0,w,0)$, $|w|\le l/2$. At time $t$ the ideal oriented contour $C(t)$ comprises only the rail portions $a_0\le s\le x(t)$, that left side, and the sliding bar centerline $(x(t),w,0)$. Give it normal $e_3$, hence traverse the bar in the $+e_2$ direction. The rails and closing side have material velocity zero; the bar velocity is $v_b(t)=x'(t)e_1$. These are separate segment velocities with sliding contacts; endpoint values at the contacts are taken independently on each segment. Define the contact-model emf as the sum of its four segment integrals $\sum_\gamma\int_\gamma(E+v_\gamma\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r$ in [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. This is not a single-valued smooth moving material sheet of [[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]]. The external test field is $E=0$, $B=B_0e_3$; all self-fields are neglected.

For force bookkeeping choose an actual finite-volume homogeneous bar, separate from the ideal centerline: fix $d,h>0$ with cross-section area $A=dh$ and set $K_t=[x(t)-d/2,x(t)+d/2]\times[-l/2,l/2]\times[-h/2,h/2]$, so $\lambda_3(K_t)=Al$. For each frozen time prescribe the uniform current density $j_t=(I(t)/A)e_2$ on its interior, with the ideal local conductor-matter coupling of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii) applied there. Its extension to the boundary is used only for the volume integral; contacts/end faces have zero volume and no additional contact force is included. The same signed lumped current runs around the contour. The local force-law adoption and prescribed current do not assert a total Maxwell or matter-dynamical solution.

(a) The rectangular flux is $\Phi(t)=B_0l(x(t)-a_0)$ and the segmentwise emf is $\mathrm{emf}(t)=-B_0lx'(t)=-\Phi'(t)$. Its magnitude is $B_0l|x'|$, including either motion direction and $B_0=0$.

(b) The finite-volume force is
$$F(t)=\int_{K_t}j_t\times B\,d\lambda_3=I(t)B_0l e_1.$$

(c) The signed instantaneous balance is
$$F(t)\cdot v_b(t)+\mathrm{emf}(t)I(t)=I(t)B_0lx'(t)-B_0lx'(t)I(t)=0.$$
It is ideal mechanical/electrical transfer bookkeeping with prescribed motion and current; no dissipative, radiation or field-storage term is included. A support enforcing the motion may supply the opposite mechanical power.

(d) This is a hypothetical conditional sliding-contact model with no measurement. Self-fields, radiation, friction, contact resistance, deformation and constitutive details are neglected; no bar equation of motion, physical realization, or total Maxwell solution is asserted. The strict $C^2$ material-sheet theorem remains a separate result under its own hypotheses.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the laboratory frame and units, the constants $l>0$, $B_0\ge0$, $d,h>0$, $A=dh$, the $C^1$ motion $x:J\to(a_0,a_1)$ with $|x'|<c$, currents $I(t)$ of the lumped model and the contour and bar data of the Statement.

[A1] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, says every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The line integral of a continuous vector field along a piecewise $C^1$ path is the sum of the integrals $\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt$ over an admissible partition. ([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]).

[F2] The cross product in coordinates is $(u\times v)_x=u_yv_z-u_zv_y$ and cyclically; the standard basis satisfies $e_1\times e_3=-e_2$. ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[F3] The Euclidean inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_kx_ky_k$, in particular $\langle e_2,e_2\rangle=1$. ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F4] For a measurable $f$ and measurable $E$, $\int_Ef\,d\mu=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu$. ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

[F5] For a nonnegative simple measurable function $s=\sum_jc_j\chi_{E_j}$, the simple integral is $\sum_jc_j\mu(E_j)$, and the nonnegative integral of a nonnegative simple function equals its simple integral. ([[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F6] The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1$. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F7] Every set between the open and closed box forms is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(R)=\prod_i(b_i-a_i)$ ; in particular closed boxes have the product volume and their faces are null when some side degenerates. ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F8] If $f,g$ are differentiable at $c$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are differentiable at $c$ with the sum, scalar and product rules. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F9] Fields are maps $\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$; $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$, $B$ carries T. ([[def-em-fields]]).

[F10] The framework adopts the SI constants including $c>0$ and the units V, T; the emf unit is the volt. ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F11] The adopted continuum matter coupling gives the force density $\rho E+J\times B$ (N m$^{-3}$) for matter interacting with the field through an explicitly stated matter model. ([[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]).

[F12] A moving material circuit of the strict branch is a $C^2$ embedded sheet with a single-valued $C^1$ material velocity; the strict theorem on this page applies only to such sheets. ([[def-em-moving-circuit-geometry]]).

[F13] The laboratory region, its chart and the spatial frame are those of the laboratory geometry; laboratory fields are maps on $\Omega\times I$ with the spatial coordinates of the frame. ([[def-em-lab-geometry]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $t\in J$. By [F1] the contact-model emf is the sum of the four segment integrals of $E+v_\gamma\times B$ with the segmentwise velocities. On the two rail portions and the left closing side the material velocity is zero and $E=0$, so the integrand vanishes identically and each of those three integrals is $0$. On the bar, parametrized by $s\mapsto(x(t),s,0)$ with $s$ from $-l/2$ to $l/2$ in the $+e_2$ direction, the velocity is $v_b=x'(t)e_1$, so [F2] gives $v_b\times B=x'(t)e_1\times B_0e_3=-B_0x'(t)e_2$ and [F3] gives $\langle v_b\times B,e_2\rangle=-B_0x'(t)$; the bar integral is therefore $\int_{-l/2}^{l/2}(-B_0x'(t))\,ds=-B_0lx'(t)$. Hence $\mathrm{emf}(t)=-B_0lx'(t)$ for every $t\in J$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 For the force let $j_t=(I(t)/A)e_2$ on the interior of $K_t$ and extend it by zero outside that interior, the difference with any boundary extension being confined to the null faces of $K_t$ by [F7]. By [F2] the force density is $j_t\times B_0e_3=(I(t)B_0/A)e_1$, a constant vector on the interior; hence, using [F4], [F5] and [F6] applied to the constant integrand and [F7] for the volume $\lambda_3(K_t)=dlh=Al$,
$$F(t)=\int_{K_t}j_t\times B\,d\lambda_3=\frac{I(t)B_0}{A}e_1\,\lambda_3(K_t)=I(t)B_0le_1 .$$
The integral is absolutely finite. This is the prescribed local matter coupling [F11] applied to the declared current density; it asserts no force on an arbitrary source without such a matter model. [F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, F11, algebra]

2.1 The flux through the frozen rectangle $R(t)=[a_0,x(t)]\times[-l/2,l/2]\times\{0\}$ with normal $e_3$ is the surface integral of the constant field $B_0e_3$, that is $\Phi(t)=B_0\,\lambda_2(R(t))=B_0l(x(t)-a_0)$ with $\lambda_2$ the two-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the plane; by [F7] applied to the rectangle with sides $x(t)-a_0$ and $l$ this is the stated value (and it is $0$ when $x(t)=a_0$, where the rectangle is degenerate). Since $x$ is $C^1$ on $J$ with the prescribed neighbourhood extension, [F8] gives $\Phi'(t)=B_0lx'(t)$ on the interior of $J$ and one-sided at the endpoints of $J$, hence $\mathrm{emf}(t)=-\Phi'(t)$ by step 1.1; the magnitude is $B_0l|x'(t)|$ because $B_0\ge0$ and $l>0$. [F7, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The signed power balance is immediate from steps 1.1 and 1.2 and the Euclidean pairing: with $v_b=x'(t)e_1$ and $\langle e_1,e_1\rangle=1$ by [F3], $F(t)\cdot v_b(t)=I(t)B_0lx'(t)$ and $\mathrm{emf}(t)I(t)=-B_0lx'(t)I(t)$, so the sum is $0$ for every sign of $I(t)$ and of $x'(t)$, including the zero values. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The three displayed conclusions are established by steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2. The fields and units are those of [F9] and [F10]; the model is the hypothetical sliding-contact model of the Statement, not a single-valued smooth material sheet of [F12], and its strict theorem is not used; the laboratory reading is that of [F13]. No measurement, self-field, radiation, dissipative or dynamical conclusion is asserted, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only through the explicitly cited box-measure and integral interfaces. [A1, F9, F10, F12, F13, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Source notes

Griffiths §7.1.3, printed pp. 294-296, presents the primitive generator: a loop pulled at speed $v$ through a uniform field, emf $=vBh$, the flux rule $\mathcal E=-\mathrm d\Phi/\mathrm dt$ for motional emf and the work/power discussion; Tong §4.1.1 and §4.1.3, printed pp. 69-77, gives the sliding bar $\mathcal E=vBd$, the Lorentz force $F=IBd$ on the bar and the coupled motion with the resistor. The present thought experiment extracts only the instantaneous idealised statements: the segmentwise emf, the flux function and its derivative, the adopted finite-volume force integral and the signed power balance. The coupled bar dynamics and the Joule-heating energetics of the sources are not reproduced, because they require a mechanical mass model and a dynamical circuit solution that this item does not adopt.

No physical leakage or loss mechanism and no measurement is asserted.'

## Example

Assume the lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $L=\begin{pmatrix}L_1&M\\M&L_2\end{pmatrix}$ be a constant symmetric block of its inductance matrix with $L_1,L_2>0$. Let $I_1,I_2:J\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ currents on an interval $J$ (each extending to a $C^1$ map on an open interval containing $J$, as in the model's conventions) with terminal voltages $V_\alpha=\sum_\beta L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\beta$. Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the realization and bounded-linking clauses (b), inherited from the linkage and energy suppliers.

(a) [Energy and instantaneous power] the stored inductive bookkeeping energy is
$$W(t)=\tfrac12L_1I_1(t)^2+\tfrac12L_2I_2(t)^2+MI_1(t)I_2(t),$$
and $V_1I_1+V_2I_2=\dot W$ by part (a) of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]]; the mutual term increases the energy for currents of the same sign and decreases it for opposite signs (as the sign of the product $I_1I_2$ indicates when $M>0$).

(b) [Perfect linkage and the bound] if the two currents are realised by fixed compact smooth conserved profiles of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b) with linkage matrix $L$ as in [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]], then $W(t)\ge0$ for all currents, and evaluating the quadratic form on both $(\sqrt{L_2},-\sqrt{L_1})$ and $(\sqrt{L_2},+\sqrt{L_1})$ gives the bound
$$|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2};$$
moreover if $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ with $s\in\{+1,-1\}$ (perfect linkage), the null direction $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-s\sqrt{L_1})$ has $J_I=0$ pointwise by the vanishing clause of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]](c).

(c) [Ideal common-flux model] if $M=\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, choose any $\Lambda>0$ and set $N_1:=\sqrt{L_1/\Lambda}$, $N_2:=\sqrt{L_2/\Lambda}$; then $L_1=\Lambda N_1^2$, $L_2=\Lambda N_2^2$ and $M=\Lambda N_1N_2$. Writing $\Phi_c:=\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)$ for the common flux linkage, the terminal voltages are
$$V_1=N_1\dot\Phi_c,\qquad V_2=N_2\dot\Phi_c,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{V_1}{N_1}=\frac{V_2}{N_2}=\dot\Phi_c,$$
and the stored energy is $W=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$; equivalently the induced emfs $e_\alpha:=-V_\alpha$ satisfy $e_1/N_1=e_2/N_2=-\dot\Phi_c$. This is the explicitly adopted common-linkage ('ideal transformer') model with turns ratio $N_1:N_2$.

(d) [Limitations] for an imperfect realized linkage, $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, the perfect common-flux voltage ratio is not an identity for all current histories; a particular history can nevertheless satisfy that ratio accidentally (including both voltages zero). Reversing the second winding retains $s=-1$: with $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ put $\Phi_c=\Lambda(N_1I_1+sN_2I_2)$ and obtain $V_1/N_1=V_2/(sN_2)=\dot\Phi_c$, with the same energy $\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$. The positive-orientation model (c) remains as stated. Winding resistance, hysteresis and core loss, stray capacitance, magnetising current and finite permeability are outside the declared model and are not inferred from it. No measurement is involved; the statements are conditional computations in the ideal model. Regularity on a non-open interval uses the stated $C^1$ neighbourhood extension; if the interval is a singleton its terminal-voltage jets are those of a specified extension, not derivatives inferred from its value restriction.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct expansion, the reciprocity theorem, and an explicit derivative-vector contradiction for the strict-linkage non-identity.

**Given:** The lumped model data, the constant symmetric block $L=\begin{pmatrix}L_1&M\\M&L_2\end{pmatrix}$ with $L_1,L_2>0$, the interval $J$, the $C^1$ currents $I_1,I_2$ with open-neighbourhood extension, the terminal voltages $V_\alpha=\sum_\beta L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\beta$ and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for clauses (b).

[A1] Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, says every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function. ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The adopted lumped model carries the Faraday branch relation $V=L\dot I$: each terminal potential is the rate of change of the branch flux linkage $LI$; the matrix and terminal data are declared model data. ([[post-em-circuit-approximation]]).

[F2] For constant symmetric $L$ and a $C^1$ current $I$ with open-neighbourhood extension, $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V,I\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle$ with $V=L\dot I$, and for a smooth compact conserved-profile realization the quadratic form equals the frozen magnetic field energy $\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|B_{J(t)}|^2$ at each time. ([[pthm-em-inductor-energy]]).

[F3] For fixed compact smooth conserved profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$ with linkage matrix $L=(L_{\alpha\beta})$ one has $U(I)=\frac12\int\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int|B_{J_I}|^2\ge0$, and $U(I)=0$ exactly when $J_I=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha=0$ pointwise; the matrix is positive definite exactly when the profiles are pointwise linearly independent. ([[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]).

[F4] The compact smooth current class consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. ([[def-em-steady-current-regime]]).

[F5] The Euclidean inner product is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_kx_ky_k$; in particular for $I=(I_1,I_2)$ and the block $L$ one has $\langle I,LI\rangle=L_1I_1^2+2MI_1I_2+L_2I_2^2$. ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F6] Sums, scalar multiples and products of differentiable functions are differentiable, with the sum, scalar and product rules. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F7] The SI units are those of the framework: $V$ in volts, $I$ in amperes, $t$ in seconds, $L$ in henries and $M$ in henries. ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

1.1 Clause (a): by [F5], $\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12L_1I_1^2+MI_1I_2+\frac12L_2I_2^2$, which is the displayed $W(t)$. Differentiating termwise with the product and scalar rules of [F6] gives $\dot W=L_1I_1\dot I_1+M(\dot I_1I_2+I_1\dot I_2)+L_2I_2\dot I_2=(L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2)I_1+(M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2)I_2=V_1I_1+V_2I_2$, since $[L\dot I]_\alpha=V_\alpha$; the sign reading of the mutual term is immediate from $W=\frac12L_1I_1^2+\frac12L_2I_2^2+MI_1I_2$ for $M>0$. [F1, F2, F5, F6, algebra]

1.2 Clause (b): under the realization hypothesis, $W(t)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)=U(I(t))\ge0$ at each $t$ by [F3], the block $L$ being by hypothesis the linkage matrix of the two profiles. Substituting $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-\sqrt{L_1})$ gives $W=L_1L_2-M\sqrt{L_1L_2}\ge0$, that is $M\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; substituting $I=(\sqrt{L_2},+\sqrt{L_1})$ gives $W=L_1L_2+M\sqrt{L_1L_2}\ge0$, that is $M\ge-\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; together, $|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$. If $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ and $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-s\sqrt{L_1})$, the same expansion gives $W=L_1L_2-sM\sqrt{L_1L_2}=L_1L_2-L_1L_2=0$, so by the vanishing clause of [F3] the associated current $J_I$ vanishes pointwise. [A1, F3, F4, algebra, cases]

1.3 Clause (c): with $N_1=\sqrt{L_1/\Lambda}$ and $N_2=\sqrt{L_2/\Lambda}$ one has $L_1=\Lambda N_1^2$, $L_2=\Lambda N_2^2$ and $M=\sqrt{L_1L_2}=\Lambda N_1N_2$ because $N_1N_2=\sqrt{L_1L_2}/\Lambda$. Hence, using $V_\alpha=\sum_\beta L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\beta$, $V_1=L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2=\Lambda N_1(N_1\dot I_1+N_2\dot I_2)=N_1\dot\Phi_c$ and $V_2=M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2=\Lambda N_2(N_1\dot I_1+N_2\dot I_2)=N_2\dot\Phi_c$ with $\Phi_c=\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)$; dividing by $N_1,N_2>0$ gives the common ratio, and $e_\alpha=-V_\alpha$ reverses the common sign. For the energy, $W=\frac12L_1I_1^2+MI_1I_2+\frac12L_2I_2^2=\frac12\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)^2=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$ by the displayed relations and the binomial expansion. [F5, F6, algebra]

1.4 Clause (d), strict-linkage non-identity: suppose $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ and $V_2=kV_1$ held for all $C^1$ currents on $J$; then $\sum_\beta L_{2\beta}\dot I_\beta=k\sum_\beta L_{1\beta}\dot I_\beta$ for every such current. Fix any point $t_0\in J$ (any point when $J$ is a singleton) and, for each vector $a=(a_1,a_2)\in\mathbb R^2$, take the affine history $I(t)=c+(t-t_0)a$ (any fixed $c\in\mathbb R^2$) on $J$, which is the restriction of the affine map of $t$ on $\mathbb R$ and hence carries the stated $C^1$ open-neighbourhood extension with $\dot I\equiv a$; substituting gives $(L_{21}-kL_{11})a_1+(L_{22}-kL_{12})a_2=0$ for all $a$, hence $L_{21}=kL_{11}$ and $L_{22}=kL_{12}$, i.e. $\operatorname{row}_2L=k\operatorname{row}_1L$. Then $L_1k=M$ and $L_2=kM=M^2/L_1$, so $L_1L_2-M^2=0$, contradicting $L_1L_2-M^2>0$ from $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; hence no such $k$ makes the ratio a universal identity. Accidental satisfaction occurs: any history with $\dot I$ in the kernel of the nonzero functional $a\mapsto(L_{21}-kL_{11})a_1+(L_{22}-kL_{12})a_2$ satisfies $V_2=kV_1$ at every time, that kernel being nontrivial because one linear equation in two unknowns always has a nonzero solution; in particular the constant currents give $V_1=V_2=0$. For the reversed winding with $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, put $\Phi_c=\Lambda(N_1I_1+sN_2I_2)$; then $V_1=L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2=\Lambda N_1(N_1\dot I_1+sN_2\dot I_2)=N_1\dot\Phi_c$ and $V_2=M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2=\Lambda sN_2(N_1\dot I_1+sN_2\dot I_2)=sN_2\dot\Phi_c$ because $s^2=1$, so $V_1/N_1=V_2/(sN_2)=\dot\Phi_c$, and $W=\frac12\Lambda(N_1I_1+sN_2I_2)^2=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$. [F5, F6, algebra, cases]

2.1 Steps 1.1-1.4 establish (a)-(d): steps 1.1-1.2 give (a) and the bound and null-direction clauses of (b), and steps 1.3-1.4 give the common-flux model (c) and the limitations (d). The computation is conditional on the adopted lumped model [F1], its units are [F7], and no leakage, loss, material or measurement claim is added; the terminal-voltage jets on a singleton interval are those of the specified extension. Countable Choice is used only through the realization clause (b), via [F3]; the algebraic clauses (a), (c) and (d) are choice-free. [A1, F1, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4] ∎

## Source notes

Fitzpatrick §7.4, printed pp. 222-225, computes the two-solenoid mutual inductance and records perfect linkage $M=\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ with the leakage warning; Griffiths §7.2.3, printed pp. 310-317, derives reciprocity and the Neumann formula; Tong §4.1.2, printed pp. 71-73, identifies the mutual term in the magnetostatic energy. The example separates what is proved for the declared smooth compact profiles (the PSD bound and the null direction) from what is adopted as the common-flux ideal-transformer model, and it proves the failure of a universal voltage ratio under strict linkage by exhibiting the forced row proportionality and its contradiction; no physical transformer behaviour, loss mechanism or measurement is asserted.

## Example

In the RL branch of [[pthm-em-rl-lc-dynamics]] with the declared units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let the source voltage be the constant $V_0\in\mathbb R$, let $R>0$ and $L>0$, let $t_0\in J$ and $I_0\in\mathbb R$, with $J$ an interval and derivatives read in the model's domain-relative convention, through the stated $C^1$ open-neighbourhood extension for a non-open $J$. Then the unique $C^1$ solution of $L\dot I+RI=V_0$, $I(t_0)=I_0$, is
$$I(t)=\frac{V_0}{R}+\Bigl(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\Bigr)\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\Bigr),\qquad t\in J .$$
In particular $I(t)-V_0/R=(I_0-V_0/R)\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ and hence $|I(t)-V_0/R|=|I_0-V_0/R|\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ for every $t\in J$, with time constant $\tau=L/R$; $I\equiv V_0/R$ is the unique stationary solution; if $J$ is unbounded above, then $I(t)\to V_0/R$ as $t\to+\infty$ along $J$; and the transient part is the free decay $\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ of the initial deviation $I_0-V_0/R$. For $J=\{t_0\}$ the restriction is $I(t_0)=I_0$ and the jets are those of the same formula read through the stated extension, giving $\dot I(t_0)=(V_0-RI_0)/L$. The computation is conditional on the adopted lumped model, constant elements and fixed geometry; no measurement is involved.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** explicit differentiation of the candidate, with uniqueness inherited from the RL theorem.

**Given:** The RL branch data of the adopted lumped model with constants $V_0\in\mathbb R$, $R>0$, $L>0$, an interval $J$ with $t_0\in J$ and initial value $I_0\in\mathbb R$.

[F1] In the RL branch let $L>0$, $R\ge0$ and let $V:J\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Then the initial value problem $L\dot I+RI=V$, $I(t_0)=I_0$, has exactly one $C^1$ solution on every nondegenerate interval $J$, namely $I(t)=\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)\left[I_0+L^{-1}\int_{t_0}^t\exp(R(s-t_0)/L)V(s)\,ds\right]$; for $J=\{t_0\}$ the restriction is $I(t_0)=I_0$ and the canonical extension for the constant source $V(t_0)$ has jet $\dot I(t_0)=(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$; the RL solution uses no choice principle. ([[pthm-em-rl-lc-dynamics]]).

[F2] The real exponential is $C^\infty$ and $\exp'=\exp$. ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]).

[F3] Sums, scalar multiples and products of differentiable functions are differentiable, with the sum, scalar and product rules; the derivative of a constant is $0$ and the derivative of the identity is $1$. ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F4] If $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $g$ is totally differentiable at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ with $D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a)$. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F5] $\exp(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$ and $\exp(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$. ([[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]]).

[F6] For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and $\exp(-x)=1/\exp(x)$. ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]).

[F7] The SI units are those of the framework: $V$ in volts, $I$ in amperes, $t$ in seconds, $R$ in ohms and $L$ in henries. ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F8] A subset of $\mathbb R$ is an interval when it has one of the nine order-convex forms of the definition; an interval is unbounded above exactly when it contains a ray $[r,+\infty)$. ([[def-interval]]).

1.1 Define the candidate $\varphi(t):=\frac{V_0}{R}+\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$ on $J$. The function $t\mapsto-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}$ is affine with derivative $-\frac RL$ by [F3], and $\exp'=\exp$ by [F2], so the chain rule [F4] gives $\varphi'(t)=\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\left(-\frac RL\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)=-\frac RL\left(\varphi(t)-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)$. Therefore $L\varphi'(t)+R\varphi(t)=-R\left(\varphi(t)-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)+R\varphi(t)=V_0$ identically, and $\varphi(t_0)=\frac{V_0}{R}+\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)=I_0$. [F2, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 Stationary solutions: if $I\equiv c$ is constant, then $L\dot I+RI=Rc$, so the equation $L\dot I+RI=V_0$ holds exactly when $c=V_0/R$; since $R>0$ there is exactly one such constant, namely $I\equiv V_0/R$. [F3, algebra]

1.3 Limit statement: if $J$ is unbounded above, then for $t\in J\cap[t_0,+\infty)$ the argument $-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}$ satisfies $-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\to-\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$ because $R/L>0$, so [F5] gives $\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)\to0$ and hence $I(t)\to V_0/R$ along that ray; the time constant is $\tau:=L/R$, so the decay factor is $\exp(-(t-t_0)/\tau)$. [F5, F8, algebra]

1.4 Deviation identity: subtracting $V_0/R$ from the displayed formula gives $I(t)-V_0/R=\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$; since $\exp(x)>0$ for real $x$ by [F6], taking absolute values preserves the exponential factor, so $|I(t)-V_0/R|=\left|I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right|\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$ for every $t\in J$. [F6, algebra]

2.1 Identification of the solution: by step 1.1 the candidate $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ solution of the initial value problem (its derivative exists on all of $J$ through the stated extension convention) and by [F1] the initial value problem with the constant source $V\equiv V_0$ has exactly one $C^1$ solution on every nondegenerate $J$; hence the displayed $I$ equals $\varphi$ there and is the unique solution, and for $J=\{t_0\}$ the restriction and jets are those of [F1] with $V(t_0)=V_0$, namely $I(t_0)=I_0$ and $\dot I(t_0)=(V_0-RI_0)/L$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra, cases]

3.1 Steps 1.1-1.4 and 2.1 establish the formula, its uniqueness, the deviation identity with time constant $\tau=L/R$, the unique stationary solution, the limit behaviour on intervals unbounded above, and the singleton reading. The computation uses only the adopted lumped model and its constant positive elements, with units [F7]; no radiation, distributed-element, material or measurement claim is added, and the RL existence and uniqueness supplier is the choice-free clause (a) of [F1]. [F1, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 2.1] ∎

## Source notes

Griffiths §7.2.3, printed pp. 310-317, records the battery-plus-RL solution $I(t)=\mathcal E_0/R+k\mathrm e^{-Rt/L}$ with time constant $\tau=L/R$; Fitzpatrick §7.5, printed pp. 225-231, writes the RL equation and its exponential approach to the steady current. The example verifies the constant-source candidate by explicit differentiation and inherits uniqueness from the RL theorem; no other current history, transient measurement or numerical value is asserted.

A pair defined on a set of the form $\\mathbb R^3\\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\\mathbb R^3\\times J$ whose restriction to $\\mathbb R^3\\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\\infty$ and for the single functions $\\varphi$ and $\\chi$ below.\n\nFor a potential pair of class $C^k$ with $k\\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are\n\n$$E(\\varphi,A):=-\\nabla\\varphi-\\partial_tA,\\qquad B(\\varphi,A):=\\operatorname{curl}A,$$\n\nwhere $\\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\\operatorname{div}$ and $\\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\\varphi,A)$ and $B(\\varphi,A)$ are maps $\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.\n\nFor $k\\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function\n\n$$G(\\varphi,A):=\\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\\partial_t\\varphi,$$\n\nalso of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\\Omega$ when $G(\\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\\Omega$.\n\nFor $k\\ge2$ and a function $\\chi:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$ of class $C^k$, a **gauge function**, the **gauge transform** of the pair is\n\n$$T_{\\chi}(\\varphi,A):=(\\varphi-\\partial_t\\chi,\\ A+\\nabla\\chi),$$\n\nagain a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$.\n\nFinally, for a function $u:\\Omega\\to\\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ put\n\n$$Wu:=c^{-2}\\partial_t^2u-\\Delta u,$$\n\nwith $\\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\\Box_c$ of the wave operator $\\Box_c=\\partial_t^2-c^2\\Delta$ of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]].           "quote": "Throughout, $\\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field\n([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order\n([[def-real-order]]).\n\nA subset $I \\subseteq \\mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when\n\n$$x, y \\in I \\text{ and } x \\le z \\le y \\;\\Longrightarrow\\; z \\in I .$$\n\nThe **intervals** of $\\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where\n$a, b \\in \\mathbb{R}$:\n\n| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| $(a,b)$ | $\\{x : a < x < b\\}$ | $(a,\\infty)$ | $\\{x : a < x\\}$ |\n| $[a,b]$ | $\\{x : a \\le x \\le b\\}$ | $[a,\\infty)$ | $\\{x : a \\le x\\}$ |\n| $[a,b)$ | $\\{x : a \\le x < b\\}$ | $(-\\infty,b)$ | $\\{x : x < b\\}$ |\n| $(a,b]$ | $\\{x : a < x \\le b\\}$ | $(-\\infty,b]$ | $\\{x : x \\le b\\}$ |\n| | | $(-\\infty,\\infty)$ | $\\mathbb{R}$ |\n\nAn interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is\nfor the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\\infty)$, $(-\\infty,b)$ and $(-\\infty,\\infty)$; it is\n**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,\n$[a,\\infty)$, $(-\\infty,b]$ and $(-\\infty,\\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and\n$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.\n\n**The symbols $\\pm\\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\\mathbb{R}$.** They\nmark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right\ncolumn are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is\never performed with $\\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\\mathbb{R}$\nsilently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.\n\n**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction\nof at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \\le x$, $x < b$ or\n$x \\le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if\n$a < x$ and $x \\le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \\le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,\nby transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever\none or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \\in I$ whenever\n$x, y \\in I$ and $x \\le z \\le y$.\n\n**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly\nwhen it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower\nbound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or\nsides written with $\\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.\n\n**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,\nand **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with\nendpoints $a$ and $b$:\n\n- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \\le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly\n  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\\{a\\}$ when $a = b$.\n- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each\n  is nondegenerate.\n\nThe only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is\nthat $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because\n$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to\nboth sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside\n$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.\n\n**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \\le b$, which is\nexactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested\ninterval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always\ncarries the hypothesis $a \\le b$ in this library.\n\n**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints\n$a \\le b$ is\n\n$$\\ell = b - a \\;\\ge\\; 0 .$$\n\nLength is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the\nset: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is\n$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so\nnothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every\npoint where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.\nUnbounded intervals are assigned no length.",

This is an exterior boundary-force model: the incident vacuum field is not asserted to extend by zero across a sharp interface as a global Maxwell solution. A real absorption layer must supply a compatible material-field solution; no such realization is claimed here. Then the force per unit area is $F/A=(I/c)\\,\\hat k$: the wave pushes the absorber along its direction of propagation with pressure $I/c$. (ii) [Ideal reflector] Adopt instead (A1') the field on the material side vanishes identically while the vacuum field is the sum of the incident wave and the reflected plane wave with $k'=-k$, $e'=-e$ (so that the tangential electric field vanishes on $x_3=0$; the sum is a source-free solution by [[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), together with the same boundary-force law (A2) with zero material-side stress.     "statement": "Let $n\\ge1$, let $U\\subseteq\\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty open set, let $\\lambda_1,\\dots,\\lambda_m\\in\\mathbb C^n$ ($m\\ge1$) be pairwise distinct, and let $c_1,\\dots,c_m\\in\\mathbb C^q$ for some $q\\ge1$ (the scalar case $q=1$ included; all statements below are componentwise). Write $\\lambda_j\\cdot z$ for the componentwise bilinear extension of the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the variable $z$ remains real and $e^{iw}$ for the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] at $iw$, and consider the $\\mathbb C^q$-valued map $F(z):=\\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\\,e^{i\\lambda_j\\cdot z}$ on $U$. Then: (a) [Complex independence] if $F(z)=0$ for every $z\\in U$, then $c_1=\\dots=c_m=0$. (b) [Real-part grouping rule] if $\\operatorname{Re}F(z)=0$ for every $z\\in U$, then for every $\\nu\\in\\mathbb C^n$ the grouped coefficient $$C_\\nu:=\\sum_{\\lambda_j=\\nu} c_j+\\sum_{\\lambda_j=-\\overline\\nu}\\overline{c_j}$$ vanishes; in particular $c_j=0$ whenever $\\lambda_j\\ne-\\overline{\\lambda_j}$ and $\\lambda_j\\notin\\{\\lambda_k,-\\overline{\\lambda_k}:k\\ne j\\}$. (c) [Scope] no hypothesis beyond pairwise distinctness of the $\\lambda_j$ and nonemptiness and openness of $U$ is used; $\\lambda_j=0$ is allowed and the $\\lambda_j$ need not be nonzero, ordered or normalized. The statement concerns the open set $U$ and asserts nothing on sets with empty interior, where distinct characters can agree.",
    "strategy": "Prove (a) by induction on the dimension $n$, for complex frequencies throughout. Every factor is nonzero for distinct complex frequencies, and the complex field has no zero divisors, so vanishing of $F$ on the interval forces $c_{j_0}=0$; this uses derivatives, never a false implication from a nonzero phase difference to unequal exponential values. For $n>1$, choose an open product neighbourhood $J\\times V\\subset U$, split $z=(z_1,z')$ and group by the first complex coordinate $\\mu=\\lambda_{j1}$. Write $F(z_1,z')=\\sum_\\mu e^{i\\mu z_1}P_\\mu(z')$ with $P_\\mu=\\sum_{\\lambda_{j1}=\\mu}c_je^{i\\lambda_j'\\cdot z'}$. At each $z'\\in V$, the one-dimensional result gives $P_\\mu(z')=0$. Within a fixed group the remaining complex coordinate tails are distinct, so the induction hypothesis on the nonempty real open set $V$ forces all its $c_j=0$. This proves componentwise complex independence. For (b), at real $z$ conjugation gives $\\overline{e^{i\\lambda\\cdot z}}=e^{-i\\overline\\lambda\\cdot z}$; thus $2\\operatorname{Re}F=\\sum_jc_je^{i\\lambda_j\\cdot z}+\\sum_j\\overline c_je^{-i\\overline{\\lambda_j}\\cdot z}$. At a self-paired frequency $\\nu=-\\overline\\nu$, that coefficient is $2\\operatorname{Re}\\sum_{\\lambda_j=\\nu}c_j$, not the coefficient itself. In particular at zero frequency a purely imaginary coefficient is allowed. At a non-self-paired frequency without another equal or negative-conjugate frequency, the grouped coefficient is just $c_j$ and must vanish.     "statement": "Let $Y_1,Y_2\\in\\mathbb C$ with $Y_1+Y_2\\ne0$, and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\\in\\mathbb C$ satisfy the two linear equations $$E_i+E_r=E_t,\\qquad Y_1(E_i-E_r)=Y_2E_t.$$ Then: (a) [Solution] If $E_i\\ne0$, then $$r:=\\frac{E_r}{E_i}=\\frac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\\qquad t:=\\frac{E_t}{E_i}=\\frac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2};$$ if $E_i=0$ then $E_r=E_t=0$ and the field ratios are undefined. Let $\\omega>0$, let $\\kappa\\in\\mathbb R^{2}$ (identified with the tangential plane $\\{x_3=0\\}$) satisfy $0<|\\kappa|<K_1:=\\omega(\\varepsilon_1\\mu_1)^{1/2}$, put $k_{13}:=\\sqrt{K_1^{2}-|\\kappa|^{2}}>0$ and define wavevectors $$k_i:=\\kappa+k_{13}\\,n,\\qquad k_r:=\\kappa-k_{13}\\,n,\\qquad k_t:=\\kappa+k_{t3}\\,n,$$ where $k_{t3}\\in\\mathbb C$ satisfies $k_{t3}^{2}=K_2^{2}-|\\kappa|^{2}$ with $K_2:=\\omega(\\varepsilon_2\\mu_2)^{1/2}$ and is selected by non-growth in the $x_3>0$ half-space: $$k_{t3}=\\sqrt{K_2^{2}-|\\kappa|^{2}}>0\\ \\ (|\\kappa|<K_2),\\qquad k_{t3}=0\\ \\ (|\\kappa|=K_2),\\qquad k_{t3}=i\\beta,\\ \\beta:=\\sqrt{|\\kappa|^{2}-K_2^{2}}>0\\ \\ (|\\kappa|>K_2).$$ [This transmitted phase data is the interface-consistent, bounded choice: the propagating and evanescent branches of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](d),(e); the common $(\\kappa,\\omega)$ is declared here for each actual wave, also when a reflected amplitude is zero or the critical transmitted root is zero; the nonzero phase-matching theorem explains this matching where its hypotheses apply, and an absent reflected field has no determined phase labels.] Fix the orthonormal tangential frame $\\hat\\kappa:=\\kappa/|\\kappa|$ and $\\hat y:=n\\times\\hat\\kappa$, and consider the two polarisations: (s) [transverse electric] $e_i=E_i\\hat y$, $e_r=E_r\\hat y$, $e_t=E_t\\hat y$ with $E_i,E_r,E_t\\in\\mathbb C$, $E_i\\ne0$, and $h_j:=k_j\\times e_j/(\\mu_j\\omega)$; (p) [transverse magnetic] $h_i=H_i\\hat y$, $h_r=H_r\\hat y$, $h_t=H_t\\hat y$ with $H_i,H_r,H_t\\in\\mathbb C$, $H_i\\ne0$, and electric amplitudes $e_j:=-(k_j\\times\\hat y)H_j/(\\omega\\varepsilon_j)$ (the same computation shows that in both cases the pairs satisfy the amplitude conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b) in their media). For each polarisation define the amplitudes along the fixed tangential directions $E^{(s)}_j:=e_j\\cdot\\hat y$ and, in the case (p), $E^{(p)}_j:=e_j\\cdot\\hat x$ with $\\hat x:=\\hat\\kappa$; assume the four stationary interface identities of [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] hold on $\\mathbb R^{2}\\times I$ for a nonempty open interval $I$. Then: (a) [Amplitude system] for $\\chi=s$ in every branch, and for $\\chi=p$ when $k_{t3}\\ne0$, the tangential interface identities reduce to $$E^{\\chi}_i+E^{\\chi}_r=E^{\\chi}_t,\\qquad Y^{\\chi}_1\\bigl(E^{\\chi}_i-E^{\\chi}_r\\bigr)=Y^{\\chi}_2E^{\\chi}_t,$$ with the admittances $$Y^s_1=\\frac{k_{13}}{\\mu_1\\omega},\\qquad Y^p_1=\\frac{\\varepsilon_1\\omega}{k_{13}},\\qquad Y^s_2=\\frac{k_{t3}}{\\mu_2\\omega},\\qquad Y^p_2=\\frac{\\varepsilon_2\\omega}{k_{t3}}\\quad(k_{t3}\\ne0).$$ Write $k_{j3}:=k_j\\cdot n$ for the signed components, so $k_{i3}=k_{13}$ and $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$. Here $Y_1^\\chi>0$ uses the positive incident normal magnitude $k_{13}$, whereas the signed reflected component is $k_r\\cdot n=-k_{13}$; $Y_1^\\chi$ is not defined from that negative component. No $Y_2^p$ is defined at $k_{t3}=0$. hence, whenever $Y^{\\chi}_1+Y^{\\chi}_2\\ne0$, $$r_\\chi:=\\frac{E^{\\chi}_r}{E^{\\chi}_i}=\\frac{Y^{\\chi}_1-Y^{\\chi}_2}{Y^{\\chi}_1+Y^{\\chi}_2},\\qquad t_\\chi:=\\frac{E^{\\chi}_t}{E^{\\chi}_i}=\\frac{2Y^{\\chi}_1}{Y^{\\chi}_1+Y^{\\chi}_2}$$ ([[lem-em-admittance-interface-solve]](a)); the reflected and transmitted amplitude symbols are defined by these fixed-direction conventions, and sign conventions for full vector amplitudes may reverse a reflected amplitude relative to this convention. (b) [Propagating branch and Snell's law] if $|\\kappa|<K_2$ then all three wavevectors are real, $Y_1^s,Y_1^p,Y_2^s,Y_2^p>0$ are real, and with $\\theta_j\\in(0,\\pi/2)$ defined by $\\sin\\theta_j=|\\kappa|/|k_j|$ one has $\\theta_r=\\theta_i$ and $n_1\\sin\\theta_i=n_2\\sin\\theta_t$, $n_j=c(\\varepsilon_j\\mu_j)^{1/2}$ ([[pthm-em-phase-matching]](c), [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]); the period-averaged normal fluxes are $Y^{\\chi}_1|E^{\\chi}_i|^{2}/2$, $-Y^{\\chi}_1|E^{\\chi}_r|^{2}/2$ and $Y^{\\chi}_2|E^{\\chi}_t|^{2}/2$, so $$R_\\chi:=|r_\\chi|^{2},\\qquad T_\\chi:=\\frac{Y^{\\chi}_2}{Y^{\\chi}_1}|t_\\chi|^{2},\\qquad R_\\chi+T_\\chi=1 .$$ (c) [Brewster condition] In the finite-admittance branches, $r_\\chi=0$ if and only if $Y^{\\chi}_1=Y^{\\chi}_2$; in particular, if $\\mu_1=\\mu_2$ and $|\\kappa|<K_2$, for unequal indices $n_1\\ne n_2$, $r_p=0$ holds at exactly one admissible incidence angle $\\theta_B\\in(0,\\pi/2)$, characterised by $\\tan\\theta_B=n_2/n_1$, and $r_s\\ne0$ at that angle. For equal indices $n_1=n_2$ (and equal permeabilities), the media are identical, $Y_1^\\chi=Y_2^\\chi$ and $r_s=r_p=0$, $t_s=t_p=1$ for every allowed incidence angle; there is no unique distinguished Brewster angle. (d) [Total internal reflection] if $|\\kappa|>K_2$ (which requires $n_1>n_2$, $|\\kappa|=K_1\\sin\\theta_i$ with $\\theta_i>\\theta_c:=\\arcsin(n_2/n_1)$ in the notation of (b)), then $Y^{s}_2=i\\beta/(\\mu_2\\omega)$ and $Y^{p}_2=-i\\varepsilon_2\\omega/\\beta$ are purely imaginary, $$|r_s|=|r_p|=1,\\qquad t_s,t_p\\ne0,\\qquad |t_\\chi|^{2}=\\frac{4(Y^{\\chi}_1)^{2}}{(Y^{\\chi}_1)^{2}+|Y^{\\chi}_2|^{2}}>0,$$ the transmitted field decays as $e^{-\\beta x_3}$ and its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically while its tangential averaged flux does not vanish ([[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](e)); the reflected wave carries the whole incident normal averaged flux. (e) [Critical angle] if $|\\kappa|=K_2$ then $k_{t3}=0$: the transmitted wave travels along the interface, its tangential electric amplitude vanishes in the (p) case and $Y^{s}_2=0$ in the (s) case, and $r_s=1$, $t_s=2$, $r_p=-1$, $t_p=0$ with vanishing transmitted normal averaged flux. The critical TM branch is solved from the nonsingular equations $E_i^p+E_r^p=k_{t3}H_t/(\\omega\\varepsilon_2)=0$ and $H_i+H_r=H_t$, not by dividing by $k_{t3}$; they give $H_r=H_i$ and $H_t=2H_i$. The transmitted TM electric vector can have a nonzero normal component even though its tangential amplitude is zero. (f) [Scope] the statements are conditional on the interface identities and on the given wave data; no existence or uniqueness of interface-consistent data is claimed. Excluded: anisotropic media, complex $\\varepsilon$ or $\\mu$ and absorption in either medium (only the lossless dielectric case with the evanescent transmitted branch is covered), dispersive media, moving media, the ideal conductor, nonlinear response, and all claims about signal speeds, group velocities, information transfer or empirical data. The statements for $Y^{\\chi}_1+Y^{\\chi}_2=0$ (which cannot occur in the stated branches, where $\\operatorname{Re}Y^{\\chi}_1>0$ and $\\operatorname{Re}Y^{\\chi}_2\\ge0$) are excluded; the notation 'angle of refraction' is used only where $k_t$ is real.",
    "strategy": "Polarisation data: for (s), $e_j=E_j\\hat y$ gives $k_j\\cdot e_j=E_j(k_j\\cdot\\hat y)=0$ (because $k_j=\\kappa+k_{j3}n$ and $\\hat y\\perp\\kappa,n$); for (p), $e_j=-(k_j\\times\\hat y)H_j/(\\omega\\varepsilon_j)$ gives $k_j\\cdot e_j=0$ as well, and $k_j\\times e_j=k_j\\times\\bigl(-(k_j\\times\\hat y)H_j/(\\omega\\varepsilon_j)\\bigr)=H_j\\bigl[(k_j\\cdot k_j)\\hat y-k_j(k_j\\cdot\\hat y)\\bigr]/(\\omega\\varepsilon_j)=H_j(k_j\\cdot k_j)\\hat y/(\\omega\\varepsilon_j)=\\omega\\mu_jh_j$ using $k_j\\cdot k_j=\\varepsilon_j\\mu_j\\omega^{2}$ and $k_j\\cdot\\hat y=0$ ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]], [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b)). The flux identities are clauses (d),(e) of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]: for (s) the normal flux of wave $j$ is $|e_j|^{2}k_{j3}/(2\\mu_j\\omega)=(k_{j3}/(\\mu_j\\omega))|E_j^s|^2/2$, giving respectively $+Y_1^s|E_i^s|^2/2$, $-Y_1^s|E_r^s|^2/2$ and $+Y_2^s|E_t^s|^2/2$; for (p), $E_j^p=k_{j3}H_j/(\\omega\\varepsilon_j)$ and the normal flux is $k_{j3}|H_j|^2/(2\\omega\\varepsilon_j)=(\\varepsilon_j\\omega/k_{j3})|E_j^p|^2/2$. The latter coefficient is negative for the reflected wave; writing it as $-Y_1^p$ gives the signed reflected flux. Thus both polarisations use $+Y_1$ for incidence and $-Y_1$ for reflection, and $+Y_2$ for transmission. Substituting the amplitudes gives $R_\\chi+T_\\chi=1$ by [[lem-em-admittance-interface-solve]](b) with the real positive magnitudes $Y_1^\\chi,Y_2^\\chi$.     "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). The sine case uses the odd extension, whose character coefficients are the sine coefficients (the $k=0$ coefficient vanishes identically). (b) Orthogonality is product integration. If $f\\in L^2(R)$ is orthogonal to every $c_m(x_1)d_n(x_2)$, then for each $m$ the function $g_m(x_2):=\\int_0^{L_1}f(x_1,x_2)c_m(x_1)\\,dx_1$ is in $L^2(0,L_2)$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and Fubini ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]), and $\\int_0^{L_2}g_md_n=0$ for all $n$ by Fubini, so $g_m=0$ a.e. by (a).           "quote": "Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in its lossless isotropic scalar case at rest in the laboratory frame: constants $\\varepsilon,\\mu>0$, $\\sigma=0$, $J_{\\mathrm{ext}}=0$, the constitutive relations $D=\\varepsilon E$, $B=\\mu H$ of [[post-em-material-closure]] clause (b), read with the objects $D,H$ of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], and the macroscopic equations (b) of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with $\\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$ on the guide region; suppose also $\\varepsilon\\mu\\ge c^{-2}$ whenever the broadband interpretation of that branch is used.           "quote": "Let the laboratory region $U\\cong I\\times\\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and define $\\nabla_t f=(\\partial_1f,\\partial_2f,0)$, $\\Delta_t f=\\partial_1^2f+\\partial_2^2f$ and $\\operatorname{div}_tu_t=\\partial_1u_1+\\partial_2u_2$ for the stated regularity, using [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].\n(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\\Omega_A:=A\\times\\mathbb R$ where $A$ is either a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) or the explicit rectangular cross-section; the rectangle has corners and is treated by its open faces, not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\\{x_1=0\\},\\{x_1=a\\},\\{x_2=0\\},\\{x_2=b\\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\\Omega_c:=(0,a)\\times(0,b)\\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. The separate smooth-cavity spectral branch uses an explicitly declared bounded $C^\\infty$ domain in $\\mathbb R^3$ with its smooth PEC boundary; it is not the rectangular reflection class. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\\Omega\\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.\n(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\\times E=0$ and $n\\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $n\\cdot D=\\sigma_f$ and $n\\times H=K_f$ are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\\sigma\\to\\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.\n(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\\prod_j\\mathbb R/(2L_j\\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\\operatorname{div}E$ and $\\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions.
