## Statement

Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and clause (ii) of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are
jointly $C^1$ of [[def-em-fields]], the source fields $\rho,J$ are continuous
of [[def-em-sources]], the constants are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]],
the force density is
$f:=\rho E+J\times B$ of that clause (ii), in
$\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, and $g,\sigma,\Pi=-\sigma$ are the momentum
density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Then:

(a) [Local identity] On $\Omega\times I$, componentwise,

$$\partial_tg-\operatorname{div}\sigma=-f,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f,$$

that is, $\partial_tg_i-\sum_{j<3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}=-(\rho E_i+(J\times B)_i)$ for every $i$, with $\partial_t$ the partial derivative at fixed position and $\operatorname{div}$ taken at fixed time.

(b) [Fixed-volume identity] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with
$\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$
presentation of
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let
$t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Then for
every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and every $i$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}g_i\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j<3}\sigma_{ij}n_j\Bigr)dS-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx=-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j<3}\Pi_{ij}n_j\Bigr)dS-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx,$$

the closed-surface integrals being the finite face sums of that divergence
theorem.

(c) [Scope] The identities are conditional on the two adopted postulates. The
force density $f$ is defined only for the matter model of clause (ii), so no
claim is made about a prescribed current without such a matter model. No
conservation of the total momentum follows unless the boundary term vanishes
or is included in the chosen system. The weak branch, singular sources and
non-integrable products are excluded as in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]; no self-force, radiation reaction or
magnetic-monopole coupling is included, in accordance with the exclusions of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]. This is not an empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$; the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the jointly $C^1$ fields of [[def-em-fields]]
and the continuous sources of [[def-em-sources]]; clause (ii) of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]; the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; and
$g,\sigma,\Pi$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. In clause (b) also
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the admissible $\Omega'$ and $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$.

[F1] The four smooth-branch equations hold pointwise on $\Omega\times I$:
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$,
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, $c>0$ and $\mu_0>0$
([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F2] The fields are jointly $C^1$ on the open $\Omega\times I$: for fixed
position the component maps $s\mapsto E_i(x,s)$, $s\mapsto B_i(x,s)$ are
differentiable with derivatives $\partial_tE_i$, $\partial_tB_i$; sums, scalar
multiples and products of differentiable functions of the time variable obey
the usual rules, and components of a cross product are finite sums of
component products ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[F3] The objects $g,\sigma,\Pi$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] are of
class $C^1$ on $\Omega\times I$, with
$g=\varepsilon_0E\times B$,
$\sigma_{ij}=\varepsilon_0(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2)+\mu_0^{-1}(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2)$
symmetric, $\Pi=-\sigma$, and
$(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j<3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$ at fixed time;
the dot and cross products are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

[F4] Quadratic stress identity: for a $C^1$ field $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ on an
open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and
$Q_{ij}=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert^2$,
$\operatorname{div}Q=F\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$
pointwise ([[lem-em-quadratic-stress-identity]]).

[F5] Fixed-volume tools: for compact measurable $K$ with finite Lebesgue
measure and $f,\partial_tf$ continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$,
$t\mapsto\int_Kf\,d\lambda_n$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative
$\int_K\partial_tf\,d\lambda_n$ ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]); if $\Omega$
carries the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and
$F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then
$\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$ with faces
counted once off the edge set, under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]]); and the
boundary of such an $\Omega$ is Lebesgue-null, because its faces are compact
graph pieces of content zero
([[thm-graphs-of-continuous-functions-have-content-zero]]) and a nonnegative
measurable integral over a null set vanishes
([[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]), so signed integrals over $\Omega$
and over its closure agree.

[F6] The force density is $f=\rho E+J\times B$, a continuous map
$\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ with unit $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-3}$
([[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], [[def-em-sources]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; apply the quadratic stress identity with coefficients $\varepsilon_0$ and $\mu_0^{-1}$, substitute the four smooth Maxwell equations, identify the time derivative of the momentum density by the product rule, and integrate the resulting pointwise identity over an admissible fixed volume with the divergence theorem.

1.1 Divergence of the stress tensor: define $Q^{(E)}_{ij}=E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2$ and $Q^{(B)}_{ij}=B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2$ at fixed time. Both are $C^1$ on the open $\Omega$, and [F4] applied to $F=E$ and to $F=B$ gives $\operatorname{div}Q^{(E)}=E\operatorname{div}E-E\times\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\operatorname{div}Q^{(B)}=B\operatorname{div}B-B\times\operatorname{curl}B$; since $\sigma=\varepsilon_0Q^{(E)}+\mu_0^{-1}Q^{(B)}$ and $\operatorname{div}$ is linear in its argument, $\operatorname{div}\sigma=\varepsilon_0(E\operatorname{div}E-E\times\operatorname{curl}E)+\mu_0^{-1}(B\operatorname{div}B-B\times\operatorname{curl}B)$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 Time derivative of the momentum density: because $g=\varepsilon_0E\times B$ and the components of $E\times B$ are finite sums of products of the component functions, the product rule and linearity [F2] give $\partial_t(E\times B)=\partial_tE\times B+E\times\partial_tB$ componentwise, hence $\partial_tg=\varepsilon_0(\partial_tE\times B+E\times\partial_tB)$ pointwise. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 Fixed-volume setup: let $\Omega'$, $t_0<t_1$ be as in clause (b), fix $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and choose $a,b$ with $t_0<a<t<b<t_1$. The closure $\overline{\Omega'}$ is compact and contained in the open $\Omega$, and each $g_i$ together with $\partial_tg_i$ is continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}\times[a,b]$ by [F3]; the boundary is Lebesgue-null by the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and [F5], so integrals over $\Omega'$ and over its closure agree, and [F5] makes $t\mapsto\int_{\Omega'}g_i(x,t)\,dx$ differentiable at $t$ with derivative $\int_{\Omega'}\partial_tg_i(x,t)\,dx$. [given, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 Local identity: substitute [F1] into step 1.1: $\operatorname{div}\sigma=\rho E-\varepsilon_0E\times(-\partial_tB)-\mu_0^{-1}B\times(\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE)=\rho E+\varepsilon_0E\times\partial_tB-B\times J-(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}B\times\partial_tE$. By bilinearity and alternation of the cross product, $-B\times J=J\times B$ and $-(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}B\times\partial_tE=\varepsilon_0\,\partial_tE\times B$; hence $\operatorname{div}\sigma=\rho E+J\times B+\varepsilon_0(E\times\partial_tB+\partial_tE\times B)=f+\partial_tg$ by [F6] and step 1.2. Therefore $\partial_tg-\operatorname{div}\sigma=-f$, equivalently $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ because $\Pi=-\sigma$; this is clause (a). [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F6, algebra]

3.1 Fixed-volume identity: by steps 1.3 and 2.1, for each $i$ we have $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}g_i\,dx=\int_{\Omega'}\partial_tg_i\,dx=\int_{\Omega'}(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i\,dx-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx$; the fixed-time vector field $x\mapsto(\sigma_{i1},\sigma_{i2},\sigma_{i3})(x,t)$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}$ by [F3], so the divergence theorem of [F5] gives $\int_{\Omega'}(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\sum_j\sigma_{ij}n_j\,dS$ as a finite face sum. Substituting $\Pi=-\sigma$ turns this into the two displayed equalities of clause (b) under the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [step 1.3, step 2.1, F5, algebra]

4.1 Clause (c) records the postulational status of the two inputs, the model dependence of $f$ and of the boundary term, and the exclusions inherited from the weak branch and from the coupling; the argument used only the adopted postulates, the definitions of $g,\sigma,\Pi$, the quadratic stress identity and the integration interface, and made no empirical claim. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F3, F6] ∎

## Remarks

- **The two coefficient applications.** The identity is applied once with coefficient $\varepsilon_0$ to the electric quadratic form and once with coefficient $\mu_0^{-1}$ to the magnetic one; equivalently one applies it to the pair $(\sqrt{\varepsilon_0}E,\mu_0^{-1/2}B)$, but the displayed form keeps the SI constants in their physical places.
- **Why the magnetic curl term survives.** Unlike the energy balance, the momentum balance does not cancel the magnetic terms: $\operatorname{div}Q^{(B)}=-B\times\operatorname{curl}B$ contributes the Ampere-law current and the displacement term, whose combination with $\partial_tg$ produces the force density $J\times B$.
- **Boundary term and traction.** On a fixed volume the identity reads $dP_{\Omega',i}/dt=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\sigma_{ij}n_j\,dS-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx$, the first term being the traction of the field on the boundary; the minus sign in $\Pi=-\sigma$ fixes the sign convention of every later material balance.

## Statement

Assume the hypotheses of [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]]: the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], clause (ii) of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]], the
jointly $C^1$ fields of [[def-em-fields]], continuous sources, and the force
density $f=\rho E+J\times B$. Let $g$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$, the orbital
angular momentum density $\ell=x\times g$ and its flux $x\times\Pi$ be those
of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] relative to the origin fixed there. Then:

(a) [Local identity] On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_t\ell+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f,$$

componentwise
$\partial_t\ell_i+\sum_{j<3}\partial_j(x\times\Pi)_{ij}=-(x\times f)_i$,
where $(\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi))_i:=\sum_{j<3}\partial_j(x\times\Pi)_{ij}$
and $(x\times f)_i=\sum_{j,k<3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jf_k$ with the Levi-Civita
symbol of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial
time derivative at fixed position
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

(b) [Fixed-volume identity] Under the domain, time-interval and
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypotheses of [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]](b), and with
$n$ the outward unit normal, for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and each $i$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}\ell_i\,dx=-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j<3}(x\times\Pi)_{ij}n_j\Bigr)dS-\int_{\Omega'}(x\times f)_i\,dx,$$

the closed-surface integral being the finite face sum of the divergence
theorem used in that clause.

(c) [Scope] The identities depend on the origin fixed in
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]](e) through the explicit factor $x$; no
conservation of angular momentum follows unless the boundary flux vanishes or
is included in the chosen system. The hypotheses and exclusions of
[[pthm-em-momentum-balance]](c) are inherited. The density $\ell$ is orbital,
$\ell=x\times g$; no spin or intrinsic angular momentum of matter is defined
or claimed by this item. This is not an empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses of [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]]; the objects
$g,\sigma,\Pi,\ell,x\times\Pi$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]; and, in
clause (b), the admissible volume $\Omega'$, the interval
$(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$ and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] Under the stated hypotheses the local momentum identity
$\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ holds pointwise on $\Omega\times I$,
with $g$ of class $C^1$, $\Pi$ of class $C^1$ and symmetric, and $f$
continuous ([[pthm-em-momentum-balance]]).

[F2] The objects of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]: $g$, $\sigma$ and
$\Pi=-\sigma$ are of class $C^1$; $\Pi$ is symmetric; the orbital angular momentum density is
$\ell=x\times g$, componentwise $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k<3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$, and
its flux tensor is $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k<3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$;
both depend on the fixed origin of the spatial chart. The cross product and
the Levi-Civita symbol are those of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and of the
definition in that item.

[F3] Angular local identity of the quadratic stress lemma: if $\Pi$ is a $C^1$
symmetric tensor field on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, if $g:U\to\mathbb R^3$
is continuous, and if $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ holds pointwise on
$U$ for a continuous $f:U\to\mathbb R^3$, then
$\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f$ pointwise on
$U$, with time entering as the parameter of the fields
([[lem-em-quadratic-stress-identity]]).

[F4] Fixed-volume tools: for compact measurable $K$ with finite Lebesgue
measure and $h,\partial_th$ continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$,
$t\mapsto\int_Kh\,d\lambda_n$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative
$\int_K\partial_th\,d\lambda_n$ ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]); if $\Omega$
carries the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and
$F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then
$\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$ with faces
counted once off the edge set, under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]]); and the
boundary of such an $\Omega$ is Lebesgue-null, because its faces are compact
graph pieces of content zero
([[thm-graphs-of-continuous-functions-have-content-zero]]) and the integral of
a nonnegative measurable function over a null set vanishes
([[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]), so signed integrals over $\Omega$
and its closure agree.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; apply the angular identity of the quadratic stress lemma to the momentum balance, and integrate the result over an admissible fixed volume with compact-parameter differentiation and the same divergence theorem.

1.1 Local identity: by [F1] the hypotheses of [F3] hold at every fixed time with $g(\cdot,t)$, the $C^1$ symmetric $\Pi(\cdot,t)$ and the continuous $f(\cdot,t)$; applying [F3] pointwise gives $\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f$ on $\Omega\times I$, which is clause (a) with $\ell=x\times g$ and the component conventions of [F2]. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Fixed-volume setup: let $\Omega'$, $t_0<t_1$ be as in clause (b), fix $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and choose $a,b$ with $t_0<a<t<b<t_1$. The closure $\overline{\Omega'}$ is compact and contained in the open $\Omega$, and each $\ell_i$ together with $\partial_t\ell_i$ is continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}\times[a,b]$ by [F2] and [F3]; the boundary is Lebesgue-null by the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and [F4], so integrals over $\Omega'$ and over its closure agree, and [F4] makes $t\mapsto\int_{\Omega'}\ell_i(x,t)\,dx$ differentiable at $t$ with derivative $\int_{\Omega'}\partial_t\ell_i(x,t)\,dx$. [given, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Fixed-volume identity: by steps 1.2 and 1.1, $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}\ell_i\,dx=\int_{\Omega'}\partial_t\ell_i\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}(x\times f)_i\,dx-\int_{\Omega'}(\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi))_i\,dx$; the fixed-time vector field $x\mapsto((x\times\Pi)_{i1},(x\times\Pi)_{i2},(x\times\Pi)_{i3})(x,t)$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}$ by [F2], so the divergence theorem of [F4] gives $\int_{\Omega'}(\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi))_i\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\sum_j(x\times\Pi)_{ij}n_j\,dS$ as a finite face sum, which is clause (b) under the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, F4, algebra]

3.1 Clause (c): the identity depends on the fixed origin through the explicit coordinate factor in $\ell$ and $x\times\Pi$ (the shift law of [F2]); the boundary term is retained, and the hypotheses and exclusions of the momentum balance are inherited unchanged; no spinor or material intrinsic angular momentum enters the argument. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F2] ∎

## Remarks

- **Why symmetry of $\Pi$ is the whole content.** Contracting the momentum balance with the position vector, the term produced by the derivative of $x$ is the antisymmetric contraction $\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}$, which vanishes exactly because $\Pi$ is symmetric; the identity is therefore not a second dynamical law but a consequence of the momentum balance together with the symmetry recorded in the definition.
- **Origin dependence.** Under a shift of origin the left and right sides change in the same way, since $x\mapsto x+a$ adds $a\times(\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi)$ to the left-hand side and $-a\times f$ to the right and these are equal by the momentum balance; the displayed form nevertheless refers to the one fixed origin.

## Statement

Assume the hypotheses of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and
[[pthm-em-momentum-balance]]: the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and clause (ii) of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]] on
the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, jointly $C^1$ fields of
[[def-em-fields]], continuous sources, the constants of the framework, and the
field objects $u,S,g,\Pi$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Suppose in
addition that matter fields
$u_m:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $S_m:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$,
$g_m:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and a symmetric tensor field $\Pi_m$ on
$\Omega\times I$ are of class $C^1$ and satisfy the matter balance equations

$$\partial_tu_m+\operatorname{div}S_m=J\cdot E,\qquad\partial_tg_m+\operatorname{div}\Pi_m=f,$$

pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, where $f=\rho E+J\times B$ and $J\cdot E$ are
the coupling densities of clause (ii). Put
$u_{\mathrm{tot}}:=u+u_m$, $S_{\mathrm{tot}}:=S+S_m$,
$g_{\mathrm{tot}}:=g+g_m$, $\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\Pi+\Pi_m$ (symmetric) and
$\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}:=x\times g_{\mathrm{tot}}$. Then:

(a) [Local conservation] On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\partial_tu_{\mathrm{tot}}+\operatorname{div}S_{\mathrm{tot}}=0,\qquad\partial_tg_{\mathrm{tot}}+\operatorname{div}\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}}=0,\qquad\partial_t\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}})=0$$

componentwise in the last two identities.

(b) [Fixed-volume conservation] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with
$\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$
presentation of
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let
$t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $n$ be the outward unit normal. Then for
every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dx=-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot n\,dS,\qquad\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}g_{{\mathrm{tot}},i}\,dx=-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j<3}\Pi_{{\mathrm{tot}},ij}n_j\Bigr)dS,\qquad\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}\ell_{{\mathrm{tot}},i}\,dx=-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\Bigl(\sum_{j<3}(x\times\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}})_{ij}n_j\Bigr)dS,$$

the closed-surface integrals being finite face sums of that divergence
theorem. Consequently each of the three totals is constant on $(t_0,t_1)$ if
and only if the corresponding boundary flux integral vanishes for every
$t\in(t_0,t_1)$.

(c) [Scope] The matter balances are additional, explicitly stated assumptions,
not consequences of the Maxwell postulates: a prescribed current $(\rho,J)$
does not by itself supply matter fields satisfying them, and "closed system" is
a modelling choice about which boundary terms are included. The hypotheses and
exclusions of the two field theorems are inherited, and no empirical claim is
made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and
[[pthm-em-momentum-balance]]; the field objects of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]; and the $C^1$ matter fields $u_m,S_m,g_m$
and symmetric $C^1$ $\Pi_m$ satisfying the two matter balance equations
pointwise. In clause (b) also the admissible $\Omega'$, the interval
$(t_0,t_1)$ and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] Field balances: $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J\cdot E$ and
$\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with
$u,S,g,\Pi$ of class $C^1$, $\Pi$ symmetric, and $f$ continuous
([[pthm-em-poynting-balance]], [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]]).

[F2] Angular field balance: with $\ell=x\times g$ and $x\times\Pi$ as in
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]],
$\partial_t\ell+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f$ pointwise on
$\Omega\times I$, under the hypotheses of [F1]
([[pthm-em-angular-balance]]).

[F3] Matter balances: $\partial_tu_m+\operatorname{div}S_m=J\cdot E$ and
$\partial_tg_m+\operatorname{div}\Pi_m=f$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with
$u_m,S_m,g_m,\Pi_m$ of class $C^1$ and $\Pi_m$ symmetric; the coupling
densities are those of clause (ii) of [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]].

[F4] Sum rules: for differentiable real functions of the time variable, sums
and scalar multiples have the expected derivatives
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); and the divergence is linear in its argument,
being a finite sum of coordinate partial derivatives
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F5] Fixed-volume tools: compact-parameter differentiation
([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]); the divergence theorem on the finite
piecewise $C^1$ presentation with faces counted once off the edge set, under
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]]); the
Lebesgue-nullity of the boundary of such a domain, from the graph content-zero
theorem ([[thm-graphs-of-continuous-functions-have-content-zero]]) and the
vanishing of nonnegative measurable integrals over null sets
([[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]); and the fact that a continuous
function on an interval whose derivative vanishes at every interior point is
constant ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]).

[F6] The quadratic stress lemma in the form used for the total angular
identity: if $\Pi$ is $C^1$ and symmetric, $g$ continuous, and
$\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-F$ pointwise for continuous $F$, then
$\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times F$
([[lem-em-quadratic-stress-identity]]).

[F7] Identities of the cross product and its components used in the total flux
tensor: $(x\times\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}})_{ij}=\sum_{k,l<3}\epsilon_{ikl}x_k\Pi_{{\mathrm{tot}},lj}$
and $\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}}$ symmetric ([[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]],
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; add each matter balance to the corresponding field balance to obtain the total energy and momentum identities, obtain the total angular identity by adding the field angular balance to the angular identity implied by the matter momentum balance, and integrate with the divergence theorem.

1.1 Total energy and momentum: adding the two identities of [F1] to the two matter balances of [F3] and using the sum rules [F4], $\partial_tu_{\mathrm{tot}}+\operatorname{div}S_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S+J\cdot E)+(\partial_tu_m+\operatorname{div}S_m-J\cdot E)=0$ and $\partial_tg_{\mathrm{tot}}+\operatorname{div}\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi+f)+(\partial_tg_m+\operatorname{div}\Pi_m-f)=0$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, since $\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Pi+\Pi_m$ and the coupling terms cancel between field and matter. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 Total angular: the field angular identity [F2] reads $\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f$; the matter momentum balance $\partial_tg_m+\operatorname{div}\Pi_m=f$ of [F3], written as $\partial_tg_m+\operatorname{div}\Pi_m=-(-f)$ with the continuous $F:=-f$, enters the lemma [F6] and gives $\partial_t(x\times g_m)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi_m)=-x\times(-f)=x\times f$, where the tensor $x\times\Pi_m$ is the one defined inside [F6] for the symmetric $\Pi_m$. Adding the two with [F4] yields $\partial_t\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}})=0$ pointwise, using $\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}=x\times(g+g_m)$ and $\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}}=\Pi+\Pi_m$ as in [F7]. [given, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, algebra]

1.3 Fixed-volume setup: let $\Omega'$, $t_0<t_1$ be as in clause (b), fix $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and choose $a,b$ with $t_0<a<t<b<t_1$. The closures are compact and contained in the open $\Omega$; all six quantities $u_{\mathrm{tot}},S_{\mathrm{tot}},g_{{\mathrm{tot}},i},\Pi_{{\mathrm{tot}},ij},\ell_{{\mathrm{tot}},i},(x\times\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}})_{ij}$ and their time derivatives are continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}\times[a,b]$ by [F1], [F3] and the sum rules; the boundary is Lebesgue-null by [F5], so integrals over $\Omega'$ and its closure agree, and [F5] applies to each of the three total quantities separately. [given, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 Fixed-volume identities: by steps 1.1-1.3, $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dx=\int_{\Omega'}\partial_tu_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}S_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dx=-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot n\,dS$, and likewise for $g_{\mathrm{tot}}$ with the vector fields $(\Pi_{{\mathrm{tot}},i1},\Pi_{{\mathrm{tot}},i2},\Pi_{{\mathrm{tot}},i3})(\cdot,t)$ and for $\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}$ with $((x\times\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}})_{i1},(x\times\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}})_{i2},(x\times\Pi_{\mathrm{tot}})_{i3})(\cdot,t)$, each $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}$ and each integrated with the divergence theorem of [F5]; this proves the three displayed identities and their finite face sums. If a total function has vanishing derivative at every point of $(t_0,t_1)$ then it is constant there by [F5], and if it is constant then its derivative vanishes and the displayed identity forces the corresponding flux to vanish; this is the asserted equivalence for each of the three totals. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F5, algebra]

3.1 Clause (c): the matter balances were assumed, not derived; the coupling densities enter exactly through clause (ii) of [F3], and the boundary terms were retained, so constancy of a total requires its flux to vanish or to be included in the chosen system; the exclusions of the field theorems remain in force and no empirical content is added. [step 2.1, F3, F5] ∎

## Remarks

- **The cancellation is formal, the assumptions are physical.** The proof only adds two pointwise identities; the physical content lies in the hypothesis that a matter model exists whose balances carry exactly the coupling densities $J\cdot E$ and $f$ with the opposite signs. A prescribed current does not supply such matter fields.
- **Totality is a modelling choice.** "Closed system" here means that the chosen volume's boundary flux is either neglected because it vanishes or tracked separately; the theorem asserts the exact boundary-flux forms and nothing more.

## Example

Let $k>0$, $\omega:=ck$, $E_0>0$, and on $\Omega\times I=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
define, with $\theta(x,t):=kz-\omega t$ in the frame $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]] and the encoding of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]],

$$E(x,t):=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\,e_1=\operatorname{Re}\bigl[E_0e_1\,e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\bigr],\qquad B(x,t):=\frac{E_0}{c}\cos(kz-\omega t)\,e_2=\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\tfrac{E_0}{c}e_2\,e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\bigr].$$

The electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to one another and to the
direction $e_3$ ("crossed" fields); $E$ oscillates along $e_1$ and $B$ along
$e_2$. Then:

(a) [Field data] $E$ and $B$ are smooth fields of [[def-em-fields]] on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, and they satisfy the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho=0$ and $J=0$.

(b) [Energy density and flux] With $u$ and $S$ of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]],

$$u(x,t)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(kz-\omega t),\qquad S(x,t)=\varepsilon_0cE_0^2\cos^2(kz-\omega t)\,e_3,$$

and the local balance $\partial_tu+\partial_zS_3=0$, equivalently
$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$, holds exactly on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(c) [Finite-volume accounting] For $a<b$, $L_1,L_2>0$ and the box
$B:=(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)\times(a,b)$ with outward normal $n$, for every $t$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Bu\,dV=L_1L_2\bigl(S_3(a,t)-S_3(b,t)\bigr)=-\oint_{\partial B}S\cdot n\,dS:$$

the four faces with normals $\pm e_1,\pm e_2$ carry zero flux because $S$ is
parallel to $e_3$, and the upper face $z=b$ has outward flux
$L_1L_2S_3(b,t)$ and the lower face $z=a$ has outward flux
$-L_1L_2S_3(a,t)$. Their respective signed contributions to the field-energy
change are $-L_1L_2S_3(b,t)$ and $L_1L_2S_3(a,t)$.

(d) [Scope] The configuration is an ideal source-free plane wave; the
finite-volume accounting of (c) is the fixed-volume energy balance of this
declared solution in the sense of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]], and the example
asserts nothing about the total energy of the field over all of $\mathbb R^3$
nor any empirical realization. $E_0>0$, $k>0$ and $\omega=ck$ are the declared
parameters of the configuration.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $k>0$, $\omega=ck$ with the constant $c>0$ of the framework,
$E_0>0$, the phase $\theta(x,t)=kz-\omega t$, the fields $E,B$ defined above,
and the box $B=(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)\times(a,b)$ with $a<b$ and $L_1,L_2>0$.

[F1] The laboratory region, its chart coordinates $(t,x)$, frame basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and spatial Euclidean structure are those of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]]; the fields of [[def-em-fields]] are maps
$\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$, $E$ polar and $B$ axial, with no
value asserted at singular source support.

[F2] Encoding and its calculus: with $e:=E_0e_1$, $b:=(E_0/c)e_2$,
$\mathbf k:=k e_3$, the definition of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] gives
$E_j=\operatorname{Re}(e_j\exp(i\theta))$, $B_j=\operatorname{Re}(b_j\exp(i\theta))$;
the definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness, and
identities obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar
multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by
$\operatorname{Re}$ term by term.

[F3] Euler's formula: $\exp(i\vartheta)=\cos\vartheta+i\sin\vartheta$ for every
real $\vartheta$ ([[thm-eulers-formula]]).

[F4] The complex exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]); a complex
differentiable map is real totally differentiable with derivative equal to
multiplication by its complex derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]).

[F5] Total-derivative tools: a composite of totally differentiable maps is
totally differentiable with the composite derivative
([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); total differentiability gives
continuity ([[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]]);
if all first partial derivatives exist near a point and are continuous there,
the map is totally differentiable there with Jacobian matrix its total
derivative ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]);
the partial derivatives of a totally differentiable map are the total
derivative applied to the coordinate vectors
([[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); the
partial derivative is the derivative of the corresponding line map
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F6] $C^k$ conventions: a map into $\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when every
component is, and a map is smooth when it is $C^k$ for every $k$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); finite sums, products, scalar
multiples and composites of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$
([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]); sums, scalar
multiples and products of differentiable functions of one variable obey the
usual rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F7] Constants and units: $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with $c>0$ and
$\mu_0>0$; $E$ carries $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $B$ carries $\mathrm T$,
$u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $S$ carries
$\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]],
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]).

[F8] Inner and cross products: $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the Euclidean
coordinate inner product ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the cross product
is bilinear, alternating and right-handed in the positively oriented frame
basis, so $e_1\times e_2=e_3$, $e_2\times e_3=e_1$ and $e_3\times e_1=e_2$
([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[F9] The energy density and Poynting vector are
$u=\tfrac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\langle E,E\rangle+\tfrac{1}{2\mu_0}\langle B,B\rangle$
and $S=\mu_0^{-1}E\times B$ ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]); the smooth
branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] consists of the four equations
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$,
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ for jointly $C^1$ fields.

[F10] Fixed-volume integration: the second fundamental theorem
$\int_\alpha^\beta G'=G(\beta)-G(\alpha)$ for $G$ differentiable on
$[\alpha,\beta]$ with integrable derivative ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]); the
differentiation of compact-parameter integrals under the integral sign
([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]); the reduction of a multiple Riemann integral
over a product rectangle to iterated integrals
([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]); linearity of the multiple
Riemann integral, so a constant integrand integrates to the constant times the
volume ([[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]]), the volume of
$\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ being the product of its side lengths
([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]).

[F11] Box presentation and face flux: the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentations
of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]] consist of compact faces
meeting only in a null edge set, each carrying its actual outward unit normal;
the flux of a continuous field through a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$ is
$\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$, a scalar Riemann
integral ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]); and the
fixed-volume energy identity of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]](b) holds for
every open domain carrying such a presentation, under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
with the closed-surface integral its finite face sum.



## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct; exhibit the fields through the complex encoding, differentiate the exponential by the chain rule, verify the four Maxwell equations and the exact energy identities by substitution, and compute the finite-box ledger with the fundamental theorem, parameter differentiation and Fubini.

1.1 Explicit real form: by [F3], $\operatorname{Re}(e_j\exp(i\theta))=e_j\cos\theta$ for the real amplitudes $e=E_0e_1$ and $b=(E_0/c)e_2$, so $E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$ and $B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; in particular $E\perp B\perp e_3$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Derivatives of the exponential factor: put $G:=\exp(i\theta)$ and $L:=i\theta$, a real-linear map $\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$ whose partial derivatives are the constants $L(e_j)\in\{0,0,ik,-i\omega\}$. The map $L$ has continuous partial derivatives, hence is totally differentiable with $DL=L$ by [F5]; the exponential is real totally differentiable with derivative multiplication by $\exp$ by [F4]; so the chain rule [F5] makes $G=\exp\circ L$ real totally differentiable at every point with $\partial_jG=DG(e_j)=\exp(i\theta)\,L(e_j)$, that is $\partial_xG=\partial_yG=0$, $\partial_zG=ikG$ and $\partial_tG=-i\omega G$; being differentiable everywhere, $G$ is continuous by [F5]. [given, F4, F5, algebra]

1.3 Box presentation: $B=(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)\times(a,b)$ is nonempty open and bounded with closure $[0,L_1]\times[0,L_2]\times[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^3=\Omega$; its boundary consists of the six closed rectangles $S_1^\pm,\dots,S_3^\pm$ in the coordinate planes, with edge set the twelve edges, each face is a compact Borel subset of a coordinate-plane patch, faces meet only in the edge set, and the outward unit normal is $-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2,-e_3,+e_3$ on the faces $x=0$, $x=L_1$, $y=0$, $y=L_2$, $z=a$, $z=b$ respectively; so $B$ carries a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation in the sense of [F11]. [given, F11, algebra]

2.1 Smoothness: we show that $G$ is $C^\infty$. Every partial derivative of $G$ of order at most one is a constant multiple of $G$ by step 1.2, and those partials are continuous because $G$ is. Suppose $G$ is $C^r$ with $r\ge1$ and every partial derivative of order at most $r$ is a constant multiple of $G$; if $P=cG$ is such a partial derivative, then for each coordinate $j$ the line map $s\mapsto P(\cdot+se_j)=c\,G(\cdot+se_j)$ has derivative $c\,\partial_jG=c\,L(e_j)G$ by the scalar-multiple rule [F6], so $\partial_jP$ exists everywhere, equals the constant $c\,L(e_j)$ times $G$, and is continuous; thus every partial derivative of order $r+1$ is a continuous constant multiple of $G$, and $G$ is $C^{r+1}$. By induction $G$ is $C^k$ for every $k$, that is smooth [F6]. [step 1.2, F6, algebra]

2.2 Energy density and flux: substituting step 1.1 into [F9] and using $\mu_0c^2=\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ and $e_1\times e_2=e_3$ gives $u=\tfrac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E_0^2\cos^2\theta+\tfrac{1}{2\mu_0}\tfrac{E_0^2}{c^2}\cos^2\theta=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2\theta$ and $S=\mu_0^{-1}E_0\tfrac{E_0}{c}\cos^2\theta\,e_3=\varepsilon_0cE_0^2\cos^2\theta\,e_3$, which is clause (b) with the units of [F7]. [step 1.1, F7, F8, F9, algebra]

3.1 Field data: $E_j=E_0\operatorname{Re}(G)$ for $j=1$ and $E_j=0$ otherwise, and $B_2=(E_0/c)\operatorname{Re}(G)$ with the other components zero; since $G$ is smooth and real parts, scalar multiples and zero components of smooth maps are smooth by [F6], the maps $E,B:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ are smooth fields of [F1]. Their relevant partial derivatives are $\partial_tE_1=E_0\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega G)=E_0\omega\sin\theta$ and $\partial_zE_1=E_0\operatorname{Re}(ikG)=-E_0k\sin\theta$, and likewise $\partial_tB_2=E_0\omega c^{-1}\sin\theta$ and $\partial_zB_2=-E_0kc^{-1}\sin\theta$, all read from step 1.2. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F6, algebra]

4.1 Maxwell equations with $\rho=J=0$: since $E$ depends only on $z$ in the $e_1$ direction and $B$ only on $z$ in the $e_2$ direction, $\operatorname{div}E=\partial_xE_1+\partial_yE_2+\partial_zE_3=0$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$; the curl formulas give $\operatorname{curl}E=(\partial_yE_3-\partial_zE_2,\ \partial_zE_1-\partial_xE_3,\ \partial_xE_2-\partial_yE_1)=(0,-E_0k\sin\theta,0)=-\partial_tB$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=(0,0,\partial_xB_2-\partial_yB_1)$ evaluated as $(\partial_yB_3-\partial_zB_2,\ \partial_zB_1-\partial_xB_3,\ \partial_xB_2-\partial_yB_1)=(E_0kc^{-1}\sin\theta,0,0)=c^{-2}\partial_tE$, using $\omega=ck$; hence the four smooth-branch equations of [F9] hold with $\rho=0$, $J=0$, which is clause (a). [step 3.1, F8, F9, algebra]

4.2 Local balance: from step 3.1, $\partial_tu=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cdot2\cos\theta(-\sin\theta)(-\omega)=2\varepsilon_0E_0^2\omega\cos\theta\sin\theta$ and $\partial_zS_3=\varepsilon_0cE_0^2\cdot2\cos\theta(-\sin\theta)k=-2\varepsilon_0cE_0^2k\cos\theta\sin\theta$; their sum is $2\varepsilon_0E_0^2(\omega-ck)\cos\theta\sin\theta=0$ because $\omega=ck$, so $\partial_tu+\partial_zS_3=0$, equivalently $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$ since $S$ is parallel to $e_3$; this completes clause (b). [step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

5.1 Time derivative of the box energy: the integrand $u$ is continuous on $\overline B\times\mathbb R$ with continuous time derivative by step 4.2, so the compact-parameter differentiation [F10] applies to $K=\overline B$ and the boundary $\partial B$ is Lebesgue-null, giving $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Bu\,dV=\int_B\partial_tu\,dV$; by Fubini [F10] for the product rectangle $(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)\times(a,b)$, and because $u$ does not depend on $x$ or $y$, this equals $L_1L_2\int_a^b\partial_tu(z,t)\,dz$, and the fundamental theorem [F10] applied to $\partial_tu=-\partial_zS_3$ of step 4.2 yields $\int_a^b\partial_tu\,dz=-\int_a^b\partial_zS_3\,dz=-(S_3(b,t)-S_3(a,t))$. Hence $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Bu\,dV=L_1L_2(S_3(a,t)-S_3(b,t))$. [step 4.2, F10, algebra]

6.1 Closed-surface flux: the box is an admissible $\Omega'$ for the fixed-volume energy identity of [F11] (step 1.3), whose hypotheses are otherwise those verified in steps 3.1, 4.1 and 2.2 with $J\cdot E=0$, so $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Bu\,dV=-\oint_{\partial B}S\cdot n\,dS$. On the four faces with normals $\pm e_1,\pm e_2$ the integrand $S\cdot n$ vanishes identically because $S$ is parallel to $e_3$; on the upper face ($z=b$, outward normal $e_3$) the parametrization $\varphi(x,y)=(x,y,b)$ has $\varphi_x\times\varphi_y=e_1\times e_2=e_3$, so by [F11] the face flux is the integral over $(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)$ of the constant $S_3(b,t)$, equal to $L_1L_2S_3(b,t)$ by [F10]; on the lower face ($z=a$, outward normal $-e_3$) the parametrization $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y,a)$ has $\varphi_x\times\varphi_y=e_3$, so the oriented flux is the integral of $S(x,y,a,t)\cdot e_3=S_3(a,t)$ against the *outward* normal, equal to $-L_1L_2S_3(a,t)$. Summing the six face fluxes as the presentation requires gives $-\oint_{\partial B}S\cdot n\,dS=-L_1L_2S_3(b,t)+L_1L_2S_3(a,t)=L_1L_2(S_3(a,t)-S_3(b,t))$, the signed contributions to the field-energy change being $-L_1L_2S_3(b,t)$ on the top and $+L_1L_2S_3(a,t)$ on the bottom. [step 4.2, step 1.3, step 5.1, F10, F11, algebra]

7.1 Clause (d): the configuration solves the smooth branch with zero sources (step 4.1), its exact energy ledger is steps 2.2, 4.2, 5.1 and 6.1, and nothing was asserted about the whole-space integral of $u$ (which is not a finite energy statement here, the field being a nonzero ideal plane wave) or about any apparatus; the parameters $E_0>0$, $k>0$, $\omega=ck$ are the declared data. [step 6.1, algebra] ∎



## Remarks

- **Why no double-angle identity is needed.** The local balance is proved by differentiating $\cos^2\theta$, equivalently by the product of $\cos\theta$ and $-\sin\theta$ in each term; because $\omega=ck$ the two contributions cancel exactly at every point, which is the exact statement of the balance for this solution and requires no period averaging.
- **The face signs.** The outward normal on the lower face is $-e_3$; the statement lists the flux of the field through the face in the outward orientation as $-L_1L_2S_3(a,t)$, while the contribution of that face to the rate of change of the box energy is its negative, $+L_1L_2S_3(a,t)$. Both signs are kept explicitly.
- **No total-energy claim.** A nonzero whole-space plane wave has infinite integral of $u$ over $\mathbb R^3$; the example uses only the finite box $B$, in accordance with clause (d).

## Definition

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ in the sense of
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain, and the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a) is the one proved in
[[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] for the encoded expressions; the statement of
this definition uses that regularity and adds no further analytic property.
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

## Statement

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and the Laplacian $\Delta$ of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be
jointly $C^2$ fields of [[def-em-fields]], let $(\rho,J)$ be the source fields
of [[def-em-sources]], and let $W\subseteq\Omega\times I$ be open with
$\rho=0$ and $J=0$ on $W$ (a source-free region). Then on $W$, componentwise,

$$\Delta E=c^{-2}\partial_t^2E,\qquad \Delta B=c^{-2}\partial_t^2B;$$

equivalently each of the six Cartesian components of $E$ and of $B$ satisfies
the scalar wave equation $c^{-2}\partial_t^2v=\Delta v$ of speed $c$ on $W$.

(a) [Hypotheses actually used] The derivation differentiates the Faraday and
Ampère equations in time, commutes the time derivative with
$\operatorname{curl}$ (Clairaut's theorem, available for jointly $C^2$ fields),
uses the curl-curl identity of [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]], and
uses the two Gauss equations $\operatorname{div}E=0$,
$\operatorname{div}B=0$ on $W$. The two evolution equations alone are not
sufficient for the conclusion without the constraint equations.

(b) [One-directional] No converse is asserted. The two vector wave equations do
not imply the four source-free Maxwell equations: the constraints
$\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ and the two curl relations are not
recovered, and solutions of the six uncoupled scalar wave equations need not
lie in a source-free smooth Maxwell branch. The correctly constrained
initial-value problem is a separate result on this page.

(c) [Scope] Only the smooth branch is covered. No decay, boundedness, compact
support, finite-energy or boundary hypothesis is imposed or needed; the
conclusion is local on $W$, asserts no value of any field or derivative at a
point of singular source support, and does not cover the weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. The result is conditional on the adopted postulates
and makes no empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ and its frame, the open
set $W\subseteq\Omega\times I$ on which $\rho=0$ and $J=0$, the jointly $C^2$
fields $E,B$ and continuous sources $\rho,J$, the four smooth-branch equations
of the postulate on $U$, and the constants with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

[F1] The fields are jointly $C^2$ on $\Omega\times I$ in the class sense of
[[def-em-fields]], so at every fixed $t\in I$ the maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are $C^2$ spatial vector fields
read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], and all
second partial derivatives including the mixed time-space ones exist and are
continuous.

[F2] On $U$ the smooth branch of the postulate holds:
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, with $\rho,J$ the fields of
[[def-em-sources]] and $\partial_t$ taken at fixed position
([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); on
the open subset $W$ one has $\rho=0$ and $J=0$, so there
$\operatorname{div}E=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B=c^{-2}\partial_tE$.

[F3] The operators are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the Laplacian is that of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]; for a $C^2$ field $F$ on an open subset of
$\mathbb R^3$ the curl-curl identity
$\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F$
holds, with $\Delta F$ componentwise
([[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]]).

[F4] For a jointly $C^2$ field the mixed partial derivatives commute:
$\partial_t\partial_iF_j=\partial_i\partial_tF_j$ for every spatial index $i$
and component $j$ ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

[F5] The constants satisfy $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and hence
$c^2=(\varepsilon_0\mu_0)^{-1}$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

## Proof

1.1 On $W$ the source terms vanish, so the Faraday and Ampère equations become $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B$, the second obtained from $\operatorname{curl}B=c^{-2}\partial_tE$ by multiplying by $c^2$; both displays hold pointwise on $W$, and each side is a continuous combination of second partial derivatives of $E,B$ because $E,B$ are jointly $C^2$ there. [F1, F2, F5, given]

1.2 The conclusion is local on the open set $W$ and uses only the smooth branch: no decay, boundedness, compact-support, finite-energy or boundary hypothesis was imposed or needed, the weak branch and singular source support are excluded, and no empirical or existence claim is made. [F2, given]

2.1 Differentiating the two displays of step 1.1 in time gives $\partial_t^2E=c^2\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}B)$ and $\partial_t^2B=-\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}E)$ on $W$; by step 1.1's differentiability and [F4] the time derivative commutes with every spatial partial derivative, so $\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}B)=\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tB)$ and $\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}E)=\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tE)$; substituting the displays of step 1.1 yields $\partial_t^2E=c^2\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tB)=-c^2\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\partial_t^2B=-\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tE)=-c^2\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}B$ on $W$. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra]

3.1 Fix $(x,t)\in W$; by [F1] the spatial field $E(\cdot,t)$ is $C^2$ on the open set $\Omega$, so [F3] gives $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E=\nabla\operatorname{div}E-\Delta E$ at $(x,t)$, and the Gauss equation $\operatorname{div}E=0$ of [F2] on $W$ turns this into $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E=-\Delta E$; the identical computation with $B$ gives $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}B=-\Delta B$. Substituting these into step 2.1 gives $\partial_t^2E=c^2\Delta E$ and $\partial_t^2B=c^2\Delta B$ on $W$, that is $\Delta E=c^{-2}\partial_t^2E$ and $\Delta B=c^{-2}\partial_t^2B$ componentwise: each component $v$ of $E$ or of $B$ satisfies $c^{-2}\partial_t^2v=\Delta v$ on $W$. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 The derivation used both Gauss constraints through step 3.1; without $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ one obtains only the curl-curl forms of step 2.1. No converse holds: on $W=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the time-independent field $E(x)=(x_1,0,0)$, $B=0$ is $C^\infty$, is affine in $x_1$ so that $\Delta E=0$ and $\partial_t^2E=0$, and therefore satisfies both vector wave equations, while $\operatorname{div}E=1$ violates the constraint $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ with $\rho=0$; hence it lies in no source-free smooth Maxwell branch and the wave equations do not imply the four Maxwell equations. [step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

5.1 Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 derive the two displayed vector wave equations on $W$ from the four smooth-branch equations with vanishing sources, record the hypotheses actually used (time differentiation, Clairaut commutation, the curl-curl identity and the two Gauss constraints), and exhibit a witness showing that the implication is one-directional; step 1.2 records the scope. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 1.2, given] ∎

## Source notes

The cited treatments derive the source-free vacuum wave equation by exactly
this route: differentiate the two evolution equations, commute derivatives,
apply the curl-curl identity and use $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$
in the source-free region. The textbook statements are the motivation for the
claim; the deduction above uses only the imported divergence, curl, Laplacian,
Clairaut and curl-curl interfaces together with the adopted smooth-branch
postulate. The one-directional warning is the standard observation that
solutions of the wave equation need not satisfy the constraints.

## Statement

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The wavevector $k\ne0$, the angular frequency $\omega>0$, the
complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, the plane-wave fields $(E,B)$ of
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ with
phase $\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$, and the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]] with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

[F1] The fields are given by
$E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(e\exp(i\theta(x,t)))$ and
$B(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(b\exp(i\theta(x,t)))$ componentwise; they are of
class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, and $(E,B)$ is the
identically zero pair exactly when $e=b=0$
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]).

[F2] The smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate holds for jointly $C^1$
fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation and
continuous sources; on the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$,
$I=\mathbb R$ with the identically zero source fields $\rho=0$, $J=0$ it
consists of the four equations
$\operatorname{div}E=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$,
$\operatorname{curl}B=c^{-2}\partial_tE$ ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]],
[[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F3] On $\mathbb C^3$ the inner product and cross product are the
componentwise extensions of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]: $u\cdot v=\sum_j u_jv_j$ and $u\times v$ given by
the coordinate differences of products. The identities of
[[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]] are polynomial
identities with integer coefficients and therefore hold for complex entries as
well: the cross product is bilinear and alternating,
$\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to
$u$ and to $v$. Moreover
$|u\times v|^2=|u|^2|v|^2-(u\cdot v)^2$ for real $u,v$
([[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]]).

[F4] The operators: divergence and curl of a $C^1$ field are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]; partial derivatives are
those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]; the Laplacian is that of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. The complex exponential is entire with
derivative itself ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]),
the chain rule for total derivatives applies
([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]), complex differentiability is
equivalent to real total differentiability with a complex-linear derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real part, imaginary part and conjugation are those of
[[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], so that
$\operatorname{Re}$ is $\mathbb R$-linear and every $W\in\mathbb C^3$ has a
unique decomposition $W=A+iB$ with $A,B\in\mathbb R^3$.

[F5] The source-free wave-equation theorem
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] holds for jointly $C^2$ fields on a
source-free open region of the smooth branch, with
$\Delta E=c^{-2}\partial_t^2E$ and $\Delta B=c^{-2}\partial_t^2B$
componentwise.

[F6] Complex field arithmetic and Euler's formula: $\mathbb C$ is a field, so
multiplication is distributive and $i^2=-1$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]); for every real $\theta$,
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ ([[thm-eulers-formula]]); and
$\cos(\pi/2)=0$, $\sin(\pi/2)=1$, $\cos\pi=-1$, $\sin\pi=0$
([[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]).

## Proof

1.1 For the fields of [F1] with phase $\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$, differentiation through the real part gives componentwise $\partial_{x_j}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,k_je\,\exp(i\theta))$ and $\partial_tE=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\,e\,\exp(i\theta))$, hence $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,(k\cdot e)\exp(i\theta))$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,(k\times e)\exp(i\theta))$; replacing $e$ by $b$ gives the same four displays with $B$ and $b$. Indeed each component of $(x,t)\mapsto e_j\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is a composition of the entire exponential with the real-linear maps $(x,t)\mapsto i\theta(x,t)$ and multiplication by the constant $e_j$, so the chain rule [F4] gives $\partial_{x_j}(e_j\exp(i\theta))=e_j\exp(i\theta)\,ik_j$ and $\partial_t(e_j\exp(i\theta))=e_j\exp(i\theta)(-i\omega)$; the derivative of the real part equals the real part of the derivative because $\operatorname{Re}$ is $\mathbb R$-linear [F4], and summing coordinates with the coordinate formulas for divergence and curl [F4] and the cross-product formula [F3] gives the displays. [F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $W\in\mathbb C^3$ satisfy $\operatorname{Re}(W\exp(i\theta))=0$ for every real $\theta$. Writing $W=A+iB$ with $A,B\in\mathbb R^3$ [F4] and using Euler's formula and the field arithmetic [F6] gives $W\exp(i\theta)=(A\cos\theta-B\sin\theta)+i(A\sin\theta+B\cos\theta)$, so $\operatorname{Re}(W\exp(i\theta))=A\cos\theta-B\sin\theta$; evaluating at $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $-B=0$ and at $\theta=\pi$ gives $-A=0$, using the quarter-turn values of [F6]; hence $A=B=0$ and $W=0$. Moreover, for every $(x,t)$ the phase attains every real value: given a real $\theta$ and a time $t$, choose a coordinate $j$ with $k_j\ne0$ and let $x$ have $x_j=(\theta+\omega t)/k_j$ and $x_i=0$ for $i\ne j$; then $k\cdot x=\theta+\omega t$ by the coordinate form of the inner product [F3], so $\theta(x,t)=\theta$. Consequently a relation $\operatorname{Re}(W\exp(i\theta(x,t)))=0$ valid for all $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ forces $W=0$. [F3, F4, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2] and step 1.1, the four equations $\operatorname{div}E=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}B=c^{-2}\partial_tE$ hold on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ exactly when $\operatorname{Re}(i(k\cdot e)\exp(i\theta))=0$, $\operatorname{Re}(i(k\cdot b)\exp(i\theta))=0$, $\operatorname{Re}(i(k\times e-\omega b)\exp(i\theta))=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(i(k\times b+(\omega/c^2)e)\exp(i\theta))=0$ for all $(x,t)$; by step 1.2 each of these is equivalent to the vanishing of the complex vector it multiplies, that is to $k\cdot e=0$, $k\cdot b=0$, $k\times e=\omega b$ and $k\times b=-(\omega/c^2)e$. This proves the equivalence of (a). [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, algebra]

3.1 Assume $(e,b)$ satisfies the four amplitude equations of step 2.1 and $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$. If $e=0$, then $k\times e=\omega b$ gives $b=0$, a contradiction; hence $e\ne0$. Since $k\cdot e=0$, the triple-product expansion $k\times(k\times e)=k(k\cdot e)-|k|^2e=-|k|^2e$ (the coordinate identity of [F3]) shows that $k\times e=0$ would force $|k|^2e=0$ and hence $e=0$; therefore $k\times e\ne0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega\ne0$. Crossing $k\times b=-(\omega/c^2)e$ with $k$ gives $k\times(k\times b)=-(\omega/c^2)(k\times e)=-(\omega^2/c^2)b$, while the same triple-product identity and $k\cdot b=0$ give $k\times(k\times b)=k(k\cdot b)-|k|^2b=-|k|^2b$; hence $(|k|^2-\omega^2/c^2)b=0$ and, since $b\ne0$ and $|k|^2,c^2$ are real with $c>0$, $|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$. Equivalently, if $|k|^2\ne\omega^2/c^2$ then the only solution is $e=b=0$, because any nonzero solution would have $|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$ by the argument just given. [step 2.1, F3, algebra]

3.2 Conversely assume $|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$. For any $e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$, put $b:=k\times e/\omega$; then $k\cdot b=(k\cdot(k\times e))/\omega=0$ because $\langle k\times e,k\rangle=\det[k\ e\ k]=0$ by alternation [F3], and $k\times b=(k(k\cdot e)-|k|^2e)/\omega=-(\omega^2/c^2)e/\omega=-(\omega/c^2)e$, so $(e,b)$ satisfies the amplitude equations; by step 2.1 the corresponding plane wave lies in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch. If $e=0$ then $b=k\times e/\omega=0$, the zero wave; if $e\ne0$ then $k\times e\ne0$, since $k\times e=0$ together with $k\cdot e=0$ would give $k\times(k\times e)=k(k\cdot e)-|k|^2e=-|k|^2e=0$ and hence $e=0$, so $b\ne0$. Conversely, every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ satisfies $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$ by the amplitude equations, so on the dispersion relation the solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,k\times e/\omega)$ with $k\cdot e=0$; since $k\ne0$, the condition $k\cdot e=0$ is one nontrivial complex-linear equation in $\mathbb C^3$, whose solution space is a complex two-dimensional subspace. [step 2.1, F3, algebra]

3.3 By step 2.1 the pair $(E,B)$ satisfies the four equations of the source-free smooth branch on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, and the fields are $C^\infty$ by [F1]; the source-free wave-equation theorem [F5] applied on the source-free region $W=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ therefore gives $\Delta E=c^{-2}\partial_t^2E$ and $\Delta B=c^{-2}\partial_t^2B$ componentwise on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. [step 2.1, F1, F5]

4.1 For a solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and any $(x,t)$, the equalities $k\cdot e=0$ and $k\cdot b=0$ of step 2.1 give $k\cdot E(x,t)=\sum_jk_j\operatorname{Re}(e_j\exp(i\theta))=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((k\cdot e)\exp(i\theta)\bigr)=0$ and likewise $k\cdot B(x,t)=0$, using the $\mathbb R$-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$ and the coordinate form of the inner product [F3, F4]. [step 2.1, step 3.2, F3, F4, algebra]

4.2 For a solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ one has $b=k\times e/\omega=(|k|/\omega)(\hat k\times e)=\hat k\times e/c$, so componentwise taking real parts and using that $\hat k\times\cdot$ is a real-linear combination of coordinates gives $B(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(b\exp(i\theta))=\hat k\times\operatorname{Re}(e\exp(i\theta))/c=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$. Consequently $E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=E\cdot(\hat k\times E)/c=\det[E\ \hat k\ E]/c=0$ for every $(x,t)$, by the determinant identity and alternation of [F3], the last determinant having two equal columns. [step 3.2, F1, F3, algebra]

5.1 For a solution with $|k|=\omega/c$, step 4.2 gives $|B(x,t)|^2=|\hat k\times E(x,t)|^2/c^2$, and the Gram determinant identity of [F3] together with $\hat k\cdot E=0$ from step 4.1 and $|\hat k|^2=\langle k,k\rangle/|k|^2=1$ gives $|\hat k\times E|^2=|\hat k|^2|E|^2-(\hat k\cdot E)^2=|E|^2$; hence $|B(x,t)|^2=|E(x,t)|^2/c^2$ and, both sides being nonnegative and $c>0$, $|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. [step 4.1, step 4.2, F3, algebra]

5.2 The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch, and it asserts nothing about fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations; [F5] records the one-directional character of the wave-equation implication for general fields. The item covers ideal whole-space plane waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and is conditional on the adopted postulate. [step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, given]

6.1 Steps 1.1 and 1.2 supply the derivative formulas and the phase-injectivity fact; step 2.1 proves the amplitude-equation equivalence (a); steps 3.1 and 3.2 prove the dispersion alternative, the nonzero-solution criterion and the complex two-dimensional solution family (b); step 3.3 proves the wave-equation clause and steps 4.1, 4.2 and 5.1 prove transversality, orthogonality, the relation $B=\hat k\times E/c$ and the magnitude relation (c); step 5.2 records the scope (d). [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, step 5.2, given] ∎

## Source notes

The cited treatments obtain the amplitude equations by substituting the
monochromatic ansatz, read the dispersion relation and transversality off them,
and state the relation between the magnetic and electric amplitudes; they also
stress that solutions of the wave equation need not satisfy the full Maxwell
system. The deduction above uses the plane-wave definition, the smooth-branch
postulate and the imported complex, cross-product and vector-calculus
interfaces; the vanishing fact of step 1.2 is the elementary statement that
the real parts of $W\exp(i\theta)$ for all phases determine $W$, and the
products of amplitudes are never decomposed as if they were additive.
