## Definition

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$, let $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$,
and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave pair of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on
the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with phase
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Suppose the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold, so that $k\cdot e=0$ and
$b=k\times e/\omega$. By that theorem, if the pair is nonzero then it also
satisfies the dispersion relation $|k|=\omega/c$, while the zero pair is
permitted for every $k\ne0$ and $\omega>0$, both on and off this dispersion
relation. This item classifies the polarization of that class of transverse
plane waves; it adds no field-theoretic content.

Write $e=a+id$ with the real vectors $a=\operatorname{Re}e$ and
$d=\operatorname{Im}e$ of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
applied componentwise in $\mathbb C^3$; since $k$ is real and $k\cdot e=0$, the
real and imaginary parts of this complex equation give
$\langle k,a\rangle=\langle k,d\rangle=0$. Put $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $|\cdot|$ and $\times$ be the inner product, norm
and cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Then:

(a) [Trace] At every fixed $x$ one has
$E(x,t)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\theta=\theta(x,t)$. The curve
$\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, $\gamma(\theta):=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$,
lies in the transverse plane
$k^\perp=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:\langle k,v\rangle=0\}$; it is the image of the unit
circle $S^1=\{(u_1,u_2)\in\mathbb R^2:u_1^2+u_2^2=1\}$ under the $\mathbb R$-linear
map $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$; it is $2\pi$-periodic in the phase parameter
$\theta$ and satisfies $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$, while the map
$t\mapsto E(x,t)$ has time period $T=2\pi/\omega$. The curve $\gamma$ is
called the **polarization trace** at $x$; it does not depend on $x$, so the
classification below is the same at every point.

(b) [Classification] Exactly one of the following three cases holds.

(i) **Linear polarization**: $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$.
When $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the trace is a nontrivial closed
segment in that span, traversed twice per period; when $a=d=0$, the trace is
the single point $\{0\}$ and $(E,B)$ is the zero wave.

(ii) **Circular polarization**: $|a|=|d|>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$. The
trace is the circle of radius $|a|$ in $k^\perp$, and $|E(x,t)|=|a|$ for all
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(iii) **Elliptical (nondegenerate, noncircular) polarization**:
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$ and not (ii). The trace is a nondegenerate
ellipse centred at $0$ in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$, and the
origin lies in its interior. If in addition $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the
parametrization is along principal axes and the semiaxis lengths are $|a|$ and
$|d|$; the general principal-axis computation is not asserted by this item.

(c) [Handedness] For $a,d\in k^\perp$, the cross product $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $a$ and to $d$
([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), hence parallel
to $k$; define the **helicity sign**
$H:=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle\in\mathbb R$, whose sign is taken in the
order of [[def-real-order]]. One has $H=0$ exactly in the linear case (i), and
$H\ne0$ otherwise. This library calls the polarization **right-handed** when
$H<0$ and **left-handed** when $H>0$. Geometrically, $H<0$ means that at fixed
$x$ the electric vector rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing the
incoming wave (looking along $-\hat k$), and $H>0$ means counterclockwise;
here the screen orientation is fixed by any positive orthonormal triad
$(u,v,\hat k)$, with $u$ to the right and $v$ up for that observer.
Equivalently, $\langle E(x,t)\times\partial_tE(x,t),\hat k\rangle=\omega H$ for
every $(x,t)$. The names "right" and "left" handedness are conventional and
both conventions occur in the literature, so later statements in this library
use only the sign of $H$.

(d) [Status] This is a classification definition. It introduces the trace,
the three cases and the sign $H$, and asserts no field equation, no
propagation, energy or empirical content. The magnetic amplitude enters only
through the two amplitude conditions $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$
recalled above; the definition covers the zero wave, both on and off the
dispersion relation, and no non-plane or non-transverse field is classified.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The real vectors $a,d$ are well defined by the componentwise real and
imaginary parts of $e$; because $k$ is real, taking real and imaginary parts of
$k\cdot e=\sum_jk_j(a_j+id_j)$ gives $\langle k,a\rangle=0$ and
$\langle k,d\rangle=0$, so $a,d\in k^\perp$ and $\gamma$ takes values in
$k^\perp$. The trace formula in (a) is Euler's formula
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of [[thm-eulers-formula]] together with
the field arithmetic on the right-hand side of
$E=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)+i(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)\bigr)$
and the real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$: the real part is
$a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, while the imaginary part is not a field. Since
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\omega>0$, at fixed $x$ the map
$t\mapsto\theta$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$; hence the set traced by
$E(x,t)$ as $t$ varies is the full image $\gamma(\mathbb R)$, independently of
$x$, and $\gamma$ is $2\pi$-periodic with $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$
because $\cos$ and $\sin$ shift by a sign under $\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$. The
time period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, the least positive $s$ with
$\theta(x,t+s)=\theta(x,t)-2\pi$ for all $(x,t)$; it is distinct from the
phase-parameter period $2\pi$ of $\gamma$.

For the classification, "exactly one of the three cases holds" is checked
case by case: if $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$ then (i); otherwise
$\dim=2$, and either $|a|=|d|>0$ with $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, which is (ii),
or not, which is (iii). In case (i) with $\dim=1$, write $d=\lambda a$ with
$a\ne0$ (or symmetrically $a=\mu d$); then
$\gamma(\theta)=(\cos\theta-\lambda\sin\theta)a$, whose image is the segment
$\{sa:|s|\le\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}\}$ in $\mathbb R a$, traversed once in each
direction as $\theta$ runs over an interval of length $\pi$. In case (ii),
expanding with the bilinearity of the inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) gives
$|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2-2u_1u_2\langle a,d\rangle=|a|^2$
whenever $|a|=|d|$, $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $u_1^2+u_2^2=1$, so the image
of the unit circle under $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is contained in the
circle of radius $|a|$ in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; conversely,
for every $v$ in that plane with $|v|=|a|$ the coordinates
$u_1=\langle v,a\rangle/|a|^2$ and $u_2=-\langle v,d\rangle/|d|^2$ satisfy
$u_1^2+u_2^2=1$ and $u_1a-u_2d=v$, because $a/|a|$ and $d/|d|$ are orthonormal
and $v=\langle v,a/|a|\rangle(a/|a|)+\langle v,d/|d|\rangle(d/|d|)$; hence the
trace is exactly that circle. In case (iii) the vectors $a,d$
are linearly independent, so $T:(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is a linear
isomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$ onto the two-dimensional plane
$\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; the image of the closed unit disk under $T$ is a
compact convex subset with nonempty interior in that plane, the image of the
open disk is its nonempty interior, and the image of the unit circle is its
boundary, so the trace is a nondegenerate ellipse centred at
$0=T(0)$ with the origin in its interior. If moreover
$\langle a,d\rangle=0$, then along the principal axes $a,d$ the parametrization
$u_1a-u_2d$ has the stated axis lengths because the two summands are
orthogonal: $|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2$; no computation of
principal axes for general $a,d$ is used or claimed.

For (c), the cross product $a\times d$ is orthogonal to both factors and
alternating ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), so
$a\times d=0$ holds exactly when $a$ and $d$ are linearly dependent, that is,
in case (i); then $H=0$. Otherwise $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$, and
since $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\subseteq k^\perp$ are both two-dimensional,
they are equal; being orthogonal to $a$ and $d$, the vector $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $k^\perp$, whose orthogonal complement in $\mathbb R^3$ is the
line $\mathbb R k$, so $a\times d=\mu k$ for a real $\mu$ and
$H=\mu|k|\ne0$. For the rotation identity, differentiating
$E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ along $t$ with $\partial_t\theta=-\omega$ gives
$\partial_tE=\omega(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)$, so
$E\times\partial_tE
=\omega(a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)\times(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)
=\omega\bigl((\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)a\times d
+\cos\theta\sin\theta(a\times a-d\times d)\bigr)=\omega\,a\times d$
by bilinearity and alternation, and taking the inner product with $\hat k$
gives the displayed identity. As a concrete check of the convention, take
$\hat k=e_3$ with the positive orthonormal screen triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, so
that $e_1$ points right and $e_2$ up for the observer looking along $-e_3$;
then $e=e_1-ie_2$ has $a=e_1$, $d=-e_2$,
$E(0,t)=\cos(\omega t)e_1-\sin(\omega t)e_2$ (clockwise), and
$H=\langle e_1\times(-e_2),e_3\rangle=-1<0$, consistently with the
right-handed naming. This fixes the sign convention of the cited treatment:
the source writes $E_0=\alpha-i\beta$ and calls the polarization right-handed
if and only if $\beta=\hat k\times\alpha$, which under $a=\alpha$,
$d=-\beta$ is $H=-|\alpha|^2<0$ in the circular case.

Finally, all amplitudes $e,b$ and vectors $k,a,d$ are constant and all
quantities above are computed from them by the operations of the cited items;
no limit, no integral and no field equation is used, and the definition is at
the level of classification only.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
[[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from
[[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]. Let $t_0<T$ be real, let
$E_0,B_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^\infty$ fields
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on the whole-space laboratory
region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the
constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume the constraints
$$\operatorname{div}E_0=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B_0=0$$ on $\mathbb R^3$
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Put
$\dot E_0:=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ and
$\dot B_0:=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$. No decay, boundedness, compactness or
finite-energy hypothesis is imposed on the data. Then:

(a) [Existence and explicit representation] There are jointly $C^\infty$
fields $E,B:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R^3$ (in the extension sense of
[[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]) satisfying the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$,
$J\equiv0$ and the initial conditions $E(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$,
$B(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$, $\partial_tE(\cdot,t_0)=\dot E_0$,
$\partial_tB(\cdot,t_0)=\dot B_0$. Explicitly, each component $E_i$ is the
scalar solution $u$ of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](a) with data
$(a,b)=(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$ and $h=0$, each $B_i$ that with
$(a,b)=(B_{0,i},\dot B_{0,i})$, in the spherical-mean representation
$u=\partial_sH_a+H_b$ of that theorem, the mean being that of
[[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]].

(b) [Uniqueness] Every pair of jointly $C^2$ fields on
$\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ (in the extension sense) satisfying the same four
equations with $\rho\equiv0$, $J\equiv0$ and $E'(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$,
$B'(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$ equals $(E,B)$; the time derivatives at $t_0$ are then
automatically $\dot E_0,\dot B_0$ by the Ampere and Faraday equations.

(c) [Finite propagation and domain of dependence] If second constrained data
$(E_0',B_0')$ agree with $(E_0,B_0)$ together with all curls on the closed ball
$\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ — that is, $E_0=E_0'$, $B_0=B_0'$,
$\operatorname{curl}E_0=\operatorname{curl}E_0'$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B_0=\operatorname{curl}B_0'$ there — then the
corresponding solutions agree at $(x_*,t_*)$, for all $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and
$t_*\in[t_0,T]$. Consequently the value at $(x_*,t_*)$ is determined by the
Cauchy data on the closed backward cone
$K(x_*,t_*)=\{(y,v):|y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v)\}$ of
[[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]. In
the causal geometry of the adopted affine Minkowski model this cone is the
model's causal past cone of the event $(x_*,t_*)$ in the chart $x^0=ct$; by
the reachability objects of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]] and the
straight-segment criterion and time monotonicity of
[[thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence]], events outside it cannot
be joined to $(x_*,t_*)$ by a future causal path, so the constructed field
supplies no vacuum influence outside the model's causal cones; this
identification of the PDE cone with the model's causal cone is the modelling
statement of the item, not an additional empirical claim.

(d) [Compact support] If in addition $E_0$ and $B_0$ vanish off a compact set
$K\subset\mathbb R^3$, choose $\rho>0$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]); then for every $t\in[t_0,T]$ one has
$E(x,t)=B(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$.

(e) [Finite-energy branch] Define
$u(x,t)=(\varepsilon_0|E(x,t)|^2+\mu_0^{-1}|B(x,t)|^2)/2$ and
$S=\mu_0^{-1}E\times B$ as in [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and define total
energy by the nonnegative ball exhaustion
$\mathcal E(t):=\sup_{R>0}\int_{B_R(0)}u(x,t)\,dx\in[0,\infty]$. If
$\mathcal E(t_0)<\infty$, then $\mathcal E(t)=\mathcal E(t_0)$ for every
$t\in[t_0,T]$. More locally, for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, $r>0$ and
$t_0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\int_{B_r(x_0)}u(x,t)\,dx\le\int_{B_{r+c(t-s)}(x_0)}u(x,s)\,dx.$$
This is a branch for the same smooth constrained data with finite initial
energy; no existence result for nonsmooth finite-energy data is asserted.

(f) [Scope] This is the smooth whole-space vacuum branch with initially
constraint-satisfying data; general smooth non-decaying data may have infinite
total energy, and no boundary condition, inhomogeneous source, weak-branch
content or empirical claim is asserted. The result is conditional on the
adopted postulates and on $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the latter used through the
scalar theorem and the divergence and substitution suppliers in clause (e).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; times
$t_0<T$; $C^\infty$ data $E_0,B_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with
$\operatorname{div}E_0=\operatorname{div}B_0=0$; the derived data
$\dot E_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$, $\dot B_0=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$; the
whole-space laboratory region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ with frame
basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and constants $c,\mu_0>0$,
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$; and the operators $\operatorname{div}$,
$\operatorname{curl}$, $\nabla$, $\Delta$, $\partial_t$ and
$W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ on the slab.

[F1] Cauchy problem for the scalar wave equation
([[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]): assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, let $c>0$,
$t_0<T$, $a,b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and let $h$ be $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, and let $u$ be the
spherical-mean construction of that theorem. Then (a) $u$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, $Wu=h$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, $u(\cdot,t_0)=a$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,t_0)=b$;
(b) every $v\in C^2$ in the extension sense with the same $Wv=h$ and the same
Cauchy data equals $u$; (c) if data agree on the closed ball
$\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ and the sources agree on the closed backward
cone $K(x_*,t_*)$, the corresponding solutions agree at $(x_*,t_*)$ for every
$x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t_*\in[t_0,T]$; (d) if $a,b$ vanish off compact sets
and $h(\cdot,v)$ vanishes off a fixed compact set contained in
$\overline B_\rho(0)$, then $u(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$.

[F2] Gauss-constraint propagation ([[pthm-em-gauss-constraint-propagation]](a)):
let $E,B$ be jointly $C^2$ fields and $\rho,J$ $C^1$ source fields on the
laboratory region; assume only the evolution equations
$\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$,
$\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B-c^2\mu_0J$ and, separately, the
continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Then the defects
$D_B=\operatorname{div}B$ and
$D_E=\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0$ satisfy
$\partial_tD_B=\partial_tD_E=0$ pointwise; for each fixed $x$ both defects are
constant in time, and initial zero constraints at any $t_0$ persist at every
time.

[F3] Source-free wave equation ([[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]]): let $E,B$ be
jointly $C^2$ fields of [[def-em-fields]] on the laboratory region and let
$W'\subseteq\Omega\times I$ be open with $\rho=0$, $J=0$ on $W'$ for the
sources of [[def-em-sources]]. If the smooth branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds on $W'$, then componentwise
$\Delta E=c^{-2}\partial_t^2E$ and $\Delta B=c^{-2}\partial_t^2B$ on $W'$;
that is, each component of $E$ and of $B$ satisfies $Wv=0$ there.

[F4] Local Poynting identity ([[pthm-em-poynting-balance]](a)): for the
jointly $C^1$ fields of the smooth branch with continuous sources on the
laboratory region, the energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] satisfy
$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J\cdot E$; in particular on a source-free
region $J=0$ one has $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$.

[F5] Energy density and Poynting vector ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]): for
fields of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$,
$u=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\langle E,E\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\langle B,B\rangle$
is a nonnegative $C^k$ function, $S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}E\times B$ is a $C^k$ vector
field, and both are polynomial expressions in the components of $E$ and $B$
with no derivative used.

[F6] Parameter integrals ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]], set form): for
$K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ compact, Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$
and $f$, $\partial_tf$ continuous on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$,
the map $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with
derivative $\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx$, and has the corresponding one-sided
derivatives at the endpoints.

[F7] Change of variables
([[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]]):
under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ of open
subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ and every nonnegative Borel $h:V\to[0,\infty]$,
$\int_Vh(y)\,dy=\int_Uh(T(x))|\det DT(x)|\,dx$.

[F8] Balls, the divergence theorem and surface integrals
([[lem-euclidean-balls-are-bounded-c-one-domains]],
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]],
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]): for $n\ge2$,
$a\in\mathbb R^n$, $R>0$, the open ball $B_R(a)$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain
whose outward unit normal at $y\in\partial B_R(a)$ is $(y-a)/R$; under
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for every bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega'$ and
$F\in C^1(\overline\Omega';\mathbb R^n)$ one has
$\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega'}F\cdot\nu\,dS$;
and the surface integral over a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface is defined
as a finite sum of Lebesgue integrals of the pulled-back nonnegative function,
so for a nonnegative continuous surface function the surface integral is
nonnegative.

[F9] Null spheres, compactness and the mean value theorem
([[lem-unit-sphere-is-lebesgue-null]], [[thm-heine-borel-rn]],
[[cor-mean-value-theorem]]): the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$, $n\ge2$, has
$n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero (under Countable Choice, so the same
holds for every translated scaled sphere); a subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is compact
if and only if it is closed and bounded; and a continuous function on $[a,b]$
that is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $F'\le0$ there satisfies
$F(b)\le F(a)$.

[F10] Wave cones and causal geometry
([[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]],
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]],
[[thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence]]): the closed backward
cone with vertex $(x_0,t_0)$ and speed $c$ is
$K^-(x_0,t_0)=\{(x,t):0\le t\le t_0,\ |x-x_0|\le c(t_0-t)\}$ with base ball
$B_{ct_0}(x_0)$; in the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space the
causal relation is $p\le q\iff q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ with
$J^-(q)=q+\overline{C^-}=\{p:p\le q\}$, and a piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path $x:[a,b]\to A$ has displacement $x(b)-x(a)\in\overline{C^+}$, with
$J^+(p)=R^+(p)$ and the straight-segment criterion for reachability; in an
inertial chart the closure of the future cone is
$\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$.

[F11] Framework objects ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]](a), [[def-em-fields]],
[[def-em-sources]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]): on
the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ the smooth branch of the vacuum
Maxwell postulate holds for jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation, with
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$; a field is $C^k$ when it is
$C^k$ componentwise in the frame basis; $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and
$c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$; the whole-space choice is $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$,
$I=\mathbb R$.

[F12] Vector calculus and differentiability
([[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]],
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]],
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]],
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]): for a $C^2$ field $F$ on an
open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=
\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F$ componentwise, with
$\Delta F$ the componentwise Laplacian; divergence and curl are computed from
first partial derivatives at fixed $t$; for a jointly $C^2$ map the mixed
partial derivatives commute, $\partial_i\partial_j=\partial_j\partial_i$; sums
and real multiples of differentiable functions differentiate termwise; a
$C^\infty$ map in the extension sense on a closed slab is the restriction of a
$C^\infty$ map on an open slab.

[F13] Spherical-mean wave identity
([[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]): for $c>0$ and
$f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ the mean
$M_rf(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{S^2}f(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n)$ is smooth in $r\ge0$,
satisfies the Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity, and
$H_f(x,t)=t\,M_{ct}f(x)$ satisfies $\partial_t^2H_f=c^2\Delta H_f$,
$H_f(\cdot,0)=0$, $\partial_tH_f(\cdot,0)=f$; the identities are local and
need no decay of $f$.

[F14] The Euclidean inner product and cross product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]):
$\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_ku_kv_k$ is bilinear and symmetric with
$|u|^2=\langle u,u\rangle\ge0$, and the cross product is given by the
coordinate differences of products, so that
$|u\times v|^2=|u|^2|v|^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2$ and $|u\times v|\le|u||v|$ for
all $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Setting and construction. Put $\dot E_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ and $\dot B_0=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$, both $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3$; for each $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ apply clause (a) of [F1] on the slab $[t_0,T]$ with $h=0$ and scalar data $(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$ to obtain a $C^\infty$ function $E_i$ with $WE_i=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, $E_i(\cdot,t_0)=E_{0,i}$, $\partial_tE_i(\cdot,t_0)=\dot E_{0,i}$, and likewise $B_i$ with data $(B_{0,i},\dot B_{0,i})$; by clause (a) each $E_i$ has the spherical-mean representation $\partial_sH_a+H_b$ with mean the $M_r$ of [F13], and the construction is legitimate because all six data functions are $C^\infty$ and [F1] carries $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through [A1]. [given, A1, F1, F11, F13]

2.1 Defects and their wave equations. Define the jointly $C^\infty$ fields $R:=\partial_tE-c^2\operatorname{curl}B$ and $Q:=\partial_tB+\operatorname{curl}E$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$; the displayed derivatives exist and are continuous (indeed $C^\infty$) because the components are $C^\infty$, and $WE_i=WB_i=0$ by step 1.1. Then each component satisfies $WR_i=0$ and $WQ_i=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$: for $R_i$, $\partial_t^2R_i=\partial_t^3E_i-c^2(\operatorname{curl}\partial_t^2B)_i=c^2\Delta\partial_tE_i-c^4(\operatorname{curl}\Delta B)_i=c^2\Delta(\partial_tE_i-c^2(\operatorname{curl}B)_i)$ using $\partial_t^2E_i=c^2\Delta E_i$, $\partial_t^2B_i=c^2\Delta B_i$ from step 1.1, commutation of the mixed partial derivatives and of $\Delta$ with the first derivatives [F12], and the same computation with $E$ and $B$ exchanged gives $Q$; equivalently $R_i,Q_i$ are $C^\infty$ in the extension sense on the closed slab. [step 1.1, F12]

3.1 Initial values of the defects. At $t_0$, $R_i(\cdot,t_0)=\partial_tE_i(\cdot,t_0)-c^2(\operatorname{curl}B(\cdot,t_0))_i=\dot E_{0,i}-c^2(\operatorname{curl}B_0)_i=0$ and $Q_i(\cdot,t_0)=\dot B_{0,i}+(\operatorname{curl}E_0)_i=0$ by step 1.1 and the definitions of $\dot E_0,\dot B_0$. For the time derivatives, the component wave equations of step 1.1 give $\partial_t^2E_i(\cdot,t_0)=c^2\Delta E_{0,i}$ and $\partial_t^2B_i(\cdot,t_0)=c^2\Delta B_{0,i}$, so $\partial_tR_i(\cdot,t_0)=c^2\Delta E_{0,i}-c^2(\operatorname{curl}\dot B_0)_i=c^2\Delta E_{0,i}+c^2(\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E_0)_i=c^2(\Delta E_0+\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E_0)_i=c^2(\nabla\operatorname{div}E_0)_i=0$ by the curl-curl identity [F12] and the constraint $\operatorname{div}E_0=0$ of the Statement, and symmetrically $\partial_tQ_i(\cdot,t_0)=c^2\Delta B_{0,i}+c^2(\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}B_0)_i=c^2(\nabla\operatorname{div}B_0)_i=0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F11, F12, algebra]

4.1 The defects vanish and the evolution equations hold. By step 2.1 and step 3.1 each $R_i$ is $C^2$ in the extension sense on the closed slab with $WR_i=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$ and zero Cauchy data at $t_0$; clause (b) of [F1] applied with $(a,b,h)=(0,0,0)$ therefore gives $R_i=0$ on the whole slab, and the same argument gives $Q_i=0$. Hence $\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B$ and $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ hold pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$, the two evolution equations of the smooth branch with $J=0$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1]

5.1 The Gauss constraints propagate: all four equations hold. The fields $E,B$ of step 1.1 are jointly $C^2$ and $\rho=0,J=0$ are $C^1$ on the laboratory region, the two evolution equations hold by step 4.1, and the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ is trivially satisfied; the initial defects vanish because $\operatorname{div}E(\cdot,t_0)=\operatorname{div}E_0=0$ and $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t_0)=\operatorname{div}B_0=0$ by the constraints of the Statement. Clause (a) of [F2] therefore gives $\operatorname{div}E\equiv0$ and $\operatorname{div}B\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$, so with step 4.1 all four equations $\operatorname{div}E=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}B=c^{-2}\partial_tE$ of the source-free smooth branch [F11] hold, as does the initial-value clause $\partial_tE(\cdot,t_0)=\dot E_0$, $\partial_tB(\cdot,t_0)=\dot B_0$ from step 1.1; this proves clauses (a) and the equation part of the Statement. [step 1.1, step 4.1, F2, F11]

6.1 Uniqueness. Let $E',B'$ be jointly $C^2$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense, satisfy the four source-free equations of [F11] and have $E'(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$, $B'(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$. Then the Ampère and Faraday equations at $t_0$ give $\partial_tE'(\cdot,t_0)=c^2\operatorname{curl}B'(\cdot,t_0)=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0=\dot E_0$ and $\partial_tB'(\cdot,t_0)=-\operatorname{curl}E_0=\dot B_0$; by [F3] each component of $E'$ and of $B'$ satisfies $Wv=0$ on the whole slab, and clause (b) of [F1] identifies each component with the corresponding component constructed in step 1.1 and verified in step 5.1, so $(E',B')=(E,B)$. [step 1.1, step 5.1, F1, F3, F11]

6.2 Domain of dependence and the cone reading. Let $(E_0',B_0')$ be constrained data agreeing with $(E_0,B_0)$ and with $\operatorname{curl}E_0,\operatorname{curl}B_0$ on the closed ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$, and let $(E',B')$ be the corresponding constructed solution of steps 1.1 and 5.1, whose scalar data for the $i$-th component of $E$ are $(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$, respectively $(E'_{0,i},\dot E'_{0,i})$, with $\dot E'_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0'$. On the closed ball the scalar data agree: $E_{0,i}=E'_{0,i}$ and $c^2(\operatorname{curl}B_0)_i=c^2(\operatorname{curl}B_0')_i$; the sources are $h=\tilde h=0$ on the closed backward cone $K(x_*,t_*)$, which is exactly the cone object of [F10]. Clause (c) of [F1] applied to each of the six scalar problems therefore gives $E(x_*,t_*)=E'(x_*,t_*)$ and $B(x_*,t_*)=B'(x_*,t_*)$ for every $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t_*\in[t_0,T]$. For the model reading, put the event $q=(x_*,t_*)$ in the inertial chart $x^0=ct$ of [F10]; for an event $p=(y,v)$ with $t_0\le v\le t_*$ the displacement $q-p$ has components $(c(t_*-v),x_*-y)$, and by the closure description of the future cone in [F10] one has $p\le q$ if and only if $c(t_*-v)\ge|x_*-y|$, that is, $(y,v)\in K(x_*,t_*)$; hence $K(x_*,t_*)$ is the model causal past $J^-(q)$ intersected with the slab, and an event outside it cannot be joined to $q$ by a piecewise $C^1$ future causal path, since such a path has displacement in the closed future cone by [F10]. This is the modelling statement of clause (c) and carries no empirical claim. [step 1.1, step 5.1, F1, F10]

6.3 Compact support. Assume $E_0,B_0$ vanish off a compact $K$ and choose $\rho>0$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$, which exists because compact subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ are bounded [F9]. For $x\notin K$ the fields $E_0,B_0$ vanish on a neighbourhood of $x$, so $\dot E_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ and $\dot B_0=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$ vanish at $x$ as well: each component of the scalar data of step 1.1 vanishes off $K$, and $h=0$ vanishes off the compact set $\{0\}$. Fix $t\in[t_0,T]$ and $x$ with $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$; then for every $y\in\overline B_{c(t-t_0)}(x)$ the reverse triangle inequality gives $|y|\ge|x|-|y-x|>|x|-c(t-t_0)>\rho$, so $y\notin K$ and all six scalar data vanish at $y$, and $(y,v)\in K(x,t)$ likewise has $v\in[t_0,t]$, $|y-x|\le c(t-v)$ and hence $|y|\ge|x|-c(t-v)\ge|x|-c(t-t_0)>\rho$, so $h(y,v)=0$; clause (d) of [F1] applied to each component with $\rho$ and the compact $\{0\}$ therefore gives $E(x,t)=B(x,t)=0$, which is clause (d). [step 1.1, step 5.1, F1, F9, algebra]

6.4 Finite-energy setup and the flux bound. Let $u$ and $S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of [F5] for the fields of step 5.1; $u$ is a nonnegative $C^\infty$ function and $S$ a $C^\infty$ vector field, and by [F4] with $J=0$ the local Poynting identity $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$ holds on the whole slab. For every $x$ and $v$, the coordinate identity $|E\times B|^2=|E|^2|B|^2-(E\cdot B)^2\le|E|^2|B|^2$ of [F14] gives $|S|=\mu_0^{-1}|E\times B|\le\mu_0^{-1}|E||B|=c\,pq$ with $p=\sqrt{\varepsilon_0}|E|$ and $q=|B|/\sqrt{\mu_0}$, because $c\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}=1$ by [F11]; since $2pq\le p^2+q^2$ for real $p,q$, $|S|\le c(p^2+q^2)/2=c\,u$. [step 5.1, F4, F5, F11, F14, algebra]

7.1 Moving-ball identity. Fix $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, $r_0>0$ and $t_0\le s\le t\le T$, put $r(v):=r_0+c(t-v)$ for $v\in[s,t]$ (so $r\ge r_0>0$ and $r'=-c$), and put $F(v):=\int_{B_{r(v)}(x_0)}u(x,v)\,dx$. For each $v$, the map $T_v(y)=x_0+r(v)y$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\det DT_v=r(v)^3$, and $T_v(B_1(0))=B_{r(v)}(x_0)$; by the change-of-variables lemma [F7] applied to the nonnegative Borel function $u(\cdot,v)$, $F(v)=\int_{B_1(0)}f(y,v)\,dy$ with $f(y,v):=u(x_0+r(v)y,v)r(v)^3$, and the boundary sphere $S^2$ is Lebesgue null by [F9], so the integral may equivalently be taken over the compact set $\overline B_1(0)$. On an open neighbourhood of $\overline B_1(0)\times[s,t]$ the function $f$ and its partial derivative $\partial_vf=\nabla u(x_0+ry,v)\cdot r'y\,r^3+\partial_vu(x_0+ry,v)\,r^3+3r^2r'u(x_0+ry,v)$ are continuous, because $u$ is $C^\infty$ in the extension sense and $r$ is $C^1$; the parameter-integral lemma [F6] with the compact finite-measure set $\overline B_1(0)$ therefore gives the one-sided derivatives at the endpoints and $F'(v)=\int_{\overline B_1(0)}\partial_vf(y,v)\,dy$ for $v\in(s,t)$. Expanding and substituting back, the first and third terms are $\int_{\overline B_1}\bigl[r^3r'\nabla u(x_0+ry,v)\cdot y+3r^2r'u(x_0+ry,v)\bigr]dy=\frac{r'}{r}\int_{B_r(x_0)}\operatorname{div}\bigl((x-x_0)u(x,v)\bigr)dx$, and the second term is $r^3\int_{\overline B_1}\partial_vu(x_0+ry,v)\,dy=\int_{B_r(x_0)}\partial_vu(x,v)\,dx$; the divergence theorem [F8] applies on the ball $B_r(x_0)$, a bounded $C^1$ domain with outward normal $n=(x-x_0)/r$, giving $\int_{B_r}\operatorname{div}\bigl((x-x_0)u\bigr)=r\int_{\partial B_r}u\,dS$ and, with $\partial_vu=-\operatorname{div}S$ from the Poynting identity of step 6.4, $\int_{B_r}\partial_vu=-\int_{\partial B_r}S\cdot n\,dS$. Hence $F'(v)=-\int_{\partial B_r(x_0)}\bigl(S\cdot n-r'(v)u\bigr)dS=-\int_{\partial B_r(x_0)}\bigl(S\cdot n+c\,u\bigr)dS$ with $r=r(v)$, and the integrand is nonnegative because $S\cdot n+cu\ge-|S|+cu\ge0$ by step 6.4; the surface integral of a nonnegative continuous function is nonnegative by the definition of the surface integral [F8], so $F'\le0$ on $(s,t)$. [step 6.4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, A1, given, algebra]

8.1 Local energy estimate and the equality. By step 7.1, $F$ is continuous on $[s,t]$ and differentiable on $(s,t)$ with $F'\le0$, so the mean value theorem [F9] gives $F(t)\le F(s)$, that is, for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, $r_0>0$ and $t_0\le s\le t\le T$, $\int_{B_{r_0}(x_0)}u(x,t)\,dx\le\int_{B_{r_0+c(t-s)}(x_0)}u(x,s)\,dx$; this is the local inequality of clause (e) for the constructed pair, and the computation of step 7.1 used only the nonnegativity of $u$, the Poynting identity, the bound $|S|\le cu$ and the smoothness of the pair, so the same inequality holds for every smooth source-free Maxwell solution on a slab with its own energy density and flux. Taking $s=t_0$ and the supremum over $r_0>0$ with $x_0=0$ gives $\mathcal E(t)\le\mathcal E(t_0)$ for every $t\in[t_0,T]$. For the reverse inequality, apply the same computation to the pair $\widetilde E(x,v):=E(x,t-v)$, $\widetilde B(x,v):=-B(x,t-v)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[0,t-t_0]$: by the chain rule and the four equations of step 5.1, $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=\operatorname{div}\widetilde B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=-\partial_v\widetilde B$ and $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde B=c^{-2}\partial_v\widetilde E$, so the pair is a smooth source-free solution on that slab, with energy density $u(x,t-v)$ and Poynting vector $-S(x,t-v)$; applying the local inequality with $s'=0$ and $t'=t-t_0$ gives $\int_{B_{r_0}(x_0)}u(x,t_0)\,dx\le\int_{B_{r_0+c(t-t_0)}(x_0)}u(x,t)\,dx\le\mathcal E(t)$ for every $r_0$, so $\mathcal E(t_0)\le\mathcal E(t)$. Hence if $\mathcal E(t_0)<\infty$ then $\mathcal E(t)=\mathcal E(t_0)$ for every $t\in[t_0,T]$. [step 5.1, step 7.1, F9, algebra]

9.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 5.1 prove clause (a) with the explicit spherical-mean representation, step 6.1 proves clause (b), step 6.2 proves clause (c) including the model cone reading, step 6.3 proves clause (d), and steps 6.4, 7.1 and 8.1 prove clause (e) with the local estimate and the total-energy equality under $\mathcal E(t_0)<\infty$. Clause (f) records the scope: the argument is conditional on the adopted postulates and on $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, which is used in step 1.1 through [F1], in step 7.1 through the change-of-variables and divergence suppliers [F7, F8] and the parameter-integral lemma [F6], and in step 8.1 through the same suppliers applied to the time-reversed pair; no decay, boundedness, compactness or finite-energy hypothesis was imposed on the data of the arbitrary-growth branch, no boundary condition, inhomogeneous source or weak-branch content is asserted, and the conclusion makes no empirical claim. [step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 6.2, step 6.3, step 6.4, step 7.1, step 8.1, given] ∎

## Source notes

The two cited treatments derive the wave equation from empty-space Maxwell and
emphasise that the converse fails, but do not state the constrained whole-space
Cauchy theorem; the existence, uniqueness, finite-propagation and
compact-support content is supplied by the cited mathematical Cauchy theory
with the six scalar problems, and the constraint propagation is supplied by the
Gauss-constraint theorem of the framework. The finite-energy branch is proved
here from the local Poynting identity by a moving-ball energy estimate, without
any restriction of the arbitrary-growth existence result.

## Statement

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading] On the source-free region the local identities of
[[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this
field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The wavevector $k\ne0$, the frequency $\omega=c|k|$, the amplitude
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$, $b=k\times e/\omega$, the plane-wave pair
$(E,B)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with phase
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$, the constants of the SI conventions, and the
quantities $u,S,g,\sigma,\Pi$ of the two definition items.

[F1] Period averages ([[lem-em-period-average]]): for $\omega>0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega$ and $a,d\in\mathbb C$,
$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d)$;
for $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$ the same identity holds with the componentwise
complex-bilinear Euclidean inner product, and
$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\times\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a\times\overline d)$
componentwise.

[F2] Energy density and Poynting vector
([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]):
$u=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\langle E,E\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\langle B,B\rangle$
and $S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}E\times B$ are $C^\infty$ and $u\ge0$.

[F3] Momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux
([[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]): $g=S/c^2$,
$\sigma_{ij}=\varepsilon_0(E_iE_j-\frac12\delta_{ij}|E|^2)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}(B_iB_j-\frac12\delta_{ij}|B|^2)$
and $\Pi=-\sigma$, with $\sigma$ symmetric.

[F4] Balance identities ([[pthm-em-poynting-balance]](a),
[[pthm-em-momentum-balance]](a)): for the jointly $C^1$ fields of the smooth
branch with $\rho=J=0$ one has $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$ and
$\partial_tg-\operatorname{div}\sigma=0$ (equivalently
$\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=0$) componentwise on the whole-space
region.

[F5] Plane-wave solutions ([[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]): with
$|k|=\omega/c$, $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$ the pair $(E,B)$ lies in
the source-free smooth Maxwell branch on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; the
fields are $C^\infty$, $B=\hat k\times E/c$ pointwise and $|B|=|E|/c$.

[F6] Plane-wave encoding ([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]):
$E=\operatorname{Re}(e\exp(i\theta))$, $B=\operatorname{Re}(b\exp(i\theta))$,
$\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$, and the amplitudes determine the fields uniquely.

[F7] Fundamental theorem of calculus ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]): for $F$ of
class $C^1$ on $[0,T]$, $\int_0^TF'(t)\,dt=F(T)-F(0)$; more generally the
integral of the derivative over any interval equals the increment.

[F8] Cross and inner product algebra ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]],
[[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]],
[[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]]): the cross
product is bilinear and alternating and the inner product is bilinear and
symmetric, so the coordinate identities
$u\times(v\times w)=v\langle u,w\rangle-w\langle u,v\rangle$ and
$|u\times v|^2=|u|^2|v|^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2$ hold for real vectors, and
extend to complex entries by componentwise complex bilinearity.

[F9] Real and imaginary parts ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]):
$\operatorname{Re}$ and conjugation are $\mathbb R$-linear,
$\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$, $z\overline z=|z|^2$, and
$\operatorname{Re}(\overline z)=\operatorname{Re}(z)$.

[F10] SI constants ([[def-em-si-conventions]]):
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, so $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$ and
$1/(\mu_0c)=\varepsilon_0c$; $c>0$.

[F11] Riemann integration on rectangles
([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]],
[[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]],
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]): continuous functions
on closed nondegenerate rectangles are Riemann integrable, the multiple
integral equals the iterated integral when the sections are integrable, and
the Darboux integral of a nonnegative function is monotone in the rectangle.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Setup and componentwise averages. Fix $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and put $\alpha:=e\,e^{ik\cdot x}$, $\delta:=b\,e^{ik\cdot x}\in\mathbb C^3$, so that $E_i=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha_ie^{-i\omega t})$ and $B_i=\operatorname{Re}(\delta_ie^{-i\omega t})$ for each $i$ by [F6], with $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Applying the scalar and vector forms of [F1] with $a=\alpha$, $d=\alpha$; $a=\delta$, $d=\delta$; and the cross-product form with $a=\alpha$, $d=\delta$, and using $\alpha_i\overline{\alpha_j}=e_ie^{ik\cdot x}\overline{e_j}e^{-ik\cdot x}=e_i\overline{e_j}$ and $|\alpha_i|^2=|e_i|^2$, gives $\langle E_iE_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$, $\langle B_iB_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})$ and $\langle E\times B\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(e\times\overline b)$, and $\langle|E|^2\rangle=\frac12|e|^2$, $\langle|B|^2\rangle=\frac12|b|^2$, all independent of the starting time and of $x$. [given, F1, F5, F6, F9]

2.1 Clause (a). By [F2] and step 1.1, $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\langle|E|^2\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\langle|B|^2\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|e|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|b|^2$. Since $k\cdot e=0$, the Gram identity of [F8] gives $|b|^2=|k\times e|^2/\omega^2=|k|^2|e|^2/\omega^2=|e|^2/c^2$ because $|k|=\omega/c$; hence $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|e|^2+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|e|^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$ by $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$ of [F10]. The value is independent of $x$ (the phase factors cancel in step 1.1) and of the starting time: the integrand is $T$-periodic and continuous, so its integral over any interval of length $T$ equals $\int_0^T$ by [F7] applied to the function $G(s)=\int_s^{s+T}f$ with $G'=0$. [step 1.1, F2, F8, F10, algebra]

3.1 Clause (b). By [F2] and the cross-product average of step 1.1, $\langle S\rangle=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\langle E\times B\rangle=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}(e\times\overline b)$. Since $b=k\times e/\omega$ and $k$ is real, $e\times\overline b=\frac1\omega e\times(k\times\overline e)=\frac1\omega\bigl[k\langle e,\overline e\rangle-\overline e\langle e,k\rangle\bigr]=\frac1\omega k|e|^2$ by the triple-product identity of [F8] and $\langle e,k\rangle=0$; hence $\langle S\rangle=\frac{|e|^2}{2\mu_0\omega}k=\frac{|e|^2|k|}{2\mu_0\omega}\hat k=\frac{|e|^2}{2\mu_0c}\hat k=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$ by $|k|=\omega/c$ and $1/(\mu_0c)=\varepsilon_0c$ of [F10]. Comparing with step 2.1 gives $\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$ and $I=|\langle S\rangle|=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2=c\langle u\rangle$. [step 1.1, F2, F8, F10, algebra]

3.2 Clause (c), tensor identity. By [F3] and step 1.1, $\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=\varepsilon_0\bigl(\frac12\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})-\frac14\delta_{ij}|e|^2\bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\bigl(\frac12\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})-\frac14\delta_{ij}|b|^2\bigr)$. For the magnetic term, the coordinate identity of [F8] for the cross product applied componentwise gives $\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})=\frac{1}{\omega^2}\operatorname{Re}\bigl[(k\times e)_i\overline{(k\times e)_j}\bigr]=\frac{1}{\omega^2}\bigl[|k|^2|e|^2\delta_{ij}-k_ik_j|e|^2-|k|^2\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})\bigr]$: multiplying the coordinate formula for $(k\times e)_i$ and $\overline{(k\times e)_j}$ and summing over the repeated indices leaves exactly the three displayed contractions, using $\langle k,e\rangle=0$ and the reality of $k$, and $\operatorname{Re}(\overline{e_i}e_j)=\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$ by [F9]. Substituting, the two $\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$ coefficients are $\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}-\frac{|k|^2}{2\mu_0\omega^2}=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}-\frac{1}{2\mu_0c^2}=0$ by $|k|^2/\omega^2=1/c^2$ and [F10], and the three $\delta_{ij}$ coefficients are $-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}+\frac{|k|^2}{2\mu_0\omega^2}-\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|b|^2=-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}=0$ using $|b|^2=|e|^2/c^2$ from step 2.1; there remains $\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\frac{|k|^2|e|^2}{2\mu_0\omega^2}\frac{k_ik_j}{|k|^2}=-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2\hat k_i\hat k_j=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$ by [F10] and step 2.1, so $\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=-\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F3, F8, F9, F10, algebra]

3.3 Clause (e), zero and nonzero amplitudes. If $e=0$ then $b=k\times e/\omega=0$, so $E=B=0$ by [F6] and $u=0$ identically by [F2]; all box integrals and their supremum vanish, so the zero amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy. Assume now $e\ne0$ and write $e=a+id$ with $a,d\in\mathbb R^3$; then $u=\varepsilon_0|a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta|^2$ by [F2] and [F6], with $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Choose a coordinate $j$ with $k_j\ne0$ and put $P:=2\pi/|k_j|$; at fixed $t$ and fixed coordinates $x_i$, $i\ne j$, the map $x_j\mapsto\theta$ is affine with nonzero slope $k_j$, so over any $x_j$-interval of length $P$ the phase runs through an interval of length $2\pi$; the average $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$ of step 2.1 is strictly positive here, so $e\ne0$ gives a nonzero wave, and the $2\pi$-periodicity of $\theta\mapsto|a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta|^2$ (by [F9] and the periodicity of the trigonometric functions implicit in the encoding of [F6]) gives $\int_{x_j}^{x_j+P}u\,dx_j=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{|k_j|}\int_0^{2\pi}|a\cos\phi-d\sin\phi|^2d\phi=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{|k_j|}\bigl[\pi|a|^2+\pi|d|^2\bigr]=\frac{\varepsilon_0P}{2}|e|^2>0$, where the elementary integrals of $\cos^2$, $\sin^2$ and $\sin\cos$ over a full period are computed from their derivatives by [F7] and $\sin\cos$ integrates to zero by the symmetry $\phi\mapsto\phi+\pi$. By [F11] the continuous density is Riemann integrable on every closed box and the iterated integral equals the multiple integral, so for $R=NP$ with a positive integer $N$, integrating first in $x_j$ over the $2N$ full periods of $[-R,R]$ and then over the square $[-R,R]^2$ in the other coordinates gives $\int_{[-R,R]^3}u=(2N)\cdot(2R)^2\cdot\frac{\varepsilon_0P}{2}|e|^2=(2R)^2N\varepsilon_0P|e|^2\to+\infty$ as $N\to\infty$; since $u\ge0$, the Darboux integrals over the boxes are monotone in $R$ by [F11], so the box-exhaustion total energy $\sup_{R>0}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u$ is $+\infty$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F6, F7, F9, F11, algebra]

4.1 Momentum density and flux reading. By [F3], $\langle g\rangle=\langle S\rangle/c^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$ by step 3.1, and $\langle\Pi\rangle=-\langle\sigma\rangle$ with $\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$ by step 3.2; the period-averaged momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ is the vector with components $\sum_j\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle n_j=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i(\hat k\cdot n)$, that is $\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, with signed coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$ because $|\hat k|=1$ and $I=c\langle u\rangle$ by step 3.1. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F3, algebra]

4.2 Balance reading (clause (d)). By step 2.1 the function $u$ is $C^\infty$ on the whole-space region and $T$-periodic in $t$, so the mean of $\partial_tu$ vanishes, $\frac1T\int_0^T\partial_tu(x,s)\,ds=\frac{u(x,T)-u(x,0)}{T}=0$, by [F7]; the same computation applies to each component of $g$ by [F3] and step 3.1. The averaged fields $\langle S\rangle$ of step 3.1 and $\langle\sigma\rangle$ of step 3.2 are constant, so $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and $\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ componentwise; hence the local identities of [F4] with $f=0$ hold term by term after period-averaging, and the identification of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum densities and fluxes is exactly the interpretation stated by those two balance theorems ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]](e), [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]](f)). [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, F2, F3, F4, F7]

5.1 Conclusion. Clause (a) is step 2.1, clause (b) is step 3.1, the tensor identity of clause (c) is step 3.2 and its flux reading is step 4.1, clause (d) is step 4.2, and the zero- and nonzero-amplitude statements of clause (e) are step 3.3. The identities hold for every complex transverse amplitude $e$ because no step used reality or any relation between $a$ and $d$ beyond the amplitude conditions $k\cdot e=0$, $b=k\times e/\omega$, $|k|=\omega/c$; no detection statistics, finite-beam or empirical content is asserted, and $I$ is the intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment and the radiation-flux arguments on the companion pages. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 4.1, step 4.2, given] ∎

flux and momentum density for the monochromatic plane wave and identify

## Statement

Let $\omega>0$ and let $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|k_1|=|k_2|=\omega/c$. For $j=1,2$ let $e_j\in\mathbb C^3$ with
$k_j\cdot e_j=0$, put $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$ and let $(E_j,B_j)$ be the
plane-wave solutions of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] given by
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]. Let $a_1,a_2\in\mathbb R$ and put
$(E,B):=a_1(E_1,B_1)+a_2(E_2,B_2)$. Then:

(a) [Superposition] $(E,B)$ is a smooth source-free solution of the vacuum
Maxwell equations ([[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), and at each fixed $x$ it
can be written with a single phase,
$$E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),\qquad B(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\beta(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),$$
where $\alpha(x):=a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta(x)}$,
$\beta(x):=a_1b_1+a_2b_2e^{i\delta(x)}$ and
$\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$; constant relative phases are absorbed in $e_2$.

(b) [Averaged energy density with the coherent cross term] For every $x$,
$$\langle u\rangle(x)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha(x)|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta(x)|^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\bigl(a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2\bigr)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(W(x)\bigr),$$
where
$W(x):=\bigl(e_1\cdot\overline e_2+(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)\bigr)e^{-i\delta(x)}$.
The first two terms are the sum of the averaged energy densities of the two
waves ([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]); the third is the interference cross
term, which for a fixed relative phase does not average away.

(c) [Averaged flux and momentum; equal wavevectors] (with $u$ the energy
density and $S$ the Poynting vector of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]])
$\langle S\rangle(x)=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\alpha(x)\times\overline{\beta(x)}\bigr)$.
In particular, if $k_1=k_2=:k$ then the superposition is the single plane wave
with amplitude $a_1e_1+a_2e_2$, and
$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2$,
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2\hat k$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]).

(d) [No incoherent or statistical claim] The formulas are deterministic
identities for the specified coherent superposition; they are not an ensemble
average over phases, and no detection statistics, finite-sample visibility
estimate or empirical conclusion is drawn. The computation is a conditional
consequence of the adopted Maxwell postulate and does not by itself distinguish
classical from quantum descriptions of light.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The frequency $\omega>0$; wavevectors $k_1,k_2\ne0$ with
$|k_1|=|k_2|=\omega/c$; amplitudes $e_j\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k_j\cdot e_j=0$
and $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$; the plane-wave fields $(E_j,B_j)$ with phases
$\theta_j(x,t)=k_j\cdot x-\omega t$; real coefficients $a_1,a_2$; and the
energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]].

[F1] Linear superposition ([[pthm-em-linear-superposition]](a)): for any finite
list of field-source pairs satisfying one and the same branch of the vacuum
Maxwell postulate on the same region and real coefficients, the corresponding
linear combination of fields and sources satisfies the same branch with the
same constants; pointwise in the smooth branch.

[F2] Plane-wave solutions ([[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]): for
$|k|=\omega/c$, $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$ the plane-wave pair lies
in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch, its fields are $C^\infty$, and
$B=\hat k\times E/c$; there are no sources.

[F3] Plane-wave encoding ([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]):
$E_j=\operatorname{Re}(e_j\exp(i\theta_j))$,
$B_j=\operatorname{Re}(b_j\exp(i\theta_j))$ componentwise.

[F4] Period averages ([[lem-em-period-average]]): for $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$
and $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$\frac1T\int_0^T\langle\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t}),\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\langle a,\overline d\rangle)$
and
$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\times\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a\times\overline d)$
componentwise.

[F5] Energy density and Poynting vector
([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]):
$u=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\langle E,E\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\langle B,B\rangle$
and $S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}E\times B$.

[F6] Single-wave averages ([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]): for a single
transverse plane wave with amplitude $\tilde e$, wavevector $\tilde k$,
$|\tilde k|=\omega/c$, the period-averaged energy density and Poynting vector
are $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|\tilde e|^2$ and
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|\tilde e|^2\hat k$.

[F7] Cross and inner product algebra ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]): both products are bilinear over $\mathbb R$
and extend componentwise to complex entries as complex-bilinear maps, the cross
product is alternating, and the polynomial identity
$\langle u\times v,w\times z\rangle=\langle u,w\rangle\langle v,z\rangle-\langle u,z\rangle\langle v,w\rangle$
holds; in particular $\langle\hat k\times u,\hat k\times\overline v\rangle=\langle u,\overline v\rangle$
whenever $\langle\hat k,u\rangle=\langle\hat k,v\rangle=0$ and $|\hat k|=1$.

[F8] Complex parts and conjugation
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]):
$\operatorname{Re}$ is $\mathbb R$-linear, $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$,
$z\overline z=|z|^2$, and $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb C^3$
restricted to real vectors.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Setting. For $j=1,2$ the data satisfy $|k_j|=\omega/c$, $k_j\cdot e_j=0$ and $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$, so by [F2] each $(E_j,B_j)$ of [F3] is a $C^\infty$ source-free solution of the smooth vacuum Maxwell branch on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; put $\theta_j(x,t)=k_j\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x=\theta_2(x,t)-\theta_1(x,t)$, a function of $x$ alone. [given, F2, F3]

2.1 Clause (a). The pairs $(E_1,B_1,\rho_1,J_1)$ and $(E_2,B_2,\rho_2,J_2)$ with $\rho_1=\rho_2=0$, $J_1=J_2=0$ each satisfy the smooth branch on the same whole-space region by step 1.1, so [F1](a) with $n=2$ and the real coefficients $a_1,a_2$ gives that $(E,B)=a_1(E_1,B_1)+a_2(E_2,B_2)$ satisfies the smooth source-free branch with the same constants, and the fields are $C^\infty$ as finite linear combinations of $C^\infty$ fields. The single-phase rewriting follows from $\exp(i\theta_2)=\exp(i\delta(x))\exp(i\theta_1)$ and the $\mathbb R$-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$ of [F8]: componentwise $E=\operatorname{Re}(e_1e^{i\theta_1})a_1+\operatorname{Re}(e_2e^{i\theta_1}e^{i\delta})a_2=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta})e^{i\theta_1}\bigr)=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha e^{i\theta_1})$ by the field arithmetic of $\mathbb C$, and identically for $B$ with $\beta=a_1b_1+a_2b_2e^{i\delta}$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F8, algebra]

3.1 Clause (b). Fix $x$ and write $\theta=\theta_1(x,t)=k_1\cdot x-\omega t$, so that by step 2.1 $E=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha e^{-i\omega t})$ and $B=\operatorname{Re}(\beta e^{-i\omega t})$ with the constants $\alpha=\alpha(x)$, $\beta=\beta(x)$ (the factor $e^{ik_1\cdot x}$ being absorbed into $\alpha$ and $\beta$). The inner-product form of [F4] gives $\langle E_iE_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\alpha_i\overline{\alpha_j})$, hence $\langle|E|^2\rangle=\frac12|\alpha|^2$, and likewise $\langle|B|^2\rangle=\frac12|\beta|^2$; therefore $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta|^2$ by [F5]. Expanding the squares with the complex bilinearity of [F7] and [F8] gives $|\alpha|^2=a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_1\cdot\overline e_2e^{-i\delta}\bigr)$ and $|\beta|^2=a_1^2|b_1|^2+a_2^2|b_2|^2+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_1\cdot\overline b_2e^{-i\delta}\bigr)$. For the magnetic terms, $|b_j|^2=\omega^{-2}\langle k_j\times e_j,\overline{k_j\times e_j}\rangle=\omega^{-2}|k_j|^2|e_j|^2=|e_j|^2/c^2$ by [F7] and $k_j\cdot e_j=0$, and $b_1\cdot\overline b_2=\omega^{-2}(k_1\times e_1)\cdot\overline{(k_2\times e_2)}=\frac{|k_1||k_2|}{\omega^2}(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)=\frac{1}{c^2}(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)$; substituting and using $\frac{1}{4\mu_0c^2}=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}$ from the SI relation gives $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}(a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}(W)$ with $W=(e_1\cdot\overline e_2+(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2))e^{-i\delta}$, which is clause (b). [step 2.1, F4, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

3.2 Clause (c). At the same fixed $x$, the cross-product form of [F4] gives $\langle E\times B\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\times\overline\beta)$, so $\langle S\rangle=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\langle E\times B\rangle=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\times\overline\beta)$ by [F5], which is the first display of clause (c). If $k_1=k_2=:k$ then $\delta=0$, $\alpha=a_1e_1+a_2e_2=:\tilde e$ and $\beta=a_1b_1+a_2b_2$; by the bilinearity of the cross product [F7], $\beta=k\times(a_1e_1+a_2e_2)/\omega=k\times\tilde e/\omega$, and $k\cdot\tilde e=0$, so $(E,B)$ is exactly the single plane wave with amplitude $\tilde e$ and wavevector $k$, of the class covered by [F6]; clause (a) of [F6] gives $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|\tilde e|^2$ and clause (b) gives $\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|\tilde e|^2\hat k$. These agree with clauses (b) and the first display of (c): when $k_1=k_2=k$ the bracket in $W$ reduces to $2e_1\cdot\overline e_2$ by the identity of [F7], and $|\tilde e|^2=a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}(e_1\cdot\overline e_2)$ by [F8]. [step 2.1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion and scope. Step 2.1 is clause (a), step 3.1 is clause (b), step 3.2 is clause (c), and clause (d) is a scope qualification on the same computation: every average above is the deterministic period average at a fixed point of the specified coherent superposition, no ensemble or random-phase average, detector model, finite-sample frequency or visibility estimate is introduced, and nothing in the proof uses any property distinguishing classical from quantum descriptions of light beyond the adopted Maxwell equations and the definitions; in particular classical electromagnetic waves interfere, so these formulas do not by themselves discriminate between descriptions. The identities are conditional on the adopted postulate and make no empirical claim. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, F5, given] ∎

## Source notes

The cited treatments state the superposition principle for linear Maxwell
theory and the monochromatic amplitude representation on which the two-beam sum
is written; the interference cross term and its averaged form are proved here
from the framework's own definitions and period-average lemma. The scope
qualification (d) records explicitly that this is a deterministic field
calculation, not a detection or sampling analysis.

## Example

Use the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and the SI conventions of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix $K>0$, put
$\omega:=cK$ and $k:=Ke_3$, so that $|k|=K=\omega/c$ and $\hat k=e_3$, and let
$E_0>0$ carry the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$. For each amplitude choice
below put $b:=k\times e/\omega$; then the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold and the corresponding fields
$(E,B)$ of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] are smooth source-free vacuum
Maxwell solutions on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, with
$\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$.

(i) [Linear] $e:=E_0e_1$, $b=(E_0/c)e_2$. Here $a=E_0e_1$ and $d=0$, the
trace is the segment $[-E_0,E_0]e_1=\{se_1:-E_0\le s\le E_0\}$ traversed
twice per period, the polarization is linear and
$H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle=0$; moreover
$E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$, $B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$ and $|B|=|E|/c$.

(ii) [Circular] $e:=E_0(e_1+ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-ie_1)$. Here
$a=E_0e_1$ and $d=E_0e_2$, so $|a|=|d|=E_0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$: the
polarization is circular of radius $E_0$, with
$E=E_0(\cos\theta\,e_1-\sin\theta\,e_2)$,
$B=(E_0/c)(\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2)$, $|E|=E_0$ and $|B|=E_0/c$
everywhere, and $H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle=E_0^2>0$, so this
polarization is left-handed in the convention of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The reversed choice $e=E_0(e_1-ie_2)$
gives $H=-E_0^2<0$ and is right-handed.

(iii) [Elliptical] $e:=E_0(e_1+2ie_2)$. Here $a=E_0e_1$ and $d=2E_0e_2$ are
orthogonal with unequal lengths, so by clause (b)(iii) of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]] the trace is the axis-aligned ellipse
$E_0\cos\theta\,e_1-2E_0\sin\theta\,e_2$ with semiaxes $E_0$ and $2E_0$ along
$e_1$ and $e_2$; $|E|^2=E_0^2(\cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta)$ varies between
$E_0^2$ and $4E_0^2$; and $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-2ie_1)$, $H=2E_0^2>0$.

(iv) [Degenerate and edge cases] $e=0$ gives the zero wave, for which
$a=d=0$ and the trace is the single point $\{0\}$. For $e:=E_0(1+i)e_1$ one
has $a=d=E_0e_1$, so the polarization is linear with trace the segment
$[-\sqrt2E_0,\sqrt2E_0]e_1$ and $H=0$; the classification (b) of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]] covers this case without requiring $a$ and
$d$ to be orthogonal.

(v) [Verification and scope] In every case $b=k\times e/\omega$ with
$|k|=\omega/c$, so the amplitude equations hold and the fields are smooth
source-free solutions by [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]; the amplitudes and
the semiaxis lengths carry the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and
$|B|=|E|/c$ holds pointwise. The examples assert no empirical realization and
no measured polarization.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, the constants $c>0$ and $K>0$,
$\omega=cK$, $k=Ke_3$, the amplitude $E_0>0$ in $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$,
the five amplitude choices $e\in\{E_0e_1,\ E_0(e_1+ie_2),\ E_0(e_1-ie_2),\ E_0(e_1+2ie_2),\ E_0(1+i)e_1,\ 0\}$
with the corresponding $b=k\times e/\omega$, and the phase
$\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$.

[F1] The polarization definition fixes the trace
$E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $a=\operatorname{Re}e$, $d=\operatorname{Im}e$,
the linear, circular and elliptical clauses with their criteria, and the
helicity sign $H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle$, with $H=0$ exactly in the
linear case, right-handed meaning $H<0$ and left-handed meaning $H>0$
([[def-em-polarization-definition]]).

[F2] For a plane wave with $k\ne0$, $\omega>0$, if $|k|=\omega/c$ and
$e$ satisfies $k\cdot e=0$ then $b=k\times e/\omega$ makes the amplitude
equations hold, so the pair lies in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch;
all solution fields are $C^\infty$ and satisfy
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$ pointwise ([[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]).

[F3] The plane-wave pair is
$E=\operatorname{Re}(e\exp(i\theta))$, $B=\operatorname{Re}(b\exp(i\theta))$
with $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$, $b$ the complex magnetic amplitude, and
$\hat k=k/|k|$ ([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]).

[F4] The cross product has the coordinate formula
$u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\,u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$ on the standard
basis ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).

[F5] The Euclidean inner product is $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_k u_kv_k$,
additive and real-homogeneous in each argument, so that
$|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2-2u_1u_2\langle a,d\rangle$ for real
$u_1,u_2$ and $a,d\in\mathbb R^3$; in particular the frame basis is
orthonormal ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[F6] The SI conventions provide the propagation constant $c>0$ with its unit
and the units of $k$, $\omega$, $E$ and $B$
([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F7] The laboratory region carries the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ in which
components are read ([[def-em-lab-geometry]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Common data. With $k=Ke_3$ one has $|k|=K$, $|k|=\omega/c$ because $\omega=cK$, and $\hat k=e_3$; by [F4] and the coordinate formula, $e_3\times e_1=e_2$ and $e_3\times e_2=-e_1$. Hence for each choice $b=k\times e/\omega=(K/\omega)(e_3\times e)$: for $e=E_0e_1$, $b=(E_0/c)e_2$; for $e=E_0(e_1+ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-ie_1)$; for $e=E_0(e_1-ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2+ie_1)$; for $e=E_0(e_1+2ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-2ie_1)$; and for $e=E_0(1+i)e_1$, $b=(E_0/c)(1+i)e_2$. Also $k\cdot e=K e_3\cdot e=0$ for each of these amplitudes, since only the first two coordinates are nonzero. [given, F3, F4, F5, F7, algebra]

2.1 Case (i), linear. For $e=E_0e_1$ one has $a=E_0e_1$, $d=0$, so $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$ and clause (b)(i) of [F1] gives a linear trace, the segment $[-E_0,E_0]e_1$ traversed twice per period; $a\times d=E_0e_1\times0=0$ by [F4], so $H=0$. The fields are $E=\operatorname{Re}(E_0e_1e^{i\theta})=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$ and $B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$, whence $|B|=|E|/c$ pointwise; this also matches $b=(E_0/c)e_2$ from step 1.1 and clause (c) of [F2]. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.2 Case (ii), circular. For $e=E_0(e_1+ie_2)$ one has $a=E_0e_1$, $d=E_0e_2$, so $|a|=|d|=E_0>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=E_0^2\langle e_1,e_2\rangle=0$ by the orthonormality of [F5]; clause (b)(ii) of [F1] gives a circular polarization of radius $E_0$. The trace is $E=E_0(\cos\theta\,e_1-\sin\theta\,e_2)$ with $|E|^2=E_0^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)=E_0^2$ by [F5], and $B=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((E_0/c)(e_2-ie_1)e^{i\theta}\bigr) =(E_0/c)(\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2)$ with $|B|=E_0/c$; finally $H=\langle a\times d,e_3\rangle=E_0^2\langle e_1\times e_2,e_3\rangle=E_0^2>0$ by [F4] and [F5], so this polarization is left-handed by [F1]. For the reversed choice $e=E_0(e_1-ie_2)$ one has $d=-E_0e_2$ and $H=E_0^2\langle e_1\times(-e_2),e_3\rangle=-E_0^2<0$, which is right-handed. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.3 Case (iii), elliptical. For $e=E_0(e_1+2ie_2)$ one has $a=E_0e_1$, $d=2E_0e_2$, which are orthogonal by [F5] and have unequal lengths, and $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$; since $|a|=E_0\ne2E_0=|d|$, clause (b)(ii) fails, so clause (b)(iii) of [F1] applies and, because $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the trace is the axis-aligned ellipse with semiaxes $E_0$ and $2E_0$ along $e_1$ and $e_2$. Explicitly $E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1-2E_0\sin\theta\,e_2$ and $|E|^2=E_0^2\cos^2\theta+4E_0^2\sin^2\theta$ by [F5], which lies between $E_0^2$ and $4E_0^2$; $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-2ie_1)$ by step 1.1, and $H=\langle E_0e_1\times2E_0e_2,e_3\rangle=2E_0^2>0$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.4 Case (iv), degenerate and edge cases. For $e=0$ the fields vanish identically by [F3] (the zero wave), $a=d=0$, and clause (b)(i) of [F1] covers the trace $\{0\}$; for $e=E_0(1+i)e_1$ one has $a=d=E_0e_1$, so $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the polarization is linear, and the trace is $E=E_0(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)e_1$, whose coefficient $\cos\theta-\sin\theta=\sqrt2\cos(\theta+\pi/4)$ ranges over $[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]$; the trace is therefore the segment $[-\sqrt2E_0,\sqrt2E_0]e_1$, and $H=\langle a\times a,e_3\rangle=0$ by alternation of the coordinate formula [F4]. No orthogonality of $a$ and $d$ is used, matching the covering clause of [F1]; the corresponding $b$ is the one computed in step 1.1. [step 1.1, given, F1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

3.1 Scope check (v). In every case step 1.1 gives $b=k\times e/\omega$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $|k|=\omega/c$, so by clause (b) of [F2] the amplitude equations hold and the corresponding fields are smooth source-free Maxwell solutions; the amplitudes $e$ and the semiaxis lengths $E_0$, $2E_0$ carry $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ by [F6], and the pointwise relation $|B|=|E|/c$ is clause (c) of [F2]. The item computes only ideal field quantities and asserts no measurement or empirical realization. [step 1.1, F2, F6, given] ∎

## Remarks

- **Classification, not evidence.** The five choices illustrate clauses of
  [[def-em-polarization-definition]]; they neither predict nor report any
  laboratory measurement, and the handedness names are the conventional labels
  fixed there, not physical claims.
