## Example

Fix $K>0$, $\omega:=cK$, $k:=Ke_3$, $E_0>0$
(unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$), the amplitude $e:=E_0e_1$ and
$b:=k\times e/\omega=(E_0/c)e_2$, and let $(E,B)$ be the corresponding
plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with energy
density $u$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]; write
$\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$. Then:

(i) [Explicit density] $E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$,
$B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$ and
$u(x,t)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2\theta(x,t)$, a nonnegative function vanishing
exactly on the nodal planes $\cos\theta=0$; the period average at every fixed
$x$ is $\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2>0$, uniformly in $x$ and $t$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]](a)).

(ii) [Unbounded box integrals] Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and let
$R\ge(\omega|t|+\pi/4)/K$. On the sub-box
$Q_R:=[-R,R]^2\times[(\omega t-\pi/4)/K,\,(\omega t+\pi/4)/K]$ of the box
$[-R,R]^3$ one has $\cos^2\theta\ge1/2$, hence
$u\ge\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2$ there; both boxes are product boxes with finite
volume ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]), $u$ is continuous on
them and therefore Riemann integrable
([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]), and
monotonicity of the multidimensional Darboux integral
([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]) gives
$$\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,dx\;\ge\;\int_{Q_R}u(x,t)\,dx\;\ge\;\frac{\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{2}\,\mathrm{vol}(Q_R)\;=\;\frac{\pi\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{K}\,R^2\;\longrightarrow\;+\infty\quad(R\to\infty).$$
Consequently no finite value is attained by the box integrals as
$R\to\infty$: the ideal plane wave has infinite total energy in the
box-exhaustion sense, in contrast to the total energy of a single wave 'mode'
being finite on any bounded box.

(iii) [Contrast with compactly supported data] If instead the constrained data
of [[pthm-em-general-wave-ivp]] vanish off a compact set, then by clause (d) of
that theorem the fields have compact spatial support at each time, and the
instantaneous total energy is the integral of the continuous density $u$ over
a compact set, hence finite. So finite total energy is available for
compactly supported data, while the ideal plane wave of (i)-(ii) is not a
finite-energy configuration.

(iv) [Scope] The example is an exact computation for the ideal plane wave; it
reports no measurement, and "infinite total energy" means the divergence
statement (ii), not a claim about any laboratory field or finite beam.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The constants $K>0$, $c>0$, $\omega=cK$, $k=Ke_3$, $E_0>0$ in
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, the amplitude $e=E_0e_1$, the magnetic amplitude
$b=k\times e/\omega=(E_0/c)e_2$, the phase $\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$, the
plane-wave fields $(E,B)$, and the energy density $u$.

[F1] Plane-wave data ([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]],
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]): the fields are
$E=\operatorname{Re}(e\exp(i\theta))$,
$B=\operatorname{Re}(b\exp(i\theta))$, and with $|k|=\omega/c$,
$k\cdot e=0$, $b=k\times e/\omega$ the pair lies in the source-free smooth
Maxwell branch.

[F2] Energy density ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]):
$u=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|E|^2+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}|B|^2\ge0$ is $C^\infty$ and
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

[F3] Plane-wave averages ([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]](a)): for this class
of plane waves $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$, independent of
$x$ and of the starting time, where the average is taken over the period
$T=2\pi/\omega$; in particular the real-amplitude identity
$\frac1T\int_0^T\cos^2(\phi_0-\omega s)\,ds=\frac12$ is the scalar case of
[[lem-em-period-average]].

[F4] Integration over boxes and Jordan sets
([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]],
[[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]],
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]): a product
box $[a,b]=\prod_j[a_j,b_j]$ has volume $\prod_j(b_j-a_j)$; a continuous
function on a compact Jordan measurable set is Riemann integrable there; and
the Darboux integral of a nonnegative function is monotone under inclusion of
product boxes.

[F5] Compact-support propagation ([[pthm-em-general-wave-ivp]](d)): for
initially constraint-satisfying $C^\infty$ data vanishing off a compact
$K\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$, the solution
fields satisfy $E(x,t)=B(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$.

[F6] Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]): the norm and inner
product are the Euclidean ones, so for real vectors $v$, $|v|^2=\langle v,v\rangle$.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Explicit fields and density. Since $k\times e=(Ke_3)\times(E_0e_1)=KE_0e_2$, one has $b=(E_0/c)e_2$; by [F1] and Euler's formula in the real-part encoding, $E=\operatorname{Re}(E_0e_1e^{i\theta})=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$ and $B=\operatorname{Re}((E_0/c)e_2e^{i\theta})=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$. By [F2] and [F6], $u=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E_0^2\cos^2\theta+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\frac{E_0^2}{c^2}\cos^2\theta=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2\theta$ because $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$; the function is nonnegative and vanishes exactly where $\cos\theta=0$, the union of the nodal planes $Kx_3-\omega t=\pi/2+\pi\mathbb Z$. [given, F1, F2, F6, algebra]

2.1 Period average. At fixed $x$, $u(x,\cdot)$ is the $\cos^2$ profile $\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(\phi_0-\omega s)$ with $\phi_0=Kx_3$; the scalar case of [F3] gives $\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cdot\frac12=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E_0^2$, which equals $\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$ and is strictly positive, independent of $x$ and of the starting time. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

2.2 Unbounded box integrals. Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and $R\ge(\omega|t|+\pi/4)/K$, and let $Q_R$ be the sub-box of $[-R,R]^3$ with $x_3\in[(\omega t-\pi/4)/K,(\omega t+\pi/4)/K]$ and $x_1,x_2\in[-R,R]$. Each point of $Q_R$ satisfies $|Kx_3-\omega t|\le\pi/4$, so $\cos^2\theta\ge1/2$ and $u\ge\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2$ there, while $Q_R\subseteq[-R,R]^3$ because $|(\omega t\pm\pi/4)/K|\le R$; both are product boxes with finite volume by [F4], and $u$ is continuous on the compact boxes, hence Riemann integrable by [F4], so monotonicity of the Darboux integral gives $\int_{[-R,R]^3}u\ge\int_{Q_R}u\ge\frac{\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{2}\mathrm{vol}(Q_R)$. The volume is $\mathrm{vol}(Q_R)=(2R)^2\cdot\frac{\pi}{2K}=\frac{2\pi R^2}{K}$ by [F4], so $\int_{[-R,R]^3}u\ge\frac{\pi\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{K}R^2\to+\infty$ as $R\to\infty$; hence the box integrals are unbounded and the box-exhaustion total energy $\sup_{R>0}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u$ is $+\infty$. [step 1.1, F4, algebra]

3.1 Compactly supported data. Suppose the constrained $C^\infty$ data of [F5] satisfy $\operatorname{div}E_0=\operatorname{div}B_0=0$ and vanish off a compact $K\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$, and let $(E,B)$ be the corresponding solution; for fixed $t$ the fields vanish off the closed ball $\overline B_{\rho+c(t-t_0)}(0)$, a compact set, so $u(\cdot,t)$ is a continuous function with compact support there; by [F4] it is Riemann integrable over that compact Jordan set, and its integral is finite because a continuous function on a compact set is bounded and the set has finite volume. Thus the instantaneous total energy of the compactly supported configuration is finite, in contrast with the divergence of step 2.2 for the ideal plane wave. [step 2.2, F4, F5, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion and scope. Step 1.1 is clause (i) except for the average, which is step 2.1; step 2.2 is clause (ii) including the divergence of the box integrals; step 3.1 is clause (iii); and clause (iv) is a scope qualification: all quantities are exact ideal-field quantities of the specified plane wave, no laboratory measurement or finite beam is described, and the phrase "infinite total energy" refers to the divergence statement of step 2.2 in the box-exhaustion sense, not to any finite measured energy. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Remarks

- **Idealisation, not evidence.** The computation shows that the ideal
  whole-space plane wave is not a finite-energy configuration; it makes no
  claim about any laboratory field, and the compact-support branch of
  [[pthm-em-general-wave-ivp]] is the source of the finite-energy contrast.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
[[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which the fixed-volume clause
of the momentum balance is stated. Idealised setup: the vacuum region is
$\{x_3<0\}$ and a material body occupies $\{x_3>0\}$ with plane surface
$x_3=0$; an incident plane wave of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] with
$k=Ke_3$ ($K>0$, $\omega=cK$), $e=E_0e_1$ ($E_0>0$, unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$) and $b=(E_0/c)e_2$ propagates in the $+e_3$
direction. By [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] its period-averaged Poynting
flux is $\langle S\rangle=I\hat k$ with $I=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}E_0^2$, and
its period-averaged normal Maxwell stress is $\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle=-I/c$
([[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] for $\sigma$). All period-averaged
quantities below are independent of time. Two idealised models of the surface:

(i) [Ideal absorber] Adopt (A1) no reflected vacuum field and a zero back-face
stress for an ideal absorption layer, and (A2) the total force on the material
is given by the pillbox limit of the momentum balance, i.e. equals, per unit
area, the difference
$\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle_{\mathrm{back}}-\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle$ of
the back-face and incident-side normal stresses, with the back-face stress set
to zero by (A1). This is an exterior boundary-force model: the incident vacuum
field is not asserted to extend by zero across a sharp interface as a global
Maxwell solution. A real absorption layer must supply a compatible
material-field solution; no such realization is claimed here. Applying
[[pthm-em-momentum-balance]](b) to a fixed box inside the vacuum region with
one face at $x_3=-\delta$ and period-averaging (the time derivative of the
averaged field momentum of a periodic configuration has zero mean,
[[lem-em-period-average]] for the explicit $\cos^2$-profile) shows
$\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle$ is constant in $x_3$ in the vacuum region, so
$\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=-I/c$. Then the force per unit area is
$F/A=(I/c)\,\hat k$: the wave pushes the absorber along its direction of
propagation with pressure $I/c$.

(ii) [Ideal reflector] Adopt instead (A1') the field on the material side
vanishes identically while the vacuum field is the sum of the incident wave and
the reflected plane wave with $k'=-k$, $e'=-e$ (so that the tangential
electric field vanishes on $x_3=0$; the sum is a source-free solution by
[[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), together with the same boundary-force law
(A2) with zero material-side stress. Compute the averaged normal stress of the
standing wave directly: the real fields satisfy
$E=E_0[\cos(Kx_3-\omega t)-\cos(Kx_3+\omega t)]e_1=2E_0\sin(Kx_3)\sin(\omega t)e_1$
and $B=(2E_0/c)\cos(Kx_3)\cos(\omega t)e_2$, whose cross terms cancel
identically in $\sigma_{33}=-(\varepsilon_0/2)|E|^2-(1/(2\mu_0))|B|^2$; with
$\langle\sin^2\rangle=\langle\cos^2\rangle=1/2$ this gives
$\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=-\varepsilon_0E_0^2=-2I/c$ (the incident and
reflected waves contribute $-I/c$ each). Hence $F/A=(2I/c)\,\hat k$: twice the
absorbing pressure, because the momentum of the reflected wave is reversed.

(iii) [Status] The absorber back-face and reflector vanishing-field
idealisations (A1)/(A1') and the boundary-force law (A2) are adopted model
assumptions of this thought experiment, not derived material laws and not
observations; the deduction from them with the computed averaged stresses is
complete and conditional. The setup idealises an infinite plane beam at normal
incidence on an infinite plane surface; oblique incidence, finite beams, real
absorbers and any magnetisation/current response of a material require a
material model and are excluded. No measured pressure is reported and no
empirical or statistical claim is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the frame basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; $K>0$, $\omega=cK$, $k=Ke_3$, $E_0>0$ in
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$; the incident amplitude $e=E_0e_1$; the constants
$c,\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$; the vacuum region $\{x_3<0\}$
and the surface $x_3=0$.

[F1] Plane waves and their amplitude conditions
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]], [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]): for
$j$ indexing the incident and reflected waves, $|k_j|=\omega/c$,
$k_j\cdot e_j=0$, $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$ imply that the pair lies in the
source-free smooth Maxwell branch with
$E_j=\operatorname{Re}(e_j\exp(i(k_j\cdot x-\omega t)))$ and
$B_j=\operatorname{Re}(b_j\exp(i(k_j\cdot x-\omega t)))$.

[F2] Plane-wave averages ([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]): for a transverse
plane wave with amplitude $e$, wavevector $k$ with $|k|=\omega/c$ and
$b=k\times e/\omega$, one has $\langle S\rangle=I\hat k$,
$I=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$ with
$\langle u\rangle=I/c$, so in particular $\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle=-I/c$ for
$k=Ke_3$.

[F3] Momentum balance ([[pthm-em-momentum-balance]]): under its hypotheses and
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, for an open $\Omega'$ with compact closure in the
region, every $t$, and every component $i$,
$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}g_i\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}(\sum_j\sigma_{ij}n_j)\,dS-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx$;
locally, $\partial_tg-\operatorname{div}\sigma=-f$ componentwise, with
$f=\rho E+J\times B$ of the matter coupling.

[F4] Momentum density and stress
([[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]): $g=S/c^2$ and
$\sigma_{ij}=\varepsilon_0(E_iE_j-\frac12\delta_{ij}|E|^2)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}(B_iB_j-\frac12\delta_{ij}|B|^2)$.

[F5] Linear superposition ([[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]): a finite linear
combination with real coefficients of smooth source-free solutions is again a
smooth source-free solution on the same region.

[F6] Period averages of squares ([[lem-em-period-average]]): for
$T=2\pi/\omega$, $\frac1T\int_0^T\sin^2(\omega s)\,ds=\frac1T\int_0^T\cos^2(\omega s)\,ds=\frac12$.

[F7] Fundamental theorem of calculus ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]): for a $C^1$
function $G$ on $[0,T]$, $\int_0^TG'(s)\,ds=G(T)-G(0)$; in particular if $G$ is
$T$-periodic then $\frac1T\int_0^TG'=0$.

[F8] Rectangle volume ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]): for
$R>0$, $\mathrm{vol}([-R,R]^2)=(2R)^2=4R^2$.

[F9] SI relation ([[def-em-si-conventions]]): $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$,
so $\varepsilon_0E_0^2=2I/c$ because $I=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}E_0^2$.

[A1] Adopted ideal-absorber model: no reflected vacuum field and zero
back-face stress; the force per unit area on the material is
$F/A=\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle_{\mathrm{back}}-\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle$
along $+e_3$, a pillbox boundary-force law, not a derived material law.

[A2] Adopted ideal-reflector model: the field on the material side vanishes
identically, the vacuum field is the sum of the incident wave and the reflected
plane wave with $k'=-k$, $e'=-e$, and the same boundary-force law with zero
material-side stress applies.

[A3] The Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Incident wave data. For the incident wave $k\times e=(Ke_3)\times(E_0e_1)=KE_0e_2$, so $b=(E_0/c)e_2$, and $|k|=\omega/c$, $k\cdot e=0$; hence by [F1] the pair is a smooth source-free solution, with $E=E_0\cos(Kx_3-\omega t)e_1$ and $B=(E_0/c)\cos(Kx_3-\omega t)e_2$, fields independent of $x_1,x_2$ and $T$-periodic in $t$ with $T=2\pi/\omega$. By [F2] the averaged Poynting flux is $\langle S\rangle=I\hat k$ with $I=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}E_0^2$, and the averaged normal stress of the incident wave is the constant $\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle=-I/c$ everywhere. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Absorber: the averaged normal stress is constant in the vacuum region. Fix $R>0$ and $0<\delta<L$ and let $\Omega':=(-R,R)^2\times(-L,-\delta)$, an open box whose compact closure lies in the vacuum region $\{x_3<0\}$. On $\Omega'$ the field is the incident wave alone by [A1], a smooth source-free solution with $\rho=J=0$, so $f=0$; the momentum balance [F3](b) with $i=3$ and the hypothesis [A3] gives $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}g_3\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\sum_j\sigma_{3j}n_j\,dS$ for every $t$; extending $g_3$ and $\sigma$ by the incident-wave fields, the function $t\mapsto\int_{\Omega'}g_3(x,t)\,dx$ is $C^1$ and $T$-periodic, so its derivative has zero mean over a period by [F7]. The lateral faces contribute zero for every $t$ because $\sigma_{31}=\sigma_{32}=0$ identically: $E_3=B_3=0$ for the incident wave, so $\sigma_{31}=\varepsilon_0E_3E_1+\mu_0^{-1}B_3B_1=0$ and likewise for $\sigma_{32}$, by [F4]. On the faces $x_3=-\delta$ (outward normal $+e_3$) and $x_3=-L$ (outward normal $-e_3$) the integrand is $\sigma_{33}$ restricted to a face on which it is constant in the tangential variables, so those contributions are $4R^2\sigma_{33}(-\delta,t)$ and $-4R^2\sigma_{33}(-L,t)$ by [F8]; averaging over a period and dividing by $4R^2>0$ gives $\langle\sigma_{33}(-\delta)\rangle=\langle\sigma_{33}(-L)\rangle$. Since $0<\delta<L$ were arbitrary, $x_3\mapsto\langle\sigma_{33}(x_3)\rangle$ is constant on the vacuum region $(-\infty,0)$, and by step 1.1 its constant value is $-I/c$; hence $\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=-I/c$. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F7, F8, A1, A3, algebra]

2.2 Reflector: the standing-wave averaged stress. Adopt [A2]; the reflected data satisfy $k'\cdot e'=(-k)\cdot(-e)=0$, $|k'|=|k|=\omega/c$ and $b'=k'\times e'/\omega=(-Ke_3)\times(-E_0e_1)/\omega=(E_0/c)e_2=b$, so by [F1] the reflected pair is a plane-wave solution and by [F5] the sum $(E,B)=(E_1,B_1)+(E',B')$ is a smooth source-free solution on the vacuum side; explicitly $E=E_0[\cos(Kx_3-\omega t)-\cos(Kx_3+\omega t)]e_1=2E_0\sin(Kx_3)\sin(\omega t)e_1$ and $B=(E_0/c)[\cos(Kx_3-\omega t)+\cos(Kx_3+\omega t)]e_2=(2E_0/c)\cos(Kx_3)\cos(\omega t)e_2$ by the sum-to-product identities, so the tangential electric field vanishes on $x_3=0$. Since $E_3=B_3=0$, [F4] gives $\sigma_{33}=-\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|E|^2-\frac{1}{2\mu_0}|B|^2=-\varepsilon_0\cdot2E_0^2\sin^2(Kx_3)\sin^2(\omega t)-\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\cdot\frac{4E_0^2}{c^2}\cos^2(Kx_3)\cos^2(\omega t)$; period-averaging with [F6] and using $\frac{E_0^2}{\mu_0c^2}=\varepsilon_0E_0^2$ gives $\langle\sigma_{33}(x_3)\rangle=-\varepsilon_0E_0^2[\sin^2(Kx_3)+\cos^2(Kx_3)]=-\varepsilon_0E_0^2$, and $\varepsilon_0E_0^2=2I/c$ by [F9]; in particular $\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=-2I/c$. [step 1.1, F1, F4, F5, F6, F9, A2, algebra]

3.1 Absorber force. By [A1] the back-face stress is zero, so the force per unit area on the absorber is $F/A=\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle_{\mathrm{back}}-\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=0-(-I/c)=I/c$ along $+e_3=\hat k$, the propagation direction of the incident beam: the wave pushes the absorber with pressure $I/c$. [step 2.1, A1, algebra]

3.2 Reflector force. By [A2] the material-side stress is zero, so the force per unit area on the reflector is $F/A=0-\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=2I/c$ along $+e_3=\hat k$: twice the absorbing pressure, the momentum of the reflected wave being reversed. [step 2.2, A2, algebra]

4.1 Status and scope. The two conclusions are conditional on the adopted idealisations [A1]/[A2]: neither the vanishing of the reflected or transmitted fields nor the pillbox force law is derived from a material model, and the incident vacuum field is not asserted to extend by zero across the sharp interface as a global Maxwell solution; a real absorption layer or reflector would require a compatible material-field solution. The deduction from the adopted assumptions and the computed averaged stresses is complete, the geometry is the ideal infinite plane beam at normal incidence, and oblique incidence, finite beams, material response, radiation reaction and measurements are excluded; no measured pressure, statistical statement or empirical claim is made. [step 3.1, step 3.2, A1, A2, given] ∎

## Source notes

The cited treatments give the momentum flux $I/c$ of the incident beam and state
the absorber pressure $I/c$ and reflector pressure $2I/c$ for perfect
absorbers and reflectors; the deduction above makes the required boundary
assumptions explicit (A1)/(A1')/(A2) and computes both averaged normal
stresses from the framework's definitions, so that the textbook statements are
the motivation rather than premises. No material law, absorbed or reflected
amplitude, or observed force is asserted.

## Example

Let $K>0$, $\omega:=cK$, let $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ (half the angle between the
beams) and $\varphi\in\mathbb R$, and take the two plane waves of
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] with
$$k_1=K(\sin\alpha\,e_1+\cos\alpha\,e_3),\qquad k_2=K(-\sin\alpha\,e_1+\cos\alpha\,e_3),$$
$$e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}=E_0e_2,\qquad e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}=E_0e^{i\varphi}e_2,$$
where $E_0>0$ carries $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and both amplitudes are
polarized along $e_2$, perpendicular to both wavevectors; with
$b_j=k_j\times e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}/\omega$ and $|k_j|=\omega/c$ both pairs
satisfy the amplitude equations of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]], so the
superposition is a source-free smooth Maxwell solution
([[pthm-em-classical-interference]]). Write
$\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x=-2K\sin\alpha\,x_1$. Then:

(i) [Averaged energy density]
$\langle u\rangle(x)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\bigl[1+\cos^2\alpha\,\cos(2K\sin\alpha\,x_1-\varphi)\bigr]$
for every $x$, by clause (b) of [[pthm-em-classical-interference]] with
$e_1\cdot\overline e_2=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}$ and
$(\hat k_1\times e_1^{\mathrm{amp}})\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}})=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}\cos2\alpha$.

(ii) [Fringes and visibility] At fixed $x_2,x_3$ the averaged energy density is
periodic in $x_1$ with period $\pi/(K\sin\alpha)=\lambda/(2\sin\alpha)$, where
$\lambda=2\pi/K$; its maximum and minimum are
$\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1\pm\cos^2\alpha)$, so the visibility
$V:=\frac{\langle u\rangle_{\max}-\langle u\rangle_{\min}}{\langle u\rangle_{\max}+\langle u\rangle_{\min}}$
equals $\cos^2\alpha=\frac12(1+\hat k_1\cdot\hat k_2)$. In particular
$V\to1$ as $\alpha\downarrow0$ through crossing beams, and $V\to0$ as
$\alpha\to\pi/2$. At $\alpha=0$ with fixed relative phase the profile is
spatially constant: its spatial visibility is $0$ when its value is positive,
and the displayed ratio is undefined when the field vanishes.

(iii) [The promised copropagating amplitude law] For $k_1=k_2=k$, equal
amplitudes $E_0$ and relative phase $\Delta$ (so that the sum is the single
plane wave with amplitude $E_0(1+e^{i\Delta})$),
$\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1+\cos\Delta)=2\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(\Delta/2)\propto|1+e^{i\Delta}|^2$,
the form used in the double-slit discussion of the content model. Scanning
$\Delta$ gives phase-scan visibility $1$, distinct from spatial visibility at
fixed phase.

(iv) [Statistical qualifications] This is a deterministic prediction of the
classical wave model for the specified coherent two-wave preparation, at every
point of the ideal plane-wave field; a *measured* fringe pattern or detector
histogram would additionally require a declared measurement model (detector
response, finite bin width, background, integration time, sampling) and a
statistical analysis. The example reports no observation, no finite-sample
claim and no visibility estimate from data; in particular classical
electromagnetic waves interfere, so the prediction alone does not discriminate
between classical and quantum descriptions of light. All quantities are
idealized field quantities of the framework.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $K>0$, $\omega=cK$, $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$, $\varphi\in\mathbb R$,
$E_0>0$ in $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, the wavevectors $k_1,k_2$ and
amplitudes $e_1^{\mathrm{amp}},e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}$ above, the associated
$b_j=k_j\times e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}/\omega$, and the frame basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

[F1] Coherent interference ([[pthm-em-classical-interference]]): for two
same-frequency transverse plane waves with amplitudes $e_1,e_2$, real
coefficients $a_1,a_2$ and
$\delta(x)=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$, the sum is a smooth source-free solution and
$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}(a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}(W)$
with
$W=(e_1\cdot\overline e_2+(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2))e^{-i\delta}$;
if $k_1=k_2=:k$ the sum is the single plane wave with amplitude
$a_1e_1+a_2e_2$ and
$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2$.

[F2] Plane-wave solutions ([[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]): for
$|k|=\omega/c$, $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$ the pair lies in the
source-free smooth Maxwell branch.

[F3] Plane-wave encoding ([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]): the fields are
the real parts of $e\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))$ and
$b\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))$, and the complex amplitudes are constant.

[F4] Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]): the frame basis is
orthonormal, $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$, and
$|v|^2=\langle v,v\rangle$; in particular $\hat k_j=k_j/K$ satisfies
$|\hat k_j|=1$.

[F5] Cross product ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]): $u\times v$ is given by the
coordinate differences of products in the positively oriented basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

[F6] SI conventions ([[def-em-si-conventions]]): $\varepsilon_0$ and $c$ are
the framework's positive constants with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Setup and amplitude conditions. Since $\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha=1$, one has $|k_1|=|k_2|=K=\omega/c$ and $\hat k_1=\sin\alpha\,e_1+\cos\alpha\,e_3$, $\hat k_2=-\sin\alpha\,e_1+\cos\alpha\,e_3$; both $e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}$ are multiples of $e_2$, which is orthogonal to $e_1$ and $e_3$, so $k_j\cdot e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}=0$ by [F4], and with $b_j=k_j\times e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}/\omega$ the amplitude conditions of [F2] hold for both pairs; moreover $\delta(x)=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x=(-2K\sin\alpha\,e_1)\cdot x=-2K\sin\alpha\,x_1$, and $\hat k_1\cdot\hat k_2=-\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha=\cos2\alpha$ by [F4]. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 Clause (i). Apply [F1] with $a_1=a_2=1$ and the amplitudes $e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}=E_0e_2$, $e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}=E_0e^{i\varphi}e_2$: then $|e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}|^2=E_0^2$ and $e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}\cdot\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}}=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}$, while $k_j\times e_2$ computed coordinatewise by [F5] gives $\hat k_1\times e_2=\sin\alpha\,e_3-\cos\alpha\,e_1$ and $\hat k_2\times e_2=-\sin\alpha\,e_3-\cos\alpha\,e_1$ (using $|k_j|=K$), hence $(\hat k_1\times e_1^{\mathrm{amp}})\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}})=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}(\cos^2\alpha-\sin^2\alpha)=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}\cos2\alpha$ by [F4]; the bracket is therefore $E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}(1+\cos2\alpha)=2E_0^2\cos^2\alpha\,e^{-i\varphi}$, so $W=2E_0^2\cos^2\alpha\,e^{-i(\delta+\varphi)}$, $\operatorname{Re}(W)=2E_0^2\cos^2\alpha\cos(2K\sin\alpha\,x_1-\varphi)$, and $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}(E_0^2+E_0^2)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\operatorname{Re}(W)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2[1+\cos^2\alpha\cos(2K\sin\alpha\,x_1-\varphi)]$ by [F1] and $\cos(-\delta-\varphi)=\cos(\delta+\varphi)$; this is clause (i). [step 1.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra]

3.1 Clause (ii). By step 2.1, at fixed $x_2,x_3$ the function $x_1\mapsto\langle u\rangle(x)$ is $\varepsilon_0E_0^2[1+\cos^2\alpha\cos(2K\sin\alpha\,x_1-\varphi)]$; since $\cos^2\alpha>0$ for $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $\sin\alpha>0$, its oscillation has period $2\pi/(2K\sin\alpha)=\pi/(K\sin\alpha)=\lambda/(2\sin\alpha)$ with $\lambda=2\pi/K$, maximum $\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1+\cos^2\alpha)$ at $\cos(2K\sin\alpha x_1-\varphi)=1$ and minimum $\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1-\cos^2\alpha)$ at $\cos(2K\sin\alpha x_1-\varphi)=-1$; hence $V=\cos^2\alpha$, and $\cos^2\alpha=\frac12(1+\cos2\alpha)=\frac12(1+\hat k_1\cdot\hat k_2)$ by step 1.1. As $\alpha\downarrow0$ with $\alpha>0$ the value $\cos^2\alpha\to1$, and as $\alpha\to\pi/2$ it tends to $0$. At $\alpha=0$ one has $k_1=k_2$ and the profile is $\varepsilon_0E_0^2[1+\cos(-2K\sin\alpha\,x_1-\varphi)]$ evaluated at $\alpha=0$, which is the spatial constant $\varepsilon_0E_0^2[1+\cos\varphi]=2\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(\varphi/2)$: if this value is positive then max $=$ min and the displayed ratio is $0$, while if it vanishes (that is, $\varphi\equiv\pi\bmod 2\pi$) the ratio is the undefined expression $0/0$. [step 2.1, F4, algebra]

3.2 Clause (iii). If $k_1=k_2=:k$ with equal amplitudes and relative phase $\Delta$, then by [F1] (equal-wavevector clause) the sum is the single plane wave with amplitude $E_0(1+e^{i\Delta})e_2$, and $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|E_0(1+e^{i\Delta})e_2|^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E_0^2|1+e^{i\Delta}|^2=\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1+\cos\Delta)=2\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(\Delta/2)$ using $|1+e^{i\Delta}|^2=2+2\cos\Delta$; scanning $\Delta$ over $\mathbb R$ gives maximum $2\varepsilon_0E_0^2$ at $\Delta\equiv0$ and minimum $0$ at $\Delta\equiv\pi$ modulo $2\pi$, so the phase-scan visibility $({\max-\min})/({\max+\min})$ equals $1$, a different quantity from the spatial visibility at fixed phase. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, algebra]

4.1 Clause (iv) and conclusion. Clause (i) is step 2.1, clause (ii) is step 3.1 and clause (iii) is step 3.2; clause (iv) records that all quantities above are deterministic field quantities of the stated ideal coherent preparation, that a measured fringe pattern or histogram would require a declared detector response, finite bin width, background, integration time and sampling model together with a statistical analysis, and that no observation or finite-sample visibility estimate is reported; in particular classical electromagnetic waves interfere, so the deterministic prediction alone does not discriminate between classical and quantum descriptions of light. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, given] ∎

## Remarks

- **Prediction, not measurement.** The example computes the ideal averaged
  energy density of the specified two-wave field and its fringe geometry; a
  finite detector record is a different object requiring its own measurement
  and sampling model, and no agreement or disagreement with data is claimed
  here.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty open set, let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\in\mathbb C^n$ ($m\ge1$) be pairwise distinct, and let $c_1,\dots,c_m\in\mathbb C^q$ for some $q\ge1$ (the scalar case $q=1$ included; all statements below are componentwise). Write $\lambda_j\cdot z$ for the componentwise bilinear extension of the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the variable $z$ remains real and $e^{iw}$ for the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] at $iw$, and consider the $\mathbb C^q$-valued map $F(z):=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\,e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}$ on $U$. Then:

**(a) [Complex independence]** if $F(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$.

**(b) [Real-part grouping rule]** if $\operatorname{Re}F(z)=0$ for every $z\in U$, then for every $\nu\in\mathbb C^n$ the grouped coefficient
$$C_\nu:=\sum_{\lambda_j=\nu} c_j+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline\nu}\overline{c_j}$$
vanishes; in particular $c_j=0$ whenever $\lambda_j\ne-\overline{\lambda_j}$ and $\lambda_j\notin\{\lambda_k,-\overline{\lambda_k}:k\ne j\}$. At a self-paired frequency $\nu=-\overline\nu$ the coefficient is $2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\lambda_j=\nu}c_j$; in particular at $\nu=0$ only the real part is constrained, and a purely imaginary coefficient is allowed.

**(c) [Scope]** no hypothesis beyond pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$ and nonemptiness and openness of $U$ is used; $\lambda_j=0$ is allowed and the $\lambda_j$ need not be nonzero, ordered or normalized. The statement concerns the open set $U$ and asserts nothing on sets with empty interior, where distinct characters can agree.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $n\ge1$, a nonempty open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, pairwise distinct $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\in\mathbb C^n$ with $m\ge1$, and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in\mathbb C^q$ with $q\ge1$; the map $F(z)=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}$ on $U$, with the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

[F1] The complex exponential is the everywhere convergent series $\exp w=\sum_{n\ge0}w^n/n!$, with $\exp 0=1$, and it is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]).

[F2] Conjugation and modulus: $\overline{a+bi}=a-bi$ and $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, so $w+\overline w=2\operatorname{Re}w$ by the coordinate formulas ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]); conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism satisfying $\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w$, $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$, $\overline{\overline z}=z$, and $z\overline z=|z|^2$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F3] $\mathbb C$ is a field containing the embedded copy of $\mathbb R$, every complex number has the unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $i^2=-1$, and a product in a field vanishes only if one of its factors vanishes ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]).

[F4] The Euclidean inner product on $\mathbb R^n$ is $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$; we use its componentwise bilinear extension $\xi\cdot\zeta=\sum_{k=1}^n\xi_k\zeta_k$ to complex vectors, and for real $z$ and complex $\lambda$ the product $\lambda\cdot z$ splits as $\lambda_1z_1+\lambda'\cdot z'$ under $z=(z_1,z')$, $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\lambda')$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the extension and splitting are the same finite sum rearranged).

[F5] Real-variable calculus: partial derivatives of maps on open subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ are derivatives of line maps ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); sums, real scalar multiples and products of differentiable functions are differentiable with the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules, and quotients are differentiable where the denominator is nonzero ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); the chain rule holds for total derivatives ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; reduce to the scalar case, conjugate the exponential by its series, prove (a) by induction on the dimension using the one-dimensional annihilating operator $\prod_{j\ne j_0}(d/dt-i\lambda_j)$, then obtain (b) by applying (a) to $F+\overline F$ grouped by frequency.

1.1 Reduction to the scalar case. Both assertions are componentwise in $\mathbb C^q$: $F(z)=0$ holds if and only if every component $F_k(z)=\sum_j(c_j)_k e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}$ vanishes, and $\operatorname{Re}F(z)=0$ if and only if $\operatorname{Re}F_k(z)=0$ for every $k$, while the vector $C_\nu$ of clause (b) vanishes if and only if each of its components $\sum_{\lambda_j=\nu}(c_j)_k+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline\nu}\overline{(c_j)_k}$ vanishes. Applying the scalar assertions $q=1$ to each component function therefore yields the general assertions, so we may and do assume $c_1,\dots,c_m\in\mathbb C$ in the rest of the proof. [given, F3, algebra]

1.2 Conjugation of the exponential. For every $w\in\mathbb C$, $\overline{\exp w}=\exp\overline w$. By [F1] the complex numbers $\exp w$ and $\exp\overline w$ are the sums of the everywhere convergent series $\sum_nw^n/n!$ and $\sum_n\overline w^n/n!$, with partial sums $S_N(w)=\sum_{n\le N}w^n/n!$ and $S_N(\overline w)=\sum_{n\le N}\overline w^n/n!$; by [F2] conjugation fixes each real number $n!$ and satisfies $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$ and $\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w$, so $\overline{S_N(w)}=S_N(\overline w)$ for every $N$. Also by [F2], $\overline u-\overline v=\overline{u-v}$ and, by the coordinate formula, $|\overline u|=\sqrt{(\operatorname{Re}u)^2+(-\operatorname{Im}u)^2}=|u|$, whence $|\overline u-\overline v|=|u-v|$. Writing $d=\overline{\exp w}-\exp\overline w$, for every $N$ we have $d=(\overline{\exp w}-S_N(\overline w))+(S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w)=(\overline{\exp w}-\overline{S_N(w)})+(S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w)$, so $|d|\le|\exp w-S_N(w)|+|S_N(\overline w)-\exp\overline w|$; given $\varepsilon>0$, the definition of convergence of the two series supplies $N$ with both summands below $\varepsilon/2$, so $|d|<\varepsilon$, and since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary $|d|=0$, which forces $d=0$ by the definiteness of the modulus in [F2]. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 Characters and the annihilating operator. For $\mu\in\mathbb C$ let $\varphi_\mu(t):=\exp(i\mu t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, the one-variable restriction of the complex exponential along the real-linear map $t\mapsto i\mu t$. By [F5], the chain rule applied to that map and the entire exponential of [F1] gives $\varphi_\mu'(t)=i\mu\exp(i\mu t)=i\mu\,\varphi_\mu(t)$, and the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules of [F5] give, for any finite combination $\sum_\mu a_\mu\varphi_\mu$ with complex coefficients, derivative $\sum_\mu a_\mu i\mu\,\varphi_\mu$, hence $(d/dt-i\mu)\varphi_\mu=0$ and $(d/dt-i\mu)\varphi_\nu=i(\nu-\mu)\varphi_\nu$ for all $\nu\in\mathbb C$. Consequently, for pairwise distinct $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m$ and a fixed $j_0$, the composed operator $L_{j_0}:=\prod_{j\ne j_0}(d/dt-i\mu_j)$ is complex-linear on finite combinations and acts on $\varphi_{\mu_k}$ as multiplication by $0$ if $k\ne j_0$ and by the constant $\prod_{j\ne j_0}i(\mu_{j_0}-\mu_j)$ if $k=j_0$; that constant is nonzero because $i\ne0$ and $\mu_{j_0}-\mu_j\ne0$ for $j\ne j_0$ by pairwise distinctness, and a product of nonzero field elements is nonzero by [F3]. [F1, F3, F5, algebra]

1.4 Induction step: reduction to a product box. Let $n\ge2$ and assume assertion (a) established in dimension $n-1$ for every number of frequencies and every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^{n-1}$. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and open, fix $z^*\in U$ and, by openness, $\varepsilon>0$ with the open product box $B:=\prod_{k=1}^n(z^*_k-\varepsilon,z^*_k+\varepsilon)\subseteq U$; put $B':=\prod_{k=2}^n(z^*_k-\varepsilon,z^*_k+\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$. Write $z=(z_1,z')$ with $z'\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $\lambda_j=(\lambda_{j1},\lambda_j')$. For each value $\mu$ in the finite set $\{\lambda_{11},\dots,\lambda_{m1}\}$ put $I_\mu:=\{j:\lambda_{j1}=\mu\}$ and $P_\mu(z'):=\sum_{j\in I_\mu}c_je^{i\lambda_j'\cdot z'}$; then, by the splitting identity of [F4] and the distributivity of the finite sum, $F(z_1,z')=\sum_\mu e^{i\mu z_1}P_\mu(z')$ for every $(z_1,z')\in B$, the outer sum running over the pairwise distinct values $\mu$. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 Base case, dimension one. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty and open, so that it contains a nonempty open interval $J$; suppose $F=\sum_{j=1}^mc_j\varphi_{\lambda_j}\equiv0$ on $U$. Fix $j_0$; then $L_{j_0}F\equiv0$ on $J$, and by step 1.3 and the linearity of $L_{j_0}$ we have $L_{j_0}F=c_{j_0}\bigl(\prod_{j\ne j_0}i(\lambda_{j_0}-\lambda_j)\bigr)\varphi_{\lambda_{j_0}}$ on $J$. Evaluating at $t=0$, where $\varphi_{\lambda_{j_0}}(0)=\exp 0=1$ by [F1], gives $c_{j_0}\prod_{j\ne j_0}i(\lambda_{j_0}-\lambda_j)=0$; the second factor is a product of nonzero complex numbers, hence nonzero by [F3], so $c_{j_0}=0$ by the field property in [F3]. As $j_0$ was arbitrary, $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$; this proves (a) for $n=1$. [given, step 1.3, F1, F3]

2.2 The conjugate sum. Suppose now that $\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ on $U$, and define $\widetilde F(z):=\sum_{j=1}^m\overline{c_j}\,e^{-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z}$ on $U$. For real $z$ and every $j$, step 1.2 applied to $w=i\lambda_j\cdot z$ gives $\overline{e^{i\lambda_j\cdot z}}=\exp\bigl(\overline{i\lambda_j\cdot z}\bigr)$, and by [F2] and the reality of $z$ we have $\overline{i\lambda_j\cdot z}=\overline i\,\overline{\lambda_j\cdot z}=(-i)\bigl(\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z\bigr)=-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z$; therefore $\overline{F(z)}=\sum_j\overline{c_j}\,e^{-i\overline{\lambda_j}\cdot z}=\widetilde F(z)$ on $U$ by [F2]. Since $w+\overline w=2\operatorname{Re}w$ by [F2], the hypothesis $2\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ reads $F+\widetilde F\equiv0$ on $U$. [given, step 1.2, F2]

3.1 One-dimensional slices. Suppose $F\equiv0$ on $U$, fix $z'\in B'$ and define $G(t):=\sum_\mu e^{i\mu t}P_\mu(z')$ for $t$ in the interval $J:=(z^*_1-\varepsilon,z^*_1+\varepsilon)$. By step 1.4, $G(t)=F(t,z')=0$ for every $t\in J$, and $G$ is a finite combination of the pairwise distinct characters $\varphi_\mu$ with complex coefficients $P_\mu(z')$; the base case of step 2.1 applied on the nonempty open interval $J$ therefore gives $P_\mu(z')=0$ for every $\mu$. As $z'\in B'$ was arbitrary, each $P_\mu$ vanishes identically on the nonempty open set $B'$. [step 2.1, step 1.4]

4.1 Induction hypothesis on each group. Fix a value $\mu$. The vectors $\lambda_j'$, $j\in I_\mu$, are pairwise distinct: if $\lambda_j'=\lambda_k'$ and $\lambda_{j1}=\lambda_{k1}=\mu$, then $\lambda_j=\lambda_k$, hence $j=k$ by pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$. The function $P_\mu=\sum_{j\in I_\mu}c_je^{i\lambda_j'\cdot z'}$ vanishes identically on the nonempty open set $B'\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, so assertion (a) in dimension $n-1$ gives $c_j=0$ for every $j\in I_\mu$. Every index lies in $I_{\lambda_{j1}}$, so $c_1=\dots=c_m=0$; this completes the induction and proves (a) in every dimension $n\ge1$. [step 3.1, step 1.4, induction]

5.1 Frequency grouping and application of part (a). Let $\Phi\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be the finite set of distinct values among $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m,-\overline{\lambda_1},\dots,-\overline{\lambda_m}$, and for $\nu\in\Phi$ put $C_\nu:=\sum_{j:\lambda_j=\nu}c_j+\sum_{j:-\overline{\lambda_j}=\nu}\overline{c_j}=\sum_{\lambda_j=\nu}c_j+\sum_{\lambda_j=-\overline\nu}\overline{c_j}$. Regrouping the finite sum of step 2.2 over the distinct frequencies and using the bilinearity of the extended inner product in [F4] gives $F+\widetilde F=\sum_{\nu\in\Phi}C_\nu e^{i\nu\cdot z}$ on $U$; the frequencies $\nu\in\Phi$ are pairwise distinct by construction, so assertion (a) as proved in steps 2.1 and 4.1 applied to this finite combination gives $C_\nu=0$ for every $\nu\in\Phi$. For $\nu\notin\Phi$ both defining sums are empty, so $C_\nu=0$ trivially; hence $C_\nu=0$ for every $\nu\in\mathbb C^n$. [given, step 2.2, step 4.1, F4, algebra]

6.1 Consequences and scope. (i) If $\nu=-\overline\nu$ is self-paired, the condition $-\overline{\lambda_j}=\nu$ is equivalent to $\lambda_j=\nu$, so both sums of $C_\nu$ run over the same index set and $C_\nu=\sum_{\lambda_j=\nu}(c_j+\overline{c_j})=2\operatorname{Re}\sum_{\lambda_j=\nu}c_j$ by [F2]; at $\nu=0$ this constrains only the real part, and the constraint is genuinely not stronger: for $m=1$, $\lambda_1=0$, $q=1$ and $c_1=i$ one has $F\equiv i$, so $\operatorname{Re}F\equiv0$ and $C_0=c_1+\overline{c_1}=2\operatorname{Re}i=0$, a nonzero purely imaginary coefficient at frequency $0$. (ii) If $\lambda_j\ne-\overline{\lambda_j}$ and $\lambda_j\notin\{\lambda_k,-\overline{\lambda_k}:k\ne j\}$, then $\{k:\lambda_k=\lambda_j\}=\{j\}$ and $\{k:\lambda_k=-\overline{\lambda_j}\}=\emptyset$ (a member $k=j$ would give $\lambda_j=-\overline{\lambda_j}$, and $k\ne j$ is excluded by hypothesis), so $C_{\lambda_j}=c_j+0=c_j=0$ by step 5.1, which is the stated consequence. (iii) The scope (c) holds: steps 2.1, 1.4 and 4.1 used only pairwise distinctness of the $\lambda_j$ and the nonemptiness and openness of $U$, through the interval $J$ and the product box $B$; the frequencies were never assumed nonzero, ordered or normalized; the proof is a finite construction using complex arithmetic, the series for the exponential and its derivative, and no choice principle. No assertion is made for sets of empty interior: the openness of $U$ is used when a nonempty open interval and a product box are extracted from it, and the statement (c) records that distinct characters can agree on such smaller sets. [step 5.1, step 2.2, F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $Y_1,Y_2\in\mathbb C$ with $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$, and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ satisfy the two linear equations

$$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad Y_1(E_i-E_r)=Y_2E_t.$$

Then: (a) [Solution] If $E_i\ne0$, then
$$r:=\frac{E_r}{E_i}=\frac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad t:=\frac{E_t}{E_i}=\frac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2};$$
if $E_i=0$ then $E_r=E_t=0$ and the field ratios are undefined. Throughout (b)-(d), $r,t$ denote the displayed algebraic transfer coefficients $(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$, which are defined independently of $E_i$; when $E_i\ne0$ they equal the field ratios of (a). (b) [Normal-flux identity] If $Y_1>0$ is real (the incident side admittance), then
$$|r|^2+\frac{\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{Y_1}\,|t|^2=1,$$
and explicitly $|t|^2=\dfrac{4Y_1^2}{|Y_1+Y_2|^2}$ and $|r|^2=1-\dfrac{4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{|Y_1+Y_2|^2}$. The second summand $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ is nonnegative if and only if $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\ge0$; it is the normal-flux coefficient of a passive transmitted medium and may be negative for an active one, in which case $|r|>1$ and the identity carries no energy-conservation reading. (c) [Pure-imaginary admittance] If $Y_1>0$ is real and $Y_2$ is purely imaginary, then $|r|=1$, $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\,|t|^2=0$ and $|t|^2=\dfrac{4Y_1^2}{Y_1^2+|Y_2|^2}>0$; in particular $r\ne0$ and $t\ne0$. (d) [Real-positive specialisation] If $Y_1,Y_2>0$ are real, then $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ are real and $|r|^2+(Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$; with $Y_j=1/Z_j$, $Z_j>0$, this is $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$, $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $R+T=1$ for $R=|r|^2$, $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$, in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]. (e) [Scope] The lemma is pure algebra of $\mathbb C$; the labels 'incident', 'reflected' and 'transmitted' and the interpretation of the second summand as a flux fraction belong to the consuming physical theorem, not to this lemma.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Complex numbers $Y_1,Y_2$ with $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$ and complex numbers $E_i,E_r,E_t$ satisfying $E_i+E_r=E_t$ and $Y_1(E_i-E_r)=Y_2E_t$; the transfer coefficients $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$.

[F1] Field arithmetic in $\mathbb C$: $\mathbb C$ is a field, every element has the unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$, addition and multiplication follow the coordinate formulas, $(a+bi)^{-1}=(a-bi)/(a^2+b^2)$ for $a+bi\ne0$, and a product of nonzero field elements is nonzero ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

[F2] Conjugation and modulus: $z\overline z=|z|^2$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z|\ge0$ with $|z|=0$ exactly for $z=0$, conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism fixing every real number, and $|\overline z|=|z|$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F3] Real order: the real numbers form an ordered field with positive cone $P$ ([[def-ordered-field]]): by trichotomy a positive real is nonzero, and by closure sums and products of positive reals are positive; the same axioms give that the product of two nonzero reals of equal sign is positive and of opposite signs is negative, and that division by the positive real $Y_1$ preserves the sign of a quotient, since $a=(a/Y_1)Y_1$ has the sign of $a/Y_1$ when $Y_1>0$.

[F4] Squares in an ordered field: the square of a nonzero element is positive ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), and for $a,b\ge0$ one has $a<b$ if and only if $a^2<b^2$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[F5] The normal-incidence interface lemma [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]: for real $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$, $Z_j=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}>0$, and $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfying $E_i+E_r=E_t$ and $(E_i-E_r)/Z_1=E_t/Z_2$, one has $E_r/E_i=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$, $E_t/E_i=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$, and $R+T=1$ for $R=|E_r/E_i|^2$, $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|E_t/E_i|^2$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; solve the two linear equations by substitution, expand the moduli with $|z|^2=z\overline z$, and read the sign statements off the ordered-field structure of $\mathbb R$.

1.1 [Solution of the linear system] Substituting the first equation $E_r=E_t-E_i$ into the second gives $Y_1(2E_i-E_t)=Y_2E_t$, that is $2Y_1E_i=(Y_1+Y_2)E_t$ after expanding and collecting terms by the field arithmetic of [F1]. Since $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$ is invertible in the field $\mathbb C$ by [F1], $E_t=2Y_1E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)$, and then $E_r=E_t-E_i=\bigl(2Y_1-(Y_1+Y_2)\bigr)E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)=(Y_1-Y_2)E_i/(Y_1+Y_2)$, again by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 [Consequences of the solution] If $E_i\ne0$, dividing the two identities of step 1.1 by $E_i$ gives $r=E_r/E_i=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=E_t/E_i=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$. If $E_i=0$, the identities of step 1.1 give $E_t=0$ and $E_r=0$, so no field ratio exists; the algebraic expressions $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$ and $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ remain defined because $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$, and they agree with the field ratios whenever the latter exist. This proves (a) and the convention stated before (b). [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

3.1 [Modular expansions] For any $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $|z\pm w|^2=(z\pm w)(\overline z\pm\overline w)=|z|^2\pm(z\overline w+\overline z w)+|w|^2$, and $z\overline w+\overline z w=2\operatorname{Re}(z\overline w)$ by [F2]; hence for real $Y_1$ and arbitrary $Y_2$, $|Y_1\pm Y_2|^2=Y_1^2\pm2Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2+|Y_2|^2$, and subtraction gives $|Y_1+Y_2|^2-|Y_1-Y_2|^2=4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2$. Moreover $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$ and $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$: indeed $|zw|=|z||w|$ and $|z|^2=z\overline z$ by [F2] applied to the quotients of step 2.1 give $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}$ and $|t|^2=|2Y_1|^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}=4Y_1^2|Y_1+Y_2|^{-2}$ because $(2Y_1)\overline{(2Y_1)}=4Y_1^2$ for real $Y_1$, and the denominator is nonzero since $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$. [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 [The flux identity] Assume $Y_1>0$ real. By [F2] and [F3], $|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$, so $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$, and the identity of step 3.1 gives $|r|^2=|Y_1-Y_2|^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2=1-4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$; adding $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2$ cancels the correction and yields $|r|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$, the displayed identity and explicit formulas of (b). [step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

5.1 [Sign analysis] Still with $Y_1>0$ real: since $|t|^2>0$ by step 4.1, the second summand $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ has the sign of $\operatorname{Re}Y_2$ by [F3], so it is nonnegative if and only if $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\ge0$. If $\operatorname{Re}Y_2<0$, then $|r|^2=1-4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>1$, and since $|r|\ge0$ and $1\ge0$, [F4] gives $|r|>1$; in that case the identity of step 4.1 has a negative transmitted term and carries no energy-conservation reading, while $|r|>1$ alone is consistent with an active transmitted model. [step 4.1, F3, F4, algebra]

5.2 [Purely imaginary admittance] Assume $Y_1>0$ real and $Y_2=i\beta$ with $\beta\in\mathbb R$. Then $\overline{Y_1+Y_2}=Y_1-i\beta=Y_1-Y_2$ by [F2], so $|Y_1-Y_2|=|\overline{Y_1+Y_2}|=|Y_1+Y_2|$ by [F2] and step 3.1 gives $|r|=1$; the identity of step 4.1 then gives $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\,|t|^2=0$ (multiplying the identity by $Y_1>0$ and using $|r|^2=1$), while $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+\beta^2)=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+|Y_2|^2)>0$ by [F2] and [F3]; hence $r\ne0$ because $|r|=1$ and $t\ne0$ because $|t|>0$ by the definiteness of the modulus in [F2]. This proves (c); no division by $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=0$ is performed, and the case $Y_2=0$ is included with $\beta=0$. [step 4.1, step 3.1, F2, F3, algebra]

5.3 [Real-positive specialisation] Assume $Y_1,Y_2>0$ real. Then $Y_1-Y_2$ and $Y_1+Y_2$ are real and nonzero, so $r,t$ of step 2.1 are real by [F1], and step 4.1 gives $|r|^2+(Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$ because $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=Y_2$. Substituting $Y_j=1/Z_j$ with $Z_j>0$ real, $Y_j$ is invertible and $1/Z_1\pm1/Z_2=(Z_2\pm Z_1)/(Z_1Z_2)$ by [F1], so $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ by cancellation of the nonzero factor $Z_1Z_2$; moreover $Y_2/Y_1=Z_1/Z_2$ by [F1], so the balance is $R+T=1$ for $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$. These are exactly the solution formulas and the balance of [F5], so clause (d) is in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]. [step 4.1, step 2.1, F1, F5, algebra]

6.1 [Scope] Clause (e) holds: the entire argument is algebra in the field $\mathbb C$ together with the ordered-field arithmetic of the real scalars $Y_1,\operatorname{Re}Y_2$; no wave model, no labelling of the amplitudes and no interpretation of the second summand is used, and no choice principle occurs, all divisions being by explicitly nonzero field elements. [given, F1, F5, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], in its isotropic scalar case: the material is at rest in the laboratory frame, and the constitutive relations of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]] hold with constant scalars $\varepsilon>0$ (F$\,$m$^{-1}$), $\mu>0$ (H$\,$m$^{-1}$) and $\sigma\ge0$ (S$\,$m$^{-1}$), so that $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and the free current is $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Write $c>0$ for the exact vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and let $\omega>0$ (s$^{-1}$) be an angular frequency. Define:

**(a) [Lossless parameters]** with $\sqrt{\cdot}$ the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]],
$$v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}\quad(\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}),\qquad Z:=\Bigl(\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{1/2}\quad(\Omega),\qquad n:=\frac{c}{v}=c(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\quad(\text{dimensionless}),\qquad k(\omega):=\frac{\omega}{v};$$
$v$ is the phase speed, $Z$ the wave impedance, $n$ the refractive index relative to vacuum and $k(\omega)$ the real wavenumber of the lossless case.

**(b) [Complex propagation constant]** put $a:=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}>0$, $b:=\mu\sigma\omega\ge0$, $r:=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ and
$$p(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r+a}{2}},\qquad q(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r-a}{2}},\qquad \kappa(\omega):=p(\omega)+i\,q(\omega).$$
Then $\kappa(\omega)$ is the unique $k\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ and $k^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$; in the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $q=0$ and $\kappa(\omega)=k(\omega)=p(\omega)$ real. (The explicit formula is the one of [[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]; the verification $p^{2}-q^{2}=a$, $2pq=b$ and the uniqueness of the root with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ are recorded in the strategy.)

**(c) [Skin depth]** call $\delta(\omega):=1/q(\omega)$ (m) the skin depth if $\sigma>0$, and set $\delta(\omega):=+\infty$ if $\sigma=0$: for $\kappa(\omega)=p+iq$ and $x_3\in\mathbb R$ the modulus of $e^{i(\kappa x_3-\omega t)}$ equals $e^{-q x_3}$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]), so $\delta$ is the distance in which that modulus decays by the factor $1/e$ in the direction of increasing $x_3$; for $\sigma=0$ there is no attenuation and $\delta$ is infinite rather than a division by zero.

**(d) [Status and scope]** This item fixes objects, units, branch conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation for a solution, no attenuation of any concrete field and no material validity. The parameters are declared for the isotropic scalar constant-coefficient branch at rest in the laboratory frame; for $\varepsilon\mu<c^{-2}$ the branch is, by [[post-em-material-closure]](b), a declared finite-band effective phase-response model with no universal front-speed claim, while $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$ is the exact broadband case. No measured value, precision or empirical statement is included.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The material assumptions, the rest-frame clause, the isotropic scalar case and the finite-band caveat are those of [[post-em-material-closure]](a)-(b) read with [[def-em-polarization-magnetization|the polarization and magnetization definitions]]; the unit system and the exact constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the laboratory chart is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

The only content beyond notation is the well-definedness of $\kappa(\omega)$ in (b). With $a>0$, $b\ge0$ and $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ one has $p^{2}-q^{2}=(r+a)/2-(r-a)/2=a$ and $(2pq)^{2}=4\cdot(r+a)(r-a)/4=r^{2}-a^{2}=b^{2}$, so $2pq=b$ because $p,q\ge0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); hence $\kappa^{2}=p^{2}-q^{2}+2ipq=a+ib$, by the field arithmetic of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. The square roots of $a+ib$ are exactly $\pm\kappa$ ([[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]). If $k=u+iv$ with $u,v\ge0$ and $k^{2}=a+ib$, then $u^{2}-v^{2}=a$, $2uv=b$ and $u^{2}+v^{2}=|k|^{2}=|k^{2}|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=r$, where $|k^{2}|=|k|^{2}$ is the multiplicativity of the modulus ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and $|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ is the modulus of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]; solving gives $u^{2}=(r+a)/2=p^{2}$ and $v^{2}=(r-a)/2=q^{2}$, and since $u,v,p,q\ge0$ the uniqueness of the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) gives $u=p$ and $v=q$, so $k=\kappa$. In the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $r=a$, $q=0$, $p=\sqrt a=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}=k(\omega)$ by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. All divisions are by strictly positive real numbers, $v$ and $q$ are nonzero exactly where defined, and no choice principle is used.
