## Statement

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in its isotropic scalar case at rest in the laboratory frame, with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma\ge0$, the constitutive relations $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], the fields of [[def-em-fields]] on the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and the parameters and phase convention of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]. Consider a declared region with vanishing free charge density and no external free current, so that $\rho_f=0$ and the free current is the conduction current $J_f=\sigma E$. Let $k\in\mathbb C^{3}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,h\in\mathbb C^{3}$, and for $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R$ define $E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}\bigr)$ and $H(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(h\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}\bigr)$ componentwise, i.e. with the phase convention $e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}$ and the real-part encoding of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; put $D:=\varepsilon E$, $B:=\mu H$ and $J_f:=\sigma E$. Extend the Euclidean inner and cross products to $\mathbb C^{3}$ by the same componentwise polynomial formulas ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). Then:

**(a) [Amplitude vanishing]** if $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(w\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}\bigr)=0$ for some $w\in\mathbb C^{3}$ and all $(x,t)$ in a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R$, then $w=0$.

**(b) [Amplitude conditions]** the quadruple $(E,H,D,B)$ satisfies the four source-free macroscopic equations $\operatorname{div}D=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ on $\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R$ if and only if
$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot h=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega\mu\,h,\qquad k\times h=-(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)\,e .$$

**(c) [Structure, dispersion and solution family]** if $e\ne0$ and (b) holds, then $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)$, $k\cdot h=0$, $e\cdot h=0$ and $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega$; conversely, if $k\in\mathbb C^{3}\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$ satisfy $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega$, then for every $e\in\mathbb C^{3}$ with $k\cdot e=0$ the pair $(e,\,k\times e/(\omega\mu))$ satisfies (b), with $(e,h)=(0,0)$ if and only if $e=0$; on the dispersion relation the solution set of (b) for fixed $(k,\omega)$ is exactly $\{(e,\,k\times e/(\omega\mu)):k\cdot e=0\}$, a complex two-dimensional space when $k\ne0$; off the dispersion relation the only solution is $e=h=0$.

**(d) [Lossless propagating waves: instantaneous identities and period averages]** if in addition $\sigma=0$ and $k\in\mathbb R^{3}$ with $e\ne0$, then $|k|^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}$, $|k|=k(\omega)$ in the notation of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]], and for every $(x,t)$ $k\cdot E=k\cdot B=0$, $E\cdot B=0$, $B=\hat k\times E/v$ and $|B|=|E|/v$ with $\hat k=k/|k|$; the period-$T$ averages with $T=2\pi/\omega$ ([[lem-em-period-average]]) satisfy, for $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ and $S=E\times H$ of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]],
$$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|e|^{2},\qquad \langle S\rangle=\frac{|e|^{2}}{2\mu\omega}\,k=\frac{|e|^{2}}{2Z}\,\hat k=v\,\langle u\rangle\hat k .$$

**(e) [Evanescent waves]** if $\sigma=0$, $n'\in\mathbb R^{3}$ is a unit vector, $k=\kappa_0+i\beta n'$ with $\kappa_0\in\mathbb R^{3}$, $\kappa_0\cdot n'=0$, $\beta>0$ and $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}$ (so $|\kappa_0|^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+\beta^{2}$ and $\kappa_0\ne0$), and if $e\ne0$ satisfies $k\cdot e=0$, then the field factorizes exactly as $E(x,t)=e^{-\beta\,n'\cdot x}\,\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i(\kappa_0\cdot x-\omega t)}\bigr)$, and the time-averaged flux satisfies $\langle S\rangle=e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}\,\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(e\times\overline h)$ with normal component $\langle S\cdot n'\rangle=-\dfrac{e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}}{2\mu\omega}\operatorname{Re}\bigl[(e\cdot n')(\kappa_0\cdot\overline e)\bigr]$; this normal component is in fact zero for every such transverse amplitude. For the transverse-electric polarisation $e=E_0(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)$, $E_0\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, and for the transverse-magnetic data $h=H_0\hat y'$ with $\hat y':=n'\times\hat\kappa_0$, $H_0\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and electric amplitude $e=-(k\times\hat y')H_0/(\omega\varepsilon)$, the normal component vanishes identically, $\langle S\cdot n'\rangle\equiv0$, while the tangential averaged flux is positive: $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0\rangle=\dfrac{|\kappa_0||e|^{2}}{2\mu\omega}e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}>0$ in the transverse-electric case and $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0\rangle=\dfrac{|\kappa_0||h|^{2}}{2\omega\varepsilon}e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}>0$ in the transverse-magnetic case.

**(f) [Scope]** the four equations are verified only for the explicit ideal whole-space plane-wave fields; for $k$ with $\operatorname{Im}k\ne0$ the factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}k\cdot x}$ grows in some directions, so clauses (b)-(e) are read on regions where the model declares the field bounded (in (e), on the half-space $n'\cdot x>0$). No completeness, energy-finiteness, boundary, interface, material-validity or empirical claim is made, and the finite-band caveat of [[post-em-material-closure]](b) applies whenever $\varepsilon\mu<c^{-2}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The declared isotropic scalar Ohmic branch at rest with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma\ge0$, the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], the fields of [[def-em-fields]], and the plane-wave data $k\in\mathbb C^3$, $\omega>0$, $e,h\in\mathbb C^3$ with $E=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i\theta})$, $H=\operatorname{Re}(h\,e^{i\theta})$, $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$, $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$, $J_f=\sigma E$; the inner and cross products are extended componentwise to $\mathbb C^3$.

[F1] Real-part encoding: $E_j=\operatorname{Re}(e_j\exp(i\theta))$ componentwise; $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, with partial differentiation and with integration, and the real-part encoding of a product of two encoded real fields must not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation ([[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]).

[F2] The complex exponential and its calculus: $\exp w=\sum_{n\ge0}w^n/n!$ converges for every $w\in\mathbb C$ with $\exp 0=1$ and $\exp'=\exp$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]); the sum, real-scalar-multiple, product and quotient rules ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) and the chain rule for total derivatives ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) apply; $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$ for all complex $z,w$, and $\exp(x)=e^x$ for real $x$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]); for real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[F3] Complex field arithmetic, conjugation and modulus: $\mathbb C$ is a field, a product vanishes only if a factor does ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]); conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism fixing the reals, $z\overline z=|z|^2$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z|\ge0$ with $|z|=0$ exactly for $z=0$, and $\operatorname{Re}w=(w+\overline w)/2$ by the coordinate formulas ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F4] The divergence and curl of a $C^1$ field as coordinate expressions in the first partial derivatives, and partial derivatives as derivatives of line maps ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F5] The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_kx_ky_k$ and the cross product $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, both extended componentwise to complex vectors; the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to $u$ and $v$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]).

[F6] The material model and field equations: the elementary inertial-rest branch gives $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $J_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$ here ([[post-em-material-closure]]); with $\rho_f=0$ the macroscopic equations read $\operatorname{div}D=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ ([[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]).

[F7] Medium parameters: $v=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$, $Z=(\mu/\varepsilon)^{1/2}$, $k(\omega)=\omega/v$, and $\kappa(\omega)=p+iq$ with $p,q\ge0$ and $\kappa(\omega)^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega$ ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]).

[F8] Stored energy and flux: for the constant model, $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ and $S=E\times H$ ([[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]).

[F9] Period averages: for $\omega>0$, $T=2\pi/\omega$ and complex amplitudes $a,d$, the average over a period of $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})$ is $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d)$, with the analogous componentwise inner-product and cross-product forms; the conjugation is essential ([[lem-em-period-average]]).

[F10] Square roots: every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; exhibit the partial derivatives of the encoded fields, reduce each equation to a complex coefficient identity by the amplitude-vanishing fact, analyse the resulting algebraic system, and compute the lossless and evanescent structures with the period-average supplier.

1.1 [Derivatives of the encoded fields] For $w\in\mathbb C^3$ and $\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$, each component $x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w_j\exp(i\theta(x,t)))$ has partial derivatives $\partial_{x_l}\operatorname{Re}(w_j\exp(i\theta))=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(i\,k_l\,w_j\exp(i\theta)\bigr)$ and $\partial_t\operatorname{Re}(w_j\exp(i\theta))=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(-i\omega\,w_j\exp(i\theta)\bigr)$: indeed $\theta$ is the real-linear map $(x,t)\mapsto\sum_lk_lx_l-\omega t$ with partial derivatives $k_l$ in $x_l$ and $-\omega$ in $t$ as derivatives of line maps by [F4], and the chain rule [F2] applied to the entire exponential gives $\partial_{x_l}\exp(i\theta)=ik_l\exp(i\theta)$ and $\partial_t\exp(i\theta)=-i\omega\exp(i\theta)$, after which the real part commutes with the real-linear multiplication by $ik_l$ or $-i\omega$ componentwise by [F1] and [F3]. Consequently $\operatorname{div}D=\varepsilon\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot e\,e^{i\theta})$, $\operatorname{div}B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot h\,e^{i\theta})$, $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\times e\,e^{i\theta})$, $\partial_tB=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\mu\,h\,e^{i\theta})$, $\operatorname{curl}H=\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\times h\,e^{i\theta})$ and $J_f+\partial_tD=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\sigma-i\omega\varepsilon)e\,e^{i\theta}\bigr)$ with the componentwise complex inner and cross products of [F5] and the uniform notation $e^{i\theta}:=\exp(i\theta)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

1.2 [Nonvanishing of the exponential] For every $w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp w\ne0$: by [F2], $\exp w\exp(-w)=\exp 0=1$, and a product equal to $1\ne0$ has no zero factor in the field $\mathbb C$ by [F3]. In particular $e^{i\theta}\ne0$ for all $(x,t)$, and $e^{ik\cdot x_0}\ne0$ for every fixed $x_0$. [F2, F3]

2.1 [Amplitude vanishing, part (a)] Let $Z\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ be nonempty and open with $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ on $Z$ for a fixed $w\in\mathbb C^3$. Fix $(x_0,t_0)\in Z$; by openness of $Z$ there is $\delta>0$ with $\{x_0\}\times(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)\subseteq Z$. The components of the map $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(W\exp(-i\omega t))$ with $W:=w\,e^{ik\cdot x_0}$ vanish on that interval, and by step 1.1 its $t$-derivative is $\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega W\exp(-i\omega t))$, so at $t_0$ both $\operatorname{Re}(W\exp(-i\omega t_0))=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega W\exp(-i\omega t_0))=0$. Writing $W\exp(-i\omega t_0)=u+iv$ with real coordinate vectors $u,v$ by [F3], the first identity is $u=0$ and the second is $\operatorname{Re}(v-iu)=v=0$; hence $W\exp(-i\omega t_0)=0$, and since $\exp(-i\omega t_0)\ne0$ by step 1.2 the field property in [F3] gives $W=0$, i.e. $w\,e^{ik\cdot x_0}=0$, and $\exp(ik\cdot x_0)\ne0$ by step 1.2 gives $w=0$. This proves (a). [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, F3]

3.1 [Equations as coefficient identities] By step 1.1 the four equations of (b) are, on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, the identities $\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot e\,e^{i\theta})=0$, $\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot h\,e^{i\theta})=0$, $\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\times e\,e^{i\theta})-\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\mu\,h\,e^{i\theta})=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\times h\,e^{i\theta})-\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\sigma-i\omega\varepsilon)e\,e^{i\theta}\bigr)=0$; all fields are smooth on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, so the operators of [F4] apply. By the additivity of $\operatorname{Re}$ in [F1] and [F3], each of these is an identity $\operatorname{Re}(W_j\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for a constant $W_j\in\mathbb C^3$; by (a) of step 2.1, with the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, they hold if and only if the constants vanish. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F3, F4]

4.1 [Proof of (b)] By step 3.1, the first and second equations hold if and only if $k\cdot e=0$ and $k\cdot h=0$, since multiplication by the nonzero field element $i$ is injective by [F3]. The third holds if and only if $i\,k\times e+i\omega\mu\,h=0$, that is $k\times e=\omega\mu\,h$ after dividing by the nonzero factor $i$ and using $\omega\mu\ne0$. The fourth holds if and only if $i\,k\times h-(\sigma-i\omega\varepsilon)e=0$, because $\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\mu h e^{i\theta})=-\operatorname{Re}(i\omega\mu h e^{i\theta})$ by [F3]; dividing by $i$ and using $(\sigma-i\omega\varepsilon)/i=-(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)$ — indeed $(\sigma-i\omega\varepsilon)=i\cdot\bigl(-(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)\bigr)$ by the field arithmetic of [F3] — gives $k\times h=-(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)e$. Hence the quadruple satisfies the four equations if and only if the four displayed amplitude conditions hold, which is (b). [step 3.1, F3, algebra]

5.1 [Structure and dispersion, forward in (c)] Assume $e\ne0$ and the four conditions of (b). Since $\omega\mu\ne0$, the third condition gives $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)$; then $k\cdot h=k\cdot(k\times e)/(\omega\mu)=0$ and $e\cdot h=e\cdot(k\times e)/(\omega\mu)=0$ by the orthogonality in [F5]. Crossing the third condition with $k$ and substituting the fourth, $k\times(k\times e)=\omega\mu\,k\times h=-\omega\mu(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)e$; the vector triple-product identity $k\times(k\times e)=k(k\cdot e)-(k\cdot k)e$, a componentwise polynomial identity for the bilinear extension by [F5], together with $k\cdot e=0$, gives $-(k\cdot k)e=-\omega\mu(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)e=-(\varepsilon\mu\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega)e$, and dividing by the nonzero vector $e$ — equivalently, reading the identity coordinatewise — gives $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega$. [step 4.1, F3, F5, algebra]

6.1 [Converse and solution family in (c)] Let $k\ne0$, $\omega>0$ satisfy $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega$, and let $e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$; put $h:=k\times e/(\omega\mu)$. Then $k\cdot e=0$ and $k\cdot h=0$ by orthogonality in [F5], $k\times e=\omega\mu h$ by definition, and $k\times h=k\times(k\times e)/(\omega\mu)=\bigl[k(k\cdot e)-(k\cdot k)e\bigr]/(\omega\mu)=-\bigl(\varepsilon\mu\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega\bigr)e/(\omega\mu)=-(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)e$, so the pair $(e,h)$ satisfies (b) by step 4.1. If $e=0$ then $h=0$; conversely if $h=0$ then $k\times e=0$, so the two-vector family $(k,e)$ is linearly dependent over the field $\mathbb C$: writing the vanishing minors of $(k\ e)$ — if the coordinate $k_l\ne0$ then $e_j=(e_l/k_l)k_j$ for the two other coordinates $j$ and also for $l$ — gives $e=\alpha k$ with $\alpha=e_l/k_l\in\mathbb C$ by [F3]; then $0=k\cdot e=\alpha(k\cdot k)$ and $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2+i\mu\sigma\omega\ne0$ (its real part is $\varepsilon\mu\omega^2>0$ by [F3]) force $\alpha=0$, so $e=0$. Thus $(e,h)=(0,0)$ if and only if $e=0$. For the solution set with $(k,\omega)$ on the dispersion relation: every solution $(e,h)$ of (b) has $k\cdot e=0$ and $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)$ by step 5.1, so it lies in the displayed set; conversely every element of that set is a solution by the first part of this step, and the correspondence $e\mapsto(e,k\times e/(\omega\mu))$ is injective, so the solution set is exactly $\{(e,k\times e/(\omega\mu)):k\cdot e=0\}$. If $k_l\ne0$ the map $e\mapsto(e_j)_{j\ne l}\in\mathbb C^2$ is a bijection from $\{e:k\cdot e=0\}$ onto $\mathbb C^2$ with inverse $(e_j)_{j\ne l}\mapsto e$ where $e_l=-\bigl(\sum_{j\ne l}k_je_j\bigr)/k_l$, both maps being linear over $\mathbb C$; hence that solution space is a complex two-dimensional space. Off the dispersion relation, if (b) holds then either $e=0$, which gives $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)=0$, or $e\ne0$, which by step 5.1 forces the dispersion relation; so the only solution is $e=h=0$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F3, F5, algebra]

6.2 [Lossless pointwise identities in (d)] Assume $\sigma=0$ and $k\in\mathbb R^3$ with $e\ne0$, so the four conditions of (b) hold and (c) applies by steps 4.1 and 5.1. From $k\cdot k=|k|^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$ and $|k|\ge0$ we get $|k|=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}$ by [F10], which is $k(\omega)=\omega/v$ by [F7]. For every $(x,t)$: $k\cdot E=k\cdot\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i\theta})=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((k\cdot e)e^{i\theta}\bigr)=0$ and $k\cdot B=\mu\operatorname{Re}\bigl((k\cdot h)e^{i\theta}\bigr)=0$ by [F1] and the reality of $k$; further $B=\mu H=\mu\operatorname{Re}\bigl((k\times e)/(\omega\mu)e^{i\theta}\bigr)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((k\times e)e^{i\theta}\bigr)/\omega=k\times\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i\theta})/\omega=k\times E/\omega=(\hat k\times E)/v$ because $k$ is real and $|k|/\omega=1/v$ by [F7]; and $E\cdot B=E\cdot(\hat k\times E)/v=\langle E,\hat k\times E\rangle/v=\det[E,\hat k,E]/v=0$ by [F5] because a determinant with two equal columns vanishes. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, F5, F7, F10, algebra]

6.3 [Evanescent factorisation in (e)] Assume the hypotheses of (e). Since $k=\kappa_0+i\beta n'$ with $\kappa_0,n'\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\kappa_0\cdot n'=0$, $|n'|=1$, the bilinear extension of [F5] gives $k\cdot x=\kappa_0\cdot x+i\beta\,n'\cdot x$ for real $x$ and $k\cdot k=|\kappa_0|^2-\beta^2$ (the cross terms $2i\beta\,\kappa_0\cdot n'$ vanish), so the dispersion relation gives $|\kappa_0|^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2+\beta^2>0$ and hence $\kappa_0\ne0$. Writing $\varphi:=\kappa_0\cdot x-\omega t\in\mathbb R$ and $b:=\beta\,n'\cdot x\in\mathbb R$, the identity $i\theta=i(k\cdot x-\omega t)=-b+i\varphi$ combines with the addition law and real extension of [F2] to give $e^{i\theta}=\exp(-b+i\varphi)=e^{-b}\exp(i\varphi)$; the Cartesian form of [F2] gives $\exp(i\varphi)=\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi$, and the coordinate formula for the real part of a product in [F1] and [F3] then gives, componentwise, $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i\theta}\bigr)=e^{-\beta n'\cdot x}\bigl[(\operatorname{Re}e)\cos\varphi-(\operatorname{Im}e)\sin\varphi\bigr]=e^{-\beta n'\cdot x}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i\varphi}\bigr)$, the last equality being the same coordinate formula read backwards. This is the stated factorisation, and $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)$ by step 5.1. [given, step 5.1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

7.1 [The cross-product norm identity] For real vectors $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$ the component expansion gives $|u\times v|^2=|u|^2|v|^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2$: both sides equal $\sum_{j\ne l}u_j^2v_l^2-2\sum_{j<l}u_ju_lv_jv_l$ by the coordinate formulas of [F5]. Applying this with $u=\hat k$ and $v=E$, where $|\hat k|=1$ since $|k|=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\ne0$ and $\langle\hat k,E\rangle=(k\cdot E)/|k|=0$ by step 6.2, gives $|\hat k\times E|^2=|E|^2$, hence $|B|=|\hat k\times E|/v=|E|/v$ by step 6.2 and the positivity of $v$ in [F7]. Moreover $|h|=|k\times e|/(\omega\mu)=|k||e|/(\omega\mu)$ with $|k\times e|^2=|k|^2|e|^2-\langle k,e\rangle^2=|k|^2|e|^2$ by the same identity applied to the real vectors $k,e$ and $k\cdot e=0$, so $|h|=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}|e|/(\omega\mu)=|e|(\varepsilon/\mu)^{1/2}=|e|/Z$ by [F7]. [step 6.2, F5, F7, algebra]

7.2 [Evanescent averaged flux in (e)] By step 6.3 the fields are $E=e^{-b}\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i\varphi})$ and $H=e^{-b}\operatorname{Re}(h\,e^{i\varphi})$ with $\varphi=\kappa_0\cdot x-\omega t$, so $E\times H=e^{-2b}\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t'})\times\operatorname{Re}(h\,e^{-i\omega t'})$ evaluated at $t'=t-\kappa_0\cdot x/\omega$, and the period average in $t$ equals that in $t'$; the cross-product form of [F9] applied with $a=e$, $d=h$ gives $\langle S\rangle=e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(e\times\overline h)$. Since $\overline h=\overline{k\times e}/(\omega\mu)$ and $\overline{k\times e}=\overline{k}\times\overline e=(\kappa_0-i\beta n')\times\overline e$ by [F3], the triple-product expansion of [F5] gives $e\times\overline h=\bigl[\overline k(e\cdot\overline e)-\overline e\,(e\cdot\overline k)\bigr]/(\omega\mu)$, whose inner product with $n'$ is $\bigl[(\overline k\cdot n')|e|^2-(\overline e\cdot n')(e\cdot\overline k)\bigr]/(\omega\mu)$; here $\overline k\cdot n'=-i\beta$ and $e\cdot\overline k=\kappa_0\cdot e-i\beta\,(e\cdot n')$ by the bilinear expansion of [F5]. Hence $\operatorname{Re}\bigl[-\overline{(e\cdot n')}(e\cdot\overline k)\bigr]=-\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\overline{(e\cdot n')}(\kappa_0\cdot e)\bigr]-\operatorname{Re}\bigl[i\beta|e\cdot n'|^{2}\bigr]=-\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\overline{(e\cdot n')}\cdot\overline{(\kappa_0\cdot\overline e)}\bigr]=-\operatorname{Re}\bigl[(e\cdot n')(\kappa_0\cdot\overline e)\bigr]$, where the middle term vanishes as a purely imaginary number and the last identity uses $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$ and $\operatorname{Re}\overline\zeta=\operatorname{Re}\zeta$ from [F3]; substituting into the previous display gives the stated normal component. [step 6.3, F3, F5, F9, algebra]

8.1 [Lossless averages in (d)] With $T=2\pi/\omega$, step 6.2 gives $E\cdot E=\operatorname{Re}(e_je^{i\theta})\operatorname{Re}(e_je^{i\theta})$ summed over $j$, and its period average is $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(e\cdot\overline e)=\tfrac12|e|^2$ by the vector form of [F9] applied with $a=d=e$ (the phase $e^{ik\cdot x}$ is constant in $t$ and cancels in the product $e^{ik\cdot x}e^{-ik\cdot x}=1$ by [F2]); similarly $\langle H\cdot H\rangle=\tfrac12|h|^2=\tfrac12|e|^2/Z^2$ by step 7.1. Hence $\langle u\rangle=\tfrac12\bigl(\varepsilon\langle E\cdot E\rangle+\mu\langle H\cdot H\rangle\bigr)=\tfrac14\bigl(\varepsilon|e|^2+\mu|e|^2/Z^2\bigr)=\tfrac14\bigl(\varepsilon|e|^2+\varepsilon|e|^2\bigr)=\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}|e|^2$ because $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ is the stored-energy quantity of [F8] and $\mu/Z^2=\varepsilon$ by [F7] and [F3]. Similarly $\langle S\rangle=\langle E\times H\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(e\times\overline h)$ by the flux definition $S=E\times H$ of [F8] and the cross-product form of [F9] with $a=e$, $d=h$; substituting $\overline h=\overline{k\times e}/(\omega\mu)=(k\times\overline e)/(\omega\mu)$ for real $k$ by [F3] and using the triple-product expansion $e\times(k\times\overline e)=k(e\cdot\overline e)-\overline e(e\cdot k)=k|e|^2$ by [F5] and $k\cdot e=0$ gives $\langle S\rangle=|e|^2k/(2\mu\omega)=|e|^2\hat k/(2Z)$ because $k/(\mu\omega)=\hat k|k|/(\mu\omega)=\hat k/(\mu v)=\hat k/Z$ by [F7]; and $v\langle u\rangle\hat k=v\varepsilon|e|^2\hat k/2=|e|^2\hat k/(2Z)$ because $v\varepsilon=1/Z$ by [F7], so the three displayed expressions agree. [step 6.2, step 7.1, F2, F3, F5, F7, F8, F9, algebra]

8.2 [Vanishing on transverse amplitudes] Under the hypotheses of (e) with $k\cdot e=0$, the bilinear expansion of [F5] gives $0=k\cdot e=\kappa_0\cdot e+i\beta\,(n'\cdot e)$, so $\kappa_0\cdot\overline e=\overline{\kappa_0\cdot e}=\overline{-i\beta\,(n'\cdot e)}=i\beta\,\overline{(n'\cdot e)}=i\beta\,(n'\cdot\overline e)$ by [F3] and the reality of $\kappa_0$, and hence $(e\cdot n')(\kappa_0\cdot\overline e)=i\beta\,(e\cdot n')\overline{(e\cdot n')}=i\beta\,|e\cdot n'|^2$, a purely imaginary number; therefore its real part vanishes and step 7.2 gives $\langle S\cdot n'\rangle\equiv0$ for every transverse amplitude. [step 7.2, F3, F5, algebra]

9.1 [The polarised evanescent cases] In the transverse-electric case $e=E_0(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)$ with $\hat\kappa_0=\kappa_0/|\kappa_0|$ and $E_0\ne0$: the triple-product expansion of [F5] gives $k\times(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)=(k\cdot\hat\kappa_0)n'-(k\cdot n')\hat\kappa_0=|\kappa_0|n'-i\beta\hat\kappa_0$ because $k\cdot\hat\kappa_0=\kappa_0\cdot\hat\kappa_0=|\kappa_0|$ and $k\cdot n'=i\beta$, and $k\cdot(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)=\langle n'\times\hat\kappa_0,k\rangle=\det[n',\hat\kappa_0,k]=\det[n',\hat\kappa_0,\kappa_0]+i\beta\det[n',\hat\kappa_0,n']=|\kappa_0|\det[n',\hat\kappa_0,\hat\kappa_0]+i\beta\cdot0=0$ because a determinant with two equal columns vanishes by [F5]; so this is a transverse amplitude with $h=E_0(|\kappa_0|n'-i\beta\hat\kappa_0)/(\omega\mu)$ and $\overline h=\overline E_0(|\kappa_0|n'+i\beta\hat\kappa_0)/(\omega\mu)$. With the positively oriented orthonormal triad $(\hat\kappa_0,\hat y',n')$ where $\hat y'=n'\times\hat\kappa_0$, the cross-product relations $\hat y'\times n'=\hat\kappa_0$ and $\hat y'\times\hat\kappa_0=-n'$ hold by [F5], so $e\times\overline h=|E_0|^2\bigl[|\kappa_0|\hat\kappa_0-i\beta n'\bigr]/(\omega\mu)$ and $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0\rangle=e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}|E_0|^2|\kappa_0|/(2\mu\omega)=e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}|e|^2|\kappa_0|/(2\mu\omega)>0$ because $|e|^2=|E_0|^2\ne0$, $|\kappa_0|>0$ and $\mu,\omega,v>0$. In the transverse-magnetic case $h=H_0\hat y'$ with $H_0\ne0$ and $e=-(k\times\hat y')H_0/(\omega\varepsilon)$: the same expansion gives $k\times\hat y'=|\kappa_0|n'-i\beta\hat\kappa_0$, so $e=H_0(i\beta\hat\kappa_0-|\kappa_0|n')/(\omega\varepsilon)$; then $k\cdot e=H_0(i\beta\,k\cdot\hat\kappa_0-|\kappa_0|\,k\cdot n')/(\omega\varepsilon)=H_0(i\beta|\kappa_0|-|\kappa_0|i\beta)/(\omega\varepsilon)=0$, and $k\times e=H_0(i\beta\,k\times\hat\kappa_0-|\kappa_0|\,k\times n')/(\omega\varepsilon)$. Here $k\times n'=(\kappa_0+i\beta n')\times n'=\kappa_0\times n'=-|\kappa_0|\hat y'$ and $k\times\hat\kappa_0=(\kappa_0+i\beta n')\times\hat\kappa_0=i\beta(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)=i\beta\hat y'$ by [F5] and $\kappa_0\times\hat\kappa_0=0$, whence $k\times e=H_0\bigl((i\beta)^2+|\kappa_0|^2\bigr)\hat y'/(\omega\varepsilon)=H_0\bigl(|\kappa_0|^2-\beta^2\bigr)\hat y'/(\omega\varepsilon)=\omega\mu H_0\hat y'=\omega\mu h$, because $|\kappa_0|^2-\beta^2=k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$ by step 6.3 and [F7]; so this data satisfies the amplitude conditions by step 4.1, and $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0\rangle=e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}|H_0|^2|\kappa_0|/(2\omega\varepsilon)=e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}|h|^2|\kappa_0|/(2\omega\varepsilon)>0$ with $|h|^2=|H_0|^2\ne0$. In both polarisations the normal component vanishes identically by step 8.2. [step 6.3, step 7.2, step 8.2, step 4.1, F3, F5, F7, algebra]

10.1 [Scope (f)] Clause (f) holds: all computations were carried out for the explicit fields defined by $(k,\omega,e,h)$ on the whole space, so no existence or completeness of any plane-wave family, no energy finiteness, no boundary or interface conditions, no material validity and no empirical statement is claimed; for $\operatorname{Im}k\ne0$ the factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}k\cdot x}$ is unbounded in some directions, so the statements are read where the model declares the field bounded, and in (e) the decay factor $e^{-\beta n'\cdot x}$ is the bounded branch on $n'\cdot x>0$; the finite-band caveat of [F6] applies throughout; and no choice principle is used, every construction being finite-dimensional algebra for exhibited data. [given, step 8.2, step 9.1, F6, F7] ∎

## Statement

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the lossless isotropic scalar case: two homogeneous media at rest in the laboratory chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] (frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]), medium 1 in $\{x_3<0\}$ with constants $\varepsilon_1,\mu_1>0$ and medium 2 in $\{x_3>0\}$ with constants $\varepsilon_2,\mu_2>0$, both with $\sigma=0$, sharing the plane interface $S:=\{x_3=0\}$ with unit normal $n:=e_3$, and the plane-wave amplitude conditions and solution structure of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]] in each medium. Let $\omega_i,\omega_r,\omega_t>0$, $k_i,k_r,k_t\in\mathbb C^{3}$, $e_i,e_r,e_t\in\mathbb C^{3}\setminus\{0\}$, and put $h_j:=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega_j)$ for $j\in\{i,r,t\}$ where $\mu_i=\mu_r=\mu_1$ and $\mu_t=\mu_2$, so that each triple satisfies the conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b)-(c) in its own medium: $k_j\cdot e_j=0$, $k_j\times e_j=\omega_j\mu h_j$, $k_j\times h_j=-\omega_j\varepsilon e_j$ and $k_j\cdot k_j=\varepsilon\mu\omega_j^{2}$ with $(\varepsilon,\mu)=(\varepsilon_1,\mu_1)$ for $j=i,r$ and $(\varepsilon_2,\mu_2)$ for $j=t$. Assume the declared normal orientation conditions $k_i\cdot n\in\mathbb R_{>0}$ and $k_r\cdot n\in\mathbb R_{<0}$; no order is placed on a complex number. Tangential components may be complex. Algebraic phase matching permits every complex transmitted wavevector satisfying its amplitude conditions and dispersion relation, including a zero normal root at critical incidence. No outgoing or non-growth condition is required here. A consuming Fresnel construction may optionally select a root $k_t\cdot n$ of $(k_t\cdot n)^2=\varepsilon_2\mu_2\omega_t^2-\kappa_t\cdot\kappa_t$, where $\kappa_t:=k_t-(k_t\cdot n)n$, with $\operatorname{Im}(k_t\cdot n)\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(k_t\cdot n)\ge0$ when its imaginary part is zero. Such a selection is a declared additional branch assumption of that construction, not a restriction on this theorem or an inferred material realization. Complex tangential phases may grow along the unbounded interface; no global tangential boundedness is asserted. Define the wave fields $E_j(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j e^{i(k_j\cdot x-\omega_jt)}\bigr)$, $H_j(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(h_j e^{i(k_j\cdot x-\omega_jt)}\bigr)$, which are fields of [[def-em-fields]], and let $E:=E_i+E_r$, $H:=H_i+H_r$ on the medium-1 side and $E:=E_t$, $H:=H_t$ on the medium-2 side. [Interface hypothesis] assume that for all $(y,t)\in\mathbb R^{2}\times I$, with $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval, the one-sided traces at $(y,0,t)$ satisfy the four stationary interface identities with no free surface charge or current,
$$n\cdot\bigl(\varepsilon_2E_t-\varepsilon_1(E_i+E_r)\bigr)=0,\qquad n\cdot\bigl(\mu_2H_t-\mu_1(H_i+H_r)\bigr)=0,$$
$$n\times\bigl(E_t-(E_i+E_r)\bigr)=0,\qquad n\times\bigl(H_t-(H_i+H_r)\bigr)=0 .$$
Then:

**(a) [Phase matching]** with $\kappa_j:=k_j-(k_j\cdot n)n$ the tangential wavevector, $\kappa_i=\kappa_r=\kappa_t$ and $\omega_i=\omega_r=\omega_t$.

**(b) [Geometry]** if $\kappa_i\ne0$ then $k_i,k_r,k_t$ all lie in the complex two-dimensional subspace $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\kappa_i,n\}$ (a real plane when the wavevectors are real); if $\kappa_i=0$ then all three wavevectors are parallel to $n$.

**(c) [Propagating waves: reflection law and Snell's law]** if in addition $k_i,k_r,k_t\in\mathbb R^{3}$, then with $\theta_j\in[0,\pi/2]$ defined by $\sin\theta_j=|\kappa_j|/|k_j|$ (well defined because the real dispersion relation gives $|k_j|>0$; the incident and reflected angles are below $\pi/2$, and the transmitted angle may equal $\pi/2$) one has $\theta_r=\theta_i$ and, writing $v_j=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{-1/2}$ and $n_j=c/v_j$ for the parameters of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]],
$$n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t.$$
If $\theta_i>0$, this is equivalently $\sin\theta_t/\sin\theta_i=v_2/v_1=n_1/n_2$. At normal incidence $\theta_i=0$ it gives $\theta_t=0$ without forming $0/0$.

**(d) [Hypotheses actually used]** the proof uses only the two tangential identities $n\times[E]=0$ and $n\times[H]=0$ and the nonzero-wave hypotheses $e_j\ne0$ together with $k_j\cdot k_j\ne0$; the two normal identities are recorded because they belong to the interface model, but they are not used. If the reflected wave is absent ($e_r=h_r=0$), the same argument matches the incident and transmitted actual waves; it does not determine the absent reflected wave's frequency or wavevector, which a Fresnel construction may conventionally assign the common phase.

**(e) [Scope]** the wave data are given: no existence of interface-consistent data, no reflection or transmission amplitudes, no energy fluxes and no well-posedness are claimed. Complex transmitted wavevectors are covered by (a) and (b) (the evanescent case of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](e) satisfies $k_t\cdot n\ne0$); the physical propagating or evanescent character of the transmitted wave, the angle selection in the real case and the amplitudes are treated by the interface items that consume this theorem. The four interface identities are the stationary plane-interface conditions of the model; for compact interfaces they follow from the distributional jump theorem [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]], and on the noncompact plane they are the stated interface hypothesis. No material dispersion, absorption, anisotropy, moving medium or nonlinearity is covered, and no empirical claim is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-media lossless setting of the Statement, the six wave data $(k_j,\omega_j,e_j)$, $j\in\{i,r,t\}$, with $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega_j)$, the normal $n=e_3$, the interface interval $I$, and the interface hypothesis [A1].

[A1] The four stationary interface identities of the Statement hold for all $(y,t)\in\mathbb R^2\times I$; only the two tangential identities $n\times(E_t-(E_i+E_r))=0$ and $n\times(H_t-(H_i+H_r))=0$ are used in the proof.

[F1] Plane-wave structure in each medium: $k_j\cdot e_j=0$, $k_j\times e_j=\omega_j\mu h_j$, $k_j\times h_j=-\omega_j\varepsilon e_j$ and $k_j\cdot k_j=\varepsilon\mu\omega_j^2$ with the constants of the medium of wave $j$, and $e_j\ne0$ ([[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b)-(c)); the parameters $v_j=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{-1/2}$ and $n_j=c/v_j$ are those of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]].

[F2] The character-grouping lemma: if $F(z)=\sum_{k}c_k e^{i\lambda_k\cdot z}$ with pairwise distinct $\lambda_k\in\mathbb C^m$ and $\operatorname{Re}F=0$ on a nonempty open $U$, then for every $\nu\in\mathbb C^m$, $\sum_{\lambda_k=\nu}c_k+\sum_{\lambda_k=-\overline\nu}\overline{c_k}=0$ ([[lem-em-exponential-character-open-set-independence]](b)).

[F3] Inner and cross products: $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_lx_ly_l$, $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$, bilinear and alternating, with $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$ and $u\times v$ orthogonal to $u$ and $v$; orthogonality of the decomposition $x=x^\tau+(x\cdot n)n$ with $x^\tau:=x-(x\cdot n)n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]).

[F4] Complex arithmetic and conjugation: $\mathbb C$ is a field in which a product vanishes only if a factor does ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]); conjugation is an involutive automorphism with $\operatorname{Re}w=(w+\overline w)/2$ and $z\overline z=|z|^2$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F5] The principal inverse sine: $\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ satisfies $\sin(\arcsin y)=y$, and sine is strictly increasing on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ ([[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]).

[F6] Nonnegative square roots: every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root, and $\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt a\sqrt b$ for $a,b\ge0$ by squaring and uniqueness ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F7] The laboratory setting, fields and units are those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the material branch is the lossless isotropic scalar case of [[post-em-material-closure]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; evaluate the tangential traces on the interface as real parts of six-component characters, apply the character-grouping lemma to force equal frequencies, and read off the geometry and the real-angle laws.

1.1 [Nonzero tangential traces] For each $j$, the six-component tangential trace datum $A_j:=(e_j^\tau,h_j^\tau)\in\mathbb C^6$ is nonzero. Suppose $A_j=0$; then $e_j^\tau=0$ and $h_j^\tau=0$, so $e_j=a\,n$ with $a=e_j\cdot n$ and $h_j=b\,n$ with $b=h_j\cdot n$ by the orthogonal decomposition of [F3]. Taking the inner product of the amplitude condition $k_j\times e_j=\omega_j\mu h_j$ of [F1] with $n$ gives $0=\omega_j\mu\,b$: indeed $\langle k_j\times e_j,n\rangle=\det[k_j,e_j,n]=a\det[k_j,n,n]=0$ because a determinant with two equal columns vanishes and $\langle h_j,n\rangle=b$; hence $b=0$ and $h_j=0$. Then the amplitude condition $k_j\times h_j=-\omega_j\varepsilon e_j$ gives $0=-\omega_j\varepsilon\,a\,n$, so $a=0$, and then $e_j=a\,n=0$, contradicting $e_j\ne0$ in [F1]. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 [Interface traces as characters] For a wave $j$ and $x=(y,0)$ on the interface, $k_j\cdot x=\kappa_j\cdot y$ because $k_j\cdot n$ multiplies the vanishing third coordinate; hence at the interface $E_j(y,0,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j^\tau e^{i(\kappa_j\cdot y-\omega_jt)}\bigr)$ and $H_j(y,0,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(h_j e^{i(\kappa_j\cdot y-\omega_jt)}\bigr)$, whose normal parts are annihilated by $n\times\cdot$. The two tangential interface identities of [A1] are identities of tangential vector fields, and for a tangential $w$ the vanishing $n\times w=0$ forces $w=0$ (a vector orthogonal to both $n$ and its own cross product with $n$ vanishes by [F3]); hence they say, for all $z=(y,t)\in\mathbb R^2\times I$, that $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(A_t e^{i\lambda_t\cdot z}\bigr)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(A_i e^{i\lambda_i\cdot z}\bigr)+\operatorname{Re}\bigl(A_r e^{i\lambda_r\cdot z}\bigr)$ componentwise, with $\lambda_j:=(\kappa_j,-\omega_j)\in\mathbb C^3$ and $A_j=(e_j^\tau,h_j^\tau)$; equivalently $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(A_i e^{i\lambda_i\cdot z}+A_r e^{i\lambda_r\cdot z}-A_t e^{i\lambda_t\cdot z}\bigr)=0$ on the nonempty open set $\mathbb R^2\times I$, by the additivity of the real part in [F4] and the componentwise linearity of the tangential projection in [F3]. [given, A1, step 1.1, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 [Frequency grouping] Group the three frequencies of step 2.1 by value: let $\nu_1,\dots,\nu_M$ be the distinct values among $\lambda_i,\lambda_r,\lambda_t$ and put $c_{\nu_0}:=\sum_{j:\lambda_j=\nu_0}\epsilon_jA_j$ where $\epsilon_i=\epsilon_r:=1$ and $\epsilon_t:=-1$. Then $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{M}c_{\nu_k}e^{i\nu_k\cdot z}\bigr)=0$ on $\mathbb R^2\times I$, the $\nu_k$ being pairwise distinct, so [F2] applied to the distinct frequencies $\nu_1,\dots,\nu_M$ with coefficients $c_{\nu_1},\dots,c_{\nu_M}$ gives $c_{\nu}+\sum_{k:\nu_k=-\overline\nu}\overline{c_{\nu_k}}=0$ for every $\nu\in\mathbb C^3$. Fix $k$ and take $\nu=\nu_k$: the left sum is $c_{\nu_k}$ alone, while $-\overline{\nu_k}=(-\overline{\kappa_k},+\omega_k)$ has last coordinate $\omega_k>0$, whereas every $\nu_l=\lambda_j$ for some $j$ has last coordinate $-\omega_j<0$; hence $\nu_l=-\overline{\nu_k}$ fails for every $l$, the second sum is empty, and $c_{\nu_k}=0$. [given, step 2.1, F2, F4, algebra]

4.1 [All frequencies agree] By step 3.1, for each distinct actual frequency $\nu$ the signed sum of the tangential data of the waves with that frequency vanishes. If the three actual frequencies were not all equal, then some actual frequency would occur exactly once among $\lambda_i,\lambda_r,\lambda_t$ (a partition of three terms into at least two nonempty groups has a group of size one), and for that $\nu$ the identity $c_\nu=0$ of step 3.1 would read $\pm A_j=0$ for the corresponding single wave, contradicting the nonzero trace datum of step 1.1. Hence $\lambda_i=\lambda_r=\lambda_t$, which is the assertion (a): reading the three coordinates, $\kappa_i=\kappa_r=\kappa_t$ and $\omega_i=\omega_r=\omega_t$. [step 3.1, step 1.1, algebra]

5.1 [Geometry, part (b)] By step 4.1, $\kappa_j=\kappa:=\kappa_i$ for every $j$, and $k_j=\kappa_j+(k_j\cdot n)n=\kappa+(k_j\cdot n)n$ by the orthogonal decomposition of [F3]; hence each $k_j$ lies in the complex span of $\kappa$ and $n$, which is two-dimensional over $\mathbb C$ when $\kappa\ne0$ because $\kappa$ and $n$ are independent: if $\kappa=zn$ for some $z\in\mathbb C$ then $0=\kappa\cdot n=z\,(n\cdot n)=z$, so $\kappa=0$, contrary to hypothesis. When the wavevectors are real this span is the real plane they span. If instead $\kappa=0$, then every $k_j=(k_j\cdot n)n$ is parallel to $n$. [step 4.1, F3, algebra]

5.2 [Hypotheses used and the absent-wave case, part (d)] The argument of steps 1.1-4.1 used exactly: the two tangential identities of [A1], the nonzero amplitudes $e_j\ne0$ and the amplitude conditions with the dispersion relation $\varepsilon\mu\omega_j^2=k_j\cdot k_j\ne0$ of [F1] (the dispersion enters through the evaluation of $k_j\times h_j$ from $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega_j)$, so the role listed as $k_j\cdot k_j\ne0$ is the nondegeneracy actually used); the normal orientation conditions $k_i\cdot n>0$, $k_r\cdot n<0$, the two normal interface identities, and the optional normal-root selection rule were not used, and no outgoing or tangential-growth condition was used. If a consuming construction declares the reflected wave absent, $e_r=h_r=0$ (so that $A_r=0$ and only the incident and transmitted traces are matched), the same grouping argument applies to the two nonzero trace data $A_i$ and $-A_t$: a singleton group would give $\pm A_i=0$ or $\mp A_t=0$, impossible by step 1.1, so $\lambda_i=\lambda_t$, i.e. $\kappa_i=\kappa_t$ and $\omega_i=\omega_t$; no constraint on the labels $k_r,\omega_r$ of the absent field is produced, and a Fresnel construction may assign it the common phase as a convention. [step 1.1, step 4.1, A1, F1, algebra]

6.1 [Angles and laws, part (c)] Assume now that $k_i,k_r,k_t$ are real. For each $j$, [F1] gives $k_j\cdot k_j=|k_j|^2=\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2$ with the common $\omega=\omega_j$ of step 4.1, so $|k_j|=\omega(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}=\omega/v_j>0$ by [F6] and [F1], and $|k_i|=|k_r|$. By [F3], $|k_j|^2=|\kappa_j|^2+(k_j\cdot n)^2$, so $|\kappa_j|\le|k_j|$ and the ratio $\sin\theta_j:=|\kappa_j|/|k_j|$ lies in $[0,1]$; define $\theta_j:=\arcsin(|\kappa_j|/|k_j|)\in[0,\pi/2]$ by [F5], so that $\sin\theta_j=|\kappa_j|/|k_j|$ as in the Statement. Since $\kappa_r=\kappa_i=\kappa_t=\kappa$ by step 4.1, $\sin\theta_r=|\kappa|/|k_r|=|\kappa|/|k_i|=\sin\theta_i$; the principal inverse sine is strictly increasing on its interval because sine is strictly increasing on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ by [F5], hence injective, so $\theta_r=\theta_i$. Similarly $|\kappa|=\omega(\varepsilon_1\mu_1)^{1/2}\sin\theta_i=\omega(\varepsilon_2\mu_2)^{1/2}\sin\theta_t$, that is $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$ after multiplying by $c/\omega$ where $n_j=c(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}=c/v_j$ by [F1] and [F6]. If $\theta_i>0$ then $\sin\theta_i>0$ and division is legitimate, giving $\sin\theta_t/\sin\theta_i=(\varepsilon_1\mu_1)^{1/2}/(\varepsilon_2\mu_2)^{1/2}=v_2/v_1=n_1/n_2$; if $\theta_i=0$ then $|\kappa|=0$, so $|\kappa_t|=0$ and $\theta_t=\arcsin 0=0$, since $\sin 0=0$ and the principal inverse sine returns the unique number of $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ with sine $0$, without forming $0/0$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, F3, F5, F6, algebra]

7.1 [Scope, part (e)] The four statements (a)-(d) are conditional on the given wave data and the interface hypothesis [A1]; nothing about the existence of interface-consistent data, reflection or transmission amplitudes, energy fluxes or well-posedness is proved. All frequencies are positive, all tangential quantities may be complex, and clauses (a) and (b) cover complex transmitted wavevectors; the propagating angle selection of (c) and the amplitudes are the business of the consuming interface theorems. The interface identities on the noncompact plane are the stated hypothesis; for compact interfaces the distributional jump theorem [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]] supplies them, and no distributional or choice-theoretic clause of that theorem is used here (only complex arithmetic, the character lemma, and the real geometry of the propagating case), so no choice principle is inherited. [given, step 5.2, F2, F7] ∎

## Statement

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the isotropic scalar case at rest in the laboratory frame with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma>0$, the fields of [[def-em-fields]] on the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and the plane-wave structure of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]: let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^{3}\setminus\{0\}$, $n$ a unit vector and $k=\lambda n$, $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, and let $E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}\bigr)$ be a plane-wave field satisfying the amplitude conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b) with $k\cdot e=0$. Put $a:=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}>0$, $b:=\mu\sigma\omega>0$, $r:=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ and let $p,q>0$ be the quantities of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]. Then:

**(a) [Exact propagation constant and decay]** $\lambda^{2}=k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$, so $\lambda=\pm(p+iq)$; if $x_3':=n\cdot x$, then for $\lambda=p+iq$
$$E(x,t)=e^{-q x_3'}\,\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i(p x_3'-\omega t)}\bigr),$$
so the field oscillates with wavenumber $p$ and its amplitude decays in the direction of increasing $x_3'$ at the exact rate $q$; with $\lambda=-(p+iq)$ the exact formula is $E(x,t)=e^{q x_3'}\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i(-p x_3'-\omega t)})$, which grows in that direction, so the decaying branch is the one with $\lambda=p+iq$, in agreement with the selection rule of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]](b).

**(b) [Exact skin depth]** $q^{2}=\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}-a\bigr)/2$, $p^{2}=\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}+a\bigr)/2$, $pq=b/2=\mu\sigma\omega/2$, and the skin depth of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] equals the exact closed expression
$$\delta(\omega)=\frac{1}{q}=\frac{\sqrt{2\,(r+a)}}{b}=\frac{\sqrt{2\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}+a\bigr)}}{\mu\sigma\omega}.$$

**(c) [Good-conductor regime]** put $t:=a/b=\varepsilon\omega/\sigma>0$. For every $t\le1/4$ the exact value satisfies the explicit bounds
$$\bigl|q-\sqrt{b/2}\bigr|\le2t\sqrt{b/2}=\frac{2\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\mu\sigma\omega}{2}},\qquad \bigl|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}\bigr|\le4t\sqrt{2/b}=\frac{4\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu\sigma\omega}} ;$$
equivalently $\delta=\sqrt{2/(\mu\sigma\omega)}\,\bigl(1+O(\varepsilon\omega/\sigma)\bigr)$ in the declared regime $\varepsilon\omega/\sigma\le1/4$, with the displayed explicit remainder bounds.

**(d) [Poor-conductor regime]** put $t':=b/a=\sigma/(\varepsilon\omega)>0$. For every $t'\le1/2$ the exact value satisfies
$$\Bigl|q-\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}\Bigr|\le\frac{t'^{2}}{4}\cdot\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}},\qquad\Bigl|\delta-\frac{2}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}}\Bigr|\le\frac{t'^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}},$$
so in this regime $\delta$ is frequency-independent up to the displayed relative error $O\bigl((\sigma/(\varepsilon\omega))^{2}\bigr)$.

**(e) [Phase relation for a real amplitude]** if $e\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $\lambda=p+iq$, then
$$E(x,t)=e^{-q x_3'}e\cos(px_3'-\omega t),\qquad H(x,t)=\frac{e^{-q x_3'}}{\mu\omega}\bigl(p\cos(px_3'-\omega t)-q\sin(px_3'-\omega t)\bigr)\,(n\times e),$$
and the ratio of the quadrature to the in-phase coefficient is $q/p=\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$ with $1-2t\le q/p\le1$ for every $t\le1/2$; in particular $q/p\to1$ as $t\downarrow0$, so the magnetic scalar factor is $\sqrt{p^2+q^2}\cos(px_3'-\omega t+\eta)$ with $\eta:=\arctan(q/p)\to\pi/4$ (45 degrees), not a 90-degree quadrature phase shift. At fixed position with the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention this corresponds to the stated signed $+\eta$ phase in the decreasing phase variable.

**(f) [Limits and scope]** for $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $q=0$, no attenuation and $\delta=+\infty$, and the approximations of (c) and (d) are not applicable; the ideal-conductor limit $\sigma\to\infty$ is not covered by this theorem, which works inside the finite-Ohmic branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] (a separate boundary model is needed for an ideal conductor); the frequency dependence of $\sigma$ (Drude or other) is not supplied, and $\sigma$ is the declared constant of the branch; the conclusions are exact identities for the ideal plane-wave field and carry no empirical content, no measured conductivity and no claim about any laboratory field.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The declared Ohmic branch with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$, $\sigma>0$; the unit vector $n$, $k=\lambda n$, $e\ne0$ with $k\cdot e=0$; the plane-wave field $E=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)})$ with $H$ determined by the amplitude conditions; the numbers $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2>0$, $b=\mu\sigma\omega>0$, $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and the parameters $p,q>0$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]].

[F1] Concrete propagation data: $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega$ and $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)$ by [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b)-(c); and by [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]](b), $\kappa=p+iq$ is the unique complex number with $\operatorname{Re}\kappa\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}\kappa\ge0$ and $\kappa^{2}=a+ib$, where $p=\sqrt{(r+a)/2}$ and $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}$; also $v=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$ and $Z=(\mu/\varepsilon)^{1/2}$.

[F2] The complex exponential in Cartesian form: for real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^{x}(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^{x}$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[F3] Complex arithmetic and modulus: $\mathbb C$ is a field, a product vanishes only if a factor does, and from $z^{2}=w$ and $\kappa^{2}=w$ one gets $(z-\kappa)(z+\kappa)=0$, hence $z=\pm\kappa$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]); the modulus satisfies $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$ and $|zw|=|z||w|$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F4] Real roots and order: every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root, and $\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{ab}$ for $a,b\ge0$ follows from squaring and uniqueness ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); for $0\le a\le b$ one has $a^{2}\le b^{2}$, and for $0\le a,b$ with $a^{2}\le b^{2}$ one has $a\le b$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); if $0\le a\le b$ and $0\le c\le d$ then $ac\le bd$, and if $0<c<d$ then $1/d<1/c$ in the sense $0<1/d\le1/c$ ([[prop-of-multiply-inequalities]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]]: multiplication by a positive preserves order, and $1/c-1/d=(d-c)/(cd)>0$).

[F5] Every complex number has a square root ([[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]).

[F6] The principal inverse tangent $\arctan:\mathbb R\to(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ is continuous and strictly increasing with $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ ([[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]), and the addition formulas $\cos(\theta+\eta)=\cos\theta\cos\eta-\sin\theta\sin\eta$ hold for real angles ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]).

[F7] Trigonometry: for every real $\theta$, $\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ ([[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]).

[F8] The laboratory setting and units are those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]; the branch assumption is that of [[post-em-material-closure]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; substitute the concrete data into the medium plane-wave theorem, extract the decaying root via Euler's Cartesian form, and bound the exact radicals with elementary square-root inequalities.

1.1 [Propagation constant and decay, part (a)] By [F1], $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$, and since $k=\lambda n$ with $n\cdot n=1$ the bilinear expansion gives $\lambda^{2}=k\cdot k=a+ib$; by [F1] and [F5] with [F3], the solutions of $z^{2}=a+ib$ are exactly $z=\pm(p+iq)$. Writing $x_3'=n\cdot x$, so that $k\cdot x=\lambda x_3'$, the exponent is $i(k\cdot x-\omega t)=i\lambda x_3'-i\omega t$; for $\lambda=p+iq$ this is $-qx_3'+i(px_3'-\omega t)$, and the Cartesian form [F2] gives $e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega t)}=e^{-qx_3'}(\cos(px_3'-\omega t)+i\sin(px_3'-\omega t))$, whence $E=e^{-qx_3'}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,e^{i(px_3'-\omega t)}\bigr)$ componentwise; the amplitude factor $e^{-qx_3'}$ decreases as $x_3'$ increases because $q>0$ by [F1]. For $\lambda=-(p+iq)$ the same computation gives $i\lambda x_3'-i\omega t=qx_3'+i(-px_3'-\omega t)$ and $E=e^{qx_3'}\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i(-px_3'-\omega t)})$, which grows in the direction of increasing $x_3'$; the decaying branch is therefore $\lambda=p+iq$, matching the root selection of [F1]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 [Exact skin depth, part (b)] By [F1], $q^{2}=(r-a)/2$ and $p^{2}=(r+a)/2$ with $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$; multiplying, $(pq)^{2}=\bigl(r^{2}-a^{2}\bigr)/4=b^{2}/4$, and since $p,q\ge0$ and $b>0$ the uniqueness of the nonnegative square root in [F4] gives $pq=b/2=\mu\sigma\omega/2$. For the skin depth $\delta=1/q$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]](c): $\delta^{2}=1/q^{2}=2/(r-a)=2(r+a)/\bigl((r-a)(r+a)\bigr)=2(r+a)/b^{2}$, where $(r-a)(r+a)=r^{2}-a^{2}=b^{2}$ by [F4]; since $\delta>0$ and $b>0$, taking the nonnegative square root gives $\delta=\sqrt{2(r+a)}/b$, and substituting $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}$ and $b=\mu\sigma\omega$ gives the displayed closed form. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra]

3.1 [Ratio identities] With $t=a/b>0$ one has $r=b\sqrt{1+t^{2}}$ because $r^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}=b^{2}(t^{2}+1)$ and both sides are nonnegative, by [F4]; hence $q^{2}=(r-a)/2=\tfrac{b}{2}\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t\bigr)$ and $\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t=\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}+t\bigr)^{-1}$, the second identity because $\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t\bigr)\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}+t\bigr)=1+t^{2}-t^{2}=1$ with all factors positive by [F4] and [F1]. Moreover $q/p=\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$: indeed $q^{2}/p^{2}=(r-a)/(r+a)$, and the same rationalisation gives $(r-a)/(r+a)=\bigl(\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t\bigr)^{2}$, so the positive quantities $q/p$ and $\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$ have equal squares and are equal by [F4]. With $s=t'=b/a>0$ one has analogously $r=a\sqrt{1+s^{2}}$ and $q^{2}=\tfrac{a}{2}\bigl(\sqrt{1+s^{2}}-1\bigr)$. Writing $q_{t}:=\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}$, the identity $q_{t}=\frac{\sqrt{a}\,s}{2}$ holds: expanding $\sqrt a=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}$ and $s=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon\omega}$ by [F1] gives $\frac{\sqrt a\,s}{2}=\frac{\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\sigma}{2\varepsilon\omega}=\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}$; hence $q^{2}/q_{t}^{2}=\frac{2(\sqrt{1+s^{2}}-1)}{s^{2}}=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+s^{2}}}$ by the same rationalisation. [step 2.1, F1, F4, algebra]

4.1 [Good-conductor bounds, part (c)] For $t\ge0$ one has $1\le\sqrt{1+t^{2}}\le1+t$: the left inequality because $1\le1+t^{2}$ and both sides are nonnegative, the right because $1+t^{2}\le(1+t)^{2}=1+2t+t^{2}$, both by [F4]. Hence $\frac{1}{1+2t}\le\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t\le\frac{1}{1+t}\le1$ by step 3.1 and [F4], and $\frac{1}{1+2t}\ge1-2t$ because $0\le1-2t\le1$ and $(1-2t)(1+2t)=1-4t^{2}\le1$ for $t\le1/2$; therefore $\sqrt{1-2t}\le\frac{q}{\sqrt{b/2}}\le1$, that is $\sqrt{b/2}\sqrt{1-2t}\le q\le\sqrt{b/2}$. For $t\le1/4$ one has $1-2t\ge0$ and $(1-2t)^{2}\le1-2t$, so $\sqrt{1-2t}\ge1-2t$ by [F4], giving $\bigl|q-\sqrt{b/2}\bigr|\le2t\sqrt{b/2}$ with the stated equivalent form since $\sqrt{b/2}=\sqrt{\mu\sigma\omega/2}$. For $\delta=1/q$ one has $\sqrt{2/b}\le\delta\le\frac{\sqrt{2/b}}{1-2t}$ from the bound on $q$ and [F4]; and $\frac{1}{1-2t}\le1+4t$ for $t\le1/4$ because $1\le(1+4t)(1-2t)=1+2t-8t^{2}$, i.e. $0\le2t(1-4t)$, by [F4]; hence $\bigl|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}\bigr|\le4t\sqrt{2/b}$ with the stated equivalent form. [step 3.1, F1, F4, algebra]

4.2 [Poor-conductor bounds, part (d)] By step 3.1, $q^{2}=\tfrac{a}{2}\bigl(\sqrt{1+s^{2}}-1\bigr)$ and $q^{2}/q_{t}^{2}=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+s^{2}}}$ with $q_{t}=\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}$, $s=t'=b/a>0$. Since $\sqrt{1+s^{2}}\ge1$, the ratio is at most $1$, so $q\le q_{t}$; and $\sqrt{1+s^{2}}\le1+\frac{s^{2}}{2}$ because $1+s^{2}\le\bigl(1+\frac{s^{2}}{2}\bigr)^{2}=1+s^{2}+\frac{s^{4}}{4}$, so $q^{2}/q_{t}^{2}\ge\frac{2}{2+\frac{s^{2}}{2}}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{s^{2}}{4}}$; for $s^{2}\le1$ (which holds when $s\le1/2$) one has $\frac{1}{1+s^{2}/4}\ge1-\frac{s^{2}}{4}$ since $\bigl(1-\frac{s^{2}}{4}\bigr)\bigl(1+\frac{s^{2}}{4}\bigr)=1-\frac{s^{4}}{16}\le1$ with $1-\frac{s^{2}}{4}\ge0$; therefore $q/q_{t}\ge1-\frac{s^{2}}{4}$, i.e. $\bigl|q-q_{t}\bigr|\le\frac{s^{2}}{4}q_{t}$. For $\delta=1/q$ and $\delta_{t}=1/q_{t}$ we get $\delta/\delta_{t}=q_{t}/q\le\frac{1}{1-s^{2}/4}\le1+\frac{s^{2}}{2}$ whenever $s^{2}\le1$ (since $\frac{1}{1-s^{2}/4}\le1+\frac{s^{2}}{2}$ is equivalent to $1\le1+\frac{s^{2}}{4}-\frac{s^{4}}{8}$, true for $s^{2}\le2$), whence $\bigl|\delta-\delta_{t}\bigr|\le\frac{s^{2}}{2}\delta_{t}$; substituting $\delta_{t}=\frac{2}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu}}$ gives both displayed bounds, by [F4] throughout. [step 3.1, F4, algebra]

5.1 [Phase relation, part (e)] Assume $e\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $\lambda=p+iq$; by [F1], $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)=\lambda\,(n\times e)/(\omega\mu)$ because $k=\lambda n$ and $n\times e$ is real, and the exponent is computed as in step 1.1. Writing $\theta:=px_3'-\omega t$ and using $\lambda/(\mu\omega)=(p+iq)/(\mu\omega)$ with real $p,q$, the Cartesian form [F2] gives $\operatorname{Re}\bigl((p+iq)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)=p\cos\theta-q\sin\theta$, so $E=e^{-qx_3'}e\cos\theta$ and $H=e^{-qx_3'}(p\cos\theta-q\sin\theta)(n\times e)/(\mu\omega)$, the two displayed identities. By step 3.1, $q/p=\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$, and the bounds $1-2t\le q/p\le1$ for $t\le1/2$ are the ones established in step 4.1 for the same quantity; as $t\downarrow0$ the continuous function $t\mapsto\sqrt{1+t^{2}}-t$ tends to $1$, so $\eta:=\arctan(q/p)$ tends to $\arctan 1=\pi/4$ by the continuity of $\arctan$ in [F6]. Put $r:=q/p>0$ and $\eta=\arctan r\in(0,\pi/2)$; by [F6], $\sin\eta=r\cos\eta$, and the Pythagorean identity $\sin^{2}\eta+\cos^{2}\eta=1$ with $\cos\eta>0$ gives $\cos\eta=1/\sqrt{1+r^{2}}$ and $\sin\eta=r/\sqrt{1+r^{2}}$; equivalently $\cos\eta=p/\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}$ and $\sin\eta=q/\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}$, since $\sqrt{1+r^{2}}=\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}/p$ with $p>0$ by [F4]. The addition formula of [F6] then gives $\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}\cos(\theta+\eta)=p\cos\theta-q\sin\theta$, which is the stated form of the magnetic scalar factor. [given, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, F4, F6, F7, algebra]

6.1 [Limits and scope, part (f)] Clause (f): for $\sigma=0$ the definition of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] gives $b=0$, $q=0$, no attenuation and $\delta=+\infty$, and the divisions and bounds of steps 3.1-4.2 use $b>0$, $q>0$ and are not evaluated at zero; the limit $\sigma\to\infty$ is outside the finite-Ohmic branch and the frequency dependence of $\sigma$ is not supplied; all identities are exact for the plane-wave field and involve no measurement, material data or empirical statement, and no choice principle is used since every quantity is defined by explicit formulas in the given scalars. [given, step 4.2, F1, F8] ∎
