## Statement

Assume the following plane-interface material setting, with the same explicitly adopted stationary interface identities as [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] (including its absent-wave qualification), at normal incidence: medium 1 in $\{x_3<0\}$ with $\varepsilon_1,\mu_1>0$, $\sigma_1=0$, medium 2 in $\{x_3>0\}$ with $\varepsilon_2,\mu_2>0$ and either $\sigma_2=0$ (lossless) or $\sigma_2>0$ (Ohmic), both homogeneous and at rest in the laboratory chart, with the plane interface $S=\{x_3=0\}$ and normal $n=e_3$. Let $\omega_i,\omega_r,\omega_t>0$ and let three plane waves of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]] be given with wavevectors $k_i=k_1n$ ($k_1>0$), $k_r=-k_1n$ and $k_t=k\,n$, where for $\sigma_2=0$ one takes $k=\omega_t/v_2>0$ and for $\sigma_2>0$ one takes $k=\kappa_2(\omega_t)=p+iq$ with the complex propagation constant of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]; amplitudes $e_i\in\mathbb C^{3}\setminus\{0\}$ and $e_r,e_t\in\mathbb C^{3}$ and $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega_j)$ satisfying the conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b)-(c) in their media, and the four stationary interface identities of [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] holding on $\mathbb R^{2}\times I$ for a nonempty open interval $I$. Then:

**(a) [Common frequency]** The transmitted amplitude is nonzero and $\omega_i=\omega_t=:\omega$ for some $\omega>0$. If $e_r\ne0$, then $\omega_r=\omega$ as well; if $e_r=0$, assign $\omega_r=\omega$ conventionally, since an absent field cannot determine a frequency. Matching is proved directly from the interface characters, so the lossless-only physical scope of [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] is not used to infer the Ohmic branch.

**(b) [Amplitude system and solution]** all three electric amplitudes are tangential to $S$, and the two tangential interface identities reduce to
$$e_i+e_r=e_t,\qquad Y_1\,(e_i-e_r)=Y_2\,e_t,\qquad Y_1:=\frac{k_1}{\mu_1\omega}>0,\qquad Y_2:=\frac{k}{\mu_2\omega};$$
hence $e_r=r\,e_i$ and $e_t=t\,e_i$ with the complex scalars
$$r=\frac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad t=\frac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2};$$
in particular the reflected and transmitted electric phasors are parallel to the incident one (normal-incidence polarisation preservation), and $t\ne0$. The reflection coefficient is zero exactly when $Y_1=Y_2$, in particular at a lossless impedance-matched interface; the zero reflected field remains part of the theorem.

**(c) [Lossless transmitting medium]** if $\sigma_2=0$ then $Y_2=1/Z_2>0$ with $Z_2=\sqrt{\mu_2/\varepsilon_2}$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]], so
$$r=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_1+Z_2}\in\mathbb R,\qquad t=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}\in\mathbb R,$$
in agreement with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]; the period-$T$ averaged normal fluxes of the stored-energy model, $T=2\pi/\omega$ ([[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](d), [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]), are $\langle S_i\cdot n\rangle=\frac{|e_i|^{2}}{2Z_1}$, $\langle S_r\cdot n\rangle=-\frac{|e_r|^{2}}{2Z_1}$ and $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=\frac{|e_t|^{2}}{2Z_2}$, and with $R:=r^{2}$, $T:=\frac{Z_1}{Z_2}t^{2}=\frac{4Z_1Z_2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^{2}}$ one has $R+T=1$; $R$ is the reflected and $T$ the transmitted fraction of the incident normal averaged flux.

**(d) [Ohmic transmitting medium]** if $\sigma_2>0$ then $Y_2=\kappa_2(\omega)/(\mu_2\omega)$ has $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=p/(\mu_2\omega)>0$, and
$$r=\frac{Y_1-Y_2}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad t=\frac{2Y_1}{Y_1+Y_2},\qquad |r|^{2}+\frac{\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{Y_1}\,|t|^{2}=1 .$$
The second summand is the fraction of the incident period-averaged normal flux that enters the conductor at the interface; the transmitted field has the exact decay factor $e^{-qx_3}$ (the explicit factorization $e^{i(p+iq)x_3}=e^{-qx_3}e^{ipx_3}$) and, by the Ohmic dissipation clause of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]], the entering flux is absorbed in the conductor: the reflected fraction $|r|^{2}$ and the absorbed fraction $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^{2}$ add to $1$.

**(e) [Scope]** no existence or uniqueness of interface-consistent data, no oblique incidence, no anisotropic or dispersive media, no ideal conductor ($\sigma_2=\infty$), no nonlinear response and no empirical claim is made. The interface identities are the stationary plane-interface conditions of the model, supplied for compact interfaces by [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]; the flux identities are the model's stored-energy and Ohmic-dissipation reading, not an observational claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-media normal-incidence setting of the Statement, the wave data $(k_j,\omega_j,e_j)$ with $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega_j)$, the unit normal $n=e_3$, and the four stationary interface identities [A1] on $\mathbb R^2\times I$.

[A1] The four stationary interface identities of the Statement hold for all $(y,t)\in\mathbb R^2\times I$; the proof uses the two tangential identities and derives the normal-incidence reduction directly.

[F1] Plane-wave structure in each medium ([[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]): the amplitude conditions $k_j\cdot e_j=0$, $k_j\times e_j=\omega_j\mu h_j$, $k_j\times h_j=-\omega_j\varepsilon e_j$ with the constants of the medium of wave $j$; the solution family $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)$; and, for a lossless medium with real wavevector $k$ and $e\ne0$, the pointwise identities with $B=\hat k\times E/v$, $|B|=|E|/v$ and the period-averaged flux $\langle S\rangle=|e|^2k/(2\mu\omega)$ of the stored-energy model.

[F2] Normal-incidence instance of phase matching ([[pthm-em-phase-matching]](a)): for three nonzero plane waves in two homogeneous isotropic lossless media satisfying the amplitude conditions and the two tangential interface identities, the tangential wavevectors and the frequencies agree; at normal incidence this gives $\omega_i=\omega_r=\omega_t$ in the lossless case with all three amplitudes nonzero.

[F3] Admittance system ([[lem-em-admittance-interface-solve]]): for complex $Y_1,Y_2$ with $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$ and data satisfying $E_i+E_r=E_t$, $Y_1(E_i-E_r)=Y_2E_t$, one has $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$, $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$; if $Y_1>0$ real then $|r|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$ with $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$; and if $Y_1>0$ is real and $Y_2$ purely imaginary then $|r|=1$.

[F4] The normal-incidence interface lemma ([[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]]): for real $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$, $Z_j=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}$, and $E_i,E_r,E_t$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfying $E_i+E_r=E_t$, $(E_i-E_r)/Z_1=E_t/Z_2$, one has $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$, $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $R+T=1$ for $R=|r|^2$, $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$.

[F5] Character independence ([[lem-em-exponential-character-open-set-independence]]): a real-part-zero finite character sum on a nonempty open set has vanishing grouped coefficients; in particular if $\operatorname{Re}(c\,e^{i\lambda\cdot z})=0$ on a nonempty open set for a single frequency $\lambda$ and coefficient $c$, then $c=0$ (the $\nu=\lambda$ group has no negative-conjugate partner when the last coordinate has a definite sign).

[F6] The complex exponential: $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$ and $\exp(x)=e^x$ for real $x$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]); for real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ with $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[F7] Period averages ([[lem-em-period-average]]): the period average of $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})$ is $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d)$, with the componentwise inner-product and cross-product forms.

[F8] Stored energy and Ohmic dissipation ([[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]): $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$, $S=E\times H$, the local balance $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E$, and with $J_f=\sigma E$ and symmetric positive semidefinite $\sigma$ the nonnegative dissipation density $E\cdot\sigma E$.

[F9] Medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $Z_j=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}>0$, $v_j=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{-1/2}$, and for $\sigma_2>0$ the complex propagation constant $k=\kappa_2(\omega)=p+iq$ with $p,q>0$, whose existence and root selection rest on [[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]; for $\sigma_2>0$ also $2pq=\mu_2\sigma_2\omega$ and $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=p/(\mu_2\omega)$.

[F10] Complex arithmetic, conjugation and modulus ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), and nonnegative square roots with $\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt a\sqrt b$ for $a,b\ge0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F11] Inner and cross products: $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_lx_ly_l$ and the coordinate cross product, bilinear and alternating, with $u\times v$ orthogonal to $u$ and $v$; the decomposition $x=x^\tau+(x\cdot n)n$ with $x^\tau\perp n$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]).

[F12] The laboratory setting, fields and units ([[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]) and the declared lossless/Ohmic branches ([[post-em-material-closure]]).

[F13] One-dimensional FTC and integrability ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]), improper integrals at infinity as limits of proper integrals ([[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]]), and $e^{-2qL}\to0$ as $L\to\infty$ for $q>0$ ([[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; evaluate the normal-incidence traces as characters, apply the character lemma to the combined six-component data to force the common frequency, solve the resulting two-equation admittance system, and compute the lossless and Ohmic flux budgets.

1.1 [Transversality and the trace identity] Since $k_j\cdot e_j=0$ and $k_j\cdot n\ne0$ for each actual wave ($k_i\cdot n=k_1>0$, $k_r\cdot n=-k_1<0$, and $k_t\cdot n=k$ with $k>0$ in the lossless case or $k=p+iq$ with $p>0$ in the Ohmic case), each electric amplitude is tangential: writing $e_j=(e_j\cdot n)n+e_j^\tau$ by [F11] gives $0=k_j\cdot e_j=(k_j\cdot n)(e_j\cdot n)$. Likewise $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega_j)$ is tangential because $k_j$ is normal. Evaluating at $x=(y,0)$ gives $k_j\cdot x=0$, so $E_j=\operatorname{Re}(e_j e^{-i\omega_jt})$ and $H_j=\operatorname{Re}(h_j e^{-i\omega_jt})$ there; the two tangential interface identities of [A1] are identities of tangential fields, and for tangential $w$ the vanishing $n\times w=0$ forces $w=0$ by [F11], so with the sign convention $A_j:=(e_j,h_j)$ and $\lambda_j:=(0,0,-\omega_j)\in\mathbb C^3$ they read $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(A_i e^{i\lambda_i\cdot z}+A_r e^{i\lambda_r\cdot z}-A_t e^{i\lambda_t\cdot z}\bigr)=0$ for all $z=(y,t)\in\mathbb R^2\times I$, by the additivity of the real part in [F10]. [given, A1, F1, F10, F11, algebra]

2.1 [The transmitted amplitude is nonzero] Suppose $e_t=0$; then $h_t=k\,(n\times e_t)/(\mu_2\omega_t)=0$ and $A_t=0$, so the identity of step 1.1 has the two terms $A_i,A_r$ with nonzero frequency parts $-\omega_i,-\omega_r$. Since $-\overline{\lambda_j}=(0,0,+\omega_j)$ has positive last coordinate while every actual $\lambda_l$ has negative last coordinate, [F5] applied to the electric and magnetic traces separately gives: for each actual frequency $\nu$, the sum of the coefficients of the waves with that frequency vanishes. If $e_r=0$ then $A_r=0$ and the electric trace is a single character with coefficient $e_i\ne0$, contradicting [F5]. If $e_r\ne0$ and $\lambda_r\ne\lambda_i$, both groups are singletons and the electric trace gives $e_i=0$ and $e_r=0$, again a contradiction; hence $\lambda_r=\lambda_i$, that is $\omega_r=\omega_i$, and the electric and magnetic trace coefficients at that frequency vanish: $e_i+e_r=0$ and $h_i+h_r=0$. By step 1.1, $h_i=(k_1/(\mu_1\omega_i))(n\times e_i)$ and $h_r=(-k_1/(\mu_1\omega_i))(n\times e_r)$, so $h_i+h_r=(k_1/(\mu_1\omega_i))\,n\times(e_i-e_r)=(k_1/(\mu_1\omega_i))\,n\times(2e_i)=0$, hence $n\times e_i=0$; together with $e_i\cdot n=0$ from step 1.1 this gives $e_i=0$ by [F11], contradicting $e_i\ne0$. Therefore $e_t\ne0$. [step 1.1, F1, F5, F10, F11, algebra]

3.1 [Common frequency] By step 2.1, $A_t=(e_t,h_t)$ is nonzero; $A_i$ is nonzero because $e_i\ne0$; if $e_r\ne0$ then $A_r\ne0$. Applying [F5] to the combined six-component identity of step 1.1 and grouping as in step 2.1: for each actual frequency $\nu$ the signed sum of the $A_j$ over the waves with that frequency vanishes. If the frequencies of the nonzero-$A_j$ waves were not all equal, some group would contain exactly one of them and would give $\pm A_j=0$, a contradiction; and negative-conjugate partners cannot occur because of the sign of the last coordinate. Hence: if $e_r\ne0$, then $\lambda_i=\lambda_r=\lambda_t$, so $\omega_i=\omega_r=\omega_t$; if $e_r=0$, then $\lambda_i=\lambda_t$, so $\omega_i=\omega_t$ and $\omega_r$ is unconstrained by the absent field, matching the Statement. Setting $\omega:=\omega_i=\omega_t$, the two identities of step 1.1 with the common frequency $-\omega$ in the exponent give, after applying [F5] to the single-frequency electric and magnetic traces, $e_i+e_r=e_t$ and $h_i+h_r=h_t$. This also proves the lossless nonzero-reflected case via the normal-incidence instance [F2] of the phase-matching theorem, which is consistent with the direct argument just given. [step 2.1, step 1.1, F2, F5, F10, algebra]

4.1 [The amplitude system, part (b)] With the common frequency of step 3.1, $Y_1:=k_1/(\mu_1\omega)>0$ is real and positive, and $h_i=Y_1\,n\times e_i$, $h_r=-Y_1\,n\times e_r$, $h_t=(k/(\mu_2\omega))\,n\times e_t=:Y_2\,n\times e_t$ by [F1] and [F11]; note $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=p/(\mu_2\omega)>0$ in the Ohmic case and $Y_2>0$ real in the lossless case, so $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$ in both. The magnetic identity of step 3.1 reads $n\times\bigl(Y_2e_t-Y_1(e_i-e_r)\bigr)=0$, and its argument is tangential, so $Y_1(e_i-e_r)=Y_2e_t$ by [F11]; together with $e_i+e_r=e_t$ this is exactly the system of [F3], and since $Y_1+Y_2\ne0$ the solution formulas $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$, $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ hold with $e_r=r\,e_i$, $e_t=t\,e_i$; here $r,t$ are scalars in $\mathbb C$ multiplying the fixed nonzero vector $e_i$, so the reflected and transmitted electric phasors are parallel to the incident one. Moreover $t\ne0$ because $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$ by [F3] and [F10]; and $r=0$ if and only if $Y_1=Y_2$. [step 3.1, F1, F3, F10, F11, algebra]

5.1 [Lossless transmitting medium, part (c)] If $\sigma_2=0$ then $k=\omega/v_2>0$ by the Statement, so $Y_2=k/(\mu_2\omega)=\omega/(v_2\mu_2\omega)=1/(v_2\mu_2)=1/Z_2$ by [F9] ($v_2\mu_2=\sqrt{\mu_2/\varepsilon_2}=Z_2$), and $Y_1=1/Z_1$ similarly; hence substituting $Y_j=1/Z_j$ into the formulas of step 4.1 gives $r=(1/Z_1-1/Z_2)/(1/Z_1+1/Z_2)=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$, both real, the same formulas as in the scalar parametrisation of [F4]. The period-averaged normal fluxes at the interface: for a lossless wave with real wavevector the flux of [F1] is $\langle S_j\rangle=|e_j|^2k_j/(2\mu_j\omega)$ with $\omega$ the common frequency, so $\langle S_i\cdot n\rangle=|e_i|^2k_1/(2\mu_1\omega)=|e_i|^2/(2Z_1)$ because $k_1/(\mu_1\omega)=Y_1=1/Z_1$; similarly $\langle S_r\cdot n\rangle=|e_r|^2(-k_1)/(2\mu_1\omega)=-|e_r|^2/(2Z_1)$ and $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=|e_t|^2k/(2\mu_2\omega)=|e_t|^2/(2Z_2)$. With $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$, the identity $R+T=1$ is [F4]; since $|e_r|^2=R|e_i|^2$ and $|e_t|^2=(Z_2/Z_1)T|e_i|^2=|e_i|^2 T Z_2/Z_1$, the three fluxes are $|e_i|^2/(2Z_1)$ times $1$, $-R$ and $T$ respectively, which is the stated fraction reading. [step 4.1, F1, F4, F9, F10, algebra]

5.2 [Ohmic transmitting medium: system and budget, part (d) first half] If $\sigma_2>0$ then $k=\kappa_2(\omega)=p+iq$ with $p,q>0$ by [F9], so $Y_2=(p+iq)/(\mu_2\omega)$ has $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=p/(\mu_2\omega)>0$ and $\operatorname{Im}Y_2=q/(\mu_2\omega)>0$; the solution formulas of step 4.1 give $r,t$, and [F3] gives $|r|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$ and $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$. Since $\operatorname{Im}Y_2\ne0$, the numerator $Y_1-Y_2$ of $r$ is nonzero, so $r\ne0$ in this branch. [step 4.1, F3, F9, F10, algebra]

6.1 [Evanescent transmitted field and entering flux] With $k=p+iq$ and the common frequency, the transmitted field factorizes exactly: for $x_3\in\mathbb R$, $i(kx_3-\omega t)=-qx_3+i(px_3-\omega t)$, and [F6] gives $e^{i(kx_3-\omega t)}=e^{-qx_3}(\cos(px_3-\omega t)+i\sin(px_3-\omega t))$, so $E_t(x,t)=e^{-qx_3}\operatorname{Re}(e_t e^{i(px_3-\omega t)})$ componentwise (the exact decay factor $e^{-qx_3}$), and $H_t=e^{-qx_3}\operatorname{Re}(h_t e^{i(px_3-\omega t)})$ for the same reason since $h_t$ is a constant phasor. The period-averaged normal flux of the transmitted field is, by the cross-product form of [F7] applied to the factorized fields, $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=e^{-2qx_3}\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl((e_t\times\overline h_t)\cdot n\bigr)$; from $h_t=Y_2\,n\times e_t$ with $Y_2=(p+iq)/(\mu_2\omega)$ by step 4.1, $\overline h_t=\overline{Y_2}\,n\times\overline e_t=((p-iq)/(\mu_2\omega))\,n\times\overline e_t$ by [F10], and the triple-product expansion of [F11] gives $e_t\times(n\times\overline e_t)=n\,|e_t|^2-\overline e_t\,(e_t\cdot n)=n\,|e_t|^2$ because $e_t$ is tangential; hence $(e_t\times\overline h_t)\cdot n=(p-iq)|e_t|^2/(\mu_2\omega)$ and $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=e^{-2qx_3}p|e_t|^2/(2\mu_2\omega)=:F(x_3)$. At the interface $x_3=0$ this equals $(p/(\mu_2\omega))|e_t|^2/2$, and dividing by the incident flux $|e_i|^2/(2Z_1)=Y_1|e_i|^2/2$ of step 5.1 (which applies to medium 1, lossless) gives $\frac{p}{\mu_2\omega Y_1}|t|^2=\frac{\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{Y_1}|t|^2$, the stated entering fraction of the incident period-averaged normal flux. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F6, F7, F10, F11, algebra]

7.1 [Ohmic absorption] In the conductor the free current is the conduction current $J_f=\sigma_2E_t$ with the declared positive scalar $\sigma_2$ (the model of [F1] has no external free current), and the Ohmic dissipation density of [F8] averaged over a period is $d(x_3):=\sigma_2\langle|E_t|^2\rangle=\sigma_2|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/2$ by [F7] applied to the factorized field of step 6.1; the flux of step 6.1 is $F(x_3)=p|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/(2\mu_2\omega)$. Since $2pq=\mu_2\sigma_2\omega$ by [F9], $F'(x_3)=-2q\,p|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/(2\mu_2\omega)=-pq|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/(\mu_2\omega)=-\sigma_2|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/2=-d(x_3)$: the flux lost per unit length is exactly the Ohmic dissipation. For every $L>0$ the integrand $d$ is continuous on $[0,L]$, hence Riemann integrable by [F13], and the exponential antiderivative is differentiable through the endpoints; the fundamental theorem [F13] gives $\int_0^Ld(x_3)\,dx_3=\sigma_2|e_t|^2(1-e^{-2qL})/(4q)=F(0)-F(L)$, where the last identity uses $p/(2\mu_2\omega)=\sigma_2/(4q)$, which is $2pq=\mu_2\sigma_2\omega$ rearranged. Since $q>0$, $e^{-2qL}\to0$ as $L\to\infty$ by [F13], and defining the improper integral as the limit of the proper integrals per [F13] gives $\int_0^\infty d(x_3)\,dx_3=\sigma_2|e_t|^2/(4q)=F(0)$: the whole entering flux is dissipated in the conductor, and with the budget of step 5.2 the reflected fraction $|r|^2$ and the absorbed fraction $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ add to $1$. [step 5.2, step 6.1, F8, F9, F13, algebra]

8.1 [Scope, part (e)] All conclusions are conditional on the given wave data and the interface identities [A1]; the argument used only the two tangential identities, the amplitude conditions and dispersion of [F1], the character lemma [F5], the admittance algebra [F3], the Euler form [F6] and the period averages [F7]; the normal interface identities, the optional normal-root selection rule and any outgoing condition were not used, and the oblique-incidence theorem [F2] was cited only as the consistent lossless cross-check. Nothing about existence or uniqueness of interface-consistent data, oblique incidence, anisotropy, dispersion, ideal conductors ($\sigma_2=\infty$), nonlinear response or empirical data is claimed; the entering-flux absorption reading is the model's stored-energy and Ohmic-dissipation statement, not an observational claim. The interface identities are stated hypotheses on the noncompact plane; for compact interfaces they follow from [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]. No choice principle is used: every quantity is finite-dimensional algebra in the given data, and the only limiting passage is the explicit exponential improper integral of step 7.1. [given, step 7.1, F2, F12] ∎

## Statement

Assume the following plane-interface setting with the same stationary interface identities as [[pthm-em-phase-matching]]: two homogeneous isotropic lossless scalar media at rest (medium 1 in $\{x_3<0\}$, constants $\varepsilon_1,\mu_1>0$; medium 2 in $\{x_3>0\}$, constants $\varepsilon_2,\mu_2>0$; both $\sigma=0$), the plane interface $S=\{x_3=0\}$ with normal $n=e_3$, and the plane-wave structure of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]. Let $\omega>0$, let $\kappa\in\mathbb R^{2}$ (identified with the tangential plane $\{x_3=0\}$) satisfy $0<|\kappa|<K_1:=\omega(\varepsilon_1\mu_1)^{1/2}$, put $k_{13}:=\sqrt{K_1^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}}>0$ and define wavevectors $$k_i:=\kappa+k_{13}\,n,\qquad k_r:=\kappa-k_{13}\,n,\qquad k_t:=\kappa+k_{t3}\,n,$$ where $k_{t3}\in\mathbb C$ satisfies $k_{t3}^{2}=K_2^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}$ with $K_2:=\omega(\varepsilon_2\mu_2)^{1/2}$ and is selected by non-growth in the $x_3>0$ half-space: $$k_{t3}=\sqrt{K_2^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}}>0\ \ (|\kappa|<K_2),\qquad k_{t3}=0\ \ (|\kappa|=K_2),\qquad k_{t3}=i\beta,\ \beta:=\sqrt{|\kappa|^{2}-K_2^{2}}>0\ \ (|\kappa|>K_2).$$ [This transmitted phase data is the interface-consistent, bounded choice: the propagating and evanescent branches of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](d),(e); the common $(\kappa,\omega)$ is declared here for each actual wave, also when a reflected amplitude is zero or the critical transmitted root is zero; the nonzero phase-matching theorem explains this matching where its hypotheses apply, and an absent reflected field has no determined phase labels.] Fix the orthonormal tangential frame $\hat\kappa:=\kappa/|\kappa|$ and $\hat y:=n\times\hat\kappa$, and consider the two polarisations: (s) [transverse electric] $e_i=E_i\hat y$, $e_r=E_r\hat y$, $e_t=E_t\hat y$ with $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$, $E_i\ne0$, and $h_j:=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega)$; (p) [transverse magnetic] $h_i=H_i\hat y$, $h_r=H_r\hat y$, $h_t=H_t\hat y$ with $H_i,H_r,H_t\in\mathbb C$, $H_i\ne0$, and electric amplitudes $e_j:=-(k_j\times\hat y)H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ (the same computation shows that in both cases the pairs satisfy the amplitude conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b) in their media). For each polarisation define the amplitudes along the fixed tangential directions $E^{(s)}_j:=e_j\cdot\hat y$ and, in the case (p), $E^{(p)}_j:=e_j\cdot\hat x$ with $\hat x:=\hat\kappa$; assume the four stationary interface identities of [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] hold on $\mathbb R^{2}\times I$ for a nonempty open interval $I$. Then:

**(a) [Amplitude system]** for $\chi=s$ in every branch, and for $\chi=p$ when $k_{t3}\ne0$, the tangential interface identities reduce to $$E^{\chi}_i+E^{\chi}_r=E^{\chi}_t,\qquad Y^{\chi}_1\bigl(E^{\chi}_i-E^{\chi}_r\bigr)=Y^{\chi}_2E^{\chi}_t,$$ with the admittances $$Y^s_1=\frac{k_{13}}{\mu_1\omega},\qquad Y^p_1=\frac{\varepsilon_1\omega}{k_{13}},\qquad Y^s_2=\frac{k_{t3}}{\mu_2\omega},\qquad Y^p_2=\frac{\varepsilon_2\omega}{k_{t3}}\quad(k_{t3}\ne0).$$ Write $k_{j3}:=k_j\cdot n$ for the signed components, so $k_{i3}=k_{13}$ and $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$. Here $Y_1^\chi>0$ uses the positive incident normal magnitude $k_{13}$, whereas the signed reflected component is $k_r\cdot n=-k_{13}$; $Y_1^\chi$ is not defined from that negative component. No $Y_2^p$ is defined at $k_{t3}=0$. hence, whenever $Y^{\chi}_1+Y^{\chi}_2\ne0$, $$r_\chi:=\frac{E^{\chi}_r}{E^{\chi}_i}=\frac{Y^{\chi}_1-Y^{\chi}_2}{Y^{\chi}_1+Y^{\chi}_2},\qquad t_\chi:=\frac{E^{\chi}_t}{E^{\chi}_i}=\frac{2Y^{\chi}_1}{Y^{\chi}_1+Y^{\chi}_2}$$ ([[lem-em-admittance-interface-solve]](a)); the reflected and transmitted amplitude symbols are defined by these fixed-direction conventions, and sign conventions for full vector amplitudes may reverse a reflected amplitude relative to this convention.

**(b) [Propagating branch and Snell's law]** if $|\kappa|<K_2$ then all three wavevectors are real, $Y_1^s,Y_1^p,Y_2^s,Y_2^p>0$ are real, and with $\theta_j\in(0,\pi/2)$ defined by $\sin\theta_j=|\kappa|/|k_j|$ one has $\theta_r=\theta_i$ and $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$, $n_j=c(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}$ ([[pthm-em-phase-matching]](c), [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]); the period-averaged normal fluxes are $Y^{\chi}_1|E^{\chi}_i|^{2}/2$, $-Y^{\chi}_1|E^{\chi}_r|^{2}/2$ and $Y^{\chi}_2|E^{\chi}_t|^{2}/2$, so $$R_\chi:=|r_\chi|^{2},\qquad T_\chi:=\frac{Y^{\chi}_2}{Y^{\chi}_1}|t_\chi|^{2},\qquad R_\chi+T_\chi=1 .$$

**(c) [Brewster condition]** In the finite-admittance branches, $r_\chi=0$ if and only if $Y^{\chi}_1=Y^{\chi}_2$; in particular, if $\mu_1=\mu_2$ and $|\kappa|<K_2$, for unequal indices $n_1\ne n_2$, $r_p=0$ holds at exactly one admissible incidence angle $\theta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$, characterised by $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1$, and $r_s\ne0$ at that angle. For equal indices $n_1=n_2$ (and equal permeabilities), the media are identical, $Y_1^\chi=Y_2^\chi$ and $r_s=r_p=0$, $t_s=t_p=1$ for every allowed incidence angle; there is no unique distinguished Brewster angle.

**(d) [Total internal reflection]** if $|\kappa|>K_2$ (which requires $n_1>n_2$, $|\kappa|=K_1\sin\theta_i$ with $\theta_i>\theta_c:=\arcsin(n_2/n_1)$ in the notation of (b)), then $Y^{s}_2=i\beta/(\mu_2\omega)$ and $Y^{p}_2=-i\varepsilon_2\omega/\beta$ are purely imaginary, $$|r_s|=|r_p|=1,\qquad t_s,t_p\ne0,\qquad |t_\chi|^{2}=\frac{4(Y^{\chi}_1)^{2}}{(Y^{\chi}_1)^{2}+|Y^{\chi}_2|^{2}}>0,$$ the transmitted field decays as $e^{-\beta x_3}$ and its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically while its tangential averaged flux does not vanish ([[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](e)); the reflected wave carries the whole incident normal averaged flux.

**(e) [Critical angle]** if $|\kappa|=K_2$ then $k_{t3}=0$: the transmitted wave travels along the interface, its tangential electric amplitude vanishes in the (p) case and $Y^{s}_2=0$ in the (s) case, and $r_s=1$, $t_s=2$, $r_p=-1$, $t_p=0$ with vanishing transmitted normal averaged flux. The critical TM branch is solved from the nonsingular equations $E_i^p+E_r^p=k_{t3}H_t/(\omega\varepsilon_2)=0$ and $H_i+H_r=H_t$, not by dividing by $k_{t3}$; they give $H_r=H_i$ and $H_t=2H_i$. The transmitted TM electric vector can have a nonzero normal component even though its tangential amplitude is zero.

**(f) [Scope]** the statements are conditional on the interface identities and on the given wave data; no existence or uniqueness of interface-consistent data is claimed. Excluded: anisotropic media, complex $\varepsilon$ or $\mu$ and absorption in either medium (only the lossless dielectric case with the evanescent transmitted branch is covered), dispersive media, moving media, the ideal conductor, nonlinear response, and all claims about signal speeds, group velocities, information transfer or empirical data. The statements for $Y^{\chi}_1+Y^{\chi}_2=0$ (which cannot occur in the stated branches, where $\operatorname{Re}Y^{\chi}_1>0$ and $\operatorname{Re}Y^{\chi}_2\ge0$) are excluded; the notation 'angle of refraction' is used only where $k_t$ is real.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two-media lossless setting of the Statement, its common $(\kappa,\omega)$ and wavevectors $k_i,k_r,k_t$, the two polarisation data families, and the four stationary interface identities [A1] on $\mathbb R^2\times I$.

[A1] The four stationary interface identities of [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] hold for all $(y,t)\in\mathbb R^2\times I$.

[F1] Plane-wave structure ([[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]): the amplitude conditions $k_j\cdot e_j=0$, $k_j\times e_j=\omega\mu_jh_j$, $k_j\cdot h_j=0$, $k_j\cdot k_j=\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2$ and the solution form $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega)$; the lossless pointwise identities $B=\hat k\times E/v$ and period-averaged flux $\langle S\rangle=|e|^2k/(2\mu\omega)$ for real $k$; and, in the evanescent branch, the factorization with decay $e^{-\beta n'\cdot x}$, the vanishing normal averaged flux and the positive tangential averaged fluxes for the two transverse polarisations.

[F2] The angle laws ([[pthm-em-phase-matching]](c)): for real wavevectors at a lossless interface, $\theta_r=\theta_i$ and $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$ with the same angle conventions, together with the parameters $v_j$ and $n_j=c/v_j$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]].

[F3] Admittance algebra ([[lem-em-admittance-interface-solve]]): (a) the solution formulas for the two-equation system; (b) for real $Y_1>0$ the identity $|r|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$ with $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$; (c) for real $Y_1>0$ and purely imaginary $Y_2$ the identities $|r|=1$ and $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/(Y_1^2+|Y_2|^2)>0$; (d) the real-positive specialisation agreeing with [[lem-em-interface-wave-linear-system]].

[F4] Period averages ([[lem-em-period-average]]) and the stored-energy/flux definitions $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$, $S=E\times H$ of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]].

[F5] Geometry of the fixed frame: $\hat x=\hat\kappa=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $\hat y=n\times\hat\kappa$, with the right-handed orthonormal triad relations $\hat x\times\hat y=n$, $\hat y\times n=\hat x$, $n\times\hat x=\hat y$ and the reversed signs; the cross product is bilinear with $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to $u$ and $v$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]).

[F6] Medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $K_j=\omega(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}$, $v_j=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{-1/2}$, $n_j=c(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}$, $k_{13}^2=K_1^2-|\kappa|^2$, $k_{t3}^2=K_2^2-|\kappa|^2$ and the branch selection of the Statement.

[F7] Complex arithmetic, conjugation, modulus ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) with nonnegative square roots ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) and the existence of complex square roots ([[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]).

[F8] Trigonometry: $\sin(\arcsin y)=y$ with sine strictly increasing on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ ([[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]); $\tan$ restricts to a strictly increasing bijection $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\to\mathbb R$ with the principal inverse ([[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]); $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ ([[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]]); $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ with $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$ ([[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]); sine is strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ and cosine strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\sin 0=0$, $\cos 0=1$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]).

[F9] The laboratory setting, fields and units ([[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]) and the declared lossless branches ([[post-em-material-closure]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; verify the amplitude conditions for the two polarisation families, reduce the tangential interface identities to scalar admittance systems in the fixed frame, and read off the propagating, Brewster, evanescent and critical cases from the admittance algebra and the medium plane-wave structure.

1.1 [Both polarisation families satisfy the amplitude conditions] For (s), $k_j\cdot e_j=E_j\,k_j\cdot\hat y=0$ because $k_j=\kappa+k_{j3}n$ and $\hat y\perp\kappa,n$; and $k_j\times e_j=E_jk_j\times\hat y=E_j(\kappa\times\hat y+k_{j3}n\times\hat y)=E_j(|\kappa|n+k_{j3}\hat x)$ by [F5], which equals $\omega\mu_jh_j$ with $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega)$ by definition. For (p), $e_j=-(k_j\times\hat y)H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ and $k_j\cdot e_j=0$ because $k_j\cdot(k_j\times\hat y)=0$ by the orthogonality in [F5]; further $k_j\times e_j=-(k_j\times(k_j\times\hat y))H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)=\bigl[(k_j\cdot k_j)\hat y-k_j(k_j\cdot\hat y)\bigr]H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2)\hat yH_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)=\omega\mu_jH_j\hat y=\omega\mu_jh_j$, using $k_j\cdot\hat y=0$ and $k_j\cdot k_j=\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2$ of [F1]. Hence in both cases the pairs $(e_j,h_j)$ satisfy the amplitude conditions of [F1] in their media, with $k_j\cdot k_j=\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2$ and $k_j\cdot e_j=0$. [given, F1, F5, F7, algebra]

2.1 [The tangential interface identities in the fixed frame] By the orthogonal decomposition of [F5], the tangential parts of the electric amplitudes are: for (s), $e_j^\tau=e_j=E_j\hat y$; for (p), $e_j^\tau=(k_{j3}H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j))\hat x$ because $e_j=(k_{j3}\hat x-|\kappa|n)H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ from $k_j\times\hat y=|\kappa|n-k_{j3}\hat x$ by [F5]. Similarly the magnetic amplitudes are tangential: $h_j=H_j\hat y$ in (p), and in (s) $h_j=E_j(\kappa\times\hat y+k_{j3}n\times\hat y)/(\mu_j\omega)=E_j(|\kappa|n+k_{j3}\hat x)/(\mu_j\omega)$ with tangential part $k_{j3}E_j\hat x/(\mu_j\omega)$ and, for the reflected wave with $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$, tangential part $-k_{13}E_r\hat x/(\mu_1\omega)$. Since the interface identities hold for all $(y,t)$ with the common $(\kappa,\omega)$, each is, after division by the nonzero unit complex number $e^{i\kappa\cdot y}$ of modulus one, of the form $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(W\,e^{-i\omega t}\bigr)=0$ on the nonempty open set $\mathbb R^2\times I$ for a constant vector $W$ in the one-dimensional span of $\hat x$ or $\hat y$; the amplitude-vanishing clause (a) of [F1], applied componentwise to the single character at the fixed wavevector $\kappa$, forces $W=0$. Concretely: the tangential electric identity gives $E_i+E_r=E_t$ in (s) and $E^{(p)}_i+E^{(p)}_r=E^{(p)}_t$ in (p); the tangential magnetic identity gives $k_{t3}E_t/(\mu_2\omega)=k_{13}(E_i-E_r)/(\mu_1\omega)$ in (s) and $H_i+H_r=H_t$ in (p), where $E^{(p)}_j=k_{j3}H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ by definition, and converting $H_j=Y^p_jE^{(p)}_j$ for $j=i,t$ and $H_r=-Y^p_1E^{(p)}_r$ (the reflected sign entering through $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$) turns the last identity into $Y^p_1(E^{(p)}_i-E^{(p)}_r)=Y^p_2E^{(p)}_t$. Writing $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)$, $Y^p_1=\varepsilon_1\omega/k_{13}$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/k_{t3}$ gives the two systems of (a). [given, A1, step 1.1, F5, F7, algebra]

3.1 [Solution of the systems, part (a)] In the (s) branch, $Y^s_1>0$ is real and positive, and $Y^s_2$ is real positive for $|\kappa|<K_2$, zero at the critical point, and $i\beta/(\mu_2\omega)$ for $|\kappa|>K_2$; in every case $\operatorname{Re}(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)=Y^s_1>0$, so $Y^s_1+Y^s_2\ne0$. In the (p) branch with $k_{t3}\ne0$, $\operatorname{Re}Y^p_1=Y^p_1>0$ and $\operatorname{Re}Y^p_2=0$ or $>0$, so again $Y^p_1+Y^p_2\ne0$. The admittance lemma [F3](a) therefore applies to each scalar system of step 2.1 and gives $r_\chi=(Y^\chi_1-Y^\chi_2)/(Y^\chi_1+Y^\chi_2)$ and $t_\chi=2Y^\chi_1/(Y^\chi_1+Y^\chi_2)$; in particular $t_\chi\ne0$ because its numerator $2Y^\chi_1\ne0$. [step 2.1, F3, F7, algebra]

3.2 [Critical angle, part (e)] Let $|\kappa|=K_2$; then $k_{t3}=0$ by [F6], so $Y^s_2=0$ and no $Y^p_2$ is defined (a division by $k_{t3}$ is not performed). For (s), the system of step 2.1 reads $E_i+E_r=E_t$ and $Y^s_1(E_i-E_r)=0$ with $Y^s_1>0$, so $E_r=E_i$ and $E_t=2E_i$, i.e. $r_s=1$ and $t_s=2$. For (p), $E^{(p)}_t=k_{t3}H_t/(\omega\varepsilon_2)=0$ and $E^{(p)}_i=k_{13}H_i/(\omega\varepsilon_1)$, $E^{(p)}_r=-k_{13}H_r/(\omega\varepsilon_1)$ by the fixed-direction definitions of step 2.1; the tangential electric identity $E^{(p)}_i+E^{(p)}_r=0$ gives $H_r=H_i$, and the tangential magnetic identity $H_i+H_r=H_t$ gives $H_t=2H_i$; hence $r_p=E^{(p)}_r/E^{(p)}_i=-H_r/H_i=-1$ and $t_p=E^{(p)}_t/E^{(p)}_i=0$. The transmitted normal averaged flux vanishes: $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl((e_t\times\overline h_t)\cdot n\bigr)$ by [F4], and with $h_t=H_t\hat y$ and $e_t=-(k_t\times\hat y)H_t/(\omega\varepsilon_2)=-|\kappa|H_tn/(\omega\varepsilon_2)$ (because $k_t=\kappa$ and $\kappa\times\hat y=-|\kappa|n$ by [F5]), the vector $e_t\times\overline h_t$ is a multiple of $n\times\hat y$, which is orthogonal to $n$: $(e_t\times\overline h_t)\cdot n=0$. The transmitted electric vector $-|\kappa|H_tn/(\omega\varepsilon_2)$ has a nontrivial normal component whenever $H_t\ne0$. [step 2.1, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

4.1 [Propagating branch: angles and fluxes, part (b)] Let $|\kappa|<K_2$. Then $k_{t3}=\sqrt{K_2^2-|\kappa|^2}>0$ and all three wavevectors are real by [F6]; the four admittances of step 2.1 are real and positive. With $|k_i|=|k_r|=K_1$ and $|k_t|=K_2$ from $|k_j|^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{j3}^2$, the angles $\theta_j:=\arcsin(|\kappa|/|k_j|)\in(0,\pi/2)$ are well defined by [F8] since $0<|\kappa|<K_2<K_1$; then $\sin\theta_r=|\kappa|/K_1=\sin\theta_i$, so $\theta_r=\theta_i$ by the strict increase of sine and of $\arcsin$ in [F8], and $K_1\sin\theta_i=|\kappa|=K_2\sin\theta_t$, which is $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$ after multiplying by $c/\omega$ and using $n_j=cK_j/\omega=c(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}$ by [F6]; this is the same angle law as [F2]. The period-averaged normal fluxes: for (s), the flux of [F1] is $\langle S_j\rangle=|e_j|^2k_j/(2\mu_j\omega)$ with $|e_j|^2=|E^{(s)}_j|^2$ and $k_j\cdot n=k_{j3}$, so the normal fluxes are $k_{j3}|E^{(s)}_j|^2/(2\mu_j\omega)$, i.e. $Y^s_1|E^{(s)}_i|^2/2$, $-Y^s_1|E^{(s)}_r|^2/2$, $Y^s_2|E^{(s)}_t|^2/2$; for (p) the same $\langle S_j\cdot n\rangle=|e_j|^2k_{j3}/(2\mu_j\omega)$ equals $Y^p_j\,|E^{(p)}_j|^2/2$ up to the reflected sign, because $|e_j|^2=\mu_j|H_j|^2/\varepsilon_j$ and $|E^{(p)}_j|=|k_{j3}||H_j|/(\varepsilon_j\omega)$ give $|e_j|^2k_{j3}/(2\mu_j\omega)=k_{j3}|H_j|^2/(2\varepsilon_j\omega)$ for the incident and transmitted signs, while the reflected signed component $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$ produces the minus sign, as in the Statement. With $R_\chi=|r_\chi|^2=|E^\chi_r|^2/|E^\chi_i|^2$ and $T_\chi=(Y^\chi_2/Y^\chi_1)|t_\chi|^2=Y^\chi_2|E^\chi_t|^2/(Y^\chi_1|E^\chi_i|^2)$, the budget $R_\chi+T_\chi=1$ is [F3](b) applied with the real positive $Y^\chi_1,Y^\chi_2$. [step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, F6, F8, algebra]

4.2 [Total internal reflection, part (d)] Let $|\kappa|>K_2$; then $K_2<K_1$, so $n_2<n_1$, and $k_{t3}=i\beta$ with $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^2-K_2^2}>0$ by [F6]. Hence $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)=i\beta/(\mu_2\omega)$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/(i\beta)=-i\varepsilon_2\omega/\beta$ are purely imaginary by [F7], while $Y^\chi_1>0$ is real; the admittance lemma [F3](c) gives $|r_s|=|r_p|=1$ and $|t_\chi|^2=4(Y^\chi_1)^2/((Y^\chi_1)^2+|Y^\chi_2|^2)>0$, so $t_\chi\ne0$. The transmitted wave is the evanescent branch of [F1] with $n'=n$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$ and $k_t\cdot k_t=K_2^2=\varepsilon_2\mu_2\omega^2$: the field factorizes with the decay factor $e^{-\beta x_3}$, its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically, and its tangential averaged flux is strictly positive; since $|r_\chi|=1$, the reflected normal averaged flux equals minus the incident normal averaged flux, i.e. the reflected wave carries the whole incident normal averaged flux. [step 3.1, F1, F3, F6, F7, algebra]

5.1 [Brewster condition, part (c)] In each finite-admittance branch the formula of step 3.1 gives $r_\chi=0$ exactly when the numerator $Y^\chi_1-Y^\chi_2$ vanishes, i.e. $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$. Assume now $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu$ and $|\kappa|<K_2$, so that the (p) admittances are real positive. The condition $Y^p_1=Y^p_2$ reads $\varepsilon_1/k_{13}=\varepsilon_2/k_{t3}$; substituting $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$ and $k_{j3}=(\omega n_j/c)\cos\theta_j$ (from $k_{13}=K_1\cos\theta_i=(\omega n_1/c)\cos\theta_i$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos\theta_t=(\omega n_2/c)\cos\theta_t$) gives $n_1\cos\theta_t=n_2\cos\theta_i$. Together with Snell's law $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$ of step 4.1, squaring both and eliminating $\sin^2\theta_t$ gives $(n_1^2-n_2^2)\bigl[n_2^2-(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2\theta_i\bigr]=0$: indeed $n_1^2(1-\sin^2\theta_t)=n_2^2\cos^2\theta_i$ and $\sin\theta_t=(n_1/n_2)\sin\theta_i$ yield $n_1^2n_2^2-n_1^4\sin^2\theta_i=n_2^4-n_2^4\sin^2\theta_i$, i.e. $n_2^2(n_1^2-n_2^2)=(n_1^2-n_2^2)(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2\theta_i$. If $n_1\ne n_2$, division by the nonzero first factor gives $\sin^2\theta_i=n_2^2/(n_1^2+n_2^2)$; since $0<\theta_i<\pi/2$ and sine is strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$ by [F8], this determines the unique admissible angle $\theta_B:=\arcsin\bigl(n_2/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}\bigr)\in(0,\pi/2)$, at which $r_p=0$ by construction. At this angle $\cos\theta_B>0$: cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ by [F8], so $0<\theta_B<\pi/2$ gives $\cos\theta_B>\cos(\pi/2)=0$. The Pythagorean identity of [F8] then gives $\cos\theta_B=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta_B}=n_1/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}$, so $\tan\theta_B=\sin\theta_B/\cos\theta_B=n_2/n_1$ by the definition of tangent in [F8]; no other admissible angle has this tangent, because tangent is strictly increasing on $(0,\pi/2)$ by [F8]. Also $r_s\ne0$ at $\theta_B$, because $Y^s_1=Y^s_2$ would give $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ (the $\mu$ factors being equal), hence $K_1^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{13}^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{t3}^2=K_2^2$ and $n_1=n_2$, contrary to hypothesis. If instead $n_1=n_2$ and $\mu_1=\mu_2$ then $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ and the two media are identical: $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ and $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ give $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$, so $r_s=r_p=0$ and $t_s=t_p=1$ at every admissible angle (where the (p) formula applies), with no distinguished Brewster angle. ## Example

Adopt the isotropic scalar Ohmic branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] at rest and the exact quantities of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] and [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]]. Let the declared parameters be $$\varepsilon=4\ \mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \mu=1\ \mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \sigma=100\ \mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \omega=3\ \mathrm s^{-1};$$ these are declared model parameters of the illustration, not measured values of any material. The numerical evaluations below use these SI units: $a,b,r$ have unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $p,q$ have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and $\delta$ has unit m; $t=a/b$ is dimensionless. Then: (i) $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}=36$, $b=\mu\sigma\omega=300$, $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\sqrt{91296}$ and $t=a/b=3/25=0.12\le1/4$, so the good-conductor regime of [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]](c) applies; (ii) the exact propagation and attenuation constants are $p=\sqrt{(r+36)/2}$ and $q=\sqrt{(r-36)/2}$, with $pq=b/2=150$ exactly; the decimal evaluations $r\approx302.15228$, $p\approx13.00293$, $q\approx11.53586$ satisfy $q<\sqrt{b/2}=\sqrt{150}\approx12.24745$ with $$|q-\sqrt{150}|\approx0.71159\le 2t\sqrt{150}=0.24\sqrt{150}\approx2.93939,$$ and for the skin depth $\delta=1/q\approx0.08669$ against $\sqrt{2/b}=1/\sqrt{150}\approx0.08165$ one has $$|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\approx0.00504\le 4t\sqrt{2/b}=0.48\sqrt{2/b}\approx0.03919 .$$ Thus the exact skin depth satisfies the stated good-conductor bound with the margin predicted by the theorem. (iii) for $\sigma=0$ (same $\varepsilon,\mu,\omega$) one has $b=0$, $q=0$, no attenuation and $\delta=+\infty$ by the convention of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]](c); the inequalities of (ii) do not apply, consistently with the exclusion recorded in [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]](f). (iv) [Scope] the computation is an exact check of the stated inequalities for the declared model parameters (with dimensionless ratio $t$); it reports no measurement, no material identification and no empirical claim, and the decimal evaluations are displayed only as approximate illustrations of the exact expressions.

## Verification



**Proof technique:** direct substitution in the exact identities and bounds of the skin-depth theorem, with the decimal displays read as roundings of the exact radicals.

**Given:** The declared parameters $\varepsilon=4$, $\mu=1$, $\sigma=100$, $\omega=3$ as the stated dimensionless representatives of the SI quantities of the Example, the branch assumption of [[post-em-material-closure]], and the exact quantities $a,b,r,p,q,\delta,t$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] and [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]].

[A1] The declared Ohmic branch with $\sigma>0$: the plane-wave attenuation theorem [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]] holds, with its clauses (a)-(f) as stated, in particular the exact identities of (b) and the good-conductor bounds of (c) for $t\le1/4$.

[F1] The medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2$, $b=\mu\sigma\omega$, $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, $p=\sqrt{(r+a)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}$, $\delta=1/q$ for $\sigma>0$ and $\delta=+\infty$ for $\sigma=0$; $t:=a/b$.

1.1 [Substitution, clause (i)] By [F1], $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2=1\cdot4\cdot9=36$ and $b=\mu\sigma\omega=1\cdot100\cdot3=300$; hence $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt{36^2+300^2}=\sqrt{1296+90000}=\sqrt{91296}$ and $t=a/b=36/300=3/25$. The regime condition $3/25\le1/4$ is $12\le25$ after multiplying by $100$, so the good-conductor bounds of [A1](c) apply. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 [Exact identities, clause (ii)] By [F1] and [A1](b), $p=\sqrt{(r+a)/2}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{91296}+36)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{91296}-36)/2}$ and $pq=b/2=150$ exactly. Consequently $q^{2}<b/2$ because $\sqrt{91296}-36<\sqrt{91296}+36$ by the strict positivity of $36$, so $q<\sqrt{150}=\sqrt{b/2}$; and the exact bounds of [A1](c) read $|q-\sqrt{150}|\le(6/25)\sqrt{150}=\frac{2\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\mu\sigma\omega}{2}}$ and $|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\le(12/25)\sqrt{2/b}=\frac{4\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu\sigma\omega}}$. [A1, F1, algebra]

1.3 [The $\sigma=0$ exclusion, clause (iii)] For the same $\varepsilon,\mu,\omega$ and $\sigma=0$, [F1] gives $b=0$, $r=a$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}=0$ and $\delta=+\infty$ by the convention of [F1]; the identities and bounds of [A1](b),(c) carry the hypothesis $b>0$, equivalently $\sigma>0$, and are not evaluated at $b=0$, which is the exclusion recorded in [A1](f). [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 [Decimal displays and the bound comparisons] The decimal numbers displayed in clause (ii) of the Example are the stated roundings of the exact quantities $r=\sqrt{91296}$, $p=\sqrt{(r+36)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-36)/2}$, $\delta=1/q$, $\sqrt{150}$ and $\sqrt{2/300}$; reading them as roundings, the comparisons $|q-\sqrt{150}|\le(6/25)\sqrt{150}$ and $|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\le(12/25)\sqrt{2/b}$ displayed there are instances of the exact inequalities of step 1.2, and the numerical magnitudes quoted in the Example are not independent assertions of exact decimal arithmetic. In particular the inequalities hold with the margin predicted by [A1](c) for the declared dimensionless ratio $t=3/25$. [step 1.2, A1, algebra]

3.1 [Scope, clause (iv)] The computation used only the declared parameters, the branch assumption [A1] and the exact definitions [F1]; it reports no measurement, no material identification and no empirical or statistical claim, and the decimal displays of the Example are approximate illustrations of the exact expressions, as stated. No choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 1.3, A1, F1] ∎

## Example

Adopt the setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with two lossless media at rest, equal permeabilities $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu>0$ and declared refractive indices $n_1=1$, $n_2=3/2$ (declared model parameters, not optical measurements), so that $\varepsilon_j=n_j^{2}/(c^{2}\mu)$ and $K_j=n_j\omega/c$ in the notation of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]. Then: (i) [Brewster angle] by [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]](c) the TM amplitude vanishes exactly at the unique angle $\theta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$ with $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1=3/2$, i.e. $\sin\theta_B=3/\sqrt{13}$, $\cos\theta_B=2/\sqrt{13}$; the transmitted angle satisfies $n_1\sin\theta_B=n_2\sin\theta_t$, hence $\sin\theta_t=2/\sqrt{13}$, and $\theta_B+\theta_t=\pi/2$; (ii) [Amplitudes] at $\theta_i=\theta_B$ one has $Y^{p}_1=Y^{p}_2=\sqrt{13}/(2c\mu)$, hence $r_p=0$ and $t_p=1$; the remaining $s$-amplitudes are $Y^{s}_1=2/(\sqrt{13}c\mu)$, $Y^{s}_2=9/(2\sqrt{13}c\mu)$ and $$r_s=\frac{2/\sqrt{13}-9/(2\sqrt{13})}{2/\sqrt{13}+9/(2\sqrt{13})}=-\frac{5}{13},\qquad t_s=\frac{8}{13};$$ (iii) [Flux budget] with $R_s=|r_s|^{2}=25/169$ and $T_s=(Y^{s}_2/Y^{s}_1)|t_s|^{2}=(9/4)(64/169)=144/169$ one has $R_s+T_s=169/169=1$ exactly, while the TM channel has $R_p=0$, $T_p=1$; (iv) [Scope] the numbers are declared model parameters; the example is a deterministic computation of the classical interface model, reports no measurement, and a pure TM incident wave has zero reflected field at the Brewster angle. For incident data with a nonzero TE component, the surviving reflected field is TE-polarised because $r_p=0$ and $r_s\ne0$; no unpolarised-beam statistics are modelled here.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct substitution in the oblique-incidence theorem and the medium parameters, with all numerical values kept exact.

**Given:** The lossless two-media setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with $\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu>0$, $n_1=1$, $n_2=3/2$, $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$, and the Brewster angle $\theta_B$ of [A1](c).

[A1] The oblique-incidence theorem [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]]: its clause (a) gives the two admittance systems with $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)$, $Y^p_1=\varepsilon_1\omega/k_{13}$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)$, $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/k_{t3}$ and the amplitude formulas; clause (b) gives the angle law $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$, the normal fluxes $Y^\chi_1|E^\chi_i|^2/2$, $-Y^\chi_1|E^\chi_r|^2/2$, $Y^\chi_2|E^\chi_t|^2/2$ and $R_\chi+T_\chi=1$ with $R_\chi=|r_\chi|^2$, $T_\chi=(Y^\chi_2/Y^\chi_1)|t_\chi|^2$; clause (c) gives the unique Brewster angle with $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1$ for $n_1\ne n_2$ and the nonzero $s$-reflection there.

[F1] Medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $K_j=\omega(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}=\omega n_j/c$ for $\mu_j=\mu$, $k_{13}=\sqrt{K_1^2-|\kappa|^2}=K_1\cos\theta_i$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos\theta_t$ for $|\kappa|<K_2$, and $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$.

[F2] Trigonometry: $\sin(\arcsin y)=y$ with sine strictly increasing on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ ([[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]); $\tan$ the strictly increasing principal inverse on $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ with $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ ([[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]); $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ ([[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]]); $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$ ([[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]); sine strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]); and $\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x$ ([[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]).

1.1 [The Brewster angle and its sine and cosine, clause (i)] Since $n_1=1\ne3/2=n_2$ and $\mu_1=\mu_2$, [A1](c) gives a unique Brewster angle $\theta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$ with $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1=3/2$. By [F2], $\sin^2\theta_B=\tan^2\theta_B/(1+\tan^2\theta_B)=(9/4)/(13/4)=9/13$; since $\theta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$ and sine is strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$, $\sin\theta_B>0$, hence $\sin\theta_B=3/\sqrt{13}$; and $\cos\theta_B=\sin\theta_B/\tan\theta_B=(3/\sqrt{13})/(3/2)=2/\sqrt{13}$. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 [Transmitted angle and the right-angle relation, clause (i)] Snell's law $n_1\sin\theta_B=n_2\sin\theta_t$ of [A1](b) gives $\sin\theta_t=(2/3)(3/\sqrt{13})=2/\sqrt{13}$. Since also $\cos\theta_B=2/\sqrt{13}=\sin\theta_t$ and $\sin(\pi/2-\theta_B)=\cos\theta_B$ by [F2], the equality $\sin\theta_t=\sin(\pi/2-\theta_B)$ holds with $\theta_t,\pi/2-\theta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$; sine is strictly increasing on that interval, hence injective, so $\theta_t=\pi/2-\theta_B$, i.e. $\theta_B+\theta_t=\pi/2$. [step 1.1, A1, F2, algebra]

3.1 [The admittances, clause (ii)] By [F1], $K_1=\omega/c$, $K_2=3\omega/(2c)$, $k_{13}=K_1\cos\theta_B=(\omega/c)(2/\sqrt{13})$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos\theta_t=K_2\sin\theta_B=(3\omega/(2c))(3/\sqrt{13})=9\omega/(2\sqrt{13}c)$. With $\varepsilon_1=1/(c^2\mu)$ and $\varepsilon_2=9/(4c^2\mu)$, the admittances of [A1](a) are $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu\omega)=2/(\sqrt{13}c\mu)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu\omega)=9/(2\sqrt{13}c\mu)$, $Y^p_1=\varepsilon_1\omega/k_{13}=\sqrt{13}/(2c\mu)$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/k_{t3}=(9/(4c^2\mu))\omega\cdot2\sqrt{13}c/(9\omega)=\sqrt{13}/(2c\mu)$, so $Y^p_1=Y^p_2$ exactly. [step 1.1, step 2.1, A1, F1, algebra]

4.1 [The amplitudes, clause (ii)] By [A1](a) and step 3.1, $r_p=(Y^p_1-Y^p_2)/(Y^p_1+Y^p_2)=0$ and $t_p=2Y^p_1/(Y^p_1+Y^p_2)=1$. For the $s$-channel, factoring the common positive scale $1/(\sqrt{13}c\mu)$ from numerator and denominator, $r_s=(2-9/2)/(2+9/2)=(-5/2)/(13/2)=-5/13$ and $t_s=2\cdot2/(2+9/2)=4/(13/2)=8/13$. [step 3.1, A1, algebra]

5.1 [Flux budget, clause (iii)] By [A1](b), $R_s=|r_s|^2=25/169$ and $T_s=(Y^s_2/Y^s_1)|t_s|^2=(9/4)(64/169)=144/169$, so $R_s+T_s=(25+144)/169=169/169=1$ exactly; and in the TM channel $R_p=|r_p|^2=0$, $T_p=(Y^p_2/Y^p_1)|t_p|^2=1$, so $R_p+T_p=1$ as well. [step 4.1, A1, algebra]

6.1 [Scope, clause (iv)] All quantities are declared model parameters and the computation is exact rational or quadratic-irrational algebra of the interface model; no measured refractive index, no absorption, no unequal-permeability interface, no unpolarised-beam statistics and no empirical claim is used. Since $r_p=0$ and $r_s\ne0$ at $\theta_B$, an incident wave with a nonzero TE component has a surviving reflected TE component; no statement about random or unpolarised beams is made. No choice principle is used. [given, step 5.1, A1] ∎

## Example

Adopt the setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with equal permeabilities $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu>0$ and declared indices $n_1=3/2$, $n_2=1$ (declared model parameters, not measurements), choose the tangential wavevector $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$, so $\hat\kappa=e_1$ and $\hat y=n\times\hat\kappa=e_2$, and take the transverse-electric polarisation $e_j=E_j\hat y$. Let the incidence angle be given by $\sin\theta_i=4/5$, which exceeds the critical angle $\theta_c$ with $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1=2/3$, so $|\kappa|=K_1\sin\theta_i=(6/5)(\omega/c)>(\omega/c)=K_2$. Then with $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^{2}-K_2^{2}}=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$ and $k_{13}=(\omega/c)(3/2)(3/5)=(9/10)(\omega/c)$: (i) [Reflection] $Y^{s}_1=9/(10\mu c)$, $Y^{s}_2=i\sqrt{11}/(5\mu c)$ and $$r_s=\frac{9/10-i\sqrt{11}/5}{9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5},\qquad |r_s|=1,\qquad t_s=\frac{9/5}{9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5},\qquad |t_s|^{2}=\frac{324}{125};$$ the reflection factor is the phase $r_s=e^{-2i\varphi}$ with $\varphi=\arctan\!\bigl(2\sqrt{11}/9\bigr)\approx0.63514703$ (about $36.39124^\circ$), i.e. the reflected wave acquires the phase $-2\varphi\approx-1.27029406$ (about $-72.78249^\circ$); (ii) [Transmitted field] the transmitted field is $E_t(x,t)=e^{-\beta x_3}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(E_t\hat y\,e^{i(|\kappa|x_1-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with $\beta=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$: it decays by the factor $e^{-\sqrt{11}/5}\approx0.51514$ when $x_3$ increases by $c/\omega$, its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically, $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle\equiv0$, while its tangential averaged flux is positive, $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}\,\frac{(6/5)(\omega/c)|E_t|^{2}}{2\mu\omega}=e^{-2\beta x_3}\frac{3|E_t|^{2}}{5\mu c}$; (iii) [Flux budget] $|r_s|^{2}+(\operatorname{Re}Y^{s}_2/Y^{s}_1)|t_s|^{2}=1+0=1$, so the whole incident normal averaged flux is reflected, while the evanescent field carries a tangential averaged flux only; (iv) [Scope] the example is an exact deterministic computation of the lossless interface model for declared parameters; it reports no measurement, and the presence of a tangential evanescent flux is not a claim about information speed or signal propagation.

## Verification



**Proof technique:** direct substitution in the oblique-incidence and medium plane-wave theorems with exact rational and quadratic-irrational arithmetic, and an explicit phase computation via Euler's form.

**Given:** The lossless two-media setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with $\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu>0$, $n_1=3/2$, $n_2=1$, the tangential wavevector $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$, the transverse-electric data $e_j=E_j\hat y$ with $\hat y=e_2$, and the incidence data $\sin\theta_i=4/5$.

[A1] The oblique-incidence theorem [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]]: clause (a) and (d) give $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)$, the amplitude formulas, and in the evanescent branch $|r_s|=1$, $|t_s|^2=4(Y^s_1)^2/((Y^s_1)^2+|Y^s_2|^2)>0$ together with the flux budget; clause (d) also records that the transmitted field decays and its normal averaged flux vanishes.

[A2] The medium plane-wave structure [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]: the transmitted evanescent field of clause (e) with the substitution $n'=n$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$: the exact factorization, the vanishing normal component $\langle S\cdot n'\rangle\equiv0$ and the positive tangential averaged flux $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0\rangle=|\kappa_0||e|^2e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}/(2\mu\omega)$ for the transverse-electric data $e=E_0(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)$.

[F1] Medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $K_j=\omega(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}=\omega n_j/c$, $k_{13}^2=K_1^2-|\kappa|^2$, $\beta^2=|\kappa|^2-K_2^2$, $k_{t3}=i\beta$ and $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$.

[F2] Complex arithmetic and modulus ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]): $\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w$, $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z|^2=z\overline z$ and $|z|\ge0$ with $|z|=0$ only for $z=0$; in particular a complex number of modulus one is nonzero and the sum of a complex number and its conjugate is twice its real part.

[F3] Trigonometry and phases: $\arctan$ is the principal inverse tangent with $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ ([[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]); $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ ([[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]]); $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$ ([[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]); cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]); and for real $y$, $\exp(iy)=\cos y+i\sin y$ with $|\exp(iy)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

1.1 [The geometry and the evanescent data] With $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$ one has $\hat\kappa=e_1$, $|\kappa|=(6/5)(\omega/c)$ and $\hat y=n\times\hat\kappa=e_3\times e_1=e_2$; $K_1=(3/2)(\omega/c)$, $K_2=\omega/c$ by [F1], so $|\kappa|=K_1\sin\theta_i$ with $\sin\theta_i=4/5$, and $|\kappa|>K_2$ because $6/5>1$. Hence the evanescent branch applies: $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^2-K_2^2}=\sqrt{(36/25-1)}(\omega/c)=\sqrt{11/25}\,(\omega/c)=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$ and $k_{13}=\sqrt{K_1^2-|\kappa|^2}=\sqrt{(9/4-36/25)}(\omega/c)=\sqrt{81/100}\,(\omega/c)=(9/10)(\omega/c)$; the critical angle satisfies $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1=2/3<4/5=\sin\theta_i$, both angles being in $(0,\pi/2)$. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 [Admittances and reflection data, clause (i)] By [A1](a) and [F1], $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)=9/(10\mu c)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)=i\beta/(\mu\omega)=i\sqrt{11}/(5\mu c)$ and $t_s=2Y^s_1/(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)=(9/(5\mu c))/((9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5)/(\mu c))=(9/5)/(9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5)$; the numerator $9/10-i\sqrt{11}/5$ of $r_s=(Y^s_1-Y^s_2)/(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)$ is the complex conjugate of its denominator, so $|r_s|=1$ by [F2] (and [A1](d)). For the transmitted modulus, $|t_s|^2=4(Y^s_1)^2/((Y^s_1)^2+|Y^s_2|^2)$ by [A1](d); computing $(Y^s_1)^2=81/(100\mu^2c^2)$ and $|Y^s_2|^2=11/(25\mu^2c^2)=44/(100\mu^2c^2)$ gives $|t_s|^2=(324/100)/(125/100)=324/125$. [step 1.1, A1, F2, algebra]

2.2 [The transmitted field and its fluxes, clause (ii)] By $|t_s|^2$-normalised data we take the transmitted electric amplitude $E_t\hat y$ with $E_t=t_sE_i$; the evanescent structure of [A2] applied with $n'=n=e_3$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$, $\beta$ as in step 1.1 and $e=E_t\hat y=E_t(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)$ gives exactly $E_t(x,t)=e^{-\beta x_3}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(E_t\hat y\,e^{i(|\kappa|x_1-\omega t)}\bigr)$, the identity $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle\equiv0$, and the tangential averaged flux $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}|\kappa||E_t|^2/(2\mu\omega)$; substituting $|\kappa|=(6/5)(\omega/c)$ gives $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}(6/5)(\omega/c)|E_t|^2/(2\mu\omega)=e^{-2\beta x_3}3|E_t|^2/(5\mu c)$. The decay over a distance $c/\omega$ is the factor $e^{-\beta c/\omega}=e^{-\sqrt{11}/5}$, whose decimal display in clause (ii) is the stated rounding. [step 1.1, A1, A2, algebra]

3.1 [The reflection phase, clause (i)] Put $Y_1:=9/10$ and $\beta':=\sqrt{11}/5$ in the units $1/(\mu c)$ and $\alpha:=\beta'/Y_1=2\sqrt{11}/9$, so that $r_s=(1-i\alpha)/(1+i\alpha)$; let $\varphi:=\arctan\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $w:=1+i\alpha$, $|w|=\sqrt{1+\alpha^2}$. By [F3], $\tan\varphi=\alpha$ and $1+\tan^2\varphi=\sec^2\varphi$, so $\cos^2\varphi=1/(1+\alpha^2)=1/|w|^2$; since $\cos\varphi>0$ (cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ and $\varphi\in(0,\pi/2)$), $\cos\varphi=1/|w|$ and $\sin\varphi=\alpha\cos\varphi=\alpha/|w|$. Euler's form of [F3] then gives $w=|w|(\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi)=|w|e^{i\varphi}$ and $\overline w=|w|e^{-i\varphi}$ by [F2], so $r_s=\overline w/w=e^{-2i\varphi}$. The decimal values displayed in clause (i) are the stated roundings of $\varphi=\arctan(2\sqrt{11}/9)$ and of the reflected phase $-2\varphi$. [step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 [Flux budget and scope, clauses (iii)-(iv)] By [A1](d), $|r_s|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y^s_2/Y^s_1)|t_s|^2=1$; here $\operatorname{Re}Y^s_2=0$ by step 2.1, so the identity reads $1+0=1$: the whole incident normal averaged flux is reflected, while the tangential averaged flux of step 2.2 is positive and transports no normal flux. All quantities are declared model parameters; the computation is deterministic classical interface algebra, reports no measurement, and neither the tangential evanescent flux nor the reflection phase is a claim about information speed, signal propagation or empirical data. No choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 2.2, A1, F2] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega_t\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open, let $\beta\in\mathbb C$, $\omega>0$, and let $\tilde F,\tilde G:\Omega_t\to\mathbb C^3$ be $C^1$ maps (componentwise, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write $\theta(x_3,t):=\beta x_3-\omega t$ and define $F:\Omega_t\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by $F(x_1,x_2,x_3,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i\theta(x_3,t)}\bigr)$ componentwise, and $G$ likewise from $\tilde G$; here $e^{i\theta}$ is the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] and $\operatorname{Re}$ the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Then $F$ is $C^1$ and, for every point of the domain:
(a) $\partial_{x_j}F=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\partial_{x_j}\tilde F\,e^{i\theta}\bigr)$ for $j=1,2$, $\partial_{x_3}F=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(i\beta\tilde F e^{i\theta}\bigr)$, $\partial_tF=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(-i\omega\tilde F e^{i\theta}\bigr)$, where the divergence and curl are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]];
(b) $\operatorname{div}F=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\partial_1\tilde F_1+\partial_2\tilde F_2+i\beta\tilde F_3)e^{i\theta}\bigr)$;
(c) $\operatorname{curl}F=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\partial_2\tilde F_3-i\beta\tilde F_2,\; i\beta\tilde F_1-\partial_1\tilde F_3,\; \partial_1\tilde F_2-\partial_2\tilde F_1)e^{i\theta}\bigr)$;
(d) [amplitude injectivity] if $C\in\mathbb C^3$ and $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(Ce^{i\varphi_1}\bigr)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(Ce^{i\varphi_2}\bigr)=0$ for two real phases with $\varphi_1-\varphi_2\notin\pi\mathbb Z$, then $C=0$; consequently, if $F=G$ on a nonempty open subset $U$ of $\Omega_t\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$, then $\tilde F=\tilde G$ on the projection of $U$ to $\Omega_t$ (a nonempty open subset of $\Omega_t$).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open set $\Omega_t\subseteq\mathbb R^2$; complex numbers $\beta=p+iq$ ($p,q\in\mathbb R$) and $\omega>0$; $C^1$ maps $\tilde F,\tilde G:\Omega_t\to\mathbb C^3$, with real functions $a_l:=\operatorname{Re}\tilde F_l$ and $b_l:=\operatorname{Im}\tilde F_l$ for $l=1,2,3$; the phase $\theta(x_3,t)=\beta x_3-\omega t$; and the fields $F,G$ of the Statement.

[F1] A map into $\mathbb R^n$ is $C^k$ when each component is, and a $C^1$ component has continuous first partial derivatives; the $j$th partial derivative $\partial_jf(a)=D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the derivative along the coordinate line $t\mapsto f(a+te_j)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F2] $\mathbb C$ is a field with $i^2=-1$, every $z$ has the unique form $z=\operatorname{Re}z+i\operatorname{Im}z$ with real parts, and $\operatorname{Re}$ is $\mathbb R$-linear; in particular $\operatorname{Re}(i\zeta)=-\operatorname{Im}\zeta$, $\operatorname{Re}(-i\zeta)=\operatorname{Im}\zeta$, and for real $a,b,\varphi$ the cartesian multiplication gives $(a+ib)(\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi)=(a\cos\varphi-b\sin\varphi)+i(a\sin\varphi+b\cos\varphi)$, so $\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+ib)(\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi)\bigr)=a\cos\varphi-b\sin\varphi$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

[F3] For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]); the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]).

[F4] The real exponential is $C^\infty$ with $(\exp)'=\exp$ ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]) and $\exp x>0$ for real $x$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]); $(\sin x)'=\cos x$ and $(\cos x)'=-\sin x$ ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]); sums, scalar multiples and products of differentiable real functions satisfy the sum, scalar and product rules and composites satisfy the chain rule for total derivatives, which applies to the affine substitutions $x_3\mapsto\pm qx_3$ and $x_3,t\mapsto px_3-\omega t$ composed with the outer exponential, sine and cosine ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F5] For all real $A,B$, $\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B$ and $\cos(A+B)=\cos A\cos B-\sin A\sin B$ ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]); $\sin(-A)=-\sin A$, $\cos(-A)=\cos A$ and $\sin^2A+\cos^2A=1$ ([[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]); finally $\sin x=0$ if and only if $x\in\pi\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]).

[F6] For a $C^1$ field $F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_1F_1+\partial_2F_2+\partial_3F_3$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=(\partial_2F_3-\partial_3F_2,\ \partial_3F_1-\partial_1F_3,\ \partial_1F_2-\partial_2F_1)$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct: reduce the complex phase to real cartesian factors, differentiate the explicit components along coordinate lines with the real one-variable rules, assemble the divergence and curl, and settle the injectivity clause by a two-phase linear system.

1.1 [Reduction of the phase and of the components] Since $\beta=p+iq$ and $i^2=-1$, $i\theta=i(\beta x_3-\omega t)=i(px_3-\omega t)+i(iqx_3)=-qx_3+i(px_3-\omega t)$; with $\varphi:=px_3-\omega t$ the cartesian form [F3] gives $e^{i\theta}=e^{-qx_3}(\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi)$. By [F2] the component of $\tilde Fe^{i\theta}$ with index $l$ is $e^{-qx_3}\bigl[(a_l\cos\varphi-b_l\sin\varphi)+i(a_l\sin\varphi+b_l\cos\varphi)\bigr]$; taking real parts, $F_l=e^{-qx_3}(a_l\cos\varphi-b_l\sin\varphi)$. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 [The two-phase system] For clause (d), write $C=a+ib$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R^3$. By [F2], $\operatorname{Re}(Ce^{i\varphi_j})=a\cos\varphi_j-b\sin\varphi_j$ componentwise, so $\operatorname{Re}(Ce^{i\varphi_1})=\operatorname{Re}(Ce^{i\varphi_2})=0$ is the system $a_l\cos\varphi_1=b_l\sin\varphi_1$ and $a_l\cos\varphi_2=b_l\sin\varphi_2$ for every $l$. Multiplying the two equations of index $l$ by $\cos\varphi_2$ and $\cos\varphi_1$ and subtracting gives $b_l(\sin\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2-\cos\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2)=0$, and multiplying them by $\sin\varphi_2$ and $\sin\varphi_1$ and subtracting gives $a_l(\cos\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2-\cos\varphi_2\sin\varphi_1)=0$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 [The phase factor and its derivatives] By step 1.1 the real and imaginary parts of $(x_3,t)\mapsto e^{i\theta}$ are $e^{-qx_3}\cos\varphi$ and $e^{-qx_3}\sin\varphi$, which are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^2$ by [F4] (the chain rule applied to the affine substitutions $x_3\mapsto-qx_3$ and $x_3,t\mapsto px_3-\omega t$ composed with the outer exponential, sine and cosine, together with the sum, scalar and product rules), with $\partial_{x_3}e^{-qx_3}=-qe^{-qx_3}$, $\partial_te^{-qx_3}=0$, $\partial_{x_3}\cos\varphi=-p\sin\varphi$, $\partial_{x_3}\sin\varphi=p\cos\varphi$, $\partial_t\cos\varphi=\omega\sin\varphi$ and $\partial_t\sin\varphi=-\omega\cos\varphi$. Pairing these, $\partial_{x_3}e^{i\theta}=(-q+ip)e^{i\theta}=i\beta e^{i\theta}$ and $\partial_te^{i\theta}=-i\omega e^{i\theta}$ by [F2], while $e^{i\theta}$ does not depend on $x_1,x_2$, so $\partial_{x_j}e^{i\theta}=0$ for $j=1,2$. [step 1.1, F2, F4]

2.2 [Transverse derivatives] Fix $j\in\{1,2\}$ and $l\in\{1,2,3\}$. Along the $x_j$-coordinate line the factors $e^{-qx_3}$, $\cos\varphi$ and $\sin\varphi$ of step 1.1 are constant, so the derivative of the partial application is $e^{-qx_3}\bigl[(\partial_ja_l)\cos\varphi-(\partial_jb_l)\sin\varphi\bigr]$ by the sum and scalar rules [F4], the derivatives $\partial_ja_l,\partial_jb_l$ existing by [F1]; by the expansion of step 1.1 applied to $\partial_j\tilde F_l$ in place of $\tilde F_l$, this number is $\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\partial_j\tilde F_l)e^{i\theta}\bigr)$. Hence $\partial_{x_j}F=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\partial_{x_j}\tilde F\,e^{i\theta}\bigr)$ componentwise for $j=1,2$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F4]

2.3 [Injectivity] By the addition and parity formulas [F5], $\sin(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)=\sin\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2-\cos\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2$ and $-\sin(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)=\cos\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2-\cos\varphi_2\sin\varphi_1$. Since $\varphi_1-\varphi_2\notin\pi\mathbb Z$, [F5] gives $\sin(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)\ne0$, so the two equations of step 1.2 force $b_l=0$ and $a_l=0$ for every $l$, that is, $C=0$. [step 1.2, F5]

3.1 [Longitudinal and time derivatives] Fix $l$. Along the $x_3$-line the amplitudes $a_l,b_l$ are constant, so the product and scalar rules [F4] and the derivatives of step 2.1 give $\partial_{x_3}F_l=-qe^{-qx_3}(a_l\cos\varphi-b_l\sin\varphi)+e^{-qx_3}(-pa_l\sin\varphi-pb_l\cos\varphi)$; by [F2], $i\beta(a_l+ib_l)=(-qa_l-pb_l)+i(pa_l-qb_l)$, so $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(i\beta\tilde F_l e^{i\theta}\bigr)=e^{-qx_3}\bigl[(-qa_l-pb_l)\cos\varphi-(pa_l-qb_l)\sin\varphi\bigr]$, which is the displayed expression. Along the $t$-line the amplitudes and $e^{-qx_3}$ are constant, so $\partial_tF_l=e^{-qx_3}(a_l\omega\sin\varphi+b_l\omega\cos\varphi)$; by [F2], $-i\omega(a_l+ib_l)=\omega b_l-i\omega a_l$, so $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(-i\omega\tilde F_l e^{i\theta}\bigr)=e^{-qx_3}(\omega b_l\cos\varphi+\omega a_l\sin\varphi)$, the displayed expression. Assembling the components gives $\partial_{x_3}F=\operatorname{Re}(i\beta\tilde Fe^{i\theta})$ and $\partial_tF=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\tilde Fe^{i\theta})$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F4, algebra]

4.1 [Regularity] Every partial derivative displayed in steps 2.2 and 3.1 is continuous on $\Omega_t\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$: the partial derivatives $\partial_ja_l,\partial_jb_l$ ($j=1,2$) are continuous by [F1], the factors $e^{-qx_3}$, $\cos\varphi$, $\sin\varphi$ and their displayed partial derivatives are smooth by step 2.1, and each displayed formula is a finite sum of products of such continuous functions. Thus all first partial derivatives of $F$ exist and are continuous, so $F$ is $C^1$. [step 2.2, step 3.1, F1, F4]

4.2 [Divergence] By [F6] and steps 2.2 and 3.1, $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_1F_1+\partial_2F_2+\partial_3F_3=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\partial_1\tilde F_1+\partial_2\tilde F_2+i\beta\tilde F_3)e^{i\theta}\bigr)$: indeed, for complex $\zeta_l$ the $\mathbb R$-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$ and distributivity in $\mathbb C$ [F2] give $\operatorname{Re}(\zeta_1e^{i\theta})+\operatorname{Re}(\zeta_2e^{i\theta})+\operatorname{Re}(\zeta_3e^{i\theta})=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\zeta_1+\zeta_2+\zeta_3)e^{i\theta}\bigr)$. [step 2.2, step 3.1, F2, F6, algebra]

4.3 [Curl] Similarly, [F6] together with steps 2.2 and 3.1 gives the three components of $\operatorname{curl}F$ as $\partial_2F_3-\partial_3F_2=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\partial_2\tilde F_3-i\beta\tilde F_2)e^{i\theta}\bigr)$, $\partial_3F_1-\partial_1F_3=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((i\beta\tilde F_1-\partial_1\tilde F_3)e^{i\theta}\bigr)$ and $\partial_1F_2-\partial_2F_1=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\partial_1\tilde F_2-\partial_2\tilde F_1)e^{i\theta}\bigr)$, since [F2] gives $\operatorname{Re}(\zeta e^{i\theta})-\operatorname{Re}(\eta e^{i\theta})=\operatorname{Re}((\zeta-\eta)e^{i\theta})$ for complex $\zeta,\eta$. This is clause (c). [step 2.2, step 3.1, F2, F6, algebra]

5.1 [Open-set consequence] Let $U\subseteq\Omega_t\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ be nonempty open with $F=G$ on $U$. Its projection $\pi(U)$ to $\Omega_t$ is nonempty and open. Fix $x_t\in\pi(U)$; the fibre $\{(x_3,t):(x_t,x_3,t)\in U\}$ is a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, so there are $x_3\in\mathbb R$ and an open interval $J$ of $t$-values on which $(x_t,x_3,t)\in U$; choose $t_1,t_2\in J$ with $0<\omega|t_1-t_2|<\pi$. Put $C:=(\tilde F(x_t)-\tilde G(x_t))e^{i\beta x_3}$. For $j=1,2$, the $\mathbb R$-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$ [F2] and $F=G$ on $U$ give $\operatorname{Re}(Ce^{-i\omega t_j})=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((\tilde F-\tilde G)(x_t)e^{i\theta(x_3,t_j)}\bigr)=F(x_t,x_3,t_j)-G(x_t,x_3,t_j)=0$. The phases $\varphi_j:=-\omega t_j$ are real and $\varphi_1-\varphi_2=-\omega(t_1-t_2)\notin\pi\mathbb Z$, so step 2.3 gives $C=0$. Finally $e^{i\beta x_3}=e^{-qx_3}\bigl(\cos(px_3)+i\sin(px_3)\bigr)$ by step 1.1, where $e^{-qx_3}>0$ by [F4] and $\cos(px_3)+i\sin(px_3)\ne0$ because its real and imaginary parts have $\cos^2(px_3)+\sin^2(px_3)=1\ne0$ [F5]; since a product of nonzero elements of the field $\mathbb C$ is nonzero [F2], $\tilde F(x_t)=\tilde G(x_t)$. As $x_t\in\pi(U)$ was arbitrary and $\pi(U)$ is nonempty open, this is the stated consequence. [step 2.3, F2, F4, F5, algebra] ∎
