## Example

Assume the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]], the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$, and the straight-guide, TEM and separated-phasor conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]]; put $Z:=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$ and $v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$.
(a) [Potential form] Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain and let $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb C)$ (with real-valued potentials included) satisfy $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$ (the plane Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]; a $C^2$ function with $\Delta\varphi=0$ is called harmonic). For either sign $\zeta\in\{+1,-1\}$ define $\tilde E:=-\nabla\varphi$, $\beta:=\zeta\omega/v$ and $\tilde H:=\zeta e_z\times\tilde E/Z$; then the separated real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(\tilde Ee^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(\tilde He^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)})$ satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations with $E_z=B_z=0$ (TEM), and the PEC condition on a smooth wall with unit normal $n$ is equivalent to $\partial_\tau\varphi=0$ along that boundary curve, so that $\varphi$ is constant on each connected component of $\partial A$. Moreover, if $A$ is star-shaped ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), every separated TEM phasor with $C^1$ transverse amplitudes has on the interior a complex harmonic potential $\varphi\in C^2(A;\mathbb C)$, obtained by applying [[cor-closed-exact-and-conservative-equivalence-on-star-shaped-domains]] to the real and imaginary electric amplitudes separately. If the field is nonzero, the equations force $\beta^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$, hence $\beta=\pm\omega/v$, and $\tilde H=\beta e_z\times\tilde E/(\omega\mu)$, giving the two displayed signs. If the field is zero, $\tilde E=\tilde H=0$ solves the equations for every longitudinal label $\beta$, with no dispersion conclusion. The boundary potential description requires the stated continuous differentiable boundary trace (in particular the initial $C^2(\overline A)$ potential has it); the interior exactness supplier alone is not asserted to produce a real potential or automatic boundary extension.
(b) [Single-conductor obstruction] If in the potential-form setting $\partial A$ is connected, then $\varphi$ is constant on $\partial A$, hence $\varphi$ is constant on $\overline A$ by the two-dimensional classical Dirichlet uniqueness [[cor-uniqueness-for-the-classical-dirichlet-problem]], applied to its real and imaginary parts with their respective constants as second solutions, and therefore $\tilde E=\tilde H=0$: a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the potential form. The same potential-form obstruction applies to a rectangular cross-section with a potential in $C^2(A)\cap C(\overline A)$ having constant boundary trace, because this uniqueness supplier does not require a $C^1$ boundary. For rectangular separated TEM amplitudes that are $C^1$ on the interior and continuous on the closure with the classical PEC traces on open edges, the star-centre radial primitive extends continuously to the rectangle closure. The edgewise tangential derivative is the electric trace, so PEC makes the potential constant on each open edge and continuity joins those constants at the corners. Thus this stated rectangular class has no nonzero TEM field.
(c) [Coaxial example] For the following Lebesgue polar-coordinate energy calculation assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<a<b$, $A:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:a<|x|<b\}$ (two boundary components), fix $V\in\mathbb R$, choose the forward label $k:=\omega/v$, and define $\varphi(x):=V\ln(b/|x|)/\ln(b/a)$, so that $\tilde E=V e_r/(|x|\ln(b/a))$ with $e_r:=x/|x|$ and $\tilde H=(V/(Z|x|\ln(b/a)))e_\varphi$ with $e_\varphi:=e_z\times e_r$. Then $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$: indeed $\partial_i\ln|x|=x_i/|x|^2$ by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]), and the second partial derivatives sum to zero; hence $\varphi$ is constant on each boundary circle (values $V$ at $|x|=a$ and $0$ at $|x|=b$), the fields satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations and the PEC conditions, and the relation $k=\omega/v$ is nondispersive with no cutoff. The amplitude integrals computed in polar coordinates with [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] (the Jacobian factor $r$ is read from that formula) are $$W_e:=\tfrac12\varepsilon\int_A|\tilde E|^2\,dA=\tfrac12CV^2,\qquad W_m:=\tfrac12\mu\int_A|\tilde H|^2\,dA=\tfrac12CV^2,\qquad C:=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)};$$ the instantaneous per-length energies are $\tfrac12CV^2\cos^2\theta$ and $\tfrac12LI^2\cos^2\theta$ with $\theta=kx_3-\omega t$; equivalently, with $L:=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)$ and the boundary-current amplitude $I:=2\pi V/(Z\ln(b/a))$ one has $W_m=\tfrac12LI^2$ and $LC=\varepsilon\mu$. The two boundary components carrying distinct constants are exactly what the single-conductor obstruction excludes.
(d) [Scope] The obstruction clause (b) is proved for the continuous-boundary harmonic-potential form. The star-shaped interior classification in (a) covers both signs and the zero field, with boundary conclusions under the stated potential-trace hypotheses; the general reduction of an arbitrary TEM field to the potential form on a merely simply connected non-star-shaped cross-section is not asserted here. The coaxial clause is an explicit conditional computation in the declared model with no empirical content; no lossy, radiation or signal-speed claim is made.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and relations $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$; the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$; the straight-guide, TEM and separated-phasor conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]]; $Z:=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$ and $v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$; a bounded connected $C^1$ domain $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and, in the star-shaped clause, a star-shaped such $A$; a potential $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb C)$ with $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$ (the plane Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], a $C^2$ function with $\Delta\varphi=0$ being harmonic); for the coaxial clause $0<a<b$, $A=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:a<|x|<b\}$, real $V$, and Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The declared real fields satisfy the source-free equations of [F1] of the theorem page exactly when their complex amplitudes satisfy $\widehat{\operatorname{div}}(\tilde E)=0$, $\widehat{\operatorname{div}}(\tilde H)=0$, $\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}(\tilde E)=i\omega\mu\tilde H$, $\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}(\tilde H)=-i\omega\varepsilon\tilde E$, where $\widehat{\operatorname{div}}(w)=\partial_1w_1+\partial_2w_2+i\beta w_3$ and $\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}(w)=(\partial_2w_3-i\beta w_2,\ i\beta w_1-\partial_1w_3,\ \partial_1w_2-\partial_2w_1)$ ([[lem-em-separated-phasor-calculus]], [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] clause (b), [[post-em-material-closure]] clause (b)); a nonzero separated real field has nonzero amplitude, and a separated real field vanishes identically exactly when its amplitude does ([[lem-em-separated-phasor-calculus]] clause (d)).

[F2] Transverse vector identities: for a transverse vector $v$, $e_z\times(e_z\times v)=-v$, $e_z\times v$ is transverse and $|e_z\times v|=|v|$; and $\operatorname{div}(e_z\times\nabla_th)=0$ for $C^2$ $h$ ([[lem-em-transverse-vector-identities]] (a), (c)). Cross-product and scalar-triple-product manipulations are those of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]: $a\cdot(b\times c)=\det[a\ b\ c]$ and $a\times b\perp a,b$.

[F3] Plane harmonic components are smooth, indeed real analytic, in the interior ([[thm-plane-harmonic-functions-are-smooth-and-real-analytic]]); a $C^2$ function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$ has equal mixed partials ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

[F4] Classical Dirichlet uniqueness: if $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, is bounded, nonempty and open and $u,v\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ satisfy $\Delta u=\Delta v$ in $\Omega$ and $u=v$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $u=v$ on $\overline\Omega$; the statement requires no regularity of the boundary ([[cor-uniqueness-for-the-classical-dirichlet-problem]]).

[F5] On an open star-shaped $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a $C^1$ field is closed exactly when it is exact, and exactness uses a $C^2$ potential ([[cor-closed-exact-and-conservative-equivalence-on-star-shaped-domains]], [[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]).

[F6] One-variable and measure tools: for a differentiable function on an interval a vanishing derivative makes it constant, and $\int_a^bG'=G(b)-G(a)$ for $G$ with integrable derivative ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]); $\log'(x)=1/x$ and $\log x=\int_1^xdt/t$ for $x>0$ ([[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]); composites obey the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); the polar-coordinate formula integrates continuous functions on the annulus with Jacobian factor $r$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]), the omitted radial segment being Lebesgue null ([[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]); positive square roots exist and are unique ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F7] In the lossless branch the stored-energy density and flux are those of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]; only its local positive reading is used.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct: verify the potential-form amplitudes against the four amplitude equations and the PEC traces, classify an arbitrary $C^1$ TEM amplitude by the transverse curl components, apply two-dimensional Dirichlet uniqueness to the constant-boundary potentials, and compute the coaxial integrals in polar coordinates.

1.1 [Potential form and the PEC boundary equivalence] Let $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb C)$ with $\Delta\varphi=0$, fix $\zeta\in\{+1,-1\}$, and put $\tilde E:=-\nabla\varphi$, $\beta:=\zeta\omega/v$, $\tilde H:=\zeta e_z\times\tilde E/Z$, with real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(\tilde Ee^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(\tilde He^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)})$. Then $\tilde E_3=0$ and $\tilde H_3=0$ because $e_z\times\tilde E$ and $\nabla\varphi$ are transverse [F2], so $E_z=B_z=0$ (TEM); and the four amplitude equations of [F1] hold: $\widehat{\operatorname{div}}(\tilde E)=-\Delta\varphi=0$; $\widehat{\operatorname{div}}(\tilde H)=\frac{\zeta}{Z}\bigl(\partial_1(-\tilde E_2)+\partial_2(\tilde E_1)\bigr)=-\frac{\zeta}{Z}\operatorname{curl}_2\tilde E=0$ because $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi$ has equal mixed partials [F3]; $\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}(\tilde E)=(i\beta\partial_2\varphi,\ -i\beta\partial_1\varphi,\ \operatorname{curl}_2\tilde E)=i\beta e_z\times\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H$, using $\tilde H=\frac{\beta}{\omega\mu}e_z\times\tilde E$, which holds because $\frac{\beta}{\omega\mu}=\frac{\zeta\omega/v}{\omega\mu}=\frac{\zeta}{v\mu}=\frac{\zeta}{Z}$ since $v\mu=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}=Z$; and $\widehat{\operatorname{curl}}(\tilde H)=i\beta e_z\times\tilde H=i\beta\,\frac{\zeta}{Z}e_z\times(e_z\times\tilde E)=-\frac{i\zeta\beta}{Z}\tilde E=-i\omega\varepsilon\tilde E$ by [F2] and $\frac{\zeta\beta}{Z}=\frac{\omega/v}{Z}=\frac{\omega}{vZ}=\omega\varepsilon$ because $vZ=1/\varepsilon$. Hence the real fields satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations by [F1]. If the potential has a differentiable boundary trace on a smooth wall of $A$ with outward unit normal $n$ (an in-plane unit vector) and tangent $\tau:=e_z\times n$, then $n\times\tilde E=(0,0,n_1\tilde E_2-n_2\tilde E_1)$ and, since $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi$, $n_1\tilde E_2-n_2\tilde E_1=n_2\partial_1\varphi-n_1\partial_2\varphi=-\nabla\varphi\cdot\tau=-\partial_\tau\varphi$, so $n\times\tilde E=-e_z\partial_\tau\varphi$ (only the vanishing of this normal-cross field is used below); likewise $n\cdot\tilde H=\frac{\zeta}{Z}n\cdot(e_z\times\tilde E)=\frac{\zeta}{Z}\tilde E\cdot(n\times e_z)=-\frac{\zeta}{Z}\tilde E\cdot\tau=\frac{\zeta}{Z}\partial_\tau\varphi$ by the scalar triple product and $n\times e_z=-\tau$ [F2]. Since a separated real field vanishes identically exactly when its amplitude does [F1], the PEC conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ hold exactly when $\partial_\tau\varphi=0$ along the wall. [F1, F2, F3, F6, algebra]

1.2 [Converse classification and the star-shaped potential] Let $(\tilde E,\tilde H)$ be $C^1$ transverse amplitudes of a separated TEM field satisfying the four amplitude equations of [F1]. The third components of the two curl equations read $\operatorname{curl}_2\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H_3=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}_2\tilde H=-i\omega\varepsilon\tilde E_3=0$, while the two divergence equations read $\operatorname{div}_t\tilde E=0$ and $\operatorname{div}_t\tilde H=0$ (the $i\beta$-terms vanish with the third components). The transverse part of Faraday reads $(0,0,0)$ in its third component and $(-i\beta\tilde E_2,\ i\beta\tilde E_1,0)=i\beta\,e_z\times\tilde E$ in its transverse components, so $i\beta\,e_z\times\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H$ and, since $\omega\mu>0$, $\tilde H=\frac{\beta}{\omega\mu}e_z\times\tilde E$ with no division by $\beta$. Substituting into the transverse part of Ampere and using $e_z\times(e_z\times\tilde E)=-\tilde E$ [F2] gives $-i\frac{\beta^2}{\omega\mu}\tilde E=-i\omega\varepsilon\tilde E$, that is $(\beta^2-\varepsilon\mu\omega^2)\tilde E=0$. If $\tilde E\ne0$ then $\beta^2=\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$, so $\beta=\pm\omega/v$ by [F6]; if $\tilde E=0$ then Faraday gives $\tilde H=0$, and the zero field solves the equations for every longitudinal label $\beta$ with no dispersion conclusion. Finally, if $A$ is star-shaped and $\tilde E$ is a $C^1$ transverse closed field ($\operatorname{curl}_2\tilde E=0$), then its real and imaginary parts are closed $C^1$ fields on the star-shaped domain, so [F5] supplies $C^2$ potentials for each, hence a complex $\varphi\in C^2(A;\mathbb C)$ with $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi$ after a sign change, and $\operatorname{div}_t\tilde E=0$ makes $\Delta\varphi=0$; no real-only or boundary-extension conclusion is inferred from interior exactness. [F1, F2, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 [Single-conductor obstruction] Suppose $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb C)$ is harmonic on the bounded connected domain $A$ and has constant boundary trace on each connected component of $\partial A$, with the PEC potential description of step 1.1 available. If $\partial A$ is connected, the trace is a single constant $c$, and applying [F4] to the real and imaginary parts of $\varphi$ and of the constant function $c$ gives $\varphi=c$ on $\overline A$; then $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi=0$ and $\tilde H\propto e_z\times\tilde E=0$. For a rectangular cross-section with a potential in $C^2(A)\cap C(\overline A)$ having constant boundary trace the same argument applies, because [F4] requires only a bounded nonempty open set and no boundary regularity. For rectangular separated TEM amplitudes that are $C^1$ on the interior and continuous on the closure with the classical PEC traces on the open edges, let $\psi$ be the radial primitive of the closed field $\tilde E$ from a star centre of the rectangle; it is $C^2$ on the interior with $\nabla\psi=\tilde E$, and since $\tilde E$ is continuous on the closure it extends continuously to the closure and its tangential trace on an open edge is the tangential electric trace, which PEC makes zero; by the one-variable constancy of [F6] the potential is constant on each open edge, and continuity at the corners joins those constants, so the trace is constant on $\partial A$ and [F4] gives $\psi$ constant, hence $\tilde E=0$ and $\tilde H=0$. Thus a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the stated potential form, and the same holds for the stated rectangular class. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6]

2.2 [Coaxial annulus: potential and fields] In the annulus $A=\{a<|x|<b\}$ put $\varphi(x):=V\ln(b/|x|)/\ln(b/a)$ and choose the forward label $k:=\omega/v$ (so $\zeta=+1$). Since $\partial_i\ln|x|=x_i/|x|^2$ by [F6] and the chain rule, $\partial_i\partial_i\ln|x|=1/|x|^2-2x_i^2/|x|^4$ and $\Delta\ln|x|=2/|x|^2-2/|x|^2=0$, so $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$; also $\varphi=V$ on $|x|=a$ and $\varphi=0$ on $|x|=b$, so the trace is constant on each boundary circle. The constructed fields of step 1.1 are then $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi=V e_r/(|x|\ln(b/a))$ with $e_r=x/|x|$, and $\tilde H=e_z\times\tilde E/Z=\bigl(V/(Z|x|\ln(b/a))\bigr)e_\varphi$ with $e_\varphi:=e_z\times e_r$; by step 1.1 they satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations and the PEC conditions, and the longitudinal label satisfies $k=\omega/v$, nondispersive with no cutoff, so $k$ is real and nonzero for every $\omega>0$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F6, algebra]

3.1 [Coaxial energies in polar coordinates] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. With $W_e:=\frac12\varepsilon\int_A|\tilde E|^2dA$ and $W_m:=\frac12\mu\int_A|\tilde H|^2dA$, the polar formula of [F6] (Jacobian $r$; the omitted radial segment is null) and $|\tilde E|^2=Z^2|\tilde H|^2=V^2/(|x|^2\ln^2(b/a))$ give $\int_A|\tilde E|^2dA=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_a^b\frac{V^2}{r^2\ln^2(b/a)}r\,dr\,d\theta=\frac{2\pi V^2}{\ln(b/a)}$, using $\int_a^b dr/r=\ln(b/a)$ by [F6]. Hence $W_e=\frac12\varepsilon V^2\frac{2\pi}{\ln(b/a)}=\frac12CV^2$ with $C:=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)}$, and $W_m=\frac12\mu\frac{V^2}{Z^2}\frac{2\pi}{\ln(b/a)}=\frac12CV^2$ because $\mu/Z^2=\varepsilon$. With $L:=\frac{\mu\ln(b/a)}{2\pi}$ and $I:=\frac{2\pi V}{Z\ln(b/a)}$ one gets $\frac12LI^2=\frac12\frac{\mu\ln(b/a)}{2\pi}\frac{4\pi^2V^2}{Z^2\ln^2(b/a)}=\frac12\frac{2\pi\mu V^2}{Z^2\ln(b/a)}=\frac12CV^2=W_m$, and $LC=\frac{\mu\ln(b/a)}{2\pi}\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)}=\varepsilon\mu$. The instantaneous per-length energies are $\frac12CV^2\cos^2\theta$ and $\frac12LI^2\cos^2\theta$ with $\theta=kx_3-\omega t$, by the definitions of $E$ and $B$ and the identity $\operatorname{Re}(we^{i\theta})^2+|{\operatorname{Im}}(we^{i\theta})|^2=|w|^2$; for $V=0$ all fields and energies vanish. The two boundary components carry the distinct constants $V$ and $0$, which is exactly what the single-conductor obstruction of step 2.1 excludes. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F1, F6, F7, algebra]

4.1 [Scope] Clause (a) is steps 1.1 and 1.2: the potential form gives TEM fields satisfying the equations and turns PEC on a smooth wall into the vanishing tangential potential derivative, the converse classification gives the two nonzero signs $\beta=\pm\omega/v$ and the unrestricted label for the zero field, and the star-shaped interior exactness is used only with the stated potential-trace hypotheses for boundary conclusions. Clause (b) is step 2.1, proved for the continuous-boundary harmonic-potential form and the stated rectangular class; the general reduction of an arbitrary TEM field to the potential form on a merely simply connected non-star-shaped cross-section is not asserted. Clause (c) is steps 2.2 and 3.1: the coaxial computation is conditional, in the declared lossless model, with the polar-measure branch the only place Countable Choice is used, and no lossy, radiation, empirical or signal-speed claim is made. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

This definition fixes the framework's report-record vocabulary; it selects no experiment, records no value, evaluates no indicator and asserts no measurement.\n\n(a) [Primary source] A *primary source* is a declared bibliographic identification of a report (author, title, date, publication, and the identification of the passages actually inspected) together with the declared limits of the reading: which parts of the report were read, which were not, and any carrier defects (for instance corrupted optical-character-recognition text of formulae or tables).\n\n(b) [Comparison quantity and measurand] Let $d\\ge1$ be an integer. These may include the values of $E,B,\\rho,J$ at declared events, the charge parameter $q$, and the declared charge or current integrals of [[def-em-sources]]; declared field circulations and surface fluxes on the admitted fixed geometries of [[def-em-fixed-test-geometry]]; and declared finite-time or period averages of specified derived field quantities, including $u$ and $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]. A declared detector-response integral may be used only when its declared model and integral suppliers establish a finite real value. An extended nonnegative integral with value $+\\infty$ is not a component of this real-valued comparison map or a recorded finite rate.         "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Choice as carried by [[lem-em-exterior-vector-helmholtz-mixed-boundary-existence]], whose variational, Sobolev-compactness and compact-spectral steps use it; the algebraic computations below use no further choice. Let $O\\subset\\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set with $C^\\infty$ boundary, $D:=\\mathbb R^3\\setminus\\overline O$ connected, $k>0$, $\\omega:=ck$ with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and $R>0$ with $\\overline O\\subset B_R(0)$; let $V\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\\overline D\\subseteq V$, and let $(\\widetilde E_{\\rm inc},\\widetilde B_{\\rm inc})$ be a $C^\\infty$ frequency-$\\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pair on $V$ ([[def-em-monochromatic-source-free-phasors]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]). Plane-wave instances are provided by [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]: if $\\kappa\\cdot e=0$, $b=\\kappa\\times e/\\omega$ and $|\\kappa|=\\omega/c$, then $(\\widetilde E_{\\rm inc},\\widetilde B_{\\rm inc})(x)=(e\\,e^{i\\kappa\\cdot x},b\\,e^{i\\kappa\\cdot x})$ satisfies the four phasor equations on $\\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]). Adopt the ideal perfectly conducting (PEC) boundary model: the tangential component of the total electric field vanishes on $\\partial O$. This is a declared idealization of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]] with vanishing fields inside the conductor; it is not one of the finite-conductivity branches of [[post-em-material-closure]], and the induced surface charge and current are neither prescribed nor determined here. Let $e_T$ be the tangential projection of $-\\widetilde E_{\\rm inc}$ on $\\partial O$, and let $\\widetilde E_{\\rm scat}$ be the unique $C^\\infty$ field on $\\overline D$ of [[lem-em-exterior-vector-helmholtz-mixed-boundary-existence]] with $(\\Delta+k^2)\\widetilde E_{\\rm scat}=0$ and $\\operatorname{div}\\widetilde E_{\\rm scat}=0$ on $D$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]), tangential trace $e_T$ on $\\partial O$ and that lemma's outgoing modal condition on $S_R$. Set $\\widetilde B_{\\rm scat}:=(i\\omega)^{-1}\\operatorname{curl}\\widetilde E_{\\rm scat}$ and, on $D$, $\\widetilde E_{\\rm tot}:=\\widetilde E_{\\rm inc}+\\widetilde E_{\\rm scat}$, $\\widetilde B_{\\rm tot}:=\\widetilde B_{\\rm inc}+\\widetilde B_{\\rm scat}$. Then: (a) [Phasor Maxwell] $(\\widetilde E_{\\rm scat},\\widetilde B_{\\rm scat})$ and $(\\widetilde E_{\\rm tot},\\widetilde B_{\\rm tot})$ are $C^\\infty$ frequency-$\\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pairs on $D$; and for every $C^\\infty$ frequency-$\\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pair $(\\widetilde E,\\widetilde B)$ on an open set $O'\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$, the associated real fields of [[def-em-monochromatic-source-free-phasors]] satisfy on $O'\\times\\mathbb R$ the smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\\rho\\equiv0$ and $J\\equiv0$. Consequently the associated real total fields $E_{\\rm tot},B_{\\rm tot}$ satisfy those source-free equations on $D\\times\\mathbb R$. ## Postulate

Adopt as a physical assumption of this framework the following solution-selection rule for the classical vacuum model on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the constants and SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]] (so $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$).

(a) [Formulation] In the potential formulation of [[pthm-em-lorenz-gauge-wave-form]] with the conventions of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], for a $C^2$ potential pair in Lorenz gauge the sourced Maxwell system of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] is equivalent to the decoupled sourced wave equations $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. The wave expression $W$ is invariant under $t\mapsto-t$; where explicit retarded or advanced constructions for a prescribed history exist, they give distinguished particular solutions built from the corresponding forward or backward fundamental kernels. Every other solution differs from a chosen particular solution by a source-free addition; retarded and advanced particular solutions also differ by such an addition. This describes the affine free-solution freedom, not a claim that arbitrary histories have exactly two solutions or that either construction always exists.

(b) [Adopted rule] The framework adopts the retarded branch with no free field added: the physical potential pair of the model is the retarded one, that is, the one whose support and propagation lie in the forward light cones of the source and which carries no field arriving from the past independently of the source. For the zero-incoming model the selected sourced solution has no independently prescribed homogeneous addition. If nonzero Cauchy data are instead prescribed, their compatible homogeneous addition is a separate initial-data model; it is not equivalent to setting every free addition to zero. The advanced construction and independent incoming free fields are excluded by the present retarded selection.

(c) [Status and scope] This is an adopted extra temporal condition carrying the model's arrow-of-time content. It is not a theorem, not a consequence of the time-symmetric wave or Maxwell equations (which admit advanced and free solutions as mathematical objects), and not a deduction from experiment; it asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity, support or decay for any source class, all of which must be supplied separately by theorems of this page. It selects a solution only of the models to which it is applied; it introduces no product of distributions, no source model, no self-force, no radiation reaction, no measured signal and no statistical claim. The retarded compact-source branch to which this selection applies is developed on this page as a conditional theorem, and the point-source branch is developed later on this page; neither existence statement is part of this postulate. For the separately declared point-source branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as in its exact source/field interfaces, and adopt the same no-free-addition retarded selection in the weak equations of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], for the locally integrable field and proper point-current types of [[def-em-weak-sources]]. This extends the selection's model scope explicitly; neither existence nor an arbitrary convolution of noncompact distributions is postulated.

## Source notes

The classical treatments cited above display the retarded and advanced Green functions of the wave operator and then identify the choice of the retarded branch as additional structure imposed on the time-reversal-symmetric equations; they support the formulation of clauses (a)-(b) and the honest non-theorem status recorded in clause (c). They are not evidence for the physical correctness of the choice, and this postulate reports no experiment, measurement or statistical inference. The exact interfaces of the wave form, the gauge conventions, the smooth Maxwell system and the separately adopted weak singular-source equations are those of the cited framework items; the weak point-source extension is an explicit physical selection on the already-adopted singular-source equations, not a deduction from the smooth-only potential theorem, and a consuming theorem must construct its actual history integrals and prove weak admissibility.

## Definition

Let the laboratory region, inertial chart, spatial Euclidean structure and SI units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], in particular $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. A **retarded point-geometry datum** consists of a real charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ in coulombs ([[def-em-sources]](a)) and a prescribed map $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) together with a constant $0\le v_*<c$ such that $|z'(s)|\le v_*$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the spacetime curve $s\mapsto(z(s),s)$ is the laboratory reading of a prescribed massive future timelike worldline of the physical model ([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]]), and $v_*$ is a declared bound on its coordinate speed, not a measured quantity. Write $\Gamma:=\{(z(s),s):s\in\mathbb R\}$ and $D:=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R:x\ne z(t)\}$ for the open off-worldline observation domain. Then:

(a) [Retarded root] For every observation event $(x,t)\in D$ there is exactly one $s=s(x,t)<t$ with $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$; the map $s:D\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^3$, and with the data of (b) below one has $\partial_ts=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$ ([[lem-em-global-retarded-root]], whose $C^3$ branch applies because $z$ is $C^3$ and uniformly subluminal).

(b) [Retarded data] For $(x,t)\in D$ define $R:=x-z(s(x,t))$, $r:=|R|>0$, $n:=R/r$, $\beta:=z'(s(x,t))/c$, $\kappa:=1-n\cdot\beta$, $\dot\beta:=z''(s(x,t))/c$; then $r=c(t-s)$ and $\kappa\in[1-v_*/c,\,1+v_*/c]\subseteq(0,\infty)$. On $D$ the objects $r$ and $n$ are of class $C^3$, $\beta$ and $\kappa$ are of class $C^2$, and $\dot\beta$ is of class $C^1$ (each is a composition of the $C^3$ root with $z$ or its derivatives).

(c) [Emission-event data and emitted spheres] At an emission event $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and a direction $n\in S^2$ put $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$, $t_r:=s_0+r/c$ for $r>0$, and $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $\kappa_0:=1-n\cdot\beta_0$. Then $(x_r,t_r)\in D$ and $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$ for every $r>0$: the sphere $\{x_r\}$ at observation time $t_r$ is emitted at the single event $s_0$.

(d) [Branches and scope] Only the all-time uniformly subluminal branch (a)-(c) is defined by this datum. For a curve prescribed on a finite interval $J$ the same formulas define retarded data only at observation events for which the root equation has a solution $s\in J$; each consumer must assume that cone intersection explicitly. Pointwise subluminality $|z'(s)|<c$ for every finite $s$ does not imply (a): the companion example on the examples page exhibits a smooth curve with $|z'|<c$ pointwise for which the retarded equation has no root at some event, so the uniform bound $v_*<c$, or an explicit cone-intersection hypothesis, is part of the datum. This definition is kinematic: it fixes the root, the retarded data and the notation, and asserts no field, no dynamics, no force law, no self-force and no empirical content. The identification of these data with the emission data of the physical field is made by the selection postulate [[post-em-radiation-selection]] together with the theorems of this page.

## Well-definedness notes

Clauses (a)-(b) are exactly the all-time uniformly subluminal $C^3$ branch of [[lem-em-global-retarded-root]]: that lemma supplies, for every event of $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, existence and uniqueness of the root, the identity of the equality case $s=t$ with $x=z(t)$, the strict inequality $s<t$ on $D$, the derivative formulas with $1-v_*/c\le\kappa\le1+v_*/c$, and the $C^k$ regularity of the root on $D$ for a $C^k$ trajectory; no new analysis is introduced here. Clause (c) is the elementary root check $t_r-s_0=|x_r-z(s_0)|/c=r/c$ combined with the uniqueness in clause (a); no boundedness of $z''$ is used. Clause (d) records the branch boundaries honestly: the finite-history and nonuniform cases are left to consumers, and the failure of existence under mere pointwise subluminality is exhibited on the examples page rather than asserted here. The phrase 'prescribed worldline' is licensed by [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]](a) and (c), which relate chart readings $t\mapsto r(t)$ of massive worldlines to the condition $|r'(t)|<c$. The definition introduces no physical field, so no Maxwell, self-force or empirical assertion is made; the cross-reference to [[post-em-radiation-selection]] records that the retarded root is the kinematic object that the adopted selection turns into an emission time. No choice principle beyond the countable choice already carried by the cited root lemma is used.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), as carried by the surface-measure interface below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on the unit sphere $S^2\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]), let $e_3:=(0,0,1)$ and write $n_3=n\cdot e_3$ for $n\in S^2$. Then:

(a) [Zonal identity] for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$, $$\int_{S^2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}f(u)\,du.$$

(b) [Linear weighted moment] for every continuous $f$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^3$, $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)\,f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\,a_3\int_{-1}^{1}u\,f(u)\,du.$$

(c) [Quadratic weighted moment] for every continuous $f$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^3$, $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^2f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\,a_3^{2}\int_{-1}^{1}u^{2}f(u)\,du+\pi\,(a_1^{2}+a_2^{2})\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^{2})f(u)\,du.$$

(d) [Moments] $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, $\int_{S^2}n\,d\sigma=0$, $\int_{S^2}n_in_j\,d\sigma=(4\pi/3)\delta_{ij}$, and for every $a\in\mathbb R^3$ $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^2d\sigma=\frac{4\pi}{3}|a|^2,\qquad \int_{S^2}|n\times a|^2d\sigma=\frac{8\pi}{3}|a|^2,$$ where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker symbol and $\times$ the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

(e) [Scope] (a)-(d) are identities for the polar surface measure of the unit sphere with only the stated continuity of $f$; they assert no physical field, flux or radiation statement. The measure is finite, so all displayed integrals are absolutely convergent; $f$ need not be nonnegative. For the uses on this page $f$ is a rational function with denominator bounded below by $1-b>0$, hence continuous on $[-1,1]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the polar surface measure $\sigma$ on $S^2$; a continuous $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$ and $a\in\mathbb R^3$; $e_3=(0,0,1)$ and $n_3=n\cdot e_3$; the chart $X$, the parameter region $D$ and the reflection maps $\eta_1,\eta_2,\eta_3$ introduced in steps 1.1 and 2.1.

[F1] For Borel $E\subseteq S^2$, $\sigma(E)=3\lambda_3\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}$; under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $\sigma$ is a finite Borel measure on $S^2$. ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]])

[F2] The chart surface measure on $S^2$ equals $\sigma$; orthogonal transformations of $\mathbb R^3$ preserve $\sigma$; and $\sigma(S^2)=3|B_1|$. ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]])

[F3] For a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface $S$, the chart integral over finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations with a subordinate ambient partition defines a finite Borel measure $\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ independent of the presentation; the same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]])

[F4] A regular parametrized surface patch is a $C^1$ map $X$ from a compact Jordan parameter region $D$ (the closure of its nonempty connected interior) with $X_u\times X_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ$ and no interior parameter point sharing its image with a distinct point of $D$; seam identifications and rank failures may occur on the boundary. For continuous $q$ on the patch image, $\int_Sq\,dS=\int_D(q\circ X)J_X$ with $J_X=|X_u\times X_v|$, and boundary values may be changed on the content-zero parameter boundary without changing the integral. ([[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], [[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], [[lem-parameter-boundary-exceptions-do-not-affect-surface-integrals]])

[F5] Sine and cosine are differentiable with $\sin'=\cos$, $\cos'=-\sin$, $\sin0=0$, $\cos0=1$; $\sin(\pi/2)=1$, $\cos(\pi/2)=0$, $\sin\pi=0$, $\cos\pi=-1$; $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, $\cos(-x)=\cos x$, $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$; sine is strictly increasing on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ and strictly decreasing on $[\pi/2,3\pi/2]$, cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[\pi,2\pi]$, both have range $[-1,1]$; the addition formulas $\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y$, $\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y$ hold; and $\sin x=0$ if and only if $x=m\pi$ for some integer $m$. ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]])

[F6] If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $P(u)=\int_0^uf$, then $P'=f$ there; if $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ with integrable derivative, then $\int_a^bG'=G(b)-G(a)$; and the chain rule holds for composites of totally differentiable maps. ([[thm-ftc-first-part]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

[F7] In $\mathbb R^3$ with the Euclidean inner product and norm, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2$. ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]], [[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]])

[F8] Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and composites of composable $C^k$ maps are $C^k$; $C^k$ means continuous partial derivatives up to order $k$. ([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])

[F9] On the finite measure space $(S^2,\sigma)$ a bounded Borel function $g$ with $|g|\le M$ is integrable, since $\int|g|\,d\sigma\le M\sigma(S^2)<\infty$; the integral is linear in the integrand. ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]])

[F10] For a bounded Jordan set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and a Riemann integrable $g$ whose sections outside a content-zero exceptional set are Jordan measurable with integrable section functions, the iterated integral over either coordinate block equals $\int_Eg$. ([[thm-jordan-fubini-by-sections]])

[F11] $\sigma$ is invariant under the reflection $\omega\mapsto-\omega$, and the substitution identity $\int g\,d\sigma=\int g\circ\eta\,d\sigma$ for a $\sigma$-preserving bijection $\eta$ holds for indicators by definition, extends to simple functions by linearity and to bounded Borel functions by the approximation used in that proof; the first moment satisfies $\int_{S^2}\omega\,d\sigma=0$. ([[lem-first-moment-of-the-unit-sphere-vanishes]])

[F12] $V_3(1)=\pi^{3/2}/\Gamma(5/2)$; $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$ for $s>0$ and $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$, so $\Gamma(5/2)=3\sqrt\pi/4$ and $V_3(1)=4\pi/3$. ([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]], [[cor-real-gamma-one-half-is-root-pi]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; the sphere integral is reduced to the standard rectangular chart, evaluated by Fubini and the fundamental theorem, and the weighted moments are obtained by reflection substitution.

1.1 Define $X(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta)$ and $D:=[0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]$. Then $D$ is a compact Jordan parameter region, being a closed bounded rectangle and the closure of its nonempty connected interior $D^\circ=(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$, and $X$ is $C^1$ on the open neighbourhood $\mathbb R^2$ of $D$ because its components are finite sums and products of the $C^1$ functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ [F5, F8]. Its partial derivatives are $X_\theta=(\cos\theta\cos\varphi,\cos\theta\sin\varphi,-\sin\theta)$ and $X_\varphi=(-\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\sin\theta\cos\varphi,0)$, and the coordinate formula for the cross product gives $$X_\theta\times X_\varphi=(\sin^{2}\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin^{2}\theta\sin\varphi,\ \sin\theta\cos\theta)=\sin\theta\,X(\theta,\varphi),$$ since $\cos^{2}\varphi+\sin^{2}\varphi=1$; also $|X(\theta,\varphi)|^{2}=\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$ [F5, F7]. Hence $X_\theta\times X_\varphi=0$ exactly when $\sin\theta=0$; on the interior $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ one has $\sin\theta>0$ by strict monotonicity and the values $\sin0=\sin\pi=0$ [F5], so the parameter cross product is nonzero on $D^\circ$. [F4, F5, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 The chart covers the sphere and is injective in its interior. If $n\in S^2$, strict monotonicity of cosine on $[0,\pi]$ with range $[-1,1]$ gives a unique $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta=n_3$, so $\sin\theta=\bigl(n_1^{2}+n_2^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$ because $\sin\theta\ge0$ on $[0,\pi]$ and $\sin^{2}\theta=1-\cos^{2}\theta$ [F5]. If $\sin\theta=0$ then $n=\pm e_3=X(0,0)$ or $X(\pi,0)$; otherwise put $c:=n_1/\sin\theta$ and $s:=n_2/\sin\theta$, so $c^{2}+s^{2}=1$, and choose $\varphi\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\varphi=c$ when $s\ge0$ and $\varphi\in[\pi,2\pi]$ with $\cos\varphi=c$ when $s<0$, possible because cosine has range $[-1,1]$ and is strictly monotone on each interval; then $\sin\varphi$ has the sign of $s$ there and $\sin^{2}\varphi=1-c^{2}=s^{2}$, so $\sin\varphi=s$ and $n=X(\theta,\varphi)$. Thus $X[D]=S^2$. Conversely, if $X(\theta,\varphi)=X(\theta',\varphi')$ with $(\theta,\varphi)\in D^\circ$ and $(\theta',\varphi')\in D$, then $\cos\theta=\cos\theta'$ with both angles in $[0,\pi]$, so $\theta=\theta'$ by strict monotonicity; then $\sin\theta>0$ and the first two coordinates give $\cos\varphi=\cos\varphi'$ and $\sin\varphi=\sin\varphi'$, hence $\cos(\varphi-\varphi')=\cos\varphi\cos\varphi'+\sin\varphi\sin\varphi'=\cos^{2}\varphi+\sin^{2}\varphi=1$ [F5]. Writing $x:=\varphi-\varphi'\in(-2\pi,2\pi)$ and using $\cos x=1-2\sin^{2}(x/2)$, we get $\sin(x/2)=0$, so $x/2=m\pi$ for some integer $m$ and $x=2m\pi$; since $|x|<2\pi$ this forces $x=0$, that is $\varphi=\varphi'$ [F5]. Therefore no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of $D$, and $(D,X)$ is a regular parametrized surface patch with image $S^2$. [step 1.1, F4, F5, algebra]

3.1 Reduction to the chart. By [F2] the polar measure $\sigma$ is the chart surface measure of [F3], and by the restriction clause of [F3] applied to the compact Borel face $S^2=X[D]$ carried by the regular patch $(D,X)$ of step 2.1, the chart formula computes the $\sigma$-integral of a continuous (hence bounded Borel) function $q$ on $S^2$: $\int_{S^2}q\,d\sigma=\int_D(q\circ X)J_X$, and by [F4] with the computation $J_X=|X_\theta\times X_\varphi|=\sin\theta$ of step 1.1 and the content-zero boundary convention, $$\int_{S^2}q\,d\sigma=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi}q\bigl(X(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi,$$ the right-hand side being an ordinary integral of a continuous integrand over the rectangle. In particular $n_3(X(\theta,\varphi))=\cos\theta$, so for the integrand $q=f\circ n_3$ of (a) $$I:=\int_{S^2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi.$$ [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

4.1 Conclusion of (a). The function $g(\theta,\varphi):=f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta$ is continuous on the rectangle $D$ [F5, F8], hence Riemann integrable, and its sections in $\varphi$ are continuous; [F10] therefore gives $I=\int_0^{\pi}\bigl(\int_0^{2\pi}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\varphi\bigr)d\theta=2\pi\int_0^{\pi}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta$. Let $P(u):=\int_0^{u}f$ on $[-1,1]$; by [F6] $P'=f$, and the chain rule [F6] with $\cos'=-\sin$ [F5] gives $(P\circ\cos)'(\theta)=-f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta$ on $[0,\pi]$. Since this derivative is continuous, the second fundamental theorem [F6] applies and $$\int_0^{\pi}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta=-\bigl[P(\cos\theta)\bigr]_0^{\pi}=P(1)-P(-1)=\int_{-1}^{1}f(u)\,du,$$ because $\cos0=1$ and $\cos\pi=-1$ [F5]. Combining with step 3.1 gives $\int_{S^2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}f(u)\,du$, which is (a); all integrands here are continuous on the compact sets in question, so the displayed integrals are finite. [step 3.1, F5, F6, F10, algebra]

5.1 Conclusion of (b). Let $\eta_1(n_1,n_2,n_3):=(-n_1,n_2,n_3)$ and $\eta_2(n_1,n_2,n_3):=(n_1,-n_2,n_3)$. Each is an orthogonal bijection of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\eta_i[S^2]=S^2$, so each preserves $\sigma$ [F2]; by the substitution identity of [F11], applied to the bounded Borel function $g_i(n):=n_if(n_3)$ and the fact that $g_i\circ\eta_i=-g_i$, we get $\int_{S^2}n_if(n_3)\,d\sigma=-\int_{S^2}n_if(n_3)\,d\sigma$, whence $\int_{S^2}n_if(n_3)\,d\sigma=0$ for $i=1,2$ (finiteness of both integrals is [F9]). For the third component, (a) applied to the continuous function $u\mapsto uf(u)$ gives $\int_{S^2}n_3f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}uf(u)\,du$. Since $n\cdot a=a_1n_1+a_2n_2+a_3n_3$, linearity of the $\sigma$-integral [F9] gives $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\,a_3\int_{-1}^{1}uf(u)\,du,$$ which is (b). [step 4.1, F2, F5, F9, F11, algebra]

5.2 Conclusion of (c). Expanding the square, $(n\cdot a)^{2}=\sum_{i,j=1}^{3}a_ia_jn_in_j$, and by linearity [F9] the integral is the finite sum $\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j\int_{S^2}n_in_jf(n_3)\,d\sigma$. For $i\ne j$ the function $n_in_jf(n_3)$ changes sign under $\eta_i$ (or $\eta_j$), so the substitution identity of [F11] gives $\int_{S^2}n_in_jf(n_3)\,d\sigma=0$. For the diagonal terms, the swap $\eta_3(n_1,n_2,n_3):=(n_2,n_1,n_3)$ is orthogonal and preserves $\sigma$ [F2], so the substitution identity gives $\int_{S^2}n_1^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=\int_{S^2}n_2^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma$; with $n_1^{2}+n_2^{2}=1-n_3^{2}$ [F5] and linearity, $$2\int_{S^2}n_1^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=\int_{S^2}\bigl(1-n_3^{2}\bigr)f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^{2})f(u)\,du$$ by (a) applied to the continuous function $u\mapsto(1-u^{2})f(u)$; and (a) applied to $u\mapsto u^{2}f(u)$ gives $\int_{S^2}n_3^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}u^{2}f(u)\,du$. Substituting into the expansion yields $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^{2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma=2\pi\,a_3^{2}\int_{-1}^{1}u^{2}f(u)\,du+\pi\,(a_1^{2}+a_2^{2})\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^{2})f(u)\,du,$$ which is (c). [step 4.1, F2, F5, F9, F11, algebra]

6.1 Conclusion of (d) and scope (e). Taking $f=1$ in (a) gives $\sigma(S^2)=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}du=4\pi$; independently [F2] gives $\sigma(S^2)=3|B_1|=3V_3(1)$, and [F12] evaluates $V_3(1)=\pi^{3/2}/\Gamma(5/2)$ with $\Gamma(5/2)=(3/2)(1/2)\Gamma(1/2)=3\sqrt\pi/4$, so $V_3(1)=4\pi/3$ and the two routes agree. Taking $f=1$ in (b) gives $\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)\,d\sigma=0$ for every $a$, hence $\int_{S^2}n\,d\sigma=0$, and taking $f=1$ in (c) gives $\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^{2}d\sigma=2\pi a_3^{2}\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}+\pi(a_1^{2}+a_2^{2})\cdot\tfrac{4}{3}=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}|a|^{2}$; choosing $a=e_i$ and $a=e_i+e_j$ for $i\ne j$ reads off $\int_{S^2}n_i^{2}\,d\sigma=4\pi/3$ and $\int_{S^2}n_in_j\,d\sigma=0$ for $i\ne j$, that is $\int_{S^2}n_in_j\,d\sigma=(4\pi/3)\delta_{ij}$. Finally the norm identity of [F7] gives $|n\times a|^{2}=|n|^{2}|a|^{2}-(n\cdot a)^{2}=|a|^{2}-(n\cdot a)^{2}$ for $n\in S^2$, so by linearity [F9] and the value just computed $\int_{S^2}|n\times a|^{2}\,d\sigma=4\pi|a|^{2}-\tfrac{4\pi}{3}|a|^{2}=\tfrac{8\pi}{3}|a|^{2}$. This proves all identities of (d); every integrand is continuous on the compact $S^2$ and $\sigma$ is a finite Borel measure by [F1], so the integrals are absolutely convergent, $f$ need not be nonnegative, and no physical interpretation is asserted, which is (e). [step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2, F1, F2, F5, F7, F9, F11, F12, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by the retarded-kernel and Cauchy suppliers below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let the laboratory region, chart and units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], so that $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]. Let $a>0$, $t_0<T$ and let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $J:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] that are jointly of class $C^\infty$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], vanish identically outside the compact set $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$, and satisfy the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ everywhere --- the compatibility condition that [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] shows to be forced by the Maxwell system, here assumed for the prescribed source. Define the retarded potentials by the explicit retarded integrals

$$\varphi(x,t):=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho\bigl(y,t-|x-y|/c\bigr)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad A(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J\bigl(y,t-|x-y|/c\bigr)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$

and put $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=\nabla\times A$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]]). Then:

(a) [Smoothness and wave equations] $\varphi$ and each component of $A$ are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, and $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$ pointwise.

(b) [Lorenz gauge] With $G:=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ one has $G=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: the retarded pair is in Lorenz gauge, and this is exactly where the continuity hypothesis is used.

(c) [Maxwell fields] $E$ and $B$ are of class $C^\infty$ and the tuple $(E,B,\rho,J)$ satisfies the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the whole of $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\nabla\times E=-\partial_tB$, $\nabla\times B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$.

(d) [No field before the source] $E=B=0$ at every event with $t<t_0$ (indeed $\varphi=A=0$ there): the selected retarded solution carries no field from before the source acted.

(e) [Zero-data Cauchy identification] For every $t_1<t_0$ the pair $(\varphi,A)$ restricted to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_1,\infty)$ is the unique $C^2$ extension solution of the wave Cauchy problem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] at time $t_1$ with zero Cauchy data and sources $\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\mu_0J$.

(f) [Total charge] The total charge $Q(t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y,t)\,dy$ is zero for every $t$: a source that is smooth, compactly supported in space and restricted to a compact time interval and satisfies continuity carries zero total charge, so this branch does not model an eternal isolated nonzero charge.

(g) [Scope] This is the compact smooth branch with an adopted causal selection; it asserts nothing about point, line or sheet sources, about weak or distributional branches, about finite-energy or decay properties, about radiation reaction or self-force, and no empirical claim. In particular the fields of a prescribed isolated point charge with an eternal worldline are not covered by this theorem and are supplied separately by the point-source items of this page.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the laboratory chart and SI constants of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]; constants $a>0$, $t_0<T$; a jointly $C^\infty$ source pair $(\rho,J)$ vanishing outside $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$ and satisfying $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; the retarded integrals $\varphi,A$ of the Statement, with $K$ denoting the retarded kernel of [F1] so that $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}(K*\rho)$ and $A_k=\mu_0(K*J_k)$.

[F1] Retarded kernel: for every $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ the function $(K*h)(x,t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/(4\pi|x-y|)\,dy$ is well defined (absolutely convergent), of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, and satisfies $W(K*h)=h$ pointwise. ([[lem-em-retarded-wave-kernel]] (b))

[F2] Gauge identities and the decoupling definition: for a potential pair of class $C^2$ jointly on an open set, $\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG$ and $\operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G$ hold there, the source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ hold automatically for any potential pair, and if in addition $G=0$ then the sourced Maxwell system of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds if and only if $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $WA=\mu_0J$; the fields $E,B$, the Lorenz divergence $G$ and the wave expression $W$ are those of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], and field regularity classes are those of [[def-em-fields]]. ([[pthm-em-lorenz-gauge-wave-form]] (a),(c))

[F3] Cauchy uniqueness: if $v\in C^2(\mathbb R^3\times[t_1,T'])$ is of class $C^2$ in the extension sense, satisfies $Wv=h$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_1,T')$ with $h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_1,T'])$ in the extension sense, and has prescribed Cauchy data at $t_1$, then $v$ equals the solution constructed there. ([[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] (b))

[F4] SI constants: $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, so $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$; $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$. ([[def-em-si-conventions]])

[F5] Source fields: smooth source fields $(\rho,J)$ with their units, the continuity equation and the compact-support convention are those of [[def-em-sources]]; the standing hypotheses of this theorem are as stated in the Given. ([[def-em-sources]])

[F6] $C^1$ change of variables for $L^1$: for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ of open sets and $f\in L^1(\lambda_n)$, $\int_Vf=\int_U f\circ T\,|\det DT|$. ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]])

[F7] Differentiation under the integral sign: if $x\mapsto f(x,s)$ is integrable for every $s$ in an open interval, $s\mapsto f(x,s)$ is differentiable for almost every $x$, the extended partial derivative is measurable in $x$, and $|\partial_sf(x,s)|\le g(x)$ for an integrable $g$ independent of $s$, then $\int f(x,s)\,dx$ is differentiable with derivative $\int\partial_sf(x,s)\,dx$. ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]])

[F8] Polar coordinates: for every nonnegative Borel $f$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\,d\lambda_3=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^2}f(r\omega)r^2\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$; in particular $\int_{B_s(0)}|z|^{-1}\,dz=4\pi\int_0^s r\,dr=2\pi s^2<\infty$. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]])

[F9] Linearity of the integral on $L^1$. ([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]])

[F10] Divergence theorem for a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain $\Omega$ and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$: $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$ with outward normal. ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]])

[F11] Parameter integrals: if $K$ is compact measurable of finite measure and $f,\partial_tf$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$, then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx$ is differentiable there with derivative $\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx$. ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]])

[F12] $C^k$ means continuous partial derivatives up to order $k$; finite sums and products of $C^k$ maps are $C^k$. ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])

[F13] The framework adopts the retarded branch of [[post-em-radiation-selection]]: the selected physical potential pair is the retarded one with no free addition, and the theorem below computes exactly that branch; it asserts no existence of its own. ([[post-em-radiation-selection]] (b),(c))

[F14] For $C^2$ fields and $C^1$ sources satisfying the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], the continuity equation is forced; here continuity is assumed for the prescribed source. ([[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] (a))

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; identify the potentials with the retarded kernel of [F1], differentiate the kernel pairing to obtain the Lorenz gauge from continuity, read off the Maxwell system from [F2], localize the retarded integrals for the vanishing and Cauchy claims, and integrate the continuity equation for the total charge.

1.1 Smoothness and wave equations. The source pair $(\rho,J)$ is jointly $C^\infty$ and vanishes outside the compact set $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$, so $\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and each $h=\mu_0J_k$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ [F5, F12]. Applying [F1] to these functions and using the identification $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}(K*\rho)$, $A_k=\mu_0(K*J_k)$ of the Given gives that $\varphi$ and every component of $A$ are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, with $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $WA=\mu_0J$ pointwise. This is (a). [F1, F4, F5, F12]

1.2 Derivative identities for the retarded kernel. Fix $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$. For fixed $(x,t)$ the change of variable $y\mapsto z=x-y$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^3$ with $|\det D(x-\cdot)|=1$, is legitimate for the integrable function $y\mapsto h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/(4\pi|x-y|)$ [F6], so $(K*h)(x,t)=\int h(x-z,t-|z|/c)/(4\pi|z|)\,dz$. For a compact parameter block $|x|\le R$, $|t|\le R$ and any first partial derivative of $h$, the differentiated integrand $z\mapsto(\partial h)(x-z,t-|z|/c)/(4\pi|z|)$ (zero at $z=0$) is dominated by $M_R\mathbf 1_{B_{2R}}(z)/|z|$ with $M_R$ the supremum of the relevant derivative of $h$ on the compact set $\{|y|\le R+a+1,\ t\in[-R-1,R+1]\}$, because the numerator vanishes whenever $|x-z|>a$; that majorant is integrable by [F8] (in three dimensions $\int_{B_{2R}}|z|^{-1}dz=2\pi(2R)^2$). The derivative is measurable as a limit of measurable difference quotients, so [F7] applies once per parameter $x_1,x_2,x_3,t$ with the other three parameters held fixed, and gives $\partial_{x_i}(K*h)=K*(\partial_{y_i}h)$ and $\partial_t(K*h)=K*(\partial_th)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, where $\partial_{y_i}h$ is the partial derivative of $h$ in its $i$-th spatial argument. [F6, F7, F8]

1.3 No field before the source. Suppose $t<t_0$. For every $y$ the retarded argument satisfies $t-|x-y|/c\le t<t_0$, where $\rho$ and $J$ vanish identically by the support hypothesis; hence both integrands in the definitions of $\varphi$ and $A$ vanish for every $y$, and $\varphi(x,t)=0$, $A(x,t)=0$ [F9]. Therefore $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA=0$ and $B=\nabla\times A=0$ at every event with $t<t_0$, which is (d). [F4, F5, F9, algebra]

1.4 Total charge. By the support hypothesis, $Q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y,t)dy=\int_{B_a(0)}\rho(y,t)dy$ for every $t$, and $Q(t)=0$ for $t<t_0$; the integral depends smoothly on $t$ with $Q'(t)=\int_{B_a(0)}\partial_t\rho(y,t)dy$ by [F11] applied to the fixed compact $B_a(0)$ (the integrands $\rho,\partial_t\rho$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline B_a(0)\times[t]$) [F5, F12]. Fix $t$ and $R>a$; the continuity equation and the divergence theorem [F10] give $\int_{B_a(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=\int_{B_R(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=\int_{\partial B_R(0)}J(y,t)\cdot\nu\,dS=0$, because $J$ vanishes outside $\overline B_a(0)$ and $R>a$; hence $Q'(t)=-\int_{B_a(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=0$. Thus $Q$ is constant on $\mathbb R$ and, being zero at times before $t_0$, is identically zero, which is (f). [F5, F9, F10, F11, algebra]

2.1 Lorenz gauge. By step 1.2 applied to each component $J_i$ and to $\rho$, together with linearity of the integral [F9], $$\operatorname{div}A=\mu_0\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_{x_i}(K*J_i)=\mu_0\sum_{i=1}^{3}K*(\partial_{y_i}J_i)=\mu_0\,K*(\operatorname{div}J),\qquad c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}K*(\partial_t\rho)=\mu_0\,K*(\partial_t\rho),$$ the second equality using $c^{-2}\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\mu_0$ [F4]. Adding, $G=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=\mu_0K*(\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J)=0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ by the assumed continuity equation and linearity of the kernel integral [F9]. This is (b), and it is the only place where continuity is used. [step 1.2, F4, F5, F9, algebra]

2.2 Zero-data Cauchy identification. Fix $t_1<t_0$ and $T'>t_0$. By step 1.3, $\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$, $A(\cdot,t_1)=0$ and also $\partial_t\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$, $\partial_tA(\cdot,t_1)=0$ (the same vanishing argument applies to the time derivatives, whose integrands contain $\rho_t,J_t$, vanishing for retarded arguments $<t_0$ as well). By step 1.1 the pair is $C^\infty$, hence $C^2$, on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_1,T']$ in the extension sense and satisfies $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_1,T')$; [F3] (with its final time renamed $T'$ and its Cauchy data $a=b=0$) therefore identifies each component with the zero-data solution constructed there. As $T'>t_0$ is arbitrary, the identification extends to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_1,\infty)$, which is (e). [step 1.1, step 1.3, F3, F12, algebra]

3.1 Maxwell fields. $E$ and $B$ are $C^\infty$ because $\varphi$ and $A$ are [step 1.1, F12]. By [F2] with the Lorenz divergence $G$ of step 2.1, $\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG=\rho/\varepsilon_0-0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G=\mu_0J+0$; the two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ are automatic for the potential pair [F2]. Hence the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds for $(E,B,\rho,J)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with $E,B$ of class $C^\infty$, which is (c). The remaining clause (g) is scope bookkeeping: every hypothesis used above is one of the displayed compact smooth source hypotheses, no point, line, sheet or distributional source is involved, no product of distributions or self-field is formed, no finite-energy, decay, self-force or measurement claim is made, and the only choice assumption is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ carried by the kernel, polar and Cauchy suppliers. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, F2, F13, F14, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the setting and hypotheses of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by its suppliers: $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$, $t_0<T$, jointly $C^\infty$ fields $\rho,J$ vanishing outside $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$ and satisfying $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; let $\varphi,A$ be the retarded potentials and $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=\nabla\times A$ the fields, with $S:=E\times B/\mu_0$ ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]]). Adopt the causal selection [[post-em-radiation-selection]]: these retarded fields are the fields of the source model (the compact smooth instance established by [[pthm-em-retarded-potentials]]). Define the **time-dependent electric dipole moment**

$$p(u):=\int_{B_a}y\,\rho(y,u)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3$$

(componentwise, about the fixed chart origin of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; it is the fixed-time analogue of the static source moment of [[def-em-electric-moments]]), and, as in the asymptotic theorem, $I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$, $V(n,u):=\partial_uI(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and

$$D(u):=\frac{a}{c}\int_{B_a}\sup_{|v-u|\le a/c}|J_{tt}(y,v)|\,dy.$$

Then:

(a) [Moment identities] $p\in C^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$, $p'(u)=\int_{B_a}J(y,u)\,dy$, $p''(u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u)\,dy$, $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u)\,dy=0$ and the total charge $\int_{B_a}\rho(y,u)\,dy$ vanishes for every $u$.

(b) [Dipole replacement error] $|V(n,u)-p''(u)|\le D(u)$ for every $n\in S^2$ and every $u\in[t_0,T]$: the explicit absolute error of the dipole approximation to the source's transverse current moment.

(c) [Leading fields] With $\Gamma_E$, $\Gamma_B$ the constants of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]](b) (depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and the listed source suprema), for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$, $r\ge2a$:

$$\Bigl|E\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p''(u))\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0D(u)}{4\pi r},\qquad \Bigl|B\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)-\frac{n\times E(rn,u+\tfrac rc)}{c}\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_B+\Gamma_E/c}{r^2}.$$

The leading far field is the electric-dipole field, with amplitude proportional to $p''(u)$; all errors are uniform in the direction $n$ at fixed $u$.

(d) [Retarded-time radiated power] The limit of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]](c) equals $\mu_0|p''(u)|^2/(6\pi c)+R(u)$ with the explicit absolute error

$$|R(u)|\le\frac{\mu_0\bigl(2|p''(u)|D(u)+D(u)^2\bigr)}{4\pi c},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)d\sigma=\frac{\mu_0}{6\pi c}|p''(u)|^2\ \text{ whenever } D(u)=0.$$

The evaluation uses the sphere moment $\int_{S^2}|n\times p''|^2d\sigma=(8\pi/3)|p''|^2$ of [[lem-em-sphere-zonal-moments]](d). The limit is at fixed retarded time $u$, not at fixed observation time.

(e) [Scope] The compact smooth source branch only; the dipole error is absolute and explicitly controlled by $D(u)$, and no assertion is made that slow or 'nonrelativistic' source motion alone makes $D(u)$ small -- that is a hypothesis on the source's time variation. No point charge, no moving point source, no radiation reaction, no self-force and no empirical or measurement content; the failure of the correspondence with an oscillator for rapidly varying sources is retained through $D(u)$. Separately retain the sharper actual source estimate $|B(rn,u+r/c)-n\times E_{\rm lead}(n,u,r)/c|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$, with $E_{\rm lead}=\mu_0n\times(n\times V)/(4\pi r)$; the bound against the actual E uses the combined constant displayed in (c).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the hypotheses of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]]: constants $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$, $t_0<T$, jointly $C^\infty$ sources $(\rho,J)$ vanishing outside $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$ and satisfying $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; the retarded potentials and fields with $S=E\times B/\mu_0$; the dipole moment $p$, the moments $I,V$ and the error coefficient $D$ of the Statement.

[F1] Far-zone expansion of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] (b): with $\mathbf I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy$, $\mathbf V=\partial_u\mathbf I$, $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathbf V(n,u))$ and $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$ constants depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and the source suprema, for all $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$, $r\ge2a$ one has $|\mathbf E(rn,u+r/c)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)|\le\Gamma_E/r^2$ and $|\mathbf B(rn,u+r/c)-n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)/c|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$. ([[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] (b))

[F2] Retarded-time flux limit of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] (c): for every $u\in[t_0,T]$, $\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+\tfrac rc)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2\,d\Omega(n)$, a limit at fixed retarded time; $d\Omega$ is the sphere surface measure, which equals the polar measure $\sigma$ on $S^2$. ([[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] (c))

[F3] Energy flux reading: $S=E\times B/\mu_0$ is the Poynting energy-flux density of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and the fixed-volume Poynting balance of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] reads the boundary flux $-\oint S\cdot n\,dS$ as field energy leaving the volume. ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]])

[F4] Source moments: the static dipole moment and total charge of a compactly supported charge distribution about the chart origin are those of [[def-em-electric-moments]](a); the present $p(u)$ is the fixed-time analogue for the moving source. ([[def-em-electric-moments]])

[F5] Parameter integrals over a fixed compact set: if $f,\partial_tf$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times J$ with $K$ compact measurable of finite measure, then $t\mapsto\int_Kf$ is differentiable with derivative $\int_K\partial_tf$; iterating gives $C^\infty$ dependence for $C^\infty$ integrands. ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]])

[F6] Divergence theorem on a bounded $C^1$ domain: $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$ for $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$. ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]])

[F7] Mean value theorem: if $f:[s_1,s_2]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and differentiable in the interior, then $f(s_2)-f(s_1)=f'(s_*)(s_2-s_1)$ for some interior $s_*$. ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]])

[F8] Cauchy-Schwarz: $|e\cdot w|\le|e||w|$ for $e,w\in\mathbb R^3$. ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]])

[F9] Integral triangle inequality and monotonicity: $|\int f|\le\int|f|$ for integrable $f$, and $0\le f\le g$ gives $\int f\le\int g$ for the nonnegative integral. ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]])

[F10] Cross product identities: $u\times v$ is bilinear and alternating, $n\cdot(u\times v)=\det(n,u,v)$, and for $|n|=1$ one has $n\cdot(n\times w)=0$, $n\times(n\times w)=n(n\cdot w)-w$, $|n\times(n\times w)|=|n\times w|\le|w|$; and for $a_\perp:=a-(n\cdot a)n$ one has $a\cdot b-(n\cdot a)(n\cdot b)=a_\perp\cdot b_\perp$. ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]])

[F11] Shifted source moments: $V(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy=\partial_uI(n,u)$. ([[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] (a),(b))

[F12] Sphere moment: $\int_{S^2}|n\times a|^2\,d\sigma(n)=\frac{8\pi}{3}|a|^2$ for every $a\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$. ([[lem-em-sphere-zonal-moments]] (d))

[F13] Compact smooth branch: for the same source class the retarded fields satisfy the smooth vacuum Maxwell equations and the total charge vanishes: $\int_{B_a}\rho(y,u)dy=0$ for every $u$, and the retarded pair is the adopted selected branch. ([[pthm-em-retarded-potentials]] (b),(f), [[post-em-radiation-selection]])

[F14] Source support and regularity conventions: $(\rho,J)$ are the smooth source fields of [[def-em-sources]], with the support hypothesis of the Given. ([[def-em-sources]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; obtain the moment identities by differentiating the dipole integral and integrating the continuity equation by parts, bound the moment replacement by the mean value theorem, transfer the far-zone expansion of [F1] to the dipole fields, and evaluate the flux limit of [F2] using the exact sphere moment [F12] and the pointwise replacement bound.

1.1 Moment identities (a). The moment $p(u)=\int_{B_a}y\,\rho(y,u)dy$ is the fixed-time analogue of the static source moment of [F4], a convention about which moment is computed and not a dynamical identity. Since $\rho$ is jointly $C^\infty$ and supported in the fixed compact set $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$, repeated application of [F5] to $u\mapsto p(u)$ shows $p\in C^\infty$ with $p'(u)=\int_{B_a}y\,\rho_t(y,u)dy$ and $p''(u)=\int_{B_a}y\,\rho_{tt}(y,u)dy$ [F14]. For the first derivative, fix $u$ and $R>a$: the continuity equation gives $\int_{B_a}y_i\rho_t(y,u)dy=-\int_{B_a}y_i\operatorname{div}J(y,u)dy$, and since $\operatorname{div}(y_iJ)=J_i+y_i\operatorname{div}J$, the divergence theorem [F6] on $B_R$ gives $\int_{B_R}\operatorname{div}(y_iJ)dy=\int_{\partial B_R}y_iJ\cdot\nu\,dS=0$ because $J$ vanishes on $\partial B_R$; hence $\int_{B_a}y_i\operatorname{div}J\,dy=-\int_{B_a}J_i\,dy$ and $p_i'(u)=\int_{B_a}J_i(y,u)dy$ [F9]. Differentiating this identity once more with [F5] gives $p''(u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u)dy$, the displayed second moment identity. The same divergence theorem with weight $1$ gives $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u)dy=-\int_{B_a}\operatorname{div}J(y,u)dy=0$, and the vanishing of the total charge is clause (f) of [F13] for this source class. This is (a). [F4, F5, F6, F9, F13, F14, algebra]

2.1 Dipole replacement error (b). Fix $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$ and $y\in B_a$, and put $s_1:=u$, $s_2:=u+n\cdot y/c$, so $|s_2-s_1|\le a/c$; the map $s\mapsto J_t(y,s)$ is $C^1$ [F14]. If $\Delta:=J_t(y,s_2)-J_t(y,s_1)\ne0$, apply [F7] on the closed interval between $s_1$ and $s_2$ to the scalar function $s\mapsto e\cdot J_t(y,s)$ with $e:=\Delta/|\Delta|$: there is $s_*$ between $s_1$ and $s_2$ with $e\cdot\Delta=(e\cdot J_{tt}(y,s_*))(s_2-s_1)$; if $\Delta=0$ the same bound holds trivially. By [F8], $|e\cdot J_{tt}(y,s_*)|\le|J_{tt}(y,s_*)|$, so $|\Delta|\le(a/c)\sup_{|v-u|\le a/c}|J_{tt}(y,v)|$ (the point $s_*$ lies within $a/c$ of $u$). Integrating over $B_a$ with the integral triangle inequality and monotonicity [F9], and using $V(n,u)-p''(u)=\int_{B_a}\bigl[J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)-J_t(y,u)\bigr]dy$ from step 1.1 and [F11], gives $|V(n,u)-p''(u)|\le D(u)$. This is (b). [step 1.1, F7, F8, F9, F11, F14, algebra]

3.1 Leading fields (c). By [F1], for $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$, $r\ge2a$ write $E(rn,u+\tfrac rc)=E_{\rm lead}(n,u,r)+\rho_E$ with $|\rho_E|\le\Gamma_E/r^2$ and $E_{\rm lead}=\mu_0\,n\times(n\times V(n,u))/(4\pi r)$. Substituting $V=p''+(V-p'')$ and using the identity $|n\times(n\times w)|=|n\times w|\le|w|$ of [F10] together with the bound of step 2.1, $$\Bigl|E\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p''(u))\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|V(n,u)-p''(u)|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0D(u)}{4\pi r},$$ which is the first displayed bound. For the magnetic field, [F1] gives $|B(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-n\times E_{\rm lead}/c|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$, and $|n\times(E-E_{\rm lead})|/c\le|E-E_{\rm lead}|/c\le\Gamma_E/(cr^2)$ by [F10], so the triangle inequality [F9] gives the second displayed bound $(\Gamma_B+\Gamma_E/c)/r^2$; the sharper source estimate against $n\times E_{\rm lead}/c$ is the supplier's own $\Gamma_B/r^2$ bound retained in (e). This is (c), uniformly in $n$ at fixed $u$. [step 2.1, F1, F9, F10, algebra]

4.1 Retarded-time radiated power (d). By [F2], the limit of $\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+\tfrac rc)d\sigma$ as $r\to\infty$ equals $\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times V(n,u)|^2d\sigma$ at fixed $u$; here the polar measure and the sphere surface measure coincide, and [F3] identifies the surface flux with the field-energy flux. For the replacement $V\mapsto p''$ put $a_\pm:=V\pm p''$; by [F10] the pointwise difference satisfies $|n\times V|^2-|n\times p''|^2=a_+\cdot a_--(n\cdot a_+)(n\cdot a_-)=(a_+)_\perp\cdot(a_-)_\perp$, so its absolute value is at most $|a_+||a_-|\le(|V|+|p''|)|V-p''|\le(2|p''|+D)D=2|p''|D+D^2$, using [F8], the bound of step 2.1 and monotonicity of the norm. Since $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ [F12], the integral changes by at most $4\pi(2|p''|D+D^2)$ in absolute value [F9], so the limit equals $\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times p''(u)|^2d\sigma+R(u)$ with $|R(u)|\le\frac{\mu_0(2|p''|D+D^2)}{4\pi c}$. The exact integral is $\int_{S^2}|n\times p''(u)|^2d\sigma=\frac{8\pi}{3}|p''(u)|^2$ by [F12], so the exact term is $\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\cdot\frac{8\pi}{3}|p''(u)|^2=\frac{\mu_0}{6\pi c}|p''(u)|^2$; whenever $D(u)=0$ the error vanishes by the displayed bound. This is (d). The scope clause (e) is bookkeeping: the limit is at fixed retarded time, the error is controlled by the source's time variation through $D(u)$ alone, and no point source, no observer-time power, no radiation reaction, no self-force and no measurement claim is introduced; the only choice assumption is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, inherited from the supplier. [step 2.1, F2, F3, F8, F9, F10, F12, algebra] ∎
