## Statement

The finite-interval Riemann particle-sector calculation is choice-free: the
field-sector Countable Choice convention of
[[def-em-field-action-definition]] is not used here. Let worldlines,
four-velocities and proper times be those of
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]], let $F$ be the electromagnetic
two-form with the component and potential dictionary of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and let $m>0$ and $q\in\mathbb R$ be the
framework's external rest-mass and charge parameters ([[def-em-sources]] (a)).
Let $[a,b]$ be a nondegenerate compact interval, let $X:[a,b]\to A$ be a $C^2$
future timelike massive worldline (clause (a) of
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]]), let $A_\mu$ be a $C^2$ covector
field - the prescribed external four-potential - on a neighbourhood of the
image of $X$, and let $S_{\rm pt}$ be the particle functional of clause (c) of
[[def-em-field-action-definition]], i.e. the functional
$-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,ds+q\int_a^bA_\mu(X)\dot X^\mu\,ds$ of
[[lem-em-particle-curve-variation]].

Then, under the adopted stationary-action model for the particle sector
([[post-em-stationary-action-model]] (ii)), for every fixed-endpoint $C^2$
variation $h$ with $h(a)=h(b)=0$ the curve $X+\varepsilon h$ is future
timelike for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$, and the following are
equivalent: (i) $X$ is stationary for $S_{\rm pt}$ under all such variations;
(ii) $m\,dU_\nu/d\tau=qF_{\nu\mu}U^\mu$ on $[a,b]$, where $F=dA$ and $\tau$ is
the proper time of $X$; (iii) the four-force equation
$m\,dU/d\tau=q\,\Phi(U)$ of the framework's adopted covariant coupling
[[pthm-em-relativistic-lorentz-force]], where $\Phi$ is the raised-index field
operator $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$. In particular the stationary-action
formulation of the particle sector is equivalent, for prescribed external
potentials, to the adopted Lorentz coupling; the coordinate equations
$\frac{dp}{dt}=q(E+v\times B)$ and
$\frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}=qE\cdot v$ of
[[pthm-em-relativistic-lorentz-force]] then hold wherever the laboratory
reading is $C^2$.

Scope: the potential, hence the field, is prescribed and external to the
particle; the particle's own field, radiation reaction and self-force are
excluded, as are magnetic monopoles, zero or variable mass, coupled
particle-field existence and any approximation of the trajectory over a time
interval. The equivalence is conditional on the adopted postulates and makes
no empirical claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nondegenerate compact interval $[a,b]$; a $C^2$ future timelike
massive worldline $X:[a,b]\to A$ with four-velocity $U$ and proper time
$\tau$; a prescribed $C^2$ covector field $A_\mu$ on a neighbourhood of the
image of $X$; the rest-mass and charge parameters $m>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$; the
electromagnetic two-form and its potential and index dictionary; the particle
functional $S_{\rm pt}$ with its fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations; and the
adopted particle-sector stationary-action principle.

[F1] The particle functional is
$S_{\rm pt}[X]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,ds+q\int_a^bA_\mu(X)\dot X^\mu\,ds$
on the declared class, with admissible variations the fixed-endpoint $C^2$
variations $h(a)=h(b)=0$ of [[lem-em-particle-curve-variation]]
([[def-em-field-action-definition]] (c)).

[F2] The curve-variation lemma states that for a $C^2$ future timelike curve
$X:[a,b]\to A$ and a $C^2$ covector field $A_\mu$ on a neighbourhood of its
image, for every fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variation the curve $X+\varepsilon h$
remains future timelike for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$, and
stationarity of the displayed functional under all such variations is
equivalent to
$m\frac{dU_\nu}{d\tau}=qF_{\nu\mu}U^\mu$, $\frac{d\tau}{ds}=\frac{\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}}c$,
$F=dA$, with the four-velocity $U$ and proper time $\tau$ of the
observer-decomposition theorem ([[lem-em-particle-curve-variation]]).

[F3] A massive worldline is a future timelike worldline of class $C^k$,
$k\ge1$; its four-velocity $U$ and four-acceleration $A$ satisfy
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ and $\eta(U,A)=0$ by the observer-decomposition theorem
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] (a)-(b)).

[F4] The observer-decomposition theorem states (clause (a)) that for a $C^1$
future timelike worldline with four-velocity $U$ one has
$\eta(U(s),U(s))=-c^2$ for every $s$
([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]).

[F5] The antisymmetric-contraction lemma states that for a skew form $F$ on
the four-dimensional Minkowski vector space there is exactly one linear
$\Phi$ with $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, and that in the fixed basis
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]).

[F6] The two-form definition states that the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
the antisymmetric-contraction lemma satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, and that if a $C^1$
covector field satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$
then the recovered fields obey $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and
$B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with $\varphi:=-cA_0$
([[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] (c)-(d)).

[F7] The framework takes a real charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ in coulombs
and a rest-mass parameter $m$ carrying the kilogram ([[def-em-sources]] (a),
[[def-em-si-conventions]] (c)).

[F8] The relativistic Lorentz-force theorem states that, for a future timelike
$C^2$ massive worldline in a prescribed $C^1$ field generated externally to
the particle, the adopted equation of motion
$m\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\Phi(U)$, $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ implies, wherever the
worldline is $C^2$, the coordinate force and power laws
$\frac{dp}{dt}=q(E+v\times B)$ and
$\frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}=qE\cdot v$, with $p=m\gamma v$ and
$U=\gamma(c,v)$ ([[pthm-em-relativistic-lorentz-force]]).

[F9] The adopted particle-sector principle states that the motion is
dynamically admissible exactly when the worldline is stationary for the
particle functional under all fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations
([[post-em-stationary-action-model]] (ii)).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; verify the hypotheses of the curve-variation
lemma for the framework's data, transport its equivalence to the framework's
four-velocity and proper time, and identify the lowered coefficient equation
with the adopted raised-index coupling.

1.1 The data meet the hypotheses of [F2]: $[a,b]$ is a nondegenerate compact interval, $X$ is a $C^2$ future timelike curve by [F3] and the statement's class, and $A_\mu$ is $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of the image of $X$ by assumption; the functional of [F1] is literally the functional of [F2] in the framework's conventions. Hence for every fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variation $h$ the curve $X+\varepsilon h$ remains future timelike for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$, and stationarity of $S_{\rm pt}$ under all such variations is equivalent to $m\frac{dU_\nu}{d\tau}=qF_{\nu\mu}U^\mu$ with the four-velocity $U$ and proper time $\tau$ supplied by the observer-decomposition theorem; this is a finite-interval Riemann calculation in ZF and consumes no field-sector choice convention. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 The curve $X$ of step 1.1 is the framework's massive worldline by [F3] and the functional $S_{\rm pt}$ is the framework's particle functional by [F1]; the four-velocity $U$ and proper time $\tau$ occurring in the coefficient equation of [F2] are the four-velocity and proper-time parameter of that same curve, the objects to which [F2] refers through the observer-decomposition theorem, and they satisfy the framework's norm $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ by [F4]. Hence condition (ii) is stated with the framework's $U$ and $\tau$, and step 1.1 proves (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii). [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4]

3.1 Lowering the index in [F5], $(\Phi(U))_\nu=\eta_{\nu\mu}\Phi(U)^\mu=\eta_{\nu\mu}\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}U^\beta=F_{\nu\beta}U^\beta=F_{\nu\mu}U^\mu$, and [F6] identifies this $\Phi$ and the potential relation $F=dA$ with the framework's two-form; since $u\mapsto\eta(u,\cdot)$ is injective (the form is nondegenerate), the component equation $m\,dU_\nu/d\tau=qF_{\nu\mu}U^\mu$ holds for every $\nu$ if and only if $m\,dU/d\tau=q\,\Phi(U)$ in $V$. Hence (ii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii). [step 2.1, F5, F6, algebra]

4.1 Under the adopted coupling (iii), [F8] applies with the prescribed external field of [F6] and the $C^2$ worldline of the statement, so the coordinate force and power laws $\frac{dp}{dt}=q(E+v\times B)$ and $\frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}=qE\cdot v$ hold wherever the laboratory reading is $C^2$, with $p=m\gamma v$ and $U=\gamma(c,v)$ as recorded there. [step 3.1, F6, F8]

5.1 The equivalence (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iii) was obtained by instantiating the choice-free finite-interval curve lemma [F2], identifying the framework's worldline objects through [F3] and [F4], and lowering the index through [F5] and [F6]; the potential is prescribed and external, the particle's own field, radiation reaction and self-force are excluded, and the whole statement is conditional on the adopted stationary-action principle [F9] of the particle sector and on the adopted coupling [F8], with no empirical claim and no use of the field-sector Countable Choice convention. [given, step 4.1, F2, F7, F8, F9] ∎

## Source notes

The prescribed-field particle action and its reduction to the Lorentz force
are Tong §5.5.1-§5.5.2 (printed pp. 118-124), Landau–Lifshitz §16 and Binney
§3.1, each in its own conventions; the covariant functional, the fixed-endpoint
variation class and the resulting equation are restated here in the
framework's $(-,+,+,+)$ dictionary, and the exact coefficient implication is
supplied by the in-run mathematical curve-variation lemma rather than accepted
from the sources' informal boundary-term step.

## Example

Assume Countable Choice, inherited from the field-action measure suppliers
([[def-countable-choice]]); no additional choice is used. Work in
[[def-em-field-action-definition]] with the coordinate box $U=(-1,1)^4$ lying
compactly inside the chosen laboratory chart, constants $c,\mu_0>0$,
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]]) and $j=0$.

(a) [Coordinate and physical forms] With $x^0=ct$, set
$U_t:=\{(t,x):(ct,x)\in U\}=(-1/c,1/c)\times(-1,1)^3$. The exact field
dictionary gives

$$S[A]=\frac{1}{2c\mu_0}\int_U(|E|^2/c^2-|B|^2)d\lambda=\frac12\int_{U_t}(\varepsilon_0|E|^2-|B|^2/\mu_0)dt\,d^3x.$$

Also $S[\lambda A]=\lambda^2S[A]$ for every real $\lambda$.

(b) [Stationarity] $A=0$ is stationary: the actual first-variation coefficient
of [[lem-em-compact-field-variation]] is
$-\mu_0^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu h_\nu+j^\nu h_\nu$, and the action variation
is $c^{-1}$ times its integral. Both terms vanish at $F=0$, $j=0$.

(c) [Positive direction] Choose $\theta\in C_c^\infty(U)$ with
$\nabla_x\theta\not\equiv0$. Set the covariant components $h_0=\theta$, $h_i=0$,
equivalently the contravariant variation $h^0=-\theta$, $h^i=0$. Then
$E=c\nabla_x\theta$, $B=0$, and

$$S[h]=\frac{1}{2c\mu_0}\int_U|\nabla_x\theta|^2d\lambda>0.$$

(d) [Negative directions with a fixed compact support] Choose nonzero
nonnegative smooth bumps $\eta,\varphi,\psi_2,\psi_3\in C_c^\infty((-1/2,1/2))$
using [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]. Extend them by
zero to $\mathbb R$. For integers $N\ge1$ define the contravariant variation
with only its second spatial component nonzero:

$$h^{(N)2}(x)=\eta(x^0)\varphi(Nx^1)\psi_2(x^2)\psi_3(x^3).$$

All supports lie in one fixed compact subset of $U$. Writing
$f_N=h^{(N)2}$, its fields are $E=-c(\partial_0f_N)e_2$ and
$B=-(\partial_3f_N)e_1+(\partial_1f_N)e_3$. Define finite constants, with all
one-dimensional integrals over $(-1,1)$,

$$C_E=\Bigl(\int\eta'^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\varphi^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\psi_2^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\psi_3^2\Bigr),\qquad C_B=\Bigl(\int\eta^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\varphi'^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\psi_2^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\psi_3^2\Bigr)>0,$$

$$C_3=\Bigl(\int\eta^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\varphi^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\psi_2^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\psi_3'^2\Bigr)\ge0.$$

Exact substitution and Fubini give

$$\int_U|E|^2/c^2\,d\lambda=C_E/N,\qquad\int_U|B|^2d\lambda=C_BN+C_3/N,$$

$$S[h^{(N)}]=\frac{1}{2c\mu_0}\Bigl(\frac{C_E-C_3}{N}-C_BN\Bigr)\longrightarrow-\infty.$$

Thus a fixed sufficiently large $N$ supplies one negative direction $h_-$; the
direction $h_+$ of (c) is positive. For nonzero $\lambda$, their rescalings
keep their respective signs, and each action tends to zero in absolute value
as $\lambda\to0$. A single fixed negative direction is not claimed to change
sign under rescaling.

(e) [Every usual neighbourhood] Fix those two directions before rescaling.
For each derivative multi-index, every compact-set supremum of a derivative of
$\lambda h_\pm$ is $|\lambda|$ times the finite supremum for that fixed smooth
compactly supported direction. Thus both tend to zero in the usual $C^k$,
smooth compact-convergence and fixed-support and LF test-function topologies
([[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]],
[[def-test-function-topology]]) (and in any usual function-space topology with
continuous scalar multiplication). Every such neighbourhood of zero therefore
contains configurations of positive and negative action, arbitrarily small in
magnitude. The stationary zero is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum.
This is a computation in the declared smooth finite-region model, not a claim
about actual fields or measurements; other sources or boundary/variation
restrictions require their own analysis.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the field-action definition
with $U=(-1,1)^4$, smooth $A,j$ on an open neighbourhood $N$ of $\overline U$,
constants $c,\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the source-free case
$j=0$; the component and invariant dictionaries of the electromagnetic
two-form; and the test-function class $C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^4)$.

[F1] The field action is
$S[A]=c^{-1}\int_U\bigl[-(4\mu_0)^{-1}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}+j^\nu A_\nu\bigr]d\lambda$
with $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, compactly supported
smooth variations and the stationarity predicate
([[def-em-field-action-definition]]).

[F2] The compact-variation lemma states: $S[A]$ of the lemma is a finite real
number; its first variation at $A$ in the direction $h$ is
$\int_U\bigl(-\kappa^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu h_\nu+J^\nu
h_\nu\bigr)d\lambda$; and $A$ is stationary if and only if
$\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=-\kappa J^\nu$ on $U$ for every $\nu$
([[lem-em-compact-field-variation]]).

[F3] The observer decomposition of the electromagnetic two-form gives
$\tfrac12F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$
([[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] (b)).

[F4] The component dictionary is $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$,
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$, with
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] (a)).

[F5] The electric constant is $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, so
$\varepsilon_0\mu_0c^2=1$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F6] The laboratory chart has $x^0=ct$, so the chart image of the laboratory
region is $cI\times\Omega$ and constant-$t$ slices correspond to fixed $x^0/c$
([[def-em-lab-geometry]]).

[F7] In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$
open there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on
a neighbourhood of $K$
([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F8] Substitution: if $\phi:[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable with
$\phi'$ integrable and $f$ is continuous on an order-convex set containing
$\phi([c,d])$, then
$\int_{\phi(c)}^{\phi(d)}f=\int_c^d(f\circ\phi)\phi'$
([[thm-substitution]]).

[F9] Under Countable Choice, a bounded Borel real function on a nondegenerate
box that is Riemann integrable is Lebesgue integrable with the same integral;
in particular this applies to smooth compactly supported integrands
([[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F10] Fubini's theorem for $L^1$ functions on a sigma-finite product: the
multiple integral equals the iterated integrals
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F11] The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F12] Derivatives satisfy the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F13] The chain rule holds for composites of differentiable functions
([[thm-chain-rule]]).

[F14] For nonnegative measurable $f\le g$ one has $\int f\le\int g$, and for
$c>0$, $\int cf=c\int f$
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F15] Assume Countable Choice: if a continuous $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ on an open
$U$ satisfies $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained
in $U$, then $g=0$ on $U$ ([[lem-em-continuous-localization]]).

[F16] If $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and
$f$ is a Riemann-integrable extension of $G'$ from $(a,b)$, then
$\int_a^bf=G(b)-G(a)$
([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

[F17] For compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ the fixed-support seminorms are
$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|$
([[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]).

[F18] In the test-function topology a seminorm satisfies
$q(av)=|a|q(v)$, and zero-neighbourhoods contain finitely many bounds
$q<\varepsilon$ ([[def-test-function-topology]]).

[F19] Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the statement that every
sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F20] For every $\varepsilon>0$ in a complete ordered field there is a natural $n\ge1$ with $1/n<\varepsilon$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]]).

[F21] The adopted field sector states that a smooth field is dynamically
admissible exactly when it is stationary for the field action under all
compactly supported smooth variations
([[post-em-stationary-action-model]] (i)).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct; substitute the component dictionary into the
box action, compute the first variation at zero, and exhibit one positive and
one fixed-support negative direction whose rescalings stay in every usual
neighbourhood of zero.

1.1 In the source-free case $j=0$, [F3] turns the density of [F1] into $-(4\mu_0)^{-1}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=|E|^2/(2\mu_0c^2)-|B|^2/(2\mu_0)$, so linearity of the integral gives $S[A]=(2c\mu_0)^{-1}\int_U(|E|^2/c^2-|B|^2)d\lambda$; writing the time coordinate as $t=x^0/c$ multiplies the one-dimensional time integral by $c$ and carries $(-1,1)$ to $(-1/c,1/c)$ by [F6] and [F8], while the spatial coordinates are unchanged, so $S[A]=\tfrac12\int_{U_t}(\varepsilon_0|E|^2-|B|^2/\mu_0)dt\,d^3x$ by [F5]; and since $A\mapsto F(A)$ is linear in $A$ and $S$ is quadratic in $F$, $F(\lambda A)=\lambda F(A)$ gives $S[\lambda A]=\lambda^2S[A]$ for every real $\lambda$. [given, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, F10, F11]

2.1 At $A=0$ one has $F(A)=0$ and $j=0$, so the first-variation coefficient $-\mu_0^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu h_\nu+j^\nu h_\nu$ of [F2] vanishes identically for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^4)$; the action variation is $c^{-1}$ times its integral by [F1] and [F2], hence every compact first variation of $S$ at $A=0$ is zero and $A=0$ is stationary. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 By [F7] with $\Omega=U$ and $K=\{(0,0,0,0)\}$ there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(U)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ near the origin; then $\theta:=x^1\chi$ lies in $C_c^\infty(U)$ and $\partial_1\theta(0)=\chi(0)+0\cdot\partial_1\chi(0)=1$, so $\nabla_x\theta\not\equiv0$. With covariant components $h_0=\theta$, $h_i=0$ the dictionary [F4] gives $F_{0i}=-\partial_i\theta$, hence $E=c\nabla_x\theta$ and $B=0$; step 1.1 then gives $S[h]=(2c\mu_0)^{-1}\int_U|\nabla_x\theta|^2d\lambda$. The integrand $g:=|\nabla_x\theta|^2$ is continuous, nonnegative and nonzero at the origin; if $\int_Ug\,d\lambda=0$, then for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$ monotonicity [F14] would give $\int_Vg\le\int_Ug=0$ with $\int_Vg\ge0$, so [F15] would force $g=0$ on $U$, a contradiction; hence $\int_Ug>0$ and $S[h]>0$, one positive direction. [step 2.1, F4, F7, F14, F15, algebra]

4.1 Apply [F7] with $\Omega=(-1/2,1/2)$ and $K=\{0\}$ four times (or once, taking all four bumps equal) to obtain nonzero nonnegative $\eta,\varphi,\psi_2,\psi_3\in C_c^\infty((-1/2,1/2))$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R$; define $f_N(x):=\eta(x^0)\varphi(Nx^1)\psi_2(x^2)\psi_3(x^3)$ for integers $N\ge1$ and let $h^{(N)}$ have $h^{(N)2}=f_N$ and all other contravariant components $0$. Since $\operatorname{supp}\varphi(N\cdot)\subseteq(-1/(2N),1/(2N))\subseteq(-1/2,1/2)$, every $h^{(N)}$ is smooth with support in the fixed compact set $(-1/2,1/2)^4\subset U$. The product and chain rules [F12] and [F13] give $\partial_0f_N=\eta'(x^0)\varphi(Nx^1)\psi_2\psi_3$, $\partial_1f_N=N\eta(x^0)\varphi'(Nx^1)\psi_2\psi_3$ and $\partial_3f_N=\eta(x^0)\varphi(Nx^1)\psi_2\psi_3'$; since $f_N=h^{(N)2}$ and $h^{(N)0}=h^{(N)1}=h^{(N)3}=0$, the dictionary [F4] gives $E=-c(\partial_0f_N)e_2$ and $B=-(\partial_3f_N)e_1+(\partial_1f_N)e_3$. [step 3.1, F4, F7, F12, F13]

5.1 Because all integrands below are smooth with support in the fixed compact subset $(-1/2,1/2)^4\subset U$, [F9] lets each Lebesgue integral be computed as the equal Riemann integral, and Fubini [F10] together with linearity [F11] factors each product of one-variable functions into a product of one-dimensional integrals: $\int_U|E|^2/c^2\,d\lambda=\int(\eta')^2\cdot\int\varphi(Nx^1)^2dx^1\cdot\int\psi_2^2\cdot\int\psi_3^2$ and $\int_U|B|^2d\lambda=\int\eta^2\cdot\int\varphi(Nx^1)^2dx^1\cdot\int\psi_2^2\cdot\int\psi_3'^2+\int\eta^2\cdot\int(N\varphi'(Nx^1))^2dx^1\cdot\int\psi_2^2\cdot\int\psi_3^2$. By [F8] with the affine map $y=Nx^1$ on $[-1,1]$, $\int_{-1}^1\varphi(Nx^1)^2dx^1=N^{-1}\int_{-N}^N\varphi(y)^2dy=N^{-1}\int_{-1}^1\varphi(y)^2dy$, the last equality because $\varphi$ vanishes outside $(-1/2,1/2)$; the same identity holds for $\varphi'$. Hence $\int_U|E|^2/c^2\,d\lambda=C_E/N$ and $\int_U|B|^2d\lambda=C_BN+C_3/N$ with the stated constants, and $C_B>0$: if $\varphi'$ vanished identically then [F16] would make $\varphi$ constant on $\mathbb R$, hence zero by compact support, contradicting the nonzero choice, so $\varphi'^2$ is a continuous nonnegative nonzero square, and together with the nonzero bumps $\eta,\psi_2,\psi_3$ the same argument as in step 3.1 with [F14] and [F15] gives each of the four one-dimensional integrals in $C_B$ strictly positive. [step 4.1, F8, F9, F10, F11, F14, F15, F16, algebra]

6.1 Step 1.1 with $j=0$ and [F3] expresses $S[h^{(N)}]=(2c\mu_0)^{-1}\int_U(|E|^2/c^2-|B|^2)d\lambda$, so step 5.1 gives $S[h^{(N)}]=(2c\mu_0)^{-1}\bigl((C_E-C_3)/N-C_BN\bigr)$; since $C_B>0$, choose $N\ge1$ with $C_BN>(C_E-C_3)/N$: if $C_E-C_3\le0$ every $N$ works, while if $C_E-C_3>0$ then $\varepsilon:=C_B/(C_E-C_3)>0$ and [F20] provides $n\ge1$ with $1/n<\varepsilon$, that is $n>(C_E-C_3)/C_B$; setting $N:=n$ gives $C_BN>C_E-C_3\ge(C_E-C_3)/N$ because $N\ge1$. For that fixed $N_0$ one has $S[h^{(N_0)}]<0$, giving one fixed-support negative direction $h_-:=h^{(N_0)}$. [step 5.1, F1, F3, F20, algebra]

7.1 For every real $\lambda$ the scaling law of step 1.1 gives $S[\lambda h_+ ]=\lambda^2S[h_+]$ and $S[\lambda h_-]=\lambda^2S[h_-]$, so the signs of the two directions are preserved for nonzero $\lambda$ and both action magnitudes tend to $0$ as $\lambda\to0$. In the fixed-support space [F17] each seminorm satisfies $p_m(\lambda h)=|\lambda|p_m(h)$ by definition of the maximum and supremum, and in the LF topology [F18] every seminorm satisfies $q(\lambda h)=|\lambda|q(h)$ and a zero-neighbourhood contains finitely many bounds $q<\varepsilon$; hence $\lambda h_\pm\to0$ in both topologies, and in any usual topology with continuous scalar multiplication the map $\lambda\mapsto\lambda h_\pm$ is continuous at $0$. Therefore every such zero-neighbourhood contains configurations $\lambda h_+$ with $S>0$ and $\lambda h_-$ with $S<0$, with $|S|=\lambda^2|S[h_\pm]|$ arbitrarily small: the stationary configuration $0$ is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum. [step 3.1, step 6.1, F17, F18, algebra]

8.1 Every object above is smooth and compactly supported in the box $U$, all integrals are the declared finite-region Lebesgue integrals, and the arguments used exactly [F7], [F8], [F9], [F14], [F15], [F16] and [F20]; Countable Choice [F19] enters only through the measure interface of [F9] and [F15], as inherited from the field-action sector. The computation concerns the adopted functional [F21] and asserts nothing about physical fields, measurements, existence of stationary configurations beyond the exhibited zero, or any other region or variation class. [given, step 7.1, F19, F21] ∎

## Source notes

Landau–Lifshitz §27 (printed p. 67 and eqs. (27.4)-(27.6)) ties the sign of
$(\partial A/\partial t)^2$ to a minimum requirement for $S_f$; the exact
computation above shows that with the framework's adopted sign and
normalisation the stationary point of the source-free box functional is a
saddle rather than a minimum, so the source's minimum wording is not adopted.
Tong §5.5.3 (printed p. 124) expands the action to
$\int dtd^3x\,(\varepsilon_0E^2/2-B^2/(2\mu_0))$ and reads the electric term
as kinetic and the magnetic term as potential; the explicit compact
variations of this example are the framework's own witnesses and are not a
numbered result of either source.

## Example

Assume Countable Choice, inherited from the cited theorems. Work in the
field-action setting of [[def-em-field-action-definition]] with $U=(-1,1)^4$,
constants $c,\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$
([[def-em-si-conventions]]), and the component dictionary of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]: $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F^{0i}=E_i/c$,
$F^{10}=-E_1/c$.

(a) [Source-free zero field] For $j\equiv0$ and $A=0$ the first-variation
coefficient (whose integral is multiplied by $c^{-1}$)
$-\mu_0^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu h_\nu+j^\nu h_\nu$ of clause (a) of
[[lem-em-compact-field-variation]] vanishes identically for every
$h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^4)$, because $F(A)=0$ and $j=0$; hence every
compact first variation of $S$ at $A=0$ is zero and $A=0$ is stationary.

(b) [A non-trivial compact test variation] Let $A$ be the smooth potential with
$A_0(x)=x^1$ and $A_1=A_2=A_3=0$, and let $j\equiv0$. Then
$F_{01}=-\partial_1A_0=-1$, $F^{01}=+1$, $F^{10}=-1$ and all other components
vanish, so the represented field is $E=(c,0,0)$, $B=0$ (clause (b) of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]]) and $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=0$ on $U$. By
the equivalence of [[pthm-em-action-maxwell-variation]], $A$ is stationary;
directly, for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^4)$ the first variation of $S$
at $A$ is

$$\frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}S[A+sh]=-\frac{1}{c\mu_0}\int_U\bigl(\partial_0h_1-\partial_1h_0\bigr)d\lambda=\frac{1}{c\mu_0}\int_U\bigl(\partial_1h_0-\partial_0h_1\bigr)d\lambda=0,$$

where each of $\int_U\partial_0h_1\,d\lambda$ and $\int_U\partial_1h_0\,d\lambda$
vanishes by the fundamental theorem in one variable combined with Fubini, and
no boundary term appears because $h$ is compactly supported in $U$
([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]],
[[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

(c) [Gauge-source sign check with actual overlap] Independently choose the
smooth prescribed source $j^0=c\rho(x^0)$, $j^i=0$, with nonzero nonnegative
$\rho\in C_c^\infty((-1/4,1/4))$ extended by zero. Choose
$0\le\zeta\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$ with $\zeta=1$ near $[-1/2,1/2]$, and nonzero
nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty((-1,1)^3)$, supplied by
[[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]. Put
$\varphi_\pm(u)=(2\pm u)\zeta(u)$ and
$\chi_\pm(x)=\varphi_\pm(x^0)\psi(x^1,x^2,x^3)$. Both $\varphi_\pm$ are
nonnegative compact bumps, but they are not globally monotone: on the entire
support of $\rho$ their derivatives equal $+1$ and $-1$, respectively. Use the
contravariant gauge variations
$(\partial^\sharp\chi_\pm)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu\chi_\pm$ from
[[pthm-em-action-gauge-source-compatibility]]. Then, for every smooth potential
$A$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline U$,

$$S[A+\partial^\sharp\chi_\pm]-S[A]=\Bigl(\int_{-1}^1\rho\varphi_\pm'\,dx^0\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_{(-1,1)^3}\psi\,d^3x\Bigr)=\pm\Bigl(\int\rho\Bigr)\Bigl(\int\psi\Bigr),$$

which is strictly positive for $+$ and strictly negative for $-$, since both
factors are positive. Integration by parts gives exactly the same value as
$-c^{-1}\int_U(\partial_\mu j^\mu)\chi_\pm d\lambda$ with
$\partial_\mu j^\mu=c\rho'$. This verifies the relative sign of the
$+j^\mu A_\mu$ coupling, the raised-vector/covariant-lowered gauge shift and
the conservation condition, using explicitly overlapping supports. If instead
$\rho$ is constant on the whole neighbourhood, the source is conserved and
every compact gauge difference is zero. No compact nonzero globally increasing
or decreasing function is used.

(d) [Scope] The example is an exact computation in the declared smooth
finite-region model; it asserts no existence of sources or fields, no numerical
value of $\mu_0$, and no global gauge statement.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the field-action definition on the box
$U=(-1,1)^4$ with smooth $A,j$ on a neighbourhood $N$ of $\overline U$,
constants $c,\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the component
dictionary; the linear potential $A_0=x^1$ of part (b); and the compactly
supported data $\rho,\zeta,\psi$ and gauge directions
$\partial^\sharp\chi_\pm$ of part (c).

[F1] The field action is
$S[A]=c^{-1}\int_U\bigl[-(4\mu_0)^{-1}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}+j^\nu A_\nu\bigr]d\lambda$
with $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, compactly supported
smooth variations and the stationarity predicate
([[def-em-field-action-definition]]).

[F2] The compact-variation lemma states that the first variation of its
functional at $A$ in the direction $h$ is
$\int_U\bigl(-\kappa^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu h_\nu+J^\nu h_\nu\bigr)d\lambda$,
and that $A$ is stationary if and only if
$\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=-\kappa J^\nu$ on $U$ for every $\nu$
([[lem-em-compact-field-variation]]).

[F3] The action-stationarity theorem states that, on the smooth class,
stationarity of the field action under all compactly supported smooth
variations is equivalent to $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=-\mu_0j^\nu$ on $U$ for
every $\nu$ ([[pthm-em-action-maxwell-variation]]).

[F4] The gauge-source theorem states: the field term is gauge invariant and
$S[A+\partial^\sharp\chi]-S[A]=c^{-1}\int_Uj^\mu\partial_\mu\chi\,d\lambda$,
with the equivalent distributional expression; for smooth sources, invariance
under all compact gauge variations is equivalent to
$\partial_\mu j^\mu=0$ on $U$
([[pthm-em-action-gauge-source-compatibility]] (a)-(b)).

[F5] The component dictionary is $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$, $F^{0i}=E_i/c$,
$F^{i0}=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$
([[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] (a)).

[F6] The electric constant is $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$
([[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F7] The four-current convention is $j=(c\rho,J)$ ([[def-em-sources]]).

[F8] In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$
open there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on
a neighbourhood of $K$
([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F9] If $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and
$f$ is a Riemann-integrable extension of $G'$ from $(a,b)$, then
$\int_a^bf=G(b)-G(a)$
([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]).

[F10] Fubini's theorem for $L^1$ functions: the multiple integral equals the
iterated integrals
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F11] The Lebesgue integral is linear on $L^1$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

[F12] If $u,v$ are differentiable on $[a,b]$ with integrable derivatives, then
$\int_a^buv'=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^bu'v$
([[thm-integration-by-parts]]).

[F13] For nonnegative measurable $f\le g$, $\int f\le\int g$
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F14] Assume Countable Choice: if a continuous $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ on an open
$U$ satisfies $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained
in $U$, then $g=0$ on $U$ ([[lem-em-continuous-localization]]).

[F15] Coordinate partial derivatives are the directional derivatives in the
standard directions, and $\partial_0$ is the derivative in the $x^0$
direction ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

[F16] Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the statement that every
sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; evaluate the first-variation coefficient at the
two configurations and compute the exact gauge difference for the signed
source model.

1.1 With $j\equiv0$ and $A=0$ one has $F(A)=0$ by [F1], so the coefficient $-\mu_0^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu h_\nu+j^\nu h_\nu$ of [F2] vanishes identically on $U$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^4)$; the first variation is $c^{-1}$ times the integral of that coefficient by [F1], hence it is zero for every $h$ and $A=0$ is stationary. This is part (a). [given, F1, F2, F6]

1.2 For the potential $A_0=x^1$, $A_1=A_2=A_3=0$ of part (b), [F15] gives $\partial_1A_0=1$ and $\partial_0A_1=0$, so the dictionary [F5] yields $F_{01}=\partial_0A_1-\partial_1A_0=-1$; raising indices with $\eta^{00}\eta^{11}=(-1)(1)=-1$ gives $F^{01}=+1$ and $F^{10}=-1$, and all remaining components vanish because the other $A_\nu$ are constant; the inverse dictionary of [F5] then gives $E_1=-cF_{01}=c$ with $E_2=E_3=0$ and $B=0$, so $E=(c,0,0)$ and $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=0$ on $U$ because every component of $F$ is constant and only the two nonzero components $F^{01}$, $F^{10}$ occur, whose coordinate derivatives vanish. [given, F5, F15, algebra]

1.3 For part (c), apply [F8] with $\Omega=(-1/4,1/4)$ and $K=\{0\}$, with $\Omega=(-1,1)$ and $K=[-1/2,1/2]$, and with $\Omega=(-1,1)^3$ and $K=\{0\}$; this gives nonzero nonnegative $\rho\in C_c^\infty((-1/4,1/4))$, $\zeta\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$ with $\zeta=1$ near $[-1/2,1/2]$, and nonzero nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty((-1,1)^3)$, all extended by zero. Set $\varphi_\pm(u):=(2\pm u)\zeta(u)$ and $\chi_\pm(x):=\varphi_\pm(x^0)\psi(x^1,x^2,x^3)$; then $\varphi_\pm$ is a nonnegative compactly supported smooth function with $\varphi_\pm'(u)=\pm\zeta(u)+(2\pm u)\zeta'(u)$, which equals $+1$ and $-1$ respectively on a neighbourhood of $[-1/2,1/2]$ and in particular on the whole support of $\rho$. [given, F8, algebra]

2.1 With $j\equiv0$ the equation $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=-\mu_0j^\nu=0$ of step 1.2 is exactly the coefficient equation of [F3], so [F3] gives that $A$ is stationary; directly, for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^4)$ the first variation is $c^{-1}\int_U\bigl(-\mu_0^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu h_\nu\bigr)d\lambda=-(c\mu_0)^{-1}\int_U\bigl(F^{01}\partial_0h_1+F^{10}\partial_1h_0\bigr)d\lambda=-(c\mu_0)^{-1}\int_U(\partial_0h_1-\partial_1h_0)d\lambda$ by [F2] and step 1.2. Each of $\int_U\partial_0h_1\,d\lambda$ and $\int_U\partial_1h_0\,d\lambda$ vanishes: Fubini [F10] writes the first as the iterated integral whose inner $x^0$ integral is over a continuous compactly supported one-variable function, whose value is $0$ by the fundamental theorem [F9], and symmetrically for the second; hence the first variation is $0$ for every $h$ and the direct computation confirms stationarity with no boundary term. This is part (b). [step 1.2, F1, F2, F3, F9, F10]

2.2 For every smooth potential $A$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline U$, [F4] gives $S[A+\partial^\sharp\chi_\pm]-S[A]=c^{-1}\int_Uj^\mu\partial_\mu\chi_\pm\,d\lambda$; with the source $j^0=c\rho(x^0)$, $j^i=0$ of step 1.3 and the convention [F7], the integrand is $j^0\partial_0\chi_\pm=c\rho(x^0)\varphi_\pm'(x^0)\psi(x^1,x^2,x^3)$, whose support lies in the compact box $[-1/4,1/4]\times(-1,1)^3$; Fubini [F10] factors the integral as $c^{-1}\cdot c\bigl(\int_{-1}^1\rho\varphi_\pm'\,dx^0\bigr)\bigl(\int_{(-1,1)^3}\psi\,d^3x\bigr)$, the factors being finite Lebesgue integrals of continuous compactly supported functions; and since $\varphi_\pm'=\pm1$ on $\operatorname{supp}\rho$ by step 1.3, $\int\rho\varphi_\pm'=\pm\int\rho$ with $\int\rho>0$, while $\int\psi>0$: each positivity follows because the integrand is continuous, nonnegative and nonzero, so if the integral over the ambient open box vanished then monotonicity [F13] would give vanishing over every compactly contained ball and [F14] would force the integrand to vanish identically, a contradiction. Hence $S[A+\partial^\sharp\chi_\pm]-S[A]=\pm(\int\rho)(\int\psi)$, strictly positive for $+$ and strictly negative for $-$. [step 1.3, F4, F7, F10, F11, F13, F14, algebra]

3.1 For the same data, the second form of [F4] gives $S[A+\partial^\sharp\chi_\pm]-S[A]=-c^{-1}\int_U(\partial_\mu j^\mu)\chi_\pm\,d\lambda$; here $\partial_\mu j^\mu=\partial_0(c\rho(x^0))=c\rho'(x^0)$ by [F7] and [F15], so the right-hand side is $-\int_U\rho'(x^0)\varphi_\pm(x^0)\psi\,d\lambda=-\bigl(\int_{-1}^1\rho'\varphi_\pm\,dx^0\bigr)\bigl(\int\psi\bigr)$ by Fubini [F10]; the one-variable integration by parts [F12] applied to $\rho$ and $\varphi_\pm$ has vanishing endpoint terms because both are compactly supported, giving $\int\rho'\varphi_\pm=-\int\rho\varphi_\pm'=\mp\int\rho$, which reproduces exactly the value $\pm(\int\rho)(\int\psi)$ of step 2.2. If instead $\rho$ is constant on the whole neighbourhood, then $\partial_\mu j^\mu=c\rho'=0$, and [F4] (b) gives $S[A+\partial^\sharp\chi]=S[A]$ for every compact gauge variation $\chi$; no globally monotone compact function occurs anywhere. [step 2.2, F4, F7, F10, F15, algebra]

4.1 The computation used exact substitutions in the declared box functional, the one-variable fundamental theorem for compactly supported functions and the factoring of the four-dimensional integral by Fubini; it used no existence of sources or fields, no numerical value of $\mu_0$, no global gauge statement and no globally monotone compact function. All integrals are the finite-region Lebesgue integrals of the definition, and Countable Choice [F16] enters only through the inherited measure statements [F14] and the cited theorems; this is part (d). [given, step 3.1, F1, F6, F16] ∎

Tong §5.5.3 (printed pp. 125-126) discards the total derivative in the

## Definition

Let $\omega>0$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set, and let $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be the vacuum constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; put $T:=2\pi/\omega$.

**(a) [Phasor encoding.]** For every pair of $C^\infty$ maps $\widetilde E,\widetilde B:D\to\mathbb C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) define the **associated real fields** $E,B:D\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\widetilde B(x)e^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\qquad((x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R),$$

with the complex exponential and real part of [[def-complex-exponential]] and [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. This is the encoding convention of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] specialized from plane-wave amplitudes to a general $C^\infty$ amplitude, and the complex fields are not themselves physical fields.

**(b) [Source-free class.]** The pair $(\widetilde E,\widetilde B)$ is called a **frequency-$\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pair on $D$** when it is $C^\infty$ and satisfies, on $D$,

$$\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\widetilde B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=i\omega\widetilde B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\widetilde B=-i\omega\varepsilon_0\mu_0\widetilde E=-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde E,$$

with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied componentwise to the complex fields. The word "source-free" records that the displayed equations carry no charge or current term; the associated real fields are read as an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]], $\omega$ is the angular frequency and $T$ the period.

**(c) [Status and scope.]** This item fixes the encoding, the four phasor equations and the terminology only. It asserts no equation for the associated real fields, no outgoing or boundary condition, no existence or uniqueness statement, no energy or flux reading and no empirical content. In particular the deduction that the associated real fields satisfy the smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations with zero sources is not part of this definition; for the pairs used on the exterior-scattering page it is established by the exterior-scattering theorem recorded there. Only $C^\infty$ pairs on an open set are defined, so no boundary trace, weak or distributional class is introduced here.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The componentwise reading of the two complex fields is the one of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: $\widetilde E$ and $\widetilde B$ are $C^\infty$ exactly when their six real coordinate maps $\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k$, $\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k$ ($k=1,2,3$) are $C^\infty$ on the open set $D$. The real and imaginary parts and the complex exponential of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and [[def-complex-exponential]] are total on $\mathbb C$, so the associated real fields are defined for every $C^\infty$ pair, with no equation assumed and no regularity asserted of them by clause (a). Clause (b) is the subclass cut out by the four displayed equations: the divergence and curl of a $C^\infty$ complex field are the componentwise extensions of the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] to $\operatorname{Re}$ and $\operatorname{Im}$ parts, evaluated on the open set $D$, and the right-hand sides use only complex scalar multiplication by the constants $i\omega$ and $i\omega\varepsilon_0\mu_0$. In particular $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=c^{-2}$ by [[def-em-si-conventions]], a positive scalar parameter; all four equations are pointwise, so no selection of data and no choice principle enters the definition.

The units are inherited from [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]: $\widetilde E$ and $E$ carry $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\widetilde B$ and $B$ carry the tesla $\mathrm T$, the wavevector-like spatial variable $x$ carries $\mathrm m$, $t$ carries $\mathrm s$, and $\omega$ carries $\mathrm s^{-1}$. The complex fields are auxiliary amplitudes encoding the real fields; the quotient $(\widetilde E,\widetilde B)\mapsto(E,B)$ forgets the imaginary part only in the combination $e^{-i\omega t}$, and clause (b) is a condition on the complex representatives, not a new physical assertion about the real fields.

## Statement

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, $c>0$ and $\omega>0$, and let $\widetilde E,\widetilde B:D\to\mathbb C^3$. Define $E,B:D\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by $E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and $B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde B(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]; [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] for the classes). Then: (a) [Calculus] if $\widetilde E,\widetilde B$ are $C^1$, then $E,B$ are $C^1$ and at every $(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R$: $\partial_tE(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$; for each $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\partial_jE(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\partial_j\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$; and with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] acting on the spatial variable, $\operatorname{div}E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{div}\widetilde E)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, $\operatorname{curl}E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$. (b) [Injectivity] if $w\in\mathbb C^3$ and $\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})=0$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$, then $w=0$; more generally, if $w:D\to\mathbb C^3$ is continuous and $\operatorname{Re}(w(x)e^{-i\omega t})=0$ for all $(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R$, then $w\equiv0$ on $D$. (c) [Equivalence] if $\widetilde E,\widetilde B$ are $C^1$, the phasor system $$\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=0,\quad\operatorname{div}\widetilde B=0,\quad\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=i\omega\widetilde B,\quad\operatorname{curl}\widetilde B=-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde E$$ holds on $D$ if and only if the real system $$\operatorname{div}E=0,\quad\operatorname{div}B=0,\quad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\quad\operatorname{curl}B=c^{-2}\partial_tE$$ holds on $D\times\mathbb R$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An open set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, reals $c>0$ and $\omega>0$, complex fields $\widetilde E,\widetilde B:D\to\mathbb C^3$, and the associated real fields $E,B:D\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ of the Statement. Components are indexed by $k,j\in\{1,2,3\}$.

[F1] Complex exponential and Euler form: $\exp$ is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ and satisfies $\exp(z+u)=\exp z\,\exp u$; for real $\theta$ one has $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, so $e^{-i\omega t}=\cos\omega t-i\sin\omega t$ and $e^{-i\pi/2}=\cos(\pi/2)-i\sin(\pi/2)=-i$; $\sin'=\cos$ and $\cos'=-\sin$ on $\mathbb R$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]).

[F2] Real and imaginary parts: $\operatorname{Re}(a+bi)=a$, $\operatorname{Im}(a+bi)=b$; $\operatorname{Re}$ and $\operatorname{Im}$ are $\mathbb R$-linear; $(a+bi)(s+ti)=(as-bt)+(at+bs)i$; in particular $\operatorname{Re}((a+bi)(c-is))=ac+bs$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega(a+bi)(c-is))=\omega bc-\omega as$ for real $a,b,\omega,c,s$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]).

[F3] Complex differentiability and real differentiability: complex differentiability at a point is equivalent to real total differentiability there with the derivative given by multiplication by the complex derivative; hence $\exp$ is real totally differentiable everywhere with real derivative the multiplication map $h\mapsto e^z h$, and the chain rule for total derivatives applies to real-differentiable compositions ([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F4] One-variable and componentwise rules: sums, scalar multiples and products of differentiable real functions are differentiable with the usual derivatives ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); partial derivatives are coordinate-line directional derivatives, so $\partial_jg(x)$ is the derivative at $0$ of $h\mapsto g(x+he_j)$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); a map $U\to\mathbb R^q$ on an open $U$ is $C^k$ when every component's iterated partials up to order $k$ exist and are continuous, and a complex field is $C^1$ exactly when its six real coordinate maps $\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k,\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k$ are $C^1$, with complex partials $\partial_j\widetilde E_k=\partial_j(\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k)+i\,\partial_j(\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

[F5] The divergence of a $C^1$ real field $F$ on open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_k\partial_kF_k$, and the curl on $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ is $\operatorname{curl}F=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$; both are linear in $F$ with real scalars, and on complex fields both are applied componentwise to real and imaginary parts ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]).

[F6] Continuity toolkit: continuity is the metric notion of [[def-metric-continuity]], and on $\mathbb R^m$ the Euclidean topology agrees with the product-of-$\mathbb R$ topology ([[lem-product-topology-on-rn]]); projections from a product are continuous and a map into a product is continuous exactly when all its components are ([[thm-product-universal-property]]); compositions of continuous maps are continuous ([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); finite sums, products, maxima, minima and quotients of continuous real-valued maps on a topological space are continuous ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]]); and a function differentiable at a point of its domain is continuous there ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]). Consequently, if $g:D\to\mathbb R$ is continuous then $(x,t)\mapsto g(x)$ is continuous on $D\times\mathbb R$, if $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is continuous then $(x,t)\mapsto h(t)$ is continuous on $D\times\mathbb R$, and finite sums and products of such maps are continuous on $D\times\mathbb R$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; expand the encoding in real components, differentiate along the time and coordinate directions with the one-variable rules, read the divergence and curl off the componentwise formulas, and obtain the equivalence from the injectivity of the real-part evaluation proved at the two phases $t=0$ and $t=\pi/(2\omega)$.

1.1 [Encoding] For every $k$ and every $(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R$, [F1] and [F2] give $E_k(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E_k(x)e^{-i\omega t})=(\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k(x))\cos\omega t+(\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k(x))\sin\omega t$, and the same display with $\widetilde B_k$ in place of $\widetilde E_k$ gives $B_k(x,t)$; moreover, since $\widetilde E$ and $\widetilde B$ are $C^1$, their six real coordinate maps and all first partials are continuous on $D$ and the complex partials are $\partial_j\widetilde E_k=\partial_j(\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k)+i\,\partial_j(\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k)$, by [F4]. [given, F1, F2, F4]

1.2 [Injectivity] Let $w\in\mathbb C^3$ satisfy $\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})=0$ for every real $t$. At $t=0$, [F1] gives $e^0=1$, so $\operatorname{Re}w=0$; at $t=\pi/(2\omega)$ one has $e^{-i\pi/2}=-i$ by [F1], so $0=\operatorname{Re}(-iw)=\operatorname{Im}w$ by [F2]; hence $w=\operatorname{Re}w+i\operatorname{Im}w=0$. If $w:D\to\mathbb C^3$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}(w(x)e^{-i\omega t})=0$ for all $(x,t)$, applying the preceding conclusion at each fixed $x\in D$ gives $w(x)=0$ for every $x$, so $w\equiv0$; no continuity of $w$ is needed for this conclusion. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 [Time derivative] Fix $x$ and $k$. The map $t\mapsto\widetilde E_k(x)e^{-i\omega t}$ is the composition of the real-linear map $t\mapsto-i\omega t$ (which is differentiable on $\mathbb R$ with derivative $-i\omega$ and real-linear, so totally differentiable with that derivative) with $\exp$, which is real totally differentiable everywhere with derivative the multiplication $h\mapsto e^z h$ by [F3], followed by multiplication by the constant $\widetilde E_k(x)$; the chain and product rules of [F3], [F4] give derivative $-i\omega\widetilde E_k(x)e^{-i\omega t}$. Taking real parts by [F2] and inserting the display of step 1.1, $\partial_tE_k(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\widetilde E_k(x)e^{-i\omega t})=\omega(\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k(x))\cos\omega t-\omega(\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k(x))\sin\omega t$ for every $(x,t)$; the same computation with $\widetilde B$ gives $\partial_tB_k(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\widetilde B_k(x)e^{-i\omega t})$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.2 [Spatial derivatives] Fix $(x,t)$ and indices $j,k$. The map $h\mapsto E_k(x+he_j,t)$ equals $h\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E_k(x+he_j))$ times $\cos\omega t$ plus $h\mapsto\operatorname{Im}(\widetilde E_k(x+he_j))$ times $\sin\omega t$ on a neighbourhood of $0$ small enough that $x+he_j\in D$, by step 1.1. By [F4] the coordinate-line maps $h\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k(x+he_j)$ and $h\mapsto\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k(x+he_j)$ are differentiable at $h=0$ with derivatives $\partial_j\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k(x)$ and $\partial_j\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k(x)$, so the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules of [F4] give $\partial_jE_k(x,t)=(\partial_j\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k(x))\cos\omega t+(\partial_j\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k(x))\sin\omega t$, which by [F2] and step 1.1 equals $\operatorname{Re}((\partial_j\widetilde E_k)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$; the same computation with $\widetilde B$ gives $\partial_jB_k(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}((\partial_j\widetilde B_k)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$. [step 1.1, F2, F4]

3.1 [Divergence and curl] By [F4] the divergence and curl act componentwise on real and imaginary parts of complex fields; hence, summing step 2.2 over $k$ and using $\mathbb R$-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$ [F2], $\operatorname{div}E(x,t)=\sum_k\partial_kE_k=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{div}\widetilde E)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and for the third curl coordinate, in the naming of [F5], the alternating sum of the displayed partials and [F2] give $(\operatorname{curl}E)_z(x,t)=\partial_xE_y-\partial_yE_x=\operatorname{Re}((\partial_x\widetilde E_y-\partial_y\widetilde E_x)(x)e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E)_z(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, the other two coordinates being identical by cyclic relabelling of the indices; the linearity of [F5] organizes these componentwise identities into the displayed formulas, and the same argument with $\widetilde B$ gives those for $B$. [step 2.2, F2, F4, F5]

4.1 [Regularity] Each of the displayed first partials of $E$ and of $B$ in steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 is a finite sum of products of the maps $(x,t)\mapsto g(x)$ for $g$ among $\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k,\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k,\partial_j\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k,\partial_j\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k$ (and the $\widetilde B$ analogues), each continuous on $D\times\mathbb R$ by [F6] since its one-variable factor is continuous on $D$ by [F4], together with the maps $(x,t)\mapsto\cos\omega t$ and $(x,t)\mapsto\sin\omega t$, continuous on $D\times\mathbb R$ by [F1], [F6]; the fields $E_k,B_k$ themselves are of the same form by step 1.1. By the sum-and-product clause of [F6], all these functions are continuous on $D\times\mathbb R$; hence every first partial of $E$ and $B$ exists and is continuous there, so $E$ and $B$ are $C^1$ by [F4], with the partials displayed in steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1. This proves (a). [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, F1, F4, F6]

4.2 [(i) implies (ii)] Assume the phasor system of (c) holds on $D$. Then for every $(x,t)$: $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{div}\widetilde E)e^{-i\omega t})=0$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$ by step 3.1 and $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=\operatorname{div}\widetilde B=0$; $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E)e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{Re}(i\omega\widetilde B e^{-i\omega t})=-\partial_tB$ by steps 3.1, 2.1 and $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=i\omega\widetilde B$; and $\operatorname{curl}B=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{curl}\widetilde B)e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde Ee^{-i\omega t})=c^{-2}\partial_tE$ by steps 3.1, 2.1 and $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde B=-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde E$. Hence the real system holds on $D\times\mathbb R$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra]

4.3 [(ii) implies (i)] Assume the real system of (c) holds on $D\times\mathbb R$. The fields $u:=\operatorname{div}\widetilde E$, $v:=\operatorname{div}\widetilde B$, $w:=\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E-i\omega\widetilde B$ and $z:=\operatorname{curl}\widetilde B+i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde E$ are continuous $\mathbb C^3$-valued maps on $D$ by step 1.1 and [F4], [F5], and steps 2.1 and 3.1 give $\operatorname{Re}(u(x)e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{div}E=0$, $\operatorname{Re}(v(x)e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{Re}(w(x)e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}(z(x)e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=0$ for all $(x,t)$; step 1.2 then forces $u=v=w=z=0$ on $D$, which is exactly the phasor system. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 [Conclusion] Steps 2.1, 2.2, 3.1 and 4.1 prove the calculus and $C^1$ clauses of (a); step 1.2 proves the injectivity clause (b); steps 4.2 and 4.3 prove both directions of the equivalence (c). All assertions are pointwise identities on the open domain $D\times\mathbb R$, no existence theory for partial differential equations, no boundary condition and no choice principle are used, and the argument rests only on the cited complex, real-analysis and topological continuity suppliers. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 4.3, given] ∎

## Remarks

- The two evaluation points $t=0$ and $t=\pi/(2\omega)$ are the whole content of injectivity; no integration or orthogonality argument is needed, and the field version of (b) does not use the continuity hypothesis, which is recorded only because the Statement carries it.
- The equivalence (c) concerns the four source-free equations only. It says nothing about boundary conditions, energy, uniqueness of solutions or existence; those belong to the consuming items.
- The proof uses no choice principle: all steps are pointwise computations with explicit finite data, and the continuity conclusion only composes explicitly given continuous maps.

## Statement

Let $\omega>0$, $T:=2\pi/\omega$, $n\ge1$ and $w\in\mathbb C^n$; use the real part and complex exponential of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and [[def-complex-exponential]]. Define $z_p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ by $z_p(t):=\operatorname{Re}(-w\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise ([[def-derivative]] for the derivative below). Then:

(a) $z_p$ is $C^\infty$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) and satisfies $z_p''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$; it is $T$-periodic.

(b) every $C^2$ solution $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of $z''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ on $\mathbb R$ has the form $z(t)=z_p(t)+a+bt$ with unique $a,b\in\mathbb R^n$.

(c) such a solution is $T$-periodic if and only if $b=0$; the $T$-periodic solutions are exactly $z_p(t)+a$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, and their oscillating part has complex amplitude $-w/\omega^2$.

(d) [Local solutions and exact global extension] Let $I$ be any nonempty open interval, $t_*\in I$, and let $z:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ with the same harmonic equation on $I$. Then $z=z_p+a+bt$ on $I$ for a unique pair $a,b\in\mathbb R^n$, with $b=z'(t_*)-z_p'(t_*)$ and $a=z(t_*)-z_p(t_*)-bt_*$. The same explicit formula defines its unique global harmonic-ODE extension $Z$ on $\mathbb R$. This extension is $T$-periodic exactly when $b=0$, equivalently $z'(t_*)=z_p'(t_*)$; when $b=0$ its mean over every complete period is $a$. For general drift, the mean of its global extension over $[t,t+T]$ is $a+b(t+T/2)$. Thus periodic preparation can be imposed on the global response without requiring a driven nonlinear family to exist on $\mathbb R$. If $I$ contains at least one pair $t,t+T$, equality at that pair forces $b=0$. If $I$ contains no such pair, a condition expressed only as $z(t+T)=z(t)$ wherever both arguments belong to $I$ is vacuous and does not imply periodicity of the global extension. All affine-drift local solutions remain classified, and the original global branches (a)-(c) remain intact.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real $\omega>0$ with $T=2\pi/\omega$, an integer $n\ge1$, a vector $w\in\mathbb C^n$, and the map $z_p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of the Statement with components $z_{p,j}(t)=\operatorname{Re}(-w_j\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})$.

[F1] Complex exponential and Euler form: $\exp$ is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ and satisfies the addition law $\exp(z+u)=\exp z\,\exp u$; for real $\theta$ one has $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, and the complex exponential extends the real one; $\cos 0=1$, $\sin 0=0$, and $\sin(m\pi)=0$ for every integer $m$, so $\sin2\pi=0$; both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]).

[F2] Real and imaginary parts: for real $a,b$ one has $\operatorname{Re}(a+bi)=a$ and $\operatorname{Im}(a+bi)=b$; $\operatorname{Re}$ and $\operatorname{Im}$ are $\mathbb R$-linear; complex multiplication in real coordinates is $(a+bi)(c+si)=(ac-bs)+(as+bc)i$; conjugation is a real-field automorphism with $\overline{z+u}=\overline z+\overline u$ and $\overline{zu}=\overline z\,\overline u$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]).

[F3] One-variable calculus rules on $\mathbb R$: $\sin'=\cos$ and $\cos'=-\sin$; sums, scalar multiples and products of differentiable functions are differentiable, with $(f+g)'=f'+g'$, $(\lambda f)'=\lambda f'$ and $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$; the chain rule holds for compositions; the identity map has derivative $1$ and $t\mapsto\omega t$ has derivative $\omega$ ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[def-derivative]]).

[F4] Shift and period formulas: $\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x$ and $\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x$ for every real $x$, and both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$: $\sin(x+2\pi)=\sin x$ and $\cos(x+2\pi)=\cos x$ ([[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]).

[F5] Zero-derivative corollary ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]): if $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is order-convex ([[def-interval]]), $f:J\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $J$ and differentiable at every interior point of $J$ with $f'=0$ there, then $f$ is constant on $J$; if $f,g:J\to\mathbb R$ are continuous on $J$ and differentiable at every interior point of $J$ with $f'=g'$ there, then $f-g$ is constant on $J$. The interior of $\mathbb R$ is $\mathbb R$, the interior of every nonempty open interval is itself, and every point of a nondegenerate interval that lies in its interior is an interior point ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-interval]]).

[F6] Integral calculus: if $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ (one-sided at the endpoints) and $f:=G'$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a)$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]); a real function continuous on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]); a function differentiable at a point of its domain that is a limit point of that domain is continuous there, so a function differentiable on an interval is continuous on it ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).

[F7] Class conventions: a map $U\to\mathbb R^q$ on an open $U$ is $C^k$ when every component is, and $C^\infty$ when it is $C^k$ for every $k$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); the componentwise rules of [F3] show that sums, scalar multiples, products and compositions of smooth real functions are smooth.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct; expand the complex encoding in real components, use the elementary antiderivative $\frac{d}{dt}e^{-i\omega t}=-i\omega e^{-i\omega t}$ componentwise, classify solutions by the zero-derivative corollary, and compute the period means with the fundamental theorem of calculus.

1.1 Write $w_j=\alpha_j+i\beta_j$ with $\alpha_j=\operatorname{Re}w_j$, $\beta_j=\operatorname{Im}w_j$ real and fix the component index $j$; by [F1] $e^{-i\omega t}=\cos\omega t-i\sin\omega t$, so the product rule of [F2] with $(a,b)=(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$ and $(c,s)=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t)$ gives $z_{p,j}(t)=\operatorname{Re}(-w_j\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})=-\omega^{-2}(\alpha_j\cos\omega t+\beta_j\sin\omega t)$ for every real $t$. The maps $t\mapsto\omega t$, $\sin$ and $\cos$ are smooth, and the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules of [F3] give the derivatives of finite combinations, so each $z_{p,j}$ is $C^\infty$ and hence $z_p$ is $C^\infty$ by [F7]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F7]

2.1 Differentiating the display of step 1.1 componentwise with the rules of [F3] gives $z_{p,j}'(t)=\omega^{-1}(\alpha_j\sin\omega t-\beta_j\cos\omega t)$ and $z_{p,j}''(t)=\alpha_j\cos\omega t+\beta_j\sin\omega t=\operatorname{Re}((\alpha_j+i\beta_j)(\cos\omega t-i\sin\omega t))=\operatorname{Re}(w_je^{-i\omega t})$ for every $j$ and every real $t$, the middle equality by the product rule of [F2] and the last by [F1]; hence $z_p''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3]

2.2 Since $\omega(t+T)=\omega t+2\pi$, the display of step 1.1 and the period formulas $\cos(\omega t+2\pi)=\cos\omega t$, $\sin(\omega t+2\pi)=\sin\omega t$ of [F4] give $z_{p,j}(t+T)=z_{p,j}(t)$ for every $j$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$, so $z_p$ is $T$-periodic; with steps 1.1 and 2.1 this is claim (a). [step 1.1, F4, given]

3.1 Let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ with $z''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ on $\mathbb R$ and set $h:=z-z_p$; by step 2.1, $h''=0$ on $\mathbb R$. Fix $j$; the component $h_j$ is $C^2$, so $h_j'$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ by [F6] and differentiable at every point of $\mathbb R$, which is the interior of $\mathbb R$ by [F5], with $(h_j')'=h_j''=0$; [F5] applied on the order-convex interval $\mathbb R$ therefore makes $h_j'$ a constant $b_j\in\mathbb R$. The map $h_j-b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ by [F6] and differentiable at every point with derivative $h_j'-b_j=0$, the derivative of $b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ being $b_j$ by [F3]; [F5] makes $h_j-b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ a constant $a_j$, so $h_j=a_j+b_jt$ and $z=z_p+a+bt$ with $a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$, $b=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$. If also $z=z_p+a'+b't$ on $\mathbb R$, evaluating at $t=0$ gives $a=a'$ and then differentiating at $t=0$ gives $b=b'$, so the pair $(a,b)$ is unique; this is claim (b). [step 2.1, F3, F5, F6, given]

4.1 Let $z=z_p+a+bt$ be a solution as in step 3.1. If $b=0$, then $z=z_p+a$ is $T$-periodic by step 2.2. Conversely, if $z$ is $T$-periodic, then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the equality $z(t+T)=z(t)$ together with $z_p(t+T)=z_p(t)$ of step 2.2 gives $b(t+T)=bt$, hence $bT=0$ and $b=0$ because $T>0$. The $T$-periodic solutions are therefore exactly the maps $z_p+a$ with $a\in\mathbb R^n$; their oscillating part is $z_p$ itself, whose defining formula $z_p(t)=\operatorname{Re}(-w\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})$ exhibits the complex amplitude vector $-w/\omega^2$; this is claim (c). [step 2.2, step 3.1, given]

4.2 Let $I$ be a nonempty open interval, $t_*\in I$, and let $z:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ with $z''=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ on $I$; put $h:=z-z_p$ on $I$. Fixing $j$ and repeating the argument of step 3.1 on the order-convex interval $I$, every interior point of which lies in $I$ where the assumed derivatives exist, gives a constant $b_j$ on $I$ equal to $h_j'$, then a constant $a_j$ with $h_j=a_j+b_jt$ on $I$; hence $z=z_p+a+bt$ on $I$. Evaluating at $t_*$ gives $b=z'(t_*)-z_p'(t_*)$ and $a=z(t_*)-z_p(t_*)-bt_*$, and conversely those values reproduce $z$ on $I$, so the pair $(a,b)$ is unique. Define $Z(t):=z_p(t)+a+bt$ for all real $t$ with these $(a,b)$; by steps 2.1 and 2.2, $Z$ is a $C^\infty$ solution on $\mathbb R$ extending $z$. If $\tilde Z$ is any global $C^2$ solution on $\mathbb R$ agreeing with $z$ on $I$, then step 3.1 writes $\tilde Z=z_p+\tilde a+\tilde bt$ with a unique pair $(\tilde a,\tilde b)$; restricting to $I$ and using the uniqueness just proved gives $\tilde a=a$ and $\tilde b=b$, so $\tilde Z=Z$ and the extension is unique. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, F5, given]

5.1 For $Z$ as in step 4.2, step 4.1 gives that $Z$ is $T$-periodic if and only if $b=0$, which by step 4.2 is equivalent to $z'(t_*)=z_p'(t_*)$. If $t$ and $t+T$ both lie in $I$, then $Z(t+T)-Z(t)=bT$ while $Z$ agrees with $z$ at those two arguments, so equality $z(t+T)=z(t)$ forces $bT=0$ and $b=0$. If $I$ contains no such pair, then the condition "$z(t+T)=z(t)$ whenever both $t$ and $t+T$ lie in $I$" has empty scope and is satisfied vacuously; the extension with any fixed nonzero $b$ obeys it and is not $T$-periodic, so the condition determines nothing about periodicity of the global extension. [step 4.1, step 4.2, given]

6.1 Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and a component index $j$ and define $G_j(s):=-\omega^{-3}(\alpha_j\sin\omega s-\beta_j\cos\omega s)$ for $s\in[t,t+T]$; by the rules of [F3], $G_j$ is differentiable at every point of $[t,t+T]$ with $G_j'(s)=-\omega^{-2}(\alpha_j\cos\omega s+\beta_j\sin\omega s)=z_{p,j}(s)$. The map $z_{p,j}$ is differentiable on $\mathbb R$ by steps 1.1 and 2.1, hence continuous on $[t,t+T]$ by [F6], hence Riemann integrable on $[t,t+T]$ by [F6]; the fundamental theorem [F6] therefore gives $\int_t^{t+T}z_{p,j}=\omega^{-3}[\beta_j(\cos(\omega(t+T))-\cos\omega t)-\alpha_j(\sin(\omega(t+T))-\sin\omega t)]=0$, the vanishing because $\cos(\omega t+2\pi)=\cos\omega t$ and $\sin(\omega t+2\pi)=\sin\omega t$ by [F4] and $\omega T=2\pi$. Summing over $j$ and dividing by $T$ gives mean zero for $z_p$ over $[t,t+T]$. For the affine part put $P(s):=as+bs^2/2$, differentiable with $P'(s)=a+bs$ by [F3]; the same fundamental theorem, the integrand $s\mapsto a+bs$ being continuous, gives $\frac1T\int_t^{t+T}(a+bs)\,ds=\frac{P(t+T)-P(t)}T=a+\frac{b((t+T)^2-t^2)}{2T}=a+b(t+\frac T2)$. Adding the two computations, the mean of $Z$ over $[t,t+T]$ is $a+b(t+T/2)$ for every real $t$, and it equals $a$ for every $t$ exactly when $b=0$, which by step 5.1 is exactly the periodicity condition; then the mean over every complete period is $a$. This completes the proof of (d) and of the lemma. [step 5.1, F3, F4, F6, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

- The proof uses no choice principle: the exponential, sine and cosine interfaces, the real-linear algebra of $\operatorname{Re}$ and $\operatorname{Im}$, the zero-derivative corollary and the fundamental theorem are all constructive, and the only selections made are of finitely many components of the fixed vectors $a$ and $b$.
- The affine drift is deliberately retained: the lemma does not assert that every solution family is periodic, only that a specified periodic preparation selects the solutions with $b=0$, and that this selection can be imposed on the unique global extension of any local solution even when no global driven nonlinear family is available.
- The local-interval clauses are not cosmetic. For an interval $I$ shorter than $T$ the equation $z(t+T)=z(t)$ is never instantiated inside $I$, so it cannot test periodicity; the global extension and its mean are the exact objects that the periodic-preparation hypothesis constrains.

## Definition

Let $\omega>0$, $k:=\omega/c$ with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\mu_0>0$ the vacuum permeability of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and $p_0\in\mathbb C^3$ (the complex dipole-moment amplitude, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m$). Define, on the punctured space $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and all times $t\in\mathbb R$,

$$E_{\rm d}(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(-\frac{\mu_0\omega^2}{4\pi r}\,n\times(n\times p_0)\,e^{i(kr-\omega t)}\Bigr),\qquad B_{\rm d}(x,t):=\frac1c\,n\times E_{\rm d}(x,t),$$

where $r:=|x|$ and $n:=x/r$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), with the real part and complex exponential of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and [[def-complex-exponential]] and the componentwise real-part encoding convention of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] (the spatial amplitude here varies with $x$; no plane-wave instance is asserted). Call $(E_{\rm d},B_{\rm d})$ the **ideal harmonic electric-dipole radiation model of frequency $\omega$ and amplitude $p_0$**, and call $S_{\rm d}:=E_{\rm d}\times B_{\rm d}/\mu_0$ its model flux ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]); the model fields are read as an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]].

### Adopted status

This is an explicitly adopted ideal radiation-law model, fixed by the following declarations.

1. It is the leading transverse far-zone field of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]](c) evaluated at the harmonic transverse moment $V(u)=\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, i.e. at $p''$ for the waveform $p(u)=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u})$: by part (a) of [[lem-em-harmonic-forcing-periodic-response]] the second derivative of that explicit $C^\infty$ waveform is $\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, and substituting $u=t-r/c$ into $\mu_0\,n\times(n\times V(u))/(4\pi r)$ gives exactly $E_{\rm d}$, because $e^{i(kr-\omega t)}=e^{-i\omega(t-r/c)}$.
2. The model contains no independent magnetic-dipole or higher-multipole radiation, no near-zone or static field and no other radiating component.
3. It is not asserted to solve the vacuum Maxwell equations at finite $r$, to be the field of any actual source, to satisfy any boundary condition or to have finite total energy on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$.
4. For compact smooth conserved sources, comparison with these prescribed model fields uses the actual source's moment $p_{\rm act}(u)$ of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]], the harmonic waveform $p_{\rm h}(u)=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, their second-derivative mismatch

$$M(u):=|p_{\rm act}''(u)-p_{\rm h}''(u)|,$$

and the explicit $D,\Gamma$ bounds of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] (b), (c) and (e). A bound depending only on that source's $D$ and $\Gamma$ is valid when $M\equiv0$ on the observation window, in which case the theorem's leading fields for the source's moment coincide with the model fields; for $M\not\equiv0$ the comparison carries the additional mismatch term. The source's moment is not automatically the independently prescribed $p_0$. These actual-source comparisons assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) carried by the cited theorem. The explicit ideal fields themselves and their pointwise flux definition remain choice-free.

No measured, empirical or material-response content is adopted: $p_0$ is prescribed model data, not a derived polarizability.

### Well-definedness and conventions

On the declared domain $r>0$, so $r=|x|$ is the positive Euclidean norm and $n=x/r$ is a unit vector; $n\times(n\times p_0)$ and its real part are defined componentwise, and $E_{\rm d}$, $B_{\rm d}$ are $C^\infty$ on $(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R$ because $r$ is $C^\infty$ there and the real and imaginary parts of $-\frac{\mu_0\omega^2}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p_0)e^{i(kr-\omega t)}$ are smooth combinations of the smooth functions $r^{-1}$, $x_i$, $\cos(kr-\omega t)$ and $\sin(kr-\omega t)$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). The field is transverse in the sense that $E_{\rm d}\cdot n=0$ and $B_{\rm d}\cdot n=0$, because $n\times(n\times p_0)$ is orthogonal to $n$ and $n\times E_{\rm d}$ is orthogonal to $n$ by [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]] applied separately to real and imaginary parts, and $B_{\rm d}=n\times E_{\rm d}/c$ holds by definition with $|B_{\rm d}|=|E_{\rm d}|/c$. The model is meaningful at $p_0=0$, where both fields and the flux vanish identically. The varying radial amplitude $1/r$ is not a plane-wave amplitude, and the componentwise real-part convention is that of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; the cross product, inner product and norms are those of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. No equation of motion of any source, no determination of $p_0$ from any charge distribution and no energy or flux reading beyond the pointwise definition of $S_{\rm d}$ in [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] is part of this item.
